The SARS-CoV-2 Pandemic


	Quarraisha Abdool Karim, Fran Baum, and Roger Detels





Summary


	The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic is the most recent and challenging pandemic facing humanity in the twenty-first century. While it is a reminder of our global interconnectedness and shared vulnerabilities, it has also highlighted the stark inequities within and between countries that render some more vulnerable than others. The disruptions to the economy and loss of lives unmasked yet again the intersection of race, gender, displacement, and poverty as well as the differing vulnerabilities of those who could not pivot to remote working, access health services, ensure food and income security, or implement public health measures, and those who could.
	In the words of António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General at the 2021 High Level Political Meeting on Accelerating progress on the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):
	 	This crisis is a wake-up call to do things differently. We need a recovery based on economic and social justice since response gaps in pandemics, whether HIV or COVID19, lie along the fault lines of inequality.
	Country responses to this pandemic, identified in early 2020, provide important insights on political leadership and commitment in the face of an emergent crisis and balancing or prioritizing saving lives, livelihoods, and interrupting chains of viral transmission. The returns on investments in epidemic preparedness including modernized health information systems, access to healthcare, critical care capacity, investments in science and technology, and/or bulk manufacturing and distribution capacity enabled some countries to respond more rapidly. Trust in government continues to influence individual-level decisions on the adoption of public health and social measures. The rate of knowledge generation has been unprecedented, for example, the identification of the causative organism within weeks; the development of diagnostic assays; development of six highly efficacious vaccines in 2020; and the importance of oxygen and dexamethasone for survival in the face of severe disease. Many political leaders have had their responses guided by the science despite substantial scientific uncertainty. Others have ignored scientific advice causing their countries to suffer rapid transmission, rampant infections, and death overwhelming their healthcare systems. This ongoing pandemic provides opportunities to reflect on the strengths and weaknesses of global and country responses to SARS-CoV-2 and the need to respond to multiple parallel pandemics. The hope emanating from vaccines informed by mimicking natural recovery from infection has been dampened by inequitable access as a result of vaccine nationalism. The ongoing emergence of new variants of concern of SARS-CoV-2, even in the face of high vaccine coverage rates in some countries, highlights the need to better understand viral immune escape and redefine what epidemic control needs to look like. At the time of writing (August 2021) it is evident from the emergence of the Delta variant, the most transmissible variant of concern, that the pandemic is far from over. The reluctance of many to accept vaccination; the third and fourth waves/surges of infections in mid-2021; the growing cohorts of long COVID19 patients are sobering reminders of how little we know about SARS-CoV-2 and COVID19, and how uncertain the future is in terms of when countries can safely implement their post-COVID-19 social and economic recovery plans. This chapter highlights key elements of the biology of SARS-CoV-2 infection; effective responses to SARS-CoV-2; the interaction between SARS-CoV-2 and HIV; and the opportunity and importance of control of existing noncommunicable diseases and other serious communicable diseases in the face of the pandemic. It illustrates the application of basic and more advanced epidemiological concepts of pandemics; public health responses; communication strategies, case identification, isolation, and quarantine; incidence and prevalence; principles of screening in use of diagnostic assays; herd immunity; transmission dynamics; molecular surveillance and use of genomics and meta-data. The pandemic underscores the challenges of responding effectively to global emergencies and disasters and the need for solid investments in epidemic and pandemic preparedness. SARS-CoV-2 provides an opportunity to rethink global health, the importance of partnerships and collaborations between countries and between governments and the public; revisiting intellectual property rights in relation to the public good in the context of global emergencies and disasters; and opportunities for accelerating progress on the UN 2030 Sustainable Development Goals through addressing the root causes of inequalities.





1. The emergence of a new pandemic


	On 27 December 2019, a physician in Wuhan, China reported seeing an unusual pneumonia to the Jiangshan District Center for Disease Control. Within four days an epidemiologic alert had been raised by the local health authority, and the Chinese Center for Disease Control initiated an investigation. Initially suspicion involved a seafood market as the source of cases and the Huanan Seafood Market in Wuhan was closed down immediately. But by then, secondary cases without a history of contact with the market were already occurring. By 3 January 2020, China notified the World Health Organization (WHO) and other countries that an epidemic of an unknown disease was occurring in the Wuhan area (1). By 7 January 2020, a corona virus, named by WHO, the severe acute respiratory coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), was identified as the cause of the corona virus disease 2019 syndrome (COVID19) (2). Remarkably, within three days the genetic sequence of the virus was elucidated and shared with WHO and, through open-source access, facilitated the development within days of a diagnostic polymerase chain reaction test in Germany to identify infected individuals (3).
	By 17 January 2020, most countries had started to implement some form of port of entry (thermal and/or symptom) screening for COVID19. By 21 January and 24 January 2020, the first cases were reported in the United States and Europe, respectively. On 20 January 2020, COVID19 was added to the WHO list of notifiable diseases and three days later, on 23 January 2020, Wuhan was placed on lockdown, cases isolated, and contacts quarantined. On 30 January 2020, WHO declared the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic a Public Health Emergency of International Concern that was followed by similar national declarations in several countries around the world (4).
	The early action by the government of China successfully slowed the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in China but at the cost of limiting civil liberties through rapidly enforced isolation of cases, quarantine of contacts, and forceful implementation of ‘lockdown’ regulations. These important milestones and timelines are captured in Figure 1.
	Figure 1 Timeline for the emergence of a new pandemic in China and key milestones.





2. The first 18 months of the pandemic


	As the virus started to spread beyond China, countries started to implement national programmes to respond to the emerging epidemics within their countries, some guided by the Chinese government response. There were wide variations in responses that were influenced by, among others: political leadership; public fear and anxiety of the unknown; economic and human rights considerations that had implications for the epidemic trajectory within a country as well as for the global trajectory of SARS-CoV-2 infections (5). From mid-January 2020 to mid-March 2020, return from travel to countries with identified COVID19 cases was viewed as the main risk factor for infection and diagnostic testing was restricted to symptomatic individuals who had recently returned from a country with COVID19 and their close contacts. In contrast to China, Singapore, New Zealand, and South Korea, most governments spent days and weeks debating issues like isolation, quarantine, banning or restricting large gatherings, criteria for eligibility for diagnostic testing; mandatory wearing of masks, social distancing, and lockdown regulations which, combined with a lack of national leadership, allowed the virus to spread largely unchecked within communities. Delays in the implementation of prevention strategies; lack of unity in action; poor preparedness of health facilities for hospitalization of severe cases; supply chain challenges for personal protective equipment; access to reliable diagnostic tests and/or reagents; capacity to identify, isolate, and quarantine cases contributed to the success or failure to contain the spread of the virus and the COVID19 mortality rates at a country level. By April 2020 most countries had established special COVID19 Science Advisory Groups or COVID19 Task Forces, instituted declarations of COVID19 as a public health emergency and introduced restrictions against large gatherings; school closures; curfews, and were implementing public health and social measures such as mask wearing; social distancing and isolation of confirmed cases. The goal of most country responses was to slow down the spread of SARS-CoV-2 and prepare health facilities to manage the care of severely ill COVID19 patients.
	The United States of America (USA), United Kingdom (UK), and Italy suffered among the highest incidence and mortality rates globally (6, 7). After an initial delay, the UK subsequently implemented strong responses and Neil Ferguson is quoted as saying ‘institution of a national lockdown one week earlier would have reduced the COVID19 mortality rates by 50% in the UK’ (8). The anticipated high rates of COVID19 in most low-and-middle-income countries (LMICs) did not unfold in the first half of 2020. Over the past 18 months we have seen the emergence of waves/surges of infections every 90–120 days with the most recent (fourth wave) occurring even in countries with high vaccination coverage rates. By early 2021, as the high death rates in the USA started to decline we saw substantial increases in cases in Brazil, India, and Indonesia. As of mid-August 2021, globally there were 207 million cases of COVID19 and 4.3 million COVID19-related deaths and most countries have been experiencing a new surge of infections (6, 7).
	As the virus has continued to spread unrelentingly and with high speed in the past 18 months, our knowledge and understanding of this new pandemic has grown in parallel and continues to grow as described by some as analogous to ‘building the ship while it is sailing’.





3. Biology of SARS-CoV-2


	Coronaviruses are a very diverse family of enveloped, single-stranded ribonucleic acid (RNA) viruses (9, 10). Coronaviruses, first discovered in the 1960s, are found in birds and mammals, especially in bats, civets, camels, and rats. Coronaviruses constitute the subfamily Orthocoronavirinae, family Coronaviridae, and order Nidovirales, which is further subdivided into four genera (Alpha-, Beta-, Gamma-, and Delta-). SARS-CoV-2 is a beta-coronavirus (β-CoV) and is the seventh coronavirus known to infect humans. Notwithstanding restricted geospatial transmission, SARS-CoV-1 (Asia) in 2003 and MERS-CoV (Middle East) in 2012 caused serious disease. Coronaviruses HKU1, NL63, OC43, and 229E are associated with mild symptoms and represent about a fifth of ‘common colds’ in most parts of the world. SARS-CoV-1 caused a much smaller pandemic and ultimately has disappeared globally. MERS-CoV has caused localized epidemics in the eastern Mediterranean area, Korea, and Thailand and is still present in camels in the Middle East. MERS has a case fatality ratio of over 30%. Both SARS-CoV-1 and MERS are thought to have originated in bats, which are immunologically very permissive, and gone through an intermediate animal host—for SARS-CoV-1, civets and for MERS, camels. SARS-CoV-2 is thought to have undergone a similar process originating in bats but an intermediate animal host has not been identified (9, 10).
	The inability to identify a likely animal intermediary host has resulted in considerable controversy about the origin of the virus, much of which involves international politics (11). The true origin of SARS-CoV-2 in humans remains to be established. Phylogenetic analysis (the study of evolutionary relationships among biological entities, often species, individuals, or genes, where viruses isolated from humans and or other animal species are sequenced and compared to identify common ancestry or where differences exist between species) suggests that bats are the most likely original host. Phylogenetic analyses show that the pangolin coronavirus is genetically related to the SARS-CoV-2 and other bat coronaviruses. It carries the same receptor binding domain as does SARS-CoV-2 but the rest of the virus is only 90% genetically similar. Pangolins may therefore not be the intermediary host. SARS-CoV-2 binds with high affinity to human angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE-2) as its cellular receptor and uses it as an entry point to invade target cells in humans. ACE-2 receptor expression is much higher in the lower lobes of our lungs compared with the upper respiratory tracts (12).
	SARS-CoV-2 has four structural proteins: spike (S), membrane (M), envelope (E), and nucleo-capsid (N) (9, 10). The spikes on the surface of SARS-CoV-2 virus particles each comprise three identical subunits, each of which, in turn, is made up of two functional components; the S1 part is responsible for binding to the host cell receptor and the S2 part is for the fusion of the viral and cellular membranes. The spike protein binds to the cellular ACE-2 receptor of the cell by which it gains entry into a cell through a process of fusion to the cell membrane and uncoating of the virus in the cytoplasm of the cell. Unlike retroviruses, the intracellular process of replication of coronavirus does not involve entry of viral material into the nucleus and genetic DNA of the host cell. Once in the cytoplasm of the cell the infecting virus is subject to a series of complex steps resulting in the expression and replication of messenger RNA and genomic RNA to produce full-length copies that are incorporated into the newly produced viral particles which are secreted and released by exocytosis.
	Despite the RNA proofreading function of the virus, the high incidence of infections in humans provides opportunities for mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 virus genome and the development of variants (distinct viruses with a specific combination of mutations) that is discussed further in Section 10.3.





4. Transmission of SARS-CoV-2


	Transmission in most instances takes place via inhalation or contact with mucosal surfaces of respiratory droplets (generated through coughing and sneezing) or the much smaller and lighter respiratory aerosols (generated by normal breathing, talking, or singing), and by direct transfer of virus particles from contaminated surfaces to the mouth, nose, or eyes (13). Airborne transmission is most likely to occur at short range, but longer-range transmission can occur in poorly ventilated spaces. Transmission also occurs through direct contact with still-active virus left on surfaces in the immediate environment of, or on objects used by, actively infected persons. The stability of the virus in air and on various surfaces varies widely. For example, on copper it is 4 hours, 24 hours on cardboard, 48 hours on stainless steel, and 72 hours on plastic.
	The virus is usually detectable in the nasopharynx/oropharynx 1–3 days before the onset of symptoms (13). The viral load peaks around the time of symptom onset. Viral loads are generally higher in sputum specimens than in nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal swabs. The virus is detectable by PCR in the nasopharynx/oropharynx for ≥7 days after the onset of illness in most cases, but culturable virus appears to be rare after day 7. Presymptomatic transmission is an important contributor to community transmission, estimated to be up to 50%. Transmission occurs from symptomatic cases in the first few days of symptoms. Transmission after 7 days of illness is likely to be rare. The diagnostic test positivity rate is recommended by WHO as a proxy marker of transmission rates and test positivity rates of <5% is considered as a marker of low levels of transmission (14).
	Two studies provided important insights on viral transmission very early on in the pandemic (15, 16). The first are data from a cruise ship, the Diamond Princess, that showed that for every 100 symptomatic cases, there were an additional 19 asymptomatic cases. The overall test positivity rate was 19% in the sample of the total population on the cruise ship. In contrast, data from the US aircraft carrier, Theodore Roosevelt, demonstrated that there could be as many as 120 asymptomatic cases for every 100 symptomatic cases. The test positivity rate was 15% in this cohort. An important confounder in the data from these two ships is age, with the Diamond Princess having many more older people in contrast to the younger cohort of military personnel on the Theodore Roosevelt.
	Transmissibility can be described with the basic reproduction number (R0), which was estimated at between 2 and 3 for the original Wuhan strain of SARS-CoV-2 (and is now estimated to be 6–8 for the Delta variant, highlighting the increased transmissibility of the Delta variant) (17). This can be contrasted to seasonal influenza with an R0 around 1.3. R0 simply expresses how many people on average will be infected by each patient, and it is calculated with the product of the probability of transmission, the number of contacts per unit time, and the duration of infectiousness (18). Thus, interventions aimed at reducing the rate of spread to less than 1 need to influence one or more of these variables. Typically for herd immunity to be reached, R0 has to be <1, or in other words, each person infected is unlikely to spread infection to anyone else. To create a time-dependant reproductive number, a new approach was adopted called Rt. Rt. is important as it takes into account the lag between cases and provides a more accurate estimate of the quantity of viral spread. Rt cannot be measured but it can be estimated for any period of time, with 7 and 14 days being the time periods of interest for Sars-CoV-2 (19, 20). Further Rt, takes into account vaccination coverage rates and adoption of other prevention measures.
	The virus spreads easily and remains viable outside the body for several hours or days depending on the way it leaves and the material of any surfaces it lands on (13). Stopping spread is complicated as the virus is highly infectious and spreads even before an infected person has symptoms (presymptomatic spread) and, further, the majority of exposed and infected individuals remain asymptomatic. The transmission rate is high, on average one person infects between two and three others; but, in the circumstances in which spreading is most effective (closed, unventilated spaces with many people not wearing masks and talking or singing, etc.), superspreading can occur with tens or hundreds of people being infected in a single event (21). It is estimated that about 80% of transmissions take place at such superspreading events from less than 10% of infected individuals. Even when substantial reductions in new infections have been achieved, there can readily be a resurgence of infection. The virus replicates and spreads rapidly within a matter of days. This rapid spread and surge of infections can easily overwhelm health services and divert attention from other serious health problems, resulting in higher death rates (22). During winter it is challenging to differentiate between flu and COVID19.





5. Temporal trends in SARS-CoV-2 infections and national responses


	The global numbers of SARS-CoV-2 cases and COVID19 deaths masks wide variations within and between countries in terms of magnitude of epidemics, severity of disease presentation and mortality rates (Figure 2) (6, 7). For example in Africa, while there have been 6.2 million cumulative cases representing 3.2% of global cases by mid-August 2021, it has a high case fatality rate of 2.5% (158,697 deaths) translating to approximately 3.8% of global deaths in 15% of the world’s population (6, 7). By the beginning of August 2021, most countries had experienced at least three surges or waves of infections with brief respites of between 90–120 days between surges. Some countries are now experiencing a fourth wave of new infections (6, 7).
	Figure 2 Temporal trends in global distribution of COVID19 infections.
	National responses to the pandemic have varied considerably and with the ongoing pandemic and waves of resurgences at a national level, continued to evolve in the first six months of the pandemic. Those countries, such as Australia, New Zealand, China, South Africa, and South Korea, that implemented strict national lockdown measures and closed ports of entry, were able to avoid widespread transmission whereas other countries, like the United States and Brazil, where limiting personal freedom was avoided on political grounds, experienced severe epidemics (23).
	In September 2019, the Global Health Security Index (24) predicted that the world in general was not well prepared for the pandemic but did not predict individual country preparedness. In contrast to other pandemics and most diseases, in the first year of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic rich countries suffered a higher burden of disease and death than most middle-and low-income countries (25). An analysis of the factors that appear to affect country epidemic trajectories and resilience indicates that the following factors were important:
	 	i. The extent of globalization and geography: Most rich countries were more highly globalized and linked. Geography itself was a determinant such that island countries and those with only one border were more protected.
	ii. Health system capacity: Nations with universal publicly funded health systems that were not financially distressed and had strong public health capacity, appear to have been relatively well prepared for COVID19, including Australia and New Zealand. Conversely, the pandemic highlighted the weaknesses of fragmented systems relying on for-profit healthcare providers, such as the USA.
	iii. Political leadership: Those countries with leaders who denied the scientific advice (including Brazil and the USA) fared badly. Others that acted on scientific advice fared better (e.g. South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand).
	iv. A country’s wealth was not the only or main determinant of health security. Some lower-income countries made a conscious decision to allocate their scarce resources to prioritize their COVID19 response including taking out loans to cover the increased debt resulting from the pandemic measures implemented (26, 27).
	v. The extent of inequalities within countries also affected how well a country managed the pandemic. Those with high levels of inequities appear particularly vulnerable, as is discussed next.
	vi. Social security provisions to protect people from losing their jobs and homes was a vital part of pandemic responses (28)
	vii. An active civil society also played an important role in improving a country’s pandemic responses. social solidarity built on civil society engagement offered protection even where trust in government was weak. For example, in South Africa, community action networks worked to both ameliorate the consequences of lockdown and reduce local transmission prevention (29). Using social media, they built local relationships based on trust and created a collective consciousness for responses to COVID19 which has challenged divisive individualism.





6. Preventing the spread of SARS-CoV-2


	Prior to the development of efficacious vaccines in November 2020, the only strategies effective in slowing the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 were the classical public health strategies of identification and isolation of cases and quarantine of contacts. The collection of prevention measures to minimize the spread of SARS-COV-2, also sometimes referred to as the ‘COVID19 prevention toolbox’ includes: symptom screening; staying home if symptomatic; hand sanitizing; regular cleaning of frequently touched surfaces and objects; use of face masks (cloth or medical masks) when interacting with others or in closed spaces; and maintaining social distance (>2 metres) (30). All healthcare workers need personal protective equipment (PPE), which includes combinations of respirators, surgical masks, face shields, goggles, gloves, plastic gowns or aprons depending on the risk of exposure in care provision.
	Early in the pandemic, national lockdowns were an extreme form of social distancing used by some countries to slow down the spread of SARS-CoV-2 and utilize the time to prepare healthcare facilities to cope with the anticipated increase in patients with severe disease. Another form of social distancing adopted was remote working or schooling that was also referred to as voluntary ‘stay at home’ strategies. Restrictions on movement included policies against social gatherings including political rallies, sports events, and religious gatherings, entertainment venues, closing of shopping malls, and other circumstances or places in which people would come in close contact with others. In other situations where exposure to other people could not be avoided, especially in health facilities and other essential service points, masks and protective gear were strongly advised or mandated. The adoption of these prevention measures nationally or for individuals became a political issue; for example, in the United States of America the wearing of a mask was considered by many to be an expression of political affiliation (31). The implementation of any level of lockdown caused severe economic hardship, with many persons losing employment and many businesses closing down (32). In other settings, the enforcement of mandatory national lockdowns with curfews resulted in severe violations of human rights including loss of lives. Regardless of the measures adopted, the COVID19 pandemic has resulted in the most severe economic and social disruptions and has resulted in societal divisions in many settings (33). Twenty months into this pandemic, implementation of national lockdowns is considered very parsimoniously by most governments and in fact the focus now is on striking a better balance between saving lives and livelihoods and living with the virus in our midst, implemented through varying degrees of restrictions based on magnitude of surges or declines of new infections. Notwithstanding the public health rationale, we continue to see public protests, particularly in industrialized countries, when any form of lockdown measures are instituted.
	The only way to identify someone who is infected is through viral diagnostic testing (21). The early development of diagnostic tests facilitated identification of cases. There are currently two types of diagnostic tests available for COVID19 viral tests—polymerase chain reaction assays and rapid antigen tests. The timing of testing is critically important; testing too early after exposure or after the peak stage of infection, yields a negative test result (21) (Figure 3). The molecular real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) test detects the virus’s genetic material collected from respiratory specimens, such as nasopharyngeal, nasal, or oropharyngeal swabs, or sputum. False-positive results can occur with PCR tests, because non-viable genetic material may linger in the body long after recovery from an infection. False-negative results from antigen tests may range from 20 to 30%. Importantly, even in symptomatic individuals and their contacts a negative viral test only indicates that in that individual the virus is not detectable and repeat testing is necessary to accurately measure infection and contain further spread.
	An antibody test confirms past infection and provides important individual or population level data of prior infection. It can take 1–3 weeks post-infection for detectable antibodies to emerge. Some serological assays differentiate between different classes of immunoglobulins with IgM detected earliest during infection followed by IgG. IgA is detectable at mucosal surfaces (26). Given that SARS-CoV-2 is a new virus, we are still learning about immune response and the durability of protection including vaccine-induced immunity. While it was initially thought that immunity from natural infection offered protection against re-infection for several months, the repeated waves/surges of infection and the emergence of variants of concern even in countries with high vaccination coverage rates indicate a more complex interplay between host immune responses and the evolution of viral immune escape. Anti-spike antibody tests are used to detect vaccine-induced immunity and are different from antibody tests used to detect natural infection.
	Figure 3 Detecting SARS-CoV-2 infection—viral and antibody kinetics.
	Source: Senthuraman N, Jeremiah SS, Ryo A. Interpreting diagnostic tests for SARS-Cov-2. JAMA 2020, 323(22):2249–51.
	Several factors contribute to the challenges of containment of SARS-CoV-2. These include:
	 	i. Presymptomatic infectiousness where individuals unknowingly are spreading the virus prior to developing symptoms;
	ii. Asymptomatic infectiousness where individuals are unknowingly spreading the virus without ever knowing they have the infection;
	iii. Rapid spreaders/superspreaders where an infected person infects more than one other person or at events, such as large gatherings, where several hundred or thousand people can get infected from a few infected persons; for example, patient 31 in South Korea who through her social interactions infected over 1,000 people in a few days;
	iv. Repeated waves or resurgence of infections where after the initial epidemic is controlled a new surge of infections occurs creating an ever-present risk of new epidemics;
	v. Emergence of new variants of concern that are able to escape natural or vaccine-induced immune responses.
	Efforts to test both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals through contact tracing and community testing in most countries were constrained by logistics, capacity, and delays in undertaking large numbers of RT-PCR tests; the need for repeated testing, the high cost of testing; supply chain issues and access to test kits due to global demand and travel/flight restrictions. In many settings, contact tracing had to be abandoned as diagnostic kits were correctly prioritized for confirmatory testing of hospitalized COVID19 patients (34). The emergence of rapid, point-of-care diagnostic viral tests has assisted with rapid screening of large numbers of individuals leading to better surveillance and containment of viral spread in some settings. Measures of voluntary isolation of confirmed cases and a 10-day quarantine of potential contacts is commonly instituted to assist with viral containment efforts.





7. The natural history and disease progression of COVID19


	Infection with the SARS-CoV-2 results in a range of clinical manifestations ranging from asymptomatic infection to death. Figure 4 is a schematic representation of the natural history of COVID19, from onset to recovery or death (35). There are basically three stages or phases in the natural history of COVID19: the first phase is related to the onset of the disease and is generally characterized by the development of influenza-like symptoms from mild to moderate. Some individuals recover and some progress to the second phase. Depending on the severity of phase 2, patients can improve or worsen with the necessity of intubation and mechanical ventilation. Phase 3 is characterized by hyperinflammation and sepsis of lungs. Patients with severe disease require treatment in an intensive care unit (ICU) and most of them, unfortunately, cannot overcome the infection and may eventually die.
	Figure 4 Natural history of COVID19 infection.
	Source: Brogan G et al. Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID19). https://litfl.com/coronavirus-disease-2019-covid-19/.
	In the asymptomatic or presymptomatic stage, the individual has a positive nucleic acid amplification test but no symptoms consistent with SARS-CoV-2 infection. The individual may either resolve the infection or progress to a more serious stage of infection. An individual in the asymptomatic or presymptomatic stage can transmit the virus complicating surveillance and contact tracing. Some infected individuals progress to the mild stage, manifested by a range of symptoms including fever, cough, nausea, vomiting, malaise, headache, and diarrhoea and in some individuals loss of smell (anosmia) and/taste (ageusia) (Table 1) (36). Once the individual has developed shortness of breath, dyspnoea, and signs of lower respiratory disease with an oxygen saturation level of 94% or higher, they are considered to be in the moderate stage of disease. Once their oxygen saturation level falls below 94% and they have a breathing frequency greater than 30 breaths per minute they are considered to have severe disease. In the critical stage patients progress to respiratory failure, septic shock, and death. The likelihood of serious disease is greater in individuals 65 years or older and those with underlying conditions including obesity, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, lung disease, smoking, cancer, kidney disease, or if immunosuppressed. The majority of SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals, particularly, younger individuals, recover completely. A proportion of infected persons go on to suffer from long COVID that manifests as varying persisting signs and symptoms of infection for weeks to months after infection. Long COVID disease can follow either subclinical or clinical disease (37).
	 	Table 1 Severity of disease presentation
	 			Severity of disease presentation
	Signs and symptoms
			Mild
	Fever, cough, fatigue, anorexia, shortness of breath, myalgia. Other non-specific symptoms, such as sore throat, nasal congestion, headache, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, anosmia, and ageusia
		Moderate
	Above symptoms with clinical signs of pneumonia and SpO2 >90%
		Severe
	Respiratory distress with SpO2 <90%
		Critical
	Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
	Adapted from: WHO clinical guidelines of grading, 2020.
	While not everyone who gets infected gets sick; not everyone who gets ill develops acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) requiring mechanical ventilation. While bilateral multilobular lung involvement was very common in the early cases of COVID19, we now know that COVID19 is a multisystem disease affecting human beings from head to toes (Table 2) (38). SARS-CoV-2 is capable of infecting and affecting any organ in which its receptor is present. Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE-2) embedded in the surface membrane of many cells is the functional receptor for SARS-CoV-2 to gain access to human cells. The ACE-2 receptor is highly expressed in lung epithelial cells, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, liver, vascular endothelial cells, and arterial smooth muscle cells. Thus, all of these organs and systems with high expression of ACE-2 receptors are targets for SARS-CoV‐2 infection. COVID19 may induce a widespread inflammatory response involving all these organs. (39)
	 	Table 2 Multisystem involvement of COVID19: a disease from head to toe
	 			Organ system
	Signs and symptoms
			Neurologic
	Headaches, dizziness, encephalopathy, Guillain–Barre, ageusia, myalgia, anosmia, stroke
		Thromboembolism
	Deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, catheter-related thrombosis
		Renal
	Acute kidney injury, proteinuria, haematuria
		Cardiac
	Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, myocardial injury/myocarditis, cardiac arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, myocardial ischaemia, acute cor pulmonale
		Hepatic
	Elevated aminotransferases, elevated bilirubin
		Endocrine
	Hyperglycaemia, diabetic ketoacidosis
		Gastrointestinal
	Diarrhoea, nausea/vomiting; anorexia, abdominal pain
		Dermatological
	Petechiae, livedo reticularis, erythematous rash, urticaria, vesicles, pernio-like lesions
	Adapted from: Feng, Z., et al Nature Communications, 2020, 11(1), pp.1–9.





7.1. Predictors of severe disease and mortality: age and comorbidities


	There is growing evidence that COVID19 can also itself either cause or exacerbate metabolic syndrome (pre-diabetic condition) and hypertension (40). Clinical management for hospitalized patients with COVID19 is focused on supportive care for complications, including supplemental oxygen and advanced organ support for respiratory failure, septic shock, and multiorgan failure. Most mortality attributable to SARS-CoV-2 infection occurs through the development of viral pneumonia-induced ARDS. While the exact mechanisms through which SARS-CoV-2 causes ARDS and how certain host factors confer an increased risk of developing severe disease remains unclear, one factor has emerged as a dominant predictor of disease severity and risk of mortality—which is age (41). In an analysis of more than 44,672 confirmed cases by the Chinese Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, the case fatality rate was <1% among <60 years old; 3.6% for those 60–69 years; 8.0% in people 70–79 years; and 14.8% among those 80 years or older (41). Other predictors of disease progression include malnutrition (both underweight and overweight/obesity), and noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), including hypertension and diabetes (40, 42).
	Infection with SARS-CoV-2 triggers an inflammatory process that can lead to direct or indirect insults to the lung. About 5–15% of patients with COVID19 infection require intensive care monitoring and ventilatory support, mainly for severe hypoxemia (43, 44). The goal of treatment is maintenance of oxygen saturation >90%. That means supplementation of oxygen via several ways. There are no clear evidence-based guidelines for the ideal time to proceed to mechanical ventilation in patients with COVID19. Availability of ventilators, intensive care capacity, considerations of palliative care, and end-of‐life resources as well as individual patient characteristics all play a role in decisions to institute mechanical ventilation. There are several strategies for delivering oxygen as presented in Table 3.
	 	Table 3 Strategies for delivering oxygen in moderate to severely ill COVID19 patients
	 			Strategies for delivering oxygen
	Indication
			Nasal cannula
	Effective for mildly hypoxic patients, supplemental oxygen delivered by nasal cannula can induce significant dispersion of exhaled air, even at low flow rates. Supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula provides up to about 5–6 L/min
		Simple face mask
	Oxygen supplementation via simple mask is only marginally greater than that of nasal cannula. Simple masks provide supplemental oxygen with flow rates up to approximately 5–10 L/min
		Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
	Delivers pressure through all phases of the respiratory cycle. The patient continues to breathe spontaneously both with and against the positive airway pressure
		Mechanical ventilation
	Endotracheal tube for patients may be necessary for patients with frank respiratory failure or multisystem organ dysfunction. The machine takes over completely or supports the patients spontaneous breathing
		High flow oxygen system
	High flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) includes high flow nasal cannula and high velocity nasal insufflation. High flow oxygen systems provide oxygen-rich heated humidified gas to the patient’s nose at flow levels sufficient to deliver a constant, precisely set high FiO2





7.2. Clotting and strokes


	Strokes occur when the brain’s blood supply is interrupted, usually by a blood clot. COVID19 causes complications to younger patients being hospitalized for, and sometimes dying from, serious strokes (45, 46). It is unknown if coronavirus itself stimulates blood clots to form, or if they are a result of an overactive immune response to the virus. These strokes are found in patients who test positive for coronavirus but who do not have any traditional risk factors for stroke. They tend to have no COVID19 symptoms, or only mild symptoms. The type of stroke occurring in these patients typically occurs in much older patients. COVID-related strokes occur because of a body wide increase in blood clot formation, which can damage any organ, not just the brain. A blood clot in the lungs is called pulmonary embolism and can cause shortness of breath, chest pain, or death; a blood clot in or near the heart can cause a heart attack; and blood clots in the kidneys can cause kidney damage requiring dialysis.





7.3. Long COVID


	Fatigue, muscle weakness, insomnia, anxiety, loss of smell or taste persist beyond several weeks for a significant proportion of those infected, including those who were mildly symptomatic. Persistent cardiac symptoms have also been observed. A Norwegian (47) study found at 6 months, 61% (189/312) of all patients had persistent symptoms. Given the short experience (less than two years) with SARS-CoV-2 disease there is still uncertainty about the frequency, manifestations, and severity of persisting COVID19 disease/long COVID or its management (37). Given the growing cohorts of persons with long COVID, this is becoming an area of increasing concern and requires urgent attention.





7.4. Children and COVID19


	To date, data on COVID19 in children and adolescents remain scarce. Young people can be asymptomatic or may present with fever, respiratory, and/or gastrointestinal symptoms. Recent studies have demonstrated that COVID19 is generally a mild disease in children when compared with older patients. It is not yet known what the reasons for the difference in severity of disease are, but three possibilities exist (48): i. Children may have lower viral loads even if they get COVID19. There may be a correlation between the severity of COVID19 and the viral loads (or the duration of virus-shedding period); ii. Children have lower expression levels of ACE2, when compared to adults, and, therefore, have fewer receptor sites for the SARS-CoV-2 to bind to; iii. There may be a simultaneous presence of other viruses in the mucosa of the lungs and airways, common in young children, and these viruses may compete with SARS-CoV-2 virus and limit its growth.
	A small proportion of children develop a rare, COVID19 associated multisystem inflammatory syndrome which appears to develop after the infection rather than during the acute stage of COVID­19. The clinical features of these paediatric cases are both similar and distinct from other well-described inflammatory syndromes in children, including Kawasaki disease, Kawasaki disease shock syndrome, and toxic shock syndrome. This COVID19­associated multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children and adolescents is referred to interchangeably as paediatric inflammatory multisystem syndrome temporally associated with SARS-CoV-2 (PIMS­TS) or multi­system inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS­C) associated with COVID­19 (49). Symptoms of MIS-C in children include: conjunctivitis; loss of appetite; red, cracked lips or red tongue; enlarged lymph nodes; prolonged fever over several days; diarrhoea and/or vomiting; urticaria; abdominal pain; swollen hands and feet. Of greater growing concern for children is the impact of the death of parents and the increased numbers of orphaned children.





7.5. Treatment


	The priority in treatment has been saving the lives of those with severe illness. Currently there are a limited number of drugs that have clinical trial level evidence against SARS-CoV-2. A comparison of the WHO clinical care guidelines (50) to the NIH panel recommendations for treatment of SARS-CoV-2 (Table 4) (51) highlights huge disparities in what drugs can be accessed where leading to huge differences in COVID19 mortality rates between industrialized countries and LMICS.
	The recommendations from the NIH Panel on Treatment for SARS-CoV-2 in terms of the treatment strategy and recommended drugs is dependent on the stage of disease (51). Most infected individuals will have few symptoms and will require primarily symptomatic treatment including rest, fluid replacement, and pain management with non-opioids such as acetaminophen. They do not require hospitalization but may require monoclonal antibodies if at risk of progression. Patients developing respiratory distress and shortness of breath, chest pain, new onset confusion, inability to stay awake, a bluish caste to their face and other signs of hypoxia require hospitalization. Treatment of individuals with more severe disease is based on physician judgement and it may be necessary to put patients on artificial ventilators and oxygen therapy.
	 	Table 4 NIH panel recommendations for treatment of SARS-Cov-2
	 			Patient condition
	Treatment recommendation
			Mild to moderate symptoms, not requiring hospitalization or supplemental oxygen but at risk of progression
	Anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibody products such as casirivimab plus imdevimab or sotrovimab. Do not use dexamethasone or other systemic glucocorticoids
		Discharged from hospital despite requiring new or increasing need for supplemental oxygen
	6 mgs of dexamethasone once daily for duration of supplemental oxygen but less than 10 days
		Hospitalized but does not require supplemental oxygen
	No corticosteroids. If at high risk for progression may use remdesivir
		Hospitalized and requires supplemental oxygen
	Remdesivir, remdesivir plus dexamethasone if increasing need for oxygen, dexamethasone if remdesivir not available or contraindicated
		Hospitalized and requires oxygen through high flow ventilator
	Dexamethasone or dexamethasone plus remdesivir. If systemic inflammation, add baricitinib or tocilizumab
		Hospitalized and requires intensive mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation
	Dexamethasone. If within 24 hours of admission plus tocilizumab
	Adapted from NIH guidelines (https://www.covid19treatmentguidelines.nih.gov).
	Given the burgeoning of the antiviral drug field in recent years, it was natural for researchers to turn to proven agents successful against other viruses to attempt to treat COVID19. Data from small observational studies of chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine (CQ and HCQ) looked promising but the UK’s adaptive multiarmed randomized controlled trial, RECOVERY (52), and the WHO’s multicountry Solidarity treatment trial demonstrated that neither HCQ nor lopinavir/ritonavir had any effect in reducing mortality in COVID19 (53).
	The RECOVERY trial did have a COVID19 treatment breakthrough in demonstrating that dexamethasone reduced mortality in hospitalized patients on supplemental oxygen. Patients requiring ventilation had a 33% reduction in death. Dexamethasone or its equivalent, e.g. prednisone, is now standard of care for severe, hospitalized COVID19 patients, worldwide. Hopes for remdesivir, a repurposed antiviral nucleoside analogue first used in Ebola patients, were also high following a US study that showed that it significantly reduced recovery time if people were treated early (11 days vs. 15 for untreated) but was less effective in severely ill patients (54). The Solidarity therapeutics trial demonstrated no effect of remdesivir on mortality rates in severe COVID19. There have also been reports of success in reducing the death rate among in severely ill patients by use of infused convalescent plasma, which prompted the FDA in the USA to issue an ‘emergency use authorisation (EUA)’ to allow hospitals to use it (55).
	Monoclonal antibodies are recommended for mild-to-moderate disease but cost and access remain barriers to widespread access. The RECOVERY trial also showed mortality benefit for REGEN-CoV in hospitalized adults (56), RECOVERY (57), and REMAP-CAP (58) have shown benefit of tocilizumab.
	There remains controversy about drug use and at what stage of disease they should be used. Of concern is the promotion through social media platforms and by some clinicians of several unproven drugs notably ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine.
	As data from rigorously and robustly conducted trials emerge, the current WHO and NIH treatment guidelines will change. The challenge for benefit will be access. Importantly, in contrast to the substantial investments and advances made in vaccine development (Section 10.2), treatment has had less attention or investments.





8. Social and economic impact of the pandemic


	The dichotomy of this pandemic lies in the struggle between saving lives and saving livelihoods. With 90% of the world’s countries in recession there has been an unprecedented economic downturn, possibly exceeding even that of the great depression in the 1930s. Some indication of the severity of the social and economic impact of COVID19 can be gleaned from this quote from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD): ‘The COVID19 pandemic has triggered the deepest economic recession in nearly a century, threatening health, disrupting economic activity, and hurting well-being and jobs. Extraordinary policies are required to walk the tightrope towards recovery, which will shape the economic and social prospects of the coming decade’ (59).
	The COVID19 pandemic has created an unprecedented economic and public health crisis. The economic impacts have resulted from reduced productivity, loss of life, business closures, trade disruption, interruption of global supply chains and decimation of the travel and tourism industry (60). The US Congressional Research Service (61) estimates that ‘… the virus reduced global economic growth in 2020 to an annualized rate of –3.4% to –7.6%, with a recovery of 4.2% to 5.6% projected for 2021. Global trade is estimated to have fallen by 5.3% in 2020 but is projected to grow by 8.0% in 2021’. Further, it notes that the recovery is likely to remain uneven among countries with differences driven by the extent of SARS-CoV-2 vaccine rollout, ability to provide fiscal and monetary support, the extent of hard-hit sectors (especially tourism) and predict that emerging economies will face the most problems because they do not have access to COVID19 vaccines and have lower resources, providing some indication of how COVID19 will entrench and deepen existing global economic inequity (Figure 5). While virtually every country covered by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) posted negative economic growth in 2020, the downturn was more pronounced in the poorest parts of the world (62, 63).
	Figure 5 Global GDP growth 2020.
	A McKinsey survey of executives in June 2021 (64) showed that those countries with ‘developed’ economies were more optimistic about the risk posed by the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic to their domestic growth than those countries with ‘emerging’ economies—an about turn from their projections in June 2020. This is most likely because more OECD countries have higher vaccination rates than LMICs.
	Yeyati and Filippini (65) note that the pandemic triggered an unprecedented fiscal response in terms of speed and magnitude. Globally, the fiscal support reached nearly USD 16 trillion (around 15% of global GDP) in 2020. They point out that the capacity of countries to implement such measures varied significantly and noted the different capacities country have to support households and firms which depended on access to international financial markets. They also noted that the capacity of states to rapidly and efficiently implement policies to support household and firms, requires substantial state capacity and well-developed tax and transfer infrastructures, which many LMIC do not have.
	The report goes on to note that the fiscal and monetary policies of government meant the 2020 economic turndown was not as severe as forecast. These policies included support for businesses to retain workers and additional support for those who were or became unemployed. For instance in March 2021, the UK Government announced a £65 billion stimulus package over two years to revive the UK economy through various business incentives and worker income support measures to be followed by tax increases starting in 2023 (66). At the same time the US Congress passed a $1.9 trillion economic stimulus bill, designated the American Rescue Plan (67). Such moves demonstrated the ways in which the pandemic upended the neoliberal consensus that has been in ascendance since 1990 when UK Margaret Thatcher and US President Regan instituted neoliberal policies which drastically cut public spending and ‘rolled back the state’. This illustrates to what extent a public health crisis can have a dramatic impact on the economic policy of a country.
	A congressional report also noted in July 2021 that new variants of the COVID19 virus and a surge in diagnosed cases in countries like India and Indonesia and resistance to vaccinations among some populations in developed economies means it was hard at that point to predict the speed and strength of an economic recovery.
	During the pandemic there were passionate debates about whether the economic sacrifice necessary to impose public health control measures would create more health problems than the pandemic (68). Such dilemmas are not new in public health where those who perceive a loss of profits often oppose public health constraints. The experience of countries where public health measures were not taken (e.g. Brazil and the USA in 2020) demonstrate that the result is a very high death toll and causes extreme pressure on health systems. Ultimately the decision of whether to protect health rather than profits is a moral one. Public health ethics dictate that health is the primary consideration.
	The COVID19 pandemic has laid bare the many inequities that existed before it started. The Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response report in May 2021 (69) captures this as follows: ‘The lack of planning and gaps in social protection have resulted in the pandemic widening inequalities with a disproportionate socioeconomic impact on women and vulnerable and marginalized populations, including migrants and workers in the informal sector’. These inequities concern those within as well as between countries and reflect structural drivers of ill-health. The inequities between countries have been most noticeable in the vaccine distribution, drugs, and equipment necessary to diagnose, prevent, and treat COVID19; this is discussed in greater detail next. Vaccine inequities, for example, will lead to a range of social and economic inequities affecting countries’ ability to return to more normal life, thereby exacerbating the existing inequities between these countries.
	Within countries inequities were also apparent according to: ethnicity and race; being a migrant or refugee; employment and economic status; gender. While limited data are available largely from small studies with several confounders the intersection of race, gender, and deprivation or marginalization is not surprising.





8.1. Ethnicity and race


	Globally, COVID19 has shown a strong tendency to affect minority populations more than other groups. Table 5 shows that in the US while Black, Indigenous peoples, and Hispanic or Latino populations were only slightly less likely to get COVID19, they were much more likely to be hospitalized or die from it. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) notes that race and ethnicity are risk markers for other underlying conditions that affect health, including socioeconomic status, access to healthcare, and exposure to the virus related to occupation, e.g. frontline, essential, and critical infrastructure workers. In the UK the ethnic and racial differences have been reported as being even greater, as illustrated in a prospective cohort study that demonstrated a more than 4-fold higher risk of COVID hospitalization for Blacks vs. a 2-fold increased for Asians and other non-white groups compared to whites, after adjusting for age and sex (70).
	Indigenous peoples are at greater risk of harm from COVID19 primarily because of their existing poorer health status, and because ‘they have been made fragile by the legacy and persistence of colonial practices’. In Brazil, where the overall death rate was already one of the highest in the world, for Indigenous people the death rate was even higher (71). It is notable that Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services in Australia have been very successful in protecting the health of Aboriginal people, especially those living in remote areas through developing a range of resources and a National Management Plan for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples (72). This suite of measures to protect population groups with many vulnerabilities has been demonstrably effective.
