8.2. Migrants and refugees


	Refugees and migrants have been disproportionately affected by the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. WHO reported that the pandemic has triggered many different adaptation policies related to international migration that affect public health, directly or indirectly. They note that the overall picture is ‘highly complex and disparate, as national reactions to the global pandemic vary considerably in both nature and scale, impairing, in turn, a truly coordinated and consistent public health response’ (73). In addition to experiencing a range of health conditions including NCDs, mental health, and a high rate of injuries, they also may also experience highly insecure living conditions and lifestyles. Very often they also suffer discrimination, poverty, poor housing and education, poor employment practices, often without access to essential health and other services including to COVID19 vaccines. WHO stresses that better international coordination is required to safeguard the human rights of refugees and migrants and this is particularly the case given the additional stress of the COVID19 pandemic.





8.3. Employment and economic status


	The International Labour Organisation reported in 2021 that the COVID19 pandemic has caused unparalleled disruption to employment and livelihoods worldwide. Workers whose labour market position was disadvantageous prior to the crisis—women, young people, migrants, informal workers, and workers in lower-skilled occupations—suffered disproportionately (74). People working in casual and informal employment have been more likely to be exposed to COVID19. Some forms of work pose multiple risks (see Figure 6 for the example of meat workers). The case of meatworkers highlights the ways in which a range of vulnerabilities—casual work, migrant status, low wages, home environment, low occupational health and safety conditions—converge to make a particular group of workers very vulnerable to COVID19.
	Figure 6 Meatworkers and susceptibility to COVID19





8.4. Gender


	A study in China found (83) that while men and women have the same prevalence, men with COVID19 are more at risk for worse outcomes and death, independent of age. A global data base (84) reveals that females are more likely to get tested (57% of those tested are female), equally likely to be diagnosed with COVID19 (50% of cases), less likely to be hospitalized (48% of hospitalizations), less likely to be admitted to an ICU (31% of admissions), and less likely to die (43% of deaths) compared with males. In terms of social determinants (which will affect health in the longer term) the impacts of pandemic-induced social and economic change appear more severe for women. Nearly 40% of employed women work in the hardest hit industries including the informal sector, which is dominated by women workers (85). There are approximately 740 million women working in the informal sector and their incomes saw a 60% reduction in the first month of the pandemic (86). Other affected female-dominated sectors include arts and entertainment, accommodation and food services, wholesale and retail trade and manufacturing (garment industry). Women also provide three-quarters of unpaid care work that has increased due to closure of schools and childcare services, increased care needs for aged and overwhelmed health systems (87). A UN Women report (88) highlights the intensification of violence against women as a result of COVID19 containment measures and as the economic impact starts to unfold. Of concern is that globally 243 million women and girls aged 15–49 years have been subjected to sexual or physical violence perpetrated by an intimate partner and describe this surge in violence against women and girls as a ‘shadow pandemic’ linked to COVID19 and call for national COVID19 responses to include services to mitigate this pandemic.





8.5. Healthcare workers


	Health workers are one group of workers who are at high risk of contracting COVID19. The Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response (69), notes that at least 17,000 health workers died of COVID19 in the first year of the pandemic and said this underscored the need for countries to do much more to support and protect them. Of note is that 70% of those employed in health and social work are women and they often hold lower-skill and lower-paying jobs. Their working conditions put them at greater risk of infection, especially in LMICs (89). Community health workers (CHWs) are mostly women, and often from rural and lower socioeconomic backgrounds, paid irregular salaries/stipends/incentives, especially in LMICs. CHWs have been an essential part of the pandemic response and they have played a crucial role in public health systems. They have undertaken COVID19 surveillance, contact tracing, monitoring quarantine and isolation, along with their regular tasks. Despite the high risk, they often work without adequate PPE or training (90, 91, 92).





8.6. Children


	UNICEF estimates 42–66 million children could fall into extreme poverty as a result of the pandemic adding to 386 million children already in extreme poverty in 2019 (93). With the second, third, and fourth surges mortality rates have increased in 40–60-year-old people who are typically the main breadwinners and likely have young children. The impact of premature loss of lives on child orphans remains to be quantified.





8.7. Digital divides


	When many are confined to the home and many workplaces are forced to convert employees to working from home, the divide between those with internet access and the necessary technology to continue their work remotely and those that don’t becomes even more pronounced. Under the circumstances of the COVID19 pandemic, individual access to information is critical for coping both with work for breadwinners, and with education for young children looking to further their prospects in life. Roughly 60% of the global population has internet access however, in sub-Saharan Africa, 82% of students do not have internet access and 90% don’t have access to a household computer (94). Putting percentages into more direct numbers, there are more than twenty-one million people in South Africa alone who do not have internet access. (95).





8.8. Mitigating the impact of COVID19


	A Congressional report (96) estimates that 95 million people may have entered into extreme poverty in 2020 with 80 million more undernourished compared to pre-pandemic levels. The International Labour Organization (ILO) (97) identifies four pillars of action designed to lessen the impact of COVID19 on businesses, jobs, and people in vulnerable circumstances: i. Stimulation the economy and jobs; ii. Supporting enterprises, employment, and incomes; iii. Protecting workers in the workplace; iv. Using social dialogue between government, workers, and employers to find solutions. The ILO views these pillars as vital to using the response to COVID19 as a chance to ensure decent working conditions.





9. The colliding pandemics of HIV and SARS-CoV-2


	SARS-CoV-2 is one of several pandemics facing humanity today. Here we focus on HIV noting that advancing HIV disease is closely intertwined with Tuberculosis and sub-Saharan Africa bears a disproportionate 70% of the global burden of HIV infection (see Chapter 8.13, Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome [AIDS], for more details). Importantly, in recent times, the global response to the HIV pandemic set a precedent in responding to pandemics, for example, the establishment of UNAIDS (the joint United Nations Programme for HIV/AIDS). This new global solidarity to responding to global health crises supplemented with substantial multilateral and bilateral collaborations and capacity building efforts enabled global equity for access to affordable life-saving antiretroviral treatment that transformed AIDS from an inevitably fatal condition to one that is chronic and manageable. Substantial increases in life expectancy in excess of 12–15 years particularly in countries in Africa have been achieved since the establishment of the Global Fund for AIDS, TB, and Malaria and the USA President’s Emergency Program for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) (98). In 2020 there were approximately 38 million people living with HIV, 690 thousand deaths, 1.5 million new infections, 32 million HIV-infected individuals on treatment and transmission rates to infants reduced to <2% (99). Despite predictions early in 2020 that sub-Saharan Africa would be devastated by SARS-CoV-2 that did not happen during the first surge of infections (6, 7). However, since the latter half of 2020, with each new surge of SARS-CoV-2 infections the impact on sub-Saharan African countries has worsened. The ongoing HIV pandemic in the midst of the emerging and evolving SARS-CoV-2 pandemic provides important insights on addressing parallel pandemics and the potential cost and short-sightedness of abandoning work on an existing pandemic in favour of a new pandemic.





9.1. The use of existing resources


	The technology, infrastructure, and systems developed to control and treat HIV served as a springboard to accelerate the response to COVID19 in Africa. For example, diagnostic equipment such as PCR and gene-expert platforms have become commonplace in primary healthcare clinics and other health settings for HIV viral load testing and enabled the rapid rollout of SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR diagnostic testing. The community outreach programmes developed for HIV and TB contact tracing and case management enabled the rapid mobilization of hundreds of thousands of healthcare workers in Africa to assist in COVID19 education, screening, testing, contact tracing, isolation, and quarantine efforts. Similarly, the overall strengthening of healthcare delivery systems and human resource capacity to enable massive rollout of antiretroviral (ARV) treatment for AIDS patients facilitated rapid pivoting in health facilities to deal with the large numbers of severely ill COVID19 patients. Clinical staff already trained in infectious diseases meant that there was a critical mass of skilled personnel who could and did provide expert advice to guide national and local responses to COVID19 across Africa. The same genetic sequencing platforms designed to monitor trends in ARV drug resistance and understand HIV viral transmission dynamics (100) enabled a faster and more reliable identification of variants of SARS-CoV-2 and rapidly strengthen molecular surveillance efforts including for outbreak investigations (101, 102). Clinical trial infrastructure developed to evaluate HIV prevention technologies, including potential HIV vaccines, pivoted rapidly to evaluate COVID19 vaccine trials and establish COVID19 vaccine rollout platforms (103).





9.2. The complications of two concurrent pandemics


	In many countries in Africa, interventions to prepare for the anticipated increase in hospitalization for severe COVID19 cases or to slow the spread of SARS-CoV-2 such as national lockdowns had unanticipated negative effects on responses to HIV. For example, testing and treatment for both HIV and TB dropped substantially as patients were apprehensive about visiting a clinic or hospital where they faced the risk of acquiring SARS-CoV-2 or where access to these services were restricted. This increases the risk of new infections, and/or the emergence of drug-resistant variants of HIV because of ARV treatment interruptions. While there is limited data to quantify the magnitude of these effects, a study undertaken in South Africa during national lockdown showed that weekly testing for HIV viral loads dropped by 22%, and CD4+ cell count monitoring dropped by 33% (104). In addition to this impact on HIV patients in care in public sector health facilities, the number of new HIV tests being done each month declined nearly 50% during lockdown, as did the number of antiretroviral treatment (ART) initiations negatively (105) impacting the country’s efforts to reach the ‘90–90–90’ targets towards achieving the UN 2030 goal of achieving epidemic control of HIV (106). Notably there were no marked changes in ART collections suggesting that those patients already on medication remained adherent (105). Access to other essential services such as pre-natal care, access to sexual reproductive health services, and other chronic conditions were also severely restricted. However, innovations of multi-month dispensing, community collection points for medication, and community-based buddy/peer adherence support clubs ensured continuity of care and minimized treatment interruptions for HIV and other chronic conditions (107).





9.3. Does HIV enhance the risk of acquiring SARS-CoV-2?


	Given that HIV attacks the immune system of infected individuals, this is an important question. The answer to this question was a bit more complicated for several reasons. Firstly, in contrast to Africa, industrialized countries have low HIV infection rates that are concentrated in key populations (99). Therefore, in the first half of 2020 little data was available on whether HIV was a risk factor for SARS-CoV-2 infection. Secondly, 65% of the population in Africa is under 35 years old and for most of 2020 for SARS-CoV-2 infection, older age was regarded as an important risk factor and this partly explained why the number of infections in Africa remained relatively low (6, 7). However, as SARS-CoV-2 infection became more established in Africa, data on HIV risk has started to emerge (108, 109, 110). These data suggest that HIV positive individuals (PLHIV) who are virally suppressed as a result of being an ART and who have immune reconstitution viz a CD4 count >500 have a similar risk of acquiring SARS-CoV-2 as HIV uninfected persons. However, PLHIV who are not on ARV treatment or have treatment interruptions, or have low CD4 counts (i.e. severely immunocompromised) and high HIV viral loads were more likely to acquire SARS-CoV-2 infection; shed SARS-CoV-2 for longer durations and experience a more severe clinical course of COVID19 (108). Specifically, PLHIV with low CD4 cell counts, or untreated HIV infection have higher mortality rates, and those with CD4 counts<200/ml have higher rates of ICU admissions that require mechanical ventilation. A retrospective study conducted in the USA (109) found a 2.9-fold higher death risk for patients living with HIV, with a 2–4-fold confidence interval. Of note in this study was that individuals in this cohort who were Black, male, and economically deprived, had 4.3-fold higher mortality rate compared to the 1.8-fold higher mortality rates noted for other HIV infected persons (109). At least 8% of COVID19 deaths are attributed to co-infection with HIV (111, 112, 113).





9.4. Uncontrolled HIV infection fuelling the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and compromising vaccination efforts


	Individuals with advanced HIV and ART failure or who are on treatment but still immune-compromised (i.e. CD4<500) are likely to have prolonged COVID19 infection. This extended COVID19 infection can be reduced with effective HIV ARV treatment and once immune reconstitution reaches CD4 counts >500 it results in clearance of SARS-CoV-2 infection (114). However, while HIV infection persists, SARS-CoV-2 replicates freely and mutations constantly emerge within those immunocompromised patients. This is clearly demonstrated in the early emergence of the N501Y transmissibility substitution and escape mutations such as the E484K substitution HIV infected patients (114). A HIV stratified analysis in a matched case-control study demonstrates that substantially lower concentrations of both IgG and pseudovirus neutralizing antibody titres after SARS-CoV-2 infection in PLHIV, that might explain the diminished immune response to SARS-CoV-2 infection (115).
	What are the implications of a compromised immune response in HIV infected for vaccine efficacy? Preliminary data from a longitudinal analysis of a severely compromised HIV infected patient with uncontrolled viraemia (VL >800,000 copies; CD4< 20 cells/ml) showed no response after two doses of the BNT162b2 vaccine (116). The patient had no IgG reaction against the spike protein, no SARS-CoV-2 specific neutralization, and no quantifiable spike protein specific T cells. Given the high burden of HIV infection in sub-Saharan Africa, this has important implications for COVID19 vaccination efforts suggesting that an additional vaccine dose is needed in this group and should be considered in the ongoing responses to the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. Of note is more recent data demonstrating that with well-controlled HIV, similar immune responses are observed as in HIV uninfected persons (117, 118) underscoring the importance of strengthening efforts to increase HIV testing, treatment initiation in those infected with HIV, and ensuring viral suppression rates in those initiated on treatment as we increase SARS-CoV-2 vaccination efforts.





10. Ending SARS-CoV-2: An evolving endgame


	As many countries have pondered their post-COVID-19 recovery plans, the public health goal has shifted from herd immunity, that is, sufficient numbers of individuals being exposed to SARS-Cov-2 and who have recovered; to high vaccination coverage rates combined with natural immunity to stop community spread; to natural immunity, vaccination, and slowing the emergence of variants of concern. Each of these key concepts are elaborated on next in relation to COVID19. For now, the virus appears to have the upper hand but we need to continue our efforts to get ahead of it. With pandemics in the past such as smallpox or polio, global efforts with vaccine availability have focused on elimination of the presence of the organism in humans. In the case of SARS-CoV-2, will the goal be epidemic control as with the UN2030 HIV goal, i.e. the numbers of infection reach sufficiently low levels for it to no longer pose a public health threat? The repeated surges of infection globally usually triggered by the emergence of a variant of concern, each more infectious than the last, suggests that we are dealing with greater complexity of transmission dynamics than we have ever known.





10.1. Role of herd immunity


	Herd immunity is an inflection point in an epidemic or pandemic where sufficient people in a country or globally are protected from a disease and the virus can no longer spread within a population. This can result from natural recovery from infection and/or from vaccination and/or from the adoption of other public health and social interventions as described in section 4, earlier. Early in the pandemic some countries such as Sweden (119) used the concept of natural recovery from infection to define their SARS-CoV-2 response. A challenge with natural immunity or vaccine-induced immunity is that we don’t yet know for how long that protection lasts. In mid-2021 some reports of re-infection with COVID19 started to emerge (120). We now know that there is wide variability in SARS-CoV-2 transmission depending on the environment and R0 only applies to a population that has no natural or vaccine-induced immunity or widespread adoption of other prevention measures such as mask wearing; physical distancing; and hand washing that reduce the risk of getting infected and the rate at which people get infected. In 2020 using the highest transmission rate estimate of 3 for COVID19; a herd immunity level of 67% was estimated to be needed to slow down viral spread within the community (121). But, because viruses evolve over time, have different levels of infectiousness and new variants emerge, and we don’t have vaccines that are 100% efficacious or prevent infection, R0 is not static, and the herd immunity level will need to be higher than 67%, some estimate closer to 100%.





10.2. Vaccines


	Based on prior experience with pandemics, the development and rollout of an efficacious vaccine was regarded as the most effective approach to control the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic (122). During the early stages of the pandemic, many expressed scepticism that an effective vaccine would soon become available, pointing out that time period from initial vaccine development through a series of trials and finally to approval often takes over a decade. Yet despite the many obstacles, several highly efficacious and safe vaccines have emerged in less than a year (123, 124, 125). A major reason for this is that pharmaceutical companies, in many instances with substantial financial support from governments, have compressed the timeline by overlapping many of the phases of this process through novel adaptive study designs. To facilitate access, the infrastructure for producing vaccine in massive quantities was put in place even before the success of clinical trials was demonstrated, and actual production in mass quantities of vaccine preceded approval and, in some cases, the final results of clinical trials. From a financial point of view, such a compressed timeline entails considerable extra risk, in case the vaccine fails. But many governments were willing to subsidize these risks given the considerable social and economic losses that result from a continuation of the pandemic.
	The accelerated development for COVID19 vaccines was also made possible because several scientists had already been working either with related coronavirus vaccine candidates, for example the Middle Eastern respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) or the original severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-1) and were able to rapidly replace inserts of SARS-CoV-2 genes or proteins; or had well-developed vaccine ‘backbones’ like those for measles and flu vaccines, making it easy to adapt them for COVID19 (126). These factors, and the willingness to adapt the traditional clinical evaluation pathway to allow concurrent Phase 1/2 and 2/3 testing, meant that development time could be reduced to as little as 10 months to a year. Thus, within less than a year of the global report of the pandemic, several effective vaccines had been developed by several corporations in collaboration with the US, the UK, and other government agencies globally. Over 150 vaccines were under development in 2021 (127).
	Several approaches have been used by different producers including: i. Genetic vaccines, consisting only of RNA or DNA encoding the spike protein, or the main virus particle outer protein; ii. ‘Killed’ or inactivated whole virus particle vaccines; iii. Subunit, or nanoparticle, vaccines, which consist only of the spike protein made in a recombinant expression system; iv. Live virus vaccines, such as several different kinds of adenoviruses or measles vaccine or vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV, also used for Ebola) that carry the gene for spike protein; and v. Attenuated vaccines, with the live modified SARS-CoV-2 virus itself.
	Table 6 presents vaccine efficacy by vaccine type. The AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson (J&J) vaccine efficacy varied by trials and country in which the trials were conducted (128, 129).

10.2.1. Vaccination and global equity in access to vaccines


	The increasing number of safe and efficacious vaccines are an important starting point to control of the pandemic. However the potential of vaccines can only be realized by global equity in access and ensuring the sufficient numbers of individuals globally are vaccinated.
	Notwithstanding the many formidable challenges of developing, testing, and licensing a vaccine we now have a growing number of safe and efficacious vaccines (Table 1). Continuing large-scale manufacture and distribution requirements pose new and equally formidable challenges depending on the types of vaccines. Those merely requiring a live virus to be grown, such as the adenovirus-based candidates, are probably the easiest to produce as the volume of material to be produced is less than for subunit vaccines, which typically require much more material to be made and purified as they are not infectious. Killed vaccines are one of the quickest ways to make the product, but this requires that a very large amount of live, virulent SARS-CoV-2 be grown. This is problematic due to the stringent safety requirements imposed when working with live unmodified virus (131). The production volumes required for the non-live vaccines are such that the world may simply not have the capacity to make the required amounts in less than a couple of years to protect the majority of persons globally (132).
	Distribution is also potentially a problem, as certain of the vaccines require refrigeration to as low as –80° C for storage and transport, which may pose a serious obstacle for rolling these out to remote locations especially in LMICs. Of note is that with the exception of the J&J vaccine, which requires only a single dose, most of the other available efficacious vaccines require at least two doses for full protection. It remains to be seen how manufacturing capacity is scaled up and the geopolitical issues of vaccine distribution are handled (133).
	The rapid dissemination of the vaccines, primarily in wealthy countries, has had a dramatic effect in reducing the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 and has caused the lifting of lockdowns in many areas. An expected surge in transmission accompanied the loosening of restrictions has occurred but the surge is higher in communities with low vaccination rates. Although the level of persons vaccinated has not reached a level to achieve ‘herd immunity’, the dissemination of vaccinations has had a dramatic effect at reducing the transmission of SARS-CoV-2. Underscoring the importance of being vaccinated, 99% of persons dying in the United States in mid-2021 had not received a vaccination (134). Data from the UK demonstrates substantial reductions in mortality rates in the current wave of infections compared to the second wave that correlates with their high vaccination coverage rates (Figure 7) (135). If a vaccinated person gets infected, while they may not experience severe disease they may unknowingly transmit the virus, especially if they are asymptomatic. Some emerging data underscore the importance of vaccination for breaking chains of transmission, for example, in a study from Israel that included 253,564 individuals in 65,624 households there was a 79% reduction in infection in those exposed to vaccinated household contacts compared to unvaccinated infected household contacts (136). At a community level there is evidence that with each 20% increase in vaccination there is a 50% decline in test positivity rate in unvaccinated people (137). These data underscore the importance of enhancing access to vaccines and high vaccination coverage rates in our efforts to curb the spread of SARS-CoV-2 and have some return of ‘normality’ globally.
	Figure 7 Impact of vaccination on hospitalization rates in the UK with circulation of Delta variants.
	Adapted from: UK Open National Statistics.
	Unfortunately, in some countries where vaccines are available, a substantial proportion of the population is reluctant to be vaccinated. Some of the reluctance stems from hesitancy emanating from the rapid production of the vaccine (138). However, as increasing numbers have been safely vaccinated confidence in their safety is growing and many have become vaccinated. Various forms of incentives are also having an impact on those who are hesitant. In some settings such as workplaces or travel to other countries, evidence of vaccination is becoming a requirement. While no country has yet made vaccination mandatory, an increasing number of sectors have started to institute vaccine mandates.
	Of greater concern is the ‘anti-vaxxer’ movement whose anti-vaccine stance preceded SARS-CoV-2 and has now become more complex (139). At heart are underpinnings of mistrust in government, science, supremacy, and interpretation of individual rights. While their presence was initially observed in industrialized countries the dissemination of misinformation about vaccines and vaccinations spread through the social media platforms and conservative news stations is expanding to LMICs (140). Of concern are ‘anti-vaxxer’ rallies and marches occurring in many countries with a disregard for any of the public health preventative measures particularly use of masks and social distancing.
	Politics and panic have caused major disruptions in the distribution of vaccines to where they are needed with vaccine nationalism at the forefront. Vaccine nationalism involves: buying more vaccines than necessary; striking deals with pharma to redirect doses away from equity groups; negotiating bilateral deals and queue skipping by paying more and thus pushing prices higher; rushed regulatory approval of vaccines despite inadequate data available; and bans on export of vaccine by the manufacturing countries. These actions and the diversion of vaccines away from LMICs will cost rich countries the most. Review of the global vaccine rollout in mid-2021 reveals that just 10 countries have received 75% of the vaccine doses that have been administered, while the remaining 170 countries share only 25% of global vaccine doses (141) (Figure 8). Only a small fraction of the world’s population has been vaccinated, even in the affluent developed countries. The fraction of people having received at least one vaccine dose in the USA and the UK are 49.6% and 41.8%, respectively, whereas in Africa it is <2% (142). By 15 August 2021, 4.7 billion vaccine doses were administered and 1.9 billion people were fully vaccinated (143).
	Figure 8 Vaccine nationalism defining who has vaccine access
	Source: Official data collated by Our World in Date. This data is only available for countries which report the breakdown of doses administered by first and second doses.
	Civil society groups around the world and some LMIC countries have been campaigning for a waiver to the World Trade Organization’s intellectual property rights through a waiver of the Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) agreement (144). A major boost was given to their campaign when President Biden announced that the USA would support the waiver and more recently his commitment to distributing over 200 million doses of vaccines to LMICs through Covax are important contributions to increase vaccine access to LMICs. Yet the world continues to be starkly divided in terms of equal access to vaccines and civil society groups continue to advocate for more equitable access. On Twitter, the hashtag #vaccineequity has been trending demonstrating the moral concern about the maldistribution of the vaccine. Laudable access efforts include the European Union’s commitment to building vaccine production capacity in Africa in partnership with the African Union through the Africa CDC bringing some hope for future pandemic preparedness and represents an important commitment for building global capacity and strengthening local resilience. Notably it highlights recognition by wealthy countries of their global responsibilities (145). Notwithstanding, bilateral and public-private agreements, a recent New York Times report that of 90% of J&J vaccine produced in South Africa was shipped to Europe contrary to pre-production commitments made to the South African government in their export permit applications that indicated that export permit waivers were needed to facilitate vaccine distribution in LMICs through Covax (146). This type of corporate greed contributes to distrust in the public and LMIC governments in industry.
	Notwithstanding efforts to bridge global disparities in vaccine access, the hope and optimism from vaccines as a gateway to return to pre-COVID-19 normality is being further compromised by the emergence of new and more potent variants of concern that are infecting fully vaccinated individuals, which is described next.





10.3. Variants of concern


	For viruses, mutations occur naturally during replication. The majority of these mutations are minor and do not impact viral functioning or structure. However, sometimes the mutation can result in a substantive structural or functional change to the virus that enhances transmissibility, virulence, or alternatively leads to extinction of the virus.
	With the rapid transmission of SARS-CoV-2 resulting in millions of replication events many variants have evolved in several areas of the world. For example, the Alpha variant first described in the UK, the Beta variant first described in South Africa, the Gamma variant first described in Brazil, the Delta variant first described in India, and the Epsilon variant first described in California (147, 148, 149). Variants can occur via multiple pathways. Naturally SARS-CoV-2 has a slow genetic drift of 1–2 mutations a month, occasionally this same genetic shift will incorporate multiple mutations and thus create a variant. Persistent long-term active infection in immunocompromised individuals is an important source of new variants wherein antibody treatment or vaccination can create variants with immune escape. The majority of new variants have no functional advantage and so die off before spreading widely, though occasionally a new variant does have a functional advantage such as higher transmissibility that allows it to spread faster and become the dominant variant. These new variants may also be more pathogenic for humans.
	Variants have been classified into two categories (150): i. variants of interest (VoI), and ii. variants of concern (VoC). A VoI can be raised to a variant of concern if it spreads faster and causes more serious cases or deaths. Typically, identification of VoI is based on a laboratory identification of biological mutation that may potentially causes infectiousness or severe disease in a small number of patients. A VoI can be recategorized as a VoC when it spreads more widely within populations; spreads faster, or causes more cases of death, and/or infects large proportions of vaccinated people.
	Variants of interest have been identified in the USA, the UK, Brazil, and India. Variants of concern have been identified in the UK, South Africa, and Japan, and Brazil. The range of reductions in neutralization activity to convalescent sera relative to the original Wuhan strain have ranged from <2-fold to as high as 12-fold (151). The vaccine efficacy against individual variants has ranged from 10% (AstraZeneca) to 90% (Pfizer) depending on the variant, the country reporting, and the outcome being measured, e.g. mild–moderate or severe disease (152). The current vaccines are thought to provide an adequate level of protection against the currently known variant strains although there is concern about the need for ongoing surveillance for variants that may escape in vaccinated individuals as well as immunocompromised individuals (153).
	In November 2020, scientists in South Africa identified the 501Y.V2, B.1.351, or the Beta variant that coincided with the emergence of the second surge of SARS-CoV-2 infections in South Africa that was worse than the first wave of infections. The E484K mutation that resulted in the Beta variant occurs at the binding domain and helps the virus to evade antibodies produced by the body’s immune system. This immediately raised questions around whether current vaccines will work to protect people from the Beta variant and its implications for continued spread. The Beta variant can significantly evade immunity from previous infection thereby resulting in many cases of re-infections and increased household transmission resulting in higher rates of hospitalizations from severe disease. In other words, the rise of new variants poses a problem for reaching herd immunity, as the more infectious the virus becomes, the more people need to be protected in order to stop the virus from spreading. There are also implications for vaccine-induced immunity. This was, for example, seen in the trials for the AstraZeneca and J&J vaccines that were undertaken while the Beta variants were in circulation in South Africa (154). The rapidity of the spread of the Beta variant across Africa within a matter of weeks also highlight our interconnectedness and vulnerability and why we need equity in access to and coverage rates of interventions such as vaccines. Only a handful of COVID vaccine manufacturers have released results from their clinical trials and received emergency use approval in countries such as the United States, Israel, and the UK. All of these vaccines rely on our bodies identifying the spike protein on the surface of the coronavirus as a way of producing an immune response. We are starting to see second-and third-generation variants emerge, e.g. the Delta variant is a variant to the Beta variant.
	From March to June of 2021, a severe outbreak of the Delta variant in India resulted in a substantial surge in India followed by noticeable increases in infections globally even in countries with high vaccination coverage rates. The new surges in infection experienced globally in 2021 are being driven by the Delta variant (6, 7). In the USA for the first time since February 2021, there were more than 100,000 cases per day reported in August 2021. Similar scenarios are emerging in Australia, New Zealand, China, and several countries in Africa. There was initial evidence suggesting that the variant reduces vaccine efficacy. Preliminary data from England shows that the effectiveness of both the Pfizer and AstraZeneca vaccines had been lowered after one dose from 51.1% to 33.5% that was offset following the second dose—the AstraZeneca vaccine efficacy was reduced from 66.1% to 59.8% and for the Pfizer vaccine it dropped from 93.4% to 87.9% (155). These data suggest that for the two dose vaccines, there is sufficient protection against the Delta variant for those who are fully immunized. The rapidity of the emergence and transmission of VoC underscores the importance of higher global vaccination coverage rates globally and that existing non-pharmaceutical interventions such as wearing masks and physical distancing need to continue. There is also some evidence of reduction in vaccine protection against mild–moderate symptomatic disease, but high levels of protection against severe disease and death seem to be maintained.
	Should herd immunity be dismissed now, what is the role of vaccines, should we be giving booster doses of vaccines, are we likely to see more VoC and how many more? What we know is that the interplay between natural immunity, vaccine-induced immunity, and VoC is complex and we have much to learn. We know that there are individual level and population level benefits from vaccines but that the population level benefit is dependent on many factors, particularly R0 and the extent to which infected vaccinated individuals transmit the virus. Vaccination coverage for herd immunity varies and we do not currently know what levels are needed to reach this goal. In terms of viral transmission we are seeing similar viral loads in vaccinated and unvaccinated cases (156) [median Ct values: 21.9 (n = 80) vs. 21.5 (n = 65)]. New variants have changed the game with their higher transmissibility and/or immune escape, making reaching herd immunity much more difficult and we don’t know what the next variants will look like (157).
	Several rich countries, e.g. Israel, France, and Germany, are giving third–dose boosters when many poor people have not yet received their first dose of vaccine, spurring WHO to place a moratorium on boosters based on global disparity in vaccine access. We see corporate greed manifestations through vaccine manufacturing companies promoting the administration of booster doses of vaccines using arguments such as inadequate vaccine responses, waning antibody levels (homologous boosts), and variants escaping vaccine immunity need for heterologous boosts. To date, we have no correlate of immunity, nor do we know how much antibodies are required for protection. We do know from prior experience—for example, older people who had Spanish flu—that antibody levels decline over time but that memory B cells in lymph nodes can regenerate antibodies very quickly and therefore a homologous boost adds little value. Thus far, all mRNA vaccines remain effective against all current variants, displacing the argument that a heterologous vaccine boost is needed to enhance vaccine immunity against new mutated forms of the virus. There is no clinical trial evidence currently to justify booster doses. The three-dose vaccination dose schedule for persons with autoimmune disease or who are severely immunocompromised to enhance immune responses to date is the only clear justification for an additional dose of vaccination.
	Finally, the hybrid immunity resulting from natural immunity with vaccine-induced immunity appears to be higher and more durable than either on its own (158) (Figure 9), providing a strong rationale for rapidly increasing vaccine coverage rates globally to limit the emergence and transmission of VoC and achieving some level of epidemic control.
	Figure 9 Hybrid immunity is much better than natural immunity.
	Source: Crotty S, Science 2021.





11. Lessons learned and the way forward


	The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has affected virtually every aspect of life on Earth: physical and mental health economies, national well-being, social interactions, political fortunes, and exacerbated global, national, and local inequalities. The pandemic has underscored the importance of public health principles and applications and the interconnectedness of all persons whether in wealthy or poor countries or conditions. We know that attaining a high level of community immunity to SARS-CoV-2 will reduce the threat and spread of the infection. Due to the reluctance of many persons to get vaccinated and the failure of the world’s institutions to provide vaccine equity, the pandemic continues. In rich countries where people have the opportunity to have a vaccine some people, choose not to be vaccinated. Thus, the pandemic is now a pandemic of the unvaccinated who refuse to acknowledge their community responsibility to protect their fellow humans. Their argument that their ‘human rights’ are being violated ignores the human rights of their fellow humans to not be infected. Further, the human rights of people in LMICs are denied because they have not been given the chance to be vaccinated because of the system of ‘intellectual property’ laws which protects the profits of corporations at the expense of lives and health.
	The pandemic has exacerbated existing inequalities that intersect with race, gender, and social and economic marginalization. In all countries, people living in economically deprived circumstances have been more affected by COVID19. Crowded housing, insecure employment, care work, work in the retail and manufacturing sectors, being a migrant or Indigenous person have meant more exposure to the virus and less ability to cope with its impact. Strong healthcare delivery systems with universal health coverage and access have been shown to be most effective in protecting people from the impact of COVID19.
	The impact of the pandemic has been mitigated to some extent by our experience with the previous epidemic of HIV/AIDS, which through global solidarity ensured access to the scientific advances that has resulted in for example AIDS being transformed from an inevitably fatal condition to a chronic one. That solidarity emanated from the synergy of years of activism and advocacy from affected communities and scientists, strong public engagement and communication, and demand for accountability from politicians. Collaborations between scientists across different regions and countries resulted in the development of new methods of diagnostic testing, prevention, and treatment and infrastructure to undertake cutting edge research and clinical trials in most affected populations. The implementation of these advances strengthened health systems, improved health information systems, and enabled innovation in delivery of interventions.
	The rapid pace of knowledge generation with COVID19 was possible because of prior investments in science and technology. For example, the decades of investigations from several research centres on other coronavirus epidemics enabled an accelerated pathway to vaccine development and evaluation into the arms of people in less than a year. This unprecedented rapid response to SARS-CoV-2 needs to be applied to existing challenges and provides important lessons for confronting future pandemics.
	The pandemic also demonstrated the importance of strong political leadership in ensuring that responses are guided by science, as uncertain and evolving as it may be. We have seen the dual facets of public health, namely science and social justice, become more politicised on ideological grounds by both politicians and some of the public. Public health practitioners have a responsibility to inform decision-makers, political leaders, and the public and to ensure science-based policy promulgation and implementation. Ongoing public communication and engagement has become even more important in the current era of modern formal and informal rapid communication and the rapid expansion of social media platforms. Public health must develop strategies to counter misinformation and negative messages. Parallel to the COVID19 pandemic, a pandemic of misinformation and distrust has flourished and undermined effective responses to COVID19.
	We can be confident that there will be future pandemics, some possibly involving coronavirus, and likely other disease agents. To mutate a virus must replicate. The more people who are infected the more replications that will occur, each with a probability of mutating. Although the majority of these mutations will be non-pathogenic, some will increase their adaptability to humans and will demonstrate even greater transmissibility and pathogenicity. Thus, ongoing molecular surveillance and laboratory predictions of new and mutating agents such as Sarbecovirus is important and key for adequate pandemic preparedness and expanding the protective benefits of current vaccines.
	Above all, the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has demonstrated the complexities of disease transmission and control in a rapidly changing world. To confront the next pandemic, as well as to have a greater impact on the current pandemic it is necessary to muster all our resources: public health, political, scientific, and social, and to recognize our interconnectedness. We hope that this chapter will help understanding of and responses to the current pandemic and provide a path forward for future pandemics.
	We would like to end with an exhortation from Pope Francis:
	 	The pandemic has exposed the paradox that while we are more connected we are also more divided … To come out of this crisis better we have to recover the knowledge that as a people we have a shared destination. The pandemic has reminded us that no one is saved alone. What ties us to one another is what we commonly call solidarity. Solidarity is more than acts of generosity, important as they are, it is the call to embrace the reality that we are bound by bonds of reciprocity.

1.1


The scope and concerns of public health


	Roger Detels and Chorh Chuan Tan





Introduction to the scope and concerns of public health


	There have been many definitions and elaborations of public health. The definition offered by the Acheson Report (Acheson 1988, p. 1) has been widely accepted:
	 	Public health is the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting health through the organized efforts of society.
	This definition underscores the broad scope of public health and the fact that public health is the result of all of society’s efforts viewed as a whole, rather than that of single individuals.
	In 2003, Roger Detels defined the goal of public health as:
	 	The biologic, physical, and mental well-being of all members of society regardless of gender, wealth, ethnicity, sexual orientation, country, or political views. (cited in Detels 2009, p. 3)
	This definition or goal emphasizes equity and the range of public health interests as encompassing not just the physical and biological, but also the mental well-being of society., This is in keeping with the spirit of the 1948 United Nations declaration that health is a basic human right, and the declaration of the United Nation’s Millennium Development Goals. These have now been superseded by the declaration of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in 2012. The 17 SDG goals focus on a broad range of topics including inequalities, poverty, climate change, and other areas essential for achieving optimal health of the public. The SDGs underscore public health as being concerned with more than mere elimination of disease, and place public health issues as a fundamental component of development.
	To achieve the World Health Organization (WHO) goal of ‘health for all’, it is essential to bring to bear many diverse disciplines to the attainment of optimal health, including the physical, biological, political, and social sciences. The field of public health has adapted and applied these disciplines for elimination and control of disease, and promotion of health.





Functions of public health


	Public health is concerned with the process of mobilizing local, state/provincial, national, and international resources to assure the conditions in which all people can be healthy (Detels and Breslow 2002). To successfully implement this process and to make health for all achievable, public health must perform the functions listed in Box 1.1.1.
	 	Box 1.1.1 Functions of public health
	 	1. Prevent disease and injuries and their negative outcomes
	2. Promote healthy lifestyles and good health habits
	3. Identify, measure, monitor, and anticipate community health needs (e.g. surveillance)
	4. Investigate and diagnose health problems, including microbial, societal, and chemical hazards
	5. Formulate, promote, and enforce essential health policies
	6. Organize and ensure high-quality, cost-effective public health and healthcare services
	7. Reduce health disparities and ensure access to healthcare for all
	8. Promote and protect a healthy environment
	9. Disseminate health information and mobilize communities to take appropriate action
	10. Promote health
	11. Plan and prepare for natural and man-made disasters
	12. Reduce the impact of interpersonal violence and aggressive war
	13. Conduct research and evaluate health-promoting/disease-preventing intervention strategies
	14. Develop new methodologies for research and evaluation
	15. Train and ensure a competent public health workforce
	16. Continually evaluate the effectiveness of existing public health programmes
	Source: data from the Office of the Director, National Public Health Performance Standards Program, 10 Essential Public Health Services, Centers for Disease Control, 1994, available from https://www.cdc.gov/od/ocphp/nphpsp/EssentialPHServices.htm.
	Public health identifies, measures, and monitors health needs and trends at the community, national, and global levels through surveillance of disease and risk factor (e.g. smoking) trends. Analysis of these trends and the existence of a functioning health information system provide the essential information for predicting and anticipating future community health needs.
	In order to ensure the health of the population, it is necessary to formulate, promote, and enforce sound health policies to prevent and control disease, and to reduce the prevalence of factors impairing the health of the community. These include policies requiring reporting of highly transmissible diseases and health threats to the community and control of environmental threats through regulation of environmental hazards (e.g. water and air quality standards and smoking). It is important to recognize that influencing politics and promoting sound health policies is an essential function of public health at the local, national, and global levels.
	There are limited resources that can be devoted to public health and the assurance of high-quality health services. Thus, an essential function of public health is to effectively prioritize, plan, manage, coordinate, and administer cost-effective health services, and to ensure their availability to all segments of society. In every society, there are health inequalities that limit the ability of some members to achieve their maximum ability to function. Although these disparities primarily affect the poor, minority, rural, and remote populations and the vulnerable, they also impact on society as a whole, particularly in regard to infectious and/or transmissible diseases. Thus, there is not only an ethical imperative to reduce health disparities, but also a pragmatic imperative.
	Technological advances and increasing commerce have done much to improve quality of life, but these advances have often come at a high cost to the environment. In many cities of both the developed and developing world, the poor quality of air—contaminated by industry and commerce—has affected the respiratory health of the population and has threatened to change the climate, with disastrous consequences locally and globally (Fig. 1.1.1). We have only one world. If we do not take care of it, we will ultimately have difficulty living in it. Through education of the public, formulation of sound regulations, and influencing policy, public health can contribute much to the protection and monitoring of the environment to ensure that it is conducive for the population to live healthily.
	Fig. 1.1.1 Air pollution—the silent killer.
	From http://www.euro.who.int/en/health-topics/environment-and-health/air-quality/news/news/2018/5/over-half-a-million-premature-deaths-annually-in-the-european-region-attributable-to-household-and-ambient-air-pollution/infographic-air-pollution-the-silent-killer
	Behavioural patterns account for about 40% of all deaths in the United States, while social circumstances and environmental factors account for 15% and 5%, respectively (Schroeder 2007). To ensure that each individual in the population functions to his or her maximum capacity, public health needs to educate the public, promote adoption of behaviours associated with good health outcomes, and stimulate the community to take appropriate actions to ensure the optimal conditions for the health of the public. This is vital since the majority of public health problems are linked to human behaviour and lifestyles. Ultimately, public health cannot succeed without the support and active involvement of the community.
	We cannot predict and rarely can we prevent the occurrence of natural and man-made disasters, but we can prepare for them to ensure that the resulting damage is minimized. Thus, disaster preparedness is an essential component of public health, whether the disaster is an epidemic such as influenza or the occurrence of typhoons and other natural disasters.
	Unfortunately, in the modern world, interpersonal violence and war have become common. In some segments of society (particularly among adolescent and young adult minority males), violence and suicide have become leading causes of death and productive years of life lost. Public health cannot ignore the fact that violence and wars are major factors dramatically reducing the quality of life for millions.
	Many of the advances in public health have become possible through research. Research will continue to be essential for identifying and anticipating health problems and the optimal strategies for addressing them. Strategies that seem very logical may, in fact, not succeed for a variety of unforeseen reasons. Therefore, public health systems and programmes cannot be assumed to function cost-effectively without continuous monitoring and evaluation. Thus, it is essential that new public health strategies undergo rigorous evaluation before being scaled up, and once scaled up, are periodically reviewed to ensure their continuing effectiveness in diverse groups and populations.
	Over the last century, the quality of research has been enhanced by the development of new methodologies, particularly in the fields of epidemiology, biostatistics, social, and laboratory sciences. Rapid advances in computational hardware, software, and techniques, including artificial intelligence, have greatly increased our ability to analyse massive amounts of data that incorporate thousands of variables, and to use multiple strategies to aid in the interpretation of data. It will be a major challenge to keep pace with the explosive growth in the volume and complexity of data being generated, driven by a range of factors from the pervasive use of the internet, social media, and mobile phones, to the masses of data from population studies (e.g. census), molecular biology, and whole genome sequencing studies. To glean valuable insights pertinent to public health from these huge data sets will require new approaches, strategies, and methodologies, such as further development of machine (computer) learning techniques for finding associations with public health outcomes of relevance and discovering patterns such as geographic distributions of relevant variables within geographic subunits that can be targeted for implementation of specific interventions. The increasing use of robotics and artificial intelligence will have a huge impact on public health in the coming decades. Increasingly humans in the workforce will be replaced by robots, especially for performing dangerous and repetitive jobs. These technologic advances are likely to affect low level workers disproportionately. Thus, there will be an increasing demand for training in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM disciplines) which are essential for designing and programming of robots and other technology advances. It is essential that public health continues to use leading-edge technologies to develop more sophisticated research strategies to address current and future public health issues.
	A major problem in public health has been translating research advances into effective health practice and policy in a timely manner. A recent area of research, implementation science, attempts to delineate barriers to and factors that facilitate rapid translation of scientific advances into improvements in health practice and development of more effective policies promoting health.
	The quality of public health is dependent on the competence and vision of the public health workforce. Thus, it is an essential function of public health to ensure the continuing availability of well-trained and competent professionals at all levels, including leaders with the vision essential to ensure the continued well-being of society and the implementation of innovative, effective public health measures.
	Finally, a common thread that runs through all these functions is the necessity for much greater international collaboration in data sharing, policy formulation and implementation, and management of specific public health issues. With globalization, the rapid flow of information, people, goods, and services across national boundaries means that many public health concerns and issues are interconnected in complex ways. Effective solutions will therefore often depend on joint action between different countries. In addition, now more than ever, there are many opportunities for major public health attainments to be made through cooperative action at the global level, as has been demonstrated in the past by milestones such as the eradication of smallpox. The media can play an important role in educating the public and in facilitating public health interventions, but often must be educated about public health strategies and goals.





Contemporary health issues


	Underlying the bulk of the public health problems of the world is the issue of poverty. More than half of the world’s population (more than 3 billion, with one-third being children) live below the internationally defined poverty line of less than US $2.50 per day, with 1.3 billion on less than US $1.25 per day (World Bank 2012). Although the majority of the world’s poor live in developing countries, there are many poor living in the wealthiest countries of the world, underscoring the disparity of wealth between the poor and the rich in all countries (United Nations Development Programme 2014). In the United States, 40.6 million Americans were living below the official poverty level in 2016. The proportion was highest among African-Americans and Hispanic-Americans (23.2%). Unfortunately, the disparity between the rich and the poor is increasing within countries (US Census Bureau 2016). Poverty causes a cascade of problems leading to poor health (Table. 1.1.1). Worldwide, 844 million people do not have access to clean drinking water, and at least 2 billion use a drinking water source contaminated with faeces, which causes diarrhoea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid, and polio (WHO Drinking Water). It is incumbent on public health to work to reduce the impact of these disparities to ensure that all members of the global society share in a healthy quality of life.
	The population of the world is changing. In 2017 the global population was over 7 billion people. By 2050 it is estimated to be more than 9 billion. Population growth will be flat in many areas of the world, but in the African countries the population will continue to increase changing the relative distribution of population across the globe. Meeting these changes will be a challenge for assuring the health of the global population.

	The twentieth century witnessed the transition of major disease burdens, defined by death from infectious and/or communicable diseases, to noncommunicable diseases (NCDs). In 1900, the leading causes of death in the United States and other developed countries were reported to be pneumonia and influenza. By the beginning of the twenty-first century, diseases of the heart and other chronic diseases were the leading causes of death, and pneumonia and influenza were no longer among the top ten causes of death and primarily affected the elderly (Fig. 1.1.2).
	Fig. 1.1.2 Top 10 global causes of deaths, 2016 (WHO Global Health Estimates).
	Reproduced with permission from World Health organization. (2018) The top 10 causes of death. Copyright (c) 2017 WHO. Available at http://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/the-top-10-causes-of-death
	The prevalence of chronic diseases will continue to increase further stressing the healthcare system. It also underscores the need for cities, which will accommodate an ever increasing proportion of the population, to innovate and adapt in order to facilitate health promotion, e.g. through providing conducive walking paths and stairs, and supporting those with reduced function and mobility or who have disabilities.
	Reductions in communicable diseases were not primarily due to development of better treatments, although vaccines and antibiotics played an important role in the second half of the twentieth century. Instead, public efforts to reduce crowding and improve housing, enhancing nutrition, and providing clean water and safe disposal of wastes were key to reducing communicable diseases.
	By 1980, many leading public health figures felt that infectious diseases had been eliminated as a primary concern for public health; however, the discovery and expanding pandemic of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in the early 1980s, and subsequently, outbreaks of the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), Ebola, and Zika in the early twenty-first century underscored the fallacy of these declarations as do the persisting high rates of infectious diseases, particularly in Africa.
	Although communicable diseases persist as a major public health concern, globally, NCDs have become the leading health challenge, accounting for 40 million or 71.4% of all deaths in 2016 (Fig. 1.1.3). Even in poor developing countries, NCDs are a dominant and growing concern. In 2015, 30.7 million NCD deaths occurred in low-and middle-income countries (World Health Organization 2017b). The age-standardized death rate due to NCDs among males in low-and middle-income countries was 65% higher, and among females, 85% higher than for men and women in high-income countries. This figure is particularly disturbing because low-and middle-income countries have far fewer resources and capacity to address the epidemic of NCDs. Communicable diseases, however, still accounted for almost 30% of the burden of disease worldwide, but caused a majority of deaths only in Africa. The majority of communicable diseases are now preventable through vaccines, improved sanitation, behavioural interventions, and better standards of living, although new diseases emerge that will require public health action.
	Fig. 1.1.3 Deaths due to noncommunicable diseases, 2015.
	Reproduced with permission from World Health organization. (2017) Deaths due to noncommunicable diseases: age standardized death rate (per 100 000 population). Copyright (c) 2017 WHO. Available at http://gamapserver.who.int/mapLibrary/Files/Maps/Global_NCD_deaths_2015.png
	Compounding the global shift to NCDs is the rapidly rising age of populations in many countries, due to increased longevity (71.4 years globally) and dramatically decreased birth rates (United Nations 2015a). Population growth is already below replacement in many countries, both developed and developing. This demographic shift to an ageing population has widespread and profound implications (Fig. 1.1.4). It will increase the burden of chronic disease in these countries, place increasing demands on healthcare and social support services, and strain public financing systems. This will occur as the proportion of the population in the productive ages decreases, which in turn will impact economic growth. The low-and middle-income countries in particular will be affected by the ageing of their populations.
	Fig. 1.1.4 Percentages of population aged 65 and over in 2015 and 2050.
	Source: data from US Census Bureau, 2013, 2014a, 2014b, International Data Base, U.S. Population Estimates and U.S. Population Projections.





Measuring disease occurrence


	An essential step in defining health is to identify appropriate methods for measuring it. Traditionally, public health has defined disease in terms of mortality rates because they are relatively easy to obtain and death is indisputable. The use of mortality rates, however, places the greatest emphasis on diseases that end life, and tends to ignore those which compromise function and quality of life without causing death. Thus, the problems of mental illnesses, accidents, and disabling conditions are seriously underestimated if one uses only mortality to define them.
	Two other strategies to measure health that evolved in the last half of the twentieth century have been ‘years of productive life lost’ (YPLL) (Lopez et al. 2007) and ‘disability-adjusted life years’ (DALYs) (Murray and Lopez 1997). The former emphasizes those diseases that reduce the productive lifespan (currently arbitrarily defined as 75 years), whereas the latter emphasizes those diseases that compromise function and also includes a measure of premature mortality. Using either of these alternatives to define health results in very different orderings of diseases and/or health problems as public health priorities.
	Using death to identify disease priorities, the leading cause is NCDs, which account for 70% of diseases worldwide (Fig. 1.1.3). Among the chronic diseases, cardiovascular diseases account for half of the deaths. The proportion, however, varies markedly by regions of the world and level of affluence of the countries. Communicable diseases remain the major cause of death only in Africa, although they account for a significant proportion of deaths in Southeast Asia and the eastern Mediterranean. The majority of victims of these communicable diseases are infants and children under 5 years old. The persistence of communicable diseases in these areas represents a continuing major public health challenge.
	DALYs and YPLL may be considered better measures of the quality of life and functioning capacity of a country than mortality (Figs. 1.1.5a, 1.1.5b, and 1.1.6). Using DALYs to establish global disease priorities emphasizes communicable diseases and injuries, which tend to disproportionately affect the young, and reduces the relative importance of cardiovascular diseases and other chronic diseases that primarily affect the elderly. The WHO has projected that the ranking of total DALYs for neuropsychiatric disorders, injuries, and noncommunicable and/or chronic diseases will increase by 2020, whereas the ranking for communicable diseases will decline. Communicable diseases, which currently account for 39% of global DALYs, are expected to decline to 30% by 2030 (Mathers and Loncar 2006).
	Fig. 1.1.5 Global burden: disability-adjusted life year (DALY).
	From https://ourworldindata.org/health-meta under the CC BY 4.0 license.
	Fig. 1.1.6 YLL (potential years of life lost): estimator of the impact of premature death by world regions.
	From https://libguides.acomedu.org/GlobalHealth.
	According to projections by the WHO, while lower respiratory infections and diarrhoea remain the most prevalent communicable diseases, infections such as HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria will rise in terms of YPLL per 1,000 population by 2030, even as other communicable diseases will yield to intervention efforts and account for progressively fewer YPLL (World Health Organization n.d.). The YPLL per 1,000 population due to NCDs that primarily affect older people, however, is projected to remain constant, perhaps reflecting the optimism regarding the development of strategies for earlier diagnosis, better health habits, and better drugs to sustain life in patients with these conditions.
	In the 1990s syndemicity introduced the concept that diseases occur in specific contexts. These include such factors as the environment (physical and social/psychologic) in which disease occur and the concept that there are interactions between diseases which affect vulnerability and severity. This theory emphasizes that disease occurs as the result of a constellation of factors, only some of which are biologic (see Fig 1.1.7). This theory, thus, suggests the need for a broader approach to public health promotion and disease intervention (Mendenhall 2017).
	Fig. 1.1.7 The convergence model.
	Reprinted from Smolinski, S.M., Hamburg, M.A., Lederberg, J. (editors) (2003). Microbial Threats to Health: Emergence, Detection, and Response, Institute of Medicine, Board on Global Health, Committee on Emerging Microbial Threats to Health in the 21st Century, Figure ES-1, p. 5, with permission from The National Academies Press.





Communicable diseases


	Many new vaccines against infectious agents have been and are being developed, and many have become more affordable (Qadri et al. 2016). The WHO’s regional offices working with individual countries have conducted intensive immunization programmes against the major preventable infectious diseases of childhood, but there are significant barriers to complete coverage, including poverty, geographic obstacles, low levels of education affecting willingness to accept vaccination, logistical problems, civil unrest and wars, corruption, and mistrust of governments. Poverty, weak governments, and misuse of funds have also prevented control of disease vectors that play a key role in diseases such as malaria and dengue, provision of clean water, and safe disposal of human waste, all of which are essential for control of communicable diseases.
	Another major factor in the rapid spread of communicable diseases has been the rapid growth in transportation. It is now possible for an individual with a communicable disease to circumnavigate the globe while still infectious but asymptomatic. Thus, cases of SARS were reported throughout Southeast Asia and as far as Canada within weeks of the recognition of the first cases in Hong Kong (Lee 2003). Similarly, due to the extensive global food supply chains, food-borne infections can spread rapidly within and across countries.
	Another source of communicable diseases is the continuing emergence of new infectious agents, many of them adapting to humans from animal sources. Box 1.1.2 lists new disease outbreaks from 1994 to 2019, including newly drug-resistant variants of new diseases and emerging infections such as MERS, Zika, and SARS-CoV2 occurring worldwide. Changes in food production, crowding of animals, mixing of live animal species in ‘wet markets’ (selling live animals for food) in Asia and elsewhere, and the introduction of hormones and antibiotics into animal feed have all contributed to the emergence of these new diseases.
	In early January 2020 a new agent, SARS-CoV2, was recognized. The virus rapidly spread globally from China to cause a pandemic which, in the first 4 months since its identification, caused over 3.25 million cases and over 226,000 deaths severely impacting the global economy and the way society functions (Wu and McGoogan 2020; Singhal 2020). As the seventh edition of the Oxford Textbook of Global Public Health goes to press, many key characteristics of the virus are unknown making predictions difficult, although it is clear that the pandemic will have a major impact on the future of the planet (Chapter 8.13).
