	In addition to the diseases listed in Box 1.1.2, antibiotic-resistant strains of known agents have emerged rapidly due, in part, to the widespread inappropriate use of antibiotics (see also Box 1.1.3). Thus, resistant strains of gonorrhoea, Staphylococcus, tuberculosis, and malaria have become major problems, with the latter two being among the most important infectious disease problems globally. Development of drug-resistant malaria has been compounded by the emergence of vectors resistant to the commonly used chemical insecticides. The frightening potential for rapid and dangerous spread of antibiotic resistance through genetic elements that are transmissible between different bacterial species was highlighted by reports of the speed and extent to which New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase (NDM-1), which encodes multiple-antibiotic resistance, spread to many different countries (Moellering 2010).
	More than one billion people, one-seventh of the world’s population, suffer from one or more tropical disease, including Buruli ulcer, Chagas’ disease, cholera, dengue, dracunculiasis, trypanosomiasis, leishmaniasis, leprosy, lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis, helminthiasis, and trachoma (World Health Organization 2015). The functional ability of those afflicted is severely compromised, in turn affecting the economic competitiveness of the poorest countries, which suffer the greatest burden of these tropical diseases. However, major strides have been achieved in reducing the burden of diseases such as leprosy, guinea worm disease, and lymphatic filariasis. Continuing efforts are needed to further reduce the impact of these and other tropical diseases.
	 	Box 1.1.3 Factors contributing to the emergence or re-emergence of infectious diseases
	 	1. Human ‘demographic change’ by which persons begin to live in previously uninhabited remote areas of the world and are exposed to new environmental sources of infectious agents, insects, and animals
	2. People living in close proximity to domestic animals and poor animal husbandry in many parts of the developing world, leading to zoonotic infections
	3. Breakdown of sanitary and other public health measures in overcrowded cities and in situations of civil unrest and war
	4. Economic development and changes in the use of land, including deforestation, reforestation, and rapid urbanization
	5. Climate changes causing changes in the geographic range of agents and vectors
	6. Changing human behaviours, such as increased use of child-care facilities, sexual and drug-use behaviours, and patterns of outdoor recreation
	7. Social inequality
	8. International travel and commerce that quickly transport people and goods vast distances
	9. Changes in food processing and handling, including foods prepared from many different animals and transported great distances
	10. Evolution of pathogenic infectious agents by which they may infect new hosts, produce toxins, or adapt by responding to changes in the host immunity (e.g. influenza, HIV)
	11. Development of resistance of infectious agents such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae to chemoprophylactic or chemotherapeutic drugs
	12. Resistance of the vectors of vector-borne infectious diseases to pesticides
	13. Immunosuppression of persons due to new medical treatments or new diseases that result in vulnerability to infectious diseases caused by agents not usually pathogenic in healthy persons (e.g. leukaemia patients, AIDS)
	14. Deterioration in surveillance systems for infectious diseases, including laboratory support, to detect new or emerging disease problems at an early stage
	15. Illiteracy limiting knowledge and implementation of prevention strategies
	16. Lack of political will—corruption, competing priorities
	17. Biowarfare/bioterrorism—an unfortunate potential source of new or emerging disease threats (e.g. anthrax)
	18. War, civil unrest—creating refugees, food and housing shortages, increased density of living, etc.
	19. Famine
	20. Declining immunization rates (e.g. measles, mumps)
	We now recognize that we will continue to see new human pathogens emerge in the future, and need to be prepared to contain them. Unless the world realizes the consequences of not protecting the environment in which we live and acts upon it, newly emerging diseases will continue to plague us.





Noncommunicable diseases


	With increasing control of communicable diseases and increasing lifespan, NCDs have emerged as the major global health problem in both developed and developing countries. Even in developing countries, NCDs have assumed greater importance. The prevalence of type 2 diabetes in rural India is 7.3% (Anjana et al. 2017). Cardiovascular diseases have become a major cause of death in China. During 2000–2008, the incidence of stroke in low-and middle-income countries exceeded that in high-income countries by 20% (Feigin et al. 2009).
	The causes of NCDs are many and complex. Although the immediate causes are factors such as elevated blood pressure, increased blood glucose, abnormal lipids and fat deposition, and diabetes, the underlying causes are behavioural and social. These behavioural factors include unhealthy diets that substitute pre-packaged and fast foods high in fats for a balanced diet, physical inactivity, and, especially, tobacco use; these in turn are the products of social change, including globalization, urbanization, economic improvement, and ageing. The WHO estimated that globally, insufficient physical activity contributes to 3.2 million deaths and 69 million DALYs annually (Barreto 2013), and that obesity contributes to 2.8 million deaths and 35.8 DALYs globally (World Health Organization 2017b). Some NCDs have been associated with infectious disease agents. For example, Chlamydia pneumoniae has been implicated in the development of atherosclerosis (Kuo and Campbell 2000), hepatitis C is a leading cause of hepatocellular (liver) cancer, and human papilloma virus (HPV) is the major cause of cervical cancer. Recently, an effective vaccine against HPV was developed that protects against cervical cancer, but it is expensive, must be administered before sexual activity begins (i.e. early adolescence) and requires multiple injections.
	Fig. 1.1.8 shows the global distribution of deaths from NCDs, demonstrating the higher rates of death from NCDs in developing countries, especially in Africa. Another aspect of NCDs is the increasing survival of treated individuals who would not have survived as long previously. Many of them are left with disabilities that require modified environments to allow a reasonable quality of life and to realize their full potential in order to contribute to society. Most NCDs can be reduced by a combination of healthy behaviours, including not smoking, moderate alcohol use, and exercise (Breslow and Breslow 1993). Many developed countries have been promoting healthy lifestyles, but there is a need for greater emphasis and development of these programmes in developing countries, where the major global burden of chronic diseases exists.
	Fig. 1.1.8 Percentage of deaths from noncommunicable diseases by country, 2013.
	Reprinted from Mokdad A. (2016) “Global noncommunicable disease prevention: Building on success by addressing an emerging health need in developing countries” The Journal of Health Specialties 4(20: 92–104), with permission from Wolters Kluwer: Medknow.





Mental illness


	Public health professionals have only relatively recently recognized the importance of addressing the mental health needs of society on a global scale, partly due to the difficulties in defining it. It is now estimated that 1.1 billion people suffer from mental health problems, and that psychiatric disorders account for 15.5% of the global burden of disease (Collins et al. 2011) (Table 1.1.2). Mortality rates seriously underestimate the burden of mental health on society and the true extent of mental illness is probably greater.

	Updates of global provisions for treatment of mental illness are still significantly below what is necessary to adequately address the problem. The global median mental health expenditure per capita is US$ 2.5. Based on the WHO Global Health Expenditure database, the global median of domestic general government health expenditure per capita in 2015 was US$ 141, thus making government mental health expenditure less than 2% of global median of government health expenditure, with large variations between world regions. Levels of public expenditure on mental health are very meagre in low and middle-income countries, and more than 80% of these funds go to mental hospitals. Seventeen per cent of WHO Member States reported that persons pay mostly or entirely out of their own pockets for mental health services and 18% pay for psychotropic medicines themselves. The highest rates for out-of-own-pocket expenditures on mental health were noted in African and Southeast Asian regions. Globally, the median number of mental health workers is 9 per 100,000 population, but there is extreme variation (from below 1 in low-income countries to 72 in high-income countries) (World Health Organization 2017a). Of those with mental illness in developing countries, 76–85% do not have access to appropriate care. Although 87% of the world’s governments offer some mental health services at the primary care level, 30% of them have no relevant programme and 28% have no budget specifically identified for mental health. Mental illness robs society of a significant number of potentially productive persons. With the diminishing proportion of productive people of working age and the increasing proportion of elderly dependents, it is important to assist those who are not productive because of mental illness to become healthy, productive members of society.





Population projections


	Although the rate of growth of the world’s population has slowed in the latter half of the twentieth century, the world’s population, currently (2018) over 7.6 billion people, is still estimated to grow to 9.8 billion by 2050 (World Health Organization 2017b). An increasing proportion of the population will be mostly among the elderly and the old elderly (those over 80 years of age).
	The well-being of society is dependent on the ratio of those who produce to those who are dependent. Improved technology and strategies will be required to increase worker productivity. The majority of the population growth in the coming decades will be among the old and old elderly, not through increasing birth rates, and will result in a diminishing proportion of producers and an increasing proportion of dependents. It is expected, however, that more of the elderly will need to continue to be economically productive for longer periods of time. In 2017, the proportion of the world’s population that was 60 years and older was close to 1 billion (13% of the global population and doubled since 1980), and is growing at approximately 3% each year, with the total expected to double to 2 billion by 2050 (World Population Prospects: the 2017 Revision). East Asia and the Pacific have the greatest increases in ageing populations. This will be further exacerbated because the majority of the oldest elderly will be single women who traditionally have more limited resources and lower levels of education, particularly in developing countries. The productivity and efficiency of those who produce must increase if we are to sustain and improve the quality of life for all.
	The occurrence of disease in old age is directly correlated with unhealthy behaviours developed in early life. Unfortunately, concurrent with population growth, there has been a worldwide epidemic of obesity and decreased physical activity, which has increased the proportion of elderly who suffer from chronic debilitating diseases in both the developed and developing world. Thus, unless efforts to promote healthy lifestyles are successful, not only will there be an increase in the proportion of elderly, there will also be an increasing proportion of them who will require assistive care, placing a further economic and social burden on families and society.
	As the population grows, there is increasing pressure to provide food, water, and other necessities to maintain a high quality of life. Shifts in dietary preferences in developing countries towards greater meat consumption also put additional strains on food production. Fertile farmlands are increasingly being converted to residential, commercial, and industrial use. Thus, more people will effectively need to be supported on less arable land. Food security will hence be a key issue for the future and this will be affected by a multitude of factors, most notably, insufficient water resources and whether there will be major increases in agricultural productivity. It is not clear how large a population planet earth can sustain.





Other public health issues


Nutrition


	Appropriate nutrition is essential for health. In many developing countries (as well as among the poor and homeless in developed countries), undernutrition is a problem. Beyond access to nutritious and safe food, many of the poor have little knowledge about what constitutes a healthy diet, compounding the difficulties. At the same time, in developed and many rapidly developing countries such as China, overnutrition and obesity are a major problem underlying the current epidemic of diabetes. Industrial sectors have been more effective in promoting calorie-dense, salt-rich, and unhealthy foods than the efforts of public health professionals to champion healthy food choices consumed in reasonable quantities. This has particularly been the case for the young, and has contributed to rising childhood obesity in many countries, including the more affluent in developing countries.





Oral health


	Good dental health is essential for maintaining adequate nutrition and a good quality of life. Worldwide, however, 60–90% of school children and nearly 100% of adults have dental cavities. About 30% of adults aged 65–74 years have lost all of their teeth. It was also estimated that globally, there was an average of 1.6 decayed, missing, or filled teeth among children aged 12 years old (FDI World Dental Federation, 2015). These high rates of dental problems reflect poor dental hygiene and preventive care (Pine and Harris 2007). Unfortunately, many people believe that dental care is an expendable luxury, and that visits to dentists are only necessary when there is a problem. Oral cancers are the eighth most common cause of cancer globally and the third most common in Asia. The estimated incidence, mortality and 5-year survival due to lip and, oral cavity cancer in world is 300,373 (2.1%) 145,328 (1.8%) and 702,149 (2.2%), respectively (Gupta et al. 2016). Approximately 90% of all oral cancers are squamous cell carcinomas, and the 5-year survival rate of oral cancer is estimated to be 50% globally (FDI World Dental Federation, 2015). Worldwide, approximately 450,000 new cases are found each year. Death rates are high, due to the disease usually being found in late stages (Oral Cancer Foundation). Poor dental hygiene is an important risk factor, together with smoking, as well as the habit of betel nut chewing, which is common in parts of Asia. Clearly the public health message regarding the importance of good dental hygiene, regular brushing of teeth, and regular dental check-ups is not reaching the majority of the people.





Injuries


	Injuries and violence cause about 5.8 million deaths annually (about 10% of all global deaths), nearly 1.7 times the number of fatalities that result from HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria combined, of which about one-third are due to interpersonal violence, one-quarter to traffic accidents, and 15% to suicide. Tens of millions of people suffer non-fatal injuries that require treatment. Deaths due to injuries are almost three times greater in developing than in developed countries. Furthermore, they occur more commonly among younger persons and children; for those aged 5–44 years, injuries are the third leading cause of death (World Health Organization 2014a). Injuries can be broadly categorized into the following groups: motor vehicle accidents, suicide, homicide, and unintentional injuries, including occupational injuries and falls. Motor vehicle accidents account for the largest proportion of deaths due to injury (23%; over 3,400 deaths each day), and tens of millions of people are injured or disabled every year (World Health Organization 2014b). Falls, particularly among the elderly, are also a major cause of DALYs.
	Unintentional injuries are largely preventable through community and governmental intervention. Thus, improved roads, separation of different modes of transportation, enactment, and enforcement of seat belt and helmet laws, implementation, and enforcement of safe practices at work, and improved designs of houses, automobiles, ladders, and other equipment and tools have all been shown to significantly reduce injuries and deaths due to accidents.





Homicide, violence, and suicide


	Homicide, violence, and suicide represent a growing problem, particularly among the young. Homicide and suicide are among the leading causes of death globally. In some minority groups in the United States, homicide and violence are the leading cause of death of youth, followed by suicide. Globally, approximately 30% of women have experienced physical and/or sexual violence from their intimate partners (World Health Organization 2014d). In China, suicide remains the leading cause of death among women in rural areas. Globally, the WHO predicts that homicide and suicide will account for an increasing proportion of deaths.





Vulnerable populations


	Public health has always been concerned with the health and well-being of vulnerable groups who require special attention. The definition of a vulnerable population varies by time, situation, and culture, but the common characteristic across all vulnerable groups is their special susceptibility to poor health and quality of life. The list of vulnerable groups includes the poor, minorities, women, children, the elderly, the handicapped, the illiterate, orphans and street children, immigrants, rural-to-urban migrants, refugees and displaced people, the homeless, and the mentally ill. In certain situations, other groups may be considered vulnerable. For example, in the face of epidemics such as HIV/AIDS, one should also consider adolescents to be a vulnerable group. Often vulnerable individuals live at the margins of society and have difficulty accomplishing the basic functions of living and accessing healthcare. Thus, they require assistance. In many societies, particularly in developing countries, the family acts as the safety net for these groups, but if the family itself is vulnerable or dysfunctional, this safety net is compromised. Societies with sufficient resources have developed social support programmes that assist the vulnerable, but these programmes seldom cover the full range of vulnerable groups, and may not adequately support those whom they target. Universal access to healthcare is one component of assisting the vulnerable, but presently, even in wealthy developed countries such as the United States, healthcare is not available to all, and strategies to fund universal healthcare are difficult to implement.
	In almost every country, developed and developing, there are homeless people, many of whom suffer from multiple problems, including mental illness. The ability to function adequately and achieve good health among many vulnerable groups, including the homeless, mentally ill, alcoholics, and drug addicts, is adversely impacted by additional factors such as poverty, prejudice, and stigmatization by society. The US is experiencing an epidemic of overuse of opioid drugs, due to overprescribing. Thus, programmes to assist the vulnerable need to also encourage society to take supportive action in order to be optimally effective. This is a particular challenge in respect to persons with handicaps. Many developed countries have provisions for persons with handicaps, but in poorer countries, those with handicaps face substantial difficulties to function in society, and many do not survive.
	Over the last decade our understanding of the diversity of society has increased as we have recognized, for example, that gender encompasses more than the dichotomy of male and female and is actually a spectrum of sexual orientations and behaviours. Traditionally society has either ignored or ostracized groups that deviate from the ‘norm’. In order to achieve true equity it is incumbent on public health to champion diversity and equality as we recognize more diverse subgroups in our society.
	In designing programmes for vulnerable groups, a further complication is the fact that the specific problems and needs of each of these groups differ, and they thus require public health actions which are tailored to their requirements. For some of these groups, such as mothers and children and the handicapped, there are well-established programmes, although coverage is far from complete and the quality of these programmes varies widely. For others, such as illiterate persons and migrants, there are fewer established programmes. If we are to meet the public health goal of ‘health for all’, we need to identify and assist the vulnerable groups within societies to achieve their maximum possible health and function.





The environment


	 	Environmental health comprises those aspects of human health, including quality of life, that are determined by physical, chemical, biological, social, and psychosocial processes in the environment.
	Draft definition developed at a WHO consultation in Sofia, Bulgaria, 1993 (WHO Regional Office for Europe 1994)
	Currently, one of the major problems that the world faces is deterioration of the environment caused by the increasing numbers of people and the accumulation of wastes produced by them, their vehicles, and the industries they support. Thus, the quality of the air that we breathe has declined, especially in developing countries where rapid economic growth has been achieved at the expense of the environment (Table. 1.1.3). The most polluted cities of the world are concentrated in developing countries, which often have the least capacity and political will to reduce pollutant levels. Pollution of the world’s oceans, which receive massive amounts of biological and chemical wastes daily, affects not only the quality of the water, but also the ability of the ocean to sustain marine life, an important source of food.
	The number of known chemicals globally exceeds 14 million, of which over 60,000 are commonly used. All of these ultimately end up in the environment. They are the result of the huge proliferation of industry, technology, and automobiles in the twentieth century. The full health effects of many of these chemicals are still unclear and difficult to establish. Twenty-three per cent (23%) of all deaths globally are attributable to the environment (approximately 12.6 million deaths annually) (WHO Environmental Impacts on Health). As the twenty-first century progresses, the number of pollutants will continue to increase. Exposure to ambient PM 2.5 (particles with diameters of less than 2.5 microns) was ranked fifth of all global risk factors in 2014. It is estimated that it caused 4.2 deaths and 103 million DALYs globally (4.2%) in 2015, with attributable deaths increasing from 3.5 million in 1990 to 4.2 million in 2015 (Cohen et al. 2017).
	Problems of the environment occur at the personal level (at home and the workplace), the community level (e.g. air and water pollution), and globally (e.g. global warming, hazardous and radioactive waste). Although these problems may be viewed separately, they are in fact all global issues affecting both local and remote populations. Thus, slash-and-burn agricultural practices in Indonesia result in periodic and sometimes severe air pollution problems in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia. Industrial pollutants released in the industrial states of northeastern United States cause acid rain, which adversely affects crops and people in the midwestern United States and southern Canada. Pollution of rivers upstream can adversely affect communities and countries downstream, as happened in 2005 when nitrobenzene was released into the Songhua River in Heilongjiang, China, contaminating drinking water downriver in both China and Siberia, Russia.





Air pollution


	The rapid increase in automobiles and industry has caused widespread air pollution in most urban areas of the world, with the worst occurring in the developing countries that have rapidly industrialized at the expense of their environment (Table. 1.1.3). The main pollutants are ozone, particulate matter, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, sulphur dioxide, and lead. Now, in the early part of the twenty-first century, many of these countries are realizing the need to protect the environment. Unfortunately, reversal of decades of pollution is far more difficult and costly than prevention.

	The harmful effects of air pollution extend beyond the environment. Many members of society, including asthmatics and persons with chronic respiratory disease, are vulnerable to even relatively low levels of pollutants. Levels of pollutants observed in many developing countries, especially in China and India, are considerably higher than in developed countries. A study carried out in China in 2015 (Levin 2015) estimated that 1.6 million deaths per year in China are attributable to air pollution, and cancer rates have increased dramatically (as much as fourfold in industrial provinces), with an estimated 4 million cases in 2015 that resulted in nearly 3 million deaths (Carney 2016). However, the true cost of uncontrolled industrialization and pollution in these countries is not fully known.
	Indoor pollution is a particular problem in developing countries, where cooking is typically fuelled by coal or charcoal fires in poorly ventilated houses. However, it is also a problem in wealthier countries in which harmful chemicals are used for cleaning and household construction.





Water pollution


	The main types of water pollutants are mercury, nitrates, phosphorous, faecal coliform, and bacterial pollution. Those who live in developed countries take the provision of safe drinking water for granted, but 40% of the world’s population does not have access to clean drinking water, a basic necessity of life. As the world population expands, production of waste increases, and the problem of protecting water supplies also rises. Approximately 60% of the world does not have adequate facilities for waste disposal. Even in leading cities in developed countries, pollution of the water supply can occur. The increased rate of upper respiratory infections and gastrointestinal disorders among surfers and others using the ocean for recreational purposes has been well documented. Beaches in most urban areas are frequently closed when the sewage disposal systems that drain into the vicinity become overwhelmed. Acid rain from industrialization has caused acidification of lakes, making them inhospitable for fish and other marine life, thus compromising the food supply. Recently there has been discussion about whether the benefits of omega-3 fatty acids found in fish outweigh the risk of mercury poisoning among those who eat large quantities of fish. Ensuring a safe adequate water supply for people in both developed and developing countries must remain a public health priority.





Other pollutants


	The most common types of soil pollutants are heavy metals such as cadmium, chromium, copper, zinc, mercury, pesticides or herbicides, organic chemicals, oils and tars, explosive or toxic gases, combustible or radioactive materials, biologically active compounds, and asbestos; these pollutants can enter the soil through poor agricultural practices, industrial runoff, mining, landfill leakage, littering, or the improper or illegal dumping of household or industrial waste materials. As the population of the world rapidly increases and technology produces new substances and processes, not only the amounts of pollutants, but also increased varieties of pollutants. As new substances are developed, it would be ideal if their use was not permitted until plans and provisions are developed and implemented for their safe disposal. However, this is often not the case in practice.
	Biodegradable pollutants have a limited lifespan in the environment, but there is increasing production of non-biodegradable substances such as plastics, which are now ubiquitous, and hazardous materials such as radioactive wastes that persist for generations. The problem of discarding these materials safely has become a major public health issue. In some cases, developed countries are paying developing countries to accept their hazardous waste products. This strategy does not solve the problem, but shifts it to those countries that have fewer resources with which to deal with the challenge, and which are increasingly reluctant to accept wealthy countries’ garbage.
	In the past decade, nanoparticles (1 nanometre is 1 billionth of a metre) have been increasingly used in the production of foods, drugs, cosmetics, and other products used by humans. Particles of this small size become reactive in the body and, according to reports (Li et al. 2009), can cause serious damage to lung, liver, and brain cells. Given this problem, it is important that the use of nanoparticles in products intended for human use be regulated.





Climate change


	One of the most serious, long-term challenges of the twenty-first century is global warming due to the release of carbon dioxide and other ‘greenhouse gases’. Climate changes affect the social and environmental determinants of health, including safe homes, clean air, safe drinking water, sufficient food, and safe homes. Climate change may affect health through multiple ways, such as increased frequency and intensity of heat waves, reduction in cold-related deaths, increased natural disasters such as floods and droughts, changes in the distribution of vector-borne diseases, and effects on the risk of disasters and malnutrition. There is growing evidence that the consequential climate change will be associated with increased public health risks such as heat-related disorders, infectious diseases, respiratory and allergic disorders, malnutrition, mental health problems, and violence (Patz et al. 2005).
	A major review by WHO to assess the public health impact of anthropogenic climate change to date, estimated that from the mid-1970s, climate change might already have contributed to 150,000 deaths and about 5 million DALYs per year. These are largely related to increased incidence of conditions such as malnutrition, diarrhoea, and malaria (World Health Organization 2014c). Mitigating the health impact of global warming and climate change at the regional level is a major public health issue for this century, which unfortunately has been politicized.





Rescuing the environment


	To prevent further degradation of the environment and to tackle the threat of global climate change, strong political will is required of the countries of the world. For example, while the United States is one of the world’s major producers of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, in 2017, President Trump refused to endorse the Paris Accord on Climate Change, an international treaty aimed at stabilizing global greenhouse gases at levels that would avoid dangerous climate change.
	From a public health perspective, it is unrealistic to expect that the risks from environmental pollution and hazardous waste can be reduced to zero. Instead, the concept of ‘acceptable risk’ will continue to be a part of the process. Determining the level of acceptable risk will probably be arrived at through an interplay of the scientific data and evidence, with policy and political considerations. Public health professionals and researchers must play a strong role in these determinations.





Occupational health


	 	Occupational diseases are different from other diseases, not biologically, but socially.
	Henry Sigerist, 1958 (Sigerist 1958–1961)
	The International Labour Organization’s Health and Safety Programme estimated that each year globally there are over 2 million work-related deaths, over 300 million suffering from work-related diseases, and approximately 3.7 million fatal and non-fatal work-related injuries. In some developing countries, child labour is still the norm. Twelve million serious injuries occurred among young workers in 2011. This affects more people than those who have myocardial infarcts (heart attacks), strokes, or newly diagnosed malignancies annually. A significant proportion of these deaths and injuries are preventable by improving safety in the workplace. However, safeguarding the health of the worker often receives less priority than the need to produce goods cheaply, especially in developing countries, despite the increase in workplace fatalities in low-and middle-income countries in four of the six WHO regions (Hamalainen et al. 2017) (Table 1.1.3).
	The nature of the workplace is constantly changing, with increasing proportions of workers being involved in service industries rather than in manufacturing. Over the last decade particularly, production of goods has shifted rapidly to developing countries, where labour costs are lower. The manufacturing industries in these countries are often subject to fewer and less comprehensive safety regulations, and in some cases, are associated with low salaries and few or low healthcare benefit provisions for workers, especially for migrant workers from rural areas. Increasingly, women are entering the workforce and must manage both work and family. Larger numbers of workers are being employed on an informal part-time basis. While this reduces labour costs for industry, these informal part-time workers do not usually receive work-related benefits such as retirement and health insurance. They now represent 50% or more of the workforce globally. This segment of the workforce is particularly vulnerable to injury and limited access to healthcare.
	As noted earlier, the population is ageing, and the proportion of the population that is economically active is diminishing. In response to this change, the age of eligibility for social security benefits in the United States is increasing, and mandatory retirement is being phased out. It is now projected that the proportion of workers over the age of 60 will increase to 20% in Japan and 10% in the United States by 2030 (Population Projections 2000). The United Nations report on World Population Ageing 2015 noted that among individuals aged 65 years or over, 30% of men and 15% of women were active in the labour force (United Nations 2015b). The needs of older workers are different and greater than those of younger workers. Thus, the changing nature of the workforce will require corresponding changes in work safety regulations and health benefits to ensure a healthy, productive workforce.





Provision of and access to healthcare


	Access to preventive and curative care is a requirement for health in every society, whether rich or poor. Access to affordable healthcare has long been a problem for the poor and for rural residents, especially in developing countries. Even in the United States, full access to healthcare remains a problem. Health insurance is prohibitively expensive and beyond the reach of many in the middle classes, unless it is subsidized by employers or government. Increasingly, employers are attempting to free themselves from the cost of health insurance for their employees through a variety of strategies. The elderly also have problems with healthcare; because healthcare utilization and costs tend to increase with age, insurance companies have been less willing to cover the elderly, and many governments, even in developed countries, do not provide adequate support for the elderly. The Affordable Care Act enacted under President Obama extended coverage significantly, but President Trump and the Republican Congress have undermined it, causing 13 million Americans to lose their coverage. In developing countries, the rural poor are particularly at risk. Few health professionals are willing to work in rural areas, and the cost of providing care in less populated areas, even in wealthier countries, is greater than in urban areas. Innovative strategies are needed to promote universal coverage and ensure that the rural poor and elderly have access to reasonable healthcare.





Bioterrorism and war


	The history of use of biological weapons in war extends back for hundreds of years. In the Middle Ages, corpses of plague victims were catapulted into castles under siege. In more modern times, anthrax was used to contaminate the US postal system, resulting in several deaths. The WHO and public health agencies of individual countries have developed plans to quickly diagnose and control bioterrorist incidents. However, these threats to the health of the public will continue until the underlying causes of terrorism and bioterrorism are addressed.
	Few actions can have the magnitude of negative impact on the health of the public that war has. Men, women, and children are killed, children are forced to serve as soldiers, homes are destroyed, major segments of the population become displaced refugees, women are raped, and the social and/or economic fabric of the countries involved is destroyed. Recovery usually takes years to decades. The outside world, particularly those countries adjacent to warring nations, must cope with the huge influx of displaced persons, and action needs to be implemented to help those still in the country suffering from the impact of the war. The consequences of war are so severe and wide-ranging that it is imperative that better ways be reached to resolve international conflicts. The resources ploughed into armed conflict could be better deployed on humanitarian and public health support.





Ethics in public health


	Although ethical issues are implicit in the delivery of public health, it was only after the Second World War and the recognition that ‘scientific experiments’ in Nazi Germany violated human rights that an emphasis was placed on recognizing the ethics of public health actions, particularly research. The Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association 2002), the Belmont Report (US National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research 1979), and the Council for International Organizations of Medical Science (2002) have promulgated ethical guidelines for research and the establishment of institutional review boards worldwide to ensure that medical and/or public health research is conducted ethically and does not violate human rights. However, there are inherent ethical conflicts in many public health actions. For example, some consider that the human rights of ‘typhoid Mary’, a typhoid carrier who insisted on working as a cook in the early twentieth century, were violated when she was incarcerated to prevent her from continuing to prepare food that initiated typhoid epidemics. Protecting the human rights of a man to refuse testing for HIV may result in him unknowingly infecting his wife, yet-to-be-born children, and other sexual contacts. By protecting his human rights, the human rights of his wife or partner and future family will be violated, underscoring the complexity of human rights issues.
	Implementing public health programmes and research often results in ethical conflicts and the need to balance the good of society against potential harm to the individual. It is imperative to inform society, particularly those who will be involved in the public health programmes or research, about the nature of the ethical conflicts inherent in action. For example, a trial evaluating the effectiveness of prophylactic treatment to prevent HIV infection in sex workers in Cambodia was stopped by the prime minister, who felt that the prevention trial exploited Cambodian sex workers. A more intense effort on the part of the researchers to inform the public and politicians about the nature of the study and the potential benefit to sex workers, not only in Cambodia, but globally, might have averted this unfortunate outcome.





Public health interventions


	One important task of public health professionals is to raise the level of anxiety of the public about public health problems to the level at which they will be willing to take an appropriate action. In this, an appropriate balance must be struck, since raising the level of anxiety too little will result in inadequate or no action, while raising it too high may promote a fatalistic attitude and, as in the case of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, may promote stigmatization and isolation of affected individuals, seriously complicating the task of intervention. The difficulty for the public health professional is creating the level of anxiety that results in the required action while minimizing unintended consequences.
	Public health interventions can be divided into four categories: social/biological/environmental, behavioural, political, and structural. The public health professional must use strategies in all four categories to achieve the maximum health of the public.





Social, biological, and/or environmental interventions


	The strategy that has had the greatest impact on improving the health of the public has been an improved standard of living, including provision of clean water and safe disposal of wastes. Unfortunately, these interventions have not reached much of the world where crowding, unsafe and insufficient water, accumulation of wastes, inadequate housing, and lack of economic development persist.
	The most cost-effective biological intervention strategy is immunization, in part because it requires minimal behavioural change and usually involves only a single series of actions. The WHO has taken the lead in promoting vaccine coverage worldwide through its Expanded Programme on Immunization. The appropriate use of vaccines has reduced the majority of childhood infections in developed countries, and significantly reduced them in most developing countries. Smallpox, a major infectious disease problem until the latter half of the twentieth century, has now been eliminated. The WHO has now targeted polio, but more challenges, such as hepatitis, tuberculosis, and measles, remain. However, it is important to realize that development and production of a vaccine is only the first step. An effective vaccine against smallpox was available for over 150 years before smallpox was eliminated. The key was the strategy of vaccine coverage, ‘search and contain’, together with adequate political will and funding that permitted global elimination of that disease. Thus, the strategy for utilizing the vaccine is perhaps equally important as the efficacy of the vaccine itself. Public education and engagement must continue to be a major priority. Recently, attacks from the media, particularly social media, have caused acceptance of vaccines to decline, reducing the level of ‘herd immunity’ required to prevent epidemics (Karlamangla 2018).
	Another biological strategy is to eliminate the vectors of disease, the major approach currently in use for the control of dengue, arboviral diseases, and many of the parasitic diseases. However, overzealous use of pesticides can also create problems. For example, dichloro-diphenyl-trichloroethane (DDT), used widely in the twentieth century as an insecticide, still contaminates the food supply, creating other health problems, including the risk of malignancy.
	Treatment can also be considered a biological intervention strategy. To confront tuberculosis, one of the major infectious diseases of the twenty-first century, directly observed treatment short course (DOTS) has been successfully implemented in countries where the disease persists, and reduces transmission and development of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (TB). Treatment of sexually transmitted infections and contacts to reduce the reservoir of infectious people is a major strategy for control of transmission, but has yet to prove effective in stopping the current epidemic. ‘Treatment as prevention’ has become a mantra of HIV/AIDS control.





Behavioural interventions


	Most public health interventions depend ultimately on behaviour change, whether it is personal or community behaviour. At the personal or individual level, promotion of good health habits, including avoidance of smoking and excessive alcohol use and other dependency disorders are important interventions that have a major impact on health. At the community level, confronting attitudes towards acceptable sexual behaviour and persons with dependency disorders and stigmatizing diseases are key to establishing community ‘norms’ that promote a healthy lifestyle and include all segments of society. However, modifying individual behaviour and community norms is difficult, and it is even more difficult to ensure persistence of the modified behaviour. However, the majority of the public health interventions will not be successful unless they are embraced and sustained by the community at the individual, local, national, and international levels, and accompanied by appropriate regulations and policies. The success of the antismoking campaigns in the United States and Britain and population control in China (the one-child policy) affirm that it is possible to change community norms.
	Many theories identifying strategies to modify behaviour have been proposed. One of the most interesting is the Popular Opinion Leader model (Kelly 2004), which utilizes the natural leaders found in any social group as agents of change. In the United States, this strategy has been demonstrated to change behaviour in groups of men who have sex with men, and has been evaluated in other populations worldwide (Rotheram-Borus et al. 2011). Ultimately, if public health interventions are to be effective, they must be adopted by the community. The media can play an important role in facilitating these interventions and assuring that they become community norms.





Political interventions


	Public health is politics. Any process that involves obtaining the support of the public will involve politics and differing points of view. For example, the campaign to stop smoking was strongly opposed by the tobacco industry, which spent millions of dollars trying to counter the many reports on the adverse health effects of smoking. Countering the efforts of the tobacco industry required obtaining the political support of the public in order to pass laws and regulations limiting smoking, placing health warnings on cigarette packages, and raising taxes on cigarettes. Many needed regulations transcend boundaries and require international cooperation (e.g. regulation of greenhouse gases).
	If we are to succeed in safeguarding the oceans, inland waters, and the air we breathe, it will be through political process requiring global coordination and joint action. This process has already begun in many developed countries, which have passed strong laws regulating emissions from automobiles and factories, although they are constantly under attack. Now this process must be expanded to the developing countries, where the worst pollution is currently occurring.
	One of the most urgent issues before the public today is the battle over emission of ‘greenhouse gases’, which are causing a rise in temperatures globally. This temperature rise will adversely affect the quality of life of our children, grandchildren, and their grandchildren. Unfortunately there is still political action in the US to not take the necessary steps to arrest or reverse this detrimental warming trend.
	It is important that the political process puts in place measures to improve the health of the public, based on sound scientific evidence. Pushing agendas not based on sound scientific evidence will undermine the credibility of public health professionals and our ability to accomplish our legitimate goals. Obtaining this evidence is not always easy. For example, accumulating evidence on the long term (induction period of years to decades) impact of adverse exposures is not easily established, and often requires extrapolation from data from the impact of acute high-dose exposures to lower long-term doses. This often requires relying on models that are difficult for the public to understand, and are often subject to debate, even within the scientific community.





Structural interventions


	An important end-point of the political process is the passage of laws and regulations. This action, if implemented, can have a very significant impact on the improvement of the health of the public. The passage and enforcement of helmet laws for motorcycles in Indonesia, the US, and Vietnam reduced the incidence of associated brain injuries and deaths. The incidence of lung cancer and heart disease among men has been significantly reduced, partly due to the laws regulating smoking in public spaces and the high taxes imposed on cigarettes. In 2013, China began very strong antipollution measures, particularly to stop use of coal, and the air quality in China has now greatly improved (Economist 2018). Many of the current public health problems of the world, particularly those involving protection of the environment, can best be addressed through structural changes requiring passage and implementation of laws and regulations. To accomplish this will require changing the attitudes and behaviour of the public and ensuring that public health regulations and laws are enforced.





Private support of public health


	Private support has played an important role in the development of public health, especially in the twentieth century. The Rockefeller Foundation supported the first school of public health in the United States at Johns Hopkins University; set up the International Health Commission in 1913; established the China Medical Board in 1914, which established the first public health university in China, the Peking Union Medical College, in 1921; and has continued to contribute to global health since its founding in 1913 (Brown 1979; Berman 1983). Other foundations, including the Gates, Ford, Carnegie, and Robert Wood Johnson Foundations, have made similar significant contributions to public health.
	Private support of public health has been implemented through three strategies: establishment of charitable foundations by industry; development of international, national, and local non-governmental organizations (NGOs); and direct contributions by industry. Each makes and can continue to make a significant contribution to the health of the public.
	Foundations have contributed enormously to the advancement of public health, but most identify their own priorities for funding. Usually they provide support for important public health needs, but foundations and public health leaders do not always agree on what the most important priorities are. Massive infusions of money into public health by organizations such as the Gates Foundation, which makes contributions to fight HIV, malaria, and tuberculosis, can have a significant positive impact, but they also tend to influence public health priorities. Some argue that developing strong public health infrastructures in developing countries will have a much greater impact on improving health than focusing funds on specific health issues (Garrett 2007).
	NGOs tend to focus on specific health problems (e.g. American Cancer Society), specific health issues such as refugee health or medical care for the underserved (e.g. Doctors without Borders), and specific populations (e.g. drug users and sex workers). Often they can be more effective in reaching vulnerable populations and addressing specific health problems and issues because they are closer to the problem than health professionals who must handle a broad range of concerns. Public health programmes can increase their cost-effectiveness by cooperating with NGOs in addressing specific issues, health problems, and populations.
	Industry is often viewed as part of the problem. Public health needs to convince industry to temper its profit motive to incorporate responsible citizenship at all levels. Industry is frequently a significant contributor to public health problems (e.g. air and water pollution). On the other hand, economic development can lead to an improved economic situation that reduces poverty and benefits all of society. Industry, particularly advertising, has clearly demonstrated that they are better at creating demand and influencing lifestyles than public health professionals. Thus, it behooves public health organizations to learn from industry and to work with industry to develop and implement healthy economic growth, while safeguarding the environment and benefiting the public.
	Private support greatly benefited public health in the twentieth century. The challenge for the twenty-first century is for public health and private support to agree on the most effective use of private funds for achieving the greatest public health advances.





Social activism


	Action by groups within society has led to improvements in the health of the public. Social activism by workers and others in the nineteenth and early twentieth century in England and the United States resulted in improved working conditions for workers in a variety of industries and to development of the field of occupational health. More recently, social activism by social groups adversely affected by HIV/AIDS led to the policy to provide access to treatment for all with HIV infection and the need to recognize the human rights of marginalized groups in both developed and developing countries. Demands for better health conditions led by society itself are most likely to result in positive changes.





The future of public health


	Public health does not lack challenges requiring solutions. Poverty is the major cause of poor health globally, yet income disparities in most countries of the world continue to grow. Developing countries must continue to cope with infectious diseases while confronting the epidemic of NCDs, further compounded by the threat of emerging diseases such as new variants of influenza. Rapid communications and transportation greatly increase the likelihood that local problems will quickly become global problems. This underscores the urgent need for much better international cooperation. An increasing proportion of the world’s population will live longer. We have been successful at adding ‘years to life’, but chronic diseases such as Alzheimer’s have reduced the quality of some of the years of life added. We must now concentrate on adding ‘life to years’, helping older people to continue to be healthy and productive.
	We cannot afford to continue to ignore the quality of the environment. Continuing contamination of the air and water will not only cause and/or exacerbate chronic and infectious diseases, but will also compromise global food production. The world’s population is still growing and, together with increasing urbanization, will further exacerbate the problem of environmental degradation.
	Despite the economic and health advances of the past century, disparities between the rich and the poor in many countries are widening. This gap needs to be narrowed, not at the expense of those who are better-off, but by improving the economic situation and health of the poor and disadvantaged. The rising cost of healthcare will make closing the gap in access to healthcare even more challenging.
	Injuries and violence are robbing an increasing number of people of their ability to function and to enjoy a reasonable quality of life. Injuries can be easily prevented through a variety of preventive strategies, including better design of the workplace and tools, as well as behavioural and structural approaches.
	Violence and war present a particularly great challenge, and will require new strategies not hitherto widely used in public health. Public health must contribute to strategies to resolve differences between countries by promoting cross-national and international cooperation in confronting global health problems, and contribute to strategies to implement successful conflict resolution.
	It is clear that the pandemic of SARS-CoV2, which has caused many deaths globally, has severely impacted the global economy and the ways in which society functions. As of this writing it is difficult to predict what those changes will be, but we must be prepared to deal with them.
	Public health must convince people and provide the environment that allows them to adopt healthy lifestyles. The major strategies to combat the current epidemic of NCDs are regular exercise, a healthy diet, and development of good health habits.
	Much is known about what needs to be done to significantly reduce the incidence of NCDs such as cardiovascular diseases, stroke, and cancer, but much more effective ways are needed to effect the necessary changes in personal and community behaviour, and to promote healthy lifestyles. The growing prominence of data analytics, artificial intelligence and technology raises the promise of more effective identification of at-risk groups in the general and patient populations, and more targeted and effective interventions. However, these need to be well integrated into broader public health goals and strategies.
	Tremendous strides have been made to improve the health of the public, but the challenge to do better remains. In subsequent chapters, public health experts discuss the challenges and potential solutions in greater detail.

1.2


The history and development of public health in developed countries


	Simon Szreter





Introduction: prioritizing the public’s health and engendering economic development


	It has been conventional to locate the origins of public health in early efforts to combat epidemics and to regulate the sanitary environment accompanying urban life and to trace its history in the gradual evolution of such measures in relation to politics, administrative practices, public laws, and medical science’s changing aetiology (Rosen 1993; Porter 1994). Such an historical account provides important insights and understanding but it is also de-limited in one significant sense. Public health is cast in a responsive role in relation to the processes of economic development. However, the nature of the relationship between public health and global economic development can appear very differently when it is viewed over the long-term, encompassing the whole process of modern economic transformation from the singular matrix of its origins in the early modern society and economy of England, c.1600–1800.
	This chapter will show that state policies to promote the social order, security, and health of the population in fact pre-date and crucially underpinned the process through which the modern world’s economic transformation originated—in early modern England. Furthermore, the relationship has since remained an interdependent and dialectical one. Economic development has required healthier and more productive citizens to sustain both the supply and the demand sides of the growing economy. Furthermore, as Amartya Sen has recently had to remind the discipline of economics, the purpose of economic growth is to enhance human capabilities and functioning, not simply to amass a global stock of capital, regardless of welfare and distributional issues (Sen 1999).





The historic origins of public health policies in ensuring food security and preventing epidemics


	Public health is a term which refers to a complex body of scientific expertise, policies, laws, and behavioural norms which have evolved in relation to a changing knowledge base about the prevention of harm and the promotion of health among human communities. It is also a term which refers to the observable state of relative health in those communities. Wise statecraft in the past dictated that a secure leader or government ruling over a robust polity aimed for the populace to be at least as vigorous and economically productive as those of rival states. The most elementary public health policy pursued by leaders throughout history has therefore always been the search for food security.
	Given the vagaries of climate and weather, food security has posed a fundamental problem of potential disorder for leaders of settled human groups of any significant size. Threats of dearth and famine are literally Old Testament biblical themes. The importance of the relationship between sound statecraft and ensuring the public’s health through food security is encapsulated in Genesis 41 in the story of Joseph’s interpretation of the Pharaoh’s dream of the seven fat years to be followed by seven lean years and the institution of state granaries in Egypt to preserve the people and the ruler. Ancient Chinese doctrine of an emperor’s ‘Mandate of Heaven’ enshrined the legitimacy of popular uprising against a ruler who could not protect his people from natural disaster, including from famines. Most ancient civilizations which were sufficiently successful to have endured across many generations and to have supported the elaborate cultural productions which we now marvel at in museums, such as that of the Egyptians or the Chinese, the Incas, or the Romans, also solved this basic public health problem of food security through state-controlled granaries.
	Inadequate food is the most elementary of public health threats, but sufficient and clean water is not far behind. Most historic settlements could only prosper and expand where water supplies were adequate to their needs. However, the Romans (and quite independently in South America, e.g. the Moche-Chimú and the Incas) famously developed impressive hydraulic technological solutions which allowed settlements and cities to grow to sizes way beyond their immediately accessible water supplies. Their irrigation channels, aqueducts, public fountains, and bathing facilities were publicly funded engineering feats supplying dense populations with secure and clean water supplies, separated from the equally necessary sanitary waste systems.
	Two other crucially important measures in the modern public health armamentarium which also have their genesis in much earlier practices—from the late fourteenth century onwards in Ragusa (Dubrovnik) first and then across Italy—are, firstly, the policy of physical segregation of those believed to be carrying a life-threatening communicable disease. This practice is generally known as quarantine, signalling its historic association in Europe with efforts to ward off plague outbreaks (40 days free from disease was found to be the required period to clear infected ships). It is closely related to the later practice of isolation of the infected, which lay behind the creation of separate fever wards and hospitals. Secondly, the administrative practice of counting burials, as an early warning system to monitor signs of epidemic disease outbreaks within urban populations. Also first observed in Italian city states, the most developed of these were London’s weekly Bills of Mortality, which publicized the data collated from its parishes sporadically in the sixteenth century and then continuously from the early seventeenth century onwards, when they also began to include information on attested causes of death. This provided the basis for the beginnings of epidemiology in the analysis pioneered by John Graunt in his Natural and Political Observations of 1662 (although information on age at death was lacking until the eighteenth century).1
	Thus, most of the key principles and policies which inform the preventive practices of ‘modern’ public health—and which cause it to have an integral relationship with the capacity of populations to attain high densities of settlement and associated sophisticated levels of commercial and cultural development—can be found repeatedly in history long before the advent of the most recent era of global industrialization (on earlier globalizations in history, see Hopkins 2002).





The emergence of the world’s first universalist social security system in England c.1530–1830: facilitator of labour mobility, economic growth, and the public’s health


	Between approximately 1600 and 1850 English society experienced a transformative rise in the material productivity of its people and economy that was without historical precedent in its speed and global reach; and it is from the proliferation of this process that all of today’s developed economies and countries have emerged. Economic historians will no doubt continue to debate till the end of time the relative importance of all the different factors, both within British society and through its relationships within an expanding European, trans-Atlantic, and also global set of trading networks, which have contributed to explaining how this extraordinary process unfolded during these two centuries.2
	However, one crucially important part of the story of this initiating episode of modern, industrial economic development relates intimately and directly to the history of a peculiarly English variant of the long-standing preoccupation of sovereign rulers with preserving and promoting the health of their subject populations. The strategy for doing this took an important, entirely innovative turn in England during the course of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, with extraordinary, novel implications for the productivity of the economy.
	During the fateful decade of the 1530s Henry VIII broke with the Catholic Papacy in Rome, proclaiming himself head of the Church of England. One of the prime functions of the mediaeval church all across Europe had been to dispense alms to the needy, fulfilling its Christian vocation to offer mercy and charity. As the new head of the Church in England the ultimate responsibility to provide alms to the indigent poor now rested with the Crown. The Tudor state therefore needed to find an alternative, practical means to fulfil its Christian obligations to support the poor without bankrupting the Crown’s limited resources, having sold off much of the rent-generating Catholic church’s estates, which previously funded this activity. A sequence of experiments during the rest of the sixteenth century by Henry and his successors finally culminated in a system for placing this practical responsibility primarily on the approximately 10,000 individual parishes of the new Church of England, using the funds generated by a progressive tax rate levied on the value of land occupied by individuals within the parish. This was the famous Elizabethan or ‘Old’ Poor Law, enacted by statutes in 1598 and 1601. Buttressed also by a reforming 1601 Charities Act, these Acts established an absolute right to ‘relief’—a universal social security entitlement—for every Anglican subject of the Crown in all circumstances. Parish officials (usually unpaid) had the duty, overseen by local Justices of the Peace—answerable ultimately for the fair administration of the system to the Crown—to ensure that nobody starved due to lack of work, being orphaned, old age, or illness.3
	The parish-administered Poor Laws became the all-purpose social security and antifamine system for England and Wales, preserving the public’s health throughout the ensuing two centuries. It proved so effective it enabled the entire population to avoid completely the fundamental insecurity of famine and starvation-related disease deaths throughout this period, achieving a unique level of protection from the perennial threat which still afflicted the rural populations of the continent. The key difference in England and Wales was that every rural parish had its Poor Law fund and officers (Solar 1995). This necessitated an associated scale of public expenditure on the rural poor which French observers in the eighteenth century found literally incredible (Smith 2011). Whereas on the continent of Europe episodes of dearth resulted in raised death rates as hungry, workless, diseased rural refugees tried to make for urban centres with their grain stores, in England and Wales cash relief to purchase food was doled out to all in need in their own parishes. Unlike in the rest of Europe, after the 1620s there is no further evidence that high food prices caused peaks in death rates across England (Galloway 1988; Healey 2014). As Paul Slack has pointed out this approach to preserving social order by stabilizing the populace in times of potential disruption was also followed through in relation to the great epidemic threat of plague, where Tudor practices of isolating infected families by shutting them up in their houses, while continuing to supply them with food, were consolidated in the 1604 Plague Act (Slack 1985).
	Quite unlike previous, successful antifamine strategies, as for instance that of the state granary system of the Qing dynasty in China at this very same time (Wong 2011), the English parish Poor Law did so without interrupting the normal commercial functioning of the market economy. Even when food prices were high, rather than interdicting the market price, the poor received adequate financial support to maintain them; and producers continued to make their profits.4 The continuity of markets gave greater confidence to landlords and farmers making major investments to promote higher productivity. This raised the overall productivity of British agriculture, enabling it successfully to feed a population of increasingly landless, urban workers which grew to proportions of the national total never previously sustained (Wrigley 1987, ch.7).
	The absolute commitment, given in black-letter statute law, to maintain at parish expense all subjects of the Crown, including not only the unemployed but also the ill, orphans, and the old, was a most extraordinary mandate laid on the collective funds of each community to maintain the health of all, including a duty of care for the vulnerable—both young and old. This was an incipient free healthcare system, a comprehensive, if embryonic, public health policy. It did indeed lead to the largest proportion of the regular expenses of many parishes being consumed in supporting the incomes of the elderly in pensions, and in the building of almshouses to accommodate them and payments for doctors’ fees in attending them (Williams 2011: 161–2). The most comprehensive recent study of healthcare under the Poor Law in seven provincial counties has found 15% of Poor Law funds spent on medical care throughout the period 1750–1834 (King 2018). London’s largest parishes, charged under the Poor Law with caring for the vulnerable, were operating large infirmaries giving free treatment to patients throughout the eighteenth century (Siena 2004; Reinarz and Schwarz 2013). The link between illness and liability to support the poor was sufficiently obvious that leading figures across England were founding voluntary subscription hospitals at a rate of one every two years during the period 1720–75 (Slack 1990: 19, 50–1). The provincial city of Chester, for instance, was where the physician, Dr John Haygarth, trained under the great William Cullen at Edinburgh, innovated in 1783 the practice of segregated fever wards, by having a top-floor extension constructed for the Chester Infirmary; he was also an active promoter of smallpox inoculation in the region and conducted a pioneering census of the city to estimate more accurately the prevalence of different diseases. Enlightenment principles of systematic observation were leading physicians towards preventive conceptions for collective promotion of the public’s health (Risse 1992).
	It has been estimated that Poor Law transfer payments amounted to approximately 1% of gross national product (GNP) by 1696 and this had further risen to 2% by the 1780s (Slack 1990, Table 1). The Poor Law’s primary virtue, in terms of promoting economic development, was that by underwriting security for the older generation, it released a historically novel degree of voluntary labour mobility among the younger generation. During the initial, gradual stages of commercial expansion in the world’s first industrializing economy the most important factor of production was flexible labour power, free to migrate to wherever nodes of growing labour demand were located. Between 1600 and 1800, the single statistic which consistently marked-out English society as exceptional from the rest of Europe and the world was the rapidity with which its rising generations were consistently moving, decade by decade, to urban places of manufacturing and commerce, leaving behind their ageing, landless parents secure in the knowledge that their parishes would support them (Wrigley 2004: Fig. 3.8). Parish pensions provided the elderly with an alternative security to the small subsistence patrimonies handed down from one impoverished generation to the next, as in much of the rest of Europe, including France, where the immiseration of morcellement is widely considered one of the underlying causes of the 1789 Revolution. Throughout history honouring and looking after elders had gone with a general need to maintain close geographic proximity; the parish Poor Law of England released the younger generation from this constraint to pursue their best options for income-earning. Furthermore, the absolute entitlement to community support muted the political consequences of the grievances of the rural poor at the productivity-raising enclosure of commons lands and the buying-up of smaller farms by larger, more commercial enterprises.
