The birth of the modern Public Health movement: minimizing the costs of disease prevention


	Although the Elizabethan Poor Law was the midwife to England’s labour mobility and, thereby, its economic dynamism, during the second half of the eighteenth century its costs were rising as the industrializing economy disrupted and drew workers from ever larger proportions of its rural hinterland. The British economy’s globally expansionary growing pains were also involving the nation increasingly in foreign wars during this same period and so the Poor Laws were picking up the indirect domestic social costs of migration, overseas trade, and war, rising 8-fold in cost c.1750–1815. It was the search by the governing class for containment of the rising costs of managing these disruptions, within a continuing commitment to universal social security, which was to dictate the shape of the world’s first public health administration during the formative period c.1834–1914.
	This directly resulted in the first ever national Public Health Act passed in 1848, the same year in which the continent of Europe was convulsed in republican rebellions violently put down by reactionary monarchical regimes. By contrast, Britain’s 1848 reconfirmed a further stage in the evolution of the exceptionally devolved governance system the Tudor Crown had first instituted to deal with the public policy issues of social order and social security. Although important scientific initiatives and policy ideas, relevant to the overall unfolding history of public health, can be identified as occurring in several other countries, too, such as in Austro-Hungary, France, Germany, and Sweden, it was primarily in Britain, the most economically dynamic, rapidly urbanizing, and wealthy state, that a public health administration—gradually and contestedly—first came into existence as a nationwide institution over the half-century following the 1848 Act.
	Influential advocates for Poor Law reform included Adam Smith and Thomas Malthus, though their detailed arguments have been demonstrated by modern historians to have been unevidenced and incorrect.5 Strongest support for reform in Parliament came from those seeing themselves as paying disproportionately for the Poor Law, who were principally the tax-rated landowners and farmers of the nation, not the urban industrialists (Mandler 1987). Eventually in 1834 a radically reformed New Poor Law was enacted. Jeremy Bentham’s amanuensis, Edwin Chadwick, deployed his master’s individualist and behaviourist pain-pleasure principle of ‘scientific’ government to redesign deterrence into the nation’s social security system.
	The new ideology of free markets and individual pursuit of self-interest deemed the collectively funded parish Poor Law an inefficient creator of dependency and pauperism and so insisted on cut-backs and deterrence. The state was attempting to withdraw systematically from intervention in society and economy, following the logic of political economy and rationalist utilitarianism replacing mercantilism and Christian mercy as guides to public policy. Although the state would continue to honour the right to relief of all subjects of the Crown, this would now only be available to those entering a workhouse to earn their keep by hard labour, with the sexes kept segregated to ensure the idle poor had no inducement to reproduce further at the expense of the community. Henceforth outdoor relief (cash doles handed to the unemployed in their homes) were supposed to cease, except for the old and the sick who genuinely could not work.
	Globally expanding free trade, promoted by an increasingly dominant Royal Navy able to enforce British trading wishes even as far away as China, also brought with it more intensive intercontinental exchange of diseases, signified for Europe in the sequence of cholera pandemics, 1829–49, 1852–9, 1863–79, 1881–96, 1899–1923, each originating in India, the prize colony in Britain’s expanding commercial empire. The successive epidemics, reached Britain itself in 1831–2, 1847–8, 1853–4, and 1866–7, provoking fear and panic, even among the property-owning section of society, who increasingly sought refuge in the suburbs for their families, away from the filth and poverty of the urban centres where their wealth was manufactured.
	The public health tool of information collection and dissemination, used for centuries to warn of such epidemics, was developed further, initially in post-Napoleonic France to promote public awareness of the scale of truly shocking quantities of non-epidemic, premature mortality afflicting the poorest districts of Paris, increasingly revealed from 1829 onwards in the pages of the new journal, Annales d’Hygiène Publique et de Médecine Légale (Coleman 1982; La Berge 1992). The pioneering French studies then inspired new official analyses beginning a decade later in Britain. William Farr had studied in 1829–30 in the Paris of the pioneering investigative hygienists such as Louis-René Villermé and Alexandre Parent-Duchâtelet and the great exponent of the numerical method, Pierre Louis, and this influenced his own statistical approach to medicine. On appointment to the new post of Medical Superintendent of Statistics at the General Register Office in 1839, Farr began to analyse the whole nation’s newly instituted civil death registers to conduct a classic public health information campaign bombarding the British public and its newly freed-up provincial and national press with evidence of the egregious scale of preventable deaths occurring in the industrial cities. He innovated graphic survival tables which aimed to shock, in demonstrating that half of all infants failed to reach their fifth birthday in Liverpool and Manchester; and he went on to devise league tables of death rates to goad city’s elected representatives to take action (Eyler 1979; Szreter 2005, ch.8).
	From quite distinct premises Edwin Chadwick was himself coming to parallel conclusions about the costs of disease. He was vexed to find that his deterrent workhouses were not, after all containing Poor Law costs. His investigations in East London convinced him that this was because disease caused incapacity to work and hence dependence of the sick on the Poor Law (Hamlin 1997). As Hamlin points out, there were other medical leaders at this time, notably W.P. Alison in Edinburgh, who championed the more radical argument that poverty—inadequate pay and insecure employment– caused the disease revealed by Farr’s statistics. The great German medical scientist, Rudolf Virchow, having concluded from his pioneering studies of typhus among starving Polish peasants in Silesia in 1847–8 that it was due to the exploitative conditions imposed by the German aristocratic landowners, also backed socially radical policies to address workers’ wages and living conditions in his new weekly journal, Die Medicinische Reform. However, the flawed Smithian wages fund theory prevailed at this time in Britain and increasingly across Europe, with its claim that any rise in one set of workers’ wages could only be at the expense of others. It was endorsed also by the French hygienists, who accepted the Revolution’s principles regarding the sanctity of private property (against monarchical despotism) and the necessity of a market economy, championed in France by J.-B. Say (Ramsey 1994, p. 57). The wages fund theory was not to be abandoned by the Victorian high priest of economic orthodoxy, J.S. Mill, until 1869. As Hamlin has shown, Chadwick’s Public Health Act did not question economic orthodoxy and was devised as a pragmatic, sanitary engineering solution to specific problems he had diagnosed with the practical operation of his masterly New Poor Law.
	In medical terms Chadwick’s ‘Sanitary Idea’ was premised on the obsolescent miasmatist theory—that bad smells given off by decaying organic matter—caused disease. The notion that cleanliness was close to godliness was, however, a conventional homily of the period, appealing to MPs’ common sense and to evangelical religionists (Smith 2007). The proposal to cleanse the city with an inflow of constant pressure, clean water, and an outflow of the used water through a self-scouring arterial sewers system (with the product sold to farmers as night-soil to help defray the cost) passed parliamentary scrutiny and became law. It would engineer the sanitized city, remove disease, and thereby minimize poverty and claims on the Poor Law, without in any way impugning the laws of the free market in labour.
	Chadwick’s sanitary city was still going to be extremely expensive to build. Westminster envisaged that most of the money would come from local taxation—rates levied on urban property values. Proud ‘traditions’ of liberty, sanctity of private property, and local self-government were all now mobilized against the will of Edwin Chadwick. As James Hanley’s important recent study has shown, when it came to implementing the spirit of the 1848 Public Health Act or its watered-down successor, the 1858 Local Government Act, the legal battles that ensued between private landowners and urban and other corporations, were many and protracted (Hanley 2016). The net effect was to delay by as much as a whole generation—until the 1870s—the implementation in many of Britain’s fast-growing towns and cities the kind of ambitious public health scheme envisaged in Chadwick’s blueprint. While urban water supplies improved somewhat after 1848, especially in textile towns where millowners wanted increased supply because of their industrial needs, it was often the sewering dimension which was neglected. Partial sewering in the better-off districts was initially left to discharge into inland rivers until this polluting practice was legally addressed through mandating treatment and filtration plants from the 1880s (Hassan 1985; Luckin 1986; Szreter and Mooney 1998).





The nineteenth-century public health movement in other developed countries


	However, for all the gradualness and delay, most historians who have studied the distinctive evolution of public health history in other, comparable major countries also undergoing rapidly urbanizing economic growth, tend to portray the British as relatively hyperactive and, overall, endowed with a more effective set of institutions. In his meticulous and wide-ranging comparative examinations of England and nineteenth-century Germany, E.P. Hennock finds a relative disinterest in Germany in its appalling urban death rates and notes that the more radical German medical reformers, like Virchow, had been politically incapacitated and excluded from power by prematurely tying their flag to the failed 1848 republican revolutionary movement (Hennock 1984; 2000). By contrast Chadwick’s ‘Sanitary Idea’ was politically brilliant, as Hamlin has put it (Hamlin 2015: 27), because it was ideologically safe. When, later in the 1880s, Bismarck initiated innovative compulsory accident and health insurance, the spirt of 1848 was long past and his primary motive was to promote productivity of the German industrial economy (Hennock 2007: 94–6).
	Hygiène publique in France had been the standout scientific and intellectual leader in the wake of the French Revolutionaries’ inclusion of health within their Declaration of the Rights of Man. However, the Revolution’s commitment also to the sanctity of private property and an acceptance of J.-B. Say’s liberal political economy became the over-riding, safe consensus of post-Napoleonic French policy, surviving all subsequent regime changes through to 1945 (Ramsey 1994: 50, 57, 70, 82–3). There was suspicion and rivalry almost everywhere between medical professionals selling their therapeutic services in the market-place and preventive public medicine, which would seemingly undercut their market. In France this exerted an exceptionally strong influence impeding the emergence of a public health medical administration. Despite the scientific achievements of bacteriology and the Institut Pasteur in France, the power of the incumbent private practitioners ensured that even when finally a national Public Health act arrived in 1902 it did not produce a salaried public health profession—by contrast with the UK’s hundreds of trained MOHs all across the country by this time. Ramsey concludes that the French medical profession has been the most privately dominated of any modern society, apart from USA’s (Ramsey 1994: 99).
	Indeed, in addition to USA, none of the Anglophone, developed countries beyond Europe—Canada, Australia New Zealand—followed the British lead during the nineteenth century, either in terms of a universal social security system or in creating a national cadre of medically trained public health officials with enforceable powers (Bryder 1994; Fee 1994). The thrust of the foregoing analysis is that in fact the latter absence followed from the former. Like USA, these were all frontier societies of opportunity and immigrant settlers, who bridled at paternalist authorities and associated taxes necessary for collective provision, preferring to take their chances and retain the profits of their own individualist enterprise. This meant that in the various states of Australia, although public health acts were passed, the same factors which had militated against their effectiveness in mid-Victorian Britain were even more of an impediment: local authority jurisdiction countermanding central executive initiatives in the name of upholding private property rights; disinclination to self-tax; and consequently inadequately remunerated health officials and lack of legal enforcement agencies. For instance, though Victoria passed a Public Health Act in 1854, ‘marvellous Melbourne’ was still a deadly city lacking a sewers system until 1897; New South Wales was unable to pass its own first Public Health Act until the year after it finally and reluctantly introduced its first Income and Land Tax Acts in 1895 (Lewis 2003: 70–90).
	In the USA, despite its large number of urban centres, public health medicine was not integrated into urban government as in Britain. Although the foundation of the APHA (American Public Health Association) dates from 1872, it was initially short of medically trained members and was relatively easy to tar with the brush of being unscientific, paternalist do-gooders when the majority of American medical practitioners subscribed to conventional individualist, free market values. New York city, having commenced the nineteenth century with a colonial inheritance of a municipally organized food supply, deregulated its public food markets in 1843 in response to commercial private interests and promptly unleashed rising inequalities in food access and quality to compound the inequalities of unregulated housing conditions, from which landlords benefitted while immigrants suffered sanitation and crowding diseases (Baics 2016). Although major cities like Chicago and New York did subsequently invest—out of sheer necessity—in municipal water and sanitation projects, nationally there was no co-ordination; not even an investigative Public Health Service until 1912. There was also no universal death registration system until 1926, the essential foundation for intelligent public health work.
	Sweden was the principal other European state which did, unlike France and Germany, institute effective public health policies already in the nineteenth century. Sweden was also an early modern unified state with a Protestant established church of loyal local priests, as in England. The Swedish Crown had first become concerned to take measures to boost its population after absorbing in 1748 the disappointing results of its then-new parish population registers, the Tabellverket, showing a population of just two million. The following decades saw royal decrees that parishes create poorhouses and over 20 locally financed and state-subsidized hospitals were built so that illness no longer robbed the Crown of productive subjects (Johanisson 1994: 166–8). This pro-populationist public health policy was informed by mercantilism, the dominant economic orthodoxy in this era. This held that successful sovereigns accumulated the limited stock of the world’s gold and silver (necessary to employ armies) through the capacity of a large and productive population to sell abroad more products than were bought-in. The mercantilist Swedish public health efforts culminated in the 1815 smallpox legislation and in the same year a unique nationally funded system to care for patients with venereal diseases—many of whom were young men of prime productive and military age, of course (Sköld 1996; Lundberg 1999).
	An ambitious state public health policy could be justified on mercantilist grounds and the most comprehensive blueprint for this was the Medicinische Polizey, famously laid out in minute detail across nine volumes, 1779–1827, by the eminent German physician, Johann Peter Frank (Rosen 1993: 137–43). When he had begun his publications in the 1770s he had been addressing Europe’s enlightened despots, such as Joseph II of Austro-Hungary. This was at a time when for instance, Austro-Hungary maintained a 1,000-mile militarized cordon sanitaire, the Militärgrenze, against plague incursion from the Ottoman empire (Flinn 1981, ch.4). However, neither the enlightened despots of Prussia or Russia, nor even Joseph II of Austro-Hungary actually implemented Frank’s autocratic and expensive masterplan. It is generally considered that the Swedish state’s policies represent the furthest practical elaboration of such mercantilist-inspired state public health measures (Porter 1994: Introduction; Sundin and Willner 2007). As with England, Sweden’s historical social-inclusionary commitment to promote the population’s health also fed through into early adoption of collectively funded preventive sanitary investment. Sweden’s 1874 Public Health Act was strongly influenced by British experience but was passed sufficiently early in Sweden’s trajectory of industrialization that it successfully prevented Sweden’s urbanizing population from suffering the same epidemiological consequences as those of Britain, France, Germany, and the USA (Nelson and Rogers 1994).
	Thus, among the leading industrializing countries during the nineteenth century it was mainly in Britain that important scientific advances led also to practical public health interventions, though these only really began to be extensively funded from the 1870s, when a provincial movement to promote municipal sanitation finally took-off, led by Joseph Chamberlain’s mayorship in Birmingham, 1873–6 (Hennock 1973; Szreter 2005, chs.7, 9). The French had pioneered comparative epidemiology in the 1820s but it was in Britain that comparative death rates subsequently became a motivator for a nationwide movement towards the adoption of sanitary measures. Scientific leadership in the application of germ theory to identify the pathogens of communicable diseases clearly occurred first in France (The Institut Pasteur) and in Germany (Koch and the Prussian Institute for Infectious Diseases), yet it was in Britain that an extensive public system for the notification of infectious diseases was developed before the end of the century. Why was this?
	Here, once again, the influence of the unusual, universal social security system of England and Wales, even though it was now in its reformed, deterrent variant of the post-1834 New Poor Law, still continued to provide a crucial influence and explanatory context. We have already seen that it was the encompassing Poor Law statutory assumptions of universalist responsibility for the poor which repeatedly led the responsible authorities into innovative forms of healthcare provision, with the building of parish almshouses followed in the eighteenth century by workhouse infirmaries and subscription hospitals; and that the need to constrain costs had led Chadwick to argue the case for sanitary investment to prevent diseases. Exactly the same logic of Poor Law cost containment, while still adhering to principles of universal provision, drove the precocious investment in disease notification in the last decades of the nineteenth century.
	The moralizing aim of the New Poor Law was to end outdoor relief and drive all able-bodied workers into the labour market; however, the law recognized that the sick should instead be paid for in their own homes, not in the workhouse, as their incapacity to work was not due to idleness and in any case workhouse infirmaries did not want the risks of infectious patients. Chadwick had tried to reduce the costs of illness by sanitation in 1848. But incapacitating diseases were due to more than unclean water. Two decades later Sir John Simon, the nation’s chief medical officer, was able to demonstrate statistically that infected individuals left in the community to spread their afflictions were driving up Poor Law costs and that it would be far more efficient to make a range of such diseases compulsorily ‘notifiable’ and to then remove the sufferers to isolation facilities (Mooney 2015: 11–12, chs. 1, 3). Mooney points out it was this administrative efficiency reasoning (and the moral and economic ideologies standing behind it), as much as microbial science, which resulted in compulsory notification for various lethal diseases with identifiable causes, such as scarlet fever, diphtheria, enteric fever (typhoid) and smallpox, beginning in London in 1889—following experiments in certain other cities—and then throughout the country with the Infectious Disease (Notification) Act, 1899. In England and Wales unavoidable fiscal responsibilities, dating back to 1601, were laid on local authorities for their sick and poor; and it was crucially this economic and politically generated framework of accountability which enabled bacteriological science to be turned into a practical, funded regime. Doctors, though they were not even state officials, were legally compelled to notify infectious disease cases; and cities had to invest in freely provided isolation hospital facilities to make the system work as efficiently as possible while meeting its universalist commitment.





Public health in the twentieth century


	Sustained global economic growth in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries has, of course, contributed a sequence of important scientific developments, with a range of potential implications for the enhancement of the public’s health, such as antitoxins (diphtheria was the first in the 1890s), chemotherapies (salvarsan and neo-salvarsan to treat syphilis was the first in the 1910s), antibiotics (penicillin from the 1940s) and vaccinations (enabling smallpox to be globally eradicated in the 1970s). At the same time economic growth has contributed major new epidemiological challenges, notably the tobacco and obesity epidemics due to insufficiently regulated marketing of profitable, addictive products, HIV-AIDs, and most recently the COVID-19 pandemic, global warming, and various pollutions of land, water and air, due both to industrial practices and to affluence; and also a range of mental health-related conditions such as anorexia and depression. None of these—neither the challenging new afflictions, nor the scientific breakthroughs to counter them—can be simply attributed to the unmediated effects of economic growth on the public’s health. Ideology, culture, and politics, interacting with contingent major events such as the World Wars, the Great Depression, and the Cold War, have in all cases been involved as crucial socially and politically determining influences over the exact way in which the public’s health and economic growth have co-evolved differently in each distinct national polity.
	Most southern and eastern European states, such as Spain, Italy, Greece, Yugoslavia, or Poland, for instance—and also those populations in the Far East, such as Japan, Singapore, and Korea, which became developed countries in terms of per capita income levels in the course of the twentieth century, did so after many of the scientific breakthroughs had been made to deal with communicable diseases and the sanitary problems of dense, urban living. In some cases, such as pre-war Japan or Franco’s Spain, these advances were driven by authoritarian regimes, others were more liberal and democratic, such as postwar Japan and Italy. Provided governments promoted universal access to the necessary primary care and public health services, their populations could achieve better health outcomes while their economies were still growing from a relatively low per capita income level, as the famous Preston curves first demonstrated (Preston 1975). The interwar period also saw the emergence of ambitious public international bodies, notably the League of Nations Health Organization and US philanthropics, such as the Rockefeller Foundation, seeking to promote public health initiatives internationally (Weindling 1995). This pattern has since expanded further in the postwar era to include the World Health Organization (WHO), World Bank, the Gates Foundations, and many other western governmental departments such UK’s DfID (Packard 2016; Cueto et al. 2019). However, since Preston’s publication of 1975 new global problems of growing inequality and antibiotic resistance and, most especially, pollutants and climate change are proving to be enormous health challenges for all developed and developing societies, alike. Indeed, many species are now threatened, not only poor humans. It is proving extremely challenging for national governments and powerful corporations to set aside their short-term interests to engage in a new level of global civic and political commitment to effective action, with the UN Climate Summit of 2019 the latest in a series of only partially successful attempts to bring this about. The Montreal protocols of 1987 (to address the human threat to stratospheric ozone) still remains the only such UN treaty ratified by all the world’s states.
	Although democracies have been strongly associated with the rise of welfare states among the economically most advanced societies since the Second World War, it is recognized that these welfare states have taken on many diverse forms influenced by their historical inheritances (Esping-Andersen 1990; Castles 2010). Germany had pioneered state social insurance in the 1880s, whereas in USA there was no nationwide Social Security Act until half a century later in the depths of the Great Depression in 1933. The Second World War, as elsewhere, further empowered public health in Roosevelt’s New Deal, as the poor health of many GI recruits was revealed. However, the subsequent Cold War fears of Soviet rivalry enabled the commercial, insurance and medical vested interests once again to reassert a dominant role for private medicine in postwar USA at a time when most European developed countries were endorsing universal compulsory insurance models of healthcare for their new, fully, democratic electorates (Fee 1994: 241, 246, 249, 254). Unlike in McCarthyite USA, these were predominantly seen in western Europe, in the long tradition established by Bismarck’s pioneering ‘state socialism’, not as ‘red’, but as the best antidote to communism: social democratic methods to ameliorate working-class insecurity and grievances in a free market economy.
	The UK went further than most. The principles of 1601 re-emerged, once those of 1834 were abandoned. Beveridge’s welfare state was once again unconditionally universalist, supporting in principle all the vulnerable—old, young and unemployed—and was to be funded by national progressive taxation. In fact, as early as 1917 the UK government had endorsed a free national public health service, but only for venereal diseases (STIs), thereby adopting Sweden’s precocious policy of a century earlier, in the interests of protecting its conscripts (Eyler 1987). From 1948 onwards the NHS meant that in principle the entire population was entitled to receive the best preventive and therapeutic medical care the nation could afford for all diseases, not just for syphilis and gonorrhoea. For instance, BCG vaccination against tuberculosis, which had been adopted in Sweden since the 1920s, now became a public health policy protecting the whole British nation (Bryder 1988: 139, 253–4).
	With such universalist welfare and public health systems, national average life expectancy among most developed nations now rose above 60 for the first time in history in the immediate postwar decades as most of the sanitary and infectious diseases were tamed. Expectation of life at birth has since risen even above 80 in many advanced nations, though notably not in USA where a system of universal healthcare insurance was only introduced in 2010 and remains politically contested. The stalling of population health improvements in USA both before and since President Obama’s 2010 Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, a stalling also seen to a lesser extent in UK under the Conservative government’s decision to impose an austerity policy of cuts on public services rather than additional taxes on the financial sector (despite the uncontested culpability of the latter for the financial crash of 2007–8), has drawn attention to the importance for public health of trends in socio-economic inequality. These are the two developed societies in which economic inequality and its justifying ideology of economic liberalism have had most impact on public policy during the period since c.1980, with regimes in power extolling the virtues of low-taxation and negative liberty (in Isiah Berlin’s sense of individual-and therefore corporate—freedom from government regulation and intervention).
	As the foregoing has shown, public health does not progress simply because of scientific medical advances or directly because of increases in average per capita income. Economic growth does not necessarily translate into public health. Ideologies which favour private, individualist wealth accumulation over more universalist, more egalitarian distribution militate against providing the funding necessary for effective public health policies. These require collectively funded measures both to prevent those with less private resources from exposure to harm in their environment, and to make available relatively equally the health-enhancing advances of the bio-medical sciences. They attempt to redress what are now termed the social determinants of health (Marmot 2008). Alternative, individualist approaches focus on behaviours and ‘lifestyle risks’, appearing to presume that the major causes of ill-health in developed societies today are amenable to a significant degree to personal control, even though these notably include cancers, heart disease, obesity, mental afflictions, and dementias.





Conclusions


	While it is possible to produce an account of public health history in terms of a sequence of scientific advances, it is more important to examine carefully when, where, and how such advances were adopted into public health practice. Due to the complex administrative and substantial financial resources required to translate medical science into enhancements in the public’s general state of health—most particularly in the highly disruptive conditions of living provoked by continuous economic growth—major conflicts of interests, ideologies, and ethics are all involved. This has meant that public health has tended to be promoted most effectively in societies subscribing to collectivist principles of welfare provision. England and Sweden were two Protestant confessional states initially influenced by mercantilist and humanist ideologies, which were historically innovative in adopting universalist principles of policy in relation to social security and health. This endowed both countries with a profoundly pro-public health commitment which has endured through different forms across the centuries. Other developed countries, both the other monarchies of Europe and the individualist, settler societies of ‘neo-Europe’, have only acquired such collectivist and universalist dispositions towards their citizens’ health claims much later in their histories and in the case of USA incompletely so even until the twenty-first century.
	The history of public health in developed countries across the whole era of modern economic history thus reveals several major features, of which all current practitioners need to be fully aware. Firstly, the continuing long-term productivity of all modern national economies, as each century in world history has passed, has always required an ever more well-educated and generally healthy populace, not only to justify, but also both to produce and to consume an increasingly diverse and complex range of goods and services. Secondly, both the public’s health and the institutional practice of public health has always been and necessarily always will be interrelated to the prevailing, wider social security system (or lack of it) in the country in which it functions. Thirdly, that this combined social security and public health matrix has enormous generative significance for the potential and the patterns of economic growth achievable in any national context. Public health, efficiently managed, is far more than a cost-burden on the economy; it is an integral, productive constituent of the character of both citizens’ and the economy’s future growth potential (Keating and Hertzman 1999). Finally, the public health apparatus extant in any national polity is intimately related to its political and fiscal sensitivities. These, in turn, are subject to a process of historical conflict and negotiation over the balance to be struck between Isiah Berlin’s (1969) concepts of positive and negative freedoms. To what extent, within a democratic polity respectful of the rule of law, do its citizens place their trust (and taxes) in collectively provided social, environmental, and health services, as against reliance on their own private resources to purchase commercially provided variants of such services? (Nathanson 2007)
	With its universalist and progressive taxation principles, the Elizabethan Poor Law statutes are, in effect, jointly the world’s first social security and Public Health Act because of their coverage of the sick, the ‘lame, impotent, old, blind’ as well as those ‘not able to work’ (ER 43, cap.2 first paragraph). This extraordinary innovation may still provide a fruitful resource of ideas and administrative practices to return to, when considering the relationship between statecraft, economic development, and public health in the future of the world’s developed societies.

	1As Cipolla carefully pointed out, although the governments of several Italian city states began collating burials in ‘Books of the Deceased’ from as early as the fourteenth century, they did not seek to make the information public in ‘Weekly Bills’ circulated to the population. Since the Italian data subsequently ‘remained buried … in the cities’ archives’ it did not contribute to the early development of demography, which occurred when John Graunt set in train a scientific public discourse based on his systematic analysis of the London Bills (Cipolla 1978: 543; Kreager 1988).
	2For a review of the range of such interpretations, see Ahearn (2014) and Mokyr (1990: 3–6) on Solovian, Smithian, Boserupian, and Schumpeterian causes of growth.
	3See Slack (1990: 57) on the reasons for the failure of a similar, effective parish scheme to develop in the course of the seventeenth century in Scotland (Ireland was not part of the United Kingdom until 1801).
