1.3


The history and development of public health in low-and middle-income countries


	Than Sein





Introduction to the history and development of public health in low-and middle-income countries


	Historically, public health interventions are those actions to promote and protect people’s health, and are chiefly undertaken by the governments. The notion of public, within the term public health, encompasses actions for health development by the people themselves individually and collectively. Public health interventions not only deal with the control and management of both communicable and non-communicable diseases, but also address the promotion, prevention, or reduction of risks and root causes of these diseases. Fundamental characteristics of public health actions lie primarily on the social and other determinants of health that fall outside the domain of the government’s health sector—and also beyond the individual’s action. The majority of people in low-and middle-income countries are still living in poverty with very low health status. According to the United Nations (UN) classification of countries by their development as measured by per-capita gross national income (GNI) in 2017: countries that have per-capita GNI below US$1,005 are designated as low-income countries (32 in total); those which have per-capita GNI between US$1,006 and US$3,955 are lower-middle-income countries (38 in total); and those between US$3,956 and US$12,235 as upper-middle-income countries (42 in total). Countries with per-capita GNI of more than US$12,235 are categorized as high-income countries (UN 2018a).
	This chapter describes the history and development of public health in 112 countries, classified as low-, lower-and upper-middle-income countries, also referred to as low-and middle-income countries (LMICs). The population of LMICs (excluding those of Brazil, China, and India) is around three billion (about half of the world’s population); thus, the advancement of health development in LMICs has a major impact on the health of the world. The present chapter provides an updated review of the history and development of public health in LMICs, covering the key factors and events of the last decade.





Historical development


	The majority of LMICs came under the colonial territories during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and some have not yet been independent until near the end of the twentieth century. The initial foundation for public health was formally laid down through the intensification of international and local public health actions by the colonialists in their territories, including international health diplomacy among themselves from the eighteenth century onwards. The United States and the European countries applied protective legislative measures and preventive actions through several series of international sanitary conventions. Soon after the League of Nations and its health organization were founded, the consciousness on public health prevention and control at the international level became more realized. The World Health Organization (WHO), the first truly international and intergovernmental agency, was founded in 1946. Its two main functions were to direct and coordinate international health work and cooperate with the Member States and partners in international health development. After WHO, several international agencies had come up under the UN to deal with health, social and economic development, such as UN Development Program (UNDP), UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), UN Population Fund (UNFPA), UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), UN AIDS, etc. The original mandates for establishing these agencies have improved and changed over time. By the late 1990s, several international philanthropies and international civil societies had come out as major financing and development partners.





Control and eliminating old scourges


	While effective prevention and control measures for old scourges like smallpox, cholera, plague, and yellow fever, that are major cripplers and killers over the last 500 years, are available in high-income countries for centuries, a substantial portion of the world’s population living in LMICs have not been able to gain access to these measures. The control of smallpox in LMICs after the invention of smallpox vaccination in the early nineteenth century in Europe was hindered by several factors, such as: impurity and variable potency of the vaccine; insufficient quantities of heat-stable vaccine; poor vaccination technique; poor coverage by the health workers due to lack of appropriate human resources; lack of commitment by the colonial administration; and lack of confidence in vaccination among the local populace. The continued global advocacy and provision of technical, material (heat-stable freeze-dried vaccines), financial, and human resources support from WHO, UNDP, and many donor countries had led to successful containment of the disease by the mid-1960s. Combined strategies of routine vaccination of children and mopping up mass vaccination, coupled with intensive case-detection, contact tracing, isolation of cases, and vaccination of individuals in the vicinity who could have been exposed to the infection, had managed to control smallpox epidemics and cut the transmission. After the last naturally acquired human smallpox case in Somalia in October 1977, in May 1980 the world was declared free from natural transmission of the smallpox virus. An international arrangement was made to create an emergency stockpile of over 60 million doses of the first-and second-generation smallpox vaccine in safe and secure places, to be used for the effective control of any smallpox outbreak that might occur (WHO 2011a; WHO 2016a). Since smallpox has been used historically as a notorious biological warfare agent, and it is easier than ever to create and spread such a deadly pathogen, the world has been warned that a bioterrorist attack that could wipe out 30 million people is becoming increasingly likely to happen (The Telegraph 2017). The 1980 eradication of smallpox by natural transmission stands out as the most successful public health intervention achieved globally in the twentieth century.
	Another devastating disease, cholera, occurred worldwide for many centuries due to its severity and quick and easy spread across borders. Although it was identified as a globally notifiable disease under the old version of the International Health Regulations (IHR), report on its occurrence was no more required under the new version of IHR except in a public health emergency. Cholera remains a significant global public health problem, since 38 countries reported a total of 132,121 cases including 2,420 deaths, resulting in an overall case fatality ratio (CFR) of 1.8% in 2016. The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, Kenya, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Yemen accounted for 80% of all cases (WHO 2017a). Local armed conflicts, mass urbanization, climate change, continuing unsanitary practices (e.g. open defecation), and growing competition for water resources may, in fact, contribute to the high disease burden. Effective emergency outbreak control with good personal hygienic practices and safe water supply and sanitation remain the best preventive and control measure. Properly administered rehydration therapy and oral vaccination at the time of outbreaks could save thousands of lives. Around 20 countries affected by cholera pledged to eliminate the disease by 2030 and reduce the deaths by 90% in 2030 (WHO 2017b).
	Human plague, a bacterial infection mainly affecting small mammals and transmitted by fleas but infecting humans, is often considered a problem of the ancient disease. Between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2015, more than 3,200 cases of human plague were reported, resulting in 584 deaths, mainly occurring in 11 countries of Africa, Asia, and America. A recent outbreak of human plague with a higher frequency of pneumatic form in Africa has illustrated the breakdown of health systems due to social and political crises. The occurrence of human plague clearly demonstrates the need for strengthening surveillance on rat falls (deaths of rats around human habitats), early diagnosis and prompt treatment of human plague cases, and improved preventive and control measures in endemic countries. All these require an effective public health system (WHO 2016b). Human plague is still a global challenge as a scourge of humanity in the twenty-first century.
	Another old scourge, yellow fever (YF), has been almost eliminated in several parts of Africa and South America with an effective vaccination programme, together with vector control and widespread adoption of personal protection measures. Since there is no effective specific treatment, immunization is the only means of protection against YF. The disease remains endemic in many LMICs, with an estimated 200,000 cases worldwide each year due to declining population immunity to infection, deforestation, urbanization, population movement, and climate change. While YF spreads in historical times from the original sites in Africa to the Americas, it has never established itself in Asia, where suitable conditions for the vectors and hosts exist (WHO 2017c). The reasons for this are not well understood; hence, it is difficult to assess the probability of YF establishing itself in Asia in the near future. It could have serious consequences, given the large and dense immune-naive rural and urban population in Asia. The ongoing circulation of wild YF virus, coupled with low vaccination coverage and the presence of vector mosquitoes around the world, means that YF remains an important threat for international spread in the twenty-first century.





Elimination of childhood vaccine-preventable diseases


	After increasing availability and accessibility of improved vaccines for major infectious diseases affecting infants and young children, all LMICs have commenced national immunization programmes in mid-1980, under the sponsorship of the global Expanded Program of Immunization (EPI). This global EPI initially planned to control a few childhood vaccine-preventable diseases with the ultimate aim of eliminating or eradicating them. With the continuous technical, material, and financial inputs by the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (later known as the GAVI Alliance) since early 2000, immunization coverage has been expanded both by population and antigens. Globally over 116.5 million children (85%) received a third dose of DPT (diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus) (DPT3) in 2016, compared to 24.2 million in 1980. Measles vaccine coverage was around 70% in Africa, whereas it was over and around 90% in Europe, Asia, and the Pacific. While bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG) and poliomyelitis vaccination remained over 80% in all WHO regions, the coverage for third doses of hepatitis B (HepB3) and H. Influenza (Hib3) remained below 80% in Africa (WHO 2017d). This situation highlights the need to address limited national and community resources, competing health priorities, poor health systems management, and inadequate monitoring and supervision. Despite these challenges, many public health professionals have considered the global EPI initiative a silent revolution in public health. Figure 1.3.1 shows the immunization coverage of major childhood vaccine-preventable diseases by WHO regions in 2016.
	Fig. 1.3.1 Vaccination coverage of major vaccine-preventable diseases by vaccines and WHO Regions, 2016.
	Abbreviations: BCG = bacille Calmette–Guérin; DTP3 = 3 doses of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis vaccine; Polio3 = 3 doses of polio vaccine; MCV1 = 1 dose of measles-containing vaccine; HepB3 = 3 doses of hepatitis B vaccine; Hib3 = 3 doses of haemophilus influenza type B vaccine. WHO Regions: AFR = WHO African Region; AMR = WHO American Region; EMR = WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region; EUR = WHO European Region; SEAR = WHO South-East Asia Region; and WPR = WHO Western Pacific Region.





Source: Data from World Health Organization, Global routine vaccination coverage, 2016, WER 92(46), 701–16.


	Among the vaccine-preventable diseases, the goal of eliminating poliomyelitis, an acute potentially paralysing disease of children, was launched in 1988 under the Global Eradication of Poliomyelitis programme. In the beginning, the wild poliovirus was circulating in more than 125 countries on five continents, disabling more than 1,000 children every day. With concerted efforts and additional support from the GAVI Alliance, the global coverage of polio immunization over the next two decades had reached around 80% in all WHO Regions. WHO Region of the Americas (AMR) was certified polio-free in 1994, followed by WHO Western Pacific Region (WPR) in 2000, and then European Region (EUR) in 2002. After several rounds of vaccination against polio with designated national immunization days (NIDs), many countries were able to announce the interruption of indigenous polio transmission (WHO 2012). By 2014, the WHO South-East Asia Region (SEAR) was certified polio-free. This achievement of the majority of WHO regions marks a significant leap forward in global eradication, with 80% of the world’s population now living in certified polio-free places. More than 16 million people are able to walk today who would otherwise have been paralysed. By 2018, only three countries, viz. Afghanistan and Pakistan in Asia, and Nigeria in Africa, had endemic infections due to indigenous transmission of wild polioviruses. These countries had accounted for 90% of all new cases of poliomyelitis. Failure of the global polio eradication effort, while seemingly unthinkable, would result in the return of polio infection worldwide and constitute the most expensive public health failure in history. If and when the world successfully eradicates wild poliovirus, this would represent a major milestone of public health success in the twenty-first century. Figure 1.3.2 shows the trends for the coverage of poliomyelitis immunization (three doses) for infants by WHO Regions, in 1980, and 1990 to 2016.
	Fig. 1.3.2 Poliomyelitis immunization (three doses) coverage for <1 year of age by WHO regions, 1980 and 1990–2016.
	Abbreviations: WHO Regions: AFR = WHO African Region; AMR = WHO American Region; EMR = WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region; EUR = WHO European Region; SEAR = WHO South-East Asia Region; and WPR = WHO Western Pacific Region





Source: Data from WHO Global Health Observatory Data Repository, Copyright World Health Organization 2017.


	Measles is an easily transmitted viral infection responsible for around 10% of deaths from all causes among under-five children globally, and could easily be preventable by immunization. Measles control was included as part of the routine EPI programme in LMICs since mid-1980. By 2000, 72% of the world’s children received at least a single dose of measles vaccine (MCV1) (against 16% in 1980). The entire American continent had eliminated measles infection (i.e. no indigenous case for more than 12 months) by 2002. This successful experience had prompted other continents to launch similar measles elimination campaigns. From 2000 to 2016, MCV1 coverage had increased globally from 72% to 85%. The number of measles cases reported annually worldwide decreased from over 854,000 cases in 2000 to 132,000 in 2016. For the same period, the number of measles deaths declined from 550,100 in 2000 to 89,780 in 2016 (WHO 2017e). While it may not be possible for many LMICs to eliminate measles in the near future, maintaining the high level of coverage of measles immunization of all infants (more than 85%) is nevertheless highly beneficial in reducing sickness, lifelong disability, and deaths at early ages.
	High coverage of immunization with tetanus toxoid (TT) to all women of childbearing age and high coverage of DPT vaccine for infants and with boosters among school children, are the simplest and most cost-effective ways to reduce tetanus infection in women and neonates, as well as deaths due to neonatal tetanus (NNT). Efforts have been made since 1989 to eliminate the disease (i.e. reducing the level of incidence of one NNT case per 1,000 live births in all districts of the country). However, by 2016, around 25 countries of the world, all from LMICs, remained tetanus endemic.
	Immunization against hepatitis B (HepB), another highly prevalent viral infection of the liver that could lead to cirrhosis and cancer, was introduced as part of a routine EPI programme in 183 countries since early-1990. Approximately 257 million people live with hepatitis B virus infection (defined as hepatitis B surface antigen-positive). In 2015, hepatitis B resulted in 887,000 deaths, mostly from complications (including cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma). For the last 25 years, almost all LMICs have used both plasma-derived and recombinant HepB vaccines, achieving over 80–90% coverage globally in 2016 (WHO 2017f). If the continuous vaccine supply can be ensured and the high coverage maintained, HepB infection could be under control and even eliminated within the next two decades.
	A potent vaccine against another viral infection caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b or Hib has been available since mid-1990, being introduced under routine immunization programmes in 189 countries. Global coverage with three doses of Hib vaccination was estimated at around 52%, while some regions have better coverage of over 90% (WHO 2006a).





Control of neglected tropical diseases


	A group of infectious diseases that cause illness and death of thousands of people living in the tropical zones worldwide have been neglected for various reasons for complete prevention and control. Leprosy, the most neglected tropical disease (NTD), has been put under control by accelerated efforts in the last 25 years with the introduction of multidrug therapy (MDT). By 2001, 107 of 122 endemic countries were able to achieve the global target of leprosy elimination (i.e. reducing the prevalence to a level below one case per 10,000 people). Globally, the number of new leprosy cases reported from 143 countries had come down from a peak of over 775,000 cases in 2001 to 214,783 in 2016. Over 90% of the new cases during the last decade were represented from 22 priority countries in Asia, the Pacific, and Africa (WHO 2017g). If the current trend in disease reduction in endemic countries is well sustained with full support from the Global Alliance, the incidence and total burden of leprosy could be further reduced in the near future. Leprosy elimination could be another public health landmark during the twenty-first century.
	Trachoma is a chronic infection of the eyes by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis, mainly affecting poor people and children living in 41 tropical countries of Asia and Africa, especially in areas where unhygienic personal practices still prevail and inadequate access to safe water supply, and is responsible for the blindness or visual impairment of about 1.9 million people. Under the national integrated trachoma control programme, many endemic countries implemented the WHO-advocated SAFE strategy (surgery, antibiotics, facial cleansing, and environmental improvement). In 2016, 190.2 million people still lived in trachoma-endemic areas and are at risk of trachoma blindness. Global-level antibiotic coverage was 44.8%, a considerable increase compared to the 29.6% achieved in 2015. As of 1 July 2017, 10 countries (Cambodia, China, Gambia, Ghana, Islamic Republic of Iran, Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Mexico, Morocco, Myanmar, and Oman) had reported achieving elimination goal, which signifies a major milestone in the campaign to eliminate trachoma (WHO 2017h).
	The global effort for eradicating yaws, another disabling NTD, has been launched in many LMICs around the world in the last five decades through mass vaccination programmes and effective mass treatment. However, sporadic epidemics and scattered foci of infection persist in some parts of Latin America, the Pacific, and South and South-East Asia. Extensive surveillance and case finding, use of newer antibiotics, and follow-up of treated cases and contacts became important strategies for the eradication of yaws in the remaining endemic countries.
	Visceral leishmaniosis or kala-azar, another NTD, has been put under control by using an oral medication, Miltefosine. Until newer medicines and appropriate vaccine(s) are available at affordable prices, and made accessible to the mass population in the endemic countries, the misery and suffering of thousands of people from visceral leishmaniosis would continue.
	Onchocerciasis, also known as river blindness, is another parasitic infection still endemic in 37 countries in Africa and Latin America. A million people are visually impaired, and over 300,000 people are blind due to this disease. The Global Onchocerciasis Control Program launched in 1974 had tried to reduce severe pathological manifestations through community-based mass management with a microfilarial drug (ivermectin) combined with vector control. Although the disease is a preventable cause of blindness and its elimination goal is achievable, there is a great deal of work to be done by the health systems in endemic countries (Diawara et al. 2009).
	Dracunculiasis is a vector-borne guinea worm infestation, but an eradicable disease, as diagnosis is easy and unambiguous, and control interventions are simple, cost-effective, and relatively easy to implement. The disease has limited geographical distribution and transmission is seasonal. Many endemic countries in Asia and Africa with strong political commitment from governments were able to achieve the global eradication target set in 2004 by reducing the annual incidence from 3.5 million in 1986 to less than 1,100 cases in 2011 (WHO 2011b). As of 31 December 2015, 196 countries, territories, and areas have been certified free of dracunculiasis transmission. By 2016, the disease was confined only to three endemic countries (Sudan, Chad, and Ethiopia), where less than 30 cases were reported (WHO 2018). The challenge for eradication efforts in these countries is the emergence of another host, i.e. domestic dogs (Molyneux and Sankara 2017). If concerted efforts continued, eradication of dracunculiasis could be achieved in the near future without any use of vaccine and medicine.
	Lymphatic filariasis (LF) is also a disabling NTD caused by blood-borne infection of microscopic thread-like parasitic worms—microfilariae. The global programme to eliminate LF through mass drug administration (MDA) was launched in 2000. With 556 million people in 39 of 73 endemic countries treated during 2015, the cumulative total of MDA now exceeds 6.2 billion. A total of 18 countries have halted MDA nationwide and six of these (Cambodia, Cook Islands, Maldives, Niue, Sri Lanka, and Vanuatu) were acknowledged by WHO as having eliminated LF as a public health problem. Nonetheless, 2738 implementation units across 54 countries, with approximately 946 million people, are still considered to require MDA to achieve elimination targets (WHO 2017i).





Controlling non-communicable diseases


	While communicable diseases continue to be major public health problems, chronic non-communicable diseases (NCD) are emerging in LMICs as public health challenge for the 21st century. In 2015, an estimated 40 million deaths occurred due to NCD, accounting for 70% of the overall total of 56 million deaths. The majority of such deaths were caused by the four main NCD, namely: cardiovascular disease—17.7 million deaths (accounting for 45% of all NCD deaths); cancer—8.8 million deaths (22%); chronic respiratory disease—3.9 million deaths (10%); and diabetes—1.6 million deaths (4%) (WHO 2017j). Many large-scale, well-designed population-based control programmes had shown that lowering the common risk factors like tobacco and alcohol use, high sugar or salt including unhealthy diets, can reduce morbidity and deaths from NCDs. The dual approach of early screening and mitigating risk factors, and promoting population-wide preventive measures like policy and legislation is an appropriate strategy for LMICs.
	Diabetes mellitus, either insulin-dependent (Type 1) or non-insulin-dependent (Type 2), has affected around 200 million people of above 20 years of age worldwide. Gaps in early diagnosis and treatment of diabetes in LMICs are the biggest challenges, and health systems are not well-prepared for narrowing these gaps. The number of patients with diabetes may increase to 370 million by 2030, if proper promotive, preventive, and control strategies are not in place. With early screening and diagnosis followed by effective management with diet, exercise, and essential medicines, diabetes, and its complications can be potentially controlled.
	Cancer is a well-known NCD and a leading cause of death worldwide, with more than 70% of all cancer deaths occurring in LMIC. Liver cancer affects approximately 5.5 million people, predominantly caused by viral hepatitis B and C. Stomach cancer caused by Helicobacter pylori infection could be easily prevented by early prevention and control of infection with appropriate medicines. The global burden of cancer in women has recently received much attention, but there are few comprehensive reviews of the burden and policy approaches to reduce it. Early detection with proper screening and improved breast cancer treatment has reduced mortality by 45% in women above 50 years of age. Cancer of the uterine cervix, which is prevalent among women of childbearing age, is mainly due to chronic infection with sexually transmitted human papillomavirus (HPV). In LMICs, cervical cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in women, and 91% of global estimated HPV-related cancer deaths are due to cervical cancer. HPV vaccines are very effective at preventing the disease, and the protection lasts for at least 5 years (WHO 2009). Pap smear screening and early treatment also significantly reduced mortality from cervical cancer.
	There are examples of proven public health interventions with a particular focus on the primary prevention of risk factors. Many of these measures are extremely cost-effective, especially in the case of tobacco control and vaccination against cancer-causing diseases. LMICs must prioritize efforts to reduce known cancer risk factors and make prevention and treatment accessible to all. Early diagnosis, effective treatment, and palliative care are also required. Expanding population-based cancer registries and research in LMICs are needed to set cancer control priorities and determine the most effective interventions.





Environmental health promotion


	For centuries, the promotion of environmental health, including public housing, public water supply, personal hygiene, and sanitation, has been recognized as key elements for public health development. Despite legislative measures supplemented by public health education campaigns, public subsidy support, and private donation, the progress in environmental health (specifically safe water supply and sanitation) in LMICs has not been satisfactory. According to WHO, the population using improved drinking-water sources in LMICs had increased from 70% in 1990 to 87% by 2010, while the population using improved sanitation in the same group of countries in 2010 was still less than 50% (WHO 2017j). About 2.4 billion people around the world, mostly in Asia and Africa, were still lacking access to improved sanitation facilities, mainly due to low priority given to the sector, inadequate financial resources, and lack of sustainable public water supply and sanitation services, especially the existence of unimproved sanitation and open defecation, and poor personal hygienic practices.
	The situation is exacerbated by inadequate provision of public water supply and sanitation facilities, even in public places like wet markets, parks, movie theatres, schools, hospitals, health centres, offices, and religious places. Providing access to low-cost, adequate, and simple, improved drinking-water sources and improved facilities for sanitary disposal of excrement, and promoting sound hygienic behaviours among the general population in LMICs is of critical importance in reducing the burden of communicable diseases. Given the current economic growth prospect, LMICs have the challenge of getting additional financial support from external agencies, in order to achieve the UNSDG for environmental health improvement (WHO/ UNICEF 2017).
	The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) on health has a target that by 2030, there will be substantially reducing the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and air, water, and soil pollution and contamination. Around 4.5 million deaths occur every year as a result of household exposure to smoke from dirty cook stoves and fuels, and 3 million deaths every year as a result of exposure to ambient (outdoor) air pollution. Most air-pollution deaths are premature deaths, largely as a result of increased mortality from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections. People living in LMICs disproportionately experience the burden of outdoor air pollution, with 87% of the 3 million premature deaths (WHO 2016c). Policies and investments supporting cleaner transport, energy-efficient housing, power generation, industry, and better municipal waste management, agricultural waste incineration, forest fires, and certain agro-forestry activities (e.g. charcoal production) would reduce key sources of urban outdoor air pollution.





Climate change and its impact


	Climate change is now affecting every country on every continent. It is disrupting national economies and affecting lives, costing people, communities, and countries dearly today and even more tomorrow. People are experiencing the significant impacts of climate change, which include changing weather patterns, rising sea levels, and more extreme weather events. The greenhouse gas emissions from human activities are driving climate change and continue to rise. Without action, the world’s average surface temperature is projected to rise over the twenty-first century. It is likely to surpass 3ºC this century—with some areas of the world expected to warm even more. Implementation of the Paris Agreement adopted in 2015 provides a roadmap for climate actions that will reduce emissions and build climate resilience (UN 2018b).





New generation of health systems reforms


	For effective control of both communicable and NCDs and their risks, there is a need to have viable and efficient health systems. Historically, many LMICs tried to establish their healthcare facilities and public health measures, based on the models of their colonial masters. In general, these health systems were publicly funded, except in some African countries where basic healthcare relied upon health facilities and staff supported by non-governmental organizations. Several medical schools and paramedical training institutes, public health training and research institutions and healthcare facilities were later added with technical and financial assistance from their colonial rulers.





Health systems development in the twenty-first century


	Until mid-1970, many LMICs had weak health infrastructure for maternal and child health (MCH) care and communicable disease control, leading to high mortality and morbidity from maternal and childhood illnesses. Immunization coverage for children was very low, and essential MCH care had to rely on poorly trained human resources at hospitals and hospital-based clinics, located mostly in urban areas. It was later realized that the vertical approach of opening MCH centres and deploying MCH workers alone did not achieve the purpose of expanding MCH care. In 1980–1990, many LMICs started adopting comprehensive population policies and family planning services as part of MCH care to address both demographic challenges and maternal health problems. Even though simple and effective family planning techniques were available and within reach globally, only a fraction of women in LMICs could have access to these services.
	Another critical challenge is making essential medicines affordable and accessible for needy patients. While many newer food supplements, medicines, and vaccines have been made available to the vast population, the control of substandard, spurious, falsely labelled, falsified, or counterfeit medical products has become a big challenge. LMICs must continually strengthen their food and drug regulatory agencies to ensure effective implementation, especially control of these counterfeit, substandard, spurious medicines. With the expansion of the private sector and health insurance, ensuring access to, and—in particular—affordability of essential medicines and vaccines become more vital.
	Healthcare systems utilizing varieties of health professionals and allied health workers, hospitals and modern allopathic medicine intended to benefit the whole population barely existed a century ago in many LMICs. To date, major responsibility for healthcare provision in LMICs is through the publicly financed health facilities in conjunction with private healthcare providers. The development of infrastructure for public health, mainly for prevention and control of communicable disease, solely depended upon the support and expansion of vertical disease control campaigns such as vaccine-preventable diseases, HIV/AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis, or reproductive health, supported with international funds.
	There are glaring contrasts between high-income countries and LMICs as well as among LMICs themselves in achieving a higher level of health status. The average life expectancy at birth in 2015 in low-income countries was around 62 years, and that of lower-middle-income countries was around 66 years, while the data for upper-middle and high-income countries ranged from 74 to 80 years (WHO 2017j). Many low-income countries still have an under-five mortality rate of above 120 per 1000 live births.
	At the turn of the twenty-first century, while some countries still concentrated on vertical campaigns for expanding personal healthcare interventions like MCH, family planning, growth monitoring, breastfeeding, and immunization, as well as vertical disease control campaigns for malaria, HIV/AIDS, TB, etc., other LMICs tried to implement comprehensive health programmes including health legislative and health finance reforms. There was inadequate coordination and collaboration among specific health intervention initiatives, like immunization or specific disease campaigns or capital investment for hospital care on the one hand, and the development of basic health systems infrastructure on another. This dichotomy situation resulted in the inadequate involvement of communities in their health development efforts and the slow pace of integrating vertical disease control campaigns into the basic health services. It was compounded by weak planning and management of health development, especially at the operational levels at districts and below, and the imbalance and inappropriateness of some human resources for health.
	Some LMICs acknowledged that their health development programmes utilizing the conventional approach of merely expanding basic health services were inadequate. The public sector could not bear the cost of expanding basic healthcare services to the entire population in the face of existing resource constraints. Thus, many countries sought partnerships with private healthcare providers, worked with community-based civil society organizations, and deployed a large number of community-based health workers, who were volunteers and trained for short periods to serve as a third workforce of human resources for health (Sein 2006; WHO 2007). The increasing use of community-based volunteers in health development had proved successful for quickly expanding essential healthcare coverage in many countries. With the involvement of private healthcare providers and community-based health workers, many essential public health interventions were enhanced, especially in disease prevention and control, health promotion, maternal and child healthcare, information gathering and surveillance, treatment of minor ailments, and environmental health promotion.





Health policy, planning, and financing


	The centrally directed health planning framework applying country health planning (CHP) or national planning process for health sector development, supported by WHO and UN agencies during 1970–1990, had moved many LMICs to a higher level of health attainment. It was highly successful when the health development programmes based on selective healthcare interventions, like immunization, malaria, leprosy, HIV/AIDS, or tuberculosis control, or selective maternal and childcare and family planning, growth monitoring, were promoted on the national scale through centrally controlled, externally funded programmes. In the late 1990s, the development partners moved their financing aid from planning multiple vertical health development projects, to integrated sectoral planning of comprehensive health development programmes.
	Around 2005, the UN introduced the principle of delivering as one (DaO), basically covering four areas—one leader, one budget, one programme, and one office, especially to integrate multiple UN-supported national programmes under one umbrella. The UN also worked with multiple development partners to establish the multi-donor trust fund (MDTF) mechanism by pooling multiple donor-supported funds into one integrated plan, and getting more partners to support a single national strategy in selected LMICs (UNDG 2010). A group of development partners, led by WHO and the World Bank that share a common interest in improving health services and health outcomes for LMICs, in 2007 launched another global initiative called the International Health Partnership plus related initiatives (IHP+). An interagency working group of IHP+ had developed a joint assessment tool for national health plans and strategies (JANs) and associated guidelines in 2009. Since 2010, the JANs tool was applied in several LMICs as part of the national health policy development and planning process (WHO 2015b). The national health planning processes now cover a comprehensive, balanced, and evidence-based assessment of the country’s health and health system challenges. Many LMICs tried to strengthen their institutional capacity to harmonize and align donor programmes with their national policies, strategies, priorities, and plans.
	LMICs, while struggling to improve their health systems, increasingly realized the value of financially protecting their own people in the fairest way possible. The key challenge of reform in health financing in LMICs, particularly the collection of revenue and pooling and use of financial resources, is to find a good balance between affordability and fairness to the people while providing appropriate incentives to healthcare providers. This is in keeping with the ideal for universal coverage, which means equity of access to key promotive, preventive, curative, and rehabilitative health interventions for all at an affordable cost (WHO IBRD/WB 2017).
	In 2015, the world had spent US$ 7.3 trillion on health, close to 10% of the global gross domestic product (GDP). In fact, high-income countries with only 16% of the world’s people account for 80% of global health spending. Conversely, 76% of the world’s people living in middle-income countries accounted for less than 20% of global health spending, and the low-income countries with more than half a billion people accounted for less than 1% of the world’s health spending. In 2015, the global average health spending per capita was US$ 1,011, which conceals a very large difference between the highest and lowest spending countries, ranging from over US$ 9,000 to less than US$ 20 per capita. People spend more on health through out-of-pocket payment (OOP) in constant absolute terms for all income groups. Today, there are one billion people living in countries where out-of-pocket spending is 50% or more (WHO 2017k).
	The way healthcare is financed varies considerably across countries. Middle-income and high-income countries tend to have a higher share of health spending funded from compulsory prepaid sources, such as government budgets (from various types of taxes) and/or social health insurance contributions. Many LMICs still rely heavily on external assistance to health expenditure, estimated at about 33% on average. Middle-income countries with high reliance on external resources are almost all exclusively small states. There is evidence of the fungibility of external funds, particularly in low-income countries. In addition, there is evidence of non-additionality of development assistance for health, where development assistance is spent in the health sector, but the recipient government re-allocates its own resources to fund other priorities (WHO 2017k). The proliferation of bilateral and multilateral donors, multiple global initiatives, and international non-governmental agencies (NGOs) also generates the potential to weaken health systems rather than strengthen them, allowing countries to avoid issues like long-term sustainability.





Strengthening health workforce for 2030


	One key factor for success in public health and health system development is having a critical mass of competent health workforce. As human resources consume as much as 60–70% of the public health expenditure, they need to be fully developed and optimally utilized. The World Health Report 2006 had provided a global analysis and identified effective strategies to strengthen the development of appropriate human resources for health (WHO 2006b). There is an anticipated mismatch between demand, need, and supply. In addition, there is an acceleration of domestic and international migration of all types of the health workforce. Furthermore, the challenge of deploying and retaining health professionals in rural, remote, and underserved areas is truly global. The major reasons for the health workforce shortage, while varying greatly among LMICs, include inadequate numbers of human resources due to under-investment in basic undergraduate and graduate education and training; loss of existing workforce due to emigration to other countries; mismanagement and coordination; and inefficient planning. Newer models of deployment, health workers’ education, and management are in need (WHO 2016d).
	Some of the impediments to the development of a relevant and adequately sized public health workforce are lack of incentives and career structure for public health professionals, public health training being seen as an extension of the biomedical model of clinical training, and the inclusion of many training courses and core curriculum which are either obsolete or irrelevant to the public health needs of the countries. Several networks, both formal and informal, among public health education institutions in Asia and Africa have been established to collaborate and support exchange programmes for faculty members and students, sharing of curriculum and training materials, and organizing joint research studies.





Health research and development


	While science and technology research and development and their application have advanced rapidly in high-income countries, these disciplines have remained rudimentary in LMICs. Many LMICs must rely on the results of research and development on pharmaceuticals and vaccines from high-income countries, and in fact, many breakthroughs have been contributed by the experiences gained and the studies carried out in LMIC. In many LMICs, there are very few health research and development institutions as well as poor career prospects for researchers.
	Joint collaborative studies between LMICs, especially upper-middle-income countries, and the high-income countries, are carried out for the development and use of medicines and vaccines for infectious diseases, promotion of human health and reproduction specifically on contraception and other fertility control measures, strengthening of health systems, promotion and protection of environmental health, and control of NCDs, and development of essential healthcare technologies. Considerable progress has been made in capability strengthening for promoting health systems research, which has further paved the way for developing effective national health research systems.
	In recent years, the development of health research has been promoted through international exchanges of experience and expertise among the networks such as INCLEN Trust, Asia-Pacific Health Research System Network and African Health Research System Network. A major issue faced by LMICs today is that while scientific advances and technological development of the high-income countries provide them with vast opportunities for their overall economic development, many people in LMICs are still suffering from preventable NCDs, neglected tropical diseases, and under-nutrition.





Strive for social determinants of health


	Many LMICs are particularly susceptible to the negative impact of socially determined health inequities due to heavy exposure to health risks, social exclusion, and other broader determinants associated with health risks, including low-income, unsafe living conditions, poor work environment, unsafe sex, and changing consumption patterns of food, water, and information. LMICs considered the need to build up their national capacities to address advocacy, intersectoral action, evidence gathering of health inequity, and social determinants across sectors.





Reducing tobacco and alcohol use


	Tobacco is the most common risk factor for many NCDs. In 2015, more than 1.1 billion people smoked tobacco, with far more males than females currently engaging in this behaviour. Tobacco-related illnesses and deaths had increased globally during the past decades with seven million deaths every year, and if no proper control measures are instituted, the death toll may go up to 10 million in the next decade. In LMICs, the increasing use of betel-quid (betel leave combining betel-nut, slake-lime, and tobacco) has become a major issue, since it causes oral, laryngeal, and gastrointestinal cancer, and cardiovascular diseases. After adoption in May 2003 of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (WHO FCTC), LMICs have either adopted or amended their tobacco control legislation, conforming to the provisions of the WHO FCTC. By 2017, 180 parties to WHO FCTC had ratified the Convention, and adopted tobacco control measures called MPOWER (M for monitoring tobacco use, P for protecting people from tobacco smoke, O for offer help to quit, W for warning about dangers of tobacco, E for enforcing ban on tobacco advertising, promotion and sponsorship, and R for raising tax for tobacco), the six best-buy strategies promoted by WHO and adopted by all parties to WHO FCTC. Around 4.77 billion people are covered by at least one best practice policy intervention at the national level, a substantial increase from nearly two billion people (WHO 2017l). There is also an urgent need to make effective control for e-cigarettes, water pipes, and heated tobacco products, as they became newer forms of tobacco marketed to LMICs. It is critical that all countries act urgently to protect their people more effectively with evidence-based tobacco control policies at the most comprehensive level.
	Worldwide consumption of alcohol has increased from 6 litres of pure alcohol consumed per person aged 15 or older, in 2008, as compared to 6.4 litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15 years or older, with considerable variation between WHO regions, in 2016. A large portion of this—28.6% or 1.76 litres per person—was homemade, illegally produced or sold outside normal government controls (WHO 2017j). Harmful use of alcohol is a major factor contributing to premature deaths and avoidable disease worldwide. A wide range of policy options and interventions for reducing public health problems caused by the harmful use of alcohol was advocated for all countries.





Preventing injuries


	Injuries, caused intentionally and non-intentionally, have emerged as a major public health problem in the twenty-first century. Globally, road traffic injuries claim more than 1.2 million lives each year and greatly impact health and development. The rapidly rising number of motor vehicles (48% of the world’s vehicles are registered in LMICs), and motorcycles (adding more than a million a day on the roads) has led to an equally rapid increase in traffic-related injuries and deaths. LMICs have a higher road-traffic-related death rate of over 20 per 100,000 population, and accounted for over 90% of the world’s fatalities.
	They are the leading cause of death among young people aged between 15 and 29 years, and cost governments approximately 3–5% of GDP. The rise in global road traffic deaths has been largely driven by the escalating death toll on roads in LMICs—particularly in emerging economies where urbanization and motorization accompany rapid economic growth. In many LMICs, necessary infrastructural development, policy changes, and levels of enforcement have not kept pace with increasing vehicle use. Introduction and upgrading of safe public transport, improvement of road signs and pedestrian crossings, compliance with traffic legislation like wearing helmets and seatbelts, and avoiding speeding and drink-driving, are important measures for reducing road traffic injuries (WHO 2015). In addition to deaths on the roads, up to 50 million people incur non-fatal injuries each year as a result of road traffic crashes, while there are additional indirect health consequences that are associated with this growing epidemic. The UN SDG3 target aims to halve the number of global deaths and injuries from road traffic crashes by 2030, while SDG11 relates to providing access to sustainable transport systems for all, improving road safety, and expanding public transport (WHO 2016d).





Nutrition promotion


	Despite the significant steps taken towards promoting nutrition and reducing associated health burdens over recent decades, the global community is grappling with multiple burdens of malnutrition. Global Nutrition Report (2017) showed that 88% of countries face a serious burden of either two or three forms of malnutrition (i.e. childhood stunting, anaemia in women of reproductive age, and/or overweight in adult women). It also indicated that progress on global nutrition targets is slow or moving backwards. Around 2 billion people lack essential micronutrients like iron and vitamin A in their daily diet, 155 million children have stunted growth, 52 million children are wasted, while 41 million children are obese. 88% of 193 UN member countries have faced a serious burden of either two or three forms of malnutrition (Development Initiatives 2017). There is an opportunity to identify—and to take—double-duty actions at once which tackle more than one form of malnutrition. These will increase the effectiveness and efficiency of the investment of time, energy, and resources to improve nutrition. Likewise, triple duty actions which tackle malnutrition and other development challenges could yield multiple benefits across the UN SDGs.





Social medicine and public health


	The initial idea of social medicine or the social dimensions of public health had emerged in the early twentieth century. The concept of social medicine was developed as a new public health discipline in the late 1940s. At that time, the leaders of both clinical medicine and public health questioned the perceived polarization of curative medicine and preventive medicine. The situation was exacerbated by continued specialization and the lack of cross-disciplinary interaction (Ko Ko 2011).
	The social and behavioural aspects that influenced illness and well-being are recognized again, and revisited during the dawn of the twenty-first century. Many social and personal behavioural interventions are introduced as part of health promotion and disease prevention. Many universities and medical schools converted their departments, faculties, or schools of hygiene and public health into those of preventive and social medicine from the 1960s. Instead of integrating curative and preventive medicine in the teaching of social medicine, educational institutions equated public health and hygiene with preventive and social medicine, and conventional public health teaching still has a primary focus on the prevention and control of infectious diseases and hygiene. The general population is now becoming increasingly aware of the social and economic determinants impacting health. As a result, national debates at both public and political levels on health linkages with social, environmental, economic, and political factors are needed. There are more discussions at the global level to give a wider political and social dimension to international public health.
	The history of public health development has shown the need for increased cooperation between high-income and LMICs to promote the total health and well-being of all world citizens. Over the past 50 years, many international, intergovernmental, bilateral, and multilateral development agencies and organizations, as well as professional and technical alliances, have emerged out of necessity to deal with international health developmental issues both in policy and programme terms. Partnerships could be established to sustain and support health system development so that equitable health outcomes are achieved and the needs of the people are met. More recently, debates have intensified around global public health development and the global governance of health (Kickbusch and Gleicher 2012).





Whither to new public health


	Now, entering the twenty-first century, many LMICs move towards another era of public health development with new thoughts from a narrow view of vertical disease control interventions to a wider perspective of multisectoral interventions beyond the health sector. Besides the usual public health measures undertaken by the governments, an increasing number of NGOs and the private sector agencies, both at the local and global level, were involving in public health development. In addition to external financing and technical support by traditional international agencies like WHO and UN, bilateral aid agencies from high-income countries and multilateral financial institutions like the IBRD, the World Bank, and Regional Development Banks, there are a myriad of multinational foundations, international funds, and financing groups like the GAVI Alliance and the Global Fund, as well as private international foundations like Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation or Bloomberg Philanthropies, etc., that have transformed international health support and governance on national and international health cooperation.





Globalization of public health


	The UN had launched the Joint UN Program on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) in January 1996, with the UN-wide mission to lead, strengthen and support an expanded response to HIV/AIDS. Another UN initiative was the adoption of UN Millennium Development Goals (UN MDG), with targets for 2015, representing the world’s commitment to deal with global poverty and health in several dimensions (UN 2011). After reviewing the progress of UN MDG, the UN Summit in 2015 adopted a development agenda titled—Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which contained the UN SDG to be achieved by 2030. The SDG positions health as a key feature of human development in a more integrated manner than was the case for the MDG. Certain important health issues that were not addressed in the MDG now have targets in the SDG, such as mental health, substance abuse, health impact from hazardous chemicals, water, and soil pollution and contamination and the effective implementation of the WHO FCTC (UN 2018c).
	By the start of the twenty-first century, several series of analyses of the impact of rapid globalization on public health are available in many health and development literature. They all revealed that the global trade, finance, information and people flows, governance, and security could contribute to improving the health of people everywhere. The threats to and opportunities in public health, including cross-country control of infectious diseases and international governance, have been analysed extensively within the context of globalization (Fidler 2004). An updated version of IHR is a guide for all countries to prevent, protect against and control, and provide a public health response to the international spread of a disease or diseases, in various ways that are commensurate with and restricted to public health risks, and that avoid unnecessary interference with international traffic and trade. The UN SDG outline the need to support countries to detect and manage health risks, build resilient health systems, and focus on protecting the most vulnerable populations.





Addressing healthy ageing


	Many LMICs have experienced an expansion of the proportion of people above 60 years of age, from 1.2 billion in 2015 to 2 billion in 2050. They have started paying attention to dealing with older people’s health by adopting appropriate comprehensive national policies and related legislation. They have focused on creating closer linkages between social welfare and health, providing care at home and in the community, promoting traditional family ties, optimizing the use of existing healthcare delivery systems and setting up elderly care homes. Access to essential healthcare for older people is still inadequate in many LMICs, since knowledge and skill among health and social workers for specific needs of older people is minimal. The economic, social, and health status of the fast-growing elderly population in LMICs poses a great challenge to all sectors.





Looking ahead


	LMICs have undertaken a series of health reforms by improving the content of essential health packages and introducing a new way of financing. Many health financing models either at national or local levels were developed, including reforms in expanding social health insurance. Another global trend in health development is the increasing role of the private sector, both for-profit and non-profit. It is not a simple solution that can fit within a country’s existing socioeconomic, political, and health situation. The extent of the national health plans ensures that wider reforms would address the gaps in healthcare and create a pro-poor health system.
	A multiplicity of new actors in national and international health arena had redefined the boundaries of the health sector. Groups of individuals, united to a particular cause, such as patient groups or civil societies both at national and international levels, have become major players for policy and programme development in public health by creating powerful lobbies and raising public awareness. A new paradigm in health development, in countries that must rely heavily on external aid for health in earlier years and even now, has led to a complex relationship among traditional and new players in international health and health-related development, for effective planning and use for resources, and the need for delineation and harmonization of responsibilities.





Conclusion


	The history and development of public health in LMICs shows that important breakthroughs in public health interventions have led to great improvements in economic development. Health determines economic productivity and prosperity, and the physical and emotional well-being of the people. The mindset of the population afflicted with a high infant mortality rate usually lacks the secure knowledge of its children’s longevity, witnesses higher fertility rates, and experiences the quality-quantity trade-off in child-rearing. Ever since the health-for-all movement was initiated over three decades ago, health, equity, and social justice remain the main themes of social and health policy. It is essential for all public health professionals to sustain these values, especially those in LMICs and the international community.

1.4


Public health priorities in countries undergoing economic transition


	The middle-income countries
	Stephen Tollman and Jessica Price





Introduction


	Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3 highlights the range of health challenges which continue to reduce quality of life, extending the horizon of global health well beyond maternal and child health, HIV, and malaria—which dominated the Millennium Development Goals—to include non-communicable diseases, mental health, injuries, and exposure-related illnesses. SDG 3 further addresses the goal of universal health coverage (UHC) (World Health Organization n.d., b). However, if SDG 3 targets are to be met, the complex health challenges accompanying social and economic transitions in middle-income countries (MICs) must be confronted.
	MICs are diverse in geography, population size, politics, and economic activity. The World Bank defines lower MICs as countries with a gross national income (GNI) per capita of $1,006 to $3,955 (currently 47 countries), and upper middle-income economies as those with a GNI per capita between $3,956 and $12,235 as of 2018 (60 countries) (The World Bank in Middle Income Countries 2018).
	MICs are of special interest to public health researchers, practitioners, and policy makers first, because of the sheer number of people living in them—5 of the world’s 7 billion; second, because despite rapid economic growth, many MICs remain highly unequal—reflected by a high GINI index and widespread persistent poverty; and third, because prolonged economic and social transitions drive a series of health transitions. These in turn put a premium on adaptive health systems able to respond to changing health needs (The World Bank in Middle Income Countries 2018).
	Economic transition refers to structural, organizational, and institutional changes in national economies that affect their growth paths, policy context, and private sector evolution. Changes to the job market include growing numbers of skilled jobs and a rise in women’s participation in the formal economy (with a move from unpaid home and care work to paid formal employment), increased labour-related migration, the establishment of new microeconomies, and rising expectations of standards of living, government services and social protection (International Monetary Fund 2000). Economic transitions are broadly separated into those required to boost countries from low-to middle-income (industrialization, greater privatization, movement to market-based economies); and transition from middle-income to high-income (characterized by a move from industrial to knowledgebased economies). Countries which transition successfully to middle-income, but fail to transition to high-income nations are said to be caught in a ‘middle-income trap’. This describes the slowing of economic growth in MICs that are unable to develop new growth models and institutions required to drive knowledgebased economies (Gill and Kharas 2007). The ‘middle-income-trap’ is an important reminder that despite being described as linear processes, economic transitions are typically prolonged, heterogenous and non-linear with some countries even regressing to a lower income status—as in Argentina which was classified as high-income in 2014 and 2018, but as upper middle-income 2015–2017 and again in 2019 (World Bank 2019).
	The upstream changes associated with economic transition lead to far-reaching behavioural transitions which feed through to health, risk and disease profiles—outcomes directly influenced by greater urbanization, changes in diet and physical activity, as well as educational and infrastructure development. Economic and social transitions have important downstream health system effects: management of diseases improve as numbers of health professionals increase with the upskilling of the population, and increased spending on healthcare as gross domestic product (GDP) grows. Positive effects on the social determinants of health include better female education, improvements in sewage and hygiene, and introduction of social protection policies—accompanied by declining maternal and child mortality, and infectious disease. However, offsetting impacts on health arise from overcrowding, air pollution, physical inactivity, alcohol and tobacco consumption, and high fat, sugar and salt diets often linked with hyperaccessibility to ‘fast foods’ (Miranda et al. 2019). This tends to manifest in growing burdens of non-communicable diseases: diabetes, cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, and cancers. These changes in disease burden have been termed health transitions (Beaglehole and Bonita 2004).
	In this chapter we start by reviewing the relationship between the economy and health, looking at changes in health outcome as income increases, demographic transitions related to economic growth, and the impact of urbanization on health outcomes. We then review major health challenges facing MICs, including the triple burden of disease, multimorbidity, mental health across the life course and the impacts of migration, climate change, and antimicrobial resistance. Finally, we discuss health system challenges and the importance of building resilient and ‘learning’ health systems with the agility to adapt to meet MICs’ evolving health needs. We discuss strategies to achieve universal health coverage in MICs and the importance of intersectoral collaboration in promoting health. The key messages are outlined in Box 1.4.1.
	 	Box 1.4.1 Key messages
	 	1. MICs are countries undergoing social and economic transitions, which can be prolonged and non-linear.
	2. Economic and social transitions have profound effects on the health burdens and related health behaviours in MICs. This is compounded by greater vulnerability to health impacts from climate change, migration, and antimicrobial resistance.
	3. MICs are best served by resilient and ‘learning’ health systems, able to respond with agility to the changing health needs of the population.
	4. Policies designed to enable universal health coverage and intersectoral collaboration can position MICs to meet the complex health needs of their populations.





Health and the economy


Income and health


	Growth in per capita GDP is associated with improved health outcomes at a national level. This association was described by Samuel Preston in 1975, who showed that life expectancy at birth was higher in wealthier nations, but that the relationship flattens at higher incomes (Preston 1975). As shown in Figure 1.4.1 using 2012 data, in countries with a GDP per capita of up to ~$4,000 small increases in gross domestic product (GPD) are associated with large increases in life expectancy. At higher levels of GDP per capita the association weakens (Biciunaite 2014). Rising GDP per capita is also associated, in aggregate, with declining neonatal, infant and under-5 mortality (Pritchett and Summers 1993). As income rises and under-5 mortality falls, neonatal deaths typically account for a greater proportion of all under-5 deaths.
	Fig. 1.4.1 Preston curve 2012: change in life expectancy at birth by per capita GDP (from Euromonitor International). Note: GDP based on purchasing power parity (PPP) and takes account of differences in pricing between countries.
	Reprinted from Biciunaite A (2015) ‘Economic Growth and Life Expectancy—Do Wealthier Countries Live Longer?’ Euromonitor International ©Euromonitor.
	While the relationship between income and health outcomes holds across countries, national averages can mask significant differences in outcomes between the wealthy and the poor within the same country. This is especially problematic in MICs, many of which remain highly unequal. A recent review found that in India, a child in the poorest socioeconomic quintile is over 2.5 times more likely to die as one from the wealthiest quintile, with a difference in the under-5 mortality rate of over 30/1,000 live births. The ratio of under-5 mortality in the poorest quintile compared to the wealthiest in Brazil exceeded 2.5, and is above in South Africa (Chao et al. 2018). Table 1.4.1 illustrates differences in infant and child mortality by socioeconomic quintile for selected MICs where Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) data is available (World Health Organization, n.d., a; Hosseinpoor et al. 2016).

Income and demography


	In essence, demographic transition can be understood as a change in population dynamics from high mortality and birth rates (fertility), to low mortality and fertility as socioeconomic development (notably female education) occurs. The demographic transition results in changes to population age structure, with implications for labour capacity, child and older adult dependence, and disease and disability burdens (Coale 1989).
	As a group, MICs span multiple stages of demographic transition (Table 1.4.2): those at an earlier stage of transition experience a growing proportion of young people in the population; while at later stages, fertility declines and population size stabilizes. Concurrent declines in mortality and fertility can produce a ‘demographic dividend’ with greater productivity of adults in the labour force resulting from fewer child dependents (so a decline in the dependency ratio) (United Nations Population Fund, n.d.). A greater proportion of economic resources can therefore be invested to speed development. However, the benefits of a demographic dividend are not guaranteed: in addition to education and health systems to support more productive working populations, the demographic dividend requires a buoyant economy that can withstand shocks. In contrast, in countries with high youth unemployment, economic growth remains slow even as the dependency ratio falls (Table 1.4.2). In addition, where economic benefit is realized, this can be short-lived: as the population ages greater care burdens are place on the state and on working adults to care for older generations. Growth in the population 65 years and older results in a rise in the old-age dependency ratio and is generally associated with a slowing of per capita income growth (United Nations Population Fund n.d.).
	Although characterized as a linear transition with sequential stages, the reality of demographic transitions in MICs is generally more complex. In southern and east Africa, the HIV epidemic resulted in rising mortality in the 1990s and early 2000s despite a continued decline in fertility. AIDS-related mortality mostly affected adults age 30–44 (i.e. the working generation) resulting in significant burdens placed on older persons to take over the roles of primary caregiver and breadwinner (with households increasingly dependent on old-age pensions as sources of income) (Hosegood et al. 2007). Although demographic transitions tend to accompany economic transition, it is possible for demographic transitions to continue despite economic stagnation.
	Table 1.4.2 provides trend data for selected MICs from 1997 and 2017, demonstrating the heterogeneity of demographic transitions across countries.
