Urbanization and health


	Urbanization is arguably the most ubiquitous and powerful social transition with mixed effects on personal and population health. On one hand, given the concentration of services, urbanization can support marked health gains through improved access to education, healthcare, and employment. However, when urbanization occurs in a rapid, unplanned, and uncontrolled manner—as seen in the creation of urban slums—urbanization itself can become a risk factor for poor health outcomes (Patil 2014).
	Urban slums are overcrowded with a lack of proper hygiene and sanitation systems, informal housing, and unreliable water and energy supply. While some slums have a quasi-permanent character, others have high turnover of residents (Ezeh et al. 2017). As a result of poor living conditions, slum-dwellers are at risk of infectious diseases such as TB, acute respiratory infections, diarrhoea, and vector-borne diseases including malaria (Elsey et al. 2019). Conditions of poverty including a lack of food put children of the urban poor at increased risk of undernutrition and stunting (Patil 2014).
	Behaviour changes influenced by urbanization include dietary preferences, tobacco, and alcohol consumption and physical activity—contribute at population level to a rising incidence of non-communicable disease and risk including obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Urbanization has also been shown to negatively affect mental health—with increasing stress and social isolation, and higher levels of violence and injury (Patil 2014). Changes in household structure—tending to more households of smaller size occur in rural and urban areas (Wittenberg et al. 2017) and exacerbate the loss of social support (Patil 2014).
	Increasing pace of migration—whether unidirectional or circular—of sizeable numbers to cities increases demands on transport and leads to more (often less roadworthy) vehicles. Furthermore, vehicles in low-and middle-income countries are typically more polluting than those in high-income countries (HICs). Combined with rapid industrialization, this contributes to worsening air pollution1 which in turn may exacerbate chronic respiratory conditions and contribute to cardiovascular events and cancers. In 2018, air pollution was assessed the fifth leading risk factor for death globally, and the third and fourth leading risk factor for mortality and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) combined in India and China respectively (Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) 2018; Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) 2018b; Health Effects Institute 2019).
	Finally, urbanization is associated with localized rises in temperature relative to surrounding areas—known as the ‘Urban Heat Island’ effect. This results from increased heat production, reduced surface evaporation, changing thermal characteristics and rising air pollution (Grover and Singh 2015). The negative impacts of rising temperatures, including heat stroke, cardiovascular and respiratory mortality, are discussed in the following section on climate change and health.
	1Air pollution is measured using particulate size >25 µm (PM2.5). Over the past 30 years, PM2.5 concentrations have increased by ~25% across South Asian cities. Furthermore, growth of urban populations means more people exposed to harmful levels of air pollution (Miranda et al. 2019).





Health challenges in MICs


Triple burden of disease


	The triple burden of disease describes the concurrent, often interacting health burdens of (1) communicable, maternal, neonatal, and nutritional disease (CMNN); (2) a rising burden of non-communicable disease; and (3) substantial morbidity and mortality from injuries.
	As seen in Figure 1.4.2, non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are now the leading cause of death and account for the largest proportion of DALYs globally and in MICs (Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) 2018c). This reflects changes in the social determinants, risk factors, and behaviours associated with the economic and social transitions occurring in MICs, as well as the impact of demographic transitions—with growing proportions of the world population over 65 years (Table 1.4.2). According to figures from the Global Burden of Disease study, stroke, ischaemic heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and lung cancer were leading causes of DALYs in China in 2017. This marks a significant change from 1990 when lower respiratory infections and neonatal disorders were first, followed by stroke and COPD (Zhou et al. 2019). In India, leading causes of death in 2017 were ischaemic heart disease, COPD, and stroke (IHME 2018); and in Mexico ischaemic heart disease, chronic kidney disease, and diabetes remained the leading causes of death from 2007 to 2017 (IHME 2018d).
	Fig. 1.4.2 Causes of DALYs across World Bank Income groups, 2017.
	Data from Global Burden of Disease study 2017 (IHME 2018c).
	However, MICs continue to face a substantial burden from infectious disease, maternal, neonatal, and nutrition-related conditions (Fig. 1.4.2) (Bawah et al. 2016; IHME 2018c). This despite improvements in hygiene and sanitation, declining fertility rates, greater female education, and targeted interventions resulting in increased vaccination rates, skilled birth attendants at delivery and the use of artemisinin-based treatment for malaria among others. Furthermore, there is growing recognition of the interaction between infectious and NCDs, especially cancers (e.g. human immunodeficiency virus and Kaposi’s sarcoma as well as lymphomas, human papilloma virus and cervical cancer, and chronic hepatitis B infection and liver cancer).
	Finally, injuries (from road traffic accidents, interpersonal violence, homicides, and self-harm) continue to account for approximately 10% of the global burden of disease and the same is true in MICs (Fig. 1.4.2). However, the impact of DALYs from injuries are disproportionately felt in MICs (and low-income countries) where car ownership is rising rapidly, preventive strategies are less developed, traffic and alcohol regulations are poorly enforced and health systems are less prepared to manage injury emergencies (Gosselin et al. 2009).
	South Africa—along with many countries in southern and eastern Africa—is described as having a quadruple burden of disease (Groenewald et al. 2017) so recognizing the impact of HIV and TB. HIV/AIDS remains the leading cause of death in South Africa in 2017, as well as the leading cause of premature death and disability (IHME 2018f).
	The complexity of disease burdens facing MICs is also reflected by the concurrence of risk factors that promote both communicable and non-communicable disease. This is best highlighted by the coexisting epidemics of underweight and overweight populations within the same country (Manyanga et al. 2014; Ford et al. 2017). Furthermore, both epidemics are typically experienced by the poorest socioeconomic quintiles, with wealthier quintiles having better health outcomes across all risk factor and disease groupings. In addition to changing nutritional patterns—driven in part by the expansion of multinationals into MICs and the hyperaccessibility of ‘fast foods’ (Miranda et al. 2019)—increased consumption of tobacco and alcohol, high blood pressure, raised glucose and air pollution are among the leading risk factors contribution to DALY’s across the BRICS nations and many other MICs (IHME 2018; IHME 2018a, 2018e, 2018b, 2018f).





Multimorbidity


	A consequence of these complex, sometimes interacting infectious, non-communicable and injury-related disease burdens, is the growing challenge of multimorbidity—referring to the presence of two or more chronic conditions in the same individual (Academy of Medical Sciences 2018). Increasingly individuals in MICs have coexisting conditions which manifest at younger ages. Thus multimorbidity is not only due to population ageing, but also because of the premature growth in prevalence of NCDs, and persistence of communicable disease including HIV and TB (Academy of Medical Sciences 2018). See Box 1.4.2.
	 	Box 1.4.2 Multimorbidity
	Multimorbidity refers to the coexistence of two or more chronic conditions, each one of which is either:
	 	• A physical non-communicable disease of long duration, such as a cardiovascular disease or cancer.
	• A mental health condition of long duration, such as a mood disorder or dementia.
	• An infectious disease of long duration, such as HIV/AIDS or hepatitis C.
	The World Health Organization (WHO) Study on global AGEing and adult health (SAGE)—which considered non-communicable conditions in China, Ghana, India, Mexico, Russian Federation and South Africa—found that NCD-related multimorbidity affected 19% of the adult population (compared to 17% with only one NCD). Furthermore, 17.43% of 18–49 year olds already had 1 NCD with 9.27% having two or more NCDs. This burden only grows as the population ages: a third of 50–64 year olds had two or more NCDs (Sum et al. 2019).
	Though recognition of the impact of multimorbidity on treatment requirements, patient outcomes, and health system demands is growing, there remains limited evidence about the most common clusters of chronic conditions and the relevance of the different combinations. In attempting to group coexisting conditions, those which are similar in their origin and/or treatment requirements have been termed concordant multimorbidities (e.g. ischaemic heart disease and stroke are both related to hypertension), while those which differ in their origin and treatment are classified as discordant multimorbidities (e.g. ischaemic heart disease and depression) (Academy of Medical Sciences 2018). Contrasting patterns of multimorbidity have also been described, a European pattern reflecting combinations of two or more NCDs (that may be similar to China, South Asia, and South America), whereas multimorbidity patterns including HIV/AIDS or TB and non-communicable disease is common in African settings. Successful antiretroviral treatment programmes and subsequent rise in life expectancy of people living with HIV means that multimorbidity including HIV/AIDS will become more prevalent (Bawah et al. 2016).
	There is evidence to suggest that the different chronic disease dyad and triad combinations have different health system implications; for example, patients with multimorbidity including depression having fewer outpatient visits but more hospitalizations and generally reporting a lower quality of life (hypothesized to result from limited use of primary care services and delayed presentation to more specialized care leading to hospital admission (Sum et al. 2019)). Work from South Africa suggests that HIV positive patients on antiretroviral therapy (ART) have better outcomes across a range of coexisting conditions including better blood pressure control and lower blood glucose. The ‘ART advantage’ is thought to arise through increased healthcare utilization in people living with HIV/AIDS (Manne-Goehler et al. 2017; M’yambo Magodoro et al. 2019).
	However, the health system implications of multimorbidity extend beyond utilization rates: these patients contribute to an excessive workload and cost (beyond simply the sum of treating the individual conditions). Vertically designed programmes tend to be specialized and may miss opportunities to manage concurrent conditions—though further data is needed to assess the contrasting impacts of vertical, horizontal, and diagonal health system designs (Academy of Medical Sciences 2018).
	The impact of ART on life expectancy is resulting in rising prevalence of HIV/AIDS in ageing populations also at risk of other chronic NCDs (Bawah et al. 2016; Chang et al. 2019). The implications of managing patients’ concurrent HIV and NCD treatment needs demand greater consideration, particularly in southern and eastern Africa which account for almost 60% of all people taking ARVs globally (Chang et al. 2019).
	Finally, despite evidence that multimorbidity and associated risk affects both adolescent and ageing populations, most health systems are poorly configured to meet the needs of these key groups. Notably, in adolescents, emphasis on preventive strategies and behaviour change interventions will be required (e.g. promoting healthier lifestyles and reducing obesity which will pay dividends later in life) (Patton et al. 2016).





Mental health across the life course


	The burden from mental, neurological and substance use disorders continues to grow globally, in part reflecting demographic and epidemiological transitions as well as greater awareness. Mental health across the life course is a particular concern for MICs as known social determinants of mental illness and substance use disorders include inequality, poverty, childhood adversity, displacement, and violence (Patel et al. 2018). As such, mental health status is an important pathway in the cycle of intergenerational poverty (Fig. 1.4.3) (Leon and Walt 2000; Patel et al. 2018).
	Fig. 1.4.3 The cycle of poverty and mental illness. From poverty, inequality, and mental health in developing countries (2000).
	Reprinted from Leon, D. A. and Walt, G. (2000) ‘Poverty, inequality, and mental health in developing countries’, in Leon, D. and Walt, G. (eds) Poverty, Inequality, and Health. Oxford University Press, with permission from Oxford University Press.
	A life course approach highlights critical periods which increase the risk for mental ill-health and require multilevel preventive and treatment strategies (Patel et al. 2018). Similarly, the concept of allostatic load (McEwen and Seeman 1999) recognizes the impact of cumulative psychosocial stresses which in turn lead to physiological ‘wear and tear’ contributing to negative health outcomes, including poor mental health.
	Childhood experiences of early life stresses associated with low socioeconomic status and lack of stimulation in infancy are shown to increase the risk of mental health problems in later life. The presentation of mental disorders in adolescents is partly explained by the centrality of peer opinions which tend to replace those of parents and family and can be influenced by complex patterns of brain and cognitive development (Patton et al. 2016). This is a challenge in MICs where health systems seldom meet the health needs of adolescents despite growing adolescent and young adult populations. In older adults, mental health outcomes often relate to earlier life experiences, and a lack of formal education increases the chances of cognitive decline. Furthermore, cognitive impairment is associated with depression over the life course and so societies more exposed to risk factors for depression may experience increased burdens of dementia as populations age, a concern for MICs (Patel et al. 2018).
	In addition, significant treatment and care gaps exist and surveys from China and India suggest that over 80% of people with a mental or substance use disorder did not seek treatment (Wei et al. 2013; Murthy 2017). Lack of access to care partly reflects underspending on mental health, with MICs spending approximately 2% of health budgets on mental health despite mental illness accounting for almost 30% of DALYs. Furthermore, most of this is spent on tertiary centres and inpatient institutions with little investment in community-based and primary care interventions (Patel et al. 2018).
	Quality of services also tends to be poor: the World Mental Health Surveys report that only 11.4% of patients living with major depressive disorder in upper MICs receive minimally adequate treatment, and this drops to 3.7% in lower MICs (Thornicroft et al. 2017). Regarding substance use disorders, only 4.3% of patients in upper MICs and 1% of patients in lower MICs receive minimally adequate treatment (Degenhardt et al. 2017).





Migration


	Most global migration occurs within LMICs (Abubakar et al. 2018). There were an estimated 258 million international (cross-border) migrants in 2017 (UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs Population Division 2017). However, internal migration—referring to movement within national borders—accounts for far more movement globally with over 740 million internal migrants in 2009 (four times the number of international migrants in the same year) (UNDP 2009). Internal labour migration may be from rural to urban areas (accounting for much of urban growth in MICs), or from rural to rural areas based on work opportunities in agriculture or mining (with the proportion of female migrants growing substantially in recent decades. Importantly, evidence is strong that labour migrants, whether international or internal, generally contribute positively to a host country’s economy. There are also consistently more internally displaced people in LMICs (due to conflict or natural disasters) than refugees or asylum seekers (being forced international migrants) (Abubakar et al. 2018). While it remains challenging to assess the full range of migrant health needs due to limitations in data quality, migration should be recognized as a core determinant of health in MICs.
	The UCL-Lancet Commission on Migration and Health (2018) highlighted that migration is rarely a single journey (Abubakar et al. 2018)—with patterns involving variable distances within and across borders, temporarily or permanently, and often multiple times. Migration may involve several phases (Fig. 1.4.4) (Abubakar et al. 2018), each of which poses particular health risks relevant to planning health systems in MICs. Health of individuals pre-departure may be poor; the mode of transport can pose risks of injury or exposure, as can environmental and pathogen exposures on the journey. In the new country or region of residence, migrants face different infection and occupational exposures. And when returning to their origin home, the health risks may increase—some having lost immunity to local pathogens or having returned home following injury or disability without being able to access the necessary services (Abubakar et al. 2018).
	Fig. 1.4.4 The migration cycle.
	Reprinted from Abubakar A et al. (2018) ‘The UCL-Lancet Commission on Migration and Health: the health of a world on the move’. The Lancet 392(10164):2606–54, with permission from Elsevier.
	Mortality rates among migrants have been studied in various settings. While a ’healthy migrant effect’—whereby health among migrants tends to be better than expected with lower risk for disease—the theory overlooks the diversity among migrant groups, and that the health benefits of migration may reduce over time. Data on mortality among migrants in MICs is limited however work in sub-Saharan Africa concluded that internal migrants often display higher mortality than long-term residents. This health disadvantage arose due to both infectious and non-communicable disease, and was likely linked to poor social integration and access to care, and inadequate living conditions (Abubakar et al. 2018; Ginsburg et al. 2018).
	Evidence on the relationship between migration and mental health is mixed: international migrants, particularly asylum seekers and refugees, tend to have higher rates of depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder. This often reflects differences in the precipitating risk factors such as experience of violence and traumatic events (Patel et al. 2018). The economic and psychosocial stresses of migration and urbanization may place migrants at greater risk of poor mental health outcomes (Ginsburg et al. 2018). Finally, migration appears linked to mental health outcomes in children: both in children who migrate, where research suggests they are more likely to have depression, anxiety, aggression, or hyperactivity, and among children left behind. A meta-analysis of studies on left-behind children suggested they are at increased risk of depression (RR 1.52, 95%CI 1.27–1.82), anxiety (RR 1.85, 1.36–2.53), substance use (RR 1.24, 1.00–1.52) and suicidal ideation (RR 1.70, 1.28–2.26) (Patel et al. 2018).
	In South Africa, internal ‘circular’ labour migration—whereby workers move to town but maintain regular contact with their rural home—was an important factor in propagating the HIV epidemic: migration led to an increased risk of HIV infection, though acquisition and transmission could be bidirectional, e.g. from migrants to their rural partners, and from rural residents to their migrant partners (Lurie et al. 2003). As migrant labourers developed AIDS (or other serious chronic condition), becoming too sick to work, they chose to ‘return home to die’ (Welaga et al. 2009), with significant attendant care burdens and health-related costs borne by their households during their final stage of illness.
	As a principle, consistent with the goal of UHC, health systems need to incorporate the competencies required to address the specific health needs of the migrant population, whether citizens or not. Furthermore, health systems need to strengthen their capability to provide services to highly mobile groups unlikely to access care from the same place consistently over time.





Climate change and health


	MICs include countries heavily affected by climate change through altered temperature and rainfall patterns coupled with extreme weather events resulting in widespread health, social, and economic impacts. MICs are at risk of climate-related health effects for three reasons: (1) geography viz. a higher concentration of heatwaves, adverse weather events such as droughts and floods, and loss of labour capacity especially in areas close to the equator; (2) national systems lack the resilience needed to adapt to persisting weather changes, respond to disasters, or diversify food sources—with single crop markets at particular risk; (3) less developed regulatory frameworks to limit key drivers of climate change such as fossil fuels, and provide incentives for clean energy.
	Climate change has both direct and indirect health impacts. Direct effects include exposure to heat waves and rising temperatures, as well as weather-related disasters. Indirect effects are those mediated through changes in ecosystems, land use, air pollution and water quality (Fig. 1.4.5).
	Fig. 1.4.5 The direct and indirect effects of climate change on health and wellbeing. From Lancet Commission on Health and climate change: policy responses to protect public health.
	Reprinted from Watts, N., et al. (2015) ‘Health and climate change: policy responses to protect public health’, The Lancet. 386(10006), pp. 1861–914, with permission from Elsevier.





Direct health effects


	Increased temperature and heatwaves can exacerbate chronic conditions, lead to new cardiovascular and renal conditions, and provoke dehydration—to which older persons are especially prone. Furthermore, when combined with urbanization and air pollution, not only is the temperature rise amplified, but acute and chronic respiratory disease tends to worsen (Watts et al. 2015).
	The impact of heat exposure is also evident in the fall in outdoor labour productivity (some 5.3% decline worldwide 2000–2016—with the greatest reductions in countries worst affected by rising temperatures, many of which are MICs). The decline in outdoor labour productivity is paralleled by both a rise in health burden and reduction in economic output—of particular concern for MICs where much of the labour force continues to work in industry (Watts et al. 2015, 2018).
	Concern around climate-sensitive diseases is growing: greater exposure to UV rays resulting from damage to the ozone layer is leading to rising incidence of malignant melanoma (Watts et al. 2018); and climate-related weather disasters result in direct morbidity and mortality, and can cause mental health disorders linked to the trauma of the extreme weather events (Watts et al. 2015).





Indirect health effects


	Most climate-related health risks are mediated through ecological and social processes. Food insecurity is among the greatest impacts of climate change and arises through multiple pathways including crop failure, reduced food production, extreme weather events, increased food-borne and other infectious diseases, and civil unrest. While severe food insecurity and hunger are associated with undernutrition, wasting, and stunting in children, mild to moderate food insecurity has been associated with obesity in vulnerable populations (Swinburn et al. 2019), a paradox of concern in the context of high inequality and rising NCDs in MICs.
	Diseases related to water quality (e.g. cholera) and vector spread (including malaria and dengue fever) are impacted by rising temperatures and changes in rainfall patterns. Warmer temperatures promote cholera bacterial growth, while droughts and extreme weather events can limit access to safe drinking water. In areas previously protected by lower temperatures, climate change is affecting the range and reproductive rate of malaria-carrying mosquitoes, even at higher altitudes, with growing risk of new malaria epidemics (Watts et al. 2015). This increase in vector capacity also contributes to the climbing incidence of dengue fever with an estimated 58.4 million cases in 2013 (95%CI 23.6 million –121.9 million) accounting for some 10 000 deaths and 1.14 million DALYs. Much of this burden is in the Asia-Pacific, Latin American and Caribbean regions—mostly MICs. The A aegypti and A albopictus mosquitoes which transmit dengue are also vectors for emerging and re-emerging arboviruses including Yellow Fever, Chikungunya and Zika virus (Watts et al. 2018).





Antimicrobial resistance


	MICs face a paradox when it comes to antimicrobial use: on one hand, infections continue to account for a significant burden and are the leading cause of death in some countries, notably in children under-5. An estimated 445, 000 pneumonia-related child deaths could be averted through universal provision of antibiotics (Laxminarayan et al. 2016). On the other hand, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing problem, driven largely by increasing and inappropriate use of antibiotics (Miller-Petrie et al. 2018). With regard to neonatal mortality alone, resistant sepsis infections kill approximately 214, 000 neonates each year primarily in India, Pakistan, Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and China (four of these five countries are MICs) (Miller-Petrie et al. 2018).
	Tackling antimicrobial resistance in MICS is challenging for several reasons:
	 	1. Increasing consumption of antibiotics: although per capita antibiotic use remains lower in MICs than HICs, MICs saw the highest growth rates in antibiotic consumption 2000–2010 and have higher drug resistance indices (Klein et al. 2019). In part this is due to rising income and greater access to antibiotics, however, it also reflects supply-side problems including: lack of enforcement of prescribing regulations, high rates of over-the-counter purchasing, and a lack of incentives for rational prescribing, all of which lead to inappropriate antibiotic use. Substandard and falsified medications are also a concern; while this is common in India, the WHO estimates that it affects 7% of antibiotics globally (Miller-Petrie et al. 2018; World Health Organization 2018b). Lastly, changing patterns of antibiotic use have resulted in increased consumption of broad-spectrum antibiotics including cephalosporins, broad-spectrum penicillins, and fluoroquinolones, as well as increased use of last-resort antibiotic classes (carbapenems and polymixins) (Laxminarayan et al. 2016).
	2. Antimicrobial use in animals: two-thirds of all antibiotic use, including antibiotics to treat infections in humans, are used in animals at subtherapeutic levels to promote growth and prevent disease, and at therapeutic levels to treat infection in livestock (Laxminarayan et al. 2016). Estimated use of antibiotics in food production is expected to virtually double (98% increase) in BRICS nations (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa) by 2030, including a projected 312% increase in India alone (Laxminarayan et al. 2016). Widespread use of antibiotics in farming creates strong selection pressure, encouraging the development of resistant infections (Miller-Petrie et al. 2018) which will have impact human and animal health (encompassed in the concept of One Health). However, few MICs regulate or monitor the use of antimicrobials in animals—or have adequate capacity to do so (Hu and O’Neill 2019).
	3. Lack of antimicrobial resistance surveillance programmes: Accurate data on AMR is required to effectively design programmes to prevent the spread of infection and tackle inappropriate prescribing practices. However, few MICs have managed to establish routine antimicrobial surveillance systems. And where these do exist, data is usually publicized in annual reports of resistance profiles, making it difficult to respond rapidly to changes in resistance and outbreaks of resistant organisms (Perez and Villegas 2015). Furthermore, no AMR surveillance programmes in MICs include data on antimicrobial use and antibiotic resistance in agriculture and livestock (World Health Organization 2014). A global AMR surveillance system (GLASS) is being developed by the WHO to support the global action plan on antimicrobial resistance, and aims to improve surveillance capacity and data quality particularly in LMICs (World Health Organization 2018a).
	4. Lack of data from primary care settings: Where data on AMR is available—whether from surveillance programmes or specific research studies—this tends to focus on resistance in hospital settings and is extrapolated to estimate the community prevalence of AMR (World Health Organization 2018b). However, the impact of antibiotics used in farming and the environment, substandard and falsified medications, and self-medication with antibiotics are more likely to affect community-acquired infections. Most patients with bacterial infections sensitive to first line antibiotics will improve with treatment at primary care level and not present to higher levels of care. As a result, extrapolating trends in AMR from hospital level data could over-or underestimate AMR in the community, and resistant strains may vary between hospital and community settings.
	The consequences of AMR can be more severe in MICs (and low-income countries (LICs)) than HICs. Mortality from resistant infections may be higher—due to a lack of access to newer and more effective drugs, compounded by poorer social determinants of health (World Health Organization 2018b). Where second-and third-line drugs are available they tend to be more expensive: the World Bank estimates that AMR could push 28 million people into poverty by 2050 (World Bank 2017). Furthermore, the growth of fluoroquinolone resistance is of particular concern as fluoroquinolones are used in the treatment of multidrug resistant TB which remains a priority in many MICs (Hu and O’Neill 2019).
	Finally, strategies to limit AMR include preventing infection with regular hand washing and infection control in health facilities (Miller-Petrie et al. 2018), practices which tend to be less well implemented in MICs compared to HICs. Similarly, vaccinations can protect against common infections, reducing the need for antibiotics (Miller-Petrie et al. 2018). However as MICs graduate from GAVI, the Vaccine Alliance, they will need to take on higher vaccine costs—as of December 2020 only India, Nigeria and Indonesia will remain eligible for assistance out of the nine BRICS and MINT (Mexico, Indonesia, Nigeria, Turkey) nations (Hu and O’Neill 2019).





Health systems in MICs


	Given the complex and heterogeneous health challenges facing MICs as a consequence of the evolving, dynamic transitions underway, it is critical that health systems in these countries adapt to respond to societies’ changing health needs. This cannot be achieved by simply improving the efficiency of current approaches; rather it requires an all-round rethinking of health systems in these settings, taking cognisance of inevitable resource constraints. We suggest the following tenets underpin future-oriented health systems in MICs—that they
	 	• be resilient and learning health systems
	• strive to provide UHC
	• focus on the quality of health services in addition to their availability
	• take into account the contributions possible from intersectoral collaboration.





Resilient and learning health systems


	‘Resilience’ describes the degree to which health systems can absorb shocks and adapt to provide the required services (Kruk et al. 2015; Massuda et al. 2018). Although the phrase gained traction following the 2014–2016 Ebola crisis in West Africa, there is growing recognition of the importance of everyday resilience in resource-constrained health systems which experience repeated shocks (such as funding shortages, unreliable staffing, changing policies and guidelines, and growing administrative burdens) (Gilson et al. 2017; Massuda et al. 2018).
	Resilient health systems can be characterized by five elements: (1) awareness of available assets and vulnerabilities (human, physical, informational); (2) capacity to address a diversity of health needs across communities (measured in part by the degree to which universal health coverage has been achieved); (3) self-regulation with the capability to rapidly identify and contain new health threats while continuing to provide other essential health services; (4) integration of health services with other sectors to maximize the innovation in solutions to health challenges (which requires clear communication and information sharing); (5) adaptation to meet new health needs, both in response to emergencies and slower changes in evolving disease burdens (Kruk et al. 2015).
	A learning health system is also one which has as a central tenet, a focus on routinely collected data as a basis for continuous improvement integrated into the everyday functioning of services (English et al. 2016)—in this way, learning health systems can ore rapidly adjust their practices to adopt new evidence and improve the quality of patient care.
	Both resilient and learning health systems depend on accurate and up-to-date data upon which to base decisions, evaluate progress, and adapt in response to available evidence. To-date, many MICs lack comprehensive civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems. Investment in routine information systems is necessary as MICs endeavour to strengthen their health systems. Doing so as part of initial health system strengthening can prove far more cost-effective than retro-fitting data collection systems later (English et al. 2016).





Universal Health Coverage


	In 2005, all WHO member states committed to working to achieve UHC, i.e. that all people are able to access high-quality health services when needed (including preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative and palliative services) without risk of financial hardship (WHA58.33 Sustainable health financing, universal coverage, and social health insurance 2005). UHC is a particularly powerful and unifying principle for health systems in MICs: systems designed around the provision of essential care to all regardless of citizenship, nationality, age, or gender should be far better placed to address the complex disease burdens and provide integrated care for patients with multimorbidity, often at young adult ages. UHC is also a critical element in strategies to better provide migrant health services by lowering barriers to care related to entitlement to use services, where and which services, and essential information sharing between providers when patients routinely do not attend the same clinic.
	While few MICs can claim to have achieved UHC, some have made substantial strides as detailed in the World Bank’s Going Universal report (Cotlear et al. 2015). Although approaches vary, key features include increased health spending, pooling of funds, decentralization of care management, effective private–public partnerships, and expansion of comprehensive primary care services (Cotlear et al. 2015; Castro et al. 2019). Box 1.4.3 details elements of the Brazilian effort to achieve UHC.
	 	Box 1.4.3 Achieving UHC in Brazil
	The basis of UHC in Brazil is the Sistema Unico de Saúde (SUS)—a unified health system established in 1990 following the enshrining of health as universal human right in the Brazilian constitution of 1988. SUS decentralized health programme financing and management, sharing power between federal and municipal structures. All citizens are entitled to services provided by SUS, however the purchasing of private insurance by higher income groups means that SUS services are largely utilized by poorer and uninsured members of the population.
	As explained by Castro and colleagues (2019), SUS changed the model of healthcare delivery, expanding comprehensive primary care services and investing in the Family Health Strategy (a community-level health delivery platform) which increased service provision from some 7 million people (4% of the population) in 1998, to 130 million people (62% of the population) in 2018. In addition, mental health services, emergency care services, and specialist outpatient services were developed. Private–public partnerships were established to boost access to specialist care whereby the public sector funds service and facilities, but management and staff are provided by the private sector (Castro et al. 2019).
	The SUS is credited with significant improvements in health outcomes including rising life expectancy at birth, a fall in under-5 mortality from 64/1,000 live births in 1990 to 15/1,000 in 2015, and increased immunization coverage. SUS enabled Brazil to meet the rapidly changing health needs of its population, driven by migration from rural to urban areas, re-emerging infectious disease due to expanded human occupation of regions of the Amazon, rapid demographic and epidemiological transitions resulting in an increasing burden from non-communicable diseases (Castro et al. 2019).
	However, Brazil also serves as a warning to MICs of the fragility of health gains, and the ease of reversal when political leadership changes and investment in health systems decline. Introduction of austerity measures in 2016, including capped increases in health spending, and changes to reproductive and adolescent health services which threaten to limit access to care (given fear of promoting abortion), failure to explicitly include the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and questioning (LGBTQ+) community in ministerial mandates (claiming instead that ’diversity policies have threatened the Brazilian family’), education policies which prevent teachers from discussing gender, identity, and sexuality, amendments to gun laws which will increase their availability, and possible reductions in tobacco taxation all threaten to reverse—at least in part—the hard won health gains of the past 30 years (Castro et al. 2019).
	Although the principle of UHC is increasingly accepted, financing remains more controversial. The move towards UHC will see countries increase total health expenditure even in scenarios where there are significant efficiency gains. Ability to afford this increase is largely driven by economic growth and so increased available national income. However, in addition to increased spending, UHC requires pooled spending with criteria for contributions distinct from criteria for use (which is simply health need). Different strategies to pool spending are available (Schuster et al. 2018): some countries use general taxation; however, this can be challenging in countries with high unemployment and small tax bases (which may already be heavily taxed). Some countries have used compulsory payroll contributions (Hong 2009), while others have targeted public health insurance to the most vulnerable groups who do not meet criteria for employment-based schemes (such as the Seguro Populare programme in Mexico (Frenk et al. 2006)).
	Countries also need to resolve what health services to fund (often referred to as a ‘minimum benefits package’). This too will vary depending on what countries can afford. However, the Disease Control Priorities Project (3rd ed.) recommended standardized essential care packages that all countries should strive to provide based on value for money, disease burden and feasibility of implementation (Watkins et al. 2017).
	There is ongoing debate on the extent to which migrants gain access to the various models of UHC emerging. Thailand is among the best-known examples of migrant-inclusive policies: migrants with work permits are fully covered by the Thai social security scheme which is funded through mandatory payroll taxes including contributions from the employer, employee, and government. However, the majority of migrants in Thailand are undocumented and so ineligible for social health insurance. Therefore, in 2001, Thailand established a migrant health insurance scheme which migrants (documented or not) could join through a voluntary annual prepayment premium. The scheme was later extended to cover migrants’ dependents. Furthermore, Thailand invested in innovations to create migrant-friendly health services, including use of volunteer community workers to assist with health education, mobile clinics, and bilingual signposts. These efforts have served to increase access care for migrants, improve diagnosis and treatment, and reduce financial risk from large out-of-pocket payments, though work remains to increase the proportion of migrants enrolled (Tangcharoensathien et al. 2017).





Quality healthcare services


	The quality of care is as important as the extent of care provided: the Lancet Global Health Commission on High Quality Health Systems in the SDG Era found that improving quality of care could save an estimated 8 million lives in LMICs each year. Furthermore, promoting quality care can be expected to increase patient trust and improve patients’ experience of engaging the healthcare system (Kruk et al. 2018). However, health systems in MICs remain underresourced relative to the need and so innovative strategies are required to deliver quality care at an affordable cost. Task shifting and digital technologies are strategies increasingly used to extend high-quality healthcare in MICs.





Task shifting


	Task shifting, an approach that is widespread in global health, refers to the process of redistributing tasks to less specialized healthcare workers (World Health Organization 2007) and was successfully employed at scale in response to the HIV epidemic in sub-Saharan Africa: counselling and testing ‘shifted’ from nurses to lay counsellors or community health workers (CHWs); treatment initiation and monitoring transferred from doctors to nurses as did diagnosis and management of opportunistic infections; and management of advanced disease shifted from infectious disease specialists to non-specialist physicians (World Health Organization 2007).
	Task shifting has been employed in prevention and management of cardiovascular disease (Ogedegbe et al. 2014) and to improve maternal and child health outcomes, with CHWs tasked to provide health education to pregnant women and new mothers, identify high-risk pregnancies for referral to medical centres, conduct newborn checks, treat newborn infections and refer for further care where necessary, and monitor growth and vaccinations among others (Balsari et al. 2017). In global surgery, obstetrics, and anaesthetics, associate clinicians are increasingly tasked with operations and anaesthesia in place of doctors (Federspiel et al. 2018).
	While multiple trials have demonstrated the success of task shifting in expanding access to care without sacrificing the quality of care, there is less evidence to show which factors are critical to maintaining quality of care when such interventions are scaled-up. However, supervision, clear guidelines, adequate initial training, and regular retraining all appear important elements of successful programmes (Mason et al. 2006; World Health Organization 2008).





Digital health technologies


	Digital technologies are increasingly included in studies that: address coverage gaps, increase communication with patients, improve diagnosis and treatment, improve data management, and assist in financial transactions (and limit fraud and abuse) within the healthcare system. Technologies include mHealth (mobile health) and computer-based information applications. With rapidly rising access to mobile phones and the internet, delivering health interventions using mobile technologies is increasingly feasible (Lewis et al. 2012).
	There is now evidence to demonstrate the value of mHealth interventions across LMICs. SMS reminders have been shown to improve treatment adherence and care seeking as seen with regards to ARVs and malaria diagnostics (Liu and Modrek 2016; Amankwaa et al. 2018); and educational interventions such as MomConnect have been effective at delivering targeted health promotion messages to pregnant women (Seebregtsi et al. 2016). Technology has also enabled task shifting with mobile or tablet-based applications designed to assist health workers in diagnosis and treatment in the field or in primary care (Lewis et al. 2012). Virtual consultations reduce the need for in-person visits to clinics and so increase access to care where geography, transport and financial barriers might exist (Lewis et al. 2012). Furthermore, virtual consultations may be preferred by patients who experience stigma and resist accessing care for fear of being ostracized. In contrast, the use of information system interventions, including electronic health records and data management systems is less well established in MICs.
	Despite successful pilot studies, few programmes have been scaled successfully (exceptions including MomConnect in South Africa (Seebregtsi et al. 2016) and the mDiabetes project in Senegal (World Health Organization 2017)). Scaling digital interventions often requires additional investment; electricity and internet access are inconsistent and mobile data is expensive; and there remain cultural and generational barriers to widespread adoption of technological interventions (Lewis et al. 2012; Labrique et al. 2018). Furthermore, despite the imperative for data that underpin learning health systems, many MICs are not making use of available technologies to assist in data collection and management (Lewis et al. 2012).





Intersectoral collaboration


	The impact of social and economic transitions on disease burdens and outcomes highlights the multidimensional nature of health and points to the value of intersectoral collaboration in tackling major public health challenges. We have noted the importance of functioning CRVS systems and regular health outcome reporting which often falls outside the remit of health departments; improvements in housing, water, and sanitation are critical to reducing the burden of communicable disease. Intersectoral collaboration is required to tackle persistent inequality in many MICs: targeted social welfare policies seek to support the large ‘tail’ of the population still to emerge from poverty. These tend to be high health burden populations, and policies which redistribute wealth across socioeconomic quintiles assist in lessening the burden on the next generation. The South African non-contributory old-age pension and child support grants are exemplars of pro-poor policies where positive externalities have included health gains beyond the direct grant recipient (Aguero et al. 2006; Case and Menendez 2007).
	Conditional cash transfers have been used to address the burdens of poverty and incentivize health behaviours in high-risk populations: in Indonesia, conditional cash transfers improved vaccination rates by up to 30% (Kusuma et al. 2017). while the Oportunidades CCT programme in Mexico and the Bolsa Família programme in Brazil have been associated with improved child health, growth, and development, and increased care seeking among other positive health and education outcomes (Fernald et al. 2008; Shei et al. 2014).
	Finally, national taxation policies and regulation of nutrient content in foods are powerful tools for addressing public health burdens. Excise taxes on tobacco, alcohol, and sugar-sweetened beverages are effective strategies to reduce consumption with an ensuing decline in risk, morbidity, and mortality from related diseases (including cardiovascular disease, cancers, interpersonal violence) (Task Force on Fiscal Policy for Health 2019). Mandated salt targets in processed foods are expected to further reduce death rates from heart disease (Webster et al. 2017). Such policies demonstrate the value in governments becoming more adept at nudging their populations to make healthy choices, and suggest that similar approaches can be applied to other products. See Box 1.4.4 for a discussion of tobacco.
	 	Box 1.4.4 The power of tobacco, alcohol, and sugar-sweetened beverage excise taxes
	Excise taxes on tobacco have been used effectively in MICs including Brazil, South Africa, Ukraine, Turkey, and the Philippines (Task Force on Fiscal Policy for Health 2019), though there remains room for further increases to meet the WHO recommendation of a 70% excise tax on tobacco (World Health Organization 2010). Figure 1.4.6 shows changes in per capita cigarette sales as prices rose in Brazil: over 2006–2011, the real price of cigarettes rose by 34% per pack, with a corresponding fall of 19% in per capita cigarette consumption. In 2012–2016, the real price of cigarette packs rose by a further 33%, corresponding to an overall decline of almost 50% in cigarette consumption per adult (Task Force on Fiscal Policy for Health 2019).
	Russia continues to have one of the highest alcohol consumption rates in the world. However in 2004, laws banning alcohol advertising, restricting availability, and taxing alcoholic beverages were introduced and resulted in a decline in alcohol consumption by a third by 2014 (Task Force on Fiscal Policy for Health 2019). In Mexico the introduction of a 10% sugar-sweetened beverage tax is credited with reducing consumption of sugary drinks by 7.6% over the first 2 years of the tax, with the largest reductions noted among the poorest socioeconomic groups (Colchero et al. 2017). Further projections suggest the tax will prevent 189,300 incident cases of type 2 diabetes, 20,400 strokes and heart attacks and 18,900 deaths in adults 35 years and older between 2016 and 2026 (Sánchez-Romero et al. 2016). A similar policy (Health Promotion Levy) was introduced in South Africa in 2018 and is projected to prevent 8,000 diabetes-related premature deaths over the coming 20 years (Saxena et al. 2019).
	Fig. 1.4.6 Cigarette Prices and Per Capita Cigarette Sales, Brazil, 2000–2016.
	Reprinted from Health Taxes to Save Lives (2019) Task Force on Fiscal Policy for Health (2019) ‘Health Taxes to Save Lives: Employing Effective Excise Taxes on Tobacco, Alcohol, and Sugary Beverages’. New York: Bloomberg Philanthropies.





Discussion


	MICs are diverse in geography, politics, and population size—but all are undergoing social, economic and health transitions which necessitate adaptations of their health system to meet changing needs across the life course. Investing in resilient and learning health systems based on the principle of UHC should enable MICs to deliver care in a context of heterogeneity of outcomes related to persistent inequality in MICs, a triple (or quadruple) disease burden, growing prevalence of multimorbidity, mental and substance use disorders, and the health impacts arising from migration, climate change, and antimicrobial resistance. There is every likelihood that failure to adapt current health system functioning will lead to a divergence between health spending and outcomes—with increased spending failing to generate increased impact. Moreover, the nature of health profiles and burdens evolving in transitioning countries also requires interventions beyond the health sector, highlighting the value of collaboration across sectors and reinforcing a ‘health in all policies’ approach.
	While much of the chapter is focused on the health transitions that accompany economic growth, there are of course economic effects from changing health status: with improved health comes greater productivity and reduced treatment costs (and conversely poor health negatively impacts economic growth). Investment in effective preventive and promotive strategies can be extremely cost-effective across the life course and translate with time into enhanced education and livelihoods. However there is a tension between prioritizing spending on prevention of future disease in the face of prevalent burdens requiring immediate attention. Furthermore, many preventive strategies require investment beyond the health sector—to alter more upstream social, structural, and environmental determinants of health. UHC and intersectoral collaboration are key to managing these competing priorities in order to meet the health needs of transitioning populations given the resources available.
	Achieving the necessary health system reforms across MICs will require sustained investment in research and cognisance of the complexity of cultural and contextual ‘fit’. We have highlighted a number of areas where further research is needed: accurate data on risk, morbidity, and mortality patterns is critical to designing and monitoring interventions. Better understanding of multimorbidity is urgent, with particular focus on adolescent and young adult populations, both poorly served by existing health infrastructure. The full impact of migration, climate change, and antimicrobial resistance on primary healthcare and agriculture are research agendas which warrant ongoing attention. Research is also necessary to evaluate interventions and generate the data to drive learning health systems—including questions of cultural acceptability and contextual fit which will influence the effects of interventions, and strategies to scale-up. Implementation scientists can advise on integrating routine data into evaluation of health systems performance, and how to effectively convert evidence into practice and policy.
	Costs are a challenge facing all countries and a particular challenge for MICs. Health costs will grow as life expectancy increases and disease burdens evolve, and intervention strategies will likely differ for communicable, non-communicable and injury-related burdens—with the implication that parallel investments are required. The suggestion that MICs strive to achieve UHC places further demands on national health services—and an imperative to set priorities. The reality, however, is that MICs will be unable to cover all interventions for all conditions for all people. This is true of even the largest economies (such as China, India, and Brazil) which remain vulnerable to the pressures inherent in the global financial system including trade wars, depressions, and recessions. Many MICs require external support and investment—from bilateral donor countries, philanthropies, and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank, and UN system—to meet immediate costs and support investment in systems strengthening and health promotion which yield health benefits in the future.
	The leadership demands posed by the health challenges facing MICs in transition are substantial with few tried and tested leadership strategies that guarantee improved health outcomes. The challenges highlighted in this chapter impose leadership requirements across all levels of the health sector and spill over into other sectors (including infrastructure, water, social development, housing, education, environmental policy, city planning, legislation, and policing). Successful leaders will be able to influence the political agenda towards achieving UHC, while balancing the challenges of competing interests, and using evidence to buttress policy decisions.
	Good policy, though necessary, is not sufficient. Governance—being the capability to strategically implement policy, achieve buy-in, monitor compliance, and hold parties to account—is critical. Although many MICs need to build institutions and strengthen their capacity to monitor public health legislation, successes such as the enforcement of tobacco legislation in Brazil and South Africa can serve as motivation to further develop governance structures.





Conclusion


	MICs are countries undergoing complex, often rapid economic and social transitions. Such transitions are typically prolonged and non-linear and pose major challenges to the conventional organization of health systems. Innovative policies should focus on building resilient and learning health systems better able to deliver UHC, capitalize on intersectoral collaboration, and make use of task shifting and digital health technologies to deliver high-quality care. Investment in further research—to generate new data and better translate evidence into policy and programmes—and enhanced leadership and governance will support MICs in meeting their populations’ changing health and development needs.

1.5


Globalization


	Kelley Lee





Introduction


	‘Globalization’ is a term associated with varied changes to our world, and the net balance of the costs and benefits of these changes to specific individuals and populations remains fiercely debated. There is now substantial scholarship on the links between globalization and public health, explaining how increasing flows of people, other life forms, economic activity, and information worldwide are influencing health determinants and outcomes (Lee 2003b; Labonte et al. 2012; Hanefeld 2015). The greater scale and geographical reach of these flows pose three core challenges for the public health community: how can the evidence base concerning the causal relationship between globalization and health continue to be strengthened; what effective policy responses are needed to optimize globalization’s benefits, and minimize its costs, to population health; and how can these policy options be practically and effectively implemented?
	This chapter begins by defining the concept of globalization, and the nature of the changes taking place in the contemporary world as a result. The most prominent feature of globalization—the emergence of a global economy—is then described. The chapter then focuses on how selected public health functions might take account of the changes posed by globalization. Many of the challenges raised in this chapter are addressed in more detail elsewhere in this textbook, reflecting how globalization has come to influence the full spectrum of public health functions. The chapter concludes by considering the prospects for global health governance as the means for strengthening collective action to protect and promote population health. While the public health community is often on the frontline of responding to health risks arising from globalization, it has played only a limited role to date managing and shaping globalization processes and outcomes. The chapter concludes that addressing the public health impacts of globalization through effective collective action remains essential to the future sustainability of globalization.





What is globalization?


	The widespread use of the term ‘globalization’ has been accompanied by variation in its definition. In many cases, the term ‘global’ is used interchangeably with ‘international’ (subjects that concern two or more countries). At other times, globalization is used to refer to specific phenomena such as the spread of fast food restaurants beyond western societies, the worldwide popularity of Hollywood films, or the vast quantities of information digitally available through the internet. Alongside definitional vagueness lie marked differences in how globalization is normatively assessed. Some observers believe globalization as highly desirable for generating economic growth and prosperity for millions (Feachem 2001; Bhalla 2018). Others argue that globalization is a contemporary form of colonialism creating new patterns of inequality within and across countries (Cornea 2001; Labonte et al. 2011). There are contrasting values and assumptions underpinning these starkly different perspectives, resulting in highly contested debates within the research, policy, and advocacy communities.
	While it is beyond the scope of this chapter to review the nuances of these debates in detail, an important starting point is to approach the term with a critical lens. In the broadest sense, globalization has become widely understood as the closer integration or interconnectedness of human societies across geographical or territorially-defined boundaries. While this has arguably been occurring over millennia, what is distinct since the late twentieth century has been the vast increases in the types, scale and speed of transboundary flows, and the reach of their consequences. Held et al. (1999) write that it is this greater intensity and extensity of interconnectedness of human societies that distinguish contemporary globalization.
	More specifically, the flows associated with globalization can be understood as leading to three types of changes to human connectedness (Lee 2003a). Spatial change refers to how people organize and interact across physical or territorial space. The concept of a ‘global village’ derives from the increased capacity for people to conduct social relations across vast distances because of the greater availability and affordability, for example, of information technologies and long-haul flights. Similarly, the reorganization of the world economy by globalization has enabled ready consumer access to many goods and services produced in faraway locations. This ‘death of distance’ (Cairncross 2001) includes the formation of new human geographies, such as virtual communities in social media, by which individuals come together across territorial space to interact, exchange, and form identities. In short, the spatial changes resulting from globalization are profoundly shifting how people define, occupy, and navigate geography.
	A second, and closely related consequence of globalization, is temporal change which concerns how we think about and experience time. The modern world is characterized by an acceleration of the timeframe in which many phenomena occur. For instance, global financial transactions such as foreign exchange, buying and selling equities (stocks and shares), and securing credit can take place in a matter of seconds. New modes of transportation have enabled larger numbers of people to travel greater distances in shorter amounts of time. Mechanization and digitalization have sped up processes of resource extraction, manufacturing, and distribution. The capacity for certain tasks to be done faster, in turn, has driven accelerated change in some parts of society such as business, communications and transportation (Friedman 2012).
	Third, globalization is leading to cognitive change—how we think about ourselves and the world around us. The production, dissemination, and adoption of new knowledge, ideas, values, and beliefs has become global as a consequence of mass and social media (including the advertising industry), research, and educational institutions, thinktanks, consultancy firms, religious organizations, and political parties. The ascendance of English, as the preferred language for diplomacy, business, and science, is also a reflection of cognitive globalization. Huntingdon (2011) cast such changes within a terrain of epic conflict, a historic ‘clash of civilizations’ between western and other world views. In contrast, many raise concerns that globalization is leading to western-dominated cultural homogenization, threatening diversity by eradicating local cultures, languages, and belief systems. Others argue that globalization is enabling cultural links across diverse societies to be negotiated, focused on shared ideas and values such as human rights, gender equity, and environmental and labour standards. Still others see new cultures emerging, a global mélange from processes of hybridization and fusion (Pieterse 2012). Together, spatial, temporal, and cognitive are closely intertwined, creating complex and dynamic impacts on societies worldwide, with both positive and negative consequences.
	As well as the nature of the changes caused by globalization, the drivers of globalization have also elicited substantial debate. Mass access to certain technologies, led by information and communication technologies, and transportation, are clear enablers of transboundary flows (Rossignoli et al. 2017). For example, declines in transport costs per ton by sea, due to larger ships, more efficient container management, and consolidation of the industry has been central to the large-scale shift in manufacturing (offshoring) to lower-cost countries (Wright 2017). Similarly, between 1997 and 2015, the Consumer Price Index for personal computers and peripheral equipment declined by 96% (US Department of Labor 2015).
	For some writers, however, technology is the enabler, but not driver, of globalization. They argue that the underlying factors driving such technological changes are economic in nature. The global spread of capitalism has been spurred, on the one hand, by producers seeking cheaper inputs (i.e. raw materials, labour, research and development, transport, and communications), more efficient (and greatest) economies of scale, and ultimately profitable markets. Billions of consumers around the world, on the other hand, fuel this process by demanding higher quality, quantity, and range of goods and services at lower prices. The resulting economic transactions, guided by what eighteenth-century economist Adam Smith called the ‘invisible hand’ of the market, are described as the real force behind globalization (Schuh 2007; Dicken 2015). Globalization, in this sense, is seen as a largely economic and market-driven process of change.
	A further perspective rejects globalization as essentially technology or economics-driven process which implies a degree of rationality and progress. Instead, current forms of globalization are arguably driven by particular ideologically-based values and beliefs broadly referred to as neoliberalism. The global spread and dominance of this ideology from the 1980s, and its embedding within global institutional arrangements has, for instance, defined the industrial policies facilitating the development of such technologies (e.g. the promotion of an information economy through deregulation and privatization of the telecommunications sector), and their dissemination for particular purposes (e.g. deregulation of financial markets). Neoliberalism has also defined economic policies which encourage trade liberalization, market-based competition, and foreign direct investment (e.g. tax incentives), while advocating a minimal role for the state at the expense of social welfare and environmental protections (Slobodian 2018).
	Differing perspectives about the drivers of globalization, in turn, underpin varying beliefs about whether, on balance, global changes are leading to net costs or benefits to people and societies. ‘Globalists’ (supporters of contemporary globalization) anticipate positive benefits overall—a world of shared identities, greater efficiency and productivity, economic growth, and rising prosperity. While a period of transition is recognized, during which accrued benefits may be unevenly distributed, including temporary inequalities in wealth within and across countries, globalists believe that the globalization process is progressive in the longer term, bringing the greatest benefits to the greatest numbers of people. In sharp contrast, opponents hold that there are fundamental flaws underpinning the market-driven logic of contemporary globalization. This logic is producing stark inequalities in wealth and power which are neither temporary nor just. The result is a world increasingly structurally skewed in favour of a relative minority (e.g. those with access to technology, education, capital, and gainful employment) at the expense of a majority disproportionately bearing the costs of globalization (e.g. those with insecure or unsafe employment, low wages, low education). Thus, while globalization may be generating large-scale wealth, critics challenge the assumption that this new wealth will eventually ‘trickle down’ the global pecking order. Without a strong commitment to redistributive policies, and meaningful social and environmental protections, neoliberal globalization is seen as widening the gap between the ‘haves’ and ‘have nots’ (Mittelman 2002). The greater concentration of the world’s wealth in ever fewer hands—the richest 1% increased their share of the world’s wealth between 2008 and 2016 from 42.5% to 50.1% (Credit Suisse Research Institute 2017)—is seen as evidence of the structural inequities created by contemporary globalization.
	From a public health perspective, there is substantial evidence that globalization is creating diverse and complex changes to health determinants, resulting in both positive and negative health outcomes for specific individuals and populations. Policies to minimize the costs to and maximize the benefits for health, as well as measures to ensure that these costs and benefits to public health are equitably distributed within and across societies, are arguably central to the longer-term sustainability of globalization (Bacchetta and Jansen 2011). Towards the development of effective policy measures, a fuller understanding of the public health impacts of globalization is required.





The public health implications of a global economy


	Economic globalization is characterized by the steady restructuring of production, distribution, and consumption into systems organized on a worldwide scale. While economists disagree about the precise timing of this restructuring, most agree that this has led to a fundamental transformation of the world economy by the latter part of the twentieth century. Key features of this ‘global shift’ have been the liberalization of capital flows; rise of transnational corporations in major industrial sectors; and the emergence and spread of global production networks. Each of these has implications for public health determinants and outcomes.
	The first major pillar of the globalized world economy, the liberalization of capital flows, was introduced in the United States from the mid-1970s. Historically, banks, insurance companies, investment companies, and brokerage firms have been subject to heavy regulation. Deregulation of financial markets, such as the removal of restrictions on the types of securities that financial institutions could trade, levels of interest that could be paid on specific types of securities and bank accounts, and types of institution entitled to act as financial intermediaries, was introduced to increase competition and encourage capital flows within and across countries. Information and communication technologies enabled high-speed electronic-based transactions which eventually linked financial markets across countries. The result has been a globally integrated financial market capable of 24-hour trading in foreign exchange, commodities, capital, and other financial assets (Valdez 2006). The world’s financial assets have correspondingly boomed, from US $136 trillion in 2005 to US $294 trillion in 2014 (Witkowski 2015). By 2020, this is expected to rise to US $371 trillion, with one-third accounted for by emerging economies (Roxburgh et al. 2011).
	A second key pillar is the increased international trade of goods and services. While trade has been the lifeblood of commerce for thousands of years, it is the global restructuring and integration of production, accompanied by the increased scale and scope of trade, which characterizes the world economy since the late twentieth century. Historically, trade among countries has been dominated by raw materials and natural resources (e.g. oil, timber), commodities (e.g. grains, metals), or manufactured products (e.g. textiles and clothing, food products). In 1948, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) was established as an agreement under which signatories could negotiate reductions in tariffs on traded goods. Eight trade rounds were carried out between 1948 and 1994 by which thousands of tariff reductions were negotiated. During this period, membership grew from 23 countries in 1947 to 125 countries in 1994, thus establishing a worldwide trading system.
	The growth of international trade led to renewed support for a permanent organization, resulting in the creation of the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 1995. As of 2018 there are 164 member states and 23 observer states, many of which are seeking accession. Moreover, the WTO’s remit embraces trade in services, agriculture, intellectual property rights, government procurement, and other areas (Wilkinson 2014). The overall effect has been that world trade grew faster than world output. Between 2006 and 2016, for example, world merchandise exports increased from US $8 to US $11 trillion (37.5%), and commercial services exports from US $2.9 to US $4.8 trillion (66%) (WTO 2017a), between 1.1 and 2 times faster than global gross domestic production (GDP). The global financial crisis beginning in 2008 led to a significant downturn in trade volumes, with trade eventually growing slower than global GDP in 2016. Nevertheless, since 2017 the overall trend in world trade has once again been growth (WTO 2017b; WTO 2018).
	The global restructuring of production and exchange processes has been an integral part of this boom in international trade. In many sectors, transnational corporations (TNCs) have emerged which have relocated components of their business to different parts of the world. Thus, resource extraction may take place in one country, manufacturing in another, and research and marketing in still others (Dicken 2015). The targeted consumers have also changed, with TNCs seeking markets worldwide for global brands. According to the European Brand Institute (2017), the ten most valuable global brands are Apple, Google, Microsoft, Coca Cola, AT&T, Amazon, Johnson & Johnson, China Mobile, Verizon, and Facebook.
	Global economic restructuring can be observed in many industrial sectors posing distal or proximal impacts on health determinants and outcomes. One important example is the pharmaceutical industry which has become dominated globally by large companies formed through mergers and acquisitions. This includes the buying of domestic generic and manufacturing companies to access emerging markets, and the consolidation of the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries. Table 1.5.1 describes the largest pharmaceutical companies in 2016 by revenue. In 1992, the ten largest companies accounted for one-third of global revenue (Tarabusi and Vickery 1998). By 2016, this had increased to 40%. This consolidation of the market has been driven by intense competition, the high cost of research and development (R&D), economies of large-scale manufacturing, and the need for capacity to market and distribute worldwide (Wright 2017). For example, the reported cost of developing and bringing a new prescription drug to the market is now around US $2.6 billion, a 145% increase since 2003 (Mullin 2014). Success in the pharmaceutical sector amid globalization requires large companies with global reach and access to considerable resources.
