	The alcoholic beverages industry, worth an estimated US $645 billion in 2017 and projected to reach US $1,594 billion by 2022 (Allied Market Research 2017), is another health-related example of the global restructuring of the world economy. As market saturation and increased regulation may moderate growth in North America, Europe, and Australia/New Zealand, the industry has turned to emerging markets notably in Asia (Esser and Jernigan 2018). The ability to compete globally, in turn, is prompting mergers and acquisitions, and the increasing domination in parts of the industry by transnational alcohol companies (TACs). For example, beer manufacturing is led by Anheuser-Busch InBev, Heineken and Carlsberg which produced 38% of global supply in 2016. The spirits and wine sectors are less concentrated to date, but further globalization of production, distribution, and consumption is expected to be spurred by intensifying competition for new markets, new product development and marketing, and trade and investment liberalization (Mitchell and Casben 2016).
	The direct public health consequences of economic globalization arise from changes in the production, distribution, and consumption of either health promoting or health harming products and services. Where a product is inherently health harming, such as tobacco, an increase in risk is posed to public health. This is not withstanding the use of non-combustible nicotine products such as electronic cigarettes, increasingly produced and marketed by the tobacco industry itself, to potentially mitigate although not remove such risks if used exclusively instead (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine 2018). For other potential health harming products, such as alcoholic beverages, food and drink, the level of risk depends on the specific product or amount consumed. Globalization, in this case, may create a mixture of benefits and harms. For example, many products of the pharmaceutical industry are essential to healthcare worldwide. The increased production and affordability of such products, through improved economies of scale to serve larger markets, increased spending on R&D, and innovations in distribution would accrue benefits to health. However, the competitive pressures caused by economic globalization can also lead ‘Big Pharma’ to unduly focus on the most profitable products and markets to recover investment or maximize returns for shareholders. This can skew production decisions away from diseases and populations deemed to offer insufficient financial returns (Trouiller et al. 2002), and allow companies to price their products beyond the affordability of many who need them. This lack of access to patent-protected medicines has led to ongoing tensions worldwide between ensuring an economic return for Big Pharma and enabling equitable access to improve health outcomes. The Treatment Action Campaign initiated in South Africa in 1998 by HIV/AIDS activists, which has pressed the government to make various drug treatments more readily available in the country (Heywood 2009), and the licensing of generic drug production by the Thai government despite industry pressure to enforce patent protections under the TRIPS agreement (Yamabhai et al. 2011), illustrate this tension between private and public interests.
	More indirectly, the global economy can adversely impact human health by enabling conditions that pose new risks. These risks can arise in several ways. First, economic globalization has encouraged unprecedented population mobility. Population movements are not new—humankind has been on the move since Homo erectus migrated out of Africa in about 1 million BC. What characterizes population mobility since the late twentieth century has been its volume, geographical reach, speed, and frequency. Globalization is what Castles and Miller (2009) call the ‘age of migration’. In 2017, the number of international migrants reached 258 million people, an increase from 173 million in 2000. By 2017, 244 million people lived outside their country of birth, compared with 156 million in 1990 (UNDESA 2017). The reasons why people migrate are diverse. For the relatively educated, highly skilled, and mobile, economic globalization offers new training and employment opportunities. For the lower educated and skilled, work opportunities in places of ‘global employment’ may beckon, such as the offshore factories of TNCs, fields of cash crops grown by the agri-food industry, or the extraction sites of the natural resources industries. Changing patterns of population mobility and settlement may contribute benefits to health through, for example, providing new training opportunities to health workers or enabling vulnerable populations to move from locations posing risks. Increased population mobility may also generate new risks by, for example, heightening the risk of communicable disease outbreaks where refugee settlements do not have adequate housing, water, and sanitation; facilitating the spread of communicable disease outbreaks globally via long distance travellers; or weakening healthcare systems in low and middle-income countries (LMICs) through the depletion of domestic healthcare workers.
	Second, economic globalization can increase environmental health concerns, ranging from local, small-scale factors (e.g. household exposures) to widespread exposures affecting whole populations. The possible impacts of globalization on environmental health are wide-ranging, potentially affecting populations at the global, regional, community, occupational, and household levels. These impacts can be direct, such as through the dumping of hazardous waste across borders, relocation of risky occupations (such as ship breaking or asbestos disposal), and damage caused by cross-border pollution or contamination. Economic globalization, in which companies compete on a worldwide scale to increase returns, is raising concerns that profit-maximization motives can undermine environmental health. Governments, seeking to attract foreign direct investment or unleash market competition to fuel economic growth and generate employment, are accused of engaging in a ‘race to the bottom’ by offering reduced tax rates, lower wages, or weaker environmental, labour, and health and safety protections (Mosley and Uno 2007). A change in investment or lending policy at the global level can also have health consequences for local communities. For example, policy conditions set by the World Bank, or requirements to repay substantial sums of foreign debt, can restrict the public expenditure of borrowing countries on environmental protection or investment in basic infrastructure, such as water and sanitation. A cholera outbreak in South Africa in 2000–2001, which led to around 120,000 cases and 265 deaths, has been blamed on the introduction of user fees following the privatization of water utilities as part of the country’s structural adjustment programme. As water supplies were cut to poor people unable to pay for the new charges, many resorted to using polluted river water (Anonymous 2006). The World Bank (2000) argues that ‘[e]very society has to decide for itself on the relative value it places on economic output and the environment’. Others argue, however, that there are substantial inequities in terms of who bears the environmental costs of globalization (Wiedmann and Lenzen 2018).
	Third, the rapid growth, open nature, and regulatory challenges of the global economy have led to a substantial growth in illegal products, many of which pose risks to human health. The illicit tobacco trade, for instance, is believed to account for 9 per cent of retail sales, increasing access to lower-priced and unregulated cigarettes (WHO n.d.). Around 5 per cent of the global population aged 15–64 have used illicit drugs at least once in 2015. The production, distribution, and consumption of such drugs, since the late twentieth century, have been transformed by transnational networks of criminal organizations (UN Office on Drugs and Crime 2017). A related problem is the global business of counterfeiting which was worth US $1.2 trillion in 2017 (Research and Markets 2018). Many counterfeits are health-related or affecting products, notably pharmaceuticals, and food and beverage products. WHO estimates that one in ten medical products circulating in low-and middle-income countries is either substandard or falsified (WHO 2017a). Counterfeit baby milk powder containing melamine reportedly caused 50 child deaths and acute malnutrition in more than one hundred others in rural China (Watts 2004). Deaths from counterfeit alcohol products have led to hundreds of deaths in countries worldwide including Indonesia (Faridz and Griffiths 2018), Russia (Reevell 2016), Ireland (McNamee 2016), and Mexico (ACS Sensors 2018). Economic globalization has flourished through the creation of special economic zones, global financial systems, worldwide transportation networks, and internet sales. The same systems have been harnessed by criminal organizations to produce and distribute illicit goods with health harming effects. As discussed next, in relation to global health governance, within efforts to strengthen the regulatory frameworks managing globalization, there is much need for increased measures to protect and promote population health.





Globalization and essential public health functions


	Public health is concerned with protecting and promoting the health of whole populations within and across countries. Since the late twentieth century, there have been efforts in many countries to reinvigorate public health systems. The Institute of Medicine, for example, initiated debate in the United States through its reports, The Future of Public Health (Institute of Medicine 1988), and The Future of the Public’s Health in the 21st Century (Institute of Medicine 2002), with the latter identifying the need to address ‘emerging threats’ caused by rapid changes to the nation’s social, cultural, and global contexts, scientific and technological advances, and demographic shifts (Institute of Medicine 2002). Given an inadequate capacity to response to the SARS (severe, acute respiratory syndrome) in 2003–2004, the Canadian government formed the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC). Correspondingly, the creation of the European Centre for Disease Control (ECDC) in 2004 was to strengthen the capacity of European Union countries to respond to infectious disease outbreaks. Over the past decade, there has also been similar investments to build public health systems in such countries as India (Planning Commission of India 2011), Brazil (Jerberg 2008), and China (Liang and Burns 2017).
	While disease outbreaks prompted renewed attention to public health systems in many countries, WHO and national policy makers now recognize the need to adapt a fuller range of essential public health functions (EPHFs) to meet the challenges of a globalizing world (Martin-Moreno et al. 2016). As described earlier, spatial, temporal, and cognitive changes arising from globalization are having important impacts on a broad range of population health determinants and outcomes. The remainder of this chapter describes how globalization has implications for three EPHFs identified by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO 2002)—monitoring, evaluation, and analysis of health status; public health surveillance; and health promotion—and how the public health community might effectively adapt to these impacts (see Box 1.5.1).
	 	Box 1.5.1 Essential public health functions

Monitoring, evaluation, and analysis of health status


	Assessing the health of a given population is the starting point for a wide range of public health actions including priority setting, resource allocation, the design and implementation of interventions, and programme evaluation. There are well-recognized steps for assessing population health status:
	 	• Define the purpose of the assessment.
	• Define the population concerned and any comparator population.
	• Define the aspects of health to be considered.
	• Identify and review existing data sources.
	• Select the most appropriate existing data (Gentle 2001).
	However, assessing population health status within the context of globalization presents two key challenges. First, there remains variable capacity within and across countries to collect and manage the essential health information needed. In many LMICs, in particular, inadequate health information systems results in data of variable quality or incomplete regarding selected populations and health conditions. According to WHO (2006a):
	 	A country health information system comprises the multiple subsystems and data sources that together contribute to generating health information, including vital registration, censuses and surveys, disease surveillance and response, service statistics and health management information, financial data, and resource tracking. The absence of consensus on the relative strengths, usefulness, feasibility, and cost-efficiency of different data collection approaches has resulted in a plethora of separate and often overlapping systems.
	To address this problem, the Health Metrics Network (HMN) was formed in 2005 as a global partnership hosted by WHO to advocate for the strengthening of health information systems in LMICs. Funded by the Gates Foundation and other donors, the partnership was comprised of governments, multilateral and bilateral development agencies, foundations, global health initiatives, and technical experts that aimed to increase the availability and use of timely, reliable health information. In 2013, the WHO Executive Board decided to discontinue the HMN because the network was deemed to have ‘fulfilled its time-limited and catalytic role’ of ‘raising the profile of health information systems, helping countries to assess and strengthen their systems and accelerating improvements to country civil registration and vital statistics systems’ (WHO 2013). The focus has turned to harnessing the capacity of global information and communication systems for a wide range of health applications including monitoring, evaluation, and analysis of health status (de Fatima Marin et al. 2017). While improvements in health information systems have been achieved across many LMICs, including the innovative application of mobile technologies, resource constraints continue to pose the largest problem.
	A second challenge is the limitations of existing health information systems for capturing health status and needs that do not conform with, or cut across, national boundaries. For each country, health data is collected and managed by local and national health departments and associated institutions. The WHO Statistical Information System (SIS), now part of the Global Health Observatory (GHO), in turn, collates this data to produce aggregated health indicators, mortality and health status, disease statistics, health system statistics, risk factors and health service coverage, and inequities in health from member states. These data are compiled in the World Health Statistics. Governments, donors, and other organizations may use these data to identify health priorities.
	The impacts of globalization on health, however, are by definition transcendent of national borders such that new health and disease patterns may be emerging that may not be captured by aggregated or disaggregated national data. A good example is the complex pattern of rising overweight and obesity rates. In high-income countries, obesity is rising rapidly across all socioeconomic groups but is particularly associated with social deprivation. In the United States, for example:
	 	CSD [community socioeconomic deprivation] was associated with higher BMI [body mass index] at average age [of study cohort] (10.7 years) and with more rapid growth of BMI over time. Children born in communities with greater CSD had steeper increases of BMI at younger ages. Those born into the poorest communities displayed sustained accelerated BMI growth. CSD remained associated with BMI trajectories after adjustment for a measure of household socioeconomic deprivation. (Nau et al. 2014)
	In France, Romon et al. (2005) found that genetic predisposition influences the prevalence of obesity and changes in BMI among children from the higher social class. For children within the lowest social class, which has seen an increase in BMI across the whole population, environmental factors appear to have played a more important role. In LMICs, the total number of obese or overweight people has grown rapidly in such diverse countries as Kenya, China, India, and Brazil, notably among a rising middle class. This includes a 10-fold increase in obese children and adolescents in LMICs (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration 2017). At the same time, many urban populations within the lower social classes are experiencing rising rates of overweight and obesity, now exceeding rates of undernutrition (Ford et al. 2017). Trends in over/undernutrition, in other words, are complex and dynamic, requiring detailed and comparable data across population groups defined along variables such as age, gender, socioeconomic status, geography, and occupation.
	The challenges of monitoring, evaluating, and analysing health status, within the context of globalization, can be illustrated by a wide range of other examples. The emergence of a global economy dominated by TNCs, for example, has restructured employment around global value chains as leading modes of production, distribution, and consumption. This has led to the employment of millions of factory workers throughout the world, creating new sources of employment, but often under conditions of weak social and environmental protections (Phillips 2017). How might we measure the changing health status of these workers over time and place? What public health needs do these workers share across domestic jurisdictions which arise, not from their nationality, but from their conditions of employment? The unprecedented movement of people across national borders also requires appropriate ways to understand the health status and needs of varied types of migrants such as tourists, refugees, overseas workers, and trafficked people. Some patterns of migration will not be captured by aggregated national data, thus obscuring the public health needs arising for home and host populations. Similarly, the public health impacts on population health from climate change need to use measures beyond national data given the planetary scale of the environmental effects taking place. These examples illustrate the need for methods that identify new population groups arising from globalization’s impacts which do not conform to national borders, and enhanced health information systems which generate corresponding data to monitor, evaluate, and analyse the health status of these populations.





Public health surveillance, research, and control of risks and threats to public health


	The just-described need for genuinely global health data, beyond aggregated national level data, underpins the core public health function of preventing, controlling, and responding to public health risks. Traditionally, this function has focused on disease outbreaks and epidemics. Historically, risks from disease-causing microbes have long mirrored the migration and settlement patterns of human species. The shift from hunting-gathering to agrarian societies and the domestication of animals, between 8000 and 3500 BC, for example, brought new risks from zoonotic diseases (Swabe 1999). The so-called ‘Columbian exchange’, following the arrival of Christopher Columbus in the Americas, is noted for the widespread exchange of plants, animals, foods, human populations (including settlers and slaves), and ideas that followed. Diseases, such as cholera, influenza, measles, malaria, smallpox, and tuberculosis, were also exchanged, resulting in the decimation of Indigenous peoples (Crosby 1972). The influenza pandemic of 1918–1919, which killed around 25 million people worldwide, was undoubtedly enabled by the large-scale population movements and devastation caused by the First World War. The changing structures of human societies over time and place, in short, give rise to particular health risks.
	In this context, contemporary globalization can be understood as altering the structure of human societies once again in ways that pose new risks to human health. First, globalization may alter the population size at risk due to patterns of settlement. The world’s urban population will almost double, from 3.3 billion in 2007 to 6.3 billion in 2050, with most of this growth in cities within the developing world. Rapid urbanization has been accompanied, in many cases, by poverty, inadequate housing, limited access to clean water and sanitation, or basic healthcare. This has created larger populations now vulnerable to infectious disease risks (Alirol et al. 2010). One of the factors attributed to the unprecedented magnitude of the Ebola virus outbreak in West Africa during 2014–2015, for instance, is that the continent has had the world’s highest urban growth rate for 20 years. Rapid urbanization, prompted in large part by war and poverty, may explain how Ebola shifted from relatively small outbreaks at village level to a much larger outbreak putting millions at risk (Mackenzie et al. 2014).
	Moreover, globalization has increased the size of populations at risk due to far greater mobility of human and animal species. Diseases have a greater capacity to spread more rapidly and further afield in a more interconnected world. Some infections, such as tuberculosis and cholera, are historically associated with poverty but may now pose new patterns of risk due to globalization (Gushulak and MacPherson 2004). United Nations peacekeepers from Nepal arriving in earthquake-affected Haiti in 2010 are alleged to have caused a devastating cholera outbreak within an already highly vulnerable population (Gladstone 2017). In other ways, globalization is ‘democratizing’ disease risks. The spread of SARS in 2002–2003, from China to around 25 countries within weeks, posed a threat to populations rich or poor in a world of migrant workers, business travellers, and long-haul flights. The human health risks potentially arising from highly pathogenic pandemic influenza would be truly global by virtue of the widespread lack of immunity, and rapid person-to-person transmission facilitated by highly mobile human populations. Further concerns relate to the global spread of antimicrobial drug-resistant organisms and drug-resistant infectious diseases by mobile human populations. As MacPherson et al. (2009) write: ‘Current population movement dynamics rapidly and effectively link regions of marked health disparity, and these linkages can be associated with risk for importation of drug-resistant infectious diseases.’
	Second, globalization may influence the prevalence (number of people with a disease within a given population) and incidence (number of new cases of a disease in a specified period of time per total population) of certain diseases. De Vogli and Birbeck (2005) argue that vulnerability to HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria is closely linked to poverty, gender inequality, development policy, and health sector reforms that involve user fees and reduced access to care. Dorling et al. (2006) similarly argue that ‘global inequality in wealth will have compounded the effects of AIDS on Africa’, notably caused by globalization-related policies such as structural adjustment programmes. Changing employment patterns and conditions, arising from economic globalization, have also had epidemiological consequences. Moody (2007) describes the globalization of the mining industry and its impact on local communities. Basu et al. (2009) observe how tuberculosis incidence among southern African miners is ten times greater than the general population, with migration to and from mines amplifying tuberculosis epidemics in the general population.
	Third, globalization is increasing the risks from emerging and re-emerging diseases. Environmental degradation, such as rainforest destruction and intense farming methods, can bring human and animal populations into closer contact. Sixty per cent (60%) of emerging infectious diseases that affect humans are zoonotic (originating in animals), and more than two-thirds of those originate in wildlife including HIV and AIDS, West Nile, Ebola virus, Lyme disease and possibly SARS-CoV-2. The detection and rapid spread of a novel coronavirus, the Middle East Respiratory Syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), from Saudi Arabia to South Korea in 2012, illustrated what Gannon (2015) calls ‘a general archetype for emerging infectious diseases: zoonotic in origin, carried across continents by an infected air traveller, initially undiagnosed, bringing fear and economic disruption, and spreading most quickly through vulnerable populations’. Moreover, evidence by Smith et al. (2014) suggest that ‘the total number and diversity of outbreaks, and richness of causal diseases increased significantly’ from 1980 to 2013.
	This heightening of public health risks within a globalizing world has prompted efforts to improve capacities in surveillance, research, and control measures. Globalization offers opportunities, for instance, to harness information and communication technologies to enable faster, cheaper, and more efficient gathering and worldwide sharing of knowledge. ProMEDmail (see Box 1.5.2) and regional disease surveillance networks have facilitated the collection and reporting of epidemiological data. The lessons learned from SARS prompted renewed WHO efforts to revise the International Health Regulations (IHR), which came into effect in 2007, including the harnessing of a broader range of information sources. The expanded scope of the IHR beyond a handful of named diseases, to the broader concept of ‘public health emergencies of international concern’ also reflected recognition of the need for collective action on a more diverse range of global health risks. Global technologies are also enhancing research capacities in data analysis, such as genomics, and the use of so-called ‘big data’ source including the innovative harnessing of non-health global scale data. For example, the use of airline travel data to model transmission dynamics and potential impact of the West African Ebola virus outbreak provided lessons for enhancing real-time epidemiological assessment in future outbreaks via improved data collection and analyses (Cori et al. 2017). There remain critical challenges to harnessing big data, to improve the capacity of countries to respond to global public health risks, namely better understanding of what big data is most useful, how to accurately interpret such data for public health purposes, and how to protect individual privacy and the proprietary interests of data holders (Lazer and Kennedy 2015).
	 	Box 1.5.2 Programme for Monitoring Emerging Diseases (ProMEDmail)
	ProMED—the Program for Monitoring Emerging Diseases—is an internet-based reporting system dedicated to rapid global dissemination of information on outbreaks of infectious diseases and acute exposures to toxins that affect human health, including those in animals and in plants grown for food or animal feed. Electronic communications enable ProMED to provide up-to-date and reliable news about threats to human, animal, and food plant health around the world, 7 days a week. By providing early warning of outbreaks of emerging and re-emerging diseases, public health precautions at all levels can be taken in a timely manner to prevent epidemic transmission and to save lives.
	ProMED is open to all sources and free of political constraints. Sources of information include media reports, official reports, online summaries, local observers, and others. Reports are often contributed by ProMED subscribers. A team of expert human, plant, and animal disease moderators screen, review, and investigate reports before posting to the network. Reports are distributed by email to direct subscribers and posted immediately on the ProMED web site. ProMED currently reaches over 70,000 subscribers in at least 185 countries.
	Reproduced with permission from the International Society for Infectious Diseases, About ProMEDmail, Copyright © 2018 International Society for Infectious Diseases. All rights reserved. Available from http://www.promedmail.org/aboutus/.





Global health promotion


	There is now substantial evidence of a marked rise in the global burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) since the 1980s. This includes an almost quadrupling of the total number of adults worldwide with Type 2 diabetes (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration 2016) since 1980, and a tripling of the rate of obesity since 1975 (WHO 2017b). In 2017, NCDs killed 40 million people worldwide and accounted for 70% of all deaths. Cardiovascular diseases accounted for most NCD deaths (17.7 million people annually), followed by cancers (8.8 million), respiratory diseases (3.9 million), and diabetes (1.6 million) (WHO 2017c). WHO predicts that, while infectious diseases like malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS will largely decline, cancers and ischaemic heart disease, as well as cerebrovascular disease, will continue to steadily rise from 2015 to 2030 (WHO 2018a).
	The clarity of evidence about this rapid rise in NCDs across societies at all levels of development, and within populations spanning varying levels of socioeconomic status, has been attributed in part to changes associated with globalization. As Gostin (2014) writes:
	 	Rapid travel, mass migration and the globalization of culture are known to fuel the spread of infectious diseases. The same factors are also increasing the incidence of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) such as cancer, diabetes and heart disease. As developing countries prosper, these conditions are a by-product of rising air pollution, physical inactivity, and consumption of alcohol, tobacco and excess calories.
	This association, in turn, has prompted greater efforts to strengthen collective action on NCDs including global health promotion. Health promotion is the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health (WHO 1986). Interventions address three areas of activity to prevent disease and promote the health of a community: communication, service delivery, and enabling factors (individual and structural) which influence the chance of an intention being carried out and a behaviour sustained. Individual enabling factors include communication skills and literacy; structural enabling factors include social supports, income level and cultural attitudes (Walley et al. 2001, p. 147). A global approach to health promotion takes account of the ways in which globalization may be influencing the social determinants of health, and in turn health behaviours, as well as, offers opportunities for providing appropriate interventions. The Bangkok Charter for Health Promotion in a Globalized World adopted in 2005 recognized the major challenges posed by globalization, and the actions and commitments needed to address the determinants of health in a globalized world by reaching out to people, groups, and organizations that are critical to the achievement of health. To galvanize concerted action by governments, three UN General Assembly High-Level Meetings have been held on the prevention and control of NCDs. The first adopted a Political Declaration on NCDs (2011), and the second followed with an Outcome Document on NCDs (2014), with the target of reducing premature NCD mortality by 25% by 2025 (WHO 2018b). However, the virtual absence of heads of state at both meetings was a disappointment for the NCD Alliance (largely composed of civil society organizations). A 2017 progress report revealed ‘uneven and insufficient’ progress in most countries in meeting globally agreed targets including a substantial number of countries without NCD national plans and targets (Ravelo 2017). To address the lack of political will, and propose ‘bold and practical actions steps to scale up prevention and treatment of NCDs and provide health for all’ (WHO 2018c), WHO appointed an Independent High-Level Commission on Noncommunicable Diseases, co-chaired by the heads of state of Uruguay, Sri Lanka, Finland, Russia, and Pakistan. The challenges faced by the Commission in its deliberations, and for societies worldwide seeking to tackle NCDs, is well-illustrated by two of the leading risk factors—obesity and tobacco use.
	The rapid increase in overnutrition and obesity, among adults and children, has attracted substantial public health concern in recent years (Fig. 1.5.1). According to WHO (2017b), around 1.9 billion people worldwide are overweight, of which around 650 million people worldwide are obese (BMI >30). At least 340 million school-age children are overweight or obese. The number of overweight or obese infants and young children (aged 0 to 5 years) increased from 32 million globally in 1990 to 41 million in 2016, and expected to rise to 70 million by 2025 (WHO 2017d). Importantly, while obesity rates are higher in wealthier countries than LMICs, these changes span populations in diverse settings and income levels, including such wide-ranging countries as India, Nigeria, Mexico, and China. The association to globalization of obesity and overweight populations began to be identified in the 1990s. For example, Drewnoski and Popkin (1997, p. 32) write:
	 	Whereas high-fat diets and Western eating habits were once restricted to the rich industrialized nations … the nutrition transition now occurs in nations with much lower levels of gross national product (GNP) than previously … First, fat consumption is less dependent on GNP than ever before. Second, rapid urbanization has a major influence in accelerating the nutrition transition.
	Prentice (2006, p. 93) attribute these trends to the globalization of food production and lifestyles:
	 	The pandemic is transmitted through the vectors of subsidized agriculture and multinational companies providing cheap, highly refined fats, oils, and carbohydrates, labour-saving mechanized devices, affordable motorized transport, and the seductions of sedentary pastimes such as television. This trend has been linked to the globalisation of sedentary lifestyles alongside changes in food production and consumption.
	Beyond anecdotal and descriptive evidence, Goryakin et al. (2015) undertook extensive econometric analyses of several datasets, using a series of new proxies for different dimensions (social, political, and economic) of globalization potentially affecting overweight in up to 887,000 women aged 15–49 living in 56 countries between 1991 and 2009. They found that both political and especially social globalization dimensions appear strongly positively related to the greater overweight risk, while the association with economic globalization countries is dependent on ‘country-specific factors such as economic development and infrastructure, education, attractiveness of economies to investors, as well as the size of the market’ Goryakin et al. (2015, p. 74). Overall, this evidence supports the hypothesis that the multitude of yet interrelated changes in diet, levels of physical activity, and the built environment associated with globalization are substantial and significant explanations for the sharp rise in obesity and overweight worldwide since the 1980s.
	Fig. 1.5.1 Worldwide age-standardized prevalence of overweight (upper) and obesity (lower) in adults 20 years and older by country in 2005.
	Reproduced with permission from Kelly, T. Global burden of obesity in 2005 and projections to 2030. International Journal of Obesity, 9(32). Copyright © Springer Nature. Available at https://www.nature.com/articles/ijo2008102
	The few measures adopted to address so-called ‘globesity’ (Costa-Font and Mas 2016) to date have focused on modifying individual behaviours or lifestyles. These measures emphasize public health education led by healthy eating initiatives and the promotion of increased physical activity. However, more comprehensive approaches to global health promotion are increasingly recognized as necessary. This includes addressing the structural factors that constrain or enable healthy eating, and adopting both supply and demand-side measures concerning what and how food is produced, marketed, and consumed. For example, the Institute of Medicine (2005) report, Food Marketing to Children and Youth: Threat or Opportunity? recognizes that dietary patterns begin in childhood and are shaped by the interplay of genetics and biology, culture, and values, economics, physical and social environments, and commercial media environments. The report includes a comprehensive review of the scientific evidence on the influence of food marketing on diets and diet-related health of children and youth. It concludes that environments supportive of good health require leadership and action from the food, beverage, and restaurant industries; food retailers and trade associations; the entertainment industry and the media; parents and caregivers; schools; and governments. Prior to the Second UN High-level Meeting on NCDs in 2014, WHO Director-General Margaret Chan stated, ‘The globalization of unhealthy lifestyles is by no means just a technical issue for public health. It is a political issue. It is a trade issue. And it is an issue for foreign affairs’ (WHO 2014). Similarly, following its initial technical consultation in 2018, the WHO Independent High-level Commission on NCDs has argued for a whole-of-society approach (WHO 2018b).
	The regulation of the agri-food industry amid globalization, however, remains a major challenge. The concentration of ownership in the food industry, to be dominated by a small number of large transnational food companies, has been achieved by greater economies of scale, lower-cost production methods, and heavy marketing of high-profit foods. This has led to a substantial increase in the production and consumption of highly processed foods which contain industrially-produced ingredients such as high-fructose corn syrup and palm oil. The marked rise in hypertension, heart disease, and type 2 diabetes worldwide, coinciding with the ready availability and affordability of food products produced from such ingredients, continues to be studied (Bray 2013; Ismail et al. 2018). In the meantime, debates about the regulation of such ingredients have intensified. Many public health advocates call for governments to adopt improved and mandatory labelling, and even restrictions on their use. At the global level, WHO called for the adoption of a Global Strategy on Diet, Physical Activity, and Health. However, these efforts were hindered by the agri-food industry’s opposition to explicit recommendations on healthy levels of salt, sugar, and fats intake, and subsequently given no regulatory ‘teeth’ by member states (Lang et al. 2006; Johnson 2012). Instead, the agri-food industry has promoted voluntary self-regulation such as limits on the targeted marketing of processed food products at children and corporate social responsibility initiatives. The industry has also emphasized the importance of protecting consumer choice, and the primary importance of non-food factors such as physical activity as a health concern. However, Lang et al. (2006) assessed compliance by 25 of the world’s largest food manufacturers and retailers to recommendations concerning ingredients, advertising, portion size, and labelling. Only a small proportion of companies voluntarily reduced salt, sugar, and fats in their products. In Spain, León-Flández et al. (2017) found a decline in compliance with the Spanish code of food and drinks advertising directed at children under 12 since 2008. In the US, as Kelly (2005) advises:
	 	So far the U.S. government has declined to regulate the aggressive ways in which food producers market high-energy, low-nutrition foods to young people. That public-health responsibility has been left to an industry-created scheme of self-regulation that is deeply flawed; there is a compelling need for government involvement.
	Similar lessons for global health promotion can be drawn from tobacco control.
	Like the agri-food industry, the tobacco industry has globally restructured and is now dominated by a small number of large TNCs. Industry consolidation has been achieved, for example, by the establishment of global value chains, development of ‘global drive brands’, and intense marketing in emerging markets (Lee et al. 2016). As WHO Director-General Gro Harlem Brundtland (2000, p. 2) stated, in initiating the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) negotiation process in the 1990s:
	 	[O]ver the past fifteen years, we have seen that modern technology, has limited the effectiveness of national action. Tobacco advertising is beamed into every country via satellite and cable. Developing countries are the subject of massive marketing campaigns by international tobacco companies. In the slipstream of increasing global trade, new markets are opened to international tobacco companies which see these emerging markets as their main opportunity to compensate for stagnant or dwindling markets in many industrialized countries.
	The negotiations faced intense efforts by the tobacco industry to limit stronger regulation by participating in some national delegations, lobbying leaf-producing countries and farmers, orchestrating criticism of WHO, and even challenging the science on tobacco and health (Wipfli 2015). Despite industry opposition, the FCTC was signed in 2003 and came into effect in 2005. As of 2018, 181 countries are parties to the treaty. Importantly, the FCTC remains the most prominent example of collective action across WHO member states to address a significant public health problem worsened by globalization. This required participation by a broad spectrum of national, regional, and global stakeholders. The mobilization of public health advocates worldwide, led by the Framework Convention Alliance, was greatly facilitated by the use of the internet (focused on the Globalink network) which enabled stakeholders to follow negotiations, organize advocacy activities, and share experiences (Collin et al. 2004). While the final treaty was weaker on some key challenges posed by globalization than initially hoped, such as setting aside tobacco from international trade agreements, the possible negotiation of additional protocols was to address these transboundary issues. To date, only the FCTC Protocol to Eliminate Illicit Trade in Tobacco Products has been signed, and will come into effect when ratified by 40 states parties (WHO 2015).
	In summary, globalization has coincided with the rise of NCDs worldwide across diverse populations, posing new challenges for public health. In many cases, powerful vested interests within key sectors of the world economy oppose stronger action to prevent and control NCDs. Initiating collective action, such as the WHO Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of NCDs 2013–2020, can serve to make NCDs a higher priority. However, past experience shows that international agreements are only the starting point. Effective implementation of commitments requires sustained mobilization of political will, resources, and technical capacity to translate strategies into results (Ravelo 2018). A key lesson from efforts to date to address the risk factors of obesity and tobacco use in some countries, is that globalization needs to be better harnessed for health promotion. Worldwide consumer boycotts of TNCs, such as Nestlé and McDonalds, have been organized via social media by civil society organizations to pressure companies to change their practices (Swinburn et al. 2015). The public health community has also drawn attention to the dangers of illicit products through global campaigns (Fig. 1.5.2). These examples of collective action across societies, to harness globalization to counter continued high rates of tobacco use, obesity, and other risk factors behind the rising trends in NCDs, offer important examples to build upon.
	Fig. 1.5.2 World No Tobacco Day 2015.
	From https://blogs.worldbank.org/health/world-no-tobacco-day-2015-illicit-trade-and-taxes





Harnessing global information and communication technologies for public health


	A defining and enabling feature of contemporary globalization has been rapid advances in information and communication technologies (ICTs), spurring the transformation of societies worldwide. From the personal computer in the 1980s, the progressive development of ICT devices with ever faster processing speeds and larger storage capacity has enabled a wide range of applications at affordable prices. Investments in ICTs not only generate economic impacts, they served as core infrastructure for the global economy as a whole. Global ICT networks underpin global supply chains, transportation systems, 24-hour financial trading and vital information networks (Baller et al. 2016).
	The globalization of ICTs may lead to profound changes in the health sector including research, diagnostics, patient care, planning and management, informatics, and health promotion. Often known as eHealth (or electronic health), technological change has been spurred by the increased complexity of health systems, need to manage ever larger and more complex datasets, rising cost of healthcare, need to provide longitudinal and comprehensive health records for individual patients, and increased mobility and/or geographically dispersal of many patient populations and healthcare providers. ICTs have been identified as particularly effective, for example, at reaching more individuals with effective health-related advice and information at a very low cost (Bloom et al. 2017).
	The use of mobile and wireless technologies in health (known as mHealth), in particular, has grown rapidly with advances in technologies and applications (or ‘apps’), the declining cost of handsets and data transmission, and growth cellular network coverage. According to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), subscriptions grew 20% annually from 2012 to 2017, reaching 4.3 billion globally by 2018 (ITU 2017). LMICs have seen the highest rate of growth where the potential for mHealth to improve healthcare, hindered in the past by a lack of infrastructure, is most promising (Silva et al. 2015).
	Social media, ‘interactive platforms via which individuals and communities create and share user-generated content’ (Kietzmann et al. 2011, p. 241), has also seen the blossoming of health-related applications. A systematic review of social media and public health messages finds that, as more consumers turn to the internet for health-related information, health organizations have begun to use social media for connecting with the public For example, health insurance companies are applying social media, health gaming apps, and other mobile apps to increase patient engagement in their own healthcare. Evidence suggests considerable reach associated with social media applications, and the potential for engaging specific target audiences, although efficacy of public health messaging requires further investigation through controlled studies (Ventola 2014).
	Overall, ICTs offer much promise to enhancing core public health functions. There continues to be substantial investment in such technologies by the public and private sectors, and their application to a wide range of health applications. However, systematic reviews of the use of eHealth technologies in behavioural interventions (Oosterveen et al. 2017) and mental health (Stratton et al. 2017), for instance, cast doubt on the longer-term efficacy and cost-effectiveness of using such technologies.
	Importantly, there has also been an increased use of ICTs for commercial purposes to shape consumer choices and behaviours. The online marketing, promotion and distribution of health-affecting products and services has spread rapidly and, in most cases, remain weakly regulated. The global reach of direct-to-consumer marketing of pharmaceuticals (genuine and counterfeit), supplements, food and beverages, and tobacco products (including electronic nicotine delivery systems) via the internet has been a particular source of regulatory concern (Freeman et al. 2014). For national authorities, the challenge of regulating the internet arises from the global nature of ICTs. How to strengthen global regulatory mechanisms, notably in countries where such goods originate, has been the focus of growing policy debate (Institute of Medicine 2012). Collective action to regulate the global use of ICTs, to protect and promote population health, remains much needed.





Strengthening the governance of global public health


From international to global health governance


	Governance broadly concerns the agreed actions, rules, and means adopted by a society to promote collective action and solutions in pursuit of common goals. Governance takes place whenever people seek to organize themselves to achieve a shared end through agreed rules, procedures, and institutions. This can take place at different levels of decision-making and action. In public health, if a local community decides to initiate a campaign to slow traffic speed and improve road safety, this requires some form of governance to organize the effort. If a national policy is adopted to improve food labelling and increase the taxation of unhealthy foods, governance is needed to set the agreed labelling standards and rates of taxation, as well as enforce compliance. If a global campaign is initiated to strengthen tuberculosis control, an agreed form of governance is needed to take decisions, for example, on agreed treatment, resource mobilization, and implementation of agreed actions across countries. To what extent is there need for more effective governance to protect and promote public health within an increasingly globalized context?
	The existing institutional arrangements for collective action among countries have historical roots dating from the International Sanitary Conferences of the nineteenth century. This series of meetings, largely dominated by European countries and the US, focused on protecting their economic and political interests from epidemic diseases such as cholera and plague. The institutions eventually created, such as the Office International d’Hygiène Publique, were primarily concerned with collecting and disseminating epidemiological data on these diseases (Fidler 2001). The creation of the WHO as a specialized agency of the United Nations in 1948 was intended to universalize membership, and broaden the scope of, international health cooperation. Its objective, ‘the attainment by all peoples of the highest possible level of health’, was reflected in the vast array of programmes initiated under WHO’s auspices (Lee 2008).
	Recent decades have seen challenges to WHO’s designated role as ‘the directing and co-ordinating authority on international health work’ (WHO Constitution, Article 2(a)). In part, this has arisen from differences in perspective on whether WHO should be biomedically (disease) focused, or whether the organization should address the broad social determinants of ‘health for all’. These debates have been accompanied by rapid changes in WHO’s operating environment, with the ascendance of new institutional players with often competing resources, technical expertise, and normative perspectives (McInnes and Lee 2012). From the 1980s, the World Bank became a major influence as the biggest source of financing for health development (Buse 1994), while other UN bodies such as the UN Children’s Fund and UN Development Programme (UNDP) expanded their health portfolios. The 1990s saw the creation of numerous global public–private partnerships for health which attracted additional resources, but rendered the policy environment far more complex and crowded (Buse and Walt 2000). Charitable foundations, led by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, have since become the biggest players in the funding of health development (Birn 2014). This influx of institutions and resources has, on the one hand, reflected the higher priority to health development given by governments, corporations, and civil society organizations (CSOs). On the other hand, there is substantial evidence of overlapping mandates, duplication of effort, and, above all, a lack of consensus about how to effectively tackle the collective public health challenges posed by globalization (Gostin 2017).
	The governance of global public health can thus be understood as undergoing a period of transition, from international (state-based) to global (state and non-state-based) collective action. In principle, leading institutions formally responsible for governing public health remain governmental. Public health authority lies within the ministries of health of each WHO member state, and collaboration across countries and regions is expected to take place on a wide range of functions through governmental bodies. However, as described in this chapter, intensified flows of people, other life forms, goods and services, capital, and knowledge are creating transboundary health determinants and outcomes that can transcend state capacity to manage them. This is due, in part, to differences in perspective about what priority goals and actions should be pursued, the capacity of governments to act, and even a willingness to act collectively. Where governments cannot or will not assume a global health governance role, non-state actors in the form of CSOs, charitable foundations, and even corporations have been looked to as potentially filling this governance gap. Many scholars of global governance point to the need for new institutional arrangements to enable more effective action in the face of urgent need. Examples described in this chapter—such as tobacco control, obesity, and infectious disease outbreaks—demonstrate the need for innovation but also the political challenges posed.





Strengthening legal and regulatory frameworks for global health


	Globalization is now an established subject of discussion and debate at public health meetings around the world, and there has been no shortage of commitments to addressing its impacts. Efforts to do so through stronger regulatory frameworks have yielded mixed results. The FCTC is seen as a successful example of WHO member states coming together to address a major global public health problem through the creation of a legal instrument requiring signatories to adopt a minimum package of measures. The revision of the IHR in 2005 was also an important step towards the creation of legal frameworks for global health groups (GHGs). Collective action was furthered on access to medicines through the 2001 Doha Declaration on Intellectual Property Rights and Public Health, followed in 2003 by the WTO’s Decision on Implementation of Paragraph 6, both intended to clarify flexibilities in the Agreement on Trade-Related Intellectual Property Rights permitting member states to take measures, such as compulsory licensing, that improves access to medicines (Kerry and Lee 2007). The Report of the WHO Commission on Intellectual Property Rights, Innovation and Public Health (WHO 2006b) sought to address the tensions between economic and health equity goals by reviewing ‘current incentive and funding regimes, including intellectual property rights, designed to stimulate the creation of new medicines and other products, and facilitate access to them’ (p. iv).
	Beyond the health sector, however, to what extent is there recognition of the need to govern globalization differently? The foremost challenge, perhaps, remains the governance of the world economy in ways that are ecologically sustainable, and bring the most benefits to the most people. The global financial crisis beginning in 2007 revealed fundamental regulatory weaknesses—the availability of easy credit, incentives to undertake high-risk lending and borrowing, poor fiscal management by governments, and rampant speculative investing. The reforms that followed have sought to ‘fix’ selected parts of the global financial system. However, critics argue that the parts addressed are those which enable the ‘haves’ in the global economy to have more. The further concentration of global wealth in ever fewer hands—1% of the world’s population owned 50% of global wealth by 2017 (an increase from 42.5% in 2008)—sharply questions the social, political, and environmental sustainability of current forms of economic globalization (Credit Suisse 2017). The rise in populist movements worldwide, many opposing globalization, reflect this discontent.
	In relation to public health, more fundamental reforms in the governance of the global economy are required which recognize the profound consequences of insecure employment, stark inequalities in wealth, large-scale corporate tax evasion, and environmental degradation on human health. As heads of state, ministers of trade and investment, and corporate executives ponder the future of economic globalization, the public health community can seek to play a bigger role in creating the necessary checks and balances for the global economy to function sustainably. Public health representation in policy debates on trade and finance to date has been limited. WHO, public health institutions, and civil society organizations have remained at the margins of key decision-making forums such as the WTO, World Economic Forum and Group of Seven (G7) meetings. The substantial concerns by citizens and consumers worldwide about the social and environmental footprints of global products and services, the looming economic time bomb of NCDs, and the potential costs to the global economy of a highly lethal infectious disease pandemic may be leverage points for finding common ground between public health and economic policy. A global public goods for health approach, for example, addresses globalization and health from an economic perspective. The concept identifies where a good or service (such as knowledge of an infectious disease outbreak), which would be of benefit globally, will not be produced or disseminated if left to the market because no one can be excluded from accessing the good, and thus no charge can be levied for its use and no costs recouped. There may even be economic disincentives to produce certain goods, such as outbreak reports, because of resultant negative economic consequences. At the national level, the production of these goods is usually ensured by government intervention, but at the global level there remains no ‘global government’ to undertake this role. Certain functions of public health may be classed as global public goods (e.g. immunization programmes, disease surveillance), which require collective action to overcome market failures (Smith et al. 2005). The concept might thus be an appealing rationale to non-health policymakers shaping global change. The potential role of health impact assessment for informing policy proposals is another such approach (Friedman and Burci 2017). Most importantly, the long-term sustainability of globalization requires public health to be a core part of any efforts to build better global governance.





Conclusion


	This chapter has described key ways in which globalization is relevant to the theory and practice of public health. There are both risks and opportunities arising from the complex and diverse changes being created by globalization, with current forms of market-dominated globalization characterized by an inequitable distribution of winners and losers. For the public health community, there is a need to understand and contribute to more effective management of the rapid changes taking place. Greater attention to these public health impacts will, in turn, contribute to more sustainable forms of globalization.

2.1


Determinants of health


	Overview
	Matthew Fisher, Belinda Townsend, Patrick Harris, Ashley Schram, and Fran Baum





Introduction


	Determinants of health have been defined as ‘the range of personal, social, economic and environmental factors which determine the health status of individuals or populations’ (Nutbeam and World Health Organization 1998). An understanding of determinants of health accepts that human health is affected by multiple factors operating at different levels and interacting in complex ways. Determinants of health are classically grouped into four categories of biological, behavioural, environmental, and social determinants (Remais and Jackson 2016), although other classifications are available which incorporate categories such as ‘knowledge, attitudes and beliefs’ (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2008). Determinants of health are understood through a combination of research methods, investigating associations between specified factors and disease or disease risk in populations, and investigating mechanisms by which particular factors affect the health status of individuals (Rose 1985).





Biological determinants


	Biological determinants are endogenous features of the human body that affect health. They include the genetic structures that play a central role in the development of body and brain in early life and may render a person more or less susceptible to particular diseases. Age is also identified as a biological determinant of health recognizing, for example, that deterioration of cell functions in old age may increase susceptibility to disease. Arguably, the category of biological determinants is limited by its attention on physical attributes and overlooks the role that neuropsychological states play in affecting health; a matter we will discuss further later in the chapter.





Behavioural determinants


	Behavioural determinants notably include the widely recognized ‘lifestyle’ factors of tobacco smoking, use of alcohol and other drugs, and diet and exercise. Tobacco smoking is known to increase risk of a range of respiratory and cardiovascular diseases and several forms of cancer, and contributes to around six million premature deaths globally each year (World Health Organization 2015). Diet and exercise affect health in a range of ways, but most notably influence the development of overweight and obesity, which increase risk of conditions such as type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, musculoskeletal disorders, and some cancers. Prevalence of obesity worldwide had tripled since the 1970s, and represents a growing risk to health in many countries (World Health Organization 2017). As we discuss later, this category is regarded by some as too limited because it overlooks the role that social and commercial factors play in influencing health behaviours (Baum and Fisher 2014).





Environmental determinants


	Environmental determinants are factors in the physical environment that affect health, including features of human-made environments such as air pollution or availability of sewerage systems, and feature of natural environments such as weather events, insect-borne disease vectors, or availability of fresh water. The characteristics of foods such as their nutritive properties or presence of food-borne pathogens are important environmental determinants of health. For example, a lack of naturally occurring iodine in soil—and thus in the food it grows—impairs mental function in adults and during pregnancy can compromise foetal development. Diarrhoeal disease caused by contaminated water or food is a major cause of illness or death in children under 5 years, especially in low-income countries (LICs). Clearly, human activities are increasingly shaping ‘natural’ environments in a variety of ways with implications for human and ecological health such as land clearing and agriculture, commercial fishing, and use of fossil fuels contributing to global warming. Air pollution is an environmental determinant of growing concern. Recent analysis from the World Health Organization (WHO) indicates that each year around 4.2 million deaths result from ambient air pollution and 3.8 million deaths from household air pollution from cooking fuels (World Health Organization 2018).





Social determinants: an introduction


	Social determinants of health (SDH) have been defined as including both the daily social and economic conditions in which people live, and the higher-level socioeconomic and political factors that affect distribution of power, money, and resources, within or between countries (Commission on the Social Determinants of Health 2008). Factors in daily life that affect health include living and working conditions, availability of healthy foods, and access to healthcare. The higher-level factors, such as the decisions of governments or the structures of a market economy, are understood to distribute the social conditions that positively or negatively affect health; working through key mediating mechanisms of power, income/wealth, education, and employment (Commission on the Social Determinants of Health 2008). Where these processes produce inequalities in access to conditions supportive of good health, or in exposure to conditions that adversely affect health, then (socially determined) inequalities in health are the likely result. For example, political and economic conditions within a particular country may be such that relatively wealthy, urban populations enjoy better access to good quality food, medical care, and housing than impoverished rural populations, leading to higher rates of infant mortality in the latter group. This multilevel understanding of SDH is illustrated in Figure 2.1.1.
	Fig. 2.1.1 Social determinants of health and health inequities.
	Adapted with permission from Solar, O. & Irwin, A. (2010). A Conceptual Framework for Action on the Social Determinants of Health: Social Determinants of Health Discussion Paper 2. Geneva: World Health Organization. Copyright © 2010 WHO.
	Not all health inequalities between populations are socially determined. Women have much higher rates of breast cancer than men but this is thought to result from biological differences, rather than differences in social conditions. (However, equally, socioeconomic factors may determine that some women have access to screening or treatments for breast cancer while others do not.) Health inequalities that are understood as socially determined may also be regarded as unfair or unjust. Those taking this view argue that health inequalities arising from structural social and economic inequalities could be reduced or eliminated, if governments and societies made different choices. To not do so, then, is regarded as unfair to those who (unnecessarily) are subsequently subjected to higher rates of disease and shorter lives than others (Whitehead 1992). Those who accept such arguments may refer to socially determined health inequalities as ‘health inequities’ (Baum 2016) to signal their ethical stance; a position we will adopt in this chapter. Such arguments can appeal to evidence showing that across different countries both overall health outcomes and the extent of health inequalities vary widely, in ways that relate to differences in political, social, or economic conditions (Commission on the Social Determinants of Health 2008). In the next section we discuss some commonly identified SDH in more detail.





Social determinants of health


	Many features of human societies are identified as SDH (Marmot et al. 2008). Here we discuss some standard items in classifications of SDH and some issues that have come to prominence more recently, as shown in Table 2.1.1. It is useful to note that there are different pathways and mechanisms by which social factors get ‘under the skin’ to affect individual or population health. Some of these are predominantly physical in nature, such as poor working conditions in mining leading to exposure to dust, contributing to lung disease. Other pathways involve psychological states. In particular, recurrent exposure to social environments perceived as threatening or demanding can cause psychological distress and chronic arousal of stress physiology, leading to adverse effects on mental or physical health (Fisher and Baum 2010).

	 			• Healthcare services

		• Environments for early child development
	• Urbanization and health

Healthcare services


	Access to healthcare services is widely recognized as an SDH, supporting health and preventing disease by providing trained advice and support, preventative interventions such as vaccination, and medical treatments for disease or injury; when these are needed. Research suggests that universal access to primary healthcare (PHC) is an important step in improving population health and health equity in all countries (World Health Organization 2008). A comprehensive approach to PHC combines first-level medical care with strategies to promote health, prevent disease, engage communities, and address other determinants of health within local spaces (Baum 2016).





Environments for early child development


	Environments affecting the early emotional, cognitive, behavioural, and physical development of children, say from conception to 7 years of age, are crucial in determining health prospects over the life-course (Irwin et al. 2007). Social factors involved here include: access to material resources during pregnancy to promote good health; opportunity to undertake and continue breastfeeding; nurturing and stimulation; interaction to develop socialization and language; housing conditions; and access to clean water (Maggi et al. 2010). Higher-level economic and social policies shaping issues such as minimum wages, parental leave provisions and welfare provision, or inequalities in income, differentially affect the lives and circumstances of families and other proximal conditions of child development, contributing to inequities in child health (Irwin et al. 2007).





Income, education, and employment status


	These three factors are central to contemporary understanding of SDH and health inequities within and between countries (Baum 2016). Clearly they are related: for example, education is likely to affect employment status, which affects income, which in turn affects educational opportunities across generations. Income, education, and employment are key mechanisms by which hierarchical societies distribute resources, thereby affecting differences in living and working conditions, and ability to afford essential goods and services. Some evidence suggests that, in addition, the psychological experience of being in a lower position within a status hierarchy can itself have adverse consequences for health (Wilkinson and Pickett 2009). Income, education, and employment status are commonly used as measures of socioeconomic status (SES), and research shows that health inequities do not just manifest as poorer health among those at the ‘lowest’ end of the SES scale, but often follow a gradient pattern whereby average health status decreases incrementally at each step down the SES scale, from ‘highest’ to ‘lowest’ (Fryers et al. 2003; Marmot and Friel 2008). Furthermore, among developed countries those with higher levels of inequality tend to have worse health across all SES levels, compared to more equal societies (Wilkinson and Pickett 2009). Thus, arguably, social and health inequities are a concern for all. Figure 2.1.2 presents an example of social gradients in child mortality within five countries. Note that there are also inequities between these countries.
	Fig. 2.1.2 Under-5 mortality rate per 1000 live births by level of household wealth in five countries, between 1998 and 2004.
