Employment conditions


	Aside from the role of employment in determining SES, the conditions of employment and unemployment are also important SDH. Work may provide many benefits for health, including financial security, social relationships, a sense of purpose, and opportunities for learning. However, workplace conditions may also involve exposure to health-damaging substances, physical demands causing injury, or psychosocial demands causing chronic stress (Marmot et al. 2008). In many countries the nature of work is changing under pressures from (inter alia) globalization, neoliberal ‘austerity’ politics, financial crises, technological change, declines in trade unions, and growth in casual and informal work and self-employment. Economic inequalities between countries create incentives for permanent or temporary migration to seek work, and these workers may be at higher risk of exploitation. According to the International Labour Organization (2015), in 2013 around 150 million people migrated for reasons of work. These changes risk an expanding divide between the ‘haves and have-nots’ in work status, security, and remuneration—within and between countries—with the potential to exacerbate health inequities.





Gender


	In most parts of the world women tend to live longer than men despite reporting more ill health. Explanations for women’s longer lifespans have included biological differences, the more dangerous nature of male employment, the tendency for women to seek healthcare more readily, and the greater social attachments women have (Baum 2016). However, gender inequities unfavourable to women have a range of adverse impacts on health by placing women and girls in cultural, social, or economic positions of lesser status compared to their male counterparts. Gender inequities affect health in a variety of ways, contributing to violence against women, discrimination against female children, unfair divisions of work, lower wages, and restricted access to education and healthcare (Marmot et al. 2008).





Social and cultural determinants of Indigenous health


	Indigenous peoples are defined as the descendants of ‘those who inhabited a country or … region at the time when people of different cultures or ethnic origins arrived, [who then] became dominant through conquest, occupation, settlement or other means’ (United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Peoples 2018). Although data on the health status of Indigenous peoples is uneven, in countries where it is available the story is often the same: Indigenous peoples have significantly worse health than the non-Indigenous population (Anderson et al. 2016). While Indigenous health is no doubt influenced by ‘general’ determinants such as income, scholars now identify a range of determinants affecting Indigenous peoples more particularly. These include health-promoting factors such as strong cultural identity and community control over resources and, on the negative side of the ledger, processes of colonization such as dispossession of traditional lands, discriminatory policies such as removal of children, and exposure to racism (Carson et al. 2007).





Determinants of mental health


	Common forms of mental illness (including substance abuse disorders) account for around 20% of the total global burden of disease in terms of years lived with disability (Whiteford et al. 2013), equating to many millions of people whose ability to gain an education, keep a job, or maintain social relationships may be compromised. Depressive disorders alone are a major and growing cause of disease burden globally and contribute to the approximately 800,000 suicides that occur each year. Many of the SDH we have discussed may adversely affect mental health by causing chronic stress (Fisher and Baum 2010). Social factors affecting use of alcohol and other drugs also play a significant part. Chronic physical ill health may also contribute to poor mental health. Major events such as wars or natural disasters are likely to have significant impacts on stress and mental health by destroying basic infrastructure and causing dislocation of populations. As with other health conditions, rates of common forms of mental illness are typically inversely related to SES (Fryers et al. 2003).





Urbanization and health


	A growing proportion of populations globally and within countries are living in cities. In 2008, for the first time in human history, the majority of the world’s population lived in urban environments, and the decade since has seen an upsurge in interest in the links between cities and health. There is now broad acceptance that urbanization itself is a determinant of health and of health inequities within and between urban populations.
	To understand urbanization as a determinant of health, there is now evidence of the full causal chain from urban system policies to health outcomes such as injuries, respiratory diseases, stress and mental illness, and infectious disease; and to quality of life outcomes such as well-being and liveability (Giles-Corti et al. 2016). Risk exposures cluster around environmental conditions (air, noise, and traffic), human factors (social isolation and safety), and behaviours (healthy eating, physical activity) (Giles-Corti et al. 2016). Although these factors have tended to be described as health-related features of the ‘built environment’, health is also affected by the social and economic make-up of cities. Here it is important that basic goods such as sanitation, education, healthcare, and social services are provided in ways, ‘that are socially cohesive, that are designed to promote good physical and psychological well-being and that are protective of the natural environment’ (Friel et al. 2011, p 863). At the same time it is now understood that urbanization is in large part contributing to global issues like climate change and migration.
	In terms of action, the alignment of the determinants of health within urban planning policy systems is crucial. A century ago planning was strongly aligned with public health objectives to prevent the spread of infectious disease. This close relationship was not sustained, however, as planning became a specific policy sector in most developed countries with narrower aims related to setting strategic direction for cities, assessing and approving developments, and other local issues to do with zoning and urban design. While planning and public health are gradually realigning, full realization of the potential of urban planning to prevent disease and reduce health inequity requires substantial shifts in the policy systems that govern the built environment (Friel et al. 2011). From an SDH perspective, the challenge is to align the broad interests of a public health agenda with those of urban planning—tricky in countries where there are well-developed urban planning sectors, and even more difficult in resource-poor settings where regulatory frameworks governing city planning may not exist. Evidence on health impacts alone is unlikely to suffice given that city planning is closely linked to competition between cities globally and thus is strongly influenced by local politics and perceived economic imperatives. Rather than prioritizing health, concepts like ‘agglomeration’ have come to dominate urban planning, whereby urbanization creates local centres for production activity that require servicing to function effectively. However it is important to recognize that considerations of health and economic vitality are not incompatible, given that well-planned cities that are more liveable and equitable in terms of offering jobs, goods, and services are likely to be more competitive economically.
	Questions of scale ought to dominate thinking about urbanization as a determinant of health. Urbanization itself is uneven across countries even as cities become central to the global economy; massive slums dominate some cities and can even exist alongside affluent suburbs, whereas others are characterized by urban sprawl. Within cities the need to plan at varying scales is fundamental to managing urbanization and population growth at regional and city levels down to local places and spaces. These issues of scale are replicated in the various governance arrangements that dominate how cities are developed and planned. Local government has long been recognized as politically powerful, for instance by the Healthy Cities movement, and the ‘local’ scale is seen by some as an important venue for action on SDH and health equity, able to mitigate some effects of determinants operating at a national or global scale. There are also a range of actors—public and private—engaged in planning for and delivering urban environments ranging from large city-wide infrastructure projects to precincts to buildings. Action to ensure these varying governance regimes and networks continue to engage with ideas about urbanization as profoundly influencing health are essential.





Globalization and commercial determinants of health


	Globalization facilitates increasing interconnectedness between national economies, societies, and cultures, shaping the upstream determinants of health. Arguably, globalized economic activity has produced some benefits for health through increased living standards, although this proposition is contested (Baum 2016). However, globalization has also facilitated widening income inequality. Income inequality has increased in nearly all regions of the world over recent decades, although at different speeds (Alvaredo et al. 2018). Globalization therefore presents risks and challenges for population health and health equity within and between countries.
	In the last two decades, intensified movement of capital and expanded trade and investment has facilitated the growth and size of transnational corporations (TNCs); those firms with manufacturing, production, and marketing operations across multiple countries. TNCs like Coca-Cola have production sites on every continent and extensive supply chains across the world. TNCs have also become significant economies on their own. In 2016, of the top 100 world economies, only 31 were countries. Most of the world’s largest economies are now TNCs such as Walmart, Royal Dutch Shell, and Exxon Mobile, and technology firm Apple.
	TNCs have become powerful actors, with significant economic resources, influencing global policymaking. For example, global pharmaceutical firms played a key role in shaping the World Trade Organization’s Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights Agreement (TRIPS) which requires signatories to provide a minimum of 20-year protections on patents (Sell 2003). TNCs, alongside other industry bodies, have pushed for an expansion of the issues covered under trade and investment agreements between countries. While trade agreements once covered commitments to reduce tariffs, they increasingly include rules for domestic regulatory issues, such as intellectual property, competition, technology, and rights for investors.
	There are several pathways through which these trade agreements can impact on health. Trade agreements can have a positive effect on health through increased access to technologies and health-promoting products and services. But they can also create negative consequences. The extension of intellectual property rights in trade deals, for example, can delay the market entry of cheaper generic medicines, reducing affordable access (Townsend et al. 2016). Trade agreements also promote greater market liberalization which facilitates the availability, affordability, and accessibility of unhealthy commodities such as ultra-processed food, tobacco, and alcohol—three key risk factors for noncommunicable diseases (NCDs). Simultaneously, these agreements secure greater access for TNCs in domestic regulatory policymaking, which can increase the time and resources required for governments to regulate these products, as well as the influence of industry on the selected regulatory approach (Schram et al. 2017). Trade deals can therefore serve as enabling mechanisms for the commercial drivers of NCDs. The costs associated with the negative effects of products such as cheap ultra-processed foods (most significantly an increase in NCDs) is externalized to governments.
	The ‘commercial determinants of health’ is a recent term in public health used to refer to the practises and strategies of corporations involved in driving risk factors for NCDs (Kickbusch et al. 2016). In addition to influencing trade and investment deals, companies that manufacture and trade in unhealthy commodities such as tobacco, alcohol, and ultra-processed food utilize a number of strategies to promote greater uptake of their products and undermine public health regulation. Documented strategies by firms include marketing strategies targeting young people, lobbying, and donating to political representatives, partnering with governments, funding biased research, co-opting health professionals and policymakers to promote industry objectives, and sponsoring campaigns to favourably influence public opinion (Kickbusch et al. 2016). The regulation of unhealthy commodities industries has therefore become a key challenge for global public health. Public health researchers have criticized the continuing participation of alcohol and food industries in global health policymaking. For example, despite strong financial motivation to promote the consumption of sugary drinks, Pepsi-Co and Coca-Cola contributed to the recommendations of the 2011 UN High-Level Meeting on NCDs (Buse et al. 2017).
	Public health campaigns have successfully intervened in the commercial determinants of health, most notably in tobacco control. Following decades of collecting and disseminating evidence and advocacy from health practitioners and policymakers, the first global treaty on tobacco—the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC)—was adopted in 2003 and has since been ratified by 181 countries. The FCTC explicitly prevents parties from engaging with tobacco companies, and offers a strong example of regulation to prevent industry interference. The case of tobacco illustrates that public health advocacy can be channelled to counter industry power and profits.





Social determinants of health behaviours


	Ultimately, improving the health of populations may require changes in behaviour. On the face of it doing this appears relatively straightforward, in that there are a range of behaviour change techniques to assist. However, behaviours are socially structured and so it follows that changing these behaviours requires changing the structures within which behaviours occur. Despite mounting evidence to support the importance of structure in shaping behaviours, behaviourism is still often promoted as a solution to ‘lifestyle’ diseases while paying little attention to structures. Ideologies influence these policy choices, as Tesh (1988) noted some time ago. Her analysis of US public policy demonstrates that there is a strong ideology of individualism which undermines appreciation of the role of structural factors, meaning that behaviourism is often privileged despite a weak evidence base for its effectiveness. There is a strong inherent logic to behaviour change strategies (Baum and Fisher 2014). If the problem of smoking is seen as one of people choosing to smoke and obesity as one of people overeating, then telling them not to do this seems to make sense.
	There are many theories grounded in social psychology which aim to assist individuals to change their behaviours. These include social learning theory (Bandura 1977) and the health belief model (Becker 1974). Each tackles individuals’ underlying beliefs and their motivations to change their behaviours. Such theories underpinned a generation of heart health programmes in the 1970s and 1980s. These started with great promise but in the main have been shown not to be successful. Their major limitation is that these models pay scant attention to the social, economic, and cultural environments in which people’s behaviours occur. One of the few heart health programmes to succeed was the Finnish North Karelia programme. Its evaluation reported greater changes in chronic heart disease (CHD) risk factors than for the Finnish population as a whole, and in CHD male mortality (Puska et al. 2009). The relative success in North Karelia was not mainly a result of individual increase in health knowledge, but rather of community-level strategies—including provision of PHC services and involvement of community organizations—and policy changes, such as the reduction of fat in food.
	The accumulated experiences with unsuccessful health promotion programmes directed at individual behaviour change reinforces the importance of the social determinants of behaviour. Many behaviours judged to be bad for health are often those that help people cope with stressful circumstances or are simply a response to an unhealthy environment. Thus the high smoking rates among Australian Aboriginal people reflect, in part, a means of coping with the racism they experience in their daily life. The increase in overweight and obesity is primarily because the marketing and supply of high fat and sugar foods in many countries has made these foods attractive, available, and affordable. As we saw in the previous section, trade agreements have made it much easier for transnational food companies to gain access to food markets and undermine healthy food supply. Thus individual behaviours reflect social, cultural, economic, and physical environments in which people live. Changing behaviours requires changing these environments.
	Changing environments is particularly important in achieving health equity. Behaviour makes the most difference to people’s health status when other conditions in their life are favourable. So, if someone is not poor in relation to the society they are living in, if they are not living in absolute poverty, have a supportive social network, are reasonably free of disease, then behaviour change strategies might make some difference to their health status; but such strategies alone are likely to increase rather than decrease health inequities.





Climate change and social determinants of health


	Anthropogenic global warming leading to climate change is having significant, adverse effects on human health that are only likely to increase in the future. While climate change is an environmental rather than a social determinant of health, human societies as currently configured are the primary cause of global warming, and the effects of climate change also intersect with SDH in ways that significantly shape health and health equity outcomes (McMichael 2017). Climate change can adversely affect health in a variety of ways including: the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events; sea level rise and associated flooding in low-lying islands or coastal areas; changing vectors of contagious disease; loss of arable land; and reduced access to fresh water. In many cases the health impacts of these events are likely to fall most heavily on countries, and population groups within countries, that are also subject to socially determined health inequities. Social impacts of climate change include the possibility of environmental refugees, forced to move in response to extreme weather events or changed environmental conditions, who will be highly vulnerable to poor health. Health impacts of climate change may also increase demand on under-resourced healthcare systems in LICs. For all these reasons, climate change—intersecting with SDH—presents risks of increased health inequities globally and within countries over time.





The complexity of determinants and their interactions


	The complex and multiscaled nature of determinants of health presents a number of complications for understanding and action, whether by researchers, healthcare practitioners, civil society organizations, governments, or international agencies.





Temporality


	In epidemiology, the concept of relative risk is used to express a causal link between a particular social or environmental determinant and the health of an individual or population group: that is, the likelihood or risk that people exposed to condition x will go on to develop disease y, relative to others not exposed. For example, in Australia, a current smoker is nine times more likely to develop lung cancer than a non-smoker. However, these equations on their own do not convey the temporal nature of the relationships between determinants and health or disease (Remais and Jackson 2016). A clinically recognizable effect on health arising from exposure to a particular determinant may take years to emerge. Exposure of young children to abuse or neglect is understood to increase the risk of conditions such as depressive disorders, drug use, and sexually transmitted infection (Norman et al. 2012), but these conditions generally develop in adolescence or adulthood. Along the way, other mediating factors may intercede to mitigate or exacerbate the risk. This kind of life-course perspective offers significant potential for primary prevention of multiple health problems, and possible gains in health equity, by acting on the common, underlying risk factor of child maltreatment (Irwin et al. 2007). However, for researchers, long time-lags between exposures and health effects complicate the challenge of investigating and demonstrating the links (Remais and Jackson 2016).
	The dynamic, temporal nature of the relationships between determinants and health are also expressed over longer periods, and at larger scales. A combination of improvements in medical care, urban environments, nutrition, and living conditions is likely to have contributed to the so-called epidemiological transition in many countries, where rates of infectious diseases (IDs) have declined, while NCDs have increased (Wahden 1996). In part, the increased prevalence of NCDs is a by-product of longer lifespans and ageing populations; because incidence of NCDs (such as heart disease and cancer) increases later in life. However, IDs do not go away, and may continue to have significant, adverse impacts among populations subject to disadvantage, producing what has been referred to as a ‘double burden of disease’, while having only small effects on overall population health (Wahden 1996).





Multiple scales and multiple determinants


	As was alluded to earlier, relationships between determinants of health and health problems can be understood as spanning multiple mechanisms and events operating at different scales; from individual biology, psychology, and behaviour to social or environmental conditions at a local, national, and international scale. This understanding is represented in the nested models of SDH presented in the literature, such as Dahlgren and Whitehead’s famous ‘rainbow’ model (2006). Thus, the health status of a particular individual or population group at any point in time is very likely to have been shaped by multiple factors. This presents challenges for research because more factors affecting health will be drawn into consideration, the farther ‘out’ from individual biology and behaviour one looks. The link between smoking (as a behavioural determinant) and risk of lung cancer can be established fairly readily, but if we ask why one population group has a smoking rate of 20% and another a rate of 5%, the determinants to consider expand accordingly. The nested nature of SDH also presents challenges for action. Healthcare practitioners seeking to reduce smoking rates might find it easier to focus on approaches targeting individual behaviour change such as nicotine therapy or health literacy, rather than worrying about broader determinants such as the lobbying practices of tobacco TNCs (Remais and Jackson 2016). Policymakers aiming to address increased rates of type-2 diabetes linked to obesity might find it easier to implement a social marketing campaign encouraging healthy food choices, than to tackle powerful interests determining the availability and marketing of ultra-processed, energy dense foods. The general argument from an SDH perspective is to look ‘upstream’ from biology and behaviour and address the higher-level environmental and social determinants, the ‘causes of the causes’ (Commission on the Social Determinants of Health 2008); because they are the key to prevention rather than cure, and because even modest changes in social or environmental factors operating across whole populations will produce far larger gains for population health than interventions with high-risk individuals (Rose 1985).
	In response to the complexity of social determinants, integrative theories have been put forward, explaining how the many factors, operating at different levels interact to produce health inequities. For example, Singh-Manoux and Marmot (2005) argue that health inequities are socially produced (and reproduced) via processes of ‘socialization’, whereby social class positions people within certain social milieu, which shape their psychology, attitudes, behaviours, and living conditions related to health.





Cross-boundary effects


	Understanding environmental and SDH means that questions about the role and responsibilities of national governments cannot be avoided (Commission on the Social Determinants of Health 2008). However, it is also the case that many public health issues transcend national borders and policies and require processes of global governance (Marmot et al. 2008), presenting challenges to international organizations such as the United Nations and its health body the WHO. No public health challenge exemplifies this level of international and global concern more than the profound and entrenched social and economic inequalities within and between nations (Alvaredo et al. 2018), which are the underlying cause of health inequities. Similarly, climate change is surely a matter of global concern requiring a global response, including not just the obvious imperative to reduce greenhouse gas emissions but also consideration of the potentially complex repercussions of national policy responses. For example, policy decisions by wealthy nations to increase use of bio-fuels may create incentives in LMICs to shift agricultural production from food crops to bio-fuel crops such as palm oil. This in turn can lead to increased prices for food staples on global markets, contributing to undernutrition among people with lower incomes (Remais and Jackson 2016).
	Another major public health issues transcending national boundaries is the movement of migrants and refugees across borders, whether stimulated by the desire to find work or to escape oppression or the violence of war. It is estimated that the Syrian civil war alone has led to over 5 million refugees leaving the country and another 6 million people displaced within Syria. The repercussions of these events for health will inevitably be substantial and long-lasting, in Europe and the Middle East, and around the world.





Political challenges


	National governments now operate within a global, neoliberal economic environment that prioritizes free trade, private profit, and economic growth and promotes these as vehicles for meeting human needs and reducing poverty. In this context, the role and capacity of national governments to regulate markets in ways conducive to public health, or tax and spend to deliver universal public services that contribute to health may be compromised in a variety of ways. Depending on the political and economic circumstances of the country in question, these challenges may take a variety of forms: governments adopting neoliberal or antidemocratic political values, weak or stagnating public revenues, influence of the private sector on policy, out-migration of skilled workers, or domestic political corruption just to name a few. Here we discuss two challenges for national governments in low, middle, and high income countries in taking action on SDH to improve public health and reduce health inequities.





Economic growth


	The Preston Curve (Bloom and Canning 2007) indicates that, for LICs in particular growth in national income from a low base is often associated with marked increases in average life expectancy (although the benefits decline as national income continues to increase). Such health gains may well be influenced by improvements in determinants such as nutrition, access to clean water and safe sanitation, and PHC (Bloom and Canning 2007). The pathway to economic growth for LICs—as perceived by a national government, or promoted by international agencies—has commonly been seen as one of foreign investment for industrialization of mining, agriculture, or manufacturing for export, facilitated by low labour costs, urbanization, fossil fuel-based electricity generation, limited regulation and environmental protections, or tax concessions (Remais and Jackson 2016). Development loans to LICs from agencies such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have cultivated this approach by imposing conditions of economic liberalization and reduced government spending. However, this neoliberal model of development may involve adverse changes in determinants of health and health equity such as: poor nutrition or reduced access to healthcare; increased income inequalities; environmental degradation and pollution; poor urban living conditions; low wages and poor working conditions; displacement of population groups; and loss of agricultural production to meet domestic need.





Healthy public policy


	The accumulated evidence on SDH along with a concern for health equity leads compellingly to the conclusion that health as a policy concern cannot be confined to the health sector alone but should involve all sectors and levels of government (Marmot et al. 2008). Such thinking has led to innovative strategies such as the ‘Health in All Policies’ approach in South Australia and elsewhere (Baum 2016). However, calls for a whole-of-government approaches to health face both institutional and political obstacles. On the former point, one issue identified is the ‘siloed’ structure of large government agencies, meaning the structures of decision-making, funding and accountability are organized vertically within departments and thus discourage ‘horizontal’ collaboration. On the political front, a raft of incentives may come into play encouraging decision makers (despite the evidence) to adopt a narrow biomedical and behaviourist view of health and illness, and thus focus their policy attention for ‘health’ on systems of acute care for illness, or on individualized, behaviour change strategies such as social marketing. As noted earlier the incentives at work here may variously include: (again) neoliberal, individualist political values; the power and lobbying efforts of TNCs in sectors such as food, soft drink or alcohol; and the influence of the medical profession or the media on health policy (Baum and Fisher 2014; Tesh 1988).





Conclusion


	In this chapter we have provided an overview of contemporary evidence and understanding of biological, psychological, behavioural, social, economic, and environmental determinants of health. Identifying particular categories of determinants can be very useful for analysis and research. Research focused on isolating and understanding the effects of particular factors on the health of individuals or populations has contributed to rich and detailed body of evidence on determinants of health and health inequities now available (Commission on the Social Determinants of Health 2008). Given this evidence, it is clear that governments and societies concerned with improving health cannot limit their attention to healthcare services, important as these may be. Neither can they reasonably believe that the adverse health impacts of (inter alia) tobacco, ultra-processed food, or alcohol are adequately understood as purely matters of individual ‘lifestyle’ choice. We have discussed the complexity of determinants and their interactions, and this might seem to suggest that determinants of health and health inequities are just too complex for governments to address successfully. However, this is not so: although the political challenges are no doubt significant, in principle what is required is to understand that addressing determinants of health to improve population health and reduce health inequities require multiple forms of action, at different scales, in different domains, and giving attention to different phases of the lifespan.

2.2


Politics of public health


	Kaitlyn B. McBride and Linda Rosenstock





Introduction to the Politics of Public Health


	The aim of public health is to improve and protect individuals and their communities, as well as promote evidence-based policy to drive decision-making across the larger health system. Researchers in academic institutions, government agencies, and the private sector provide the science to help policymakers make evidence-based health policy decisions, such as interventions to increase smoking cessation, or policies to improve access to preventive care services. Despite the proliferation of evidence-based policy research, and significant advances in both the prevention and treatment of disease, there has been consistent efforts to suppress and distort scientific research, as well as prevent the creation, implementation, and enforcement of laws to protect the public health of individuals and their communities.
	Fig. 2.2.1 A formula to guide the analysis of politics in the policy process.
	Evaluating politics in the policy process can be reduced to the following components of the formula: Science + Politics = Policy (see Fig. 2.2.1). In an ideal world, science (or evidence) drives policy, with politics playing a minimal or enabling role. However, this formula recognizes that public health policy is not only decided based on science (or evidence), but science itself is increasingly vulnerable to the political process, and to attacks by a wide array of players (e.g. politicians, industry leaders, and interest groups) that have vested interests to undermine scientific evidence in order to thwart the actions that would credibly follow that knowledge. Put differently, politics are key—and can be systematically analysed—in advancing or thwarting evidence-based policy.
	Unfortunately, the adoption of evidence-based research and practices is increasingly subjected to complex strategies—including economic manipulation, delays, harassment, and rhetoric—which weaken evidence-based policy (Rosenstock and Lee 2002; Rosenstock 2006). The politics in this arena involves significant trade-offs, and political leaders may elect to not support objective or scientific evidence, due to many factors, including biases (e.g. ideology and religion), fear of losing political capital (e.g. votes from constituents), loss of financial or political support from powerful organizations, or strong partisanship.





Framework for evaluating the politics of the health policy process


	To examine the politics of the health policy process, our framework is a guide to evaluating how the role of politics influences the adoption of public health policy. To analyse this process, we will assess specific examples in a case-based approach, by expanding on the following domains:
	 	1. Define the problem and evidence for policy interventions (The What)
	2. Understand the roles and the players (The Who)
	3. Understand motivations (The Why)
	4. Understand strategies and tactics (The How)





The problem and the evidence (The What)


	Defining the public health problem is the first step in ‘the what’. For example, the problem might be that preventive care services are not sufficiently utilized. Once the problem has been identified, it is imperative that there is strong empirical evidence in support of a public health strategy to advance and improve the public health. For example, reducing an individual’s out-of-pocket expenses (e.g. through added fees such as deductibles or co-pays) is an effective strategy for increasing preventive care utilization.
	In this context, the collection of accurate data and objective, unbiased research is essential for establishing evidence-based policy (Choi, 2005). Additional components of high-quality scientific evidence include a sound analysis, comprehensive synthesis of findings, appropriate translation of results, and accessibility of information, either for policymakers, government officials, or for the general public (Choi 2005). An evidence-based approach in health policy can lead to both direct and indirect benefits, such as increased utilization of preventive health services, improved productivity among the workforce, and better quality of care for patients (Brownson et al., 2009).
	The politics of the health policy process can best be analysed in focusing on steps 2–4 of the framework: The Who, The Why, and The How:





The players (The Who)


	Policymaking is influenced by a myriad of players, including elected political leaders, public health officials, corporations, key interest groups, the media, and research institutions. In some settings, judicial review is key. In general, policymaking is often driven by legislators and elected officials who shape the law. Understanding who the key players are, and how they work together, or in opposition to one another, is a key step in recognizing the role of politics in the policy process.





Motivations (The Why)


	The motivation for pursuing a public health policy should ideally be driven by evidence-based public health research that results in policy that advances the public good. But health policy is also driven by economic, ideological, religious, and emotionally-held beliefs that are not always based on sound science. As such, motivations beyond those to increase the public good are key to understanding the role of vested interests—where one’s interest, such as economic, may override the drive towards evidence-based policy.
	For example, in many countries, elected leaders have prioritized ideology over sound empirical evidence in support of needle-exchange programmes (NEPs), a harm reduction strategy aimed to reduce the harms accompanied by risky health behaviours and illicit drug use. Arguments against needle-exchange programmes have been tied to moral and religious philosophies, which purport that harm reduction approaches, such as NEPs, condone amoral behaviour, and increase violence in communities. Despite the abundant evidence in support of NEPs in improving outcomes and decreasing disease burden, public officials continue to misrepresent and ignore scientific evidence for ideological purposes (Hwang 2007).
	Laws restricting access to abortion are another example of public health policy driven by political, religious, and moral beliefs, rather than scientific evidence. Research has shown that laws restricting access to abortion and reproductive healthcare are harmful to women’s health and well-being, and actually increase risk of injury or death; however, many countries have laws that criminalize abortion, as well as restrict access to reproductive health services, such as family planning (Berer 2017).





Strategies and tactics to undermine science and evidence-based policy (The How)


	Strategies and tactics are key to advancing evidence-based policy, but all too often they are employed to thwarting policy that would protect the public good. One key strategy is simply to attack the underlying science (or evidence), taking advantage of the distraction that claiming scientific uncertainty creates (Rosenstock and Lee 2002). A key example is climate change, where some question the mainstream of scientific opinion in order to undermine steps to mitigate climate-related adverse health effects. Economic manipulation is another tactic commonly used by politicians, interest groups, and corporations. For example, insufficient funding of regulatory and health agencies can limit the effectiveness of the policy apparatus. In addition, industry-sponsored research—especially in the US—is playing an increasingly large role as a source of funding, with a range of potential effects of altering the nature of the research itself to altering the dissemination of research results. In particular, the tobacco industry has used its financial ties to pressure health insurance companies to reduce consumer incentives to quit smoking (Shamasunder and Bero 2002). Due to these financial conflicts of interests, industry-sponsored research may lead to a suppression of study findings, prioritization of projects to produce economic gains, or biased interpretation of results by investigators (Okike et al. 2008).
	Corporations, politicians, and vested interest groups also use delay and harassment tactics to forestall the release of sound science. Delay tactics includes funding of parallel studies (with the aim to confound the understanding of the original data), threats to sue, initiation of litigation, delay of hearing of the facts, and legislative barriers to prevent policies from being implemented. These vested interest groups have also been known to harass researchers and federal agencies to suppress scientific findings and prevent publications that support research in opposition to their economic interests (Rosenstock and Lee, 2002).





Conclusion


	To be able to respond to attacks on science that are the underpinning of blocking evidence-based policy, the scientific community must increase its awareness of potential manipulation, distortion of empirical evidence, and conflicts of interest. This practice will hopefully encourage researchers and investigators to not only be vigilant about the potential consequences of undertaking industry-sponsored research but to understand their role in advocating for evidence-based policy.





Harm reduction strategies: needle-exchange programmes


	An estimated 13 million people worldwide inject drugs—and 10% of HIV infections are attributed to injection drug use (IDU) (World Health Organization 2016). Use of contaminated needles is the primary mode of transmission of blood-borne viruses, such as HIV, hepatitis C (HCV), and hepatitis B (HBV), and is a significant contributor to worldwide morbidity and mortality (Degenhardt et al. 2017).
	NEPs have shown to be an effective strategy to reduce transmission of infection among injection drug users. NEPs were first introduced in Amsterdam in the early 1980s by a group known as the Junkie Union. The primary purpose was to prevent the transmission of hepatitis B and HIV among injection drug users (Jarlais 2006). Studies later demonstrated a reduction in drug injection and HIV transmission among the programme’s participants (O’Gurek and Kirchner 2010). NEPs were quickly adopted throughout Europe as a principal HIV prevention initiative and began to spread in US cities amidst the growing HIV/AIDS epidemic in the 1980s. During this period, NEPs gained support from several global institutions and non-governmental organizations, including the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS.
	NEPs vary considerably in their design, services provided, programme policies, and daily operations (Fernandes et al. 2017). In addition to giving clean needles, the majority provide free testing for infectious disease (e.g. HIV and HCV), advice on safe injection and disposal practices, referrals to drug treatment programmes, such as opioid substitution therapy, and other supplies, including alcohol pads, and condoms.
	NEPs are considered a harm reduction initiative aimed at mitigating risk among IDUs and reducing transmission of infectious disease (Clark and Fadus 2009). The term ‘harm reduction’ was first introduced in 1974 by the 20th WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, referring to strategies aimed at reducing adverse consequences associated with drug use (Ball 2007). The concept and theoretical framework for the application of harm reduction strategies began initially with a defined focus on drug-related abuse; however, harm reduction policies have more recently been applied in response to broader public health issues ad not only drug-related harm, including alcohol abuse and sex trafficking (Myers et al. 2004).
	From a public health perspective, harm reduction is a strategy that aims to reduce the harms that are accompanied by risky health behaviours. In the case of NEPs, these initiatives are a proven, practical public health approach to reduce injection-related infections, while not leading to an increase in injecting drug use (Witteveen and Schippers 2006). The science behind the effectiveness of NEPs has been well-established. Several studies have shown that these programmes lead to positive health outcomes among NEP participants, including reductions in needle sharing and injection frequency. Reviews of international evidence by the WHO and Institute of Medicine (IOM) have consistently found evidence in support of the effectiveness of NEPs in reducing the spread of HIV, and other risk behaviours, including syringe sharing among IDUs.
	NEPs have been implemented in several countries, including Australia, Canada, Norway, Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, United Kingdom, China, and Malaysia. Despite the proliferation of empirical evidence and global support for NEPs– significant challenges remain in the global health response to the rapid spread of disease among IDUs. In 2016, of the 158 countries with reported injecting drug use, only 90 countries have implemented NEPs (Stone 2016).
	The harm reduction strategy remains extremely controversial and underfunded in parts of the world, including Eastern Europe, Asia, and particularly in the United States. Opponents argue that NEPs lead to an increase of illicit drug use and perpetuate the cycle of addiction (Wodak and Cooney 2006). Others critique the philosophy of harm reduction, stating that harm reduction strategies condone immoral and illicit behaviour. These opponents support incarceration and punishment for IDUs, although there is no empirical evidence to suggest that this strategy leads to decreased use of illicit drugs, reduces crime, or prevents the spread of disease.
	 	Case study Federal funding for needle-exchange programmes in the United States
	In the United States, opposition to NEPs has historically been rooted in conservative and Republican ideology and moral philosophy, which purports that harm reduction initiatives such as NEPs, promote drug use, increase injection of illicit drugs, and lead to increased violence in communities. Although hundreds of needle-exchange programmes operate across the country, the United States has one of the lowest rates of needle-exchange availability and is one of the only countries to ban federal funding for NEPs (Coleman, 2015). Consequently, ongoing programmes have limited resources to provide basic services, and must rely on private donations to operate. Lack of federal funding has also stalled widespread adoption of NEPs.
	The debate over federal funding for NEPs has remained a steady battle between Republicans and Democrats since the introduction of NEPs in the 1980s. In 1988, during the height of the HIV epidemic in the United States, a federal funding ban for NEPs was put in place by Congress, which could only be lifted if it was determined that NEPs were effective ‘in reducing drug abuse and transmission of HIV infection’ (US Code Title 42: The public health and welfare). This 1988 ban set the stage for decades of policy driven by politics, not science, and an ideological war against providing clean needles for IDUs (Weinmeyer, 2016). Since the introduction of the federal funding ban, efforts by Democratic leaders to finance NEPs with federal dollars were defeated by five presidential administrations, regardless of the growing body of scientific evidence in support of NEPs, and increases in in intravenous drug use accompanied by a rise in transmission of HIV and HCV through shared needles (Mathers et al. 2013).





Fear tactics


	In the United States the sharing of needles is due to fear of arrest for needle possession or violation of state laws and ordinances (Vlahov and Junge 1998).
	Some law enforcement authorities resorted to scare tactics to demonstrate their opposition to needle exchanges. Officers threatened patrons at local NEPs and IDUs were afraid of being arrested if found exchanging old syringes for new ones. Other law enforcement associations lobbied against any legislation that would protect IDUs against the possession of illicit syringes (Cohen, 2003; Beletsky et al. 2011).





Attacks on science


	Conservative interest groups and policy organizations have continued to oppose harm reduction policies with arguments tied to symbolism and moral philosophy. For example, the Drug Free America Foundation is a well-known group particularly adamant against harm reduction initiatives, including NEPs. They framed their arguments on the notion that needle exchanges promote drug use and enable drug users (Drug Free America Foundation, 2020). Other conservative groups also propagated the perception that injection drug users were not as important or worth saving as other members of society (Brownstein, 2016).
	Opponents of NEPs also reference and misinterpret studies to show the failures by NEPs to curb drug use, even though subsequent research always upheld the views of the scientific community (Drug Policy Alliance, 2012). One study conducted in Montreal was repeatedly mentioned since it indicated that NEPs increased HIV transmission rates. However, the authors later claimed that the participants were not a representative population, and a large majority had a higher risk of infection (O’Gurek and Kirchner 2010). Despite the negation, Republicans, and opposition groups used these studies to add greater legitimacy to their support of the federal ban.





Policy window for federal funding


	Republican leaders avoided addressing the growing public health crisis or legislation associated with NEPs, until the epidemic hit in their own states among their own constituents. At this time, the United States was experiencing rapidly increasing addiction rates, accompanied by a surge in HCV and HIV infections, predominantly affecting the Midwestern and Southern states, especially Kentucky, Indiana, and Tennessee (Zibbell et al. 2015). These states also had the strictest laws against NEPs and prevention initiatives like HIV testing.
	In early 2015, Scott County, a region in southeastern Indiana, had a massive outbreak of HIV infections linked to IDUs injecting prescription opioids (Conrad et al. 2015). Republican Governor Mike Pence authorized a needle-exchange programme to stall the HIV outbreak, effectively overriding state laws that prohibit syringe programmes (Rich and Adashi 2015). During the same period, Kentucky saw a surge of hepatitis C infections in nearly 54 counties, also linked to IDU. With this latest outbreak, a window of opportunity opened for bipartisan legislation to end the decades long ban for NEPs. Two Republican leaders from Kentucky ensured language was included in the 2016 legislative spending bill to end the federal funding ban. Some members of Congress who had historically supported the ban, finally acknowledged that legislation was necessary to counter the growing public health crisis.
	At first glance, it finally looked like a win for advocates and Democrats, however, the federal funding ban was not fully repealed. The bill currently includes language that will allow state and public health departments to use federal funds for NEPs, ‘as long as the federal funds do not purchase the syringes’ (Consolidated Appropriations Act 2016). Federal funds for NEPs can also only be used in areas with high rates of IDU, deemed eligible by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Furthermore, the bill does not guarantee any more federal funds for NEPs, just a shift in funding.
	Although though it took nearly three decades, the lifting of the ban in 2016 signals a shift in conservative politics towards implementing evidence-based preventive harm reduction policies.





The politics of women’s reproductive health


	Tremendous improvements globally have been documented in recent decades in women’s reproductive health and related quality of care. From 1990 to 2015, maternal mortality dropped by about 44% worldwide (Alkema et al. 2016). Despite this progress, significant challenges remain in meeting the reproductive healthcare needs for women and girls. Access to family planning services, including contraception, is still significantly limited in many low-and middle-income countries, and those countries bear a disproportionate burden of maternal mortality and morbidity. Recent estimates indicate that nearly 810 women die every day from preventable causes associated with pregnancy and childbirth, such as high blood pressure, delivery complications, and unsafe abortions; and approximately 94% of maternal deaths worldwide occur in low and-middle income countries (World Health Organization 2019).
	The accessibility and availability of quality family planning and reproductive health services, including safe abortion services and effective contraceptive methods, are key components to preventing maternal mortality and morbidity (Filippi et al. 2016). A recent study of 172 countries found contraceptive use in one year avoided approximately 272,040 maternal deaths (a 44% reduction), and would have prevented an additional 102,000 deaths (29% reduction) if the unmet need for contraceptives been addressed (Ahmed et al. 2012). Research has further shown that the use of effective family planning and contraception methods decreases the number of unintended pregnancies, including among adolescent girls, results in significantly fewer unsafe abortions, and is also an effective approach to reducing costs associated with HIV/AIDS (World Health Organization 2018a).
	Although access to effective sexual and reproductive healthcare has been shown to reduce national and global rates of maternal mortality, as well as pregnancy-related health risks, many countries fail to provide these services, and women face significant barriers to accessing them. It is estimated that about 225 million women of reproductive age in developing countries lack access to birth control and effective family planning services primarily due to cultural or religious opposition, poor access to quality health services, or restrictive laws and regulations (Sedgh et al. 2016).
	The US, because of its own domestic policy debates, has played a disproportionate role in curtailing access to and information about safe abortions globally. One policy, created by executive mandate of the US President without congressional approval, and that affects countless women worldwide, is the ‘Mexico City Policy’, also known as the Global Gag Rule. This rule initially implemented under the Reagan administration in 1984, curtailed US Agency for International Development family planning funds going directly or indirectly to non-US-based non-governmental organizations (NGOs) (international or regional NGOs located outside the United States and local NGOs) that provided information efforts, or counselling about or access to safe and legal abortions (Crane and Dusenberry 2004). The Gag Rule policy established a dangerous precedent for curtailing women’s rights for safe and effective sexual and reproductive healthcare worldwide—effects well beyond the intended restriction on provision of abortion information and services—and which has caused significant damage towards women’s access to services.
	Research on the impact of the Global Gag Rule found evidence that the Mexico City Policy, because of its overall effect on the NGO community including limiting access to family planning services, is associated with increases in abortion rates in several sub-Saharan African countries. One study found that abortion rates rose dramatically in countries with high exposure to the Gag Rule (namely, those most vulnerable to the funding restrictions) compared to those with low exposure (see Fig. 2.2.2) (Bendavid et al. 2011).
	Fig. 2.2.2 Abortion rates in 20 sub-Saharan African countries, by exposure to Gag Rule, 1994–2008.
	Reprinted from Bendavid, E., Avila P., and Miller, G. United States aid policy and induced abortion in sub-Saharan Africa. Bull World Health Organ. 2011. Vol. 89. Number 12. doi: 10.2471/BLT.11.091660. Figure used under Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 IGO licence (CC BY 3.0 IGO).
	The Gag Rule has historically been supported by Republican Presidents (and removed by Democratic ones), reflective of highly partisan views (in part driven by moral and religious ideologies) of women’s reproductive rights in the United States. The policy was recently reinstated by President Trump in January 2017 (Congressional Budget Office 2017), and as with many such policies in this administration, broadened even further than previous norms. Currently, the scope of the Gag Rule goes beyond US AID family planning funding (about $700 Million USD per annum) to include most US Government global health funding (about $9 Billion USD per annum). The consequences of this broadly expanded Global Gag Rule are as yet unmeasured, but are likely to include far more negative consequences than during previous Republican administrations.
	 	Case study Reproductive health rights for women in the US
	Despite formidable odds, President Barack Obama signed the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA) on 23 March 2010. This historic legislation also marked a new era of partisanship in Washington as well as the beginning of endless Republican congressional efforts to repeal the law. Prior to the implementation of the ACA, access to healthcare and preventive services was a significant challenge for millions of Americans. Following the law’s passage, millions more gained health insurance, along with coverage for preventive care services without out-of-pocket costs to the consumer. The original legislation did not include key preventive service coverage for women. This was addressed by an amendment to the ACA that resulted in the formation of a review process led by the Institute of Medicine (now, National Academy of Medicine) to identify gaps in coverage for women that should be included as benefits (Council 2011). After a contentious roll out of these added benefits, the small but vocal opposition was largely focused on the decision to include the full range of US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved contraceptives. Soon coined by opponents as the ‘contraception mandate’ (no more a mandate than any of the other listed evidence-based preventive measures similarly offered without cost-sharing, such as screening colonoscopy or mammography), the inclusion of family planning services as an insurance benefit has been strongly opposed by most Republicans, some employers, and many social conservative and religious organizations.





The science


	There is significant research to indicate that expanded family planning coverage has largely benefited women and teens of reproductive age in the United States. Following the implementation of the policy of expanded insurance coverage, the number of US abortions decreased by more than 132,000 between 2011 and 2014 (the abortion rate fell to 14.6 abortions for every 1,000 women between the ages of 15–44, a 14% drop since 2011) (Dreweke 2017). In addition to the health benefits of reductions in unintended pregnancies and concomitant abortions, there are other health benefits including decreased maternal morbidity and likely benefits to both mother and child of more optimal birth spacing (Cleland et al. 2012). Contraception use also confers several economic benefits; for example, prior to the ACA’s mandate, out-of-pocket expenses for contraceptives was a large portion of women’s medical expenditures, amounting to about 21 percent of their total out-of-pocket healthcare spending (Taylor and Mhatre, 2017). Recent evidence indicates that women saved $1.4 billion in out-of-pocket payments in 2013 resulting from the ACA’s inclusion of family planning as a covered preventive service (Polsky 2015).





The players (The Who)


	The ACA family planning benefits expansion drew a broad array of opponents despite broad support among the population. Opponents include religious organizations (notably, Catholic-affiliated organizations and employers), antiabortion groups, and the majority of Republican lawmakers. Reproductive health access opposition was driven by several components, based on religious, ideological, and political grounds.
	Those in support of greater access to contraception and reproductive health rights for women in the United States tend to include most Democrats along with women’s health advocacy groups, and pro-choice organizations. Universal access to contraception in the United States is also largely supported by key professional and academic organizations, including the National Academy of Medicine, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the American Public Health Association.





United States Supreme Court and the ‘contraception mandate’


	The Supreme Court has played a significant role in the contraception debate in the United States In 2012, Hobby Lobby, an arts and crafts company founded and owned by the Evangelical Christian Green family, filed a lawsuit against the United States over the new regulation requiring health insurance be provided to cover the full range of contraception methods, citing objections to the inclusion of emergency contraception (often known as Plan B or the ‘morning after’ pill) and intrauterine devices (IUDs). In the Supreme Court Case (Burwell vs. Hobby Lobby, decided in July of 2014), a divided court 5–4 struck down the ‘contraception mandate’ for family-owned businesses, based on alleged violation of the federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act (Luchenister 2015). This was the first time in US history that the court ruled that a private corporation can claim to have religious beliefs and deny employees a federal benefit.





Attacks on science


	Several tactics were used by opponents to undermine the science behind the family planning rule; challengers attempted to weaken support for the evidence-based policy with conservative rhetoric and delay tactics through litigation, motivated by ideology and partisan politics. For example, religious organizations and social conservatives, as well as the owners of the Hobby Lobby, erroneously equated emergency contraception drugs with abortion (Carroll 2014). Although this was unsupported by any empirical evidence, religious leaders and conservative lawmakers continue to spread the notion that certain family planning methods and contraception options, such as IUDs, are a form of abortion and thus constitute a violation of faith; this rhetoric was used to garner support from their constituent-base and antiabortion activist groups.





The future of women’s reproductive health rights


	Although the majority of the American public support mandated coverage of birth control in health plans, the law’s family planning inclusion as a preventive benefit remains a politically polarizing and controversial topic, primarily along partisan lines (Moniz et al. 2014). Republican party leaders and lawmakers are increasingly gaining support to restrict reproductive rights for women; Republican-leaning states have also slowly eroded women’s access to safe abortions and reproductive health rights in recent years; between 2011 and 2016 states enacted nearly 334 abortion restrictions (Nash 2016). There are now new efforts to reduce reproductive health funding and access for women under President Trump, and conservative lawmakers continue to attack the ACA’s contraception coverage and funding for women’s health. Although not a problem unique to the United States, as other countries are in general broadening access to such services, the United States is experiencing a serious erosion of women’s sexual health and reproductive rights.





Evidence-based policy challenged by politics: income inequality and health


	Despite recent increases in overall economic growth, global income and wealth inequality have been rising steadily since 1980; for example, the wealthiest 1% have increased their total wealth twice as much as the poorest 50% of the world’s population (Alvaredo et al. 2018). In some countries, including India, China, and the United States, growth in income inequality between 1980 and 2016 has increased exponentially, as a result of various factors-including educational inequalities, tax policies, and deregulation. Conversely, the rise in inequality has grown only moderately across continental Europe, primarily attributed to social, educational, and tax-related policies that favoured the middle-and lower-classes (Alvaredo et al. 2018).
	There are several methods for assessing the level of inequality in society. One widely accepted global measure is the GINI index, which is used for evaluating the level of income inequality within and across different countries (De Maio 2007); the index is a statistical measure to represent income (or wealth) distribution in a country. A coefficient of 1 (or 100%) represents maximum inequality (e.g. all wealth in one individual), while perfect equality is represented by a coefficient of 0.
	Using the GINI index from World Bank estimates, South Africa and Zambia, as shown in Table 2.2.1, are among the most unequal countries in terms of income distribution—while Ukraine, Sweden, and Norway are among the most equal nations in the world. China and the United States have similar levels of income inequality and fall in the middle of country rankings in terms of inequality (World Bank 2018).
	 	Table 2.2.1 Global income inequality using the GINI Index

	Substantial evidence shows that poverty in and of itself is a significant risk factor for poor health. In recent decades, evidence is accumulating that shows income and wealth inequality, in addition to poverty per se, are independent drivers of mortality and morbidity (Pickett and Wilkinson 2015; Williams and Rosenstock 2015). The additional role of another socioeconomic status indicator, namely, wealth and income inequality, is not surprising in the context of a Social Determinants of Health Framework, which posits a wide array of factors beyond biology and access to healthcare that have outsized influence on health throughout the life cycle (Friedman and Starfield 2003).
	A WHO Commission employed this framework to elucidate the main pathways through which social, economic, and political mechanisms influence socioeconomic status and social positions, inequities in education and household wealth, and how this shapes health status and vulnerabilities to specific health conditions. Social position and socioeconomic status are also influenced by income, since poor health status may affect employment, or other opportunities in various social and economic structures (Solar and Irwin 2010).
	A substantial body of literature demonstrates that from a population level-perspective, economic and social deprivation have a direct link on incidence of disease. Several studies have evaluated the relationship between low socioeconomic status and increased risk of morbidity and mortality (Brown et al. 2004; Bosworth, 2018). This evidence is reflected in life expectancy across countries-income inequality (as measured by the GINI coefficient) is one factor in explaining differences in life expectancy. Individuals living in nations with lower levels of inequality have been shown to have longer life expectancies (Deaton 2003). In 2016, the average life expectancy in Sweden is 82.4 years (one of the most equal countries), the US average life expectancy is 78.5, and South Africa is 63.6 years (one of the most unequal countries) (World Health Organization 2015).
	Evidence also shows that child and adolescent mortality is higher in countries with increased income inequality. One study found, using the GINI coefficient, that income inequality was positively associated with increased all-cause and communicable disease mortality in both males and females (Ward and Viner 2017). Additionally, researchers have also found evidence to suggest direct links between wealth inequities and mental health and overall psychological well-being; a recent review evaluating the association between income inequality and depression found that countries with larger gaps between the rich and poor have a higher incidence of mental illness (Patel et al. 2018).
	In sum, the evidence supports that higher stress and depression, and higher rates of morbidity and mortality, occur among countries with significant income inequity. Evidence further indicates that greater income equality leads to slower economic growth, and leaves countries more vulnerable to political corruption.





Case study The politics of US income inequality in a global context


	By several measures, income inequality in the United States has risen since 1980. The wealth gap in the United States has also increased steadily in the past few decades, and is currently the highest in the country’s history. As of 2016, the wealthiest 1% of Americans own nearly 40% of the nation’s wealth (Wolff 2017).
	The relation between income inequality in select developed countries and an index of social, economic and health outcomes (including mental illness, obesity, imprisonment, education, and social mobility) is shown in Figure 2.2.3. There is a clear correlation between rising inequality and poor outcome, with the United States an outlier in both measures.
	The US is the only advanced economy without universal healthcare; the country also performs poorly on several indicators, compared to other nations, including maternal mortality, and life expectancy. Among the 37 countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the US ranks 28th in life expectancy at birth (OECD 2020).
	In addition to the growing gap between rich and poor, the US is also experiencing a dramatic reduction in the size and standing of the middle class. Middle-class Americans have experienced a much greater decline compared to other advanced economies across continental Europe (Kochhar 2017). Research also shows growing income disparities by race and ethnic groups—the racial and ethnic disparity in wealth holdings widened considerably between 2007 and 2016 (Wolff 2017).
	Fig. 2.2.3 Index of health and social problems.
	Reprinted from Wilkinson RG, Pickett KE. 2009. The Spirit Level: Why More Equal Societies Almost Always Do Better. London: Penguin with permission author.





The political context of rising inequality in the US


	Although inequality has been rising for decades in the US among both Republican and Democratic administrations, there is a clear partisan divide about perception of the issue and responses to it. Republicans are more likely to associate a person’s financial standing to his/her own hard work, and are also less likely to favour taxes for the wealthy that mitigate inequality, or advocate for policies to raise the minimum wage; however, Democratic counterparts tend to argue that social and economic determinants, and institutional factors embedded in society, such as structural racism, are the primary drivers of poverty and inequality. Democrats also favour policies aimed to support lower and middle-class families (Smith 2017).





Partisan divide over solutions for inequality


	This partisan divide towards solutions to address the widening income gap are ever more apparent in two recent legislative bills: The Patient Protection and ACA, passed in 2010, and the recent Republican Tax Bill of 2017.
	The ACA was passed by President Obama and Democrats in 2010. This remarkable legislative achievement—the first major health and social legislation in decades—had a significant impact on inequality for the nation. The goal of the ACA was to make health insurance more affordable for low-and moderate-income families. Following the law’s implementation, nearly 20 million more Americans gained health insurance, reducing the uninsured rate to the lowest level on record (Cohen and Martinez 2016). It also reduced inequality (increased high earning taxes) and redistributed benefits, made many more families financially secure (blunting for lower-income shocks of healthcare cost), and lowered the federal deficit. A recent report found healthcare access for people in lower socioeconomic strata improved following ACA implementation and reduced disparities, with the gap in insurance coverage between higher-and lower-income households falling (Griffith et al. 2017).
	In contrast, President Trump and Republican lawmakers passed the ‘Tax Cuts and Job Act of 2017’, the largest tax reform in decades, which effectively redistributed wealth to leading corporations and the wealthiest Americans. President Trump and Republicans claimed several victories in passing this bill: lowered the individual top tax to 37% (from 39.5%), lowered corporate tax rate to 21% from 35%, and repealed the ACA individual mandate (the mandate not only assured through penalties broad participation and hence stabilization in the insurance markets, but also banned health insurance companies from discriminating against individuals with pre-existing conditions). Although the 2017 tax legislation does reduce taxes, if only slightly, across all income groups, the bill will continue to increase income inequality; higher income households will receive larger average tax cuts as a percentage of after-tax income; the biggest cuts as a share of income will go to taxpayers in the 95th to 99th percentiles of the income distribution, and the wealthiest will receive the largest cuts of all (Tax Policy Center 2018).





Solutions to address global inequality


	Substantial evidence indicates income inequality across regions and countries is driven by a multitude of social and political factors—as well as disparities in educational and economic opportunities. The downstream effects of increasing inequity not only harm individuals and their surrounding communities, as evidenced by worse health outcomes, increased crime rates and political instability, but impede investments in education and training programmes for future generations.
	To address the rapidly increasing structural inequities, the WHO recently identified several evidence-based policy options, with a particular focus to improve social determinants of health within the four following areas: childhood education and development, fair employment, social protection (e.g. cash transfers), and living and environmental conditions (e.g. housing affordability, legal protections) (Saunders et al. 2017). The various mechanisms to address systematic inequities in education, health, food security, etc., integrate several policy frameworks; however the underlying construct through which equity can be obtained is through short-and long-term investments in social determinants of health. With a more explicit policy focus to address upstream factors, such as economic stability and physical environment, regions and countries will see improvements in long-term economic growth, as well as improvements in health outcomes for the population (Nichols and Taylor 2018).





Conclusion


	Decision makers can mitigate threats to science (the public health evidence-base) by recognizing that broad-based support and public education are key to enacting and enforcing effective health policies, on both a domestic and global scale. The mainstream media as a purveyor of trusted information to the public needs to be protected from politically motivated attacks (e.g. in both the US and globally, the rhetoric in some quarters about false vaccine-related threats to health are aided when the public no longer knows who to trust).
	The role of science in public health today is critical for evidence-based policy, and crucial for improving public health worldwide. Advancement of policy based on sound science will continue to be necessary to combat growing global public health crises and respond effectively to new public health threats. Understanding the players, their motivations, and tactics used, is fundamental to analysing the role of politics in the process.

2.3


Poverty, justice, and health


	Ronald Labonté, Fran Baum, and David Sanders





Introduction to poverty, justice, and health


	Poverty has to be understood not just as a disadvantaged and insecure economic condition, but also as a shameful and corrosive social relation. (p. 7, emphasis in original)
	Lister, R., Poverty, Polity Press, Copyright © 2004.
	Poverty has long been a concern in public health. Not only do people living in poor circumstances generally suffer higher burdens of disease, but during periods of infectious epidemics or pandemics they are perceived as posing a risk to others as well. Studies even suggest that high poverty and disease rates together can contribute to social unrest and ‘failed’ (or failing) states (Cheek 2001; Hotez 2002; Singer 2002; Peterson and Shellman 2006). Apart from these more ‘public’ (or population) health risks, the persistence of poverty has also led many public health theorists and practitioners to ask why poverty continues to exist in times of great global wealth, and to argue that a socially just society would seek to eliminate poverty. The reasons for the persistence of poverty lie in how societies’ economic and political systems allocate the opportunities and resources people need to be ‘non-poor’ and healthy, or intervene to reduce inequities (avoidable inequalities) in their access to services and resources. Thus, any discussion of poverty, and of its impacts on health, unavoidably intersects with understanding how inequalities arise in the distribution of income and wealth, and of the material and psychosocial resources these socioeconomic privileges accord. As the British economist-cum-philosopher, Adam Smith, known best for his writings extolling the virtues of free markets, noted:
	 	Wherever there is great property, there is great inequality. For one very rich man, there must be at least five hundred poor, and the affluence of the few supposes the indigence of the many. (Smith 1776, p. 419)
	To further our understanding we need to answer the question of what poverty is exactly? How is it affecting health, and ill health affecting poverty? And what theories or practices of justice should guide public health interventions based on poverty’s persisting health risks? These three questions form the basis of the chapter that follows.





What is poverty?


	At first glance, it may seem simple to define poverty: the inability of people to provide for the basic necessities of life. But there are actually many forms of poverty, all of them important to public health and to public policy; and the concept of poverty itself is ‘highly contested’ (Alcock 1993). Its contestation is not simply theoretical (what does it mean?) or empirical (how do we measure it?) but also political, since it is the same sociopolitical structures and economic arrangements that give rise to both poverty and affluence.





Absolute poverty


	There are people in the world so hungry, that God cannot appear to them except in the form of bread.
