It was formed following the First People’s Health Assembly in 2000 and its political position is outlined in the People’s Charter for Health (People’s Health Movement 2009) and summarized in the Preamble as:
	 	Health is a social, economic and political issue and above all a fundamental human right. Inequality, poverty, exploitation, violence and injustice are at the root of ill-health and the deaths of poor and marginalized people. Health for all means that powerful interests have to be challenged, that globalisation has to be opposed, and that political and economic priorities have to be drastically changed.
	Reproduced with permission from People’s Health Movement, The People’s Charter for Health, Copyright © 2009.
	The Charter goes on to call for much broader political, economic, and social participation from poor people. Since 2000 the PHM has grown to encompass around 80 national circles of varying size and weight which are organized into regional networks. A Right to Health campaign, whose parameters have been defined at a global level but whose country-level activities vary according to context and conjuncture, has placed the responsibility for poverty reduction and the reduction of health inequities firmly on the shoulders of national states and international organizations. PHM has also collaborated with other organizations to produce five editions of the publication, ‘Global Health Watch’ (http://www.ghwatch.org), which present alternative and more progressive versions of the World Health Reports produced by the WHO. The GHWs provide a critical ‘watch’ on international organizations relevant to global health policy and governance including the World Bank, the WHO, and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation; offer evidence-informed critiques of neoliberal globalization; and argue strongly for its replacement by a more just and equitable system of global governance and economic system to achieve poverty eradication and health equity.





Conclusion


	This chapter has analysed the various definitions of poverty and considered their philosophical and political implications. We have examined a variety of explanations for why poverty affects health adversely. On the basis of this examination we concluded that poverty reflects structural features of global and national economic and social systems and, in particular, that unequal societies give rise to greater poverty and suboptimal health outcomes. We examined the norms of justice that can guide policy interventions to reduce poverty and its causes. We argued that both equality of opportunity and outcome are essential considerations in public policy and that confronting inequalities in initial conditions is vital. Political responses to poverty reflect philosophical and ideological positions. Social democratic and socialist responses place emphasis on tackling the underlying structural causes of poverty and seek to provide non-stigmatizing supports to those living in poverty. Socialism also seeks to replace capitalist modes of production with those that socialize both production and profits and argues that a transition to such an economy would result in a significant reduction in poverty. Despite the efforts of many civil society groups around the world, poverty or near poverty, and its health consequences, although showing recent decline, are still the reality for about half of the world’s population. This fact, together with growing economic inequities, does suggest that a new world economic and social order is required to dramatically reduce or eliminate poverty and the adverse health outcomes to which it gives rise.

2.4


Socioeconomic inequalities in health in high-income countries


	The facts and the options
	Frank J. van Lenthe and Johan P. Mackenbach





Introduction to socioeconomic inequalities in health in high-income countries


	In the first decades of the twenty-first century, socioeconomic inequalities in health still represent one of the greatest challenges for public health worldwide. This chapter aims to review the available evidence on the magnitude and explanation of these health inequalities (the ‘facts’), and to present the available evidence on what can be done to reduce health inequalities (the ‘options’). Socioeconomic inequalities in health will be defined as systematic differences in morbidity or mortality rates between people of higher and lower socioeconomic status, as indicated by, for example, level of education, occupational class, or income level.
	This chapter only deals with the situation in high-income countries. Wherever possible, we will draw upon international overviews, such as comparative studies, in order to avoid biases related to the selective experiences of single countries. Most of the illustrations will be drawn upon the European experience, which has become very well documented in the past three decades.
	An active interest in health inequalities in Europe can be linked to the publication of the Black Report in England in 1980 (Department of Health and Social Services 1980), which has been followed by an enormous rise of descriptive studies in many other countries, testifying to the existence of substantial inequalities in health in all countries with available data. Gradually the emphasis of academic research in this area has shifted from description to explanation, not only to satisfy scientific curiosities, but also to find entry-points for policies and interventions to reduce health inequalities. As a result, our understanding of the causes of socioeconomic inequalities in health has expanded tremendously, and has allowed interested policymakers to start searching for strategies to reduce these inequalities. The World Health Organization has actively promoted the issue of health inequalities by creating a Commission on Social Determinants of Health that has issued a major report urging policy action to ‘close the gap in a generation’ (Commission on Social Determinants of Health 2008). In some countries political windows of opportunity have arisen which have led to national programmes to tackle health inequalities. Evaluations of the most ambitious of these programmes (the ‘English strategy’) point to a need to double our efforts to find effective interventions and policies that can be implemented on a sufficiently large scale to achieve population-wide impacts (Mackenbach 2011).





The facts: description


	Socioeconomic status (SES) should preferably be measured by individual-level indicators like education (e.g. highest completed level of education), occupation (e.g. occupational class), or income (e.g. household income adjusted for household size). Usually, all these indicators point in the same direction, with health being worse for those in lower socioeconomic groups, but there is often substantial variation between indicators in the strength of the association, suggesting that the underlying etiological mechanisms are different as well. There is no ‘best single measure’.
	The magnitude of socioeconomic inequalities in health can be measured in different ways, ranging from simple measures like rate ratios and rate differences (indicating relative and absolute differences in morbidity or mortality rates between two contrasting groups), to more complex measures like the relative index of inequality and the slope index of inequality (indicating relative and absolute differences in rates between those with the lowest and highest SES, taking all groups into account and calibrating the social position of each group to its relative size) (Mackenbach and Kunst 1997). Although the choice of measure will partly depend on technical considerations, each emphasizes different aspects of health inequalities, often at the expense of others, and it may therefore be important to combine different measures.
	Socioeconomic inequalities in health usually present themselves as a gradient, in the sense that there is a stepwise increase of rates of morbidity and mortality with every step down the social ladder, implying that social inequality affects the health of nearly everybody, not only the worst-off.





Mortality


Total mortality


	Evidence shows that mortality rates are higher among those in less advantaged socioeconomic groups. According to a cross-national comparative study, the relative index of inequality is greater than 2 for men in a number of European countries in the period around 2005–2009, indicating that mortality rates are twice as high for those in the lowest as compared to the highest educational groups (Table 2.4.1). For women, relative inequalities are reasonably similar or slightly lower (Mackenbach et al. 2016).

	The magnitude of these inequalities varies substantially among European countries. For example, in the period around 2005–2009, the relative index of inequality for men is less than 2 in Scotland, whereas it is more than 3 for men in Lithuania. Education-related relative inequalities in mortality are smaller than the European average in all southern European populations and larger than average in most countries in the eastern and Baltic regions. Similar patterns are seen for occupation-related inequalities in mortality among middle-aged men (Mackenbach et al. 2008).
	Within Europe, the international pattern observed for relative inequalities in mortality also applies to absolute inequalities in mortality, as indicated by the slope index of inequality. This is because countries with larger relative inequalities in mortality, i.e. those in the eastern and Baltic regions, also tend to have higher average rates of mortality. As a result, the range of variation of absolute inequalities in mortality is even larger than that seen for relative inequalities, suggesting an enormous scope for reducing inequalities in mortality (Mackenbach et al. 2016). While the mortality rates of the higher educated are rather similar in different countries, the mortality rates of the lower educated are much more variable, and higher in countries with larger inequalities in mortality. In other words, the mortality rates among the lower educated drive the magnitude of inequalities in mortality in a country, suggesting that the lower educated are more vulnerable to unfavourable national conditions (van Raalte et al. 2011).





Cause-specific mortality


	Across Europe, rates of mortality from ischaemic heart diseases (IHD) are higher among lower as compared to higher socioeconomic groups (Kulhanova et al. 2016). The highest mortality rates in the lowest educational group are observed in the eastern European countries included. In fact, eastern European countries with high inequalities in IHD mortality rates show higher mortality rates in all educational groups. Unfavourable material circumstances, lack of control over life circumstances, and (a culture that approves) hazardous drinking seem to have affected health of the entire population, and those in the lowest education groups specifically (Mackenbach et al. 2008). Southern European countries never witnessed an ‘epidemic’ of IHD mortality, and inequalities in IHD mortality have not arisen.
	Consistently higher mortality rates among those in lower as compared to higher socioeconomic groups are also found for stroke. Again, eastern European countries show above-average absolute inequalities in stroke mortality (Mackenbach et al. 2016). Although absolute mortality rates are substantially lower among women, higher absolute inequalities in stroke mortality are found in women in eastern European countries as well (Mackenbach et al. 2008).
	Inequalities in mortality from cancer are often large among men, partly because of the excess lung cancer mortality in lower socioeconomic groups (Van der Heyden et al. 2009). Inequalities in cancer mortality are often smaller in women; sometimes they are really small or even have a ‘reverse’ direction, with higher mortality among the higher educated, particularly in Southern Europe (Mackenbach et al. 2008). This is because lung cancer mortality does not (yet) have the same negative association with SES status among women as it has among men, and because the most important cause of cancer mortality among women, breast cancer, often had a ‘positive’ association with SES. However, some evidence suggests a change in the direction of the association, with positive associations no longer being significant (Gadeyne et al. 2017). For lung cancer, there are similar indications for a future change in gradient among women (Van der Heyden et al. 2009).
	External causes of injury are another important contributor to socioeconomic inequalities in mortality, particularly (but not exclusively) in Eastern Europe. Mortality from road traffic accidents, from suicides and from homicides is higher in lower socioeconomic groups among men, but not or less clearly so among women (Lorant et al. 2005; Stickley et al. 2012). The larger inequalities in injury mortality in Eastern Europe are likely to be related to higher rates of excessive alcohol consumption (Mackenbach et al. 2008).





Trends


	Socioeconomic inequalities in mortality are not a static phenomenon. In addition to the already mentioned change in the direction of the association between SES and breast cancer mortality, this can be illustrated for IHD. In many countries, particularly in the North of Europe, mortality from IHD increased substantially after the Second World War. In the North of Europe, during the 1950s and 1960s IHD mortality was higher in the higher socioeconomic groups, leading to the notion of IHD being a ‘manager’s disease’. It was only during the 1970s, coinciding with the start of the decline of IHD mortality in the population as a whole, that the current inverse association emerged (Gonzalez et al. 1998).
	In the past two decades, absolute declines in all-cause mortality became larger among lower socioeconomic groups, and contributed to the smaller absolute inequalities in mortality in men and women in some North-European countries (Mackenbach et al. 2016). As a result of economic and social developments after political changes around 1990, Eastern European countries witnessed a widening of the gap in death rates (Leinsalu et al. 2009). Recent evidence, however, shows that the initial increase in mortality rates among lower educated men in many countries in Eastern Europe were followed by a decrease around 2008 (Mackenbach et al. 2018).
	The latter finding of a decline in mortality among the lower educated across Europe deviates from the situation in the United States. Specifically, mortality rates for white non-Hispanic US 45–54-year-old adults in the lowest educational group increased (Case and Deaton 2015), which has been mainly attributed to increases in mortality from external causes (drug and alcohol poisoning and suicides).





Life expectancy is shorter in lower socioeconomic groups


	As a result of these differences in the risk of dying, people from lower socioeconomic groups live considerably shorter lives than those with more advantaged social positions (Stringhini et al. 2017). Again, this difference varies by country. Whereas the difference in life expectancy between primary or lower secondary educated on the one hand and tertiary educated persons on the other hand is relatively small in Italy (2.3 years among men and 0.6 among women), it is large in Lithuania (9.2 years among men and 4.7 among women) (Mäki et al. 2014).
	Again, the United States and Europe seem to deviate when it comes to recent trends. A decrease in life expectancy among the lowest educated contributed to an increase in absolute inequalities in life expectancy between 1990 and 2008 in the United States (Olshansky et al. 2012).





Morbidity


Inequalities in generic health indicators


	For one indicator, self-assessed health (measured with a single question on an individual’s perception of his or her own health), the availability of data is almost as great as that for inequalities in mortality (Fig. 2.4.1).
	Fig. 2.4.1 Absolute and relative inequalities in self-assessed health across Europe.
	Reprinted from Hu, Y. et al. (2016) ‘Trends in socioeconomic inequalities in self-assessed health in 17 European countries between 1990 and 2010’. Journal Epidemiology Community Health 70: 644–52, with permission from the BMJ Publishing Group Ltd.
	The overall pattern is clear again: prevalence rates of less than ‘good’ self-assessed health are higher in lower socioeconomic groups, resulting in both absolute and relative inequalities (Hu et al. 2016a, b). Although self-assessed health is a good predictor of mortality, trends in inequalities in mortality and in ‘less than good’ self-assessed health do not correspond exactly. Specifically, whereas absolute inequalities in mortality declined in many countries, they remained rather stable in less than ‘good’ self-assessed health (Hu et al. 2016a, b).





Inequalities in diseases and disabilities


	Socioeconomic inequalities can also be found for many specific indicators, including objective measurements of the incidence or prevalence of diseases and disabilities. Many studies have shown socioeconomic inequalities in the incidence and prevalence of cardiovascular diseases (Manrique-Garcia et al. 2011). Although the size of absolute and relative inequalities seem to differ by diagnosis, substantial inequalities are found for coronary heart diseases, acute myocardial infarction, stroke, and heart failure (Christensen et al. 2016). In addition to a higher incidence, lower socioeconomic groups also tend to have a higher case fatality (Yang et al. 2012).
	Similarly, inequalities in cancer mortality reflect inequalities in both incidence and survival. Many cancers, particularly those associated with smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, and other lifestyle factors, such as cancers of the respiratory and upper digestive tract, have a higher incidence in the lower socioeconomic groups, whereas risks of cancer of the prostate, breast, ovary, and colon, and malignant melanoma are often less clear, absent or positive (Aarts et al. 2010). That the prevalence of cancer tends not to be different between socioeconomic groups (Dalstra et al. 2005) is perhaps because longer survival of higher SES patients ‘compensates’ their lower incidence. Whereas the incidence of breast cancer has been higher for women in higher socioeconomic groups, case fatality rates are higher in lower socioeconomic groups (Lundqvist et al. 2016). Similarly, survival of prostate cancer is lower among patients in lower socioeconomic groups (Klein and Von dem Knesebeck 2015). As suggested by data on mortality from suicide (see earlier), mental ill health tends to be more prevalent in lower socioeconomic groups (Lorant et al. 2007). The higher prevalence of mental illness in lower socioeconomic groups is likely to have a complex explanation. In psychiatric epidemiology, there is a long tradition of looking at the possible effects of mental health problems on downward social mobility. This ‘drift hypothesis’ has indeed found some support, for example, in the case of schizophrenia, whose onset usually occurs in adolescence and young adulthood, and which may consequently interfere with school and early work careers. On the other hand, incidence studies have also found higher rates of many mental health problems among those who are currently in a lower socioeconomic position. It seems likely that this at least partly reflects a causal effect, perhaps through a higher exposure to psychosocial stressors and/or a lack of coping resources (Lorant et al. 2007).
	As a result of the higher frequency of physical and mental health problems in lower socioeconomic groups, the prevalence of limitations in functioning and various forms of disability also tends to be higher. This applies to many aspects of functioning (mobility, sensory functioning, grip strength, walking speed, etc.) and is particularly evident among the elderly (Stringhini et al. 2018).





‘Healthy life expectancy’ is shorter in lower socioeconomic groups


	The fact that mortality and morbidity rates (among those who are still alive) are higher in lower socioeconomic groups contributes to even larger inequalities in ‘healthy life expectancy’ (the number of years which people can expect to live in good health). Inequalities in the number of years lived in good health are often seen of more than 10 years (Majer et al. 2011).





The facts: explanation


	During the past decades, great progress has been made in unravelling the determinants of health inequalities in high-income countries, and here we will summarize the evidence under three headings: ‘selection’ versus ‘causation’, ‘specific causal pathways’, and ‘overarching ideas’.





‘Selection’ versus ‘causation’


Early debates


	Selection explanations imply that health determines SES. Because of the occurrence of ‘social mobility’ (changes in SES during a person’s lifetime) there is ample scope for selection processes: health problems may lead to downward social mobility, and upward mobility may be more likely for those with above-average health.
	The occurrence of health-related selection is undisputed: during social mobility, some degree of selection on (ill) health does indeed occur, with people who are in poor physical or mental health being more likely to be downwardly mobile (e.g. get a lower status job, or lose income) and less likely to be upwardly mobile (e.g. finish high-level education, or obtain a highly paid job), than people who are in good health. The contribution of health-related selection to the explanation of socioeconomic inequalities in health is small, at least when occupational class or education is used as an indicator of SES (Bartley and Plewis 1997). This is because most health problems occur in late middle or old age, after people have reached their final level of education and main occupational status.
	Income, however, is much more sensitive to health status than education or occupational class. For example, poor self-perceived health is an important determinant of transitions into disability pensions, unemployment, and early retirement (Van Rijn et al. 2014), and as such presumably to a decrease in income. In a study using a more objective indicator of health, employees with an unscheduled hospitalization that could not be postponed experienced a drop in income 2 years later, as compared to matched employees who were not hospitalized. The same absolute reduction in income between the poorest and richest meant that the relative impact of the hospitalization was larger among the poorest (García-Gómez et al. 2013). There is also scope for an impact of what has been called ‘indirect selection’—that is, selection on determinants of health. For example, some evidence suggests that obesity affects social mobility, perhaps because of discrimination during recruitment for jobs or promotion (Karnehed et al. 2008).
	Selection on the basis of personal attributes, such as cognitive ability, coping styles, control beliefs, personality, and bodily and mental fitness, is also important. These attributes may influence educational and occupational achievement, and at the same time determine later health, either directly or through health-related behaviour. Empirical studies have found associations between many of these personal attributes and social mobility (Lounsbury et al. 2003), and some studies suggest that factors like personality and cognitive ability do indeed contribute to the explanation of health inequalities (Bijwaard et at al. 2015).





Disentangling causal effects


	Confounding by both measured and unmeasured variables, and the exclusion of reverse causation are major problems in disentangling the causal impact of SES on health (see Chapter 5.14). Because randomization by SES is not possible, situations have been sought that mimic experimental manipulation (see Chapter 5.10). In lotteries for example, large amounts of money are allocated randomly. Evidence suggests that the impact of winning substantial lottery prizes on mortality, healthcare utilization, and child development outcomes is weak (Cesarini et al. 2016).
	Historical changes in the age of compulsory education have been used to study the causal effect of education on mortality. In the United States, between 1915 and 1939, at least 30 states changed their compulsory schooling laws. A comparison of later-life mortality of children attending school just before and just after the changes took effect showed that 1 year of extra schooling reduced mortality substantially (Lleras-Muney 2002). Such results have also been reported for other countries (Kippersluis et al. 2011; Lager and Torssander 2012). A study using state-level school laws and school characteristics to predict years of education, reported that the variation in predicted years of education was inversely related to the risk of dementia (Nguyen et al. 2016). Together, these studies seem to suggest that a causal effect of education is more likely than a causal effect of income and wealth on health outcomes.





Specific causal pathways


	The findings summarized in the previous paragraph suggest that socioeconomic inequalities in health at least partly reflect a causal effect of SES on health. The debate on the relative contribution of such causal mechanisms, however, is far from closed. That also applies to the exact nature of these causal mechanisms, which are likely to be largely indirect, by raising the prevalence of specific determinants of morbidity or mortality in lower socioeconomic groups.
	Many risk factors for morbidity and mortality are more prevalent in lower socioeconomic groups. Three groups of explanatory factors are likely to explain the bulk of health inequalities in high-income countries: material, psychosocial, and behavioural risk factors (Van Oort et al. 2005). Healthcare may also play a role. Figure 2.4.2 provides a schematic representation of these mechanisms.
	Fig. 2.4.2 A possible model for the explanation of health inequalities.
	Reproduced with permission from Commission on Social Determinants of Health, Closing the gap in a generation: Health equity through the social determinants of health, World Health Organization; Geneva, Switzerland, Copyright © 2008, available from http://whqlibdoc.who.int/publications/2008/9789241563703_eng.pdf. Adapted with permission from Solar, O. and Irwin, A., A conceptual framework for action on the social determinants of health: Discussion paper for the Commission on Social Determinants of Health, World Health Organization; Geneva, Switzerland, Copyright © 2007.





Material factors


	There is no doubt that financial resources and related unfavourable material living conditions are very unevenly distributed between people with a lower and higher SES, even in high-income countries with strong egalitarian traditions. For example, in 2014, the average disposable income of the richest ten percent was about 9.5 times higher than that of the poorest ten percent in Europe (OECD 2017).
	Financial disadvantage may affect health through various mechanisms. The lowest possible costs for healthy living (as defined by health-based needs for nutrition, physical activity, housing, medical care, social needs, hygiene, and transport) tend to exceed minimum benefit levels (Morris et al. 2007). Yet, for some health behaviours, the cheapest option is also the healthiest, which is obvious in the case of smoking. That smoking is more prevalent among those in the lowest income groups has been attributed, among other factors, to the stress resulting from living in poor material conditions (Beenackers et al. 2018).
	Other ‘material’ risk factors that tend to be more prevalent in lower socioeconomic groups include occupational health risks (exposure to chemicals, accident risks, physically strenuous work, etc.) (Costa and D’Errico 2006), health risks related to housing (crowding, dampness, accident risks, etc.) (Dunn and Hayes 1999), and environmental health risks (air pollution, traffic noise, etc.) (Kruize et al. 2007). Some of these factors have been shown to make important contributions to the explanation of health inequalities (Marmot and Wilkinson 2006).





Psychosocial factors


	The second group of specific determinants which contribute to the explanation of health inequalities are psychosocial factors. Those with a low SES on average are exposed to more psychosocial stressors, in the form of negative life events, daily hassles, an ‘effort–reward imbalance’ (high levels of effort without appropriate material and immaterial rewards), and a combination of high demands and low control both in the workplace and beyond (Siegrist and Marmot 2004).
	At the same time, they also tend to have lower levels of social support (Stansfeld 2006), as well as less effective coping styles (Kristenson 2006) and a weaker sense of control over their life and living conditions (Bosma et al. 1999). This combination of a higher exposure to psychosocial stressors and less capacity to remove or buffer these exposures may explain part of the higher frequency of health problems in the lower socioeconomic groups. This has been best documented for psychosocial factors related to work organization, such as job strain, which have been shown to play a role in the explanation of socioeconomic inequalities in cardiovascular health (Marmot et al. 2006).
	Two possible pathways may be involved. According to the increasingly popular ‘scarcity-theory’ (Mullainathan et al. 2013) stress from exposure to poor material circumstances (such as financial stress) limits individuals’ ‘cognitive bandwidth’, probably leading to less self-control and ultimately unhealthy behaviour (Beenackers et al. 2018). The second is a biological pathway. The experience of stress affects the neural, endocrine, and immune systems of the body, and chronic stress may lead to maladaptive responses in the form of, for example, high blood pressure, a prolonged high level of cortisol, higher blood viscosity, or a suppression of the immune response, which may in their turn increase the susceptibility to a range of diseases (Brunner 2017). In this context, studies also refer to the concept of ‘allostatic load’, e.g. the cumulative physiological burden of exposure to stressful circumstances (the bodies’ ‘wear and tear’). Socioeconomic inequalities in cardiovascular, metabolic, and inflammatory markers used to measure allostatic load, have been explained by stressful living conditions (Robertson et al. 2015), and as such provide an explanation how unfavourable material and psychosocial factors ‘get under skin’.





Health-related behaviours


	The third group of contributory factors are health-related behaviours, such as smoking, inadequate diet, excessive alcohol consumption, and lack of physical exercise (Oude Groeniger et al. 2016, 2017). In many developed countries one or more of these ‘lifestyle’ factors are more prevalent in the lower socioeconomic groups. As we have already seen, many of the disease-specific patterns of health inequalities also suggest a substantial contribution of health-related behaviours to inequalities in mortality.
	By far the most widely available data on a specific determinant of health inequalities relate to smoking. The prevalence of smoking differs strongly between socioeconomic groups in many European countries (although variations in the magnitude of these inequalities between countries have been reported), so one can safely assume that it plays an important role in generating health inequalities (Huisman et al. 2005). The prevalence of smoking has declined over the past decades in many countries, at least among men. In the first decade of this century, the proportion of quitters among ever-smokers was higher among those in higher than in lower socioeconomic groups, leading to a widening of relative inequalities in smoking (Bosdriesz et al. 2015).
	Socioeconomic inequalities in alcohol-attributed mortality suggest an important contribution of excessive alcohol consumption to inequalities in mortality (Probst et al. 2014), particularly in Eastern Europe (Mackenbach et al. 2015a). Indeed, excessive alcohol consumption is more frequent among those with a lower SES, and increases mortality risks (Woods et al. 2018). Alcohol, however, is a complex factor in this context: abstinence, which is more frequent in lower socioeconomic groups, is often associated with a higher mortality risk, as compared to light alcohol consumption in observational epidemiological research (Woods et al. 2018). Moderate alcohol consumption is more frequent in higher socioeconomic groups, and often associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease mortality (Ronksley et al. 2011). Methodologically stronger evidence, however, challenges the protective effect of light-to-moderate as compared to non-drinking, and suggests that a lower mortality risk results from residual confounding by for example factors directly related to SES (Holmes et al. 2014).
	Socioeconomic inequalities in diet, particularly in fruit and vegetable consumption and fat intake, are well-established (Giskes et al. 2010). Only a few comparative studies have been conducted, and these show that men and women in lower socioeconomic groups tend to less frequently eat fresh vegetables, particularly in the North of Europe. Literature reviews have shown that it is likely that many other aspects of diet, such as consumption of meat, dairy products, and various fats and oils, also are socially patterned in many European countries, and that these social patterns differ between countries (Lopez-Azpiazu et al. 2003).
	Socioeconomic patterns in physical activity depend on the type of activity. A lack of leisure-time physical activity tends to be more common in the lower socioeconomic groups, whereas occupational physical activity is less common among higher socioeconomic groups (Beenackers et al. 2012). High levels of occupational physical activity, however, are related to early mortality (Coenen et al. 2018) and as such may contribute to socioeconomic inequalities in mortality.
	A lack of physical activity and an unhealthy diet are the main determinants of obesity. The increase in the prevalence of obesity over the past decades is, beyond doubt, among the major challenges in public health. Interestingly, this is one of the very few health aspects where patterns of social variation are clearer for women than for men. Among women, overweight and obesity are more prevalent in lower socioeconomic groups in European countries with available data, with clearly large inequalities in overweight and obesity in Southern Europe (Roskam et al. 2010). Recent evidence suggests a widening of absolute inequalities in obesity in many countries in Europe, but not of relative inequalities, both among men and women (Hoffmann et al. 2017).
	The systematic nature of these differences in health-related behaviour clearly demonstrates that these are not a matter of free choice. While there is evidence of socioeconomic inequalities in intrapersonal determinants of behavioural changes, such as attitudes towards health behaviour (Kamphuis et al. 2009), such findings still do not provide an answer to the question why these determinants are socioeconomically patterned. As a result, the attention shifted towards the role of physical and sociocultural environmental conditions which are at least partly beyond the control of the individual (Van Lenthe et al. 2005).
	With regard to the physical (‘built’) environment, empirical evidence testing the ‘deprivation amplification’ hypothesis, according to which lower socioeconomic groups are exposed to contextual disadvantages in terms of the availability and accessibility of health enhancing facilities and healthy products produced inconsistent findings, at least in many European countries (Macintyre 2007). There are indications that built environmental characteristics play a more important role in the United States, suggesting again that macro-level processes leading to socioeconomic patterning of these characteristics are involved in generating the inequalities (Cummins and Macintyre 2006). Overall however, there remains an important knowledge gap if and how built environments contribute to inequalities in health behaviour.
	With regard to the sociocultural environment, evidence suggests that social capital and social resources, such as membership of support-providing networks and perceived social support, are associated with health behaviour (Conklin et al. 2014). Their contribution to socioeconomic inequalities in health behaviour is less clear. Scholars also explored the role of ‘cultural capital’, e.g. culture-based resources that shape and influence people’s habits, values, norms, knowledge, and preferences, and that are acquired mostly through social learning, with learning conditions varying between socioeconomic groups and milieus (Bourdieu 1984). Bourdieu argued that food and sport preferences may become part of an identity and can be used as a distinction mechanism between social groups. Emerging evidence suggests that cultural capital is a promising explanation for socioeconomic inequalities in healthy behaviour (Oude Groeniger et al. 2017).





Healthcare


	Unequal access to effective healthcare could theoretically also play a role in the explanation of health inequalities. Most high-income countries, however, have healthcare financing systems that have reduced inequalities in access to rather low levels. This is clear from studies of healthcare utilization, which typically show that lower socioeconomic groups tend to use more care than higher socioeconomic groups in accordance with their higher levels of need, and that relatively low use of specialist care in lower socioeconomic groups goes together with relatively high use of primary care (van Doorslaer et al. 2006).
	Studies of variations in healthcare outcomes do suggest that there may be inequalities in quality of care that are not captured by studies of global indicators of healthcare utilization. As was mentioned earlier, survival after a cardiovascular event or after a diagnosis of cancer is often shorter for patients in lower socioeconomic groups. Some studies have found higher rates of utilization of surgical and non-surgical interventions among hospitalized patients with a higher socioeconomic position (Stirbu et al. 2012). Like inequalities in survival after myocardial infarction, inequalities in survival of cancer patients are likely to be partly determined by inequalities in comorbidity or other risk factors for mortality independent of care received, but there is some emerging evidence that inequalities in treatment may also play a role, for example, in the case of breast cancer (Aarts et al. 2012).
	At the population level, mortality from causes of death that have become amenable to medical intervention also is higher in lower socioeconomic groups. Inequalities in mortality from these conditions are often substantial, and contribute between 11 and 24% to inequalities in partial life expectancy between the ages of 30 and 64 (Stirbu et al. 2010). To what extent these inequalities really reflect inequalities in healthcare access or quality is, however, uncertain. Countries with larger inequalities in healthcare utilization have not been found to also have larger inequalities in amenable mortality (Plug et al. 2012).





A role for genes?


	In intriguing question is whether genes contribute to health inequalities. Genetic factors do not easily fit into ‘causation’-type explanations, because temporally a person’s genotype precedes his/her SES, and a causal effect of the latter on the first is therefore logically impossible (Mackenbach 2005). In fact, genes which are both more frequent in lower than in higher socioeconomic groups and predispose to health, would confound the association between SES and health outcomes. This situation is not entirely unlikely: genes may be more frequent in lower socioeconomic groups when they predispose to health outcomes, which subsequently lead to social mobility. For example, genes may predispose to personal attributes such as cognitive ability or personality traits, which may lead to downward social mobility and may affect health. A ‘contribution’ of genes to health inequalities may however, come from ‘gene-environment’ interactions, whereby the health (dis)advantages of higher and lower socioeconomic groups differ between those with different genes. SES may also change gene functioning (e.g. the process of DNA methylation) in absence of changes in DNA sequences (‘epigenetics’), and as such contribute to health inequalities (Fiorito et al. 2017).





Overarching ideas


	What has emerged from recent research efforts is a rather complex picture of how individuals in the lower socioeconomic strata are exposed over their lifetime to a wide variety of unfavourable and interacting material, cultural, and psychological conditions, and how these exposures lead to ill health—either directly, or indirectly through unhealthy behaviours or psychosocial stress. Various attempts have been made to combine these factors and pathways into overarching theories. We discuss some of these attempts in the following sections.





Life course perspective


	In a life course perspective, health, or disease risk in lower socioeconomic groups later in life result from socially patterned exposures during gestation, childhood, adolescence, young adulthood, and later adult life (see Chapter 5.20). Different life course models have been developed, of which the ‘critical period’ model and the ‘accumulation’ model are most prominent.
	In a critical period model, SES has an exclusive effect on health in later life in a short and specific period in life, but not in other periods of life (Mishra et al. 2013). One example of a ‘critical period’ model relates to the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ hypothesis. According to this hypothesis a low birth weight is not only associated with infant health, but also with adult health, e.g. coronary heart disease, stroke, hypertension, and diabetes, probably due to ‘fetal programming’ of growth patterns and related metabolic and endocrine processes (Barker and Robinson 1992). Robust evidence exists of socioeconomic inequalities in unfavourable birth outcomes, including a low birth weight, preterm birth, babies born small for gestational age (Blumenshine et al. 2010). To the extent that fetal programming results in persistent and structural changes, a low socioeconomic status in pregnancy can be seen as a critical period.
	According to the accumulation model, different forms of material and immaterial disadvantage tend to cluster in the same persons, either uncorrelated or with one disadvantage increasing the likelihood of another one at a later point in time. Empirically, accumulation is often tested by investigating dose–response relationships between socioeconomic status at different periods in life and health outcomes in later life (Pollitt et al. 2005). Indeed, risk of disease and mortality increases with an increase in exposure to a low socioeconomic status during life (Mishra et al. 2013).
	Accumulation models can be refined to take into account chains of events reinforcing each other. Interestingly, this also resolves the ‘selection’ versus ‘causation’ debate, because a low socioeconomic status in one stage of the life course may translate into a health disadvantage in the next, which may then lead to a still lower socioeconomic status some years later, and so on. Health-induced downward social mobility then becomes just another form of accumulation of disadvantage.
	Clearly, the implicit assumption in accumulation models of an equally strong impact of socioeconomic status at different periods of life may be invalid. In a ‘sensitive period’ model exposure to a low socioeconomic status at different periods in life exerts different effects on health in later life. Although disentangling life course models empirically is complex, evidence suggests that a sensitive period model, in which a low socioeconomic status later in life is more strongly related to mortality than a low socioeconomic status earlier in life, best describes the effect of socioeconomic status in mortality across the life course (Mishra et al. 2013).





Fundamental causes


	The theory of ‘fundamental causes’ stipulates that it is the social forces underlying social stratification which ultimately cause health inequalities, and not exposure to the proximal risk factors which are usually studied by social epidemiologists (like smoking, psychosocial stress, working conditions, etc.). According to this theory, the persistence of health inequalities in different time-periods and different national conditions is due to the fact that a person’s socioeconomic status provides him or her with ‘flexible resources’. These include ‘knowledge, money, power, prestige, and beneficial social connections’ which can be used ‘to avoid disease risks or to minimize the consequences of disease once it occurs’ regardless of the prevailing circumstances. The association between SES and health ‘is reproduced over time via the replacement of intervening mechanisms’, and as opportunities for avoiding disease continue to expand so will health inequalities continue to exist (Phelan et al. 2010).
	This theory provides an elegant summary of all the more specific explanations, which fail to explain why health inequalities are seen in all countries with available data, and persist over time, regardless of variations in the proximal determinants of health. Existing empirical tests tend to be in line with the theory (Mackenbach et al. 2015b), Yet, how additional resources of higher socioeconomic groups do protect against prevailing health risk needs further exploration (Mackenbach et al. 2017). The theory is, however, a useful reminder that in the end the existence of health inequalities depends on the existence of socioeconomic inequalities.





Health inequalities and the welfare state


	The persistence of socioeconomic inequalities in health is one of the great disappointments of public health. All countries, including those ranking high on indices of economic prosperity and human development, have systematic inequalities in mortality and morbidity between citizens with a higher and a lower socioeconomic position, as indicated by education, occupation, income, or wealth. This also applies to the highly developed ‘welfare states’ of Western Europe. All Western European countries have created extensive arrangements aiming to reduce socioeconomic inequality and its various consequences. With notable variations all these ‘welfare regimes’ include measures to redistribute income (e.g. by progressive taxation and social security) and a range of collectively financed provisions (e.g. public housing, education, healthcare, access to culture and leisure facilities) (Esping-Andersen 1990).
	There is good evidence that welfare policies have contributed to a reduction of inequalities in income, housing quality, healthcare access, and other social and economic outcomes (Kautto et al. 2001), but they have apparently been insufficient to eliminate health inequalities. The explanation of this paradox has puzzled observers (Bambra 2011), and several hypotheses have emerged. Three circumstances may help to explain the persistence of health inequalities despite attenuation of inequalities in material conditions by the welfare state: (1) inequalities in access to material and immaterial resources have not been eliminated by the welfare state, and are still substantial; (2) due to greater intergenerational mobility, the composition of lower socioeconomic groups has become more homogeneous with regard to personal characteristics associated with ill health; and (3) due to a change in epidemiological regime, in which consumption behaviour became the most important determinant of ill health, the marginal benefits of the immaterial resources to which a higher social position gives access have increased (Mackenbach 2012).





The options: how to build a strategy to reduce inequalities in health?


	With all these advances in our understanding of health inequalities, we are now in a much better position than, say, in 1980 when the Black Report appeared (Department of Health and Social Services 1980), to develop rational strategies to tackle them. Bringing together evidence from around the world, the World Health Organization has called upon all countries to ‘close the gap in a generation’ (Commission on Social Determinants of Health 2008).





Normative assessment of health inequalities


	Reducing inequalities in health, by levelling up the health status of those in lower socioeconomic positions, has thus become an important policy goal in many high-income countries. One reason is technical: potential health gains are larger in lower socioeconomic groups, and raising their health status may therefore be a very effective way to improve average population health. Another reason is normative: health inequalities are widely perceived to be ‘unjust’. One particularly striking illustration of this perception can be found in the report of the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health, which stated that ‘[p] utting right these inequities is a matter of social justice. Reducing health inequities is an ethical imperative. Social injustice is killing people on a grand scale’ (Commission on Social Determinants of Health 2008).
	It is important, however, to outline the reasoning behind this move from ‘inequalities’ (a term with ethically neutral connotations, like ‘disparities’ or ‘variations’) to ‘inequities’ (a term which implies that these variations are ‘unjust’). This was first done by Whitehead in a simple but effective scheme consisting of two criteria: ‘avoidability’ (are health inequalities caused by changeable social conditions, and therefore unnecessary?) and ‘unfairness’ (do health inequalities result from conditions out of people’s direct control, not from free choice?) (Whitehead 1992).
	According to these criteria, health inequalities caused by exposure to health hazards in the environment, or by restricted access to healthcare, would be considered unjust, as would health inequalities caused by health-damaging behaviour restricted by socioeconomic factors. On the other hand, health inequalities caused by natural biological variation (e.g. genetic factors) or freely chosen health-damaging behaviour would not (Whitehead 1992). Application of this scheme thus requires empirical evidence on the determinants of health inequalities, and on the role of free choice versus ‘conditions out of people’s direct control’—evidence that is actually hard to obtain, although it is hard to imagine that systematic differences in behaviour between socioeconomic groups are based on truly free choice.
	Attempts to further formalize the normative assessment of health inequalities have tried to use Rawls’s influential ‘theory of justice’ (Daniels et al. 1999) or Sen’s capability theory (Venkatapuram 2011). The latter theory has become especially popular among social epidemiologists because, in contrast to other theories of justice, it gives a central place to health. It argues that all human beings are entitled to a certain set of ‘capabilities’, such as the ability to live a life of normal length, to have good health, to have emotional attachments to others, and to participate effectively in political decisions. From this perspective, tackling health inequalities should be a central objective of all governments pursuing justice (Venkatapuram 2011).





Policy development vis-à-vis health inequalities


	In reality, different countries are in widely different phases of awareness of, and willingness to take action on, socioeconomic inequalities in health. Common milestones in policy development are: high-profile independent reports recommending research or policy on health inequalities; national research programmes on health inequalities; government advisory committees recommending policies to reduce health inequalities; and coordinated government action to reduce health inequalities (Mackenbach and Bakker 2003).
	Whitehead has proposed a schematic ‘action spectrum’ to characterize the stage of diffusion of ideas on socioeconomic inequalities in health (Fig. 2.4.3). Starting with a primordial stage in which socioeconomic inequalities in health are not even measured, the spectrum covers the stages of ‘measurement’, ‘recognition’, ‘awareness’, ‘denial/indifference’, ‘concern’, ‘will to take action’, ‘isolated initiatives’, ‘more structured developments’, and ‘comprehensive coordinated policy’ (Whitehead 1998).
	Fig. 2.4.3 Whitehead’s action spectrum.
	Reproduced from Whitehead, M., Diffusion of ideas on social inequalities in health: a European perspective, Milbank Quarterly, Volume 76, Issue 3, pp. 469–92, Copyright © 1998 Milbank Memorial Fund, with permission from John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
	Some countries entered a ‘more structured developments’ stage, with national research programmes as well as high-level advisory committees that have issued comprehensive policy advice on how to reduce socioeconomic inequalities in health, and fewer have started a ‘comprehensive coordinated policy’ (Whitehead 1998; Mackenbach and Bakker 2003). A rational approach to tackling health inequalities should be based on logical reasoning: dependent on the causes of the problem, and on what is known about possible ways to address these causes, interventions and policies should be developed and tested for effectiveness, and then implemented systematically on the scale required to have population-wide impacts (Whitehead 2007). A possible typology of actions to tackle health inequalities is: (1) strengthening individuals (e.g. improving individuals’ abilities to make healthy lifestyle choices); (2) strengthening communities (e.g. community development initiatives to create healthier conditions in neighbourhoods); (3) improving living and working conditions (e.g. improve access to adequate housing and eliminate work-related health risks); and (4) promoting healthy macropolicies (e.g. reduce income inequalities) (Whitehead 2007).
	Within high-income countries, there is considerable diversity in the way scientific evidence is being used to underpin policies to reduce health inequalities. Often, most of the evidence used relates to the contribution of specific factors to the explanation of health inequalities, not to the effectiveness of policies and interventions tackling them (Macintyre et al. 2001). It is only rarely that strategies are developed primarily on the basis of evaluation studies of various intervention options (Mackenbach and Stronks 2004). As we will see in the next section the evidence base is still very limited, and opinions differ on what type of evidence is needed to underpin policies and interventions in this field.
	There are those who argue that in view of the urgency of starting to tackle health inequalities (‘doing nothing is not an option’) (Petticrew et al. 2004), one should be prepared to start intervening on the basis of plausibility. Political ‘windows of opportunity’ are usually short, for example, 4 years at most, and they may be closed before careful evaluation studies have been conducted (Whitehead et al. 2004). A parallel has been drawn with nineteenth-century public health interventions for which controlled intervention studies have never been done, but which were implemented on the basis of plausibility and have proven to be highly successful (Davey Smith et al. 2001). Under the pressure of politicians wanting to see rapid results, the best that can be achieved in terms of scientific evaluation may then be large-scale implementation accompanied by a ‘real-time’ evaluation study of the intervention, concurrent with its implementation, using some quasi-experimental design (before–after study, interrupted time-series study, and so on) (Macintyre 2003).
	On the other hand, there are those who argue that this is a strategy with serious risks. Like in other areas of social and health policy, the actual results of policies and interventions to reduce health inequalities could easily be counterintuitive. There are many historical examples of ‘plausible’ interventions and policies that did not work, or actually had adverse effects (Macintyre et al. 2001). In addition to that, one could argue that any investment in reducing health inequalities should be justified on the basis of a comparison of its cost-effectiveness with that of other possible investments in health and well-being, and that producing credible evidence is therefore essential (Oliver 2010).
	Another issue for debate is what types of evidence are best suited to underpin policy decisions in this area. Clearly, randomized controlled trials will not always be feasible, particularly for the evaluation of policies and interventions that are applied on a population-wide scale. Sometimes, community intervention trials, in which groups of people (school classes, neighbourhoods, etc.) instead of individuals are allocated to the intervention and control condition, will then be a good alternative. But in many circumstances one will have to rely on quasi-experimental or even observational designs to inform policymakers on the effectiveness of new approaches. Controlled before–after studies or interrupted time-series designs could then be used, or observational studies of ‘natural experiments’, for example, by making comparisons between countries (Thomson et al. 2004). Useful guidance has been developed to support further research in this area (Craig et al. 2011), including the application of techniques applied in economics and econometrics (Hu et al. 2017). Also, a Cochrane and Campbell Equity Methods group has been set up to ensure that research about differential effectiveness of health interventions is available worldwide (http://equity.cochrane.org/).
	A complicating factor in evaluating the effectiveness of policies and interventions to reduce health inequalities is that this effectiveness should be measured in terms of favourably changing the distribution of health problems in the population, not of reducing the rate of health problems in a particular group. A ‘full’ study design therefore requires the measurement, in one or more experimental populations and one or more control populations, of changes over time in the magnitude of health inequalities. Any other design, such as an experimental study of changes over time in the rate of health problems in lower socioeconomic groups only, requires rather strong assumptions to be made, in this case on the absence of health effects in higher socioeconomic groups (Mackenbach and Gunning-Schepers 1997).





Approaches to reduce health inequalities


	A number of approaches to reduce health inequalities have been developed, for which there is at least some empirical evidence suggesting that they can help to reduce health inequalities.
	In general, there seems to be an ‘inverse evidence law’, in the sense that more is known about small-scale interventions with potentially little population-level impact, and less is known about interventions and policies with a potentially large impact (Nutbeam 2003). A few promising approaches using different entry-points, are discussed here.
	Governmental (social) policies at the national and local level affect education, income, and related material living conditions. If such policies effectively improve the conditions for those in lower socioeconomic groups specifically, and (as a result) lead to improvements in health, health inequalities will be reduced. For example, the United Kingdom introduced a national minimum wage in 1999, resulting in an increase of the lowest incomes. A comparison of those exposed to this increase with a group who earned just more than the minimum wage before and after the introduction or those who experienced no increase, revealed a significant improvement in mental health, but not in health behaviour, in the ‘intervention’ group (Reeves et al. 2017). Despite the potential to tackle health inequalities via social interventions covering housing, work, transport, unemployment, food, and education, a differential impact on socioeconomic groups is only occasionally studied. To the extent it has been done, work interventions showed some evidence for an effect on reducing inequalities (Bambra et al. 2010).
	The important contribution of health behaviour to health inequalities makes health promotion among lower socioeconomic groups a potentially effective approach. One way to classify interventions for this purpose is to assess the degree of choice for individuals, resulting in ‘structural’ interventions (in which individual choice is removed), ‘agento-structural’ interventions and ‘agentic’ interventions (in which individuals are required to make independent choices) (Backholer et al. 2014). Of these, structural interventions seem to be best able to reduce inequalities in health behaviour. Fiscal policies are a good example of a structural intervention with a potentially larger impact on lower than higher socioeconomic groups. Indeed, the effects of raising taxes on tobacco is effective in reducing smoking among lower socioeconomic groups particularly (Main et al. 2008). Recent evidence suggests that a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages is either equally effective across socioeconomic groups or more effective among lower socioeconomic groups (Backholer et al. 2016). Such policies, however, are sometimes criticized for their regressive nature, meaning that the same tax takes a proportionally larger part of lower than higher incomes. One potential way to overcome this criticism is to use these tax revenues for public health investments for the lowest socioeconomic groups. Instead of taxing unhealthy products, there are also indications that lowering costs for healthy products contributes to a reduction of inequalities in health behaviour. A Norwegian experiment showed a large change in the uptake of fruits and a larger decline in the consumption of unhealthy snacks after the introduction of free fruit at schools (Øverby et al. 2012).
	Agento-structural interventions target both environmental and individual conditions. They can be implemented in neighbourhoods, but also in schools or workplaces. While the evidence of a reduction of inequalities in health behaviour is not overwhelming, this type of project does have more potential than single interventions. Indeed, an equity specific re-analysis of obesity-related lifestyle interventions showed that intensive and long-lasting community-based projects are potentially able to reduce inequalities in health behaviour (Magnée et al. 2013).
	Agentic interventions, entirely relying on individual choice, run the risk of widening instead of closing the gap between socioeconomic groups. This is perhaps, because the cognitive resources needed to fully benefit from these interventions are more prevalent among the higher educated (Magnée et al. 2013).





Comprehensive strategies: evidence from the English strategy


	The Black Report, commissioned by a Labour government to investigate the causes and possible remedies for Britain’s undiminished social class inequalities in mortality, had proposed a radical change in social and healthcare policies but disappeared into a desk drawer after the Conservatives won the 1979 elections (Department of Health and Social Services 1980). However, research continued and when Labour came back into power almost 20 years later, it again commissioned an expert report to bring together all the evidence—the Independent Inquiry into Inequalities in Health (Department of Health 1998)—and developed a comprehensive programme to tackle health inequalities.
	This programme consisted of a range of new government policies including the introduction of a national minimum wage, higher benefits, and pensions, and substantially increased spending on education, housing, urban regeneration, and healthcare. It also announced a number of specific initiatives including the ‘Sure Start’ programme (free child care, early education, and parent support for low-income families), ‘Health Action Zones’ (local strategies to improve health in deprived areas), and a series of antitobacco policies (including free nicotine replacement therapy for low-income smokers) (Department of Health 1999). In a further evolution of the programme two quantitative targets (to narrow the socioeconomic gap in life expectancy and that in infant mortality by 10% in 2010) were added, and priority was given to key interventions expected to contribute to closing the life expectancy gap, such as reducing smoking in manual social groups, managing risks for coronary heart disease and cancer (poor diet and obesity, physical inactivity, hypertension), and reducing accidents at home and on the road (Department of Health 2003). The total budget exceeded £20 billion (Table 2.4.2).
	The strategy came to an end with the 2010 parliamentary elections and the formation of a Conservative/Liberal Democrat coalition government. An extensive review of the achievements of the programme showed that it had been a mixed success: despite positive effects in some areas (e.g. reduction of child poverty, improvements in housing, better uptake of influenza vaccination) most indicators showed a widening instead of a narrowing of health inequalities, and the programme missed its targets (Department of Health 2010). Further analyses showed that the failure to achieve the targets was due to the fact that the strategy had not sufficiently focused on the most relevant entry-points, that effective policies were unavailable at that point in time, and that the scale of implementation had not been sufficient for achieving population-wide impacts (Mackenbach 2011).

Conclusion


	Whether it will actually be possible to substantially reduce socioeconomic inequalities in health remains an open question. The good news, however, is that there has been enormous progress in explanatory research, and that this has identified a large number of targets for policies and interventions to tackle health inequalities. There has also been a beginning of research and development for effective interventions and policies to tackle health inequalities. While this is still a modest beginning, it does put us in a better position to reduce socioeconomic inequalities in health in the coming decades. A number of innovative approaches have been developed for which there is at least some evidence of effectiveness. Comprehensive packages have been developed in several countries that have a sound theoretical basis and clear inspirational value.
	Developing effective strategies to reduce health inequalities is a daunting task. No single country has the capacity to contribute more than a fraction of the necessary knowledge. This is a matter not only of restricted manpower or financial resources for research, but also of restricted opportunities for implementing and evaluating policies and interventions. Some policies can be implemented and evaluated in some countries and not in others, either because they have already been implemented or because they are politically infeasible. International exchange is therefore necessary to increase learning speed.
