2.5


Reducing health inequalities in developing countries


	Romulo Paes-Sousa, Paulo M. Buss, and Mauricio L. Barreto





Introduction


	Human society is divided into a number of characteristics. Many of these divisions are the result of adaptive, biological, or geographical processes, and others are created in the course of historical, social, economic, or cultural processes. Some of these could be merely differences (e.g. men and women), others are purely social or historical as with the social classes. The importance is that inequalities very often are upgraded to inequities as they define relationships that are essentially based on power and the access to, and the possession of, goods, services, and wealth. Consequently, the fruits of the societal efforts accumulated over generations are unequally distributed (General Assembly 2000; UNDESA 2018). The more visible face of inequality is the existence of people with different level of access to the wealth, and this was observed in all four country income groups—high, upper-middle, lower-middle, and low.
	However, an important difference is that social inequalities in both low-and lower-middle-income countries are very often associated with a high level of poverty. While different, there is some overlapping in these two concepts and its consequences and both inequality and poverty has been given very high importance in the study of the social determinants of health. While social inequalities and poverty are both in general higher in lower-middle-income countries when compared with high-income countries, the health literature has in westernized, rich countries emphasized the study of inequalities and health, and the study of poverty and health has great emphasis in lower-middle-income countries. Therefore, while there is an accumulated body of evidence that inequality and poverty have isolated effects on health, in lower-middle-income countries less is known on the effect of inequalities on health and yet less on the joining effect of inequalities and poverty (UN General Assembly 2000a, b, 2015).
	Poverty is an absolute term that defines the lack of resources necessary to have a decent way of life. Certainly, the necessary resource to achieve a decent life vary in time and across different societies. Then, despite the effort to have universal definitions and measures of poverty making easier comparisons among nations, it is in fact very much contextual. In the effort for universal measure, the World Bank uses cut-off values corrected by purchasing power parity-PPP and defines extreme poverty as living on less than US$1.90 per day per capita, and moderate poverty as less than $3.10 a day per capita. In another aspect, inequality is a relational concept related with the distribution of the societal wealth among its members. A commonly used measure of inequality in the GINI Index (GI) that vary from 0 (zero) to 1 (one), where 0 is the situation where the wealth is equally distributed among all members (situation that maybe existed in very primitive societies) and 1 is the maximum of concentration where a member accumulated all the wealth. In present times, HICs with more fair societies have GI below or around 0.3, while the low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) are very often above 0.4 or 0.5, but a few arrive at 0.6 or above. A country can be poorer but less unequal, for instance, India has great poverty than Brazil, but it is less unequal. In 2011, the World Bank estimated 0.549 as the GINI Index of Brazil and 0.341 to India 34.1, while the prevalence of extreme poverty (% of the population living below US$ 1.9/day) was 11.1% and 21.1% in Brazil and India, respectively (UN General Assembly 2012).
	As you can see, inequalities within a country relate to the distribution of the accumulated wealth (World Bank, 2018). But, the consolidation of that situation and to transform inequalities in inequities, is dependent on how that society is politically organized and the power and social relations established among its various strata. It is defined by the political organization historically moulded in each society, and how the state redistributed the nation wealth through fiscal and transfer systems, generating greater or lesser distributive distances between existing social groups. Cultural elements are also important regarding amplifying and consolidating some existing inequalities. Inequalities consolidated in the social realm are often visible and sometimes enhanced when the object of study is health, meaning the health conditions or the access to the health services and resources reflect the way the wealth is distributed in that specific society or nation. Health inequalities generate different chances of exposure to the factors that determine health and disease, different chances about illness and death, as well as unequal possibilities about the ability to take advantage of scientific and technological advances for health. In the same way that social inequalities have persisted in all countries, regardless of their level of development, health inequalities persist in the same fashion (Deaton 2013; Marmot 2015). Given their development stage inequalities are associated with high levels of poverty and extreme poverty and other historical and cultural prejudices that create other dimensions of the inequalities such as the ones related to ethnicity or gender.
	Among countries poverty and inequality levels, while correlated, are not similar. Among the lower-middle-income countries, higher levels of inequalities are observed in Latin American countries while higher levels of poverty are observed in other continents in particular, in Africa. It gives a complex picture of the lower-middle-income countries poverty and inequality distribution. For instance, in the effort to understand the reasons why LA countries have great levels of inequalities three axes were explored: its position within the global economic system, the internal colonialism that maintains racial categories and the underdevelopment of state structures (Hoffman and Centeno 2003).
	In the current international context of economic globalization, discussions have highlighted inequalities within the same country but also inequalities between countries. Inequalities between countries are related to the differences in economic and social development achieved by different countries, which are generated by the position that these countries have occupied during different phases of history within the global productive system. The latter reflect historical aspects, and the international economic and political environment in relation to each country’s share of global resources and development opportunities.
	More recently, the concept of global inequality has arisen, which involves the combined effects of these two types of inequalities (Milanovic 2016). Global inequality is the result of inequalities both between and within countries, and it is therefore defined by the interaction of the determinants of each. The availability of international data has made it possible to conduct empirical studies regarding the issue of global inequality. For example, when the GINI Index, which is one of the most frequently used methods to measure social inequality within a country, is calculated globally it results in even higher levels than those found in nations with the highest levels of social inequality. In recent years, the GINI indices of countries with the highest levels of inequality have been around 0.60 (1 = maximum inequality and 0 = total equality), while the global GINI Index is close to 0.70. The global GINI Index captures the extremes of the poorest strata of the poorest countries (low-income countries) and the richest strata of the richest countries (high-income countries), which translates into a higher level of inequality than when measured in each country separately.





Health inequalities


	Poverty associated with an unfair wealth distribution in LMICs effects on health are staggering. It generates an estimated 800 million people chronically hungry, makes one in six children underweight, and more than one-third of deaths among children under 5 years to be attributable to malnutrition (Stiglitz 2012; FAO 2015; Johnston 2015). Insufficient access to safe and nutritious food exists despite the fact that global food production is sufficient to cover 120% of global dietary needs. Within each of these lower-middle-income countries social inequalities are observed among regions, inside regions, inside cities etc, or when societal or individual characteristics are considered (social class, ethnical groups, gender, etc.).
	Looking overall the level of inequality (as measured by the GINI Index) is strongly correlated with different health indicators being life expectancy at birth, infant mortality, different infectious diseases incidence, non-communicable chronic diseases (NCD) report, or violence. For instance, the global average of the life expectancy at birth in 1990 was 64 years, while in 2013 that number had increased by seven years to 71 years. However, as averages these values conceal a series of inequalities. For example, at country level, in 2013, the average life expectancy at birth ranged from a minimum of 46 years (38 in 1990) in Sierra Leone (a low-income country), to a maximum of 84 (79 in 1990) in Japan (a high-income country). By 2013, life expectancy had increased in both countries and although the gap has narrowed slightly (from 41 to 38 years) they are still at unacceptable levels (WHO 2015).
	Children are especially sensitive to social and environmental adversities. Despite advances in recent decades, it is estimated that 6.3 million children under the age of five died in 2013, mostly due to preventable causes in poor or developing countries. Children in low-income countries from sub-Saharan Africa are 15 times more likely to die before their fifth birthday than children in high-income countries. In 2015, the highest mortality rate was observed in Afghanistan (115 deaths per 1,000 live births) and the lowest was in Monaco (1.8 deaths per 1,000 live births) (Requejo et al. 2015). From 1990, when the Millennium Development Goals were established, to 2015 the global infant mortality rate fell from 62 to 32 deaths per 1,000 live births. Despite this substantial reduction (around 50%), the established target was not reached, which was to reduce the 1990 rate by two-thirds.
	Today, infectious diseases continue to be the leading cause of death for children, and they are also a major cause of death in adults. Globally, three of the top ten causes of death are infectious diseases. These also account for 16% of deaths each year. Most of these deaths occur in poor and developing countries, and they are attributable to preventable or treatable diseases such as diarrhoea, respiratory infections, HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria. Although there have been significant advances in interventions to prevent and treat most of these diseases, such interventions are not always available for the populations that need them. Taking the example of tuberculosis, which is a disease highly linked to the conditions in which afflicted populations live and whose occurrence changes rapidly when these conditions change, in 2013 it was estimated that nine million people became sick with tuberculosis worldwide, with most of these cases (56%) occurring in Southeast Asia and the Western Pacific. However, Africa had the highest incidence of tuberculosis, with 280 cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Of these cases, around 500,000 were caused by multidrug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) bacilli, which, in addition to causing more severe diseases, often increase treatment costs, making them prohibitive for the majority of patients living in poverty. In the same year, the estimated total number of deaths from tuberculosis was 1.5 million. Of these deaths, more than 95% occurred in developing countries, although the death rate fell by 45% between 1990 and 2013 (WHO 2014). NCDs as a whole are responsible for a significant proportion of the world’s burden of diseases, accounting for almost two-thirds of global deaths (36 of the 57 million deaths in 2008). The main health problems in this group are cardiovascular diseases, cancers, chronic respiratory diseases (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma) and diabetes. Although other diseases, such as mental and neurological diseases (including various forms of dementia), contribute to the high burden of morbidity (lower mortality), they have not been prioritized in global plans. NCDs are increasing rapidly in developing countries, where they impose large-scale human, social and economic costs, many of which could be avoided with well-known, cost-effective, and feasible interventions. Although they were initially associated with wealth, evidence shows that about 80% of NCD deaths occur in lower-middle-income countries. Even in sub-Saharan nations, where communicable diseases, maternal and perinatal issues, and nutritional deficiencies are still more important when taken together, they are in decline, whereas cases of NCDs are growing rapidly. This picture has resulted in projections that by 2030 NCDs will be the most frequent cause of death on the African continent (Rasella et al. 2013; WHO 2013; Worku and Woldesenbet 2015).
	It is estimated that more than five million (9%) of deaths occurring globally are related to various forms of violence. Approximately a quarter of these deaths result from suicide and homicide, and traffic accidents are responsible for another quarter. The various types of violence vary in different regions of the world, but, in general, their rates are always higher in poor and developing countries.
	Within countries this difference is observed being gradients of health status, measured by different outcomes, or the access and utilization of health services are observed for among regions, among social or ethnical groups.





Development and inequalities in health: the role of the Agenda 2030


	The Agenda 2030 recovers a fundamental debate on health justice. The Goal 3 ‘Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages’ implies a health standard which can be globally recognized. The target 3.8 ‘Achieve universal health coverage, including financial risk protection, access to quality essential health care services and access to safe, effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all’ is not explicit in relation to the role of the public sector as the main provider of health goods and services. However, it states that healthcare is local and global social concern, indicating that healthcare is related to social justice. The concept of social justice is explored in Chapter 2.3 (‘Poverty, justice and health’) in this Textbook (Labonté et al 2015). There is an important convergence for significant part of the moral philosophers in relation to healthcare as an essential component of the well-being and the societies have the moral obligation to make them accessible and affordable for all individuals (Ruger 2004). That leads the debate to another dimension: the need of a global health justice framework, which could direct global institutions and norms towards a globally shared principle of global heath obligations and rights (Ruger 2016).
	Health and development are deeply interrelated issues: without a healthy population, a society will hardly achieve development, as will an incomprehensible paradox if a society does not include the health of its population among the main objectives of its development.
	Both issues have been on the United Nations’ global agenda since its inception in 1945. In the 1960s, anticolonialist liberation struggles, which resulted in the independence of several African countries and other regions, gave renewed impetus to both issues. However, successive economic crises and strategies formulated in the 1970s and 1980s did not live up to the ‘right to development’ expectations of most underdeveloped countries. In health, the strategy of primary healthcare was drawn up since 1975, with its culmination in the Alma Ata Conference and Declaration in 1978. The relative failure of development policies led the United Nations to make efforts in practically all its agencies to review their policies and practices in the 1990s by holding international conferences to ‘prepare the world for the 21st Century’ (UNDESA 2018).
	In 2000, at its headquarters in New York, the United Nations held the Millennium Summit (General Assembly 2000), which issued the Millennium Declaration (General Assembly 2000) with a set of eight Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and 21 development goals to be achieved by the year 2015, measured by 60 indicators. Despite some recognized progress to many authors and the United Nations itself the major development goals were not achieved. Despite this, taking on the ‘unfinished agenda of the MDGs’, the United Nations and its Member States insisted on the process, replacing in 2015 the Millennium Development Agenda with the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda (General Assembly 2015), with its 17 goals and 169 targets to be met by 2030, compliance with which will be measured by 232 indicators.
	The Rio + 20 Conference, held in Rio de Janeiro in 2012 (UN General Assembly 2012), builds the political foundations of Agenda 2030 and its Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), whose central mantra ‘leave no one behind’ clearly indicates the radical political rhetoric of the UN and its Member States by the reduction of inequalities between and within countries. The concept of managed sustainable development indicates that it will be realized through the articulation of its three dimensions—economic, social, and environmental—to be realized in the global, national, and local plans. There are reasonable degrees of freedom for each country to seek on the ‘menu’ of Agenda 2030 and its SDG to set up its own Development Agenda.
	It can be said that Agenda 2030 and its SDG are potentially the most relevant global public policy underway to overcome inequalities in society, including in the field of health.
	Funding for global development is suggested in the Addis Ababa Agenda for Action (AAAA) (UN General Assembly 2015a, b). The final text of the outcome document, adopted at the Third International Conference on Financing for Development (Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 13–16 July 2015) and endorsed by the General Assembly in its resolution 69/313 of 27 July 2015, was one of the changes in relation to the Millennium Agenda. While it was basing its funding strategy on building a global development alliance in which official development assistance (ODA) gained importance, the AAAA stipulates that development must be pursued by each country for the openness, albeit asymmetrical, of its markets to international capital investments, which would inevitably lead to development. Numerous experts (including ourselves) doubt that simple trade liberalization can induce sustainable and equitable development, as advocated by Agenda 2030; in fact, the induction and participation of the democratic state is essential in the formulation and implementation of equitable and inclusive development policies.
	Overcoming health inequalities is clearly stated on the SDG 3: ‘Ensuring health and promoting well-being for all ages’, but this concept does not translate into a set of proposed goals and means of implementation capable of achieving the goal.
	This gap between the intention of the goal in health and the means to achieve it is perhaps the main weakness of the Agenda in this area. It is a considerable task for United Nations sectorial agencies in the area—made up of the World Health Organization (WHO), its regionals, and the countries’ Ministries of Health—to be able to find, with the support of civil society and users, the ways to adequately translate the politically powerful and far-reaching Objective into achievable goals and indicators that can measure the effective achievement of overcoming health inequalities, particularly in developing countries.
	Among the proposed strategies are Health in All Policies (WHO, 2013) with the understanding that given the multidimensional nature of human health, governments need to assess the positive and negative effects of economic, social, and environmental policies on health, including in reducing inequalities. This strategy is supported by the highest policy body for conducting SDG implementation at the global level, the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF), with its ‘From silos to integrated policy making’ orientation, which explicitly recommends the adoption of integrated multisectoral and harmonious policies for achieving sustainable development, in accordance with the precepts of equity and inclusion.
	The political rhetoric of Agenda 2030 and its SDG, including SDG 3, for health, establishes high-level global agreements for reducing health inequalities in developing countries. However, its concrete implementation will depend on the effective political will of the whole society and government—executives, legislators, judiciaries, and civil society—to translate into national development plans designed as a strategy for sustainable development in almost all countries.





Urban transition and health inequality


	Demographic and epidemiological transitions are shaping and being shaped by urbanization. The demographic aspects combined with the urban built environment have influenced the conditions of living and, therefore, becoming ill or dying.
	Fertility and mortality trends influence the age composition of populations, which, consequently, influences morbimortality patterns. The links between morbimortality patterns and population dynamics are commonly studied within the epidemiological transition theory. In emerging countries for example, three components of the population dynamics (fertility, mobility, and mortality) seem to be strongly associated with urbanization. Urbanization presents controversial impacts on health. If on the one hand the urban citizens are more likely to be reached by health, hygiene policies, and food availability, on the other they are also exposed to risks related to industrial sources, overfeeding, violence, and psychosocial factors. This means that a contradictory scenario tends to take place in the cities, especially, in developing countries (Eckert and Kohler 2014).
	Since the mid of 20th Century, the emerging urban population has faced dramatic changes in morbimortality patterns. When compared to rural areas, emerging cities present lower levels of morbimortality due to infectious diseases and undernutrition, while presenting higher levels of morbimortality due to chronic diseases (Eckert and Kohler 2014). In the cities the levels of fertility have declined largely in the last 50 years as well. This suggests that the urban population tend to present better conditions in terms of sanitation and medical care and more exposed to widespread ideas on birth control (Bongaarts 2017).
	However, mortality rates due to infectious diseases (including neglected diseases) and undernutrition vary within the city, suggesting that the gains of urbanization are not equally distributed among all settlers. When examining disaggregated data, intraurban variations expose the health inequality patterns across the urban territories (Hotez 2017). Socioeconomic differences and uneven morbimortality patterns have been a usual scenario in emerging cities.





Migrations and the limits of human movements


	Since time immemorial, sectors of populations or even whole populations have moved to new destinations for various reasons. In 2013, it was estimated that 232 million people—3.2% of the world’s population—lived outside their country of birth, and another 700 million were internal migrants in their own country of birth (UNDESA 2013). The patterns and motives for these migratory movements have changed greatly over time; however, it is clear that the majority of migrants who cross national borders do so in search of better economic and social opportunities. In recent decades, exacerbated disparities between nations, global economic expansion, geopolitical transformations, wars, ecological disasters, and many other occurrences have had, and will continue to have, a profound impact on people’s decisions to move to other nations. The recent phenomenon of the massive migration from some Arab countries to Europe is an example of the explosive and uncontrolled possibilities that the migratory issue can generate (Social Europe 2018).
	The migratory issue introduces an important point into the debate on inequalities. Estimates show that social inequalities between countries account for a larger share of global inequalities than inequalities within countries. While inequalities within nations are much more related to class issues and other processes of social stratification, inequality between nations raises the issue of place of birth, or what has been termed the ‘citizenship prize’, which is related to history and the overall process of development of nations. Taking the question of life expectancy, a child born in Sierra Leone in 1990 only had an average life expectancy of 38 years, which was less than a child born in Japan in the same year (46 years compared with 84 years). Therefore, the issue of where one is born takes on great importance, and the migratory movement is defined by this attempt to change what was to some extent established by one’s place and moment of birth. However, in a globalized world, in which capital, commodities, and human beings circulate, there are serious limitations on the movement of people, especially when they wish to move between nations.





Defining contexts on health inequalities


	The essence of the health inequality is the uneven variation of health indicators among the individuals due to their social characteristics. That variability can be accessed through the stratification of the individuals according to available social characteristics data. Evans and Brown (2003) described the most used social characteristics in health inequality studies. It is summarized by the acronym PROGRESS, relating to first letter of the following set of variables: Place of residence (rural, urban, etc.); Race or ethnicity; Occupation; Gender; Religion; Education, Socioeconomic status; and Social capital or resources. That comprehensive list of equity stratifiers for studying health risks and morbimortality does not consider some characteristics that are present in the literature. Age for example can be an equity stratifier if that condition is associated with unfair access to health services, as it occurs in many countries where adolescents have no access to contraceptive methods (WHO 2013). The relevance of each stratifier varies on time and space. In the recent years, large-scale involuntary migration emerged as one of the most relevant political items in the agenda of many countries, producing important shifts on national politics and international aid priorities in Europe. As a consequence, the health researchers elected health inequalities associated with race and ethnicity as a relevant investigating topic. Some findings revealed the impact of anti-immigration politics on health systems. In Barcelona in 2012, changes in the legal framework constrained immigrants to access health services (Castano 2016). In the Latin America and the Caribbean countries, race and ethnicity are relevant for observing the unfair distribution of health goods and services among national groups.
	However, the migration is not frequently considered neither a prevalent nor a relevant topic on population health studies. Data availability and scientific tradition also interfere in the preference for some stratifiers. In Brazil, income is a very commonly used stratifier, while in South Africa, multivariable indicators, such as household socioeconomic status, are most popular. A common criticism related to the use of equity stratifies is the narrow representation of the social vulnerability captured by a single social dimension associated with one health indicator (WHO, 2013). In fact, vulnerable contexts (such as poverty in poor countries) encompass a large number of stratifiers which are entangled producing a complex picture of this vulnerability.





The growth in health inequalities: possible solutions


	The construction of a more equitable world has been the aspiration of different political movements which understand that reducing inequalities in the various spheres of human life is essential and guarantees the existence and sustainability of human society. Health inequalities expose one of the facets of inequalities that are prevalent among human beings, the cruel and damaging effects on one’s own existence, which is reflected in the immense differences in life expectancy or the burden of disease and suffering.
	The evidence of the importance of social determinants in explaining health inequalities is compelling. However, although there are clear academic and political arguments that favour the implementation of actions to redress the determinants of health inequalities, policies to mitigate these inequalities have been scarcely implemented as part of the public policies of national governments, and still less to alleviate inequalities between nations. There are several reasons for this lack of political motivation; however, some aspects have been recurrent in the literature regarding health inequalities.
	One of the first aspects to consider is the consolidation of a health system based on biomedical knowledge and the resulting technologies, together with strong industrial and service sectors. These forces tend to generate and consolidate health systems that are only slightly affected in conceptual and structural terms, or favour actions directed at the social determinants of health.
	It is worth noting that the existence of inequalities, and their magnitude, does not immediately result in moral imperatives or generate political action within a society. In some societies, relatively small levels of health inequalities have generated strong policy actions to reduce them (e.g. some Scandinavian countries), while others, with broad levels of health inequality, are not motivated to alleviate them as happen in a major part of the LMICs.
	In poor and developing countries, where health inequalities are of the highest magnitude, there are few examples of the latter being among the priorities of public policy. For example, following the establishment by the WHO of its Commission on Social Determinants of Health, Brazil, which is a country with immense social and health inequalities, created its own national commission. However, after 2 years of work this commission produced a report which, in the main, was not assimilated into government actions (CNDSS 2008). Nevertheless, over the past two decades the implementation in many developing countries of redistributive policies such as income-transfer and micro-credits (von Gliszczynzki 2015), which are non-health policies, have had positive effects on health inequalities (Rasella et al. 2013). With regard to inequalities between countries, the proposals and actions have been even more timid. For example, the final report of the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health (CSDH 2008; Landmann-Szwarcwald and Macinko 2016) places great emphasis on inequalities within a particular society and less on inequalities between nations. It has a chapter dedicated to the issue of health inequalities in the global sense, which focuses on the need to strengthen so-called global governance and explains the need for coordination among various intergovernmental agencies. Some of these ideas were subsequently deployed in policies, such as the MDGs, which focused on the eradication of extreme poverty from 2000 to 2015 and their successor, the SDGs, which include the additional aspiration of sustainable development in its three forms (economic, social, and environmental) during the period 2016–2030.
	More recently, another group (The Lancet, the University of Oslo Commission on Global Governance for Health) (Ottersen et al. 2014) has made advances in understanding and proposing actions about global inequalities. The latest document produced by this group entitled ‘The Political Origins of Health Inequity: prospects for change’ is intended to ‘convey a strong message to the international community and to all actors who influence global governance processes: we must no longer simply consider health to be a biomedical, technical issue; we recognize the need for multisectoral and global actions and justice to address health inequalities’ (Ottersen et al. 2014, p. 631).
	In conclusion, although interest in the issue of health inequalities has increased from the academic point of view, this interest has only had a limited impact on public policies aimed at improving the health of populations. Social inequalities in health are a global problem that, to a greater or lesser extent, affects all human societies. They are mainly due to the inequalities that exist between the different social groups in each society. Although the inequalities that exist between different societies and nations are relevant, and are often of a greater magnitude, they are not always considered to be unjust, and as such they are subject to political actions. The most plausible theory that has been put forward to solve the latter type of inequalities has been to improve the mechanisms of global governance, insofar as this includes an understanding of how nations were historically founded and the effect of the position of each country in the productive global system (Robinson and Acemoglu 2012).





How to reduce health inequalities in developing countries?


	Combating health inequality demands an articulation of different actions that are associated with its determinants. A comprehensive approach should consider: (1) To be a distinguished goal of the national health policy; (2) To intervene on social determinants of health inequality; and (3) To improve living conditions and to overcome the exclusions mechanisms related to barriers for reaching the health systems.
	It is difficult to access the national commitment on converting a public goal into effective policies. In Latin America, the concept of ‘social institutionalization’ has been used to access such degree of governmental commitment. According to Repetto (2004), social institutionalization refers to a set of formal and informal norms, including routine and organizational behaviours, necessary to process and to prioritize the social problems, delimiting the content and the political and administrative dynamics of social policies.
	Cruces and Machinea (2010) have highlighted some institutional attributes that can be amplified to state level scale while defining a strategy for fighting health inequality: clear norms and goals, and sustainable policy. The issue of health inequality should be intrinsically part of the health policy with clear and stable norms and goals based on explicit political agreements and legal framework, with its sustainability been assured by adequate funding policy.
	Martínez (2017) has performed an extensive review of the Latin American literature on social institutionalization. The following list highlights selected components based on aforementioned authors’ reviews that tend to be relevant on the subject of reducing health inequality:
	 	1. Consistent and sustainable long-term strategy. That indicates a resilient policy with the capacity to go beyond electoral cycles and ready to respond to economic and political shocks.
	2. Social justice approach, as just explained.
	3. Coordination Fora. Health inequality policy requires a large number of actions from different areas and levels. The coordination of different actors from different loci and interests requires specific spaces of horizontal and vertical coordination with mandate and capacity for easing divergences and identifying the best cost-effective solutions.
	4. Development of technical capacities. A great limitation for implementing any action is the lack of qualified professional for implementing the adequate procedures. In developing countries, that is aggravated by the high turnover of the limited trained personnel as a consequence of precarious labour contracts and low incomes.
	5. Social participation. That comment is strongly associated with the long-term sustainability of policy and programmes and will be further explored in the next section.
	Interventions on social determinants of health inequalities are strongly associated with the reduction of morbimortality in vulnerable populations. Currently, the most effective approach to reduce poverty, extreme poverty, and social inequality is the use of articulated interventions to confront different factors associated with population vulnerabilities. Investment on education, labour policies, social protection, gender policies, and housing, compose the set of public policies that are often associated with the promotion of health equalitarianism. Ideally, a combined approach would seek to:
	 	1. Promoting social development. Restoring the broader dimension of the concept of development in order to integrate an excluded population into the national and local economic and social dynamics.
	2. Promoting equity. Using public policies to reduce unjustifiable differences and fighting discrimination. Reducing the poverty gaps faced by minority groups such as: black, indigenous, and traditional populations.
	3. Generating opportunities. Human capital development considering gender, place of residence (urban or rural), and cultural context.
	4. Improving quality in the delivery of public goods and services. The main deficit faced by the vulnerable populations is lack of access to quality public services.
	5. Developing a sustainable policy. The endogenous and exogenous factors that can affect the programmes and policies sustainability should be considered while developing the model.
	Box 2.5.1 presents the recent change in the Mauritian strategy to fight poverty and extreme poverty named as The Marshal Plan. An observation of its components can be useful for countries with some capacities but with huge social inequality.
	 	Box 2.5.1 Marshall plan against poverty in Mauritius
	Mauritius is implementing the Marshall Plan, aiming to fight poverty and inequality using an articulated set of 39 interventions from the areas: social protection, employment, social housing, education, health, environment, and equity in service delivery. The success of the plan lays on: (1) mobilizing all sectors, including private sector to reduce poverty and inequality; (2) produce institutional arrangements of public sector in order to avoid redundancy, overlapping responsibilities and waste of resources; (3) empowering the public institutions responsible for promoting community-based approach; (4) setting official poverty line for harmonizing the concept across public institutions; (5) improving technological capacity for accessing the needs and service performance; (6) developing creative mechanisms for funding pro-poor actions.
	The first intervention is to fill the poverty gap in the whole country using conditional cash transfers. Many specific interventions on the poor areas are expected to produce positive impacts on the reduction of the health inequality, such as: dismantling of asbestos housing in 5 years; implementing community-based childhood care and education services; implementing community schools to promote emotional, physical, and creative learning.
	One group of interventions was designed to reduce the barriers to access basic health services. The implementation of mobile clinics for youth-friendly and stigma-free healthcare services for providing sexual and reproductive healthcare services for youth, sex workers, people living with HIV/AIDS, people who inject drugs, and men who have sex with men.
	Other community-based environmental interventions were designed to improve the sustainability in the poor areas. They comprise: increase waste recycling; producing income generating green jobs in textiles and manufacturing; developing alternative livelihoods from coastal and marine zones in management of communal forests and sustainable collection of native plant species; and to enhance ecotourism.
	A third layer of policy interventions refer to improve living conditions and to overcome the exclusions mechanisms related to barriers for reaching the health systems. Living conditions encompasses a wide list of factors such as health behaviours and the hazards present in the working place. In relation to health behaviours is well known that tobacco consumption and poor diet are associated with socioeconomic status both in developed and developing countries. Thus, price interventions can reduce health inequalities, such as increasing taxation on unhealthy habits (alcohol and tobacco consumption) or providing subsidy to stimulate the healthy ones (Hill et al. 2014; McGill et al. 2015). Interventions to control diseases associated with poverty are also part of the strategy to reduce health inequality. More challenging is to promote the reduction of the barriers to access the health services. Kidd (2017) has used the concept of social exclusion to identify the main barriers of access to social policy services, as ‘the process through individuals or categories of the population are wholly or partially excluded from full participation in the society in which they live’. He identifies three dimensions that restrict or block the access of vulnerable populations to diverse social programmes. He three dimensions require specific strategies for dealing with associated problems. The Kidd’s social exclusion dimensions are described below, with focus adjusted on main problems and practical policy responses present in health sector:
	 	1. Exclusionary forces. It is related to the view from those sectors that hold major share of power in the society over marginalized groups. Civil servants and institutions become embedded by discriminatory practices, institutional blindness, and no recognition of claims demanded by some groups. A large number of populations groups can be affected by discriminatory practices, such as: indigenous populations in Latin America, religious minorities in Asia, women in Arabic countries, Albinos in Africa, and disabled population in many continents. Recent interventions in Mauritius (Box 2.5.1) and Bangladesh (Box 2.5.2) have aimed to remove the barriers to health services and social protection schemes.
	2. Structural disadvantages. They comprehend infrastructure deficits (such as roads, transportation, health facilities), lack of telecommunications systems, exposure to natural disasters (such as water crisis), and low levels of economic activity, interfering in all provision of services market. They are very associated with geographical factors and low economic dynamism of the areas located is the countryside of developing countries. Botswana (Box 2.5.3) have promoted an extensive shift on health programmes in order to improve the infrastructure of health services in poor rural areas. Brazil (Box 2.5.4) also present a relevant experience of how the interactive effects of primary healthcare and social transfers programmes can reduce morbimortality related to poverty-related diseases.
	3. Limitations in capabilities. Some individual states or attributes may reduce the capacity to engage with public authorities and civil servants. The list of conditions is extensive, such as: disabilities, mental disorders, low education (literacy and numeracy), poor linguistic fluency, being exposed to domestic violence and abuse, low self-confidence, lack of available time, care responsibilities for children, elderlies, and ill persons.
	 	Box 2.5.2 Reducing poverty-related diseases in Bangladesh
	Bangladesh is one of the most populated, dense, and disaster-prone country in the world. With a territory of almost the size of England and Wales together, it accounted for 163 million people in 2016. In the last 20 years, it has achieved remarkable results on improving child and women health, despite of its modest public spending in health (2.6% of GDP in 2015), with meagre domestic general government health expenditure (0.39% % of GDP) in the same year according to the World Bank. The impressive health achievements at low cost turned Bangladesh in a role model for developing countries in the region (WHO 2015).
	A mix of actors (public, private, and NGO) have contributed for the achievements on rapidly improvement of health indicators, such as infant mortality, under-5 mortality, and maternal mortality rates, morbidity rates from some infectious diseases including malaria, tuberculosis, diarrhoea, visceral leishmaniosis, HIV/AIDS, nutritional deficiencies, immunization coverage, and access to medicine (WHO 2015). Between 1990 to 2015, the under-5 mortality rate and maternal mortality ratio fell, respectively, to 73.8% and 69.1% (Ahmed 2016). The fall in mortality has produced significant impact in both life expectancy at birth and in fertility rate. Between 1990 and 2016, the total life expectancy at birth jumped from 58.4 to 72.49. When stratified by gender, that gains are greater for women. For men, the variation for this indicator in the period was from 58.05 to 70.89, while for women it moved from 58.78 to 74.29. Between 1990 and 2016, the total fertility rate declined from 4.49 to 2.1 (World Bank 2018). The demographic indicators suggest significant improvement of health conditions for women. That is a remarkable achievement for a patriarchal society with a tradition of gender disparities in all areas.
	The results are associated with actions from different sectors, including health, education, social protection, infrastructure, and economic development. Some health programmes achieved international recognition such as: expanded immunization programme, oral rehydration, prevention, and treatment of targeted infectious diseases and undernourishment. An interdependent set of determinants are associated with these heath gains, such as the increase in female schooling, which in turn was strongly stimulated by the Female Stipend Programme designed to increase female secondary education and to delay marriage and childbearing (Hahn 2018).
	 	Box 2.5.3 Fighting poverty as part of development strategy in Rwanda
	After violent conflicts in Rwanda in the mid-90s, that included a genocide in 1994, the country experienced a rapid and sustained growth, sharp poverty reduction, and reduced inequality. According to Verpoorten (2014), among the most relevant drivers are: massive aid; increased public investment on health, education, and agriculture; the fertility transition; and the rise in international prices of the commodities.
	The World Bank Open Data allows for comparison between the immediate post-conflict period with the current context. The net official development assistance received by the country increased from USD$321 million (2000) to USD$1.148 billion (2016). The secondary school enrolment (% gross) increased from 11% (2000) to 37% (2016). The health indicators presented substantive improvement, such as: the total life expectancy grew from 48 years at birth (2000) to 67 years (2016), and the total fertility rate declined from 5.6 births per woman to 3.9, respectively, in the same years of reference. Its economic prospects are marked by the real GDP growth averaged at about 8% per year (between 2001 and 2015).
	The development policy of Rwanda is shaped by the Vision 2020 (long-term) and the second Economic Development and Poverty Reduction Strategy—EDPRS 2 (medium-term). They stress the combination of economic with social goals, such as: economic transformation with poverty reduction, e.g. moving the country from agriculture-based economy to knowledge-based and service-oriented-economy while reducing the percentage of population living on poverty from 30% by less than 9% by 2020 (World Bank 2017).
	Rwanda also promoted a health sector reform that produced a relevant impact on maternal and infant health. According to Bucagu (2012), between 2006 and 2010, the improvements on the heath sector was particularly high in rural areas as a consequence of scaling up of facility-based childbirth policy based on: the heath workforce skills, performance-based financing, community-based health insurance, better governance.
	The data compiled by the World Bank Open Data accounts that under-5 mortality rates per 1,000 live births fell from 195 in 2000 to 39 in 2016. That is strongly correlated with the rise in the coverage of the proportion of births attended by skilled health staff, which raised from 31% (2000) to 91% (2016). The DHS 210 allowed for comparison between the top and bottom quintile of wealth, indicating small difference on health indicators between the two groups, such as: antenatal care (at least one visit), DPT3 and measles immunizations, full immunization coverage (1 year), early initiation of breastfeeding, vitamin A supplementation (WHO 2013). The difference in percentage points between the two groups (top/bottom) varied from –1.6 (early initiation of breastfeeding) to 8.6 (full immunization coverage). At that time, the biggest difference was related to births attended by skilled health staff. The access of the bottom quintile was 61.2% while top quintile was covered by 85.9%. The subsequent progress on the indictor had reduced that gap.
	 	Box 2.5.4 The interactive effects of primary healthcare and social transfers on the reduction of health inequalities in Brazil
	From 1981 to 2014, Brazil presented one of the most remarkable drops in poverty in the world. According to the World Bank Data (2018), the poverty head count ratio at US$ 1.90 a day (2011 PPP) fell from 21.4% to 2.8% of the population in the period. The indicator refers to the population classified as ‘extreme poor’. From 1980 to 2014, according to the Brazilian Census Bureau (IBGE), the infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live birth) fell from 69.12 to 14.4, suggesting that the gains on poverty reduction influenced the improvement of public health indicators, as it is largely described in the scientific literature in relation to different countries. What is surprising is the fall of the GINI Index that was long stabilized from 1981 to 2003 around 58, reaching 51.3 in 2015 (World Bank 2018). Three determinants seemed to be associated with the reduction of poverty and inequality: the rise of the formal employment and the minimum wage, and the fast increase of the coverage of the social transfer programmes, which Bolsa Familia Programme is the major one in Brazil. The former was particularly relevant for protecting the extreme poor population against socioeconomic adversities, accounting for 66% in the reduction on the severity of poverty (Tesouro Nacional 2016).
	The Brazilian primary healthcare programme (Family Health Strategy, FHS) is the biggest of its kind in the world. In 2018, it covered 206 million people (98.5% of the Brazilian population). More than 263,000 community health agents, organized in more than 42,000 teams, deliver a comprehensive and preventive healthcare services to the local populations. There is strong evidence of the contribution of the FHS on the reduction of infant mortality, in particular post-neonatal mortality due to diarrhoea and respiratory infections, also improving oral health, and increasing the detection of neglected disease and the reporting of vital data (Macinko and Harris 2015). Despite being a universal programme, its presence is more relevant to poor populations that use only the public health system, which contributes to the reduction of health inequalities. The FHS has contributed to the reduction of the disparities between Black/Pardo and White populations in relation to deaths due to ambulatory-care-sensitive conditions (Hone et al. 2017).
	The effect of the poverty alleviation (including better nutrition) component of the Bolsa Familia with the incentive for accessing FHS is associated with the reduction of under-5 years of age mortality (Rasella et al. 2013), and the incidence of tuberculosis (Nery et al. 2017) and leprosy (De Andrade et al. 2018), among the poorer municipalities.
	The interactive effects of social transfer and high coverage primary healthcare programmes are not only effective, but also very efficient. In 2017, the investment on Bolsa Family Programme represented only 0.43% of the Brazilian GDP, while FHC responded for just 0.31 of the GDP (Senado Federal do Brasil 2018).





Social participation


	Social participation is usually indicated as a condition for the sustainability of health inequality interventions in terms of funding, content, and governance. When active, it can prevent political interference on the health systems, specially under the shift of governments. It is considered a fundamental component of the institutionalization process and referred in many targets of the Agenda 2030. However, social participation refers to a wide set of engagements of representatives on policy fora, including inequalities of access to decision-making processes.
	Arnstein (1969) described the participatory process as a ladder with eight steps, which social participation would vary from information to citizen control, e.g. different degrees of access to power from convening only to inform about decision taken elsewhere to effective participation.
	Gaventa (2006) suggests a more complex model (cube shape), which participation can vary in three different levels (local, national, and global). The spaces for participation can be closed, invited, or claimed/created. And forms of power per se can be:
	 	1. Visible, if the decision-making process is observable;
	2. Hidden, if the setting of the political agenda is controlled by powerful individuals and institutions;
	3. Invisible, if the controllers operate through psychological or ideological mechanism, preventing the appreciation of inconvenient topics.





Conclusions


	In the recent decades, poverty has presented a sharp decline in all regions. However, in Africa, Asia, and in the Americas, poverty is still a vulnerability experienced by large parts of the population. That risk is exacerbated by economic crises that exterminate jobs, and shrink the fiscal space, thus compromising the countries’ level of social protection and safety nets. The face of poverty and the extreme poverty is changing, becoming more urbanized and affecting the older population, while remaining highly concentrated in rural areas and among children. If poverty is moving down, socioeconomic inequality is growing in size and complexity. Global and national wealth concentrations challenge the capacity of the states to produce equity, integration, and the feeling of living in a fair society.
	Both poverty and inequality are no longer isolated national issues. The degree of economic and cultural integration at the global level shows how the prosperity of some social groups across the planet may be connected, through a complex web of economic unfair advantages, to the unfavourable condition of far larger population groups. The migration crisis faced specially in Africa and Asia, and secondarily in Europe illustrates that natural disasters, political conflicts, economic crises, religious or ethnical rivalries can drive masses of destitute people towards safer areas, expanding the effects of a context, which combines recent crisis with historical poverty to other regions.
	Poverty and inequality interfere on the health dimensions: determinants of health, access to promotive and preventive actions, and health intervention. As a consequence, an inequal health patterns of diseases, deaths, and disabilities flows across the different population groups. Health inequality is present across the planet with far more intensity on the poorer areas and dwellings.
	Policies for fighting poverty and inequality require local, national, and global approaches. The Agenda 2030 is a laudable initiative for presenting a multisectoral approach for confronting simultaneously health problems and their social determinants. The commitments of the countries encompass fighting poverty, hunger, health problems, and inequalities in articulation with environmental and economic interventions. However, the lack of a clear funding strategy limits its feasibility.
	National and local interventions have decisively contributed to reducing health inequalities. Leveraging social participation has helped to promoting public policies for reducing health inequalities. Different health and other social policy initiatives from countries such as Bangladesh, Rwanda, Brazil, and Mauritius show alternatives ways for improving the health status of the population while reducing health inequalities.
