2.6


Genomics and public health


	Veron Ramsuran and Tulio de Oliveira





Introduction


	In the last two decades there have been several significant advances in the field of genomics. Some of these advancements include, the completion of the Human Genome Project in 2003, use of genomic tools to diagnose patients at point-of-care facilities, and the use of gene editing technology to cure several diseases. The discipline of ‘public health genomics’ emerged as a need to provide ‘responsible and effective translation of genome-based knowledge and technologies for the benefit of the population’ (Bellagio 2005, in Bellagio 2019). It is becoming increasingly accepted that the one size fits all approach is going to be outdated soon. Targeted personalized medicines, therapies, and interventions approach will be the preferred form of treatment in the not too distant future (Molster et al. 2018).
	Genomics has served as the platform for ‘precision medicine’, which utilizes the advances made by genomic technologies to provide information that is person centric. Determining the interactions of an individual’s genes, environment, and lifestyle to deliver a targeted intervention specific to that person (Khoury et al. 2017). The rapid advancement of genomic technologies has led to significant volumes of individual and population level data. Combining data generated, at the individual level on genes, environment, behaviour, and other social and economic determinants of health, provide a useful new approach of utilizing big data to guide the right intervention to the right people at the right time, has been termed ‘precision public health’ (Khoury et al. 2017).
	The fields of public health genomics, precision medicine, and precision public health have proven important aspects in improving population health. However, despite the advancements made, there are still improvements that need to be implemented to significantly improve health, especially within the developing countries. In this chapter we discuss the advancements made within the field and highlight challengers or future directions.
	Genetic variation has been shown to associate with a number of clinical outcomes. These variations could be single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), combinations of SNPs within a gene or in multiple genes and chromosomal aberrations (Molster et al. 2018). Genetic testing can be used as a diagnostic or a predictive tool to screen individuals who present with or are at risk for a particular disease or to determine a suitable course of treatment through pharmacogenomic studies. As a predictive tool, it allows for newborn screening of metabolic diseases such as phenylketonuria, it can be used to determine if individuals are carriers of a recessive trait which can be passed on to offspring, it allows non-invasive testing of foetuses for genetic disorders or chromosomal abnormalities and it can also be used during in-vitro fertilization to test if an embryo has a particular genetic or chromosomal abnormality. Genetic testing methods vary depending on the question being asked. Simple tests such as SNP genotyping and target gene capture with sequencing are used for single-gene disorders or Mendelian diseases. Chromosomal disorders on the other hand are abnormalities of the chromosome structure or number and these are detected usually through karyotype analyses which reveals minimal information about the genetic code itself. Finally, there are the polygenic diseases that are caused by a collection of mutations that may occur across a number of different genes contributing to a given phenotype (Khoury et al. 2017). For example, there are several combinations of mutations that can lead to hypertension, coronary artery disease, and neuropsychiatric disorders. Testing for these disorders can sometimes be more complicated especially when the causative genes are unknown. When the causative genes are known, targeted sequencing of specific genes can be performed. However, when they are unknown it becomes more beneficial to perform whole exome (WES) or whole genome sequencing.
	The era of genome-wide association studies has allowed us to identify variants across the genome that contribute to a disease phenotype. Many of the variants identified that reach genome-wide significance are found within the non-protein coding regions of the genome. One of the major benefits of performing whole genome sequencing (WGS) is that it covers variation in the coding and noncoding regions of the genome. Another is that WGS data from an individual does not change over time and contains a plethora of invaluable information about the health outcomes one might experience in their lifetime (Molster et al. 2018).





Public health genomic tests currently in use


	The rapid proliferation of genetic tests has made it possible to detect a range of health problems at the clinic level or direct-to-consumer for personal genetic tests. According to the Genetic Testing Registry (GTR) (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gtr/), a central location of submitted genetic test information hosted by the National Institute of Health, has 60,027, 11,971 conditions, 18,631 genes from 526 labs across the world (last accessed 16 August 2019) (NCBI 2019). The United States still dominates the number of labs contributing to the GTR, about 50% of the information submitted originates from a United States-based laboratory. The conditions reported range from several rare diseases to a variety of common diseases. The risk assessment, predictive, diagnostic, and prognostic are described for the tests. The information provided on the GTR is voluntary based submissions and is not verified for accuracy (NCBI 2019). The application of these tests ranges from diagnostic, predictive, and reproductive genetic testing, which could be used in response to a specific clinical problem or as a screening tool.





Diagnostic genomic testing


	The diagnostic genomic testing is often used to confirm a clinical diagnosis. The genetic information obtained proves valuable to relatives and for monitoring of treatment. The finding of genetic makers observed within an individual that is linked to an inherited disease should encourage their family members to perform the diagnostic test (Molster et al. 2018).





Predictive genomic testing


	Genetic variants linked to a person’s risk of developing heritable disorders are used as predictive tools or biomarkers. There are a few tests that have received significant attention due to their usefulness for screening before signs or symptoms appear. These predictive tests include screening for cancers, newborn diseases, and pathogen detection.





Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer


	More than 50 hereditary cancer syndromes have been reported and genetic predictive testing is available for most of these cancers (NCI 2019). Mutations within the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes have been associated with Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer (HBOC). These genes have tumour suppressor abilities and serve the function of repairing damaged DNA. Therefore, mutations within these genes inhibits the overall functioning. In breast cancer mutations account for 5% of all cases, while within ovarian cancer mutations account for 10–15% of cases (Armstrong et al. 2019). Women with BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations have a significantly higher lifetime risk of developing breast cancer (about 50–85%) and ovarian cancer (about 15–40%) chance. There are several thousand mutations that have been identified within the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes (BRCA 2019). Many of these mutations do not contribute towards cancers, while certain mutations have the ability to cause truncated proteins when translated. Understanding the genetics basis of mutations with regards to HBOC from diverse ethnic backgrounds around the world is the aim of collaborative efforts like the BRCA Exchange programme (BRCA 2019). Resources that provide clinical significance of genetic variants specific to the country and ethnicity an individual originates from has greater relevance to the patient than general information.
	Apart from BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, which show the strongest lifetime risk for developing breast cancer, other human genes have also been linked to breast cancer predisposition. The genes identified and the lifetime risk for breast cancer are TP53 (50–80%), PTEN (50–85%), CDH1 (39–52%), STK11/LKB1 (35–50%), PALB (20–30%), CHEK2 (15–25%), NF1 (15–25%), and p16 (15–25%) (NCI 2019). Risk genes for ovarian cancer include BRIP1, RAD51C, and RAD51D (NCI 2019). Genomic testing is currently being offered direct to consumers or through healthcare providers and genetic counsellors.





Newborn screening


	Infants that are a few days old undergo predictive testing as a form of newborn screening (NBS). A growing list of NBS tests provide predictive evidence that an infant is at risk for certain metabolic, hormone, and genetic diseases (Therrell et al. 2015; Urv and Parisi 2017). The metabolic disorders NBS examines includes; phenylketonuria (PKU), methylmalonic acidaemia, maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), tyrosinemia, citrullinemia, and medium chain acyl CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency. Congenital hypothyroidism and congenital adrenal hyperplasia are the hormone disorders tested. Some of the other disorders tested can include sickle cell disease, haemoglobin SC disease, beta thalassemia, galactosemia, biotinidase deficiency, cystic fibrosis, severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II), mucopolysaccharidosis type 1, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and spinal muscle atrophy (SMA) (Therrell et al. 2015; Urv and Parisi 2017). Results from these tests provide information for diagnosis, treatments, follow-up, and evaluation. Most the genetic testing performed for NBS is performed on mass spectrometry, which allows multiple conditions to be screened for at once. Traditional genetic testing, such as next-generation sequencing is not recommended as the initial technique for NBS, mainly due to the time taken to receive results (Berg et al. 2017; Ceyhan-Birsoy et al. 2017). Currently, researchers are exploring alternate DNA-based genetic tests to complement existing NBS methods (Friedman 2015).





Preimplantation and prenatal genetic testing


	Genetic testing that determines if an embryo possesses genetic abnormalities prior to in-vitro fertilization is termed preimplantation genetic testing. This screening test decreases the chance of having a child with genetic abnormalities, since only embryos ‘passing’ the test are implanted into the uterus. Whole genome and exome sequencing are used to screen the embryos.
	Another test, which examines genetic changes present within genes and chromosomes from a foetus is termed prenatal genetic testing. This test allows for detection of disorders such as Down’s syndrome and neural tube defect. Results from this test provide parents with information to prepare for the child’s care after birth, some parents choose termination of pregnancy. Novel testing methods have been evolving to detect genetic abnormalities, which include whole genome or exome sequencing (Vora and Wapner 2018). Measuring the cell-free DNA (cfDNA) from the foetus, which circulate in the mother’s blood, serves as a form of non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) (Vora and Wapner 2018). NIPT whole genome or exome sequencing have also been reported (Fan et al. 2012; Kitzman et al. 2012), however, these techniques still possess a few limitations (i.e. cost of sequencing, limited cell-free placental DNA, and requirement of paternal DNA to determine the fetal genome).





Pathogen genomics


	The use of genomics within pathogen detection, specifically infectious diseases, has made the greatest advances in genomics of public health. Advances in molecular technologies and bioinformatics have allowed researchers to examine pathogen genomes more rapidly, which has led to altering both medical and public health practice (Gwinn et al. 2019). Some of the public health applications for pathogen genomics, as described by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), are diagnosing infection, investigating outbreaks, describing transmission patterns, monitoring antimicrobial resistance, and developing interventions, including vaccines (CDC 2019). The CDC has an advanced molecular detection (AMD) programme that uses the latest technology to examine the key areas of pathogen genomics and has committed to making genomic data freely available. Access to pathogen genomic data is key to understanding pathogen mutations that could threaten public health, identifying new pathogens, development of diagnostic tests and determining and monitoring outbreaks (CDC 2019). Increasing the number of countries that subscribe to the data sharing model will dramatically improve pathogen genomics.
	Next-generation sequencing is currently being used for pathogen genomics which provide rapid and reliable results compared to traditional clinical diagnostics. A new sequencing method, nanopore sequencing, has the potential to be the biggest game-changer for public health genomics. The first available commercial instrument has unrivalled portability (i.e. sequencing can be performed at any location, even from the outbreak site). This was demonstrated by studies that used nanopore sequencing in a mobile genomics laboratory that travelled through rural Brazil monitoring the genetic diversity of Zika virus (Faria et al. 2017) and yellow fever virus (Faria et al. 2018). The sequences produced from these studies were analysed in real time, which allowed for the generation of pathogen diversity, distribution, and transmission data. Apart from the device portability, nanopore sequencing has a number of other benefits such as fast sample preparation, flexibility, long sequence reads, and relatively low cost. These benefits make this technology an attractive option as a first line strategy for pathogen sequencing in clinical and public health settings (Besser et al. 2017; Quainoo et al. 2017; Gwinn et al. 2019).
	Technologies aiming to be implemented within a clinical health setting need to meet certain criteria in order to be fully utilized and provide public health benefit. Some of these criteria include, ease of use, cost-effectiveness, rapid results, minimized risk to patients, extended shelf life of reagents and the ability to function within resource-limited settings (i.e. interrupted electricity and extreme temperatures). The GeneXpert MTB/RIF test is one example where the technology has tremendous potential due to the ability to detect tuberculosis (TB) and the multidrug resistant form with very high sensitivity and specificity. However, this test does not meet some of the requirements to function effectively within a resource-limited setting, which has a large proportion of the TB infected patients (Evans 2011; Van Rie et al. 2011). It is therefore suggested that new technologies targeting diseases prevalent within resource-limited settings carefully consider the criteria to achieve maximum impact on public health.





Evaluation of genetic testing


	Genetic testing is a rapidly expanding area with many clinical applications. As mentioned earlier the GTR (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gtr/), there are serval genetic tests currently being used around the world. While the introduction of new genetic tests creates tremendous potential for improving patient care, it is essential to evaluate these tests thoroughly to ensure that they are accurate and lead to improved patient outcomes when used in clinical practice settings. Therefore, methods have been developed to guide stakeholders (patients, clinicians, healthcare system policymakers, payers, and public health officials) in the assessment of tests, including genetic tests, in a broad array of clinical settings. The process of implementing a molecular genetic test for diagnostic use is complex and involves many levels of assessment and validation. The key components of the process, as detailed by the ACCE framework, are analytical validation, clinical validation, clinical utility, and consideration of the ethical, legal, and social implications of the test (Pitini et al. 2018). Analytical validity and clinical validity are the two main measures of accuracy that apply to genetic tests. Another measure of the quality of a genetic test is its usefulness, or clinical utility (Holtzman and Watson 1999).
	 	• Analytical validity refers to how well the test predicts the presence or absence of a particular gene or genetic change (Teutsch et al. 2009), i.e. can the test accurately detect whether a specific genetic variant is present or absent?
	• Clinical validity refers to how well the genetic variant being analysed is related to the presence, absence, or risk of a specific disease (Teutsch et al. 2009; Wylie Burke 2014).
	• Clinical utility refers to whether the test can provide information about diagnosis, treatment, management, or prevention of a disease that will be helpful to a consumer (Teutsch et al. 2009; Wylie Burke 2014).
	The Agency of Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) report evaluated the four commonly used methods that cover the principal domains of test evaluation used in the environment of genetic testing. The four methods include; the US Preventative Services Task force (USPSTF) method (Harris et al. 2001; Trinite et al. 2009), the Fryback Thornbury hierarchy (Fordyce and Douglas 2017), the ACCE model and the Evaluation of Genomic Applications in Practice and Prevention (EGAPP) model (Teutsch et al. 2009). Framework such as Fryback–Thornbury hierarchy provide general conceptual guidance, analytic framework such as USPSFT and EGAPP provide additional benefit for important questions regarding the relevant population. A framework of interest was the McMaster University evaluation due to its thoroughness and richness in detail for making decisions about genetic testing (Giacomini et al. 2003). Also reviewed was the Genetic Testing Evidence Tracking Tool (GETT). GETT allows (1) researchers to summarize the current evidence and to identify knowledge gaps for further research, and; (2) stakeholders to collect data related to a given molecular test and improve their decision-making process (Rousseau et al. 2010).
	In the USPSTF method, the purpose is defined as preventive interventions in primary care. It provides a formal analytic framework; evidence assessment related to key questions to establish a chain of evidence. The downfall of focusing on preventive services results in a focus on clinical utility outcomes that are not relevant to all clinical applications (Sawaya et al. 2007). In contrast, the Fryback–Thornbury hierarchy, recognizes the clinical value of diagnostic efficacy and diagnostic thinking. It provides a hierarchic representation of levels of efficacy for medical tests, which allows an evaluator to determine what evidence types need to be assessed for a given test purpose or desired outcome (Morrison and Boudreau 2012). However, this method lacks a formal evidence-based assessment procedure. ACCE is an analytic process for evaluating evidence on genetic tests. It has a standard set of 44 questions that are organized according to different evidence types (analytic validity, clinical validity, clinical utility, ELSI) (Sanderson et al. 2005). This method provides a highly granular approach to assessing different evidence types. However, ACCE does not provide details on evaluating the strength of evidence. It was developed for single-gene tests and may be difficult to extend to multigene panels or genome-scale sequencing test. EGAPP has a systematic approach to evidence-based assessment of genetic tests (Teutsch et al. 2009).
	A hybrid approach using analytic framework similar to USPSTF and the evaluation of evidence types articulated by ACCE might provide an enhanced method. The flexibility of this framework allows to evaluate different topics in genetic testing including a wide array of potential outcomes of interest, and integration of formal evidence-based reviews (Sanderson et al. 2005). The downside is the flexibility to evaluate different topics in genetic testing focus on single-gene tests that may be difficult to extend to broader genomic technologies. GETT provides structure for systematic identification and organization of published evidence on genetic testing. GETT comprises 72 clearly defined items/questions, grouped into 10 categories and 26 subthemes, including an overview of disease epidemiology and genetics, the available diagnostic tools, and their analytical and clinical performances, availability of quality control programmes, laboratory, and clinical best practice guidelines, clinical utility, impact on healthcare, and psychosocial, ethical, and legal implications. The method helps stakeholders to determine whether the knowledge base is sufficient for genetic technology assessment (Rousseau et al. 2010). The disadvantage of this method is the lack of details on evaluating the strength of evidence; developed for single-gene tests and may be difficult to extend to multigene panels or genome-scale sequencing tests. The McMaster University framework is an evaluation model to guide public coverage for new predictive genetic tests in Ontario, Canada (Giacomini et al. 2003). This method combines technology assessment with coverage decision-making from payer’s perspective. It defines criteria for determining coverage, anticipates the need for payers to identify evidentiary thresholds, and considers conditional coverage scenarios. Since it is developed for the Canadian health system, it lacks a formal evidence-based assessment procedure.
	In order to achieve the full potential of genetic tests and to avoid inappropriate use, genomic tests need to be broadly understood and a dialogue between different types of clinicians, researchers, and drug companies needs to be facilitated. The frameworks mentioned earlier are intended to facilitate ongoing discussion and developmental activities among manufacturers, test researchers, systematic reviewers, regulators, and other policymakers. These discussions need to then facilitate understanding among clinicians and patients. Future frameworks should be broad enough to be applied to a wide variety of genomic testing. It is appreciated that the complexities and rapid advances within genomics (next-generation sequencing) and related fields (proteomics, metabolomics) will necessitate re-evaluating and tailoring frameworks over time.
	Future aspects require examining patient outcome efficacy to determine if patients benefit from the test and if patients that take the test do better than similar patients who do not. Another aspect is observing at societal level, it should be noted that genetic testing should have a favourable effect on the health and allow effective health interventions throughout the entire population (Hall and Olopade 2005; Phillips et al. 2014). It is also important to examine ethical, legal, and social implications of genomic medicine (ELSI) and the effects of applying genetic technologies on a large scale (Clayton 2003). Technical efficacy for accurate detection of genetic variants, analytic, sensitivity, and specificity also include therapeutic and management efficacy as well as diagnostic thinking efficacy. This reflects a useful synthesis of existing frame working efforts to date, it may allow more consistency in definitions for terms and concepts going forward and provide a platform for future collaborative efforts.





Pharmacogenomic testing


	The combination of pharmacology and genomics has led to the new field termed pharmacogenomics, which essentially examines the effects a person’s genes have on response to drugs. Tailoring effective, safe medications and doses according to the genetic makeup is one of the major goals of precision medicine. Most of the drugs currently available and being produced are designed as ‘one size fits all’, however, increasing evidence has demonstrated that drugs do not have the same effect on everyone.
	Pharmacogenomics involves DNA and RNA influence on drug efficacy whereas pharmacogenetics only involves DNA and is usually observed for single genetic variants rather than a combination of variant effects. Pharmacogenomics is a relatively new field of research which is gaining momentum due to the variable effectiveness of drugs between individuals and it is an area of study that shows promise for the design of safe and efficacious treatments in a dose dependent manner according to an individual’s genetic makeup (Roden et al. 2019). The majority of the drugs available today have been created without taking pharmacogenomics into account. These drugs have been created with a one drug fits all approach. Furthermore, many of the drugs that have passed clinical trials have been tested in mostly American/European Caucasians, some Asians, and a few individuals of African descent, therefore, extending these treatments to individuals from developing countries does not always prove successful. One of the major problems with using these non-tailored drugs are the adverse drug reactions (ADRs). ADRs occur at alarming frequencies and are well documented in developed countries. Most clinicians today use a trial and error approach when prescribing drugs. Usually, when an individual fails treatment due to ineffectiveness or the occurrence of a negative reaction the drug dosage is altered, or the drug is changed. This process is time-consuming, costly, and the potential of untimely death. In the US alone it is estimated that more than 100,000 individuals die from serious adverse events every year (Tan et al. 2016). Within developing countries, it is estimated that death by ADRs greatly exceeds that of developed countries. This is mainly due to the genetic variation unaccounted for during drug development. The interindividual genetic diversity within individuals of African descent is several folds higher than other ethnic groups (Masimirembwa et al. 2014), which highlights the dire need for pharmacogenomic drug development within Africa.
	Two major considerations should be considered when establishing whether a drug will prove efficacious in an individual, i.e. pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Pharmacokinetics is the process of absorption, transport to target site, metabolism, and excretion (Roden et al. 2019). Pharmacodynamics is variability in drug action that is not contributed by drug concentrations, and represents changes of the interaction of active drug with its effector molecules or other mechanisms such as variability in disease mechanisms (Roden et al. 2019). A large part of pharmacogenetic traits identified to date have a pharmacokinetic controlling mechanism.





Pharmacokinetic mechanism


	There are two main scenarios that demonstrate how single gene variants affect pharmacokinetics that could lead to large effects. The first example requires the use of bioactivation pathways to achieve the desired therapeutic effects. Changes caused by mutations in the drug metabolizing enzyme can decrease or block the drug effect. An example includes codeine that gets bioactivated to active metabolite morphine with the CYP2D6 gene (Roden et al. 2019). The majority of the variants identified offer partial or complete loss of function. There are fewer variants that lead to gain of functions within the bioactivation pathways, which subsequently leads to excess drug response. An example of gain of function variants include the CYP2C19*17 that was linked to bleeding during clopidogrel therapy (Sibbing et al. 2010).
	The second scenario is demonstrated when pharmacokinetic variants apply large effects during the administration of a drug that possesses a narrow therapeutic range of activity, that leads to either optimum activity or toxic doses. This is mainly through the elimination by a single drug metabolizing system. An example of this scenario is demonstrated by the antileukaemic drug 6-mercaptopurine that gets bio inactivated by thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) and xanthine oxidase. Individuals that are homozygous for the loss of function variants within TPMT exhibit life-threatening bone marrow toxicity (Relling et al. 2019).
	Transporter molecules, responsible for moving drugs into and out of cells, are affected by mutations that possess the capability of altering drug levels at target effector sites. An example of an efflux transporter gene that is affected by variants is the OATP1B1 encoded by SLCO1B1, which are shown to be variable in individuals of African descent (Naidoo et al. 2018; Naidoo et al. 2019).





Pharmacodynamics mechanism


	Some of the initial well-described syndromes affected by pharmacogenetics are from the pharmacodynamics area. The anticoagulant drug warfarin is a well-studied pathway that acts by inhibiting the production of vitamin K dependent clotting factors in order to treat thrombotic disorders. The drug dosage is influenced by genes encoding the cytochrome P450 family (CYP2C9, CYP4F2, CYP2C) of enzymes responsible for the metabolizing the drug as well as a VKORC1 which recycles vitamin K in the body (Belley-Cote et al. 2015; Nagai et al. 2015). Testing for variation within these genes allow clinicians to make informed decisions when administering warfarin. If the drug is administered at a standard dose without testing for variation in these genes it may result in either too much drug in the bloodstream which can lead to excessive bleeding and death or not enough drug which could lead to thrombosis.
	Another example can be observed during HIV treatment, where a combination of antiretrovirals are administered. One such drug known as abacavir has shown serious adverse reactions ranging from fever, nausea, vomiting, and death. Studies have shown that administering abacavir to individuals carrying the HLA-B*57 allele results in increased hypersensitivity and therefore testing for HLA-B*57 is recommended prior to administering abacavir (Sousa-Pinto et al. 2015; Illing et al. 2017). The allele frequency of HLA-B*57 in Caucasians is approximately 6% while in African Americans it is between 2% and 3%. However, in native Africans the allele frequency is much lower. Another HLA-B allele (HLA-B*15:02) has also shown an effect on Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN). HLA-B*15:02 confers risk of the disease mainly within southeast Asian populations, in which the allele is found in relatively high frequencies (Chung et al. 2004). However, a different HLA allele (HLA-A*31:01) has been linked to the SJS/TEN disorder within individuals from European ancestry (McCormack et al. 2011). These studies reporting differing alleles contributing to SJS/TEN highlights the need to examine the genetic profiles for each population the drug is being administered to. However, there is much controversy about whether enforced HLA-B*15:02 testing is cost-effective (Rattanavipapong et al. 2013; Chong et al. 2017). The implementation of a testing campaign, within Hong Kong that examined more than 100,000 patients, showed a decrease in the prescription of carbamazepine and a decrease in related SJS/TEN (Chen et al. 2014). However, the prescription of other antiseizure medications increased in this study and examining this group showed no overall change in SJS/TEN (Chen et al. 2014). The authors report, clinicians preferring antiepileptic drug (AED) therapy that do not require genetic screening are preferred, this exemplifies the need for educational programmes to supplement the implementation of testing programmes.
	An example of the type of infecting organism found within a person also plays a role on the type of drug administered. Maraviroc, an HIV drug that binds onto the HIV entry receptor, CCR5, prevents the virus entering into the cell for viral replication. However, the desired effect of maraviroc is achieved within individuals that possess only the CCR5 receptor strain of HIV. The virus also uses CXCR4 to enter into the cell. Maraviroc does not function with CXCR4 strains of HIV, therefore, health providers need to determine the receptor usage before prescribing the drug (Ryst 2005).





Pharmacogenomics and drug development


	A huge amount of effort and resources goes into the development of drugs to treat a range of diseases and disorders, however, the number of drugs candidates entering clinical trials are very small in number. Increasing evidence suggests that studies examining the human genetic components of the drug have an increased likelihood of successful marketing than those drugs not testing the genetics (Sanseau et al. 2012; Nelson et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2015). Drugs that have proved to be successful in clinical trials still have remarkable failure rates when these drugs are given to the target audience. Since most of these trials are being performed in developed countries and do not take into account the genetic effect on individuals from underdeveloped countries not knowing the human genetics within these populations hinders the desired effect of the drug.
	Ideally, when a drug is created for an individual or individuals within a population, their genetic diversity must be considered. Since the assembly of the first human genome there has been an explosion in the generation of genomic data with projects providing full length whole genome sequences that are curated and annotated. Using this data, there is evidence that the haplotype frequency and overall genetic diversity is much higher in Africans than Caucasians and Asians (Rotimi et al. 2017). Furthermore, within Africans there is an additional spread of genetic diversity which suggests that drugs need to be designed for specific populations. For example, a drug created to treat African individuals from Northern Africa should be reconstructed to treat African individuals in Southern Africa due to their genetic differences. In regions where there is minimal diversity, genetic screening can be used to test whether a drug is suitable for that candidate.
	Currently, there are a number of platforms that offer the ability to test the suitability of a drug. The cheapest and smallest scale screening is the genotyping approach which works using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology to determine the presence of single variants. This can be used when a single SNP has an effect on drug efficacy. Another approach is the use of genome-wide association study (GWAS) to identify the variants carried by an individual. This test provides a more comprehensive picture than the single variant genotyping. Special chips can be designed to suit a specific population or trait. WGS provides the maximum genomic information for an individual. Patients who screen their whole genome can be assessed not only for genetic variants that alter drug efficacy but also a myriad of information such as their susceptibility to infectious diseases as well as the likelihood of developing heritable diseases.
	Pharmacogenomics is a step in the direction towards precision medicine and may help to reduce the burden of disease by improving outcomes with specialized drugs. The epigenome has been shown to have a significant effect on gene regulation and interactions between the genome and epigenome may provide an additional layer of complexity to the field of pharmacogenomics. The use of WGS and whole genome methylation in conjunction with pharmacology will allow us to understand much more about the landscape for treating disease.





Epigenetic therapy


	The field of epigenetics has rapidly expanded in the past few decades to the extent that novel forms of therapy are emerging from this field that warrant discussion in this chapter. It is well established that epigenetic changes contribute to the development of human diseases such as cancer, autoimmune disease, as well as neurodegenerative and psychological disorders (Hahn and Weinberg 2002; Jones and Baylin 2002; Zoghbi and Beaudet 2016). Epigenetics refers to all heritable alterations in gene expression and chromatin structure due to chemical modifications that do not involve changes in the primary nucleotide sequence (Strahl and Allis 2000; Jenuwein and Allis 2001; Nightingale et al. 2006; Bernstein et al. 2007). Epigenetic mechanisms have the ability to either appropriately regulate cell growth (Portela and Esteller 2010; Moosavi and Motevalizadeh Ardekani 2016) or in contrast, dysregulation of epigenetic patterns lead to induction and propagation of disease states (Hahn and Weinberg 2002; Jones and Baylin 2002; Feinberg et al. 2006).
	There are several factors that contribute to epigenetic alterations, the factors with the strongest contribution include DNA methylation, histone modifications, and noncoding RNAs. All of these are crucial mechanisms that ensure the stable propagation of gene activity from one generation of cells to the next (Jenuwein and Allis 2001; Feinberg et al. 2006). Disruption of any of these three distinct and mutually reinforcing epigenetic mechanisms leads to inappropriate gene expression, resulting in cancer development and other ‘epigenetic diseases’ (Jones and Baylin 2002; Egger et al. 2004; Feinberg et al. 2006). In some instances, pathogens have been able to take advantage of epigenetic alterations for their propagation.
	In recent years, scientific interest in epigenetics has increased substantially so that this field represents an important new avenue to advance our understanding of pathogenesis and to help in the development of strategies for disease. It is hoped that by understanding epigenetic mechanisms effective therapies would soon become available. Epigenetic therapy, a relatively new outlook to treatment, involves the use of drugs or epigenome altering tools to change the non-DNA environment to treat medical conditions. There are about 191 clinical trials around the world involving epigenetic therapy, according to the NIH clinical trials database, indicating the potential of this rapidly growing field (NIH 2019). Most of these clinical trials have targeted different forms of cancer, however there are several other diseases which also have been targeted. Drug reposition efforts have been launched to explore epigenetics therapies for non-oncology conditions (Best and Carey 2010). Some of these conditions include diabetes mellitus, depression, rheumatoid arthritis, schizophrenia, etc.





Clinical conditions treated with epigenetic therapy


	DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) enzymes are responsible for the addition of methylation to DNA, these enzymes are inhibited with the drugs 5-azacytidine and 5-aza-20-deoxycytidine. Both drugs have been approved for use by the FDA for the treatment of various forms of cancer. These drugs have been shown to reactivate the cellular antitumor systems repressed by the cancer, enabling the body to weaken the tumour (Foulks et al. 2012; Vendetti and Rudin 2013; Li et al. 2014; Wells et al. 2014). Zebularine, an activator of a demethylation enzyme, has also been used with some success (Kowluru et al. 2013). The wide-ranging effects of these drug on the entire genome may result in major side effects, however, survival rates are significantly increased when the drugs are used for treatment.
	The largest class of epigenetic therapies is inhibitors of histone-modifying enzymes. These include drugs that inhibit histone methyltransferases (HMTs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs) and are the most prevalent form of epigenetic therapy. In addition, there are several compounds that activate HDACs or inhibit HDMs, currently being developed. These include inhibitors of the H3K79 methyltransferase DOT1L for the treatment of Mixed-lineage leukaemia (MLL)-rearranged leukaemias (Barski et al. 2007). The treatment of non-Hodgkin lymphoma involves the inhibitors of the H3K27 methyltransferase EZH2, which form the catalytic component of the PRC2 complex (Bradley et al. 2014). Use of HDAC inhibitors, specifically HDAC6, are being explored for the treatment of certain cancers such as multiple myelomas and a wide variety of haematologic malignancies (Li et al. 2018). Epigenetic therapy also includes the use of bromodomain and extraterminal motif (BET) bromodomain inhibitors. Bromodomains are evolutionary conserved protein-protein interaction modules that preferentially recognize acetylated chromatin (Fujisawa and Filippakopoulos 2017). The use of BET bromodomain inhibitors that possess broad binding specificity have been tested for treatment of advanced haematologic and non-haematologic malignancies (Sanchez and Zhou 2009).
	Treatment of diabetic retinopathy using epigenetic therapy has also been explored. One therapeutic approach includes inhibition of methylation within manganese superoxide dismutase (SOD2) and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP-9). The DNMT inhibitors 5-azacytidine and 5-aza-20-deoxycytidine inhibit the SOD2 and MMP-9 methylation patterns and have been reported to reduce diabetic retinopathy symptoms (Kowluru et al. 2013). Limited success has also been reported for the treatment of this disorder with histone acetyltransferase (HAT) inhibitors epigallocatechin-3-gallate, vorinostat, and romidepsin (Kowluru et al. 2013).
	The epigenetic mechanisms of lupus have been studied in detail, which has assisted the use of epigenetic-based therapies into clinical trials against lupus. A cytidine analogue, Cytarabine, reported to increase DNA methylation, was used for treatment of refractory cutaneous lupus in a human clinical trial (Mishra et al. 2003). Results showed relapse of disease during the fourth week in two-thirds of tested cases, however, treatment with Cytarabine also showed rapid improvement of refractory cutaneous lupus in treated patients (Yung and Richardson 1995).
	There have been many experimental drugs that target epigenetic mechanisms against rheumatoid arthritis (RA). DNMT inhibitors such as 5-azacytidine was used to treat normal synovial fibroblasts and this reproduced RA synovial fibroblasts phenotypes (Kooistra and Helin 2012). Trichostatin A (TSA) and nicotinamide, both HDAC inhibitors, were separately used to reduce TNF-α which in turn reduces IL-6 expression in macrophages isolated from PBMCs of RA patients (Gillespie et al. 2012). Other studies have shown that targeting HDACs, using HDACi such as valproic acid, can mitigate the severity of murine chronic inflammatory arthritis in part via improving regulatory T-cell function (Chung et al. 2003; Saouaf et al. 2009). These show potential therapeutic value, due to their ability to reduce or disrupt the production of inflammatory signals that fuel RA disease activity. Another promising study silenced SIRT1 and promoted apoptosis in RA synovial fibroblasts from synovial tissues and cells from RA patients (Niederer et al. 2011).
	Multiple sclerosis (MS) is another clinical disorder for which investigators have considered epigenetic therapy for treatment. Histone deacetylases inhibitor, such as TSA, has reduced spinal cord inflammation, demyelination, neuronal and axonal loss in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) models, and thus serves as a potential treatment option for MS (Camelo et al. 2005). However, HDAC inhibitors used at the systemic level have shown to negatively affect the generation of new myelin, since HDAC is crucial to developmental of myelination (Marin-Husstege et al. 2002; Shen et al. 2005). Chirivi et al. have proposed citrullination as a target for epigenetic intervention in MS and other inflammatory diseases (Chirivi et al. 2013). The authors also postulate that shielding citrullinated histone epitopes, which play a large role in NET formation, can help prevent the intensification of the inflammatory response in MS and other inflammatory diseases (Chirivi et al. 2013).





Advantages and disadvantages of epigenetic therapy


	Unlike genetic defects, epigenetic defects are potentially reversible and are therefore more amenable to corrective therapeutic reversal. This realization has driven the rapid emergence and expansion of epigenetic drug discovery, and drug-targeting epigenetic enzymes are in the clinic for the treatment of human disorders, especially for clinical management of haematological malignancies and neurological disorders. However, treatments with epigenetic drugs still need to overcome the challenge of avoiding off-target effects. It should be considered that multiple epigenetic enzymes are contained in chromatin complexes, and as a result the inhibition of an epigenetic enzyme can result in changes in other members of the same protein complex. For example, treatment with the HDAC inhibitor sodium butyrate alters the acetylation level of histones, but also affects their methylation status. In addition, drug development based on epigenetics is difficult and expensive similar to other drug targets.





Epigenomic technologies


	Similar to GWAS, epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) could be a diagnostic tool for screening epigenetic disorders. An EWAS is an examination of a genome-wide set of quantifiable epigenetic marks, such as DNA methylation, in different individuals to derive associations between epigenetic variation and a particular identifiable phenotype/trait (Flanagan 2015). Bisulfite conversion is used for the detection of DNA methylation levels, methylated cytosines are saved from conversion to uracil and thus measured using WGS. Whole genome and RNA sequencing are valuable tools for the screening of noncoding RNAs. Continued study of genome sequences can help determine whether new genetic variations are associated with health conditions.





Epigenetic therapy in the future


	Future studies may be able to identify methods for recognition response mechanisms by combining genomic sequencing and gene expression profile. In addition, DNA could also undergo histone modifications, phosphorylation, ubiquitination, sumoylation, and acetylation. Each of these mechanisms could provide novel opportunities for epigenetic therapies in the future. The use of noncoding RNA (ncRNA) is also an avenue that is currently being explored. MicroRNAs (miRNA), a class of ncRNA, that are about 19–24 nucleotides long, prevent the translation of mRNA and protein production (Nam et al. 2009). As miRNAs play critical roles in regulating functions of the cells, disruption in their structure and turnover can cause diseases. There are 651 miRNA clinical trials reported on the NIH clinical trials database (NIH 2019) highlighting the growing interest of this avenue for treatment of clinical disorders. The use of specific miRNA mimics and inhibitors that modulate miRNAs and regulate gene expression could be an attractive avenue for future research. miRNA mimics have shown therapeutic benefit in mouse models of lung cancer (Trang et al. 2011; Kasinski et al. 2015). Therapeutic delivery was demonstrated using mimics of the tumour suppressors, microRNA-34a (miR-34a) and let-7, both of are often downregulated in lung cancer. Specifically, mice treated with miR-34a displayed a 60% reduction in the tumour area compared to mice treated with a miRNA control (Trang et al. 2011). Similar results were obtained with the let-7 mimic. As a single miRNA may be able to target more than one gene it would be interesting to combine several microRNA with different targets so that various proteins involved in different steps of a disease can be regulated, enabling a combinatorial, multitarget approach that could complement combination drug treatment.
	Long noncoding RNA (lncRNAs) should be taken into account as future advances in epigenetic therapy, since lncRNAs could also be regulated by epigenetic mechanisms, including CpG methylation as well as histone marks (Kung et al. 2013). They are involved in chromatin remodelling, as well as transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation, through a variety of chromatin-based mechanisms and via cross-talk with other RNA species (Zampetaki et al. 2018). There are currently 32 clinical trials for lncRNA according to the NIH clinical trials database (NIH 2019). The data gathered so far concerning the involvement of lncRNA in epigenetic regulation is still the tip of the iceberg of this emerging field, and further expansion of these data may reveal untapped targets and pathways amenable to epigenetic therapy. In addition, as mentioned earlier, screening for epigenetic diversity across diverse populations prior to administering epigenetic therapies will assist with the success of the treatment.





Genome editing and public health


	Genome or gene editing provides the ability to edit an organism’s genetic material to achieve a desired trait. Using genome editing technologies researchers can modify precisely specific additions, deletions, and alterations to specific sites within the genome. There are several tools used for genetic editing, however since the advent of clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) there has been much excitement. The reason for the excitement is mainly due to CRISPR being faster, cheaper, increased in accuracy and efficiency when compare to the existing genome editing methods. Some of the common methods used prior to the arrival of CRISPR include meganucleases, zinc fingers nucleases (ZFNs), and transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENS).





Meganucleases


	These are endonuclease molecules, also called homing endonucleases, that can be grouped into five families (Pingoud and Silva 2007). The large recognition site, that is rarely found within an entire genome, allows this tool to function highly specifically for the editing of genomes. The meganucleases carry the genetic portion that influences recombination during homing (Orlowski et al. 2007). Meganucleases have been implemented in an industrial scale to target research, bio-manufacturing, bio-production, and have a potential role in human healthcare. A limitation of this tool is that small sequences that may play a role in disease outcome are not targeted.





Zinc finger nucleases (ZFNs)


	ZFNs are fusion proteins that have been adapted from zinc finger containing transcription factors, which possess numerous site-specific DNA-binding domains. These fusion proteins are linked to the bacterial FokI restriction enzyme, which forms the endonuclease domain (Gupta and Musunuru 2014). A single zinc finger domain possesses the ability to recognize and bind a 3-to 4-bp DNA fragment, the combination of domains allows for the ability to detect a large target DNA sequence. Cleavage of a site in the DNA sequence is bi-directional using two flanking sequences. Once the ZNFs are bound at a specific site in the genome, the two FokI domains dimerize and cuts the DNA, which generates a double stranded break (Urnov et al. 2010; Gupta and Musunuru 2014). A major limitation of this tool has been found to be the off targets effects. For a more precise edit, more zinc finger domains are required, which increases costs of the application (Urnov et al. 2010).





Transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENS)


	This endonuclease has a similar mechanism of action to ZFN. However, instead of ZFN binding to three nucleotides (codon), each nucleotide has its own zinc finger protein (33 to 35 amino acids), which are much larger than ZFNs (Gupta and Musunuru 2014; Miller et al. 2010). In addition to the length advantage, TALENS are also easier to design and have fewer constraints of site selection than the ZFNs. Limitations of TALENS is the large size and their highly repetitive nature (Gupta and Musunuru 2014).





CRISPR-Cas9


	CRISPR is a gene editing tool based on the bacterial adaptive immune system. Bacterial cells retrieve protospacers from invading bacteriophages and incorporates them within their genomes. These protospacers are then used as short guide RNAs by a CRISPR-cas system and target any foreign DNA possessing the matching incorporated protospacer sequence. The invading DNA is cut using the cas9 enzyme, which enables cutting of the double stranded DNA. The CRISPR-Cas9 currently being used in research labs is mimicked from the bacterial system (Hsu et al. 2014). Several versions of a modified Cas9 protein exists, which enables CRISPR gene editing system to be the most versatile and precise tool on the market.





CRISPR-based clinical trials


	CRISPR has the potential to be used as an editing tool for genetic diseases. Recently, a group of scientists produced CRISPR engineered mouse pluripotent stem cells, which are resistant to proinflammatory cytokines. Not only do these engineered cells prevent inflammation, they also alleviate inflammation in chronic inflammatory diseases such as arthritis (Brunger et al. 2017). In 2018, the mutated DMD gene, which causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy, was edited in dogs using the CRISPR-Cas9 system and delivered using an Adeno-associated virus. As a result of CRISPR-Cas9 mediated editing, dystrophin expression was restored in a canine model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Duan 2018).
	Following the success of CRISPR as a therapy against disease in animals, many human clinical trials against various diseases have been initiated. According to the NIH clinical trials database (www.clinicaltrials.gov), a total of 28 CRISPR-based clinical trials are underway by multiple groups targeting a range of diseases including HIV-1 and other viral infections, sickle cell disease, thalassemia, Kabuki syndrome, Leber congenital amaurosis (blindness), malignant hyperthermia, various leukaemias and lymphomas, as well as various cancers (NIH 2019).
	Interest was sparked in 2016, the first phase I pre-clinical trial involving CRISPR gene editing technology in cancer research in China, as well as the second CRISPR initiative in the treatment of two debilitating inherited blood disorders, beta thalassemia (TDT) and sickle cell disease (SCD), both in the United States and by the Swiss (Baylis and McLeod 2017; Nasdaq:CRSP 2019). Currently, these two CRISPR trials are being approved to edit immune cells against tumours and to activate genes that are inactive, making these the initial two out of several human trials that are underway. These treatment approaches may become a novel and powerful therapeutic intervention against various other diseases as well.
	The trial entitled CTX001-121 aims to treat various hemoglobinopathies such as severe SCD and thalassemia. The first patient to be treated with the CTX001 drug had a form of thalassemia. Following treatment, the patient reportedly did not require any blood transfusions (the usual treatment for thalassemia) for 4 months. The first patient with severe SCD was also treated with CXT001 in 2019 (NIH Clinical Trials 2019). There are also plans by the companies behind this trial to run gene therapy trials on patients suffering with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and myotonic dystrophy type 1 (MD1) (Wang et al. 2018).
	In addition to CRISPR, the FDA has approved other gene-based therapies to treat an array of diseases. These include (1) Luxturna, used for the treatment of a different form of Leber congenital amaurosis (blindness—retinal dystrophy) (Maeder et al. 2019); (2) Zolgensma, approved for the treatment of SMA, a leading cause of infant mortality (Pena et al. 2020); and iii) Kymriah, which is an approved cell based therapy for the treatment of some blood cancers such as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) (Montano et al. 2018).
	CRISPR’s potential to hit drug markets as a prescribed therapy against not only genetic but also against infectious diseases is huge. HIV is one infectious disease that has been targeted by CRISPR technology. Using the Cas9/sgRNA parts of the HIV genome was targeted for cleavage in an attempt to decrease the replication of the virus, however, the virus was able to overcome CRISPR editing by escape mutations located within the cas9 cleavage site of the virus (Wang et al. 2016a, b). The therapeutic potential of CRISPR needs further exploration and it is estimated within the next few decades the genome editing tool will play a major role in personalized and public health.





Advantages and limitations of CRISPR


	The important advantage of the CRISPR Cas9 system over other gene editing technologies is the simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and efficiency. In addition, the technology has the potential to be applied directly to embryos to modify target genes, which enables rapid desired affects when compared to alternative gene editing technologies that require use of embryonic stem cells. Another benefit of the CRISPR system is the improved bioinformatic tools that are available to design guide RNAs. Optimizing of experimental conditions is simple and robust, which almost guarantees introduction of the desired edit will be successful. Furthermore, CRISPR can edit virtually any genome, this provides it with the capability to treat diseases, destroy infecting microorganisms, resurrect species, and create healthier foods without the use of antibiotics (Omodamilola and Ibrahim 2018). Additionally, the CRISPR tool proves to be far superior to competitors, due to its ability to modify multiple genes in a single experiment, up to 25 targets have been reported successfully (Campa et al. 2019). CRISPR possesses yet another benefit over competing gene editing technologies with its ability to alter the epigenetic environment. This is achieved by using a deactivated form of the cas9 protein, which does not cut or edit the DNA sequence but instead changes the surrounding epigenetic environment with accessory molecules attached to deactivate cas9 (Bae et al. 2019).
	One of the main limitations of the CRISPR technology is the off-target effects. The guide RNA, which is intended to bind onto a specific target may also bind on other unintended sites resulting in unplanned altering or deactivating of genes, thus producing side effects. The simplicity of the CRISPR tool may also be its downfall, questions about the tools ability to create bioweapons or designer babies are raising significant ethical concerns.





Ethics of CRISPR


	The CRISPR technology received a significant amount of negative attention from November 2018, after the first human babies created from edited embryos were revealed to the world by the Chinese scientist, Dr Jianku He. This sent the scientific research community into debates regarding the ethical, legal, and social implications regarding the germline editing (Kleiderman and Ogbogu 2019). The research has violated Chinese regulations and international bioethical standards. The Chinese regulations on gene editing seem to align with international standards (Isasi et al. 2016; Kleiderman and Ogbogu 2019). In addition to the ethics concerns of the ‘CRISPR babies’ experiment, researchers have also questioned the soundness of the research conducted. The gene targeted for editing, CCR5, is required for viral entry only for the CCR5 strain of the virus, however the CXCR4 viral strain can still be transmitted despite altering the CCR5 gene. There is currently a drug, maraviroc, against CCR5 that has been used in numerous HIV clinical trials. Individuals with mutated forms of CCR5 have an increased risk of symptomatic West Nile virus infection (Glass et al. 2006). These events have certainly created more focused attention on human genetic editing, despite this study not being the first to edit human genes in an embryo (Bonora et al. 2015). Researchers in 2015, reported CRISPR/Cas9-mediated editing of endogenous beta-globin gene in human embryos (Liang et al. 2015). The authors also reported unplanned off-target effects as determined by whole exome sequencing and cautioned the pressing need to further improve the fidelity and specificity of the CRISPR/Cas9 platform (Liang et al. 2015).
	Any future clinical trials aiming to alter human embryos should be subject to much discussion, especially for the need of such an experiment. Due to the simplicity of the technique, potential to leap into the public platform, and the convincing potential applications, it probably wouldn’t be too long before another unorthodox individual announces the results of their human embryo editing experiments.
	The US National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Medicine constituted a multidisciplinary, international committee to review the current status and make recommendations based on the ethical concerns raised (Coller 2019). The report makes recommendations, which include experimental germline genome editing that is subject to restrictions that include research focused on preventing transmission of a serious disease or condition, modification of well-documented DNA changes associated with disease, and research conducted under a set of stringent ethical and regulatory guidelines (Coller 2019). However, with simplicity of use and easy accessibility, mail-order do-it-yourself CRISPR kits are currently available for a few hundred US dollars, experts are concerned about what amateur scientists may achieve with the powerful tool (Sneed 2017). Is the world ready to implement such strategies or should CRISPR remain in a laboratory setting until future stable gene editing techniques are developed? There is also the growing concern of CRISPR being used as a biotechnological threat (Vogel and Ouagrham-Gormley 2018). This technology can make a treatable pathogen become deadly by altering the drug target sites.
	Another major concern is, if CRISPR germline editing eventually becomes regulated and allowed in the future, who will the technology be accessible to? Will it simply be for the rich and famous? The main challenge for nations experimenting with gene editing is to come up with feasible, rational, and ethical guidelines for its practical implementation. CRISPR is still a developing technology, which provides a strong foundation for the development of new advanced tools in the field of gene editing.





Ethical implications of genomics and public health


	The rapid advances in the field of genomics and public health arises with a new set of ethical problems that need to be addressed. A framework by Burke et al. highlights several important aspects of improved population health (Burke et al. 2006). These include engaging with a range of stakeholders that are within and external to the public health and scientific communities. The aim is to provide a support of core activities, some of these include; advising on public policy; design, implementation, and evaluation of preventive and clinical health services; communication and stakeholder engagement; and finally dissemination of knowledge via education and training (Burke et al. 2006). Roberts and colleagues have reviewed in detail some of the emerging issues in public health genomics (Roberts et al. 2014). We provide an updated summary of these emerging issues in this chapter.





Informed consent


	Genomic testing can provide specific confirmation or diagnosis as described earlier, however in certain instances genomic testing may raise more questions, i.e. some tests may not provide meaningful information within the present setting. However, after ongoing interpretation of the results, researchers may find relevant information in the future, therefore the informed consenting process needs to be adequate to deal with these wide range of outcomes (Horton and Lucassen 2019). Several researchers believe we are not achieving valid consent in the genomic setting, since the consent to be valid ‘the patient needs to be competent; they need to be appropriately informed; and their consent needs to be voluntarily given’ (Horton and Lucassen 2019). The process of informing a patient appropriately means possessing a clear understanding of the genetic results obtained, this is in most instances not the case. Even within experts in the field, as demonstrated by the APOE status of Dr James Watson, one of the first people to be sequenced. He released his sequenced genome to online public databases, except for apolipoprotein E (ApoE), which was redacted due to its linkage with Alzheimer’s disease, Dr Watson preferred not to know his status (Nyholt et al. 2009). However, based on linkage information found throughout the rest of the genome, the Alzheimer’s information could be ascertained. The linkage information located in other parts of the genome was only discovered later (Nyholt et al. 2009; Horton and Lucassen 2019). Does this mean the informed consent was violated? If so, what could have been done to better protect Dr Watson? These are some of the questions that should be asked in future when achieving consent in the genomic setting. Dr Watson’s case is just one of many scenarios where public health genomics have left patients with undesirable outcomes. Patients who participate in genomic research should also be informed of both the risks and benefits of testing (Department of Health et al. 2014; Miller et al. 2008).





Prenatal screening


	Within the United States alone, nearly all the 4 million infants born a year are screened for rare genetic diseases (Roberts et al. 2014). Genetic screening has enabled parents to make informed choices regarding the welfare of their child’s health. Testing for Down’s syndrome is especially common in pregnant women over 50 years of age as there is an increased risk of non-disjunction during meiosis resulting in ova that could lead to the birth of a child with Down’s syndrome (Reynolds 2003; Dukhovny and Norton 2018). Some of the symptoms of Down’s syndrome include learning disabilities, stunted or delayed growth as well as characteristic facial features, however, many of the more serious health problems associated with this disease can be treated. The life expectancy of children with Down’s has increased dramatically as there is now reduced stigma and better healthcare available. Genetic testing provides the ability for a positive Down’s syndrome infant to be treated earlier, however, certain parents choose the option of premature pregnancy termination (Dukhovny and Norton 2018). As the number of prenatal genetic tests become available, there needs to be a balance of autonomy and distributive justice (Dukhovny and Norton 2018).





Data storage and sharing


	Sharing of genomic data has become an actuality with the advent of genomic databases that allow access to thousands of whole genome sequences for the purpose of scientific advancement (Mathaiyan et al. 2013; Dijkers 2019). At the point of data collection, is the participant privy to their own information? Does that information remain within the institute or is it shared with other institutes or companies? As WGS becomes more affordable the risk of data sharing with employers and health insurances or medical aids becomes a potential problem. If an individual who works in a laborious field is predicted to develop Parkinson’s, sensitive information such as this may lead the employer to retrench him/her due to this information. Additionally, information like this may cause their insurance premiums to skyrocket or medical aid be denied or delayed. Access to such sensitive data can lead to its abuse allowing government, employers, and companies to exploit individuals (Dijkers 2019).
	The need for confidentiality cannot be disputed when performing genomic research. The genetic data from WGS gives important information about current or potential diseases as well as risk of disease. In the case of rare diseases, it may be easy for the identity of the patient to be leaked because of the rarity of the disease itself (Dijkers 2019). The breach of confidentiality could expose the individual to discrimination in the workplace as well as in social settings. Proper channels for blinding patient data are necessary similar to what is performed during clinical trials, however, there needs to be additional measures to ensure that there is no leak in data.





Storage of samples


	Biological specimens can be frozen for many years at a time. Researchers use these samples to answer many questions and may store them for use in future studies. Indefinite storage of samples means that the research being conducted on these samples will never end (Vaz and Srinivasan 2014). Although consent may be given by the participant for a particular study or overall type of study there is no definite way for them to know what will be done on the samples in the future (McGuire and Beskow 2010). Generally, when consent is given there is very little a patient can do regarding the studies being performed on their samples. Considering the stability of DNA, these risks to privacy of genetic and personal information does not decrease with time. Considering the long-term storage and dissemination of samples, should researchers constantly request updated consent, where the patient is informed of new or ongoing studies and recompensated (Haga and Beskow 2008)?





Conclusion


	The field of public health genomics has been growing rapidly over the past few years and is projected to increase steadily in the future. The significant improvement of new technologies has made genomics accessible within the public health setting. An explosion of genetic tests examining conditions that range from several rare diseases to a variety of common diseases have started to reach the market. Caution should be implored when a new genomic test reaches the market. Each test needs to meet certain diagnostic requirements within a target population before it is implemented as a genomic test within the public health sector. In addition, pharmacogenomics testing is encouraged before a new drug is administered within diverse ethnic groups.
	Advancements in the field of epigenetics has led to new therapeutic treatment options against a range of conditions. Epigenetic therapy is in its early stages and has enormous potential for future applications. Despite setback within the field, gene therapy is still argued to be the treatment of the future. Significant policies and ethics guidelines are required to be reviewed and implemented for gene therapy to be utilized as a therapeutic tool in the future. Public health genomics is an exciting area that can benefit a larger segment of the population by bringing the right interventions to the right population at the right time.
