2.8


Food and nutrition


	Roger Shrimpton, David Sanders, and Anne Marie Thow





Introduction


	Nutritional science concerns the study of nutrients in food, how the body uses nutrients, and the relationship between diet, health, and disease. In previous centuries the focus was more on identifying the nutrient components in the diet, and single nutrient deficiencies, such a scurvy caused by vitamin c deficiency, beriberi caused by thiamine deficiency, and goitre caused by iodine deficiency. By the end of the Second World War, virtually all the nutrients had been identified and the work was thought to have been completed (Carpenter 2003). Early nutrition programme efforts around the turn of the millennium focused on tackling child undernutrition especially, but in more recent times nutrition science has begun to study population-based evidence for the relationships between specific dietary patterns, nutrient intakes, and the noncommunicable diseases of obesity, cancer, diabetes, and atherosclerosis.
	Nutrition paradigms have shifted in the last few decades, and now there is an urgent need for the policy discourse and public health practice to catch up. Effective public health policy and practice responses to nutrition depend on an accurate understanding of the problem of ‘malnutrition’, its implications for human health, and its underlying causes. They also depend on the political economy of nutrition policy—including policies relating to food environments and the global food system. The aim of this chapter is to map out the public health dimensions of food and nutrition problems that increasingly assail the world as well as to provide some guidance on the population-based interventions necessary for diet-related diseases to be contained.





The double burden of malnutrition


	Malnutrition refers to nutritional excesses of macronutrients and micronutrients as well as deficiencies (WHO 1995). Undernutrition is the result of insufficient intake, poor absorption, and/or poor biological use of the nutrients. This can result in impaired body functions, impaired growth, and underweight. Excess or imbalanced nutrient intakes can result in impaired body functions, as well as overweight and/or obesity. The double burden of malnutrition (DBM) was presented as a ‘new paradigm’, at the 1992 International Conference on Nutrition (ICN), a member state meeting jointly hosted by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Health Organization (WHO). It was subsequently recognized that DBM occurs not only in the same populations, but also in the same households, and even the same individuals (Shrimpton and Rokx 2012). At the population level women are the most affected by DBM, with most low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) having problems of both overweight and underweight women (Jaacks et al. 2015). The most common form of DBM at the household level is stunting in children and overweight/obesity in women (Garrett and Ruel 2005). For individuals the most common form of DBM is overweight and iron deficiency (Zhao et al. 2015). Furthermore, new evidence emerged suggesting that maternal and foetal undernutrition increased susceptibility to overweight and obesity and diet-related noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) in adulthood. Consequently, the understanding of the causal links to overweight and obesity evolved to reflect the double burden causality across the ‘life course’ (Darnton-Hill et al. 2004). Separating the treatment and/or prevention of nutritional deficiencies and excesses was therefore no longer considered sensible.
	Most countries are now grappling with multiple burdens of malnutrition, and globally overnutrition is increasing faster than undernutrition is decreasing. Estimates are that at least 88% of countries face a serious burden of either two or three forms of malnutrition, i.e. childhood stunting, anaemia in women of reproductive age and/or overweight in adult women (Development Initiatives 2017). Two billion adults were overweight or obese globally in 2017 (a third being obese), while 815 million people were still going to bed hungry and 2 billion people lacked key micronutrients like iron and vitamin A. Furthermore 155 million children were stunted, and 52 million children were wasted, while 41 million children were overweight. Obesity prevalence more than tripled from 3.2% to 10.8% among men and more than doubled (6.4–14.9%) among women from 1975 to 2014. By comparison, the prevalence of underweight people decreased from 13.8% to 8.8% among men and 14.6% to 9.7% among women (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration 2016). Between 1975 and 2016 the prevalence of moderate and severe underweight in girls decreased from 9.2% to 8.4% and from 14.8% to 12.4% in boys (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration 2017). More than 20 million infants worldwide, representing 15.5% of all births in 2000, were born with low birthweight, 95.6% of them in LMICs (UNICEF/WHO 2004). Accurate monitoring is challenging, since nearly half of the world’s infants are not weighed at birth, but this situation does not seem to have improved. Iron deficiency is the most common and widespread nutritional disorder in the world, being common in both high and low-income countries.





Measuring nutritional status


	Methods of defining nutritional status and describing the size of nutritional problems have evolved considerably in the last few decades. Until the turn of the millennium the focus of nutrition programme efforts was on child undernutrition, the population estimates of which largely relied on the adequacy of weight-for-age in children under five. These efforts essentially focused on trying to understand the aetiology of the severe forms of undernutrition, kwashiorkor, and marasmus, trying to prove the hypothesis that these were protein deficiency and energy deficiency diseases (Scrimshaw and Viteri 2010). There was little awareness at that time that non-severe forms of malnutrition existed, and that their consequence for a population perspective was of immense importance. During this era, much was achieved in terms of definitions for undernutrition. Moderate malnutrition was defined as between 2 and 3 Z scores, and severe malnutrition was more than 3 Z scores, below the median of the Harvard growth standard (Jelliffe 1966). However, as noted by Waterlow (1973), a deficit in weight-for-age conceals two different conditions, a deficit in height-for-age or ‘stunting’ and a deficit in weight-for-height or ‘wasting’. It is important that these conditions should be differentiated and assessed separately, because they reflect different underlying problems: stunting tends to reflect chronic undernutrition, and wasting, acute undernutrition.
	Recognizing the needs for more representative references for child growth and nutrition, WHO developed the WHO International Growth Reference (de Onis et al. 2006), constructed by measuring the growth of cohorts of well-fed children from several nations. This was essentially to demonstrate that in the right circumstances, i.e. healthy environments, children grew similarly independent of their ethnic differences or geographical location. Indeed, this is now the growth standard children of all nations should attain.
	In the years since the pioneering work on child undernutrition, it has become increasingly obvious that the burden of malnutrition is changing, with dietary risk factors for overweight and NCDs becoming more and more of a problem. In consequence increasing effort has gone into better defining and measuring overnutrition. Overweight and obesity are most commonly measured in adults with the body mass index (BMI), which is weight divided by height squared. A BMI greater than 25 is regarded as overweight and greater than 30 is obesity. Child overweight is also defined as a weight-for-height greater than +2 standard deviations of the WHO Child Growth Reference (WHO 2017a). The World Health Organization has also recommended BMI cut-offs for overweight and obesity be 23 kg/m2 and 27 kg/m2, respectively in Asia, lower than the cut-offs used in Caucasian populations (WHO 2004). Further measures of adiposity include waist circumference and skinfold thickness, but these are more often used for individual than population assessments.





Nutrition and health


	Nutritional diseases are caused by both under and overnutrition and affect people throughout the lifecourse. Undernutrition, including foetal growth restriction, suboptimal breastfeeding, stunting, wasting, and deficiencies of vitamin A and zinc, caused 45% of child deaths, resulting in 3.1 million deaths annually in 2011 (Black et al. 2013). Breastfeeding is the most important start to life in terms of feeding patterns (Victora et al. 2016). Appropriate breastfeeding practices prevent child morbidity due to diarrhoea, respiratory infections, and otitis media. Where infectious diseases are common causes of death, breastfeeding provides major protection. Despite these benefits, in 2013, only about two-fifths of infants in LMICs were exclusively breastfed for the first 6 months of life, and three-quarters were still being breastfed at 12–15 months (Rollins et al. 2016). Rates in high income countries (HICs) are less sure but are much lower at all ages.
	At least a third of the world’s population, some 2 billion people, are anaemic, many due to iron deficiency, and in resource-poor areas, this is frequently exacerbated by infectious diseases. Maternal anaemia, especially during the first trimester of pregnancy, can be considered as a risk factor for many pregnancy outcomes including low birth weight (Rahmati et al. 2017). High BMI accounted for 4 million deaths globally in 2015, nearly 40% of which occurred in persons who were not obese but overweight (The GBD 2015 Obesity Collaboration 2017). More than two-thirds of deaths related to high BMI were due to cardiovascular disease. Furthermore, Asians at any given level of adiposity have a much greater predisposition to cardiometabolic disorders than Caucasians (Haldar et al. 2015).
	Increasingly, diet-related metabolic risk factors and NCDs are becoming the major driving force behind the global burden of disease. NCDs accounted for 64 % of the attributed risk factors for deaths in 2016 (GBD 2016 Risk Factor Collaborators 2017). High blood pressure was the fourth-leading risk factor for both men and women in 1990 and had risen to be the second leading risk factor for men and the leading risk factor for women by 2016. High fasting plasma glucose (FPG) was the third leading risk factor for deaths and the fourth-leading risk factor for disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). Diabetes was the largest source of DALYs attributable high FPG. The global prevalence of diabetes has nearly doubled since 1980, rising to 8.5% in the adult population, with 422 million so affected, three times more than in 1980 (WHO 2016). By increasing the risks of cardiovascular and other diseases, diabetes, and high FPG caused 3.7 million deaths, with 43% of these occurring before the age of 70 years. The percentage of deaths attributable to high FPG or diabetes that occurs prior to age 70 is higher in LMICs than in HICs.
	Systematic reviews find that red meats, processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, high glycaemic load foods, transfats, and sodium are the principal dietary factors that increase the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes (Micha et al. 2017).





Changing dietary patterns


	Globally, food consumption per person measured as dietary energy intake, increased by 15% in the 30 years up to 2000 (Kearney 2010). In the same period annual meat consumption in LMICs rose from 10 kg to 26 kg per person (WHO/FAO 2003). Global consumption of milk and dairy products also doubled to 45 kg, and the average global supply of fat increased by 20 g per capita per day. The type of carbohydrate in the diet also changed, with decreases in complex carbohydrates such as starchy foods (for example, whole grain cereals and legumes) and an increase in refined sugar. The average global consumption of fish increased from 13.4 kg per capita in 1990 to 16.3kg per capita in 1999 (FAO 2003). The concept of this ‘consumption’ is more related to food purchased than intake, as it doesn’t take into consideration food waste. Food lost and wasted along the way from field to fork may be as much as a third, amounting to about 1.3 billion tonnes per year (FAO 2011).
	WHO recommends that adults and children should maintain a reduced intake of free sugars over the life course, and this should be less than 10% of total energy intake (WHO 2015). Global assessments of sugar intake as a percentage of energy intake range from 20.0% to 38.4% in young children and 13.5–24.6% in adults (Newens and Walton 2016). Various systematic reviews and meta-analyses provide evidence that consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) (Malik et al. 2006) or free sugars (Te Morenga et al. 2012) promotes weight gain in adults and children. Per capita sugar consumption is strongly associated with the prevalence of diabetes mellitus in a 165-country analysis, with the strongest association found in the Asia region (Weeratunga et al. 2014). Another problem is that many processed foods have a high glycaemic index (Fardet et al. 2017), with blood sugar levels remaining high for a long period after the food is eaten. Consumption of higher glycaemic index foods are associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Bhupathiraju et al. 2014) and coronary heart disease (CHD) (Fan et al. 2012).
	The proportion of energy contributed by dietary fats exceeds 30% in the HICs, and in nearly all other regions this share is increasing, even though the WHO recommendation is for not more than 30% (WHO/FAO 2003). Thinking has now changed however, and fat intake is regarded as less important in the genesis of obesity and cardiovascular disease with calls to revise the dietary guidance (Willett 2011; Harcombe et al. 2016). Contrary to popular commentary regarding the fat intake being bad for health, a recent dynamic time series analysis of US and global population data sets suggests that while increases in carbohydrate consumption are associated with increasing weight, increases in fat consumption are associated with decreasing weight (Riera-Crichton and Tefft 2014). Similarly, a cohort study in 18 countries from five continents has also found that high carbohydrate intake was associated with higher risk of total mortality, whereas total fat and individual types of fat intake were related to lower total mortality (Dehghan et al. 2017). Alongside this changing understanding of the impact of fat and carbohydrate (particularly sugar) intakes on health has been increasing evidence for the role of ‘ultraprocessed’ foods in contributing to diet-related NCD risk (Fardet 2016; Fiolet et al. 2018).
	It is increasingly recognized that what is eaten is as important as how much is eaten in the causality of obesity and cardiovascular disease. Traditional thinking that ‘eating too much’ and ‘moving too little’ are the causes of the rising global obesity problem is increasingly coming under scrutiny (Shrimpton et al. 2017). Average adult weight began to increase by 1.5 kg a year in the early eighties in the United States and the main drivers were the consumption of processed foods, and especially of potato chips and SSBs (Mozaffarian et al. 2011). This suggests that relatively minor changes in diets—for example, marginal increases in energy intakes due to increased discretionary food intake—can have significant impacts on body weight and health over the long term.





The food environment


	These dietary changes have occurred during a time of systemic changes to the food environments in which people make decisions about what—and how much—they eat. The food environment acts as an important interface between the wider food system and peoplés food acquisition and consumption through continuous and complex interactions between external and personal food environments. The external food environment domain relates to the world of opportunities and constraints that exists within a given context, and includes exogenous dimensions such as food availability, prices, vendor and product properties and marketing and regulation. The personal food environment domain includes a set of endogenous dimensions including food accessibility, affordability, convenience, and desirability (Turner et al. 2017).
	Processed foods now account for 80% of country food sales (Mazzocchi et al. 2012), that is foods sold through retail outlets. Ultraprocessed products are becoming dominant in the global food system, including in LMICs where they have become ubiquitous, especially in urban areas (Igumbor et al. 2012; Monteiro et al. 2013). These foods are formulations of several ingredients which, besides salt, sugar, oils, and fats, include food substances not used in culinary preparations in the home, such as flavours, colours, sweeteners, emulsifiers, and other additives. They contribute almost 60% of the energy and 90% of added sugars consumed by the USA population (Martínez Steele et al. 2016). Chemical food additives are used to make processed foods look, smell, and taste better, as well as to improve their shelf life. These include a large assortment of colourings, preservatives, antioxidants, emulsifiers, stabilizers, anticaking agents, and flavour enhancers. In 2000, the food industry spent US$20 billion on such additives, and the average consumption was 7 kg per person a year in industrialized countries (Millstone and Lang 2003).





Changing food systems


	Changes to food environments reflect broader changes to food systems, that have revolutionized how food is produced, processed, and marketed. Global food production has outpaced rising demand based on population growth rates during the last four decades (FAO 2002). The number of farms globally is around 570 million, and of these 83% are small farms of less than two hectares (Lowder et al. 2016), which operate about 12% of the world´s land. Despite the population almost doubling, the per capita supply of energy from food for human consumption rose by just over 20% between the early 1960s and the late 1990s. The greatest growth came from increases in the production of wheat, vegetable oils, sugar, and meat.
	The increase in global food production has been largely attributed to the green revolution (Pingali 2012). The production of cereal crops tripled in the last 50 years with only a 30% increase in land area cultivated. Using petroleum-based fertilizers and chemical pesticides, expanded irrigation, and genetically modified disease-resistant cultivars, cereal production (wheat, rice, maize) doubled in Asia between 1970 and 1990. This success was concentrated in areas where irrigation water, infrastructure (roads) and access to markets (input and output) as well as credit were well developed. In areas without these conditions, such as in most of Africa, the impact of the green revolution was less impressive.
	Of the 446 million small farms, the majority (87%) are in Asia, and only 8% are in Africa and 1% in the Americas. About a half of small farms are pre-commercial, i.e. not benefitting from productivity enhancing technologies, financing, and market access. While these small farms of the peasant food web provide 70% of total food eaten globally (ETC Group 2015) and harvests 60–70% of food crops from 20% to 30% of arable land, the larger farms of industrial agriculture food system provide 30% of all food consumed globally and uses 70–80% of world’s arable land. Even where the green revolution was successful in raising productivity this was concentrated in the richer larger landholders, as the poorer farmers of the peasant food web could not afford to pay for these inputs. The green revolution thus gave impetus to the development of agribusiness (Engdahl 2007), designed to increase the flow of food crops from the places of production through the food system, to the place of consumption.
	The number of actors providing the inputs needed to achieve increased production through the industrial agricultural system is very limited (ETC Group 2013). A few big multinational conglomerates, including Monsanto and DuPont, Syngenta and Bayer, Dow, and BASF, control 75% of all private sector plant breeding research, 60% of the commercial seed market and 76% of global agrochemical sales. About a third of global cereal production and just over 90% of soybean production is used to feed farm animals, mostly in factory farms of the industrial agriculture food system (FAO 2002).
	Around 56 billion land animals are estimated to be reared and slaughtered for human consumption annually (Koneswaran and Nierenberg, 2008). These estimates vary considerably however, largely depending on terminology and definitions used. It is agreed that factory farms are the most rapidly growing system of farm animal production (FAO 2009), providing 72% of poultry, 43% of eggs, and 55% of pork globally. Furthermore, capture fisheries production increased from 69 million to 93 million tonnes during the last three decades, while world aquaculture production increased from 5 million to 63 million tonnes (World Bank 2013). Aquaculture will provide close to two-thirds of global food fish consumption by 2030 as catches from wild capture fisheries level off and demand from an emerging global middle class, especially in China, substantially increases
	Food is now a major component of international trade, accounting for 10% of all global trade (FAO 2011a), and the aggregate value of agricultural exports passing through the international food system was expected to reach a record US$1.29 trillion in 2011. The amount of food calories traded on the international market is about 20% and had more than doubled between 1986 and 2009 (D’Odorico et al. 2014). Much of the increases in global food trade have been in highly processed commodities. Since the early seventies and the development of the Washington Consensus on the conditionality for structural adjustment programmes (SAPs) from the World Bank, and the ‘standard prescription’ by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), LMICs have been increasingly encouraged to liberalize trade and investment, privatize national industries, and reduce state support to local agricultural production (Weis 2007). The Washington Consensus also bolstered the global free trade negotiations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), which eventually resulted in the creation of the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 1994. Alongside this, multilateral, regional, and bilateral trade agreements, such as the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), have proliferated in the past 30 years.
	The WTO, World Bank, and IMF are thus key institutions governing trade in the modern global food system. All these institutions have mandates that include food security to some extent—but this inclusion has been along economic lines, focused on calorie availability at the national level, and paying little attention to inequalities and sociocultural aspects of food production and distribution (Rosset 2006; Margulis 2013). Another key actor in global food governance is the Codex Alimentarius Commission, which sets food standards, including approval for use of food additives. The Codex is recognized by the WTO as an international reference point for the resolution of disputes concerning food safety and consumer protection, thus lending it greater authority (Halabi 2015). However, while Codex is a member state organization, under the WHO and UN FAO, it is also a standards-setting body with open membership. This means that industry actors can act as formal observers and has resulted in standards that often preference trade interests over public health (Downes 2014).
	Growing industry concentration has led to a situation where just a few companies control large shares of the flow of food through the global food system (FAO 2002). In 2003 just four firms controlled 73% of the global grain trade (Murphy et al. 2012). Furthermore, these multinational corporations are highly diversified and integrated both vertically and horizontally; for example, Cargill, ADM, and Bunge not only account for more than 60% of total financing of soy production in Brazil, but they also provide the seed, fertilizer, and agrochemicals to the growers, and subsequently buy the soy and store it in their own facilities (Murphy et al. 2012). In the USA Cargill is number one in terms of domestic grain handling, as well as grain and soybean exports but also the second largest compound feed producer and the number three turkey producer. Policies of trade liberalization have facilitated the rising availability and consumption of relatively cheap meat, dairy products, and processed foods in LMICs (Thow and Hawkes 2009). Imported foods tend to be cheaper because of continued state support to the industrial agriculture system in HICs, and their dumping of cheaper food commodities onto the world market.
	Notwithstanding the increasing production of food globally, food prices have risen sharply since 2006, impacting most negatively on the poor. The main drivers of food price rises are the increasing use of land for biofuel production in the face of rising energy costs, and greatly increased speculative acquisition of land, as well as financial speculation on food futures (McMichael 2012). Speculative acquisition of land, sometimes termed ‘land grabbing’ authorizes large-scale removal of rural populations from (often) ancestral lands to install ‘agriculture without farmers’, i.e. agro-industrialization. It sacrifices land and its inhabitants in favour of what is a necessary global good (food yields, green fuels, and carbon offsets). For example, in Colombia between 2001 and 2005, 263,000 peasant families were expropriated from 2.6 million hectares by agrobusiness and/or paramilitaries interested primarily in palm oil development. (McMichael 2012).
	Another recent and major contributor to rising food prices is financial speculation in food. The deregulation of commodities derivatives markets in 2000 as part of financial liberalization allowed large institutional investors to enter these markets. Between 2003 and 2008 commodity index holdings increased from $13 billion to $317 billion (McMichael 2012). Already in 2006, Merrill Lynch Wealth Management and Financial Services estimated that speculation was causing commodity prices to trade at 50% higher than if they were based on fundamental supply and demand (De Schutter 2010). The increase of the agricultural commodities futures between March 2003 and March 2008 was accompanied by price increases during the same period for coffee with 167%, for soybean oil with 199% and for wheat with 314% (Kerckhoffs et al. 2010).
	Global food retail sales are about US$4 trillion annually, with supermarkets accounting for the largest share of sales (Meade 2017). The urban demand for food in LMICs is expected to more than double in the next decade. It will be responsible for almost the entire growth in global food demand, spiking from about 40% to some 60% by 2050. The emergence of supermarkets in LMICS is leading to a radical change in the global food marketing and distribution system (Reardon et al. 2015). Structural changes in the food distribution system, which took 50 years to unfold in the United States, have taken place in little more than a decade in Latin America. In China, where no supermarkets existed in 1989, annual supermarket sales were US$100 billion in 2008 (Reardon and Gulati 2008). Unlike HICs, where supermarkets are often the principal, if not only, source of fruits and vegetables (Larson et al. 2009), supermarkets in LMICs are often distribution channels for cheap processed foods including less than healthy snacks and ‘junk’ food, as well as being venues for fast food chains.
	Given the changing nature of the food system one of the greatest challenges to improving nutrition is how to deal with the burgeoning private sector. The food industry is now a massive business, with ten big food and beverage companies generating revenues of more than US$1.1billion a day (OXFAM 2013). Together they are part of an industry valued at US$7 trillion, larger than the energy sector and representing roughly ten percent of the global economy. Although spending on processed foods is still lower in LMICs (US$143 per capita per year in middle-income countries and US$63 per capita in low-income countries), it is growing at 28% and 13% a year respectively in those country groups.





The political economy of food and nutrition


	The economic consequences of the DBM across the life course are massive. Estimates are that more than 200 million stunted children under 5 years of age in LMIC countries that survive growth failure in the first 1,000 days, are not developing to their full potential, and that this is associated with more than a 20% deficit in their income as adults (Grantham-McGregor et al. 2007). It is hard to put a single figure on this, but in comparison with the costs of over nutrition they are likely to be small. Current trends project 65 million more obese adults in the United States and 11 million more obese adults in the United Kingdom by 2030, consequently accruing an additional 6–8.5 million cases of diabetes, 5.7–7.3 million cases of heart disease and stroke, 492 000–669 000 additional cases of cancer, and 26–55 million quality-adjusted life years forgone for United States and UK combined (Wang et al. 2011). Combined medical costs associated with treatment of these preventable diseases are estimated to increase by $48–66 billion/year in the United States and by £1.9–2 billion/year in the UK by 2030. Over the next 20 years, the cost of treating NCDs and cumulative output losses globally are likely to be at least US$30 trillion and US$47 trillion, respectively, representing 48% and 75%, respectively, of global GDP in 2010 (Bloom et al. 2011). Of course, the great majority of these NCDs are diet-related.
	At the turn of the millennium the prospects for eliminating young child malnutrition were considered grim. An assessment done by the World Bank and UNICEF (Gillespie et al. 2003) revealed that nutrition was improving slowly in some regions but was stagnant in others and was often side-lined in poverty agendas despite its potential to improve health, mental development, and productivity. Although nutrition professionals broadly agreed on key interventions and on success factors for implementation, this was not reflected in action. Few large-scale programmes were rigorously monitored and evaluated and inadequate capacity to tackle malnutrition was a major factor limiting progress.
	The publication of the Lancet Nutrition Series in 2008, including an article with a package of low cost efficacious interventions for tackling maternal and child undernutrition (Bhutta et al. 2008), stimulated a tremendous increase in political commitment to the reduction of child undernutrition. In consequence most development agencies revised their strategies to address undernutrition and focused on the 1,000 days during pregnancy and the first 2 years of life. National commitment in LMICs grew, donor funding rose, and civil society and the private sector were increasingly engaged. However, despite this ‘awakening’, progress in tackling stunting was still considered insufficient 5 years later (Black et al. 2013). In 2012, the World Health Assembly endorsed a comprehensive implementation plan on maternal, infant, and young child nutrition which specified six global nutrition targets for 2025. The first target is a 40% reduction in the number of children under-5 who are stunted. The global prevalence of stunting in children under-5 declined 36% during two decades—from an estimated 40% in 1990 to 26% in 2011 (UNICEF 2013), hence the likelihood of a further 40% reduction by 2025 seems remote.
	Translating the evidence, interest, and government concern regarding nutrition into action on the ground has proved challenging—often as the result of politico-economic challenges (Balajaran and Reich 2016). One such challenge is that the nutrition system and community are fragmented from global to community level. Among the various subgroups at the country level are clinic-based medical nutritionists, academic nutritionists, development economists, and planners, social scientists, public health nutritionists, and agricultural specialists. Building coalitions across these different groups is challenging and time-consuming. Furthermore, this multiplicity of stakeholders creates multiple narratives concerning nutrition approaches, which can lead to contention and rivalry. All these challenges are compounded by a limited capacity among nutritionists, be it to engage in the broader political dynamics of managing nutrition policy or the delivery of interventions by multiple actors/sectors.
	The private sector must surely play a role in controlling the malnutrition problem, but this will require balancing public health needs with commercial interests and managing conflicts of interest requires transparent systems and mechanisms (Hawkes and Buse 2011). Efforts to achieve some balance have been developed though the scaling up nutrition (SUN) initiative (Bezanson and Isenman 2010), with countries increasingly looking to the private sector to join national SUN multistakeholder committees. Recent evaluations of SUN suggest that it is still far from being successful in achieving any impact however (Mokoro 2015). The challenge facing policymakers trying to integrate business into national nutrition strategies remains and mistrust and opposition to the private sector are the hardest challenges. Until now the SUN ‘movement’ has been largely focused on maternal and child undernutrition, but whether and how it can evolve to include overnutrition and the metabolic and NCDs remains to be seen, as the potential for conflict of interest are obviously enormous.
	Multinational retailers have introduced into LMICS the types of supply chain seen before in HICs, based around tight vertical coordination, centralized purchasing, and sophisticated marketing (Mazzocchi et al. 2012). They accelerate the rate at which local firms adopt these strategies and tailor them to local needs, and in doing so provide employment and generate income locally. Most of the profits however still revert to the head office of the chains located in HICs (Hawkes 2005). These trends risk eroding the more traditional access to fruit in urban areas of LMICs, such as in South Africa for example, where it is primarily through the informal market; in particular, wet markets or stalls and street vendors. Specific policy opportunities that could increase access to fruit and vegetables in South Africa and other LMICs are: targeted support for periurban farmers to access urban markets (e.g. transport); including food production considerations in initiatives for urban greening; and, initiatives that could increase access to, or incentivize the sale of, fresh fruit and vegetables by street vendors (Thow et al. 2017)
	The food industry spends at least US$ 40 billion a year globally on advertising processed foods (Millstone and Lang. 2003). The evidence indicates that unhealthy food and beverage marketing increases dietary intake and preference for unhealthy food and beverages. Marketing of unhealthy food and beverages increased dietary intake and influenced dietary preference in children during or shortly after exposure to such advertisements (Sadeghirad et al. 2016). Exposure to child-targeted fast food TV advertising is positively associated with fast food consumption among children of pre-school age (Dalton et al. 2017). Trade liberalization is considered to be driving the NCD epidemic in Asia (Baker et al. 2014). Evolving layers of the international and regional trade regimes have facilitated increased market penetration by transnational tobacco, alcohol, and ultraprocessed food corporations and thereby driven consumption of these unhealthy commodities in Asia especially.





Challenges to taking action


	Nutrition has been identified as a ‘chosen issue’, meaning that champions are required to put it on the policy agenda (Garrett et al. 2011). Moreover, the implementation of multisectoral approaches for maternal and child undernutrition (MCU) improvement demands strong and sustained support from high levels of government (Levinson and Balarajan 2013), and this is no different for overnutrition. Accelerating progress in nutrition through multisectoral approaches requires building leadership at nationally and locally.
	The lack of a natural institutional home in government is a challenge, as nutrition doesn’t fit cleanly into any single government agency, with health or agriculture usually nominated as a ‘home’ agency—but both departments are usually unable to lead cross-sectoral action across government. To surmount this problem many countries have created a ‘home’ for nutrition in suprasectoral bodies such as the prime minister’s office or the ministry of planning. Giving high profile leaders—such as Prime Ministers and Mayors—a central role in driving initiatives has been shown to be a key factor in bringing different actors together to collaborate towards NCD prevention goals (Meiro-Lorenzo et al. 2011).
	Nutrition capacity is often weak in many countries and in LMICs especially. This is largely related to the absence of a common understanding of the malnutrition problem (Heaver 2005). This lack of understanding as well as the relatively recent development of public health nutrition (PHN) science have undoubtedly contributed to the shortage of professionals capable of developing population-based approaches for the prevention of all forms of malnutrition as opposed to (or in addition to) a cadre capable of treating the consequences in individuals. Indeed, in most African countries nutrition programmes and interventions are led by nurses whose nutrition knowledge is generally very limited. Typically, other development actors look to the health sector for nutrition guidance, while health sector workers’ nutrition training is all too often woefully outdated and clinical.
	A consensus is growing that a robust and knowledgeable workforce is essential for PHN policy implementation (Yngve et al. 2012). How to build that capacity is the question that still needs to be answered, especially in LMICs. A hybrid distance learning model for PHN workforce managers’ in-service training is urgently needed, especially in LMICs (Shrimpton et al. 2016), and unless increased priority and funding is given to building capacity for SUN programmes in LMICs, MCU rates are likely to remain high and nutrition-related NCDs to escalate.
	The World PHN Association has placed considerable emphasis on improved definition of the nutrition capacity and how to build it since its inception in 2008. A competency framework was first developed (Hughes et al. 2012) which described the core functions of PHN practice, and the work done at different levels of the public health system. Subsequently a nutrition capacity assessment framework was proposed (Shrimpton et al. 2013) to guide the systematic assessment of capacity development needs at system, organizational, workforce, and community levels. While nutrition has to be everybody’s business at the district level, somebody has to be in charge. That is the role proposed for the public health nutritionist.
	Another serious challenge that faces nutrition is demonstrating the effectiveness of policies and programmes. Improving nutrition in practice is complicated and context specific, since it requires careful strategic planning, informed by the situational analysis and prioritization of programmatic interventions to be funded with limited resources (Balajaran and Reich 2016). There is a growing repertoire of efficacious nutrition interventions for maternal and child undernutrition but translating that knowledge into practice and demonstrating tangible results at scale is still difficult to achieve (Leroy and Menon 2008). It is easier for academic experts in nutrition to get funding for carrying out research than for programme evaluations.
	While intervening in the first 1,000 days is critical, addressing the DBM requires expanding the focus of nutrition interventions to cover the rest of the life course and the food system (Fig. 2.8.1). The importance of employing multisector policies and interventions for improving nutrition outcomes has been widely agreed during this last decade (World Bank 2006). Indeed, these nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive interventions need to be continued across the school years into adulthood and the workplace (Shrimpton and Rokx 2012). Moreover, in order to tackle the double burden a range of policy interventions and programmes are needed to address the overall food environment (Shrimpton et al. 2016) and concerted efforts are needed from the health, education, agriculture, industry, social protection, and water and sanitation sectors as shown in Figure 2.8.1.
	The nutrition-specific interventions directed at immediate levels of causality are mostly delivered through the health sector, while nutrition-sensitive interventions directed at the underlying and basic levels of causality are often delivered through other sectors such as education, agriculture, water and sanitation, and social welfare. Scaling up the priority nutrition-specific interventions through the health sector to cover 90% of the population in the 36 countries with 80% of the global stunted children will only reduce stunting by 20% (Bhutta et al. 2013), still short of the WHO CIP target for 2025. Scaling up the nutrition-sensitive interventions through other sectors is therefore required to achieve these MCU targets and perhaps as important, do so in a sustainable way. Although the evidence base doesn’t yet permit precise estimation of the contribution of nutrition-sensitive interventions to stunting reduction, early indications are that social protection, agriculture, and water and environment, and public health can all greatly contribute to the acceleration (Fanzo et al. 2013).
	Fig. 2.8.1 Framework of sectoral actions and systems strengthening efforts needed for a multisectoral response to the double burden of malnutrition.
	Reprinted from Shrimpton R, Mbuya NK, Provo AM (2016) ‘The Double Burden of Malnutrition in East Asia and the Pacific: Evidence and Lessons for a Multisectoral Response’. Washington: World Bank under a CC BY 3.0 IGO license.
	The estimates of impact of the various packages of nutrition interventions assumes that all are delivered together. Rather than joint programme implementation, the various sectors need to converge their programme interventions to be delivered together as a package. This process is essentially the responsibility of local government and is facilitated by decentralization (Shrimpton 2002). Community-based programmes are of importance here, especially if they have the essential elements of community ownership, adequate population coverage, targeting, and central support for supplies and training (Mason et al. 2006). The promotional activities, which aim at ensuring optimal growth of the foetus/infant from conception through to 2 years of age, i.e. the first 1,000 days, typically include: treating maternal anaemia; treating infections such as intestinal parasites and avoiding/treating malaria; monitoring growth of the infant; promoting breast feeding and adequate complementary feeding; using oral rehydration for diarrhoea, and getting children immunized.
	In a typical community-based programme, community ‘mobilizers’ take on the task of looking after households in their neighbourhood, allowing whole communities to be mapped and covered. A certain level of intensity of effort must be ensured, with optimal ratios of not more than 20 mobilizers per facilitator and not more than 20 households per mobilizer. If these levels of intensity of effort with a sufficiently wide coverage are not ensured, no impact will be seen in the population, and the resources invested will be largely lost. A key challenge for scaling up such community-based programmes lies in institutionalizing and mainstreaming community participation (Lehmann and Sanders 2007).
	As no single sector alone can solve the problem of undernutrition, neither can a health-centric approach reverse the growing trend of overnutrition. Multiple sector contributions are needed, and the necessary actions range from national and district level policies to creating supportive community environments and supporting individuals to change their behaviours. National level political support—through taxation, regulation, and/or subsidization—is necessary to ensure social environments that support healthy decisions as the default. Interventions are needed beyond the realms of ‘self-will’: ensuring that physical activity is facilitated and easily available and access to quality diets is affordable, without the promotion of unhealthy products and habits through the media. The education sector has an important role to play in nurturing the development of children who graduate from school with adequate life skills and appropriate habits that help them avoid these risks in adulthood. The health sector must do more to deliver the messages and screening that can contribute to primary and secondary prevention, particularly for adults.
	There is clear evidence that policy intervention that fosters a food environment in which the healthy choices are more available and affordable than the unhealthy choices, and in which marketing and point of sale incentives do not preference unhealthy foods, can support consumers to make healthier choices (Hawkes et al. 2015). Macro, or environment-focused, policy intervention can help to correct for existing incentives in food environments which incentivize the purchase of highly processed (and highly profitable) unhealthy foods and beverages. For example, fiscal policy interventions, including taxes and subsidies, can help to incentivize consumption of healthier, rather than unhealthy foods (Thow et al. 2018). Similarly, nutrition labelling interventions are critical in supporting healthier point-of-purchase decision making, by clear external labelling detailing the internal properties of the foods (Cecchini and Warin 2016).
	The WHO recommendations for childhood obesity prevention programmes include key points which have population-wide relevance (WHO 2016a). These recommendations include: use a mixture of ‘top-down’ and community-based actions, employ a range of policy instruments, establish cross-sectoral platforms and a multisectoral approach; promote interventions across a range of settings, including early childcare settings, schools, workplaces, and community organizations; and leverage legislative and financial tools to ensure availability and affordability of healthy foods and physical activity opportunities. Similarly, for reducing the risk of chronic NCDs, WHO has found multicomponent interventions that are adapted to the local context to be the most successful (WHO 2013a, 2013b). Interventions that used the existing social structures of a community, such as schools or the weekly meetings of older adults, reduced barriers to implementation. Effective interventions invariably involved participants in the planning and implementation stages, such as involving the workers themselves in workplace interventions, and the leaders of the range of civil society organizations in the community.
	In 2015 the United Nations adopted a set of goals to be achieved by 2030 with the aim of ending poverty, protecting the planet, and ensuring prosperity for all as part of a new sustainable development agenda (UN 2015). While considerable progress has been made over the past decade across all areas of development, the pace of progress observed in recent years is insufficient to fully meet the sustainable development goals (SDGs) and targets by 2030 (UN 2017). One of the seventeen SDGs is directly related to food and nutrition, namely SDG 2 which is to end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture. While some progress has been made to reduce hunger and malnutrition, it is not enough to meet the goal. Failure to achieve SDG2 will also make other SDGs difficult to achieve, since the pervasive negative influence of our current food system endangers many others (Shrimpton 2017). The SDGs provide an exciting opportunity to achieve global nutrition targets while catalysing other development goals through ‘double duty’ actions (WHO 2017b). These include interventions, programmes and policies that have the potential to simultaneously reduce the risk or burden of both undernutrition (including wasting, stunting and micronutrient deficiency or insufficiency) and overweight, obesity, or diet-related NCDs.





Learning from success


	Examples of successful programmes are not easily found, but experiences gained in Brazil with undernutrition and France with overnutrition offer some important insights.
	In Brazil the Bolsa Familia Programme (BFP) is part of the National Food and Nutrition Security System (SISAN), which has evolved over the last two decades to become a very effective large-scale multisectoral nutrition programme. The principal sectors participating in SISAN include the Ministries of Social Development, Health, and Education. At national level SISAN is overseen by the National Council on Food and Nutrition Security (CONSEA). CONSEA is a deliberative body with two-thirds of its members made up of civil society, and that is linked to the President’s Office. Coordination and implementation of SISAN is carried out by an interministerial chamber on food and nutrition security (CAISAN) which is located in the Ministry of Social Development (Chmielewska and Souza 2011).
	The BFP targets the mothers and children of poor families across Brazil, with some 12 million families and 48 million beneficiaries in 2010 (Lindert et al. 2007). The conditionality of BFP includes either school attendance of children aged 5–18, or regular health check-ups for mothers and their children aged under 5 years of age. At the municipal level there are councils and committees that oversee the conditionality requirements of BFP, with the creation of registries of poor families (Cadastro Unico) that are requirements for a family to become BFP beneficiaries. The delivery platforms at the municipal level are the family grant that is dispensed through the banking system based on the family being in the ‘Cadastro Unico’. The conditionality of the BFP through the health system includes regular pre-and postnatal care, growth monitoring, immunization, and participation in nutrition education seminars. These services are largely provided through the Family Health Programme (Programa de Saude da Famila or PSF) of the Ministry of Health. Together, a doctor, nurse, nurse auxiliary, and four to six community health workers (CHW) comprise a multidisciplinary family health support team working in health units in defined geographic areas covering no more than 5,000 residents. (Harris and Haines 2010). There are some 250,000 CHWs. These CHWs must live in the area they work, are responsible for up to 120 families in a defined area and perform home visits to each family once a month.
	The PSF provides primary healthcare services in 95% of all 5,564 municipalities, covering 55% of the population or some 85 million people. Coverage of PSF is not universal as it is targeted at poorer areas. Since 2008 the PSF has included a nutritionist in the family health support teams to strengthen nutrition capacity (Jaime et al. 2011). The SISAN also includes the school meal programme (Programa Nacional de Alimentaçâo Escolar or PNAE) through the Ministry of Education, and the Food Acquisition Programme (FAP) through the Ministry of Social Development. There is a requirement that 30% of food used in schools be locally produced, and the Ministry of Agriculture oversees the production, with funds transferred to municipal governments. The FAP primary focus is on small farm families and gives special attention to native fruits and places a high premium on diversified production and consumption by small producer families. School meals are required to be healthy, using fruits and vegetables produced by local farmers and minimizing the use of ultraprocessed foods.
	The interventions delivered through the various delivery platforms of SISAN including the BFP, PSF, FAP, and PNAE are largely targeted at mothers and their children in poor families. The BFP monthly cash transfers range from $US7 to US$45 per family depending on eligibility (very poor and moderately poor). The health conditionality means that BFP beneficiaries are most likely going to be PSF clients. The PSF CHW’s primary concern is maternal and child health: they provide counselling on maternal and infant and young child feeding, ensure adherence to micronutrient supplementation and immunization, as well as provide guidance on oral rehydration in the treatment of diarrhoea as appropriate. Increasingly CHWs are involved in curative care, triage, and referral to the health unit and health promotion for chronic diseases.
	The impact of the various component parts of the SISAN has been quite remarkable in the last decade. The BFP has contributed to reduction of poverty with those on less than US$ 1.25 a day falling from 25.6% in 1990 to 4.8 percent in 2008. Estimates are that the BFP contributed to about 35% of the reduction of the extreme poverty gap. Although there is limited rigorous evidence that the BFP resulted in improved nutrition outcomes (Martins et al. 2013), there is considerable ecological evidence that it contributed to national reductions.
	National stunting rates in young children fell from 37.1% in 1974–5 to 7.1% in 2006–7, accompanied by a narrowing of the difference in stunting rates between poor and rich quintiles. The steepest decline was in the last 10 years of that period (Monteiro et al. 2010). In the Northeast of Brazil, the prevalence of child undernutrition fell by one-third between 1986 and 1996 and by three-quarters between 1996 and 2006 (de Lima et al. 2010). The improvements in the first period were mostly associated with improvements in maternal schooling and in water and sanitation coverage, whereas in the second period increasing purchasing power of the poorer families as well as maternal schooling were the strongest associations. Quite remarkably the median duration of breastfeeding in Brazil increased from 2.5 months in 1970 to 14 months in 2006–7 (Victora et al. 2011). Furthermore, it seems likely that PSF has also contributed to the dramatic decreases in infant mortality seen in Brazil in the last few decades (Aquino et al. 2009)
	In France, the ‘Ensemble Prévenons l’Obésité Des Enfants’ (EPODE) was first developed in 2003, with the aim to reduce the prevalence of obesity in children under 12 years of age. The institutional arrangements include a central coordination in the Ministry of Health in Paris which liaises with the office of the Mayor in the cities that are involved, where there is a local project manager that works with a local steering committee. EPODE is a large-scale, coordinated, capacity-building approach for communities to implement effective and sustainable strategies to prevent childhood obesity (Borys et al. 2011). EPODE is designed to involve all relevant local stakeholders in an integrated and concrete prevention programme aimed at facilitating the adoption of healthier lifestyles in everyday life (Van Koperen et al. 2013). The delivery platforms include local crèches, health clinics, sports facilities, cultural associations, supermarkets, restaurants, school catering services, school recreation facilities, local parks, and gymnasiums. The activities developed and supported include advocacy and social mobilization through local media campaigns, together with capacity building and coaching of local actors, as well as the monitoring and evaluation of these activities.
	The initial evaluations of the first ten EPODE cities gave encouraging results with ten to 20% reductions in obesity prevalence (Romon et al. 2009). EPODE now extended to nearly 1.8 million inhabitants in 167 French cities, 20 cities in Spain, and 8 cities in Belgium. In June 2008 the first EPODE Mayors’ Club European congress was held. Success to date is measured by a large field mobilization in the pilot cities and by the encouraging reduction of the BMI of children in France within the pilot cities (European Public Health Alliance 2008).
	The sale of sugary soft drinks and vending machines was also banned in all schools across France. A tax on sugary soft drinks was introduced in 2012, which has led to companies making demands at the EU for evidence of the impact of such taxes. The resulting study found that food taxes achieve a reduction in the consumption of the taxed products and, in some cases, product reformulation aimed at reducing the sugar, salt, and fat levels of the product. It is also found that product substitution takes place, both through an increase in the consumption of taxed products from cheaper brands and non-taxed or less-taxed product substitutes. To what extent such changes in consumption lead to public health improvements was still considered inconclusive however (Ecorys 2014).





Conclusion


	Shifting the paradigm for addressing the DBM will require attention to the common drivers of malnutrition. In particular, translating the science into interventions that support and empower people to consume diets of high nutrition quality. The DBM is not two separate problems, but the product of inadequate access to affordable, quality sufficient foods. However, transitioning to a food system that delivers foods of high nutritional quality across the population will require addressing the politico-economic factors that shape food production, processing, distribution, and retail. It will also require re-visioning nutrition interventions to consider implications for undernutrition as well as risk factors for overweight and NCDs. For example, programmes like Bolsa Familia and the Mexican Opportunidades have been associated with weight gain and consumption of sugar and SSBs (de Bem Lignani et al. 2011). To address these global challenges adequately, a key enabler will be strategic investment in PHN capacity at the local, national, and global level. Among the key aims should be promoting exclusive breastfeeding and adequate complementary feeding in children up to 2 years of age, as well as promoting the local production of fruits and vegetables and increasing their availability in local markets and reducing the supply of ultraprocessed foods.

	Willett, W.C. (2011). The great fat debate: total fat and health. Journal of American Dietetic Association, 111(5), 660–2.
	Yngve, A., Tseng, M., Haapala, I., and Hodge, A. (2012). A robust and knowledgeable workforce is essential for public health nutrition policy implementation. Public Health Nutrition, 15, 1979–80.

2.9


Climate change and human health


	Alistair Woodward and Alex Macmillan





Introduction to the environment and climate change


	This chapter aims to introduce readers to the basic science underlying climate change, to explore the links between climate change and health, and examine the implications of this knowledge for public health policy and practice.
	As a start, readers are invited to check their understanding of climate science against the multiple-choice questions in Box 2.9.1. (The answers are shown at the end of the chapter.)
	The Earth has an average surface temperature suitable for life that is the product of a number of natural influences on the balance of radiation (radiative ‘forcing’ at the top of the atmosphere). These include solar activity (the amount of energy produced by the sun), the tilt and orbit of the planet, volcanic activity that injects gases and ash into the upper atmosphere, other dusts and aerosols that block incoming solar radiation, and the amount of reflection (‘albedo’) by clouds, ice, and snow. Also important is the concentration of so-called ‘greenhouse’ gases. These gases are transparent to relatively high-frequency incoming solar radiation in the visible spectrum. However, when this radiation is absorbed on the surface of the Earth it is re-emitted in the infra-red range, which is trapped by the greenhouse gases. This action is similar to the effect of a pane of glass in a greenhouse (or the window of a car sitting in the sun). Without the blanket for the planet that is provided by the greenhouse gases, the Earth would be approximately 30°C colder than it is at present. Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the most abundant of these heat-trapping gases. Other important greenhouse agents include methane, nitrous oxide, black carbon, and manufactured halocarbons (e.g. chlorofluorocarbons or CFCs).
	CO2 levels in the atmosphere vary over long timescales due to transfers from the atmosphere to the biosphere and the oceans, and from the oceans carbon is eventually sequestered in sedimentary rocks. In the very long term, carbon from the Earth’s crust is ejected by volcanic eruptions into the atmosphere, and the cycle begins again.
	What has changed in the last 200 years or so is the large-scale emission of CO2 (and other heat-trapping gases) as a result of human activities, such as clearing of forests and burning of fossil fuels. This process began in pre-industrial times as a relatively minor addition of carbon to the atmosphere but has escalated rapidly in the last 50 years. In 2017, about 37 giga-tonnes (Gt) of CO2 were released into the atmosphere each year, roughly 150 times more than the amount emitted in the middle of the nineteenth century. CO2 is a long-lived greenhouse gas: about half of the carbon that is emitted into the atmosphere is taken up by natural sinks within 30 years, but about 30% will persist in the atmosphere for centuries. Nitrous oxide and methane are much more potent heat-trapping gases, but are emitted in lesser quantities. Nitrous oxide remains in the atmosphere for about a hundred years; methane is short-lived, and is mostly removed within about 12 years.
	The concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere rose steadily from about 280 parts per million (ppm) in pre-industrial times, to 315 ppm in 1960 when direct measurements were first made. Since then the level has increased 2–3% per year, reaching a global average concentration of 403 ppm in 2017. Indirect measures, using ice cores and other indications of historic conditions, tell us that present levels are higher than at any time in the last 5 million years (IPCC 2013).
	Consequences of these changes in atmospheric chemistry are evident in the recent temperature records at or close to the Earth’s surface, sea level rise, reduced snow and ice cover, and increased ocean acidity. The year-to-year variability in average global temperatures is dominated by natural factors such as the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), so the effect of persistent, external forcing such as steadily rising greenhouse concentrations is seen most clearly on longer timescales. Indeed each of the last three decades has been warmer than all previous decades in the last 150 years and in early 2018 NOAA reported the 5 warmest years on record have occurred in the last 10 years (Climate Central 2018). This rise in global average temperatures has occurred in every region, over both land and ocean, and cannot be explained by time trends in solar activity and other natural forces. On the other hand, climate simulations that include anthropogenic contributions (i.e. the increase in CO2 and other greenhouse gases) fit well with the last 40 years of temperature records (Fig. 2.9.1).

	 	A. Stratospheric warming
