	E. Dilution of the oceans making them less acidic
	Other evidence of global warming includes the predominance of highest ever temperatures in the record of temperature extremes (in the western United States, record high temperatures now outnumber record low measurements each year by about three to one) (Meehl et al. 2009), and the unique combination of warming in the troposphere (the lower atmosphere) and cooling at higher levels (due to trapping of heat in the greenhouse layer, and less heat radiating into space). Summertime Arctic sea ice is reducing year on year, and global average sea level is rising at about 3.0 mm/year (twice the rate observed before 1990) (Australian Academy of Sciences 2010).
	Fig. 2.9.1 Observed and simulated climate change.
	Reproduced with permission from Climate Change 2013: The Physical Science Basis. Working Group I Contribution to the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Figure SPM.6. Cambridge University Press.
	Since the 1960s, emissions of greenhouse gases have tracked upwards, the rise halted only briefly by major economic disturbances, such as the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s (Peters et al. 2011). Emissions in the first 15 years of the twenty-first century have matched, or exceeded, the figures forecast by the most extreme of the climate scenarios reported in the IPCC’s Third Assessment Report in 2001.
	What about the future? The 5th Assessment Report of the IPCC forecast that if there was essentially no restriction on the burning of fossil fuels or harmful land use changes (the Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5), atmospheric CO2 would double pre-industrial levels sometime between 2050 and 2100, and global average temperatures would rise as a result by 3.2–5.4°C relative to 1850–1900 by 2100 (IPCC 2013).
	The increase in average temperatures will be accompanied by a marked increase in the frequency of very high temperatures. It has been projected that ‘mega-heatwaves’ of the kind that caused more than 50,000 excess deaths in Russia in 2010 may increase by a factor of 5–10 in Europe, within the next 40 years (Barriopedro et al. 2011). As average temperatures rise, the incidence of cold events is likely to fall, all else being equal, although there may be unexpected effects in some regions due to feedback loops and critical tipping points. In one example, melting of the Arctic ice has disturbed the high-level jet stream over Europe and North America, re-distributing very cold air masses and leading to the apparently paradoxical phenomenon of warm polar seasons and extreme cold events further south (Liu et al. 2012).
	The effects of warming and changes in rainfall will be unevenly distributed, geographically. For instance, a global average of 4°C of warming may be associated with an increase in temperatures in the Arctic of 10°C or more, a decline in rainfall by 40–50% in North Africa, droughts threatening the viability of rainfed agriculture in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa by the end of the century, and much of south-eastern Australia experiencing extreme fire risks as often as every second summer (4°C and Beyond 2009).
	In summary, the greenhouse effect is long known and well described. The rate at which greenhouse gas levels in the atmosphere are increasing is unprecedented, and absolute concentrations are presently higher than at any time since the Pleiocene. In association with these changes, the world is warming, in a manner that carries a discernible human ‘fingerprint’. For instance, the mix of carbon isotopes in the atmosphere has changed with the rising contribution of CO2 from burning of fossil fuels (in which the lighter isotopes especially 12C predominate) (IPCC 2013).
	Why is this a public health issue? It is important to recognize that for human health, variability and frequency of extreme events are often more important than average conditions. On exposure to heat or cold, it is deviations from usual or most commonly experienced temperatures that carry the greatest risk.
	While humans may be able to cope with modest increases in baseline temperatures, there are physical and ecological systems of importance to health that are exposed to environmental change and may be exquisitely sensitive to temperature rise. Agriculture generally operates as an open system, directly exposed to the weather, with very few buffers against extreme events or long-term shifts in ambient conditions. Warming of 2–4°C in the global average would lead to substantial falls in productivity in some parts of the world. In much of sub-Saharan and southern Africa, it has been projected that an increase of 5°C in the global average would reduce the growing period for some staple crops by more than 20%, threatening the coping capacity and resilience of hundreds of millions of people (Thornton et al. 2011). A small degree of ocean warming above certain threshold limits may lead to death of coral and increased rates of ciguatera (fish poisoning) (Tester et al. 2010). Mosquitoes and other disease vectors also respond acutely to small shifts in temperature and rainfall, and increases in average temperatures will increase the potential for disease transmission in some populations (Wandiga et al. 2010). Conversely, disease risks may be reduced in areas where conditions are presently close to the upper limits of vector survival (Gething et al. 2010). Perhaps as important, historical improvements in health have been built on stable governance, liberty, and relative protection from extreme violence.
	Another mechanism by which climate change may affect human health is through conflict, disorder, and displacement of populations. There are many examples in history of social disruption caused by rapid fluctuations in temperature and extremes in precipitation (McMichael 2017). Although the sudden variations in climate in the past resulted from natural causes, such as volcanic eruptions and long-term climate cycles, the consequences resemble what may occur due to anthropogenic climate change. Indeed, the risks may be even higher now, given the scale and speed of change that is projected.





Observational studies of weather, climate, and health


	A great deal has been written about variations in weather (day-to-day conditions) and climate (average weather over a period of decades), and their relationship with health outcomes. One of the exposures most closely studied is temperature, which may be expressed in many ways, commonly as the daily average or maximum temperature, with or without an adjustment for humidity. Figure 2.9.2 shows a pattern that is frequently observed—a J-shaped relation between temperature and health outcomes (in this case, mortality excluding accidental deaths). The optimal temperature (the point at which mortality is lowest) differs from one setting to another. In the case of Haerbin, a city located in the far north of China, the number of deaths is at its lowest when the average temperature is close to 0°C (Yang et al. 2007). In cities located closer to the equator, the optimal temperature tends to be higher (Fig. 2.9.2). The overall shape of the curve relating temperature to mortality remains similar, but the point of inflection on the curve moves towards the right in cities where high temperatures are more commonly experienced (McMichael et al. 2008). This is a reminder that populations do adapt to their ecological context, physiologically and socially. What is less clear is how quickly this adaptation can occur, if people move, or the climate changes. Another important question is: what are the limits of adaptation? how much heat is tolerable (Box 2.9.2)?
	 	Box 2.9.2 Too big? Or too big to ignore? The challenge of scale
	Climate change is fundamentally different from most other environmental problems that public health has faced. It is a matter of scale. Climate change is a global problem, not only because the effects are widely distributed, like acid rain, or influenza epidemics, but because the underlying cause is a breakdown of Earth’s homeostatic systems. Other examples of environmental changes that threaten a ‘safe operating space’ planet-wide include the depletion of high-level atmospheric ozone by chlorofluorocarbons and loss of biodiversity (Steffen et al. 2015). Climate change moves on prolonged timescales. For instance, the full effects of a spike in greenhouse emissions on warming of the deep ocean and associated sea level rise may not be apparent for 5,000 years or more (Stouffer 2012). This provides a serious challenge to public health scientists. In the last hundred years, with advances in exposure assessment and better knowledge of cellular and molecular mechanisms, the focus has shifted to finer-grained explanations of disease. However the contexts in which chemical reactions occur, microbes multiply, and individuals make their decisions is key to understanding both risk and resilience. For example, mortality in the 1995 Chicago heatwave was a function of both individual-level variables (such as age and income), and the qualities of neighbourhoods. The poor and the elderly were at much greater risk during the heatwave if they lived in areas with rundown businesses, abandoned housing, and degraded public spaces (Klinenberg 2002). Climate change represents a particularly stark example of a big-picture problem, featuring extended timescales, ubiquitous exposures, and the confounding effects of human adaptation. In response, public health must move upstream, beyond studies of the variations between individuals to investigations of causes on a larger scale (Pearce 2011), and pay greater attention to the ecologic perspective on human disease and injury (Krieger 2015). This will very likely require refinement of established methods of public health inquiry (such as time series analysis, and population-level research designs); an understanding of climate science and meteorology; the creative use of analogues; and the application of relevant modelling methods from other disciplines (e.g. system dynamics modelling) (Rutter et al. 2017).
	Fig. 2.9.2 Average daily apparent temperature and total mortality: Santiago (33 degrees S), São Paulo (24 degrees S), and Mexico City (19 degrees N). Solid lines show central estimate, dashed lines the 95% confidence intervals. Adjusted for particulate pollution and ozone levels.
	Reproduced from Bell ML et al., Vulnerability to heat-related mortality in Latin America: a case-crossover study in São Paulo, Brazil, Santiago, Chile and Mexico City, Mexico, International Journal of Epidemiology, Volume 37, Issue 4, pp. 796–804, Copyright © The Author 2008, with permission from Oxford University Press.
	Higher temperatures have been linked with a range of health outcomes including deaths and hospital admissions for respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. In heatwaves, which may be defined as prolonged exposure to temperatures in the top 5–10% of the range for that location, the effects appear to be greater than would be expected by simply extrapolating the temperature–health outcome relationship (Anderson and Bell 2011; Rocklöv et al. 2012). Duration of heat, frequency of heatwaves, and timing (early or late in the season) all appear to modify the effects of high temperatures. High levels of air pollution amplify the damaging effects of heat (Qin et al. 2017).
	There is considerable variation within populations in vulnerability to heat. Older people (70 years and over) and children are generally at greater risk. There is no consistent pattern with gender. Men were found to be at greater risk in São Paulo and Santiago (Bell et al. 2008); whereas a study in Brisbane, Australia reported a more marked increase in mortality risk for women than men (Huang et al. 2012). In many countries, low socioeconomic status (SES) has been associated with increased risk of heat-and cold-related poor health (Qin et al. 2017), but again, this is not universal. There is, for example a greater variation by SES in heat mortality in the United States than in England, perhaps because the use of air conditioning is distributed differentially in the United States but not so much in the United Kingdom (where few houses have artificial cooling and there is much less social variation) (Armstrong et al. 2011). Vulnerability is also expressed spatially (Uejio et al. 2011) reflecting the geographical distribution of individual and household characteristics (such as prevalence of chronic diseases, housing design, and poverty) and also district-level variables (urban form, quality of services).
	It is not just the maximum or average temperatures that affect health. Variability is important as well. In 135 United States cities, for example, the standard deviation of summer temperatures was associated with mortality of older people suffering from chronic disease, after adjustment for a wide range of risk factors including average temperature (Zanobetti et al. 2012).
	As with many climate change impacts, more is known about the effects of high temperatures in high-income countries than in the developing world, although the problem is likely to be more severe in the latter, given the high temperatures that already apply in many low-latitude countries, the very large populations, often with multiple health problems, that are exposed, the large number of outdoor workers and the low quality of housing and urban environments.
	The effects of heat on the health of workers has emerged as an important issue, given the large number of people who may be affected, and the multiple adverse consequences of reduced productivity and loss of livelihoods (Lucas et al. 2014). This is especially significant in equatorial countries where high temperatures already place severe restraints on the duration and intensity of outdoor work (Kjellstrom et al. 2013).
	The effects of climate on infectious disease have long been known (see Box 2.9.3). The first textbook of tropical medicine, by Patrick Manson, was published in 1900, and was called A Manual of the Diseases of Warm Climates (Manson 1900). Manson wrote principally of infectious diseases but he recognized that few conditions were peculiar to the tropics. In other words, he understood that climate variables such as temperature and precipitation play an important part in, but are seldom the entire explanation for, the distribution and occurrence of disease.
	The mosquito-borne diseases are good examples. In warmer conditions, vectors such as Aedes aegypti (responsible most commonly for the transmission of dengue fever) develop more quickly from the immature stage (Tun-Lin et al. 2000). In tropical countries in which temperatures vary little through the year, the transition from a time of low rainfall to the rainy season may act as a powerful climatic trigger for outbreaks of dengue (Schreiber 2001). But other factors are important also. Urbanization and the quality of housing, for instance, modify the effect of climate on dengue risk (Wu et al. 2009). Overall, it is projected that climate change will extend the present geographic range of dengue and threaten populations which do not currently experience local transmission of the disease (Ebi and Nealon 2016).
	 	Box 2.9.3 Plague and climate
	Plague is caused by infection of humans with Yersinia pestis. The organism is established in rodent populations in parts of Asia, Africa, and the Americas, and periodically causes outbreaks of disease in local populations. The prevalence of Yersinia in animal hosts is climate sensitive. For example, a study of gerbils in Kazakhstan found the risk of disease was increased by warmer springs and wetter summers (Stenseth et al. 2006). An increase of 1°C in spring was associated with an increase of more than 50% in the prevalence of animals infected with Yersinia. Climate also affects the abundance of rodent hosts and flea vectors, as well as the chances of humans coming into contact with the pathogen. Consequently, it is not surprising that many historical studies have shown a link between climate and plague epidemics (McMichael 2017). As one example: a study of plague in China between 1850 and 1960 found the number of cases per year was positively related to rainfall, although extremely high precipitation in the wetter parts of the country led to lower than expected plague intensity (Xu et al. 2011).
	There are many ways by which physical and mental health may be affected by variations in climate or weather. In the south-western part of Australia, the prevalence of depression has been related to the severity of long-term drought (measured as dry-land salinity) (Speldewinde et al. 2009). The physical degradation of environments following climate change has been linked to loss, grief, separation, and self-questioning in many environments (Berry et al. 2010; Cunsolo and Ellis 2018). Non-communicable diseases may be affected: in Bangladesh the dry season is marked by increasing salinity and rising temperatures of the ground water, and it is thought these changes are linked to marked seasonal variations in the incidence of high blood pressure and eclampsia in pregnancy (precipitated by increases in sodium loading) (Xun et al. 2010). Cholera is another marker in Bangladesh of warming and salt intrusion, but indeed all the vibrio pathogens (including vulnificus and parahaemolyticus as well as cholerae) are temperature sensitive and have been described as ‘microbial barometers of climate change’ (Baker-Austin et al. 2017).
	In summary, humans have adapted to local conditions during a period of relatively stable climate (the Holocene epoch),but are susceptible to ill-health caused by rapid changes in temperature and precipitation. The connection between extremes of cold and heat on mortality is well established, and many infectious diseases also vary with climate.





Attribution—present impacts of climate change


	In 2013 the Fifth Assessment Report of the IPCC concluded that ‘It is extremely likely more than half of the observed increase in global average surface temperature from 1951 to 2010 was caused by the anthropogenic increase in greenhouse gas concentrations and other anthropogenic forcings’ (IPCC 2013, p. 17). In the IPCC lexicon, ‘extremely likely’ means the probability is more than 95%.
	The IPCC assessment reports have described many changes in physical and biological systems that are consistent with global warming. For example, during the last one hundred years the distribution of North Sea cod has changed dramatically, with fish moving northwards and into deeper waters, largely as a consequence of ocean warming (the other influence being the pressure of commercial fishing) (Engelhard et al. 2014). In the Alsace region of France, in association with higher summer temperatures, the potential alcohol content of Riesling grapes, at harvest, increased by almost 1% per year (Duchêne and Schneider 2005). It is not difficult to attribute changes such as these to climate change, as there are few alternative plausible explanations.
	The story of tick-borne diseases, including Lyme disease and tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) illustrates well the complexities of attribution. In the last decade of the twentieth century the vector for TBE moved northward across the Baltic and Scandinavia, in association with warming that has been most marked in winter and early spring (Lindgren and Gustafson 2001). The incidence of TBE surged in the early 1990s in the Baltic states, but this did not fit closely with climate. There were considerable variations within the Baltic in TBE rates, and although warming continued after 2000, TBE rates fell (Sumilo et al. 2007). Clearly there are other factors that are important besides the arrival of a climate that was more favourable for transmission of the TBE virus. When the Soviet Union broke up in 1989, many collective farms ceased to operate, areas that had been used for pasture and agriculture were left untended, and these provided new habitat for rodents and deer. At the same time, during a period of economic disruption and transition, people were more dependent than before on wild food sources, including mushrooms and small game, and as a result spent more time in the countryside. In combination these changes, climatic and non-climatic, may have increased tick abundance and boosted, for a short time, the exposure of humans to tick-borne diseases (Sumilo et al. 2007).
	Lyme disease emerged in the United States in the 1970s, most likely due to socioeconomic changes and transition of farmland in the north-east to forests (Ebi et al. 2017). The disease was slow to get established in Canada, although the local habitat was suitable and there was movement of natural hosts, vector, and pathogen (Borrelia burgdorferi) across the border from the United States. It is likely that temperature was the limiting factor. Since 2000, in the same period as lower Canada has warmed, local populations of the tick vector have established, and the number of cases of Lyme disease has increased. The links between environmental change, the shift of vectors, and the onset of disease suggest that the spread of Lyme disease, in this region, is due in part to climate change (Ebi et al. 2017).
	In public health, attribution involves probabilities, based on the risk of an event occurring following a particular exposure, compared with the probability of the same event taking place without the exposure. The inability to attribute a particular instance of lung cancer to cigarette smoking is quite consistent with a firm conviction that smoking causes the majority of such cancers in populations in which tobacco use is common. Such an approach is applied also in climate sciences to make judgements about the causes of extreme events. For instance, a study of cyclones in the north Pacific in 2015 concluded the extreme energy levels that were observed were highly likely to be due to human-induced climate change (Woodward and Samet 2018). A study of the 2003 European heatwave concluded it was very likely (probability greater than 90%) that human influences on climate had more than doubled the risk of such an extreme event (Stott et al. 2004). Note that a relative risk of more than 2.0 means it is more likely than not that the outcome is attributable to the exposure.





Forecasting


	To attribute past and present morbidity and mortality to climate change is not straightforward, but future attribution presents even greater difficulties. There is no certainty about how much the climate will change in the future, or what the consequences will be, but it is clear that the most important risks lie ahead of us. Present-day effects of climate change on health may be miniature versions of future effects, or perhaps not: future challenges may be threshold-crossing novelties. For this reason, a great deal of effort has been applied to attempts to project future climates and the consequent impacts through modelling studies. One approach is to attempt to isolate the effect of an altered climate on specific diseases by holding all other independent variables constant. We will look at examples of this approach using several diseases known to be highly climate sensitive. Since climate change acts as a multiplier of disadvantage, ideally studies would go further and ask: how are the ‘baseline’ risks likely to change in the short to medium term? This is a difficult undertaking but could, potentially, provide a more accurate description of future impacts of climate change on human health. Modelling studies that have taken this approach are less common and require methods not so familiar to epidemiologists—methods that can deal with significant levels of complexity, non-linear interactions, and feedback dynamically over time.
	A study of future impacts of climate change on the ‘potential transmission’ of malaria in Zimbabwe attempted to isolate the effects of climate between 2000 and 2050, by assuming there would be no other changes (Ebi et al. 2005). The suitability of the climate for stable transmission of Plasmodium falciparum malaria was related to mean temperatures, winter minimum temperatures, and monthly rainfall, based on outputs from the MARA (Mapping Malaria Risk in Africa) project. On this basis the researchers reported that within 50 years malaria could be established in the densely populated and presently malaria-free highlands of Zimbabwe. The model used in this study was risk based (suitability varied from 0 to 1), was explicitly projecting the potential for disease, rather than predictions of disease occurrence, and set aside the question of how other influences on malaria, apart from climate, might differ in 2050 from the present day.
	In a less common non-communicable disease example, a study in the United States modelled the current relation between mean annual temperature and hospital admissions for stones in the urinary tract in the United States. In general, nephrolithiasis is more common in populations living in warm climates, and this trend is apparent in the United States. The authors applied projections of mean annual temperatures in the future and calculated the potential increase in hospital admissions and associated costs (Brikowski et al. 2008). Since both linear and non-linear relationships between temperature and risk fitted the present data, both forms were modelled. Projections were based on one of the IPCC’s intermediate severity climate change scenarios (SRES A1B).
	Even more challenging is to model the future burden of disease due to climate change impacts on the upstream determinants of health. Crucially, the effects of climate change on the global food system may have far-reaching effects on health. To investigate this issue, researchers linked models that projected food supply under different climate scenarios with estimates of the effects of changes in fruit and vegetable consumption, red meat intake and bodyweight (Springmann et al. 2016) (Fig. 2.9.3). The study was the first to assess the effects of changes in diet composition (e.g. intake of fruit and vegetables), and found that this was more important in terms of health outcomes than simple loss of calories. It was assumed that recent improvements in most parts of the world in food security and nutrition-related health outcomes would continue, so the main effect of climate change would be to act as a brake on progress. Limitations in this assessment include the relatively short timeframe (up to 2050 only), inability in a global assessment to accurately capture local conditions and the particular difficulties faced by some populations (e.g. those on lowlying Pacific islands), and the possibility that wide-ranging mitigation policies might themselves threaten the production and distribution of food (Woodward and Porter 2016).
	Fig. 2.9.3 Climate-related deaths (in thousands) in 2050
	Reproduced from Springmann et al. (2016) ‘Global and regional health effects of future food production under climate change: a modelling study’, Lancet, with permission from Elsevier.
	Demographic projections are important, since climate change impacts will depend on the size, structure, and health status of world populations. The mid-range estimate is for the world population to increase from about 7.6 billion presently to around 9.7 billion by 2050, with most of the growth occurring in developing countries (United Nations 2015b). The proportion of the population in older age groups is likely to increase, almost everywhere, although the average years of life remaining will change much less (Lutz et al. 2008). Mortality is projected to decline, in most countries, leading to increases in life expectancy at birth of around 5–6 years by the mid-century (World Health Organization 2011). Assuming that present trends of social and economic development continue, illness rates will also decline, and it has been estimated that the overall burden of disease (measured in disability-adjusted life years) will be reduced by about 30% by 2030 (World Health Organization 2008). Child mortality is falling, worldwide, with no sign of a reduction in the rate of improvement (You et al. 2015). However, there are still very large differences between countries, and some, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, are improving slowly, if at all (World Health Organization 2011).
	How could it be that health statistics are improving around the world while pressures mount on the global environment, from climate change and other big-picture problems (e.g. loss of biodiversity, overloading waterways and soils with nitrogen and phosphorus)? We have no clear reference point of course: mortality may have fallen more rapidly, child stunting may have diminished sooner, if climate change was not acting. But the more important point relates to timing. There is good reason to believe the full costs of large-scale human exploitation of the planet have not yet become apparent (McMichael 2017): human populations have been ‘eating the future’ by headlong clearing of land, burning of fossil fuels, and drawing down on sources of fresh water.
	Whether social and economic development continues on the present trajectories is of course unknown, but is fundamental to projections both of climate change and vulnerability to its effects. In turn, uncertainty about the pace of social and economic development stems, in part, from the possible effects of climate change on societies and economies, and on the pathways we take in responding. Furthermore, health is sensitive to the manner in which economic growth occurs. If development is not inclusive, then vulnerability to the effects of climate change may not improve. India, for instance, has taken great strides, economically, in the last 20 years, but the health problems of poverty persist for many people. The prevalence of child underweight and stunting fell modestly between 1992 and 2005 (from 49% to 40% underweight, for instance), but there was no relation, at the state level, with income growth (Subramanyam et al. 2011). Child health measured in this way advanced no faster in the richest states than the poorest.
	These examples demonstrate the intertwined nature of climate change and development and serve as an entry point to understanding that climate change and our actions to address it are issues of social and environmental justice, equity, and human rights. The highest income countries have achieved substantial improvements in life expectancy, health, and quality of life, in significant part due to fossil-fuel dependent economic development. Up to 2010, the most developed countries had contributed more than half of all anthropogenic emissions, despite being home to only 17% of the global population (den Elzen et al. 2013). On the other hand, we have already demonstrated that the impacts of climate change are being, and will continue to be borne, by the lowest income countries and populations within countries who are already experiencing socioeconomic inequities. The relationship between climate change and human rights is discussed further in Chapter 2.9. Indigenous peoples are both particularly vulnerable to the health impacts of climate change and have specific resilience capabilities and knowledges for mitigation and adaptation (Ford 2012). These are discussed in detail in Chapter 10.6.
	Will there be positive effects of climate change, and if so, how will they balance the negative impacts? This is not a straightforward question to answer. It is likely there will be some positive effects in the short term, but it is difficult to judge their magnitude. For instance, it is likely that modest warming will boost agricultural yields in temperate parts of the world, increasing food production in these regions. Moreover, food crops such as wheat, rice, barley, and oats, tend to grow more quickly in higher levels of CO2. Together, these effects may reduce the risk of food shortages and undernutrition caused by lower production in hot, low-latitude countries (Gornall et al. 2010). The balance of gains and losses will depend on whether populations at risk of food shortages can in fact get access to the climate dividend, and the relief may be temporary: the increase in crop yields in temperate zones will almost certainly diminish as warming continues (Teixeira et al. 2011). In tropical developing countries, where food insecurity is greatest, the impact will be most severe. In sub-Saharan Africa, where the caloric intake of 60% of the population in the late 2000s was insufficient for an active life, 5 degrees of warming (global average) is projected to cut maize yields by 19% and beans by 68% (Thornton et al. 2011).
	Where disease vectors and pathogens are already close to the upper temperature limit for reproduction and transmission, further warming is likely to reduce the risk of disease. In parts of equatorial Africa, for example, projected temperatures will exceed the optimal settings for both the vector and the parasite, and the potential for malaria transmission will rapidly diminish (Ebi et al. 2017).
	The effects of cold and heat on mortality have been closely studied, and shed some light on the matter of balancing gains and losses with global warming (Ebi and Mills 2013). The J-shaped relation between ambient temperature and mortality suggests that warming will lead to fewer cold-related deaths, and greater heat-related mortality. This curve is rarely symmetrical—in cooler locations, the right-hand arm of the curve (associated with heat) tends to rise more rapidly, and the opposite is true for populations living in relatively warm conditions. This means that if there is a trade-off of gains and losses with warming, the balance will depend on the initial conditions. But it is more complicated still—it is not clear whether cool-location populations will retain their (relatively greater) tolerance for cold as temperatures rise, or whether the shape of the temperature–mortality curve will change. Also, it is uncertain how many of the deaths that occur at colder times of the year are in fact due to low temperatures, rather than other phenomena that vary with season (such as infectious disease epidemics). Many populations in colder parts of the world, where the most affluent and best buffered populations in the world are located, have adapted to a large extent to cold, and the impacts of both cold spells and ambient low temperatures have much reduced over time. Consequently, the added benefits of global warming in these locations may be modest, and outweighed by the additional burden of heat-related ill-health in the much larger and more vulnerable populations living in low latitudes (Kinney et al. 2015).
	It is important to identify the most important sources of uncertainty in projections. A study of diarrhoeal disease attempted to distinguish the effects of uncertainties in temperature changes and the exposure–response function (change in disease incidence per unit warming) (Kolstad and Johansson 2011). The focus in future-oriented studies tends to be on the climate modelling, given the many assumptions that have to be incorporated. However in this case it was evident that uncertainty associated with the risk coefficient (which varied almost fourfold between studies) caused more variation in the outcome than the choice of climate change model. Another study in the United States examined the effects of modelling choices on national mortality attributable to low-level ozone, in the presence of climate change (Post et al. 2012). Results varied from about 600 deaths per year avoided as a result of climate change to 2,500 deaths attributable to climate change (although most models projected increases in mortality). The most influential analytic steps were the choices of climate change scenario and air quality model. It should be noted also that the ozone studies, and many other investigations of climate impacts, have tended to project effects based on mid-range climate scenarios, when the globe is in fact tracking on a steeper trajectory for emissions, one that fits more closely with the high-range models. This highlights the issue of thresholds and tipping points—as we move further away from familiar environments and encounter more extreme exposures, it becomes less certain that present exposure–response relations will apply in the future.
	There are two ways of responding to climate change: adapt to the new environment (analogous to secondary prevention) and mitigate (primary prevention—take whatever steps are needed to avoid further, increasingly dangerous climate change occurring). Primary prevention is necessary from a public health perspective, but there are strong imperatives for now also investing in adaptation: in particular, the world is committed to warming as a result of greenhouse gases already emitted, due to the long time-course of global carbon cycles and heat transfers. This is regardless of future emission trajectories. Both adaptation and mitigation have implications for health, and we deal with each in turn.





Adaptation to expected climate change


	The importance of adaptation is proportional to the extent and momentum of climate change—when there are very long lag times in the climate system then interventions to reduce emissions will take a very long time to have their full effect, and in the meantime, steps must be taken to cope with changes that are, in effect, unavoidable. The IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report estimated the Earth has already warmed by 0.85°C on average, compared with the late 1800s, with a resulting decrease in cold days and nights, a likely increase in both heat waves and heavy rainfall events (particularly in North America and Europe), and sea level rise of about 20 cm (IPCC 2013). It has been estimated that we are already committed to further warming of at least 0.7°C over the next 30 years because of the greenhouses gases that are now in the atmosphere. Also in the atmosphere are airborne pollutants, many of which have a cooling effect, and are tending to dampen down the global warming signal. It is difficult to determine the size of this effect, but it may be as much as 0.2°C of latent warming that will be expressed when local air pollution is better controlled and fossil fuel use declines (IPCC 2013).
	Then there is the question of future emissions. In 2015, the United Nations adopted the Paris Agreement, since signed by all member states and ratified by 175 of 197 members, including the United States and China (the two single largest emitting countries, responsible for 45% of global emissions). The Agreement commits parties to increasing cuts to emissions to keep average global warming to below 2°C (the globally agreed threshold for ‘dangerous’ climate change), while aiming for no more than 1.5 degrees to protect the most vulnerable lowlying island states from devastating sea level rise. While not legally binding, the Paris Agreement is the first truly global instrument to address climate change, and recognizes both the need to protect health, and the opportunity for health co-benefits in well-designed climate action (United Nations 2015a). At present, global emissions are close to 50 Gt CO2 equivalent per year, about 14% higher than the level required to hold warming to around 2°C. Following decades of rapid growth, the years 2014–2016 saw global emissions plateau for 3 years but in 2017 emissions rose again, to an historic high. This resulted from increasing energy demand and a slowdown in energy efficiency improvements (International Energy Agency 2018). There is a mixed picture emerging internationally. Some countries (including the United States and members of the European Union) are tracking steadily downwards, while emissions continue to rise in large, rapidly-developing countries such as China. The year of peak global emissions is critical. The sooner greenhouse emissions worldwide begin to fall the less painful the pathway to climate targets. For example, if global emissions did not peak until 2025 and then reduced by 3% per year, global average surface temperatures would rise by as much as 4 degrees C by the end of this century. More severe reductions, about 8% per year, would be needed to stay within 2°C (Hausfather and Pearce 2017).
	On the one hand, there are strong forces driving emissions upwards. These include population pressures (a 50% increase projected worldwide in the next 50 years) and economic development ‘catch up’: 90% of the growth in emissions this century will come from states that are presently in the low-and middle-income categories. On the other hand, there is some evidence that economic development and emissions are beginning to ‘decouple’, especially in South America (Hausfather and Pearce 2017). Further, there is increasing global political leadership from many of the high-income countries responsible for the majority of emissions, as evidenced by the Paris Agreement. Even in countries where there is a lapse of national-level leadership (such as the US president’s threats to leave the Paris Agreement), local and state-level governance continue to be committed to reducing emissions in line with obligations. There are also some helpful feedbacks at play. For example, as alternatives to fossil fuel energy generation such as solar panels and wind turbines become more popular, the price of these alternatives fall, making them even more attractive. Both onshore wind and photovoltaic solar generation now have cheaper lifecycle costs than the marginal cost of continuing to generate electricity by burning coal in existing power plants (International Renewable Energy Agency 2018).
	Locked-in climate change and the risk of mitigation failure are both compelling reasons to find options for coping with climate change impacts, particularly adaptation to increasing average and extreme temperatures, as well as resilience to storms, flooding, sea level rise, and disruption to agricultural production and distribution. Here we will examine some of the opportunities for adaptation, ranging from individual behaviours to neighbourhood interventions, to sector-wide changes. Some of the available options for adapting to climate change can also assist with climate change mitigation, or have other co-benefits for health and equity, while others may hamper efforts in these areas. We cover some examples relating to heat and storm events.
	At an individual level, improving the body’s physiological response to temperature extremes can assist with adaptation. Increasing physical activity, reducing obesity, and improving diabetes control have many benefits to health, including enhanced capacity to deal with heat (Kenny and Jay 2013). Clinical trials have shown that short-term endurance training increases sweat rate and peripheral blood flow and leads to more effective control of body temperature during exercise (Ichinose et al. 2009). Overweight military recruits in the United States were found to be seven times more likely to suffer heat illnesses during training than their colleagues (Bedno et al. 2010). Work of this kind indicates that public health programmes to promote physical activity, prevent unhealthy weight gain, and reduce the prevalence of obesity are likely to reduce vulnerability to heat.
	Community-oriented interventions have promise, since risk factors for heat-attributable deaths tend to cluster spatially. For instance, studies in New York City found that poverty, ethnicity, poor housing, exposure to greenspace, and the prevalence of hypertension were all associated with heat wave mortality, and vulnerable census tracts may be identified through a comprehensive neighbourhood heat vulnerability index (Madrigano et al. 2015).
	Although air conditioning has been advocated by some as an important measure for coping with high temperatures (Ostro et al. 2010), it brings vulnerability, as well as consuming large amounts of (often fossil fuel-based) electricity, and transferring further heat outdoors. Artificial cooling relies on a consistent power supply, and heatwaves may trigger electricity outages due to air conditioning demand overload (Anderson and Bell 2011). In these circumstances, populations accustomed to living with air conditioning may be at increased risk of ill-health due to high temperatures. Buildings designed for air conditioning are often poorly designed in other ways to deal with heat (with large, exposed surfaces of glass, and minimal natural shade, for instance). Also, physiological adaptation requires some exposure to heat strain, that is, an increase in body temperature (Maloney and Forbes 2011). Populations with around-the-clock access to air conditioning are less likely to develop the capacity to respond to extreme temperatures, when and if this occurs. Since most deaths during heat waves occur inside buildings, a focus on passive building and surrounding measures that don’t rely on energy use will be vital for equitable heat wave survival (‘passive survivability’) (Baniassadi and Sailor 2018). These include window design, balancing insulation for cold and heat, and balancing tensions between well-designed ventilation and shading, and energy efficiency through all seasons.
	Cities are significantly warmer than their surrounding rural areas (the urban heat island effect) due to darkly paved surfaces and dense anthropogenic heat generation (e.g. from vehicles and buildings). City-level interventions to reduce the health risks due to high temperatures will therefore be important (Phelan et al. 2015). Designing cities to reduce the heat island effect can also make them safer during times of high temperature. A study in Phoenix, Arizona estimated the reduction that could be made in heat-related emergency calls by an urban re-design package (Silva et al. 2010). This included changes in building and road materials to increase heat flows, more urban green spaces, rooftop treatments, and widespread application of reflective paints. In combination, the authors estimate, these interventions could reduce inner-city temperatures sufficiently to almost halve the number of annual heat-related emergency calls.
	Measures at a city-level to manage high temperatures when they do occur include heat-health early warning systems, better cooling of at-risk environments (such as residential care facilities for the elderly), identifying the isolated and most vulnerable citizens, and improving the preparedness of the healthcare sector. In France, many such changes to heatwave responsiveness were made following the severe heatwave in 2003. When another heatwave occurred in July 2006, the question asked was: did the country cope better this time than it did in 2003? In July 2003, the increase in daily temperatures was theoretically sufficient to increase daily mortality by about 230%, according to the long-run (1975–1999) relationship between temperatures and daily deaths (Fouillet et al. 2008). But a 290% increase was observed, an excess of more than 15,000 deaths. In 2006, the heatwave temperatures were not as high as 3 years earlier, and it was theoretically projected to raise mortality by about 60%. In fact, the death rate increased by only 14%. One possible explanation is that the 2003 disaster brought forward many deaths in relatively frail individuals, greatly reducing the pool of susceptibles in 2006. However, the mortality trends indicate the 4,600 fewer-than-expected deaths in July 2006 were indeed evidence of more effective adaptation.
	The contrast between more aggressive air conditioning and greater provision of green space in cities is an example of how ‘business as usual’ approaches can miss important opportunities (Hess et al. 2012). On the one hand, enhancing air conditioning helps to protect some of the most vulnerable individuals from high temperatures, though it carries a heavy cost in power consumption. On the other hand, a radical expansion in urban green spaces and street trees may bring a range of benefits (in addition to cooling), including carbon sequestration and health benefits due to reduced air pollution, better mental health, and more opportunities for physical activity (Salmond et al. 2016). But these ‘win-win’ interventions are seldom straightforward: green spaces on their own may not be sufficient to achieve health gains. A study of the 49 largest cities in the United States (Richardson et al. 2012) compared the extent of green space with all-cause mortality, adjusting for important social and demographic differences, but not for measures of urban density. They found, against expectations, that health appeared to be worse in greener cities, and this was explained by the negative effects of factors associated in the United States with green suburbs, mainly sprawling land use and high car dependence.
	Another important area for adaptation is in preparedness and resilience to severe storms and flooding. Most climate change models project an increase in the intensity of tropical storms, though it is less clear whether the frequency of storms will change. These extreme events already cause substantial loss of life and economic damage. For example, in Burma in 2008, Cyclone Nargis caused approximately 138,000 deaths and US $10 billion damage (Fritz et al. 2009); in the United States, Hurricane Katrina in 2005 was responsible for about 1,200 deaths (Blake and Gibney 2011) and direct losses of over US $130 billion (Field et al. 2012). Yet, in almost all regions more recent storms of similar or greater severity have seen lower event mortality rates, despite increasing populations living in vulnerable coastal zones globally. Southeast Asia is an important exception to this, due to frequent cyclones, very dense coastal cities and variable preparation and warning systems (Bouwer and Jonkman 2018). There are examples of countries with an improved record for managing the health risks of storms and cyclones. Cuba was struck by four destructive hurricanes (category 2 or greater) between 1998 and 2002. While tens of thousands of homes were damaged and hundreds of thousands of people were evacuated, there were very few deaths (12 in all) (Thompson and Gaviria 2004). While Hurricane Katrina killed many in the United States, no deaths resulted in Cuba from the same storm, despite 20,000 homes being destroyed. The large number of deaths associated with Hurricane Katrina in the United States was a result of serious deficiencies in the public health system, and lack of protection for the poorest and most marginalized social groups in the city (Brunkard et al. 2008).
	In contrast, Cuba invests heavily in traditional civil defence activities, including stockpiles of equipment, clothing, fuel, and food. There are effective storm warning systems, and good means of communicating information to the public. Other factors that contribute to resilience are high levels of literacy, provision of basic facilities in all rural areas, and a comprehensive and accessible primary healthcare system. An Oxfam analysis of disaster preparedness in Cuba found there was strong community engagement, so that populations that are threatened can be mobilized rapidly, and protection extends to all social groups, not just those with personal resources (Thompson and Gaviria 2004). These more immediate disaster preparedness activities are complemented by longer term shifts in the built environment, involving housing construction, land use, and urban planning (Lizarralde et al. 2015). The Cuban example is salutary for climate change adaptation for public health. Building resilience to protect health from climate change will require co-ordinated actions by central and local government, health, and other sectors, as well as communities.

	There are other opportunities to learn from the variability in past experience of coping with climate-related health problems. For instance, enteric infections such as that caused by Salmonella tend to be more common at higher temperatures, but the size of the increase in disease rates for a given amount of warming varies from one site to another. A study of the five largest Australian cities found that all showed an increase in Salmonella notifications with monthly mean temperature, but one city stood out as following a much steeper trajectory than the others (D’souza et al. 2004). Perhaps aspects of the food safety programmes present elsewhere are missing in this apparently particularly temperature-sensitive city.
	There is no doubt that climate change acts principally as a risk multiplier. The greatest impact will occur in populations that, for other reasons, already have the worst health statistics, while patterns of economic development now also shape future climate change vulnerability. The World Bank in its landmark 2010 report on climate change and development concluded that ‘baseline health status is the single most important determinant of both future losses, and the cost of adaptation’ (World Bank 2009). It follows that adaptation must include improvements in the social determinants of health, including social safety nets, as well as essential public health services. But is it true that this is all that is needed? In other words, is ‘business as usual’ development, the package of improvements that we would want to be making anyway, sufficient preparation for climate change?
	Together with leading economists (Fankhauser and Stern 2016), we argue that ‘business as usual’ patterns of economic development will not be sufficient. Climate change is unique in geographic scale, long time lags, and momentum. Impacts accumulate and progress with such long lag times (sea level rise is a good example) that the process must be regarded as irreversible over our usual public health timescales. This is not a one-off event, but a new environmental dynamic, with enormous momentum. We are likely to be pushed to the edge of what is familiar, and beyond, leading potentially to abrupt and radical changes in Earth systems (Lenton and Ciscar 2013). In epidemiological terms, even if the trends in exposures (rising temperatures, changing patterns of precipitation) remain the same, it may be difficult to anticipate the dose–response relationships that apply in the future, due to unforeseen tipping points, thresholds, and non-linearities. The much greater than expected damage caused by unprecedentedly intense bushfires in Victoria, Australia in 2009 is a good example (Teague et al. 2010).
	Climate change does not only multiply existing risks. It may contribute to new risks where ecosystems are pressed beyond significant thresholds. This may happen on the edges of areas affected by climate-sensitive diseases. One example is the acute illness that occurs after eating sea-foods contaminated with Vibrio parahemolyticus. The organism is temperature sensitive, and until 2004 no instances of this particular food poisoning had been reported in North America above the US/Canada border. In that year there was an outbreak of cases on a cruise ship in Alaska, linked to shell-fish from a local oyster farm in Prince William Sound. On investigation, it was found that water temperatures at the farm (and the surrounding ocean) had been rising steadily for a decade, and presumably had crossed a critical boundary beyond which the organism could be sustained in local shell-fish (McLaughlin et al. 2005).
	Altogether, these unique aspects of climate change require special responses to meet health in development goals. In particular, agricultural investments and rapid urban infrastructure development will need to simultaneously be resilient to climate change impacts, low-carbon, and health-promoting, requiring unprecedented partnerships across sectors—signalled by SDG 17.
	Finally, it is crucial to note the limits to adaptation (Dow et al. 2013), emphasizing the need to address the root cause of climate change (anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions). These limits include human physiological tolerance to extreme heat; limits to the geographical and physiological adaptation of other species on which we rely (such as food plants and pollinators); financial limits to disaster protection, response and recovery; and socio-political limits to governance under multiple stressors, leading to conflict and mass migration.
	In summary, given the extent of committed warming, and the difficulty of achieving substantial reductions in emissions, the world almost certainly faces large changes in the next half century. Improving baseline health status is fundamental to adaptation, but not sufficient—there are distinctive features of climate change that have to be taken into account. Discussions about adaptation also help us to understand the limits to adaptation and the importance of urgent action to reduce the future extent of climate change (Evans et al. 2014) (Box 2.9.4).
	 	Box 2.9.4 Health sector action on climate change
	The health sector itself will need to take both adaptation and mitigation actions in direct response to climate change, over and above the general strengthening of public health activities and improving access to healthcare. In addition, the sector will need to adapt to the necessary reduction in the availability, and increase in price, of fossil fuels (and oil-based products such as plastics) that must occur in order to reduce greenhouse emissions substantially.
	Adaptation actions will need to be shaped locally or regionally to respond to contextual variations in climate-related disease risk, available resources, and uncertainty (Confalonieri et al. 2015). For example, the US Resilient Hospital Dashboard (Four Twenty Seven 2016) uses localized climate and healthcare data to inform adaptation and resilience decisions.
	However, some generalizable areas for consideration have been recently described in the World Bank’s 2017 report on Climate Smart Healthcare. These encompass infrastructure, material resources, and supply chains, workforce planning, and resource allocation to particular services.
	Decisions on location and design of new hospitals and healthcare facilities must incorporate local information about climate impacts, including flood risk, wind, and sea level rise. The Climate Smart Healthcare report includes detailed considerations for climate resilient design of healthcare facilities. Existing healthcare buildings and infrastructure (e.g. water and energy supplies) need to be assessed for their vulnerability to extreme weather and sea level rise, with responses ranging from alterations, adaptive usage plans, to planning for retreat and replacement (Wardekker et al. 2012). For example, as part of the PAHO/WHO Smart Hospitals initiative, Georgetown Hospital in St Vincent and the Grenadines has had roof repairs, solar panels installed, upgraded plumbing, water storage, and energy systems to improve its resilience to hurricanes in the Caribbean that are becoming increasingly severe, while at the same time, reducing energy consumption. In 2013, the newly refurbished hospital (Fig. 2.9.4) remained open when a severe storm closed most other health services. Georgetown Hospital continued to function, while also supplying clean rainwater to local community members (Pan American Health Organization & Regional Office for the Americas of the World Health Organization, n.d.).
	Fig. 2.9.4 Georgetown Hospital, St Vincent, and the Grenadines (PAHO/WHO).
	The need for increased service investment in public health early warning systems for heatwaves and other climate-related hazards has already been highlighted. Context-specific responses specifically related to infectious disease have also been developed (Confalonieri et al. 2015). These include enhanced disease surveillance, epidemic early warning systems, and new wider control efforts such as mosquito surveillance and standing water management which perhaps have not previously been needed. Changing patterns of disease may also require re-balancing of the healthcare workforce, as well as workforce re-training about new diseases.
	Greater attention has been paid to reducing the health sector’s own substantial greenhouse gas emissions. Although much of the focus has been in high-income countries, the Climate Smart Healthcare report points out the contribution that low-carbon changes can make to improving access to healthcare in low-income, energy-insecure settings. England, the United States, and Australia have all estimated the total emissions footprint of their healthcare sectors, with findings ranging from 3% to 10% of total national emissions (Malik et al. 2018). While the scope of these assessments varies, emissions come mainly from hospital energy use, the procurement of material resources (particularly pharmaceuticals), and healthcare-related transport. Hospitals and health boards are often the largest employers and procurers in a region, and can therefore influence local government policy, large numbers of employees, and wider supply chains, putting them in positions of significant regional leadership.
	In England, the National Health Service has a dedicated Sustainable Development Unit, whose task it is to reduce the overall environmental pollution from healthcare, with a focus on climate pollution. By taking a systematic approach to measuring emissions, setting long-term and intermediate targets, and taking action on energy, travel, reducing waste in procurement and influencing supply chains, emissions reductions have been achieved, coupled with financial savings of about GBP30 million per year (NHS Sustainable Development Unit 2016). Despite an 18% increase in inpatient admissions between 2007 and 2015, NHS England reduced its greenhouse gas emissions by 11%. Their ‘wedges’ approach demonstrates how within-health sector measures will need to be coupled with partnerships beyond the health sector to achieve required reductions (Fig. 2.9.5). The NHS England example also demonstrates the importance of the national regulatory context—in this case the UK Climate Change Act 2008 has set a consistent regulatory framework requiring all sectors to reduce their emissions by 80% by 2050 (Climate Change Act 2008 (c.27) 2008).
	Fig. 2.9.5 NHS England, public health and social care system ‘wedges’ to 2050.
	Reprinted from NHS Sustainable Development Unit. (2016). Sustainable development in the health and care system. Health check 2016, under the Open Government License v3.0.





Mitigation: scale, possible co-benefits, and unintended harms


	To avoid dangerous climate change, greenhouse gas emissions must fall to net zero in the coming decades, requiring an industrial and energy revolution. In the past, energy revolutions have been disruptive. They have caused serious environmental damage, increased social inequalities, and shortened life expectancy. Are there paths to a low-carbon future that can achieve the opposite result—simultaneous improvements in the quality of the environment, public health, and health equity? We will review the evidence for common solutions and discuss ways in which ‘co-benefits’ might influence policy settings for climate change.
	If warming by the end of the century is to be contained to below 2°C, then CO2 emissions must be reduced to around 14 Gt per year in 2050, less than a quarter of ‘business as usual’ projections. This is a tall order, and if reductions of such magnitude are going to be achieved, there will need to be radical changes in the way humans use energy across all sectors, including housing, transport, industry, and food and agriculture. It will require deeper social changes than merely identifying and bringing forward renewable technologies. Despite rapid growth in alternative energy sources, over the last 50 years each added unit of energy from wind, hydro, and other renewables has displaced only a quarter of a unit of energy obtained from fossil fuels and has had an even smaller impact on electricity generation (York 2012). In order to meet greenhouse targets, there must be serious deterrents to fossil fuel use, including prices that reflect the full environmental and social cost.
	The 2010 World Development Report talked about changes that are so large they constitute ‘an energy revolution’. Revolutions may re-orient society in a way that is beneficial, in the long run, but they tend to be disruptive and harmful in the short term. The last energy revolution began in England in the nineteenth century and ushered in what has been in many respects a golden age of industrialization and improvements in life expectancy. But England, and every other country that went through the process, also experienced the ‘four Ds’—disruption, deprivation, disease, and death (Szreter 2004). In the large English cities in the 1840s, crowding, pollution, and social upheaval affected everyone, but particularly those at the bottom of the social hierarchy. Life expectancy at birth fell to medieval levels, less than 30 years among the working classes in many cities (Szreter and Mooney 1998).
	The challenge with climate change mitigation will be to disrupt present patterns of energy use, while avoiding the very high and inequitable social and health costs that were carried by nineteenth-century cities. Early experience with alternative energy sources has not been altogether reassuring. One stark example is the encouragement of biofuels, which exemplifies the potential for health, equity, and environmental co-harms in a poorly designed low-carbon transition. There have been large-scale moves to use food and vegetable oil crops for bioethanol and biodiesel, often with substantial government subsidies: in 2009 about a quarter of all US corn was diverted to biofuel production as a result of federal intervention. Their effectiveness for reducing greenhouse gas emissions is questionable, and their encouragement has increased competition for food staples such as soybeans, maize, and cereals—increasing biofuel demand accounted for between a quarter and a third of the rise in global grain prices in the early 2000s, and played a significant role in the 2006–2008 food price crisis (Malins 2017). It remains to be seen whether second-generation biofuels, extracted from non-edible plants such as jatropha that are grown on marginal lands and don’t compete directly with food production, will bring the same energy benefits without the health risks.
	It is possible to identify low-risk transitions to zero carbon that can enhance rather than worsen health and equity. One easy example is provided by the link between short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs) and air quality. Black carbon (soot) particles, ozone, and methane have stronger heat-trapping properties than CO2 on a weight-for-weight basis, but have much shorter atmospheric life spans (from days to decades) (Kerr 2013). SLCPs, especially black carbon and ozone, are also responsible for a large proportion of the 7 million deaths globally due to air pollution.
	The United Nations Environment Programme estimated what could be achieved by widespread application of measures that are proven to reduce black carbon and methane (United Nations Environment Programme 2011). These measures include particle filters for disease engines, clean burning biomass cook stoves, and bans on the open field burning of agricultural waste. Assuming full implementation by 2030, the effects compared with ‘business as usual’ emissions amounted to saving 0.5°C of warming in 2050, while the reduction in local pollution would save about 50 million tonnes per year of lost crop yields, and avoid about 2.5 million premature deaths worldwide. The World Health Organization built on this work to identify priority policies with the best co-benefits for health and climate change mitigation through reductions in SLCPs. They identified four mitigation strategies with the greatest potential to effectively reduce SLCPs and achieve large health benefits: supporting active travel including through rapid mass public transport; promoting healthy plant-based diets; low-emission cook stoves and reducing household solid fuel use; and stricter vehicle emissions and efficiency standards, including for freight vehicles (World Health Organization 2015).
	More broadly than just SLCPs and air pollution, there are potential health and equity co-benefits from well-designed climate action across all the major emissions sectors. Transport and housing are two sectors where health co-benefits have been well studied, but where there is also a risk of adverse consequences for health and/or health equity if interventions are not carefully designed. One example is the health and energy efficiency benefits of home insulation and efficient heating. In New Zealand, although the climate is moderate, many homes are relatively cold and damp owing to a lack of insulation, ineffective heating, and poor building design. A randomized community trial tested the effect of home insulation on indoor temperatures, energy consumption, and respiratory health (Howden-Chapman et al. 2007). Insulated homes were found to be warmer, drier, used 20% less electricity than the control homes, and children in them were sick less frequently (Table 2.9.1). The findings led subsequently to a national roll-out of insulation subsidies and installation.
	However, alterations to improve the energy efficiency of housing may increase a range of other health risks. For example, there is a balance in houses between airtightness and ventilation that provides for efficient warming while allowing for adequate air flow to reduce indoor air pollution and prevent moisture from reaching levels conducive to mould growth (Shrubsole et al. 2014). The complex connections between housing, health, health equity, and energy efficiency require methods that allow for policies to be tested against their integrated impacts over time, as has been recently successfully tested for UK policies about housing (Macmillan et al. 2016) (Table 2.9.2).
