2.11


How access to healthcare affects population health


	Yvonne Inall, Rachel Lamdin Hunter, Stephen Leeder, and Angela Beaton





Introduction


	This chapter explores access to healthcare—the timely availability of professional health services to prevent, diagnose, and treat illnesses and to preserve or improve the health of individuals—and its consequences. The interplay between access to care and population health has been seen dramatically in the Covid-19 pandemic. Systems of care have been stressed to breaking point with loss of life and failure of confidence in the public health system.
	Access varies among and within countries. The challenge of providing access in relation to both communicable and non-communicable diseases is formidable (The Economist Intelligence Unit 2017).
	Providing access is complex. Which groups or organizations are responsible for provision (the enablers), and how might access be financed? More people are living longer, with long-term comorbidities. The disease burden in developing countries is shifting. By 2020, non-communicable diseases are likely to account for approximately 70% of preventable, premature deaths (WHO 2018). How much care should be provided, and at what level? Is access confined to a minimum set of services or does it include more expensive and innovative treatments?
	Countries and their governments vary in their political and social attitudes to access. Those with a strong social welfare agenda might focus attention and budgets on social factors such as education and social welfare; these not only determine health, but also access to care. Others, regarding healthcare as the individual’s concern, might give these factors less weight. These variations in response have been apparent in the Covid-19 pandemic.
	Despite this complexity and much national variation, access depends, in general, most often on good primary healthcare, public investment, and political will, availability of data to guide resourcing decisions, and the development of a well-trained, integrated workforce with appropriate supporting infrastructure.





Definitions


Primary healthcare


	Our working definition of primary healthcare is ‘the first point of contact an individual has with the healthcare system’. It might be provided by a physician, community nurse, or by other clinical or non-clinical allied health professionals.
	Effective primary healthcare provides accessible, comprehensive, culturally acceptable, community-based services to meet the health needs of individuals throughout their life-course—from family planning and infant immunizations to management of the comorbidities of the elderly and to palliative care. It also serves as the entry point for care in manging endemic and epidemic infectious disease, such as Covid-19, including vaccination.
	The watershed WHO Conference on Primary Health Care held at Alma-Ata in the then USSR in 1978 defined primary health as the first level of contact with a healthcare system:
	 	Essential healthcare based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable methods and technology made universally accessible to individuals and families in the community through their full participation and at a cost that the community and country can afford to maintain at every stage of their development in the spirit of self-reliance and self-determination. It forms an integral part both of the country’s health system, of which it is the central function and main focus, and of the overall social and economic development of the community. It is the first level of contact of individuals, the family and community with the national health system bringing health care as close as possible to where people live and work, and constitutes the first element of a continuing health care process. (WHO 1978)
	The breadth of services and professions which fall within the definition means that the nature of the services might vary substantially between and within countries. This variability creates major challenges for data collection and assessment, financing, policy development, and decision-making.





Guiding principles in primary healthcare


	Convened by Dr Halfdan Mahler, then Director-General of the World Health Organization, the Alma-Ata conference was a response to the social target set the previous year at the Thirteenth World Health Assembly, calling for ‘the attainment of all citizens of the world of a level of health that will permit them to lead a socially and economically productive life’ by the year 2000 (WHO 1988). Representatives from 134 UN member states and 67 UN organizations attended this seminal meeting. The objective was to agree on a set of principles for primary healthcare, to be endorsed by WHO and UNICEF. The principles agreed at Alma-Ata included:
	 	• accessibility and fairness;
	• relevance of the service to the needs of the population;
	• cost effective use of technology;
	• integration between primary, secondary, and tertiary care;
	• encouragement of self-care;
	• community involvement in the planning and provision of health services;
	• collaboration between the health and other sectors in addressing underlying causes of ill-health; and
	• redistribution of healthcare resources to primary healthcare, in rural and economically disadvantaged areas.
	These aspirations were widely endorsed (Bhutta et al. 2018), but 40 years after Alma-Ata, primary healthcare remains inaccessible to at least 400 million people. The reasons include:
	 	a. a lack (or misdirection) of public investment;
	b. provision of inappropriate service models; and
	c. disproportionate concentration of workers and resources in urban areas.





Secondary healthcare


	We define secondary healthcare as care by specialists to whom patients are referred by a primary health carer. Depending on the field of specialist practice, it might take place in a hospital, a stand-alone purpose-built, or modified facility, or the specialist’s consulting rooms. Obtaining secondary care can be challenging, depending on geography, transport, and funding (Araujo et al. 2018).
	The relationship between primary and secondary care providers operates both ways. Patients might not only be referred to secondary care providers by primary health carers, but secondary healthcare providers might refer patients to (or expect them to utilize) primary healthcare services following discharge from hospital, or as part of a coordinated care plan, drawing upon both primary and secondary services.
	A study of the relationship between primary and secondary care provision in Norway showed that primary healthcare workers felt that hospital-based carers ‘do not speak [our] language’ (Araujo et al. 2018). Breakdowns in communication were common. Primary and secondary carers had different ways of understanding patients’ needs. Efforts to improve coordination revealed problems relating to information technology, municipal, hospital and fiscal policy, and resistance to cultural change, all of which adversely affected attempts at harmonization.





Equity


	Equity in healthcare can be evaluated in several ways (Table 2.11.1). An important distinction, attributed to Aristotle, is between horizontal and vertical (Gillon 2005). Horizontal equity requires that equals should be treated in proportion to their equality, while vertical equity requires that unequals should be treated in proportion to their inequality.
	In vertical equity, those with the greatest needs receive the greatest attention. Horizontal inequality, like inequality in income or health, is often measured using Gini-like metrics known as concentration indices (Mackenbach and Kunst 1997). In reality, different groups in a population have different needs and require appropriately differentiated services; for example, the healthcare needs of indigenous Australians, whose life expectancy at birth is some 10.6 years less than that of the general population (AIHW 2018). Mooney (1996) has asked about a fair distribution of health resources, given this large difference in health status?
	There is little consensus on the vertical dimension of equity. Marginalized groups, such as indigenous populations, new migrants, immigrants who have not mastered the language of the host country, poorly educated people, the disabled, homeless, or prisoners might be regarded as ‘hard to reach’ or at least ‘underserved’ by standard services. In such cases, there might be a case for targeted services. There is, however, a concern that such targeted services can be seen as ‘poor services for poor people’, with the attached stigma. More generally, there is an increasing emphasis on designing local services to meet locally expressed needs, leading to greater variation in organization and delivery, contrasting with the uniform approach implied by the pursuit of horizontal equity.
	In the United Kingdom, the tension between these two dimensions of equity was addressed through the introduction of national level service specifications, which accommodated local discretion in implementation. However, the National Health Service (NHS) has come under increasing pressure resulting from austerity economic cuts to funding, staffing shortages, an ageing UK population and increasing social inequality (Iacobucci 2019).
	Ivan Illich, a radical critic of Medicine, claimed, ‘a vast amount of contemporary care is incidental to the curing of disease, but the damage done by medicine to the health of individuals and populations is very significant’ (Illich 1976). He acknowledged that Medicine, using vaccinations and antimicrobial drugs, aids in preventing and curing infectious diseases, but he argued that big reductions in mortality from infectious diseases in high-income countries had already occurred before these technologies became available. In his opinion, treatment of non-communicable diseases, such as cancer and cardiovascular disease, was of negligible benefit and indeed might cause considerable harm.
	Richard Smith, former editor of The British Medical Journal, an iconoclast and a fan of Illich, put it this way:
	 	Health, argues Illich, is the capacity to cope with the human reality of death, pain, and sickness. Technology can help, but modern medicine has gone too far—launching into a godlike battle to eradicate death, pain, and sickness. In doing so, it turns people into consumers or objects, destroying their capacity for health.
	Limits to medicine. Medical nemesis: the expropriation of health. R Smith http://dx.doi.org/10.1136/jech.57.12.928
	Illich’s opinion was supported by the controversial English physician, historian, and epidemiologist Thomas McKeown, in his analysis of historical trends in mortality in Britain (McKeown 1979). This analysis identified the limited role of Medicine as a past determinant of health. For example, relative reductions in mortality between 1881 and 1950 ranged from 30-fold for tuberculosis, 20-fold for digestive diseases, and 15-fold for respiratory diseases (ONS 1998). Most of these reductions occurred before the widespread use, after 1945, of disease-specific antimicrobial treatment.
	Archie Cochrane, famous today for his advocacy of the use of the randomized trial (RCT) in assessing the effectiveness of therapy, developed a somewhat similar argument in Effectiveness and Efficiency (Cochrane 1972). Cochrane advocated the now generally accepted view that, if at all possible, all care interventions should be tested in RCTs, and that the results of all such trials should be systematically collected, analysed, and implemented in clinical practice. Only recently, with the advent of genetic-based ‘precision medicine’, has a serious advance been made over RCTs in assessing the utility of proposed new therapies. Precision medicine, unlike RCTs, is specific to individuals.
	 	Table 2.11.1 Aspects of equity in health and healthcare
	 			Term
	Meaning
			Equity
	Fairness, or justice, in respect of treatment of different individuals or groups (Last 2007)
		Horizontal equity
	The extent to which equals are treated in proportion to their equality
		Vertical equity
	The extent to which unequals are treated in proportion to their inequality
		Equity in financial contribution
	The extent to which individual or household payments for care or health insurance are consistent with their capacity to pay
		Equity in access to healthcare
	The extent to which there is a fair distribution of access to healthcare in relation to need
		Equity in health
	The extent to which there is a fair or just distribution of opportunities for health among individuals and groups in a population
		Effective coverage
	The proportion of the population in need of an intervention that has received it (Shengelia et al. 2005)





Access to primary healthcare


	In general terms, ‘access to healthcare’ is said to exist when individuals or families can physically get to the services they need to treat illness or to maintain health (Gulliford et al. 2002). An ongoing debate seeks to distinguish access from use of services. At the simplest level, having access might be assessed in terms of the ready availability of services (Table 2.11.2).
	Obstacles to use include cost; physical barriers, including distance or difficulties of travel; personal barriers, when services are not felt culturally appropriate, socially acceptable, or not consistent with personal beliefs; or organizational barriers, such as difficulties obtaining a consultation, or delays because of waiting lists or the limited capacity of services (Aday and Anderson 1981; Pechansky and Thomas 1981). Utilization offers benefit only when effective care is relevant to needs (Table 2.11.2).
	‘Access’ has recently been reappraised. It is proposed that access be understood in terms of individuals’ ‘candidacy’, namely their eligibility for healthcare (Dixon-Woods et al. 2006). Candidacy is defined both by individuals’ perceptions of their own concerns, as well as by health providers’ views of the appropriateness of their services to meet those concerns. In short, ‘access’ is meaningful when a person perceives a need and care is available.
	 	Table 2.11.2 Dimensions of access to healthcare
	 			Dimension of access
	Meaning
	Potential indicators
			Availability
	Whether or not there is an adequate supply of health services in an area
	 	 	• Number of physicians or nurses per 1,000 population
	• Number of hospital beds per 1,000 population
	• Distance to nearest primary healthcare provider
	• Distance to nearest hospital
		Utilization
	Whether or not health services are utilized
	 	 	• Primary healthcare consultations per l,000 population
	• Hospital admissions per 1,000 population
		Relevance to need
	Whether or not appropriate services are received by the people who need them
	 	 	• Proportion of births attended by a trained healthcare professional
	• Proportion of individuals with known hypertension who are being treated
		Outcomes
	Whether achievable health outcomes are realized
	 	 	• Maternal mortality rates are improved
	• Mortality rate from appendicitis is improved





Access to secondary healthcare


	No matter how enthusiastically primary healthcare is developed and made accessible, the range of care provided stops short of major surgery, complex obstetrics, intensive medical care, sophisticated rehabilitation services, and long-term accommodation-based care.
	In many low-resource settings, where community primary healthcare is rudimentary and where access to quality care is limited, the emergency departments of hospitals overflow with patients who might otherwise be cared for in primary healthcare.
	At any of these institutions in resource-poor countries, we find mothers with sick (or very sick) children. They might have travelled days from remote villages to urban hospitals. The hospital becomes a de facto primary health carer. Nor is this phenomenon unique to low income countries. In resource-rich countries, care given to patients with serious and continuing illnesses is being reviewed to see if it could be given more efficiently through primary healthcare, especially when the services in both settings are linked and managed as a unit. Treatment for such patients is judged to be inappropriate when they receive expensive hospital care as a substitute for primary healthcare. There is no simple answer: primary healthcare services are increasingly limited to daytime working hours. At other times, the emergency department can, by default, offer primary healthcare.





Changing global and community disease burdens


	The health gain of resource-rich countries in the twentieth century is well documented. A snapshot of the interval between the Second World War and now would also show improvements in health outcomes in developing countries, in parallel with increased education, sanitation initiatives, and improved local oversight of public health (Bollyky 2018). These improvements were closely related to rising prosperity and urban development. With money to spend, many such governments invested in potable water and in sewerage disposal. In turn, a healthier workforce contributed to prosperity.
	A new set of problems has come with these advances. Chronic illnesses, once the scourge of advanced nations, are now prevalent in low-and middle-income countries. This reflects changes in food supply (including a greater proportion of highly processed foods), increasing availability of tobacco, and housing shortages. Many less economically developed nations face a loss of productive workforce in middle age due to chronic non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. It has been projected that, by 2040, 80% of premature deaths and disability in developing countries will be caused by heart disease, cancer, and other non-communicable diseases (Bollyky 2018).
	In low-and middle-income economies, healthcare expenditure per capita remains relatively low and much chronic illness is untreated. Many less developed nations spend about US$30 per person annually on healthcare, contrasted with US$5,400 in the United States and US$3,800 in the United Kingdom (Bollyky 2018). The opportunities for primary and secondary prevention through primary healthcare are often lost.
	This change in the pattern of illness has slowly been recognized. The shift in funding away from preventing and treating communicable diseases to treating and managing the growing burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) is also noteworthy. Initiatives, like the Global Alliance Against Chronic Disease, are addressing the threats posed by NCDs. This body has ‘arranged three of its four funding rounds by disease’ (Fairall et al. 2018). But, as has been seen with efforts to control HIV, the difficulties imposed by health systems which do not integrate care for the whole individual can be almost as troublesome as the underlying disease. In the case of NCDs, the usual pattern is of an individual having multiple disorders (diabetes, heart, and lung disease, for example) which need linked care. Ideally, services should respond to multimorbidity rather than to individual diseases.





Citizens’ ‘right to healthcare’


	Does any individual (or community) have a ‘right to healthcare’ or a right to access to care? Answers to this question are generally approached from either a utilitarian or human rights-based viewpoint. Another, objectivist view, sees healthcare as a commodity, to be bought or sold in an open market. This section will consider these different perspectives in the context of access to healthcare.
	Human-rights-based approaches to a right to healthcare draw on two core documents: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights (ICESCR). Rights to medical care are recognized under Article 25 of the UDHR:
	 	Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and of his family, including food, clothing, housing and medical care and necessary social services, and the right to security in the event of unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood in circumstances beyond his control. (UN 2007)
	The UDHR was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, in the wake of the atrocities perpetrated during the Second World War. It is not a legally binding document, although it is generally accepted as holding status as customary international law, which is, regrettably, hard, if not impossible, to enforce. Enforcement is generally limited to violations linked to war and armed conflict (Gunning 1991; Henckaerts 2005).
	Article 25 ties health and medical care directly to living standards and social services, welfare, and security, but without explicitly stating which governing entity should be responsible for funding and provision.
	The International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights (ICESCR adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1966, and in force since 1976) expands upon the UDHR, requiring party states to ‘recognize the right of everyone to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health’ and to create ‘conditions which would assure all medical services and medical attention in the event of sickness’ (Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights 2007); see also Chapter 3.3).
	Unlike the UDHR, the ICESCR is a ‘binding treaty’, which, as of December 2018, has been ratified by 169 member nations (United Nations Human Rights, Office of the High Commissioner n.d.). Four nations, including the United States of America, have signed (but not ratified) the treaty. States party to the treaty have agreed to submit a compliance report to the ICESCR 5-yearly. Alleged violations might be referred to the ICESCR committee for investigation. However, agreement on how violations should be recognized or quantified is lacking, and enforcement is non-existent (Kalantry et al. 2010).
	Taken together, the UDHR and ICECSR do not guarantee access to necessary services for every individual but, as statements of political and social intent, they offer an important degree of hoped-for protection for marginalized and vulnerable groups and individuals. There can, of course, be no guarantee of limitless care for any individual, nor does the resolution overcome the tyranny of distance where rural dwellers cannot access health services in the big cities. But the ICECSR places responsibility on governments to facilitate the healthcare of their citizens (discussed further in Section E). Ultimately, however, human rights, including the ‘right to healthcare’, are weakly protected at the international level.
	Human rights-based approaches to access to healthcare link to concepts of equity and draw upon social contract theory and theories of ethics. These approaches favour a just or equitable distribution of healthcare over the maximization of potential health gains for a favoured minority.
	American moral and political philosopher John Rawls’s theory of justice and fairness, proposes that a just society will be arranged so as to achieve fair equality of opportunity (Rawls 2007) not equality of achievement (for example, equal health outcomes from a particular treatment, which can never be guaranteed). Although saying little about health, Rawls envisioned his theory of justice as an extension of the social contract, as understood by Locke, Rousseau, and Kant (Rawls 2007).
	Norman Daniels, an eminent American political philosopher and philosopher of science, has been more explicitly concerned with health than was Rawls (Daniels 2008). He argues that health is an important determinant of the extent of an individual’s opportunities and that it therefore requires careful consideration if one wishes to establish a fair society. From Rawls and Daniels, equity stands out as a major ‘ethical value’, one which healthcare services should strive to promote (Braveman et al. 2001).
	Cruess and Cruess, an orthopaedic surgeon and an endocrinologist at Canada’s McGill University, respectively, have written extensively on medical professionalism, acknowledge that the relationship between the medical profession and the social contract remains poorly defined, emphasizing that ‘the social contract between medicine and society differ between countries, being influenced by cultural, economic, and political factors’ (Cruess and Cruess 2008).
	In direct contrast to rights-based and social contract theory approaches to healthcare stands the objectivist position in which healthcare is not a ‘right’, but rather a ‘service’ offered by trained professionals. Rather than focussing on the ‘rights’ of the recipient of care, this approach considers the ‘rights’ of those who provide care. In this approach, healthcare is a commodity provided by trained persons who can expect remuneration and respect for their services, and who have the right to practise their profession where and when it is legal to do so. They also are entitled to withhold those services. They have the same entrepreneurial legal rights as any non-medical professional.
	This objectivist approach to healthcare resonates especially in the United States, where it was clearly articulated by Robert Sade, an American surgeon and bioethicist, in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1971 (Sade 1971). Sade argued ‘the concept of medical care as a right of the patient entails the use or threat of violence against physicians [by the state]’. In Sade’s view, the rights of the physician to remuneration for service, and freedom to choose to whom to provide it, exceed the individual’s right to care. Gaffney describes this contrast as the ‘rights-commodity dialectic’, drawing on Gøsta Esping-Andersen’s arguments around the de-commodification of welfare services, facilitating subsistence without reliance on markets (Esping-Andersen 1990; Gaffney 2018). Sade came to describe this same contrast as one between ‘central planning’ and the ‘free market’, driven respectively by beliefs that ‘healthcare is an entitlement that must be provided by society and that obtaining healthcare is the responsibility of individuals’ (Sade 2012).
	Adam Gaffney, an instructor in Medicine at Harvard Medical School and a pulmonary and critical care doctor at the Cambridge Health Alliance, is president of the advocacy organization Physicians for a National Health Program. Writing about the history of healthcare as a right, he saw these two opposing positions as mutually exclusive (Gaffney 2018). Similarly, Sade’s recent work posits that government regulation of healthcare and ‘everything else that contributes to good health’ is ‘inconsistent with the notion of a free society’, arguing that regulations and the funding of services via taxation impinge on the freedoms of individuals (Sade 2012).
	Much of the debate around the rights and provision of healthcare, vis-a-vis the rights of the provider, centre specifically on the role and remuneration of physicians, as clearly encapsulated in Sade’s position (Sade 1971). Allied health professionals are largely absent from the debate. Cruess and Cruess are properly concerned that the medical profession is viewed, almost in parody, as a homogenous monolith, rather than a complex, heterogeneous matrix of interlinked professionals, whose needs, desires, and expectations might not be unified (Cruess and Cruess 2008).
	Gaffney notes a further complication in the discussion about the rights of the recipient of care and the provider. Whereas Sade ‘envisions healthcare sold by the individual physician to the individual patient’ (that is, an autonomous, sole-trader provider), the reality is that healthcare is more likely today to be provided by a state or a corporate entity, which employs providers, whose work may be constrained by corporate/government policy.
	Similarly, healthcare providers are accountable, not only to their patients, but also to regulatory bodies, government and corporate agencies, including insurers (Cruess and Cruess 2008). Sade’s articulated right to withhold care might also collide with antidiscrimination legislation, if withholding care could be considered illegal because it was judged to be discriminatory. Ultimately, Sade’s hypothesized example does not readily align with health systems, nor with the provision of healthcare as it is practised across the developed world. Sade himself acknowledged in a 2012 article, following the introduction of the Affordable Care Act (informally known as ‘Obamacare’) in the United States, that government had increasingly taken control of healthcare, policy development, and regulation of the health system, although he continues to argue that deregulation will facilitate innovative free market solutions ‘guided by the ethical principle of non-interference’ (Sade 2012). This libertarian perspective continues to appeal, particularly in the United States, although many such arguments fail to recognize that many corporations now rival nations in terms of their power, influence, and interference in the lives of private citizens (Babic et al. 2017). Indeed, a 2012 article in the British Medical Journal introduced the term ‘commercial determinants of health’ into the lexicon, sitting alongside the social determinants, in recognition of the ‘increasingly unhealthy dominance of corporate marketing’ (Hastings 2012). Each side of the rights-commodity divide sees fundamental flaws in the opposing position’s arguments—a gulf which is unlikely to be reconciled in the foreseeable future, and a debate with which each community and nation must continue to struggle.
	Utilitarian perspectives on access to care contend that health services should maximize the health gains obtained by all individuals. This idea is summed up by the slogan ‘the greatest good for the greatest number’, sometimes regarded as ‘the guiding principle for many of the decisions and actions of public health professionals’ (Last 2007). The objective of maximizing the health gains to be achieved from available resources is closely related to the economic principle of efficiency, which is the focus of Chapter 6.6 of the current volume. Resources for healthcare will be used most efficiently when health gain is maximized. Equity and efficiency are often viewed as conflicting objectives. For example, delivering equitable access to specialist services in sparsely populated rural areas might compromise efficiency.
	The utilitarian approach raises problems because it requires only that the sum of health gains in a population should be maximized. The individual is not of ultimate concern to the utilitarian. This could result in inefficient allocation of healthcare to individuals with greater needs; the lesser needs of many might be met instead.
	By contrast, approaches based on concepts of human rights and social justice view each individual as having a right to healthcare—those needing more will have greater access to care. Proportionality of access was a key concern of the late health economist Gavin Mooney for whom ‘equal access to equal care for equal need’ served as his definition of equity, a definition with which we agree. It was not a guarantee of equal outcomes, biologically impossible to promise, but of equal access.





Responsibility and role of governments


	Under the terms of the ICECSR treaty, participating governments bear some responsibility for providing a measure of healthcare to their citizens. However, the treaty does not prescribe how this should be organized, or to what extent governments should fund health systems. The United Nations’ resolution on 12 December 2012 on Global Health and Foreign Policy encourages member states to promote universal health coverage in foreign policy development. The resolution highlights, in particular, the impact of the high cost of care as a barrier to access (UN 2012). Ultimately, each sovereign government must determine how, and to what extent, it is willing or capable of organizing and funding healthcare. The result, globally, is a mix of private, public, and co-payment systems, some tightly controlled by governments and others with minimal regulation or government direction.
	The United Nations Sustainable Development Summit, held in New York in 2015, ushered in a series of Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) (UN 2015), (the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) (UN n.d.) having run their course), which addressed a raft of global challenges to be met by 2030. Target 3. aims to:
	 	Achieve universal health coverage, including financial risk protection, access to quality essential healthcare services and access to safe, effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all. (United Nations (UN), Sustainable Development Goals)
	The SDGs call for greater national investment in health and in improvement and maintenance of the health workforce. Success will depend on the extent to which countries ratify the goals, invest in them, and implement strategies to achieve them.
	John McDermott, an expert on public health, agriculture, nutrition and health in Africa, wrote in 2018 ‘universal healthcare is both desirable and possible, even in low income countries’ (McDermott 2018). Stigler et al. propose that universal healthcare is not possible without adequate primary healthcare, which they see as ‘the backbone of an effective healthcare system’ (Stigler et al. 2016).
	The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) report, Global Access to Healthcare: Building Sustainable Health Systems (2017) mentions primary healthcare as the ideal basis for a country’s health system—a point where governments can control funding (The Economist Intelligence Unit 2017). Starfield et al. note that health systems which emphasize primary healthcare are more efficient, widen access, reduce inequality, and lower the overall costs of care, while producing better population health and reduced rates of mortality—findings applicable in both national and cross-national analyses (Starfield et al. 2005).
	Atun et al. charted the path to universal healthcare in Latin America from the 1980s, through to the early twenty-first century (Atun et al. 2015). Health reforms in Latin America were heavily influenced by the Alma-Ata declaration and therefore placed a strong emphasis on the role of primary healthcare (WHO 1978; Atun et al. 2015). The design and implementation of these universal healthcare systems (UHCs) and the means by which they were funded varied significantly.
	With a significant surplus of physicians, the Cuban National Health Service, unlike the healthcare services in Venezuela (see next) has been particularly successful. Following the 1959 revolution, the right to healthcare was enshrined in Cuban law, and universal health services, financed via taxation, began to be developed in the 1970s. Although private healthcare is illegal in Cuba, private spending makes up approximately 10% of all healthcare expenditure. Comprehensive primary healthcare is the lynchpin of the system, with 80% of health problems being managed through healthcare networks centred on polyclinics (Atun et al. 2015).





Extended value of primary health services


	Broad definitions of primary healthcare include ‘all the activities whose primary purpose is to improve or maintain health’ (Murray and Frenk 2000), including sanitation, road safety initiatives, or the education of girls. Such multisector interventions, while generally considered to contribute to a community’s health, do not contribute to the care of individuals.
	Primary healthcare yields benefits beyond individual recipients. The treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis, for example, reduces the spread of the disease. Such positive ‘externalities’ (outcomes resulting from an intervention in one area but which affect other areas), might be more beneficial for communities than for individuals. Countries might facilitate access to these benefits as ‘merit goods’, underproduced if individuals valued only their own personal benefits.
	Extending this argument, it might be desirable to organize care so that it benefits all. For example, the eradication of infectious diseases, or the control of antimicrobial drug resistance, offer benefits extending beyond national boundaries (Smith et al. 2003).





Importance of policy


	Section 2 of the current volume examines themes surrounding the determinants of health and disease. Chapter 2.1 examines, in depth, the social determinants of health and Chapter 2.2 explores the relationship between politics and public health. Health inequalities, in both the developed and the developing world, were scrutinized in Chapters 2.4 and 2.5. Health policy has a role to play in each area. Chapters 3.5 and 3.6 examine health policy in greater detail. In this section, we examine the role of health policy as it relates to access to care.
	Policies should aim at overcoming barriers to access, many of which intersect with the broader social determinants of health. Poverty, social inequality, location—especially rurality and environment—all affect access.
	Low-and middle-income countries wishing to achieve SDG 3.8—the provision of universal healthcare (UHC)—will need policies to lead them towards that goal. Reich et al. examined 11 countries’ pathways towards UHC. These offer lessons for future transitions (Reich et al. 2016). The policy challenges are substantial and wide-ranging. Reich et al. underscore the need for policymakers’ ‘vision and commitment’ to ensure the successful and sustainable introduction of UHC (Reich et al. 2016). Policies need to address medical and allied health worker training, accreditation, and regulation; service provision; taxation; building the public’s trust; and commitment from the public. Starfield et al., also in a comparison of 11 nations, found that ‘adequate delivery of primary healthcare services was associated with supportive governmental policies’ (Starfield et al. 2005).
	To give an indication of the vital importance of policy, we briefly examine the case of Venezuela. During the 1990s, Venezuela began to reform its health system. In 1999, the Venezuelan Constitution recognized healthcare as a fundamental human right (Atun et al. 2015). Funding policies drew on a number of sources, pooled to fund healthcare for the poor, the unemployed, and the rural population. The system was a mix of public and private funding, but with out-of-pocket expenses accounting for more than 50% of health expenditure (Atun et al. 2015). From 2003, a primary healthcare model, Barrio Adentro, was introduced, which, for a time, expanded access and resulted in better health outcomes for Venezuela’s poorest citizens (Atun et al. 2015). Life expectancy rose and infant mortality dropped dramatically.
	By 2013, however, the system was faltering, and by 2016 it was, and still remains, in crisis (Editorial 2018). Economic collapse followed the decline in world oil prices from 2008. For this and other reasons, government spending on public health dropped from 9.1% in 2010 to 5.8% by 2014 (Editorial 2018). The result has been a devastating increase in out-of-pocket payments—a barrier to access for poorer citizens. Maternal and infant mortality have increased. Access to medicines, even for the wealthiest citizens, has diminished due to significant shortages of medications (Fraser and Willer 2016; Editorial 2018). Rather than acknowledge the crisis, the government has ceased gathering data; nor has it, since 2016, reported on the state of the system. Offers of international aid have been declined. The wilful refusal to acknowledge or address the crisis exemplifies a spectacular policy failure. Costing lives it serves as a reminder of the importance and impact which policy implementation can have on access to even the most basic healthcare services.





Financing primary healthcare


	Where governments assume a funding role for primary healthcare, policy becomes extremely important. Sustainability is a recurrent challenge. Reich et al. observed that sustaining coverage was a financing and policy issue for each of the 11 nations included in their study (Reich et al. 2016). Decisions undertaken during the development of Ghana’s National Health Insurance System resulted in a fee-for-service model, which has proven unsustainable. Ten years after the adoption of the system, the government had to reassess a financially unsustainable system, which did not cover 64% of the population (Reich et al. 2016). Spain implemented a tax-based funding system during the 1980s and 1990s to both expand primary healthcare and ensure the sustainability of the system as a whole (Starfield et al. 2005). Cuba and Brazil similarly fund their universal health system via taxation (Atun et al. 2015).
	Cuba has supplemented their taxation funding for healthcare through the provision of healthcare workers to Brazil and Venezuela in exchange for contracted fees paid to the Cuban government (Atun et al. 2015).





The distribution and organization of the healthcare workforce, both state-certified and non-regulated


	The Institute for Health Improvement’s Triple Aim (Institute of Healthcare Improvement 2009) supports, across differently-resourced regions and populations, the judicious use of ‘regulated’ (state-certified) and ‘non-regulated’ health workers. The latter include pharmacy technicians, community health staff, and volunteers.
	Throughout the twentieth century, health services have largely been provided by regulated practitioners, such as nurses, midwives, and doctors. But, with need outstripping supply, this workforce is now inadequate, overtrained, and expensive to educate and remunerate. Consequently, workforce development strategies have been developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to include unlicensed healthcare workers, trained to perform set tasks under the direction and supervision of regulated practitioners. For example, regulated Nigerian health workers make use of churches, mosques, and the premises of their civic organizations as their clinics. Traditional birth attendants assist at childbirth. Community support is strengthened by recruiting community leaders and prominent citizens as their advocates (Gyuse et al. 2018).
	In New Zealand, regulated practitioners, including nurses, midwives, and doctors, may be scarce in rural and remote areas, so the Ministry of Health’s strategies make extensive use of non-medical personnel. For example, ‘Quitline’ advisors available by telephone, text and online, provide smoking cessation advice; and over 50,000 community-based Kaiāwhina, or non-regulated care workers and assistants (mainly women), support people with disabilities or chronic illnesses (Health Workforce New Zealand 2018).
	Similarly, sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI) has been a leading cause of preventable death, the number of SUDI deaths reduced from 250 per year (over 4.4 per 1,000 live births) in the 1980s, to 44 deaths in 2015 (0.92 per 1,000 live births). Although SUDI rates have reduced significantly, they did not fall equitably across the population. The SUDI risk for Maori and Pasifika babies has remained consistently higher than for non-Maori, non-Pasifika babies. Identifying and promoting more effective, culturally appropriate ways of engaging, and staying engaged, with women most at risk of SUDI early in their pregnancies is crucial. A focus on this has resulted in the integration of Kaiiiwhina as community educators into Ministry of Health-directed policy and practice (Health Quality and Safety Commission New Zealand 2017). Likewise, initiatives, including the construction of wahakura (woven baskets) for infants to sleep in beside their mothers or other carers, have strengthened community networks for improving health (Abel and Tipene-Leach 2013). Ideally, non-regulated workers belong to the communities of the people they serve, thereby avoiding cultural gaps.
	With adequate remuneration, training, and supervision, sufficient resourcing, defined agreed-upon tasks and the support of the community and colleagues, non-regulated workers can successfully manage outbreaks of illnesses such as malaria, and provide preventive care, including vaccination, perinatal care and health promotion (Haines et al. 2007). In a poor rural community in Pakistan, with little access to mental healthcare, integration of a cognitive behaviour therapy-based intervention into the routine work of community health workers more than halved the rate of depression in prenatally depressed women compared with those receiving enhanced ‘usual’ care (Rahman et al. 2008). These types of initiatives demonstrate the potential to integrate similar roles for community health workers into other health systems, particularly in resource-poor settings.
	In 2010, WHO called for the more effective use of non-regulated healthcare workers. It stressed an urgent, global need to strengthen primary healthcare, to integrate interprofessional education and collaborative practice into service, education, and health policy. That need has not abated.
	In the light of budgetary constraints, primary healthcare remains one of the best investments governments can make (The Economist Intelligence Unit 2017; Mossman et al. 2017). For example, initiatives to tackle the dearth of medical practitioners in rural areas can focus on non-medical providers (Sanne et al. 2010; Fairall et al. 2012), such as nurse practitioners, to provide certain types and levels of care. New Zealand, with a population of nearly five million, including 15,000 doctors, employs more than 300 nurse practitioners throughout the country. Nurses qualify as practitioners upon gaining a clinical master’s degree in addition to the three-year bachelor’s degree. Those in primary healthcare can diagnose, treat, and prescribe and, like general medical practitioners, might be the lead healthcare provider. Each costs a fraction of the cost of educating and maintaining a medical practitioner. These nurses are often residents of the rural communities and small towns to which, following education and registration, they return.
	Technology can support access to primary healthcare. For example, the Mohalla clinics in Delhi operate low-cost kits for common medical tests (Lahariya 2017), reducing the costs of screening and treatment for diabetes, dengue fever, and hepatitis. In Rwanda and many other countries, telehealth is being trialled to carry medical advice to rural and remote patients (The Economist Intelligence Unit 2017). Like the Royal Flying Doctor Service of Australia, one of the largest and most comprehensive aeromedical organizations, telehealth is an important mechanism for enhancing access, team-based care, and quality of care for patients in rural and remote Australia (Bradford et al. 2016).
	Services such as the North Star Alliance, based in sub-Saharan Africa, support low-level continuing care, delivered via programmes which align with patients’ experiences in a culturally responsive way, providing local support, which requires less travel, resulting in shorter waiting times. The North Star Alliance also uses clever branding and marketing to reach patients and the communities they interact with. Their not-for-profit network includes more than 30 roadside health clinics at disease hotspots on major transport routes used by mobile workers, travellers, and displaced persons who frequently cross borders, thereby increasing the risk of disease spreading across borders (North Star Alliance 2018). Such services offer the convenience of enabling the patient’s daily life to continue.
	The Le-Nest initiative in Shanghai offers an inexpensive service for patients whose diabetes and hypertension can be managed in primary healthcare (International Partnership for Innovative Healthcare Delivery 2014). Such services are readily accessible for either an acute, minor problem, or a flare-up of a long-standing illness. Similarly, the Practical Approach to Care Kit (PACK) programme, offered through The British Medical Journal, offers non-physician clinicians in low-and middle-income countries a suite of checklists and algorithms for screening, diagnosis, and treatment for a range of commonly presented symptoms, acute and chronic conditions that can be managed within the community (Fairall et al. 2018).





The role of data in planning, monitoring, and evaluating services


	To try to assure the quality of primary healthcare, health key performance indicator (KPI) data are used internationally. They allow comparison of performance among different locations as well as system-wide improvements and reforms. They can establish goals for access to care and specify the extent, type, and cost of care (Hibbert et al. 2013). They can be linked to clinical and financial measures of achievement and outcome. The range of KPIs is widening as a result of the introduction of new technologies, and of expanding the expectations of those who use and pay for services.
	The place of KPIs in assessing the managerial machinery, clinical processes, and financial performance of healthcare systems is deeply entrenched. They have tended to relate to everything except the details of what the health system achieves in improving health and quality of life of patients. These provoke profound clinical scepticism, especially when accompanied with demands for copious data collection by busy clinicians. There is a tendency to measure what can easily be measured. Important qualitative aspects are pushed aside by narrow quantitative measures. This often reduces the focus to concerns with process and activity rather than with access or outcome.
	Despite these limitations, the need for KPIs is clear. Comprehensive primary healthcare using integrated, team-based services for those with multiple comorbidities is short on evidence of its effectiveness. Evaluation using performance indicators, reflecting both equity, outcome, and accessibility of care, will be crucial to advancing the effectiveness of primary healthcare (McDonald 2016).
	Several serious questions should be asked of policymakers who increasingly make use of the collected data for measuring performance:
	 	• What is the purpose of the service whose performance is being assessed?
	• Do the KPIs relate clearly and unambiguously to that purpose?
	• How are performance measures being used in practice?
	• What are the consequences of poor performance? Education? Penalties? Dismissals?
	• What changes in funding, system and outcomes have occurred as a result of spending time and treasure in obtaining and analysing performance data?
	• What could improve the use of performance measures and the data they generate?
	Although outcome data are difficult to procure and contain no magical answers, appropriate publication of such data drives improvements in the quality of care (Fung et al. 2008).
	The New Zealand Health Quality and Safety Commission recently launched a dashboard of healthcare system quality indicators (Health Quality and Safety Commission New Zealand 2018). This provides data on 60 measures for each local district. Quality measures include timely access, safety, effectiveness, patient-centredness (including satisfaction) and equity. These measures and scales, which compare each district with the national average, support continuous improvement.





Conclusion


	Regardless of a country’s wealth, political commitment and public investment make the difference between sustainable and unsustainable access to healthcare. While less affluent countries are more likely to struggle with the sustainability of such developments, several are improving impressively.
	A commitment by leadership—within countries, governments, and health organizations—to improving healthcare access is crucial if progress is to occur.
	While overcoming geographical and financial barriers is important, so is a focus on workforce initiatives. Many of these seek to improve access to primary healthcare through intermediaries such as community health workers and health practitioners, who have the time to build trusted relationships with communities and patients.
	Healthcare systems can support access by articulating a narrative which explains and inspires, designating expectations through strategy, policy, and funding formulas, to ensure that communities are engaged in the development, implementation, and monitoring of improvements to healthcare access. When informed by the analysis and use of local data to plan and monitor services, models of care can more closely fit the demand and the need for good access to care.
	Access to healthcare is not only about entry to the healthcare system, but also about the journey through it. Committed and responsive staff is vital. For all these reasons, organizing optimal access to primary, secondary and tertiary services, in combination, warrant further research and development to achieve optimal management of communicable and NCDs, and to promote health through frontline preventive services.
