The first are general thematic reports (for example, corruption and the right to health (UNGA 2017) or the SDGs and the right to health (UNGA 2016)); secondly, the Special Rapporteur undertakes visits to countries, following which a country report is written on the right to health, or specific elements of the right, with a view to holding the country to account for its right to health obligations. When rapporteurs encounter specific issues on which the existing jurisprudence gives little guidance, they offer their interpretations of the international right to health (Hunt 2016).
	Civil society is encouraged to engage in all of these reporting processes, and provide shadow reports, as a means of keeping the processes transparent and meaningful.
	Human rights obligations, including duties relating to the right to health, extend beyond states to members of society (UN 1948, preamble; UNCESCR 2000, para. 42). This includes health workers, families, communities, inter-and non-governmental organizations, civil society groups, and businesses including multinational and transnational companies, for example, pharmaceutical companies. One of the human rights responsibilities of states is to provide an environment in which the actions of all these individuals and groups is in accord with their human rights duties, and where people are able to claim their human rights entitlements.
	When states enter into bilateral, multinational, or global agreements, including trade agreements, they are duty bound to ensure such agreements respect and protect human rights. The SDGs, adopted by all UN Member States in 2015, explicitly refer to human rights in their preamble, stating, ‘The 17 Sustainable Development Goals … seek to realize the human rights of all and to achieve gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls’ (UNGA 2015). Furthermore, this global initiative uses as its catchphrase the mission to ‘leave no one behind’. This echoes the human rights imperative of equality and non-discrimination, and the public health commitment to reduce inequities.





Human rights are not without controversy


	The right to health—like other economic, social, and cultural rights—does not escape controversy and ideological objections. Some states are reluctant to see it as a right of similar weight to others, such as the right to a fair trial. However, under international law, the right to health is an integral part of the international code of human rights, a right that is interdependent and indivisible from other rights and must be given equal treatment and attention (UN 1993, para. 5).
	Despite the promise of human rights, they cannot by themselves resolve many of the complex problems pertaining to their realization. For example, despite human rights accountability mechanisms, there is little that most states can do to force other states to meet their human rights duties. Furthermore, in our globally interconnected world, where transnational companies control and own much of our health and general information, nation states remaining the primary human rights duty bearers has severe limitations. Nor do human rights present easy solutions to decisions to guide the prioritization of scarce health resources. However, the human rights principles of equality, non-discrimination, participation, and accountability are useful to guide responses to these challenges.





What is the right to health?


	The right to health does not mean a right to be healthy (UNCECSR 2000, para 8). It is however, as recognized in international law, the right to facilities, goods, services, and conditions that are conducive to the realization of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. In some quarters, there has been a presumption that the right to health relates to personal health services. Such a narrow definition is in fact inconsistent with international human rights law, which encompasses clinical care, public health, and the determinants of health, such as access to water, sanitation, nutrition, housing, and education, as confirmed by Article 12 of ICESCR and Article 24 of CRC.
	Under the right to health people have freedoms, such as the freedom from discrimination or non-consensual medical treatment and experimentation. They also have entitlements including to maternal, child, and reproductive health services; healthy workplaces and environments; the prevention, treatment, and control of diseases, including access to essential medicines; and access to safe and potable water and sanitation.
	The right to health is closely related to and dependent upon the realization of other fundamental human rights contained within international law. The rights to education, an adequate standard of living, life, privacy, and access to information, as well as other rights and freedoms, relate to and address integral components of the right to health.





International human rights law


	The origins of the right to health in international law can be traced back to the 1946 World Health Organization’s (WHO) Constitution which says: ‘The enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being without distinction of race, religion, political belief, economic or social condition’ (WHO 1946). Two years later, article 25(1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights laid the foundations for the international legal framework for the right to health. Since then, the right to health has been codified in legally binding international and regional human rights treaties, and enshrined in many national laws, some of which are signalled in the following paragraphs.
	The cornerstone protection of the right to health in international law is found in Article 12 of ICESCR. By 2018, 164 states had ratified this treaty, legally binding themselves to its implementation (OHCHR 2018).
	Additional right to health protections are contained in international treaties that address issues specific to marginalized groups, or groups whose health is at risk from the effects of marginalization.1 All countries have ratified at least one treaty with right to health provisions and with the exception of the United States, all countries have ratified the CRC (OHCHR 2018).
	Authoritative and interpretive guiding principles of several of these treaty provisions on the right to health shed further light on the parameters and content of the right generally, and in relation to the application of the right to specific groups. Of special relevance are General Comment 14 on the right to the highest attainable standard of health adopted in 2000 by the UN treatybody responsible for monitoring ICESCR (UNCESCR 2000); General Comment 15 on the right of the child to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health adopted in 2013 by the UN treatybody responsible for monitoring the CRC (UN CRC 2013); international guidelines on HIV/AIDS and human rights (OHCHR and UNAIDS 2006); the Technical Guidance on the Application of a Human Rights-Based Approach to the Implementation of Policies and Programmes to Reduce Preventable Maternal Morbidity and Mortality (UN OHCHR 2012b); the Technical Guidance on the Application of a Human Rights-Based Approach to the Implementation of Policies and Programmes to Reduce and Eliminate Preventable Mortality and Morbidity of Children under 5 years of age, (UN HRC 2014); and Ensuring Human Rights in the Provision of Contraceptive Information and Services: Guidance and Recommendations (WHO 2014).
	Far-reaching commitments relating to the right to health have been made in the outcome documents of numerous UN and WHO world conferences, such as the Alma-Ata Declaration (WHO 1978), the International Conference on Population and Development (UN 1994), the Fourth World Conference on Women (UN 1995), the Bangkok Charter for Health Promotion in a Globalized World (WHO 2005), the Rio Political Declaration on Social Determinants of Health (WHO 2011), the SDGs (UNGA 2015), and the Action Agenda from the Second Global Conference on Climate and Health (WHO 2016). These conferences and global commitments have helped to place international problems—including issues such as maternal mortality, mental health, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), health inequities, and poverty—on global agendas and their outcome documents influence international and national policymaking. Several refer to the right to health and/or health-related rights.
	The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (DRIP) has particular importance. For indigenous peoples, colonization has often led to dispossession from their lands and territories; cultural subjugation; social, economic, and political marginalization; and consequential serious harm to their health. DRIP recognizes that for indigenous peoples, well-being is shared, holistic, and includes the relationship between people and environment, and is aligned with indigenous models for public health (see Chapter 10.6) (United Nations General Assembly 2007).





Siracusa Principles


	Tragically, there have been situations such as the United States Public Health Service ‘Tuskegee Study of Untreated Syphilis in the Negro Male’ that began in 1932 and continued for 40 years (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2013) in which public health objectives have been used to justify what have been human rights violations, such as the withholding of information and treatment to develop an understanding of a disease. There are some occasions in which the public health measures necessary to respond to a serious threat to the health of a population or individual do require the limitation of other human rights. International human rights law sets out narrowly defined standards, called the Siracusa Principles (UN Commission on Human Rights 1984), as to when such limitations may be implemented legitimately. Such measures should only be taken when they are: necessary for the promotion of the general welfare; provided for in law and carried out according to the law; there is no other less intrusive and restrictive alternative; reasonable, based on evidence, and not discriminatory in any other way; subject to review; and of limited duration (UN ECOSOC 1985, Annex; UNCESCR 2000, paras. 28–9).





Regional human rights law


	The right to health is recognized in human rights treaties adopted and monitored by regional human rights systems. These have effect only in their respective regions and include: the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (Article 16); the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (Article 14); the Additional Protocol to the American Convention on Human Rights in the Area of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, known as the ‘Protocol of San Salvador’ (Article 10); and the European Social Charter (Article 11). Other regional instruments, such as the American Convention on Human Rights (OAS 1969) and the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (Council of Europe 1950), also provide, through health-related rights and other provisions, protection of the right to health.
	At the regional level there are also judicial and other mechanisms that adjudicate cases involving the right to health. A notable case in 2002 was the finding by the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) of a violation of the right to health by the Federal Republic of Nigeria, on account of violations against the Ogoni people in relation to the activities of oil companies in the Niger Delta (ACHPR 2001). In 2009, the same tribunal held that Sudan had violated the right to health as a result of exposing members of indigenous tribes in the Darfur region to serious health risks by destroying homes, livestock, farms, and poisoning wells. In so doing, the Commission recognized that the right to health extends to underlying determinants of health, including access to safe water, adequate and safe food, and housing (ACHPR, Sudan Human Rights Organisation, et al. v. Sudan Comm. No. 279/03-296/05 (2009).
	Another important development has come from the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) which expressed its willingness to ‘take into account’ provisions of the regional treaty (the Protocol of San Salvador) related to the right to health when analysing the merits of a case, even though it lacked competence to determine violations under these provisions (IACHR 2000). In the case of Gonzales Lluy et al. v. Ecuador, 2015, the American Court of Human Rights (IACtHR) recognized that the state has an obligation to supervise and monitor not only public hospitals but also private entities in the healthcare sector. The Ecuadorian government was found negligent in its supervisory duties for failing to properly test blood banks leading to a child becoming infected with HIV after a blood transfusion. It was found to have violated both the right to life and the right to humane treatment. Finally, in a recent case, Poblete Vilches et al. vs. Chile, the IACtHR ruled that ‘the right to health is an autonomous right protected by Article 26 of the American Convention’ and that the state was responsible for violations in relation to rights within article 26 (IACtHR 2018).





National laws


	A study has shown that 55% of the constitutions of all nations have provisions regarding health rights (Heymann et al. 2013). In addition, 27 states have provisions regarding sexual and reproductive health and rights, and nine of these explicitly link the right to sexual and reproductive health to the rights to education, science, and/or to make autonomous decisions about sexuality and reproduction (Pizzarossa and Perehudoff 2017).
	In some jurisdictions, these constitutional provisions have generated significant jurisprudence. The Constitutional Court of South Africa in Minister for Health v. Treatment Action Campaign, illustrated at the start of this chapter, is such an example. In many South American countries, with the right to health guaranteed in their constitutions, there has been ‘an ‘explosion’ of litigation … (thousands of cases in Costa Rica, and hundreds of thousands in Colombia and Brazil) and a heightened disposition of judges to enforce the right to health through strong remedies in comparison to non-Latin American countries’ (Ferraz 2018).
	These and numerous other laws and decisions at the international, regional, and national levels confirm that the courts have an important role to play in the protection, and fulfilment of the right to the highest attainable standard of health.





Key features of the right to health


	In recent years, the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, WHO, Special Rapporteurs on the right of everyone to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health, human rights experts, civil society organizations, academics, and many others, have developed ways of ‘unpacking’ or analysing the right to health with a view to making it easier to understand and apply to health-related policies, programmes, and projects in practice.
	Accordingly, the following paragraphs set out 10 key features of the right to health. Some of the features overlap, for example, accessibility (in key feature nine) overlaps with non-discrimination (in key feature two). Also, some of the features have technical names, such as ‘obligations of immediate effect’, which reflect their legal provenance. Nonetheless, the features also reflect an emerging discourse for understanding some of the key characteristics of the right to health. ‘The right to health in practice’ applies these features, by way of illustration, in a more practical, operational way to the three case studies that follow on.





Laws, norms, and standards


	As explained in greater detail, international, regional, and national laws, norms, and standards relevant to the particular issue, programme, or policy must be identified. These will include both general standards relating to the right to health, in addition to instruments that relate to specific groups and contexts (UNCHR 2003a, Annex 1).





Dignity, equality, and non-discrimination


	Non-discrimination and equality are fundamental to all human rights, and to achieving the core human right entitlement of being treated with dignity. These entitlements are conferred from the first two articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: ‘All persons are born free and equal in dignity and rights’ and ‘Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this Declaration, without distinction of any kind … ’ (UDHR, Arts 1, 2).





Participation


	Participation is grounded in internationally recognized human rights, such as the rights to participate in the formulation and implementation of government policy (CEDAW, Article 7(b)), to take part in the conduct of public affairs (ICCPR, Article 25(a); UN 1966a), and to freedom of expression and association (ICCPR, Articles 19 and 22). All individuals and communities are entitled to active and informed participation on issues relating to their health, including policy making and accountability. Health professionals, and their associations, are also entitled to participate in decisions that will affect their employment and the work they do.





Accountability


	Accountability lies at the heart of human rights where it has two main components: addressing past grievances and correcting systemic failure to prevent future harm (Tech Guidance HRC14/39, par 33.) Without accountability, human rights obligations can become empty promises. Accountability mechanisms provide individuals and groups (people with rights entitlements) with an opportunity to understand how states and others with human rights obligations (duty bearers) have discharged their obligations, and it also provides duty bearers with an opportunity to explain their actions. In this way, accountability mechanisms are transparent, and they help to identify policy or programme adjustments that are necessary to realize human rights entitlements. Accountability also tends to encourage the most effective use of limited resources, as well as a shared responsibility among all parties. Sometimes accountability is conflated with monitoring but monitoring is only one step towards accountability. Accountability can be understood as monitoring, review (including independent review) in relation to human rights and other standards, and remedial action (Williams and Hunt 2017). Transparent, effective, and accessible accountability mechanisms are among the most crucial characteristics of human rights and they should extend to clinical care, public health, and the determinants of health.





International assistance and cooperation


	In line with obligations envisaged in the UN Charter and some human rights treaties, such as the ICESCR (Article 2) and the CRC (Article 4), countries that need international support to meet their right to health obligations have a responsibility to seek cooperation and international assistance, and states that can provide such assistance have responsibilities to do so (Hunt et al. 2010; Maastricht Principles on Extraterritorial Obligations of States in the Area of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights 2011). Global inequality cannot be reduced without such support, as explained in the Alma-Ata Declaration, and this is also acknowledged in the SDGs (Agenda 2030, par 17.9). In times of emergency, people are entitled to disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, including public health services. States have a responsibility to cooperate in providing this support, as well as assistance to refugees and internally displaced persons (UNCESCR 2000, para. 40).





Respect, protect, fulfil all human rights


	States have obligations to respect, protect, and fulfil all human rights, including the right to health, as explained and used by CESCR, the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), the Technical Guidance on the reduction of preventable maternal morbidity and mortality, among others (UN Human Rights Council 2012). These concepts are also enshrined in the Constitution of South Africa.
	With regard to the right to health, the obligation to respect places a duty on states to refrain from interfering directly or indirectly with the enjoyment of the right to health. The obligation to protect means that states must prevent third parties from interfering with the enjoyment of the right to health. The obligation to fulfil requires states to adopt the necessary measures, including legislative, administrative, and budgetary measures, to ensure the full realization of human rights, including the right to health.
	This feature also draws attention to the indivisibility of human rights, and highlights the need to acknowledge the broad cross section of civil, political, social, economic, and cultural rights that underpin the wider determinants of health. Efforts to fulfil one right do not justify a failure to respect or protect other rights.
	As we have explained, the right to health encompasses medical care and public health (see ‘What is the right to health?’ earlier) including the determinants of health. However, there is a tendency to give more attention to medical care and to neglect determinants. Because of that, in the application of this feature (see ‘The right to health in practice’, to follow) we give particular attention to determinants to ensure they are not neglected, marginalized, or overlooked.





Resource constraints and progressive realization


	International human rights law recognizes that the realization of the right to health is subject to resource availability. Thus, what is required of a better resourced state today is of a higher standard than what is required of a poorer-resourced state. However, a state is obliged—whatever its resource constraints and level of economic development—to realize progressively the right to the highest attainable standard of health (UN 1966b, Art. 2(1)). In essence, this means that a state is required to be doing better in 2 years’ time than it is doing today. In order to measure progress (or the lack of it) over time, indicators and benchmarks must be identified, and public health has a lot of experience in developing such tools. Progressive realization often involves making difficult decisions to ensure priority goes to those who are most disadvantaged. In human rights, it is not permissible for states to take steps that reverse human rights achievements. For example the present levels of service provision in healthcare may not be reduced, the current level of access to health services may not be lowered, and so on. If this situation, called retrogression, occurs, states must explain to UN monitoring committees why it has happened, as it is impermissible unless the state had no alternative actions available to it.





Obligations of immediate effect


	Despite resource constraints and progressive realization, the right to health also gives rise to some obligations of immediate effect, such as the duty to avoid discrimination (UNCESCR 2000, para. 43). These are obligations without which the right would be deprived of its raison d’être and as such they are not subject to progressive realization, even in the presence of resource constraints (UNCESCR 1990, para. 10). Guidelines adopted by the UN monitoring committees are helping to clarify what these might be and have highlighted: agreement of a national plan of action relating to health, including sexual and reproductive health; provision of essential drugs as identified by WHO; provision of reproductive, maternal, and child healthcare; immunization against major infectious diseases; prevention, treatment and control of epidemic and endemic diseases; and training of health personnel. Clarification of minimum core obligations remains an ongoing and important debate.





Available, accessible, acceptable, and good quality


	All health services, goods, and facilities should comply with each of these four requirements. For example, all essential immunizations should be available within the country. Additionally, they should be accessible. Accessibility has four dimensions: accessible without discrimination, physically accessible, economically accessible (i.e. affordable), and accessible health-related information. As well as being available and accessible, immunization campaigns should be provided in a culturally acceptable manner. This requires, for example, planning and coordination with community leaders. The good quality element will require, for example, ensuring the integrity of vaccine cold chains.
	Note the similarity between these requirements and the four ‘As’ of public healthcare envisaged since the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration: geographical accessibility, financial accessibility, cultural accessibility, and functional accessibility (WHO 1978b).





Strengthening health systems


	At the heart of the right to the highest attainable standard of health lies an effective and integrated health system, encompassing healthcare and the underlying determinants of health, responsive to national and local priorities, and accessible to all (UN HRC 2008). The right to health cannot be fulfilled without a well-functioning health system (Backman et al. 2008). In essence, this means that the six components of a health system as identified by WHO—service delivery, health workforce, information, medical products, vaccines, and technologies, financing, and leadership and governance—are available, accessible, acceptable, and of quality to all, without discrimination. However, a health system is more than simply these six components. It also includes the people for whom it exists and a human rights perspective of a health system keeps these people at its centre. As Alicia Ely Yamin has written, ‘If health systems are understood as core social institutions, it follows that the choices to be made cannot be seen just as technical choices but rather as reflecting and embedding values and norms of the larger society, including in relation to equality, dignity, and human rights’ (Yamin 2016, p. 104).





The right to health in practice


	The key features of the right to health underscore what the right to health contributes to public health. The preoccupation with dignity, equality, and non-discrimination requires a state to take effective measures to address the health inequities that characterize some populations. The focus on active and informed participation requires a state to adopt, so far as possible, a ‘bottom–up’ participatory approach in health-related sectors. The requirement of accountability can help to ensure that health policies, programmes, and practices are observant of human rights, and offer remedy when necessary.
	Crucially, the key features of a right-to-health framework are not merely to be followed because they accord with sound management, ethics, social justice, or humanitarianism. States are required to conform to the key features as a matter of binding law. Moreover, they are to be held to account for the discharge of their right-to-health responsibilities arising from these legal obligations.
	Having looked at the legality of human rights, the meaning of the right to health, and having identified its key features, we now turn our attention to what this means in practice. We apply this approach to critically important global public health issues—the impact of climate change on children’s right to health, the digitization of health through Big Data, and overseas development assistance.
	 	Case Study 3.3.1 The Impact of Climate Change on Children’s Right to Health
	Climate change is an enormous threat to global health (see Chapter 2.9). The greatest burden of climate change is borne by low resource countries and especially by poor children (Smith 2014). Children are especially vulnerable because of their growth and development, unique physiology and metabolism, reliance on adults and families, and the conditions in which they live, learn, work, and play. Consequently their health is at greater risk from climate-related events, infections, and pollutants, with the youngest and most disadvantaged children being most vulnerable (Ahdoot et al. 2015).
	Climate change impacts on children’s right to health and indeed all their human rights–their rights to life, survival, development, health, food, water, sanitation, a healthy environment, family, education, housing, safety, protection, participation, culture, heritage, and so forth (Knox 2016; United Nations General Assembly 2017). Without effective mitigation and adaptation strategies, climate change has life-long consequences for today’s children and brings increasing harm to future generations of children. However, well-designed climate-related actions bring opportunities to improve the health and well-being of children and future generations (Hosking et al. 2011).





Laws, norms, and standards


	Human rights laws, norms, and standards are used to reduce the harm that climate change causes on the well-being of children. Under the United Nations CRC, children are entitled to special protection measures and assistance to ensure their survival and development and that they are treated as human beings equal in dignity and worth with adults. Their evolving capacities as they grow and develop require different priorities and approaches at different stages of development throughout their childhood to ensure their right to health. Children’s best interests should be central in considering all decisions that may affect their health and development (United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child 2013). There are obligations in international law for actions that protect the rights and best interests of children, including their right to health, from the impact of climate change (United Nations General Assembly 2017).
	The Paris Agreement on climate change recognizes the rights of children and people in vulnerable situations, intergenerational equity, and the right to health in its preamble (Conference of the Parties 2015). In its General Comment on the rights of the child to health, the UN Committee for the Rights of the Child included their right to a healthy environment and said climate change ‘is one of the biggest threats to children’s health and exacerbates health disparities. States should, therefore, put children’s health concerns at the centre of their climate change adaptation and mitigation strategies (para. 50)’ (United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child 2013). The UN Committee regularly makes recommendations about climate action in its in reviews of states’ progress.





Dignity, equality, and non-discrimination


	The burden of climate change is spread inequitably within and between countries. Those who have done the least to cause climate change are the worst affected and yet have the least economic and infrastructure resources for adaptation. Mothers and children, especially girls, are particularly affected (Metcalfe 2015). Climate change aggravates existing inequities, even leading to violent conflict over reduced resources and forced migration (Watts et al. 2015) and compounding other discrimination and injustices experienced by children.
	If all children are to equally enjoy their right to health free of discrimination, climate-related actions must prioritize those children who are most disadvantaged, so that they are among the first to benefit. In practice this may require changing current priorities and ensuring more resources for these children, especially those experiencing multiple discrimination and living in vulnerable situations.





Participation


	It is only recently that international climate negotiations have considered the rights of children and children have had some—albeit limited—opportunities to be heard. Children, especially those most affected, have the human right to participate and contribute to decision-making about matters which affect them and their health in accordance with their age and maturity. This requires having safe, child-friendly, and age-appropriate processes to support children to have their views heard and taken seriously. It may include them participating in legal and policy processes about health and the environment; priority-setting; the development and delivery of mitigation and adaptation policies and programmes; and accountability mechanisms. Participation has practical benefits: if children are involved in the development, delivery, and evaluations of programmes, the programmes are more likely to be effective (Children in a Changing Climate 2015).
	Public health services should support children and their families’ participation, including in the design, development, and evaluation of programmes. For example, although in times of extreme weather events and other disasters children carry out family and community duties, it is uncommon for them to be involved in disaster risk reduction planning. Yet their practical and creative ideas and unique knowledge of local environments mean they can make important contributions (Mudavanhu et al. 2015).
	Many children are active environmental advocates. In several countries children are taking legal action, arguing that the state’s obligations to hold some resources in common for all people, includes an obligation to protect the earth’s atmosphere for children now and in the future. For example, Rabab Ali, a 7-year-old girl in Kawachi, petitioned Pakistan’s Supreme Court about plans to develop a coal field, saying that atmospheric pollution harms and threatens the rights of Pakistani children and future generations, including their right to mental and physical health (Sabin Center for Climate Change Law 2016).





Accountability


	There are some opportunities to hold states accountable at an international level for the impact of their climate-related actions on children through mechanisms under the Paris Agreement and the SDGs. These are weak mechanisms, especially for the magnitude of the task. The human rights mechanisms of the UN Human Rights Council, human rights treaty monitoring bodies and special procedures are also weak but can supplement the others. As countries develop and strengthen national mechanisms for accountability there will be increasing opportunities to hold people, businesses, and other organizations accountable for the impact of actions on children.
	Accountability mechanisms at international, regional, national, and local levels should include opportunities for the participation of children and child-friendly processes, and for consideration of the right to health of future generations of children. Unless data are disaggregated by age, sex, and other characteristics, it is not possible to hold states accountable in relation to their health rights obligations for all children.
	Accountability requires consideration of the differentiated responsibilities for climate change and remedial action. High-income countries have benefited economically from their high greenhouse gas emissions. It is plainly unfair that the health of poor children throughout the world suffers the consequences. Countries with the highest emissions for their population must rapidly reduce their own emissions as part of remedying past, present, and future injustices against children. They also have urgent human rights duties to provide remedial action (including finance) for losses and damage suffered already by climate vulnerable countries and support their adaptation efforts (Hunt and Khosla 2009; Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights 2015).





International assistance and cooperation


	Unprecedented international cooperation is needed to reach the Paris Agreement’s aspirational goal of limiting global warming below 1.5° and avoid catastrophic damage to global health. The human rights responsibilities of states include actively supporting—and not obstructing—the realization of the right to health for people in other countries. This requires working for an equitable international order and healthy environmental conditions for all including measures that will stop and reverse climate change (Hunt and Khosla 2009).
	Human rights require states to act to the ‘maximum extent of available resources’. High-income countries have a human rights obligation to share resources with less resourced countries so they have the resources they need to address climate change. Considerable increases in international assistance are needed to build climate-resilient health services and programmes. Health adaptation has however been largely overlooked in international assistance: between 2003 and 2017 less than 1% of the development funds available for adaptation through global climate change financing mechanisms, was for health sector adaptation (Watts et al. 2018). International assistance for health adaptation should pay special attention to poor children in low-income countries because they bear the greatest health impact of climate change.





Respect, protect, and fulfil all human rights


	Tackling the impact of climate change on children’s right to health requires action on determinants to respect, protect, and fulfil all of children’s human rights. For example, for indigenous peoples, including children, climate change may mean displacement from their traditional lands and resources; disruption of their heritage, family life, cultural identity, and knowledge, and spiritual relationship with the natural environment; increasing poverty and marginalization; and direct and indirect harm to their health (Jones et al. 2014). Climate-related actions have potential to support or harm the well-being of indigenous peoples: for example, forced displacement of indigenous peoples from their traditional lands to build hydroelectric dams has caused serious human rights violations (Tauli-Corpuz 2017). When a state respects the right of indigenous peoples to guardianship of their forests; ensures the right is protected from interference by others (for example, multinational logging companies), and takes the legal, administrative, and budgetary measures necessary to fulfil the right, then this also respects traditional health practices and other health-related rights—as well as benefiting global climate mitigation.
	Mitigation and adaptation plans made by states, regional, and intergovernmental organizations should address the human rights impacts of climate change, with a strong focus on respecting, protecting, and fulfilling the rights of children and other vulnerable groups. Plans should include progressive improvements for child health services and programmes and the underlying determinants of health (Williams 2015). Climate-related actions should not cause retrogression of human rights: for example, the intention of increasing biofuel crop production may be to reduce use of fossil fuels but if done by displacing poor farmers from their land, may cause serious human rights violations, including of children’s rights to health, food, education, a family environment, an adequate standard of living, safety, and so forth.





Available, accessible, acceptable, and good quality


	There is considerable potential for public health co-benefits from climate-related actions (Watts et al. 2015). Climate-related public health services and programmes should be available to children, especially children living in climate vulnerable countries and situations. They should be accessible. This means prioritizing those children experiencing the greatest disadvantage; ensuring that access is not affected by physical barriers from location, distance and so forth, or economic cost; and enabling children to easily access information about health and climate change (for example, in the school curriculum). They should be provided in ways that are appropriate for the age and culture of the children served, i.e. acceptable. They should be informed by evidence, of sound quality, and provided in ways that support the best interests of children. In doing this, services should recognize the diverse needs of children—for example, protocols should include availability, accessibility, acceptability, quality criteria (AAAQ) for children who live with disabilities or whose caregivers do, and child-headed families.





Strengthening health systems


	Health services can contribute to mitigation through reducing their own greenhouse gas emissions. This can include ways that come with co-benefits for the children: for example, when clinics are held in communities, travel-related emissions are reduced and physical accessibility and affordability can increase; and when hospitals stop using coal as a source of power, children are less exposed to harm from air pollution.
	Health systems face considerable challenges in adaptation to climate change. Climate resilience has to be operationalized into each of WHO’s six building blocks of health systems (World Health Organization 2015). The basic public health actions that are the most effective immediate general adaptation measures—such as vaccination, essential child health services, clean water, and sanitation, increasing disaster risk management capacity, and reducing poverty (Smith 2014) are all key to improving child health.
	 	Case Study 3.3.2 An Impact Assessment of Big Data Using the Right to Health
	Big Data is beginning to radically transform healthcare in multiple ways—through its use in electronic health records, data sharing, diagnostic tools, and treatment. These new technologies are changing the health and public health landscapes. Examples of the roles of digitization in healthcare include personalized medicine (a patient’s treatment can be specifically tailored to their genetic, genomic, social and environmental profile) (Parry and Greenhough 2018), DNA sequencing (where the resulting vast amount of data is stored in bio banks), forensic, genetic or medical databases, including all the data from public health studies and clinical trials—and all of which can be re-purposed for various technical inventions. These large data sets are driving the burgeoning artificial intelligence (AI) industry in healthcare. Where available and accessible these technologies offer improved public health, clinical care, and patient management; where they are not, inequities in health will likely result.
	Blockchain technology also plays a role in health, with the technology, previously more associated with crypto currencies, being used to keep large health data sets more secure when data is shared. A focus on data security, although crucially important, must not become a distraction from other right to health threats posed by Big Data. In particular these threats may arise from data ownership and how equitably data will be used in the future.
	Here we examine Big Data through a right to health lens and identify opportunities and threats to health equity and to the right to health in a new data-driven economy. We suggest that just as governments have been expected to carry out human rights impact assessments prior to adopting and implementing policies (MacNaughton and Hunt 2009; MacNaughton and Hunt 2011), so they should before embarking on the use of Big Data in health and other domains.





Laws, norms, and standards


	While some health data sets are collected and controlled nationally, particularly people’s medical records, much of the data feeding into global databases is derived from individuals contributing their own data to organizations beyond the borders of their resident state. This includes fitness and lifestyle data derived from wearable devices, or personal information uploaded into Facebook and other social media, as well as far more clinical and medically detailed data such as DNA sequencing, or clinical trials information. The rules, regulations, and laws governing how data can be used, and how individuals providing the data are protected, are not universal, although there are some regional regulations, for example, the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) https://www.eugdpr.org/. Collection and use of data for Big Data sets may be overseen by professional ethics, developed to guide fair use of data, but such codes of ethics are not legally binding.
	National laws need to ensure that personal data is collected, stored, and used in ways that respect, protect, and fulfil human rights entitlements; but how can this be achieved beyond national borders? International human rights law provides such a facility. All use of Big Data, however the data sets were developed, even if ethically or with individual consent, must not subsequently be used in ways that violate human rights, including the right to health. For example, this means that, as a matter of law, Big Data must not be used, either when gathered or at a later time, to discriminate against people in terms of their right to health, including their participation in the health system, or to increase health inequities.





Dignity, equality, and non-discrimination


	There are vast global inequalities in relation to data: from the personal (being literate, owning mobile phones, having internet access), to national information systems (functional national statistical offices, electronic information systems, electronic health information systems, a Big Data-driven sector that uses and develops electronic applications). Those countries, usually low-income countries, without sophisticated and extensive electronic infrastructure will be left further behind from the benefits of data-driven health gains, resulting in increased global health inequality, unless there is specific international assistance and technical support provided from high-income countries to address information systems deficits. There are great risks that, for example, wealthy people in high-income countries will have access to personalized medicine, tailored to their own genomes, while millions in poor countries continue to die prematurely from neglected tropical diseases, and other conditions of poverty. This is an example of gross inequity in public health, and a human rights failing at an international level, which requires urgent remedy.
	Big Data enthusiasts cite its usefulness in many health domains, aside from clinical purposes. These uses include social media’s role in monitoring and tracking epidemics and monitoring SDGs (Harvard Humanitarian Initiative, MIT Media Lab, and Overseas Development Institute 2016). Because of the human rights imperatives that inequality must not increase and there is no discrimination in the delivery of healthcare, it is vitally important to disaggregate data collected by not just looking at the data to determine the characteristics of those who contributed to the data sets, but also to understand who has not. When considering the use of Big Data to track epidemics, for example, there are still large pockets in the world where communities live without internet access (Williams and Hunt 2017). The percentage of the global population with access to the internet at the end of 2017, was 54.4%, ranging from 95% in North America to 35.2% in Africa (Internet World Stats 2018). Even these statistics require far greater disaggregation: for example, several African nations have less than 10% internet coverage, with Eritrea the lowest on 1.4%. If there is a global shift to monitoring epidemics through social media, widely considered more efficient and accurate than traditional health surveillance, those communities or countries living beyond internet penetration are at risk of invisibility during health or humanitarian crises.
	As discussed earlier in ‘Key features of the right to health’, there are national and international human rights obligations to address these inequalities and discriminations, including through international assistance and cooperation (see ‘Dignity, equality, and non-discrimination’ and ‘International assistance and cooperation’)





Participation


	The human right to participation means people are entitled to be part of decision-making processes that affect their lives and their health, and also to decision-making processes about health policy. At the least, when it comes to the use of their own data, people have the right to decide whether or not their data can be used for any purposes beyond the stated reason for its collection. Ownership and terms of use of the data must be clear and obvious, so that contributors to data sets are not later surprised to find their provision of personal information has been used to discriminate against them. This could, for example, occur if details of a person’s dietary or other lifestyle factors, gleaned from social networks or sporting achievements applications, are shared with agencies that could withhold services on the basis of this information, or charge varying rates for the service on the basis of this information which was not provided directly to the service provider. Health insurance premiums could be an example of this.





Accountability


	Over the past few years, use of Big Data has been plagued with scandals: for example, in the United Kingdom in 2016 over one million confidential patient files were given freely, and without hiding personal identities, to a Google-owned company to develop privately owned apps for clinical use; throughout 2016–2018 details were released about the extent of data mining through Facebook networks to influence voters and US and Brexit election results. As mentioned already, rules have now been introduced to control aspects of data collection, to protect privacy. However, such rules focus more on rights to privacy than they do on the longer-term consequences, for example, on who will own this data in its re-purposed presentations in the future. It is difficult to predict how data collected now will be used in the future, but our social and economic transactions, and healthcare, are now completely dependent on data. In order to protect social rights, such as the right to health, use of Big Data must be transparent, and there must be accountability for the human rights implications of how this data is subsequently used. Data processors need to be held to account for the human rights implications of the products they develop: for example, will data be gathered in discriminatory ways (perhaps from poorer communities and countries who use public health services), but will the resulting products be used only by individuals or their insurers who can afford to pay for them? As discussed earlier, human rights require that duty bearers are held accountable by way of a process which includes monitoring, review against human rights and other standards, and remedial action (see ‘Key features of the right to health’).





Respect, protect, and fulfil all human rights


	Big Data arises from multiple data sets in social, economic, and political domains. It is imperative that people’s rights in each of these domains are respected and protected during the collection and use of data, and that the integrated data are not used to discriminate against anyone in each of the domains. For example, domains of data about ethnicity, poverty, and crime might be combined in order to locate emergency health services where they are most needed which would be advancing equitable access to healthcare. However, the data could also result in biased algorithms that lead to disproportionate policing in areas where a minority population resides, leading in turn to increased arrests in that area. This could be discriminatory, and a violation of people’s rights to privacy and to justice.





Available, accessible, acceptable, and good quality


	The benefits of Big Data should be available, accessible, and acceptable and based on good quality information and methodologies. When a state has determined, in a participatory way, the health services and facilities that can be provided from its maximum available resources, it is then obligated to ensure these are of good quality and available, accessible (including financially accessible), and acceptable to all. This covers such issues as ensuring that the datasets from which applications develop are built from quality, robust data, with privacy protected. Is the use of the data agreed to and acceptable to the people from whom the data was collected? Health services that arise from the use of Big Data, for example health apps to assist with diagnosis of diseases, or personalized medicine based on a person’s genome, must meet the ‘available and accessible’ criteria and avoid increasing inequities. For example, if patient information and notifications switch to digital systems, does this discriminate against people without smart phones, and result in them losing access to these services?





Strengthening health systems


	The health system is the core institution through which the right to health can be fulfilled. Data is an essential component of health systems, used for improving patient management, providing health information, and importantly, to monitor the health system’s performance. As data sets increase in size, and as multiple data sets are integrated, it is essential to monitor and review that this use of Big Data continues to strengthen the health system. Right to health impact assessments should be undertaken before installing or implementing data-driven new technologies. Assessments are needed to question whether such technologies are protecting and respecting people’s rights; they can guide their use so technology strengthens, not weakens, health systems and thereby can fulfil people’s health rights entitlements. Questions about Big Data-driven technologies and their impacts on health systems would cover both technical infrastructure aspects, such as the robustness of the new systems and their vulnerability to hackers or power outages, through to ownership of the systems and the data contained within them.
	 	Case Study 3.3.3 International Assistance and Cooperation and the Right to Health
	One element of the right to health pertains to the obligation on states to provide international assistance and cooperation. It is incumbent upon states that can afford to do so, to offer assistance and cooperation to states who request it in order to meet their human rights obligations. States have an obligation to seek such assistance when they do not have available resources to meet their right to health duties. There are also global aid agreements arising from the Alma-Ata Declaration, the SDGs, and a commitment made by OECD countries in 1970 to spend 0.7% of gross national product (GNP) on aid (OECD, n.d.). Most OECD countries have not yet achieved that level of expenditure on aid, although global health spending has increased dramatically since 2000. WHO estimated $19 billion was spent on development assistance for health (DAH) in 2015. After a decade of rapid growth from 2000 to 2010 (up 11.4% annually), DAH grew at only 1.8% annually between 2010 and 2016. In low-income countries, DAH made up 34.6% of total health spending in 2016 (IHME 2016; WHO 2017). This is partially in response to the attention brought to global health and other inequalities from the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), and SDGs, but also because of funding from global health initiatives such as The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, TB and Malaria, Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (GAVI) and the Gates Foundation. Non-government organization (NGO) funding made up 30.1% of total DAH disbursed in 2016, whereas in 1990 it contributed only 7.6% of total DAH funding. NGOs collectively disbursed more funds than any other group by a wide margin (IHME 2016, pp. 32–3). Usually NGO funding is directed to the health initiatives pertinent to their own missions. The capacity of such organizations, and the non-state sector as a whole, to have an impact of people’s right to health entitlements is therefore considerable.
	In addition to the international human rights obligation to seek and provide international assistance and cooperation, when such assistance and cooperation is provided its delivery must conform to the requirements of human rights law. In this case study, we use the right to health framework to explore issues that global partners must consider when shaping aid interventions, so they comply with duties to respect, protect, and fulfil health rights.





Laws, norms, and standards


	Development assistance must be compliant with international human rights law, as well as national laws and regulations. In the former, this pertains to such considerations as delivering assistance without discrimination (see next section), and at the national level, it will mean ensuring that, inter alia, health personnel will not be trained to deliver services beyond their regulatory scope. An example might be not training nurses to provide minor surgery if they are not permitted to perform such procedures.
	A human rights-based approach to health recognizes that health is a right, and people have human rights entitlements to health services. International providers of assistance for health services are therefore assisting the fulfilment of people’s rights, and empowering people to recognize and claim these rights entitlements. This is a different conceptualization of aid initiatives from ones of charity or philanthropy where beneficiaries may be viewed as fortunate to receive services but are not considered to have equal rights to them.





Dignity, equality, and non-discrimination


	Assistance must not be provided in a discriminatory way, even when national law results in such discrimination. Examples of discrimination in health can be found when only married women can receive some health services, or husbands’ permission is required for services, or services are prioritized for people working in the formal sector, and so on.
	International actors must therefore examine issues of inequality and discrimination in the countries they work to identify where interventions are most needed to reduce health inequities in that country. Treating all people with dignity is a fundamental value on which all human rights are based, and in aid programmes, that extends to the way in which people are presented in fundraising activities in donor countries.





Participation


	When providing assistance and cooperation, international agencies need to ensure there is participation at many levels: that the state welcomes and invites their support, that local partners are leaders in the design and implementation of support, and the people for whom services will be provided have contributed meaningfully to all aspects of the initiative and its delivery.





Accountability


	Human rights require effective accountability arrangements to be put in place for the human rights obligations arising from international assistance and cooperation. Accountability in aid initiatives is frequently limited to financial accountability, but human rights accountability is much more than this. People have human rights entitlements to know how decisions are made about the health system and provision of services. This includes for international assistance, at the least, transparency around: approval processes for international assistance support; the nature of services, products, or funds being delivered; location of services; how the quality of health services will be monitored; and whether services are provided in a non-discriminatory and equitable way. Human rights accountability necessitates the use of transparent processes to check that aid initiatives respect, protect, and fulfil human rights, remembering that rights are indivisible—so it is not acceptable to promote one health service at the expense of other health or other services, unless this is an agreed approach to the national plan. (For example, a country as a whole may decide to forego some tertiary level care to ensure primary healthcare reaches everyone). This is explained in ‘Strengthening health systems’.





Respect, protect, and fulfil all human rights


	Health aid cannot be sustainable without considering the broad determinants of health and their related rights. For example, assistance to improve a healthcare service such as child health is of limited use if children live in communities that do not have potable water, sanitation systems, or schools. Similarly, health aid programmes to educate midwives are unlikely to succeed in the long term if midwives are not paid adequately or if they are subject to violence at home or at work. It is therefore important that determinants and related human rights are assessed as part of international assistance and cooperation, and ways of addressing these rights are identified.





Available, accessible, acceptable, and good quality


	International assistance and cooperation for health must be delivered or directed so that their support for health services meet the AAAQ criteria.
	 	• Under availability, questions should be asked about what is required to make a health service fully available. This is not just about where the service is to be provided, but, for example, what medicines and other supplies are needed, and how will they be made available in a sustainable way. Similarly, how will staff be trained and employed so they are available for these services?
	• Under accessibility, aid initiatives might consider who can access the service in terms of gender, disability, place of dwelling, or knowledge of such services. Care must be taken that groups, for example, indigenous people, are made aware of services and are helped to access them.
	• Acceptability calls for culturally appropriate care to be made available. For example, are new services planned to be delivered in a way that is acceptable to women in minority or indigenous communities? Will health workers speak the languages spoken by disadvantaged groups?
	• Quality healthcare is critically important and lower standards are not acceptable simply because recipient countries have fewer economic resources. This means that health workers must be well trained and supported, medicines must be within use-by dates, and countries that receive assistance should not be treated as dumping grounds for obsolete second hand equipment that will not be serviced, or as a means of claiming tax rebates on the ‘value’ of the goods donated.
	Donors of health aid should include a right to health impact assessment of their initiatives before implementation, to consider the possible impact of a new or expanded service on the AAAQ of other health services. For example, well-funded stand-alone interventions for some health services may draw health professionals and other resources to them, weakening other core services—thereby resulting in a reduction in availability and quality (Williams and Brian 2013). At all times, donors must consider the sustainability of any interventions, in order to avoid commencement of services that will not endure, thereby later contributing to a regression in health rights fulfilment.





Strengthening health systems


	Because the health system is the key institution through which the right to health can be realized, international assistance must take care to work in ways that promotes the long-term sustainability of the system. Initiatives must work in keeping with the national health plan. They should also strengthen the health system’s capacity to provide quality health services for all, addressing inequities so that the most disempowered and worst off have their rights fulfilled first. Health impact assessments should be undertaken before implementing aid initiatives to systematically check the health system will be strengthened, not weakened, by international assistance.





Conclusion


	We began this chapter with illustrations of successful right to health initiatives from around the world in high-, middle-and low-income countries, and concluded with detailed case studies demonstrating the right to health in practice. Together, these are examples of human rights supporting global public health.
	The right to health entitles all people to a package of health services, facilities, and goods, extending to healthcare, and public health, including the underlying determinants of health, such as access to safe water, adequate sanitation, and health-related information. This package must be available, accessible, and of good quality. Also, it must be sensitive to different cultures, thus, acceptable. Health systems are the key institution through which healthcare and public health are delivered. They must be sites of inclusion, where people can participate in policy making and planning. In this way, health systems will have many features that are common to all countries, but there will also be differences between countries that will reflect their different disease burdens, determinants of health, cultural contexts, resource availability, and people’s priorities.
	Whichever approach and combination of approaches is employed, the objective is to respect, protect, and fulfil people’s right to health.





Key points


	 	• The right to the highest attainable standard of health is enshrined in several international treaties and numerous national constitutions.
	• International law recognizes that all people have human rights entitlements and states have binding obligations to uphold these rights.
	• Public health and the right to the highest attainable standard of health are natural allies both seeking effective, integrated, responsive health systems that are accessible to all.
	• The key features of the right to health assist in understanding and responding effectively to public health issues and reducing global and national inequities.
	• The right to the highest attainable standard of health can be understood as a right of everyone to public health and health services and the underlying determinants of health.
