It is important to remember that infant and under-five mortality estimates frequently differ between censuses and surveys as surveys usually use full birth histories which tend to underestimate infant and under-five mortality, while censuses use indirect methods which tend to slightly overestimate infant and under-five mortality.
	Substantial progress was made in achieving the MDGs. Maternal mortality fell by almost 44% worldwide, from 385 deaths to 216 deaths per 100,000 live births over the period 1990 to 2015 (WHO 2015). This translates into an average annual rate of reduction of 2.6 percent. Although this was a substantial decline, it was less than half of the 5.5 percent rate needed to achieve the three-quarters reduction in maternal mortality targeted for 2015 in MDG 5. In general, the ignominy of poverty has not ended at all. In 2016, members of the United Nations agreed on 17 SDGs to be achieved by 2030. This new set of goals aims to complete the agenda of the MDGs so that no country is left behind. Health is the third goal of the SDGs; one of its targets is to reduce the maternal mortality ratio to less than 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030 (WHO 2016).





Nutrition


	An essential ingredient in the improvement of maternal child health is the improved nutritional status of these individuals.
	Attention to maternal and child undernutrition—stunting, underweight and wasting, and deficiencies of essential micronutrients—increasingly focuses on the crucial period from conception to the child’s second birthday, the 1,000 days during which the nutritional status of mothers and children have lasting effects on the life of the child.
	The Lancet Maternal and Child Nutrition Series, 2008 and 2013 (Bhutta et al. 2008; Black et al. 2008; Ruel 2013; Black et al. 2013; Bhutta 2013; Victora et al. 2013) underlines these lifetime effects of nutritional conditions during this critical period, plus the adolescent period for girls, and reviews the evidence supporting interventions seeking to address the undernutrition problem.
	The series also focuses on the so-called ‘double burden of malnutrition’—these undernutrition problems coupled with problems of overweight and obesity, occurring in the same geographic areas, and with the latter sometimes a consequence of the former.
	Increasingly, it is understood that, undernutrition problems, rather than being encompassed within the confines of public health, are multisectoral in their causality and, in turn, require multisectoral interventions. Where combinations of multisectoral interventions are put in place in vulnerable areas of developing countries, the effects on nutritional status have been found to be synergistic and often highly impressive. Figure 3.5.2, often referred to as the UNICEF Conceptual Framework, summarizes these multisectoral relationships (https://www.unicef.org/nutrition/training/2.5/4.html, accessed September 2018).
	Fig. 3.5.2 Conceptual framework for the causes of malnutrition in society.
	Reprinted from United Nations Children’s Fund. UNICEF’s approach to scaling up nutrition for mothers and their children. Discussion paper. Programme Division, UNICEF, New York, June 2015.
	As indicated in the diagram, malnutrition is the result of some combination of inadequate dietary intake and infectious disease. These, in turn, are the result of a series of vitally important ‘underlying causes’—which, depending on their relative importance in a given geographic area, require effective interventions. Accordingly, nutrition policies and strategies often include project activities addressing food insecurity and poverty, behavioural change communications, health service delivery and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions, plus maternal and child feeding and micronutrient provision which address the ‘immediate causes’.
	Interventions addressing undernutrition that fall outside of the health sector are generally referred to as nutrition sensitive, addressing, primarily, the determinants of undernutrition (Pinstrup-Anderson 2013). Examples of these are:
	 	In the agricultural sector—homestead gardens, small livestock, and small pond fish farming.
	In the education sector—inclusion of essential nutrition information in primary and secondary school curricula, and, more generally, generating increases in female enrolment and attendance at both levels.
	In the social protection sector—the coupling of social protection benefits with counselling that facilitates the translation of income supplements into improved nutrition and health status.
	In the WASH sector—assurance that these services are provided to those households at highest risk, and that the physical infrastructure provided is accompanied by adequate counselling on its use.
	In the health sector, nutrition-related interventions are often described as nutrition specific, addressing more directly the effects of undernutrition with a particular focus on prevention. These interventions include child feeding, behavioural change communications with special attention to optimal breastfeeding and complementary feeding practices, micronutrient supplementation and fortification, and the treatment of severe acute malnutrition.
	Such nutrition-specific interventions in the health sector are particularly important given existing problems. Despite improvements in some countries, breastfeeding practices continue to be highly problematic and contribute significantly to high child mortality rates. Deficiencies of vitamin A, iron, iodine, and zinc adversely affect maternal and child health, while addressing these problems through supplementation and fortification have been found to be among the most cost-effective interventions functioning in developing countries.
	Overall, over 165 million children in these countries suffer from stunted growth. The highest prevalence of stunting is found in eastern and western Africa and in South Asia. The largest number of children affected by stunting, over 70 million live in South Asia. The numbers of stunted children in Africa has actually been increasing in recent years (Black 2013). When micronutrient deficiencies are added in, undernutrition, resulting both in losses in cognition and reduced schooling has been found to reduce the economic growth of a developing nation by at least 8% through productivity losses (Horton 2013).
	There has been a significant response to these problems from governments, international and bilateral assistance agencies, and non-governmental organizations. These interventions, however, are unlikely to achieve the target of the World Health Assembly calling for a 40% reduction in stunting in children under age 5 between 2010 and 2025 (Black 2013).





Actors in health policy


	Governments in developing countries play a primary role in the formulation of health policy formation and its implementation, often with the support of development partners. These partners include United Nations (UN) agencies, other international and bilateral donors, and international and domestic non-governmental organizations. International and national donors provide financial as well as technical expertise, often with an eye on international targets such as the SDGs set for the year 2030 (Koduah et al. 2015).
	National governance and the orientation of key national political leaders inevitably have considerable influence on both the direction of health policies and their implementation (Shiffman and Smith 2007; Erasmus and Gilson 2008; Gilson et al. 2014; Koduah et al. 2015). At the same time, the role of officials and institutions at subnational levels, the extent of community involvement, and the capacity and commitment of front-line workers can be critical in this regard (Erasmus et al. 2017).
	Multiple studies have highlighted the gaps and challenges in health policy implementation in developing countries (Belaid and Ridde 2012; Lehmann and Gilson 2013; Gilson et al. 2014). These shortcomings often relate to financial shortfalls or to the inadequate authority or commitment of implementing actors (Belaid and Ridde 2012). Limited responsibility and discretionary power at subnational levels have proven to be a particular liability (Lehmann and Gilson 2013; Gilson et al. 2014). More successful health policy implementation has often come on the heels of health sector reform including some combination of structural changes, e.g. decentralization, and changes in the model of healthcare delivery system (Atkinson et al. 2005).
	Increasing attention also is being given to the role of social media in health policy. Where there are limitations on media freedom and, in turn, on government transparency, or on the activities of civil society advocacy organizations there have usually been consequences (Ha et al. 2010; Green et al. 2011). By contrast, social media have played key roles in the success of behavioural change efforts relating to the consumption of alcohol and tobacco products and to traffic accidents (Grilli et al. 2002; Elder et al. 2004; Bala et al. 2013). Effective health policies generally include the role of social media in disseminating key elements of these policies and in providing the public with essential health information (Roland 2017).
	Policy agenda setting is usually determined by combinations of health sector data (ideally disaggregated by geographic area), by the availability of funding, and by the orientation of policymakers themselves (Koduah et al. 2015). As indicated, donor agencies often have a key role in both policy formation and in its implementation (Grépin et al. 2017). The nature and scope of donor influence at different levels of policymaking have been well documented in Pakistan and Cambodia (Khan et al. 2018). Primary influences often include the utilization of financial resources and mechanisms to assure adequate monitoring and evaluation of policies and programmes (Hafner and Shiffman 2013; Khan et al. 2018).
	Two other important influences on health policy development are the international agenda (e.g. SDGs), and the availability and quality of scientific evidence (Wallace et al. 2012).
	Reviews in some African countries and in Myanmar have recommended an upgrading of evidence-based decision-making and policy development, and have underlined the vital importance of increased receptivity to such evidence, and of universities in the necessary capacity development (Lavis et al. 2005; Orton et al. 2011; Young et al. 2016; Ellen et al. 2018). To fill gaps in essential knowledge transfer, such training is necessary both for policymakers and research organizations, and improved communication between the two should be encouraged (Whitehead et al. 2004).





Political and economic impacts on health systems


	Government health systems are significantly affected by the country’s economy, and by its political structure and orientation. Where political instability exists, political systems are weak (e.g. overly centralized, bureaucratized decision-making, weak regulations), economic growth is sporadic, or welfare systems are dysfunctional, health consequences are inevitable (Guha-Sapir and D’Aoust 2010).
	In some countries with strong political commitment to reduce hunger, poverty, or inequality, the health status of citizens has improved markedly even without highlighted attention to health and nutrition. This has been seen during particular periods of recent history in China and Cuba, and during the early years of the Lula presidency in Brazil (Field and Levinson 1975). In Vietnam, health sector management until the mid-1980s was state–socialist or universalist. Health expenditure emanated both from the central and subnational governments and from other local resources. All citizens could enjoy preventive and curative healthcare free of charge as citizens’ rights. As a result, child mortality rates dropped markedly. Unfortunately, in some regions of the country with more limited resources, health improvement was less dramatic and was often characterized by inequality in service delivery (London 2008).
	Commercialization in the healthcare sector began in the mid-1980s. Often resulting from macroeconomic reform, such commercialization often led to a lower quality of healthcare delivery particularly in public hospitals where, despite an outward appearance of free services, the informal fee charges levied—emanating from the new profit orientation of these hospitals, often reduced hospital utilization by the poor. Similarly, financial decentralization in the social sector as a whole often resulted in inadequate budgetary allocation for actual health services at subnational levels, with most of the funding going for high level medical staff salaries, and more sophisticated equipment rarely available to those most in need (Forsberg 2011). The associated poor management and weak regulatory systems have usually led to reduced immunization rates and to the increased prevalence of particular infectious diseases.
	In South Africa, racial discrimination was the primary cause of poor health services for the African population along with inequality in most services during the Apartheid period. The Bantustan regions set aside for large segments of the African population had their own healthcare systems which were invariably inadequate and resulted in high mortality rates (Maillacheruvu and McDuff 2014).
	In 1994, with the election of Nelson Mandela and the end of Apartheid, a new National Health Plan was developed with comprehensive primary health services (Coovadia et al. 2009). Many health sector challenges persisted, however. With inefficiencies in the health system, the percentage of Gross Domestic Product devoted to health was much higher than in most developed countries but without the quality of service delivery desired, and the expansion of health infrastructure resulted in an overly heavy work load for the often underpaid healthcare professionals—many of whom left the government for better jobs elsewhere. Meanwhile, continued poverty and health illiteracy among large segments of the population resulted in low immunization rates and high use of tobacco and alcohol. Over time, new economic policies emerged with a focus both on economic growth and redistribution, and results have improved accordingly (Mayosi and Benatar 2014).
	With these new policies in South Africa, improved benefits for health staff reduced migration to the private sector (George 2013), and intensified community mobilization significantly increased awareness of communicable diseases, particularly HIV/AIDS and tuberculosis (TB). The country’s Strategic Plan addressing HIV/AIDS 2007–2011 served as a model for many other countries (South Africa Department of Health 2007). At the same time, a new council of healthcare professionals became the regulatory body for new drug approval (Coovadia et al. 2009).
	In sum, even countries with similar geographical conditions are likely to have marked differences in their health outcomes depending on the political and economic systems functioning and their quality (Chongsuvivatwong et al. 2011) In general, socio-democratic political systems with redistributive policies result in improved coverage of health systems and better health outcomes (Borrell 2007).





Challenges in implementing global and national health policies


Governance: responsibility and accountability


	Public health policies in developing countries need to be compatible both with regional and global policies to increase cohesiveness, integration, and support. Where this is done, national policies will better assure that health priorities in local settings are addressed, and that international support can support health sector priorities. With the creation of MDG and now SDG goals, more attention is being given in these countries to policies and programmes which are results-and outcome-oriented. There remains, however, a tendency in many countries to be satisfied with the achievement of input and activity targets (more easily achieved and less threatening to health system management likely to be concerned about the extent to which these activities actually will achieve outcome targets—- and the repercussions should these outcome targets not be achieved). There also is a tendency for health systems to address only disease symptoms and not their underlying causes.
	Even where outcome targets are pursued and underlying determinants are identified, a country’s ability to address these adequately is often limited by financial capacity.
	Using the analogy of building a sound physical structure, a national health system needs to ensure a concrete foundation with (a) a clear understanding of its population’s socio-cultural norms and its health problems—both symptoms and causes (disaggregated by geographic area), and of existing population disparities and inequalities, and (b) a functioning system of governance and accountability.
	Accountability has to exist both in national and subnational governance, and applies both to financial disbursements and to health service delivery staffing and infrastructure. These, in turn, require skilled management.
	Sound strategy development, actions plans, and programmes plus effective review processes might constitute the first layer of building blocks above the foundation. These can be problematic when they are formulated by a limited inner circle of officials and do not take into account the needs of local governance and communities, the latter, as indicated, often diverse in their socio-cultural norms and values. Even where efforts are made to involve communities in decision-making and to elicit their responsibility, those representing the communities are often only persons from upper income groups and (where relevant) from more advantaged religious groups, races, or castes.
	The second layer of building blocks (above the foundation) would be the programme administrators, managers and service providers/front-line workers, with these persons fully cognizant of the building structures below them, clear about their own responsibilities (and, where relevant, their own accountability), competent to perform their tasks, and able to avail of the necessary resources to accomplish them.
	The cement, if you will, holding these building blocks together and firmly attached to the foundation, consists of such values as honesty, vision, and the ability to keep results and outcomes in sight, fairness, mutual respect, adherence to commitments, motivation, and sound judgement, the ability to instil confidence in others, and, perhaps binding these together, a sense of ownership of the undertaking as a whole. Exemplifying such cementing qualities might be segments of the health sector professionals in Brazil in recent years, believing so firmly in their country’s healthcare pursuits that they regularly eschewed more lucrative offers from the private sector (Levinson and Balarajan 2013).





Health financing and the utilization of existing resources


	The maximum utilization of existing resources through leveraging and aligning these interventions among stakeholders are necessary steps in health system modernization. These often can be accomplished by eliminating wasteful expenditures, reducing the cost of service provision, and encouraging new and more efficient means of providing care. Modernized healthcare also requires effective information technology (IT), which provides a base upon which to build managerial, staffing, and financial suprastructures. At the same time, cost-effectiveness studies comparing treatment and prevention modalities offer providers with valuable information to use in the selection of these modalities.





Health information


	Health information system (HIS), which is an integral part of the health system strengthening needs a strong institutional regulatory framework. It is also an entry point into the health sector reform through provision of information and knowledge on the quantity as well as quality of health services. It is of paramount importance to have the reliable, relevant, and real-time information in order to make proper decision for improving the quality of services through proper and effective allocation of available resources.
	Fragmentation of HIS is hampered further as donor funding sometimes targets specific areas and creates new information systems which are not integrated with the existing HIS (Braa Jørn et al. 2007). The role of the HIS in the health system is not just routine collection of health services data and reporting to higher levels of the healthcare system, but to be used by the health staff at various level and apply and facilitate evidence-based decision-making at all levels, most importantly at the point of collection but it is not usually the case in real life situation. Moreover, health policies and plans should be based on such information, which also needs to be ensured to be aligned with the needs at the operational level. Many developing countries are still facing with the issues of data privacy versus data sharing as both are equally important and supportive to each other in realizing its function effectively. Proper regulation of the creation and use of healthcare information is imperative to everyone in the system.
	It is crucial to strengthen health information including human resource for long-term cost-effectiveness in spite of having potential resistance to change and cost issues (Mpofu et al. 2014). Improved health worker capacity to monitor and evaluate programmes would improve data quality, management, and reporting, which further increased use of health data for disease surveillance and planning purposes. Quality data within the health sector itself is crucial for monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of health programme performance and for developing appropriate policies, plans, and strategies to ensure quality health services. It usually covers the dimension, comprised of data accuracy, reliability, completeness, timeliness, precision, and integrity (USAID 2007). Many developing countries experience challenges related to producing quality health data (Chaulagai et al. 2005). The contributing factors include weak linkages between M&E systems and data generation points and inadequate harmonization of multiple data collection and reporting systems (UNAIDS 2010). Additional challenges include poorly coordinated M&E systems characterized by duplication of data collection and underutilization of nationally-defined tools [12–15]. A frequently documented challenge related to producing quality health data in low and middle-income countries is the shortage of trained human resources (UNAIDS 2010). In addition, improved data quality better informed evidence-based planning at the all level. One approach that has been effectively used to address skilled health workforce shortages is task shifting (WHO 2008). In Botswana case, the district M&E officers took on M&E responsibilities that were previously conducted by nurses and other health workers as secondary activities to core programme and clinical responsibilities. This allowed such health workers to concentrate on delivering quality clinical services and focusing on implementation of quality, priority health programmes (Mpofu et al. 2014).
	Several other studies also indicated that data quality improved by addressing human resource capacity issues, mainly through training of health workers on the importance of public health information and regular feedback (Mphatswe et al. 2012). In Malawi and South Africa, it was found that data quality improved through provision of supportive supervision (Mate et al. 2009) and institutional research (Harries et al. 2011). Other initiatives, such as the transition from paper-based to electronic records, have also been shown to improve data quality (Ekouevi et al. 2011).





Infrastructure, technology, medical supplies, and logistics


	Healthcare infrastructure must be adequate to ensure a reduced burden of diseases and an improvement in the health status of the population. A solid broad-based health infrastructure is composed of necessary physical structures accessible to the entire population served; other support facilities including laboratories, medical record systems, and transport; and a competent health workforce supported by systematic and effective resource allocation practices, supervision, and supportive monitoring. An effective healthcare infrastructure needs to be both human-centred and client-responsive. The proper location and management of health infrastructure components are essential to the health system’s effectiveness in order to achieve the desired ‘universal health coverage’ and to meet basic health needs, primary healthcare centres should be within the reach of the entire community and fully cognizant of prevailing disease patterns. These primary, secondary, and tertiary healthcare centres, in turn, require the necessary facilities and equipment, competent and efficient staff, and the ability to deliver an essential health services package at affordable costs. These centres also should be characterized by a welcoming environment for both clients and service providers.
	Proper formative research and area-specific baseline information on disease prevalence, collected through necessary surveys and research, should be in place prior to the formulation of actual health plans in order to determine the optimal location of each type of health centre, the anticipated workload, and the transportation that will be necessary. Often the establishment of fewer more efficient tertiary centres at strategic locations, with transportation available to assure access by more remote population groups, can provide greater benefit than establishing a larger number of tertiary centres with insufficient infrastructure and human resources. In the building of hospitals and other health facilities, a premium must be placed on proper design facilitating cost-effective, quality-assured service delivery, and should include durable, built-in water and sanitation facilities which are adequately equipped.
	The global trend towards high-end medical technologies presents a different type of challenge for developing countries, which, on the one hand, would wish to improve the quality of treatment by using these modern technologies—and save more lives in the process, but recognize also the exorbitant costs associated with much of this technology. Where resources are limited, and they usually are, choices often have to be made between acquiring such equipment—likely to benefit a relatively small portion of the population, and using available resources to upgrade the quality and availability of health services and preventive public health utilized by larger portions of the population. High-end medical technology also needs a cadre of sophisticated medical practitioners requiring high salaries, and well-equipped maintenance staff to keep the equipment functioning properly.
	Some middle-income countries have found a workable balance in working with these choices. A prime example is Turkey, which has managed to expand high-quality diagnostic and curative services efficiently and effectively but without spending on them a disproportionate percentage of the country’s health budget. This has been done, in part, by successfully enlisting the involvement of the private sector including pharmaceutical companies, as well as biomedical engineering societies and philanthropic organizations. Turkey also has put in place a reasonably effective referral system—including timely transportation arrangements—to increase the likelihood that those most in need of this more sophisticated technology will be able to benefit from it. See Case Study 3.5.1.
	 	Case Study 3.5.1 Turkey’s Health Reform
	It shows an evidence of how a poor health system with health indicators below par changed into an improved system with population satisfaction for the health services they received. The fruitful outcomes within a decade were attributable to the decisive political action and effective reform, resulting from wisdom and forward thinking vision of health minister in 2002. Today, it has improved its health outcomes, achieving health-related Millennium Development Goals well before the 2015 deadline. The number of women dying from pregnancy-related causes more than halved since 1990 to about 20 per 100,000 live births in 2013. The number of infants dying before their first birthday dropped from 55.7 in 1990 to 16.5 per 1,000 live births in 2012.
	Strong economic growth and political stability were also found contributed a lot to the strategic directions and its implementation in health reform. A tactful confidence building and support by doing ‘easy first and difficult later’ reform interventions was very thoughtful and noteworthy.
	Major success reasons: Country-led strategic directions and realistic goals, embedded in a strategic management framework with effective implementation and M&E system.
	Emergency Action Plan of the 58th Government, which under the heading Health for All was adopted shortly after the elections on 3 November 2002, contains 11 dimensions of reform and on the basis of the Emergency Health Action Plan, the HTP was prepared in early 2003 under eight themes. It had been transformed from working as provider of health services to steward of the health sector. Turkey’s Health Transformation Programme met health-related MDGs quite ahead of the 2015 deadline. The lessons learned from Turkey centre on the importance of the sequencing of health reforms and their rapid implementation, and the benefits of primary healthcare reforms. The ‘patient-centredness’ of the Turkish system with a strong emphasis on health as a right was the cornerstone of reform.





Policy lessons


	 	• Effective sequencing in health reform steps by ensuring a good start and winning people’s hearts
	• Rapid and timely interventions with right pace for future policy shift, for example dual practice of physicians
	• Expanding public health expenditure and giving a space for non-contributory insurance scheme for the poor
	• Ending fragmentation and duplication in public sector service delivery and introduction of family medicine programme
	• Unification of various health insurance schemes and health financing reforms along with the changes in health service delivery
	(http://www.worldbank.org/en/news/feature/2015/02/17/lessons-from-turkey-how-bahrain-is-looking-to-improve-its-healthcare)





(http://www.euro.who.int/__data/assets/pdf_file/0017/272321/Strategic-Planning-for-Health_Turkey.pdf)


	An effective health workforce requires adequately detailed job descriptions, and then training to assure that these positions can be professionally met. Pre-service as well as in-service training needs to be both job-based and results-oriented. At the same time, supportive supervision and M&E systems are always necessary. As in the case of equipment support discussed previously, the private sector may, at times be in a position to support or augment a health workforce, although effective regulations and systems of accountability must be in place to assure that such a private sector role not being solely profit-oriented.
	Retention of public health staff is often as important as recruitment and training. Cases exist in numerous countries of health professionals who are trained for public service and then, utilizing such training, seek better paying jobs in the private sector. Accordingly motivation through recognition and incentives is often a vital pre-requisite for sustaining an effective workforce. These should be systematically included in protocols, guidelines, and standard operating procedures (SOPs).
	The allocation of a country’s health budget reveals much about a government’s orientation, priorities, and level of commitment to its population as a whole. Where budgets are disproportionately weighted towards high-end urban hospitals and health services and with poor access to quality services by rural and lower income population groups, the overall health status of the country is likely to suffer. Responsible allocation should be based largely on the burden of diseases in the country, and on the relative urgency of preventing and combating each disease category. This, in turn, requires proper disease surveillance and antibiograms, effective treatment guidelines, and the use of generic drugs wherever possible. Prevention itself deserves high priority in a country’s health budget, and involves health education, effective food and drug regulations, and attention to safe water, hygiene, and sanitation plus interministerial collaboration to assure, for example, adequate efforts to reduce road traffic accidents.
	The existence of affordable health insurance systems can, in many country contexts, assure that adequate medical care can be provided for population groups across the income spectrum.





Service delivery—overcoming geographical factors and conflict


	In most developing countries, the majority of the population still live in rural areas, even with rapid urban migration. Rural areas have higher death rates from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, suicide, and unintentional injury compared to highly urbanized counties (Eberhardt 2001). As indicated, it is essential that this population have access to affordable quality both through health centres and some combination of health extension personnel and community health workers. Included in this health delivery should be pertinent behavioural change counselling, preventive health screening, and the opportunity to avail of low-cost health insurance. The active engagement of the population in these processes and some level of social cohesiveness also have been identified as important ingredients in health sector success stories and is a key element of the Alma Ata Declaration.
	One of the primary causes of development failure and, in turn poor health status is conflict. Paul Collier notes that nearly 75% of people in the ‘bottom billion’ countries are engaged in a civil war or have recently been through one. (Collier indicates that the primary factors that make a country prone to civil war are low-income, slow economic growth, and dependence upon primary commodity exports.) Increases in disease prevalence resulting from such conflict are likely to continue well after the fighting has ceased (Collier 2007). Accordingly, health plans in such areas need to include the capacity for emergency responses followed by sustained health delivery. At the same time, it is clear that no health policy is capable of adequately responding to a sustained environment of conflict such as that found in Libya (Nathan 2005). Overall, responses to armed violence and its prevention require intense efforts involving criminal justice, public health, anthropology, journalism, human rights, and education (Lemard 2004; Kaldor 2007; Arya 2008).
	The direct consequences of armed violence pose multifaceted challenges for the health system (Valenti et al. 2007). The economic and human costs significantly burden resource-limited services. This correlates with a reduced capacity for quality health service provision in the post-conflict environment (Kopel 1995). The indirect effects of armed violence include the disruption of livelihoods through population displacement leading to pervasive insecurity and adverse health consequences. Moreover, such factors as psychological trauma, inadequacy of essential services, and a resurgence in vaccine-preventable disease adversely affect security, health, and development (OECD 2009; Krause et al. 2011). Globally, armed violence control is increasingly recognized as a public health asset, especially in the post-conflict environment (Gilligan 2000; Krug et al. 2002).





The health workforce


Workforce development


	A well-built health workforce is essential to overcome the complex threats of rapidly spreading infectious diseases, emerging and re-emerging disease and the increasing trend of NCDs in a developing country—these NCDs spreading as a result of globalization and interdependence among countries, changing lifestyles, and the improper use of chemicals and medicinal products. The unfinished agenda of the MDGs regarding infectious diseases, malnutrition, and maternal complications persists in a diversity of settings. These are further jeopardized by the emergence of chronic vascular disease, diabetes, cancers, and lower respiratory conditions, which now often constitute the most common causes of death. Significantly, there also are sharp increases in accidents and injuries, and a growing recognition of mental illness and its consequences (Adjuik et al. 2006; Tollman et al. 2008).
	Globally, countries are facing a Human Resources for Health (HRH) crisis. However, those likely to suffer most are the underserved poor, rural, and marginalized individuals and groups in the rural areas of developing countries. The development of quality HRH takes time and requires careful needs-based planning, access to skills-based knowledge, and effective training.
	Health workforces often can be divided into three basic categories: (a) community-based health workers (CHWs); (b) mid-level workers (MLWs); and (c) health workers with particular expertise on an aspect of health delivery. CHWs are involved in providing preventive medical services, monitoring the community’s health, identifying patients at particular risk, and sometimes providing basic curative services. These CHWs are referred to by a variety of names: health auxiliaries, health volunteers, health promoters, family welfare educators, village health workers, and community lay health aides. These are often volunteers with limited training in commodity and information dissemination and disease prevention efforts with the associated behavioural change counselling (Tollman 2008).
	In many low resource countries, MLWs are the backbone of their health service. Studies on the contribution of mid-level providers indicate that they often play a pivotal role in improving access to care for underserved populations, a role also seen in some higher income countries (Keni 2006; Staton et al. 2007). Indeed the significantly increased access to HIV treatment in most African countries was achieved through the use of MLWs—and in some instances, by staff with even less formal training (Médicins Sans Frontières 2007).
	These MLWs are certificated individuals who have been trained to provide primary healthcare services at the community level, to diagnose and treat common health problems, to manage emergencies, to refer appropriately, and to transfer the seriously ill or injured for further care. These workers go by a range of titles depending on the country in which they work. In Myanmar, health assistants, lady health visitor, and midwives provide preventive services and the management of minor ailments; lady health workers in Pakistan provide maternal and child health services; técnicos de cirugía in Mozambique provide surgical care; clinical officers in East African countries provide diagnostic and treatment services at the primary care level and in hospitals. In Nepal, health assistants staff health posts while auxiliary health workers are responsible for subhealth posts. In the United States, physician assistants provide a range of specific services (Lehmann 2008; McAuliffe et al. 2009).
	The training of these MLWs is likely to vary considerably. Those who enter this work with pre-existing medical training, often nurses, are likely to require only ‘top-up’ training which is likely to be relatively brief in duration. Those without such a background receive training that usually ranges from 2 to 4 years including some that is field-based with supervision (Lehmann et al. 2008).
	The third category, health workers with particular expertise in particular aspects of health delivery, represents an essential ingredient in the management of specific diseases, such as tuberculosis and malaria, for highly specific tasks such as the use of DOTS (Directly Observed Therapy, Short-course) in tuberculosis management, and in management of chronic diseases.
	Building the human resource base for health delivery requires, in addition to physicians and nurses, these categories of health workers in order to provide the necessary services and to respond to changing health conditions in a country. Policies are therefore necessary to address the dynamics of the health labour market and the development and management of a skilled health workforce.
	The challenges faced in optimizing these HRH are numerous and include carefully synchronizing a country’s health workforce with its primary health needs and the inherent geographic variations in these needs (Dussault and Franceschini 2006).
	With such training, health staff is often able to assume higher level responsibilities. In Rwanda, sets of tasks in HIV management have been transferred from physicians to nurses trained in HIV management. Subsequent analysis found that improvements in CD4 count, correct prescriptions, patient monitoring, and overall survival rates were similar between these nurses and the physicians they replaced in this work (AIDSMap 2010). In Malawi, clinical officers carry out nearly 95% of major obstetric operations in government hospitals with no significant differences in postoperative outcome, well-being, stillbirths, or neonatal mortality, compared with such operations carried out by medical officers. Evaluations of the performance of MLWs in Mozambique showed no significant difference in outcome when compared to that of medical specialists.
	Finally, there is often a critical shortage, particularly in developing countries of professionals trained in medical and nursing schools, of health managers and researchers trained in the schools of public health and of MLWs, lay community health workers, midwives, and other healthcare providers. (These shortages are also affected by those trained professionals who emigrate to higher income countries or seek employment in better paying private sector jobs.) Addressing these shortages often requires the attention and explicit involvement of the political leadership in these countries (Speybroeck et al. 2006).





Way forward and strategies to improve health policy and status of health in developing countries (recommendations)


	This section recommends strategies to improve health policy and the overall status of health in developing countries. These recommendations are listed as follows and will be explored in turn.
	 	1. Risk pooling to minimize catastrophic out of pocket expenditure
	2. Forging and strengthening public-private partnerships
	3. Evidence-based decision-making, strengthening of public providers in reporting and the introduction of updated technology
	4. Decentralization and triage of workload, implementing proper referral system, empowering community healthcare and capacity building
	5. Training, capacity building, and investment in infrastructure
	6. Reducing disparities and inequity in minorities and other vulnerable population groups
	7. Achieving Universal Health Coverage and the SDGs





Risk pooling, minimizing catastrophic out of programme experience (OOPE)


	Risk pooling aims to achieve equitable access to health services with financial protection. It allows for redistribution of prepaid resources to individuals with the greatest health needs. The concept is that money flows from richer to poorer, and from healthier to sicker. When a poor or socially vulnerable person becomes ill or injured, the entire household can become trapped in a downward spiral of lost income and high healthcare costs. Poor people are more vulnerable to this downward spiral as they are more prone to diseases and have more limited access to healthcare and social insurance. These catastrophic out of pocket payments arise under the conditions outlined in Figure 3.5.3.
	Fig. 3.5.3 Risk pooling.
	As a consequence of inability to pay, households may refrain from using services. This will adversely impact their health, and this morbidity will adversely impact their earning potential. Reduced earnings have a knock on effect throughout the household. Not only the ill person is affected; their family and future generations can be affected too. High expenditure can result in reduced food and clothing purchases, and reduced investment in education, with associated sequelae.
	Risk pooling addresses this point. Pooling of funds occurs through various prepayment mechanisms, which come in many forms. For instance there is tax-based financing of healthcare by governments, compulsory insurance contributions, external sources, and social health insurance. These mechanisms are common within developed nations, for instance the use of the Bismarck model in Europe. The Bismarck model uses an insurance system and is usually financed jointly by employers and employees through payroll deduction. Bismarck-type health insurance plans do not make a profit and must include all citizens (Wallace 2015). A larger and more diverse risk pool is more favourable. To create diversity compulsory participation in a health coverage scheme is required; if participation was to be voluntary there would be less likelihood of healthier individuals contributing, which ultimately would limit cross subsidy from healthy to sick and would undermine the financial stability of the system (OECD 2003).
	When risk pooling, care needs to be taken to avoid fragmentation which can result in system inefficiency. Fragmentation is noted to take multiple forms, for instance local government health agencies, externally funded vertical programmes and overlapping and uncoordinated projects between different funding agencies such as Ministry of Health and health insurance funds.
	Ultimately, health systems requiring lower out-of-pocket payments for healthcare offer better protection to the poor against catastrophic spending. Prepayment entails predictable expenditure for a given set of services. This allows opportunity to budget for healthcare and share risk with those more able to pay (e.g. as a ‘Sin Tax’; see Case Study 3.5.2). There is a reduced need for sudden acquisition of funds, and the payments required are reduced.
	It is important to note that a prepayment model will not eliminate catastrophic out of pocket payments, as other factors; for instance health services offered and copayments; need to be accounted for. Additionally, catastrophic expenditures do not automatically disappear with rising income.
	 	Case Study 3.5.2 Philippines Sin Tax
	In 1995, the Government of the Philippines set up the National Health Insurance Programme ‘PhilHealth’. All Filipinos are automatically enrolled in and therefore entitled to benefits of the programme. There are formal and informal groups, and the formal are obliged to pay a premium, which essentially cross subsidizes other members. All senior citizens are mandatorily covered.
	PhilHealth is mandated with improving access to quality care and reducing OOPE. To achieve this, it introduced a ‘Sin Tax’ in 2012. The basic premise is that taxes on alcohol and tobacco are earmarked for expenditure, mostly on healthcare:
	 	• 85% of revenues are allocated for health, of which:
	• 80% are for achieving UHC
	• 20% for medical assistance and improvement of health facilities
	Within its first year, Sin Tax raised more than 1.2billion USD, allowing enrolment of an additional 14 million families—totalling 45 million Filipinos—into PhilHealth.





What can be learned from PhilHealth?


	PhilHealth is an example of a sustainable financing mechanism for healthcare, providing an alternative to out of pocket payments. Research suggests that even at low levels of public spending, countries can make significant steps towards UHC. Revenue raising needs to be coupled with the pooling of funds and the purchasing of health services; it is the combination of reforms which drive improvements in health system performance (Jowett et al. 2016).
	The Programme has confirmed the need both to understand history and local environment, and to use a clear technical framework when analysing and assessing key drivers and impediments towards achieving UHC. There will be a struggle to attain UHC without a basic sense of solidarity in the community.





Criticism


	While the country’s UHC agenda is commendable for its pro-poor approach, other PhilHealth members must be kept in mind and feel the benefits of PhilHealth to ensure political support and stability. In this regard PhilHealth and the accredited hospitals need further strengthening to increase patients’ access to and utilization of quality health services and establish transparent and fair provider payment processes.
	Additionally, facilities need to be technically and managerially competent and empowered to respond to PhilHealth in its role as a powerful purchaser. Facilities should be held accountable for the delivery and quality of care that they provide.





Private–public partnership and strengthening


	It is widely accepted that private–public partnerships are essential in the journey towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC). Governments are encouraged to recognize that they cannot achieve UHC on their own (OECD 2003).
	UHC requires a resilient health system, one that is strong and responsive. Engagement between public and private sectors to achieve these qualities can take multiple forms, for instance capacity development, innovations, outsourcing, and consulting-all with varying degrees of commitment and financial risk sharing. Engagement of the private sector should ideally maximize strategic areas such as those shown in Figure 3.5.4.
	Fig. 3.5.4 Strategic areas to the engagement of the private sector.
	Source: data from Ota, M.O.C., et al. (2018) ‘Proceedings of the first African Health Forum: effective partnerships and intersectoral collaborations are critical for attainment of Universal Health Coverage in Africa’. BMC Proceedings, 12 (Suppl 7):8, 1–8.
	Ultimately, governments can use the private sector to increase healthcare service provision. When embarking on these partnerships governments need to ensure that there are adequate regulatory frameworks, policies, and protocols in place to facilitate good communication across sectors. Poor communication may hinder engagement which subsequently risks poor understanding of government policies and procedures. In addition to communication, central to fostering enduring private–public partnerships is building trust between sectors. The potential benefits of collaboration are vast, and it would be a pity to lose out on such due to a failure by policymakers to ensure this trust. This could be facilitated by an organizational culture of openness and sharing.
	The private sector has different needs to the public sector, which entails need for regulatory frameworks and accreditation systems to aid collaboration and foster partnerships. Literature suggests that development of protocols for communication across sectors could make coordination of projects smoother and more efficient (Suchman et al. 2018). To this effect, the private sector should be afforded regular opportunity to input into policy design, and both public and private entities should have standardized processes in place for when they collaborate. Shared goals, mutual understanding and structured ongoing communication that facilitates a strong working relationship when collaborating is crucial in making these endeavours a success (Baicker and Chandra 2017).
	Considering achievement of the MDGs, a challenge was the limited focus on interventions that affect health however are not within the remit or oversight of the respective Ministry of Health, such as infrastructure. What should be learned from this in pursuit of UHC and the SDGs is the importance of partnerships and intersectoral collaboration (Garg 2018).
	Of course private–public partnerships are not without challenges. Literature to date has highlighted a number of areas for improvement, notably:
	 	• Lack of information sharing
	• Weaknesses in management capacity
	• Funding insecurity
	• Mismatched organizational styles and differing priorities
	• Corruption (Suchman et al. 2018)





Evidence-based decision-making, strengthening of public providers in reporting, introduction of updated technology


	Evidence-based policymaking has a fundamental role in improving the health status of countries. Evidence facilitates decision-making for the achievement of goals. Goals need to be clear, and it must be accepted that a rich body of evidence does not guarantee that these goals will be achieved. Often, the process of evidence-based policymaking will be uncertain (Baicker and Chandra 2017). As important as evidence is to sound policy choices, goals are determined based on values and priorities—a given body of evidence can be used to support very different policy positions.
	The role of technology in healthcare improvement should not be underestimated. The literature highlights multiple applications:
	 	• Telemedicine
	• Training
	• Health education dissemination
	• Behaviour change promotion
	• Vaccination
	• Drug inventory and storage (Garg 2018)
	Other applications of technology within developed nations are Electronic Patient Registries (EPR) and Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS). EPR benefits include greater accuracy, a higher proportion of correct information, time saved in locating information, more economical use of financial resources, greater ease, and speed of recovery of patient data. CDSS has been found to result in increased physician adherence to standardized treatment plans, cost reduction, easier standardization and regulation of requests for secondary and tertiary healthcare and examinations, thus reducing variability between services. From an administration point of view, it is possible to obtain greater adherence to public policies. Standardized programmes for earlier detection of diseases tend to have greater diagnostic value thereby contributing towards the promotion of equity, and the reduction of complications and costs related to more complex treatments (Tomasi et al. 2004).
	Countries should adopt an open data sharing policy and develop a supportive legal framework to facilitate sharing and use of data in accordance with agreed standards for confidentiality and data sharing.
	In general there is greater efficiency of management processes within the primary healthcare setting as a result of technology. Of course there is the issue of security and training to use systems. Ultimately, harnessing the opportunity that modern technology presents is key to improving the health status of countries.





Decentralization and triage of workload, implementing proper referral system, empowering community healthcare and capacity building


	Health status and policy can be improved from the community level by empowering communities to take responsibility for their healthcare services.
	According to the WHO,
	 	community empowerment is the process of enabling communities to increase control over their lives … It is the process by which they increase their assets and attributes and build capabilities to gain access, partners, networks, and/or a voice, in order to gain control … It assumes that people are their own assets and the role of the external agent is to catalyse, facilitate or accompany the community in acquiring power … Community empowerment implies community ownership and action that explicitly aims at social and political change … a process of re-negotiating power to gain more control … power is a central concept in community empowerment and health promotion invariably operates within the arena of a power struggle … seeks to build partnerships with other sectors in finding solutions.
	The WHO concludes that empowerment can reduce health disparities (WHO 2018).
	Globalization adds another dimension to the concept of community empowerment; the local and global settings are inextricably linked. Community empowerment recognizes and strategically acts upon this interlinkage and ensures that power is shared at both local and global levels.
	Key to achieving community empowerment is communication. Approaches that encourage discussion and debate result in increased knowledge and awareness, and a higher degree of critical thinking. Critical thinking enables communities to understand the interplay of forces operating on their loves and helps them take their own decisions (WHO 2018).
	Technology can help communities and individuals to develop opportunities, capacities and tools that benefit them and it can ensure that communities can mobilize targeted populations to obtain needed health resources by fostering awareness of a given problem (WHO 2018).
	Policymakers must recognize and facilitate empowerment at a variety of levels. This can be done by involving community members and the underserved in the initiation and implementation of policy, as well as by relying on people who hold more traditional power. It is a responsibility of policymakers to achieve shared policymaking, to increase the sustainability of these advances towards improved health status and ultimately UHC (Thompson et al. 2016).





Training, capacity building, and investment in infrastructure


	Central to improved health status and UHC is quality care. Quality matters as we are seeing a shift in disease burden to more complex conditions which require greater utilization of a health system and its services. These conditions are becoming an increasingly bigger influence on population health, which makes addressing them an increasing priority. Countries require the appropriate infrastructure to meet quality standards, and governments are encouraged to establish a national quality guarantee for healthcare services. Literature states that poor quality care is now a bigger barrier to reducing mortality than insufficient access (Kruk et al. 2018).
	For a health system to function and develop a quality service, there needs to be an adequate workforce. This can be achieved by increasing the number of training places for given professions, leveraging technology to provide required training, and ensuring respect for and good morale among staff. A concern however is brain drain. The workforce needs to be available, accessible, and have the capacity to deliver quality integrated care. Investment in primary healthcare is most needed and is recognized as the most cost-effective investment in improving equity in access to essential health services (Garg 2018).
	Development agencies can play a significant role in increasing focus on human resource strategies—which are integrated into the health sector in wider civil service reforms—by:
	 	• Analysing the mix of personnel and skills
	• Reorienting training
	• Addressing pay and non-pay incentives
	• Improving job opportunities and conditions
	• Improving and expanding the use of information and communications technology in training and education programmes (OECD 2003)
	Development agencies also have an interest in capacity building to enhance the effectiveness of their partnerships and to aid achievement of pro-poor health objectives.
	Capacity building is necessary for multiple players within the healthcare arena. Taking research for example, it is crucial to align priorities and strategies of those investing in such, ensuring that programmes are coordinated and resources not wasted due to duplication. It is desirable to be able to detect and track research and innovations to facilitate progress. Health systems need to develop the capacity to measure and use data to learn. Additionally, countries should make it a priority to ensure sustainable financing mechanisms to optimize function. With investment in appropriate infrastructure and human resources, research priorities can be addressed (Ota et al. 2018).
	Ultimately, capacity building should go beyond the health sector. It requires viewing pro-poor health approaches in a larger context of:
	 	• Political and economic restructuring
	• Fiscal policy
	• Administrative reform
	• Strengthening of participation and democratic systems (Ota et al. 2003)
	Next there is investment in infrastructure. Looking at this from a health system perspective, the literature suggests various key facets of a high-quality health system. A commission by The Lancet concluded that high-quality health systems should be informed by four values—they are for people, equitable, resilient, and efficient (Kruk et al. 2018).
	The WHO building blocks of a health system are shown in Figure 3.5.5.
	Fig. 3.5.5 System building blocks.
	Source: data from World Health Organization (2010) Monitoring the building blocks of health systems: a handbook of indicators and their measurement strategies. Geneva, Switzerland: WHO.
	It follows from this that strengthening these aspects will result in stronger health systems. Stronger health systems with strong infrastructure will help to provide quality care and UHC. By contrast, poor-quality health systems are posited to result in catastrophic expenditures and waste of resources.
	The Lancet Global Health Commission 2018 endorses four universal actions to raise quality across health systems
	 	1. Health system leaders need to govern for quality by adopting a shared vision of quality care, a clear quality strategy, strong regulation, and continuous learning. Ministries of health cannot achieve this alone and need to partner with the private sector, civil society, and sectors outside of health such as education, infrastructure, communication, and transport.
	2. Countries should redesign service delivery to maximize health outcomes rather than geographical access to services alone.
	3. Countries should transform the health workforce by adopting competency based clinical education, introducing training in ethics and respectful care, and respecting all workers to deliver the best care possible.
	4. Governments and civil society should ignite demand for quality in the population to empower people to hold systems accountable and actively seek high-quality care (Kruk et al. 2018).
	These improvement efforts should ideally be adapted for local context and monitored, in a bid to achieve sustainable change (Kruk et al. 2018).
	Ultimately, national governments need to invest in high-quality health systems for their own people and make such systems accountable to people through legislation, education about rights, regulation, transparency and greater public participation (Kruk et al. 2018) Countries need to innovate to determine how they can efficiently utilize the available limited resources to provide access to essential healthcare services while exploring domestic sources of revenue to finance UHC. In achieving such, limited complexity and fragmentation is desirable. See also Case Study 3.5.3.





CASE STUDY 3.5.3 Ayushman Bharat programme, India


	India is a vast, diverse, and a highly populated country. Its problems are complex and unique to itself. It is a challenge to reach out to vast different regions across India as local beliefs, culture, and practices influence every region’s outlook.
	On 1 February 2018, the Indian Government announced two major initiatives in the health sector, as part of the Ayushman Bharat programme.
	The initiatives intervene to address health holistically at the primary, secondary and tertiary levels, and incorporate both disease prevention and health promotion. They are expanded on as follows:
	 	1. Health and Wellness Centres
	 	a. India’s National Health Policy 2017 envisaged Health and Wellness Centres as the foundation of India’s health system, bringing the system and its services closer to the homes of people. The centres are intended to provide medical care to the poor, providing comprehensive healthcare ranging from diagnostic services to free essential drugs—including the realms of NCDs and maternal and child health. The national budget has set aside funds for this project, in addition to contribution of the private sector through CSR (?) and philanthropic institutions. To disseminate their services optimally, the centres must be accessible and appealing, providing a sense of comfort and belonging to the people of the regions where they are located.
	2. National Health Protection Scheme
	 	a. This is the world’s largest government funded healthcare programme Launched on 15th August 2018 and providing cover to more than 10 crore poor and vulnerable families. Coverage is up to 5 lakh rupees per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization. Adequate funds have been set aside to facilitate smooth implementation of the scheme. Benefits of the scheme are available across the country and a beneficiary covered under the scheme will be allowed to take cashless benefits from any public or enrolled private hospital.
	b. In partnership with think tank NITI Aayog, a robust, modular, scalable, and interoperable IT platform has been made operational, entailing a paperless, cashless transaction.
	In order to further enhance accessibility of quality medical education and healthcare, 24 new Government Medical Colleges and Hospitals will be set up, by upgrading existing district hospitals in the country. This would ensure there is at least 1 medical college for every 3 parliamentary constituencies and at least 1 government medical college in each state of the country.
	The aim of the Ayushman Bharat programme is to build a New India by 2022 and ensure enhanced productivity, well-being, and avert wage loss and impoverishment. These schemes will also generate jobs, especially for women.





Reducing disparities and inequity in minorities, vulnerable population


	Health policy can be utilized strategically to target vulnerable population groups in society. Those identified as vulnerable populations are indigenous populations, minority and socially excluded groups, refugees, or displaced persons, the mentally or physically disabled and people living with HIV AIDS. These groups are among the poorest of the poor in many societies and require special attention in policy action for poverty reduction (OECD 2003).
	A pro-poor health approach is one that gives priority to promoting, protecting, and improving the health of the poor. It builds on health systems, health financing and key policy areas beyond the health sector promoting policy coherence global public goods (OECD 2003).
	Benefits of investing in the health of the poor include:
	 	• Higher labour productivity
	• Higher rates of domestic and foreign investment
	• Improved human capital
	• Higher rates of national saving
	• Demographic change (OECD 2003)
	In addition to their beneficial macroeconomic impact, health improvements have intergenerational spillover effects (OECD 2003).
	Gender inequality is a major determinant of poverty and ill health. Poor women and girls are worse off in relation to assets and entitlements; within the household and in society. Socio-cultural beliefs regarding the roles of men and women contribute to this inequality. Women are also major producers of healthcare through their roles as household managers and carers. But their health, including reproductive health suffers from inadequate nutrition, heavy workloads, and neglect of basic healthcare, factors aggravated by exposure to sexual abuse and interpersonal violence. Action on gender inequalities is therefore an essential element of a pro-poor approach to health.
	It must be noted that focusing solely on the poor may not achieve desired results. Common shortcomings include that benefits packages with only limited services and high copayments. This supports focus on elderly, disabled, and those with chronic health diseases.





Ways to UHC and SDGs


	UHC is a target of the 2015 SDGs. As defined by the WHO:
	 	UHC means that all individuals and communities receive the health services they need without suffering financial hardship. It includes the full spectrum of essential, quality health services, from health promotion to prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and palliative care. (WHO 2017)
	It is widely accepted that countries who make progress towards UHC will as a consequence make progress towards other SDGs.
	The rationale behind seeking UHC is avoidance of people being pushed into poverty due to unexpected illness that requires them to use up savings or sell assets. This can have catastrophic consequences for the current generation and indeed future generations. UHC exists to protect people from adverse financial consequences of utilizing health services. Good health allows children to learn and adults to earn, helps people escape from poverty, and provides the basis for long-term economic development (WHO 2017).
	Components of UHC are shown in Figure 3.5.6.
	Fig. 3.5.6 Components of Universal Health Coverage.
	Taking steps towards UHC means steps towards equity, development priorities, and social inclusion and cohesion. UHC requires quality care, a clear quality strategy, strong regulation, and continuous learning. Many countries are already making progress towards UHC. All countries can take actions to accelerate the process or to maintain gains already made. Ways to UHC encompass what has already been explored in this chapter:
	 	1. Strengthening health systems, ensuring robust financing and risk pooling. Limited complexity and fragmentation.
	2. Workforce to improve health service coverage and health outcomes.
	3. Good governance.
	4. Sound systems of procurement.
	5. Adequate supply of medicines—use of generics to ensure this.
	6. Utilizing advances in health technologies.
	7. Well-functioning HISs.
	8. Addressing vulnerable groups.
	(WHO 2017)
	When developing healthcare services social and cultural norms need to be accounted for. Incorporating traditional medical services organized around the comprehensive needs and expectations of people and communities will empower communities to take a more active role in their health and health systems.
	As developments in healthcare take place, it is essential that progress is measured. In the case of UHC this can be done by measuring:
	 	• Proportion of population that can access essential quality health services
	• Proportion of the population that spends a large amount of household income on health (WHO 2017)





Conclusion


	An effective health system, especially in developing countries, needs strong health policy as a basic foundation. The chapter has highlighted the stages of health transition, which led to health activities and health policy development in both developed and developing countries.
	Milestones of global health policy and global trends of health policy shifting were also described given its importance in changing global health trends from primary healthcare in the 1970s, global health initiatives in 1990s, the MDGs in 2000s, and then to current era of SDGs. How global health policy and globalization impact and shape the health of people in developing countries were discussed through various health policies, health outcomes and achievements, and current health challenges and problems. The three case studies were chosen, namely Turkey’s health system reform, the Philippines’ Sin Tax, and the Ayushman Bharat programme, India, from which impressive information and inputs were received to be considered in formulation of health policies with a notion of country’s adaptation wherever necessary.
	Implementation of global policy as well as country’s own health policy has challenges and pitfalls in various settings. It was explained within the context of health system building blocks and other related issues. Policy recommendations were made as way forward and strategies to improve health policy and status of health in developing countries in terms of; risk pooling, minimizing catastrophic OOPE; private–public partnership and strengthening; evidence-based decision-making, strengthening of public providers in reporting, introduction of updated technology; decentralization and triage of workload, implementing proper referral system, empowering community healthcare and capacity building; training, capacity building, and investment in infrastructure; reducing disparities and inequity in minorities, vulnerable population and ways to UHC and SDGs.
	Policymaking for the effective, efficient, and equitable health systems in developing countries is more critical than ever to be realized through its optimal matrix of strategic plans and implementation modalities. New challenges are being addressed, including SDGs. We hope that this chapter will contribute the information for policymakers to be able to formulate not only knowledge-base, but also results-orient policy design.

3.6


Public health policy in developed countries


	John Powles † and Hebe Gouda
	… the best strategy to identify the social and political processes that drive change in public health policies is by cross-national comparison. (Nathanson 2009)





The nature and scope of public health policy


	The scope and purpose of public health policy may be seen as implicit in widely used definitions of public health. Winslow’s definition, as adapted by the Acheson Report in England, is: ‘The science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through organised efforts of society’ (Secretary of State for Social Services 1988).
	Public health policies might thus be thought of as the policies that guide these ‘organized efforts’ to protect and improve health. The scope of such policies depends a good deal, however, on what is considered to be entailed by ‘organized efforts’ and on how centrally ‘organized efforts’ are understood to be related to efforts that are more decentralized, more informal, less organized, perhaps even ‘spontaneous’. The relative importance and legitimacy of centralized versus decentralized uses of knowledge in protecting and enhancing health is a common underlying theme in discussions of public health policy.
	We need first to define our geopolitical scope by deciding which countries are currently classifiable as ‘developed’. Many answers are clearly possible, but for the purposes of this chapter the boundary will be drawn as follows: the 33 members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) not qualified as ‘emerging’ (OECD n.d.) plus 5 member states of the EU that are not included in the OECD list (indicated by (EU), plus Singapore. These 39 countries are grouped as follows: 21 in Western Europe (Austria, Belgium, Cyprus (EU)), Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, Malta (EU), Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom (plus Israel); 11 in Eastern Europe (Bulgaria (EU), Croatia (EU), Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania (EU), Slovakia, Slovenia); 3 in Asian Developed (Japan, South Korea and Singapore); 3 in Other Developed (Canada, Australia, New Zealand). To reduce potential heterogeneity in the last group, and because of its geopolitical importance, we treat the United States (USA) separately.
	As a topic, policy gains interest from the assumptions that it guides action and that deliberate actions to protect and enhance health are major determinants of actual health trends. A brief review of health trends sets the context for our consideration of health policy.





Context: survival trends since 1950


	The unit of analysis for policy is typically the nation state. Estimates are available from the Global Burden of Disease project for trends in child mortality (risk of death before the fifth birthday) and premature adult mortality (risk for a 15-year-old of dying before 60, if age specific mortality rates were to remain unchanged) from 1950 to 2017.





Child survival


	See Figure 3.6.1.
	Fig. 3.6.1 Risk of death before the fifth birthday, unweighted means of four groups of countries with the USA shown separately, 1950–2017. For membership of country groups see Section 1.
	Source: data from Global Burden of Disease Collaborative Network (2017). (Seattle, United States: Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME)).
	The most salient finding is the marked and widespread gains in child survival achieved since the mid-twentieth century, extending the even larger gains of the first half of the century. Risks of death before the fifth birthday have fallen, in proportional terms, by a remarkable average of around 95% since 1950—in absolute terms, from around 7.5% to around 0.04% (unweighted averages across included countries). These transformations suggest continuing pervasive improvements in the determinants of child health. Around the central trend there is also some interesting variation across country groups, brought out by the log scale used in Figure 3.6.1: most improved are the Asian Developed countries, moving from highest to lowest for group averages; least improved is the USA, moving from lower than any of the group averages in 1950 to higher than any in 2017. The East European group, which also started with high risks, improved rapidly to the mid-1960s and again from the mid-1990s, with a period of stagnation between.
