	Source: data from Global Burden of Disease Collaborative Network (2017). (Seattle, United States: Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME)).
	The trends for premature mortality in Figure 3.6.2 and Table 3.6.1 reveal some striking divergences: From the mid-1960s mortality in the East European group rises substantially in men and stagnates in women before resuming declines from the mid-1990s. Also striking is the stagnation in adult mortality decline in the USA, apparent from the early 1980s. In relative terms this is more notable for women: By 2017 only in Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, and Bulgaria were rates of premature mortality in women higher than in the USA—which were about twice the median levels of all the other country groups apart from Eastern Europe.
	Declines in risks of premature death in adults have been less profound and less uniform than the declines in child mortality. Overall risks roughly halved between 1950 and 2017 for both women and men. For men, proportional reductions were greatest in the Asian Developed group (almost 85%) compared with 36% for men in East Europe and 45% in men in the USA. In 2017 the risks for men ranged from around 8% in the Asian Developed, West European, and Other Developed groups to twice that in the USA and Eastern Europe.
	Some qualitative similarities can be seen in the trends in child and adult survival: the USA and Eastern Europe each show lags relative to other groups—but with the lags occurring in different periods. In Eastern Europe, improvements were rapid until the mid-1960s after which they slowed (for children), stagnated for adult women and reversed (in some cases catastrophically) for adult men. From the mid-1990s these adverse trends in Eastern Europe changed course but with rates of improvement increasingly diverse for countries within the group.
	These manifest changes in survival provide much food for thought. The part played by ‘policy’ is not self-evident and nor are the roles played by governments at different levels nor by officials, experts, and citizens considered as individuals, nor as collectivities such as state and professional organizations, corporations, social movements, and households.





Institutions, knowledge, and policies


Institutions


	Because national (and subnational) boundaries separate populations with distinctive health trends, such trends can be assumed to reflect not just the characteristics of the individuals constituting such aggregates but also the differing national and subnational institutional contexts in which the individuals live. Here we understand institutions to be not just formally constituted organizations, such as those of states, but also the less formal and more fundamental rule-based structures which pattern social life (Searle 2005, 2010). Such institutional structures may have their own, typically longer term, patterns of evolution, in many cases beneath the surface of overt developments in the political realm (Williamson 2000; Thelen 2004).
	Constance Nathanson has produced a monumental, systematic study comparing responses in the USA, Canada, Britain, and France, to two public health challenges in the early 20th century—infant mortality and tuberculosis—and two late in the century—cigarette smoking and HIV infection in injecting drug users. Her study brings out the diversity, complexity, and richness of societal responses to risks to health (Nathanson 2009). In spite of the widespread assumption that the agency of the state has been central to public health responses, she finds no simple relationship between the strength of state institutions (presumptively high in France, low in the USA) and the nature and strength of societal responses to risks to health. Her work helps to clarify the relationship between state and non-state ‘actors’, bringing out the often limited contribution of the former, at least during the earliest, creative phases when the societal responses to health hazards are just beginning to take shape.
	 	… in only one of the eight contemporary country-case combinations (AIDS drugs in Canada) did leadership in recognizing and addressing a serious public health issue come from local public health officers or departments. (p. 254)
	At a national (as distinct from subnational) level she does find one striking example of rapid and successful state-initiated action in the face of a public health crisis—the British government’s response to the threat of HIV/AIDS in injection drug users (p. 181). Although the contributions of state actors may be limited in the earliest phases they are typically engaged dynamically with civil organizations as soon as the policy process begins to evolve. State agencies usually lead in programme implementation.
	Nathanson invokes three broad determinants of public health action: ‘states, collective actions, and constructions of risk’ and sees her task as understanding ‘how structure, opportunity, and human agency interact to create, or inhibit, the possibility of change’ (p. 203). Writing as a ‘social constructivist’, narrating public health ‘stories’, she makes little attempt to assess effects on objective health trends and pays little attention to the advance of objective knowledge about the causes of disease and injury. She concentrates instead on ‘constructions of risk’ which follow their own timetables, somewhat independent of advances in objective knowledge. In relation to the earlier influence of the germ theory of disease, she notes
	 	French public health was reenergized in the late nineteenth century, due in large part to the extraordinary impact of Pasteur on French medicine and science … Nevertheless, apart from the campaign against infant mortality, which had relatively little to do with Pasteur, the consequences on the ground were minimal. (p. 35)
	While her approach serves well to bring out the importance of human agency and the ways in which social mobilization has taken place in response to public health challenges, her relative neglect of the escalating output and diffusion of new knowledge and her sketchy coverage of the links between actions and outcomes leaves her interpretation incomplete.





The growth of knowledge


	The modern era has been characterized by an enormous increase in the production of new knowledge and this process has tended to accelerate through time. Global scientific output is estimated to be now doubling every 9 years (Bornmann and Mutz 2015). Medical research output has been highest in the USA and other English-speaking countries and in Scandinavia. This remains true when adjusted for population size. Research output in public health sciences follows a similar overall pattern but also with notably low outputs in Eastern and Southern Europe (Clarke et al. 2007).





Knowledge: ‘interventions’ plus less direct effects


	The broad temporal coincidence between the increase of knowledge and the improvement of health suggests that the former is likely to be a fundamental cause of the latter. But the question of just how the advances in knowledge have actually contributed to gains in health remains unclear. One prominent idea is that the most important uses of knowledge are those embodied in ‘interventions’. The increasing use of idea of ‘interventions’ is linked to increasing reliance on randomized controlled trials to provide trustworthy evidence on ‘what works’. In each field of activity, summaries of the evidence identifying ‘effective interventions’ are marshalled for the benefit of ‘policymakers’.
	The implication here is that the experimental arms of controlled trials provide a model for understanding how knowledge brings benefits in populations at large. But the ways in which knowledge about the causes of disease and injury is used in everyday life often differ from what happens in the experimental arm of a controlled trial. In a controlled preventive experiment, agency—the capacity to decide ‘what is to be done’ and the execution of that decision—rests with the ‘intervenor’. The idea of ‘interventions’ thus carries with it the idea that agency lies with the ‘intervenors’, that is, with professionals and officials. In this framework, all that is needed is for ‘policymakers’ to take heed of what the experts are telling them about the scope for ‘effective interventions’ for the benefits of existing knowledge to be realized. This interpretation is inadequate.
	Issues of agency are central to thinking about public health policy. They came the fore earlier in debates provoked by Thomas McKeown’s thesis on the causes of rapid mortality decline in England and Wales in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century. McKeown noted, in a series of publications, that there were no new effective interventions (‘medical measures’ in his terminology) that could explain the favourable shifts in mortality. The shifts must have been due to something else. His deus ex machina was improved nutrition. He justified his choice by invoking the logic of Sherlock Holmes: ‘When you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth’ (McKeown 1988, pp. 9–10, italics in original).
	McKeown’s implicit, though fallible, logic was: if not ‘knowledge as embedded in interventions then not knowledge’. His choice of improved nutrition as the alternative explanation has been judged implausible by social, demographic, and economic historians. These critics have noted the lack of evidence for sudden changes in diet and emphasized instead the importance of changes in civic and state organizations facilitating sanitary reform (Szreter 1988), and in risk reducing changes in childrearing practices implemented by households. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth century households were key actors:
	 	The revolution was not just in the way physicians thought about disease, but in the growing awareness that households could control their destinies by their own actions and prevent disease by avoiding certain well-understood sources of infection. (Mokyr 2002, p. 206)
	The nature of the relevant changes in childrearing practices during the period of rapid mortality decline has been documented further in Mokyr and Stein (1997, pp. 143–205), Cowan (1983), Tomes (1998), and Preston and Haines (1991).
	The acceptance of new knowledge by households was not automatic, but depended on persuasion:
	 	Persuasion requires shared standards of evidence, chains of authority, networks of trust, and accepted rules of logic and evidence. Changes in the rules of discourse and communication, no less than the knowledge unearthed by science, are the background to the changes in health and longevity that are the mark of the ‘modern’ age. (Mokyr 2002, p. 180)
	Put another way: it is not just the development of knowledge that is important but also the diffusion of knowledge and the associated evolution of institutions which increase receptivity to new knowledge and facilitate its use.
	The economic historian Simon Kuznets saw the advance of knowledge as fundamental to modern economic development (Kuznets 1973); Mokyr (2002) and Deaton (2013) each see economic development and health improvement as the joint but distinct products of advancing knowledge, propelled in separate ways by advances in knowledge, and not always in synchrony with each other.
	Two important conclusions, relevant to the understanding of more recent trends, thus emerge: (1) the advance of knowledge (understood broadly as ‘useful knowledge’, extending beyond the content of textbooks to knowledge useful in everyday life) has been fundamental to the improvement of health by both direct and indirect pathways; and (2) the persuasiveness of relevant knowledge has depended on institutional contexts evolving in ways that enhanced receptivity to new ideas.





Causes of health trends


Child health


	Trends in child mortality have not exhibited the large swings and reverses seen in adult survival and are now in asymptotic approaches to very low levels. Measures to reduce risks to the health of children have generally faced little resistance and have been widely accepted and applied. A partial exception is the antivaccination movement’s effects on immunization coverage with associated rises in measles incidence and deaths (Kmietowicz 2018).
	Although absolute risks of death before the fifth birthday are now small, relative differences remain appreciable. Within Western Europe risks are almost twice as high in the United Kingdom as in Sweden. Most of this difference has been related to ‘birth characteristics’ such as prematurity and birthweight (Zylbersztejn et al. 2018). These are more related to differences in the health of mothers than to professional services provided after birth. The ‘biological standard of living’ (Komlos 1993) of mothers is important and differences of this kind are likely to have origins that are embedded in the social structure.





Adult health


	The large differences in long-term trends and recent levels of premature mortality in adults between different groups of countries shown in Figure 3.6.2 resist easy explanation. The Global Burden of Disease project produces estimates of the contributions of proximate causes (risk factors) but the role of more distal causes, such as policies, and the institutional supports for those policies, remains poorly understood.
	We shall proceed by considering parts of this complex picture. The reduction of health losses from tobacco, traffic injuries and cardiovascular disease have accounted for a substantial part of the total health gains since the mid-twentieth century. They are relatively well documented, as are the collective measures that have sought to achieve these outcomes. Case studies of these may provide some insights into the links between advancing knowledge, institutional evolution, and health outcomes.





Tobacco


	The first English language demonstrations of the quantitative relationships between smoking and lung cancer risk were reported in 1950 (Doll and Hill 1950; Wynder and Graham 1950). By 2012, all of the 39 developed countries except the USA and Switzerland had ratified an international treaty on tobacco control, committing themselves to a full repertoire of evidence based measures to reduce tobacco smoking (Conference of the Parties to the WHO FCTC 2003). Over a 60 year interval, the currently established repertoire of measures for tobacco control were invented, tested, and refined—ultimately gaining political support at the highest level.
	The early 1950s to the 1970s was a period of gradual clarification at a scientific, professional, political, and public level of the nature and meaning of the health risks arising from tobacco use. The epistemology of professional medicine was still pre-quantitative. As reports from epidemiological studies accumulated, high level policy debates continued to revolve around a largely illusory search for ‘proof of causation’ (Pollock 1999). Many physicians remained unconvinced of the hazards. In the USA a 1960 poll found that only one-third of physicians were convinced that smoking was a ‘major cause’ of lung cancer and 43% were still regular smokers (Proctor 2011). In the United Kingdom, physicians and public health professionals who appreciated the magnitude of the risks and who were in a position to do something about it struggled to find a way forward.
	In the late 1950s, George Godber was Deputy Chief Medical Officer in Britain and was very keen to help reduce harm from cigarette smoking. But his superior, the Chief Medical Officer, did not want to take the matter forward with the Minister of Health who was known to be unenthusiastic about taking on the Chancellor of the Exchequer (Treasurer). The Treasury was keen to protect the 15 or so per cent of central government revenue provided by tobacco tax (Berridge 2007). Godber visited Charles Fletcher, a respiratory physician, at a London teaching hospital and invited him to his club for lunch so that they could discuss strategies. They decided on working through the Royal College of Physicians in order to by-pass the Chief Medical Officer. The College took up the matter energetically and decided to produce a report aimed at a large audience. In 1962, Smoking and Health appeared and quickly sold out (Pollock 1999), (Lock et al. 1998). The United States followed suit and in 1964 the Surgeon-General’s report on The Health Effects of Smoking appeared. The mass media covered these reports extensively and Pierce and colleagues have shown that smoking cessation rates in US middle-aged adults moved in synchrony with the news coverage (Pierce and Gilpin 2001). Coverage of the Surgeon-General’s report was not the beginning of mass media coverage of smoking and health in the USA—as early as 1946 a news magazine story ‘Cigarettes cause cancer?’, based on experimental work on the carcinogenicity of cigarette tar was ‘widely read’ (Proctor 2011). However, there is good reason to see the Surgeon-General’s report as a turning point in increasing public awareness in the USA of the hazards of smoking.
	A major difficulty, in the 1950s, was that public health authorities were reluctant to tell adult men how they should behave. Reluctance of this kind had not previously inhibited anti-spitting campaigns to reduce risks of transmitting a communicable disease (tuberculosis). Nor had it inhibited strong and detailed directions to mothers, early in the twentieth century on how they should care for their children (Lewis 1980). But advising adult men to abandon a widely accepted habit was seen as different. Crossing this frontier would ultimately change ‘the discourse of public health’ in Britain and legitimize government activity to promote health favouring lifestyles (Berridge 2007).
	In Britain, early tobacco control activism was largely confined to professional and political elites who aimed to build constituencies ‘from above’ in support of action by parliament. This turned out to be a slow process. Kenneth Robinson who was health minister through the mid-1960s said that lack of public support had prevented him acting (Berridge 2007). In 1971 the Royal College of Physicians established a pressure group—Action on Smoking and Health—‘to make non-smoking the norm in society and to inform and educate the public about the death and disease caused by smoking’ (Action on Smoking and Health 2017). Most of the early office holders were activist physicians.
	Major breakthroughs in mobilizing a broader base of public support came in the mid to late 1980s in Victoria, Australia. The 1987 Victorian Tobacco Act was the first to secure a tax hypothecated to health promotion—in this case to the Victorian Health Promotion Foundation (Vichealth). Vichealth then used this money (AUD 23m per year—about USD 7 per person per year) to buy out tobacco sponsorship of sporting and arts events and to fund health promotion programmes. The close passage of this Act was the outcome of careful planning, initially conducted in strict secrecy in order to catch the tobacco industry off-guard and prevent it deploying its enormous resources against the Act. Once the campaign was public, the large contributor base of the Anti-Cancer Council of Victoria was mobilized. Newspaper coverage was sympathetic—the main morning paper reported more correspondence on the topic than any other in the paper’s history (Borland et al. 2009). Over 150,000 letters of support were sent to state politicians and church leaders were engaged in the campaign. The idea of an hypothecated tax was taken to California and included in Proposition 99 which won voter approval in November 1988.
	Nathanson notes the marked differences between countries in the groups who led the opposition to tobacco. In the USA ‘lay activists’ led the way. In California, an early victory was the passage in 1977 by the Berkeley City Council of an ‘indoor air ordinance’ instigated by the local branch of GASP (Group Against Smoke Pollution). (GASP had been launched nationally in 1970 by environmental activist Clara Gouin who attributed her father’s death a year before to smoking.) From the 1970s local groups, many now constituted, in California, as Americans for Nonsmokers Rights, had achieved 117 local tobacco control ordinances by 1986 (Glanz and Balbach, p. 39). In the lead in to the Proposition 99 referendum, private polling commissioned by the Tobacco Institute reported as its ‘bottom line’ that ‘people do not like smoking or smokers’ (V. Lance Tarrance and Associates (1987) cited in Glanz and Balbach, p. 42, italics in original). It was against this background that the 1988 vote was won, despite industry spending to defeat it being 13 times greater than the spending in support (Glanz and Balbach, p. 72).
	The formal state-wide tobacco control programme mandated by Proposition 99 was funded by a 25c per pack levy on cigarettes, sufficient to pay for mass media campaigns and to fund activities developed and run by local groups. It did not fund professional and pharmacological assistance for smoking cessation. During the 1990s it was noted by programme evaluators that a substantial fraction of households were reporting that they had decided to make themselves ‘smoke free’ even though this had never been promoted by the formal programmes. This imitation by households of ‘clean air ordinances’ enacted for public venues provides a nice illustration of the complex decentralist—centralist dynamic at the heart of the California’s response to the challenge of tobacco (Pierce et al. 2010).
	From the 1990s the tobacco industry has suffered further losses of legitimacy and support in the developed world. In the USA, the 1998 Tobacco Master Settlement Agreement between 46 states and the largest cigarette manufacturers, resulted in the industry agreeing to restrict some marketing practices, to dissolve its three main front organizations and to pay the states $206 billion (sic) over 25 years to compensate for the extra state medical expenditures attributable to cigarette smoking. Interpretation of the potential effects on the Settlement on tobacco control have been mixed (Schroeder 2004) but the public release of previously secret industry documents during the discovery phase of the litigation has led to further damage to the industry. Proctor used these documents to show how the industry deliberately and secretly modified the composition of cigarettes to make the smoke more inhalable and the smoker more dependent (Proctor 2011).
	In 2006 Philip Morris was convicted by a US federal court under legislation designed to counter organized crime (the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act) for having: falsely denied that they market to youth, falsely denied that they manipulated cigarette design, falsely represented that light and low tar cigarettes deliver less nicotine and tar, falsely denied that ETS (second-hand smoke) causes disease and suppressed documents, information, and research (Proctor 2011). In November 2012 they were ordered to make public statements admitting that they had lied to the public (Associated Press 2012). Elsewhere, the closing off of marketing opportunities in high-income countries was taken one step further when, in December 2012, Australia enacted a law requiring that all cigarettes be sold in plain standardized packaging. As of mid-2018, seven more countries had followed suit: France, United Kingdom, Norway, Ireland, New Zealand, Hungary, and Slovenia.
	The tobacco wars are not over yet. Despite declining deaths from smoking, tobacco was still ranked first for men and fifth for women among causes of lost healthy life in ‘high socio-demographic index’ countries in 2017 (GBD Compare 2018). Deaths from lung cancer provide a robust and comparable indicator of health losses from tobacco and those at younger ages reflect more recent trends in tobacco exposure. Table 3.6.2 gives years of life lost from lung cancer deaths in men and women under the age of 50. It shows that, for men, progress was almost universal between 1990 and 2016 with only Portugal and Cyprus showing increases. Reductions, both proportional and absolute, were biggest in the post-communist countries, with the Czech Republic and Hungary both showing very large reductions (from 659 to 143 and from 922 to 436 respectively). Trends for women are lagged relative to those for men with 21 out of 39 countries showing increased lung cancer mortality between 1990 and 2016. Meanwhile, the tobacco industry has moved its focus from developed countries to emerging markets in low and middle-income countries where prevalence rates are high and, in some cases, growing.

	The century long epidemics of cigarette smoking and its consequent disease burdens illustrate the time frame over which chronic disease determinants may rise and fall, making campaigns to reduce them into long wars of attrition. Tobacco control also illustrates how the development of quantitative methods has supported appropriate policy responses. With increased acceptance of epidemiological reasoning and its transmission to political and wider publics (for example, Peto et al. 2013), quantitative assessments have become more central to policy deliberations, facilitating effective institutional responses, locally, nationally, and globally.





Traffic injuries


	Deaths from traffic injury per unit of exposure (e.g. per 10,000 vehicles per year) have fallen up to 10-fold in many developed countries since the mid-twentieth century. Despite this outstanding success, traffic injuries still ranked sixth among causes of lost healthy life in males and fourteenth in females in 2017 (GBD Compare 2018). Because of the visibility of control measures and the short time lags between their implementation and their effects, traffic injury control provides a sensitive field in which to explore the relationship between policy adoption, programme implementation, and health effects.
	First, it is appropriate to note that success has not flowed exclusively from centrally initiated policies, especially in the early decades of motorization. Smeed writing in the early 1970s showed that deaths from traffic crashes in relation to the number of registered vehicles had followed a general, and pronounced, downward trend as the number of motor vehicles increased in relation to population (Smeed’s Law: Deaths/vehicle = 0.0003 (vehicles/population)−0.66) (Smeed 1972). However, over the past four or five decades organized policy responses have clearly made a bigger contribution. The Australian state of Victoria has been a pioneer in traffic injury control and its experience will be briefly reviewed here.
	Consistent with Smeed’s prediction, deaths per 10,000 vehicle years fell in Victoria as the number of vehicles increased in relation to population—from over 20 in the 1930s to about 9 in the early 1960s. During these early decades, Victoria generally had rates in excess of Smeed’s prediction. The recurrent funerals resulting from avoidable deaths in young adults provoked a growing conviction that ‘something needed to be done’. Early policy responses relied on exhortation—for example, encouraging motorists to sign a pledge to abstain from ‘careless and discourteous behaviour’ on the roads. This approach was not successful. A campaigning young police surgeon engaged journalists in the cause by taking them to the scenes of alcohol related accidents on Friday and Saturday nights. At this time, the editor of ‘The Age’ a Melbourne daily newspaper threw the paper’s weight behind the campaign. A committee of the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons made a case before the parliamentary committee on road safety for more rigorous surveillance and for compulsion. In 1970, these submissions convinced the main political parties to support legislation, the first in the world, compelling Victorians to fit and wear seat belts. Compliance with the new law was high and road deaths fell. In 1976, the Victorian parliament was the first in the world to legislate for random breath alcohol testing, responding again to advice from professionals. Deaths declined over the following decade. In 1986 a Transport Accident Commission was established, with secure funding from the compulsory third party injury insurance levy on motorists being made payable to it. The Commission is required to pay no-fault compensation to those injured, giving it a financial incentive to reduce injuries. A specified proportion of its spending is required to be spent on programme evaluation—thus supporting the development of an independent accident research institution. In late 1989, after traffic deaths had begun to rise again, it launched one of the most intensive mass media campaigns ever run in Australia—combined with intensified police enforcement (Davison and Yelland 2004, ch 6). In 2009 police performed 1.24 million random breath tests in a total population of 5.4 million persons (Transport Accident Commission 2013). Since 1960 traffic fatality rates in Victoria have fallen to levels that are among the lowest of the developed world.
	Local historians commented in 2004:
	 	Probably nowhere else in the world was the conduct of the individual motorist more closely monitored or more rigorously controlled. Yet, with only occasional grumblings, motorists overwhelmingly accepted these measures.
	(Davison and Yelland 2004, p. 166)
	These strategies of education and enforcement were combined with those of engineering. In 1965, Ralph Nader denounced US cars as ‘unsafe at any speed’ (Nader 1965). In Australia, the national government negotiated against the resistance of the international automobile industry for ‘design rules’ to make cars safer—e.g. collapsible steering columns, shatter-proof windshield glass and the removal of dangerous protrusions from the passenger cabin (personal communication: Tony Ryan). For the US, Robertson has documented the continuing resistance of the motor industry to manufacturing safer cars (Robertson 2010).





Cardiovascular disease


	Cardiovascular diseases, mainly ischaemic heart disease and stroke, remain the leading causes of lost life years in developed countries. The overall change from 1990 to 2016 in the level of lost life years from these diseases in our 39 countries is shown in Table 3.6.3. The median reduction was 58%. In both time periods Japan, France, Spain, and Switzerland occupy the top four ranks (i.e. have the lowest mortality). In 1990 the Eastern European countries were at the bottom of the ladder. Over the 26-year interval reductions are largest in South Korea (76%) and Israel (71%). The post-communist group shows increasing heterogeneity with Slovenia and the Czech Republic showing above average declines while, at the other end, Bulgaria and Lithuania only achieved half the average reduction. In 2016 rates of lost life years in Bulgaria were over three times those in Slovenia. The USA also performed poorly with a reduction of just 39%, falling in rank from thirteenth to twenty-eighth.

	These trends prompt three policy-related questions:
	 	1. What have been the main contributors to reductions in cardiovascular mortality over recent decades?
	2. Why have the trends in the post-communist group been so diverse?
	3. Why has the USA been less successful?
	As with road traffic injuries and tobacco caused disease, endeavours to control circulatory diseases have been pursued in conjunction with determined attempts to better understand their causes. In the United States, President Harry Truman signed the National Heart Act in June, 1948. Between 1950 and 2018 the budget of what was to become the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute rose from US$10 million to US$3,380 million (NIH, n.d.). The deliberate rapid expansion of research into the causes of ischaemic heart disease contributed strongly to the modernization of the scientific base of public health, including the emergence of modern epidemiology and the concept of ‘risk factors’.
	The causation of these diseases has turned out to be complex but much of the variation in cardiovascular risk, at individual and population levels, continues to be explicable by the three classic risk factors—blood pressure, blood cholesterol concentration, and cigarette smoking—whose quantitative relationship to risk is now well understood. Smoking epidemic in young adult males before 1980 in most of the developed countries. Less data is available on trends in blood pressure and blood cholesterol concentrations. Where documented, trends in both sexes in developed countries have tended to follow a broadly similar time course to those of cigarette smoking in males—that is, to have been generally favourable, especially since around 1990 (Danaei et al. 2013). The development of drugs that are effective in lowering blood pressure and blood cholesterol concentrations has enabled clinicians to also make an important contribution to the prevention of these diseases. More effective treatments for heart attacks and for precursor coronary artery disease also mean that the trends in mortality from heart attack reflect not only the extent of success in preventing disease onset but also in reducing the risk of death after onset.
	In seeking to characterize societal responses to heart disease and stroke one might start with an hypothetical chain from the advance of scientific knowledge to increased professional and public knowledge, advocacy, and constituency building by activists at all levels, enactment of policy, programme implementation, changes in risk factors, and finally changes in disease incidence. However such sequences cannot be easily documented or established in a convincing way. Early phases of development were often marked by the formation of physician-led voluntary organizations which sought to mobilize public support for research, prevention and treatment in many countries: The American Heart Association (founded 1924), the National Heart Foundation in Australia (founded 1959), and the British Heart Foundation (founded 1961). The European Heart Network now unites 29 member organizations from 24 European countries. In Australia the National Heart Foundation, with extensive public support, was rich enough to actually lead in establishing national risk factor surveys during the 1980s. In Finland the local government of North Karelia, a district with extremely high risks of premature death from vascular disease, petitioned the national government for support in reducing their disease burden. From this emerged the North Karelia project which spanned epidemiological investigation and mass mobilization to promote dietary change. Finland became an exemplar in the implementation, at community level, of science-based policies to reduce vascular risk (Puska 2005).
	Few countries have long time series of data on public knowledge of risk factors or of risk factor levels. However, there are indications—not least in the salience of health claims in television advertising for foods—that public awareness of the determinants of cardiovascular risk has increased over time. By the mid-1990s a vast majority (96%) of men and women in England correctly identified at least three ways of achieving a healthier diet (Bridgwood et al. 1996, p. 62).
	One assessment of associations between risk factor changes and declines in mortality from cardiovascular diseases plus diabetes in 26 ‘industrialized’ countries (including Chile, Argentina, and Brazil but no post-Communist country in Europe) found that ‘trends in body mass index (BMI), blood pressure, serum cholesterol, and smoking together may have alone accounted for nearly one-half of the decline in men and about 40% in women’ (Di Cesare et al. 2013, p. 847). However, many of the risk factor estimates in this study were imputed using hierarchical Bayesian imputation.
	Capewell and colleagues have shown, in a series of studies, that favourable shifts in risk factors contributed much more than clinical measures (pharmacoprevention plus treatment) to the reductions in years of life lost from ischaemic heart disease in Scotland (1975–1994), USA (1980–2000), Ireland (1985–2000), and England and Wales (1981–2000) (Gouda et al. 2012).
	To all of these activities intended to reduce disease risk must be added other background factors. As early as the 1960s, results from the study of ‘Coronary Heart Disease in Seven Countries’ confirmed that local food cultures varied markedly in their association with coronary risk—protective in the Mediterranean area and in Japan (once traditional high sodium intakes were abandoned) while being adverse, for example, in Northern Europe (Keys 1980). Favourable trajectories in mortality from circulatory diseases in countries such as France, Spain and Japan may owe a good deal to protective food cultures as well as deliberate efforts to reduce risk. While the effects of rising incomes on animal fat and cigarette consumption may have been adverse in the early decades of the twentieth century, once the associated risks were understood, rising incomes will have brought benefits, for example via the ability to support further scientific research the dissemination of findings and by the diversification of food supplies—reduced fat dairy products, margarines with low trans-fat content, year-round supplies of fresh fruit and vegetables, etc. Richer populations can also afford the relatively expensive strategy of controlling blood pressure and high cholesterol by long-term medication. These changing patterns of association between vascular risk factors and national income levels have recently been described (Danaei et al. 2013).





Large scale failures of public health policy


Eastern Europe 1965–1990: a pervasive failure of institutional adaptation


	In the period up to the mid-1960s premature adult mortality fell at least as fast in Eastern as in Western Europe (Fig. 3.6.2). The Soviet model of health service organization (named after Semashko, the first commissar of health) dealt well with the main public health problems it was designed for—notably communicable diseases and maternal and child health (Field 1967). But when faced with the challenge of tackling noncommunicable disease not only did things go badly wrong but these regimes appeared incapable of changing course in the face of manifest failure.
	The communist-ruled countries with transplanted Soviet public health institutions, failed to build modern scientific foundations for responding to noncommunicable diseases: they did not invest in developing modern epidemiology and they failed to make good use of international findings. The early years of the Soviet regime had been characterized by an enthusiasm for science but subsequent developments were not favourable to population based research in medicine. According to Terris, the policy of Semashko, of integrating prevention and treatment led, in practice, to the domination of Soviet medicine by clinicians rather than by public health experts (Terris 1988). Later, the legacies of the ‘Lysenko affair’1 weakened all biological sciences (Krementsov 1997) and the control of science through hierarchical systems of research institutes limited innovation. Soviet economic philosophy also saw the route to human betterment through the physical domination of nature, not by attending to biologically based needs. The physical sciences and engineering (related, in Soviet economic theory, to the ‘productive sector’) were valued and rewarded more than medicine (seen as part of the ‘unproductive sector’). The idea that ‘dietary affluence’ could harm health was denounced as a capitalist ruse. These adverse internal characteristics were augmented by the isolation of the cold war years; at late as 1988, Terris observed that there were no Soviet members of the International Epidemiological Association. The transformative potential of the quantitative revolution in medicine and, in particular, of the randomized trial, was not realized (McKee 2007). Finally, there were problems of the supply of healthy foods: systems for counter-seasonal supplies of fresh fruit and vegetables were not developed (as in the west) and these foods tended to disappear from the shops in winter and spring. Such circumstances would not have provided a propitious background for programmes promoting dietary fruit and vegetable consumption.
	In some of the ‘laggard’ post-communist countries, public awareness of risk factors has been notably low. When survey respondents in northeast Bulgaria were asked an open-ended question (in 2000 and 2003), why they thought stroke was so common in their region, high blood pressure and cigarette smoking accounted for less than 3% of all reasons offered (Dokova et al. 2005).
	As shown in Figure 3.6.2, the East/West gap in Europe was mainly created by favourable changes in the West that were not matched in the East. This point has been somewhat obscured by the focus on ‘things going wrong in the east’, for example, the catastrophic effects of binge drinking in Russian men in the 1990s. But if we take for illustration, say, cardiovascular mortality in middle-aged women in Hungary and Spain (among whom binge drinking and heavy smoking were not especially prevalent): all of the increased difference between Spanish and Hungarian mortality levels from the 1950s and the 1990s—from Hungarian levels being 1.5 times Spanish levels to being 4.5 times—was created by decreases in mortality in Spain that were unmatched in Hungary (personal calculations using data from the World Health Organization (WHO) mortality database (WHO n.d.)). What mainly needs to be explained is the absence of favourable changes in the East.





The surprising underperformance of the USA


	The public health failure of the United States is extraordinary on many counts. It is contrary to expectations based on national income and schooling levels. It is occurring in the face of national strengths in medical and public health science. It is occurring in spite of prodigious levels of spending on clinical medicine. And, far from showing any early effects of corrective action, US mortality trajectories continue to deviate further from trends elsewhere in the developed world.
	There is also surprising ethnic selectivity. Hispanics are largely spared, with midlife death rates 30–40% below those for non-Hispanic whites (Woolf et al. 2018)—despite median household wealth just one-tenth that of non-Hispanic whites (Taylor et al. 2011). Mortality among US blacks, though substantially higher than in whites has also been declining faster, with reducing black white differences. It is thus among non-Hispanic whites that trends deviate furthest from expectation. The USA has also experienced large increases in economic inequality, and while these are important in themselves (and dealt with elsewhere in this textbook, in Chapter 6.3), it is not clear that they can explain the unfavourable trends in average health levels (Panel on Understanding Cross-National Health Differences Among High-Income Countries 2013) (Lynch et al. 2004).
	The relative failure of health improvement in the USA since the 1980s constitutes an enormous loss. Writing in 2002, the US economist Nordhaus asked his readers to consider the following choice (Nordhaus 2002):
	 	You must forgo either the health improvements over the last half-century or the non-health improvements. That is, you must choose either (a) 1948 health conditions and 1998 non-health living standards or (b) 1998 health conditions and 1948 non-health living standards. Which would you choose?
	Respondents to his straw poll tended slightly to favour b), a result consistent with his more formal analyses:
	 	The major result that comes through using all techniques is that the value of improvements in life expectancy is about as large as the value of all other consumption goods and services put together.
	Applied to the present, the implication is that the USA is losing the equivalent of a substantial fraction of its national income. It cannot be ‘great again’ without finding the means of closing the health gap with the generality of developed countries.
	Although the US failure is generally pervasive across child and adult health and across major disease groups and injuries, it does appear that a higher prevalence of obesity and increased consumption of opioids, are making notable contributions (Jeffery et al. 2018; Preston et al. 2018). In this case, the puzzle is pushed one link further back in the causal chain: why are excess adiposity and the liberal prescription of opioids more prevalent in the USA than in Other Developed countries?
	Fig. 3.6.3 Years of life lost in the US and four constituent states from six causes, age-standardized estimates for both sexes, 2016.
	Source: data from U. S. Burden of Disease Collaborators (2018), ‘The State of US Health, 1990–2016: Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Among US States. JAMA, 319 (14), 1444–72.
	So far we have been discussing the USA as though it were spatially homogeneous. In fact it is a very large country with marked internal heterogeneity in health experience across states and counties (see Fig. 3.6.3). Primary responsibility for public health programmes resides with the states (Institute of Medicine 2003, p. 102). The success of Californians in reducing health losses from tobacco have already been noted. This is now reflected in lung cancer mortality, at all ages, being one-third below the national rates (U.S. Burden of Disease Collaborators 2018, Fig. 6)—with even greater differences at the youngest ages. Between 1990 and 2016 California moved from twenty-fourth to second rank for life expectancy at birth. New York state, containing New York City, noted for its vigorous chronic disease prevention programmes (Ong et al. 2017), moved from thirty-ninth to fifth. (The magnitude of these movements will have been exaggerated by the larger than average effects of the HIV epidemic in these two states in 1990.) By contrast, in 21 ‘downwardly mobile’ states, mortality at ages 20 to 55 actually increased over this period: In Kentucky, Oklahoma, New Mexico, West Virginia, and Wyoming, the increases in mortality exceeded 10%. Comparing lost life years by cause across the states of the USA in 2016 it is apparent that levels of the major causes tend to vary together. Thus rates in California and New York for 16 and 15, respectively, out of 20 causes considered in the GBD study are significantly below national rates. Similarly, states with above average rates of years of life lost tend to have high losses from most causes. The risk factors for premature mortality thus appear to vary together. Figure 3.6.3 illustrates the contribution of major preventable causes to differences in premature mortality between two low mortality states—California and New York—and two high mortality states—West Virginia and Mississippi.
	In Eastern Europe there had been state-imposed embargoes on both knowledge and action to counter chronic disease risks; but in the USA relevant knowledge-based institutions are strong. The block in not on knowledge; it is on action. Characterizing institutional differences between countries is not straightforward, but some cross-national comparisons are suggestive.
	Programmes to reduce traffic injury are relatively easy to identify and observe, as are their effects. The authors of the US National Academies report, Shorter lives, poorer health (Panel on Understanding Cross-National Health Differences Among High-Income Countries 2013) noted with some enthusiasm a study of traffic injury control in the USA and five comparison countries (Transportation Research Board [TRB] 2011): ‘ … the panel was struck by how closely the [Transport Research Board] committee’s overall findings parallel those documented in Part 1 of this report … ’ (p. 226). The TRB report noted how jurisdictions in the USA resist the application of measures proven effective elsewhere for reducing drink driving, increasing seatbelt and motorcycle helmet use, and controlling speed. It provides a detailed comparison of driving speed management in France, the United Kingdom, and Australia with the USA, using as subheadings ‘management and planning’, ‘technical implementation of countermeasures’, and ‘political and public support’. The USA came out poorly under all three heads. The TRB report concluded that ‘Most U.S. state and local transportation safety agencies lack the institutional and technical capacities required to apply the management techniques observed in the benchmark countries’ (p. 4).
	Scientific evidence and expert opinion often carry less weight in political deliberations in the USA than in Western Europe. Nathanson contrasts the situation in Britain where ‘[c]redible scientific knowledge is monopolized and deployed by closely linked experts based within and outside the government—medical civil servants, the British Medical Association, the Royal Colleges, and government appointed advisory bodies’ with the situation in the USA where experts ‘enjoy no comparable authority’ (p. 223).
	One of the two dimensions on which the World Values Survey ranks countries from traditional/religious values at one end to secular-rational values at the other. Among developed countries, the USA is placed towards the traditional/religious end of this scale (World Values Survey 2017). Substantial proportions favour creation over evolution as an explanation of human origins (Swift 2017). Arguments based on orthodox interpretations of scientific evidence may face more competition than they would elsewhere. The much delayed uptake in the USA of syringe exchange programmes to help reduce HIV transmission in injecting drug users is often cited as an example of conservative morality blocking effective evidence based measures. It was not until December 2015 that a federal funding ban on these programmes was lifted. This happened after the prescription opioid epidemic led to new epidemics of injecting drug use and HIV transmissions in Republican Party constituencies that happened to be poor and rural, and not in Democrat voting cosmopolitan coastal cities (Showalter 2018).
	Commercial interests are powerful and politically well-organized. Lobbying is a $4b ‘industry’ with one study identifying 37,000 (sic) lobbyists active at federal level in the decade to 2008 (Bertrand et al. 2014). The chronicles of California’s tobacco wars provide insight into the challenges of operating in such an environment. The tobacco industry’s carefully planned strategy for ‘neutralizing’ the participation of the California Medical Association to the Proposition 99 campaign in 1987–88 is very sobering (Glanz and Balbach 2000, pp. 46–9).
	Responsibilities for public health programmes (like those already noted for traffic injury control) rest at state level. It is likely that the weaknesses noted in traffic injury control apply in other areas of disease and injury prevention at state level including: failure to marshall strong political and community support for preventive programmes; limited managerial capacity and accountability for achieving programme goals; and lack of longer-term planning horizons. In 2003 an Institute of Medicine report on The Future of the Public’s Health in the 21st Century concluded that ‘the nation’s entire governmental public health infrastructure—its human resources, information systems, and organizational capacity—must be revitalized and strengthened’ (Institute of Medicine 2003, p. 169). Evidence that this is underway is awaited.





Emulation and globalization of public health strategies


	In the previous section, ‘Large scale failures of public health policy’, we discussed the early, creative phases of societal responses to hazards such as tobacco and traffic injury. However, institutions evolve. For example, opportunities for discussion and comparison of early national experiences in tobacco control were created by the founding of world conferences: the first in New York in 1967, the second in London in 1971—a series that continues to the present with the seventeenth held in Capetown in 2018. The journal Tobacco Control was founded in 1992 and has since attained one of the highest impact factors among all public health journals. Knowledge of ‘what works’ in tobacco control has evolved in parallel with tobacco control activity.
	Over time the number and range of civil, professional, and scientific organizations actively supportive of stronger measures to reduce tobacco consumption has grown as has support at the level of national governments and intergovernmental bodies. In the late 1990s these trends coalesced in negotiations which led to the unanimous adoption of the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control at the World Health Assembly of 2003 (Studlar 2006). This has been ratified by all but two of our included countries (USA and Switzerland).
	The WHO website now presents a distillation of expert consensus on ‘best practice’ in tobacco control, summarized in the acronym MPOWER:
	 	Monitor tobacco use and prevention policies
	Protect people from tobacco use
	Offer help to quit tobacco use
	Warn about the dangers of tobacco
	Enforce bans on tobacco advertising, promotion, and sponsorship
	Raise taxes on tobacco.
	The website includes 12 page profiles on each of over 190 countries, tracking their compliance with the MPOWER framework—conveniently and conspicuously summarized in a colour-coded bar (WHO n.d., Tobacco).
	Global processes of emulation and policy convergence are not confined to tobacco. Also to be found on the WHO site are a ‘Global Status Reports’ on Alcohol and Health and on Road Safety (each with single page profiles for all countries) and ‘More Active People for a Healthier World’ (without country profiles).
	Of our group of 39 developed countries, 28 are (currently) members of the European Union. From the late 1980s the European Commission began its engagement with public health by working on a directive to regulate tobacco advertising. This faltered due to member state resistance (especially from Germany) and adverse judicial rulings (Duina and Kurzer 2004). However such a directive was finally passed in 2002, and since then the EU has expanded its engagement in public health, extending from tobacco to alcohol, nutrition, and physical activity along with its previously established role in communicable disease control (European Commission n.d.). It is also active in promoting traffic safety—through the transport portfolio.
	For the post-communist countries of Eastern Europe and for ‘latecomers’ such as the Asian Developed countries, the products of these supranational institutions provide practical guidance and models of ‘best practice’ for national emulation. They will be contributing, for example, to the recent above average declines in deaths from smoking in the younger cohorts in Eastern Europe—presaging further substantial declines in tobacco attributable mortality as these cohorts age.
	The Asian Developed group—Japan, Singapore, and South Korea—have been late starters (with the partial exception of Japan) and rapid improvers for child and adult survival (Fig. 3.6.1 and Table 3.6.1). They have followed technology-intensive development strategies with high investments in schooling and in research. They have been moderate to good adopters of international best practices in tobacco control and traffic safety (based on WHO score cards). They too can be assumed to be benefitting from supranational developments.
	Recognizing that healthy populations are not the result of hospitals and health systems alone, other initiatives which address social determinants of health also have had increasing influence in developed countries. Health in All Policies (HiAP) was developed by the European Union and subsequently shaped by the Commission on the Social Determinants of Health and has been adopted across developed, and more recently, developing countries Kickbusch 2013). Furthermore, the Healthy Cities programme, which was launched over 30 years ago, was a WHO strategy designed to bring Health for All to the local level and recognized the importance of developing enabling environments for healthy lives (Tsouros 2015).





Reflections and prospects


	In the period following the Second World War, the developed world faced a continuation of the challenges of communicable disease against which it had enjoyed substantial success earlier in the century and for which it now had new weapons (antibiotics and new vaccines). The momentum of post-war reconstruction provided a favourable political context. In the following decades continuing marked success in reducing deaths from communicable disease in children and adults has been universal.
	But in this post-war period new challenges were to emerge for which existing knowledge and institutional forms were not adequate—conditions such as lung cancer, road traffic injuries, and ischaemic heart disease. Strategies that were ultimately to succeed included the building of new scientific bases for tacking noncommunicable disease and injuries combined with what turned out to be cumulative piecemeal changes to social institutions related to health damaging behaviour patterns. Especially in their early phases, the actual form and content of the latter varied markedly between countries. Over time, as knowledge deepened and extended, and practical experiences in areas such as tobacco control, traffic injury reduction, and heart disease prevention were compared, it became possible to identify ‘best practice’ strategies and to codify these at an international level. Within countries, such institutions evolved over time, increasingly subject to scientific and public scrutiny. Since the mid-twentieth century risks of premature death have more than halved.
	Where political regimes blocked these developments—as in the communist-ruled countries of Eastern Europe—the health of adults either failed to improve, or, especially in the case of men, deteriorated. With the end of communist party rule, these countries have, to varying extents, resumed improving adult mortality trajectories. Countries such as the Czech Republic and Slovenia have been rapid improvers and now have adult male mortality levels that lie within the range of other developed countries and that are only half of those of laggards such as Latvia and Lithuania.
	The poor performance of the USA is noteworthy and puzzling. Adult mortality levels (at ages 15–60) are now around twice those of the best performing countries and the gap has continued to widen. Given the several background conditions favourable to the attainment of higher levels of health, suspicion falls on institutional obstacles to more effective action. There is now evidence that some other countries may be joining the US in experiencing slowdowns and reversals of previous mortality declines (Ho and Hendi 2018).
	Respect for science, objectivity, and expertise have, in combination with a sense of human solidarity, provided the foundation for major health gains over the past several decades. They are currently under challenge from the upsurge of populism, so the prospects for successfully reversing recent adverse trends remain unclear.
