5.6


Qualitative research imagination


	Jennie Popay and Fran Baum





Introduction


	In his classic book The Sociological Imagination C. Wright Mills (1970) argued that ‘imagination’ is the creative force that transforms social enquiry from the mundane application of particular techniques into a process that has the potential to generate new ways of thinking about the social world producing new knowledge of both theoretical and practical use. From this perspective, though it may seem counterintuitive, maximizing the contribution to global public health of any type of research requires imagination alongside technical competencies. Imagination enables scientists to envision the potential impact of their research on policy and practice and to ensure it is relevant and high quality. In this chapter we will consider what the qualitative research imagination ‘is’—touching on key questions that should be addressed by all researchers regardless of their approach (see Box 5.6.1). In the first part of the chapter we will consider the first two questions focusing on the type of ‘knowledge’ generated by qualitative research and in the second part on questions about the range of approaches that can be taken to data collection, analysis and interpretation, and the role of theory.
	 	Box 5.6.1 Four key questions for researchers
	 	1. Ontological perspective: What is the nature of the ‘social phenomena’ I wish to investigate?
	2. Epistemological perspective: What might represent knowledge/evidence about these phenomena?
	3. Theoretical perspective: What is the intellectual puzzle I wish to ‘explain’ and what research questions flow from this?
	4. Methodological perspective: What approach should I use to collect and analyses data about these phenomena?





What is the qualitative research imagination?


	Qualitative research is underpinned by a social constructivist philosophy. it assumes that the ‘reality’ or phenomena being studied are subjective: the product of people’s interpretations informed by their perceptions, beliefs, and experiences. These subjective phenomena are rich, diverse, and fluid. Rather than trying to control them through experiment and measurement, qualitative research therefore studies social phenomena in naturally occurring settings and seeks to develop concepts and theories that help us to see these phenomena from the point of view of the people being studied.
	The central question for qualitative research is why individuals, collectives and/or organizations ‘act’ or ‘behave’ as they do (what social scientists refer to as agency) (Mallinson et al. 2014). It seeks to answer this question by studying the relationship between ‘agency’ and social context, including in particular social structures associated with social class, gender, ethnicity, sexuality, etc. and by illuminating the understandings and meanings people attach to these actions and experiences. Qualitative research can also illuminate power relationships and how these affect the distribution of resources in a society, including the extent of equality in health status between different groups. Concepts are the basis for analysis of qualitative data, rather than numbers, and theory is the basis for explanation and generalization rather than statistical probability.
	Given the assumption that the ‘reality’ or ‘phenomena’ being studied is socially constructed, a research event, such as an interview, is not viewed as a method for gaining a ‘slice of reality’ but as a process of contextually bounded ‘meaning-making’ between the researcher and the researched. The context, perspective and position of the researcher is therefore understood to be an inevitable influence on the findings of qualitative research. So, rather than seeking to eliminate sources of potential bias, the aim is to make them visible. Processes of reflexivity and transparency are used by the qualitative researcher to identify relevant aspects of their beliefs/perceptions etc, to consider how these may have influenced the research process and to record this so that readers can assess the strengths, weaknesses, and relevance of a study.
	The rest of this chapter is divided into three parts. First, we discuss the type of knowledge produced by qualitative research. We then discuss the potential for community/public involvement as ‘partners’ in qualitative research and finally consider key methodological issues in the conduct of qualitative research.





What knowledge or evidence can the qualitative research imagination contribute to public health policy and practice?


	Armstrong (2000) has written about the separation of two ways of understanding the world: ‘mythos’ and ‘logos’ and the limits this imposes on our ability to ‘imagine’ action for health. improvement. Logos concerns the rational world—how we might understand how the world works, how we solve problems, and grasp causal processes. It is mundane and concerns both logical argument and the accumulation of facts. Mythos, on the other hand, is concerned with meaning: it is what gives life its telos or purpose. It is often expressed in different forms, through metaphor, poetry, visual arts: resources commonly used to express the emotional life and our relationships to others (Richards 2011). The point is not that one ‘way of knowing’ is better than the other but that knowledge itself becomes impoverished by this separation, often unwittingly, because of the narrow disciplinary confines in which people work and their assumption that their expertise marks them out as separate from the everyday. From this perspective, it is vital that global public health is able to access knowledge about both ways of understanding the world: the quantitative and the qualitative (Baum 2016).
	The qualitative research imagination can be used to address a wide range of questions (Popay and Williams 2009). These can be groups into four broad domains critical to global public health policy and practice:
	 	• Preparing the ground for other forms of enquiry: addressing different kinds of questions and generating hypothesis to be tested by other study designs.
	• Adding theoretical and/or empirical depth to understandings of pathways to population health and health equity.
	• Illuminating barriers and enablers to effective policy and practice.
	• Contributing to greater social justice by addressing inequities between different forms of knowledge and between researcher and researched and by contributing to critical thinking on action for population health and health equity.





Preparing the ground for other enquiries: Imagining public health evidence beyond lifestyles


	A large number of qualitative studies relevant to public health focus on the meanings people attach to behaviours/lifestyle. It has been argued that this research, ‘tends to produce bland accounts of social life, in which it is difficult to assess the import of things for people’ (Sayer 2011, p. 6). To avoid this limitation qualitative research has to provide explanations rather than descriptions: exploring the relationship between the social/material context of people’s lives and individual behaviours such as smoking and poor diet and revealing the strategies people develop to cope with risks and exposures over which they may have little control. By doing this the qualitative research imagination provides an understanding of ‘private troubles’ as ‘public issues’ and reframes the space for action beyond the individual (Wright Mills 1970); see also, Burawoy (2005) on ‘public sociology’. For example, qualitative research embedded in a trial aimed at reducing smoking in early teenage years through a ‘peer-led’ intervention found that some young people continued to smoke, despite having knowledge of the health risks, in order to maintain social relationships with peers, revealing the complex risks assessments involved in individual decision-making processes (Campbell et al. 2008).





Adding depth to understanding pathways to population health and health equity


	A recurring finding from qualitative research into the meanings people attach to their actions is the purposeful development and/or maintenance of valued social identities in situations that threaten to undermine their moral worth. Importantly this body of research often highlights ‘fault lines’ between lay and professional understanding about health and illness that can impact adversely on the success of policies/practices. For example, on the basis of a synthesis of multiple qualitative studies Graham and McDermott’s (2006) argue that teenagers pursued motherhood as a pathway into a valued adult identity—or social inclusion—in the face of limited alternative pathways to adulthood. In contrast, professionals see education and employment as the pathway to adulthood. They fail to see the positive values and identities affirmed through teenage motherhood constructing it as a pathway to social exclusion and lifelong disadvantage. A more recent qualitative study (Wekesa and Coast 2013) highlighted the extent to which stigma and discrimination affected the responses of people living in an informal settlement in Nairobi to a diagnosis of HIV/AIDS. The study showed the need to ask broad questions about the experience of living with HIV/AIDS and the importance of paying attention to structural factors including poverty, gender, and sociocultural norms.





Illuminating barriers and enablers to effective policy and practice


	Qualitative research is now a common element of research evaluating the impact of public health policies and practices and factors impinging on successful implementation: either embedded in a mixed method evaluation or stand alone. The qualitative research by Roberts et al. (2004) embedded in a RCT of the installation and use of domestic smoke alarms explored people’s perceptions of the risk of fire and barriers and enablers to the installation and maintenance of domestic smoke alarms. The results revealed, for example, that people disabled alarms because they went off when they were cooking or eating. Similarly, using examples from African research Camlin and Seeley (Camlin and Seeley 2018) illustrate how qualitative research conducted within trials of HIV/AIDS treatments can: (i) reveal vital contextual factors that influence implementation and outcomes; (ii) enable an informed adaptation of trials as they are being conducted; and (iii) can lead to the formulation of theory regarding the social and behavioural pathways to outcomes of interventions. This study design can also enable community engagement in trial design and implementation. Qualitative research conducted independently has also be used to better understanding the results of multiple RCTs. For example, Noyes and Popay (Noyes and Popay 2007) conducted a systematic review of qualitative research on help seeking behaviour in an effort to explain the diverse results of six trials of TB treatment interventions.





Contributing to greater social justice


	Public health research has long mapped the processes of exclusion and privilege that create social inequities in the experience of health and illness across and within societies (Dorling 2011; Thomas and Dorling 2011). However, these maps typically do not capture the ‘experiences of hardship, subjugation and alienation which cannot easily be … weighed via ratios, metrics and indices’ (Trahair 2014, p. 6), but about which people have points of view. These ‘knowledgeable narratives’ (Williams 2000) people’s ‘practical wisdom’, as Aristotle described it, can be accessed through qualitative research. For the philosopher Martha Nussbaum (1990, p. 55) people’s practical wisdom provides a ‘profound alternative’ to the power of ‘scientific’ knowledge that pervades ‘almost every area of human social life’. Without an understanding of this knowledge, public health policy/practice risks reducing people to unthinking bearers of various risks, deficits or assets and seriously limits the ‘evidence’ available to improve health and reduce health inequalities.
	A particularly important aspect of the experiential knowledge revealed in qualitative research is the emotion it can embody. Conventionally emotion is seen as antithetical to scientific rationality, whereas the Aristotelian view articulated by Nussbaum is that emotions, and the imagination fed by them, are central to a fuller and more grounded understanding of how knowledge of human predicaments is articulated. Rather than bracketing emotions out as residuals in the analysis of health inequalities, it would be more fully rational to include them as components in a ‘passionate epistemology’ for a critical public health (Krieger 2000). The emotionality embedded in lay knowledge about the experience and consequences of ill-health points to the significance of these experiences for individuals, but can also highlight causal pathways within which different kinds of intervention or action might be developed (Popay et al. 2003a; Eades et al. 2008).
	Finally, qualitative research can contribute to the development of the theory and practice of transformative action by illuminating both the need for, and barriers to, collective action as strategies to improve population health and reduce health inequalities (Elliot et al. 2015). Currently, prominent theories in the public health field focused, for example, on social capital, social cohesion, resilience, community assets, etc, describe the way things are, and suggest interventions that help people cope with current conditions but offer limited insight into how to overcome the threats themselves. For example, in their literature review Elliot et al. (2011) found that while most contemporary community-based public health interventions were potentially transformative for individuals they failed to support communities to acquire the collective social/political power they need to change the determinants of health and health inequities.
	Recent work by the New Economics Foundation (Coote and Angel 2014) points to the need for further critical qualitative research in this field, arguing that while concepts such as social capital are about ‘the glue’ that holds people together, ‘solidarity’ concerns ‘momentum’ and the conditions for change. This conceptual reframing locates the sources of transformative action in civil society, but also highlights the need for better understanding of barriers and enablers to such action. One important contribution qualitative research has made to this understanding is to reveal how the strategies people develop to manage their lives can undermine solidarity. For example, Popay et al. (2003b) and Ruston (2009) in the United Kingdom and Bustos Castro and Lindbladh (2004) in Sweden have described how residents of low-income neighbourhoods frequently withdraw from the public sphere and adopt strategies of avoidance, surveillance, and fortification in order to distance themselves for the stigma attaching to living in these neighbourhoods.
	Public/community involvement in research can also contribute to the development of capabilities for transformative action in public health. Health researchers have argued for decades that, whenever possible, research should be participative (Wadsworth 1984; Feuerstein 1986; Baum 1988; Bruce et al. 1995; de Koning and Martin 1996; Minkler and Wallerstein 2003; Popay 2010). Participative approaches to research have tended to be associated with qualitative research methods. In Australia the National Lowitja Institute—the National Institute for Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander Health Research—has developed supports to guide participatory and ethical research with Indigenous peoples (Laycock et al. 2011). Similar participatory approaches have been encouraged in Canada (Canadian Institutes of Health Research 2014).
	Minkler and Wallerstein (2003) have developed a practice of community-based participatory research and described its growth and increasing acceptability in the past years. However, as Oakley (1989) has argued, quantitative methodologies, such as randomized control trials, can be emancipatory in practice and could be designed to involve research participants more than at present. Today, though still underdeveloped in the public health field, the active involvement of ‘lay people’ (e.g. residents of low-income neighbourhoods, users of services, or people with particular health conditions) as partners in research is a requirement of major funding bodies in many countries. In the United Kingdom, for example, the National Institute for Health Research has published National Standards for Public Involvement in research and expects this to be adequately funded in proposals.1 The Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) requires researchers to demonstrate the degree to which Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people have been involved in the planning and will be involved in the execution the research (National Health & Medical Research Council 2003).
	The movement for more participative research approaches partly reflects the increasing recognition that lay people can offer unique expertise. In addition, it reflects a growing commitment to democratize the research process. While participants in all types of research have the right to receive information about the research, formally agree to their participation and withdraw at any time, traditional research models involve what Wadsworth (1984) called ‘data raids’. In this approach, researchers swooped down from their ivory towers, collected data, returned to their towers, and never communicated the results of the raid to the subjects. In contrast, the new public health is calling for a more meaningful form of involvement, including involving the public/communities in defining research questions, determining methods, collecting and analysing data, interpreting findings, and deciding how they could be reported back in a readily comprehensible way. In particular, there is an increasing emphasis on approaches, such as action research, that enable traditionally marginalized groups and communities to become full partners in gaining and creating knowledge and mobilizing for change. AS we have noted a participative research approach is essential when conducting Aboriginal research given the history of the use of research as part of the processes of colonization and inhumane treatment of Indigenous peoples. The People’s Health Movement conducted participative research to examine its own form of collective action to improved health and has suggested this approach presents particular methodological challenges (Bodini et al. 2019). These concerned the following issues: making meaning; aligning research and action; managing power relations; valuing experiential knowledges, chaos, and contingency; challenging preconceptions. Specific approaches to participative research are discussed in more detail in the next section of the chapter (see also Minkler and Wallerstein 2003, p. 2).





Doing qualitative research


	In this section we move on to consider the range of study designs that can be used in qualitative research, the specific methods, or tools, available for data collection, and approaches to analysis. Patton (2014) suggests that qualitative data can be grouped into three categories:
	 	• in-depth, open-ended narrative data collected from individuals or groups;
	• direct observation and description of people’s activities, behaviours, actions, and interactions, including audio-and video-taped material. Kellehear (1993) extends the definition to include the study of ‘material culture’ (graffiti, garbage, cemeteries);
	• written data, usually excerpts, quotations, or entire passages from organizational, clinical, or programme records, personal diaries, official records or publications, and open-ended written responses to questionnaires.
	These data can be collected in the context of different study designs the main ones being:
	 	• ethnographies (based on observations);
	• interview-based studies (individual or group based);
	• case studies (which may involve both qualitative and quantitative methods and most commonly use in-depth and/or focus group interviews to collect qualitative data);
	• document-based research and content analyses;
	• participative action research (using a variety of methods).
	Next we discuss the first four of these study designs, the methods available to collect qualitative data, approaches to analysing these data and how ‘quality’ in qualitative research can be assessed. Approaches to participative action research and then discussed and described in the final section of the chapter.





Study designs and data collection methods


Ethnographic approaches and observation


	Ethnographers seek to immerse themselves in a study context to study ‘everyday’ activities and practices in their natural setting in order to develop a holistic, in-depth, understanding of the ‘way of life’ of a group, institution, and/or community. Denzin (Denzin 1989, p. 83) described this as producing a ‘thick description’, which:
	 	goes beyond mere fact and surface appearances. It presents details, context, emotions, and the webs of social relationships that join persons to one another. Thick description evokes emotionality and self-feeling. It inserts history into experience. It establishes the significance of an experience, or the sequence of events, for the person or persons in question. In thick descriptions, the voices, feelings, actions and meanings of interacting individuals are heard.
	Two ‘classic’ ethnographies in the health field are Asylums (Goffman’s (1961) study of a single mental hospital for which he posed as a member of staff for over a year) and Boys in White (Becker et al.’s 1961 study of medical education). Reading these studies, which have had profound impacts on health policy and practice, is a good way of becoming familiar with the methodology.
	Ethnographers used a range of methods but participant observation, where the observers are fully active members of the activities being studied is the central method of data collection. Observational approaches to data collection are, however, used in other study designs, often less intensively when the observer may be non-participant (maintaining distance by not having a formal role in the activities there). Observation typically involves the use of field diaries to record data, though video and audio recording may be used. Field notes are written up as soon as possible after the observation and include description of events that occurred (who, what, when, where, how), theoretical notes that try to derive meaning from the descriptive observation and notes on methodological issues that may impinge on the credibility of the research. As in all qualitative research observers are typically reflecting continually on the meaning of their observations during fieldwork and beginning to analyse by generating categories and ideas.
	The ethical challenges of being an observer have been a source of debate as have the methodological issues: researcher presence may change the context under investigation. Building trust between researcher and researched, important to the quality of all empirical research, is vital. However, a balance has to be struck between building trust, understanding issues through the eyes of the researched and maintaining a critical observer stance.





Interview-based studies


	Interviews are an almost ubiquitous element of qualitative research but they can take various forms: individuals or groups; short informal conversation or long sessions over many hours; one-off or longitudinal. They are a way of gaining a more ‘in-depth’ perspective on experiences than that provided by more structured forms of research (Olesen 1994). They are typically used to explore people’s understanding or experience of a phenomenon (e.g. poverty or housing quality), the meanings they attach to these experiences and the impact on their lives. An example of this type of research is Williams and Elliot’s Health Impact Analysis (Elliott and Williams 2008) of plans to demolish substandard housing in a South Wales community, which included a qualitative study involving both individual in-depth interviews and focus groups. The qualitative findings revealed that despite recognizing housing problems residents and local professionals were ambivalent and uncertain about the developments because of the potential disruption to social and family networks. Payment of expenses (travel and childcare) may often be necessary, especially for people on low incomes. However, payment of a fee as an inducement to participate in individual or group interviews, which is becoming more common, raises ethical questions. Some ethics committees are uncomfortable with the practice. In terms of validity, payment may encourage people to take part primarily to earn the money, possibly even claiming membership of a group in order to qualify.
	In-depth interviews are either unstructured (e.g. oral history or life history) or guided by a set of topics to be used flexibly with each interviewee. Interviewees are encouraged to express ideas and experiences in their own words, generating. ‘textual’ or ‘narrative’ data. Interviews are usually tape recorded and transcribed for analysis. Respondents are often selected purposively or ‘theoretically’ to reflect a range of experience of the phenomenon of interest (e.g. a health condition, an intervention, a place). Sample sizes vary but typically would be around 20–30 interviewees. Decisions about the style of interview to use will be influenced by the:
	 	• Topic of the research. More sensitive research topics (e.g. fertility) demand longer interviews than others.
	• Resources available. Long, in-depth interviews are costly to conduct, transcribe, and analyse. Tape recording is the preferred option (assuming respondents agree): responses can be handwritten but this is hard work as the interviewer also has to concentrate on maintaining eye contact and responding appropriately.
	• Tolerance of the interview group. In-depth interviews can be quite intrusive. People also have to give up time, possibly 2 or 3 hours. This may be easier for some people. Health professionals may be less willing, but older people are often more willing to spend time being interviewed.
	In-depth interviewing is a skilled process but all members of a team doing research involving in-depth interviews should do at least some of the interviewing. Textbooks dealing with in-depth interviewing contain a considerable amount of advice for researchers (Glesne and Peshkin 1992; Seidman 2005; Minichiello et al. 2008). It is important to consider issues of gender, culture, language, and social class when planning interviews and in addition to establishing rapport, researchers need to: be able to explain the purpose of the research clearly; to keep an open mind and see ‘the respondent as teacher’ (Glesne and Peshkin 1992, p. 81); to learn and adapt as the interviews proceed; and to adopt an analytical approach from the beginning of the research. In-depth interviewing has also been used to good effect to study policy processes such as Townsend et al. (2019) study of how paid parental leave was able to get in the policy agenda.
	Focus groups are interviews with groups of people on a particular focused issue typically for up to 2 hours. They are often used to develop questionnaires for quantitative research or to obtain participants interpretation of results from the analysis of other data/studies. Increasingly, however, they have been used as a self-contained means of qualitative data collection. For example, Davidson, Kitzinger, and Hunt (2006) used 14 focus group discussions in Scotland and the north of England to explore views on health inequalities among people from different socioeconomic background. Focus groups are also commonly used in health promotion needs assessment. Similarly, Cortie et al. (1996) used four focus groups (stratified according to low and high socioeconomic status and extent of physical activity) to determine the factors in a local community that determine people’s decision to exercise or not while Jacobs and Roberts (2004) used focus groups to collect data from health professionals on approaches to addressing malnutrition in Cambodia.
	As Brown et al. (1989, p. 40) comment focus group ‘are not just a convenient way to accumulate the individual knowledge of their members. They give rise synergistically to insights and solutions that would not come about without them’. They also enable participants to control the agenda and formulate opinions in a way that would not be possible in individual interviews (Morgan 1988, p. 28) and to explore topics in an open format at the beginning of research. Researchers also need to be aware of potential problems including:
	 	• ‘Group think’ which may discourage individuals from expressing opinions at odds with the majority: ‘devil’s advocates’ may overcome this tendency (MacDougall and Baum 1997).
	• Dominant individuals who can influence results: skilful moderation to minimize this risk is vital.
	• Less control by the researchers over the data that are generated.
	• Challenges associated with recording discussions.
	The number and size of focus groups will be determined by research goals and available resources. Krueger and Casey (2009) recommends using groups of between 5 and 10 but say size can be as few as 4 to as many as 12: the key point is that the group must be small enough for everyone to have an opportunity to provide insights and yet large enough to give a range of perceptions. As with individual interviews, the number of group interviews required to answer the research question cannot always be predicted in advance. It will also be necessary to decide how to divide the ‘population’. For instance, if gender is likely to be a significant variable, it may be appropriate to have separate groups for men and women. In an evaluation, more ‘honest’ discussion may ensure if for example the providers of services are in a separate group from users. The research topic will usually determine how easy it is to recruit people for focus groups. Generally, the more sensitive the topic, the more challenging is recruitment.
	As with all interviews, the quality of data obtained from focus groups is dependent on how they are run. Skills in facilitation, knowledge of groups dynamics and an understanding of the research area (so that interesting ‘leads’ are followed up in the discussion) are essential. For Morgan (1988) the role of the facilitator is to set up the group with instructions and then move to the side, intervening only if it goes badly off track. The venue will also be important: participants need to feel comfortable and relaxed and it needs to be suitable for achieving high-quality recordings. The data from a focus group are most easily recorded on audio tapes or digital media. It is usual to have one researcher facilitating the group and another taking notes. Depending on the research it may be sufficient to have a co-researcher take notes during the focus group, merely supplementing them with a recording but if more detailed content analysis is required then the recording would be transcribed verbatim. Focus group information, like other textual data, may be analysed according to its content and themes drawn out as discussed in the next section.





Case studies


	Case studies involve the systematic study of an individual, group or community, an institution, or an event with a view to understanding why something happens in a particular context. Typically case studies place less emphasis on members’ tacit knowledge than in ethnography, involve less intensive fieldwork, and are more likely to combine quantitative and qualitative methods. Data is usually collected from a variety of sources, including in-depth individual or group interviews, self-completion surveys, and documents. Single or multiple cases can be studied, they can be descriptive or explanatory and may involve testing hypotheses.
	Case studies were once seen as an exploratory phase of research, but are now widely accepted as evaluation tools in their own right (Stake 1995; Yin 2018). They are used extensively by development agencies such as the World Bank and US AID because ‘it is more desirable to have a few carefully done case studies with results one can trust than to aim for large, probabilistic, and generalizable samples with results that are dubious because of the multitude of technical, logistic and management problems in third world settings’ (Patton 1990, p. 100) Policymakers and politicians may relate to a case study and its story better than to a set of statistics so potentially increasing the likelihood that the research will be impactful. Combining statistics with case studies may be a particularly effective way of politicians. The Healthy Cities project is an international initiative based on the evaluation of international case studies. A summary evaluation of The Noarlunga Healthy Cities initiative (Baum et al. 2006a), for example, involving a narrative review of findings from a number of reported qualitative case studies of initiative activities and other project documents identified nine factors that lead to the initiative’s sustainability over 18 years. Case studies have also been used to study the extent to which primary healthcare services are comprehensive and highlight the value of comparative case studies (Baum et al. 2013).
	According to Yin (2018, pp. 242–7) criteria for exemplary case studies include: significance (i.e. focused on issues that are unusual and of general public interest, or important in theoretical, policy, or practical terms); completeness (i.e. having clear boundaries and giving full attention to all relevant evidence); consider alternative perspectives on how the data should be interpreted; provide a sufficiency of evidence to allow readers to judge the quality and robustness of conclusions; and use engaging approaches to dissemination, such as videos.





Document-based research


	The collation and analysis of documents (such as minutes of meetings, annual reports, newspapers, etc.) is a valuable method in qualitative research. They can provide a ‘particularly rich source of information about many organizations and programs’ (Patton 2014, p. 176), and are often used in combination with other methods (Bowen 2009). Document analysis has been used to assess uptake of research evidence in health policies (Flitcroft et al. 2011; Rosella et al. 2013) and the extent to which health policies address equity issues (Keleher 2013), and is emerging as a method to assess uptake of evidence on social determinants of health and health inequities (Pinto et al. 2012; Borrell et al. 2013; Fisher et al. 2014). Document analysis is also highly relevant to the commercial determinants of health, Anaf et al. (2017; see also Anaf et al. 2019) were able to conduct corporate health impact assessments by referring to company annual reports, other corporate documents, and media analysis.
	Diaries/autobiographies are a particular form of documents used in qualitative research. Some studies make use of existing diaries other require participants to keep a diary for a set period focusing on key events they judge to be memorable. The method is particularly good for longitudinal data collection where recall may be a challenge, and where repeated interviews are not feasible. Diaries may be more or less structured and may be paper-based, computer based, or online blogs. The data are likely to be analysed in the same way as an interview transcript.





Sampling in qualitative research


	The rationale for sampling in qualitative studies is purposive rather than random as in quantitative research. The aim is to select cases that will provide the most relevant and richest data. For this reason, as Kuzel (1992, p. 41) notes:
	 	• the sample can be adjusted as the theory develops, the aim being to thoroughly explore the topic of interest and to consider as many different angles and perspectives as possible. Glaser and Strauss (1967) refer to this as ‘theoretical sampling’;
	• people/cases are selected serially and sampling continues until little new information is gained (referred to as saturation);
	• ‘negative or deviant cases’ are searched for to test ideas emerging from the analysis.
	‘Snowball sampling’ is common. It involves contacting a few members of the group that is the focus of the research, and asking them to help find others. This technique is particularly useful for reaching groups that are not readily identifiable, such as illicit drug users or voluntarily childless people. Researchers may also have to advertise. As already noted, sample size depends on what you want to know, what will be useful, what will have credibility, and what can be done with available time and resources (Patton 2014, p. 311). However, as a rule of thumb, six to eight data sources or sampling units will often be sufficient where the group is homogeneous, while up to 20 might be needed when looking for disconfirming evidence or trying to achieve maximum variation (Lincoln and Guba 1985; Patton 1990; Kuzel 1992). Qualitative researchers may be asked to specify their sample size in advance because of the requirements of a research funding body. The crucial feature is the logic underlying the sampling strategy, as this is the main criterion used to judge the strength of the sampling method. A proposal should be able to describe the sampling strategy clearly, state the selection criteria and provide an approximation of the sample size (National Health & Medical Research Council 2007).





Analysing qualitative textual data


	In qualitative research analysis is the point at which data and theory are brought together to try and generate new understandings and explanations of social phenomena. Two elements in the analysis process can be distinguished: the purpose (what is being sought) and the practice (how it is done).





The purpose of data analysis


	Although visual or audio data may be collected most qualitative research produces textual data, which typically comprise a mix of field or observational notes and transcripts from interviews or focus groups. Some examples of different approaches to analysis of these data are summarized next, but the key point is that the choice of approach to data analysis should be driven by the purpose of the research. For example, a narrative, life history, discourse, or conversation analysis can be conducted on the same extract from an interview, hence the importance of surfacing researcher standpoint and the theory driving a particular piece of research.
	Content analysis: looks at the way themes and issues arise across texts (including interview transcriptions). Analysis may focus on the context, frequency, and/or how themes are patterned by e.g. gender or ethnicity. This is a descriptive level of analysis.
	Narrative analysis: looks at the way a person constructs a ‘story’ in the light of the audience and their purpose for giving the account. There is a focus on language, imagery, metaphor, and rhetorical purpose in the story being told.
	Conversation analysis (CA): focuses on the structure of communication and conversation management such as turn taking or pausing. The aim is to reveal how meaning is constructed in interaction. CA is very specialized and marks both words spoken and how conversation proceeds (for example intonation).
	Discourse analysis: explores the way knowledge is produced in particular contexts through the use of specialized language or theories and through performances, interaction, and rhetorical devices used to persuade. A range of texts can be subjected to discourse analysis (e.g. interview transcripts, video, letters, policy documents).





The practice of data analysis


	In the broadest terms qualitative data analysis (QDA) involves the imposition of meaning and interpretation on mainly textual, usually unstructured, and unwieldy data. There are several schools of thought about methods of QDA but three theoretical traditions are particularly significant: interpretivism, social anthropology and collaborative research (Miles and Huberman 1994, p. 8). Interpretivism emphasizes the meaning of the data, and works from the premise that researchers’ perceptions and understanding are affected by, and affect, the process of research. Included within this general tradition are ethnomethodologists, phenomenologists, deconstructionists, and discourse analysts. Social anthropology, including ethnography, focuses more on the accuracy of description and less on the conceptual or theoretical meaning of the observations. There is an interest in ‘discovering’ the underlying patterns or rules in a situation, which often begins with a theory that is tested during analysis. Within this broad tradition come researchers in life history, grounded theory, and much applied qualitative research and evaluation in education and health. Finally, there is collaborative research, in which analysis is either through reflective (questioning) or dialectic (opposing) enquiry with the research participants interspersed with further rounds of data collection.
	Not-with-standing these different traditions, QDA always involves two distinct processes: description and interpretation, with the former comprising the identification of themes, concepts and categories in order to develop ideas or ‘theories’ about the data and relationships within it. There are many textbooks describing specific approaches to qualitative data but the Framework Analysis developed in the 1980s by applied qualitative researchers Ritchie and Spencer (1994) in 1994 and updated in 2011 is now extensively used. This involves the five stages briefly described next.
	Familiarization with the range and diversity of data collected. A selection of the data should be read and (if recorded) listened to. Key ideas and themes should be listed.
	Identifying a thematic framework within which textual data can be sifted and sorted. The framework should draw upon the original research ideas, theories informing the research, issues raised by respondents and themes identified during familiarization.
	Indexing is the process whereby the thematic framework is applied to the data. Each transcript or set of field notes is coded by reference to the themes, usually using a computer package. A commonly used package is NVIVO (Bazeley and Jackson 2013). The system of annotating the text means the process is visible and accessible to others, and can be checked by two or more researchers.
	Charting refers to the process of taking the data from its original context and rearranging it according to the appropriate thematic reference. Data are usually analysed by considering each theme across all respondents/cases. Charts can be produced manually but computer packages can also be used to compile all the data relating to a particular theme, which is then available for further analysis.
	Mapping and interpretation involve reviewing the themes, comparing accounts and experiences, searching for patterns and connections, and seeking explanations for them within the data: processes that require ‘leaps of intuition and imagination’ (Ritchie and Spencer 1994, p. 186).
	The use of computer packages is now common in QDA. Importantly, however, the intellectual work of description and interpretation is the responsibility of the researcher. Software cannot conduct analysis: it is simply a tool that can help make the analytical process more systematic by helping to:
	 	• Manage and keep track of all data including raw data files from interviews, survey and focus groups, or field observations, images, diagrams, audio, video, web pages, policy documents, ideas recorded as memos.
	• Organize and provide rapid access to conceptual and theoretical knowledge you generate.
	• Retrieving all relevant information from your data base in response to questions you pose. Queries can be saves and so becomes part of an ongoing enquiry process.
	• Visualize data to show the content of cases, ideas, concepts timelines, etc. and to represent these relationships visually.
	• Report from the data: including information about the original data source, the ideas and knowledge developed from them and the processes by which outcomes were reached (Bazeley and Jackson 2013, p. 3).





Assessing the quality of qualitative research


	Validity, reliability, and generalisability are concepts that enable the value of positivist research to be judged. There is uncertainty in the literature about the extent to which these concepts can be applied to qualitative research. Kirk and Miller (1986) argue that they can be adapted to qualitative research methods, but others suggest alternative terms. Lincoln and Guba (1985) suggest using the terms ‘credibility’, ‘transferability’, ‘dependability’, and ‘confirmability’.
	Credibility: Patton (2014) suggests this can be determined by reference to:
	 	• the rigour of the techniques and methods used
	• the credibility of the researcher (e.g. training, experience, track record, and status)
	• the philosophical orientation and assumptions that underpinned the study.
	Triangulation can be a useful way of increasing the credibility of qualitative research. Denzin (1978) originally defined four types of triangulation:
	 	• data source triangulation—the use of a variety of data sources
	• researcher triangulation—the use of several different researchers or evaluators
	• theory triangulation—the use of multiple theoretical perspectives to interpret the same data
	• methodological triangulation—the use of multiple methods to study a particular problem.
	To these Janesick (1994) adds a fifth type, which is relevant to public health:
	 	• interdisciplinary triangulation—having researchers from a variety of professions. This can be extended to include non-researchers who have an interest in the findings of research, such as residents of neighbourhoods receiving interventions that are being evaluated.
	The analysis of negative cases that do not fit broader patterns identified in the data is also an important way of increasing credibility. Patton (2014, p. 656) comments: ‘Dealing openly with the complexities and dilemmas posed by negative cases is both intellectually honest and politically strategic.’
	Transferability refers to the ability of qualitative researchers to extend their findings to other settings. Lincoln and Guba (1985) suggest that research reports should provide sufficient detail (about methods, parameter, setting) for other researchers and users to make judgements about transferability. The use of theory in qualitative research is central to its transferability: Hilary Graham’s (1994) research re-conceptualizing smoking among poor white women in England as a coping mechanism rather than a health damaging behaviour is an example of how the findings from qualitative research can be generalized on the basis of theory.
	Dependability and reliability refer to whether the research is likely to be consistent over time and across researchers and methods and should be considered at all stages of the research. The reliability of data depends on skills in interviewing, observing, and recording. Analysis procedures, such as having two people involving in coding of data to themes, are likely to increase the reliability of interpretation.
	Confirmability refers to the need to confirm research results with a source outside the research team and overlaps with interdisciplinary triangulation discussed earlier. De Laine (1997, p. 279) suggests that an ‘audit trail’ of sampling decisions, methods of recording, analysis, coding, construction of themes, and personal notes would enable an outsider to follow the logic of each stage and understand how and why the researchers had drawn the conclusions they had.
	There are, therefore, distinct ways of assessing qualitative research, but it is still common for the validity and reliability of public health qualitative research to be called into question by those who consider it to be subjective, and so invalid and unreliable. The issue of subjectivity and objectivity in science has been extensively debated by science philosophers, and today there are few who still maintain that positivist science is as objective as it was once thought to be, and there is broad acceptance that qualitative data can make a crucial contribution to aspects of public health. Patton (2014, p. 58) takes a pragmatic position that appears also to make sense for public health when he suggests we ‘stay out of futile debate about subjectivity versus objectivity’.





Participatory action research


	As we discussed earlier, participatory approaches are embedded in a broader movement to democratize the research process and to contribute to greater social justice. These approaches, which are not confined to qualitative research, challenge the privileged position of the professional researcher. They have drawn on the work of the adult educator Paulo Freire (1972) and place as much emphasis on the process as on the product of research.
	The term ‘action research’ is often used interchangeably with participatory research; but sometimes the two are combined into ‘participatory action research’ (PAR). In medical and public health circles action research has received more attention in recent years but it had its origins in the work of educationists during the 1940s, particularly the work of the North American Kurt Lewin and it is now an accepted and respected research tradition in educational and management research (McTaggart 1991).
	Drawing on the work of Minkler and Wallerstein (2003) and Grbich (1999) Baum et al. (2006b) define PAR as an approach that seeks to understand and improve the world by changing it. At its heart it is collective, self-reflective enquiry that researchers and researched undertake together so they can understand and improve upon the practices in which they participate and/or the situations in which they find themselves. The reflective process is directly linked to action, influenced by understanding of history, culture, and local context and embedded in social relationships. The process of PAR should be empowering and lead to people having increased control over their lives. PAR pay careful attention to power relationships, advocating for power to be deliberately shared between researcher and researched: blurring the line between them until the researched becomes the researcher. The researched cease to be objects and become partners in the whole research process: including selecting the research topic, data collection, and analysis and deciding what action should happen as a result of the research findings. PAR may use a range of qualitative and quantitative approaches to data collection.
	PAR is therefore a process that includes the generation of knowledge alongside ‘education and development of consciousness and of mobilisation’ (Gaventa 1988, p. 19). Some of the most exciting experimentation with participatory research has been in low-income countries where there is a potential to raise people’s consciousness and encourage them to become involved in actions that could liberate them from poverty and despair. Bloem and colleagues (1996), for example, describe the development of the People’s Participatory Planning (PPP) process by a non-government organization in Bangladesh in 1990. These authors stress that the PPP is not a universal panacea but overall they conclude that ‘the continual process of reflection and action can enable people to change and transform from one level of functioning to another’ (1996, p. 150). Similar conclusions were reached by Howard-Grabman (1996) in her analysis of a PAR designed to address maternal and neonatal health problems in rural Bolivia. The involvement of men and women in the project led to the development of new reproductive health practices that have seen maternal, perinatal, and neonatal mortality decline in the communities that were part of the project. Similarly, the PAR study by Hague and colleagues (2011), which found that the practice of paying for wives in rural Uganda was associated with increased domestic violence and male power over women, developed skills and capacity at the local level and made recommendations for strategies for action at both the national and the local level.
	PAR does not require the researcher to downplay their specialist knowledge but to use that knowledge in dialogue with the expert knowledge of participants in the research process. As Reason (1994, p. 328) argued ‘it is through dialogue that the subject–object relationship of traditional science gives way to a subject–subject one, in which the academic knowledge of formally educated people works in a dialectic tension with the popular knowledge of the people to produce a more profound understanding of the situation’. Similarly, PAR must avoid eulogizing the potential contribution of research participants. Just as professional researcher perspectives must be subject to critical reflection, so too must those of participants through a rigorous process of ‘critical subjectivity’ to arrive at new forms of interpretation and knowledge (Reason 1994, p. 333).
	The practice of PAR presents dilemmas in the public health domain as it does in other fields. Boutilier, Mason, and Rootman (1997, p. 76) describe a number of these and suggest that key issues to be resolved in the practice of what they call ‘community reflective action research’ relate to: whose knowledge is valued; who owns the research; why the research is being done; and recognition of the complementary skills of lay people, researchers, and practitioners. Community participation and control of research processes may also lead to tensions with the demands of scientific rigour (Allison and Rootman 1996), as participants are generally not experts in research or primarily interested in the validity of research. These tensions should be addressed so that evaluations are scientifically acceptable and ethically participatory but they are not easy to reconcile. Inevitably, then, the processes of negotiation in participatory action research can be long and complicated and may in turn conflict with the needs of funding bodies. The key point is that PAR creates new dialogical spaces in which experiential knowledge is taken seriously: contributing to the creation of a democratic public health science that builds knowledge and understanding about population health and health equity through ‘narratives of living and being’.





New directions in qualitative research


	Qualitative public health researchers have recently begun to think of more creative ways in which to engage with and represent the experiences of people and communities by, for example, working more closely with the arts and new methods including photovoice, digital storytelling and poetry which have been used to engage homeless women in research (Walsh et al. 2010). These kinds of initiatives are asking us to ‘imagine’ what cultural representations of population health and health inequity might look like, beyond the graph and the quote and they point to ways in which public health research might take more seriously the knowledge and concerns of local publics (Burawoy 2005). Working inside the fabric of everyday life can reveal the complex relationships between private troubles and local, national, and global public forces more clearly, illuminating the limits of behaviour change and demonstrating the value of experiential knowledge. This surely offers the hope of public health research with a stronger connection to broader social and political action in today’s increasingly unequal, unjust social systems.





Conclusion


	Qualitative research is vital to the study of global public health. Although primarily emanating from social epidemiology, public health research is increasingly utilizing more integrative approaches to explanation bringing together insights from different disciplines. Qualitative research has a key role to play in this context by opening up new theoretically informed analyses of the relationships between individual lives and social structures, including ‘materially-informed’ ways of thinking about the contribution of ‘individual lifestyle’ factors to health inequalities (Bartley 2004). Qualitative data can add depth to our understanding of the nature and impacts of the relationships between the social, commercial, and political determinants of population health and health inequalities described in quantitative research. Qualitative research can open up understanding of what things mean to people, what drives them to act (or not) in the situations they are in (Sayer 2011). Much public health research neglects the particulars of people’s situation and the knowledge they develop and utilize to deal with these situations. Importantly, good quality qualitative research makes theoretical connections from these ‘particulars’ to more general social structures and processes. This is illustrated by our earlier example of qualitative research in which the concept of smoking as a coping mechanism was developed to demonstrate how white working-class women caring for children while living in poverty relied on a cigarette to help them manage very stressful situations (Graham 1994). By making these connections (in this case between smoking and coping with poverty) and involving people as partners in the research process qualitative research can support public health practitioners and policymakers and the public more widely to develop new forms of solidarity: to ‘imagine’ and implement mechanisms for personal and collective change that will contribute to improving health and reducing inequities (Elliot et al. 2015)
