5.7


Methodological issues in the design and analysis of cluster randomized trials


	Kathy J. Baisley, Richard J. Hayes, and Lawrence H. Moulton





Introduction


	Randomized controlled trials are the accepted gold standard for evaluating the effects of interventions to improve health. In the majority of such trials, individuals are randomly allocated to the experimental conditions under study, for example, to treatment and control arms. However, in some situations it is more appropriate to randomly allocate groups of individuals to the treatment arms. These groups are referred to as clusters, and trials of this kind are known as cluster randomized trials (CRTs). Examples of clusters include schools, villages, workplaces, or health facilities, but there are many other possible choices. In some CRTs, all individuals within the selected clusters are automatically included. In others, there may be additional eligibility criteria. Similarly, the impact of the intervention may be measured in all individuals in the cluster, or in a random subsample. This chapter aims to discuss methodological issues that arise in the design and analysis of CRTs. Some of the content has been condensed from the textbook by Hayes and Moulton (2017).
	There are a number of reasons for using a cluster randomized design. Some interventions by their nature have to be implemented at the cluster level, such as an intervention to improve water supplies in villages. Others could in principle be implemented at the individual level, but cluster randomization may offer greater logistical convenience, or may be more acceptable to the community. Cluster randomization may help avoid contamination, where individuals in one treatment arm are exposed to or receive the treatment assigned to the other arm. CRTs are also the best design to capture the population-level effects of an intervention applied to a large proportion of a population. For example, a CRT in Uganda evaluated the effect of intermittent preventive treatment (IPT) for malaria in school children (Staedke et al. 2018). Each cluster included one primary school and 100 surrounding households. The main trial outcome was malaria parasite prevalence in the community, measured in a random sample of households in each cluster.
	When considering a cluster randomized design, the advantages need to be weighed against the limitations. The power and precision of a CRT is lower than for an individually randomized trial of the same size, and the logistical aspects of working in several different clusters may make a CRT expensive to implement. Other issues to consider are selection bias, imbalance between study arms, and generalisability, which will be discussed in this chapter.
	CRTs have become increasingly more common in health research. In the early years, the special design and analysis requirements of these trials were not always understood, and there were many trials that were designed, analysed, or reported inappropriately. However, over the past two decades, much work has been done on methods for CRTs, and the quality of these trials has improved.





Methodological implications of cluster randomization


	The design and analysis of individually randomized trials rely on individual observations being independent of one another. However, when observations are naturally grouped within clusters, this assumption of independence is violated, since observations on individuals in the same cluster are usually correlated. That is, responses among individuals in one cluster will tend to resemble each other more than the responses of individuals in different clusters. This phenomenon is termed within-cluster correlation. It can be equivalently viewed as between-cluster variation, which reflects the natural variation among clusters that exists even in the absence of an intervention effect. Therefore, within-cluster correlation and between-cluster variation can be thought of as corresponding concepts that provide two different perspectives on the same underlying phenomenon.
	Within-cluster correlation, or equivalently between-cluster variation, can occur in CRTs for three main reasons. The first reason is the most obvious, which is that health conditions tend to vary between populations, owing to differences in the individuals that make up each cluster or differences in geographical or environmental characteristics of the cluster. A perhaps less obvious point is that different clusters may respond differently to the intervention, so that there may be no between-cluster variation in the outcome of interest before the intervention, but significant between-cluster variation after the intervention is introduced. The final reason that health outcomes may be clustered is due to interactions between members of the cluster. For example, in interventions against infectious diseases, the effect of an intervention in one individual may affect the risk of contracting the disease in other individuals in the same cluster.
	The correlated nature of the data from CRTs requires careful thought at the design stage to ensure sufficient information is collected. As a result of this correlation, CRTs require larger sample sizes than conventional individually randomized trials to be adequately powered to detect treatment effects, and to obtain sufficiently precise estimates of the treatment effect.
	Since standard statistical techniques rely on the independence of individual observations, we cannot use these methods to analyse data from a CRT. Using standard statistical techniques will result in p-values that are too small and confidence intervals for the treatment effect that are too narrow. Instead, analysis techniques that account for between-cluster variability are required to analyse CRTs.





Measures of between-cluster variability


	There are two main measures of between-cluster variability, corresponding to the two ways of viewing this phenomenon: the coefficient of variation between clusters (k) and the intracluster correlation coefficient (ICC).
	Consider a CRT in which a quantitative variable, for example systolic blood pressure, is measured on each individual. The parameter of interest is the mean, μ. Suppose there are c clusters, and that the true value of the mean in the jth cluster is given by μj. We assume that the μj are randomly sampled from a probability distribution with mean E(μj) = μ and variance Var(μj) = , where represents the between-cluster variance. Then the coefficient of variation is defined as:
	If the parameter of interest is a proportion or rate, μ is replaced by π or λ, the true value of the proportion or rate, respectively. It is important to recognize that the μj represent the true value of the mean in a notional wider population in each of the c clusters. The μj are not directly observable, since we collect data only on a finite sample of individuals in each cluster. However, it is possible to use the observed values of the mean in each cluster to obtain valid estimates of , μ, and hence k, as we describe in a later section.
	The ICC, usually denoted by the Greek letter ρ, represents how much more similar outcomes are in individuals from the same cluster compared with individuals from different cluster. Another way of describing the ICC is to say that it measures the proportion of the total variance in the outcome that may be attributed to between-cluster variation. The ICC is calculated differently depending on the outcome of interest. The methods for quantitative and binary outcomes are described next. The ICC is not defined for a rate; therefore, k is used to estimate between-cluster variability when outcomes are event rates.
	For quantitative outcomes, the ICC is defined as:
	where is the between-cluster variance and is the within-cluster variance.
	For binary outcomes, where an individual either does or does not satisfy a certain condition (for example, has hypertension or does not), the objective is usually to compare the proportion of individuals with the outcome. The ICC for binary outcomes is defined as:
	where π is the true proportion for the entire population, and is the variance of the cluster-specific true proportions.
	In general the ICC will fall between zero and one. An ICC of zero implies that there is no clustering, so that individuals within the same cluster are no more similar to each other than to individuals from different clusters, in other words, there is no between-cluster variability. An ICC of one implies that individuals in the same cluster are perfectly correlated, in other words they all have the same outcome, and there is no within-cluster variability.





Design effect and effective sample size


	A CRT can be considered equivalent to collecting data from a cluster sample of individuals, rather than a simple random sample as in a conventional individually randomized trial. Cluster sampling provides less precise estimates of parameters of interest than simple random sampling. The increase in variance can be measured by the design effect (DEff) (Kish 1965):
	Since the variance for a simple random sample is inversely proportional to the sample size, the design effect also gives the effective sample size for the cluster sampling design:
	For example, if DEff = 2, this means that the cluster sample will provide the same precision as a simple random sample of half the size.
	DEff can be calculated from the ICC as follows:
	where m is the number of individuals per cluster.
	From this, we can see that the impact of clustering in a trial depends not only on the value of the ICC, but also on the size of the clusters. DEff may be substantial when we have large clusters, even if the ICC is small. A further discussion of the relationship between DEff, the ICC, and k, can be found in Hayes and Moulton (2017, pp. 19–22). A detailed discussion of how to account for the impact of clustering in sample size calculations and analyses is presented in later sections of this chapter.





Experimental and observational units


	The key difference between a CRT and an individually randomized trial is that the intervention is randomly allocated to clusters of individuals rather than to individual participants. The cluster therefore constitutes the experimental unit in a CRT. While the cluster is always the experimental unit, observations may be made at different levels so there may be several types of observational unit. In the simplest case, observations may be made only on the individual participants in each cluster. More often, data will also be collected on cluster-level variables and, in some CRTs, there may also be intermediate levels of observation. For example, in a CRT of a school-based health education programme, in which the intervention is randomly allocated to schools, units of observation might include the individual student (e.g. age, sex), class (e.g. grade, size, number of students, number of sessions delivered), and school (e.g. urban/rural, type of school, size of school). Data from all these levels may be used when making inferences about the main parameters of interest.





Design considerations in CRTs


Choice of cluster type and size


	One of the first decisions when designing a CRT relates to the choice and definition of the clusters that are to be randomized. In practice, trials have used a wide variety of cluster types, ranging from CRTs of families or households, with only a few individuals in each cluster, to CRTs of large geographical regions in which each cluster may include millions of individuals. While the general principles of CRT design may be similar for these widely varying situations, the practical aspects of implementing such trials are clearly very different.
	Having decided on the type of cluster that will be randomized, the investigator may still have some latitude in choosing the cluster size. This is particularly the case with geographical clusters, where arbitrary boundaries may be drawn. Even when we have institutional clusters, however, there may be some flexibility—for example to group neighbouring schools or health facilities into one cluster.
	A number of factors may be considered when deciding on cluster size. The formula for DEff shows that, for a given total sample size, precision is maximized with a cluster size of m = 1, corresponding to individual randomization. Assuming the ICC remains constant, DEff increases with cluster size. This implies that a large number of small clusters is statistically more efficient than a small number of larger clusters. By statistical efficiency, we mean that our estimate of the intervention effect will be more precise. However, in practice the ICC may not remain constant, and generally tends to decrease with increasing cluster size. For example, suppose the choice is between randomizing towns or neighbourhoods. There may be substantial variation in health outcomes between neighbourhoods, owing in part to socioeconomic differences. However, since each town is likely to have a mix of neighbourhoods of higher and lower socioeconomic status, the differences may average out so that there is little variation in the outcome between towns. As a result, the ICC may be larger for neighbourhoods than for towns. Thus it is important to have estimates of the ICC or k which relate to the types and sizes of cluster under consideration, when estimating the sample size of a CRT.
	Statistical issues are not the only consideration when deciding on cluster size. Although designs using a large number of small clusters are statistically more efficient, it may be logistically and financially more feasible to carry out field work in a smaller number of large clusters. The relative cost and feasibility of designs based on different cluster sizes will depend critically on the type of cluster and geographical setting.
	Contamination is another consideration in the choice of cluster size. Contamination can occur through contacts between intervention and control clusters, or through contacts between intervention clusters or control clusters and the wider population. In general, contamination is likely to decrease as cluster size increases. Rates of travel and migration across area boundaries generally decrease as the size of the area increases. Edge effects are also likely to diminish with the size of the cluster, since the proportion of the population living close to the boundary of an area decreases as the area is increased.
	One of the main strategies for reducing contamination in a CRT is to select clusters that are well-separated. This is particularly useful for reducing the level of contact between intervention and control clusters. The separation needed will depend on the intervention under study, for example, much greater geographical separation may be needed for a mass media intervention. Investigators have sometimes specified that the trial clusters should be separated by buffer zones, so that there is little or no common boundary between any two clusters. Additional strategies may be needed to reduce contact between trial clusters and the wider population.
	For example, a CRT in rural Burkina Faso evaluated the effect of a comprehensive radio campaign on key family behaviours for improving child survival (Sarrassat et al. 2018). Clusters were 14 distinct geographical areas, each centred around a community radio station, and comprising sufficient villages to provide a total population of around 40,000 per cluster. Clusters were identified using digital terrain maps, on-the-ground mapping of radio signal strength, and surveys to assess radio listenership. Clusters were selected based on their high radio listenership (>60% of women listening to the radio in the past week), and to have little or no overlap of radio signal between areas to minimize contamination.





Baseline imbalance between trial arms


	In individually randomized trials with a large number of participants, we can rely on the randomization process to provide study arms that are similar with respect to all potential confounding factors. In CRTs, owing to practical and financial constraints, the number of clusters randomized is often quite small, for example, 20 or 30. In these circumstances, randomization still has the advantages of impartiality, transparency, and justification for statistical inference as it does in individually randomized trials. However, with such a small number of randomization units, it is quite likely that there will be some imbalance on one or more potential confounding factors. While these factors can be adjusted for in the analysis, the credibility of the trial results may be weakened in the presence of such imbalances; therefore investigators may choose to employ matching, stratification, or restricted (covariate-constrained) randomization to improve baseline balance.





Matching


	Matching involves grouping clusters that are similar with respect to certain pre-defined characteristics, then randomizing one cluster in each group to each of the treatment arms. If there are two treatment arms in the CRT, clusters are grouped into matched pairs and one cluster in each pair is randomly allocated to each treatment arm. Matched trials with three treatment arms involve identifying matched triplets and so on. Matching can help to minimize differences between treatment arms with respect to baseline characteristics, and can improve the precision and power of a CRT, since it can reduce between-cluster variability in the outcome of interest.
	For example, an HIV prevention trial reported by Grosskurth et al. (1995) was carried out in 12 communities in Mwanza, Tanzania that included rural villages, settlements along a major road, and villages along the shore of Lake Victoria. Baseline HIV prevalence in these communities varied from 1.6 to 8.6%, and the primary outcome (HIV incidence) was expected to be similarly variable. When such high levels of between-cluster variability exist, the coefficient of variation in the outcome is large, which reduces the power of the trial for a given sample size. Therefore, the trial communities were grouped into matched pairs, based on baseline HIV prevalence and geographical characteristics. This helped to ensure that the two arms were similar with respect to these factors at baseline, and it was presumed that they would therefore be more similar with respect to the primary outcome. A matched analysis was employed by comparing the outcome between the intervention and control communities within matched pairs. Since the variance in the outcome within matched pairs may be considerably smaller than the overall variance, replacing the overall coefficient of variation k with the coefficient of variation within matched pairs, km, may increase the power of a trial to detect a treatment effect.
	However, there are several important disadvantages to matching. Matching is most effective if the matching variables are highly correlated with the outcome variable. In the Mwanza trial, the matching correlation coefficient was 0.94. However, this level of success in pair-matching is unusual, and indeed in some trials, efficiency may even be lost relative to that of an unmatched design. This is because of the loss of degrees of freedom associated with a matched analysis. For example, to test for an effect of the intervention, a CRT with c matched pairs of clusters is typically analysed using a paired t-test with c − 1 degrees of freedom. This is half the 2(c − 1) degrees of freedom available for an unpaired t-test. The power to show an intervention effect will depend on both the value of the t-statistic and the critical value of the t distribution, which in turn depends on the degrees of freedom. It has been shown that below a particular break-even value of the matching correlation coefficient, an unmatched design will have higher power than a matched design, because the loss in degrees of freedom will outweigh the reduction in variance (Martin et al. 1993; Hayes and Moulton 2017, pp. 80–1).
	Matching may also present problems if an entire cluster drops out of the trial. Such drop-out also reduces the power and precision of an unmatched CRT and raises questions over selection bias. However, in a matched CRT, the entire matched pair is lost, since the remaining cluster no longer has a matched cluster for comparison.
	Another disadvantage of the matched design is that it is not possible to assess whether the intervention effect varies between matched sets. This is because the difference in outcomes between clusters in a matched set depends on both the intervention effect and the intrinsic between-cluster variability within that matched set. It is impossible to separate out these two effects without making additional assumptions. This difficulty results from the lack of replication within each matched set, meaning that there is only one cluster per treatment arm in each matched set. Therefore, it is not possible to calculate the ICC or k based on data from a matched trial (unless additional assumptions are made), because the between-cluster variability is confounded with variation in the intervention effect. Although matched trials can still be analysed without an estimate of the ICC or k, the lack of a good estimate of between-cluster variation may be a limitation when investigators are calculating sample sizes for future trials.





Stratification


	Stratification is a less rigid method than matching for reducing baseline imbalance between treatment arms and reducing between-cluster variability. Stratification involves grouping clusters with similar characteristics into strata, then randomizing more than one cluster in each stratum to each treatment arm. Thus, unlike matching, stratification achieves replication within strata, which overcomes the main disadvantages of matching. For example, the HIV Treatment as Prevention (TasP) trial in rural South Africa used a stratified design to allocate 34 communities to either the intervention or control arms (Iwuji et al. 2013). The investigators created six strata on the basis of antenatal HIV prevalence. Within each stratum, communities were then randomly allocated to the two trial arms.





Restricted randomization


	Although matching and stratification may help reduce imbalances between the treatment arms, they are less useful if balance is required on a large number of variables. In these circumstances, restricted (covariate-constrained) randomization can be used to ensure an acceptable level of overall balance on a number of variables. This method uses baseline or pre-existing data from each cluster to generate a subset of possible allocations that satisfy certain predetermined balance criteria (Raab and Butcher 2001; Moulton 2004). One allocation is then randomly selected from this restricted subset. For example, the ZAMSTAR trial of a tuberculosis control intervention in Zambia and South Africa used both restricted randomization and stratification to randomly allocate 24 clusters to four intervention groups (Sismanidis et al. 2008). Stratification was by country and tuberculous infection prevalence and restricted randomization was by tuberculous infection prevalence, HIV prevalence, urban/rural, social context, and geographical location. A further overview of matching, stratification, and restricted randomization for achieving baseline balance in CRTs is provided by Ivers et al. (2012).





Choice of design strategy


	Matching and stratification are designed to achieve baseline balance and reduce between-cluster variability, so thus improve power and precision. In contrast, restricted randomization is mainly intended to achieve baseline balance.
	Matching has been most commonly used for CRTs with a small number of clusters per arm (fewer than 10–15). Unfortunately, while matching is likely to improve balance, it may reduce the power and precision of the trial if the matching is ineffective. In contrast, stratification loses fewer degrees of freedom, so power and precision are more likely to be maximized. In trials with a small number of clusters, care should be taken to limit the number of strata: as a general rule, no more than two strata should be used in trials with ≤6 clusters per arm. Although stratification loses fewer degrees of freedom compared with matching, it is less likely to achieve close balance. In particular, if balance is sought on a large number of variables, the number of strata required would result in a large loss of degrees of freedom. In this situation, restricted randomization would be more effective in achieving balance.
	Baseline balance is more likely in trials with larger numbers of clusters. However matching and stratification may still be useful to improve power and precision. In trials with many clusters, the loss of degrees of freedom has very little effect, so either method can be an effective design. In most practical situations, it is likely that stratification (with, say, three or four strata) will capture most of the additional power provided by matching unless there are matching factors that are very closely related to the endpoints of interest. Box 5.7.1 provides a summary of important points for CRT design.
	 	Box 5.7.1 Summary of important points for CRT design
	 	• In CRTs, the intervention is randomly allocated to groups of individuals, rather than individual participants
	• Observations in the same cluster are correlated; therefore, CRTs require larger overall sample sizes than individually randomized trials
	• The degree to which observations are correlated can be measured by k or the ICC
	• The design effect (DEff) measures the impact of clustering on sample size
	• CRTs often randomize a small number of clusters, so are susceptible to baseline imbalance
	• Matching, stratification, and restricted randomization can be used to help ensure balance
	• Matching and stratification may also improve power and precision
	• However, if the matching is ineffective, power and precision may be reduced in a matched CRT





Alternative trial designs


	Most CRTs involve the randomization of clusters to two parallel treatment arms. A number of alternative CRT designs exist, and may be advantageous in certain situations. However, the analysis and interpretation of trials with these alternative designs are not always straightforward. Investigators would generally be advised to use simpler deigns unless there are convincing reasons for using these more complex designs.
	Factorial designs allow the study of the independent effects of two interventions in the same trial. This has the advantage of being cost effective, and conserving sample size. The design most commonly used in CRTs takes a 2 × 2 layout resulting in four treatment arms: one arm receiving the first intervention, another receiving the second intervention, an arm receiving both interventions, and a control arm. For example, the ZAMSTAR trial evaluated enhanced tuberculosis (TB) case-finding (ECF) and a household intervention (HH) including TB screening and preventive treatment (Sismanidis et al. 2008). Clusters were randomly allocated to one of four arms: ECF, HH, both ECF and HH (ECF + HH), or control. The effect of ECF was assessed by combining the ECF and ECF + HH arms and comparing them with the combined HH and control arms. The effect of HH was assessed in a similar manner. This approach is only valid if there is no interaction between the interventions. Where interactions are expected, factorial designs can be used to identify the joint effect of two interventions; however, larger sample sizes will be required.
	The crossover design is commonly used in individually randomized trials, and has been adopted for CRTs. Each cluster receives two interventions, one after the other, in an order determined at random (Parienti and Kuss 2007). Delivery of the two interventions is separated by a washout period, to avoid any ‘carry-over’ effects. Since each cluster serves as its own control, the design has potentially greater efficiency than a parallel group CRT. However, its validity depends on the assumption that carry-over effects are absent, that is, that the estimated effects of intervention are independent of the order in which they are assigned. Even with the use of washout periods, crossover trials are still often subject to carry-over effects, particularly for interventions that aim to effect behaviour change.
	Crossover trials are also subject to ‘period’ effects, where participants respond differently in one treatment period for reasons unrelated to the intervention (e.g. because their health status has changed). A review of crossover designs is provided in Arnup et al. (2017).
	Stepped wedge trials have received increasing attention in the literature. This design is a modification of the crossover design, and involves all of the clusters beginning the trial in the control arm (Hussey and Hughes 2007). After each successive time period of the trial, one or more clusters commences the intervention and remains in the intervention arm for the rest of the trial, so that at the end of the trial all of the clusters are in the intervention arm. The order in which the clusters commence the intervention is decided randomly to avoid confounding by variables related to the order of introduction. For example, a stepped wedge trial of an intervention to reduce the risk of stillbirth was conducted in 33 maternity hospitals in the United Kingdom and Ireland (Norman et al. 2018). Hospitals were randomly allocated to one of nine intervention starting dates, approximately 3 months apart. At baseline, none of the hospitals received the intervention. Every 3 months, the intervention was implemented in the hospitals allocated to that starting date, until all of the hospitals had received the intervention. Although the stepped wedge design is becoming more widespread and there have been recent advances in the methodological literature, it is still viewed as a relatively new design with gaps in knowledge remaining around their uses, ethics, conduct and analysis (e.g. Hargreaves et al. 2015; Thompson et al. 2017).
	An important disadvantage of the stepped wedge design is that there is a systematic difference in calendar time of observation between the two treatment arms, so the design is susceptible to bias introduced through secular trends in the outcome. Stepped wedge trials often take place over a period of years, increasing the opportunity for a gradual overall improvement or deterioration in outcomes. Furthermore, it may be difficult to ascribe a particular outcome to the effect of the control or intervention, if the outcome takes a long time to occur. Similarly, there may be difficulties in interpretation when the intervention effect waxes or wanes. Further discussion of the use of stepped wedge designs in CRTs can be found in Rhoda et al. (2011), Copas et al. (2015), and Hemming et al. (2015).





Approaches for impact evaluation


	The impact of an intervention in a CRT can be evaluated either through repeated cross-sectional surveys or by following up a cohort of individuals over time. With a cross-sectional survey design, surveys are conducted at different points throughout the trial; either the entire cluster is surveyed or a random sample may be selected. Individuals who enter the cluster during the trial may be included in surveys at later time points. For example, in the CRT of a radio campaign in Burkina Faso mentioned earlier (Sarrassat et al. 2018), trial outcomes were assessed in cross-sectional surveys at 20 months and at 32 months after the trial start. In each survey, a random sample of around 360 mothers per cluster were interviewed regarding their demographic characteristics, radio listenership, and family behaviours of relevance to child survival. Cross-sectional surveys are useful for assessing the effect of an intervention on the prevalence of a binary outcome, such as hypertension prevalence, or on a quantitative outcome, such as serum cholesterol. However they are less useful for measuring incidence rates of an event of interest.
	An alternative approach is to enrol a cohort of individuals who are followed over time. Either the entire cluster, or a random sample of each cluster, may be enrolled. If the entire cluster is enrolled, the investigator must specify whether new people entering the cluster during the trial will be included (referred to as an open or ‘dynamic’ cohort) or if the cohort will be limited to those seen at baseline (a closed cohort). Cohort designs are particularly useful for measuring event rates. They also allow direct measurement of change over time, such as a change in serum cholesterol or a change in disease incidence over time. For example, a CRT in rural India of a mobile phone-based system and nurse-managed care for hypertension and diabetes randomly allocated 40 community health clinics to the intervention or control arms (Jha et al. 2017). Individuals with hypertension and/or type 2 diabetes were invited to participate in the trial. A total of 90 individuals were recruited at each clinic and followed for 12 months. The primary outcome was change in systolic blood pressure and glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) over 1 year. However, cohort designs are subject to selection bias owing to loss to follow-up, are generally more logistically complex, and may not be as generalizable since they represent the effect of the intervention in the subgroup of the population who remain in the cohort throughout follow-up. In a closed cohort, the disease incidence may decrease over time as the susceptible members acquire the disease early on and only the less susceptible members remain at risk. The choice of design will also depend in part on the primary questions of scientific interest. If interest focuses on change at the broader community level, cross-sectional designs may be the more natural choice, while cohort designs may be more appropriate if focus is on change at the individual level. Further discussion may be found in Feldman and McKinlay (1994).





Sample size determination for CRTs


Statistical approaches to estimating sample size


	The formal assessment of statistical power is a fundamental step in the design of any intervention trial. The consequences of trials that are too small for their purpose have been widely discussed in the literature. CRTs are often more costly and logistically complex than individually randomized trials, placing even more responsibility on researchers to ensure that trials are designed with sufficient power to achieve their main objectives. A fundamental principle of randomized trials is that sufficient replication is required to draw reliable conclusions. The correlated nature of the data from CRTs means that the information gained is less than that in an individually randomized trial of the same size. Even if each cluster contains a large number of individuals, the trial may be insufficiently powered if there are too few clusters. We need several clusters in each treatment arm to draw any useful conclusions about the effect of an intervention. For example, imagine an extreme case in which just two clusters are randomly allocated, one to each treatment arm. This is equivalent to a clinical trial in which just two patients are randomly allocated to the two treatment arms. Because there is no replication within each treatment arm, we have no way of measuring and taking account of between-cluster variation, and so no statistical inference is possible. Only by randomizing sufficient clusters to the different treatment arms can we obtain an accurate estimate of average response in each arm, and of differences between arms.
	Sample size formulae for CRTs are easily available in journals (e.g. Hemming et al. 2011; Rutterford et al. 2015) and textbooks (e.g. Donner and Klar 2000; Eldridge and Kerry 2012; Hayes and Moulton 2017). In their simplest form, if we have an estimate of DEff, sample sizes for CRTs can be estimated by calculating a sample size for an individually randomized trial then multiplying this by the DEff (Donner et al. 1981).
	Next we give a brief overview of formulae for a standard unmatched CRT design. The formulae assume that the cluster size is fixed, and that we need to calculate the number of clusters required per arm. This is the most useful formulation in CRTs where the sizes of the clusters are defined in advance and the outcome is measured in all individuals in each cluster. If instead the number of clusters is fixed, for example a health service intervention in a fixed number of clinics, the formulae can be rearranged to calculate the required cluster size.
	Binary outcomes are usually analysed by comparing the proportions with the outcome in the two arms of the trial. The number of clusters, c, required in each arm can be calculated as:
	where zα/2 and zβ are standard normal distribution values corresponding to the upper tail probabilities of α/2 and β, respectively, k0 and k1 are the coefficients of variation in the control and intervention arms, π0 and π1 are the true proportions with the outcome in the two arms, and m is the number of individuals per cluster.
	If we can assume that the intervention has a similar proportional effect across clusters, then the coefficient of variation for the two arms will be similar and the equation can be simplified to:
	where k is the common value of the coefficient of variation in the two arms. An important practical point is that, if the expected proportion with the outcome is above 0.50, it is usually better to work in terms of 1– π, rather than π, when calculating the sample size.
	We illustrate the calculation of sample size for a CRT using the HIV TasP trial described earlier as an example (Iwuji et al. 2013). The trial’s primary outcome was the impact of the intervention on the cumulative incidence of HIV over 24 months in adults aged ≥16 years who were HIV negative at baseline. Clusters comprised contiguous neighbourhoods in a demographic surveillance area (DSA). The study area was mapped before the trial; average cluster size was 1,000 adults. Based on previous HIV surveys in the DSA, HIV prevalence was estimated to be 20%. Allowing for 20% non-participation and loss to follow-up, the estimated mean number of HIV negative adults to be followed over 2 years in each cluster was m = 1,000 × 0.80 × 0.80 = 640.
	HIV cumulative incidence over two years in the control communities was estimated to be 5% (π0), based on surveys in the DSA. On the basis of mathematical modelling, the intervention was expected to reduce cumulative incidence by 30% (i.e. from 5% to 3.5% (π1)). A value of k = 0.25 was used, based on other studies in the region with HIV incidence as an outcome. The proportional effect of the intervention was assumed to be roughly constant over clusters so that k0 ≈ k1 ≈ 0.25. 	We would therefore select 28 clusters and randomly allocate 14 to each arm. The investigators decided to randomize 34 clusters (17 per arm), which would give them 88% power to detect an intervention effect.
	For trials in which outcomes are expressed as rates per person-year (e.g. incidence rates or mortality rates), the required number of clusters per arm can be calculated as:
	where y is the number of person-years in each cluster, and λ0 and λ0 are the true rates in the control and intervention arms, respectively. If the intervention effect is assumed to be similar across all clusters, the equation can be simplified by using a common value of k as above.
	For CRTs with quantitative outcomes (e.g. cholesterol levels), the required sample size can be calculated as:
	where μ0 and μ1 are the true means in the control and intervention arms, and σ0 and σ1 are the within-cluster standard deviations. Again, the equation can be simplified assuming a common value of k.
	Simple extensions of these formulae can be used for matched trials, using the coefficient of variation of the outcome between clusters within matched pairs, km, and adding an extra cluster to each treatment arm, to make up for the loss of degrees of freedom when using the paired t-test (Hayes and Moulton 2017, pp.141–2). Sample sizes for stratified trials can be calculated using the same equations as for matched trials. The value of km for stratified trials will generally lie between km for matched trials and the k for the unmatched design.
	Alternative formulae are available for binary and quantitative outcomes based on the ICC (Donner et al. 1981; Donner and Klar 2000). Application of these formulae generally provides very similar results to those based on the coefficient of variation.
	Our discussion so far has assumed that the number of individuals or person-years in each cluster is the same. However, in many CRTs, the cluster size may be variable, for example, because villages vary in size, or individuals in some clusters may be lost to follow-up. If the variability in cluster size is large, this should be taken into account in the sample size calculations to ensure that the power is adequate. Methods to account for variable cluster size are reviewed in Rutterford et al. (2015). Sample size calculations for more complex designs are discussed in Hayes and Moulton (2017), Campbell et al. (2007), and Rutterford et al. (2015). Sample size determination for stepped wedge trials is discussed in Baio et al. (2015), Hemming and Taljaard (2016), and Thompson et al. (2017).
	In practice sample size calculations are rarely performed by hand. Statistical packages such as R and Stata have commands to perform sample size calculations that take account of between-cluster variability. Sample size estimation by simulation is an alternative to using an analytical formula, particularly for more complex designs (Reich et al. 2012).





Obtaining estimates of k or ICC


	Sample size calculations for CRTs require an estimate of between-cluster variation in the outcome of interest. Recall that the coefficient of variation in the i th treatment arm, ki, is defined as σBi





/λi, σBi


/πi, or σBi





/μi for outcomes measured as event rates, proportions, and means, respectively. The values of λi, πi, or μi need to be specified in any case, as these are intrinsic to any sample size calculation. In addition, we need an estimate of the between-cluster standard deviation σBi in order to obtain a value for ki.


	In many cases, empirical data from which σBi can be estimated are not available at the time when a CRT is being designed. In these cases, sample sizes can be calculated using different plausible assumptions regarding k. As a rough guideline, experience from field trials suggests that k is often ≤0.25, and seldom exceeds 0.5 for most health outcomes. However, values of k in excess of 0.5 can occur, especially if the distribution of cluster values is skewed.
	Sometimes researchers may have data on between-cluster variation either from previous studies or a baseline survey. A more accurate estimate of σB 2 can then be obtained from the empirical variance s 2 of cluster-specific results. The parameter σB 2 relates to the true cluster-level values, whereas s 2 relates to the observed cluster-level values and therefore incorporates random sampling error. An estimate of this random sampling error needs to be subtracted from s 2 to get an estimate of σB 2. A detailed explanation of the approach is provided in Hayes and Moulton (2017, pp. 145–7).
	As in unmatched trials, there are often no data available on km in matched and stratified trials and so a range of plausible values must be used to estimate the required sample size. Occasionally, empirical data are available, and data on the endpoint of interest from clusters grouped according to the matching or stratification variables can be used to estimate km.
	One advantage of calculating sample sizes based on ρ is that estimates of the ICC have been published for a range of outcome variables and settings, and it is now fairly common for investigators to publish estimates of the ICC when reporting trial results. However, as with k, the ICC will depend on both the study outcome and the setting, so investigators should use caution when using published values to plan studies in different populations or with different outcomes. A range of likely values of the ICC (or k) should be explored, to ascertain the sensitivity of the sample size to these values.





Other considerations for power


	CRTs may be particularly vulnerable to problems of low power given the nature of the interventions evaluated and the heterogeneity of the populations in which they are applied. For example, many interventions are delivered to large communities with relatively little attention given to individual study participants. Thus the risk of non-compliance and loss to follow-up may be greater than in individually randomized trials.
	Since the power of a given CRT will depend on the degree of between-cluster variation, one strategy for increasing precision is to use relatively narrow cluster-level eligibility criteria. For example, in the Mwanza HIV prevention trial described previously (Grosskurth et al. 1995), clusters were deliberately selected to be similar within pairs in order to increase statistical power.
	For trials where there is some latitude in how the primary outcome variable is defined, quantitative endpoints (e.g. cholesterol level) usually lead to more statistical power than their binary counterparts (e.g. high cholesterol or not), although issues of measurement error and ease of interpretability must also be considered.
	As discussed, the statistical efficiency of a CRT is increased if we use a larger number of small clusters rather than a few large clusters. As the value of k increases, the number of clusters required increases substantially. The effect of increasing the sample size per cluster is subject to diminishing returns, particularly for large values of k. A useful rule of thumb in terms of the ICC is that very little increase in power will be obtained for a fixed number of clusters after the cluster size exceeds the value 1/ρ (Donner and Klar 2004). For example if ρ = 0.01, then the increased power obtained by enrolling more than 100 participants per cluster will be small. However, researchers will often have practical reasons for enrolling large numbers of participants per cluster, even if not needed from a statistical perspective.
	Plans to adjust for baseline covariates can lead to reduced sample size requirements. Teerenstra et al. (2012) present a simple formula for quantitative outcomes, that provides a reduction in the sample size depending on the expected correlation between the baseline and follow-up values of the outcome. However, reducing the sample size may not always be advisable, since the degree of correlation may change between the start and end of the trial.
	Once the appropriate sample size has been decided, there remains the practical problem of ensuring that recruitment targets can actually be met. Feasibility studies are essential, particularly for CRTs that involve complex intervention components. Box 5.7.2 provides a summary of important points for sample size considerations.
	 	Box 5.7.2 Summary of important points for CRT sample size considerations
	 	• Sample size calculations for CRTs require an estimate of the correlation between observations
	• Data from previous studies may be used to estimate k or ICC; however, the value may vary in different settings so a range of likely values should be explored
	• In general, power and precision of a CRT will be higher with a large number of small clusters, than with a small number of large clusters
	• CRTs tend to have diminishing returns in terms of power and precision as cluster size increases





Analysis strategies in CRTs


	A wide range of analytical methods have been proposed for the analysis of CRTs. The aim of this section is not to provide a comprehensive review of all such methods but instead to focus on a limited number of methods that are simple to understand, can be easily applied, and have proven to be robust and efficient. A detailed description of these methods, including examples of all procedures discussed in this section, is given by Hayes and Moulton (2017).





Cluster-level analysis


	There are two main approaches to the analysis of data from CRTs: analysis of cluster-level summaries, and analysis of individual-level observations. The cluster-level approach is conceptually very simple, and performs well under a wide range of conditions. It is essentially a two-stage process. In the first stage, a summary measure is obtained for each cluster, based on data collected on the outcome of interest among individuals in that cluster. Thus, the individual observations are reduced to 2c numbers, if there are c clusters in each of two study arms. At the second stage, we compare these two sets of cluster-specific measures using an appropriate statistical method. The most common approach is to use a simple two-sample t-test. Sometimes we start by applying a logarithmic transformation to the cluster-level summaries, especially if these have a skewed distribution. The t distribution can be used both to carry out a significance test of the null hypothesis of no intervention effect, and to obtain a confidence interval for the intervention effect. The methods based on the t-test have been shown to be highly robust to departures from the underlying assumptions.
	A common objection to cluster-level analysis is that information is wasted when the data are reduced to a set of summary measures. Investigators note that, in a trial with 10 clusters per arm but following many thousands of individuals, the final analysis is based on two columns of 10 numbers. This objection, however, is not valid. The power of the study and the precision of the effect estimates will depend on the observed variability in the outcome between clusters. The observed between-cluster variance will be reduced if a large number of individuals are studied in each cluster.
	As an example, we illustrate the cluster-level approach by considering the comparison of a binary outcome in an unmatched CRT with two arms, although similar equations can be used for event rates or quantitative outcomes. The first step is to calculate the proportion of individuals with the outcome in each cluster (the cluster-level summaries). Suppose that pij is the observed proportion in the jth cluster of the ith treatment arm (i = 1: intervention; i = 0: control). Then we can estimate the mean proportion in each treatment arm as

	The validity of the t-test depends on the observed cluster proportions being normally distributed. However, simulations have shown that the t-test is remarkably robust to deviations from normality, even for quite small numbers of clusters (e.g. Gail et al. 1996; Bennett et al. 2002). For CRTs with a very small number of clusters, a more conservative option is to use non-parametric methods such as Wilcoxon’s rank sum test or a permutation test (Eldridge and Kerry 2012; Hayes and Moulton 2017).
	Application of the t-test to cluster-level summaries is robust, in the sense that it provides reliable p-values and confidence intervals with approximately correct coverage. However, it may not be fully efficient in terms of providing optimal power and precision. The t-test described just now gives equal weight to each cluster, even though some clusters may be much larger than others and thus provide more information on the outcome of interest. It is theoretically possible to use a weighted t-test which weights clusters according to the information they provide. However, calculation of the weights depends on having an accurate estimate of the between-cluster variance. If the weights are not estimated accurately, the precision of the weighted analysis may be worse than for an unweighted analysis. Therefore, we would not generally recommend use of the weighted t-test.
	In addition to testing the evidence against the null hypothesis, it is important to compute a confidence interval which represents the precision in our estimate of the intervention effect. We can obtain a 95% confidence interval for the true risk difference as:

While this assumption is reasonable under the null hypothesis of no intervention effect, it may not be when there is a non-null effect. A robust alternative is to compute the variance of the risk difference based on separate estimates of the variances in the two treatment arms.

Using the logarithmic transformation


	When using cluster-level summaries to obtain estimates of the intervention effect, it is advisable to inspect the distribution of the summary measures within each treatment arm. These distributions are sometimes markedly skewed, particularly for proportions and rates. Since the statistical inference methods used assume the cluster-level summaries are normally distributed, a logarithmic transformation may be useful before analysis, if the cluster-level summaries are positively skewed. For proportions, this would involve computing the logarithm of the risk for each cluster as , then working with the which are likely to be more symmetrically distributed. It is common in statistical practice to use the natural logarithm (ln), although the choice of logarithmic base has no effect on the estimates of the intervention effect.
	We can then calculate the difference in the mean of the cluster-specific log risks (), and apply the t-test to the log-transformed values. The log transformation may help to ensure that the variances of the cluster summaries in the two treatment arms are similar as well as providing a more symmetric distribution of cluster summaries, thus improving the validity of the t-test. We can also calculate a 95% confidence interval for the difference in log risks (), and exponentiate to get these estimates on the ratio scale.





Adjusting for covariates


	In an individually randomized trial, we can expect that randomization will achieve good baseline balance between the trial arms, and the primary analysis is generally an unadjusted analysis. However, as we have seen, CRTs often randomize a relatively small number of clusters (≤30), so substantial baseline imbalance between arms is not unusual. Thus adjustment is much more important in this context and often the primary analysis would be adjusted. Furthermore, adjustment may also reduce k, by accounting for some of the variation between clusters, so may increase power and precision.
	There is limited guidance for choosing which covariates to adjust for in the analysis of CRTs. Ideally they should be covariates considered a priori to be important risk factors for the outcome of interest. These covariates must be specified in advance in a statistical analysis plan, to protect against allegations of data dredging or selective reporting. Crucially, the decision to adjust for baseline variables should not be based on the statistical significance of the imbalance between arms. Instead, the decision should depend on how strong a risk factor a covariate is thought to be, the magnitude of any imbalance, how many variables show an imbalance and the number of clusters randomized. For example, in the HIV TasP trial in South Africa described earlier (Iwuji et al. 2013), the analysis was adjusted for temporal changes in national ART guidelines, and cluster-level measures of sex (proportion female), age (proportion <30 years and >=60 years) estimated HIV prevalence, and estimated population ART coverage at baseline, all characteristics known to be associated with HIV transmission risk in the population (Iwuji et al. 2018).
	Adjustment for covariates in a cluster-level analysis can be done using a two-stage procedure. In the first stage, we carry out a standard individual-level regression analysis of the outcome, including all the covariates of interest, except for the intervention effect, in the regression model. At this stage, we ignore the effects of clustering, and use standard logistic regression for binary outcomes, Poisson regression for rates, and linear regression for quantitative outcomes. The regression model is used to obtain the expected number of events (for binary outcomes or rates) or the expected mean in each cluster, ignoring the intervention effect. After fitting the regression model, the expected and observed values are compared and used to calculate a residual for each cluster. For example, if we are interested in estimating the risk difference, we calculate the difference-residual as:
	Where dij is the observed number of events in the jth cluster of the ith treatment arm, eij is the expected number of events from the regression model, and mij is the number of individuals.
	If the rate ratio is our parameter of interest, then the ratio-residual is calculated as
	In the second stage of the analysis, the residuals take the place of the cluster-level summaries when calculating point estimates and performing statistical tests, using the methods described in the previous section. If the intervention has no effect, then the average of the residuals will be zero (for difference-residuals) or 1 (for ratio-residuals), whereas an intervention effect will result in systematic differences in the residuals between the two arms.





Individual-level analysis


	As we have discussed, the unpaired t-test is based on the assumption that the cluster summary measures are normally distributed and have equal variance. If cluster sizes vary, this latter assumption is clearly invalid, and greater power and precision would be achieved if the analysis were weighted to take into account the different variances. Such weighting is incorporated automatically when we carry out regression analyses based on individual-level data. It is essential that the regression method takes proper account of between-cluster variation. A wide range of regression methods have been suggested for this purpose, but we will focus on two approaches that have received the most attention and which have advantages over other methods: random effects regression models and generalized estimating equations (GEE).
	An advantage of individual-level regression methods over the simpler cluster-level methods is that, in an adjusted analysis, the effects of the covariates are estimated and presented simultaneously with the intervention effects. This is not the case in a cluster-level analysis, since we are comparing cluster-level residuals from which the effects of other covariates have already been removed.
	An important disadvantage of individual-level regression methods is that they do not appear to perform robustly when there are a relatively small number of clusters. Formally, both the individual-level and cluster-level methods are valid asymptotically, that is when there are a very large number of clusters per treatment arm. However, the cluster-level methods seem to perform much more robustly for small numbers of clusters.





Random effects models


	In random effects models, we take account of between-cluster variation by assuming that there are cluster-level effects (over and above the random sampling variation within each cluster) which follow a specified probability distribution. Random effect models take the general form:
	In this equation, θijk is a parameter related to the outcome of interest and refers to the k th individual in the j th cluster in the i th treatment arm. For event rate data, for example, θ might be the logarithm of the rate in that individual. The parameter βi represents the intervention effect, the γl parameters represent the effects of a set of covariates, z1, z2, … zL, each of which may be measured at individual or cluster level, and α is an intercept term representing the expected outcome in individuals in the control arm (I = 0) and with zero values for all the covariates.
	The term uij is a random effect relating to the j th cluster in the i th treatment arm, and takes account of between-cluster variation. Therefore, models of this form are known as random effects models.
	The random effects are assumed to be sampled from a probability distribution. To fit a random effects model, we need to make an assumption about the distribution of these effects, which will depend on the outcome of interest. Random effects models represent full probability models for the data and so likelihood inference is used to estimate the parameters associated with the random effects as well as the effects of the intervention and the covariates. These models can be readily fitted using standard statistical software such as R, Stata, or SAS.
	We can use random effects Poisson regression for event rates, such as disease incidence, and random effects logistic regression for binary outcomes. For quantitative outcomes, for example systolic blood pressure, these models are known as mixed effect linear regression models, because they have both fixed effects, indicated by the parameters α, βi and γl, as well as the random effects represented by uij.
	Random effect models perform well for event rate data and quantitative (normally distributed) outcomes, since the assumptions that are made about the distribution of the random effects and the variation in the outcome within clusters mean that the likelihood can be written down in analytical form. However, the likelihood for the random effects logistic regression model assumes a mixture of normal and binomial distributions, and the combination of these distributions does not provide a simple composite distribution. Therefore, numerical approximations have to be used to maximize the likelihood, and to obtain parameter estimates, confidence intervals, and significance tests. The numerical procedure used for this purpose is known as quadrature and involves approximating the normal distribution. With older versions of statistical software, the parameter estimates were not always reliable and were dependent on the number of quadrature points. However, recent advances in statistical software have resulted in significant improvements in the procedure of quadrature, so quadrature problems are rarely encountered.





Generalized estimating equations


	GEE provide an alternative method of individual-level regression modelling and make allowance for clustering without incorporating additional terms in the model (Zeger and Liang 1986). They do this by assuming that observations in the same cluster are correlated and using the data to estimate the strength of the correlation.
	While GEE models do make allowance for within-cluster correlation, they do not correspond to a full probability model for the data. For this reason, we cannot define the likelihood of the data and so we cannot obtain maximum likelihood estimators of the parameters or use likelihood ratio tests for hypothesis testing. Instead, GEE uses an iterative generalized least squares method to estimate the parameters together with robust standard errors. The Wald test can be used for hypothesis testing. As with random effects models, GEE only works reliably when there are a sufficiently large number of clusters in each treatment arm.
	For the analysis of CRTs, the usual assumption in a GEE model is that observations on individuals in different clusters are uncorrelated, while observations on individuals in the same cluster all have the same correlation coefficient ρ. In this situation an exchangeable correlation matrix is specified in the statistical model, although the method is asymptotically robust to this specification. The observed data are used to estimate the value of ρ, and this is used to obtain estimates of the regression coefficients and their standard errors that are adjusted for the correlations in the data. If ρ is large, less weight will be given to each individual in large clusters, since the outcomes within a cluster will tend to be similar. Conversely, if ρ is close to zero, this means that there is little clustering and all individuals will be given similar weight in the analysis. An excellent non-technical discussion of GEE is given in Hanley et al. (2003).
	GEE models may be fitted for event rates, binary outcomes, and quantitative outcomes. GEE models are more robust than random effects models, since they do not rely on assumptions about the distribution of the between-cluster variation. Although GEE and random effects models estimate the same parameter for the intervention effect when the outcome variable is normally distributed or an event rate, this equivalence disappears in the case of a binary outcome, and thus their interpretation is different. In a GEE logistic regression model, we are estimating a population-averaged odds ratio of the outcome, whereas with random effects models we are estimating a cluster-specific odds ratio. The cluster-specific odds ratio represents the effect on the odds of the outcome if the intervention is applied to any given cluster, whereas the population odds ratio represents the effect on the odds in the combined population of all the clusters. In many circumstances, there will be little difference between the cluster-specific and population-averaged estimates. The difference will only be large if there is substantial between-cluster variation and, in at least a proportion of clusters, the outcome is common.





Choosing an appropriate analysis


	Individual-level regression methods are popular for analysing CRTs but require a sufficient number of clusters to ensure unbiased estimates. Based on a review of simulation studies, McNeish and Stapleton (2016a) recommended that there are at least 15 clusters (8 per arm) for quantitative outcomes and 30 (15 per arm) for binary outcomes, in order to ensure unbiased estimates of the treatment effect and its standard error with random effects models. The distributional assumptions of random effects models can also be difficult to verify without large numbers of clusters.
	GEE models have been shown to have inflated type I error when there are few clusters per arm (Bellamy et al. 2000). That is, we are more likely to reject the null hypothesis, when there is no true underlying effect of the intervention. In contrast, analyses of cluster-level summaries based on the t-test provide reliable p-values, and confidence intervals with approximately correct coverage under a wide range of conditions.
	Therefore, for CRTs with a small number of clusters, less than around 15 per arm, we recommend the use of cluster-level analyses. For trials with larger numbers of clusters, either approach can be used but the individual-level regression methods are likely to be statistically more efficient than the cluster-level methods and provide greater convenience when analysing the effects of covariates. If the assumptions of the random effects models are roughly correct, we advise using these models since they are likely to be the most efficient. Another advantage of random effects models is that they provide direct estimates of the between-cluster variance, and hence the ICC, quantities which are treated as nuisance parameters using the GEE approach. If however, the assumptions of the random effects models are violated, GEE with an exchangeable correlation matrix and robust standard errors should be the method of choice. Box 5.7.3 provides a summary of important points for analysis of CRTs.
	New literature on the performance of methods for analysing CRTs is continually emerging, including methods based on restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian techniques (e.g. McNeish and Stapleton 2016b). Adjustments to GEEs for small number of clusters and variation in cluster sizes are also being investigated (e.g. Huang et al 2016). Therefore, particularly where there are few clusters or very small clusters it may be advisable to seek the advice of a statistician with experience of analysing CRTs.
	 	Box 5.7.3 Summary of important points for CRT analysis
	 	• The analysis of data from CRTs must take clustering into account
	• Analyses based on cluster-level summaries are robust and perform well under a wide range of conditions
	• Individual-level analyses have greater power and precision, but are generally less reliable when there are relatively few clusters (<15 per arm)
	• Matched designs should take account of the matching in the analysis





The matched-pair design


	Matched-pair CRTs are generally analysed using cluster-level summaries. Individual-level regression methods are usually not suitable for matched-pair designs, for reasons discussed at the end of this section.
	Some investigators have suggested that, in matched-pair CRTs with a small number of clusters, an unmatched analysis may be used, particularly when the matching correlation is not strong. This is known as breaking the matching, and helps to achieve balance while avoiding loss of degrees of freedom in the analysis. If the matching is broken, we can use either cluster-level or individual-level analytical methods (providing there is a sufficient number of clusters). However, the investigator needs to specify in advance in an analysis plan that an unmatched analysis will be conducted, resulting in a loss of power if it turns out that the matching was highly effective. If instead the investigator makes the decision based on the observed matching correlation after the trial is completed, this increases the type I error (Diehr et al. 1995). Therefore, we do not recommend this approach.
	We will begin by considering how to obtain point estimates, confidence intervals, and significance tests for pair-matched CRTs where no adjustment is made for covariates. We use the comparison of proportions as an example, but similar equations can be derived for event rates and quantitative outcomes. The simplest method of obtaining an estimate of the risk difference is to calculate the mean of the pair-wise risk differences, as follows:
