5.9


Natural and quasi-experiments


	Peter Craig





Introduction


	Natural experiments, broadly defined as events or processes outwith the control of a researcher, which divide a population into exposed and unexposed groups (Craig et al. 2012), have long been used in epidemiology and public health. John Snow’s studies of cholera in mid-nineteenth century London (Snow 1855), the most celebrated example of early epidemiology (Davey Smith 2002), exploited a natural experiment brought about by a change in domestic water supply between two cholera outbreaks. At the time, cholera was widely believed to be an airborne disease. Snow used information about cholera deaths and water supply at neighbourhood and household level to show that deaths were more likely in households whose water came from a contaminated source. Although he did not use the term, Snow clearly understood his approach as a natural experiment:
	 	No fewer than 300 000 people of both sexes, of every age and occupation and every rank and station, from gentle folks down to the very poor, were divided into two groups without their choice, and in most cases without their knowledge; one group being supplied with water containing the sewage of London … , the other group having water quite free from such impurity. To turn this grand experiment into account all that was required was to learn the supply of water to each individual house, where a fatal attack of cholera may occur. (Snow 1855)
	What makes this ‘grand experiment’ useful is that the change in exposure was well-characterized and independent of other factors that may influence the health outcome. In another important early example of turning natural experiments into account, GCM M’Gonigle compared changes in death rates among residents of an ‘Unhealthy Area’ of a town in the North East of England who were rehoused following a survey of housing conditions, with changes among residents who remained in their original houses (M’Gonigle 1933). The division of the area was, according to M’Gonigle, purely administrative, and death rates prior to rehousing in 1927 were similar among the two groups of households. In the five years following the rehousing, the death rate was markedly higher among the rehoused residents, but declined slightly in those who remained. Further investigation suggested that increased rents leading to inadequate diets among adults in the rehoused families was the probable cause.
	Despite these early demonstrations of the potential of natural experiments for addressing important public health questions, and a substantial body of epidemiological work from the 1940s onwards, including influential studies of famines and mass migrations, the methodology of evaluating natural experiments has developed piecemeal across a range of subject areas and disciplines, including psychology, economics and political science (Bärnighausen et al. 2017b). Developments in these other disciplines have been slow to permeate public health. It is only in the last ten years or so that attempts have been made to pull together the range of methods available to study the different kinds of natural experiments that are of interest to public health, and to identify the circumstances in which each method works best (Craig et al., 2012; Bärnighausen et al. 2017b; Basu et al., 2017; Craig et al., 2017). This chapter introduces the main approaches that researchers can use to evaluate natural experiments, and provides examples of their application in a wide range of contexts. It begins by setting out the advantages, and also the limitations, of a natural experimental approach. The term quasi-experiment is often used interchangeably with natural experiment, but is also used to refer to true experiments (in which there is manipulation of exposure by the researcher) which are non-randomized. To avoid confusion, the preferred term in this chapter is natural experiment.





Trials, observational studies, and natural experiments


	Randomized controlled trials and syntheses of evidence from trials occupy the top steps of the conventional hierarchy of evidence (Concato et al. 2000). The hierarchy is organized according to risk of bias, with observational studies regarded as being at higher risk because of the difficulty of isolating the effect of the exposure of interest from other factors that might affect outcomes. In a trial, random assignment of participants to treatment and control groups, plus a number of other methodological safeguards such as blinding of participants and assessors, and concealment of the allocation sequence, generates exposed and unexposed groups that are, in expectation, balanced in terms of all the factors that may influence outcomes other than exposure to the treatment. Differences in outcomes between the groups can therefore be interpreted as effects of the treatment. Outside an experimental setting, such balance is rare: individuals may be selected for treatment, or may self-select, according to characteristics that influence outcomes, leading to confounding of the treatment effect. In an observational study, statistical adjustment may be used to address such confounding, but only works to the extent that the confounders are known and accurately measured. Estimates of the treatment effect will be biased if there is ‘residual confounding’ due to unknown or imperfectly measured confounders (see Chapter 5.13). Natural experimental studies are a subset of observational studies that use the process by which exposure is determined to identify treatment effects. Understanding this process is therefore key to the design of a good natural experimental study. Because such processes rarely give rise to exposed and unexposed groups that are perfectly balanced on all of the characteristics that may affect outcomes, natural experiments also rely on statistical models that take into account both the allocation process and any observed differences between the groups in characteristics that may affect outcomes.
	Given that randomized controlled trials are such an effective way of eliminating bias associated with selective exposure to treatment, why should natural experiments be considered a useful alternative? One reason is that for many interventions a trial may not be feasible, for ethical, political, or practical reasons (Craig et al. 2012; Bärnighausen et al. 2017b; Derzon 2018). It may be regarded as unethical to withhold a treatment in order to identify its effect on health, if it clearly provides other benefits. This particularly applies to non-healthcare interventions whose main purpose is to influence some other outcome such as participation in education or in the labour market. Recipients of a conditional cash transfer benefit directly from receiving the money. If the purpose of the scheme is to reduce poverty, withholding payments from some potential recipients to study its effect on health, once its effectiveness in alleviating poverty has been established, is unlikely to be seen as fair by the losers, and may also be unacceptable to other stakeholders. Similar arguments apply to evaluating the wider, non-health-related, or long-term impacts of health interventions. The design of the intervention may make randomization impractical, at least at an individual level—as in the case of international treaties, national legislation, or taxation policies—or stakeholders may be unwilling to selectively withhold an intervention once it has been implemented, even if its effectiveness in delivering its primary outcome is uncertain.
	Natural experimental studies, which involve no manipulation of exposure by the researcher and which can be conducted retrospectively, may therefore be feasible when a prospective randomized controlled trial would not. Natural experiments may also avoid threats to validity that are specific to trials. One is the confounding of trial procedures with treatment. This may occur when methods for retaining participants in the trial also improve retention in care among patients in the control arm, leading to an underestimate of the effectiveness of treatment (Bor et al. 2017). Another is that effects on individuals observed in a trial may differ from the effect of exposing the whole population to the intervention. This may occur when interactions between recipients contribute to the overall treatment effect. To use the conditional cash transfer example again, treating a whole population may change social norms regarding the behavioural conditions, strengthening the individual incentive of the cash transfer.
	Another reason for considering alternatives to randomized trials is that minimizing bias is not the only aim of good research design. The strength of randomized controlled trials is that they permit strong causal inference with a minimum of assumptions. But additional assumptions are always needed to apply the evidence to a particular context, if it differs in any way from the settings in which the trials were conducted (Deaton and Cartwright 2018). Researchers evaluate public health interventions to provide information that is useful for decision-makers, as well as to contribute to a scientific evidence base. Precise estimates with a small amount of bias from a large natural experimental study, conducted in a relevant context, may be more useful than unbiased but imprecise estimates from an experimental study conducted in a highly artificial setting. Whether this, or any of the other reasons for considering natural experimental approach, is persuasive will depend on the details of the case. Rather than seeing trials and natural experiments as competing for position at the top of a hierarchy of evidence, researchers and evidence users should see them as belonging to a common methodological toolkit for answering important public health questions.





Natural experimental study designs


	The key methodological problem that all natural experimental studies must solve is that of selective exposure to the intervention, and the designs summarized in this section can be seen as alternative solutions to this challenge. They include some that would be ruled out by definitions that restrict natural experiments to cases where a process of ‘as-if randomization’ determines exposure (Dunning 2012), or to methods that deal with unobserved confounding as well as with confounding by observables (Tugwell et al. 2017). ‘As-if randomization’ is difficult to define, and rules out cases where the assignment process is clearly non-random, but amenable to modelling. Non-random assignment can provide useful opportunities for natural experimental studies, so long as the assignment process is well understood. None of the available methods automatically solves the selection problem. How far they do so depends on how well their underlying assumptions are met (Bärnighausen et al. 2017a). As this is unlikely to be perfect, or completely demonstrable from available data, a hard and fast distinction between methods that control for both unobserved and observed confounders, and those that only deal with observables, is unhelpful. A more inclusive list is also in keeping with the idea that the value of natural experimental approaches is that they widen the range of public health interventions that can usefully be evaluated. Because the methods originated in a number of different disciplines, terms that are readily understood by some researchers may be unfamiliar or puzzling to others. Definitions of some key terms, according to their usage in this chapter, are provided in Table 5.9.1.





‘Real-world’ randomization


	Sometimes, lotteries or ballots are used in the delivery of an intervention or implementation of a policy. A well-known example is the Vietnam-era draft lottery which has been used to identify the effects of military service on earnings (Angrist 1990). Another is the practice of reserving council seats for women in a randomly selected proportion of village elections in the Indian states of Rajasthan and West Bengal. Researchers have used the system to study the effects of women’s involvement in local government on the provision of public goods (Chattopadhyay and Duflo 2004). An example in the health field is the Oregon Health Plan Lottery in which randomly selected entrants to a public lottery were eligible to apply for health insurance. The lottery broke the link between income, prior health status and health insurance, enabling researchers to identify the effect of health insurance on use of health services and on health outcomes (Baicker et al. 2013).
	Randomization may also come about inadvertently, as a consequence of errors in policy implementation. Database errors led to some families being randomly excluded from Brazil’s Bolsa Alimentação, a conditional cash transfer programme that sought to improve child nutrition. Researchers compared the growth of children in households that were accidentally excluded from the programme and in matched households which received the payments (Morris et al. 2004). Resource constraints may sometimes limit programme reach in arbitrary ways that approximate random assignment. In Scotland’s Family Nurse Partnership, which provides teenage first-time mothers with additional support pre-natally and in the first few years of the child’s life, access to the programme is determined by the availability of specially trained nurses. When all the trained nurses have a full caseload, recruitment to the programme stops. Assignment should therefore be unrelated to characteristics of the mothers that might affect outcomes (Wimbush et al. 2015). Real-world randomization is rare, but may offer valuable opportunities for natural experiments. In studies that seek to exploit such opportunities, it is important to understand in detail how the assignment process works, and to check for self-selection by potential recipients, or manipulation of assignment by those delivering the programme.
	 	Table 5.9.1 Glossary
	 			Term
	Usage
			Assignment, allocation
	The process that determines whether units (which may be individual people, or aggregates of some kind) are exposed to the intervention that is being studied. Also referred to as the data generating process.
		Confounding, confounder (observed, unobserved)
	Confounding refers to the mixing up of the effects of the intervention with the effects of characteristics associated with exposure. Confounding by observed characteristics (i.e. those on which data is available) can be addressed using a statistical model. Some natural experimental study designs go a step further, and use a combination of assumptions about the assignment process and statistical modelling to address confounding by unobservables.
		Control, counterfactual
	Controls are unexposed units. Outcomes among the controls constitute the counterfactual, in the sense that they represent the outcomes that would occur in the absence of exposure.
		Exposure
	A general term for receipt of an intervention; effectively synonymous with treatment in natural experimental studies.
		Identification, identifying assumption
	Identification refers to the method used to obtain an estimate of the effect of the intervention. All such methods rely on identifying assumptions, such as the assumption that pre-intervention trends in outcomes will continue in the absence of intervention. Testing how well the assumptions are met is an important element of good natural experimental study design.
		Intervention
	A general term for any policy, programme, service, or treatment that is being evaluated.
		Natural experiment
	An event or process that divides a population into exposed and unexposed subpopulations. The division may be spatial, temporal, or based on the characteristics of individual units, such as test scores.
		Observational study
	A study that does not involve any manipulation of exposure for research purposes. Natural experimental studies are a subset of observational studies.
		Outcome, potential outcome
	Outcome is used as a general term for the effect of treatment or exposure to the intervention being studied. Potential outcomes are the outcomes that would occur in the absence of treatment. Comparison of actual with potential outcomes is the basis for identifying treatment effects in a natural experimental study, with potential outcomes measured in a group that is not exposed to the intervention but is otherwise similar to the exposed group.
		Quasi-experiment
	Natural experimental studies are often referred to as quasi-experiments, but quasi-experiment is also sometimes used to refer to non-randomized experiments. To avoid confusion, the term natural experiment is preferred in this chapter.
		Selection
	A process that leads exposed and unexposed units to differ in ways other than exposure to the intervention that are associated with differences in outcome. Selection is the source of confounding in natural experimental studies.
		Treatment
	Treatment is often used as a general term for exposure to an intervention, rather than to denote a medical treatment.





Controlling for observables: regression adjustment and propensity scores


	When it is plausible to expect that there are no important differences between exposed and unexposed groups a standard regression model may be sufficient to identify the effect of the intervention. The real-world randomization examples discussed in the previous section are one kind of situation in which this assumption is reasonable. Another is when randomization is built into the timing of data-gathering rather than the timing of exposure. Goodman and colleagues used this approach to evaluate a school-based cycle training scheme (Goodman et al. 2016). Parents of some children in participating schools were interviewed as part of a long-running birth cohort study before the training was implemented in their school; parents of other children in the same schools were interviewed after the training had been delivered. The researchers used Poisson regression to estimate the effects of training on cycling behaviour, with adjustment for a wide range of potential confounders. Unlike previous evaluations which compared children in participating and non-participating schools, the study found no effect of the training on cycling behaviour.
	As with real-world randomization, such opportunities are scarce but potentially highly valuable. In the example, data were gathered only from participating schools so selective participation cannot bias the estimate of effect of the programme (though may limit its generalisability). The key identifying assumption is that the timing of interviews was unrelated to delivery of training, a reasonable assumption given that the survey and the training were planned and conducted independently of one another.
	When random allocation cannot be assumed, or is known not to occur, as in the case of many social interventions that are targeted at poorer households or poorer neighbourhoods, an alternative is to model the allocation mechanism using a propensity score, defined as the conditional probability of exposure, given a number of covariates. The propensity score is usually estimated using a logistic regression model. It can be used to match exposed with unexposed units, to stratify analyses of outcomes, or as a covariate in an outcomes model. Propensity score-based methods have been extensively used to evaluate the impacts of targeted social programmes. In their evaluation of the Sure Start programme, an area-based intervention to improve the health and wellbeing of young children in England, Melhuish and colleagues calculated a propensity score from 85 area-level variables, which they used to stratify their analyses of the effects on individuals of exposure to the programme (Melhuish et al. 2008). The key identifying assumption is that the propensity score fully accounts for exposure to the programme—a strong assumption when data are sparse. Although propensity score-based methods will produce effect estimates similar to those of conventional regressions using the same covariates, they encourage a clearer conceptualization of the assignment process. A disadvantage is that units that cannot be matched on the propensity score must be omitted from the analyses.





Difference in differences and fixed effects models


	When data are available on exposed and unexposed units before and after the introduction of an intervention, the difference in the change in outcomes can be used to identify the effect of the intervention. This difference in differences (DiD) approach is one of the most widely used natural experimental study designs. Its key assumption, known as the common trends assumption, is that any group specific confounders are time invariant, and any time-varying confounders are common to all groups. Effect estimates can be obtained from a regression model with dummy variables for group (exposed, unexposed) and period (pre/post-intervention), and a group-by-period interaction term that serves as the DiD estimator. The model takes account of any differences in unobserved fixed characteristics of the groups. Additional covariates can be added to take account of observed characteristics of the groups that vary over time. Researchers have developed a range of ways in which the common trends assumption can be tested (Wing et al. 2018). With data on covariates, the standard model can be fitted with the outcome replaced by each covariate in turn to test for changes in the composition of the groups. With data on multiple time points, the outcome model can be fitted to the pre-intervention data with time as a continuous variable, to identify differences between the groups in the pre-intervention trends. The common trends assumption may also be violated by other interventions introduced at the same time as the intervention under study that affect one or other of the groups. This cannot be dealt with statistically. Instead, researchers should use specialist knowledge of the subject area to identify such threats.
	DiD methods are widely applied to the evaluation of national programmes or policies, or interventions introduced at state level within federal jurisdictions. Schram and colleagues used a DiD approach to estimate the effect of joining the World Trade Organization, and subsequent removal of controls on foreign direct investment, on sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) consumption in Vietnam (Schram et al. 2015). Models comparing SSB consumption in Vietnam and the Philippines in the pre-and post-accession periods indicated a substantially greater increase in Vietnam. The authors included gross domestic product (GDP) as a covariate in the models and fitted further models for foreign company sales growth and consumption of unprocessed foods. They found that the increase in soft drink consumption was not explained by economic growth, and was specific to products manufactured and marketed by foreign companies. The additional analyses support the conclusion that increased consumption of SSBs was the result of trade and investment liberalization.
	The two-group, two-period DiD described here can be extended to situations where there are data on multiple groups and multiple time periods. The standard approach is to estimate a regression model with a variable denoting exposure and a complete set of group and time fixed effects to take account of unobserved time invariant characteristics of the groups, and temporal trends that apply to all groups. Nandi and colleagues used this approach to evaluate the effects of paid maternity leave on infant mortality in low-and middle-income countries (Nandi et al. 2016). Their models included fixed effects of country and year, a term indicating whether countries had changed their maternity leave policies in the previous year, plus additional covariates to take account of characteristics of countries that could vary over time, such as the level of wage replacement and spending in healthcare. The research found that each month of paid maternity leave was associated with a 13% fall in infant mortality.
	Webster and colleagues used a similar approach to evaluate the impact on murder rates of withdrawing a restriction on the purchase of handguns in the US State of Missouri (Webster et al. 2014). The researchers fitted models comparing Missouri with all other US states, with fixed effects for state and year, and a range of covariates including unemployment, burglary, and incarceration rates, levels of policing, and other firearm-related legislation. They found a 16–23% increase in gun-related murders associated with withdrawal, but no change in murders by other means. As with the study of trade liberalization and soft drink consumption, this use of outcomes that are not expected to respond to the intervention in order to test the specificity of the effects helps to strengthen confidence in the conclusions.





Synthetic controls


	DiD and fixed effects approaches allow the effects of an intervention to be identified under the assumption that any differences between the exposed and unexposed groups other than the intervention are stable over time, or can be modelled using information on covariates. Choosing a comparator which is similar to the exposed group, such as a neighbouring state, or excluding groups that are known to have been affected by other interventions, can increase confidence in this assumption. An alternative approach is to create a synthetic control from a pool of potential comparators (Abadie et al. 2015). A synthetic control is a weighted composite of control units that matches the pre-intervention trend in the outcome in the exposed unit. The weights are constructed to minimize the pre-intervention differences in the outcome and observed predictors of the outcome in the exposed unit and the synthetic control. Matching on the pre-intervention outcome should also minimize differences in unobserved time-varying characteristics associated with the outcome. The difference in the post-intervention trend between the exposed unit and its synthetic control provides the effect estimate. Although standard statistical inference is not possible with this method, the estimated effect can be compared with a distribution of ‘placebo’ effect estimates obtained by swapping the intervention unit with each control unit in turn and constructing a synthetic control for each.
	The first application of synthetic control methods in public health was in a study of a tobacco control programme introduced in California (Abadie et al. 2010). Abadie and colleagues derived their synthetic control from a donor pool of other US states. After excluding those that had implemented similar programmes, the synthetic control was constructed from a weighted combination of five states. The difference in the post-intervention trend in cigarette sales between California and its synthetic control was greater than differences between the other states and their synthetic counterparts, suggesting that the programme was effective. Since that study was published, the use of synthetic control methods, often applied in conjunction with other methods, has grown rapidly (Bouttell et al. 2018). Comparing results of approaches that rely on differing assumptions is a useful way both of strengthening confidence in findings when no single method is unambiguously better, and of learning about the strengths and weaknesses of the methods.





Interrupted time series


	Alongside DiD, interrupted time series (ITS) methods are among the most widely used approaches to evaluating natural experiments. They can be used to evaluate the effect of interventions that take place at a well-defined timepoint, and affect a population for whom outcome data are available at regularly spaced intervals. Whereas in DiD studies, the pre-intervention data are used to test whether the common trends assumption is reasonable, ITS studies incorporate the data directly into the outcome model. The simplest approach is to fit a segmented regression model to the sequence of outcome data, with terms for time since start of the observation period, time period (pre/post-intervention) and time post-intervention (Bernal et al. 2017). The coefficients of these terms estimate the pre-intervention trend in the outcome, the change in level of the outcome at the point at which the intervention is introduced, and the change in trend post-intervention.
	Inclusion of the pre-intervention trend in the time series model controls for fixed characteristics of the exposed population. Additional covariates can be added and interacted with the time variables to account for observed characteristics that change more quickly, or for other interventions that might affect the outcome of interest. An unexposed group can be added to control for unobserved time-varying confounders. Outcomes that are not expected to change as a result of the intervention, but may be affected by unobserved underlying trends, can be modelled in the same way as the outcome of interest to test for specificity of effects. Similar changes seen across all the outcomes are likely to represent unobserved confounding rather than an intervention effect. Other modifications can be made to account for seasonal patterns and other forms of serial correlation which are common in time series data. Whatever approach is taken, choosing an appropriate outcome model, based on reasonable assumptions about how the intervention is likely to impact on the outcome, and what other factors need to be taken into account, is key to obtaining useful results. For example, if the effect is expected to take place after a lag, observations in the lag period can be omitted or modelled as a separate segment of the series.
	Humphreys and colleagues used a controlled ITS approach to evaluate the impact on homicide rates of a ‘stand your ground’ law enacted in the US State of Florida in 2005 (Humphreys et al. 2017a, b). Such laws, which permit the use of lethal force in self-defence, have been enacted in a number of US states, but previous evaluations had produced conflicting findings. The study used segmented regression models to analyse trends in homicide and suicide rates in Florida and four other US states for which comparable data were available, but which did not have stand your ground laws. The models assumed an immediate and permanent impact of the new law, and allowed for seasonal effects and serial correlation in the data. An interaction term was included to identify changes in homicide and suicide rates in Florida, relative to the control states. Results suggested a 24.4% increase in the monthly homicide rate but no increase in suicide rates in Florida, and no increase in either homicide or suicide rates in the control states. The specificity of the increase strongly suggests a causal interpretation.





Regression discontinuity


	DiD, fixed effects, synthetic controls, and ITS methods can be used when the introduction or, more rarely, withdrawal (Craig et al. 2018) of an intervention divides a population into unexposed (i.e. pre-intervention or post-withdrawal) and exposed subpopulations. Other approaches can be applied when the assignment process operates at an individual level, the most widely used being regression discontinuity (RD) designs and instrumental variables (IVs). RD designs can be applied when a cut-off in a continuous variable, such as age or income, is used to determine exposure. Such methods of assignment are commonly used in public policy. Examples include social security benefits awarded on the basis of a means test, school places allocated using a test of cognitive ability, and laws that define a minimum age at which people can hold a driving licence or buy alcohol. The identifying assumption is that individuals with values of the assignment variable close to the cut-off will be similar in terms of other characteristics, both observed and unobserved, that may affect outcomes, especially if there is random error in the measurement of the assignment variable. Differences in outcomes for individuals either side of the cut-off can therefore be used to estimate a treatment effect (Bor et al. 2014).
	When probability of exposure changes abruptly at the cut-off from close to zero to close to one, treatment effects can be estimated from a regression of outcomes on the assignment variable (known as the ‘forcing variable’ in RD studies), with a dummy variable denoting exposure. The coefficient of the dummy variable is the RD estimator. Additional terms may be included to allow the slopes to vary above and below the cut-off, and to control for confounders on which information is available. This is known as a sharp RD design. In many cases, known as fuzzy RD designs, probability of exposure takes intermediate values within a range of values of the forcing variable either side of the cut-off, and a two-stage approach to estimation is needed. In the first stage, probability of exposure is estimated from a regression of actual treatment on the cut-off and the forcing variable. In the second stage, the estimated probabilities of exposure replace the dummy exposure variable in the outcomes model.
	Care is needed in the interpretation of effect estimates from RD studies. In both sharp and fuzzy RD designs, the effect of exposure to the intervention is identified at the cut-off. In a sharp RD design, the effect estimate can be interpreted as the average effect of treatment across the whole population, so long as it is independent of the forcing variable. In practice, RD estimates are obtained from local regressions, using observations drawn from a narrow range of values of the forcing variable around the cut-off where the assumption of near-random assignment is most plausible. The effect estimated in a fuzzy RD design is known as a complier average causal effect because it represents the effect of exposure on those who comply with their assignment.
	A strength of the RD design is that the key identifying assumption can be tested empirically. A histogram of the assignment variable and scatterplots of the forcing variable against other covariates can be used to identify any bunching either side of the cut-off that would indicate manipulation of treatment assignment (for example, by under-reporting of income or misrepresentation of age). A scatter plot of the outcome against the forcing variable can also be used to inform decisions about the modelling approach, such as what range of data should be used, whether additional terms are needed to take account of non-linearities or changes in slopes at the cut-off. Drawbacks are that additional assumptions are needed to extrapolate effect estimates to populations far from the cut-off, and the need to restrict analyses to a subset of observations close to the cut-off, which reduces statistical power. The latter problem is less serious in studies where the effect close to the cut-off is most relevant to the research questions, such as those where the focus is on a small change in the assignment rule (Moscoe et al. 2015).
	Hainmueller and colleagues used a sharp RD design to identify the impact on child mental health of protection against deportation under the US Deferred Action on Childhood Arrivals (DACA) programme (Hainmueller et al. 2017). DACA provided renewable temporary work permits and protection against deportation for unauthorized immigrants who arrived in the US as children, and who were aged under 31 in 2012, the year in which the programme was introduced. The age cut-off determining eligibility for DACA provided the basis for a sharp RD design. Using a sample of unauthorized immigrant mothers with birthdays within 150 days of the age cut-off, drawn from Emergency Medicaid records in Oregon, the researchers found that following the introduction of the programme, children of DACA-eligible mothers were less likely than children of ineligible mothers to be diagnosed with adjustment or anxiety disorders. There was no such difference prior to the introduction of the programme. Robustness checks indicated no discontinuities in measured background characteristics, and no bunching of mothers’ birthdates around the age cut-off which would suggest manipulation of the forcing variable.
	Andalón used a fuzzy RD design to investigate the impact of Mexico’s Opportunidades programme on obesity and overweight among adolescents (Andalón 2011). Opportunidades provided cash transfers to households in rural communities below a poverty threshold, conditional on school and health attendance, plus a number of other eligibility criteria, leading to a fuzzy rather than a sharp discontinuity at the poverty threshold. Andalón used two-stage least squares regression to estimate the probability of receipt of the cash transfer as a function of poverty scores and the cut-off, and then to predict obesity and overweight as a function of the estimated probability of receipt. She found that obesity and overweight decreased among female but not among male participants. Note the difference in the interpretation of the two studies: the first estimates the effect of the DACA programme on the children of eligible mothers; the second estimates the impact on programme recipients, rather than all households below the poverty threshold.





Instrumental variables


	Fuzzy RD designs are closely related to instrumental variable (IV) methods. Both methods use the same two-stage approach to estimating treatment effects. In IV studies a potentially confounded direct measure of exposure is replaced by an unconfounded proxy measure. To solve the problem of confounding, the instrumental variable must be associated with exposure to the intervention, have no association with other factors associated with exposure, and no association with outcomes other than through its association with exposure to the intervention. Effects are estimated by first obtaining a prediction of the probability of treatment from a regression of treatment status on the instrument, plus any observed confounders. The predicted probabilities of treatment are then fitted in an outcomes model, which also includes any confounders used in the first stage model. As in the fuzzy RD design, the effect estimated is the complier average causal effect, rather than the average treatment effect across the whole exposed population.
	Reinhard and colleagues used this approach to evaluate the impact of a policy of providing free bus travel on loneliness and mental health among older people in England (Reinhard et al. 2018). Use of public transport is socially patterned but under the policy, eligibility for free travel depended solely on age. The researchers estimated the impact of the policy by regressing use of public transport on the age cut-off determining eligibility for free travel plus a range of covariates, such as employment status and pension receipt, then regressed the mental health and social outcomes on the predicted probabilities of public transport use plus the same range of covariates. They found that use of public transport was associated with fewer depression symptoms and feelings of loneliness, and higher levels of social engagement.
	The key strength of IV methods is that if the three assumptions outlined are met, the instrument controls for unobserved as well as observed confounders. The drawback is that although the first assumption can be tested empirically, it is difficult to show that the instrument has no association with any other factors that may be associated with the outcome of interest, or that it has no direct relation with outcomes other than through its association with exposure to the intervention. Critics of the use of IVs point to the lack of either an empirical or a good theoretical justification for the identifying assumptions in some applications of the method (Deaton 2010).





Conclusion—making good use of natural experiments


	Until recently, natural experiments were regarded primarily as a historical curiosity. That view no longer prevails, and natural experimental approaches are now widely, but not universally, seen as central to efforts to improve the evidence base for large-scale public health interventions. Leading national and international public health agencies have invested in initiatives to promote the use of natural experiments (Emmons et al. 2018; National Institutes of Health Office of Disease Prevention 2018; Snell et al. 2018).
	This chapter has set out the case for seeing trials and natural experimental methods as belonging to a common toolkit of approaches available to researchers, rather than as occupying separate levels of an evidence hierarchy that is stratified only by risk of bias. Exactly the same reasoning applies to the different natural experimental approaches described in this chapter. There is no single approach that is best in all circumstances. Instead, there is a range of methods that provide researchers with tools to tackle a wide array of evaluation problems. Choice of methods should depend on the specific details of the evaluation problem, rather than on more general assumptions about the superiority of some methods over others.
	Good natural experimental studies require a clear understanding of how the intervention works, and in particular of the processes that determine exposure. An explicit logic model or programme theory is a useful way of capturing this. Whatever method is chosen for identifying the effects of the intervention, careful testing of assumptions and, where possible, the comparison of results from alternative methods helps to build confidence in conclusions. Prior publication or registration of study protocols, so that it is clear which questions were theoretically motivated, rather than driven by the data, is also useful—and increasingly a requirement of journal publication.
	A key advantage of natural experimental approaches is that they can be applied retrospectively. A corollary is that they often rely on routinely collected data, from Censuses, long-running surveys, vital events registration, or monitoring carried out in the course of programme implementation. Investment in infrastructure for linking exposure and outcomes data at an individual level is opening up new opportunities for both trials and natural experiments. To enable researchers to make the most of these opportunities, information governance processes need to be rigorous, but also efficient and proportionate to the real risk of disclosure. For their part, researchers need to be alert to the opportunities provided by the withdrawal or scaling back of existing interventions, the fine details of assignment rules, or by imperfections in programme delivery, as well as by the implementation of large-scale policies or programmes.

5.10


Clinical epidemiology


	Fiona F. Stanaway, Naomi Noguchi, Clement Loy, Sharon Reid, and Jonathan C. Craig





Introduction


	Clinical epidemiology is a science that extends the principles and methods of epidemiology to clinical practice and clinical research. It incorporates the location, evaluation, and application of the best evidence to patient care by clinicians as well as the generation of high-quality research evidence by clinical researchers. Rather than being focused on health at the population level, clinical epidemiology focuses on individual patients and groups of patients. The application of the science of clinical epidemiology to patient care and its’ integration with clinical expertise and patient values is also often referred to as evidence-based medicine or evidence-based practice.
	Clinical epidemiology can make an important contribution to global public health through the application of relevant methods to public health decision-making. The field of clinical epidemiology has driven changes in the way in which evidence is generated and synthesized, and has led to more efficient approaches to the identification, retrieval, and appraisal of evidence (Sackett 2002). These methods make an important contribution to evidence-based public health, the term used to describe public health decision-making that is based on the best available evidence, availability of resources, and population needs, values, and preferences (Brownson et al. 2009). Clinical epidemiology has also contributed to the development of methods for research translation, also known as implementation science, to facilitate the rapid uptake of scientific evidence into clinical decision-making (Woolf 2008). These same approaches are being applied to the field of public health, ensuring that public health research evidence is translated into effective interventions and policies.
	Clinical epidemiology benefits global public health by its impact on improving healthcare. By providing better diagnostic and therapeutic care to individual patients and groups of patients, clinical epidemiology can contribute to health improvement at the population level. These improvements can come about through better evidence-based decision-making on the part of individual clinicians as well as health system wide approaches.
	In this chapter, we provide an overview of clinical epidemiological methods and how these approaches can be used to improve global public health. We have focused primarily on using evidence in decision-making in this chapter, rather than study design and conduct elements, such as randomized controlled trials, which are covered in detail elsewhere. Consequently, we have provided a framework for critical appraisal and reporting of relevant study designs (how to use and report), rather than a detailed discussion about how such studies should be designed and conducted (how to do).





Clinical epidemiological methods


Efficient location of research evidence


	Locating a relevant piece of evidence is the first step behind evidence-based decision-making. An important principle behind making a search for evidence efficient is starting the search with higher levels of evidence (primarily systematic reviews) and resources that have already been appraised for quality (Alper and Haynes 2016). In these ‘preappraised’ sources of evidence, the information has been critically appraised and filtered by experts, meaning that it has been appraised for risk of bias. Table 5.10.1 shows the hierarchy in terms of locating preappraised evidence. The highest level referred to as ‘systems’ is currently not applicable to public health decision-making as it involves integration of an individual’s electronic health records with computerized decision support systems. However, all of the other levels of preappraised evidence can be useful for answering public health questions. The second level of synthesized summaries for clinical reference, also referred to as point-of-care tools, although specifically aimed at clinical decision-making at the point of care, can contain useful summaries of public health-related evidence. However, an important barrier to the use of these resources is their cost as they are all subscription-based tools.
	Within the lower three levels of preappraised evidence, available content can include original reports that have been preappraised by experts (filtered content) and appraisal and extraction of key content of original reports (synopses) (Alper and Haynes 2016). Table 5.10.1 shows resources that can provide these various forms of preappraised evidence to aid public health decision-making. In addition to sites that provide one type of preappraised resource such as the Cochrane Library for systematic reviews, there are a number of search engines that search simultaneously across multiple sources and organize results according to level or quality of evidence (e.g. TRIP database and Health Evidence).
	An efficient search would start at the highest level (point-of-care tools if available) and then work down based on the availability of sources and the success of the search. Within each level, the more preappraised the material the better. For example, if searching for evidence from a guideline, a guideline that has been rated as high quality by experts would be a better start than a guideline that has not been appraised. Results of single primary studies such as a single randomized controlled trial, cohort, or case–control study should only be used to inform decision-making when no other higher-level sources are available.

Evidence synthesis


	An important part of being able to locate preappraised evidence for health decision-making is the creation of preappraised resources. A key component to this is the methodological approach to synthesizing evidence that has been developed through clinical epidemiology. ‘Evidence synthesis’ refers to the creation of an unbiased summary of all the available evidence relevant to a specific question. It involves locating all the relevant evidence for a particular question or topic, and using rigorous methods to appraise, synthesize, and present summarized information in a concise, transparent, and accessible way to inform decision-making. Synthesized summaries for clinical reference, guidelines and systematic reviews are important forms of evidence synthesis used in clinical epidemiology and the practice of evidence-based medicine. These are also important sources of preappraised information for evidence-based public health





Synthesized summaries for clinical reference


	These types of resources are also referred to as point-of-care tools (as they facilitate evidence-based decision-making at the point of care) and online, evidence-driven, clinical textbooks. A large number of these resources are available and examples are listed in Table 5.10.1. While these resources are aimed at clinical decision-making, they also provide summaries of evidence that can be relevant for public health decision-making such as evidence around smoking cessation, diabetes prevention, and vaccine effectiveness.
	Ideally, these resources should provide clear descriptions of the processes that are used to locate and appraise the evidence that forms the basis for the summarized information. In addition, there needs to be a clear process of regular updates to the resources as well as the provision of information to users about the recency of the evidence. A recent review of these resources found variation in terms of editorial quality (including items such as disclosure of conflicts of interest and regularity of updates to summaries), evidence-based methodology, and breadth of diseases covered (Kwag et al. 2016). Only three resources received scores in the top quartile across all three domains and these were BMJ Best Practice, DynaMed, and UpToDate.





Guidelines


	Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) are evidence-based statements including recommendations that aim to optimize patient care and guide healthcare decision-making for specific clinical circumstances (National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC)). CPGs typically integrate evidence from a number of different systematic reviews to assess the benefits and harms of different management options (AGREE 2018). The CPG development process involves specific methodology including a systematic method of searching for and selecting evidence, involvement of target populations so that their views and preferences can be incorporated, appraisal of the quality of evidence collected, declaration of any conflicts of interest, and clear recommendations for management based on the evidence located.
	Although developed specifically for clinical practice, CPGs can also have a public health focus such as guidelines regarding alcohol consumption and dietary recommendations. In addition to CPGs, an increasing number of guidelines are developed specifically for public health and to this end organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO 2014) and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE 2012) have developed manuals outlining the methodological approaches to guideline development for public health decision-making. Both WHO and NICE use the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach for rating evidence quality.
	An important tool for assessing the quality of guidelines is the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation (AGREE) II instrument. AGREE II provides a framework to assess the quality, development and reporting of CPGs and emphasizes the important contribution of systematic reviews in the rigour of CPG development (AGREE 2018). Although developed for appraisal of CPGs, AGREE II is a useful tool for appraising public health guidelines.





Systematic reviews


	A systematic review is an evidence synthesis of primary research studies using rigorous and clearly defined methodology. A systematic review aims to collate all empirical evidence that meets pre-specified eligibility criteria, to answer a specific research question. Systematic reviews use explicit, systematic methods to minimize the risk of bias, and aim to provide reliable findings from which conclusions can be drawn and decisions made. There are two organizations, the Cochrane Collaboration (Cochrane) and the Campbell Collaboration that produce high-quality systematic reviews that are useful for evidence-based decision-making.
	Cochrane provides an invaluable contribution to the methodological standards and dissemination of systematic reviews. The original focus of Cochrane was on systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials but over recent years the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR) has expanded to include: intervention reviews (randomized and non-randomized studies) to assess the benefits and harms of healthcare and health policy interventions; diagnostic test accuracy reviews to assess how well a test diagnoses and detects a particular disease; methodology reviews which assess issues relevant to the conduct and reporting of systematic reviews and clinical trials; qualitative reviews which consider aspects of interventions other than effectiveness; and prognosis reviews which assess the course and future outcomes for people with a particular health outcome. The Cochrane public health and health systems network includes the Cochrane public health review group which focusses on topics that address health and other outcomes at the population level and aim to help government and non-government agencies achieve population-level health, well-being, learning, and social outcomes.
	The Campbell Collaboration is a ‘sister’ organization to Cochrane for the purpose of producing systematic reviews of research evidence on the effectiveness of social interventions. Campbell systematic reviews address the effectiveness of programmes, policies, and practices in the areas of crime and justice, education, international development, and social welfare. In addition to the systematic reviews series, the Campbell Collaboration also includes: the policies and guidelines series; the methods series; and a collection of resources and tools for researchers.





GRADE and assessment of evidence quality


	Both systematic reviews and CPGs use the GRADE approach to ‘grading’ the confidence (or certainty) of evidence. GRADE classifies the quality of evidence for each outcome at one of four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. In the GRADE approach, the certainty of evidence refers to more than the risk of bias domain (internal validity) of a study. GRADE quality assessment includes consideration of the following five components.:
	 	1. Study limitations or risk of bias;
	2. Inconsistency of results;
	3. Indirectness of evidence;
	4. Imprecision; and
	5. Other considerations such as publication bias (Guyatt et al. 2008).





Risk of bias


	Bias is a kind of systematic error that leads to the results being different from the truth. Risk of bias assessment refers to the process where the risk of bias of a study is assessed in order to judge if the study’s results are trustworthy. If there is a systematic difference between the study groups not due to the intervention being studied, the truth may be distorted towards a particular direction. The domains and specific items that are important in terms of risk of bias vary between study types and the type of research question. For example, a cohort study may be used to examine questions of causality (e.g. the link between high blood pressure and stroke) and prognosis (e.g. survival following stroke), but the risks of bias domains are study design/question specific. Epidemiological study types, clinical question types, and examples of tools that can be used to appraise them are provided in Table 5.10.2.
	In general, when appraising the risk of bias of primary studies, we need to assess if: (1) the study groups remain comparable to each other throughout the research study (selection bias); (2) the participants are treated equally and their outcomes are measured in the same manner between groups (performance bias and measurement bias); and (3) if there are systematic differences in participant characteristics that can impact on the outcomes, these are taken into account (adjustment for potential confounders). Taking randomized controlled trials (RCTs) as an example, for the study groups to remain equal throughout a RCT, the study should begin with comparable groups by using an appropriate randomization method and ensuring there is allocation concealment to prevent researchers interfering with the randomization process. The groups can then be kept balanced by ensuring that loss to follow-up is minimized throughout the study and by conducting analyses by intention-to-treat, or as randomized, to preserve the effect of the randomization. Blinding is an essential component of RCTs that enables equal treatment of participants during the study and equal outcome measurement regardless of study group allocation. Confounders are factors associated with the outcome that are distributed unevenly between study groups. As randomization should ensure equal distribution of characteristics between study groups, the management of confounding is usually not needed in a RCT.
	The approach to risk of bias assessment of systematic reviews, which would be an essential part of guidelines development, is somewhat different to that of primary studies. Some of the key points in assessing risk of bias in systematic reviews are: the comprehensiveness of the search for studies including both published and unpublished research; risk of bias assessment of included primary studies; and appropriate numerical synthesis of included studies (meta-analysis).
	An important and common barrier to critical appraisal is that sufficient information may not be reported in the article to allow assessment of the risk of bias. As a result, a number of reporting guidelines have been developed that specify a set of items that authors need to report for each study type to enable risk of bias assessment. These reporting guidelines have also been listed in Table 5.10.2. It is important to note that these guidelines are reporting checklists for authors to use when preparing a manuscript and are frequently mandated by journals. They are not suitable to use as critical appraisal checklists to assess risk of bias.
