Inconsistency of results


	Within GRADE, confidence is also downgraded in the presence of unexplained inconsistency or heterogeneity in relative effects between studies (Guyatt et al. 2011c). The quality of evidence is rated down if: there is great variation in point estimates between studies; the confidence intervals around these point estimates demonstrate minimal or no overlap; and there is evidence of statistical heterogeneity in the meta-analysis through a significant statistical test for heterogeneity and a large I2 value. Inconsistency is particularly important when the variability in results would lead to different decisions. For example, it would be important to rate down evidence quality for inconsistency if some studies demonstrated large beneficial effects while other studies demonstrated large harmful effects, and there was no apparent reason for such discordance. In contrast, inconsistency would have less impact on decision-making if the inconsistency observed was quantitative only, when all studies showed benefit but varied regarding the magnitude of the benefit.





Indirectness of evidence


	Indirectness refers to the situation where the research that is being summarized in the systematic review or guideline does not directly answer the question we are interested in. This might be because the population or patients included in the study is not the population of interest. For example, studies may have all been conducted on young or middle-aged people whereas the population of interest is older people. Or, for example, in the development of the WHO guideline regarding avian influenza, evidence about the effectiveness of antivirals for avian influenza was rated down as it was based on evidence of the effectiveness of antivirals for seasonal influenza and it is possible that the avian influenza virus may not respond in the same way to antivirals (Schunemann et al. 2007; Guyatt et al. 2011b).
	Another potential reason for indirectness concerns the intervention itself. This could include consideration of situations where the same intervention may be implemented differently due to variation in the availability of technical expertise or other resources. The latter is a particularly important consideration for low-and middle-income countries.
	A third cause of indirectness is a lack of outcomes that are considered most important to patients, which may include the timing (long term versus short term) or domain (surrogate versus patient reported outcome). For example, in assessing evidence around a health condition like cardiovascular disease, outcomes such as the incidence of myocardial infarction, stroke, and overall mortality would be considered more important and relevant to patients than cholesterol levels.





Imprecision


	Assessment of imprecision in GRADE is based on confidence intervals (Guyatt et al. 2011a). However, rather than considering the width of the confidence interval alone in determining whether or not precision is sufficient, the confidence intervals relative to decision-making thresholds are regarded as more important. When the entire confidence interval lies to either side of a threshold, the imprecision has no impact on decision-making as at either extreme of the confidence interval the clinical decision would be the same—to either use or not use the intervention. However, if a confidence interval crosses the treatment threshold it would mean that decisions may be different at either extreme of the confidence interval and as a result, the quality of the evidence would be rated down for imprecision. The impact of confidence intervals on clinical decision-making in relationship to thresholds is shown in Figure 5.10.1. In study 1, the entire confidence interval is to the left of the threshold of clinical importance and therefore is sufficiently precise for decision-making. In study 2, as the confidence interval crosses the threshold of clinical importance there is a possibility that while the intervention is likely beneficial that the benefit may not be large enough to be clinically important. In this situation, therefore, we would rate down for imprecision. In study 4, even though the confidence interval is quite wide and crosses the line of no effect indicating lack of statistical significance, the entire confidence interval is to the right of the threshold of clinical importance. This means that we are confident that there is no clinically important effect and would not recommend the intervention.
	Fig. 5.10.1 Judging precision of confidence intervals in relation to clinically important thresholds
	Studies 1 and 3 are sufficiently precise as the entire confidence intervals are to one side of the threshold of clinical importance.





Study 4 is also sufficiently precise as despite lacking statistical significance, the entire confidence interval lies to one side of the threshold of clinical importance.


Studies 2 and 5 are insufficiently precise as the confidence intervals cross the threshold of clinical importance.





Publication bias


	Studies that have statistically significant results are more likely to be published than those with non-significant results. Therefore, relying solely on published studies in a systematic review may be misleading (in favour of the intervention) due to such publication bias. In addition, studies with non-significant results that are published are more likely to experience delayed publication which means that an early systematic review of a particular topic may have biased results as the negative results of these later publications will be excluded—a phenomenon described as lag bias (Hopewell et al. 2007). Publication bias can be associated with industry funding as industry sponsored trials may be less likely to publish negative or null results. A high likelihood of publication bias means that the confidence in a body of evidence about a particular topic would be rated down.





Strength of recommendations


	Using the GRADE approach, recommendations made in guidelines collapse down into two categories, ‘strong’ or ‘weak’ (also known as conditional). In addition to the confidence in the evidence determined as described earlier, the strength of recommendations also involves consideration of: uncertainty about the balance between benefits and harms associated with an intervention; uncertainty about values and preferences of target populations; and uncertainty about whether the intervention is a wise use of resources (Guyatt et al. 2008; Andrews et al. 2013). The GRADE strength of recommendations are presented in the following four categories:
	 	• Strong recommendation against using the intervention
	• Weak recommendations against using the intervention
	• Weak recommendation for using the intervention
	• Strong recommendation for using the intervention.





GRADE and public health guidelines


	The GRADE approach is readily applicable to assessment of the quality of evidence in systematic reviews and guidelines developed for public health questions and is being increasingly used in public health guidelines. WHO has adopted the use of GRADE for guidelines and NICE also uses GRADE for determining evidence certainty. However, despite this, there are still some concerns in the public health community about using GRADE (Burford et al. 2012; Rehfuess and Akl 2013). Many of the concerns are to do with the frequent need to use lower levels of evidence in public health decision-making due to the lack of availability and/or lack of feasibility of RCTs. However, it should be noted that although observational studies default to a low-confidence rating, they can be rated up if the size of the effect is large, if there is evidence of a dose-response gradient, and if all the impact of possible confounding is in the direction of reducing the observed effect (Guyatt et al. 2011d). One such example would be rating up the body of evidence from observational studies supporting smoking as a risk factor for lung cancer due to the large size of effect (RR of 5.5 overall and 16.9 for squamous cell carcinoma) and a clear dose-response gradient with greater cancer risk with the amount smoked, duration of smoking, tar level and fraction smoked (Lee et al. 2012). Moreover, many public health questions can be addressed by randomized studies, particularly with the increased use of pragmatic trials and methods such as cluster randomization or stepped wedge design.
	Other concerns about the use of GRADE in public health include the importance of taking into consideration other aspects such as cost and the legal implications of particular public health approaches. NICE, although adopting GRADE for assessment of evidence quality, also incorporates the quality of cost-effectiveness studies in the review and uses a different approach for the wording of recommendations (Thornton et al. 2013).
	The GRADE working group has taken many of these considerations into account in the development of the GRADE Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework for health system and public health decisions. In this framework, consideration is also given to the priority given to a particular problem, the impact of the proposed option on equity, and the acceptability and feasibility of the proposed public health approach (Moberg et al. 2018).





Research translation


	It has been increasingly recognized that the results of medical research are often not translated into patient care, or when they are, it is delayed. For example, as many as 8 years after a large trial demonstrated a 40% reduction in mortality from using beta blockers post myocardial infarction, this treatment was prescribed in only one-third of relevant patients in the United States. It took 20 years from the publication of the study until the rate of prescribing reached high levels and this was only after this was included as a recommendation in guidelines and became part of accreditation standards (Glasziou et al. 2017).
	The role of clinical epidemiology methods in evidence synthesis in the form of systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical practice guideline development has been outlined, but alone is not sufficient to change practice. Translating research into individual clinical practice needs to be an active process. Passive uptake of guideline recommendations can be low, even in well-resourced health systems.
	As well as failing to use interventions with strong evidence of net benefit in routine clinical care (underuse), overuse of inappropriate healthcare is also common. Overuse refers to the provision of healthcare where the harms to patients outweigh the benefits. For example, in Thailand and China, an estimated 55% of children with acute diarrhoea are reported to receive inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions (Brownlee et al. 2017). As well as non-evidence-based use of treatments, inappropriate use of diagnostic tests is also very common. For example, in the United States an estimated 36% of patients had a repeat colonoscopy that was not recommended based on guidelines and 40% had inappropriate imaging for low back pain (Brownlee et al. 2017). Research translation is concerned with both the lack of use of effective interventions and tests as well as the use of interventions and tests that are ineffective or unnecessary.
	Models of change have been developed to assist the translation of evidence into practice. These models include steps that help integrate theory with interventions to encourage change. The following steps are from a modified version of the model developed by Grol (Grol and Wensing 2004):
	 	1. Identify and measure an evidence practice gap—it is useful to choose an area of practice that is important clinically, has a good evidence base to support a particular management approach, and where current practice can be easily measured
	2. Conduct a cause analysis to determine reasons for the evidence practice gap—this can be done using tools such as fishbone diagrams or a theoretical domain framework
	3. Choose an intervention aimed at changing practice
	4. Evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention using an appropriate indicator of quality improvement
	5. Sustainability—a plan for sustainability should be incorporated into project planning from the outset as well as how sustainability will be assessed





Optimizing use of health resources


	Another area where clinical epidemiology can contribute to the functioning of the health system, is through the interpretation of evidence and, in partnership with health economists, optimization of resource use. Critical evaluation of trial data and meta-analytical techniques form the backbone of decision-making for health technology agencies. Some additional techniques used in this context include network meta-analysis (Lumley 2002) (to estimate the relative efficacy of more than two treatments to determine which intervention is likely to be the best), and a ‘linked evidence approach’ to assessing diagnostic tests (Merlin et al. 2013).
	Evaluation reports from health technology agencies not only provide local guidance, but also form a rich resource for other health systems considering adoption of new medicines. These include reports from the Food and Drug Administration in the United States (McDonagh et al. 2013), the European Medicines Agency (European Medicines Agency 2018), the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence in the United Kingdom (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence UK), and the Medicare Benefits Schedule and Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme in Australia (Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme 2018).





Applying evidence to individual patients


	As well as contributing to system wide approaches to optimizing health resource use, clinical epidemiology methods may optimize resource use through providing clinicians with skills to tailor management decisions according to the circumstances of individual patients. This process has been variously called applicability and transferability of evidence, individualizing therapy, precision medicine, and stratified care. The importance of this approach comes from an understanding that even when there is strong evidence from a trial or meta-analysis of trials that a treatment on average produces a net benefit, there may not be a net beneficial effect from the treatment in every patient in the trial(s) or in every patient in clinical practice (Glasziou and Irwig 1995). Traditionally, it has been common to use the inclusion and exclusion criteria of a trial to decide whether or not an intervention will have a net benefit in a patient. However, these inclusion and exclusion criteria for trials are primarily based upon separate considerations such as improving the power of a study to detect an effect and to maximize safety. There will be patients who meet inclusion criteria for the trial who would not receive a net benefit from the intervention and there will be those who do not meet inclusion criteria who would receive a net benefit.
	A more appropriate approach to determining which patients should receive particular interventions is a risk-benefit model approach. This process has several steps which are:
	 	• Listing all of the benefits and harms of the intervention
	• Determining if there is any heterogeneity or effect modification of the relative treatment effect and/or harms
	• Considering the impact of baseline risk on absolute benefits and harms
	• Weighing up benefits and harms taking into consideration patient values
	In the first step, a list of all patient-relevant outcomes that the intervention will have an impact on should be generated. Evidence about efficacy should come from a systematic review of RCTs. However, it may be necessary to use a cohort study or systematic review of cohort studies to obtain sufficient data about harms.
	In the second step, it is important to consider if there are subgroups of patients or particular settings in which the treatment might work differently to the estimate of effect given in the systematic review or RCT. This difference in effect can occur not only for the benefits of an intervention but also for the harms. One important cause of effect modification is socio-economic status which can be a source of variability in observed treatment effects due to resource constraints acting at the individual and/or community level. This variation in treatment effects and harms by patient subgroups will impact on the trade-off between benefits and harms.
	The next consideration is the impact of baseline risk on the benefit to harm trade-off. An important part of this step is understanding the difference between relative and absolute measures of effect. Relative risks tend to be less dependent upon baseline risk and so are commonly the measure of effect reported in clinical trials. However, the risk difference which refers to the absolute difference in incidence between groups is more useful for determining benefit to harm trade-off as illustrated in Figure 5.10.2. This figure demonstrates how the baseline risk of disease determines the size of the absolute difference given a stable relative risk. This means that if harms are constant, in those patients with a high baseline risk of disease the benefit to harm trade-off will be greater. Therefore, focussing therapy on this high-risk group would result in both better patient care and more efficient use of resources, at an individual and group level.
	Fig. 5.10.2 Change in absolute risk difference by baseline risk.
	This approach of estimating total or absolute risk of disease and tailoring management strategies accordingly is incorporated in many guidelines, such as the current WHO guidelines for cardiovascular disease (WHO 2007). It has been estimated that targeting high-risk individuals in low-and middle-income countries with evidence-based interventions to prevent cardiovascular disease could avert 17.9 million deaths from cardiovascular disease over 10 years (Lim et al. 2007).
	An essential part of a risk-benefit model approach to individualizing healthcare is having access to evidence-based information that allows clinicians to estimate absolute risk. A key part of this process is the development of valid prognostic models (variously referred to by other names including prognostic index, prediction rule, risk, or clinical prediction model and predictive model). These models can be turned into scoring systems or ‘risk calculator’ tools that are increasingly web-based and allow clinicians to estimate a patient’s absolute risk of a particular disease or outcome based on a number of predictive clinical features and test results.
	Methodological standards in prognosis research studies have lagged behind those of other areas such as RCTs and to this end the PROGnosis RESearch Strategy (PROGRESS) partnership has proposed a framework for research themes in prognosis research as well as guidance in terms of methodology. There are three main phases essential to development of prognostic models which include: development of the model, external validation of the model (ideally in a different setting), and assessment of the impact of using the model on clinical practice. Unfortunately, it is very common for only the first step to be carried out. The importance of external validation in other settings is emphasized by a study examining the performance of four commonly used cardiovascular risk prediction models in Malaysia where the performance of one of the models was found to be poor (Selvarajah et al. 2014).
	The final step of the process considers the values of individual patients as they consider potential benefits and harms. This is an essential step given existing evidence for substantial variation in patient preferences for particular treatment approaches and the varying importance placed on particular benefits and harms. For example, in a systematic review of patient preferences regarding antithrombotic therapy, included studies found substantial variation in how study participants considered the trade-off between benefits such as stroke prevention and the harm of bleeding. There was also variability in the decisions patients made when provided with evidence about the benefits and harms of treatment options (MacLean et al. 2012).





Applying evidence to individual settings


	The approach used to optimize the care of individual patients by considering benefit to harm trade-off can readily be adapted to how public health evidence can be applied to different settings. Benefits and harms of implementing a public health intervention could be considered at the country level where, in addition to benefits and harms related to the outcomes of the specific intervention, the impact on resource use also needs consideration given the constraint of fixed resources and opportunity cost. Assessing the likelihood of effect modification of the effectiveness of an intervention is a critical consideration, particularly in low-and middle-income countries. There is potential for variation in benefits and harms due to population characteristics such as socio-economic status and nutrition as well as potential variation in effectiveness due to staff training and availability and differences in infrastructure. In terms of baseline risk, rather than considering the baseline risk of an individual patient, the prevalence of disease in a particular country would provide a firm basis for determining the absolute benefit for the country in terms of health improvement that would be gained from the intervention. In the presence of a constant relative measure of effectiveness, a country with a high burden of disease will stand to receive a greater absolute benefit from an intervention targeting this disease. Finally, different values in a particular country or setting could impact on the importance placed on the potential benefits and harms of a given public health intervention, thereby influencing the benefit to harm trade-off.
	Many of these ideas are covered in the GRADE EtD framework discussed in the section ‘GRADE and public health guidelines’ in this chapter. For example, the priority given to a public health problem would be closely tied to the burden of disease. Considering the impact of the proposal on equity and considering the feasibility of the public health intervention would be considering the potential for variability in effectiveness or effect modification of the intervention. And considering the acceptability of the public health approach would involve considering the values of the population including how these impact on the benefit to harm trade-off.





Evaluation of the health system


	Clinical epidemiology methods can contribute to improved health system design. As well as optimization of resource allocation, they are also useful in health system evaluation. Analogous to methods in evaluating effectiveness of treatments for individuals, these same methods can be extended to assess system wide interventions. These methods are also frequently used in the assessment of many public health interventions that due to their complexity and breadth of focus can be difficult to evaluate using the traditional randomized controlled trial approach.





Cluster RCTs


	There are situations where a health system may wish to evaluate or randomize interventions on a work unit basis (by ‘clusters’ such as clinic, area health service or school), but also measure outcomes based on individual participant/patient outcome. These cluster RCTs may be the study design of choice because (1) the intervention applies to the entire cluster (e.g. whole-school health promotion programmes), or (2) the intervention is likely to ‘overflow’ or ‘contaminate’ non-intervention units (e.g. an educational intervention for handwashing may affect this behaviour in both the targeted health workers, as well as their colleagues who were not allocated to the intervention). An important consideration for cluster RCTs is that individual participant outcomes are likely to be correlated within each cluster. For example, patients attending the same clinic may have more similar health outcomes than patients across different clinics. This needs to be taken into account for in the planning and analysis of the study, and there are established statistical methods for doing so (Hemming et al. 2017). Protopopoff et al. is an example where the cluster randomized controlled trial design was used to evaluate insecticidal nets and indoor residual spraying, randomized to Tanzanian villages as clusters, with childhood malaria as the outcome measure (Protopopoff et al. 2018).





Stepped wedge design


	One variation to the cluster randomized trial is the stepped wedge cluster randomized trial design. This is a useful design when a health system has already decided to roll out an intervention programme, but for pragmatic reasons may only be able to roll out at one site/cluster at a time. This presents an opportunity to collect evaluation data. The stepped wedge design involves collecting outcome data at regular intervals (steps) for all clusters, starting to do so before any of the clusters has started on the intervention programme. Then at each subsequent ‘step’, a cluster is randomly assigned to commence on the intervention programme, thus adding a cluster at each step until all clusters are in the intervention programme. Analysis for stepped wedge cluster randomized trials is complex but good introductions are available (Hemming et al. 2015). Betran et al. is an example where the stepped wedge design was used to evaluate whether provision of medical supply kits improved quality of antenatal care, across 10 antenatal care clinics in Mozambique (Betran et al. 2018).





Population screening


	Population screening is defined as offering a test to all individuals in a target group in the population (e.g. a mammogram every two years, for all women aged 50–74 years) to identify people with pre-symptomatic, early disease, and offer early intervention. Recommendations for screening should be based on RCT evidence demonstrating that offering such early intervention improves outcomes (Barratt et al. 1999). The RCT design avoids two common biases that can occur in observational studies of screening: lead-time bias and length-time bias. Lead-time bias refers to the apparent longer survival of patients identified through screening due to their identification at an earlier point in their disease with a resulting longer period of follow-up. Length-time bias refers to the bias that arises due to the greater propensity of screening to identify slowly progressive disease, which will be associated with better survival. In addition to potential benefits in terms of prolonged life and improved quality of life, screening can also be associated with harms including complications from investigations, adverse effects of treatments, and psychological harms. Another harm of screening, both at the individual and population level, is the potential for overdiagnosis. This refers to the identification of disease that is inconsequential and would not have resulted in any harm if left untreated. Randomized controlled trial data may also help indicate the possibility of overdiagnosis in the screening setting (Moynihan et al. 2012).





Challenges in low-and middle-income country settings


	In this final section, some key challenges faced in terms of using the methodological approaches highlighted in this chapter are discussed along with current strategies being used to alleviate them.





Access to evidence


	An important barrier to the efficient location of research evidence in low-and middle-income settings is poor access to such evidence. This is the result of a combination of infrastructure issues around the availability of reliable internet and electricity supply in addition to reduced availability of evidence sources that are subscription based. Hinari is a programme established by the WHO that provides low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) with access to a large number of journals, ebooks, and information resources including sources of synthesized evidence such as the Cochrane Library. Hinari facilitates either full or partial access to over 250 publishers to more than 5,000 different institutions in LMICs. There are also a number of freely available sites that provide synthesized evidence for policy makers such as SUPPORT summaries that provide policy makers with structured summaries of systematic reviews of ways to organize, finance, and govern the delivery of healthcare interventions in LMIC settings and PDQ-Evidence that provides systematic reviews, syntheses of reviews, evidence-based policy briefs, primary studies, and structured summaries.





Research capacity building


	Training in clinical epidemiology provides clinicians and clinical researchers with the skills they need to effectively use and produce high-quality evidence to guide clinical decision-making. As illustrated in this chapter, training in clinical epidemiological skills also provides public health practitioners with important skills and approaches that can be used in evidence-based public health decision-making. Improving research capacity within a country or region not only increases the volume and quality of research produced but can also facilitate the setting of research priorities that are driven by local rather than global priorities.
	One important strategy to strengthen capacity in clinical epidemiology and research training in LMICs has been the establishment of the International Clinical Epidemiology Network (INCLEN) in 1982. This network has established Clinical Epidemiology Units (CEUs) and Clinical Epidemiology Research Training Centres (CERTCs) in 89 academic institutions across 39 countries. The aim of the network has been to develop and upskill patient-orientated researchers and clinician investigators, enabling them to undertake high-quality clinical research. INCLEN scholars in CEUs received training in the fields of Clinical Epidemiology, Biostatistics, Health Social Sciences, and Health Economics. Initial training was conducted at established clinical epidemiology training centres such as McMaster University in Canada, the University of Pennsylvania, and University of North Carolina in the United States, and the University of Newcastle in Australia. However, many of the originally established CEUs have now gone on to become training centres themselves. These units and centres have played a vital role in strengthening clinical research capacity, the creation of a network of researchers, and increased research output including the development of CPGs.
	The Cochrane and Campbell Collaborations also have a major focus on improving capacity in LMICs. Both have established a large network of skilled researchers and centres for producing high-quality systematic reviews that can be used to support and mentor researchers in LMICs. The Cochrane effective practice and organization of care (EPOC), equity, and public health groups are all quite involved in capacity building of LMIC researchers. For example, the Norwegian satellite of EPOC provides support to Cochrane authors in LMICs in the form of training stipends for review authors and the provision of support and instruction from the editorial team throughout the systematic review process. This satellite also helps build the capacity of policy makers to appropriately interpret research evidence for decision-making





Indirectness of evidence and transferability of guidelines


	At the present time, the majority of research evidence continues to be produced in high income settings and not all of the results will be readily applicable to LMICs. As the guideline development process is both time consuming and resource intensive, a more efficient approach would be to adapt existing guidelines to different settings. The GRADE EtD framework provides a good basis for understanding what additional pieces of evidence would be required to ensure an evidence-based adaptation process. This would include burden of disease studies that are essential for priority setting, cost-effectiveness data to quantify the impact on health resources, pilot study data examining issues of feasibility and an understanding of values in terms of the importance of particular benefits and harms.
	Owalabi et al. (2016) provides a useful example of how cardiovascular disease recommendations can be adapted for LMICs by presenting both an implementation cycle and translatable scale that is a useful approach to ranking recommendations according to how readily they may be implemented according to considerations of cost and personnel.





Conclusion


	Based on methods developed within public health, clinical epidemiology has extended these methods into new areas aimed at improving both the use of evidence in clinical decision-making and the production of high-quality evidence. Despite the clinical focus of clinical epidemiology, many of the methods are of value to public health decision-making and are being increasingly adopted by public health professionals.
