5.13


Systematic reviews and meta-analysis


	Nandi Siegfried and Lawrence Mbuagbaw





Introduction


	Systematic reviews use systematic, explicit, and reproducible methods to identify relevant studies, assess the risk of bias in these studies, extract information, and synthesize findings. Systematic reviews often employ statistical methods (known as meta-analysis) to combine data from similar studies in order to obtain more precise estimates than those derived from the individual studies included in the review.
	Systematic reviews play a critical role in guiding practitioners, policymakers, and consumers to make well-informed decisions and choices about healthcare. The massive expansion in the volume of biomedical literature, beginning in the middle of the twentieth century, has made it increasingly difficult for healthcare decision-makers to keep up with the findings of individual studies. Reviews of the literature are thus important for taking stock of existing knowledge and making informed choices about healthcare and resource allocation (Chalmers et al. 2014). Poorly conducted reviews drawing incorrect conclusions from the literature have the potential to cause serious harm to patients and populations, and waste resources (Chalmers and Glasziou 2009). This is especially important in situations where health problems are severe and the scarcity of resources makes it vital that they are not wasted (Chinnock et al. 2005).
	In this chapter we focus our discussions on the methodology of systematic reviews to evaluate the effectiveness of healthcare interventions. Reviews of effectiveness preferentially include randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and as such, most of our descriptions and examples relate to systematic reviews of RCTs. The utility of the systematic review method is increasingly applied to synthesize results from observational studies and more recently, qualitative data. The specificities related to the methods required to conduct such reviews are not covered in any detail in this chapter, and readers interested in the broader applicability of reviews are advised to expand their reading beyond what is included here. In the following pages, we outline the key steps involved in planning and executing a typical systematic review.





What is a systematic review?


	An up-to-date synthesis of the results from relevant primary studies should provide healthcare decision-makers with a strong foundation on which to base their policy and practice decisions. If due care is not paid to the methods used during the collection, identification, and analysis of results from individual studies, the final synthesis may be at risk of bias. Bias includes any distortions that occur during the investigation process and may lead to overestimating or underestimating the strength of the observed effect. The methods of a systematic review aim to reduce the risk of biases that may be present in a traditional literature review. The main biases that can affect a review are outlined next and the differences between systematic and traditional literature reviews are presented in Table 5.13.1.





Bias that may affect reviews


Selection bias


	Selection bias may occur in a review when the collection of primary studies systematically favours the identification of some studies over others. The main types of selection bias encountered in reviews are publication and language bias.
	There is robust research evidence to indicate that studies with positive results are more likely to be published than those with neutral or negative results (Hopewell et al. 2009). If unpublished, negative studies are not identified and included in a review, the synthesized results will be at risk of publication bias and may yield a false positive result (Hopewell et al. 2007). A well-conducted systematic review will attempt to seek out unpublished studies, within resource and time constraints, to reduce potential publication bias.
	English is the dominant language of publication in the biomedical literature and many authors seek to publish their work first in English-language journals. There is evidence that trials published in English are more likely to have statistically significant, positive results than studies published in German-language journals (Egger et al. 1997). Failing to include studies which are written in languages other than English, be they published or not, may lead to language bias which may affect the final synthesized results of the review, although this has not been shown consistently (Morrison et al. 2012). A well-conducted systematic review will not limit the search to a single language and review authors should recognize the need to budget for translation of articles where necessary.





Indexing bias


	Access to large volumes of literature via electronic databases has streamlined the conduct of reviews and greatly reduced the time required to conduct a systematic review of high quality. In order to accurately identify a primary study of a specific study design, the terms of the search strategy must match that of the database record. For example, for a search strategy to find a randomized controlled trial in a database, the original record must have been clearly identified or indexed as such when the record was created. An initiative to increase the precision of searches for RCTs in MEDLINE was initiated by the Cochrane Collaboration in the 1990s leading to greater accuracy when searching for RCTs in MEDLINE and Embase (Glanville et al. 2006). Systematic review team authors should note that indexing bias is likely to remain a concern when searching across other databases and when searching for observational studies and other non-randomized designs.





Information bias


	A review is dependent on the quality of the reporting of the included studies. Where reporting of a study is poor or data is lacking, a review may be at risk of information bias. During the conduct of a systematic review, the author team is encouraged to actively seek out the missing data by contacting the authors of the primary study (Young and Hopewell 2011). Where this is not possible, the systematic review team will be required to transparently report any assumptions made about the missing data and should indicate to the reader the possible effects of the missing data on the synthesized results.
	 	Table 5.13.1 A comparison of the typical characteristics of systematic versus more traditional literature reviews
	 			Systematic review
	Literature review
			States the methods of the review in a protocol
	Often does not state the methods of the review
		Answers a focused question or tests a hypothesis; usually narrow in scope
	May have a clear question but it often involves general discussion with no stated hypothesis; often very broad in scope
		Attempts to locate all relevant studies to minimize publication and other biases
	Usually does not attempt to locate all relevant studies
		Uses explicit eligibility criteria to determine which studies will be included in the review to prevent selection bias on behalf of the reviewer
	Usually does not specify why some studies are included and others excluded
		Systematically appraises the methods of the included studies to determine possibility of bias in these studies and sources of heterogeneity between the study results
	Often does not assess the risk of bias in the studies or acknowledge differences in their methods
		Bases results on studies that are methodologically sound
	Often does not distinguish between methodologically sound and unsound studies
		May combine study results statistically in a meta-analysis
	Often does not pool results in a meta-analysis
		Results illustrate level of heterogeneity of data, allowing quantification of uncertainty
	Results often presented in certain terms without indicating uncertainty or variability





Developing a protocol


	A systematic review is classified as secondary research, but it is nevertheless an original study which collects, appraises, and combines results from primary studies. For this reason, a research protocol is developed prior to the conduct of the review to ensure that the study objectives and methods are stated explicitly and to provide a template for the team to follow.
	The protocol should contain the following sections:
	 	• Background to the clinical problem and intervention under study
	• Formulation of the review question (using the PICO structure, see next)
	• Inclusion and exclusion criteria
	• Search strategy
	• Methods of study selection, data extraction, and quality appraisal
	• Methods of analysis
	• Methods of overall quality assessment (e.g. Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation, GRADE)
	Ideally the protocol should undergo peer review to ensure that it is rigorous and meets acceptable standards.
	Registration of a review on a publicly accessible platform is encouraged and is mandatory for some funders. This improves transparency and allows detection of any changes to the protocol that may have occurred during the process of the review. It may also reduce the likelihood of unnecessary duplication of effort (Straus and Moher 2010). Review protocols can be registered publicly on the freely available platform, PROSPERO (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/). PROSPERO includes protocol details for systematic reviews relevant to health and social care, welfare, public health, education, crime, justice, and international development, where there is a health-related outcome. Systematic review protocols on PROSPERO can include any type of any study design. Reviews of reviews and reviews of methodological issues that contain at least one outcome of direct patient or clinical relevance are also accepted.
	Key point: The methods of a good systematic review should be described in a protocol which is registered publicly in advance of the conduct of the review.





Formulating the review question


	The first step in conducting a systematic review is to clearly formulate the research question. A focused review question guides the selection of terms to include in the search strategy and narrows the scope of the inclusion criteria. The PICO-ST structure provides a useful framework for developing the review question:
	 	• P Populations
	• I Intervention
	• C Comparison
	• O Outcome
	• S Study design
	• T Timeframe
	The minimum structure of a PICO question is as follows:
	 	[Intervention] compared with [Comparison] for preventing/treating [Outcome] in [Populations]
	The study design (S) and timeframe (T) are optional additional components to the PICO. These allow the reader to immediately discern the design(s) of the studies included in the review (e.g. if the included studies are limited to RCTs). The timeframe component refers either to the time-point at which the primary outcome is measured, e.g. death at 1-year follow-up, or the time span of the studies included in the review, e.g. RCTs published between 1990 and 2010.
	The O in the PICO refers to the outcome designated as the primary outcome(s) in the review question. The review team should carefully consider which outcome is the most meaningful to measure for answering the clinical question and denote this as the primary outcome. Note that this may differ from the outcome(s) designated as primary outcomes across the included studies.
	Key point: The systematic review question is best formulated using the PICO structure.





Searching for studies


	The search strategy forms the foundation of a systematic review and is best prepared by a trained librarian or information specialist. A comprehensive search should be highly sensitive, aiming to identify and locate as many of the eligible studies as is feasible within the timeframe and available resources. A search should also be precise in order to reduce the need to screen vast quantities of irrelevant material. Precision is a measure of the number of records that require screening to identify a single eligible study. In practice the balance between sensitivity and precision is weighted towards high sensitivity to reduce selection bias (including language and publication bias), with low precision. Systematic review teams should generally expect to screen large numbers of records even if they will only a few studies.





Data sources to search


Published reports


	An experienced information specialist will develop a search strategy using database-specific syntax including the keywords related to the review PICO. Examples of databases are listed next. At a minimum a well-conducted review of the effects of healthcare interventions should include the first three databases.
	 	1. General electronic journal databases of published reports:
	 	• European and North American focus:
	 	■ MEDLINE (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed)
	■ EMBASE (http://www.elsevier.com/online-tools/embase)
	■ CENTRAL (Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials) (http://www.cochranelibrary.com)
	• South American focus
	 	■ LILACS (Latin American Caribbean Health Sciences Literature) (http://lilacs.bvsalud.org/en/)
	• African focus
	 	■ African Journals Online (https://www.ajol.info/)
	2. Subject-specific electronic journal databases:
	 	• Databases will be dependent on the review topic, e.g. a review of behavioural interventions may include PsycINFO (https://www.apa.org/pubs/databases/psycinfo/index.aspx)





Unpublished reports


	The so-called grey literature, such as conference abstracts, research reports, policy documents, dissertations, book chapters, and personal correspondence, should be sought by contacting authors of identified papers, experts in the field, and relevant organizations, including pharmaceutical and medical device companies, and by searching pertinent websites. These sources should be identified at the protocol stage.





Ongoing studies


	There are several prospective trials registries available which publish trial protocols and status updates of trial progress. These provide a useful source to identify ongoing studies and studies which are recently completed but not yet published. The choice of registry will be dependent on the topic.
	 	• Global focus (supported by World Health Organization)
	 	■ http://apps.who.int/trialsearch/AdvSearch.aspx
	• American and global focus
	 	■ https://www.clinicaltrials.gov
	• African focus
	 	■ http://www.pactr.org
	• Australasian focus
	 	■ http://www.anzctr.org.au/
	Within the field of observational studies, there is increasing recognition that prospective registries are important, and several small registries do exist. Review teams are encouraged to seek these out in their chosen field should they wish to include observational studies.





Methods to screen for studies


	At least two members of the review team should independently screen the titles and abstracts of the records yielded by the search and select all potentially eligible studies. The full-text article or report should then be obtained for each agreed potentially eligible study. Where disagreement or uncertainty occurs, it is advisable to adopt a conservative approach and obtain the full-text report.
	Two investigators then apply an eligibility rule based on the PICO to each full-text manuscript and determine if the inclusion criteria are met. A third member of the team can act as arbiter where there is disagreement or uncertainty. The number of records at each stage of the screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion process must be recorded in order to populate the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow diagram in the final report (see section ‘Reporting a systematic review’, later in this chapter). Reasons for excluding studies after reading the full text should also be recorded and provided in the final report.
	It is worth noting that a single study may be reported in more than one article or conference proceeding. For example, a trial protocol and a paper outlining the preliminary results of a trial may be published or presented at a conference prior to the publication of a final report of the trial results. This is viewed as legitimate publication practice. However, sometimes results are published in different articles with no cross-referencing to other relevant reports and can lead to double counting of results in meta-analyses (Abraham 2000). This phenomenon has been labelled ‘salami publication’ and is to be discouraged. The final number of included studies should therefore refer to the number of discrete studies and not the number of articles or reports identified.
	Key point: The search strategy of a systematic review requires the expertise of an information specialist and should be sufficiently comprehensive to ensure that as many eligible studies as possible are included in the review.





Data extraction


What data to collect


	The specific items of data to be collected from included studies will be influenced by the objectives of the systematic review. In general the following items should be collected:
	 	• Eligibility of the study for inclusion or reason for exclusion.
	• Study methods, such as study design and duration, as well as items that will be used to assess the risk of bias, such as sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding.
	• Data regarding participants (e.g. sex, age, ethnicity, and education level) and setting (e.g. institution and geographic location) which may influence the size of the effect estimate or assist in assessing the applicability of results.
	• The number of intervention groups and the details of the specific interventions involved. Any information relating to the fidelity with which the intervention was administered (i.e. the extent to which it was implemented as planned) should be obtained. This is particularly important in preventive or complex interventions, which are usually implemented under ‘real-world’ conditions.
	• Information regarding the outcomes such as their definitions, time points at which they were measured, and units of measurement should be collected. Usually, this is done only for those outcomes prespecified in the review protocol. However, listing all other outcomes reported in the included study may enable analysis of risk of bias due to selective outcome reporting.
	• Results should be collected only for those outcomes prespecified in the protocol. For a meta-analysis it is also necessary to collect the numerical data for analysis.
	• Other information to be collected could include funding source, details of ethics approval, name or contact details of authors, and citations.





How to collect the data


	Once the data to be collected have been determined, it is necessary to design appropriate data collection forms. These may be electronic or paper-based, depending on the preference of reviewers.
	Data extraction refers to the process of recording all the relevant data from the included studies onto data collection forms. Piloting data collection forms using a representative sample of studies is recommended. To reduce the risk of errors during data extraction, it is advisable that at least two reviewers, working independently, are involved in extracting the data. Any disagreements between the reviewers should be resolved through consensus or arbitration by a third person.
	Key point: Selection of what data to extract is guided by the objectives of the review question. Two independent investigators should extract data in duplicate to avoid errors.





Evaluation of the risk of bias


	Interpretation of the results of any type of study is dependent on how well the study was conducted. For example, a randomized controlled trial may yield a significant beneficial result, but if a large proportion of the trial participants failed to complete the trial and outcomes were not available for those lost to follow-up, we may be less likely to believe the result. Similarly, if results from several poorly conducted studies are synthesized in a systematic review, we should be concerned about the effect of the potential risk of bias on the pooled results. An evaluation of the risk of bias present in individual included studies is therefore a key part of the systematic review method.
	Risk of bias is assessed based on the information in the reports of studies. Sometimes, the reported information may be insufficient to make critical judgements about the methods of a study. In these cases, it is important to contact the study authors to clarify any issues regarding study design or missing data that are not described clearly in the report.
	There are several methods for assessing the risk of bias related to study design as outlined next.





Randomized controlled trials


	For RCTs, the Risk of Bias domain-based evaluation tool developed by the Cochrane Collaboration is in widespread use (Higgins et al. 2011). The tool requires a judgement regarding the level of risk of bias (low, high, or unclear) for each of the following six domains:
	 	• Sequence generation
	• Allocation concealment
	• Blinding or masking of participants, providers, and assessors
	• Size of, and differential loss, to follow-up
	• Selective outcome reporting
	• Other biases such as publication bias
	In the past, quality scales which provided an overall score or quality rating were in widespread use. The limitations of such scales include unreliable assessments of validity and difficulty in assigning weights to items in the scale. We mention the use of scales only to provide a complete picture for readers, but would discourage their use.





Non-randomized and observational studies


	For observational studies of interventions, the Cochrane ROBINS-I tool (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies—of Interventions) is available for the appraisal of risk of bias in estimates of the effectiveness or safety of an intervention from studies that did not use randomization to allocate interventions (Sterne et al. 2016). Studies may include observational studies such as cohort studies and case-control studies in which intervention groups are allocated during the course of usual treatment decisions, and so-called quasi-randomized studies where allocation is not fully randomized. It addresses bias due to confounding, selection of participants, misclassification of the intervention, deviations from the intervention, missing data, measurement of the outcomes, and selection of the reported result. Assessment of bias can be rated as low, moderate, serious, or critical.
	The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) is another popular tool which can be used for appraising longitudinal and cross-sectional studies (Wells et al. 2018). Risk of bias is assessed in three domains: selection of participants, comparability of the cohorts, and outcomes. The scale is based on a star system and a total of nine stars can be allocated to a study with no concerns.
	Key point: The risk of bias is essential to evaluate in the studies included in a systematic review to indicate the robustness of the results. Tools should employ a domain approach and scores from scales are to be avoided.





Data synthesis


	A good systematic review includes a detailed synthesis of the results from included studies. Synthesis may be narrative, meta-analytical, or a combination of both. The protocol of the review must identify a priori the threshold(s) for determining if a meta-analysis should be undertaken. In addition, the team should indicate in the protocol if there are important subgroups expected between studies and within the data which warrant separate analyses.





Meta-analysis


	Meta-analysis is the statistical pooling of estimates of effect from individual studies to create an overall estimate of effect from the combined studies.
	There are several benefits of doing a meta-analysis if it is appropriate so to do. It provides a more precise estimate of the treatment effect, helping one to be more confident about the size of any effect. There is more statistical power to detect small effects, which may be clinically significant; and it helps in the evaluation of the applicability of the results to other settings.
	Meta-analysis should only be conducted when the included studies are considered sufficiently similar (or homogenous) to combine together. This is a matter of judgement and systematic review teams familiar with the data should ask the following:
	 	1. Are the interventions, populations, and outcomes similar across studies or do they differ markedly? (Clinical heterogeneity)
	2. Are the methods of the studies similar or different across studies? (Methodological heterogeneity)
	3. Is there a small or large degree of variation between the results of the individual studies? (Statistical heterogeneity)
	If the studies are indeed considered sufficiently similar both methodologically and clinically, then further testing for the presence of statistical heterogeneity can be conducted during the meta-analytical procedure to assess the degree of statistical heterogeneity present. Statistical heterogeneity is quantified with the I2 statistic, which ranges from 0 to 100% (Higgins et al. 2003). The I2 statistic represents the proportion of variability between the studies that cannot be explained by chance. Higher values of I2 indicate more statistical heterogeneity.
	Meta-analyses would require the use of either the fixed effects or the random effects model, each with its own assumptions and approaches to weighting studies and generating confidence intervals.





Measures of effect


	The decision on which effect measure to use should, ideally, be taken when the systematic review is being planned. It should be based on the mathematical appropriateness of the effect measure for the type of data to be analysed. Review teams should select effect measures that are meaningful to clinicians and patients and are commonly used. For example, in a meta-analysis of studies of people living with HIV, the dichotomous outcome measure of undetectable viral load is a preferred measure to change in viral load, which requires log transformation and may not translate into a clinical benefit.
	The team should avoid conducting multiple exploratory analyses using different effect measures and then focusing on the analysis that generates their preferred result (Bender et al. 2008). However, in rare instances changing the effect measure can reduce some heterogeneity.
	For effectiveness data, combined estimates of dichotomous data are generally expressed as relative risks or odds ratios with associated 95% confidence intervals. The risk difference is an alternative which might be more appealing to a lay audience.
	Combined estimates of continuous data are generally expressed as mean differences and associated confidence intervals. Where different scales are used to measure outcomes across studies, the means and standard deviations from the different scales can be combined into a standardized mean difference (SMD) and associated confidence interval. However, the latter can be difficult to interpret clinically and review teams should endeavour to provide the reader with some indication of the clinical significance of the SMD.
	Time-to-event data (hazard ratios) can also be pooled using the generic inverse variance (GIV) method which accommodates other forms of non-standard data. The GIV uses the log transformed versions of the data to place them on a similar and symmetric scale.
	At times, data may not be usable in the reported format and it may be necessary to contact the authors of a study to obtain disaggregated data, or data may require transformation (for example, using logs, estimating means from medians and confidence intervals from p-values) to facilitate meta-analysis. In such cases, transparent reporting of changes to the planned analysis is required in the final report.





Subgroup analysis


	When statistical heterogeneity is present, this should be interrogated further according to the possible subgroups identified in the protocol. Conducting a subgroup analysis may reveal true differences in the data and provide an explanation for the observed heterogeneity. If no explanation is forthcoming, caution is required in interpreting the pooled results and a meta-analysis may not be appropriate.
	Even if there is an a priori reason to expect a subgroup analysis to show something different to the overall result, this is no guarantee that a statistically significant difference is reliable clinically. This is because the more analyses are done, the more likely it is that statistically significant results will be found, even when there is truly no difference between the subgroups. Subgroup analyses in a systematic review should be regarded as a way of showing that the direction of effect is the same across different types of patient or as a generator of a hypothesis for testing in future research. The results of subgroup analyses should be treated with caution because the effect of chance will be larger for the subgroup than for the overall result.
	It is recommended that the sources of clinical heterogeneity be determined a priori, based on clinical expertise and scientific rationale, and only focusing on variables related to the research question (participants, interventions, comparisons, outcomes). There is extensive guidance on how to conduct and interpret subgroup analyses (Higgins et al. 2002; Gagnier et al. 2013; Sun et al. 2014). Most statistical packages incorporate a formal test for subgroup effects or test of interaction. This test tells you how likely it is that the difference in effect estimates from the subgroups is due to chance.





Sensitivity analysis


	Like all statistical analyses, meta-analysis is dependent on underlying assumptions. Once the decision to conduct a meta-analysis has been made, investigators select a statistical model to underpin the analysis. Both the random and fixed effects models are widely used, with the use of a Bayesian approach also recommended for addressing heterogeneity and missing data (Higgins et al. 2009; Moreno et al. 2018). At the protocol stage, reviewers should identify the preferred model and their reasons for its selection.
	At analysis stage, a sensitivity analysis can be conducted comparing the results obtained from different models. Consistent results between models provide greater confidence in the overall pooled result; where results differ between models, investigators need to consider the underlying reasons for this and exhibit caution in interpreting the final result.
	Sensitivity analyses can also be conducted on other parameters, such as study quality. A meta-analysis of all eligible studies can be compared with a meta-analysis limited to those studies which are rated at low risk of bias. Again, investigators should think carefully about the interpretation of inconsistent results and how the inclusion of studies at high risk of bias affects the results.





Unit of analysis errors


	Trials can employ randomization at an individual, cluster, or crossover level. Combining studies with different levels of randomization in a meta-analysis can lead to unit of analysis errors and yield potentially spurious results. Analytical approaches for such data must account for the correlation between participants in the same cluster and for participants who contribute control and intervention data on crossover designs (Donner et al. 2001; Elbourne et al. 2002).





Meta-regression


	Meta-regression is another way of exploring or explaining heterogeneity in meta-analyses (Thompson and Higgins 2002). It allows us to investigate the effects of more than one categorical or continuous variable on the outcome. It is an extension of simple regression in which the outcome variable is the measure of effect and the explanatory variables are the covariates that might influence the measure of effect. Meta-regression is not recommended when there are fewer than ten studies (Thompson and Higgins 2002). The findings from meta-regression are observational and should be treated as such.





Publication bias (Funnel plots)


	Despite reviewers’ efforts to conduct exhaustive and comprehensive searches of published and unpublished data, some relevant data sources may be missed (Sedgwick 2015). The presence of publication bias plays an important role in how we appraise the completeness of a body of evidence and its quality. The presence of publication bias can be investigated using a graphical test called a funnel plot, or be statistically tested using Egger’s and Begg’s significance tests (Thornton and Lee 2000).
	The funnel plot is a plot of sample size against the effect size of the included studies. If publication bias is absent, the points on the plot would look like a funnel, with the smaller studies spread widely at the base of the funnel and the larger studies spread narrowly closer to the top. Asymmetry in the funnel plot is indicative of publication bias (Song et al. 2013) but observed asymmetry may be present for other reasons. Egger’s and Beggs’s significance tests investigate whether the study estimate is related to its size and are regression-and correlation-based, respectively (Thornton and Lee 2000).
	In Figure 5.13.1 we illustrate a forest plot of invented data. This meta-analysis includes ten studies conducted in low-income and high-income settings comparing text messaging (SMS) and cash transfers to a text messaging alone on the outcome of treatment adherence.
	Fig. 5.13.1 Forest plot of invented data, from a meta-analysis of ten studies in high-and low-income settings, comparing text messaging and cash transfers to text messaging alone on the outcome of virologic success.
	The outcome is dichotomous and measured as a relative risk. The data are pooled using the random effects approach and 95% confidence intervals are reported.
	The vertical line is the line of no difference or a relative risk = 1.
	A subgroup analyses is conducted to compare the relative merits of SMS & cash to the SMS alone, separately in the high-income and low-income settings.
	The squares represent the point estimates and the horizontal line going across them represents the breadth of the confidence interval for each estimate.
	The size of each square is proportional to the weight allocated to the study in the meta-analysis. The weight is derived from the inverse of the variance. In other words, the less precise, smaller studies with wider confidence intervals would have smaller squares.
	The diamond represents the pooled estimate. For a positive outcome, like adherence, a diamond to the right of the line of no effect would indicate that the outcome is more likely to occur in the participants who receive SMS and Cash.
	The amount of heterogeneity between all ten studies is reported as 47%; between the subgroups as 90.1%; in the high-income subgroup 0% and in the low-income subgroup 0%. The test for subgroup differences is statistically significant (p<0.001).





Narrative syntheses


	When a meta-analysis is judged to be inappropriate due to significant heterogeneity, authors are advised to present a comprehensive narrative synthesis. Presentation of the study characteristics and the data should be given the same consideration as if a numerical synthesis were conducted. Note that a narrative synthesis is not a synonym for a ‘traditional literature review’. A narrative synthesis refers to the reporting of results in a systematic review where a meta-analysis is not appropriate or possible, and employs the same rigorous systematic review methods as a review which includes a meta-analysis (Popay et al. 2006).
	Methodological and clinical heterogeneity should be reported with risk of bias and consistency in direction of estimates described. It is important to recognize that formulation of a single overall statement of the direction of benefit (or harm, or no effect) may not be possible, and caution is advised against counting studies with significant findings versus those without. Narrative syntheses contribute to the delineation of the current evidence base and can inform and influence primary studies to provide more standardized reporting of outcomes to allow for future meta-analysis.
	Key point: Meta-analysis should only be conducted when included studies are judged to be sufficiently similar, both methodologically and clinically. During meta-analysis, tests for statistical heterogeneity indicate whether the pooled results are statistically homogenous. If not, consider whether subgroup differences identified a priori explain the observed heterogeneity. Where meta-analysis is not appropriate, a detailed narrative synthesis should be reported.





Summarizing the overall quality of the evidence


	Once the results of a systematic review are available, decision-makers need to know how much confidence to place in the evidence arising from the review. This need to integrate the review results with a quality measure led to the development of several methods to present review evidence graded by a measure of strength. Current hierarchical evidence rating systems include the A to D approach used by the United States Preventive Services Task Force (U.S. Preventive Services Task Force), the Oxford Centre for Evidence-based Medicine Levels 1 to 5 (Centre for Evidence-based Medicine 2016), and the GRADE approach (Guyatt et al. 2011a). We report here in detail on the GRADE method for interventions.
	GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) provides a method to classify the overall quality of evidence arising from a systematic review as high, moderate, low, or very low (Guyatt et al. 2011a). Reviews which include several RCTs are initially graded as high quality given that the randomized design provides the highest level of evidence to support effectiveness. This level of quality may then be downgraded dependent on limitations in the included studies which include the presence of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and/or publication bias. Downgrading by a single level takes place when the limitations are judged as ‘serious’, and by two levels when judged as ‘very serious’. On the other hand, a review of observational studies is initially graded as providing low quality evidence and can in turn be downgraded for the same reasons as RCTs, or upgraded if circumstances permit (Guyatt et al. 2011e).
	Results for a maximum of seven critical outcomes are presented in a GRADE Summary of Findings table. Critical outcomes refer to those outcomes which consumers of the review—those who will be directly impacted by the results—consider most important to their health. For example, trial investigators may measure a biomarker to evaluate efficacy of a medication, but patients may be more interested in the impact of potential adverse effects of the medication on their quality of life. The systematic review team may wish to consult with consumer associations to best reflect their needs in the selection of critical outcomes.
	For each of the seven critical outcomes, the systematic review team will assess whether there is an overall risk of bias across the included studies. If a risk of bias is judged to be present, the overall quality will be downgraded (Guyatt et al. 2011f).
	When grading indirectness, the team must judge whether or not the included studies match the PICO of the systematic review, either directly or indirectly. For example, evidence may need to be extrapolated from adult studies to a PICO focused on children, where no trials of children exist. In such a case, the results would be downgraded for indirectness (Guyatt et al. 2011c).
	Results are downgraded for inconsistency where heterogeneity is present and it cannot be explained e.g. by subgroup differences. The presence of heterogeneity alone is insufficient to downgrade the results; it is the presence of unexplained heterogeneity that drives a decision to downgrade (Guyatt et al. 2011d).
	When considering imprecision, authors need to consider the width of the confidence interval around the effect estimate and determine whether this is precise or not by considering the sample size and event rate (Guyatt et al. 2011b).
	Note that judgement is required for all of the aforementioned domains, and the review team must record the rationale for each judgement in a footnote in the GRADE Summary of Findings table. This ensures transparency and allows the reader to understand the reasons for each decision.
	Once all the domains are graded, an overall quality of evidence per outcome is generated. The levels of quality are interpreted as follows:
	 	• High: We are very confident that the true effect lies close to that of the estimate of the effect.
	• Moderate: We are moderately confident in the estimate of effect: the true effect is likely to be close to the estimate of effect, but possibly to be substantially different.
	• Low: Our confidence in the effect is limited: the true effect may be substantially different from the estimate of the effect.
	• Very low: We have very little confidence in the effect estimate: any estimate of effect is very uncertain.
	It is important to recognize that the results for different outcomes may arise from pooling the results from different studies and as a result, the quality of evidence may differ across outcomes.
	Key point: GRADE is a system of quality assessment which incorporates the risk of bias, indirectness, imprecision, and inconsistency to determine the overall quality of evidence arising in a systematic review. Quality is graded as high, moderate, low, or very low.





Reporting a systematic review


	The PRISMA for reporting systematic reviews is the equivalent of CONSORT for reporting randomized trials (Moher et al. 2010) and was first published in 2009 (Liberati et al. 2009) building on the earlier QUOROM statement (Moher et al. 1999). PRISMA is an evidence-based minimum set of items for reporting in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Although PRISMA focuses on the reporting of reviews evaluating randomized trials, it can be extended to reporting systematic reviews of other types of research, particularly evaluations of interventions.
	PRISMA provides a checklist for authors to ensure that the following items are comprehensively and transparently reported:
	 	• Title
	• Abstract
	• Introduction
	• Methods
	• Results
	• Discussion
	• Funding
	The PRISMA checklist is explained in a detailed Explanation and Elaboration document which has been published in several journals (Liberati et al. 2009). A mandatory component of reporting in a systematic review is the PRISMA flow diagram which documents the stages and resultant yield of records of the search strategy.
	Several extensions to the PRISMA Statement have been developed and include PRISMA for Network Meta-analysis and PRISMA for Diagnostic Test Accuracy (see http://prisma-statement.org). Authors of systematic reviews are encouraged to report their methods and results according to the relevant PRISMA Statement.
	Key point: Systematic reviews should be reported using the structure recommended in the PRISMA Statement.





Appraising the quality of a systematic review


	A systematic review which conforms to the methods outlined in this chapter would be considered well-conducted. However, similar to the quality assessment of included studies, the quality of a systematic review can also be categorized according to whether or not a risk of bias is present. It is particularly helpful for healthcare decision-makers to know how much confidence to place in the results of a systematic review.
	Several tools exist to assess the quality of the conduct of a systematic review. The AMSTAR-2 critical appraisal tool provides a 16-item checklist incorporating the key methodological components of a review (Shea et al. 2017). The AMSTAR-2 tool does not provide a score but a rating of confidence in the results of the review based on the presence of weaknesses in critical items. It can be applied to reviews of randomized and non-randomized studies of healthcare interventions.
	The ROBIS tool was developed in 2016 to evaluate the risk of bias in reviews of most types of research questions including diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment (Whiting et al. 2016). It provides a similar judgement-based domain approach to the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for trials. Four domains include multiple questions related to the methods and the appropriateness of the study eligibility criteria, identification, and selection of studies, data collection and study appraisal, and synthesis and findings. An overall risk of bias (high, low, or unclear) is then derived from an assessment of whether the concerns raised in the four domains are addressed in the interpretation of findings, combined with an evaluation of the relevance of the included studies to the review question, and the degree to which the reviewers avoid emphasizing statistical significance.
	AMSTAR-2 and ROBIS are designed to provide a structured approach to evaluating risk of bias in systematic reviews which requires judgement. Many may find this difficult to do, and it is recommended that evaluation is completed independently by at least two investigators who have methodological and content expertise.
	Key point: The quality of a systematic review can be evaluated using a tool such as AMSTAR-2 or ROBIS, to indicate the robustness of the synthesized results.





Related approaches to evidence synthesis


Scoping reviews


	Scoping reviews are variably defined in the literature. In 2005, Arksey and O’Malley described four aims of scoping reviews viz. (1) to examine the extent, range and nature of research activity; (2) to determine the value of undertaking a systematic review; (3) to summarize and disseminate research findings; and (4) to identify research gaps in the literature (Arksey and OMalley 2005). A scoping review will generally have a broad focus compared with a systematic review which adopts a narrow focus defined by a PICO question. Given that a scoping review aims to ‘map’ the current research base on a topic, the type of included study will not be limited to RCTs but may include all forms of studies to the topic. Clearly, use of robust systematic methods would enhance the quality of a scoping review, but a scoping review may follow a more traditional review approach and categorize the results by topic area rather than present a quantitative summary or an assessment of the study quality. A 2014 scoping review of 344 scoping reviews described variability in the methodological process, terminology, and reporting of scoping reviews. The authors identified a need for methodological standardization to increase the use and the relevance of findings derived from scoping reviews (Pham et al. 2014).





Overviews of reviews


	An overview of reviews aims to identify and collate the results from relevant reviews on a specific topic (Thomson et al. 2010). An overview, also known as an umbrella review, may be conducted for several reasons. Firstly, when several systematic reviews on distinct interventions exist for the same condition, decision-makers may wish to summarize the evidence base on all relevant treatment modalities and present this in a single report. Secondly, when the number and focus of reviews on a relevant topic is not known, an overview can aid in identifying the scope of the current evidence which has undergone review.
	In an overview, the review is the type of included study design. Note that an overview may include only systematic reviews, or may include both systematic and literature reviews. Regardless of the type of included review, the methods of an overview mirror those of a systematic review with the exception that the risk of bias assessment uses the ROBIS (or similar) tool, instead of the ROB tool. There is currently no consensus regarding the application of GRADE or other ranking systems to produce an overall quality assessment in an overview.





Individual patient or participant data analysis


	This is a form of meta-analysis in which trial investigators collaborate to share individual level data from their trials, instead of aggregated data, in order to ensure that the pooled results mimic a single large trial. This allows for standardization of analyses across studies independent of how the aggregated analysis was conducted (although clustering of each individual trial must be retained rather than treated as coming from one large trial) (Riley et al. 2010). Individual participant data analysis can be very resource-intensive and is dependent on close collaboration of trial investigators, but arguably produces a more reliable estimate than a meta-analysis of aggregated data.





Prospective meta-analysis


	There is debate in the literature as to whether a single large ‘mega-trial’ conducted in trial sites around the world following an identical protocol provides better evidence than several smaller regional trials combined in a meta-analysis (Shrier et al. 2007). Concerns have been raised about the potential of increasing error when pooling aggregated results from small underpowered trials even if precision is increased. One possible solution is prospective meta-analysis in which trials are identified, evaluated, and determined to be eligible before the results of any included studies are known or published, thereby avoiding some of the potential biases inherent in standard, retrospective meta-analyses (Askie et al. 2011). This methodology provides the same strengths as a single large-scale multicentre randomized study while allowing greater pragmatic flexibility. The combined meta-analytic results using individual patient data from each trial is published when all the trials are complete.





Network meta-analysis


	Simple meta-analysis compares one intervention to another. This is a direct pairwise comparison. However, reviewers may be interested in comparing more than two treatment options. Trials may compare two treatments with each other or the treatments may have both been compared to placebo. In this instance a multiple treatment comparison, or a network meta-analysis (NMA), is possible. A NMA has the advantage of being able to provide information on the relative merits of interventions that have never been compared directly. A NMA can also increase the precision of effect estimates by using two sources of data: the direct pairwise comparisons and the indirect comparisons based on the comparisons to placebo (Mills et al. 2011; Mbuagbaw et al. 2017). Three key assumption underlie NMAs. The first is homogeneity, which simply refers to the absence of heterogeneity. The second is transitivity, which examines the validity of making indirect comparisons as all the control groups may not be identical. The third is consistency between the direct and indirect evidence (Mills et al. 2013). The results may be presented graphically or as ranks that represent the probability of an intervention being first or second and so on. NMA is a fairly novel field and guidance on how to conduct, interpret, appraise the quality of the evidence and report NMAs is becoming more available.





Diagnostic test accuracy reviews


	Reviewers may be interested in summarizing the accuracy of a diagnostic test. The searching and screening would be similar to a typical interventional systematic review, but in this case the data extracted would be the sensitivities and specificities of the diagnostic test in question as reported by the included studies (Leeflang 2014; Campbell et al. 2015). Many reviewers use the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS) tool to appraise the quality of the included studies. There are two important analytical considerations with diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) reviews. The first is the threshold effect. Tests based on continuous data (e.g. haemoglobin) require a threshold above (or below) which the test is positive. If different studies use different thresholds, this introduces heterogeneity in the review. The second issue is that sensitivity and specificity are correlated and therefore must be modelled together. The hierarchical summary ROC (HSROC) model and the bivariate model random effects model are used to address the first and second issues, respectively. Both models allow for covariate adjustment (Leeflang 2014).





Rapid reviews


	No consistent definition for rapid reviews exists in the literature and methodologies differ across published rapid reviews (Tricco et al. 2015). However, the hallmark of a rapid review is acceleration of the systematic review process, usually by simplifying or leaving out methodological stages. This allows evidence to be quickly produced for time-sensitive decision-making. Conduct of a rapid review is dependent on a highly skilled review team and urgent provision of necessary resources. With the availability of electronic database searching, computerized study selection, and shared analytical tools, stages of a review can be sped up significantly. A rapid review need not, and arguably should not, compromise on rigorous methodology, but this remains a risk when urgency prevails. We suggest that protocol templates for systematic reviews based on categories of interventions be developed in anticipation and utilized when a rapid review is required. Research to delineate the consequences of methodological shortcuts is warranted (Tricco et al. 2015).





Qualitative reviews and CERQual


	Systematic review methodology has been successfully applied to identifying and synthesizing qualitative study data. Unlike an interventional review, the aims of a systematic review of qualitative data include providing greater in-depth understanding of an issue, informing theory development, and describing major themes related to a topic. CERQual is an approach to providing a confidence rating in the synthesized qualitative evidence, based on the GRADE approach to judging overall quality (Lewin et al. 2015). Methodological limitations, relevance, coherence, and adequacy of data are considered and an overall summary of the level of confidence regarding the representation of the phenomenon of interest is produced.





Use of systematic reviews in practice guidelines


	Guidelines development should be based on evidence derived from systematic reviews. In 2007, the World Health Organization was criticised for failing to base global clinical recommendations on systematic review evidence and for an over-reliance on experts with limited methodological expertise (Oxman et al. 2007). In response, the World Health Organization (WHO) actively developed a rigorous approach to guidelines development based on the GRADE framework and outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (WHO 2014). Evidence derived from systematic reviews forms the foundation of the GRADE framework for decision-making, which is further supplemented by values and preferences, and issues of acceptability, feasibility, resource use, and equity. The process is transparent and the quality of evidence underpinning a recommendation is clearly reported as part of the overall recommendation (Andrews et al. 2013).
	Subsequent research to evaluate guidelines development within WHO has indicated that recommendations are increasingly based on systematic review evidence (Sinclair et al. 2013) but challenges remain. Active engagement between guidelines developers and systematic reviewers is to be encouraged and a certain level of tension is anticipated. Critics have identified that at times strong recommendations have been inappropriately based on low quality evidence and advocate for further training in GRADE methods for guideline panellists (Alexander et al. 2014).





What does the future hold for systematic reviews?


Living systematic reviews and artificial intelligence


	The concept of a ‘living’ systematic review grew out of the recognition that the value of a systematic review lies not only in its accuracy, but also in its currency. A living systematic review aims to continually update the evidence as new data becomes available (Elliott et al. 2017). It requires a pre-determined frequency of searching which is predictable, allowing for updating of guidelines in real time. New technologies to speed up the review process are available, for example, through machine-learning of screening for references for eligibility assessment. The accuracy of such screening classifiers can be improved by feedback models from human identification which can further be enhanced by using citizen science via crowd-funding initiatives (Thomas et al. 2017). The potential and limitations of harnessing automation to increase human responsiveness need to be carefully considered and tested to ensure the validity of results from living reviews, but offers great promise.





Mining big data


	Big data in the form of biobank development integrated with clinical data (Bouzille et al. 2018) may offer robust longitudinal data which may in time provide a substitute for data derived from RCTs. The utility may be greatest for treatment of rare diseases. However, ethical issues regarding access to the data and consent remain a subject of ongoing debate (Lipworth et al. 2017) and statistical modelling will be required to determine the key criteria for drawing causality inferences from longitudinal data derived from such databanks.





Advancing systematic review methodology


	Current efforts are underway to determine the most appropriate ways to conduct systematic reviews. In addition to independently-led methodological reviews of systematic review practices, the Cochrane Methods Groups (https://methods.cochrane.org/) and the Northern Ireland Network for Trials Methodology Research (https://www.qub.ac.uk/sites/TheNorthernIrelandNetworkforTrialsMethodologyResearch/) are actively engaged in this process.





Software and resources for systematic reviews


	Several resources exist for the conduct of systematic reviews, some of which are commercial (not reported here) and some are not-for-profit. We present a selection which readers may find useful as starting points.





Cochrane


	Cochrane (formerly, the Cochrane Collaboration) is an international voluntary organization which generates and compiles Cochrane systematic reviews, considered the gold standard of reviews. Several helpful resources are available for review authors:





The Cochrane Library


	Cochrane reviews are published on an electronic database, The Cochrane Library. Many countries provide national subscriptions to medical professionals and the general public. See http://www.cochranelibrary.com/





The Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions


	This handbook is a step-by-step guide to writing, analysing, and reporting a Cochrane review. See http://handbook-5-1.cochrane.org/





REVMAN


	This software is free and provides a text-based review template and built-in meta-analytic software. It also contains links to the Cochrane Handbook. See http://community.cochrane.org/help/tools-and-software/revman-5





The GRADE Working Group


	The GRADE Working Group continues to develop the GRADE approach and software for reviews, health technology assessment and guidelines. See http://www.gradeworkinggroup.org/





GRADEPro


	This software is free and produces Summary of Findings tables to present the overall quality of evidence based on meta-analysis. The software interfaces directly with REVMAN. See https://gradepro.org/





Rayyan QCI


	Rayyan offers free support for reference management, screening, and storage. See: https://rayyan.qcri.org/welcome





Conclusions


	In this chapter, we have provided the reader with a comprehensive approach to systematic review methodology, a guide to understanding and interpreting meta-analysis, and a synopsis of the many applications of systematic reviews and related syntheses. Although the science of systematic reviews is relatively new within epidemiology, the impact of systematic review and meta-analytic methodology has been considerable: evidence from reviews informs the direction of primary research, underpins guidelines, and provides patients, clinicians, and the general public with greater certainty regarding treatment and prevention choices. Yet it is important to remember that systematic reviews, like all studies, are subject to biases. The data generated from a review is secondary to that reported in the included studies and is thus totally dependent on the quality of the individual research studies used in the review. Users of evidence derived from systematic reviews should remember that critical appraisal remains an essential tool for the thoughtful researcher, clinician, and policymaker.

5.14


Statistical methods


	Gail Williams and Robert S. Ware





Introduction to statistical methods


	Statistics is the study of mathematically based techniques used to collect, analyse, and interpret quantitative data. In public health, this occurs in a complex of biological, clinical, epidemiological, social, ecological, and administrative systems. Sometimes we want to describe, explore, or summarize data without extending our findings beyond the coverage of the data we have—that is, the sample. More usually, however, we want to extend, or generalize, our findings from the sample to a larger group, sometimes called the ‘target’ population. In this situation, we need to consider carefully two aspects of our data collection. Firstly, what was the actual source of our data, and how did we select the sample from the population? If we deliberately excluded some people in our sampling, or made it more difficult for some rather than others to be included in our sample, then the sample may not represent the population equitably—we may have a biased sample. Secondly, we expect that if we repeat the data collection, even under identical conditions, we will get somewhat different results. This variability, called sampling variability, needs to be taken into account in deciding how precisely findings from our sample reflect what is happening in the population.
	We now have access to a wider range of statistical techniques than ever before. It is important that analytical methods used are appropriate to the sampling strategy, the type of data collected, and the research questions to be answered. We usually want to generalize our results to a population. The process of using samples to draw conclusions about populations is called statistical inference.
	In this chapter, we discuss basic concepts underpinning data analysis and statistical inference. The ideas of probability theory are heavily involved in random sampling, which takes place under the assumption that a probability model governs the selection of the sample. Probability models are also involved in helping quantify uncertainty in sample estimates. We will also discuss a range of statistical techniques in common usage, outlining the underlying assumptions, and focusing on interpretation.





Basic concepts


Populations, samples, and sampling


	For the purpose of discussing statistical methods, a population is the complete set of entities we want to consider in our enquiry. The entities may, for example, be free-living humans, hospital patients, disease vectors, communities, or health services. A sample is defined generally as a subset of a population. The sample may not be of interest in itself; its use is to provide information about the population, such as to estimate the incidence of malaria or to compare the risk of lung cancer among smokers and non-smokers. By taking a sample from the population instead of enumerating the entire population, we save resources and time. We may choose to spend some of these savings on achieving greater quality of measurement, or better follow-up of those we select. The price paid, however, is that we cannot make an absolute statement about the population; we have only an estimate—the sample incidence, or the excess of lung cancer in our sample of smokers.





Probability and random sampling


	The solution to the concerns of obtaining an unbiased estimate and being able to quantify uncertainty entails the notion of ‘fairness’ in the sample selection process. A ‘fair’ method of sampling does not favour or discriminate against any member of the population. However, if we can quantify any ‘unfairness’, we can correct for this in the analysis, and so still obtain an unbiased estimate. For example, if males are twice as likely as females to be selected from a population that contains equal numbers of each sex, we can compile the data so that females have twice the weight. Thus, what actually matters is that we know how likely it is that each individual in a population is selected for the sample—i.e. the probability of selection of each person.
	We measure probability with a single number, which has particular properties, some of which are as follows:
	 	• Probabilities lie between 0 and 1 (or 0 and 100%).
	• If the probability of the event is 0, there is no chance of the event occurring.
	• If the probability of the event is 1, the event is certain to occur.
	• The combined probability of a complete collection of events is 1.
	A process whose outcome is unpredictable and governed by rules of probability is termed random. If we are drawing random lots to select one person from 100 people, we can say (before sampling) that the probability of inclusion of an individual is 1 in 100, but we cannot predict exactly which individuals will be included. Other classic random processes are outcomes of coin tosses or rolls of a die. We know that in the long run, the chance or probability of a head is 0.5 or 50% on any one toss of an unbiased coin, but the outcome of any particular toss is unpredictable.
	The word ‘random’ as used in statistics has a specialized meaning. It is used to describe a process whose outcome (in this case, getting selected for the sample or not) is governed by the play of chance. Random does not mean ‘haphazard’ or ‘arbitrary’.
	A sample in which each person in the population has the same chance of selection is called a simple random sample. This can be achieved by listing all the members of the population (this list is called a sampling frame), applying an unbiased random process of selection, such as drawing lots or using computer-generated random numbers, and obtaining a sample of the required size. In practice, compiling a sampling frame can be difficult. More generally, a sample for which we know the probability of selection (whether the same or not) for each person in the population is called a probability or random sample.
	Recommended sampling techniques usually require identifying a population as the source of our sample. Thus, to obtain a sample of 7-year-old children to estimate the prevalence of childhood asthma, we might begin by obtaining school class lists. It is important to be clear about the population for which we want to draw conclusions. Is it the population of 7-year-old school children or is it all 7-year-olds? It may only be feasible to sample formally a restricted population (school children), but we really want to make conclusions about a wider population (all school-aged children). This wider population is sometimes referred to as the target population. Whether conclusions can be extrapolated to a wider population than actually sampled is then a matter of judgement.
	If someone has no chance of being selected in the sample, and they are different with respect to the characteristics we are measuring, or if individuals vary in both their chances of selection and the characteristics of interest, we expect to have a biased sample. We often have no way of predicting how individuals vary in the characteristics being measured, but if we can control, and therefore know, the probability of selection, we can control the potential for bias. Sampling which does not follow these rules is termed non-probability sampling. Here we do not know the probability of inclusion of population units. Sometimes we cannot define the population sampled. These methods include convenience samples (people waiting in outpatient departments) or haphazard samples (‘people in the street’).
	Critically, a sample is termed a random sample because of its method of selection. We cannot determine whether a sample is random by examining it, we must know the process by which it was obtained. Examining a sample for observations which are deviant in some respect or comparing its characteristics with those of a target population cannot ascertain randomness.
	Thus, ‘random’ does not equal ‘representative’ (although using a random method of selection, in some sense, decreases our chances of non-representativeness). In summary, the reasons for using random sampling are to:
	 	• Enable quantification of the sampling variation using probability theory.
	• Ensure that a statistically unbiased estimator of the quantity of interest is obtained.





Complex sampling


	Complex sampling is the term used to describe probability sampling which is not simple. A variety of methods, or their combination, may be used. Stratified sampling is used when the population consists of a number of subpopulations or strata which vary in the quantity of interest. We sample randomly within each stratum separately, in order to control the stratum-specific numbers, or to take into account large variability across strata. For example, typically (but not universally) urban areas have larger populations than rural areas. For sampling such a population we might first wish to stratify by rural/urban status, to achieve predetermined numbers or sampling fractions in each region. If sampling fractions differ for each stratum, the overall sample will not be a simple random sample, because the probability of selection will vary across strata; it will, however, be a probability or random sample because we can, knowing the sampling fractions within strata, calculate the probability of selection of any unit. If we control the stratum sizes to exactly reflect those in the population we can achieve greater precision than a method which ignores strata. In designing a stratified sampling scheme, we need to be clear about our priorities—do we want to disproportionately increase the numbers in a particular stratum, or do we want to control optimally for interstrata variability?
	If we select a simple random sample from a large city, individuals selected would be widely scattered and costly to reach if we have to conduct face-to-face interviews, for example. Cluster sampling involves selecting groups of individuals, rather than individuals themselves, to increase logistical efficiency. A random sample of people in a city could be achieved by first selecting a simple random sample of census collection districts, and including all people living within the selected districts. The disadvantage is that the sample may be artificially ‘homogeneous’; the selected people may be more alike than if we had used a simple random sample. This statistical inefficiency is measured by what is known as the design effect, which must be estimated in the analysis phase.
	Two-stage sampling is similar to cluster sampling except that a sample of the cluster is taken instead of the whole cluster. This helps overcome the problem of ‘homogeneity’ to some extent, but creates a more complex process, as there are two sampling stages.
	In some cases, the sampling fractions for selecting clusters and selecting from them are carefully manipulated so that the overall probability of each population unit being selected is the same. One such method is called sampling proportional to size—clusters are selected with a probability proportional to their size (larger clusters have larger chance of selection) and then a fixed number of individuals is selected randomly from each selected cluster. Another method is proportional sampling in which clusters are selected with equal probability, and a fixed sampling fraction is used to select individuals from each selected cluster. Cluster sampling and two-stage sampling do not require an explicit sampling frame for the whole population. In two-stage sampling we need a list of first-stage units (e.g. census districts) and then a list within only each first-stage unit actually selected. This is an advantage, particularly if sampling poorly documented populations. Two-stage sampling can be extended to three or more stages, for example, districts, towns, households, and individuals.
	Stratified, cluster, or multistage sampling strategies provide opportunities to measure entities at all levels. Thus, factors may be relevant at the village level (presence of a health centre, degree of remoteness), the household level (family income, access to piped water), or the individual level (age, sex).
	Complex sampling allows individuals to have different probabilities of inclusion in a sample. It is imperative that we can calculate each person’s probability of inclusion, otherwise we cannot make the necessary analytical adjustments. All information relevant to probability of inclusion must be documented in the course of the sample selection.
	Complex sampling schemes require expertise and care to design and analyse. It is usually necessary to seek advice from a professional statistician. Most statistical software has appropriate analytical procedures, and these may have particular requirements in the construction of the data set.
	We next consider the issue of characterizing information collected on our sample. This involves categorizations of variable types, crucial in deciding how to present or analyse data.





Describing variables


	A primary distinction is made between quantitative and categorical variables, because these are analysed using different techniques. The distinction is based on the kinds of values a variable may take. For the purpose of statistical analysis, what matters is the type of measurement of the variables, specifically whether they are measured on a numerical scale (such as age) or in categories (male or female). Sometimes a numerical variable (e.g. blood pressure in mmHg), is subsequently categorized (hypertensive or not hypertensive), but it is important to realize that it is the final form (numerical or categorical) of the variable that matters for analysis.





Categorical variables


	A categorical variable is one whose values are expressed in mutually exclusive categories (e.g. survival status, social class, sex, religion, extent of disability). These are further subdivided into nominal and ordinal. A nominal variable has values that are categories, with no implicit ordering of the categories (e.g. sex, religion). A variable with two levels only (e.g. sex) is referred to as a binary, or dichotomous variable. Categories of an ordinal variable have an underlying order (e.g. social class, extent of disability). Categorical variables are usually described by frequencies and percentages in each value category, and presented in tabular or graphical form, such as bar charts or pie charts. For example, a study of child mortality examined the types of birth attendant at delivery of children in the study. This can be presented in a table (Table 5.14.1), or graphically in various ways (Figure 5.14.1).

	Although the choice of graphical presentation is partly a matter of taste, bar charts tend to be used for ordinal variables (as the bars can be ordered appropriately) and pie charts used for nominal variables (to de-emphasize order).





Quantitative variables


	Quantitative variables express values in numerical measurement (e.g. height, age, number of births), and are further subdivided into discrete and continuous variables. A discrete variable takes only certain distinct values, usually whole numbers (e.g. number of births). A continuous variable takes all values within the observable range (e.g. age, birthweight, serum cholesterol). It is essential to specify units of measurement.





Frequency distributions


	Quantitative variables are usually described, at least initially, in a frequency distribution, which tabulates, in mutually exclusive and contiguous groups, the number or percentage in each group. For example, a study documents birthweights (kg) of children born at a major obstetric hospital in Brisbane, Australia, using a sample of 500 full-term babies (gestation of at least 39 weeks). A frequency distribution portrays this (Table 5.14.2), after cut-off points for groups according to birth weight are chosen.
	Choice of cut-off points for groups is to some extent arbitrary. We usually want at least eight groups, and prefer them to be evenly spaced, although this is not strictly necessary. Some recommend using √N (square root of N) groups, where N is the sample size. We may use cut-offs defined for other purposes (e.g. using 2.5 kg as a cut-off identifies ‘low’ birthweight babies, as commonly defined). If we want to compare with a frequency distribution from another study, we use the same cut-off points. A frequency distribution is often graphed in a histogram (Fig. 5.14.2a). This usually requires a large number of values to provide a picture of the shape of the distribution, which may be important when we are choosing a method of analysis. Not all distributions are symmetric. A variable may have a negatively (Fig. 5.14.2b) or positively (Fig. 5.14.2c) skewed distribution, when the peak is pushed to the right or left, respectively.
