5.16


Mathematical models of transmission and control of infectious agents


	Alex Welte and Cari van Schalkwyk





Introduction


	Indeed, the ‘heavy lifting’ of healthcare is in the care of patients, the development and distribution of vaccines, drugs and devices, and the conception and implementation of sensible systems and policies. However, in recent decades, spectacular increases in the availability of computational capacity have paved the way for mathematical modelling to play an ever-increasing role in many aspects of public health, by supporting formal analyses at various scales of the processes involved.
	The core ideas of mathematical modelling are beautiful, powerful, and simple. However, it can seem like a dark art to outsiders, distracted by the details or daunted by the considerable training and experience that appears to be required for attaining confidence, intuition, and proficiency.
	By its nature, mathematics is a broad framework, and the natural maturation of mathematical modelling lies in abstraction and generalization. Under this large and growing umbrella there is room for many mathematical ideas, approaches, and techniques. For biomedical research in general, and public health in particular, most mathematical analysis and modelling takes the form of ‘statistical’ modelling of some kind.
	In statistics, the key point is usually to understand how details of data are driven by ‘randomness’, and how, despite the randomness, when there is ‘sufficient’ data, we can learn a great deal about the underlying situations and events from which our data are generated. These ‘statistical’ methods of biomedical and public health research are the underlying mathematics that brings us such things as ‘confidence intervals’ for estimates, ‘p-values’ that express the consistency of a hypothesis with data, ‘correlation coefficients’, and so on. This health-applied statistical field, usually called biostatistics, is a major industry, and some familiarity with its key concepts is a prerequisite for reading about public health research at any depth beyond the most superficial. While we presume that the reader has some basic statistical knowledge, we will not lean heavily on this assumption.
	This chapter explores a particular kind of ‘modelling’—and it is not the common (bio)statistical kind. We focus on what we would call ‘dynamical’ modelling (as opposed to ‘statistical’ modelling, see Table 5.16.1.). This essentially entails the reduction, to mathematics, of key facts and principles inherent in the ‘processes’ or ‘mechanisms’ in an epidemiological situation. We can then manipulate these mathematical constructs, in search of insights that, while ultimately implied in the model construction, are not superficially apparent from our primary data and our intuition.
	 	Table 5.16.1 Basic features and uses of ‘statistical’ and ‘dynamical’ models
	 			Statistical Models
	Dynamical Models
			 	 	• Account for random error and bias in data to find correlations that may imply causality
	• Support assessment of relationships
	• Assume independence of individuals (sometimes independence within clusters)
	• Typical questions:
	• Is HIV status positively associated with the risk of TB infection?
	• Are insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) or indoor residual spraying (IRS) more effective for controlling malaria?
	 	 	• Systems approach—explicitly model (hypothetically ‘declare’) specific mechanisms, to explore their interactions
	• Encapsulate particular relationships between parts of the system
	• Explicitly focus on interdependence of individuals
	• Typical questions:
	• Based on increased TB risk due to HIV, how should we expect the TB notification rate to vary with HIV prevalence?
	• How do we expect the age distribution of malaria incidence to change after implementing ITNs or IRS?
	Of course, it’s not just surveys and clinical trial measurements that involve randomness. Many processes that are fundamental to epidemiology are ultimately subject to some randomness. Decapitation in an industrial accident is sure to lead to death, but even being infected with Ebola virus does not have an entirely predictable outcome. There are many levels of randomness that inevitably creep into any description of a complex situation involving biology and society. Typically, given a fully (as far as possible) specified situation and set of rules, outcomes (like infections) vary (in number), by chance, around some ‘average’, ‘mean’, or ‘expected’ value.
	Our focus, however, is on capturing and understanding the average/expected behaviour of an infectious epidemic, given some specific assumptions about the rules that govern its behaviour. This allows us to use methods of quantitative investigation that are not fundamentally dominated or complicated by randomness.
	Infections such as HIV, tuberculosis (TB), malaria, measles, dengue, zika, cholera, Ebola, etc. persist as major causes of ill health, psychosocial stress, and premature death—not to mention economic strain and impediments to development more broadly. Among the many details which are specific to each infectious agent and outbreak, an important recurring theme, in the analysis of infection moving through a population, is that there is more going on than just a collection of individuals who happen to share a ‘risk profile’ or ‘environment’. There is a fundamental difference between the risk of heart disease, driven by genetic and lifestyle factors, and the risk of tuberculosis, which depends heavily on how many TB infected people one comes into contact with. This dynamical interaction between people who have acquired, and those who are susceptible to, an infection, is the heart and soul of infectious disease epidemiology. Using mathematics to model this process provides a powerful way of elucidating concepts that can help us understand aspects of disease dynamics that would otherwise be difficult to approach intuitively.
	Aside from helping us better understand subtle collective effects, there is another fundamental aspect of the unique power of mathematical modelling: direct observation, and the application of formal experimental techniques, can only take us so far in the context of studying people, illness, care, and social systems. Ideally, scientists prefer to watch a system again and again, varying one ‘thing’ at a time (temperature, voltage, force, infectiousness, etc.) to elucidate the impact various factors have on the behaviour and/or state of a system—whether this be a solid material, a liquid solution hosting chemical reactions, or a gas trapped in an airtight container. When we want to understand a very much more complex system, comprised of many components, such as a society grappling with diseases, it’s almost too obvious to bear spelling out that we cannot just perform arbitrary experiments. Even if it were ethically/morally defensible, it would simply not be possible to learn enough, sufficiently quickly, and at feasible cost, to provide meaningful actionable insights.
	For example, we may wonder:
	 	Do we need to vaccinate everyone to prevent measles outbreaks, or is some incomplete, approximately quantifiable, level of coverage sufficient to provide ‘herd immunity’ by restricting the transmission network so that even those who are not vaccinated will be highly unlikely to encounter infectious individuals, i.e. that a single case will not plausibly lead to a wider outbreak?
	This question cuts to the heart of ‘collective’ effects in infectious spread, and it clearly cannot be answered by
	 	• isolating numerous communities with various well-defined interaction/activity networks
	• subjecting them to different (precisely measured) levels of vaccine coverage
	• introducing a case of measles into each isolated community
	• noting how big the outbreaks tend to be as a function of the vaccination coverage and social network structure
	One would have to do it all many times, to explore the many permutations of factors. Even worse, because there is inherent randomness in disease transmission in the real world, one would actually need to probe the average behaviours of any particular combinations of factors (as well as other statistical/distributional properties, such as, for instance, the worst 5% of outcomes).
	What else can we do, then, to explore such questions, which are forever and fundamentally beyond the scope of controlled experiments? This is where models come into their own. Glossing, for now, over pretty much all the details, but not, we hope, all the important concepts (which we will also revisit more thoroughly), we can summarize a model-based investigation of the measles question as:
	 	• building a model world in which we declare specific hypothetical rules about measles transmission—based on biological and health systems insights.
	(Model world construction is best done by a multidisciplinary team.)
	• capturing the states and rules of the model world in precise mathematical statements/equations/computer code
	(i.e. building a mathematical model





, using particular techniques.)


	• calibrating/fitting the model to data from past measles outbreaks with varying levels of vaccine uptake, including, crucially, no vaccine.
	(Calibration





is a process that engages heavily with biostatistics.)


	• running scenarios from various initial conditions defined by factors like which (or simply how many) population members are initially infected/infectious; and, critically, the vaccine coverage.
	(This is sometimes known as ‘





driving


’ the model.)


	• Exploring trends in the realizations of the simulated epidemics by noting how various indicators of epidemic trajectory/severity/duration depend on the simulated policies (i.e. conduct an actual investigation.)
	A model-based investigation, then, leverages our current insights, beliefs, data sets, perhaps in conjunction with some interesting ‘what if’ scenarios, and turns these into their downstream implications (sometimes referred to as ‘predictions’, causing unnecessary confusion). Some inferences are obvious, like ‘Increasing vaccine coverage reduces the size of outbreaks’. Some may be striking discoveries, like ‘essentially complete outbreak suppression can be achieved at less than complete vaccine coverage’.





The fundamentals of modelling


	The recurring central problem facing all attempts to describe the natural world, including the world of human endeavours, is this:
	 	How do we describe a particular part of the world, about which we have specific questions, without being drawn into attempting to describe so much of it that we drown in details and complexity?
	This is the recurring challenge, whether we are trying to make sense of basic physical concepts like gravity, or trying to understand why some parents decline to have their children given readily available vaccinations. Mathematical modelling is a powerful tool which can help us to make key aspects of this process explicit and clear, and to be disciplined and consistent in our investigations.
	Stepping one step further back: our current goal is to help the reader improve their mental model of the modelling process itself, without getting too far into philosophical asides. To this end, we will rely heavily on a modelling framework which, as far as we know, is the brainchild of Tony Starfield. We will call it the ‘real-world, model-world, model’ paradigm (Starfield et al. 1990). We would also like to tip our hat to the somewhat older heuristics toolbox contained in the classic How to Solve It by George Polya (Polya 1945). Polya’s ambition was far broader than our current focus on models of infectious agents, but for anyone intending to wrestle with formal problem construction and solution, it is extremely valuable, and hence paraphrased in Box 5.16.1. Starfield acknowledged Polya’s groundwork by choosing the title ‘How to Model it’ for his own excellent and entertaining guide to, in his words: ‘modelling in the computer era’ (Starfield et al. 1990).
	 	Box 5.16.1 Polya’s ‘How to Solve It’ heuristic
	 	• Understand the problem. Restate the problem in your own words (possibly to someone else); Consider whether you have enough information; Draw a picture.
	• Devise a plan. Solve a simpler problem (the simplest possible, we recommend); eliminate possibilities; guess (and check); look for patterns; Be creative!
	• Carry out the plan that you have chosen. At first, persist with your plan some through initial setbacks; If it really does not work, make another plan.
	• Review/extend. Look back at what you have done—what worked and what didn’t; Learn from this to help you solve future problems.
	Source: data from Polya, G. (1945) How To Solve It. Princeton University Press.
	Particularly striking in Starfield’s exposition (Box 5.16.2), and the main point which we would like to help make more mainstream, is the habit of taking seriously the middle ground between the external real world and mathematical details, what he calls the ‘model world’. We have found this device to be extraordinarily useful, not just pedagogically, but also as a modelling insiders’ heuristic that tangibly supports the planning and execution of model-based investigations.
	 	Box 5.16.2 Starfield’s three realms
	Real world: The world we live in: inordinately complex, only partly knowable, not under our direct control.
	Model world: Rules and ‘degrees of freedom’ are arbitrarily declared and fully known. We also have the power to declare the model world to be in any (internally consistent) particular state, without considering how such a state might have been attained.
	Model: Mathematical constructs and computer code that capture aspects of a model world—its states and rules. Models are intended to be manipulated and explored (analysed) to help understand the model world, and by extension, aspects of the real world.
	Source: data from Starfield, A. M., Smith, K. A. and Bleloch, A. L. (1990) How to model it: Problem solving for the computer age. McGraw-Hill.





The model world


	Before any mathematical equations or lines of computer code are written, there is usually some considerable, if not always explicit, mental construction of some simplified analogue of reality—a ‘model world’! In a model world which we create, the possibilities are constrained, the fundamental rules are asserted rather than discovered, and we can press rewind, change the starting point (or even the rules), and let time run again, as often as we want. This is essentially what we always do, at least implicitly, when conceiving of any object, system, or principle.
	When a bridge is designed, it does not matter exactly how many turns will be applied to each bolt—what matters is the basic structure and sufficiency of all beams and joins—although the final bridge will manifest countless minute details. All gadgets are manufactured to ‘tolerances’ which, while acknowledging the impossibility of producing an exact incarnation of a blueprint, provide guidance on the scale of acceptable deviation. When we say the word ‘house’ we have access to substantial shared meaning with all speakers of English, without having to spell out anything else, because we all carry around with us the concept; in other words, a model, of a house.
	The point of this lengthy conceptual preamble is that the first, and most important, step in practical mathematical modelling does not require any substantial detailed knowledge of the formal subject of mathematical modelling. It is an inherently interdisciplinary process, and one to which professional modellers are but one of several crucial contributing groups. The more this idea becomes accepted, the better will be the models that are implemented, and the better will be the interpretation of modelling investigations into real world action—a process lately popularly known as knowledge translation. What we are calling Starfield’s ‘three-realms’ ‘model of modelling’, then, emphasizes that before we write down equations, or generate computer code to run simulations, we need to spell out, preferably in plain English (or another natural language) and simple diagrams, which hypothetical world(s) we wish to explore. We are free to create as many new model worlds as we like. One of the most important rules of thumb in model world construction is to start as simply as possible. In other words, start by constructing the simplest model world in which anything resembling your actual question can actually be asked, even/especially if this version of your question is so simple that you can answer it.
	For example, if we wish to model the spread of seasonal influenza, we may want to explore a model world characterized by the following characteristics:
	 	• People infected with flu virus become infectious immediately, and remain infectious for precisely 7 days.
	• Any pair of individuals, regardless of infection status, have some given probability per day of coming into contact with each other in a manner that would cause transmission if one of them is infected and the other not.
	• Once people cease to be infectious after 7 days, they cannot be infected again.
	• No one dies during the timeframes under consideration (3 months of flu season).
	This relatively simple to grasp, if obviously simplistic, set of rules specifies a fully-fledged ‘model world’: a realm in which we know precisely what the rules are—because we declared them!
	The model world is further unlike the real world in that we get to choose, arbitrarily, in what state the population is at some point in time—without regard to questions about how we got there. For example, we can ‘start’ with one individual who is infected with flu, living among 1,000 who are not, and have never been; and we can do this without having to ask, much less explain, where this one person came from, or how he/she became infected with flu. Then we can ‘let four months pass’ under the rules specified earlier, and we can investigate how the world unfolds. We can ‘dilute’ the transmission process by declaring that some proportion of the individuals begin the flu season with immunity from a vaccine they took before the outbreak, and we can consider different population sizes and numbers of cases specified in the ‘initial conditions’ from which our ‘model scenarios’ start.
	To generate analysable scenarios, we usually need to go beyond conversational thought experiments. Of course, if we make a simple enough model world, we can immediately tell what will happen. Consider that aliens have landed in an isolated town of 100 people, and they exercise the arbitrary power to seize one person every day for their amusement and nourishment. It does not require mathematical skill to conclude that in at most 100 days, the town will be devoid of living people; somewhat earlier if our model world allows for other causes of death, or successful escape—but we have the power to rule these out, if we wish.
	Alternatively, perhaps the aliens need a day to recharge their stun gun. They aim at one juicy looking human early in the morning, but, alas for the aliens, the stun gun bullets are flaky and half of them misfire. Then we can no longer be sure that one person dies per day—but every day, there is half a chance of someone dying.
	Consider yet another possibility: each alien needs to eat one person each day to survive (the food on board having rotted rapidly after exposure to earth’s bacteria after landing). In fact, if the aliens aren’t doing so well themselves in the face of earthling microbes, then we would need to keep track of the number of aliens who are healthy enough to hunt, if we wish to be able to specify the number of human deaths.
	The point of this cartoonish example is to show that full specification of model world rules can take many forms, but, if done carefully, often leads to simple mathematical ideas. In the three examples of aliens hunting for humans, we have human deaths occurring, respectively:
	 	• at a steady rate of one per day;
	• randomly, but, on average, once every other day;
	• at a rate determined by the current number of healthy aliens.
	A key determinant of the satisfactoriness of a story, especially in the realm of science fiction, or fantasy, is no doubt whether the model world created by the author seems internally coherent, and whether the particular storyline (scenario) plays itself out in a manner that is consistent with various explicit and implicit rules we have discerned. Even children want to know whether and how it makes sense that Lord Voldemort was apparently killed by his own death spell, in the final climax of Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows. Fortunately, the internet provides parents with detailed analyses of the nature of wands, and wand ‘allegiance’ or ‘ownership’. Armed with this knowledge, parents can reassure their children that it’s not a case of ‘it’s complicated’, or just some arbitrarily slapped together plot holes. The natural ability of people of all ages to discuss, critique, and savour stories is ample testament to the universal capacity of the human mind to build, upload, analyse and critique model worlds by wielding substantial sophistication, insistence on internal consistency, and intuition.
	And just as the naturalistic learning and investigations of children are similar to, but not the same as, formal scientific inquiry, so creating and exploring model worlds in words, pictures, and thought, is intimately related to, if not quite the same as, quantitatively generating ‘scenarios’ through mathematical devices such as algebra and computer simulation.





Historical overview of disease modelling


	Perhaps the first application of dynamical mathematical modelling in public health was carried out in 1760 by Daniel Bernoulli to understand the efficacy of inoculating people with smallpox to prevent their developing the disease later. Bernoulli used what we would now call an ‘SR model’ (of susceptible and removed elements) to elucidate the variations in the size of susceptible and removed subpopulations over time (Bernoulli 1760; Dietz and Heesterbeek 2002; Bacaër 2010). Bernoulli concluded that, while inoculation carried some risk, it could substantially increase life expectancy, not only by trading the risks and benefits for individuals but (crucially) also by reducing overall transmission in the population.
	More than one hundred years after Bernoulli’s seminal work, Ronald Ross showed that malaria infects people through the bites of mosquitoes (Ross 1895, 1899), and for this discovery he was awarded the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine in 1902. In fact, Ross may have been a better mathematician than he was an entomologist. He developed one of the first mathematical models of disease transmission based on differential equations, to support his claim, in the face of considerable scepticism, that malaria could be eradicated by reducing the mosquito population to below a critical level, without the need to eradicate the mosquito population entirely.
	The notion that there are critical thresholds on dynamical parameters, below which disease transmission cannot persist, is perhaps the central point of mathematical models of the spread of infectious agents. This is most famously embodied in the concept of R0, the basic reproduction number, defined next.
	Another crucial example of such a ‘tipping point’, which can only be understood through the collective dynamics of a population, is the attainment of ‘herd immunity’ at partial coverage of an imperfect vaccine. Even if there are still infected and susceptible individuals in a population, if transmission is not efficient enough to replace cases as quickly as they are naturally removed, then prevalence and incidence are doomed to decline—ultimately to zero (see online appendix for more details).
	Ross’s model, published in the second edition of his book The Prevention of Malaria (Ross 1910, 1923), became the basis for subsequent modelling of vector-borne infections. He concluded, as also crucially cited in Bacaër (2010):
	 	As a matter of fact all epidemiology, concerned as it is with the variation of disease from time to time or from place to place, must be considered mathematically, however many variables are implicated, if it is to be considered scientifically at all. To say that a disease depends upon certain factors is not to say much, until we can also form an estimate as to how largely each factor influences the whole result. And the mathematical method of treatment is really nothing but the application of careful reasoning to the problems at issue.
	In the late 1920s and 1930s, William Kermack and Anderson McKendrick introduced continuous time epidemic models that incorporated stochastic (random) elements of infection and recovery (McKendrick 1926; Kermack and McKendrick 1927; Harvey 1943; Bacaër 2010). They showed how to include age, or time since infection, as continuous variables, and how to generalize models to deal with time-dependent infectiousness and recovery rates. Together with Hamer, Soper, and Ross (Hamer 1906; Ross 1923; Soper 1929), they laid the early foundations for modern mathematical modelling in epidemiology. Crucially, they realized that epidemics are driven by the rate of contact between susceptible and infectious individuals. Because the simplest models do not distinguish between individuals, all uninfected people are equally likely to be infected and the probability that a susceptible person is infected is simply proportional to the number (or proportion) of people who are already infected. This so-called principle of mass action, first formulated to model the rates of chemical reactions, now found applications in infectious disease epidemiology. It simply captures the idea of two (sub) populations being so perfectly mixed that the ‘contact rate’ is proportional to each (sub) population size (or proportion) individually.
	When considering the control of transmissible diseases, the single most important concept is the basic reproduction number, conventionally written as R0 and most commonly thought of as the number of secondary cases produced by a single primary case introduced into an otherwise entirely uninfected population. The roots of this concept can be traced through the work of Alfred Lotka, Ronald Ross, and others, but its first modern application in epidemiology was by George Macdonald (Lotka 1923; Ross 1923; Macdonald 1957), in constructing population models of the spread of malaria. The concept was extended and developed by Dietz (Dietz 1980) and by Anderson and May and their various colleagues and coworkers. The collaboration of Anderson and May culminated in their definitive book Infectious Diseases of Humans: Dynamics and Control (Anderson and May 1991).
	The number of publications applying mathematical models to answer questions regarding infectious diseases has increased dramatically in the last two or three decades, due largely to the unprecedented growth in computational power. Models are increasingly relied upon to inform public health policy and funding decisions, examples of which will be discussed later in this chapter.
	Key concepts for modelling infectious disease are outlined in Box 5.16.3.
	 	Box 5.16.3 Basic concepts crucial to the modelling of infectious agents
	(See online appendix for a more detailed treatment)
	 	• Basic reproduction number: number of new cases directly produced by one case in a purely susceptible population.
	• Disease duration: length of time individuals spend in an infected state.
	• (Disease) mortality: rate of death (usually probability per year).
	• Equilibrium: a scenario in which the state of the model world is unchanged by time.
	• Herd immunity: collective ability of a population to resist or extinguish an outbreak, despite containing susceptible individuals.
	• Incidence: rate of occurrence of infections.
	• Prevalence: proportion of a population affected by a condition at a point in time.
	• Model scenario: ‘model world’ history with fully specified initial conditions and rules.
	• Parameter: a variable which expresses a rule—a model input.
	• State variable: a variable capturing a model output.





Types of model worlds, or mathematical models


	In this section we give conceptual definitions of, and brief remarks on, some of the most important model-world/model ‘types’ encountered in disease modelling. The list is far from a systematic review, and avoids overanalysis of grey areas. The categories are cross cutting. For example, compartmental models may be deterministic or stochastic, and they may be discrete or continuous, in any combination.
	Static vs. dynamic models: In static models, the rules affecting individuals are fixed. For example, the incidence of infection is given a predetermined value, and no interaction between individuals is considered. In dynamic models, the rule defining parameters may explicitly be varied over time, and the time-dependent prevalence of an infection may be allowed to play a role in transmission of the infection. Static models, commonly used in cost-effectiveness analyses, can track individual life trajectories involving costs and benefits of health system interactions, within a context that is declared by fiat. Here static doesn’t mean that nothing happens in the model world. Rather, the term indicates that we are ignoring the emergent impact (feedback) of factors like health system interventions, or prevalence of disease, on the overall context in which individuals will find themselves. In a dynamical model world, such feedback is considered. For example, an intervention may change infectious pressure in some non-trivial way as time passes. This can be crucial to sensibly modelling long-term costs and benefits. A static model can estimate long-term costs for individuals who received the vaccine or not, but it cannot account for herd immunity—i.e. the indirect protection individuals obtain by interacting with immune individuals.
	Compartmental vs. individual-based models: In a compartmental model, population members move between compartments or health states according to rates determined by parameter values that are defined at an aggregate level. Within each compartment, all members are equal in every detail, and indeed utterly lose their individual identity. When noting how many population members flow out of a compartment, during a given period, there is no way we can even sensibly ask such questions as which population members they are, or how long they have been in the compartment they are leaving. An individual-based model (also known as a microsimulation model or agent-based model) explicitly keeps track of individuals’ particular states, and, in principle, their individually tailored tendency to experience events. Infection, relationship formation or dissolution, death, and so on, are simulated as occurring to particular individuals. A key feature of this approach is that it allows for extensive, complex, and not-consciously-predetermined heterogeneity between individuals, whereas compartmental models must explicitly enumerate all possible states in which population members may be found. Both of compartmental and individual-based types of models can be either dynamic or static.
	Deterministic vs. stochastic models: In stochastic models, there is intrinsic randomness in the occurrence of events. The key epidemiological processes, such as transmission of infection, are governed by probabilities, or probabilities per unit time (or time step). These probabilities are of course not just an expression of vagueness. They capture, or, depending on your point of view, emerge from, specific dynamical rules. In deterministic models, the future is entirely determined by the choice of a combination of ‘initial conditions’ and ‘dynamical rules’. Usually, when we construct a deterministic model world, we are actually thinking of capturing some aspects of real world dynamical processes that are at least in part stochastic. Then we usually interpret the outputs of a deterministic model to be average numbers of events (like infection or death), or average sizes of population groups (like people requiring long-term HIV treatment) that are expected (rather than strictly determined) in a model world where the dynamics are ultimately stochastic.
	Population-level vs. in vivo models. Models of biological processes within an individual, from the life cycles of cells and infectious agents to pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic processes, are often referred to as in vivo models. In contrast, population-level models focus on a higher level/scale of aggregation. Usually this point is not explicitly noted, as most epidemiological models disregard complex biological details. However, it is useful to be aware that there are interesting questions at both scales, and the fundamental modelling process is very similar, and even leads to similar structures and processes, like healthy and infected subpopulations, cycles of death and reproduction, transmission of infection status through contacts and environmental exposures, etc.
	Discrete models vs. continuous models. In discrete models, features, such as time itself, or other quantities expressing the state of the model world, jump in discrete steps. For example, individual level models always have whole numbers of people. In continuous models features vary continuously, being able, in principle, to take any value in some sensible range. We can run a continuous model until 0.4 people are left alive. It is not at all unusual for a single model to simultaneously conceive of some aspects continuously and others discretely—for example, discrete jumps in population states occurring against a continuous timeline and continuously varying risk factors.





Fundamental models


	This section aims to capture the essence of dynamical modelling by demonstrating, in considerable detail, including conceptual digressions, some very simple models. We hope to show that modelling is really not something strange or difficult, accessible only to a closed circle of initiates or specialists.
	Useful epidemiological models can be complex, and many models appearing in the literature are, we would argue, unnecessarily complex. ‘Occam’s razor’ is the tried and tested philosophical heuristic that encourages us to cut away unnecessary details and assumptions in our search for explanations, and it applies with great consistency in formal modelling. We noted earlier that one should always start with the simplest possible model worlds in which we can see any trace of the issues we are exploring—and we would now add that indeed one should also stay as simple as possible at all times. The examples next are particularly stripped down—so much so that one could be forgiven for wondering whether they are to be taken seriously, or whether they really illustrate real contemporary disease modelling. In fact, they fully illustrate a conceptual framework for approaching population dynamic models, and, in particular, disease transmission models.
	We trust readers can recall some advanced high school mathematics. Familiarity with basic calculus will greatly help. Even readers with no prior modelling experience, but a willingness to take the plunge, notepad in hand, should be able to follow most, if not all, of the details of these examples, and should find here a foundation for a deeper reading of the modelling literature.





‘Exponential’ growth or decline


	The notion of ‘exponential growth’ (or decline) is one of the most important recurring themes in all dynamical modelling—from the pure sciences like physics and engineering, to highly applied social sciences like population dynamics. Exponential growth has little to do with the popular notion that something has grown ‘exponentially’, which often simply means that something has grown ‘enormously’ (explosively?).
	Technically, exponential growth simply means that some quantity is changing (growing or shrinking) at a rate proportional to how large it currently is, with both the size and the growth continuously adjusting to maintain this relationship, at least for a while, if not indefinitely.
	Exponential growth can lead to surprisingly rapid growth in some cases, but it can also be very slow. A simple savings account that attracts a measly few percent interest per year, in a society where inflation runs in the double digits, will experience face value exponential growth in the monthly balance statements, but leave us with (exponentially) less and less purchasing power over time.
	Let’s consider a question of the most fundamental kind in population dynamics:
	 	Question 1: Given a population of 1 million individuals, with individual mortality (m) of one percent (0.01) per year, how many will (are expected to) be alive after 10 years?
	Following our noses, we now build a model world in which this question can be explored. It involves nothing more than spelling out what the rules are:
	 	• There are neither births nor migrations in or out of the population.
	• Each member of the population faces a predetermined fixed probability, m, of death each year.
	And just like that, our model world has been created. The assertion that we begin with 1 million individuals is not so much a dynamical rule, as a statement about initial conditions. To go beyond the purely conceptual, so that we can calculate something useful using the tools of mathematics, we now consider whether there is some subtlety in how we think about time.





Thinking of time as passing in discrete steps


	One view on time passing is to accept that either the model world itself, or the mathematics we are using to describe it, is somehow vague on exactly when people die, and that it is only the number of deaths in each year, or alternatively, the population size at the beginning/end of each year that is well-defined.
	Another way of spelling things out in gory detail is to come up with a quite contrived (even if absurdly comical) ‘dynamical process’:
	 	• At the beginning of each year, 1% of people are handed death notices, requiring them to report to the Grim Reaper at the end of the year.
	• Just after the deaths all occur just at the stroke of midnight on New Year’s Eve, a new round of death notices is handed out to the survivors.
	We can even ponder the possible arcane details of how the Grim Reaper’s administration works. For example:
	 	• Perhaps the death scheduler in chief does some rounding off, to the nearest whole number, when deciding, explicitly, according to a formula, how many death notices to issue each year, based on how many people are currently alive.
	• Perhaps people are required to roll a one hundred sided die, which has one side with a 0, and 99 sides with a 1. A death is scheduled for every person who rolls a zero.
	• Perhaps there really aren’t well-defined individuals here—just an annually revised declaration of the number of individuals. And perhaps we don’t much care whether this is a whole number. Then we can simply schedule (0.01)N deaths, even if N is not a multiple of 100. For example, if there are 250 people at the beginning of a year, we will let 2.5 people die that year, without worrying that this is not possible in the real world. In fact, one could argue that 2.5 deaths are not even possible in our model world. The fractional population members could be said to be a trick to create a simple mathematical approximation to what happens in our model world.
	The last of these three, even though it is in some sense the weirdest, departing even from our real world experience of people being counted in whole numbers, is actually the most simple, analytically. Allowing for non-whole numbers of individuals is an important and widely recurring device. It allows the stated individual-level risk or probability of death to be directly manifested, within each time step, as the actually realized population proportion which dies. This is the crux of focusing on ‘dynamical principles’, which are well-defined, rather than ‘actual realizations’ of a dynamical rule, which are usually subject to some sort element of randomness in the real world. This hints at a recurring theme. We can often buy a lot of analytical efficiency, not to mention simplicity and clarity, with just a little bit of abstraction, just a bit of appropriate slippage between either:
	 	• the real world and a model world, or
	• (and this is a point of view not often spelled out) a model world and a set of equations which purports to capture aspects of the model world.
	The abstraction from real to model world has at least two distinguishable aspects:
	 	1. In order to get off the ground, we need some simplification and spelling out of the basic rules that embody what the investigation is about, such as births, deaths, and infection.
	2. There is additionally often a need to decide on some very mundane details, which may at first appear irrelevant, or extraneous to the main question. Everything that can happen in the model world needs to be spelled out with sufficient specificity for the mathematics to be able to enter the discussion, and possibly, as a bonus, for the analysis not to be overly complicated.
	It is well understood among scientists, engineers, etc. that there is much value in drawing semi schematic diagrams (suggestive of key aspects of reality) to help visualize complex biological systems like cells or organs. These pictures are usually called cartoons, which is by no means a disparaging term. It’s just another example of the process building a model world to support a conversation where there are in principle many complications that we cannot possibly consider in detail. Similarly, it is absolutely normal for modellers to make up superficially silly sounding explanations for how things are decided, coordinated, implemented, and tracked, in model worlds. We enthusiastically encourage an unrestrained approach to making up model world rules, and visualizations to support thinking about all the required details.
	Having made quite a meal of the construction of this most simple model world, we are ready to assign actual mathematical relations to what is happening. We introduce the state variable, which is just the population size (N), and which we need to evaluate at discrete values of time, namely 1, 2, 3, … (years in our example, but it could be any unit of time such as days, weeks, months, even hours, and so forth). Letting Nt denote the population after t years, we can now finally proceed to build equations.
	The flipside of the declaration about the proportion of deaths, m, per year, is that (1–m) is the proportion which survives each year. Hence we have the following expressions for the population at later times, in terms of the population at the start:
	and so forth. These lead us naturally to identifying a general expression governing the population dynamic. Given the population at an arbitrary time t, we can write the population 1 year later:
	This kind of relation is called a difference equation. It tells us something about a function, intended to be evaluated/interpreted at particular steps—in this case, N, should be a whole number, interpreted as time measured in years. More specifically, this particular difference equation tells us how the function is related to itself when it is evaluated at two values separated by one time step. Even more specifically, increasing the ‘independent variable’ (time) by one (interpreted as the passing of one step of time, i.e. one year) causes the function N to change by a given multiplicative factor—which we happen to express as (1–m).
	Difference equations are a widely applicable way of capturing a range of idealized (model world) dynamical rules, like:
	 	• Each year, the staff complement of a rapidly growing company doubles.
	• Each month, my bank adds to my account 0.5% of the average value I have maintained in my account during that month.
	• Each month, the amount of money under my mattress increases by exactly the $100 I put there on payday.
	• After I reach age 65: every month, my retirement fund will be affected by two components of change: a decrease by a fixed pay out to me (my pension) and an increment of 0.5% of the value of the fund the moment before the pension pay out.
	Most people are somewhat familiar with ‘algebraic equations’. A ‘linear’ equation can be solved for a unique value of x that satisfied Ax + B = 0, for some given values of A and B (the answer is x = –B/A). A quadratic equation (AX 2 + Bx + C = 0) can be solved for potentially two values, and so on. Difference equations are not used to solve for particular values of x in this sense. The ‘solutions’ of difference equations are fully specified functions Nt, which, in order to be solutions, have to obey the difference equation for at least a specified range of values of the step variable—in our case, all positive whole (natural) numbers. It can be very challenging to solve such equations, but in this case (Equation 1), it is not difficult to figure out that the population after t years is given, completely generally, by
	Even without any substantial mathematical analysis, we should expect that, as the number of years grows indefinitely large (tends to infinity), the population in Question 1 becomes indefinitely small (tends to zero). This is reflected in key features of the model formulae:
	 	• the population size after t steps (years) is the original population size, multiplied by t copies (or t th power) of the factor (1–m), and
	• (1–m) is positive but less than one.
	An often wielded algebraic/analytical concept is that powers of any positive number less than one can be made as close to zero as we want, by taking a high enough power.
	The very particular property that in each time step the population:
	 	shrinks by a factor
	or, put differently:
	 	sheds a number of members in proportion to how large the population was at the beginning of that time step
	is known as the exponential decline of the population. Of course, we can also turn it around and define exponential growth as increasing by a certain factor in each time step.
	According to the discrete time analysis, then, the concrete answer to Question 1 is given, to the nearest whole number, by:

Thinking of time as passing continuously


	With time, t, now allowed to take any value, not just whole numbers, we want to find a fully specified function of time, N(t)which expresses, for any (positive) real number t, the population size at time t. The crucial conceptual leap here is to construct a slightly different kind of model world, still inspired by the same underlying question (the ‘Question 1’ referred to previously) but a world that fundamentally deals with time continuously. Just as we discovered some details that needed to be spelled out in the discrete time model world, here we are left with choices about the representation of the population itself. Firstly: should the population be allowed to vary continuously, or should the population jump in steps of one, at appropriate times?
	As before, we will allow no births or migration to take place in the continuous time model world. Before we confront the problem of tracking and updating the population size, we need to adapt the stated mortality dynamic as being a constant mortality rate m. In discussing what this means, and how, ultimately, to incorporate the idea into a mathematical model, we will use the language of calculus, but develop the argument intuitively rather than formally.
	The recurring elementary task, in specifying the behaviour of a continuous time model world, is to consider what happens to the system when time t advances by a very (‘infinitesimally’) small increment, usually called dt (time intervals which are not necessarily infinitesimal are usually called ∆t). The deceptively simple Figure 5.16.2, which does little more than remind us to think about a short time interval, dt, is such a useful crutch, that we in all seriousness recommend it be drawn whenever continuous models are being developed.
	Fig. 5.16.2 The fundamental diagram of dynamical modelling in continuous time. Attention is drawn to what happens during an extremely small (‘infinitesimal’) interval of time, of duration dt. In such a small interval of time, there may be some discernible, and describable, tiny (‘infinitesimal’) changes in our model world, but they will not, during this interval of infinitesimal duration, feed back into any changes in how the model world behaves. This is a fundamental technique of modelling—and thus we are able to derive differential equations, whose solution(s), which we obtain by the tools of calculus, will describe how the model world behaves over time.
	In the real world, if we were to consider ever smaller time windows, it would become more and more likely that no notable events occur in these time windows. Indeed, the very idea of a time increment, or window, of size dt, is of one that is small beyond all measurement and practical meaning. Nevertheless, it turns out to be perfectly sensible to say that the (very small/infinitesimal) probability dP of having an event occur, subject to a rate m, is just the rate itself, times the (infitesimal) size of the proposed interval, i.e.
	This could be seen as a fundamental definition of a rate, and in the minds of many modellers, it is seen just like that.
	While this is a bit abstract at first blush, it has a simplicity, and some analytical advantages, that is not as nicely manifest when accumulating events over real-sized time steps. When we want to know how many people die in a year, all sorts of complications arise. What if different times of year bring intrinsically different hazards? Or what if any of several non-lethal events (like disease acquisition), which can happen in complex ways during the year, then in turn bring with them the risk of complications and death? It can be very difficult to just write down a rule summarizing what all can all happen in a year. In fact—figuring out what can happen in a year is probably the research question, or a crucial non-trivial subquestion. We can hardly expect to get far with a method for solving this problem if that method starts by writing down the solution.
	In a sufficiently small time step, however, it becomes much simpler. A key simplifying concept is that there can be no variation in rates during the interval dt. This is the nature of infinitesimal intervals—their most important property for modelling purposes. Events may happen within infinitesimal intervals, but these events cannot provide feedback to the rules of the game quickly enough to change the rules during the very interval under consideration.
	It is in principle quite possible to construct a model world in which time passes continuously, and individuals die at well-defined points in (values of) time. These points in time can be ‘chosen according to’ (technically, ‘generated by’) a suitably well-defined (but not necessarily constant) mortality rate. We will, however, allow the population to be decreased by a continuous ‘flow’ of deaths, which is often much simpler—much like the non-whole number populations sizes we proposed in the discrete time formulation. This is usually done via a rule which forces the model world to track, at all times, the ‘average’ behaviour of a related model world with discrete jumps in population counts. For many investigations, this doesn’t imply any important loss of information or insight, and these models of continuously varying population sizes are indeed a mainstay of scenario models. They allow us to bring to bear, in a very direct and efficient way, powerful ideas and theorems of calculus, which make it possible to uncover detailed and robust analytical insights, and efficiently generate precise and informative numerical/graphical representations of very complex dynamical processes.
	We want to take the step from:
	 	• Modelling probabilities of events, to
	• Modelling a continuous flow that captures the expected accumulation of events.
	In a continuous time continuous-population-size model world, there is always something happening—populations are flowing into each other smoothly in some way. The way to turn out ideas about probabilities into population flows is as follows:
	 	• Retain the idea that every member of some population (potentially itself a subpopulation of some wider group that we are also explicitly tracking) is, by virtue of their presence in the particular population, subject to an event rate m.
	• Hence retain the idea that each population member has an infinitesimal probability, dP, of experiencing the relevant event, in a time slice dt, with dP = m * dt.
	• Crucially, declare that the (infinitesimal) proportion of population members which experience the event in the time slice dt, is precisely equal to the (infinitesimal) per-individual probability dP which we just defined as our dynamical rule in the stochastic view. This is where we build in the rule that what happens at all times is the expected/mean behaviour of a cousin model world where events are truly stochastic and fluctuations are allowed.
	• Conclude that the number of population members which experience the event in a time slice dt is given by dN = * dP.
	In an infinitesimal time slice dt, then, there will be an infinitesimal reduction in the population, due to an infinitesimal number of deaths. All the processes can now be thought of as continuous flows, just as we usually think of the flow of water as proceeding with infinite smoothness, even though we know that in the real world, there are a trillion trillion water molecules tumbling around in a small glass. It’s seldom important to know any details of how those molecules are bumping into each other.
	So we have come as far as noting that, between time t and time t + dt, there will be
	deaths. This is more usually written as:
	Which is achieved simply by:
	 	• dividing both sides of the equation by dt
	• inserting an explicit minus signs to capture that deaths lead to a reduction in the population N.
	The meaning of dN/dt, known as a ‘derivative’, is, by analogy with the concept of gradient or slope, an expression for the rate of change of N, with the passage of time, t. This equation can be solved (technically, ‘integrated’) by standard methods developed in any calculus course, to yield an expression for the population Ntafter time t:
