	This differs slightly (by about 1 part in 2,000) from the answer given by the discrete model in Equation 2, and the respective solutions will diverge further, as the time passes. This somewhat fine but conceptually interesting point is not an error per se in either method, or a sign of some fundamental incompatibility of approaches, and certainly not a reason for concern about the formal manipulations we have performed. In fact, it simply reflects our slightly casual correspondence between the notion of (cumulative) annual risk of death, and (instantaneous) probability per unit time of death (with time measured in years). This detail is explored a little more in the online appendix to this chapter, along with other fundamental modelling concepts.
	The value of m in Equation 3 in the continuous time model is the intrinsic risk per unit time. When we change our minds about the unit of time in which we want to work (days versus years, for example) then rates change their values accordingly. A rate defined per year does not take the same value as that same rate, defined per day (just like a length measured in centimetres does not assume the same value as the same physical length measured in inches). By choosing suitably different units, the value of a rate parameter can take any rate at all—as close to zero as we want, or as large as we want. However, the cumulative probability of an event occurring in a particular period, T, like one year for example, is an actual specific number between zero and one. If we now want to work in days, we should also update the question to ask what is the probability of the event occurring in 365 days, and the answer should be the same as the probability in one year. In practice, the cumulative probability of a common epidemiological event of interest actually happening to a particular individual, during an actual year of waiting, is a small number—like a few per cent. In this case, the instantaneously defined probability per year of the event happens to be a very similar number—and so subtle the difference is frequently not apparent.
	A theorem of calculus translates rates (which are measured in a way that is sensitive to our choice of time units) into well-defined probabilities of events occurring in a particular physically meaningful period T (the value of which depends on the choice of units):
	Using the corresponding value for 1–R(t), the probability of surviving for t years, in place of (1–m) in Equation 1, we can make the discrete time model solution correspond exactly to the continuous time model solution in Equation 4. All we need to do is slightly adjust the values of m to account for the fact that they mean something slightly different in the two cases. Now the only difference between the discrete time mathematical model and the continuous time mathematical model lies in the fact that we did not intended to evaluate the discrete time model for non-whole-numbered values of t—the formulae are in fact identical!
	The models we have just constructed also apply to a susceptible population being infected at a constant rate, which might then be called ‘force of infection’, ‘incidence’, or ‘hazard rate’. Similar problems may be framed in many other contexts, modelled by essentially the same equations: an infected/infectious population disappearing due to a constant rate of recovery, the mass of water remaining in a towel drying on a clothes line, the temperature (relative to room-temperature) of a cooling cup of coffee, the decaying mass of a radioactive substance. Exponential growth and decay are the fundamental recurring theme of population models, as has been pointed out extensively by Lev Ginzburg and Mark Colyvan in their book (Ginzburg and Colyvan 2004).





Know your model world building blocks


	It is not necessary here to explore in detail how continuous and discrete time models differ or correspond in more complex cases, but the following remarks may be helpful.
	 	• Continuous time models, though they may be daunting to people who are not comfortable with calculus, are in fact usually mathematically much simpler than discrete time models.
	• The rules which apply over an ‘infinitesimally’ small period of time, dt, do not need to be updated over this period of time, because the system itself accrues irrelevantly small (infinitesimal) changes in this interval. This is the key simplification offered by thinking in infinitesimal steps.
	• Hence, without much technical effort, we can usually solve for the state of the system at the end of an infinitesimal time step, relative to a specified initial state, by simply translating the rules of our model world from words into algebra.
	• Thus we derive ‘differential equations’.
	• Then, if we want to know how the system changes over a substantial period of time, we invoke the tools of calculus to ‘solve’ the differential equations.
	• ‘Solutions’ to differential equations are not values of populations at particular times, in the sense that ‘values’ are ‘solutions’ to the more familiar ‘algebraic’ equations. Solutions to differential equations are ‘functions’. This means they are fully specified formal relations between population states and time, which, to be valid solutions to differential equations, provide the values/sizes of population variables at infinitely many points in time, spanning some period over which the rules, captured in the differential equations, apply.
	• Solutions of differential equations capture internally consistent ‘histories’ of model worlds in particular scenarios.
	Discrete time step models may require either extra technical sophistication, or additional assumptions of convenience, in order for the fundamental time-step relations to be written down.
	 	• These relations are called ‘difference equations’, and their solutions too are mathematical functions (of time).
	• For functions to be solutions to difference equations, they are only required to correspond to model world states at certain discrete times.
	• Sometimes these discrete time steps need to be taken seriously, so that it may not be sensible to simply read off the system state at non-whole-number times.
	• For instance, it may be possible to build a year-on-year model of an insect population, which accounts for the net result of a brief breeding season with many births and deaths, but does not attempt, nor claim, to describe the intermediate states when many eggs, larvae, and pupae are being formed and eliminated.
	• Similarly, seasonal models of human disease may not be intended to model the details of brief outbreaks, but merely account for net impact of typical outbreaks in terms of mortality, morbidity, vaccines used, accumulated immunity, and so forth.
	Often, indeed usually, neither differential nor difference equations can be neatly solved with explicit formulae. Then it becomes necessary to use computational means to provide numerical approximations, graphical representations, and the like. These numerical methods form a mature and robust field of knowledge in their own right, and can deal routinely with most epidemiologically interesting models, so it is not necessarily a big deal if we cannot analytically solve the central equations in a model-based investigation. Of course, it is always useful to have analytical solutions, if they can be found.
	For extensive in-depth investigations, challenges may arise with computational power and run-times required. Exploring many alternative scenarios in an attempt to ‘fit’ models to data, and exploring the sensitivity of outcomes to inputs and assumptions, may involve many millions of complex calculations, and demand quite sophisticated use of data management technology and computer clusters.
	To avoid proliferation of analytical threads and details, the remaining examples in this section will be demonstrated with the continuous formulation, chosen for its conceptual clarity and pedagogic value. The development of intuition about the applicability of calculus is a powerful problem solving capacity. Now let’s return to our simple population dynamics.
	 	Question 2. What will happen to the population of Question 1, with a death rate of 1% per year, if there is immigration of individuals at an average rate of 200 per year?
	We assume a constant per capita mortality rate m (a probability per unit time of death) as before, and now, in addition, add a constant immigration rate b (a number of people coming in per unit time). In other words, in a small time increment dt, the change in population is given by:
	Hence the derivative (rate of change) is given by:
	This ‘differential equation’ can be solved, by relatively elementary methods of calculus, to yield:
	Note that the second term of the solution has the previously discussed ‘exponential decline’ structure. Whatever value is taken for the initial population N(0 ), this second term fades after a large period of time, so that, as time t tends to infinity, the population size tends to a constant equilibrium value, namely b/m which in our case is 200,000.
	The key point is that this is the eventual state of the system no matter what the (positive) initial value N(0 ) was (see Fig. 5.16.3). A corollary to this is that, for our particular original population size to be maintained, an average influx of 1,000 individuals per year would be required, since then NE = b/m = 1,000/0.001 = 1,000,000. Indeed, Equation 5 shows directly, without passing through the formalities of obtaining a solution, that the rate of change of the population will be zero when N = b/m. We need just ask what it takes to have dN/dt = 0, bearing in mind that dN/dt = b–mN. This idea of exploring the behaviour of dynamical (difference, or differential) equations in their own right, without directly constructing and manipulating potentially complicated ‘solutions’, is a normal, and very informative part of the investigation of the properties of model worlds.
	Fig. 5.16.3 Stable equilibrium of a model world population subject to a constant death rate, i.e. probability of death per unit time, given by m, and being replenished with a steady inflow of b new members per unit time. No matter what the initial population, the model world rules eventually drive the population size ever closer to the intrinsic equilibrium value .
	The volume of water in a vertical-sided tank can be used as a helpful concrete mental image for this model world. It also makes for a cheap and informative physical demonstration. Consider water in a tank, filled to some level above a small outlet, from which we declare (because we can do that, in our model world) that the rate of flow is proportional to the pressure at the outlet. Pressure in a simple liquid is just proportional to depth, and the height of the water level above the outlet is proportional to the volumeV(t) of water which stands above the outlet (see Fig. 5.16.4).
	Fig. 5.16.4 Cartoon Punctured water-tank and schematic flow diagram representation of model world population with constant inflow b and (‘linearly’) variable outflow .
	If the tap feeding into the tank is shut off, water will just run out of the tank through the hole on the side, at a rate that is always proportional to the height of the (ever declining) water level above the hole. In other words, the level will exponentially decay down to the level of the hole. If the tap produces a steady stream of water, the level in the tank will approach an equilibrium value at which the outflow (which depends on the water level) matches the inflow (which is fixed). In principle, the tank may overflow if the hypothetical equilibrium water level is higher than the top of the tank, but if we want to, we can make our model world tank automatically be big enough.
	This inflow–outflow process can be applied to the population of red blood cells in a human body. Bone marrow normally produces a roughly steady supply of about 2 * 106 cells per second, or 1,728 * 108 per day, while a nearly constant proportion of cells die daily. If we assume the body maintains an equilibrium population of about 2 * 1013 (20 trillion!) red blood cells at any moment, that mortality rate can easily be calculated from our model. (It’s really worth trying it out—the ‘real world’ answer can be looked up readily enough online)
	 	Question 3. What will happen to the population of Question 1, with a per capita death rate of 0.01 per year, if there is no immigration, but a constant per capita birth rate of 0.04?
	Once more, we assume a constant per capita mortality rate (probability per unit time of death) m. The new part is in the interpretation of fertility. Most naively, we would say that the probability of any population member giving birth to an offspring in any infinitesimal time, dt, is given by:
	This is pretty much all we can mean by constant fertility rate, and it is a rather crude model of fertility. Clearly our model world does not know about the different roles of men and women in reproduction, and there is also no concept of pregnancy or fertility variations within and between individuals. Nevertheless, the fertility rate b can be chosen to produce some reasonable dynamics. Certainly, a nuanced discussion of fertility, and other demographic processes like changing age structure of a country over time, cannot be supported by models lacking explicit age structure, but these kinds of complications are mainly about proliferation of detail, not mainly about new concepts. The conceptually important step is to translate the probability of birth, per population member, into the actually realized (infinitesimal) number of births (dB) in the generic infinitesimal time slice dt:
	Considering also the mortality, the net change in population, during dt, is given by:
	hence the derivative (rate of change) is given by:
	This can be solved to give:
	In Question 3 we proposed values of m = 0.01, b = 0.04. The model world manifests an exponential population increase when m < b, a constant population when m = b, and exponential decline when m > b (see Fig. 5.16.5). Exponential growth or decline is also called ‘geometric’ increase or decline (but less frequently, these days). When there is exponential growth, it is easy to show that there is a fixed ‘population doubling time’, and in the case of exponential decline there is a fixed population ‘halving-time’, sometimes called the ‘half-life’.
	Fig. 5.16.5 Exponential growth (m < b), decline (m > b), and equilibrium/maintenance (m = b) arising from competing replenishment and attrition, both of which proceed in direct (‘linear’) proportion to the instantaneous population size.
	That populations, even under much less simplistic assumptions, tend to increase ‘geometrically’ was first observed and studied by the great mathematician Euler in the mid-eighteenth century (Euler 1748), before being more famously explored by Thomas Malthus (Malthus 1798). Although exact exponential relations such as those presented here arise only under the idealized conditions in model worlds, their conceptual importance and wide applicability can hardly be overstated. With a technically small but far-reaching mathematical twist, exponential functions also form the basis of much modelling in pure science and engineering, including the study of oscillations and waves.





Susceptible–infectious compartmental models


	The introduction of multiple health or disease states into our model worlds is naturally crucial to modelling disease transmission and progression. We will also need to expand our options for thinking about rates. Thus far, the populations in our example models have been allowed to:
	 	• grow by fixed in-or outflows (immigration or cell generation), or
	• experience growth or decline processes scaled in proportion to the instantaneous population size (our fertility and mortality models).
	Next, we consider the most basic model of actual disease transmission, previously noted as utilizing the principle of mass action. Thus, the number of new infections occurring in a time window of duration dt is proportional to the number of infection-susceptible individuals, and, importantly, also proportional to the number of infectious individuals. To be proportional to two things at the same time requires being proportional to the product of the two.
	This means we need to choose a value for the constant of proportionality, relating the product of infectious and susceptible individuals to the rate of occurrence of new infections. This parameter can be understood to capture both:
	 	• the probability per unit time of any one member of one group coming into contact with any one member of the other, and
	• the ordinary probability (not per unit time) of such a contact leading to transmission of infection.
	If the rate of interaction is twice, in model world A, what it is in model world B, but the probability of successful transmission, given an interaction, is half, in world A, what it is in world B, then emergent value for the final model transmission rate is the same in the model equations for A and the model equations for B.
	So we have another interesting and useful aspect of introducing figurative daylight between the ‘model world’ discussion and ‘mathematical model’ analysis: we can be explicit about details in model worlds which do not directly manifest in the model equations, and we can see how some views of models (and data) cannot distinguish one dynamical rule (model world) from another. This has important consequences for interpretation of, and inferences intended to be based on, models. If we only think about equations, we will necessarily leave aspects of model worlds undetermined. This is not a problem per se, but it is good to be able to keep track of one’s mental images, assumptions, etc. and to know which rules and principles are manifesting; where, when and how, in our model worlds and mathematical equations.
	 	Question 4. How can we describe the prevalence of gonorrhoea in a closed sexually active population?
	Let S(t) and I(t) denote the numbers of susceptible and infectious people at time t. We can build a model world based on the following rules:
	 	• Individuals mix randomly, any pair of them coming together with the same probability (per unit time) as any other pair.
	• People become infectious as soon as they are infected.
	• They recover at a constant per capita rate r per day, at which point they immediately become susceptible again.
	In a small period of time, dt, the increments in numbers of susceptible and infectious individuals are:
	where K is the mass action proportionality constant. Seen from the point of view of an individual, this indicates that the probability of infection, in a small time slice dt around the time t, is given by (see also Fig. 5.16.6).
	Which can also be stated as the ‘incidence’ of infections, among susceptible individuals. This is an important measure of the intrinsic risk associated with an infectious disease epidemic.
	Fig. 5.16.6 Flow diagram of a basic transmission and recovery model. Individuals move from the susceptible class to the infected (and infectious) class with an incidence λ(t) that is explicitly allowed to vary dynamically, in order to capture potentially complex rules for contacts with individuals in the infectious class. Infected individuals move back to the susceptible state by recovering with a (constant) probability per unit time r. Equation 6 captures the dynamics for a simple gonorrhoea model by modelling contact according to the principle of mass action (i.e. perfectly random mixing).
	Another important measure of infectious risk is what is usually called the basic reproductive number, usually denoted R0. This is essentially to be understood as the number of new cases that would be produced by a single infectious person who is introduced into a large population of people susceptible to infection. The key point is that we are only counting persons infected by this artificially introduced infectious individual (sometimes called the index case), and not those infected, in turn, by others who acquire the infection over the course of the epidemic. Calculating R0 for complex model worlds can be a painful exercise in rearranging the model equations, but the important points to understand are:
	 	• If the index case is not expected to infect at least one additional individual before either recovering or dying, or somehow ceasing to be infectious, then there is no prospect of sustained spread for the infection.
	• If the index case is expected to infect numerous individuals, then there will be, in a deterministic model world, at least a period over which the number of infectious cases increases.
	Depending on the rules for transmission, there will be some dynamical feedback as the infection spreads, reducing the number of still-susceptible cases. Unless there is a mechanism to replenish the susceptible population, this group will eventually decline to the point that the infected individuals, even if there are many of them, simply don’t have enough potential contacts with susceptible individuals to sustain spread. In this case the epidemic ‘burns out’ without infecting everyone.
	Epidemic model equations can be subjected to some considerable instructive detailed analysis beyond our immediate scope. Hethcote and Yorke (Hethcote and Yorke 1984) noted that their model has prevalence declining to zero for plausible estimates of the average partner change rate, the transmission probability per partnership, and the duration of infection.
	Indeed, as just noted, model worlds involving infections for which survival or cure confers immunity, or for which infection is incurable, generically manifest epidemics that die out (potentially after rising to a peak) unless there is a sufficient source of new susceptible individuals. In our gonorrhoea model world, the cured individuals recover to be susceptible again, so, in principle, an endemic equilibrium might have been produced, though at apparently infeasible values for certain rates. As it was, the model led to a conundrum in the context of data on gonorrhoea as it could not reasonably explain the low, stable equilibrium prevalence in the United States in the 1980s.
	 	Question 5. In what kind of model world can we maintain an observed low endemic prevalence of gonorrhoea in a closed sexually active population?
	Hethcote and Yorke (1984) went on to build a further model (Fig. 5.16.7) in which they divided the sexually active population into two groups: low activity (the majority) and high activity—2% of the population with higher partner change rate. They showed that with plausible estimates of the relevant parameters they could convincingly model the low gonorrhoea prevalence shown by the data.
	Fig. 5.16.7 Flow diagram of a transmission model with simple contact heterogeneity. The population is divided into a high-and low-activity (contact rate) class. Within each, individuals move from the susceptible class to the infected class with the applicable activity-level-specific incidence λH(t) or λL(t). They move in the opposite direction through a common (and constant) recovery rate r.
	It is very common that simple first models of systems sensibly capture initial insights and data, but fail to reproduce crucial features which are known to arise in the real system. It is also very typical that one seeks to address this by identifying some important further refinement of population classes. This will require thinking about estimates of subpopulation sizes, and details of contact and mixing rules. The work of Cooke, Hethcote, Nold and Yorke (Cooke and Yorke 1973; Yorke et al. 1978; Hethcote et al. 1982; Hethcote and Yorke 1984) highlighted the importance of incorporating in modelling both risk-heterogeneity, and also of accounting for the class of asymptomatic individuals. The implications of their work helped to inform US control policy for sexually transmitted infections in the 1980s.
	Our somewhat dry technical examples have only considered:
	 	• Single populations experiencing in-and outflows.
	• Simple structured populations with susceptible and infected classes, and high or low contact tendencies.
	Other key population structures which may be important to consider are:
	 	• Sex/Gender
	• Age
	• Location
	• Relationship status
	• Finely resolved disease states such as exposed but clinically healthy and uninfectious, or
	• Detailed viral and immunological markers
	• Treatment access and utilization
	Putting to one side the list of potential complications, we want to return to our opening remarks for this section. Model building and interpretation, while deserving care and attention, and benefiting from technical skill and experience, should not be seen as obscure activities left to the obscure practices of a secret society.





Example applications


	Modelling can help us to understand the natural history of the infections or diseases that we are studying. Before we start to build models to explain these different time trends, it is essential to learn more about the biology of the disease and think of other data that is crucial in understanding the unfolding of disease incidence, such as treatment and vaccine availability and coverage.





Historically important infectious diseases


	Figure 5.16.8 shows the number of reported cases for each of four diseases in England and Wales between 1930 and 2000 (Public Health England n.d.). Before we can begin to make models to explain these different trends, we need a better understanding of the biology and control of the individual diseases.
	Diphtheria is a bacterial upper respiratory tract infection spread through contact with saliva. A vaccine has been available since the 1920s, yet the number of cases in the United Kingdom remained very high at around 60,000 per year between 1930 and 1940. Only when mass childhood immunization was introduced in 1940 did the number of cases consistently drop to effective elimination in 1950.
	Measles is highly contagious and almost everyone who come into contact with aerosols from infected people will get the disease. Survival of an infection ensures lifelong immunity and so does vaccination, which has been available since the late 1960s. In Figure 5.16.8 it is clear that England and Wales, almost without fail, experienced a measles outbreak every second year prior to vaccination. Why would this be? Since measles is an immunizing disease, a large outbreak can only occur once the pool of susceptible people has been sufficiently replenished. This implies that the birth rate in England and Wales was such that measles outbreaks occurred every second year. We can use a mathematical model to show that the interepidemic period would be longer for lower birth rates and vice versa.
	Pertussis, or whooping cough, is a highly contagious bacterial upper respiratory tract infection and those infected may cough for up to three months. Outcomes of treatment with antibiotics are poor. Before the introduction of a vaccine in the 1950s, incidence of whooping cough was very high at around 100,000 cases per year. Numbers of cases fell dramatically until unfounded beliefs that the vaccine causes brain damage led to reductions in coverage to a low of 30% in 1978. Major epidemics followed soon after and coverage gradually increased and has remained at around 90% since the 1990s. The whooping cough vaccine is ideally given in three doses to infants and one booster dose in young children due to waning immunity.
	Polio is in a race with Guinea worm disease to be the second human disease, after smallpox, to be eradicated from the world. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), only 33 cases of polio are estimated to have occurred worldwide in 2018. This viral disease is highly contagious and spreads through the oral-faecal route. The rapid rise in reported cases in the United Kingdom in 1947 remains unexplained to this day. One theory suggests that improvements in water and sanitation lead to an increase in the age of infection and adolescents are much more likely to develop severe symptoms than infants. However, age distribution of cases did not change from before to after the large outbreak. The second theory suggests that a strain of the polio virus previously not endemic to the United Kingdom caused the large outbreak, but no data are available on the circulating strains prior to the outbreak to confirm this theory (Agerholm 1953). Mass vaccination with an inactivated vaccine from 1956 and then a live, oral vaccine from 1962 lead to rapid decline in notified polio cases and the last case of wild virus polio infection in the United Kingdom occurred in 1984.
	Fig. 5.16.8 Disease incidence trends in England and Wales for diphtheria, measles, pertussis, and polio, from 1930 to 2000. The data points indicate the recorded annual number of cases in multiples of one thousand.
	Modelling can help us to understand the time trends of these four diseases and help inform decisions that policymakers need to make. All four of these diseases are preventable through vaccination. We can collect data on the coverage of vaccination over time and develop a mathematical model to see if the increase in coverage (and decrease in the case of whooping cough) sufficiently explains the trends in prevalence over time. Then we can use the model to see whether different vaccination strategies would have had similar impact. For example, would vaccination of targeted age groups have had similar impact on diphtheria and polio prevalence as mass vaccination? What impact would changes in vaccine schedule have on whooping cough prevalence?
	Application Laundry list
	The following applications demonstrate examples of mathematical modelling in the context of public health:
	 	• Encapsulating the quantifiable essence of a complex situation in a simple framework which can then be used to make estimates. Dual infection or co-infection is a good example—infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) is more likely to persist in HIV infected individuals, which may increase incidence of cervical cancer.
	• Translating descriptions of behaviour at one scale (e.g. individual-level epidemiology of a disease) into descriptions at another scale (e.g. population dynamics). The HPV vaccines used in most public health settings protect against the two oncogenic HPV types that can be found in 70% of cervical cancer cases—will this lead to a 70% reduction in population-level cervical cancer incidence in the long term?
	• Enabling extrapolation, with quantified uncertainty, from data measured over a relatively short term, to a projection of what is likely to happen in the long-term. HPV vaccines have been available since 2007 and observed efficacy is good—so far. By setting rules in our model world about long-term efficacy, we estimate impact on cervical cancer incidence, a disease that can take decades to develop from initial HPV infection.
	• Synthesizing data from different fields into a single framework, thus enabling checks on consistency. In modelling the impact of an HPV vaccine on cervical cancer incidence, in a setting with high HIV prevalence, we need clinical information concerning the rates of progression/regression of cervical disease; we need epidemiological data concerning time trends in HIV, HPV, and cervical disease; we need data on cancer screening and vaccination coverage; and we need economic data if we are to assess the cost-effectiveness of new cancer prevention strategies.
	• Providing clear guidelines for new data collection strategies when trying to answer specific questions where critical features are missing from existing data. This may include identifying what type of data, how much data, and at what temporal and spatial resolution it should be collected, within financial and operational constraints.
	• Identifying the factors that sustain the spread of infection within a population and estimating the relative importance of various factors/parameters, thus informing control and prevention programmes. In the case of HIV, factors include sexual behaviour, the use of condoms, the extent of ‘intergenerational’ sex, and age at sexual debut. Modellers might seek, for example, to compare the effects on HIV transmission of sexual heterogeneity, concurrency, and different mixing patterns.
	• Making predictions over time of the probable dynamics of prevalence, incidence, and infection-related mortality, under different interventions and comparing the impacts and synergies of different combinations of interventions.
	• Identifying threats to the success of an existing intervention. A model can be used to show that the scale-up of HPV vaccination may have a less than desired effect on cervical cancer incidence, if coverage of screening is not maintained for several more years.
	• Maximizing cost-effectiveness of interventions, hence enabling optimization of use of resources to combat an infection. Models can assist in evaluating the economics of different control strategies, and can help to decide whether programmes should re-allocate funding in response to the new data or scientific breakthroughs. Providing the new 9-valent HPV vaccine plus HPV DNA testing may be more expensive in the short term, but may reduce cancer rates, and very expensive cancer treatment, more drastically in longer term than vaccination with 2-valent vaccine and cytology based screening.





Concluding remarks


	The role of models is to formalize our understanding of, or hypotheses about, data and processes, so that we can tap into powerful tools developed by mathematicians over many years. This allows us to restate our thoughts about systems in an orderly fashion, demonstrating details of their internal workings, in the context of tough political and technical questions about investment in, and management of, public health systems.
	We hope readers of this chapter will take away the following key messages:
	 	• The conceptual heart of modelling is the construction of interesting ‘model worlds’—realms in which we declare how things work, in order to explore dynamics that, in the real world, are too complex to track in detail, or are not amenable do direct experimental control that might teach us what we are looking to learn.
	• Building model worlds is not a specialist activity to be performed only by technical modellers. Anyone who has a vested interest in a question can contribute to model world construction and exploration.
	• There are some technical details that must be faced in producing and manipulating mathematical equations of various kinds, which capture the processes we have built in to our model worlds. While this is indeed a specialist activity, there are a number of recurring themes, and even non-specialists can achieve quite a high level of familiarity with important modelling concepts.

	Online appendix: key modelling concepts
	Here we variously recap and expand on the key modelling concepts of Box 5.16.3, illustrating them by default with reference to HIV. Further elucidations of these concepts may be found in many modelling texts (see, for example, ‘Further reading’).





Basic reproduction number R0


	This very important concept is somewhat more subtle than usually noted, but there is a valid heuristic: the total number of secondary cases that arise (or are expected to arise, on average) from direct infection by one primary case introduced into a (very large) completely susceptible population.





Disease duration


	The length of time for which people have a disease, infection, or medical condition before they are treated, cured, or die. For example, without treatment, people will live with HIV for about 10 years, on average.





(Disease) mortality


	The proportion of (infected) people that die per unit of time, for instance within a year. Since HIV-positive people live for about 10 years without treatment, the mortality rate is about 10% per year, averaged over the course of disease.





Epidemic growth rate


	The rate at which the prevalence of infection rises at the start of an epidemic. For example, the prevalence of HIV initially grew at a rate of 60% per year in South Africa.





Equilibrium


	A scenario in which the state of the model world is unchanged by the passing of time. This is a subtle concept, and may refer to a scenario in which it is implicit that individuals are entering and leaving various population groups, but in such a way that the total numbers in each group (the ‘state variables’ which define the population) are unchanging. This requirement of ‘detailed balance’ between processes moving individuals into and out of population groups can only be precisely realized in a model world.
	It may appear strange or contrived to have finely adjusted all dynamical rules and state variables to achieve such a seemingly delicate balance. The key point to note here is that equilibrium can readily and naturally emerge dynamically from the system over time, even if it was not originally evident. Although real-world systems rarely display anything close to true equilibrium, the concept is very important—and not just for the purposes of formal analysis of mathematical models. Practically, the ideal of equilibrium is a useful concept that enhances insight, for example in understanding where trends, under current conditions, are in principle headed. For example, are we essentially on the way to disease elimination, or apparently doomed to high endemic persistence.





Herd immunity


	As indicated throughout this chapter, the heart and soul of dynamical modelling is the consistent propagation, through time, of rates of occurrence of epidemiological events. Crucially, these rates need to be consistently adapted as the state of the population changes from the application of the rules. The feedback loops which this implies are often characterized by critical ‘tipping points’ such as embodied in R0. One of the most important insights that comes from this kind of analysis is that it is not necessary to protect (e.g. through vaccination) every individual of a population, in order to achieve the elimination of an otherwise endemic infection. Thus ‘herd immunity’ is the collective ability to clear an existing, or resist an invading, epidemic even when some individuals are fully susceptible.





Incidence


	This can be thought of as the richly informative cousin of prevalence, and warrants a lengthier discussion because the understanding and estimation of incidence, and its susceptibility to intervention, is ultimately the central technical problem of all modelling of infectious agents. There are several valid ways to define incidence, but ultimately they all refer to the notion of the number of new cases that occur within a given population and period of time. This is sometimes stated as a raw number of cases per time window, such as 1,000 cases of severe influenza needing handling at a major hospital within a month. However, a more ‘intrinsic’ notion of incidence captures risk per unit time experienced in an exposed population. This risk is often expressed as the proportion of a susceptible group who are, or would be expected to become, infected in a period of time. When modellers and statisticians speak of event rates, in general, what they mean is the probability per unit time of an event occurring, clearly stated as referring either to an individual or to some population.
	A subtlety is that, even when we express incidence in probability per year, for example, this is not entirely the same as the probability of an infection actually occurring within a year. Firstly, risk can vary over time, but this changing instantaneous risk can still be expressed in units of probability per year. Secondly, even if the risk is constant, any particular rate (probability per unit time) can be expressed in as large, or as small, a numerical value as one wants, by choosing different units of measurement of time. This is just like noting that an object’s length can be made as large or small a number as we like, by choosing different units in which to measure length. However, the probability of an event actually occurring saturates at a value of one, which is the limit of certainty of occurrence. This is true no matter how high the rate (probability per unit time) or how long the window of time for which we wait. For hazards of no more than a few per cent, such as the annual probability of HIV acquisition in high-risk settings, the incidence as an instantaneously conceived probability per year, and the probability of infection during the course of a year, are numerically similar enough that they can be regarded as the same thing—especially when we consider the imprecision with which they can be estimated. On the other hand, a flu outbreak which brings an infection risk of 20% per week, sustained for 4 weeks, will affect about 59% (not 80%) of individuals—that is, 1—(0.08)4, or one minus the probability of escaping infection for 4 weeks. To press the point: a flu outbreak which brings an infection risk of 30% per week, sustained for 4 weeks, clearly cannot affect 120% of the population! It will affect about 76%.
	There is no simple general relationship between prevalence and incidence—a source of much inconvenience and technical pain for epidemiologists. It is simpler at equilibrium: if an epidemic of HIV reaches a ‘steady state’ so that all rates, and the resultant prevalence, are constant, then the number of new infections each year will be equal to the number of deaths. Thus the incidence, expressed in units of events per unit time per total population (as opposed to per susceptible individual) is equal to the ratio of prevalence to duration (with a consistent set of units to measure time). Hence a ‘stable’ HIV epidemic (without effective treatment—see ‘(Disease) mortality’, earlier) has a value of incidence (expressed as infection risk per year) of about one-tenth of prevalence. In reality, there is no equilibrium, and incidence and prevalence vary in complex ways as functions of both calendar time and age.





Model scenario


	Mathematical models, in the basic abstract sense, capture rules about processes in a model world, a world which by definition functions according to rules captured in certain mathematical statements. This however leaves (wide) open the question of what actually happens in this model world, as the rules by themselves do not spell out a ‘starting point’ or ‘initial condition’ from which the system is then driven by the clearly stated rules. For example, we may have captured rules about the transmission of HIV, but when applied to a population in which there is at some point no infected individual, these rules will not lead to the spontaneous appearance of an outbreak. When populations have structure, such as heterogeneity in age, gender, and various other ‘risk factors’, these also need to be specified at some initial time, in order for the rules to be applied to a concrete ‘realization’ of the model world. This fully specified realization of a possible history of a model world, in which rules as well as initial conditions are spelled out, is often called a ‘scenario’. A scenario may also involve arbitrary ‘midstride’ impositions of rule changes, such as the initiation of a vaccination or treatment campaign at some point in time. In epidemiology, such ‘interventions’ by human agency are usually treated as arbitrary changes to the model ‘rules’, rather than as events which unfold according to some complex higher level sociological rules—as this level of emergent behaviour is almost impossible to build into a model world. Model world rules are usually best kept as close as possible to rules of nature that can plausibly be modelled.





Parameter


	Any variable in a model which captures a rule about the model behaviour, such as the rate of recovery from infection, the probability that a ‘contact’ leads to ‘transmission’, and so forth. (See also ‘State variable’).





Prevalence


	The proportion of a population or group who are currently suffering from a disease, infection, or medical condition. For example, in South Africa about 10% of adults are infected with HIV.





State variable


	Any variable in a model which captures the state of the system, such as the number of living individuals, the number of people in a particular risk category, and so forth. (See also ‘Parameter’).
	Note that mathematically there may sometimes be no way to distinguish state variables from parameters in a model equation. The distinction is conceptual, and usually straightforward: parameters are usually model inputs, and state variables are usually model outputs.





5.17


Public health surveillance


	Nguyen Tran Hien, James W. Buehler, and Ann Marie Kimball





Introduction to public health surveillance


	Public health surveillance provides the epidemiological foundation for modern public health practice. The ongoing monitoring of disease or health trends within populations informs what public health actions are taken and reflects whether those actions are effective. Surveillance may involve monitoring of diseases and other health-related conditions as well as their antecedents, characteristics, and consequences. Surveillance can guide the local response to individual cases of disease or more broadly inform public health programmes and policies. A key function of surveillance is to identify circumstances that merit further public health scrutiny, such as groups or locations that are disproportionately affected or changes in disease occurrence or severity. Person, place, and time are the key epidemiological attributes of disease distribution in populations, and knowledge of these attributes afforded by surveillance allows targeting of public health programmes. General principles that underlie the practice of surveillance are essentially the same for all countries, regardless of economic development. Defining surveillance objectives depends on programme goals and on what information is needed, who needs it, and how it will be used. Desirable but potentially competing attributes of surveillance include completeness, timeliness, representativeness, high predictive value, acceptability, flexibility, simplicity, and low cost. Public health surveillance is conducted in many ways, depending on the nature of the health event under surveillance, the nature of healthcare and information infrastructures, the population involved, resources available, and information needs. The widespread and expanding use of the internet, electronic media, communication technologies, and mobile computing have enabled innovations in public health surveillance that reach far beyond traditional methods. Surveillance systems should be periodically assessed to determine whether information needs are being fulfilled and whether the resources are being used effectively. Although surveillance methods were originally developed as part of efforts to control infectious diseases, basic concepts of surveillance have been applied to all areas of public health.
	In many resource-poor countries, challenges to meeting needs for population health information are heightened and include potential tensions between the perspectives of external funders and in-country officials, between the interests of those responsible for disease-specific ‘categorical’ programmes and those interested in strengthening general surveillance infrastructures, and between advocates for using limited resources to strengthen information capacities versus those who would focus spending to address urgent service needs. At the same time, recent innovations hold promise for improving surveillance in resource-poor settings, where precedents in developed countries that can impede innovation are absent or less established.





Definition of surveillance


	People who are responsible for protecting and promoting the health of populations need ongoing, timely, and reliable information about the health of the populations they serve. The term ‘surveillance’ encompasses the multiple processes that public health agencies employ to meet this need for information. Surveillance can include information about specific diseases, health risks, or more general indicators of overall population health. As an integral part of public health practice, surveillance is an ongoing, systematic process of information collection, analysis, interpretation, visualization, dissemination, and connection to public health programmes (Thacker and Berkelman 1988). Surveillance systems are organized networks of people and activities dedicated to managing and maintaining surveillance for specific conditions. Surveillance systems can operate at various levels within countries, from local to national, or on a global scale.
	In 1963, Langmuir established the modern concept of surveillance as ‘the continued watchfulness over the distribution and trends of incidence through the systematic collection, consolidation, and evaluation of morbidity and mortality reports and other relevant data’ together with timely and regular dissemination to those who ‘need to know’ (Langmuir 1963). In 1968, the twenty-first World Health Assembly described surveillance as the systematic collection and use of epidemiological information for the planning, implementation, and assessment of disease control; in short, surveillance implied ‘information for action’ (WHO 1968). Over time, the scope and methods of surveillance have been adapted to meet the information needs of public health programmes that address a broad spectrum of infectious and non-infectious diseases and acute and chronic conditions. For brevity, the term ‘diseases’ or ‘conditions’ will be used as shorthand throughout this chapter for diseases, injuries, risk factors, and other health-related events that are the focus of public health programmes and surveillance systems.
	Surveillance can include monitoring of the incidence, prevalence, antecedents (such as behavioural risks or hazardous exposures), characteristics, and outcomes of disease and other health conditions of public health importance. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a ‘public health surveillance system is useful if it contributes to the prevention and control of adverse health-related events and can be useful in contributing to [public health programme] performance measures, including health indicators that are used in needs assessments and accountability systems’ (CDC 2001). Surveillance should begin when there exists, or is likely to exist, a public health problem that merits attention, and it should be discontinued or revamped when the information it yields is no longer needed or useful. Surveillance systems can operate at various levels within countries, from local to national, or on a global scale.
	The International Health Regulations (IHR) of 2005 provide a legal and practical framework among all World Health Organization (WHO) member countries to protect against the international spread of disease. The IHR require that all countries can detect, assess, report, and respond to public health threats that have the potential to spread across borders. So the IHR call for strengthening of national capacity for surveillance and control of public health events of national and international concerns (WHO 2016).





Establishing a surveillance system


	Establishing a surveillance system requires a statement of objectives, definition of the disease or condition under surveillance, and implementation of procedures for collecting information (or obtaining information from existing sources), managing, analysing, visualizing, interpreting, and disseminating the information. In addition, as the number of surveillance systems increases, attention should be given to whether there are multiple systems collecting information within a population and, if so, whether these systems collect common data elements and adhere to shared information standards. This is important to allow for information sharing across systems, to minimize duplication of effort, and to simplify the work of those who are asked to report to these systems. Attention should also be given to whether surveillance for a particular condition can be done similarly in different locations, increasing the likelihood that comparison of disease incidence or prevalence across multiple localities or countries is meaningful.
	Surveillance systems are information loops, or cycles, that involve healthcare providers, public health agencies, and the public in a process of information collection, analysis and interpretation, and feedback. The cycle begins when events of public health concern occur and is completed when information about these events is made available and applied in public health programmes. This may involve multiple levels that should be specified in developing a surveillance system, ranging from the anticipated local response to individuals with cases of disease to the use of information aggregated from multiple localities to inform national policies. The delivery of information to constituents and policymakers (Langmuir 1963) is essential to the completion of the surveillance cycle. To the extent that surveillance data can be released without compromising privacy or confidentiality, they should be placed in the public domain to allow full use and benefits, with appropriate documentation.
	Weaknesses in any part of the information chain can affect the entire surveillance process, and potential constraints should be anticipated. For example, when surveillance draws upon information arising from the use healthcare services, surveillance will be affected by the availability and quality of those services, including laboratory and other diagnostic services (Berkelman et al. 1994) and by the accuracy with which diagnoses are recorded or coded. No information resource is perfect, and establishing surveillance requires consideration of options, each with strengths and limitations, for how surveillance should be conducted at each step in the surveillance cycle. Having data that are complete and without error is desirable, but the effort required to obtain such data in a timely manner may not be feasible or sustainable.





Objectives of surveillance


	Goal of public health surveillance is to provide information that can be used for health action by public health personnel, government leaders, and the public to guide public health policy and programmes (Smith et al. 2013). Surveillance is essential for monitoring events that might jeopardize the health of a population so that appropriate prevention and control measures can be implemented in a timely manner. An effective surveillance system includes the following: collection, reporting, and consolidation of data; routine analysis and interpretation of data; feed-forward of surveillance data to decision makers; feedback of surveillance data to those providing the data and other interested parties; detection, evaluation, and response to unusual patterns in the data and quality assurance (PAHO WHO 2014).
	The objectives of surveillance systems will be shaped by the public health programmes they serve. For example, a programme to eradicate an infectious disease requires intensive surveillance in the later stages of the campaign that emphasizes identification of all people with the disease (Hinman and Hopkins 1998).
	The purpose of surveillance is to meet the needs of public health programmes for information about the health of the populations they serve. The following are purposes of public health surveillance:
	 	• To define public health priorities.
	• To characterize disease patterns by time, place, person, and disease characteristics.
	• To detect epidemics, health problems.
	• To monitor changes, measure trends of diseases, and health-related events.
	• To suggest hypotheses for further investigation.
	• To estimate magnitude and scope of health problems.
	• To guide and evaluate prevention and control programmes, including assessment of effectiveness and/or adverse consequences.
	Taken together, population-level measures of time, place, person, and disease characteristics can lead to an understanding of the impact of various diseases and insights into individual and social determinants of their occurrence. Surveillance might lead to hypotheses that can be tested in more definitive investigations and can identify individuals who could be enrolled in further epidemiological studies. In some instances, surveillance alone can provide compelling evidence of the impact of prevention programmes, such as the sharp decline in the incidence of a vaccine-preventable disease coincident with the widespread use of a new vaccine (Seward et al. 2002). In other situations, surveillance can contribute to evaluating the impact of interventions, but more detailed investigations are necessary to explain trends that are shaped by multiple factors. Low incidence or prevalence does not necessarily mean that certain diseases do not deserve public health attention, including continuation of surveillance, since this might reflect the impact of successful prevention efforts that must be sustained in order to prevent re-emergence. Information on disease trends gained through surveillance, when combined with other information, can also be used to predict future disease trends. For example, with the ageing of the ‘baby boom’ population in countries such as the United States, projections of disease prevalence in the elderly, such as the anticipated prevalence and cost of dementia (Hurd et al. 2013), are garnering increased attention.
	Surveillance for a disease or other health problem should have clear objectives. These objectives should include a clear description of how data that are collected, consolidated, and analysed for surveillance will be used to prevent or control the disease. When establishing the objectives of surveillance, several issues should be considered, including: health-related event and case definition; population under surveillance; data sources and data collection approach; planned uses of the surveillance data; legal authority and frequency of data collection; organization of the surveillance; integration with other surveillance and health information systems; data processing, analysis and management; information dissemination methods and ethical issues (CDC 2012c).
	An important use of surveillance is to help set public health priorities. In addition to recent measures of incidence or prevalence, other factors that can shape priority setting include likely future trends, the potential for public health or other interventions to have an impact, severity, disparities and attendant social justice concerns, and public interest. To the extent that surveillance data are used in priority setting, deliberations may give rise to concerns about surveillance methods, how surveillance data are queried and analysed, and the accuracy of estimates of disease impact. For example, even though mortality monitoring is the oldest form of surveillance and remains important in assessing the impact of different diseases (Thacker 2010), different agencies using mortality data may arrive at different conclusions, depending on the use of overall mortality measures, age-specific measures, or approaches that seek to integrate measures of mortality and wellness. Table 5.17.1 provides two estimates of the number of deaths (in millions) for leading causes of death globally in 2010, one from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) and another from the WHO (Liu et al. 2000). Such estimates from different organizations rarely line up, and disparities in estimates can cause consternation among donors and national governments seeking to prioritize interventions.
