6.5


Development and evaluation of complex multicomponent interventions in public health


	Rona Campbell and Chris Bonell





Introduction


	There have been notable advances in developing the evidence base in public health to support decision-making in policy and practice (Academy of Medical Sciences 2017; United Kingdom Clinical Research Collaboration 2018) including successful funding initiatives in the United Kingdom specifically designed to enhance the quality and quantity of public health research and to support research capacity development (United Kingdom Clinical Research Collaboration 2018; National Institute for Health Research School for Public Health Research n.d.; White 2018). Nevertheless, at a time when health systems worldwide are struggling to respond to the burden of disease and demand for healthcare, the need for innovative, cost-effective public health interventions remains (Corbett et al. 2018). Several challenges to developing and evaluating such interventions are apparent.
	Firstly, policy interventions which have the greatest capacity to improve population health (for example, increasing the price of unhealthy food or beverages to tackle obesity), are more difficult to formulate and implement than interventions merely promoting individual behaviour change because of the political commitment required (Swinburn et al. 2011). Furthermore, policy interventions are often introduced with little thought given to evaluation, missing opportunities for evaluators to work with stakeholders to identify what questions an evaluation could usefully address, collection of baseline data, identification of suitable control conditions, and the possibility of randomizing to intervention and control conditions.
	A second challenge is the need for evaluations of public health interventions to attend to the contexts in which interventions are implemented and received (Craig et al. 2018) and how this might affect their intended and unintended impacts, the latter including effects on the broader functioning of the social ‘systems’ operating within different contexts (Rutter et al. 2017), which we shall consider in more detail to follow. A third challenge is the need for the development and evaluation of interventions to involve collaboration between researchers, the public and public health policymakers, and practitioners, to maximize the relevance, acceptability, and rapid scale-ability of interventions. In this chapter, we consider how these challenges can be addressed as we describe methods for developing and evaluating complex public health interventions. We begin by examining what complexity means in the context of public health.





Definition and scope of the concept of a ‘complex intervention’


	A simple intervention is generally characterized as involving a s single component with effects unlikely to vary by context (Petticrew 2011). By contrast, complex interventions involve several synergistic interacting components whose effects are irreducible to a single ‘active ingredient’(Medical Research Council 2000). More recent literature suggests that complexity can arise from the number and difficulty of behaviours required by those delivering or receiving the intervention, the number of groups or organizational levels targeted by the intervention, the number and variability of outcomes, and the degree of flexibility or tailoring of the intervention permitted(Craig et al. 2008; Skivington et al. 2021). Accordingly, all public health interventions must be regarded as complex.





Complex interventions or complex settings, contexts, and systems


	In contrast to the aforementioned literature, it has also been recently suggested that complexity, rather than describing the characteristics of a particular intervention, actually describes how interventions interact with local contexts or ‘systems’ (e.g. family, school, community, country) (Hawe et al. 2009; Skivington et al. 2021).
	Interventions with several interrelated parts, addressing multiple levels or requiring multiple new behaviours, it has been suggested, may be more helpfully thought of as complicated rather than complex. Complexity, so the argument runs, is a property of the system that an intervention is trying to change, not an inherent feature of the intervention itself (Shiell et al. 2008). Complex systems have properties emerging from the mutual interactions of multiple ‘subunits (that are often composites themselves) whose repeated interactions result in rich, collective behaviour that feeds back into the behaviour of the individual parts’(Rickles et al. 2007, p. 933). Interventions, whether simple or complicated, can be thought of as interruptions to such complex systems, with the implication that their local impact will be context-dependent and affected by recipient or provider factors (Lewin et al. 2017). For example, Project Northland in the United States used schools as a setting for a health promotion intervention to discourage alcohol use by young people. It involved making changes to elements of the school curriculum, changing the school environment, and engagement with parents and the wider community to restrict both access to and demand for alcohol (Perry et al. 2002). The intervention is clearly a complicated one, but its impacts within schools are also complex. Schools were not simply the setting for delivery but were each complex systems, involving a whole series of different types of subunits (e.g. students, teaching staff, classes, buildings), which the intervention aimed to ‘interrupt’ in multiple ways in order to reduce alcohol use. The schools were also part of a wider community, another complex system, on which the intervention was also intended to have an impact.
	When developing a public health intervention, it can be instructive to understand something of the nature of complex systems, and to think of an intervention as something that is intended to disrupt the system. Doing so can help ensure that the likely mechanisms for achieving change, the potential consequences of disrupting the system (both intentional and unintentional), and the interaction between the intervention and the context in which it is being implemented (Moore et al. 2015) are all carefully considered from the outset.
	This increasing interest in systems science and how it might inform the development and evaluation of public health interventions results has several important implications. Firstly, those developing public health interventions should focus not merely on engendering individual behaviour change but also on transforming entire social systems (for example, urban planning, housing, and welfare policies) so that these promote rather than damage health (Rutter et al. 2017). Secondly, a focus on one or two primary health outcomes might be broadened so that evaluations explore broader impacts on system functioning and how this affects those involved in these systems. For example, evaluations of school-based health curricula might continue to examine direct effects on students’ health knowledge and behaviours but also explore how delivering the curricula affects staff workload and mental wellbeing, or student engagement with education. Thirdly, we might revise how we think of interventions; rather than discrete entities with clear starting points and modes of delivery which can ‘manualized’, public health interventions are often routine, constantly adjusted, and intermingled, so disentangling the effect of any part is difficult. Fourthly, while it remains useful to estimate intervention fidelity and effects within rigorously conducted studies, it is important to appreciate that the same fidelity and effects might not manifest when the intervention is delivered across other systems that vary across time and space. The overall implication of this is that evaluations will be most useful when they enable development and refinement of theories about how intervention can interrupt systems in ways that promote health’ (Rutter et al. 2017) and how this will vary across contexts’ (Egan et al. 2019, p. 14)
	But such theories are always likely to be imperfect because of the properties of systems. Firstly, systems are adaptive and will likely adjust in response to the implementation or even suggestion of a new intervention. For example, when the UK government announced the introduction of a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages, some producers began to reformulate the sugar content of their drinks before the legislation came into effect. Secondly, as already mentioned, systems will have emergent properties arising from dynamic interactions between their components. For example, herd immunity, where a critical mass of individuals is immune to an infection such as through vaccination, is a property of a population system arising from infection-host interactions which confers benefits on individuals who might themselves lack individual immunity. Thirdly, systems often include feedback loops, where one change enhances, balances, or diminishes another. For example, the introduction of compulsory charges on plastic bags in shops in the United Kingdom to reduce plastic pollution has led directly to a huge decline in their use and shifted cultural norms towards reuse, perhaps contributing towards the popularity of other forms of reuse and recycling. Fourthly, systems are characterized by non-linear dose-responses. For example, in an attempt to induce system level change in the secondary prevention of key non-communicable diseases in the United Kingdom, since 2009 there has been very substantial investment in the NHS Health Check programme. All those aged 40–74 years are invited to attend their general practice for checks relating to stroke, kidney disease, heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and dementia, and for measures to reduce risk of adverse outcomes to be taken. However, despite the substantial financial input (or dose) the response has been disappointing with a recent evaluation concluding that ‘program performance was substantially below national and international targets’ (Chang et al. 2016).





Standardized or flexible interventions?


	When the UK MRC first published a framework for the development and evaluation of complex interventions (Medical Research Council 2000) it adapted the phases undertaken in drug development and testing and proposed that ‘once the RCT has begun, the intervention must not evolve, as the RCT results will be unusable if later participants experience a different intervention than earlier ones. Fidelity to treatment protocols or quality standards may be essential to effectiveness’ (Medical Research Council 2000, p. 11). This emphasis on testing a standardized intervention, implemented with a high degree of fidelity, caused some concern because, it was thought, public health interventions might be maximally effective if they actively encouraged appropriate tailoring to local circumstances. Such a view led some to conclude that randomized trials were therefore not a suitable method for evaluating public health and health promotion interventions (McNulty et al. 2013). As Hawe and colleagues (Hawe et al. 2004) pointed out, however, this concern was based on a misconception of what is standardized. She argued that what should be standardized is the function of the intervention and the steps in the process by which change is to be achieved, not that all the components of an intervention have to be delivered in exactly the same way to each person, or in each setting. Hawe and colleagues did not reject the randomized trial as a method of evaluation but argued that ‘instead of mimicking trial phases which assume that the ‘best’ or the ‘ideal’ comes from the laboratory and gets progressively compromised in real world applications, community trial design would start by trying to understand communities themselves as complex systems and how the health problem or phenomenon of interest is recurrently produced by that system’ (Hawe et al. 2004, p.1562). A pragmatic solution to the problem of artificial standardization, however, is to simply embrace the idea that the interventions we develop and evaluate have adaptation and evolution built into them. This matter is discussed in further detail in the later subsection on fidelity.





Simple or complex research questions and questions from different research perspectives


	Evaluations can address simple or complex questions (Petticrew 2011). For example, a local authority commissioner might wish to evaluate an obesity prevention programme comprising multiple components: health education for pregnant women to encourage breastfeeding and healthy weaning; provision of healthy food and opportunities for physical activity among children under the care of nursery schools, child minders, and day care; classroom-based education on nutrition and physical activity in primary schools; and local spectator sports clubs encouraging fathers to be physically active and eat healthily with their children. A commissioner may simply wish to know whether or not the overall programme has been effective in reducing rates of obesity. Or she may wish to know: for which subpopulations of children and in what settings it was effective or ineffective; whether there were important secondary outcomes such as reductions in adult obesity; whether certain components interacted to achieve particularly strong effects; or whether there were broader benefits or harms, such as a reduction in the number of fast-food outlets in the locality due to a drop in demand.
	The research question might also be informed by the research perspective(s) of those doing the evaluation. The latest draft MRC guidance on the development and evaluation of complex interventions suggests four different perspectives on a continuum from efficacy to systems considerations each asking different but not mutually exclusive questions: ‘Efficacy perspective—To what extent does the intervention produce the intended outcome(s) in experimental or ideal settings? Effectiveness perspective—To what extent does the intervention produce the intended outcome(s) in real-world settings? Theory-based Perspective—What works in which circumstances, and how? and Systems perspective—How do the system and intervention adapt to one another?’ (Skivington et al. 2021)





Intervening at different levels and within systems to improve the health of populations


	The importance of multilevel and multifaceted interventions was set out in both the 1986 Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion (WHO 1986) and the later Bangkok Charter (Anonymous 2006) so that interventions should aim both to address individual, ‘downstream’ determinants of health such as knowledge and attitudes, as well as community and societal ‘upstream’ determinants, such as exposure to health benefiting and health harming goods and services, and social inequalities in wealth and power. When designing complex public health interventions, the socioecological approach to public health described by McLeroy and colleagues (Kenneth et al. 1988) with its origins in the work of Bronfenbrenner (Bronfenbrenner 1974) on ecological systems theory, can provide a useful framework for thinking about the different levels of intervention. This socioecological framework was designed to focus attention on social and environmental factors as targets for health promotion. It identifies five complementary levels of change, targets, and approaches which are set out in Table 6.5.1.
	Historical evidence suggests that the greatest improvements in public health have been achieved through non-medical interventions, such as improved sanitation, welfare benefits, and improved workplace safety (McKeown 1976). More recent evidence also indicates that multifaceted and multilevel interventions are more effective than those operating at a single level (Greaves et al. 2011), and that environmental level interventions are more likely to be cost-effective than individually targeted clinical or non-clinical prevention interventions (Chokshi and Farley 2012). Reviews of the use of socioecological models in health promotion since the late 1980s have, however, suggested that published evaluations still tend to focus on one or two levels of intervention (Richard et al. 2011; Golden and Earp 2012), although there has been a notable increase, in interventions with multiple and more ‘upstream’ targets, such as the community or political environment (Richard et al. 2011; United Kingdom Clinical Research Collaboration 2018).
	 	Table 6.5.1 Socioecological framework
	 			Level of change

		Institutional

	(United Nations General Assembly, 2015).





Health inequalities


	Public health has the dual goals of improving population health and reducing health inequalities between different populations. The United Nations’ 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development has health and wellbeing as one of 17 goals the achievement of which is integrally linked to ending poverty and hunger, planetary health, maintaining peace, ensuring prosperity, and achieving dignity and equality for all (United Nations General Assembly 2015). One approach to tackling health inequality is to target interventions at disadvantaged groups at high risk of morbidity or mortality. This can be problematic, both because it can sometimes be stigmatizing and even harmful, but also because even if effective in reducing these groups’ risk it may be insufficient in bring about substantial population-level reductions in risk because, as Geoffrey Rose pointed out (Rose 1981), where disease risks follow a bell-shaped curve (as is the case with almost all non-communicable disease), the majority of cases of a disease will arise from those at low or medium risk (because there are simply more of them). However, universalist approaches which do not address the ‘upstream’ determinants of disease and only address individual behaviour may have the potential for widening inequalities because of the ‘inverse prevention law’ (Gordon et al. 1999) whereby socioeconomically advantaged groups often benefit disproportionately from universal interventions. In particular, interventions requiring action from recipients, such as interventions to reduce obesity requiring participation in weight-loss schemes or interpretation of nutrition labelling, are likely to benefit those most able to take such action, therefore more likely to widen inequalities. Interventions less demanding of individual actions, such as governmental measures to reduce the sugar and fat content of food or increase the affordability of healthy food (Adams et al. 2016; Rutter et al. 2017) are more promising means of benefiting disadvantaged populations. Progressive universalism has been advocated, for example, by the Marmot Review, as a way of avoiding these difficulties by ensuring that action on health inequalities both addresses ‘the causes of the causes’ but also by ensuring that the scale and intensity of more downstream interventions are proportionate to the level of disadvantage (Marmot 2010).
	These matters must be examined empirically within evaluations. Evaluations of the free-swimming initiative for children in England and of the introduction of universal access to free leisure facilities in the north-west of England are good examples of evaluations examining whether the inverse prevention law was operating. In both cases findings showed that physical activity could be increased and inequalities reduced. (Audrey et al. 2012; Higgerson et al. 2018).
	When developing public health interventions, it is therefore important to consider their potential for narrowing or widening health inequalities, and to ensure that evaluations assess whether factors such as socioeconomic status, gender, or ethnicity moderate (statistically interact with) intervention effects. Both the evaluations of physical activity interventions described earlier used large administrative datasets which provided the statistical power to for such moderator analyses. It is important to pursue such analyses, even in the absence of sufficient statistical power, because the findings can contribute to the accumulation of evidence in systematic reviews of the likely impact of particular interventions on inequalities (Tinner et al. 2018).
	The PROGRESS acronym (Evans and Brown 2003) indicates disadvantage may be related to place of residence, race/ethnicity, occupation, gender, religion, education, socioeconomic status, and social capital and is a helpful prompt to thinking about which factors are relevant to the population for which the intervention is being designed. The Health Inequalities Assessment Toolkit (NIHR CLAHRC North West Coast 2017) is another useful resource for this purpose.





Stages in the development of complex interventions


	Several guides relevant to the process of intervention development have been published recently. These include a taxonomy of approaches to developing health improvement interventions (O’Cathain et al. 2019), guides to the process itself (French et al. 2012; Wight et al. 2016; Hawkins et al. 2017) guidance on considering context in relation to population health interventions (Craig et al. 2018) and a framework for reporting the details of complex interventions in a standardized way for replication, transfer and evidence synthesis purposes (Hoffmann et al. 2014). The taxonomy of approaches to intervention development is based on a systematic review and synthesis of relevant literature from which the authors identify and describe eight categories of approach to intervention development and 18 different actions which can be taken within each approach (O’Cathain et al. 2019). The strengths and weaknesses of each approach are identified. This compendium is very detailed and covers the development of clinical and patient-based interventions as well as those with a population health focus. Next we outline the key stages in the process of complex public health intervention development.





Review of existing quantitative and qualitative evidence


	A first practical step in developing a complex intervention, whether designing something new or modifying an existing approach, is to review the available evidence. If there are already relevant systematic reviews, it may only be necessary to read these or update them. But if not, a new review may be needed (see Chapter 5.13 for further information about systematic reviews). While systematic reviews of quantitative evidence of intervention effects will summarize what is known about the effectiveness of a particular intervention, it is also useful to review relevant qualitative or quantitative research on implementation, which may provide important knowledge about the contexts in which the intervention has previously been used and how context might influence the feasibility, acceptability and therefore potential impact of the intervention (Craig et al. 2018).





Public involvement from the outset


	Including potential beneficiaries in intervention development is vital in ensuring that the intervention is relevant and acceptable. In the health and social care sectors, pre-existing groups representing particular patient and client groups can be engaged as partners in research, though the extent to which they are representative of all potential beneficiaries is often uncertain. In public health, identifying representative groups, particularly for universalist interventions, may be even more challenging. There is, however, guidance available on how to approach this and examples of good practice. INVOLVE is part of the National Institute for Health Research in the United Kingdom and its role is to encourage, support and set standards for public involvement in health research (INVOLVE 2017). Its website provides ample guidance for researchers (http://www.invo.org.uk) and the public. Involvement in public health research can and should, where relevant, include children and young people (Bird et al. 2013) and there are specialist groups set up who can provide such input. The ALPHA group (Advice Leading to Public Health Advancement) is one such example. This specially trained group of young people meets monthly to provide input into research undertaken by the DECIPHer public health research centre and other research organizations (DECIPHer, n.d.).





Involving policy and practice partners from the outset


	Consulting or collaborating with those who determine policy about or actually deliver similar interventions at this early stage will also provide useful insights. Involving such stakeholders from the outset is also more likely to result in its successful translation from research into routine practice if evaluation of the intervention suggests it is effective and cost-effective. System mapping is increasingly being used in stakeholder consultations to help identify what factors are thought to contribute to the public health problem to be tackled, to consider how and where to intervene, and what resources might be leveraged and deployed to address the problem. Such system maps can also be used to guide evaluations as in the example to follow (Fig. 6.5.1), which was used to inform the design of an evaluation of the health impacts of the UK Treasury Soft Drinks Industry levy (SDIL) (White 2017).
	Fig. 6.5.1 System map for the evaluation of the health impacts of the UK Treasury Soft Drinks Industry Levy.





Importance of theory


	Pawson and Tilley (1997) suggest all interventions are ‘theories incarnate’ because they assume that a certain action (or intervention) will trigger mechanisms which, in combination with the conditions that prevail at the time (context), generate particular impacts (or outcomes). However, such assumptions may remain implicit and the opportunity for evaluation to test them and thus contribute to the refinement of middle-range theory may be lost (Moore and Evans 2017). Guidance on developing complex interventions advocates using explicit theories of change to inform their design (Campbell et al. 2007; Craig et al. 2008; Glanz and Bishop 2010; Skivington et al. 2021). While interventions formulated without recourse to theory can and do work, there is evidence that interventions are more likely to be effective when informed by theory (Noar et al. 2008; Glanz and Bishop 2010). The ASSIST peer-led smoking prevention intervention is an example of a successful theory-based smoking prevention intervention (Campbell et al. 2008). Students aged 12–13, identified by classmates at secondary school as being influential, are trained to have conversations with their peers about the benefits of not smoking (Audrey et al. 2004). The intervention was informed by diffusion of innovations theory (Rogers 1995) with the peer supporter’s role being to diffuse new attitudes and new norms of behaviour relating to smoking throughout the year group. A cluster RCT conducted in south Wales and south-west England showed a 22% overall reduction in the odds of being a smoker in intervention compared with control schools. More detailed follow-on research on the peer supporters found that those who are asked to work informally, rather than under the supervision of teaching staff, engaged more effectively with the task they have been asked to undertake and more effectively diffused the health-promotions messages, in this case smoking prevention (Audrey et al. 2008).
	The ASSIST intervention drew on a theory from the social sciences. Taking theories ‘off the shelf’ to inform intervention development is a common but potentially problematic approach because of a tendency for researchers to choose popular psychological or behavioural theories which may not be altogether pertinent to the mechanisms through which the problem is actually sustained (Moore and Evans 2017). For example, the Gatehouse whole-school intervention aimed to promote mental and physical health among adolescents by rendering school environments more inclusive and engaging but was informed by Bowlby’s attachment theory which focuses on dynamics between mothers and infants (Patton et al. 2003). This tendency is confirmed by reviews of which theories have been utilized most frequently in public health interventions. These show that the field is dominated by psychological theories (Shahidullah 1995; Glanz and Bishop 2010; Davis et al. 2014). However, as we have already indicated, effective public health intervention is likely to require action at more than just the level of the individual, needing to be informed by a clear understanding of the workings of the social system that sustains the public health problem to be tackled. Public health intervention research may therefore need to draw on theories from a variety of disciplines. There are useful resources available which provide compendia of theories but the range of theories included in each reflects the disciplines involved or the contexts examined (Glanz and Rimmer 1997; Conner and Sparks 2005; Nutbeam et al. 2010; Michie et al. 2014). It also means that stakeholders (including the public) must be included in a process of co-creating interventions to ensure that their experiential knowledge of the problem and its context can be factored into the theory of change (Moore and Evans 2017).





Development of intervention logic models


	Logic models are diagrammatic representations of the intervention theory of change and of the logical relationships, for example, between an intervention’s inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes, although there is scope for flexibility regarding the precise categories used (Cooksy et al. 2001; W.K. Kellogg Foundation 2004). Intervention theory and logic models are useful tools in clarifying how an intervention is to be delivered and to what ends, and thereby provide a focus for evaluating process (and outcomes). Figure 6.5.2 provides an example of a recent logic model. It is for the Learning Together (INCLUSIVE) intervention which was designed to reduce bullying and aggression in secondary schools (Bonell et al. 2018a). The intervention’s theory of change is informed by Markham and Aveyard’s theory of human functioning and school organization (Markham and Aveyard 2003). Its tenets inform a diagrammatic logic model consisting of inputs, processes, institutional changes, intermediate impacts, and health outcomes. Inputs include training staff in ‘restorative practice’ (RP) as an approach to preventing and managing student aggression and misbehaviour, as well as an external facilitator to convene meetings of students and staff to review data on student needs in order to plan and deliver school-specific actions. These inputs are intended to enable processes, such as improved personal, social, and health education (PSHE) and the use of RP in schools, as well as the review and revision of school policies and rules by staff and students working collaboratively. In turn these processes are intended to modify various ‘boundaries’ within the school, such as the quality of staff–student relationships, and how schooling is framed, for example, to render decision-making more student-centred. These processes are ultimately theorized as transforming the ethos of the school so that more students use their sense of agency to commit to the school’s instructional order (teaching) and the regulatory order (discipline and school sense of community) and are thus less likely to decide to commit to antischool peer groups and behaviours such as bullying and substance use which can function symbolically as alternative, antischool markers of identity and status.
	Fig. 6.5.2 Logic model for the Learning Together (INCLUSIVE) intervention.
	The intervention has been tested in a cluster RCT in 40 secondary schools in England and was shown to have a modest, but in public health terms an important, impact on bullying but no effect on aggression (Bonell et al. 2018a).
	While useful, logic models have limitations. They describe linear chains of causation, offering no indications of how intervention implementation or the mechanisms by which outcomes are generated might interact with and therefore vary by context. In the case of INCLUSIVE, the linear logic model was augmented by additional context-mechanism-outcome (CMO) hypotheses suggesting how contextual factors and intervention mechanisms might interact to generate different outcomes in different settings. A further problem with logic models is that they can sometimes lead to the variables used to measure phenomena being confused with the phenomena themselves, thus reducing social, psychological, or biological mechanisms to chains of variables with little discussion of what processes connect these. So, while logic models provide a useful summary and guide to empirical assessment, they should build on a more nuanced textual description of the theory of change (Skivington et al. 2021). In the case of INCLUSIVE, for example, the theory of change invoked concepts such as agency to make decisions as well as the symbolic meaning of risk behaviours such as bullying, to explain intervention mechanisms (Bonell et al. 2018b).
	Public health interventions, complex or otherwise, can also have unintended consequences and the potential to harm (Lorenc and Oliver 2014). Theorizing an intervention’s potential iatrogenic mechanisms and harmful effects and developing so called ‘dark logic’ models to represent these ensures that they are considered in any evaluation with a view to understanding how they might be mitigated or avoided in future (Bonell et al. 2015b).





Evaluation of complex interventions


Piloting and feasibility studies


	Before embarking on an RCT (or some other evaluation of the effects of a public health intervention), it is wise to undertake a pilot or feasibility study. Guidance on how to conduct these has been lacking but the main report from the GUEST study (Guidance for Feasibility Studies of Complex Public Health Interventions) will be published shortly (Moore et al. 2018). The terms pilot and feasibility study have tended to be used interchangeably (Arain et al. 2010) but Eldridge and colleagues (Eldridge et al. 2016) suggest that a pilot study is just one form of feasibility study. A pilot study is in effect a miniature version of the main randomized trial (or whatever design is anticipated to examine effectiveness) and is designed to test that both the intervention and the evaluation can be implemented as intended. If the pilot is successful and no changes are made, then data from it can be incorporated into the main study (this is termed an internal pilot as opposed to an external one where data cannot be incorporated into the main study because the intervention or the evaluation methods are refined between pilot and main study). In contrast, feasibility studies are intended to examine specific, discrete areas of uncertainty to decide whether an effectiveness study is feasible or worthwhile, such as the willingness of participants to be randomized, response rates to questionnaires collecting outcome data, or the standard deviation of the primary outcome measure required for the sample size calculation. Feasibility studies also provide the opportunity to test out and optimize the intervention. Such studies need not pilot every aspect of a main study, including random allocation, and will use whatever methods are required to address the identified areas of uncertainty.
	Setting predetermined criteria for progression from a feasibility study or a pilot trial to the main study of effectiveness helps bring objectivity to whether or not to proceed and may be required by research funders. Criteria may inform binary stop/go decisions or more nuanced red/green/amber with amber denoting progression contingent on some refinements. Next in Table 6.5.2 are the criteria set for progression to a full-scale RCT to test the cost-effectiveness of a secondary-school-based intervention to improve teacher wellbeing. Part of the intervention involved training a cadre of teachers in intervention schools in mental health first aid so that they could provide peer support to colleagues. Not all the criteria were met but the full trial was funded because the study authors successfully argued that what they had learnt in the feasibility study would enable them to improve the recruitment of schools and peer supporters, and increase questionnaire response rates from teachers.
	 	Table 6.5.2 Criteria for progression from a pilot to a full RCT in the WISE (Wellbeing in Secondary Schools) Study and the outcome.
	 			Criterion
	Outcome
			Recruit and maintain peer supporter teams assuming ratio of 1 peer supporter: 15 staff members
	Mean ratio of 1 peer supporter: 17 staff members
		50% schools willing to be recruited and randomized
	Wrote to 33 eligible schools: 9 requested further information, 7 met with the research team, 6 took part in the feasibility study
		Response rate of at least 75% in staff and student follow up questionnaires

	(Kidger J. 2019, personal communication).





Process evaluation methods


	Process evaluation is as important as outcome evaluation. Process evaluation can provide valuable insight not only within feasibility and pilot studies, but also within full RCTs as well as in studies examining implementation of scaled-up interventions after effectiveness trials have been completed. Process evaluations can examine how interventions are planned, delivered, and received (Bonell et al. 2006; Oakley et al. 2006).
	There is no single, agreed definition of process evaluation. The UK MRC guidance on the subject states that a process evaluation ‘is a study which aims to understand the functioning of an intervention, by examining implementation, mechanisms of impact, and contextual factors. Process evaluation is complementary to, but not a substitute for, high quality outcomes evaluation’ (Moore et al. 2015). Other priority areas have been identified. One of the most widely cited frameworks is that of Steckler and Linnan (2002) which identified priority areas for process evaluation, including fidelity (the extent to which the intervention is delivered as intended), reach (whether an intervention is received by all those it targeted), dose delivered (the amount or number of units of intervention offered to participants, dose received (the extent of participants’ active engagement in the scheme), and context (local factors which impact implementation). Thus, process evaluation can explore whether those whom an intervention targets actively engage with it, an important consideration for social interventions. The following subsections consider some of these priority areas in more depth.





Intervention delivery and fidelity


	The importance of process evaluation was increasingly recognized during the 1980s, informed by discussion of ‘type 3 error’, defined as concluding that an intervention is ineffective because of a failure of its theory of change when lack of effect reflects its not being implemented as intended (Basch et al. 1985). Initially, the main aim of process evaluations was therefore to assess intervention fidelity to determine whether outcomes evaluation could represent valid assessment of an intervention’s underlying theory. Fidelity is defined variously. Moncher and Prinz (1991) define fidelity as confirmation that manipulation of the independent variable occurred as planned. Within the context of an RCT or other comparative evaluation, this requires assessment of the integrity of both delivery within the intervention arm and its differentiation from what occurred in the control arm. Later definitions of fidelity, for example, by Lichstein and colleagues (Lichstein et al. 1994) saw this as also encompassing receipt (participant uptake of the intervention) and enactment (the extent to which participants apply the lessons of interventions into practice in their lives). But such definitions begin to blur the useful distinction between fidelity and factors such as dose, acceptability, and even outcomes, so most researchers continue to define fidelity more narrowly in terms of delivery.
	Assessments of fidelity generally involve quantitative measurement, for example, using observations, video-recording, or provider self-assessments to audit delivery against what was intended. However, fidelity should not be viewed only in terms of ticking boxes on simple checklists. Steckler and Linnan (2002) argue that when evaluating fidelity, it is also important to assess whether the ‘spirit’ of an intervention is delivered in practice, and not just its mechanics. For example, when evaluating motivational interviewing, which is counselling aimed at enabling clients to recognize their own motivations for behaviour and to modify behaviour where this is not in line with their own goals, it is important to evaluate fidelity not merely as a cookbook list of techniques, but also whether the underlying empathic, patient-centred spirit of the approach is achieved (Miller and Rollnick 2009).
	Another important consideration when evaluating fidelity is the degree to which interventions should be standardized. Advocates of strict fidelity (Mihalic 2004) argue that this is essential if effective interventions are to be replicated, especially when an intervention’s ‘active ingredient’ may not be known (or is thought to arise from synergies between all components). They present evidence which suggests that high fidelity is associated with greater impact for some interventions (Mihalic 2004). In contrast, advocates of local adaptation (Dane and Schneider 1998) argue that interventions need to be tailored to local circumstances. Durlak and DuPre (2008) propose a compromise whereby an intervention’s ‘core components’ should be delivered in standard form but less central intervention components or features can be modified to fit local needs. They present research suggesting that a balance between fidelity and adaptation is likely to be most effective, with the precise balance dependent on the specific intervention. As noted earlier in this chapter, Hawe and colleagues go further to argue that with complex interventions characterized by interactions between multiple components and between intervention and context, too much attention has been paid to standardizing the form of intervention components (what precise actions are delivered) and more attention should be given to standardizing the function of intervention components (what the aim of each component is and how it contributes to the overall aim of the intervention) (Hawe et al. 2004). Consider the case of the INCLUSIVE intervention described earlier. Fidelity of form might be measured by determining whether the training in RP was delivered as planned and whether the facilitator convened a sufficient number of staff–student meetings. In contrast, fidelity of function might be measured by determining whether teachers were equipped to deliver RP and whether staff and students felt involved in the process of reviewing school policies.





Intervention reach, dose, and acceptability


	Steckler and Linnan conceive of evaluating intervention reach and dose, and participants’ responses to an intervention largely in quantitative terms (Steckler and Linnan 2002). Reach and dose are commonly examined quantitatively using methods such as questionnaire surveys exploring participants’ exposure to and satisfaction with an intervention. However, receipt can also be seen in qualitative terms as exploring participants’ reports of an intervention in their own terms. Qualitative research can be useful in examining how participants perceive an intervention in unexpected ways which may not be fully captured by researcher-developed quantitative constructs. Qualitative research can also explore how providers or participants enact ‘agency’ (willed action) in engaging with the intervention rather than merely receiving it passively (Oakley et al. 2006). For example, process evaluation of a youth work intervention to reduce teenage pregnancy in England reported how some youth workers and teachers responded to onerous recruitment and retention targets by transforming the intervention from one delivered out of school hours to one delivered as a partial alternative to normal school time, which may have explained its ineffectiveness (Wiggins et al. 2006).





Context


	Context is a critical aspect of process evaluation. Although there is no consistent definition (Craig et al. 2018) context can be taken to mean anything that was in place before the intervention itself was implemented. This could include factors such as the needs of participants, the infrastructure within which interventions will be delivered, the skills and attitudes of providers, and the attitudes and cultural norms of potential participants. In Steckler and Linnan’s (2002) framework, context is largely considered in terms of factors which may help or hinder implementation. For example, an intervention may be delivered poorly in some areas, but well in others, because of better provider capacity or more receptive community norms in some areas. Others consider context also in terms of how it influences outcomes. For example, ‘realist’ evaluators place great emphasis on whether intervention mechanisms generate beneficial outcomes in some contexts more than others. Context can be measured quantitatively in order to inform ‘moderator’ analyses within or between trials, though the latter is rarer (Bonell et al. 2012). Qualitative research allows for a different understanding of the importance of context, for example, examining how intervention providers or recipients describe the interaction between their context and their own agency in explaining their actions (Oakley et al. 2006).





Intervention mechanism of action


	Assessing an intervention’s mechanisms of effects involves assessing the validity of the theory of change in explaining how outcomes are generated. Such analysis can explain why an intervention is found to be effective or ineffective within an outcome evaluation. This might be critically important in refining an intervention found to be ineffective or in understanding the potential generalizability of interventions found to be effective. Quantitative data can be used to undertake mediator analyses to assess whether intervention outputs or proximal outcomes appear to fully or partially account for intervention effects on distal health outcomes (Gardner et al. 2006). Qualitative data can be also used to examine such pathways in terms of how they are perceived and described by those involved, and this is particularly useful when the pathways in question have not been comprehensively examined using quantitative data, as well as when pathways are too complex (e.g. using multiple steps or feedback loops) to be assessed adequately using quantitative analyses. This was, for example, the case with an assessment of possible causal pathways underlying an intervention to modify school environments in order to reduce student substance use, which appeared to involve feedback loops whereby student participation within certain intervention activities increased student commitment to the intervention which in turn increased student participation within other components (Bonell et al. 2010).
	However, such analyses can be challenging. First, as suggested earlier, quantitative analyses require evaluators to have correctly anticipated what data are needed to examine causal pathways and to have collected these. For example, the evaluation of the youth work intervention aiming to prevent teenage pregnancy reported a higher rate of pregnancies among those receiving the intervention. It was hypothesized that this apparent adverse outcome resulted from the intervention bringing together young people engaged in risk behaviours so that pro-risk social norms were amplified. However, data on these were not collected so that this hypothesis could not be tested (Wiggins et al. 2008). A second challenge involves using qualitative alongside quantitative data to understand causal pathways. If qualitative data are analysed in order to explain quantitative findings, this may bias interpretation (Wight and Obasi 2002; Campbell et al. 2015). Furthermore, quantitative and qualitative methods originate from different research traditions. Qualitative research focuses on participants’ accounts, drawing out generalizations about meanings and agency using largely inductive methods. They offer rich insights into how actors understand social phenomena rather than trying to test hypotheses about causal associations. As Munro and Bloor (2010) put it: ‘process evaluations do indeed enrich our understanding of the social processes involved in the delivery and receipt of complex interventions’, they provide ‘interpretations to which a degree of indeterminacy is always attached that cannot be expressed in probabilistic terms. The continuing tension between positivist and interpretive paradigms within that research design pose problems of understanding and reporting. Not so much “paradigm peace” as “paradigm truce” ’.
	While we advocate process evaluation as an important evaluative tool it should not be seen as a panacea for answering all the questions an outcome evaluation cannot, nor is its use unproblematic. The range of possible domains it can focus on (delivery, fidelity, reach, dose, acceptability, context, sustainability) is wide, and resources may not be available to collect the data required to examine them all. Some may be a greater priority than others depending on the nature of the intervention and its stage of development. For example, the acceptability of an intervention is something that should predominantly be explored in a pilot or feasibility study rather than leaving it till the definitive trial, where understanding mechanism of effects may be a more pressing matter for a process evaluation to examine.





Implementation issues


Sustainability


	The implementability and sustainability of new public health interventions at a scale capable of population impact is an important consideration. For example, it may be that a group of health promotion specialists, substance misuse experts and youth workers have been specially assembled to deliver a new intervention in secondary schools to reduce substance and alcohol misuse. This intervention is shown in a cluster RCT to be effective. The issue then becomes how can that delivery model be replicated and sustained outside of the trial so that effectiveness is maintained. The ‘RE-AIM’ framework (reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, maintenance) is useful in conceptualizing this (Glasgow et al. 1999). Its originators argue that those commissioning public health services need to know not only that an intervention is effective but that it is capable of being adopted by provider agencies and implemented by them as planned, and will reach sufficient people to achieve a population health impact that can be maintained over time (Glasgow et al. 2001).





From research into practice


	The impact of research on policy and practice is increasingly recognized to occur through a gradual and indirect process of enlightenment rather than via direct effects of single studies or even reviews on single decisions (Weiss 1986; Graham et al. 2006). However, while empirically accurate, this is normatively disappointing for those advocating a more direct role for evidence in informing policy (Davies et al. 2000). Now there is recognition that to be influential, research needs to engage reciprocally with policy and practice. Earlier in this chapter we highlighted the need to consult key policy and practice stakeholders and the public early in the development and evaluation of complex public health interventions. This approach is now being extended by some into a process whereby evidence is co-produced through a knowledge exchange partnership between researchers, policymakers, and practitioners using transdisciplinary action research (Daker-White et al. 2014). This method involves academics from a variety of relevant disciplines working with policymakers, practitioners, and the public to identify what research is required, develop research questions, conduct evaluations, synthesize evidence, and implement and maintain evidence-based public health practice. The advantage of this approach is that if evaluations indicate that changes to practice are producing the desired outcomes then the capacity-building necessary to sustain that whole system change is built into the approach. There are a number of examples of promising interventions (de Silva-Sanigorski et al. 2010; Chittleborough et al. 2013), including the INCLUSIVE intervention in England (Bonell et al. 2015a; Bonell et al. 2018a) and the Gatehouse project in Australia, where this approach has been taken (Bond et al. 2001, 2004).





Discussion and future direction


	Public health interventions can comprise policy-level initiatives implemented at a national or international level, for example the World Health Organization’s Healthy Cities programme (World Health Organization, n.d.), through to brief individual behaviour change interventions to encourage reduced alcohol consumption delivered in primary care populations (Kaner et al. 2007). Interventions may be programmatic in nature with many different components such as Project Northland in secondary schools to reduce alcohol consumption, or it may be simpler, as in the example of human papilloma virus vaccination which involves three injections over a 12-month period to reduce substantially the chances of a woman having cervical cancer. Given this huge variability there is no ‘one-size-fits-all’ approach to their development and evaluation. What we have identified in this chapter are the key issues to be considered and the range of methods available to tackle them.
	We conceive of the development and evaluation of complex public health interventions as distinct elements but ideally part of an overall symbiotic and cyclical process rather than sequential phases. Knowledge exchange partnerships between researchers and public health practitioners and policymakers offer a way of achieving this ideal, but, as is sometimes the case with the interventions themselves, the evidence suggests that the effectiveness of knowledge translation varies according to context (LaRocca et al. 2012).

6.6


Economic appraisal in public healthcare: assessing efficiency and equity


	David Parkin, Stephen Morris, and Nancy Devlin





What is economic appraisal?


	Planning healthcare services to meet the health needs of a population must always recognize that availability of resources with which to meet them is a constraint on the achievement of its goals. There are many choices that must be made reflecting that constraint. For example, which public health and healthcare services should be provided, how they will be provided, and to whom they will be provided. Economic appraisal (EA) is a systematic way of analysing the consequences of such choices. It is one element of health technology assessment (HTA), the uses of which include among other things healthcare pricing and reimbursement decisions, planning the location of healthcare facilities, and setting of priorities for confronting health problems. EA is not the only element of HTA, but it is an important one.
	Similarly, the discipline of economics is not the only contributor to EA. It also requires other public health relevant disciplines such as epidemiology, statistics, and operational research. Economics contributes the rationale for EA, an overall framework for analysis, and some measurement principles and methods.
	The term ‘economic appraisal’ describes a set of techniques that weigh up the costs of an action, such as providing a particular type of healthcare to a patient or demographic group, against the benefits that it provides. The term ‘economic evaluation’ is also used. The distinction between these terms is that appraisal is undertaken before the action is taken, to help in deciding whether or not and how the action is to be done, and evaluation is undertaken after the action, to judge its effects. This distinction is often forgotten, and these terms are used interchangeably in much of health economics. The expression ‘evaluation’ is now most commonly used in the health economics literature, but appraisal is used here because that more accurately describes the main purpose for which economic analysis in healthcare is applied in practice. The usual label given to this activity in economics is cost-benefit analysis (CBA). However, that term is often reserved in healthcare EA for a particular technique, which is explained later in this chapter.
	The principles of EA can be applied to all kinds of health interventions, from individual patients’ treatments to population-based programmes, all of which may be of interest to public health practitioners. This chapter therefore does not restrict itself to activities conventionally labelled as public health, and also includes interventions that are not usually thought of as healthcare, such as health promotion. It highlights the special issues that EA faces in evaluating public health activities and finishes with a specific examination of those issues.





The economics of economic appraisal


	EA should not be confused with financial appraisal. A financial appraisal is concerned with the monetary implications of a proposed action, such as investment in a healthcare facility or the provision to a population of one or more interventions. It examines cash expenditures and available funding to ensure that the actions taken are viable and provide a reasonable return. These cash flows are measured using accounting principles. EA shares some of the methods and principles of financial appraisal, but its aim is a more general assessment of costs and benefits and has measurement principles derived from economics concepts. The most important of these are opportunity cost, social cost, marginal cost, efficiency, and equity.
	In practice, these theoretical principles are hard and occasionally impossible to adhere to, but they provide a guide as to the best sources of cost and benefit data and to the reliability of the numbers used.





Opportunity cost


	As with any goods and services that are created within an economy, production of healthcare requires resources such as personnel (often referred to as labour), equipment and buildings (often referred to as capital), land, and raw materials. There are finite amounts of such resources available to be converted into goods and services at any particular time, so it is not possible to produce everything that everyone in a population might want. Resources are therefore scarce relative to the demands for them. In the economy as a whole, there are not enough scarce resources to meet all of the wants that people have, so we have to choose which wants are met and which are not met. Similarly, in the healthcare system there are not enough healthcare resources to meet all of the health needs that people have, so we have to choose which needs are met and which are not met. Of course, it might be argued that if we cannot meet all health needs, resources should be diverted from other parts of the economy, and it is legitimate for public health practitioners to advocate that. But it would not be possible to do that indefinitely, and the consequences might be a reduction in education, welfare, and other goods and services in the public and private sectors of the economy that are not only desirable in themselves, but also contribute to maintaining and improving the health of the population.
	Economics claims that scarcity and the resulting necessity to choose are ubiquitous and unavoidable. This leads directly to an important and fundamental economics concept, opportunity cost. If scarce resources are used to produce a good or service, those resources cannot be used to produce other goods or services. There is a lost opportunity to enjoy the benefits that those other goods or services would have provided. Because there are many possible uses for resources, the opportunity cost of using resources in a particular way is defined as the benefits that would have resulted from their best alternative use.
	When economists refer to costs, they usually mean opportunity costs. This is quite different to the more familiar concept of financial costs, the costs of goods and services and of scarce resources in terms of money. Very often, financial costs are used to measure opportunity costs, but this is not always the case. Opportunity costs and financial costs are different ways of thinking about costs, rather than separate elements of overall costs; it would make no sense to calculate them separately and add them together, for example.
	Measuring opportunity costs is often difficult in practice. It is preserved in good EA practice by the separation of costing services into measuring the quantity of resources required to provide that service and calculating the value of those resources, by, for example, examining the prices of each type of resources. This is also good practice for ensuring that research can be generalized to other settings where quantities and prices may differ. For example, different countries may have very different ways of providing services, with different combinations of different kinds of personnel, facilities, and locations, as well as differing relative costs of those resources.





Social costs and benefits


	A financial appraisal of a proposed action takes into account only costs that are incurred by the person or organization taking the action and benefits to the person or those who are the organizations’ clients. These are referred to as private costs and benefits. However, in some kinds of EA it is in principle essential to take account of all costs and benefits to society, whatever they are, and whoever incurs them. In particular, it is essential to take account of social costs and benefits in a CBA that examines the impact of the action on the economy as a whole. For example, the total costs of a medical intervention would include not only costs incurred within the health sector, but also those incurred in subsequent personal care and support, whether by organizations or private carers. However, it is arguable that such wider costs should not be included for some of the EA methods discussed next, for example, in a cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA), in which the aim is to maximize healthcare outcomes within a limited budget.
	A special example of the difficulties involved in this is accounting for transfer payments, examples of which are social security payments and other state benefits paid out of taxation. Except for the costs involved in administering them, these are not costs to society as a whole. Rather, they are transfers between different members of society, since the recipients derive benefits from them that match the costs to taxpayers. However, from the state’s point of view such expenditure may be regarded as a use of tax revenues which has an opportunity cost in terms of other government expenditure.
	Again, the principle of including all social costs and benefits is almost impossible to follow perfectly because of information limitations. However, it is preserved in good practice in health EA by identifying costs and benefits according to who bears them, in three categories: the health service, patients and their families, and the rest of society. It is also embodied in the recommendation that any analysis should make clear the perspective from which the analysis is conducted, for example, society, the government, or the health sector.
	Walker et al. (2019) have argued that adoption of an abstract ‘social perspective’ is not helpful in undertaking EA in practice and have developed a framework by which these issues can be considered in a systematic way. This is further discussed next in the context of EA of Public Health interventions, where it is of special importance.





Marginal costs and benefits


	The total cost of any activity will depend on how much of it is carried out. For example, the total cost of a vaccination scheme will depend on the number of people to be vaccinated. If the total cost of the activity and the number of units of activity are known, it is possible to calculate an average cost per unit of activity, which is what accounting data usually provide. However, in some circumstances average costs may be a misleading estimate of the cost of a unit of activity, and what are required are marginal costs.
	Marginal cost is the change in cost that is caused by the smallest possible change in another variable to which it is related. The marginal cost of a good or service is usually more specifically defined as the extra cost incurred in producing one more unit of it. Note that marginal does not mean small or unimportant; instead it means at the margins of an existing condition, for example, the cost that will be incurred by changing the allocation of resources slightly. That cost could actually be large, even though the change in the amount of the good or service is small. As an extreme example, suppose that the service is a screening programme and the screening centre processing the test material has reached full capacity. Screening an extra person could only be carried out if a new screening centre was built, so its marginal cost would be very high. By contrast, the marginal cost of the last test performed within the existing capacity may have been quite small, simply the cost of performing the test. This demonstrates another important point. Marginal cost may vary considerably with respect to the same size of change in the other variable, depending on the level of that other variable, in this case the number of people screened.
	An example of the importance of looking at marginal costs is the impact of schemes designed to lower hospital inpatient surgical costs by reducing length of stay through earlier discharge. Hospitals may have information on the average cost of an inpatient stay, which can be used to calculate an average cost per day. However, the costs of an inpatient day are not constant. In particular, they may be much smaller than the average towards the end of the stay, because the average includes a share of the costs of treatment and perhaps of high dependency care that took place towards the beginning of an inpatient stay. So, reducing the number of low dependency days at the end of the stay will save far fewer resources than would be expected by examining the average. Marginal costs calculated with respect to an increase or decrease in the number of days would give a correct estimate of the likely savings.
	The same principles apply to benefits. Marginal benefits are the extra benefits obtained by consuming one more unit of a good or service. An example of the importance of looking at marginal rather than average benefits is a screening programme that can be carried out with different numbers of sequential tests. The more tests, the more cases are detected. A programme that used two sequential tests might yield 11 cases per 10,000 people tested, which could look reasonable. But suppose that a programme that used only one test would discover ten cases. The marginal benefit of including the second test is only one case per 10,000, which does not look so good.
	To give a real example, Torgerson and Spencer (1996) illustrated the importance of marginal analysis by analysing data on the cost-effectiveness of biochemical screening for Down’s syndrome as a replacement for screening by maternal age. An estimate had been published that introducing biochemical screening in a population of 20,000 pregnant women would cost £413,501 and might prevent 11 affected births, giving a cost-effectiveness ratio of £37,591 per affected foetus identified. Torgerson and Spencer pointed out that for the same number of women, existing antenatal screening procedures based on maternal age and additional tests already cost £79,500 with four births potentially prevented. So, the true cost-effectiveness of biochemical screening was (£413,500—£79,000)/(11–4) = £334,500/7 = £47,786, a much higher cost per affected foetus identified than for the estimate based on average cost.





Efficiency and equity


	Economic analysis is usually employed to judge the way in which scarce resources are employed according to two main criteria: efficiency and equity. These two concepts have technical definitions, which will be described in the following subsections, but in very broad terms efficiency refers to obtaining the greatest output for a given set of resources and equity refers to a fair distribution of that output among the population. The term ‘output’ is very general and in our context we usually mean the additional amount of healthcare or health produced.





Efficiency


	It is necessary to give a warning about definitions of efficiency. Economists, as specialists in the analysis of efficiency, largely agree about what it means and how different types of efficiency may be defined, but the labels they give to those types vary. The same concept may be given to different names and the same name given to different concepts. Here we use the labels and definitions given in Morris et al. (2012).
	Knapp (1984) gave a very broad definition of efficiency as ‘the allocation of scarce resources that maximizes the achievement of aims’. This is a useful start, because it suggests the benign nature of the desire to achieve efficiency. If we have scarce resources and competing uses for them, our aim will be to obtain the best set of uses, with ‘best’ defined in whatever way we want. If we decide that the aim of the health system is to improve the health of the population and we have a fixed healthcare budget, we will obtain the biggest health gain if the allocation of scarce healthcare resources is efficient.
	For practical purposes, we require more precise and technical definitions of efficiency. However, it is useful first to understand a slightly abstract idea, called Pareto efficiency which is also, though not consistently, called allocative efficiency. This arises from an attempt to create a widely acceptable criterion for judging different allocations of resources to different ends. The suggestion is that we would be able to say that one allocation is better than another if at least one person is better off under the first allocation and no one is worse off. This is called the Pareto criterion. Consider a change from one allocation of resources to another, for example making changes to the kind of care that is made available in the healthcare system. If some people benefit and no one is made worse off, this is described as a Pareto improvement. If it is not possible to make any such changes, then we have achieved a Pareto optimum. Another way to view the Pareto optimum is that it is a position where it is not possible to make anyone better off without making someone else worse off.
	If we aim to make people as well off as possible and are not concerned about whether some people are better off than others, then a Pareto optimum is efficient. We cannot further improve the achievement of our aim because even if we can make someone, or even many people, better off, we do not know if this is outweighed by those who are made worse off. This is not a unique position; there are many allocations of resources that would be Pareto optimal, some of which would imply great inequalities between different people. If our aims also took account of the undesirability of inequalities, then we might not view all Pareto optimums as efficient. Nevertheless, ideas of efficiency in economics derive from this concept of Pareto efficiency. Here, we define three types: technical, economic, and social.
	Technical efficiency is a concept that is used in considering how health and healthcare, or ‘outputs’, are produced from scarce resources, or ‘inputs’. There is technically efficient production if the most output possible is being produced from a given amount of inputs or the fewest possible inputs are used to produce a given amount of output. For example, the number of people that can be vaccinated against influenza in a general practice clinic depends on the number of nursing staff that are available and other inputs. If the most that can be provided by three practice nurses is 100 vaccinations each day, then it is technically inefficient if 99 vaccinations are provided by three nurses or 100 vaccinations by more than three nurses.
	Another way of viewing technical efficiency, which is consistent with Pareto efficiency, is that the practice cannot vaccinate more people without employing at least one more nurse. More generally, production is technically efficient for a given set of inputs if it is only possible to produce more by employing more of at least one input.
	In practice, EA does not directly address technical efficiency, though as will be explained it is an essential underlying assumption in most cases.
	Economic efficiency is given different labels, including cost-effectiveness, though that term should be used carefully, as will be explained next. Technical efficiency is defined with respect to the physical numbers of inputs, but economic efficiency is interested in the cost of those inputs. Economic efficiency is achieved if we are producing most output for a given cost or producing a set amount of output at the lowest possible cost. Using the earlier example, suppose that people could be vaccinated by different grades of nurses, but at least one senior nurse must be part of the team. It might be equally technically efficient for 100 people to be vaccinated each day by employing one senior and two junior nurses, one junior and two senior nurses, or three senior nurses. But senior nurses are more expensive to employ than junior nurses, so it will be economically efficient to use the first of these staff mixes. This demonstrates that although achieving technical efficiency is necessary to achieve economic efficiency, not all technically efficient ways of producing are economically efficient.
	Another way of viewing economic efficiency, which is consistent with Pareto efficiency, is that given the costs of employing nursing staff, the practice cannot undertake more treatments without them costing more to provide. More generally, production is economically efficient for a given set of input prices if it is only possible to produce more by incurring greater costs.
	In practice, economic efficiency is the dominant type of efficiency analysed in EA. However, there are different ways in which this is done, as will be explained next.
	Social efficiency is a much broader concept than technical and economic efficiency. If there is economic efficiency in production in every part of the economy, there is allocative efficiency in production for the economy as a whole. There is an equivalent concept relating to the consumption of goods and services called allocative efficiency in consumption where, given prices of goods and services, consumers maximize the benefit that they derive from those goods and services. If both of these are achieved, then there is allocative efficiency in the economy as a whole, which is also known as social efficiency. This is the same as the Pareto efficiency described earlier.
	Obviously, social efficiency according to this strict definition is not a concept likely to be of practical use in health economics. However, it is important because it underlies CBA, whose aim in theory is to move the economy closer to social efficiency.





Equity


	Equity is an important criterion for allocation of resources, and it is particularly important in health systems because it is observable that people attach more importance to fairness in health and healthcare than to the distribution of many other goods and services. Almost every healthcare system in the world has equity as an important policy objective. However, economic analysis of equity is less clear than that of efficiency, except for how equity might be measured, and there is less agreement among economists about it.
	Equity means fairness, and in the context of healthcare this means fairness in the distribution of health and healthcare between people and in the burden of financing healthcare. It is not a synonym for equality, which means an equal distribution. It may not always be fair to be equal, for example, it might be thought to be unfair if both healthy and sick people are given the same amount of healthcare. But equality is often used to define equity, as, for example, in the principles of horizontal equity—equal treatment of those who are equal—and vertical equity—unequal treatment of those who are not equal. An example often used in healthcare is the proposal that there should be equal access to healthcare for people with the same level of healthcare needs.
	That is not the only possible definition of healthcare equity, and more generally there is no single definition of what equity is. Moreover, ideas about equity are not mainly founded on economics principles, rather on philosophy, ethics, law, and other forms of enquiry. An example is the equity principle of procedural justice, which in this context might mean that the process used to decide on the allocation of healthcare resources between people should be fair. This is an important principle in deciding how HTA is applied, but it is not especially based in economics. Culyer and Bombard (2012) have suggested that one way to incorporate the plurality of approaches to equity in HTA is to use a ‘checklist’ to ensure that decision-makers take all aspects into account.
	Cookson et al. (2017) have developed a framework for examining both equity and efficiency, in terms of cost-effectiveness, in a systematic and consistent way. It uses two analytical concepts, health equity trade-offs and net equity impacts. It uses these to describe two approaches to conducting cost-effectiveness analyses that incorporate equity concerns, equity impact analysis, and equity trade-off analysis, which are described next.
	Health equity trade-offs result from the possibility that efficiency and equity may conflict under some circumstances. For example, a screening programme may be cost-effective in terms of the cost of detecting treatable cases, leading to an overall increase in health for the population as a whole, but if take-up is lower among groups who have worse overall health, this will lead to a widening of health inequalities. There are therefore four possibilities, as in Table 6.6.1:
	 	Table 6.6.1 Health equity trade-offs
	Net health impact
