6.7


Behavioural economics and health


	Alison Buttenheim and Harsha Thirumurthy





Introduction


	Among the many determinants of health outcomes around the world, human behaviour plays a central role. While resources allocated to the health sector and access to health products or services are certainly important, it is often the case that individual decision-making influences the burden of disease and the effectiveness of health services available in any given country. Examples of why human behaviour is relevant are numerous in both low-and high-income settings. Behaviours such as smoking and exercise have an impact on the burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) globally. Utilization of vaccination services and infant feeding behaviours have an impact on child health outcomes. Understanding human behaviour—specifically how people make health-related decisions—is therefore essential for explaining health outcomes around the world and also for developing solutions to leading challenges in global health. This understanding can be advanced and enriched using behavioural economics.
	Behavioural economics blends theories from the disciplines of economics and psychology to uncover key insights about human decision-making. In recent years, a rapidly expanding literature has applied behavioural economics specifically in the health domain. Behavioural economics insights have been useful for understanding why proven health interventions are not taken up at the ‘last mile’, or why it is difficult to sustain healthy behaviours like smoking cessation or medication adherence. Relevant for health policy, the field of behavioural economics has also brought to light a number of interventions that can contribute meaningfully to efforts to improve population health.
	This chapter introduces several prominent theories from behavioural economics and reviews examples of how these theories can be useful for studying global health and developing policies or programmes to improve health. We begin by reviewing the ‘standard’ theory or model of decision-making that features prominently in economics. This model posits a form of rational decision-making and offers valuable insights about what drives individuals’ decisions in various domains of life, from consumption to health. We discuss several policy implications that follow from this theory and make a case for why these are important for global health policy. We then turn to theories and principles from behavioural economics and adjacent fields that emerged from a recognition that the standard economic model of decision-making does not adequately explain many aspects of human behaviour. We discuss these anomalies—departures from rational decision-making models—and summarize behavioural economics theories that better explain human behaviour. In parallel, we draw upon empirical evidence from around the world and highlight actionable behaviour change interventions that can be useful for students of global health and practitioners alike.
	Given the breadth of behavioural economics theories and empirical evidence, we are necessarily selective in our review of this discipline and its relevance for global health. We focus on a few prominent theories of decision-making that are key to understanding and modifying human behaviour. We introduce the concept of present bias, which is particularly relevant for understanding health behaviours in which the consequences of one’s actions are not realized immediately. Present bias in individuals’ decision-making offers a compelling rationale for offering incentives—a widely-studied topic for which we summarize key studies and lessons. We also review the concepts of loss aversion, status quo bias, limited attention, and social influence, all of which have direct relevance for health behaviour and health policy. Our chapter concludes by reviewing more recent theories of the link between poverty and decision-making that offer new ways of understanding health behaviour and new opportunities for interventions that improve health.
	Empirical examples in this chapter come from diverse settings, including both low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) and high-income countries, and from diverse areas of health, from infectious diseases such as HIV and malaria for which the burden is greatest in low-income regions of the world to NCDs that are common globally.





Standard economic theories of decision-making


	To explain human behaviour and develop behaviour change interventions, the field of economics has commonly relied on a model grounded in the assumption that individuals are rational, self-interested decision makers who seek to maximize their own well-being. This workhorse model in economics offers a number of relevant insights for global health. The model posits three factors that drive choices: preferences that characterize tastes and values, the relative prices faced for the various choices available, and the constraints on available resources such as time or money. Preferences describe individuals’ likes and dislikes as well as the extent to which they value the present relative to the future and the degree of risk or uncertainty they are willing to tolerate—all of which can influence one’s propensity to make specific choices. Prices reflect the costs of purchasing products and services. And finally, resource constraints are typically denominated in income or wealth, but can also appear as time constraints. We discuss each of these in more detail next.
	Preferences are an important determinant of human behaviour that vary from person to person. For a number of health behaviours, it is easy to see why preferences might be relevant. Some individuals may place a greater value than others do on future costs or benefits of actions they take today, and as a result may be less likely to smoke cigarettes or more likely to adhere to medications. These temporal preferences have been shown to be associated with both health behaviours and outcomes in several studies (Thirumurthy et al. 2015; Bradford et al. 2017). Preferences towards risk are another relevant decision-making factor. Heterogeneity in risk preferences and the association between risk preferences and risky health behaviours have been documented in many studies (Anderson and Mellor 2008). Behavioural economics research discussed next raises doubts about the within-person stability of time and risk preferences, but standard economic theory treats risk and time preferences as not easily malleable.
	Beyond time and risk preferences, individuals’ propensity to use various health services or to engage in healthy behaviours can also be influenced by the information they possess about associated benefits (or harms). This has motivated a large literature testing whether information provision to individuals can influence decision-making, and a common approach to public health campaigns of raising awareness about the benefits of healthy behaviours or the harms of unhealthy behaviours. Empirical evidence on the effects of information provision is mixed. Some studies have documented large impacts of one-time information provision. In Kenya, informing teenage girls about the risk of unsafe sex with older men who have a higher likelihood of being HIV-positive led to sexual behaviour change and reduced pregnancy risk for the girls (Dupas 2011). Larger-scale testing of this approach in other countries has shown more muted effects, however. In the United States, researchers and policymakers have sought to influence food choices by providing caloric and other nutrition information on food items. Again, there is some evidence that this type of information provision can alter people’s preferences and ultimately, their behaviour (Wisdom et al. 2010). These examples underscore the importance of paying attention to individuals’ preferences when designing public health interventions.
	The second determinant of health behaviour—prices—is highly relevant for understanding health behaviour and continues to shape health policy in important ways. A large literature has shown that prices of health products and services influence demand. Price experiments in high-and low-income countries have shown that demand for healthcare—in much the same way as demand for consumer products—is highly sensitive to prices. The RAND health insurance experiment showed long ago that healthcare utilization is driven by the prices people face (Manning et al. 1987). In low-income countries, a series of randomized trials has demonstrated that people’s demand for life-saving health products and services is highly sensitive to prices even when prices are extremely low. One study from Zambia showed that demand for water treatment products declined substantially when going from free distribution to prices just above zero (Dupas 2014). Similarly, a recent study in Zimbabwe showed there was a 25% decline is demand for HIV self-tests among people offered self-tests for $0.50 instead of being offered them for free (Chang et al. 2019). A key lesson that emerges from these studies in low-income countries is that there is a compelling rationale for subsidizing healthcare products and services instead of charging user fees for them. This is especially the case for health products and services associated with infectious diseases, where usage by one individual can influence health outcomes of other individuals.
	In addition to public subsidies, two other policy measures also follow directly from the recognition that prices influence people’s decisions. One is the use of taxes to raise the prices faced by individuals and thereby curb certain unhealthy behaviours. Another is the provision of financial incentives to increase benefits associated with a certain health behaviour and thereby promote health behaviours. Taxes are a widely-used policy measure not only for raising government revenue but also for changing human behaviour. Cigarette taxes are perhaps the most prominent example of taxes as a lever for behaviour change in global health. Multiple studies have shown that taxes are an effective way to reduce smoking rates. More recently, in response to growing concern about rising obesity, some governments have begun to impose taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages. Studies from Mexico as well as individual cities in the United States have suggested that this is one way to reduce sugar-sweetened beverage consumption (Colchero et al. 2016; Silver et al. 2017; Roberto et al. 2019). Financial incentives (which we discuss in the next section in the context of present bias) have a clear and compelling rationale even in the standard model of decision-making. Just as subsidies lower the prices faced by consumers and thereby boost demand, incentives can offset various opportunity costs associated with seeking health services and bring down the full price faced by consumers.
	Resources available to individuals are the third and final determinant of health behaviour in standard models of decision-making. A core prediction of economic theory is that all else equal, individuals facing financial or time constraints will be less able to access healthcare than those without such constraints. This provides further motivation for interventions such as price subsidies or health insurance; in recent years there have been a number of efforts in LMICs to expand access to health insurance. Another policy response to curb the effects of poverty on health has been the provision of unconditional cash transfers. Many countries in Africa and Asia have expanded unconditional cash transfer programmes with the goal of both alleviating poverty and improving health outcomes. Later in this chapter we discuss additional ways in which poverty can influence health outcomes by summarizing recent research on the psychological consequences of poverty.





Behavioural economics insights and related interventions


	Behavioural economics theories have gained prominence in the study of health behaviour because the standard economic models of decision-making outlined earlier, while useful for explaining many facets of decision-making, fail to explain some commonly-observed patterns of behaviour. For example, even when life-saving health technologies and services are available for free or at very low prices, individuals do not utilize them at the high rates that would be predicted by standard economic theory and keenly desired by health officials. Similarly, despite medications for chronic diseases having large benefits that people recognize as important and valuable, medication adherence remains far lower than desired. These and many other behavioural ‘anomalies’ have underscored the limitations of standard models of decision-making and given rise to the behavioural economics theories that we discuss next.





Present bias and the rationale for incentives


	Perhaps the most prominent and widely discussed decision-making context is situations that involve trade-offs between present and future costs and benefits. Seeking preventive services or exercising regularly, for example, requires incurring immediate economic costs, time investment, or other disutility in order to realize health benefits in the future. For such decisions, pervasive in the health domain, individuals do not discount future costs and benefits according to a consistent discount rate, but rather do so in ways that are present-biased. Specifically, the immediacy of costs and benefits drives behaviour to a much greater extent that would be expected from the rational tendency to discount the future. Thus, even with large benefits to adopting certain health behaviours such as quitting smoking, exercising, taking medications, or seeking preventive services, individuals may fail to adopt if the benefits are delayed and the costs (in the form of economic costs, inconvenience, or psychological burdens) are immediate. Present-biased preferences have been documented in lab and field settings and go a long way towards explaining why behaviour change can be difficult when there are intertemporal trade-offs.
	An important implication of present-biased decision-making is that people can be guided towards engaging in more forward-looking, healthy behaviours if the immediate benefits of engaging in the behaviour are enhanced or the immediate costs are lowered. This insight motivates the widespread use of financial and non-financial incentives for healthy behaviours in many parts of the world. Since the future benefits of engaging in a healthy behaviour are often insufficient for promoting the behaviour, the provision of small, immediate rewards can accelerate benefits into the present and make the behaviour more likely. They can also offset the disproportionate role of immediate costs or hassle factors. A vast empirical literature has examined the effects of incentive-based interventions on behaviour change around the world. The provision of incentives by employers and governments is also widespread. A few examples illustrate the ways in which incentives and highlight the strengths and limitations of such interventions to promote better health. An early and prominent example of deploying incentives to motivate health behaviours in LMICs is the Progresa programme implemented in Mexico beginning in the 1990s and later renamed the Oportunidades programme. In this programme, low-income households could receive cash transfers from the government contingent on children in those households attending school regularly and obtaining preventive healthcare. While present-biased decision-making was not the sole rationale for the conditional cash transfers—the programme crucially also sought to alleviate poverty—the interventions succeeded in part by offering more immediate rewards to households for engaging in behaviours that would generate long-term benefits. Various studies have evaluated the Progresa programme and demonstrated that it was largely successful in promoting behaviour change (Paul Schultz 2004; Fernald et al. 2009).
	A growing number of randomized trials have also examined the effects of very small incentives in promoting individual health behaviours such as HIV testing, medical male circumcision for HIV prevention, and vaccination uptake. In many of these cases, even though the health services were provided at no cost to individuals, utilization was well below desired levels and incentives succeeded in increasing utilization rates. One study conducted in rural India examined the effects of bringing reliable, monthly immunization services closer to communities and providing caregivers non-financial incentives worth approximately $1 per immunization administered (Banerjee et al. 2010). Rates of full immunization were significantly higher in the villages randomized to receive reliable services and incentives (39%) as compared to villages that only received reliable services (18%) and to control villages (6%). Another randomized trial conducted in rural Malawi showed that small financial incentives ranging from $0.20 to $3 led to significant increase in HIV testing uptake among adults (Thornton 2008). Individuals who received some incentive were more than twice as likely to obtain their HIV test results as those who did not. Finally, several studies have also tested whether the provision of relatively small non-financial incentives increases uptake of medical male circumcision in settings with a high prevalence of HIV. Even though medical male circumcision reduces men’s risk of HIV acquisition by 60%, uptake has been low in settings where free circumcision services have been made available. Present-biased decision-making is one of several reasons why uptake may be low, as several costs of getting circumcised are relatively immediate (taking time off from work, fear of pain, and sexual abstinence for up to 6 weeks) whereas the benefits are distributed over a future time horizon. Studies in Kenya and Zambia have shown that small incentives worth as little as $9 can significantly increase uptake among adult men. One randomized trial found that uptake in a 2-month period was below 2% among men offered no incentives but considerably higher among those offered incentives of $9 and $15 (6.6% and 9.0%) (Thirumurthy et al. 2014). The use of incentives to promote specific health behaviours is by no means widespread in LMICs, but there are high-profile examples of such incentive programmes being implemented at scale. In India, for example, the government has introduced several schemes that provide pregnant women cash transfers contingent on their use of prenatal health services and contingent on facility-based deliveries.
	Incentives to promote health behaviours have not always succeeded, however, and there are a number of lessons to be learned from these examples as well. Incentives have generally been less effective in promoting sustained behaviour change. For example, medication adherence, which often requires frequent, nearly daily pill-taking is more difficult to promote with incentives that less-frequent, one-time health behaviours. A recent study in Uganda, for example, found that financial incentives did not increase viral suppression rates among HIV-positive adults taking antiretroviral therapy (ART) (Thirumurthy et al. 2019) while some other studies have shown that incentives do have promise as an adherence intervention (Linnemayr et al. 2017; McCoy et al. 2017). In practice, for incentive interventions to succeed it is important that incentive payments be delivered as close in time to the behaviours that is of interest. For example, an incentive to promote daily pill-taking is less likely to be effective if payments are not made on a nearly daily basis and instead made at the end of the month. With rising ownership of mobile phones and new technologies that make it possible to monitor behaviours like medication adherence or daily exercise (such as physical activity monitors), the potential for devising more effective incentive-based interventions is likely to grow. Costs and feasibility of implementing these interventions at scale in low-income settings remain a limitation, however. Further below, we draw attention to interventions that rely on social incentives to promote behaviour change rather than financial incentives.





Loss aversion and the endowment effect


	Another finding in the behavioural economics literature that goes against traditional economic theory is the endowment effect, which predicts that we value something we own (or have been ‘endowed’ with) more than we value the same item if we are asked to pay for it. The general principle underlying the endowment effect is loss aversion, or our tendency to weight losses more heavily than a comparable gain (Kahneman et al. 1991). We are made more unhappy by the loss of $20 than we are made happy by the gain of $20. This asymmetry also stands in stark contrast to traditional economic theory, which predicts that we should value that $20 equivalently whether it’s headed into our wallet or out of it.
	Loss aversion can be leveraged in the design of financial incentives to promote behaviour change. Instead of earning incentives prospectively (for example, receiving a weekly payment for a negative cotinine test as evidence of smoking cessation, or for meeting physical activity targets), participants can receive incentives up front (an endowment of sorts) but lose some of the incentive if they fail to meet targets. To leverage loss aversion even further, deposit contract or commitment contract schemes ask participants to put up their own funds, which they risk losing if behaviour goals are not met. In high-income settings, these types of incentives that leverage loss aversion have been shown repeatedly to be more effective than standard, gain-framed (prospectively-earned) incentives (Halpern et al. 2015). In the Philippines, the CARES programme offered smokers the opportunity to deposit funds into a savings account. If a urine test at six months showed abstinence from smoking, the savings were returned; if not, the accumulated funds were donated to charity. Among smokers who took the offer and were followed up at 6 months, 35% were biochemically confirmed to have quit smoking. While only 11% of those offered the programme took it up, quit rates among those offered the programme were 3 percentage points higher than those not offered the programme (Giné et al. 2010). The selection into such commitment contracts is of course an important aspect of these programmes, and may reveal higher levels of readiness to quit, self-awareness, or optimism about having a successful quit attempt.
	Loss aversion can also inform the design of public health information campaigns and other information-provision interventions. People respond differently to the same information when framed as a loss compared to a gain frame. In general, people tend to exhibit more risk aversion in response to gain frames and are more risk-seeking or more tolerant of risk in response to loss frames (Kahneman and Tversky 1979; Rothman et al. 1999). In a multi-country test of household use of water treatment technologies, messages that included both loss and gain messages were more motivating than gain-framed only messages (Luoto et al. 2014). Loss aversion may also shape how consumers respond to prices. For example, discounts on health-promoting items may feel like a gain and may therefore be less persuasive than taxes on unhealthy items, which may feel like a loss (Cawley 2011). Similarly, choices about purchasing or joining health insurance schemes may be shaped by the relative cost burden of premiums (a price, which may not invoke loss aversion) vs. deductibles, which must be paid following care and may feel like a loss (Rice 2013).
	Just as loss aversion can be leveraged to strengthen the effectiveness of financial incentives, other insights from behavioural economics are also relevant when designing incentive interventions. The tendency for individuals to overestimate the likelihood of low-probability events (known as base rate neglect) has been used to motivate lottery-based rewards for engaging in healthy behaviours. Several studies have tested whether lottery-based incentives are effective. One randomized trial in Lesotho found that providing lottery-based rewards to individuals if they did not obtain sexually transmitted infections (STIs) led to a large and significant reduction in HIV incidence (Björkman Nyqvist et al. 2018). Another study conducted in rural Uganda found that lottery-based incentives worth about $1 per person were more effective in increasing HIV testing uptake than standard, gain-framed incentives worth the same amount (Chamie et al. 2018). The implication therefore is that incentives may be more effective if they are offered in the form of lotteries—with some individuals receiving a large reward and others receiving a small reward or no reward. That said, the context in which incentives are provided and the specific behaviours being targeted are also relevant, as several studies have shown that lottery-based rewards are not more effective than no incentives or standard incentives (Thirumurthy et al. 2016; Buttenheim et al. 2018).





Status quo bias and defaults


	Humans have a strong tendency to stick with the status quo. We prefer the option placed in front of us—the default—over having to invest cognitive and decision-making effort to choose a different option. This so-called status quo bias explains many behaviours, from continuing magazine subscriptions that automatically renew each year to accepting the side dishes that automatically come with a fast-food meal. Status quo bias is another adaptive heuristic that can lead to suboptimal health behaviours and decisions. Status quo bias is adaptive in that it conserves limited attention span and bandwidth: if we had to thoroughly evaluate all available options for every choice we are presented with in the course of decision-rich day, we would quickly fatigue. Status quo bias can be maladaptive, however, when it causes us to remain with a preselected option purely because it is the default.
	The pervasiveness of status quo bias makes the design of default options very important in health interventions of all kinds. Of all the popular nudge approaches, defaults have consistently been shown to be the most effective and powerful. While status quo bias is likely the most powerful engine of defaults (it is simply easier to stay with the default option, and inertia will likely keep us from investing time and effort to switch), defaults are powerful nudges for other reasons as well: default options may also carry some implicit level of endorsement from the choice architect—if this is default option, someone must have thought it was a good idea. Two other behavioural economic concepts may also contribute to the power of defaults: because switching to another option from the one you already have may be perceived as a potential original option, loss aversion may come into play. Additionally, omission bias predicts that we prefer doing nothing to doing something, particularly when there may be negative consequences to our (in)action. Omission bias will make the default option seem even more attractive compared to taking action to switch to a different choice (Johnson and Goldstein 2003).
	There are many compelling empirical examples of successful defaults to change health behaviour in both high-income and LMIC settings. All opt-out screening or testing programmes employ defaults, as the patient will be automatically screened or tested unless they proactively decline. Opt-out testing for HIV has been widely scaledup across several countries in sub-Saharan Africa in diverse care settings and for different populations. In general, opt-out testing is highly effective in boosting testing rates (Steen et al. 2007) and is also feasible and acceptable (April et al. 2009). Some studies suggest that opt-out HIV testing can reduce HIV-related stigma or may be most effective in increasing testing among those with higher perceived stigma (Kaufman et al. 2017). Test-and-treat policies, in which those diagnosed with HIV immediately begin treatment with ART regardless of viral load, CD4 count, or length of time living with infection, also harness the power of defaults. When immediate initiation of treatment is framed as the default, newly diagnosed individuals do not have to make complex decisions about returning for follow-up care, repeated viral load testing, or the optimal time to begin treatment (Linnemayr and Stecher 2015).





Limited attention: availability heuristic and salience bias


	Traditional economic theories of decision-making described earlier assume that individuals have complete information about choices and can attend to and process information without constraint. In reality we live in a very information-rich environment, with many demands on our attentional and cognitive resources. To deal with this information overload, we have adaptive strategies to filter out much of the information directed at us and selectively pay attention to signals. These strategies produce predictable biases and heuristic thinking that may lead to less healthy decisions, but that can also be leveraged in health-promoting interventions.
	The availability heuristic prompts us to estimate the likelihood of an event based on how easily we can think of a recent example of that event (Tversky and Kahneman 1973). Immediately following an infectious disease outbreak, for example, people may overestimate the likelihood of future outbreak or of their own susceptibility to the disease. On the flip side, a community may underestimate the prevalence of a common but ‘silent’ or stigmatized condition such as mental illness or HIV if individuals cannot easily recall a specific instance of the illness in their network. These biased estimates of risk can then affect decisions about prevention behaviours, including screening or vaccination. A related phenomenon is salience bias, which predicts that we will focus our attention on information that is most unusual, striking, or vivid—that is, more salient. Information (visual or otherwise) that stands in contrast to the surrounding environment is particularly salient—think, for example, of a single red word on a page or a cell phone ringing in a quiet library.
	Public health interventions that rely on the provision of information to change behaviour will be most effective if they take the availability heuristic and salience bias into account. This has been shown in particularly compelling way in multiple water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions (Cole 2008; Kremer et al. 2009; Luoto et al. 2014). A study in rural India made the safety of household drinking water more salient for households in rural India by conducting a visible chemical test of water contamination in the household’s water storage containers and showing households the results (Hamoudi et al. 2012). Dangerous levels of bacterial contamination cannot necessarily be detected by sight or smell, but a chemical test strip showing presence of faecal bacteria makes this information highly salient. Households receiving this intervention were more likely to spend additional financial resources on clean water than controls, although, importantly, they did not invest more time in home-based water handling or treatment measures.
	Salience bias can also inform the design and delivery of interventions that use SMS reminders to promote attendance at appointments or adherence to medications. Messages that grab attention with relevant, personalized information that are delivered at the optimal time to promote action have been shown to be highly effective. One study conducted in Kenya, for example, examined the effects of daily and weekly text messages sent to HIV-positive adults taking ART (Pop-Eleches et al. 2011). Since adherence is important for realizing the health benefits of ART and achieving viral suppression, messages in the study were intended to remind patients to take their medications and also increase their motivation to stay adherent. Over a 12-month period, the study found that patients who received weekly text message reminders were significantly more likely to have medication adherence exceeding 90%. Another study, also conducted in Kenya, found that two-way text messages sent to ART patients on a weekly basis led to significantly higher self-reported adherence as well as higher viral suppression rates (Lester et al. 2010). These promising examples of mHealth interventions have given rise to many other interventions. While such interventions are not uniformly successful, they represent a low-cost, easily testable way to promote behaviour change.





Social norms and social influence


	We are very social creatures who look to the actions of others to guide our own decisions and behaviours. This is another adaptive heuristic mode of thinking that kicks in particularly when information is limited, choices are many, and cognitive bandwidth and attentional resources are constrained. This tendency means that social norms—standards for behaviour shared within a social group—can strongly influence behaviour, far beyond what standard economic theories of decision-making might predict. Social norms theory helpfully distinguishes between descriptive norms (what we see other people do), and injunctive norms (what others believe we ought to do) (Reid et al. 2010). For example, if you decide to take your child to be vaccinated because you observe everyone else in your community doing the same, you are acting on a descriptive norm. If you are told by others in your network that everybody ought to vaccinate their children, and you fear there will be social consequences if you don’t, you are acting on injunctive norms.
	The potential for social norms to influence behaviour is evident in an extensive literature describing correlations between descriptive norms and behaviour. An observational study of household participation in a Chagas disease vector control campaign in Peru found that participation decisions were associated with whether neighbours also participated, controlling for other predictors of participation that might also be correlated with neighbour participation (e.g. socioeconomic status, infestation status) (Buttenheim et al. 2014). Importantly, perceived norms (even if incorrect) can also predict behaviour. Men in a South African township overestimated the prevalence of risky sexual behaviour and underestimated prevalence of condom use among their peers. These behavioural norms correlated with the respondents’ own risky behaviours (Carey et al. 2011). Similarly, a study in Uganda found that village residents vastly underestimated the prevalence of HIV testing among other village members (HIV testing was actually a normative behaviour); underestimation was also associated with never having tested (Perkins et al. 2018). Multiple studies have also found a link between social norms (both descriptive and injunctive) and child marriage (Cislaghi et al. 2019).
	Of course, these relationships may reflect mere correlation or even reverse causation. Experimental trials of interventions that leverage social norms to change behaviour have had mixed results in LMICs. Two interventions informed by the descriptive work on ‘contagious’ participation in the vector control campaign in Peru that leveraged social norms in multiple ways were not able to boost household participation beyond the existing campaign (Buttenheim et al. 2018). In a randomized trial of promotion of water treatment products in Bangladesh, willingness to pay for products was not increased by observing neighbour purchases of similar products (Luoto et al. 2012). It should be noted that many of the same successful interventions mentioned earlier to improve hygiene and sanitation behaviours and reduce child marriage have also incorporated social norms as part of complex, multicomponent interventions, making the direct of effect of changing perceived norms or making norms more salient difficult to disentangle.
	Generally, there are three opportunities to deploy social norms in an intervention design to effect behaviour change. First, the intervention can make others’ behaviour more visible or salient, hopefully correcting misperceptions that shape individuals’ evaluations of the risks and benefits of the behaviour. Second, an intervention can make one’s own behaviour more observable by others, such that individuals are more likely to comply with descriptive and injunctive norms for fear of sanction. Third, respected peers or opinion leaders can promote, endorse, or request the behaviour, providing a strong signal that the behaviour is normative and will garner social approval. Recognizing the substantial variation in the effects of social norms-based interventions, Theory of Normative Spectrum posits that norms vary in their influence on behaviour along a spectrum, with the strongest norms making a behaviour obligatory and the weakest norms making a behaviour merely possible (Cislaghi and Heise 2018).





Scarcity theory and the psychology of decision-making


	This chapter has presented two overarching perspectives on human behaviour that are both useful in the real world: the rational decision-making perspective and the behavioural economics perspective. Several studies conducted in recent years provide a more nuanced view on decision-making and provide additional insight on the two perspectives we have summarized so far. By studying how being in poverty affects individuals’ decision-making, this work represents a bridge between the perspective that poverty affects behaviour because of pure constraints (not having sufficient income to access healthcare, for example) and the perspective that heuristics and biases in decision-making explain behaviour (people are present-biased in their decision-making, for example). Lab and field experiments have shown that in fact, the very condition of being poor–facing scarcity–gives rise to various features of decision-making central to behavioural economic theory such as present bias and limited attention.
	One study has shown that poverty leads to increased temporal discounting—the degree to which future costs and benefits are devalued—and also to greater present-biased decision-making (Haushofer and Fehr 2014). Using data from a randomized trial in Kenya in which some households received large cash transfers, this study was able to examine differences in time discounting and risk-taking behaviour among individuals who did and did not face extreme poverty. This study and others have also shown that poverty increases stress (Haushofer and Fehr 2014) and impedes cognitive function (Mani et al. 2013). By reducing mental bandwidth (Mani et al. 2013), poverty makes it more difficult for individuals to undertake actions that are beneficial in the long-term but lack clear short-term benefit. These and other studies revealing the psychological consequences of poverty have important implications for many domains of health in LMICs and for antipoverty programmes more generally. If poverty contributes to limited attention, cognitive capacity, and worse decision-making regarding health and other future-oriented behaviours, then programmes and policies should at the very least reduce the cognitive burdens associated with processing health information or consider using interventions such as incentives that address present-biased decision-making. Interventions such as reminders to counter the effects of limited attention also become more necessary for some behaviours such as medication adherence.
	An even stronger implication of research on the psychology of poverty is that interventions such as unconditional cash transfers may have a broad array of favourable consequences for decision-making and for health outcomes. Rather than merely bringing households out of poverty and eliminating resource constraints that limit consumption expenditures, cash transfer programme can also promote forward-looking decision-making. Recent years have seen growing consideration as well as implementation of unconditional cash transfer interventions in LMICs, sometimes under the rubric of universal basic income policies. Several evaluations of unconditional cash transfer programmes have shown largely positive effects on a broad array of health and economic outcomes. One randomized trial examined the effects of unconditional cash transfers of $400-$1,500 provided by a non-governmental organization, GiveDirectly, to rural Kenyan households and found large increases in consumption, psychological well-being, and asset holdings (Haushofer and Shapiro 2016). Several other studies have examined the effects of unconditional cash transfers provided by governments to low-income households. These studies have documented improvements in sexual and reproductive health outcomes in addition to changes in other forms of decision-making.





Moving the field forward


	Applying behavioural economics insights to global health programmes offers great potential to address the ‘last mile’ behavioural challenges to achieving better health outcomes. Researchers and practitioners from several disciplines have generated promising results in diverse settings through focused laboratory or basic science studies and through field experiments. Two important questions have been answered in the strong affirmative: first, can behavioural economics and behavioural science more broadly move the needle on behaviour change that is relevant for global health? Yes—we hope this chapter is persuasive in identifying successful interventions that leverage behavioural science to boost or supercharge existing health interventions. Second, is there continuing demand among health ministries, funders, and bilateral and multilateral development agencies for bringing a behavioural economics lens to intervention and programme development? We say ‘yes’ to this as well: a quick search of ‘behavioural insights’ and ‘health behaviour change’ will yield a rich array of initiatives in many countries, at all levels and at diverse scales, that are focused on tackling persistent global health challenges with the behavioural economics toolkit.
	That said, practitioners and researchers alike have many outstanding questions about how to incorporate behavioural economics into their global health work. Similarly, funders and government units must set strategic priorities and allocate budgets. We argue that the field is poised at a unique moment to take stock of progress and chart a path for the coming decade that will enhance and amplify this work further. As a starting point, we propose this focused list of recommendations for opportunities to move this exciting work forward:
	 	1. Continue to support and conduct rigorous field trials of promising interventions. As we write this chapter, a team of economists has just won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Economics for their efforts to use randomized controlled trials to test policies and interventions to alleviate global poverty and improve well-being. We will always need efficacy and effectiveness trials to answer the crucial ‘Did it work?’ question for interventions informed by behavioural insights. While health ministries and communities are understandably skeptical and sometimes reluctant to randomize interventions to participants and may not view evaluation investments as their highest priority, we need to ensure that we scale the interventions that work and abandon or revise those that don’t. While it’s important of course to learn about average treatment effects, heterogeneous treatment effects are also vital to answer crucial secondary questions: ‘for which subgroups, settings, and behaviours did this intervention work best?’ It is harder to power, fund, and carry out studies that pre-specify subgroup analyses, but we will learn faster how to target and tailor our behaviourally informed interventions if we do.
	2. Build capacity in behavioural science across sectors and disciplines. In our experience, frontline health programme managers and government ministry staff are eager to learn and apply behavioural science. Few will receive formal training in the theory or practice of behavioural economics, but focused capacity-building and ‘on the job’ training can infuse a behavioural science perspective vertically and horizontally across work units responsible for health programmes and outcomes. This capacity-building can be layered on to existing topical conferences, funder convenings, and other high-profile efforts for maximum leverage. While degree programmes in applied behavioural science are proliferating globally, there is also enormous scope for certifications, short courses, institutes, and initiatives that allow frontline staff and managers to get up to speed rapidly.
	3. Invite implementation science perspectives to the table. There is an extensive literature documenting the behavioural science evidence from focused efficacy and effectiveness trials. Less studied (and less resourced) are efforts to systematically study the implementation and scaling of the evidence-based interventions that emerge from those trials. Implementation science encourages us to investigate the strategies that enable behavioural economics interventions to successfully and sustainably scale. More work is needed on how to bake this perspective into existing approaches and initiatives. For example, a key strategy to implement a behaviourally informed intervention may be to build stakeholder demand and increase stakeholders’ positive appraisal of behavioural economic or nudge approaches. Empirical work that formulates and tests implementation strategies of this type is sorely needed (Trujillo et al. 2014).
	4. Consider a Nudge Unit or Behavioural Insights Team approach. The formation of units embedded within government agencies or consulted by government agencies and other health sector practitioners can foster real-world application of behavioural economics. These units, sometimes referred to as Behavioural Insights Teams or Nudge Units, typically comprise behavioural science experts who are tasked with actively engaging practitioners and jointly developing and testing low-cost interventions to improve outcomes. Governments in the United Kingdom and United States have formed behavioural insights teams to improve the performance of government agencies (Halpern and Sanders 2016). Several health systems have also established such teams to improve healthcare delivery (Patel et al. 2018). These units work best when members of the health system—from leaders to frontline healthcare workers—have opportunities to obtain basic training in behavioural insights and intervention design and can propose and prototype nudges and other interventions. Members of the nudge units themselves can further guide intervention development.
	5. Bring behavioural insights to additional health domains in LMICs. Many of the most pressing challenges in global health remain understudied from a behavioural economics perspective. A glaring case of this is the growing burden of NCDs is in LMICs. Relatively few studies or programmes have applied behavioural insights to promote the behaviour change that is needed to curb the rise of NCDs. In contrast, behavioural economics applications to health in the United States and other high-income countries have long focused on behaviours such as smoking cessation and physical activity. Just as behavioural economics research and practice has furthered our understanding of how to control HIV/AIDS and other infectious diseases in low-income settings, we see considerable potential for similar approaches in the NCD space. Another important contributor to global health outcomes that has been relatively neglected by behavioural economics researchers is the supply side of healthcare. The vast majority of nudge studies conducted and nudge interventions that have been scaledup have addressed the demand side of health, which is to say they have focused on modifying health behaviours of patients or individuals in the general population. Provider behaviour can and should equally be a target of interventions that use behavioural economics insights.
	Applying behavioural economics in isolation will not magically solve the persistent global health challenges faced by LMICs. Rather than a panacea, it is instead a promising approach that warrants further consideration and testing. No simple nudge will remove structural barriers to health behaviour change, such as limited access to healthcare or lack of affordability. While many successful behavioural interventions have been targeted at health providers, behavioural insights are not an obvious or easy path to fixing supply-side issues as well. In its most successful application, behavioural economics offers straightforward ways to boost or supercharge existing systems or interventions to promote better take up, improve engagement, reduce procrastination, or eliminate hassle factors. In the compelling example given of offering lentils and a metal plate set to parents who vaccinated their children in India, note that the other key intervention in that study was guaranteeing that vaccination camps would be functional and reliable. It is unlikely (though not tested in that study) that the incentives alone in the absence of guaranteed vaccination camps could have boosted coverage rates as much as they did.
	While this same study had a substantial effect on vaccination, many behavioural interventions will move the needle by a fairly small amount. This increases the urgency to design low-cost, light-touch interventions, and to deploy them in settings where a small effect size is still clinically or programmatically relevant if sustained. The ‘behavioural revolution’ asks us to bring a simple but powerful perspective to existing health behaviour change programmes and initiatives. If we can pay careful attention to how people actually think and behave (vs. how we hope they might optimally behave), and recognize the constraints on cognitive resources, attention span, self-control, and future orientation that poverty imposes, we can design, test, and scale interventions that will help individuals meet their health goals, and generate sustained improvements in population health and lifespan.

6.8


Governance and management of public health programmes


	Zhiyuan Hou and Na He





Introduction


	Public health programmes are diverse in scale, coverage, and complexity. They may be organized by local organizations, non-government organizations (NGOs), regional or national governments, and even involve globally (Yeoh 2015). Due to their diversity and complexity, governance and management of public health programmes become very important, and are essential to the health system performance and health outcomes (Lauer 2001; WHO 2002a, 2007; Mills et al. 2006; Institute on Governance 2011). The literature has increasingly showed the strong association between governance and health system performance (Olafsdottir 2012), and effective governance can achieve the goals of public health organizations or programmes (Institute on Governance 2011). The cross-country studies by both the World Bank and World Health Organization (WHO) found strong causal relationships between better governance and health outcomes (Kaufmann et al. 1999; Lauer 2001; Mills et al. 2006). In contrast, Gupta et al. (2000) found that corruption indicators were negatively associated with child and infant mortality, immunization coverage, and low-birthweight. Furthermore, Wagstaff and Claeson (2004) showed that health spending reduced child mortalities only in countries with high governance measures, and more spending in countries with medium and low governance measures would not reduce child mortality. The association between governance and health can operate at multiple domains, including the broader governance environment, health and general public policies, and the effectiveness of organizations within the health system (Savedoff 2011).
	Worldwide, health systems work well in some countries but not well in others. To answer the question for health system performance, the WHO builds a framework of strengthening health systems to improve health outcomes, which includes six function components: governance and leadership, healthcare financing, health workforce, medicines and technologies, information and research, and service delivery (WHO 2007). In the WHO health systems framework, governance and leadership is the central component to make the other function components effectively work together. Governance in the health system refers to ‘a wide range of steering and rule-making related functions carried out by governments/decisions makers as they seek to achieve national health policy objectives that are conducive to Universal Health Coverage (UHC)’ (WHO 2007). Good governance can enable the effective use of healthcare finances, health workforce, medicines and technologies, information, and research to deliver better health services and outcomes (WHO 2016). Overall, effective governance is central to improve the health systems performance and achieve UHC (WHO 2016).
	As the world become increasingly globalized, public health programmes are sometimes cross-border, and their governance also need to be considered at the global level. Development assistance for health has globally increased from US$7.2 billion in 1990 to US$36.4 billion in 2015 (Dieleman et al. 2016). Funds for these development assistance programmes are increasingly distributed through NGOs and bilateral assistance to governments instead of the traditional United Nations (UN) agencies. Although development assistance for health increased quickly, their effects depend on the quality of local governance and policies, especially in the resource constrained settings (Fryatt et al. 2017). On one side, many international donors question whether these development assistance programmes can reap benefits of improved health services and outcomes. On the other side, these global programmes may attract health workforce to leave local health systems, conflict with the goals of local health systems, and distort the local health priorities (Yeoh 2015). These may lead to negative effects on local health systems. Therefore, global health governance is necessary to address these problems at the global level. Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) spread across the world in 2020, which emphasis on the emergence of strengthening health governance in the global context (Phelan et al. 2020).
	In this chapter, we will discuss the following sections. First, we introduce the concepts of governance, health governance, and global health governance. Second, we introduce governance theories and a framework of health governance system, covering the actors, tools, and levels of health governance. Third, we describe in detail three governing actors—government, civil society, and private sector—and their roles in health governance. Fourth, tools of health governance are introduced to carry out the health governance functions and enable relationships among actors. Fifth, we discuss four levels of health governance: supranational, national, organization, and programme. Sixth, we summarize the assessment frameworks of health governance. Finally, we take cases for better understanding health governance.





Concepts of governance, health governance, and global health governance


	The concept of governance has evolved in the changing context of government and society. Originally, governance is described as ‘the act or manner of governing, of extending control or authority over the actions of subjects; a system of regulations’ in the Oxford English Dictionary.
	In the domain of health, WHO first defined governance as ‘stewardship’ which refers to ‘the careful and responsible management of the well-being of the population’ (WHO 2000). This definition clarifies the importance of health governance and its role in health system and population health (Mikkelsen-Lopez et al. 2011). However, because of incoherent nomenclature and the changing context, no conceptual agreement on health governance has been reached (Kickbusch and Gleicher 2012).
	The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), defines governance as ‘the exercise of political, economic administrative authority of a country’s affairs at all levels’ (UNDP 1997). This definition reveals that governance consists of the complex mechanisms, processes, and institutions through which citizens and organizations articulate their interests and rights. And it identifies the political and economic nature of social life, and the roles and interdependencies of the society, such as the government, private sector, and civil society. Dodgson and his colleagues consider health governance as ‘’the actions and means adopted by a society to organize itself in the promotion and protection of the health of its population’ (Dodgson et al. 2002). WHO refines health governance as ‘involves ensuring that strategic policy frameworks exist and are combined with effective oversight, coalition building, regulation, attention to system-design and accountability’ (WHO 2007). It characterizes the health governance as a set of processes formally or informally applied to distribute accountability among actors of a health system (Brinkerhoff and Bossert 2008). These definitions adapt a system perspective to understand the mechanisms in government, the private sector, and civil society, their complex nature and relationships, and how they influence health outcomes (Yeoh 2015).
	More recently, the necessity of strengthening health governance at the global level has been increasingly discussed due to a series of globalizing challenges. The response to global health challenges has become fragmented and ineffective without global leadership. Global health governance is then defined as ‘the action and means adopted by a society to promote collective action and deliver collective solutions in the pursuit of common goals’ (Dodgson et al. 2002). This definition admits the whole range of cooperation in global society, from informal arrangements and agreements by communities to the formalized rules and procedures institutionalized in governments. This definition also pays attention to the equal roles of the governments, private sectors, and civil society in global health governance, because health governance has become beyond the scopes of governments (Yeoh 2015). A single emphasis on the government role in health governance, neglecting the important roles of civil society and the private sector in health system, will undermine the governance capacity (Ollila 2005; Renukumar n.d.). Contributions from all governing actors for the collective actions in the pursuit of common goals are critically necessary in health governance.





Theory and framework of health governance system


Theory of governance


	There are two main theories to approach systems-level governance: principal-agent theory from the economics discipline, and theory of network governance from the public administration discipline (Greer et al. 2016). Principal-agent theory focuses on market competition, contracting, outsourcing, and incentives; and the theory of network governance emphasizes the power and effectiveness of networks, cooperation, and partnership. Both theories aim to address the interactions between organizations in governance system, including the shifting boundaries, unclear authority, and complexity of coordination, and have been widely used in health system governance.
	Principal-agent theory. Principal-agent theory illustrates the contract relationship between principals and agents. The principle hires the agent to undertake an action and pays in some certain forms such as incentives. Agents usually have more relevant information on the service than principals, thus enables them with an advantage of ‘information asymmetry’ to favour their own interests at the cost of the principal. Another feature of the principal-agent theory is that the principal does not have full control over the agent and possess only partial information about the service behaviour of the agent (Stoker 1998). Because of the distinctive features, moral hazard, and adverse selection problems may appear. The agent tends to take its own preferred actions and hide some information the principal needs to make decisions for the agent’s interest (Gailmard 2012). Taking account of the uncertainty and complexity of behavioural outcomes of the agent, principal-agent theory is used as an approach to analyse different actors in governance systems.
	Health systems are featured as purchaser–provider splits, more use of markets and contracts to encourage private sector participation, greater management autonomy for providers, emphasis on procedure control and regulation, and outsourcing ancillary functions. In health system, there are various actors—policymakers, healthcare providers and citizens, and these actors and relationships constitute the health governance system. Principal-agent theory can be used to understand these actors and relationships, and various governance frameworks for health systems are intensively developed based on principal-agent theory (Brinkerhoff and Bossert 2014). However, the relationships are mostly more about fiduciary than agency, especially for government and policymakers, and government accountability has long been questioned. Therefore, the approach to analyse the relationships among organizations should be to in the roundin their interconnections, dependencies, and accountabilities. Despite widely used in health governance, the problem with principal-agent theory is that the complex web of relationships is oversimplified to principal-agent relationship.
	Theory of network governance. Theory of network governance aims to address the complexity that principal-agent theory neglects and provide a solution to coordination dilemmas among multisector actors, in which clients, providers, and producers are linked together as co-producers. Network governance focuses on interdependence among organizations, interactions among network members, and management joint responsibilities (Rhodes 1996). Fixed organizational boundaries and roles are replaced by a new rationality of the shared aims and culture (Considine and Lewis 2003). Sørensen and Torfing (2007) defined ‘governance network’ as a number of interdependent and autonomous actors who interact through negotiations under a relatively self-regulating institutionalized framework and contribute to the production of public purpose.
	Network governance is promoted for the potential contribution to efficient governance because of its following distinctive features. First, network governance comes with a potential for identifying early stage problems and making proactive adjustment. Besides, aggregation of information, knowledge, or opinions help qualify decisions or consensus building. Finally, networks of organizations greatly reduce the risk of implementation resistance (Sørensen and Torfing 2007). While network governance is advocated to promote cooperation among multi-actor systems, there are two empirical problems with regarding governance solely as partnerships and networks. On one hand, networks and partnerships can be everywhere and nowhere, and so finding networks that actually govern and align organizations and forces can be hard. On the other hand, network governance does not simply displace hierarchy and law. In some situations, it seems that networks function best under the shadow of hierarchy to oblige them with legal force. Cross-sectional legislation could offer a general guidance for network governance in activation. However, legislation and hierarchy pose a risk to the autonomy and flexibility of the network. Still, the questions regarding decision-making and accountability can hardly be addressed by legislation (Saikku and Karjalainen 2012). The merits and problems of network governance mean that they are unlikely to be the sole basis for health system governance.





Framework of a health governance system


	A population’s health is determined together by individual factors, social and community networks, and social, economic, cultural, and environmental conditions (Commission on Social Determinants of Health 2008). The most important determinants of health are from other sectors, rather than the health sector itself. Most health challenges originate beyond healthcare, but they also depend on the global processes that drive disease outbreaks, food insecurity, climate change, urbanization, and economic inequity. This calls for a whole-of-society governance approach for health. The governments, the private sectors, communities, and citizens are required to increasingly engage in governance for health. Thus, health governance involves a wide range of actors at the level of the governments, civil society, and private sectors.
	In health governance system, the government, private sector, and civil society are the governing triangle (actors), and they are seeking public health collectively (Abimbola 2020). Each governing actor has its structures, roles in governance, governing tools, and mechanisms for interactions within and between the actors. They play health governance functions at four levels to pursue health goals: the supranational or national or organizational or programme levels. Overall, the three governing actors (triangle), their governance functions and mechanisms, and governance relationship, form a health governance system and a whole-of-society governance approach for health. A framework for health governance system can help to understand the whole-of-society governance approach for health, covering the governing actors, governance mechanisms and tools, their governance relationship, and governance at different levels (Yeoh 2015). Figure 6.8.1 summarized this framework for health governance system.
	Fig. 6.8.1 Framework for a health governance system.
	WHO proposed effective health system governance to achieve UHC, and the governing triangle can be the government, health service providers, and the citizen or civil society. The governing triangle is linked through the governance relationships, mainly principal-agent relationships (Brinkerhoff and Bossert 2014). They make or change governance rules, and these governance rules in turn influence each other’s actions and relations (Abimbola 2020). In the relationship between civil society and the government, civil society acts as the principal to express health needs and preferences to the government, and the government works as the agent to respond to these needs and preferences. In the governance relationships between the government and providers, health policymakers are principals setting up objectives and standards, providing resources, and conducting overseeing providers as their agents. In exchange for the resources, providers take health service delivery activities to meet the requirement of policymakers. In the governance relationships between the civil society and providers, civil society expresses health services needs to providers, who provide health services in turn. But this relationship is challenged by information asymmetries, capacity gaps, and moral hazard between the civil society and providers. Theories of principal-agent and network governance can help to address these challenges and complexity of networks, and better understand health governance at system level (Greer et al. 2016).
	According to the health governance system framework, the following sections will introduce each governing actor and its role in governance, the governance tools available, and the levels of governance.
