6.9


Implementation science and translational public health


	Wafaa M. El-Sadr, Judith Wasserheit, Bryan Wiener, Andrea Howard, Catherine Hankins, Patricia J. Culligan, and Katherine Harripersaud





Introduction


	The pace and scope of innovation to improve health and the potential to increase health equity have never been greater. Yet translation, implementation, and scale-up of efficacious biomedical, behavioural, and socio-structural interventions into policies and their adoption into standards of care, or large-scale programmes has remained slow and uneven. In the United States, on average, it takes almost a generation—17 years—to transform less than 15% of original research into practices, programmes, or policies that improve patient care and population health (Balas and Boren 2000). In many low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), closing this ‘know-do gap’ or the ‘knowledge to action gap’ may take far longer, although in exceptional cases ‘leapfrogging’ has been noted with rapid adoption of innovation. Furthermore, interventions that prove efficacious in randomized trials may not be effective when introduced at large scale under ‘real world’ conditions without appropriate adaptation, or stakeholder and government buy-in, particularly in fragile, overburdened health systems or new social, political, or demographic contexts (Chen et al. 2004).
	Implementation science health-related research is a rapidly emerging paradigm that addresses the urgent need to close the ‘know-do gap’ by providing new conceptual frameworks and tools to evaluate the factors that could influence the successful closure of this gap. Implementation Science uses rigorous methods from multiple disciplines and sectors to inform how best to implement and scale up evidence-based interventions, or intervention packages, in order to improve population health. Implementation science expands the opportunities and responsibilities of health researchers beyond the laboratory, bench, clinic, and bedside, by asking them to also focus on how health system, health facility, community, national, and transnational contexts impact on closing this gap (Elzarrad et al. 2013). The primary focus of implementation science has evolved differently in the United States (US) in contrast to the global health context. With growing support from the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) during the past 15 years, implementation science in the health sciences blossomed with a central focus on the translation of biomedical advances into widespread clinical practice, often working with providers and patients at health facility level (Zerhouni 2003; Glasgow et al. 2012; Neta et al. 2015). Over the same period, the primary implementation science focus globally was on translating a broad array of biomedical, behavioural, information technology and policy interventions into large-scale programmes in resource-limited settings, frequently working with policymakers and programme managers at the national or transnational level. This approach to implementation science was shaped by support from multilateral and bilateral organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the Joint United Nations Program on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the World Bank, The Global Fund for AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (GFATM), and the US NIH Fogarty International Center among other NIH institutes (Madon et al. 2007; The Global Fund to Fight AIDS Tuberculosis and Malaria USAID World Health Organization 2008; Padian et al. 2011).
	At the same time, implementation science, as a science, continues to evolve, so much so that even its boundaries are continually being demarcated. The following sections describe current thinking around defining implementation science, its governing frameworks and research designs, and the critical role of stakeholder engagement in applying implementation science.





Definitions of implementation science


	In new, rapidly evolving fields, consensus on their primary focus, core methods, boundaries, and terminology often emerge over time, as a critical mass of thought leaders are galvanized, engaged, and confronted with new challenges. This is the case for implementation science (Odeny et al. 2015). This is manifested in the diversity of definitions for implementation science which reflects both the relative youth of this field and the different factors that influence implementation of this emerging field in high-income countries and in LMICs. One early and widely cited definition from researchers based in the United Kingdom and the US frames implementation science as ‘the scientific study of methods to promote the systematic uptake of clinical research findings and other evidence-based practices into routine practice, and hence to improve the quality and effectiveness of health services’ (Eccles 2006; Eccles et al. 2009). Others have offered broader definitions that go beyond a clinical, facility-based focus on quality improvement to call for ‘applied research that aims to develop the critical evidence base that informs the effective, sustained and embedded adoption of interventions by health systems and communities’ (Allotey et al. 2008) Some characterize implementation science even more broadly as the study of the determinants and processes that influence successful integration of evidence-based innovations in specific settings, and the results of implementation and scale-up, as well as related issues such as the degree of fidelity with which core components are translated and other components are adapted as these innovations are introduced and taken to large scale (Hirschhorn et al. 2007; Rabin et al. 2008; Peters et al. 2013; Peters and Adam 2013; National Implementation Research Network 2015). Common features of all of these definitions include the following: (1) applying rigorous, systematic research methods to guide the introduction, improvement or expanded use of interventions for which there is strong evidence of efficacy from earlier phase research; (2) a multidisciplinary or transdisciplinary approach; and 3) collaboration between researchers and relevant stakeholders, prominently including programme implementers and policymakers throughout the process (Sanders and Haines 2006; Bhattacharyya et al. 2009; Knapp and Anaya 2013; Bauer et al. 2015).
	To accelerate improvements in global health and progress towards national or transnational goals such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the authors of this chapter support the following broad definition, i.e. that Implementation science is a systematic, scientific approach to ask and answer questions about how we get ‘what works’ to people who need it with greater speed, fidelity, efficiency, quality, sustainability and coverage. This definition promotes the application of at least 10 research approaches utilized by different disciplines as essential for understanding and improving the determinants, processes, and outcomes of implementation and, ultimately, scale-up and sustainability to achieve population-level health benefits (Kemp et al. 2018). These research approaches include impact evaluation, economic evaluation, qualitative health systems research, operations research, systems analysis and improvement, organizational assessment, stakeholder and policy analysis, dissemination research, social marketing, and surveillance and data systems. Although these 10 research methods are not exhaustive, together they provide a core set of tools to assess and iteratively improve implementation and scale-up of health interventions. These methods enable exploration of a synergistic continuum of three categories of outcomes for implementation science from most proximal such as acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, cost, adoption, fidelity, penetration, scale-up, and sustainability; through intermediate service delivery outcomes such as efficiency, equity, timeliness, and patient-centredness; to distal health outcomes. While improvements in service delivery and health outcomes are the ultimate criteria for evaluating the effectiveness of implementation strategies, implementation outcomes may be early signals of successful implementation, and preconditions for achieving service delivery and health objectives.
	The boundaries of the terminology of implementation science also remain to be defined, as are the boundaries of other closely related, emerging fields, such as improvement science, programme science, and delivery science, potentially creating confusion in terminology—with each aiming to improve health despite having slightly varying primary foci and approaches. For example, improvement science is primarily concerned with quality improvement, one of the 10 core implementation science methods (Foundation 2011). Programme science flips the standard paradigm of ‘getting research into practice’ and focuses on ‘getting research out of practice’ by working with programme staff to develop research questions and conduct research (Blanchard and Aral 2011). Delivery science prioritizes strengthening the capacity of health systems using intersectoral public policy and financing approaches to improve health and development outcomes (Kim 2018). Finally, the science of scale-up prioritizes policy and implementation research that focuses on the scaling of existing health tools and delivery services (Kruk et al. 2016). As these fields mature, realignments or mergers may occur, leveraging the complementary strengths and learnings.





Implementation science frameworks


	Implementation science offers several frameworks for guiding research and practice. In a 2012 review, Tabak et al identified 61 frameworks for supporting the implementation of evidence-based interventions (Tabak et al. 2012). Additional frameworks have been proposed since then. Selecting a framework can be challenging given the number of options available (Birken et al. 2017). Nilsen categorized implementation science frameworks into three types based on three common objectives for implementation science: (1) process models for describing or guiding the process of implementation; (2) determinants frameworks for identifying the factors that influence implementation; and (3) evaluation frameworks for assessing the degree of implementation success. Although specific frameworks can address more than one of these objectives, these general types of frameworks can help guide the selection of a framework for implementation research and practice (Nilsen 2015).
	The first type of frameworks, process frameworks, specify the steps, stages, or phases of implementing evidence-based interventions. Process frameworks such as the Knowledge to Action (K2A) Framework (Wilson et al. 2011) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) Model of Knowledge Translation (Canadian Institutes of Health Research) describe a sequence that begins with research on the effectiveness of interventions, then moves to the dissemination of those interventions to targeted audiences, and then moves to the implementation of those interventions in real-world settings. Other process frameworks, such as the Quality Implementation Framework (QIF) (Meyers et al. 2012), the Stetler Model (Stetler 2010), and the Ottawa Model (Logan 2010) offer practical advice for planning and carrying out an implementation effort. These frameworks are useful for guiding implementation because they not only highlight the key tasks that should be performed, but also prescribe the order in which they should be performed. The QIF, for example, delineates four phases of implementation: initial considerations regarding the host setting (Phase One), creating a structure for implementation (Phase Two), ongoing structure once implementation begins (Phase Three), and improving future applications (Phase Four). The QIF further identifies 14 critical steps across these four phases that are believed to result in high-quality implementation. Although process models describe, or in some cases prescribe, a logical sequence of steps and depict an idealized view of the implementation process, actual implementation is often nonlinear and disordered.
	Unlike process frameworks, which describe steps or stages of implementation, the second type of frameworks, determinants frameworks, identify factors that influence implementation, either positively in the case of facilitators or negatively in the case of barriers. Such frameworks are useful for assessing the context in which implementation occurs and, consequently, identifying strategies to overcome barriers or harness facilitators. They are also useful for explaining why implementation was successful or not in specific settings or why implementation success varied across multiple settings. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) is a commonly used determinants framework in implementation science, with growing use in global health (Damschroder et al. 2009). The CFIR synthesizes 19 implementation science frameworks by organizing 37 factors into five domains: intervention characteristics, outer setting, inner setting, individuals involved, and implementation processes. The attractiveness of the CFIR derives from its comprehensiveness, applicability, and flexibility; the CFIR’s developers encourage users to ‘select constructs from the CFIR that are most relevant for their particular study setting and use these constructs to guide diagnostic assessments of implementation context, evaluate implementation progress, and help explain findings in research studies or quality improvement initiatives’ (Damschroder et al. 2009). The Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) is another widely used determinants framework that, like the CFIR, synthesizes 33 psychological and behaviour change theories by organizing more than 100 constructs into 14 theoretical domains, such as knowledge, skills, intentions, goals, and social influences(Cane et al. 2012). While neither the CFIR nor the TDF hypothesizes causal relationships among determinants, both frameworks acknowledge that such relationships exist.
	Thirdly, evaluation frameworks offer a conceptual structure and a set of metrics for gauging implementation success. The two best known evaluation frameworks in implementation science are the Implementation Outcomes Framework (IOF) (Proctor et al. 2011) and Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance (RE-AIM) framework (Glasgow et al. 1999). The RE-AIM Framework is described here since the IOF was introduced earlier in this chapter. Developed for evaluating the public health impact of health promotion programmes, RE-AIM identifies five metrics that signal the applicability, scalability, potency, and sustainability of programmes or interventions in ‘real world’ settings (Glasgow et al. 1999). These metrics are as follows: the reach of the programme within the intended target population, the effectiveness of the programme, the adoption of the programme by target settings or staff, the implementation of the programme in terms of the consistency and quality of programme delivery, and the maintenance of programme delivery and programme effects. The RE-AIM Framework is particularly useful in global health because it balances classic concerns about programme effectiveness with considerations relevant to implementation and scale up, such as adoption among targeted staff, settings, or institutions and coverage (reach) within targeted populations.
	Table 6.9.1 highlights the relative strengths and limitations of the three main types of implementation frameworks described by Nilsen. Two broad observations are noteworthy. First, the different types of frameworks have complementary strengths and limitations and, thus, work well together in implementation research or practice. For example, determinants frameworks such as the CFIR or the TDF can be employed in the pre-implementation stages of process models such as the QIF to assess needs and resources, fit of the evidence-based intervention and the setting, and capacity or readiness for implementation. Likewise, determinants frameworks and evaluation frameworks can supply the independent and dependent variables in research investigating the effects of context on implementation success or failure. Second, many, if not most, implementation science frameworks have been developed in high-income countries with Western cultures. Although frameworks like the CFIR have been used in implementation science in global health, adaptation is likely needed to improve their fit with and utility for studying implementation in LMICs and countries with non-Western cultures.
	 	Table 6.9.1 Strengths and limitations of implementation science frameworks
	 			Framework type
	Strengths
	Limitations
			Process models (e.g. QIF, Ottawa model)
	 	 	• Include actionable steps, useful outside research context
	• Prescribe a sequence for performing implementation tasks
	 	 	• Describe a rational, ideal sequence rarely observed or practicable in implementation
	• Focus neither on determinants, nor outcomes
		Determinants frameworks (e.g. CFIR, TDF)
	 	 	• Include large number of potential determinants at multiple levels
	• Synthesize and harmonize prior frameworks, theories, and models
	• Include data collection and analysis tools
	• Useful for formative, concurrent, or summative evaluation
	 	 	• Provide no guidance for implementation
	• Focus on determinants, not outcomes
	• Need adaptation for use in LMIC contexts and non-Western cultural contexts
	• Include fewer determinants at higher levels (e.g. community, policy)
	• Reliable, valid measures of many constructs lacking
		Evaluation framework (e.g. IOF, RE-AIM)
	 	 	• Include multiple outcomes for evaluating public health impact
	• Differentiate implementation outcomes from effectiveness
	• Specify how outcomes can be quantitatively assessed
	• Outcomes can be measured at multiple levels
	 	 	• Provide no guidance for implementation
	• Focus on outcomes, not determinants
	• Reliable, valid measures for some outcomes lacking
	• Relations among some outcomes need clarification





Scale-up frameworks


	Although implementation science frameworks could be used to design, guide, and evaluate scale-up efforts, Barker et al. identified 45 theories, frameworks, and models that have been developed specifically for scaling up evidence-based health interventions (Barker et al. 2016). Two well-known process frameworks for scale-up are the Management Systems International (MSI) Scaling Up Management Framework for Practitioners and the ExpandNet/WHO Framework. The MSI Framework describes three main steps: developing a scale-up plan, establishing the preconditions for scaling up, and implementing the scale-up process. Within these steps, the framework offers guidance for performing 10 tasks: creating a vision, assessing scalability, filling information gaps, preparing a scaling-up plan, legitimizing change, building a constituency, realigning, and mobilizing resources, modifying and strengthening organizations, and coordinating action.
	The ExpandNet/WHO Framework outlines a nine-step process for developing a scale-up strategy and offers practical advice for conducting each step. The ExpandNet/WHO Framework also could serve, as a determinants framework. It conceptualizes scale-up as a system of five inter-related elements: (1) the innovation that is being scaled up; (2) the resource team, or the individuals and institutions that seek to facilitate the innovation’s wider use; (3) the user organization, meaning the institutions or organizations within which the innovations are expected to be widely adopted and implemented; (4) the scaling-up strategy, which designates the means by which the innovation is communicated, transferred, or otherwise promoted; and (5) the environment in which scaling up takes place. For each element, the Framework describes attributes of success, many of which correspond to the constructs found in the CFIR. For example, the attributes of success for the innovation include evidence strength and credibility, observability, relative advantage, compatibility, trialability, and complexity. The Framework’s attributes of success can be viewed as determinants that hinder or facilitate scale-up. A distinctive feature of the Framework is its delineation of strategic choices regarding the type of scaling up used; the process of communicating the innovation and preparing users in its application; the organizational options selected in implementing the process; assessing costs and resource mobilization; and monitoring and researching the process and outcomes of scaling up. Like the ExpandNet/WHO Framework, Yamey’s conceptual framework also identifies success factors (i.e. determinants) that fall into six categories representing different components of the scaling up process: attributes of the specific tool or service being scaled up, attributes of the implementers, the chosen delivery strategy, attributes of the ‘adopting’ community, the socio-political context, and the research context (Yamey 2011).
	Although there are many approaches and methods for monitoring and evaluating scale-up, including impact evaluation, no evaluation framework has emerged in global health that offers a conceptual structure and general set of metrics for evaluating scale-up efforts. While the RE-AIM Framework was developed to evaluate the public health impact of health promotion programmes in the US context, it is suitable for use as an evaluation framework beyond the US because it balances traditional concerns about programme effectiveness with considerations relevant to scale up, such as programme coverage (reach) in a targeted population, programme spread (adoption) among settings and people expected to deliver the programme, consistency and quality of programme delivery (implementation), and programme integration (maintenance) into government policies and organizational practices.





Research designs


	A wide variety of research designs have been employed in implementation science. In 2017, Brown et al. identified three broad categories of designs used in implementation science within the traditional translational research pipeline, including those that provide (1) within-site; (2) between-site; or (3) within-and between-site comparisons of implementation strategies, to determine how to make an effective clinical or preventive intervention work within community and/or service settings (Brown et al. 2017). As these designs focus on interventions that have already demonstrated effectiveness, the emphasis of such designs is on measuring (1) healthcare process, or activities undertaken by the health system, and (2) healthcare output, or observable measures of service delivery provided to the target population, as opposed to health outcomes or health-related behaviours of individuals who are the ultimate target of the intervention. Although many of these designs employ random assignment, and thus have high internal validity, some are observational or quasi-experimental, and are preferable in instances when randomization is not feasible or warranted, such as when policies are disseminated or implemented by law.
	Within-site designs evaluate implementation successes or failures by studying changes that occur inside an organization, community, or system. The simplest design is a post design, which examines healthcare process and/or utilization after introduction of an implementation strategy aimed at delivery of an evidence-based intervention in a novel health setting. On the other hand, in a pre-post design, the impact of a new implementation strategy for an existing intervention is inferred by comparing process and/or output measures prior to and following adoption of the strategy. A multiple-baseline times-series design is a variant of the pre-post design in which data are collected at multiple time points to examine whether the effects of the implementation strategy are sustained.
	Between-site designs compare healthcare process and outputs among sites that have different exposures. In a new versus implementation-as-usual design, some sites are assigned to an innovative implementation strategy while others maintain the usual condition. Process and output measures for the two strategies are then compared over the same time period. When evaluating complex, multilevel implementation strategies, a cluster-randomized design is often employed, in which sites (health facilities, communities, or organizations) are randomly assigned to either the new implementation or usual-practice condition, and endpoints are assessed for all eligible individuals in both conditions. If the implementation strategy is designed to achieve impact at a smaller unit of the organization, then randomization can occur at the level of the ward, team, or provider within each site. Individual-level randomization can also be utilized, if the intervention is delivered at the patient or individual level.
	A head-to-head randomized implementation trial design, also known as a comparative effectiveness implementation trial, tests which of two active implementation strategies is more successful in implementing an intervention, in terms of quality, quantity, or speed of intervention implementation. The same intervention is used for both study arms, and sites are randomly assigned to one of the implementation strategies. In a variant of this design, sites are randomized to one of two implementation strategies that focus on different patient populations of individuals or patients and target different outcomes. With this design, each site serves as both an active intervention and a control.
	Factorial designs evaluate a combination of two or more implementation strategies simultaneously. Each experimental factor has two or more levels (e.g. presence or absence, or low, medium, or high intensity of implementation). With a 2 × 2 factorial design, units are randomly assigned to one of four conditions (i.e. strategy 1, strategy 2, strategy 1 and 2 combined, or neither strategy), and estimates of the effect of each factor by itself and their interaction are derived. In an incomplete, or fractional, factorial design, one or more arms of a complete factorial are excluded. This design may be chosen if it is deemed unethical to withhold both implementation strategies from participating sites, or alternatively if it would be too difficult to implement both strategies at the same site.
	A multiphase optimization strategy implementation trial (MOST) design enables consideration of a large number of components that comprise an implementation strategy, including those involving leadership, the clinic level, the provider level, and key processes such as planning, training, financing, restructuring, and quality management. Testing each combination of these components is often not feasible, the MOST design can be used to identify and test an optimal intervention. This design consists of three phases: preparation, optimization, and evaluation. In the preparation phase, components are selected and pilot tested using an explicit optimization criterion. In the optimization phase, a randomized trial is conducted to assess the effectiveness of these components, using a fractional factorial design. Based on the trial’s results, the group of components that best meets the optimization criterion is identified. In the evaluation phase, a standard randomized implementation trial is conducted that compares the optimized implementation strategy with an appropriate comparison condition.
	A sequential multiple assignment randomized implementation trial (SMART) design is an adaptive approach that involves multistage randomizations such that the site-level implementation process can be modified if unsuccessful. In the latter design, the adaptation probability within each site is constant. A variant of this design is the SMART design with adaptive randomization (SMART-AR), in which the randomization probability of each strategy is updated based on the outcomes in the other sites, so that the expected outcome is optimized.
	A doubly randomized, two-level nested, or split-plot implementation design is used to assess whether experimental implementation factors directed towards two different hierarchical levels (e.g. provider and patient) have additive or synergistic effects.
	Within-and between-site comparison designs are also known as rollout randomized implementation trial designs. In these designs, sites begin in one implementation condition and cross over to another, and the timing of the start of the new implementation strategy is randomly assigned. The simplest design is a stepped wedge, or dynamic wait-listed, design, in which all sites start in the implementation-as-usual setting, and then cross over at randomly determined time intervals, until all are receiving the new implementation strategy. At each time interval, a between-site comparison of those sites assigned to the new implementation strategy and those remaining in the control condition is made. Additionally, a within-site comparison can be conducted when sites cross over from the usual practice setting to the new implementation strategy. In a head-to-head rollout trial, all sites start in the implementation-as-usual setting and then at a predetermined time, are randomly allocated to one of two new implementation strategies, which they continue until the end of the study.
	Other research designs encompass elements beyond the traditional translational research pipeline, including hybrid designs, discrete choice experiments, and designs that involve simulation. Curran et al. described three effectiveness implementation hybrid design constructs, all of which focus a priori on assessing both implementation and clinical effectiveness (Curran et al. 2012). Type 1 hybrid designs primarily test the effects of a clinical intervention on health outcomes, while collecting information on its delivery and/or its potential for implementation in a real-world setting. The latter is usually achieved through a process evaluation that ascertains barriers and facilitators to delivering the intervention, as well as potential modifications to the intervention that could be made to maximize implementation. Type 2 hybrid designs simultaneously test a clinical intervention and an implementation strategy. Type 3 hybrid designs primarily test an implementation strategy, while observing or gathering information on the clinical intervention’s impact on health outcomes.
	Another research method is discrete choice experiment approach, a health economics tool that elicits preferences from decision makers over alternatives, with each alternative consisting of several attributes. It can be used pre-implementation to elicit information from a variety of stakeholder groups, including patients, caregivers, providers, and administrators, to assess the potential acceptability or appropriateness of health services, products, or implementation strategies, in order to improve implementation (Salloum et al. 2017).
	Lastly, mixed methods designs that collect, analyse, and merge both quantitative and qualitative data are often utilized in implementation science. Typically, qualitative methods are used to identify strategies for facilitating implementation of an evidence-based intervention, or to obtain an in-depth understanding of reasons for implementation success or failure, while quantitative measures are used to test a hypothesis and assess predictors of successful implementation (Palinkas et al. 2011).
	In summary, choosing a research design for a specific context is a complex process that requires consideration of the research questions, existing knowledge base, stakeholder values, and available resources. Table 6.9.2 shows the relative strengths and limitations of various research designs.
	 	Table 6.9.2 Strengths and limitations of research designs
	Strengths
	Limitations
			Within-site designs
		Post design of an implementation strategy to adopt an evidence-based intervention in a new setting
	 	 	• Useful for assessing factors that predict programme adoption
	• Useful when new health guidelines or changes in policy occur
	 	 	• Lack of comparison group limits internal validity
		Pre-post design of an implementation strategy of an intervention already in use
	 	 	• Can be used to assess adoption of a guideline or policy by a healthcare system
	• Can examine whether an implementation strategy has sustained effects by collecting data at multiple time points

Stakeholder and community engagement


	The seeds for effective implementation science, whether it takes the form of a phase four trial, a population-level study, or other design, are sown during the conduct of the research that strengthened the scientific evidence propelling forward a line of investigation. In particular, whether effective stakeholder engagement was accomplished in the preceding trials or other research which could have a direct effect on the feasibility of conducting follow-on studies at the end of a clinical trial or other such studies.
	Transparent, mutually beneficial, respectful, sustained relationships between research funders, sponsors, researchers, implementers, community members, and other stakeholders are critical to the success of any study. These relationships set the stage for effective collaboration and shared ownership of all aspects of the research process, starting at problem formulation and in the research design stage. In the context of implementation science research, they can directly influence the relevance of the research; the likelihood that interpretable, valid data and reliable results will be produced; and the eventual uptake of study outcomes.
	The foundational principles underpinning effective stakeholder involvement, as now defined in Good Participatory Practice (GPP) guidance in several research fields, drew inspiration from the controversies and debates that arose in 2004 regarding pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) trials for HIV prevention where national political leaders in Cambodia and Cameroon opposed these trials (Mills et al. 2005; Singh and Mills 2005; Global Campaign for Microbicides 2009a; Global Campaign for Microbicides 2009b). In response, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) convened the Creating Effective Partnerships in Research process in 2005 (UNAIDS 2006) that resulted in a strong recommendation for the development of research guidelines for community stakeholder engagement.
	Following a series of regional consultations that defined the key elements needed for creating effective partnerships for biomedical HIV prevention trials, these were published as the GPP-HIV guidelines in 2007 (UNAIDS and AVAC 2007). GPP was first cited in the methodology of a scientific publication of trial results in 2010 (Grant et al. 2010). A revised edition of the GPP-HIV guidelines (UNAIDS and AVAC 2011) followed GPP application in different settings and formal consultations with stakeholder groups in Africa, the Americas, Asia, and Europe. Subsequently, the GPP guidelines were adapted for tuberculosis drug trials in 2012 (Critical Path to TB Drug Regimens 2012) and the WHO published GPP guidelines in 2016 for trials of emerging (and re-emerging) pathogens that are likely to cause major outbreaks in the future and for which few or no interventions exist (WHO 2016). Web-based training curricula, tools, application examples, and other materials are currently available to assist stakeholders to understand, implement, and monitor GPP (AVAC 2018). Further, a Centre of Excellence is under development (Coalition to Accelerate and Support Prevention Research 2017) with an implementation framework that further advances GPP practitioners’ understanding, ability, and technical skills to carry out GPP effectively.
	Determining who the relevant stakeholders are for specific implementation research study is an essential step. Broadly, stakeholders are all individuals or groups of individuals who can influence or are affected by the conduct or outcome of the research, i.e. all those who have a stake. They include national research organizations and scientific councils, Schools of Medicine and Nursing, and ministries of Health, Education, Science, and Justice as well as others that may be involved in the eventual implementation of the interventions. Importantly, an important stakeholder group is the population to be recruited, study participants, families of study participants, people resident in the area where the research is to be conducted, local support groups or networks, religious leaders, opinion leaders, media, local healthcare authorities, healthcare providers, traditional healers, private sector partners, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and community-based organizations (CBOs) including women and youth groups.
	Local contextual analysis may be needed to define such stakeholders, the optimal level of engagement needed, and the types of structures to be created to facilitate stakeholder engagement. Funding for such contextual analyses should be anticipated, with time frames determined in part by the urgency of the issue to be evaluated. Formative research, qualitative studies, geospatial mapping, key informant interviews, and other methodologies assist in defining relevant stakeholders, including community, for implementation research. In a health emergency, the formative research phase should be nimble and rapid, aiming at stakeholder engagement to identify key voices to participate from the outset in discussions of trial design (Holzer et al. 2014). In less urgent situations, communities can be engaged, for example, in the randomization process itself, as was done in the HPTN071 (PopART) Study, a cluster-randomized trial conducted in South Africa and Zambia (Bond et al. 2016).
	It should be noted that stakeholders may have competing interests and perspectives. Disagreements during implementation research may arise from power imbalances, differences in social organization, hierarchies, gender issues, relative socioeconomic disparities, and other factors. A stakeholder engagement plan, developed together by research teams and relevant stakeholders, can define the range of stakeholders to be engaged; detail the frequency and types of engagement methods to be used, such as public meetings, workshops, joint decision-making models, or delegated decision-making; and clarify the type of engagement appropriate for each stakeholder, such as being informed, consulted, collaborated with, or emancipated to make decisions (Ray and Miller 2017). Such a plan can also delineate the nature of support for initial and ongoing activities aimed at building stakeholder capacity to understand concepts, purposes, practices, and limitations of implementation research so that the ability of stakeholders to provide meaningful input to the research process will be enhanced. Importantly, it clearly describes the methods to be used for resolution of differences and lays out key principles that underpin partnerships among stakeholders, including respect, fairness, integrity, transparency, accountability, and autonomy (UNAIDS and AVAC 2011).
	Effective stakeholder and community engagement in implementation research is not only an ethical imperative, it enhances the conduct of research, contributes to robust research outcomes, and creates both impetus and support for scale-up following proven results.





Future directions


	Implementation science is an important research approach that offers the potential to bring to practice many of the discoveries that exist in scientific journals. Its focus on advancing the learning of implementation and of scale-up is directly linked to the collective ability to advance the health and well-being of populations around the world. Yet, much remains to be done to achieve broad knowledge of this approach among researchers, funders, and policymakers. The diversity of frameworks and methods put forth for implementation science also highlights the need for a maturation of the field and for consensus building among experts in implementation science. Additionally, efforts are needed to overcome some of the myths that relate to this research approach including highlighting its importance and the rigorous manner in which implementation research can be designed and conducted.
	Creating a new generation of researchers who are knowledgeable of implementation science requires an investment in specific education and training opportunities for young scholars, as well as investigators at various career stages. These training programmes should emphasize a multidisciplinary approach including how to synthesize information across disciplines, test and adjust approaches in collaboration with stakeholders, use data to inform policies, and ways to formulate scalable interventions (Means et al. 2016). Such training would allow for broad health systems perspective and understanding of multisectoral ancillary effects of health interventions and policies. Core competencies for these programmes continue to be refined and need to be foundational and responsive to advances in the field (Gonzales et al. 2012; Chambers et al. 2017). Mentorship is also a critical component of advancing this science and should accompany and supplement any formal training programmes. An evaluation of a 2-year mentorship programme focused on dissemination and implementation research for cancer prevention and control resulted in improved dissemination and implementation research competency, high satisfaction for emotional support, career planning, and sharing resources (Padek et al. 2018).
	With the adoption of implementation science as a means to help translate evidence-based-interventions related to health into positive outcomes for patients and communities, other fields have also turned to this approach as relevant for closing the know-do gap. Examples include initiatives related to special education (Cook and Odom 2013), conservation biology (Toomey et al. 2017) and environmental sustainability (Hering 2016). Thus, it is important that rather than each field developing separate frameworks and methodologies for guiding research and practice, efforts should be focused on aligning approaches and learnings across disparate fields and settings, with the ultimate goal of identifying a uniform scientific approach to close the know-do gap that is independent of setting and application.
	It is also important for global health researchers to learn from programmes focused on the translation of innovations into commercial successes. In the US, the National Science Foundation’s Innovations Corps (I-Corps) initiative is a public-private partnership aimed at equipping researchers in science and engineering with the skills and tools needed to translate their work from the laboratory to the marketplace (Robinson 2012). Akin to Innovation Science, the goal of this programme is to create an effective infrastructure for moving from basic discovery to a successful product.
	Finally, an important goal of fostering research in implementation science and translational public health, is the full engagement of the academic enterprise in solving the pressing, practical issues of the world (El-Sadr et al. 2014). By actively seeking out collaborations with other fields within and beyond academia, implementation science can inspire an expansion of the core mission of academic institutions to include in addition to the generation of new knowledge, an emphasis on the need for engagement in taking knowledge to practice.

7.1


Environmental health methods


	Chien-Jen Chen and San-Lin You





Environment and health: historical perspective


	Human beings live in a complex environment. The importance of environmental factors in human health has been recognized since antiquity (Chen 2015). Hippocrates, in his classical writing On Airs, Waters and Places, emphasized the relevance of the environment to human health. He pointed out the influence of seasons and weather, location of residence, and nature of water on human health, and the occurrence of epidemics. Since ancient times, the seasonality of infectious diseases and the geographical clustering of endemic diseases have been documented worldwide. Several hypotheses had been advanced to explain the unique distribution of various diseases in time and place. The contagion theory proposed that both direct and indirect contact with sick people or animals might transmit diseases and hence both isolation and quarantine had been suggested to prevent the spread of diseases. Although they might have reduced the risk of spread of infectious diseases by ships, the strategies evolved from the contagion theory had not stopped the outbreak of many infectious diseases.
	The miasma theory proposed that dirty living environments, unclean drinking water, and poor ventilation due to overcrowding might cause various diseases. This led to environmental sanitary reforms aimed at removing miasma by contributing to a cleaner environment in Europe. The hygienic movement emphasized the importance of implementing a safe drinking water supply and sewage disposal system. The Public Health Act enacted in Britain in 1848 was considered the first example of governmental involvement in public health affairs. However, a large outbreak of cholera still occurred in London despite its well-constructed sewage disposal system and much improved environmental sanitation in the 1850s. Through a carefully designed survey, John Snow published his famous epidemiological study on cholera in 1855 while the germ theory was still in its infancy. He identified the consumption of contaminated drinking water as the cause of the cholera outbreak. The removal of the handle which pumped contaminated water ‘magically’ prevented the spread of the disease. The relocation of sources of drinking water successfully controlled the cholera outbreak. This was a pioneering epidemiological study in the identification of environmental factors in a disease outbreak.
	In late nineteenth century, the development of germ theory led to the discovery of many specific infectious agents for human diseases. It also led to the development of several drugs for treatment of diseases, and improvements in sanitation and disinfection to control outbreaks of diseases. Robert Koch’s postulates, which emphasized a one-to-one relationship between cause and disease, were well accepted as criteria for the identification of causal agents of infectious diseases. Effective control of several infectious diseases through identification of specific agents, discovery of chemical and biological drugs, and invention of preventive and therapeutic vaccines had improved life quality and longevity of human beings. The discovery of animal reservoirs and vectors of infectious agents led to the control of vectors through environmental sanitation and disinfection. More and more biological and mechanical vectors have been identified for various viral, bacterial, and parasitic diseases since then. Control of vectors in the environment using pesticides became an important task for the prevention of infectious diseases. For example, malaria was eradicated in Taiwan through the detection and treatment of infected cases and use of the insecticide DDT. However, the widely used pesticides polluted the environment and became hazardous to wild animals and humans.
	Life expectancy in most countries increased significantly after the 1950s, when conventional infectious diseases had been controlled through the widespread use of various vaccines and antibiotics. The major diseases that threaten human life have since gradually shifted from infectious to chronic non-communicable diseases. Environmental factors exposed through lifestyle habits, dietary intakes, and environmental pollution play important roles in the development of chronic diseases such as cancers, cardiovascular diseases, and neurological disorders. There are multiple risk factors in the complex multistage pathogenesis of chronic diseases. For examples, environmental risk factors for liver cancer included hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, aflatoxins, alcohol, vinyl chloride, thorium dioxide, anabolic steroids, and fine particle pollutants (Chen et al. 1997; Chen and Chen 2002; Pan et al. 2016). Some environmental pollutants may cause several chronic diseases in multiple organ systems. For example, arsenic in drinking water has been documented to induce cancers of the skin, bladder, kidney, and lung, as well as Blackfoot disease, ischaemic heart disease, stroke, hypertension, diabetes, erectile dysfunction, mental retardation, neurological disorder, cataract, pterygium, fungal infection, chronic kidney disease, and hepatitis and cirrhosis (Chen 2014; Hsu et al. 2016a, 2016b, 2017). As most chronic diseases have a multistage pathogenesis with a multifactorial aetiology without a unique one-to-one with a specific agent, the classical Robert Koch’s postulates for judging the cause of disease are less applicable to chronic diseases. Bradford Hill’s causation criteria including the strength, dose–response relation, temporality, specificity, and biological plausibility of the association between cause and disease have been widely adopted for the identification of causal agents for various diseases.
	Endemic diseases are often characterized by their unique geographical clustering. This clustering may be associated with biological or chemical agents prevailing in local environments. Some parasitic diseases such as schistosomiasis remain endemic in areas where the ecological system maintains the life cycle of the parasites. The interruption of the life cycle through the identification and treatment of affected patients, eradication of vectors, and improvement of environmental sanitation may decrease the prevalence of these endemic parasitic diseases. Some endemic diseases such as goitre and Blackfoot disease are caused by the deficient or excessive intake of certain chemicals in the environment. The replacement of high-arsenic well water with low-arsenic surface water had decreased the occurrence of Blackfoot diseases in southwestern Taiwan. The endemic goitre caused by low dietary intake of iodine was effectively prevented by the national salt iodization programme in Taiwan.
	There has been a long-standing recognition that the workplace environment can induce occupational diseases. Bernardino Ramazzini published his seminal treatise on diseases of workers. Scrotum cancer had long been considered a disease of chimney sweeps. The poor working environment in the nineteenth century sparked reform attempts in Europe, but specific regulations to protect workers against occupational diseases were mostly implemented in the twentieth century.
	Occupational hazards may spread from the workplace to its adjacent environments. For example, a major gas and chemical leak incident in a pesticide plant in Bhopal, India in 1984, and the 1986 accident at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Ukraine resulted in environmental disasters. In addition to the immediate casualties, both events also increased the risk of a number of chronic diseases in residents living in the vicinity. The health hazards induced by long-term exposure to industrial wastes are usually more insidious than those resulting from acute environmental disasters. Environmental pollution by industrial waste has been well documented to cause Itai-itai disease and Minamata disease in Japan. Chronic poisoning by heavy metals in industrial waste has become an important issue in environmental health. Soil and water contamination by widely used agricultural chemicals have brought significant threats to human health, wild animal life, and ecological sustainability. Air pollution has increased the risk of pulmonary diseases including asthma, chronic bronchitis, ischaemic heart disease, lung cancer, and liver cancer (Pan et al. 2016).
	Natural disasters including snow-storms, hurricanes, floods, sand-storms, volcano eruptions, and forest fires have had serious consequences for public health. Other environmental disasters including earthquakes, tsunamis, and landslides are also detrimental to human health. The explosions that occurred at the Fukushima nuclear power plants in the aftermath of the major earthquake and tsunami in Fukuoka, Japan in 2011, resulted in a multiple environmental disaster. In addition to the heavy immediate casualties, natural environmental disasters threaten the function and efficiency of food, water, and electricity supply systems, ambulance and healthcare systems, sewage and waste disposal, and the control of infectious diseases. Protecting public health through proper environmental management is becoming a lasting challenge.





Causes of human diseases: host–agent interaction in the environment


	Both host and environmental factors are involved in the development of human diseases, and the relative importance of environmental to host factors varies as a continuous spectrum for different diseases. Environmental factors seem to play a small role in the development of genetic diseases compared with infectious diseases or accidents. However, exposure to environmental factors may trigger the clinical manifestation of genetic diseases such as phenylketonuria and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Environmental influences on human health are exerted through exposures to physical, chemical, and biological risk factors, and through related changes in human behavioural responses to those factors. The World Health Organization has released a country-by-country analysis of the impact of environmental factors on health (Pruss-Ustun et al. 2016). These data show that environmental risks accounted for a large fraction (23%) of the global burden of deaths and diseases. Environmental impacts on health were uneven across life course and gender. Low-and middle-income countries had the greatest share of environmental disease burden. Total environmental deaths remained unchanged from 2002 to 2012 with a strong sift to non-communicable diseases, and the evidence on quantitative links between health and environment has increased. Global health could be improved by reducing environmental risks including pollution, hazards in the work environment, ultraviolet radiation, noise, agricultural risks, climate, and ecosystem change. Proper environmental management is the key to prevent the proportion of all illnesses which are directly caused by environmental factors.
	Human beings live in environments with many causes of diseases as shown in Table 7.1.1. Environmental causes for human diseases include physical, chemical, and biological agents. The physical component includes non-ionizing and ionizing radiation, noise, vibration, pressure, humidity, temperature, earthquakes, landslides, typhoons and hurricanes, and snow-storms and sand-storms. Ionizing radiation includes alpha and beta particles, gamma rays, and X-rays. Ionizing radiation may induce spontaneous abortion, congenital malformation, cancers, and haematopoietic disorders through its effects causing DNA damage and chromosomal aberrations. Non-ionizing radiation includes ultraviolet rays, visible light, infrared rays, microwaves, and electromagnetic fields. Ultraviolet rays may induce skin cancer and cataract; while electromagnetic fields may induce some cancers. The chemical component includes heavy metals, organic solvents, agricultural chemicals, polycyclic hydrocarbons, and chlorinated organic compounds. Their health effects may be classified as acute, subacute, and chronic toxicity, carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, and teratogenicity. Some chemicals may persist in the environment and result in bioaccumulation. The biological component includes viruses, bacteria, fungi, parasites, allergens, arthropods, as well as plant and animal toxins. A number of infectious diseases of various organ systems are caused by biological agents. In addition to the acute and subacute symptoms and signs, these infectious agents may also induce chronic diseases such as cancers of the nasopharynx, stomach, liver, bladder, cervix, uteri, and lymphoid and soft tissue (Chen et al. 2014), pulmonary diseases, cardiovascular diseases, as well as neurological disorders.

	Host components in response to environmental components are also important in the determination of a number of human diseases as shown in Table 7.1.2. The genetic component includes a single gene for autosomal, X-linked, Y-linked, and mitochondrial diseases, multiple genes for common diseases such as cancers and cardiovascular diseases which run in the family, and chromosomal aberrations. There also exist gene–gene interaction and gene–environment interaction in the development of human diseases. Genetic effects may be modified by environmental factors, and environmental factors may cause genetic damages and mutations. The behavioural component includes substance use, dietary intake, personal hygiene including hand-washing and safe sex, health promotion and disease prevention practice, transportation safety practice, occupational protection practice, sports and exercise, personal communication and networking, and response to stressful life events. All these behavioural components play very important roles in the prevention of environmental health hazards. For example, using cleaner fuel such as gas or electricity, using better cooking devices, improving ventilation, or keeping children away from smoke could reduce environmental risk of respiratory infections and diseases among women and children. Enforcement of helmet and seat belt laws may significantly decrease the mortality from motor vehicle accidents. The social component of human diseases includes built environments, occupational settings, agricultural methods and irrigation schemes, transportation systems, water supply systems, sewage and waste disposal, schooling systems, healthcare systems, social welfare and criminal prevention systems, anthropogenic climate changes, and ecosystem degradation. The improvement in environmental hygiene and public health systems has increased the global health status and life expectancy significantly in the last decades.

		Anthropogenic pollution and climate changes
		Ecosystem degradation
	Several causal models have been proposed to describe the interaction between host and environment components in human health (Chen 2015). The traditional epidemiological triangle model emphasizes the equal importance of host, agent, and environment, which are located in three angles of the epidemiological triangle. This causal model emphasizes the health effects of a specific agent, especially infectious agents, may be modified by both host and environment factors. Host factors may include the biological, sociodemographic, and behavioural characteristics including individual susceptibility and immunity, age, gender, race, socioeconomic status, occupation, genetic composition, body mass index, dietary intake, lifestyle habits, personal hygiene, and social activities. Environmental factors include living and working environments such as family, school, workplace, recreation, and healthcare place, where both agent and host interact. The disease agent may spread and transmit in the environment and affect susceptible individuals. Various strategies to prevent the occurrence of the disease caused by the agent may be developed through the understanding of the epidemiological triangle model. The agent may be controlled through disinfection and sterilization, antibiotic or antiviral treatment, intervention of drug resistance, and environmental sanitation. Active and passive immunization, improvement in nutritional status, optimal rest and exercise, immunomodulation, chemoprevention, and other host factors may be strengthened to reduce the risk of disease occurrence. The environment condition may be improved to prevent the occurrence of diseases through clean housing and workplaces, safe water and food supply, hygienic sewage and waste disposal, and others.
	The epidemiological triangle model emphasizes the unique causal agent of a specific disease. This model is most appropriate for infectious diseases because the infectious agent is the necessary cause of a given infectious disease, even though the infectious agent may not be sufficient to cause the given disease. For many infectious agents, not all infected individuals will develop the disease. The one-to-one causal relation between agent and disease may not be observed under this circumstance. The triangle model is not appropriate for most chronic non-communicable diseases. Most chronic diseases have multiple causes. A single agent is neither necessary nor sufficient to cause the disease. The ecological wheel model was proposed to emphasize the host–environment interaction in the determination of human health. The ecological wheel model includes an axle (host component) surrounded by a tyre (environmental component). A disease may be caused by many environmental and host factors which are neither necessary nor sufficient causes. They are considered as contributory causes of the disease. No unique single agent is specified for a disease in this model. The environmental component included various physicochemical, biological, and social environments just described. The host component included the genetic composition located in the core surrounded with individual immunity, lifestyle, personality, dietary intake, and social networking. The ecological wheel model emphasizes the importance of ecological balance in the maintenance of the health status of a host. The relative importance of host and various environment factors varies by diseases. For example, genetic factors are most important for the highly inheritable diseases; the biological environment for various infectious diseases; and the social environment for accidents. This casual model also stresses the interactions among host and various environments.
	Neither the epidemiological triangle nor the ecological wheel takes the time dimension of disease development into consideration. The natural history of both acute and chronic diseases follows a specific temporal sequence. This usually starts from the contact of causal agent(s) with target cells, through the structural and functional changes in affected cells, the proliferation of causal agents or transformed cells, the development of lesions in target tissues or organs, the onset of clinical symptoms and signs, to the development of systemic illness. There are various agents and environment factors involved at different stages of the pathological progression. For example, the multistage process of carcinogenesis may be classified into initiation, promotion, progression, invasion, and metastasis. The development of atherosclerotic diseases includes stages of initial lesion, fatty streak, intermediate lesion, atheroma, fibroatheroma, complicated lesions, and clinical manifestation. An evolutional spiral model has been proposed to describe the disease causation through host–environment interactions over the entire natural history of the disease (Chen 1999). At the initial stage, both cause and molecular or cellular change are simple and microscopic, and the causal relationship tends to be one-to-one. With disease progression, however, the affected lesions keep expanding like a spiral with more and more complicated causal interactions between host and environment components at different stages.
	The evolutional spiral model is most appropriate for the description of multistage pathogenesis of a disease with a multifactorial aetiology. As shown in Figure 7.1.1, the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a multistage process with the involvement of multiple risk factors. There are many causes of HCC including hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), aflatoxins, alcohol, tobacco, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, diabetes mellitus, haemochromatosis, alpha 1-antitrypsin deficiency, and others. The exposure to causal agents may lead from mutations or epigenetic alterations of affected hepatocytes, through liver inflammation, chronic hepatitis, liver fibrosis, and cirrhosis, to HCC. During the hepatocarcinogenic process, the affected target starts from molecules and expands to cells, tissues, and organs like a spiral with more and more contributory causes involved to drive the progression of the disease. In addition to exposure to various chemical carcinogens, the inadequate intake of micronutrients including carotenoids and selenium is also associated with an increased risk of HCC. Host factors including humoral and cellular immunity, xenobiotic metabolism, hormones, and susceptibility genotypes can modify the risk of HCC development. Healthcare factors including immunization, antiviral therapy, liver disease screening, and other clinical interventions may be used to stop or slow the occurrence or recurrence of HCC.
	Fig. 7.1.1 Multistage hepatocarcinogenesis with a multifactorial aetiology.





Ecological studies: identification of environmental health hazards at aggregate level


	Geographical clustering of endemic diseases in a small area is the most important characteristic of environmental health hazards. An extremely high prevalence of an endemic disease in a confined area should always lead to a search for unique environmental risk factors. Ecological studies are often used to compare the morbidity or mortality of environmental disease between endemic and non-endemic areas. In ecological studies, aggregate attributes such as the morbidity of residents in exposed and unexposed areas, rather than individual attributes such as the health status of exposed and unexposed subjects, are analysed and compared. Ecological studies tend to compare health indices in areas with and without the environmental exposure, or to examine quantitatively the correlation between health indices and the magnitude of environmental exposure in many areas. Some environmental characteristics or comorbidity rates may be used as surrogate indicators of the causal agents to elucidate the relation between the disease risk and the causal agent. The interpretation of ecological studies may be limited by the potential existence of ecological fallacy, when the agent–disease correlation observed at the aggregate level may not consistently be found at the individual level. However, ecological studies are frequently used to explore the environmental component of causes for human diseases.
	As an illustrative example, Blackfoot disease is an endemic peripheral vascular disorder confined to a limited area on the southwest coast of Taiwan. Clinically the disease starts with numbness or coldness of one or more extremities and intermittent claudication, which progresses to black discoloration, ulcer, and gangrene. In end stages of the disease, spontaneous amputation of the distal parts of the affected extremities is common. The disease was hyperendemic in four neighbouring townships in southwestern Taiwan. As the water from shallow wells (6–8 metres in depth) in this area had high salinity, residents in some villages had started to use water from artesian wells (100–200 metres deep) since the 1920s. The use of artesian well water was found to be associated with the occurrence of the Blackfoot disease, and water samples from artesian wells of the endemic area were found to have high arsenic concentrations, which ranged from 0.35 to 1.14 mg/L.
	Based on the analysis of mortality data, residents in the endemic area of Blackfoot disease had significantly elevated mortality from cancers of the skin, bladder, kidney, lung, and liver as shown in Table 7.1.3. Compared with the general population in Taiwan, the age-standardized mortality ratios for cancer of the bladder, kidney, skin, and lung were threefold or greater among male and female residents in the endemic area (Chen et al. 1985), suggesting arsenic in artesian water may cause these cancers as well as Blackfoot disease. As the four townships in this endemic area had different prevalences of Blackfoot disease, cancer mortality was further compared among townships. There was a trend that the higher the Blackfoot disease prevalence of a township, the greater the age-standardized mortality ratios for cancers of the skin, bladder, kidney, and lung.

	As 84 villages in these four townships also had different prevalences of Blackfoot disease and used different types of well water, more refined analyses of cancer mortality at the village level were carried out. A significant dose–response relation between the prevalence of Blackfoot disease and the age–sex-standardized mortality ratios for cancers of the skin, bladder, kidney, lung, and liver was observed at the village level as shown in Table 7.1.4. Furthermore, biological gradients of cancer mortality were also found by the type of wells used as drinking water source with the highest cancer mortality in villages where only artesian wells were used and the lowest in villages which used only shallow wells. As both Blackfoot disease and artesian well use were significantly associated with the arsenic in drinking water, they were used as the surrogate environmental variable for arsenic exposure. It was thus implied that arsenic in drinking water might increase the risk of skin and internal cancers. However, the best way to assess the cancer risk associated with arsenic in drinking water is to obtain the arsenic levels in drinking water from wells.

	The arsenic levels in water of shallow and artesian wells in 42 villages of the Blackfoot disease endemic area were available for further analysis of the association between arsenic in drinking water and cancer mortality. The age-adjusted morality for various cancer sites and the average concentration of arsenic in water of wells in each village were derived. As shown in Table 7.1.5, there was a significant dose–response relation between arsenic level in well water and age-adjusted mortality for cancers of the bladder, kidney, lung, skin, and liver in both males and females, and prostate cancer in males at the village level (Chen et al. 1988a). In these 42 villages, a significant dose–response relation was also observed between level of arsenic in well water and age-adjusted mortality for cardiovascular diseases and peripheral vascular diseases at the village level for both males and females (Wu et al. 1989).

	In another large-scale ecological correlation study on age-adjusted cancer mortality of 314 precincts and townships in Taiwan (Chen and Wang 1990), the arsenic level in water of 83,656 wells was tested to derive the average arsenic level in well water in each precinct or township. Both cancer deaths and mid-year population in all study precincts and townships were obtained from the national death certification and household registration system. Based on the weighted multiple regression analysis, there were significant correlations between the average arsenic level in well water and the age-adjusted mortality rates of cancers of the liver, nasal cavity, lung, skin, bladder, kidney, and prostate at the precinct/township level. The increase in age-adjusted mortality per 100,000 person-years for every 0.1 ppm increase in arsenic level of well water for cancers of the liver, nasal cavity, lung, skin, bladder, and kidney, respectively, was 6.8, 0.7, 5.3, 0.9, 3.9, and 1.1 for males and 2.0, 0.4, 5.3, 1.0, 4.2, and 1.7 for females, after adjustment for indices of industrialization and urbanization. The increase in prostate cancer mortality for every 0.1 ppm increase in arsenic level in well water was 0.5 per 100,000 person-years. In these ecological correlation studies, both disease risk and environmental exposure were measured at a group (village or precinct/township) level. There exist potential ecological fallacies c and confounding effects of extraneous factors such as prevalence of cigarette smoking, alcohol drinking, environmental pollution, viral hepatitis, and others. The findings of ecological correlation studies have to be further validated by studies at the individual level.
	Ecological correlation studies have also been carried out to imply possible causal associations between infectious agents and cancer (Chen et al. 2014). The similarity in geographical variation in prevalence of oncogenic infectious agent and incidence of specific cancer was observed for HBV/HCV and HCC, herpesvirus and Kaposi’s sarcoma, human T-cell leukaemia virus and leukaemia, liver fluke and cholangiocarcinoma, as well as Helicobacter pylori and stomach cancer. For example, the incidence of liver cancer and the prevalence of HBV and HCV infection are extremely high in the East, Southeast and Central Asia, and the sub-Saharan Africa. But the etiological proportion of liver cancer attributable to HBV and HCV varies in different countries and regions. HCV is more prevalent in Japan and Central Asia, and HBV is more prevalent in Taiwan, Southeast Asia, and China. Among townships in Taiwan, a significant ecological correlation between the HCC mortality and the prevalence of chronic HBV infection was also observed. These ecological study findings suggest the importance of chronic HBV and HCV infection in the development of HCC. As around 75% of global liver cancer cases are caused by HBV and HCV. Thus, control of viral hepatitis may significantly reduce the burden of HCC globally (Chen 2018).





Cross-sectional surveys and longitudinal studies: assessment of environmental health hazards at the individual level


	Several different study designs have been applied to assess the environmental health hazards at the individual level as shown in Table 7.1.6. Based on the time of the collection of disease risk (outcome) and environmental exposure (cause) data, they may be classified into cross-sectional and longitudinal studies. Cross-sectional studies collect the data on disease and exposure at the same time. The most common type of cross-sectional studies is the environmental health survey, in which participants are enrolled from exposed and unexposed areas to collect the information on health status, exposure to environmental factors, and potential confounding factors. Morbidity estimates from cross-sectional surveys represent disease prevalence rather than incidence. As the disease and exposure data are collected simultaneously, the causal temporality of disease and exposure needs further validation. If the environmental exposure is quite consistent over a long period of time before the onset of the disease, the causal temporality may be considered correct. Longitudinal studies may be further classified into case–control and cohort studies according to the enrolment of study participants. Conventional case–control studies recruit incident cases and matched controls from healthcare institutions or community, and collect the history of exposure to environmental factors through questionnaire interviews or biomarker tests. While the causal temporality is accounted for, the information on environmental exposure history may be subject to recall loss or bias and biomarkers may not reflect a long-term exposure before the disease onset. If there were detailed records of exposure history or biomarkers of long-term exposure, the biases may be reduced significantly. Conventional cohort studies recruit exposed and unexposed healthy participants from community or workplace, and follow the cohort until an adequate proportion of participants develop the disease under study. While there is no bias of the exposure information, it may be limited by participants being lost to follow-up and resulting in the bias of disease ascertainment. If databases of disease registration, death certification, or health insurance were available, the loss to follow-up may be solved through computerized linkage with these databases.

	Returning to Blackfoot disease as an illustrative example, in a community-based cross-sectional survey of 40,421 residents in 37 villages in the endemic area in southwestern Taiwan, the relation between status of skin cancer and Blackfoot disease in participants, and arsenic in well water was examined (Tseng 1977). There was a significant dose–response relation between the arsenic concentration in the well water and the prevalence of skin cancer and Blackfoot disease for most age and sex groups. There was also a significant coexistence of both skin cancer and Blackfoot disease. In a community-based case–control study, a total of 353 pairs of Blackfoot disease cases and matched controls were interviewed (Chi and Blackwell 1968). The length of residing in the endemic villages was significantly associated with the risk of developing Blackfoot disease in a dose–response relation. While all 353 (100%) Blackfoot disease cases had ever used artesian well water as the principal source of drinking water during the 15 years before disease onset, only 233 (66%) matched controls had consumed artesian well water (p <0.001). Blackfoot disease cases had lower educational level and socioeconomic status than matched controls. In another case–control study on 241 Blackfoot disease patients and 759 matched healthy controls, questionnaire interviews were carried out to obtain information on the history of consuming artesian well water, diet, alcohol intake, and cigarette smoking, as well as the presence of arsenic-induced skin keratosis and cancer, and Blackfoot disease in first-degree relatives (Chen et al. 1988b). There was a significant dose–response relation between the risk of developing Blackfoot disease and the duration of consumption of artesian well water. In addition, arsenic-induced skin lesions, family history of Blackfoot disease, and undernourishment were also associated with the development of Blackfoot disease independent of the duration of consuming artesian well water.
	In a cohort study of cause-specific mortality of 789 Blackfoot disease patients followed for 15 years (Chen et al. 1988b), age–sex-standardized mortality ratios were derived for Blackfoot disease patients using the mortality rates of the general population in Taiwan and the Blackfoot disease endemic area as the standard rates, respectively. As shown in Table 7.1.7, patients of Blackfoot disease had increased mortality from cardiovascular disease and cancers of the skin, bladder, lung, kidney, liver, and prostate compared to two reference populations. In another case–control study on cancers of bladder, lung, and liver in the endemic area of Blackfoot disease (Chen et al. 1986), the duration of consuming artesian well water was significantly associated with three cancers in a dose–response relation after adjustment for age and sex.
