	A community-based health survey study was carried out in three Blackfoot disease-hyperendemic villages to examine the associations between arsenic in drinking water and various chronic diseases. A total of 1,571 residents aged over 30 years were interviewed by public health nurses, and 1,071 of them had health examinations. Residents in these villages started using artesian wells as the principal drinking source in early 1910s, and shifted to the public water supply system using surface water from a distant reservoir in early 1970s. The arsenic level in water of artesian wells of the Blackfoot disease-hyperendemic villages was surveyed in the early 1960s. As residents in a given village shared a few wells together, the median arsenic level of the water from the shared wells was used as the level of arsenic in drinking water for residents of the village. As a participant might migrate from one village to another, a detailed life history of residence and consumption of artesian well water was obtained through a structured questionnaire interview. The cumulative arsenic exposure was derived by the formula Σ (Ci × Di); where Ci was the median arsenic level in water of shared wells of a village in which the participant lived, and Di was the duration of drinking artesian well water in the village during the consecutive period i. The average arsenic exposure level in drinking water of a participant was derived by Σ (Ci × Di)/Σ (Di). Residents in hyperendemic villages of Blackfoot disease had a significantly higher age-specific prevalence of diabetes mellitus (Lai et al. 1994) and hypertension (Chen et al. 1995) than residents in non-endemic areas. Furthermore, there was a significant dose–response relation between the cumulative arsenic exposure and prevalence of diabetes mellitus (Lai et al. 1994), hypertension (Chen et al. 1995), peripheral vascular disease based on Doppler ultrasonography (Tseng et al. 1996), carotid atherosclerosis based on duplex ultrasonography (Wang et al. 2002), electrocardiogram-based ischaemic heart disease (Tseng et al. 2003), cataract (See et al. 2007), and pterygium (Lin et al. 2008) as shown in Table 7.1.8. Cohort follow-up studies also found a significant biological gradient of incidence of skin cancer (Hsueh et al. 1997) and lethal ischaemic heart disease (Chen et al. 1996a) with increasing cumulative arsenic exposure.
	There was another survey of well water arsenic and health status enrolling a total of 8,102 residents in four townships located in northeast Taiwan. Residents in these townships had their own tube wells in their backyards. The arsenic levels in well water of these households were tested in early 1990s. The public water supply system using surface water was introduced in this area in early 1990s, and its coverage was as high as 95% in the year 2000. There was a dose–response relation between the cumulative exposure of arsenic in well water and prevalence of cerebrovascular disease, especially cerebral infarction, which was identified from home-visit personal interviews and ascertained through the review of hospital medical records (Chiou et al. 1997). A significant dose–response association with arsenic level in drinking water was also observed for the prevalence of chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis in participants who were seronegative for hepatitis B surface antigens (HBsAg) and antibodies against HCV (Hsu et al. 2016a, b), as well as chronic kidney disease (Hsu et al. 2017).

	The occurrence of cancers of cohort participants enrolled from the endemic areas of arseniasis in southwestern and northeastern Taiwan was identified and ascertained through computerized data linkage with national cancer registry and death certification profiles. A dose–response relation was observed between long-term arsenic exposure from drinking well water and incidence of urothelial carcinoma (Chiou et al. 2001) and lung cancer (Chen et al. 2004). There was a synergistic effect on the development of lung cancer for cigarette smoking and exposure to arsenic in drinking water. Based on follow-up data from northeastern Taiwan, the cumulative lifetime (35–85 years) risk of lung cancer and urothelial carcinoma was found to increase with the arsenic concentration in well water (Yang et al. 2013). The lifetime lung cancer risk for arsenic levels in drinking water of <10, 10–99, and 100+ μg/L was 7.42%, 8.99%, and 17.09%, respectively; and the corresponding lifetime risk of urothelial carcinoma was 0.29%, 1.07%, and 3.43%, respectively. It is essential to ensure accuracy in the assessment of exposure to environmental factors in all cross-sectional surveys, case–control studies, and cohort studies in order to identify and characterize the environmental health hazards efficiently and effectively. It is also important to be aware of the possibility of temporal variations in concentration of the causal agent in various environmental media, individual variations in frequency and quantity of contact with the contaminated environmental media, and variations in detection limit of various exposure assessment methods.
	As one agent may cause many diseases like arsenic in drinking water, one disease may be caused by many agents. The multifactorial aetiology of HCC have been explored by many case–control and cohort studies (Chen et al. 1997; Chen 2018). The causes of HCC include HBV and HCV. In the 1970s, coexistence of HCC and HBsAg seropositivity, the biomarker of chronic HBV infection, was observed in several cross-sectional case–control studies. In the natural history of chronic HBV infection, spontaneous seroclearance of important milestone biomarkers including hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg), HBV DNA and HBsAg may occur (Chen and Yang 2011). HBeAg seroclearance occurs after a period of elevation of serum level of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), a seromarker of liver inflammation. The serum HBV DNA level (viral load) may remain high or gradually decline in HBeAg-seronegative patients. Seroclearance of HBsAg may occur after the serum HBV DNA level becomes undetectable. The seroclearance of these HBV biomarkers may occur before the time of HCC diagnosis. As HBeAg, HBV DNA, and HBsAg may be serocleared gradually with increasing age, their seroprevalence at the onset of HCC is much lower than that in childhood or young adulthood. It should thus be noted that cross-sectional studies might underestimate the relative HCC risk associated with the seropositivity of HBsAg, HBV DNA, and HBeAg if HCC cases and controls were not well matched on age. This may explain the wide range of relative HCC risk for HBsAg seropositivity in various cross-sectional case–control studies.
	Longitudinal cohort studies may better elucidate the HCC risk associated with these risk predictors. The causality between chronic HBV infection and HCC was first confirmed by the GECC cohort study in Taiwan (Beasley et al. 1981), the first prospective follow-up study on virus-caused human cancer. The REVEAL-HBV cohort study has documented the increased risk of HCC and cirrhosis associated with HBeAg serostatus and increasing serum HBV DNA level in HBsAg-seropositive patients (Yang et al. 2002; Chen et al. 2006; Iloeje et al. 2006). Repeated measurements of serial biomarkers during the follow-up period may help examine the causal temporality more accurately. For example, the long-term trajectory rather than baseline levels of HBV viral load has been documented to predict HCC risk more precisely (Chen et al. 2011). There was a significant dose–response relation between HBV viral load at study entry and risk of HCC newly developed during the follow-up. However, the HCC risk significantly varied among chronic hepatitis B patients with high viral loads at study entry. The HCC risk was highest for those maintaining a high viral load during the follow-up, and lowest for those whose viral load declined significantly to low levels. In other words, the follow-up biomarkers were very useful to stratify patients into more refined HCC risk groups. It has also been well documented that seroclearance of HBV biomarkers lead to a significant decrease in HCC risk (Liu et al. 2014). These observational studies suggest the most effective and efficient way to reduce the HCC risk is to eliminate chronic viral hepatitis through hepatitis B vaccination and antiviral therapy of chronic hepatitis B and C.
	Elevated serum level of aflatoxin B1-albumin adducts at study entry was found to increase the risk of cirrhosis and HCC in patients affected with chronic hepatitis B or C in case–control studies nested in the REVEAL-HBV cohort (Chu et al. 2017; Chu et al. 2018). It is important to note that the aflatoxin exposure at study entry may predict risk of end-stage liver diseases occurring within 8 or 9 years, but not those occurring afterward. In other words, aflatoxin may be a risk predictor only at the late stage of chronic liver disease development and/or aflatoxin exposure at study entry may not reflect the exposure in the long period of follow-up. This further supports the importance of serial measurements of exposure to risk predictor in cohort studies in order to elucidate the time-dependent effect of the disease predictors.





Intervention studies: validation of environmental health hazards through preventive intervention


	It is unethical to carry out experimental trials on human beings to validate the suspected effects of environmental health hazards identified from observational studies discussed earlier. However, intervention trials or programmes may be used to validate possible effects of environmental agents on disease risk by removing the exposure to agents in the environment. Intervention trials may be classified as individual or cluster trials depending on whether individual participants or clusters such as households, schools, or communities are allocated to the intervention. Intervention trials may also be classified as controlled and uncontrolled trials depending on the inclusion of a comparable control group or not. In controlled trials, the effect of the intervention on environmental health hazards is evaluated by the comparison of disease occurrence between experimental and control groups. In uncontrolled trials, the effect of intervention is assessed by the comparison of disease occurrence of the experimental group before and after the intervention.
	The implementation of a public water supply system, which used uncontaminated surface water from distant reservoirs, in the Blackfoot disease endemic area of southwestern Taiwan was started in the early 1960s and completed in the 1970s. The arsenic-induced health hazards identified from observational studies could thus be validated through the comparison of the secular changes in morbidity and mortality of arsenic-induced diseases in the endemic and non-endemic areas. In a series of studies, cause-specific standardized mortality ratios of residents in the Blackfoot disease endemic from 1971 to 2003 were calculated using the general population in Taiwan as the standard population. Cumulative sum techniques were used to detect the occurrence of changes in the standardized mortality ratios. A significant decline in mortality from ischaemic heart disease (Chang et al. 2004), renal disease (Chiu and Yang 2005), peripheral vascular disease (Yang 2006), and cancers of the lung (Chiu et al. 2004b), kidney (Yang et al. 2004), and bladder (Yang et al. 2005) was observed for both males and females in the southwestern endemic area of Blackfoot disease. A significant decline in mortality from liver cancer (Chiu et al. 2004a) and diabetes mellitus (Chiu et al. 2006) was observed for females but not males. Based on the reversibility criterion, it was concluded that associations between arsenic exposure and these diseases were very likely to be causal. Although the findings are quite consistent with observational studies mentioned earlier, there are several issues which need further clarification: (1) Classification of underlying causes of death may vary by area and time. It is necessary to examine whether the variations in the classification of underlying causes in death certificates are comparable in different areas over the study period. (2) Competing causes of death may be quite different between the endemic area and Taiwan as a whole. Arsenic has a pleiotropic health effect that induces various cancers, circulatory diseases, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, renal disease, and so forth. A person may die with several arsenic-induced diseases. It is thus difficult to select an underlying cause of death for an arsenic-exposed person. (3) Mortality associated with a disease is a function of the incidence and fatality of the disease. High mortality may imply an increased incidence and/or an elevated fatality rate. It is better to analyse incidence rather than mortality to clarify the causal association between agent and disease. (4) Risk factors other than arsenic may be important confounding factors, such as habits of cigarette smoking and alcohol drinking, chronic viral hepatitis, and obesity. They were not taken into consideration in the mortality analysis. It is thus more convincing to compare the secular changes in the incidence of arsenic-induced diseases after the implementation of public water supply system. Furthermore, age-cohort-period analysis may also help the identification of susceptible ages at exposure to arsenic and the assessment of reversibility effect of intervention.
	A nationwide vaccination programme aimed at eradicating HBV infection was launched in 1984 in Taiwan (Chien et al. 2014). It was the first universal hepatitis B vaccination programme for infants in the world. During the first 2 years (July 1984 to June 1986) of the programme, only infants born to high-risk (HBsAg-positive) mothers were vaccinated. Since July 1986, however, all new-borns were vaccinated. The programme was further extended to the preschool children who had not received vaccination as neonates since 1987. There has been a dramatic decrease in the HBsAg carrier rate and HCC incidence among children and adolescents born after 1984 demonstrating the programme not only successfully prevented the transmission of HBV but also reduced the risk of HCC (Chang et al. 1997), which is the first study to demonstrate the prevention of human cancer through vaccination. Even more striking has been the effectiveness of the national hepatitis B vaccination programme in reducing long-term risk of infant fulminant hepatitis, chronic liver disease, and HCC 30 years after its launch (Chiang et al. 2013). Through the strong evidence of a striking decline in HCC incidence of the vaccinated infants, the causal relation of chronic HBV infection with HCC is well confirmed. However, the elucidation of the failure of hepatitis B vaccination to eliminate HCC in the vaccinated birth cohort requires further study at the individual rather than national level. In a 20-year cohort study of 3.8 million vaccinees, incomplete hepatitis B immunization and maternal HBV carrier status are associated with the vaccine failure and resulting risk of acute and chronic liver diseases (Chien et al. 2014).
	Several antivirals have been approved for chronic hepatitis B therapy, Lamivudine was first approved in 1998 which was found to decrease the HCC risk of treated patients significantly with a large proportion developed antiviral-resistant YMDD mutants (Liaw et al. 2004). Newly developed antivirals for hepatitis B therapy have higher genetic barriers to induce antiviral-resistant HBV. The interferon-based therapy was the standard for chronic hepatitis C treatment before direct acting agents were launched in 2013. Several recent studies have shown the decrease in incidence of HCC in chronic hepatitis B patients treated with oral nucleoside/nucleotide analogues and in chronic hepatitis C patients who cleared HCV with direct acting agents (Chen 2018). A national programme of antiviral therapy on high-risk CHB and CHC patients was launched in October 2003 in Taiwan. A significant reduction in the burden of end-stage liver diseases through this programme has recently been documented. A total of 157,570 CHB patients and 61.823 CHC patients were treated with reimbursed antiviral therapy from 2004 to 2011. There was 22% reduction in mortality from chronic liver diseases and cirrhosis, 24% reduction in HCC mortality and 14% reduction in HCC incidence in 2008–2011 compared to the 4-year period before the programme launch, i.e. 2000–2003 (Chiang et al. 2015). The study confirmed HBV and HCV are the most important aetiology of cirrhosis and HCC in Taiwan. Recent international studies has shown the decrease in the incidence of HCC in CHB patients treated with pegylated interferon or any nucleoside/nucleotide analogues (Lin et al. 2016) or treated with entecavir or tenofovir (Papatheodoridis et al. 2017), and in CHC patients who cleared HCV with pegylated interferon with ribavirin (Huang et al. 2017) or DAAs (Ioannou et al. 2017). These studies have further confirmed HBV and HCV are the most important aetiology of cirrhosis and HCC in the world.
	Before the Second World War, endemic goitre was highly prevalent in mountainous areas in Taiwan. A national survey showed a prevalence as high as 70% in some aboriginal townships in mountainous areas. The prevalence of goitre in pigs was found to be significantly higher in the goitre-endemic area than non-endemic area. It was debated whether dietary deficiency in iodine or goitrogenic foodstuff intake was the major cause of the endemic goitre. The use of iodine tablets to supplement dietary iodine intake was found to be effective in lowering the prevalence of endemic goitre in school children, but it was considered costly and inconvenient. In order to identify an effective and efficient prevention strategy at the community level, a controlled community intervention trial on iodized salt was carried out in two townships in northern Taiwan (Chen et al. 1976). All the dietary salt used in experimental and control townships was strictly provided by the research team. Before the implementation of the community trial, the endemic goitre prevalence among schoolchildren was similarly high. One year after the trial, the prevalence of endemic goitre in the experimental township was significantly lower than in the control township. While the study did not rule out the possible effects of the intake of goitrogenic foodstuff, iodine deficiency was confirmed to be the most important risk factor for endemic goitre in Taiwan. A nationwide salt iodization programme supported by UNICEF was implemented, and the goitre prevalence has been drastically reduced since then. As there may be changes in dietary intake of iodine other than iodized salt, it is essential to monitor and adjust the level of iodine in the salt to prevent thyroid toxicity due to excessively high intakes of iodine.





Individual susceptibility to environmental health hazards: identification and application of molecular and panomic biomarkers


	The risk of developing an environmental disease may vary in different persons exposed to the same environment. In other words, there exists a host variation in the susceptibility to diseases caused by environmental factors. The individual susceptibility may come from genetic or behavioural components. For example, poor nutritional status and arsenic methylation capability may modify the risk associated with arsenic-induced health hazards including cancers and cardiovascular diseases. Multiple risk factors including cigarette smoking, aflatoxin exposure, antioxidant deficiency, and serum androgen levels are all important risk factors to HBV-induced HCC. Some environmental co-factors are difficult to detect and quantify unless biomarkers are used. Many studies have been carried out in recent decades on changes in the structures and functions of molecules, cells, tissues, and organ systems in response to exposures to environmental risk factors, to ascertain if the preclinical lesions of environmental diseases could be detected at an early stage which would allow more timely intervention. More recently, the dramatic advances in genomics, proteomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, glycomics, lipidomics, and metabolomics have enabled more extensive investigations into the genetic polymorphisms and mutations as well as epigenetic changes of host to elucidate the effects of gene–gene and gene–environment interactions more precisely.
	Various biomarkers of environmental exposure, health effect, and individual susceptibility of human diseases have been identified and applied in studies on environmental health hazards. The biomarkers for the exposure to environmental factors include molecular dosimetry of internal dose and biologically effective dose. The biomarkers for the health effect include early molecular and cellular changes, altered structures and functions of target tissues and organs, and preclinical lesions. The individual susceptibility biomarkers include both genetic and acquired susceptibility. As an illustration, since the development of chronic arsenic poisoning is a multistage pathogenesis, a series of biomarkers of arsenic-induced health hazards have been developed and applied as shown in Table 7.1.9 (Chen et al. 2005). There are several biomarkers of short-term internal dose for ingested arsenic including levels of arsenic in blood, urine, hair, and finger or toenails. Arsenic in urine, hair, and nails are better biomarkers for short-term exposure than arsenic in blood. Skin hyperpigmentation and palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, characteristic dermatological lesions induced by long-term exposure to arsenic, are excellent clinical biomarkers for long-term exposure to ingested arsenic. Patients with characteristic arsenic-induced skin lesions were found to have an increased risk of Blackfoot disease, lung cancer, and urothelial carcinoma. Inorganic arsenic is methylated into monomethylarsonic acid (MMA) and then further methylated into dimethylarsinic acid (DMA) in the human body. Monocarbon metabolism is involved in the methylation of inorganic arsenic. Genetic polymorphisms of arsenic (+3 oxidation state)-methyltransferase, purine nucleoside phosphorylase, and glutathione S-transferase (GST) omega 2 are associated with the arsenic methylation capability in humans. As MMA is more toxic than DMA, the percentage of MMA in the total urinary concentration of inorganic metabolites is considered as the biomarker for biologically effective dose of arsenic exposure. It has been well-documented that the higher the MMA percentage in the total urinary level of inorganic arsenic metabolites, the higher the risk of arsenic-induced skin cancer, bladder cancer, lung cancer, peripheral vascular disease, carotid atherosclerosis, and hypertension.
	The biomarkers of molecular changes induced by ingested arsenic include plasma levels of reactive oxidants and inflammatory molecules such as chemokine C-C motif ligand 2/monocyte chemotactic protein-1. The arsenic-induced cellular changes include sister chromatid exchanges, micronuclei, and chromosomal aberrations in peripheral lymphocytes and urothelial cells; as well as chromosomal loss and gain detected by comparative genomic hybridization and loss of heterozygosity in urothelial cells. Biomarkers of subclinical changes include carotid atherosclerosis, QT prolongation, and increased dispersion detected by electrocardiogram, retarded peripheral neural conduction, and retarded neurobehavioural function. The biomarkers of individual susceptibility to arsenic-induced health hazards include genetic polymorphisms of enzymes involved in arsenic and xenobiotic metabolism, arsenic methylation, oxidative stress, and DNA repair, as well as serum levels of carotenes, homocysteine and folate, body mass index, and cigarette smoking.

	In the multistage hepatocarcinogenesis of chronic hepatitis B, there are many other risk factors that modify the risk of developing HBV-induced HCC (Chen and Chen 2002). Biomarkers associated with HBV-induced HCC are shown in Table 7.1.10. HBV infection markers include HBsAg, HBeAg, antibodies against hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc), antibodies against HBsAg (anti-HBs), as well as serum levels of HBV DNA (viral load), HBsAg, and anti-HBc. Different HBV infection markers have different associations with the development of HCC. In addition to the seropositivity of HBsAg and HBeAg, serum HBV DNA level is associated with an increasing risk of cirrhosis and HCC in a dose–response relation (Chen et al. 2006; Iloeje et al. 2006). Different genetic characteristics of HBV are also associated with different risk of liver cirrhosis and HCC. The genotype C, basal core promoter A1762T/G1764A mutant, and pre-S mutant of HBV are significantly associated with an increased risk of liver diseases; while the precore stop codon G1896A mutant is associated with a decreased risk (Yang et al. 2008). Both quantitative and qualitative characteristics of HBV are important in the development of HCC.

	Dietary exposure to aflatoxins and habits of cigarette smoking and alcohol drinking have been found to increase the risk of hepatitis B-induced HCC. Due to the difficulties in measuring dietary intake of trace amount of aflatoxins and environmental exposures to tobacco smoke, several biomarkers are used for the molecular dosimetry of aflatoxin and tobacco smoke exposures. Aflatoxin metabolites in urine is used as a biomarkers for internal dose, and macromolecular adducts of aflatoxin as biomarkers for biologically effective dose. The hepatic DNA adducts of 4-amino-biphenyls and polyaromatic hydrocarbons are used to measure the biologically effective dose of exposures to tobacco smoke, while DNA and albumin adducts of aflatoxin B1 were used as biomarkers of biologically effective dose. There is a dose–response relation between exposure to hepatotoxins and HCC risk. There are significant synergistic effects on HCC between chronic hepatitis B and environmental hepatotoxins. The hepatocarcinogenesis progresses from asymptomatic carrier status, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, to HCC. There are several biomarkers which may be used for the detection of various precancerous lesions.
	The effect of environmental hepatotoxins on the HBV-induced HCC is modified by genetic polymorphisms of enzymes related to xenobiotic metabolism. Genetic polymorphisms of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes 1A1 and 2E1, GST M1 and T1, N-acetyltransferase 2 were found to modify HBV-induced HCC risk associated with aflatoxin and tobacco exposure. For example, a significant dose–response relation between HCC risk and serum level of aflatoxin B1 albumin adducts is observed in chronic HBV carriers with null genotype of GST M1 or T1, but no dose–response relation is observed for carriers with wild genotypes (Chen et al. 1996b). The dose–response relation between elevated serum testosterone level and HCC is much more obvious for chronic hepatitis B patients with the high-risk genotype of androgen receptor (Yu et al. 2000). Furthermore, the combination of putative high-risk genotypes of androgen receptor, CYP17, and steroid 5α-reductase is associated with highly elevated risk of hepatocellular carcinoma suggesting a significant additive effect of gene–gene interaction in the human host (Yu et al. 2001). The associations between HBV-induced HCC and low serum levels of micronutrients including carotenoids and selenium were modified by genetic polymorphisms of xenobiotic metabolism enzymes. The interactive effects on human health between biological and chemical agents in the environment are complicated and deserve scrutiny.





Risk assessment of environmental human diseases: standards of arsenic in drinking water and risk calculators for hepatocellular carcinoma in viral hepatitis patients


	In order to assure the safety of drinking water to protect public health, norms for drinking-water quality were initially recommended by World Health Organization in 1958. The International Standards for Drinking-Water established 0.20 mg/L as an allowable concentration for arsenic. The standard was re-evaluated and reduced to 0.05 mg/L in 1963. It was maintained as the ‘Guideline Value’ of World Health Organization in 1984, and many countries kept this as the national standard or an interim target. In the United States, congress directed Environmental Protection Agency to revise the standard in 1986. According to the 1993 edition of the WHO Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality, inorganic arsenic was classified as a documented human carcinogen and 0.01 mg/L was established as a provisional guideline value for arsenic. The mortality from cancers of the liver, lung, and urinary bladder from exposure to arsenic in the drinking water of 42 villages in southwestern Taiwan was intensively analysed (Morales et al. 2000). The original standard of arsenic in drinking water (0.05 mg/L) was found to be associated with a substantial increased risk of cancer and is not sufficiently protective of public health. Based on the risk assessment and cost-effectiveness analysis, a new maximal contamination level of 0.01 mg/L became effective in February 2002, and was complied with in 2006 in the United States. Several hundred million people in the world are exposed to ground water containing arsenic level higher than 0.01 mg/L. Strategies for the mitigation of chronic arsenic poisoning from drinking water may include the elimination of wells with high-arsenic water, implementation of clean water supply system to areas where the arsenic concentration in drinking water is high, monitoring of arsenic levels in agricultural products irrigated by high-arsenic water, identification, and health surveillance of exposed population, as well as detection and management of preclinical and clinical outcomes of poisoned victims.
	The prediction of disease risk is important for the planning and evaluation of public health programmes aimed at controlling the disease. Risk calculators of many diseases, especially cardiovascular diseases, have been developed and widely applied. As there are many risk predictors for most diseases, it is necessary to integrate several predictors into one measure of absolute risk using a regression model. Uncertainty about clinical interpretation of a single abnormal biomarker may be improved by the development of risk calculators based on the combination of multiple biomarkers. The risk calculator also allows for appropriate recognition of clinically important risk in persons with several but seemingly marginal risk factors that individually may otherwise not raise clinical concerns.
	As described earlier, there are several risk predictors of HCC in patients affected with chronic hepatitis B. Based on the long-term follow-up findings of REVEAL-HBV study, long-term risk of cirrhosis and HCC have been developed and validated (Yang et al. 2010; Lee et al. 2013; Chen et al. 2015). For example, a nomogram of predicted HCC risk for chronic hepatitis B patients is shown in Figure 7.1.2. Risk predictors included in this nomogram were gender, age, family history of HCC, alcohol intake, serum ALT level, HBeAg serostatus, and serum HBV DNA level. Integer risk scores were assigned to different categories of various risk predictors. The nomogram showing 5-and 10-year cumulative risk of HCC by sum of risk score. A 64-year-old man with a family history of hepatocellular carcinoma, a habit of alcohol intake, a serum ALT level > 45 IU/L, and an HBeAg-seropositive status has a risk score of 2 + 6 + 2 + 2 + 2+ 6 = 20. His cumulative risk of developing HCC after 5 and 10 years is estimated at around 90% and 100%, respectively. The REACH-B risk calculator of HCC was derived from community-based REVEAL-HBV cohort and internationally validated by hospital cohorts of chronic hepatitis B patients from Hong Kong and South Korea (Yang et al. 2011). This HCC risk calculator was found to have a high sensitivity, specificity, and discriminating capability. These HCC risk calculators may be used to assess the efficacy of antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B. It has recently been documented that antiviral therapy may decrease the HCC risk in chronic hepatitis B patients with normal to minimally elevated ALT and no cirrhosis (Hoang et al. 2016). Risk calculators for many other environmental diseases may also be developed if there were good large-scale long-term cohort studies on the diseases.
	Fig. 7.1.2 Nomogram for the predicted risk of hepatocellular carcinoma caused by chronic hepatitis B.
	From Yang HI et al., Nomograms for risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with chronic hepatitis B virus infection. Journal of Clinical Oncology, Volume 28, Issue 14, pp. 2437–744, Copyright © 2010 by the American Society of Clinical Oncology.





Promotion of global health through environmental health intervention


	With increasing globalization, environmental pollution, or infectious disease outbreaks in one country may result in environmental disasters and health hazards in both adjacent and remote countries. Public health can be promoted through environmental health interventions including the prevention of air, water, and soil pollution with chemicals or biological agents; the reduction in exposures to ultraviolet, ionizing radiation, noise, and electromagnetic fields; improvement of built environments including housing, land use patterns, and roads; minimization of carbon dioxide emission, combating global warming leading to severe climate change, and ecosystem deterioration; optimization of agricultural methods and irrigation schemes; and promotion of occupational safety and security, and so forth. Many environmental health interventions are more cost-effective compared with other kinds of health-sector efforts. These interventions often yield long-term benefits in addition to immediate health improvements. Reduction in the burden of environmental diseases may help the eradication of extreme poverty and hunger, the reduction in child mortality, the improvement in maternal health, the maintenance of environmental sustainability, and the control of epidemics including AIDS/HIV, malaria, tuberculosis, and other infectious diseases. Global partnerships need to be strengthened to achieve interrelated goals of health, environmental sustainability, and development.
