	Radiation therapy is based on the ability of ionizing radiation to kill cells, and radiation can target a particular group of cells, such as cancerous cells. Radiotherapy saves many lives every year, and in the case of palliative treatment, substantially reduces suffering. There are also some non-malignant diseases whose treatment by radiation is a method of choice. Most of the side effects of conventional radiotherapy are predictable and expected, arising from the unintentional irradiation of cells outside the target tissues, and one of the aims of modern IMRT (intensity modulated radiation therapy) is to reduce the side effects to a minimum by sparing normal tissues (Hall 2006). However, radiotherapy inevitably leads to some degree of irradiation of healthy tissues and to consequent risk of adverse health effects. This is particularly relevant for deeply-seated tumours, tumours closely located to critical organs, and paediatric tumours. One newly-emerging method is the use of charged particles (e.g. protons and 12C ions), with their positive physical and radiobiological properties, which allows highly conformal treatment of various kinds of tumours while delivering minimal doses to large volumes of surrounding healthy tissues. This means that they can cause severe damage to the DNA in cancer cells while sparing both traversed and deeper healthy tissue. This characteristic also enables them to be used for a more accurate irradiation of the tumour (Rosen 2001).





Recommendations for medical exposure


	Medical exposures are intended to provide a direct benefit to the exposed individual. If the practice is justified and the protection optimized, the dose in the patient will be as low as is compatible with the medical purposes. Therefore, dose limits are generally not applied to medical exposures. However, there is considerable opportunity for dose reductions in diagnostic radiology using the techniques of optimization of protection, and this is important since the second largest exposure to typical individuals is from medical exposures, and this is increasing particularly in the developed countries.
	The risk from diagnostic radiography is a particularly important consideration for children—they are still developing and are more sensitive to radiation-induced cancer than adults; in addition, they have a longer prospective life span, and hence, the period over which potential long-term side effects may arise is greater (Brenner et al. 2001; WHO 2005). Therefore, care should be taken to minimize the number of unnecessary X-ray examinations, including dental X-ray examinations, and in optimizing the CT exposure settings when this procedure is indicated.





Health effects (ionizing radiation)


	Ionizing radiation causes two categories of adverse health effects: tissue reactions (also known as deterministic effects) and stochastic effects (ICRP 2007). Tissue reactions are caused by the ability of radiation to kill cells—if sufficient cells are killed then the tissue reaction occurs—and tissue reactions are characterized by a threshold dose below which the effect does not occur and above which the tissue reaction increases in severity with the dose received (as more cells are affected). Stochastic effects are caused by non-lethal cell modification, which may develop into a cancer if the affected cell is somatic or into a hereditary abnormality if the affected cell is a germ cell. Stochastic effects are understood to have no threshold dose, and at low doses or low dose rates the risk is assumed to be directly proportional to the received dose, although this is not universally accepted. The overall risk of stochastic effects is dominated by the risk of cancer in the exposed individual (ICRP 2007).
	Ionizing radiation causes damage to DNA either through direct physical interaction with DNA or through the nearby creation of free radicals that then chemically react with DNA. These interactions cause strand breaks in the DNA, and ionizing radiation is particularly efficient at producing clustered (i.e. localized) damage and consequently double strand breaks. DNA repair mechanisms attempt to deal with the strand breaks caused by ionizing radiation, but double strand breaks are especially difficult to repair accurately. Heavy damage to DNA from high acute doses of radiation often leads to a loss of DNA integrity that is sufficiently serious to lead to cell death, and when a particular proportion of cells in a tissue is killed then a tissue reaction occurs; the greater this proportion the more severe the tissue reaction. A cell may survive the DNA damage caused by radiation because the DNA is repaired correctly, but a cell may also survive with the DNA damage misrepaired, and this is understood to be the origin of the risk of cancer (in somatic cells) and hereditary effects (in germ cells).
	The dose-response for stochastic effects is conventionally thought to be produced by a combination of the single traversal of the cell nucleus by a track of radiation and multiple traversals by independent tracks. The former occurs at low doses or low dose rates of sparsely ionizing radiation and produces a linear term in the dose-response, while the latter occurs at moderate and high doses delivered at a high dose-rate and leads to an upward curving quadratic term; this is the mechanistic origin of the Dose and Dose-Rate Effectiveness Factor (DDREF) of greater than 1 (conventionally, a value of 2), whereby the effect per unit dose (the slope of the dose-response) is greater at moderate-to-high acutely delivered doses. At high acute doses, cell killing becomes more likely, and the slope of the dose-response reduces as a consequence (since dead cells cannot contribute to the risk of stochastic effects). The linear no-threshold dose-response assumes that at low doses or low dose rates the risk of non-lethal DNA damage of relevance to stochastic effects is directly proportional to the dose, and therefore, to the overall number of tracks crossing cell nuclei.
	For high LET radiations, the density of ionization is such that the passage of a single particle through a cell nucleus does sufficient damage to the DNA that only a linear term in the dose-response is apparent. Indeed, at the cellular level, the passage of a single alpha-particle track is a high dose event, with a reasonable probability of inducing cell death, so the passage of two alpha-particles is most likely to kill the cell. Thus, the dose-response for high LET radiations is characterized by linearity, with a slope greater than that for the same absorbed dose produced by low LET radiations (due to the higher ionization density), followed by a reduction in slope at high doses due to cell killing.
	However, this picture is a greatly simplified version of reality, the biological mechanisms involved being very complex. For example, it assumes that DNA repair following acute low doses or low dose rates of low LET radiation, producing just a few electron traversals of a cell nucleus, is not much more efficient (conventionally, twice as efficient—a DDREF of 2) than that following acute moderate doses, producing many electron traversals, and this assumption may not be correct. Further, there is evidence that epigenetic mechanisms may play a role in radiation-induced risk, in a way that is as yet unclear, and that these mechanisms may differ between high doses and low doses.
	Some argue that since low doses produce a degree of DNA damage that is comparable to the overall level of damage that is constantly occurring through background biochemical processes, it is unlikely that low doses are harmful because the radiation-induced damage is ‘swept up’ by routine repair. Going even further, some argue that low doses of radiation stimulate the immune system, and so are beneficial because damage is repaired that would not have been otherwise (so-called radiation hormesis). Nonetheless, the ‘clustered’ nature of the damage caused by the passage of ionizing radiation through a cell nucleus must be taken into account in such a comparison. On the other hand, some mechanisms of damage may be more effective at low doses than at moderate doses, leading to a supralinear dose-response, and the bystander effect (whereby a cell hit by radiation adversely influences neighbouring cells that were not directly hit) is one example of such a mechanism because it affects more bystander cells at low doses than at moderate doses, where the effect is saturated because nearly all cells are hit. This serves to illustrate the complexity of radiobiology, and why risk estimates are still dominated by empirical epidemiological findings (ICRP 2007).
	It has been known for many decades that brief exposure to a dose of several gray leads to death through the killing of sufficient numbers of cells in vital tissues such as the red bone marrow (i.e. death is caused by tissue reactions in radiosensitive tissues). An example from recent decades is the 28 emergency workers attending the Chernobyl nuclear reactor accident in Ukraine in 1986 who died within a few months as a result of the high doses they received over a short period. Another example is the deliberate poisoning with a substantial dose of the alpha-emitter polonium-210 of Mr. Litvinenko in London in 2006. Other tissue reactions include skin burns, epilation, permanent and temporary sterility, depression of haematopoiesis, eye lens opacities and cataracts, and tissue necrosis.





Cancer (ionizing radiation)


	Radiation has always been a natural part of our environment, and the types of radiation emitted from anthropogenic sources are fundamentally the same as those emitted from natural sources. At present it is not possible to distinguish between cancers resulting from radiation exposure (whether from man-made or naturally occurring sources) and those arising from other causes (NRC 2006; ICRP 2007; UNSCEAR 2008, 2010; IARC 2012). Consequently, in the absence of being able to determine the risk to human health from exposure to ionizing radiation from fundamental radiobiological principles, risk estimates must be derived empirically from epidemiological studies of suitably exposed groups of humans, augmented by an incomplete knowledge of radiobiological mechanisms. The evidence that has been constructed from radio-epidemiological studies is substantial, and with the possible exception of tobacco, no other exposure has been studied so extensively. These epidemiological studies fall into four broad categories: studies of the Japanese survivors of the atomic-bombings, those exposed for medical purposes either therapeutically or diagnostically, occupational exposure, and those exposed environmentally (NRC 2006; ICRP 2007; UNSCEAR 2008, 2010; IARC 2012).
	The experience of the survivors of the atomic-bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945 provides the principal (but certainly not the only) epidemiological evidence on which radiation risk estimates are based. A large cohort study, the Life Span Study (LSS), was established from information gathered during the Japanese national census in October 1950, and analyses of data generated by the LSS continue today (Preston et al. 2007; Ozasa et al. 2012; Hsu et al. 2013). The LSS consists of about 93,500 survivors, around 86,500 of whom have individually estimated tissue-specific doses—considerable effort has been expended on the reconstruction of tissue-specific doses received during the bombings (mainly from γ-rays, but a component from neutrons), the latest database being the Dosimetry System 2002 (DS02), which has recently undergone a minor revision (DS02R1) (Cullings et al. 2017). Of the LSS subjects, ~48,000 received non-trivial doses (>5 mSv), and of these 18,000 received doses >100 mSv, and 2,400 doses >1 Sv; almost 2/3 of the non-trivially exposed survivors received doses <100 mSv (i.e. low acute doses). At the end of the last mortality follow-up (2003), 58% of the LSS subjects had died, and 24% of the deaths were due to cancer; 527 solid cancer deaths (8% of such deaths among non-trivially exposed survivors) are estimated to be attributable to radiation exposure during the atomic-bombings (Ozasa et al. 2012). Approaching half of the 204 leukaemia deaths before 2001 among the LSS survivors receiving doses >5 mSv have been attributed to radiation (Preston et al. 2004), so overall, around 10% of cancer deaths in the atomic-bomb survivors are estimated to have been attributable to radiation from the bombings. As well as mortality, cancer incidence is ascertained in the LSS through two specialist registries, the most recent analysis of solid cancer incidence covering the period 1958–2009 (Grant et al. 2017), while the latest findings of the incidence of leukaemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma are from an analysis covering the period 1950–2001 (Hsu et al. 2013). The latest study of solid cancer incidence has revealed a difference between the sexes in the dose-response for all solid cancers combined: for males the dose-response is curvilinear upwards while for females it is linear (Preston et al. 2007). The reasons for this difference are being investigated. In a subset of the LSS, the Adult Health Study (AHS), survivors participate in regular medical examinations to record clinical parameters such as blood pressure. Other relevant cohorts are those who were exposed in utero and the survivors’ offspring who were conceived after the bombings, the latter group providing information on the risks of the hereditable effects of exposure.
	Early support for the initial findings of the studies of the Japanese atomic-bomb survivors came from investigations of long-term health effects among patients treated with radiotherapy, in particular British patients irradiated for ankylosing spondylitis and US women treated with radiation for cancer of the uterine cervix (McLean et al. 2017; UNSCEAR 2008). Now there is evidence deriving from a wide range of radio-therapeutic treatments such as various groups of cancer survivors, children irradiated for ringworm of the scalp or haemangioma of the skin or for an enlarged thymus, and patients injected with the alpha-emitter radium-224. Patients exposed to radiation for diagnostic purposes are providing increasingly useful information as the use of CT scans increases, but those X-rayed to monitor treatment for tuberculosis or for scoliosis, and foetuses exposed during an abdominal X-ray examination of the pregnant mother have already provided valuable evidence on the risks of low-level exposures. A recent large cohort study of British children who received at least one CT scan found evidence of an increased risk of brain tumours and leukaemia that was related to the dose of radiation estimated to have been received from the scans (Pearce et al. 2012). An interesting group of patients is those injected with the radiographic contrast medium Thorotrast, which unfortunately was thorium-based and therefore radioactive and gave large doses to certain tissues, such as the liver and red bone marrow, leading to excess liver cancers and leukaemias.
	Although the findings of studies of those exposed for medical purposes form a valuable complement to the evidence from studies of the atomic-bomb survivors, medical studies need to be interpreted with care since exposure occurred due to a known or suspected disease. For example, a CT scan may have taken place because of an undiagnosed cancer, so that the cancer caused the CT scan, not the reverse (so-called reverse causation). Similarly, a certain medical condition may predispose to cancer, but may also lead to other diseases that require a greater frequency of CT scans, leading to ‘confounding by indication’. These considerations have led to difficulties of interpretation of the findings of low-dose diagnostic exposures because the predicted risk of such exposures is small relative to the background risk of cancer so that subtle biases and confounding can lead to spurious associations with radiation. Radiotherapy usually involves localized high (cell killing) doses, which can affect incidentally irradiated healthy tissues and lead to a reduction of radiation-induced cancer risk in these tissues; concomitant chemotherapy can also be a difficulty of studies of those receiving radiotherapy.
	Radiologists and radiographers have been subjects of study since the early uses of radiation in medicine, and US radiologists provided the first indication that radiation could cause leukaemia (March 1944). Of particular interest are groups of underground hard-rock miners (for example, uranium and tin miners) who inhale the radioactive gas radon and its decay products which irradiate the lungs (mainly with alpha-particles); and in the past, exposures have been high. Workers (mainly young women) who applied radium-based luminous paint to watch and instrument dials inadvertently ingested radium (an alpha-emitter) through the habit of licking the tips of paintbrushes (‘tipping’), and some workers ingested large quantities of radium, which deposits in bones and led to an excess of bone cancers. Of increasing importance is the evidence obtained from the study of groups of nuclear industry workers, especially those who worked during the early years of the industry when doses were comparatively high relative to those received today. Large worker-studies are providing valuable information on the effects of protracted low-level exposure, and international collaborations have the potential to produce statistically powerful results. The International Nuclear Workers Study (INWORKS) is a recent example of such a collaboration, and has reported radiation-related increases in the risk of leukaemia and solid cancers (Leuraud et al. 2015; Richardson et al. 2015, 2018). Special cases are those workers involved in dealing with emergencies, such as the ‘liquidators’ who were brought in to deal with the aftermath of the Chernobyl accident in 1986 (Kashcheev et al. 2015), and those from the early years of operations at the Mayak nuclear complex in Russia who were particularly highly exposed to both external sources of radiation and plutonium, an alpha-emitter that was inhaled in relatively large amounts during the early weapons production programme of the former USSR (Sokolnikov et al. 2015; Kuznetsova et al. 2016).
	Radon in homes has been a subject of substantial scientific attention because globally this is the source of the largest exposure to radiation for the great majority of people. Large case–control studies that take into account the important contribution of risk posed by cigarette smoking, have examined the risk of lung cancer arising from residential exposure to radon, and appropriately combined findings from these studies have produced radon-related risk estimates that are compatible with those obtained from underground hard-rock miners (ICRP 2010; McLean et al. 2017). Exposure to other sources of natural background radiation, in particular terrestrial gamma radiation, has also been studied, notably in those parts of the world where such exposures are materially greater than the global average. A study of cancer incidence in Kerala (India) has not found an excess cancer risk related to radiation exposure, although the power of this study is presently limited and the findings are compatible with those of the LSS (Nair et al. 2009). A large British case–control study concentrating on childhood leukaemia has found evidence of an excess risk from background gamma radiation that is consistent with risk models derived from the Japanese atomic-bomb survivors (Kendall et al. 2013), but a similar study in France did not find an excess risk (Demoury et al. 2017).
	Radioactive contamination from accidental and routine discharges from nuclear installations has been another area of study, radioactive releases from the accident at Chernobyl (UNSCEAR 2018) and substantial pollution of the Techa River by liquid effluent from the Mayak complex being notable examples (Krestinina et al. 2013; Davis et al. 2015). Radioiodine released during the Chernobyl accident in 1986 led to a large excess of thyroid cancer among those highly exposed (largely through the consumption of heavily contaminated milk) as children, and excess leukaemias and solid cancers have been found in the Techa River residents. The releases during the Fukushima nuclear reactors accident in 2011 provide another opportunity for study, although it would appear that doses are not sufficiently large for any effects to be detectable (WHO 2012a, 2012b). The Fukushima accident provides another illustration of the caution that is required in the interpretation of health data, in that the Japanese government established a health survey in Fukushima Prefecture that included a thyroid screening programme for all those at a young age at the time of the accident. An excess of thyroid cancer has been found by this screening programme, but it is most unlikely that this is as a result of radiation exposure during the accident, and probably due to screening using sensitive ultrasonography detecting cancers that would have been present but undiagnosed in the absence of the screening, an effect that has been found elsewhere (Ahn et al. 2014).
	Fallout from atmospheric nuclear weapons testing, especially at its peak in the late-1950s and early-1960s, has provided another source of exposure for study, and those resident in the vicinity of weapons testing sites (such as the Semipalatinsk Testing Site in present-day Kazakhstan) are of particular interest. Global fallout has not influenced childhood leukaemia incidence much beyond the level predicted by standard models, showing that intakes of fallout radionuclides do not have the pronounced leukemogenic effect that has been suggested by some (Wakeford et al. 2010). A group of Taiwanese residents was irradiated by gamma-rays from 60Co-contaminated steel accidentally used in building construction, and this group is being followed (Hsieh et al. 2017). There is some evidence of an excess of leukaemia and breast cancer.
	Epidemiological studies have clearly established that acute exposure to moderate and high doses of ionizing radiation (>100 mGy of sparsely ionizing radiation) increases the risk of cancer (NRC 2006; ICRP 2007; UNSCEAR 2008, 2010; IARC 2012; McLean et al. 2017) However, all types of cancer do not have equal sensitivity to radiation-induction—acute leukaemia, thyroid, and female breast cancer have a high sensitivity, whereas chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, Hodgkin lymphoma, and melanoma of the skin have a low sensitivity, with other cancers falling somewhere in between from higher (e.g. lung and colon cancers) to lower (e.g. pancreatic and prostate cancers) sensitivity. Leukaemia was the first cancer to be definitively linked to radiation exposure when a clear excess risk of the malignant disease was detected in the LSS of Japanese atomic-bomb survivors in the early-1950s (although unusually high numbers of cases were reported by alert clinicians in the late-1940s, before the LSS was established), and there had been earlier reports of elevated levels of leukaemia among radiologists (March 1944), which had been difficult to interpret at the time. As the follow-up of the atomic-bomb survivors progressed, raised mortality and incidence of other cancer sites were found to be related to exposure, and this evidence was supplemented by other exposed groups, such as an increased risk of a number of solid cancers among patients treated with radiotherapy for a variety of diseases, a marked excess of bone cancer among those groups with high intakes of radium, an excess risk of lung cancer among underground hard-rock miners exposed to radon, and an excess risk of liver cancer among the Thorotrast patients with high body burdens of thorium (McLean et al. 2017). Recently, the Chernobyl accident has produced a notable excess risk of thyroid cancer among those who as children inhaled and ingested high levels of radioactive iodine released during the accident, an excess that is compatible with that found among those exposed as children to external sources of radiation.
	The most recent analysis of leukaemia mortality among the LSS cohort found that a linear-quadratic dose-response best described the full range of data, and that the excess relative risk was 3.1 (95% CI: 1.8–4.3) at 1 Gy red bone marrow dose and 0.15 (95% CI: –0.01–0.31) at 0.1 Gy, based on 318 deaths (Ozasa et al. 2012). About half of the leukaemia deaths among the non-trivially exposed (>5 mGy) survivors are attributed to irradiation during the bombings. However, modelling demonstrates a marked variation of risk with age-at-exposure and time-since-exposure: for young children, the excess relative risk (ERR, the proportional increase in risk) rises to a peak of 50 some 7 years after exposure and then falls away to 5 some 30 years after exposure—a temporal wave of excess risk—while for exposed adults this wave is hardly apparent, with the ERR remaining below 5 at all times after exposure. From the latest data set for mortality from all solid cancers (malignant diseases other than leukaemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma) among the survivors, a linear dose–response fits the data best, with a slope of the ERR for solid cancer mortality for a survivor exposed at age 30 years and at an attained age of 70 years of 0.47 (95% CI: 0.38–0.56) Gy-1, based upon almost 11,000 deaths. The ERR coefficients for leukaemia and solid cancer incidence are similar to those for mortality (Preston et al. 2007; Ozasa et al. 2012; Hsu et al. 2013), but the latest solid cancer incidence study has found a significant difference in dose-response between the sexes (Grant et al. 2017). As mentioned earlier, there is notable variation in the ERR/Gy for individual sites of cancer, the ERR for the incidence of breast, thyroid, and non-melanoma skin cancers being high while that for cancers of the rectum and uterus are low.
	Risk models have been developed from the cancer data for the Japanese atomic-bomb survivors, supplemented by other data sources where these are found to make a useful contribution to evidence, such as for leukaemia and for thyroid and breast cancers following exposure for medical therapy. Lung cancer among radon-exposed underground hard-rock miners has provided a valuable source of information on the risk of radon-induced lung cancer, which is compatible with the risk of lung cancer among those exposed residentially to, in general, much lower levels of radon. The influence of tobacco smoke upon the risk of lung cancer is especially important to take into account in such studies, and it would appear that radiation and cigarette smoke interact to produce a combined risk of lung cancer that is more than additive, so that smokers are at a greater risk of radon-induced lung cancer than non-smokers.
	In general, the findings of the studies of the Japanese atomic-bomb survivors are compatible with those from other exposed groups, although comparisons are often not straightforward. For example, doses from radiotherapy are usually localized and high, with the objective of killing the target cells, but the unintentional irradiation of healthy cells can also lead to their being killed and thereby to a reduction in the risk per unit dose of cancer. Doses away from the target are received from scattered radiation and are difficult to compute accurately, although modern dose reconstruction methods are improving dose estimates. Of growing importance are studies of acute low doses or protracted low dose rates, because these exposure circumstances directly test the assumptions required for everyday radiological protection. Preliminary findings of such studies, e.g. of patients receiving CT scans, those living in areas affected by radioactive contamination, or nuclear industry workers, indicate that there is an increased risk from low doses/dose-rates (at least, for some types of cancer, notably leukaemia), but that this risk is not greatly different from the predictions of conventional risk models.





Other outcomes (ionizing radiation)


	Epidemiological studies have failed to produce definitive evidence that exposure to ionizing radiation increases the risk of heritable genetic effects in the descendants of those exposed (ICRP 2007). Even the follow-up of more than 30,000 offspring of the Japanese atomic-bomb survivors who were conceived after the bombings has not provided clear evidence of an inherited effect from parental exposure. Nonetheless, large experiments involving laboratory animals, mainly mice, have produced unambiguous evidence that irradiation of parents does raise the risk of hereditary effects in offspring. The risk of radiation-induced hereditary effects in humans derived from this evidence suggests that this risk is much lower than the risk of cancer in the exposed individual.
	The lens of the eye is sensitive to radiation-induced cataracts, and recent evidence indicates that the threshold for the production of cataracts, at around 500 mGy of low LET radiation, is much lower than the 5 Gy previously considered as a threshold dose (ICRP 2012). This evidence comes from the Japanese atomic-bomb survivors, the Chernobyl ‘liquidators’, and medical staff.
	The embryo and foetus are sensitive to radiation-induced developmental (teratogenic) effects, such as, early in pregnancy, congenital malformations (although death may occur before birth defects become likely) (ICRP 2007). Severe mental retardation was found among Japanese atomic-bomb survivors exposed in utero to high doses during 8–15 weeks of gestation, and less so at 16–25 weeks, and lower doses may depress IQ.
	An issue requiring resolution is whether low doses/dose-rates are capable of raising the risk of noncancer somatic diseases, in particular diseases of the blood circulatory system, such as heart attack and stroke (ICRP 2012). It has been known for some time that high doses can lead to an excess risk of these diseases, and this was attributed to tissue damage produced during such exposure, but epidemiological evidence is mounting for an effect at lower doses. However, a mechanism has yet to be identified, and the confounding effects of major (non-radiation) risk factors cannot yet be reliably eliminated as responsible for the association. Nonetheless, the potential risk of circulatory disease following low-level exposure to radiation is considered sufficiently important that significant research effort is being devoted to its investigation.





Policy and prevention (ionizing radiation)


	The International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP), in its latest assessment of evidence provides detriment-adjusted nominal risk coefficients for all cancers combined: 5.49% Sv-1 for the whole population and 4.07% Sv-1 for the working population, for low doses/dose-rates of radiation (ICRP 2007). The detriment-adjusted nominal risk coefficients for hereditary effects are: 0.2% Sv-1 for the general population and 0.12% Sv-1 for a working population. Consequently, the aggregated detriment-adjusted nominal risk coefficients for stochastic effects following low-level exposure to radiation are 5.7% Sv-1 for a general population and 4.2% Sv-1 for a working population. These risk coefficients form the technical basis of the current framework of radiological protection recommended by the ICRP, and give rise to dose limits: for workers, the limit is an effective dose of 20 mSv per year averaged over a defined period of five years (with a maximum of 50 mSv in any one year), and for the general public the limit is an effective dose of 1 mSv in a year (although in special circumstances a higher dose could be received in any one year provided the annual average is 1 mSv over a 5-year period). These limits do not apply to medical or naturally occurring sources of exposure, although residential exposure to radon and its radioactive decay products in some areas of the world are assessed to produce a sufficiently high risk of lung cancer that remediation measures are required to reduce the exposure.
	The three key principles of radiological protection remain: (1) the justification of activities that could cause or affect radiation exposures; (2) the optimization of protection in order to keep doses as low as reasonably achievable; and (3) the application of dose limits (ICRP 2007). The recommendations state:
	 	(a) No practice involving exposures to radiation should be adopted unless it produces sufficient benefit—to the exposed individuals or to society—to offset the detriment it causes.
	(b) In relation to any particular source within a practice, the magnitude of individual doses, the number of people exposed, and the likelihood of incurring exposures (where these are not certain to be received) should all be kept as low as reasonably achievable, economic and societal factors being taken into account.
	(c) The exposure of individuals resulting from the combination of all the relevant practices should be subject to dose limits, or to some control of risk in the case of potential exposures; hence, ensuring that no individual is exposed to radiation risks that are judged to be unacceptable from these practices in any normal circumstances. Dose (or risk) constraints are used to restrict to upper bounds the dose received (or potentially received) from a specific source.
	Restrictions on effective dose sufficient to ensure the avoidance of deterministic effects in all body organs and tissues, and that limit the risk of stochastic effects to acceptable levels, are shown in Table 7.2.4.

Conclusions


	The nature, frequency, and severity of adverse effects on human health caused by exposure to ionizing and non-ionizing radiation varies depending on the intensity and other exposure parameters, and is highly frequency-dependent. Potential effects range from rapidly fatal injuries to birth and hereditary defects, cancer, and other chronic diseases. Many effects occur only at high levels and are controlled or reduced by observing applicable exposure standards. In this chapter, our main emphasis is on exposures common in the everyday life and on long-term effects, which are typically of most concern to the public.
	The IARC classified ionizing radiation and ultraviolet radiation as ‘known’ or Group 1 carcinogens, while extremely low frequency magnetic fields and radiofrequency fields have been classified as a ‘possible human carcinogen’, or a Group 2B, and static fields as well as extremely low frequency electric fields have been assigned Group 3 (not classifiable as to carcinogenicity to humans). Intermediate frequencies and infrared radiation have not yet been classified as to their carcinogenic potential.
	As it is not possible to eliminate exposure to ionizing radiation, these exposures are kept to a practical minimum. Most recommend avoiding high levels of solar UV exposure in order to facilitate the prevention of skin cancers. Because of the beneficial effects of solar UV exposure it is necessary to adopt a balanced set of recommendations regarding this exposure. For ELF magnetic fields, given exposure prevalence, considerable scientific uncertainty, and limited public health impact, no or very low-cost precautionary measures are justified. For RF, potential risk could affect a large number of people because of the ubiquitous nature of the exposure. Thus, given the important gaps in knowledge and availability of no-to low-cost measures, such as use of hands-free devices to reduce exposures from mobile phones, such measures can and should be adopted.
	Rigorous studies capable of addressing knowledge gaps are urgently needed, particularly for rapidly growing technologies such as mobile phones, MRI exposures, IF antitheft, and device tagging, and modern magnetic levitation (maglev) systems.

7.3


Occupational health


	David Koh and Wee Hoe Gan





Introduction


	The World Bank Group (2017) estimated the global labour force in 2017 at 3.449 billion, about 45% of the world’s population. Females comprised 39.3% of the total labour force. In addition to workers engaged in hazardous industries, child labour, migrant workers, and those in vulnerable employment continue to be groups of concern when it comes protecting workers’ health. Rising life expectancies and declining birth rates have led to population ageing globally, which will impact the demographic profile of the workforce. The average age of the labour force is projected to increase from nearly 40 in 2017, to 41 in 2030 (ILO 2018). While this may be small from a global perspective, the proportion of aged workers will increase, especially in Europe and East Asia. This will put pressure on countries and industries to help older workers adapt physically and psychosocially to changes in the work environment.
	Occupational health is therefore a cornerstone to meet the challenges of the workforce now and in the future. The term ‘occupational health’, as defined by a joint committee of the World Health Organization (WHO) and the International Labour Organization (ILO), involves the ‘promotion and maintenance of the highest degree of physical, mental and social wellbeing of workers in all occupations’ (Forsmann 1983). This definition emphasizes the term health rather than disease, and further implies a multidisciplinary responsibility as well as a mechanism for the provision of health services for the working population. Occupational health seeks to not only maintain and promote workers’ health and working capacity, it also extends to the improvement of working environment and work to be conducive to safety and health (Coppee 2011).
	Occupational health practice encompasses the health protection, optimization, and management at the levels of the working population and individuals (Harber et al. 2010). For the former, the main components are the formulation of occupational health legislations and policies to protect the health of the workforce, the systemic reduction of risks from exposure to workplace hazards, and health promotion for those at work. Occupational health interventions at the individual level include primary prevention (e.g. occupational health training for workers, immunizations for healthcare providers), secondary prevention (e.g. pre-placement and periodic medical surveillance), and tertiary prevention (e.g. return-to-work assessments and programmes). In tertiary healthcare institutions, specialized clinical activities such as multidisciplinary management (e.g. occupational dermatology clinic jointly managed by occupational physicians and dermatologists), disability assessments, and acute management of occupational exposures (e.g. excessive mercury exposure) are undertaken (Barron et al. 2005).
	Occupational health must be practised taking the context of the worker’s job roles and environment. Both work and non-work environmental conditions can affect the health of the worker and in turn, his ability to undertake work safely and effectively. From the traditional ambit of industrial hygiene and ergonomics, the scope of occupational health practice must necessarily extend to include environmental health considerations and the holistic management of the workforce. Examples include hazardous waste management and disposal in a chemical plant, prevention of outbreaks of occupational infections in a healthcare facility, emergency preparedness and response (American College of Occupational and Environmental Health (ACOEM) 2010).





History and evolution


	The Italian physician Bernardino Ramazzini (1633–1714) is often described as the ‘Father of Occupational Medicine’. His publication, De Morbis Artificum Diatriba, is the seminal text in occupational medicine. Ramazzini stated that according to Hippocrates’ teaching, ‘When you come to a patient’s house, you should ask him what sort of pain he has, what caused them, how many days he has been ill, whether the bowels are working and what sort of food he eats’ (Ramazzini 1713/1964). Following this citation, Ramazzini wrote: ‘I may venture to add one more question: What occupation does he follow?’ Ramazzini described many occupational illnesses that are still seen today, and the principles for their control.
	The Industrial Revolution in the eighteenth century influenced the development of occupational health profoundly. Engineering and scientific innovations in the Western world, related to newly introduced industrial processes and the setting up of factories, led to dramatic social changes. Previously, work was done mainly by craftsmen in rural cottage industries. The Industrial Revolution resulted in work being carried out in factories in urban centres.
	Effects were seen both within the community, as well as in the individual worker. Family life was disrupted, with men leaving their families and moving to work in new industrial areas. In these new areas, health and social problems emerged, for example, poor housing and sanitation, alcoholism, prostitution, and poverty. Inside factories, individuals were exposed to long hours of work, uncontrolled occupational hazards, and the risk of accidents. Child labour and apprenticeship of young children were common, and there was an absence of labour legislation.
	The World Wars in the first half of the twentieth century further propelled our understanding of hazardous occupational exposures and diseases. Workers were affected with tetrachloroethylene (TCE) poisoning from applying TCE to aircraft wings, and trinitrotoluene poisoning from filling ammunition shells with little or no personal protection. Some of the phenomena seen in the Industrial Revolution are being replicated in the rapidly industrializing developing nations. Even in developed nations, similar problems are still encountered by migrant workers and other deprived sectors of the working population.





Occupational health legislation


	Occupational health legislation in many countries is one of the most important measures to protect workers’ health. For example, in the United States (US), the Occupational Safety and Health Act was passed by Congress in 1970. The United Kingdom (UK) Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 provided a broad legislative framework for the protection of workers. The European Union (EU) adopted a policy in 1989 on the ‘Fundamental Social Rights of Workers’, emphasizing the need for safety and health protection in the workplace, improvements in living and working conditions, and provision of social protection for workers.
	Internationally, there is growing recognition that a collective ownership is necessary for occupational health and safety. At the Sixtieth World Health Assembly, the WHO endorsed the global plan of action on workers’ health (WHO 2007). This calls for, among other goals, national policy frameworks on workers’ health, the protection and promotion of health at the workplace, and the improvement of access to occupational health services.





Disease burden and epidemiology


	The ILO reported that in 2015, there were an estimated 2.78 million cases of deaths from occupational causes (Hamalainen et al. 2017). The majority (2.40 million) were due to fatal work-related illnesses, while the rest resulted from work-related accidents. On average, over 7,500 work-related deaths occur every day. About 31% of work-related mortality were due to circulatory diseases, 26% due to malignant neoplasms, 17% due to respiratory diseases, 14% due to occupational injuries, and 9% due to communicable diseases. Respiratory diseases now constitute the third most common cause of work-related mortality as a result of the formal recognition of occupational exposures to a multitude of vapours, gases, dusts, and fumes as an important cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Collegium Ramazzini 2016).
	Approximately 5–7% of global fatalities are thought to be attributable to work-related illnesses and occupational injuries (Lopez and Mathers 2006). The population attributable fraction (PAF), or proportion of a disease that would be avoided in the absence of the risk factor under consideration, is often used to estimate the burden of occupational diseases. While there are several methods to estimate PAF, a commonly used approach is to multiply the relative risk from occupational exposure with the proportion exposed in the population of interest (Steenland and Armstrong 2006). The PAF should be interpreted in context because assumptions may be applied—an example is the period of cancer latency, which affect the determination of the appropriate occupational exposure period to the carcinogen of interest (Ruston 2017).
	In terms of global morbidity, an estimated 37% of back pain, 16% of hearing loss, 13% of chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases, 11% of asthma, 10% of injuries, 10% of lung cancers, and 2% of leukaemia are related to work (Concha-Barrientos et al. 2004).
	It is generally accepted that occupational and work-related illnesses are underreported. Occupational epidemiological studies are also often subjected to a selection bias known such as the healthy worker effect (HWE). HWE describes the better health status of workers relative to the general population and is often ascribed to the exclusion of unhealthy workers at employment and the study of active workers (Li and Sung 1999). Several methods have been described to minimize HWE, such as choosing active workers from another industry as the reference group instead of the general population. There is no standard solution and the approach needs to be customized for individual studies.
	Over 100 occupational diseases have been classified according to the tenth revision of the International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-10), and the list is expected to grow in ICD-11. To determine which occupational exposure leads the development of a particular occupational health condition may not be straightforward, given the multifactorial and dynamic nature of exposure-health interface in many workplaces. Recent occupational epidemiological research to map multiple occupational exposures with disease outcomes through novel models will allow better characterization and provide a clearer understanding of the multidimensional interactions between occupational hazards and ill-health (Bosson-Rieutort et al. 2018).





Estimates of costs and economic loss


	The economic cost associated with work-related disease ranges from 1.8 to 6.0% of a country’s gross domestic product (average 4%) (Takala et al. 2014). Occupational injuries and illnesses account for about US$250 billion annually to the overall national costs of all diseases, injuries, and deaths in the US (Leigh 2011). The UK estimated that the costs of workplace injuries and new cases of work-related ill-health from 2015 to 2016 to be £14.9 billion (Health and Safety Executive (HSE) 2017a).
	The main contributors are direct costs for medical care, rehabilitation, and compensation; indirect costs related to lost opportunities for the injured worker and employer comprising salary costs, administrative costs, and productivity losses; and human costs as a result of the change in the quality of life of the worker and those around him (IRSST 2013).





Major types of occupational diseases and injury


	Occupational illness can affect virtually every organ system. Occupational diseases of the lung and skin are common since these organs have substantial surface areas in direct contact with toxic substances. Noise-induced hearing loss and musculoskeletal disorders are among the most common disorders arising from physical factors in the workplace. Occupational cancer is a major concern because of its high mortality. More attention is now being channelled to the domains of psychosocial stress at work; occupational infections (especially with the emergence of multidrug-resistant organisms); and health hazards related to new agents such as nanomaterials; and maturing technologies such as the knowledge industry.





Occupational lung diseases


	The respiratory system is an easily accessible target organ for airborne toxic agents. Major categories of occupational lung disease include the pneumoconioses (‘dust diseases’ of the lungs), lung cancer, occupational asthma, chronic bronchitis and other effects of respiratory irritants, and occupational pulmonary infections.
	Silicosis is the most common form of pneumoconiosis worldwide. Exposure to silica occurs in a wide variety of occupations such as sandblasters, miners, millers, pottery workers, foundry workers, and workers using abrasives. Approximately 2.3 million workers in the US are exposed to respirable crystalline silica (RCS) at the workplace (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2017). The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified crystalline silica as a known human carcinogen (IARC 1997).
	Asbestos is another important cause of lung diseases that include mesothelioma, lung cancer, and asbestosis (a form of progressive pulmonary fibrosis). There are different forms of this group of naturally occurring fibrous minerals, with the main ones being chrysotile (white asbestos) and crocidolite (blue asbestos). All forms are carcinogenic. It is estimated that 125 million people in the world are exposed to asbestos at the workplace (WHO 2017a). Asbestos is responsible for over 100,000 deaths per year worldwide (Takala 2003), with an estimated 38,400 deaths annually due to mesothelioma (Odgerel et al. 2017). Given the long latency, the future burden of mortality resulting from asbestos will be substantial even if all future exposure were to be eliminated completely.
	Work-related asthma (WRA) comprises occupational asthma and work-exacerbated asthma (WEA, i.e. asthma not caused by, but rather worsened by an occupational exposure). At least 15% of adult asthma is thought to be work-related (Tario and Lemiere 2014), and WEA may occur in up to 25% of working persons with asthma (Henneberger et al. 2011). WRA may be caused by occupational allergens (such as inhalation of hay dust in farmers) or irritants (cleaning agents is a common group of irritants). Unlike non-WRA, the optimal management of WRA is primary prevention by eliminating or reducing occupational exposures. If the socioeconomic situation precludes total avoidance, work re-entry programmes may enable sustained employment after diagnosis (Malo et al. 2015). Prevalence studies of occupational asthma usually underestimate the number of affected workers because workers tend to quit jobs where they suffer such symptoms, although their asthma symptoms and signs may continue even after leaving work.
	Many vapours, gases, dusts, and fumes (VGDF), such as hydrogen chloride, organic solvents, and welding fumes, can cause irritant effects to the respiratory tract. Increasingly, occupational exposure to VGDF is also shown to be associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). For example, the Swedish CArdioPulmonary BioImage Study (SCAPIS) demonstrated that the PAF for occupational exposure to VGDF was 0.37 for COPD and 0.23 for emphysema (Toren et al. 2017). It is important that the occupational risk of VGDF exposure be fully appreciated so that adequate preventive measures can be put in place for workers’ protection.





Occupational cancers


	Occupational carcinogens include chemical substances, for example, benzene and asbestos; physical hazards, for example, ionizing radiation; and biological hazards, for example, viruses. It is estimated that approximately 16 million workers in the EU are exposed to carcinogens at work. The most common cancers due to these workplace exposures are cancers of the lung, bladder, skin, and liver.
	Occupational cancer accounts for about 4–20% of all cancers in developed countries. Variability in the estimates arises from differences in data sets used and assumptions applied. In the UK, 8.2% and 2.3% of mortality from cancers in males and females, respectively were occupation-related, giving an overall PAF of 5.3% (Rushton et al. 2012). Due to the complex interactions between exposure and causation in occupational cancers, the probability of causation model has, to date, been successfully applied only to occupational cancers after ionizing radiation exposure (Niu and Deboodt 2010).





Occupational and work-related skin diseases


	Skin disorders are among the most commonly reported occupational diseases. Similar to many occupational disease classifications, the main difference between work-related skin diseases (WRSD) and occupational skin diseases (OSD) is whether the occupational exposure is assessed to be partially or fully attributed to the development of the skin disorder. In Europe, the annual incidence of WRSD is estimated at 0.5–1 per 1,000 workers (Mahler 2017) with the most common condition being contact dermatitis. Although skin disorders are relatively easily diagnosed, OSD are believed to be underreported, so that the actual rate is many times higher than officially reported (European Agency for Safety and Health at Work 2008).
	WRSD/OSD are unevenly distributed between industries. Workers in agriculture, forestry, fishing, manufacturing e.g. metal workers, and some service industries, e.g. florists, hairdressers, and barbers, have a greater risk of developing WRSD/OSD. This is likely to be due to their exposure to a wider range of substances known to be irritants or allergens. With greater recognition and understanding of the role of occupational factors in skin diseases (e.g. occupational UV-induced skin cancer), there will be a revision in the Occupational Skin Diseases section of ICD-11 to provide a more comprehensive framework and facilitate precise definition and classification (Alfonso et al. 2017).





Occupational reproductive disorders


	The overall contribution of occupational exposures to reproductive disorders is not well characterized because of limited research in this area. Few studies are available, especially on physical and biological agents that may affect fertility and pregnancy outcomes in humans.
	Occupational exposure to chemical agents such as lead (Pb) and the pesticide dibromochloropropane (DBCP) have been documented to cause testicular effects with resultant reduction in sperm count. Pb can also cross the placenta in pregnant women to affect the developing foetus. Other substances associated with documented adverse reproductive outcomes include metal compounds (e.g. methyl mercury), solvents (e.g. carbon disulphide), oestrogenic agents, anaesthetic gases, antineoplastic drugs, carbon monoxide, ethylene oxide, ethylene glycol ethers, polychlorinated biphenyls, and physical agents (e.g. ionizing radiation).
	Occupational exposures can cause a wide range of reproductive disorders in both males and females (Kumar 2004; Jensen et al. 2006). Effects in males include reduced sperm count, aberrant sperm shape, altered sperm function; and lowered hormone levels or libido. Exposures in females may cause menstrual cycle irregularities, infertility, chromosomal aberrations, reduced breast milk production, early onset of menopause, and suppressed libido.
	Reproductive disorders also include adverse effects on the offspring of the exposed worker (Burdorf et al. 2011). Potential foetal and developmental effects from maternal exposures include preterm delivery, foetal loss, prenatal death, low birth weight, altered sex ratio of live births, congenital malformations, childhood malignancies, and neurobehavioral disorders in the offspring.





Occupational noise-induced hearing loss


	Exposure to excessive noise is a major occupational hazard in many industries. In the US, about 22 million workers are exposed to hazardous noise levels at work (NIOSH 2018). An estimated 16% of disabling hearing loss in adults worldwide is attributed to occupational noise (Nelson et al. 2005). In most developing countries, noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is one of the most commonly reported occupational disorders.
	Workers in manufacturing, mining, construction, transportation, agriculture, and the military are at high risk for NIHL. There is also an association between maternal occupational noise exposure and hearing dysfunction in the offspring (Selander et al. 2016). A Cochrane Review (Tikka et al. 2017) showed varying effectiveness of legislation, engineering control measures, and use of hearing protection devices in preventing NIHL. Nevertheless, the implementation of these measures has led to a systematic framework of noise hazard reduction for the at-risk industries.





Occupational infections


	Healthcare is one of several sectors whose professionals are at risk of occupational infections. In addition to blood-borne diseases such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV, airborne and droplet-borne infections such as measles, varicella, tuberculosis, and pertussis may also be transmitted from patients to healthcare workers (HCW). Many of these infections are preventable with immunizations. It has been estimated that 9–42 HCW per million die annually from occupational infections (Sepkowitz and Eisenberg 2005).
	The incidence rate of sharps injuries in HCW is about 3.7 per 100 HCW per year (Elseviers 2014), though it is known to be underreported (Elder and Paterson 2006). Needlestick injuries accounted for about 40% of hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections, and 4.4% of HIV infections in HCW (Pruss-Ustun et al. 2005). However, with the stricter implementation of universal precautions, adherence to standard operating procedures, introduction of surgical and phlebotomy devices with safety features, and availability of effective post-exposure prophylaxis for occupational infections in high risk cases, a gradual reduction in the incidence of occupational transmission is achievable.
	Transmission of M. tuberculosis is a recognized risk in healthcare facilities, and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis have re-emerged as a major occupational and public health problem. The risk of latent tuberculosis infection and tuberculosis disease is considered to be higher in HCW compared to the corresponding local communities (Baussano et al. 2011).
	Emerging infectious diseases also pose a risk to HCW. Two examples are the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) and the Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), both of which are caused by novel coronaviruses. In the 2003 worldwide outbreak of SARS, 20% of patients were HCW (Koh et al. 2003). HCW have also been shown to be the propagating vehicles for healthcare facility outbreaks (Alfaraj et al. 2018).
	Other workers besides HCW may also at risk for occupational infections. Some of the infections result directly from the work, while others are indirectly related to work. Examples include vector-borne diseases, such as malaria, dengue haemorrhagic fever, Lyme disease, and anthrax; water and food-borne diseases resulting from poor sanitation and inadequate potable water, such as cholera and typhoid; and zoonoses among veterinarians, farmers, agricultural and forestry workers, such as leptospirosis and rabies.





Occupational traumatic injuries


	These injuries include such events as amputations, fractures, severe lacerations, eye injuries, and burns. In 2014, approximately 374 million workers sustained non-fatal occupational injuries that resulted in an absence of 4 days or more from work (Hamalainen P et al. 2017). This translates to an annual accident incidence of 11,096 per 100,000 workers. In the UK, statistics of non-fatal injuries showed that the top 5 causes are—slip, trip or fall on the same level (29%), lifting/handling (22%), struck by object (10%), fall from height (7%), and acts of violence (7%) (HSE 2017b).





Work-related diseases


	Work-related diseases are diseases in which occurrence may be associated with workplace factors, but these need not be the only risk factor in each case. They occur more commonly than pure ‘occupational diseases’. The term is also used to refer to aggravation of a pre-existing medical condition by workplace factors. While prevention of occupational diseases is possible by the elimination of the workplace hazard, work-related diseases cannot be entirely prevented by only addressing occupational hazards. Common work-related diseases include hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, psychosomatic illnesses, musculoskeletal disorders, and non-specific respiratory disease. Two examples are given next.





Work-related musculoskeletal disorders


	Acute and chronic work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSD) are a major cause of morbidity affecting workers. The term encompasses a range of conditions from back pain, upper and lower limb disorders, neck and shoulder symptoms, hand–arm vibration syndrome (HAVS), carpal tunnel syndrome, repetitive strain injury, and other effects on the musculoskeletal system. There is substantive evidence to support the aetiologic importance of physical risk factors, including rapid work pace and repetitive motion, forceful exertions, non-neutral body postures, and vibration (Punnett 2014). Psychosocial factors such as high job demands, lack of job control, and monotonous work have additionally been shown to be associated with increased WRMSD risk.
	In the UK, more than 0.5 million workers suffer from new or longstanding WRMSD between 2016 and 2017, resulting in a loss of 8.9 million working days (HSE 2017c). In the US, WRMSD accounted for 34% of all lost workdays, and one out of every three dollars spent on workers’ compensation (Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) 2014). The implementation of ergonomic measures, and simple interventions such as stretching exercises may be effective in preventing WRMSD (Podniece et al. 2008; Aje et al. 2018).
	A common WRMSD is low back pain (LBP). LBP from occupational ergonomic factors accounts for about one-third of all disabilities with occupational risk factors (Driscoll et al. 2014). Given the high prevalence of back pain in the general population and its episodic nature, it is not always easy to determine the work-relatedness of this condition. While there are many studies demonstrating the association between work-related factors and the development of LBP, a recent longitudinal study showed that early exposure to heavy physical workload is associated with more than 30% risk of local and radiating LBP after a follow-up of 21 years (Lallukka et al. 2017). This highlights the importance of primary prevention even in younger workers when they enter the labour market.





Stress-related ill-health


	Work-related stress has been defined as the ‘harmful physical and emotional responses that occur when the requirements of the job do not match the capabilities, resources or needs of the worker’ (NIOSH 1999). Over the past half century, globalization and rapid technological advancements introduced significant changes to the workplace. New forms of work organization and employment patterns (e.g. more temporary and independent contracting) bring about job flexibility, yet at the same time result in lower control and a heightened sense of job insecurity. The fast pace of technological renewals enhances work efficiency, but also requires workers to constantly keep up with changes. Greater connectivity through the internet has blurred the boundary between work and personal life. Past European Working Conditions Surveys gave a prevalence of between 11.8% and 27.0% of work-related stress in the UK working population (Houdmont et al. 2010).
	The clinical manifestations of occupational stress are indistinguishable from non-occupational stress. It can present as emotional lability, anxiety, depression, insomnia, and even attempts at suicide. Adverse health outcomes of job stress are wide ranging, from increased risk of cardiovascular disease, musculoskeletal symptoms, impaired immune function, and gastrointestinal disorders (e.g. peptic ulcers and irritable bowel syndrome). The varying rates of coronary heart disease across occupations, and the link between work-related psychosocial factors and WRMSD support the role of work conditions in work-related stress (ILO 2016a). In extreme situations, work-related stress may result in karoshi (death by cerebrovascular and cardiovascular diseases due to overwork) and karojisatsu (suicide due to overwork) (Yamauchi et al. 2017).





Under-recognition of occupational ill-health


	Many countries maintain occupational disease registries. However, the lack of internationally agreed reporting standards and, in some cases, tedious notification processes result in the underestimation of the prevalence of some of the occupational diseases under surveillance (Somayeh et al. 2017).
	It is generally accepted that occupational and work-related diseases are underdiagnosed. One explanation for this is the inherent difficulty in establishing cause-and-effect relationships for occupational diseases. The link between occupation and disease may sometimes be unclear, because most occupational diseases are not distinct clinically and pathologically from diseases associated with non-occupational aetiologies. For example, skin cancer caused by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons is similar in appearance to that caused by excessive exposure to sunlight. Similarly, solvent-induced encephalopathy may easily be confused with effects of advancing age. Only for a very limited number of diseases, for example, mesothelioma (caused by asbestos), and angiosarcoma of the liver (caused by vinyl chloride monomer) are the causal association between occupational exposure and disease readily established based on strong epidemiological evidence and a good occupational history documenting exposure.
	The long latency which typically elapses between occupational exposure and onset of illness is a second factor which may obscure the occupational aetiology. For example, occupational cancers rarely appear within 10 or even 20 years of first exposure to a carcinogen. Similarly, chronic solvent-induced encephalopathy may develop insidiously only after years of exposure.
	Lack of a good understanding among health practitioners about the hazards found at work is a third cause of underestimation of occupational disease, reflecting the fact that most physicians are not adequately trained to suspect work as a cause of disease (Baillargeon et al. 2011). Technological evolutions and changes in employment patterns lead to new occupational diseases, further compounding this knowledge deficit. With competing demands for time in the medical curriculum from an increasing number of disciplines and subject areas, most medical schools now only allocate limited time to teaching medical students to take a proper occupational history, to recognize symptoms of common industrial toxins, or to recall known associations between occupational exposures and disease.
	Compounding a lack of medical awareness is the limited ability of many workers to provide an accurate report of their exposures. Workers may have had multiple toxic exposures in a variety of jobs over a working lifetime. In many developing countries today, there is still no formal requirement to inform workers of the hazard of the materials with which they work. In many instances, a patient may not know or may not be able to remember all his or her past occupational exposures.
	Finally, given the potential financial liability associated with the finding that a disease is of occupational origin, employers may be reluctant to recognize the work-relatedness of a disorder, especially in cases where personal habits or non-occupational pursuits are possible contributory factors. Since employers are often in the best position to recognize causal associations between workplace exposures and disease, this conflict of interest represents an obstacle to obtaining accurate estimates of the burden of occupational illness.
	Many of the occupational hazards today are still not fully evaluated for their potential toxicities. While it is another reason for the under-recognition of occupational diseases, there is a concerted effort globally to improve this through better classification and communication of the risk to workers.





Special populations of workers


	Workplace hazards affect some worker populations disproportionately, for example, child labourers, women employees, and impaired workers. These populations are especially vulnerable because of the interaction between their work roles and broader roles in society, as well as by their particular exposures in the workplace.





Child labour


	The ILO estimates 218 million children between five and 17 years are in employment globally, of whom 152 million are victims of child labour. Of the latter group, 73 million are engaged in hazardous work, concentrated primarily in agriculture (e.g. fishing, forestry, livestock herding). About 22,000 children are killed at work every year (International Programme on the Elimination of Child Labour (IPEC) 2017).
	Children are vulnerable to exploitation in the workplace and may be denied basic human rights, such as decent wages or access to education. Children in hazardous occupations are at greater risk of suffering ill effects than adult workers. They may have greater exposure to hazards than adult workers in the same occupation because children tend to be given the most menial jobs, which can involve higher exposures to toxic substances. Children are more susceptible to the same hazards faced by adult workers because they differ from adults in their physical, physiological, and psychological characteristics. Children using hand tools designed for adults run a higher risk of fatigue and injury. Personal protective equipment (PPE) designed for adults do not fit children, and therefore do not provide adequate protection. Furthermore, children may not be as aware as adults of workplace dangers, or as knowledgeable of precautions to be taken at work. Children are also more vulnerable to psychological and physical abuse than are adults and suffer deeper psychological damage when they are denigrated or bullied.
	In a study of more than 42,000 child labourers in Bangladesh, the incidence of injury and death among child labourers was 24 per 100,000 children-years (Dalal et al. 2016). The top three causes of injury were cuts/open wounds, abrasions/lacerations, and sprains; and the corresponding top causes of death were suicide, road traffic injuries, and electrocution. Child labour not only deprives children of education and training for a better future, it also perpetuates poverty and impacts countries’ economies through loss of competitiveness and productivity. The International Programme on the Elimination of Child Labour (IPEC), established under ILO, works with member States and partners to encourage the withdrawal of children from child labour by providing them with education, and assisting their families with skills training and employment.





Women workers


	In 2015, nearly 1.3 billion women were in the workforce compared to almost 2 billion men. As a global average, the female employment-to-population ratio was 0.46, whereas the corresponding male ratio was 0.72 (ILO 2016b).
	There is significant interplay between women’s roles in society, socioeconomic condition, and occupation. Women’s roles in traditional societies are defined in relation to childbearing and upbringing of children, and responsibility for the care and comfort of the family. Paid employment of women has increased in most countries, but this has led to a conflict between the necessity to be at work and women’s traditional home and family responsibilities. In many societies, early marriage, repeated pregnancies, large families, low educational status, and poverty all disproportionately impact on women workers. Even today, international objectives for women’s health, such as the Millennium Development Goals, are focussed on maternal-child health rather than advancing women’s intrinsic health (Mohindra 2016).
	Employment of women in most societies is characterized by occupational segregation, underemployment (often involved in doing seasonal and part-time work below their level of education), and barriers to advancement. Occupational segregation means that women tend to be clustered into a small number of occupations while being under-represented in most others. Women in developing countries tend to be employed in sectors such as agriculture, textiles and clothing, food processing, and social services. Compared with men, women work for smaller industries or organizations, and have less opportunity for work control. Women are more likely to work in the informal sector, in specific types of informal work such as domestic work, street vending, and sex work, with their accompanying low social status and lack of legislative protection. Gender differences are also observed in the rates of occupational injuries and illnesses, including the higher rates of mental disorders in females based on studies of workers’ compensation claims (Berecki-Gisolf et al. 2016).
	Increasing recognition of the importance of gender differences towards risks at work has led to gender mainstreaming in occupational health and safety (OHS). This refers to the systematic consideration of the differences between the conditions, situations and needs of female and male workers, and integrating these into the design, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of OHS (European Agency for Safety and Health at Work 2014).





Disabled workers


	A large proportion of individuals with disabilities are in the working age group, and they are able to make constructive contributions in the workplace despite physical impairment. Legislation in some countries, such as UK’s Equality Act 2010, prohibits employers from discriminating against individuals with disabilities, and encourages employers to make reasonable accommodation for those with a known impairment (HSE 2015). The Americans with Disabilities Act limits employers from asking job applicants to answer medical questions, take a medical examination, or identify a disability (US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) 2008).
	France and Germany impose quotas on enterprises to employ a certain percentage of disabled people. India and Japan use employment promotion measures to ensure workplace accessibility and provide employment services in the form of job placement agencies. Singapore provides tax reductions as a financial incentive to compensate employers for any financial burden resulting from the employment of disabled people.
	Reasonable accommodations are changes made to the work environment, job responsibilities, or conditions of work that provide opportunities for workers with special needs to perform essential job functions. The aim is to ensure that, as far as reasonably practicable, a disabled person has the same access to everything that is involved in performing and keeping a job as a non-disabled person. These measures may include technical assistance devices; customization, including PPE and clothing; and changes to processes, location, or timing for essential job functions. Many studies have demonstrated benefits of hiring people with disabilities, including improvements in profitability (e.g. cost-effectiveness); staff retention, reliability, and punctuality; employee loyalty; company image; competitive advantage (e.g. diverse customer pool, innovation); and inclusive work culture (Lindsay et al. 2018).





Migrant workers


	Migrant workers refer to all international migrants who are currently employed, or are unemployed and seeking employment in their present country of residence. The ILO estimates that there are 150.3 million migrant workers globally (ILO 2015). This forms 3.9% of the total global population and 4.4% of the global workforce. The majority of migrant workers are in the services (domestic work, food services, administrative work) sector. The other sectors significantly represented include manufacturing, construction, and agriculture.
	Migrant workers are a particularly vulnerable population. Many of them perform what are known as 3-D (dirty, dangerous, and demanding) jobs (Moyce and Schenker 2018). They may be affected by poor nutrition and endemic diseases, often have lower educational backgrounds, and are inadequately trained to deal with potential work hazards. Many face additional obstacles because they do not speak the language of the host country adequately. They are often not familiar with local health and safety practices and regulations. The accommodation available for them can be temporary and often crowded with limited shared facilities, and with restricted access to medical care and other social services. Migrant workers may encounter racism, xenophobia, and exploitation because they do not have full legal status or awareness of their rights in the host country (Holmes 2006). A review of fatal occupational injuries in the US from 2003 to 2010 found a risk difference of 15% increase in relative hazard for immigrant workers compared to their native counterparts (Byler and Robinson 2018).





Shift workers


	Shift work can take the form of fixed shifts, where workers constantly work the same shift period; or rotating shifts, where workers’ shift periods vary over time. It is estimated that in the EU, 17% of workers are engaged in shift work (ILO 2011).
	Apart from sleep deficits and suboptimal work performance, shift work has also been associated with adverse effects on psychological health (e.g. anxiety and depression), gastrointestinal disorders (e.g. peptic ulcer disease), metabolic disorders (e.g. obesity and impaired glucose tolerance), cardiovascular diseases, reproductive disorders (e.g. preterm birth), and cancer (especially breast cancer in female shift workers) (Costa 2010). The IARC classifies shift work as a Group 2A carcinogen, defining it as ‘probably carcinogenic to humans’.
	Shift work-related ill-health may also increase with time of ‘exposure’. A study found that after the first five years of shift work, the risk of cardiovascular events increases by 7.1% for every additional five years of exposure (Torquati et al. 2018). Given the complex and multifaceted interactions between shift work and health, it is important to minimize downstream consequences for susceptible workers through health surveillance, education, and proper organization of shift schedules.





Total workplace safety and health


	Work as a social determinant of health has been extensively researched. It is recognized that workload, duration, intensity, psychological stress, access to workplace health promotion resources, and other occupational-related factors have an impact on wellbeing. There is no unified definition of wellbeing. The concept of wellbeing encompasses the presence of positive emotions and moods, engaging activities and work, fulfilment, and positive functioning (CDC 2016). By integrating physical health and wellbeing into a multidimensional indicator, it provides a more holistic approach to the understanding of occupational and work-related diseases and, in turn, their prevention and management.
	Wellbeing, alongside safety and physical health, is an important outcome in occupational health and contributes to the changing paradigm of a new total workplace safety and health model. This model recognizes that in addition to addressing workplace safety issues, good workplace health (physical and psychosocial health) is equally important because it affects the worker’s overall wellbeing and therefore, his work capacity, and the overall performance of the organization.
