7.4


Toxicology and environmental risk analysis


	David Koh and Ro-Ting Lin





Introduction to toxicology and risk analysis


	Toxicology is the study of poisons. In theory, any substance can cause harm to health. To paraphrase the physician-alchemist Paracelsus, ‘It is only the dose that distinguishes a poison from a remedy’. To that we can add that the route of entry into the body can also determine the extent of injury or ill health. In practice, most poisons are either chemicals or biological materials that cause severe effects in relatively small doses. Poisonous substances that contaminate the environment can lead to an increased risk of ill health in exposed populations. The level of risk is a function of the extent of exposure and the susceptibility of those exposed. An understanding of toxicology is essential to determining and managing environmental risk.
	Risk analysis has been defined as ‘a process consisting of three components: risk assessment, risk management, and risk communication’ (Food and Agriculture Organization and World Health Organization 2009). Environmental risk analysis is a broad field, encompassing risks to ecosystems and materials as well as to human health. This chapter discusses human health risks only. The goal is to synthesize toxicology and risk analysis as a basis for evaluating risks to human health posed by hazardous agents in the environment. Other disciplines, such as epidemiology and exposure assessment, are also required to better understand risk, and for many specific agents these disciplines will provide the primary information needed for risk assessment, risk management, and risk communication.
	Toxicology has these two important roles in environmental risk analysis:
	 	1. To ascertain cause and effect relationships linking hazardous agents to adverse effects in humans or the general environment.
	2. To develop techniques capable of preventing these problems.
	Toxicologists usually approach questions of disease causation by starting with the chemical or physical agent and studying its effects in laboratory animals or in test-tube systems. Modern toxicology also develops tools, primarily through molecular biology and advanced computational techniques, capable of probing the extent to which a given disease in an individual is caused by an external agent. This reverse approach, starting with disease and moving toward determining cause, is enabled by the increasing ability of epidemiology to link subtle biological markers indicative of early effects to biological markers indicative of exposure.
	Toxicology is also an important discipline in the primary and secondary prevention of human health effects. When toxicologists understand the mechanisms by which chemical or physical agents cause biological effects, they can develop tests to help prevent further spread of harmful chemicals or promote early detection of potential adverse effects.





General concepts of toxicology relevant to risk analysis


	Knowledge about poisons extends back to the beginning of history, as humans became aware of the toxicity of natural food components. Toxicologists credit Paracelsus with the first law of toxicology, that the dose makes the poison. Two other laws underlie modern toxicology: that chemicals have specific biological effects, a maxim credited to Ambrose Pare (Goldstein and Gallo 2001); and that humans are members of the animal kingdom.





The ‘laws’ of toxicology


	The following section discusses the ‘laws’ and general concepts of toxicology pertinent to understanding how a chemical or physical agent acts in a biological system. The focus here is on the biological response to an agent, rather than on the intrinsic properties of the agent. These are the three ‘laws’ of toxicology:
	 	1. The dose makes the poison.
	2. Chemical/physical agents have specific effects.
	3. Humans are animals.





The first law: the dose makes the poison


	Exploration of the relation between dose and response is central to toxicology. There are two main types of dose–response curves (Fig. 7.4.1). One is an S-shaped curve characterized by having no observed effect at the lowest doses, gradual development of an increasing response as the dose increases followed by a linear phase of increase in relation to dose, and, eventually, a dose level at which no further increase in response is observed. Of particular pertinence to environmental toxicology is that this curve presumes that there exists a threshold level below which no harm whatsoever is to be expected. There is ample scientific basis for the existence of thresholds for specific effects. For example, one drop of undiluted sulphuric acid splashed on the skin is capable of producing a severe burn. Yet one drop of pure sulphuric acid in a bathtub of water is sufficiently dilute to be without effect. Thresholds for an adverse effect will differ among individuals based upon a variety of circumstances, some genetically determined and others representing stages of life or other specific circumstances. In the example of sulphuric acid on the skin, there are genetically determined differences in susceptibility related to the protective presence of skin and hair. Babies will be more susceptible than adults; and skin that is already damaged will be at particular risk. The S-shaped dose–response curve is assumed to fit all toxic effects except those that are produced by direct reaction with genetic material.
	Fig. 7.4.1 Dose–response curve.
	The second general type of dose–response curve covers endpoints caused by persistent changes in the genes. For example, in cancer, a somatic mutation occurring in a single cell results in a clone of cancer cell progeny. Another example is inherited mutations of the genetic components of cells involved in reproduction. It is believed that a single change in DNA can alter the genetic code in a way that can lead to a mutated cell. It follows that any single molecule of a carcinogenic chemical or packet of physical energy, such as ionizing radiation, that can alter DNA is theoretically capable of causing a persistent mutation. This presumption—that a single molecule or ionizing ray could change a normal cell to a cancerous cell—implies that there is no threshold below which the risk is zero. The resultant dose–response curve thus starts at a single molecule. As a further simplification, the shape of the curve can be linear in that the risk of two molecules of a DNA-altering chemical causing a mutation is conceivably twice that of one molecule, and so on, until a dose level results in dead cells.
	Features of both S-shaped and linear dose–response curves occur in the human body’s response to allergens. It is likely that a relatively large dose of an allergen is required to first sensitize an individual (i.e. the threshold dose for sensitization may vary with the agent and the individual). However, once sensitized, the affected individual may react to even molecules of the causative agent, with no apparent threshold for elicitation of a reaction.
	There are also a few chemicals that have a U-shaped dose–response curve, where high levels of exposure cause harm and insufficient exposure leads to a deficiency which results in ill health. Examples are fat-soluble vitamins and essential trace minerals. Excess vitamin D intake causes hypervitaminosis D, and vitamin D deficiency leads to rickets and osteomalacia. There is, therefore, an ideal range for vitamin D levels which results neither in deficiency nor poisoning.





The second law: chemicals have specific effects


	Understanding that chemical and physical agents have specific effects is in essence no different from recognizing that possession of a gun does not make one a murder suspect if the victim was stabbed to death. The law of specificity is well understood by the general public in terms of drugs: aspirin will help with your headache but is useless for constipation, while laxatives have the opposite effect. However, various surveys suggest that the selectivity of the effects of environmental chemicals is not widely understood and that many believe a chemical that can cause cancer in a particular organ can cause cancer and other diseases anywhere in the body. Some chemicals may cause malignancy in more than one body site (e.g. asbestos can cause lung cancer, peritoneal mesothelioma, and laryngeal cancer), but in general, chemical and physical agents are highly specific in their effects.
	The specificity of effects is due to both chemistry and biology. Understanding the relationship between chemical structure and biological effect has been central to both pharmacology and toxicology. Structure activity relationship (SAR) is often used as a means to design a chemical with a specific effect that might be useful as a therapeutic agent. SAR is also used to predict whether a new chemical being readied for manufacture might be of potential harm. While SAR is a useful tool being further improved through modern computational approaches, its predictive value remains too limited for use with a potentially toxic agent without recourse to additional testing. For example, only one simple methyl group separates toluene from benzene (only the latter known to cause bone marrow damage and leukaemia); ethanol from methanol (the latter causing metabolic acidosis, renal failure, and blindness); and n-hexane from either n-heptane or n-pentane (only n-hexane is responsible for peripheral nerve damage). These examples of specificity reflect both the formation of toxic metabolites, such as active species derived from the metabolism of benzene, and the interaction of a chemical or its metabolite within specific biological niches, such as the diketone metabolite (2,5-hexanedione) of n-hexane within neuronal axons.
	Specificity of effects is also conferred by cellular processes that cause certain cells to be more susceptible to environmental agents. For example, red blood cells have the iron-containing protein haemoglobin that is responsible for the transport of oxygen. Toxicity through alteration of efficient oxygen delivery occurs through certain specific mechanisms. One is through the oxidation of the reduced ferrous form to the ferric form of iron, known as methaemoglobin, which can no longer carry oxygen. This occurs with a limited number of agents (e.g. nitrates and phenols) that, once within the red blood cell, are capable of oxidizing intracellular iron. Another specific mechanism of interference is exemplified by carbon monoxide. This otherwise relatively inert gas has a physical chemistry that sufficiently resembles oxygen so that it is able to tightly combine with the oxygen-combining site of haemoglobin, thereby displacing oxygen. There are many other examples in which a normal body process is disrupted by an exogenous chemical through a specific chemical alteration, such as oxidation or covalent addition, or by fitting into a niche designed through evolution to accommodate a necessary internal chemical which it superficially resembles.





The third law: humans are animals


	The conceptual foundation for extrapolating from animals to humans is central to modern toxicology. The basic principles of cell function are common to all of biology: all cells must obtain energy, build structure, and release waste. Cell function in complex organisms, such as humans, is highly specialized, but there is still great similarity in cellular and organ function among mammals, which facilitates extrapolation from one species to another. In general, a kidney poison in one species is likely to be a kidney poison in another, although there are certainly exceptions. As an example, arsenic is a human carcinogen with a lack of evidence for carcinogenicity among other animals.
	However, despite similarities in effects, dose–response considerations often vary substantially between species, reflecting differences in absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, function, and target organ susceptibility. Understanding the factors responsible for interspecies differences greatly facilitates extrapolation from animals to humans. Once elucidated, the role of different absorption rates, metabolism, or other factors can be taken into account, often through a mathematical approximation that has come to be called physiologically based pharmacokinetics (or toxicokinetics).
	The use of alternative methods to replace animal testing is becoming popular. For example, under the 2006 Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation, and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) regulation in the European Union (EU), companies that manufacture or import chemical substances in quantities beyond a certain volume are required to submit reports of testing on vertebrate animals. To avoid unnecessary animal tests, the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) introduced the concept of alternative methods such as read-across, SAR, weight of evidence, and in vitro methods (European Chemicals Agency 2017).





Pathways of exogenous agents within the body


	Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of exogenous agents can vary greatly across individuals and within the same individual depending upon, for example, stage of life and state of health. These variations are among the major reasons for individual differences in susceptibility to risks from exposure to toxic agents. Increased understanding of how the human genotype and phenotype affect absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of exogenous agents, including foods, is providing insight into the oldest human question about disease: ‘Why is this happening to me?’ (Omenn 2000).





Absorption


	Absorption of a chemical into the body occurs through ingestion, inhalation, and skin absorption. Depending upon the specific chemical, the route of exposure can have major implications for the extent of absorption and the resultant toxicity. For example, almost 100% of inhaled lead-containing fine particles are absorbed into the body, while a much smaller percentage of ingested lead is absorbed. Internal factors also affect absorption, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract. In the case of lead absorption, both iron and calcium deficiencies increase the absorption of ingested lead. The matrix of the exposure agent also may have an effect. For example, the rate at which benzene in gasoline is absorbed through the skin is likely increased by oxygenated components of the gasoline mixture, and the absorption of dioxins from contaminated soil can vary enormously (Umbreit et al. 1986). The American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists provides a ‘skin’ notation for chemicals that can be absorbed through the skin to cause systemic effects following exposure (American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists 2013).
	Often, a single route of absorption is dominant. But in many instances, more than one route may be important. For example, exposure to chlorinated disinfection products in drinking water systems, or to gasoline contamination of well water through a leaky underground storage tank, is usually thought of solely in terms of the ingestion of water. However, during showering, there is likely to be both inhalation and transdermal absorption, and if groundwater is contaminated, there can be off-gassing from the soil into the home. Epidemiological studies of the potential adverse consequences of water contamination need to take all of these exposure routes into account (Arbuckle et al. 2002).
	Less common routes of absorption are intravenous, intramuscular, intraperitoneal, and sublingual, or via suppositories. These occur mainly in animal experiments or in human drug delivery. A novel route of absorption is the translocation of nanoparticles deposited in the nasal area via the olfactory nerves directly into the brain (Oberdorster et al. 2004). For example, inhaled airborne magnetite particulate matter (PM) has been found to cross the damaged olfactory unit, pass through the axons of the olfactory nerve, and enter the brain, which can potentially be related to neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s (Maher et al. 2016).





Distribution


	Once inside the body, chemicals are transported by the blood. Distribution is determined by factors including the route of absorption, the chemical and physical properties of the substance, and the barriers that compartmentalize the body.
	The route of absorption affects the different pathways through which chemical substances are distributed. Most compounds absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract go directly to the liver and may go no further. The liver has great capacity to detoxify many absorbed chemicals, especially when the chemical is absorbed by the digestive system and enters the hepatic portal system into the liver before it reaches the rest of the body. Enzymes in the gastrointestinal bacteria, lumen, gut wall, and liver contribute to this first-pass effect, which may greatly reduce the level at which a particular agent remains bioavailable in systemic circulation. On the other hand, inhaled agents go first to the lungs or other parts of the respiratory tract and then to general circulation, without being filtered through this ‘first-pass’ effect.
	The specific chemical and physical properties of a substance and their affinity for certain organs or tissues also affect distribution of a chemical substance. Small inhaled particles tend to be distributed deep within the respiratory tract, while larger particles are filtered out in the nose or are trapped and cleared by the bronchiolar mucociliary escalator. Chemicals that are poorly soluble in water, such as oils, usually distribute within fatty tissues. Organ-specific factors are also important. For example, a specific pump located in the thyroid gland facilitates uptake of iodine and makes the thyroid particularly vulnerable to the adverse impact of radioactive iodine.
	Some tissues, such as the blood-brain barrier and the placental barrier, limit the distribution of chemical substances. The blood-brain barrier, with its capillary endothelial cells, can protect the central nervous system. Only fat-soluble substances, such as alcohols, can cross the blood-brain barrier. The placental barrier prevents many toxicants from reaching the foetus but allows oxygen and nutrients to pass from mother to foetus (Burton et al. 2016).





Metabolism


	Metabolism, in the narrowest sense of the term, refers to alteration of chemicals by the body. The major metabolic function of the body is to alter food into energy or structural materials. Metabolism of xenobiotics is often protective, converting unwanted absorbed materials into chemical forms that are readily excretable. Thus, a fat-soluble agent can often be converted into water-soluble agents capable of being excreted in the urine. However, for certain classes of chemicals, metabolism results in conversion of relatively inactive compounds into harmful agents. For example, some carcinogens, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon components of soot and benzene, require metabolic activation to change from pro-carcinogens to ultimate carcinogens.
	All organs appear to have metabolic capability, often related both to organ function and to susceptibility to toxic agents. Understanding the specific enzymes and enzyme families responsible for metabolism within cell types is important to understanding why chemicals have specific effects in specific organs.
	In the case of inhaled benzene, about 50% of the body burden is exhaled unchanged as the parent compound, and the rest is metabolized to potentially toxic metabolites. Slowing down benzene metabolism leads to an increase in the relative amount that is exhaled rather than metabolized, and thus a decrease in bone marrow toxicity. Individuals with what appear to be genetically determined increases in benzene metabolism to toxic metabolites, or decreases in the detoxification of these metabolites experience increased haematological risk. The effects of having both polymorphisms together appear to be at least additive and perhaps multiplicative in increasing the risk (Rothman et al. 1997; Kim et al. 2007). The application of genomics and proteomics to metabolism is often known as metabolomics.





Excretion


	Excretion of chemicals from the body occurs through a variety of routes, including the gastrointestinal tract for unabsorbed compounds and for compounds dissolved in bile, and the renal tract (e.g. in urine) for water-soluble agents of appropriate molecular weight and charge. Significant excretion of volatile compounds can occur through the respiratory tract. Other routes of excretion include sweating and lactation, the latter which may put the breastfed infant at risk.





Multiple chemical interactions


	Toxicological studies of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion are often performed for single chemicals. Yet in real life, multiple and combined exposures are the norm rather than the exception. For such situations, the possibility of additive or synergistic effects, or potentiation or antagonism of effects, has to be considered. For example, exposure to two organophosphate insecticides may result in a simple additive adverse effect. In the case of exposure to carbon tetrachloride and ethanol, or asbestos exposure and cigarette smoking, the combined effects are synergistic. Antagonistic interactions take various forms. Functional antagonism is exemplified by the opposing functional effects of combined exposure to barbiturate and norepinephrine. An example of chemical antagonism is adding BAL (British anti-Lewisite) to inactivate metal ions through chelation. Dispositional antagonism is made use of when treating poisoning with charcoal, or when using an emetic or a diuretic. Receptor antagonism is seen in the case of naloxone as treatment for morphine overdose.





Risk assessment


	Risk assessment follows two separate streams of toxicological reasoning: (1) for toxic agents implicitly or explicitly assumed to have a threshold, and (2) for carcinogens. Chemical safety assessment developed from simplified approaches such as studies on laboratory animals to determine the dose (LD50, expressed usually as mg/kg body weight) or the concentration (LC50, expressed as parts per million of the substance in air or water or other medium) capable of killing 50% of the test animals. The observed LD50 or LC50 was used as a basis for extrapolating to permissible levels in humans, often using several tenfold safety factors. Such protective factors were based on the concern that humans as a species could be more sensitive than the laboratory animals; that there would be greater variability in sensitivity among humans than among genetically inbred laboratory animals all raised in a similar environment; and that there could be adverse non-lethal effects that should be avoided. A presumptive tenfold safety factor has been added specifically to protect children, in recognition of their greater risk to certain chemicals compared to adults (National Research Council 1993).
	The inherent assumption in the safety factor approach is that there is a threshold dose level below which there are no adverse effects. However, in carcinogenesis, a single mutation could be the basis for the entire cancer process. As each molecule of a carcinogen, at least theoretically, could cause this mutation, a threshold cannot be assumed, and thus, in a simplified expression, there is no level of exposure that is without risk. However, almost all DNA damage is repaired by efficient cellular processes. Some unrepaired mutations are lethal to the cell, and as dead cells do not reproduce, these mutations cannot be the basis for cancer or inherited abnormalities. The majority of mutations are silent and have no discernible effects. Accordingly, the risk of any one molecule actually causing cancer is infinitesimally small—literally trillions of molecules of carcinogens are inhaled with every cigarette, yet not all cigarette smokers develop cancer. However, the assumption that there is no zero risk in regards to chemical and physical carcinogens has a major impact on communicating to the public about cancer risk.
	There are known circumstances in which cancer causation does depend upon exceeding a threshold level of a chemical (e.g. the mechanism by which saccharin causes bladder cancer in laboratory animals appears to proceed through the precipitation of saccharin in the bladder, which requires a dose sufficient to exceed the physicochemical processes determining saccharin solubility). However, prudent management of cancer risk usually assumes that a carcinogen is ‘guilty until proven innocent’ of having no risk-free level. In essence, the burden of proof is on industry to demonstrate scientifically that a cancer-causing chemical does indeed have a threshold.
	The four major components of risk assessment are listed in Box 7.4.1.
	 	Box 7.4.1 Components of risk assessment
	Hazard identification: Determining whether a specific chemical or physical agent is causally linked to a specific endpoint of concern; that is, chemicals have specific effects, or the second law of toxicology.
	Dose–response evaluation: Determining the relation between the magnitude of exposure and the probability of occurrence of the specific endpoint of concern; that is, the dose makes the poison, or the first law of toxicology.
	Exposure evaluation: Determining who and how many people will be exposed; the routes of exposure; and the magnitude, duration, and timing of exposure.
	Risk characterization: Describing the nature and often the magnitude of the human risk, including attendant uncertainty.





Hazard identification


	Hazard is the potential for harm. It is an intrinsic property of a substance or situation. Risk is the likelihood of harm occurring (and the likely severity of the resulting effect). It is a function of both hazard and exposure: for example, asbestos fibres sealed in a ceiling of an office have the potential to cause health effects (hazard), but the likelihood of that occurring is low if the ceiling is left intact (risk). However, if the ceiling is demolished and dust containing the asbestos fibres is released, the risk to health can be considerable. The risk has changed because of the circumstances of exposure. Identifying the presence of a hazard is just one step in risk assessment; subsequent steps, such as exposure evaluation, are key to determining what preventive action needs to be taken to reduce the risk.
	Regulatory and quasi-scientific bodies often use a weight-of-evidence approach to identify a hazard. In essence, a panel of scientists judges whether sufficient evidence exists to identify an agent or condition as posing a risk of a specific effect in humans, or in some other target such as an ecosystem. In the United States, the approach to permitting the marketing of a new chemical is to have an internal Environmental Protection Agency scientific group review the chemical structure and other data submitted by industry. Similarly, the US Food and Drug Administration relies heavily on an advisory committee process to review evidence of efficacy and toxicity before approving a new pharmaceutical agent or medical device.
	Formal weight-of-evidence approaches have been particularly useful in evaluating potential human carcinogens. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) of the World Health Organization uses this approach, convening expert panels to evaluate the evidence for carcinogenicity of specific chemical compounds or defined mixtures (e.g. diesel fuel, wood dust). The focus is on the weight of the evidence for carcinogenicity based upon carefully framed criteria—considering animal toxicology, epidemiology, mechanistic information, and exposure data—but not on the potency of the compound as a cancer-causing agent. When assigning a score for carcinogenicity, IARC now includes increased weight on understanding toxicological mechanisms (Cogliano 2004). Many countries use the information produced by IARC to determine governmental regulatory approaches. In the United States, the IARC listing of carcinogens has no official status, but it carries much weight with regulators, as does a similar process used by the National Toxicology Program for its Report on Carcinogens (National Toxicology Program 2015).
	Relatively few chemicals have been reported capable of causing cancer in humans. Of the perhaps 70,000 to 100,000 chemicals in commerce, about 100 are known to be human carcinogens. To an extent, this represents the success of environmental health science in providing tools that guide chemical manufacturers away from new chemicals that are potentially carcinogenic. During the chemical development process, early application of simple test batteries that evaluate the potential for mutagenesis or other predictors of cancer causation provides a responsible chemical industry with the means to avoid producing carcinogens or other potentially harmful products—and the means to avoid the regulatory and toxic tort consequences of harming the public. The value of this primary preventive approach depends upon the availability of effective toxicological test batteries. Such tests depend upon a basic understanding of the chemical and biological processes underlying toxic effects. Unfortunately, the investment in using standardized test batteries for high-production-volume chemicals, and the major increase in such investments due to new requirements such as the EU REACH legislation (see section 5.5), has not been accompanied by recognition of the need to develop better and more effective tests to protect the public. Advances in molecular toxicology provide many opportunities to improve these test batteries (National Research Council 2007).





Dose–response evaluation


	The key issues in dose–response evaluation involve how to extrapolate from the high doses at which an effect is observed in an animal or epidemiological study to the usually much lower levels of risk which are of public or policy concern. Crucial to extrapolation are assumptions about the shape of the dose–response curve). It must be emphasized that the levels of risk desired by society (e.g. in the range of less than 1 in 10,000 to less than 1 in a million over a lifetime) are usually too low to be scientifically verifiable. This is particularly true given that the endpoints of concern cannot be attributed solely to the environmental hazard under consideration, as illustrated in Box 7.4.2.
	 	Box 7.4.2 Benzene and leukaemia in the United States
	Based upon extrapolation from both epidemiological and animal studies, an individual’s lifetime exposure to 1 microgram/m3 benzene in air is estimated to result in an increase in the lifetime risk of leukaemia of 2.2–7.8 in a million (US Environmental Protection Agency 2002). In the United States, a reasonable average outdoor level of benzene is approximately 3 micrograms/m3, which would predict a lifetime risk of 6.6–23.4 in a million caused by this benzene exposure. Regulatory approaches that decrease that outdoor background level by two-thirds to 1.0 micrograms/m3 benzene nationwide would be estimated to decrease the risk of benzene-induced leukaemia by two-thirds. This would mean that nationwide, there would be 4.4–15.6 fewer cases of leukaemia per lifetime for every 1 million Americans, or a lifetime risk of approximately 10 in a million.
	Assuming a 70-year lifetime, and 350 million Americans, one can estimate that there would be 50 fewer cases of leukaemia a year nationwide as a result of a two-thirds decrease in outdoor benzene levels. This is a very small percentage of National Cancer Institute’s estimate of 62,130 new cases of leukaemia in the United States in 2017 (http://www.cancer.gov/cancertopics/types/leukemia). While preventing 50 leukaemia cases is socially desirable, there are no current epidemiological or animal toxicology methods that could scientifically validate these assumptions. A further complication is that for most of the US population, unregulated and highly variable indoor exposure to benzene, as well as to many other volatile organic compounds, far exceeds outdoor exposure. In fact, the major reason for a decrease in personal benzene exposure in the United States has been the decline in cigarette smoking, for smokers, and its restriction from public places, for non-smokers (Goldstein et al. 2011).





Exposure evaluation


	Exposure evaluation determines the extent to which an individual is exposed to a toxic agent (i.e. determining the dose), and thus involves both monitoring of environmental and individual samples as well as modelling. This process is complicated because the selected indicators of exposure should be representative—reflecting the actual dose. Box 7.4.3 (A) demonstrates the complications of representative exposure. Note also that knowing the dose alone does not allow one to assess the risk posed by the toxic agent. The dose–response relationship may change under different exposure scenarios. Several factors related to exposure, such as timing (i.e. dose-time-response relationship), may mediate the dose–response relationship and should be considered during risk assessment, as illustrated in Box 7.4.3 (B).
	 	Box 7.4.3 Asbestos and asbestos-related diseases





(A) Measuring asbestos exposure level and assessing mesothelioma risk


	Asbestos has been classified as a Group 1 human carcinogen by the IARC. Exposure to asbestos can lead to cancer, such as lung cancer and mesothelioma. To estimate the risk of respiratory tract cancers in relation to asbestos exposure in occupational settings, airborne asbestos concentration measured by fibre per cubic centimetre (f/cc) or fibre per cubic metre (f/m3) has been widely used as an indicator. However, asbestos also exists as a health threat in the general living environment, such as in older buildings and structures. Data on residential exposure are often lacking, which limits the estimation of cumulative exposure level, let alone lifetime mesothelioma risk. Researchers have applied an alternative method to calculate individual asbestos exposure level by analysing the asbestos in a lung sample. Based on a population-based study in the United Kingdom, the lifetime risk of mesothelioma is 0.02% per 1,000 amphibole fibres per gram of dry lung tissue (Gilham et al. 2016).





(B) Dose-time-response relationship between asbestos and asbestos-related diseases


	A majority of mesothelioma cases are caused by occupational exposure to asbestos. The dose–response relationship between asbestos and mesothelioma may change with different age at first exposure. Epidemiological studies suggest that the lifetime mesothelioma risk increases with cumulative level of exposure, duration of exposure, and also the timing of first exposure. That is, early exposure to asbestos is likely to exacerbate the risk of mesothelioma and thus warrants long-term surveillance programmes that begin in childhood (Lacourt et al. 2012; Lacourt et al. 2017).
	Exposure evaluation is central to managing environmental risks. Advances in the field of exposure science are particularly crucial to understanding aggregate and cumulative risk (International Life Science Institute 2003; US Environmental Protection Agency 2003). Aggregate risk takes into account the different pathways of exposure for the same chemical. Cumulative risk describes the multiple effects of different agents through different routes. In essence, this is an assessment of the impact of the mix of external synthetic and natural chemicals in which we all live. Cumulative risk assessment is particularly pertinent to environmental justice considerations.
	The importance of exposure assessment to understanding risk is exemplified by investigations into potential adverse health consequences resulting from man-made and natural disasters. Notable examples include the attack on the World Trade Center in New York City in September 2001, and the earthquake and tsunami that destroyed the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant in March 2011. Careful evaluation of disease endpoints in relation to exposure will help unravel the highly litigious issue of whether responders or the general public have an increased incidence of disease from exposures related to an event or the clean-up process. New protocols and tools to assess exposures resulting from man-made and natural disasters may help better evaluate the exposure–effect relationship (Lioy et al. 2006).





Risk characterization


	The seemingly straightforward process of characterizing risk through hazard identification, dose–response evaluation, and exposure evaluation presents many challenges. To start with, those doing the characterization can put their own spin on the findings. For example, people are likely to respond differently to something characterized as 99% free of risk than to the numerically equivalent 1% likelihood of a serious consequence including death. Characterizing exactly who is at risk (the denominator) is also a challenge. Reporting risk in terms of the entire exposed general public can trivialize the risk experienced by a highly sensitive subpopulation, such as those with asthma.
	Risk can be displaced from one country to another. For instance, in 2006, hazardous waste illegally sent from Europe and dumped in the Ivory Coast was reported to have caused 9,000 acute illnesses and 6 deaths in Abidjan (Greenpeace 2006, 2012). The Ivory Coast, lacking internal expertise, had to use its funds to hire a European company to retrieve, ship, and process the toxic waste. The European company that dumped the waste made a series of payments to the Ivorian government and to individual claimants without admitting liability. In July 2010, a Dutch court found the company guilty of illegally exporting toxic waste from Amsterdam and concealing the nature of the cargo, and imposed a fine on the company.
	A long-standing debate exists on the extent to which numerical uncertainty, rather than a simple qualitative statement of the major sources of uncertainty, should be a routine part of risk characterization. Those in favour of routinely providing numerical boundaries that quantify the extent of uncertainty point out that the many estimates and default assumptions in a risk assessment provide wide ranges of uncertainty that should be presented to the risk manager and the general public.
	Those in favour of more restricted use of quantitative uncertainty analysis point out that most risk assessments are scoping activities aimed at considering alternatives or developing priorities. Further, major societal decisions are often made on numerical estimates for which no uncertainty factors are given (e.g. gross domestic product, unemployment estimates). Note that the qualitative issues underlying uncertainty in a risk analysis should always be transparent to the risk manager and affected stakeholders.





The future of risk assessment


	Risk assessment as a formal process for evaluating environmental agents continues to evolve, and in the last few decades, more sophisticated approaches to assessing cancer risk and cumulative and aggregate risk have been developed. The use of molecular toxicology to replace standard default assumptions is particularly promising (National Research Council 2007). Just as in other natural sciences, advances in data handling and informatics provide opportunities to assess larger and more complex databases. Advances in epidemiologic methodology using biological indicators of exposure and effect based upon ecogenetics and other molecular biological techniques may be particularly fruitful (Omenn 2000). Conceptually, our genetic makeup loads the gun, but the environment pulls the trigger. Identification of subpopulations sensitive to environmental agents will challenge regulatory and legal interpretations of the many environmental health laws aimed at protecting susceptible populations.
	Global harmonization of risk assessment has been underway for decades. This will particularly be needed to avoid the use of environmental health principles as a façade for trade barriers. Evidence-based approaches to toxicology, similar to those increasingly used in medicine, are a welcome development. It remains a challenge to use such approaches for risk assessments that depend heavily on extrapolation to levels of risk below the readily observable—that is, where evidence will be indirect.
	The regulatory approach to protecting worker health from toxic chemicals is often based upon both a measurable workplace standard and a subtle measure of effect. Thus for benzene, there is a 1 part per million, 8-hour time-weighted average workplace air standard, as well as a requirement for routine blood counts. The latter informs the former, in terms of both whether unmeasured exposures may be occurring and whether a reconsideration of the allowable external standard is needed. Red cell, white cell, and platelet counts can be affected by a variety of common conditions (e.g. infections, iron-deficiency anaemia), thus surveillance findings must be carefully evaluated before any observations are ascribed to benzene exposure.
	In contrast, environmental standards are almost always measures of external emissions or ambient levels of pollutants. Such standards are surrogates for the desired goal of avoiding adverse consequences to human health and the environment. Achieving a level of scientific knowledge that would permit direct evaluation of subtle biological precursors of adverse effects is a desired route to developing emission standards that are truly protective. There is much work in progress in this field of environmental health indicators.
	The history of protecting human life from the consequences of environmental agents is the history of catching up to the adverse effects of otherwise beneficial new technology—starting with the human use of fire. A new technology with potential for both beneficial and adverse consequences is nanotechnology. Decreased particle size can result in unexpected new physicochemical properties, in part due to a very high surface-to-volume ratio (Helland et al. 2007). There is concern about what nanoparticles may do at the cellular level and whether current toxicological testing schemes and regulatory processes are adequate to protect against potential harm.
	Multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) are a type of manufactured nanomaterial. As use of MWCNTs widens, increased exposure via raw materials and consumer products is expected. The MWCNT-7 version was classified as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B) by the IARC in 2014, following results from numerous in vivo studies (Grosse et al. 2014). In 2017, the IARC declared other MWCNTs, as well as single-walled carbon nanotubes, not classifiable for carcinogenicity to humans (Group 3) (International Agency for Research on Cancer 2017). However, toxicological principles are still relevant and central to the risk assessment process, as demonstrated in Box 7.4.4.
	 	Box 7.4.4 Potential environmental risks of carbon nanomaterials
	Scientists have identified concerns about the spread of nanomaterials in consumer products to the environment. Carbon nanomaterials (CNMs), for example, have been widely used in commercial products, such as rechargeable batteries, automotive parts, sporting goods, boat hulls, and water filters (De Volder et al. 2013). CNMs can be released into the environment via manufacturing facilities, landfills, wastewater treatment plants, or accidental release, further disrupting ecosystems (Nowack and Bucheli 2007). Several types of CNMs, such as C60 fullerene, multiwalled carbon nanotubes, and single-walled carbon nanotubes, could be adsorbed by and accumulate in plant roots where the soil or culture medium contains such CNMs.
	CNMs have both positive and negative effects on plant growth. For example, CNMs may inhibit rice growth, as measured by shoot height and root length (Hao et al. 2018). However, CNMs have also been used as fertilizer, and carbon nanotubes are used in agricultural sciences to enhance plant growth, by positioning micro-tubes inside the plant to enhance the efficiency of water uptake (Vithanage et al. 2017). Although Bjorkland et al. found low bioaccumulation of carbon nanotubes in plants, invertebrates, and non-mammalian vertebrates (Bjorkland et al. 2017), the overall health risk of CNMs to humans via plant consumption, as well as the risk from environmental exposures, needs further assessment (Guinee et al. 2017).
	Future developments in risk assessment are likely to include discovery of new risks from old agents in new forms of use, and estimation of the combined effects of low-dose exposure to mixed agents (Miller et al. 2017). With more scientific evidence showing health risks attributable to toxic agents will come more opportunities for scientists to provide timely and robust policy recommendations. To protect public and environmental health, we will need policies that promptly regulate the use and distribution of identified toxic agents. The challenge is to narrow the gaps between scientific evidence and policy application (Gross and Birnbaum 2017).
	Regulatory system design drives the ways that the risk of chemicals can be controlled. Chemical agents are used in a wide range of industries to produce consumer products, and new technology may involve new use of such agents. However, the environmental risks of most chemicals have not been quantified: industrial production processes often grow and change too fast for adequate risk assessment to be conducted. In the mid-twentieth century, there was often insufficient toxicological information to estimate the environmental health risks posed by extensive consumption of all the new chemical substances. Some regulatory schemes, such as the Toxic Substances Control Act in the United States, enacted in 1976, were developed under the assumption that ‘a substance is safe, unless it can be proven unsafe’. This placed the burden of proof on the governmental agency conducting the risk assessment. Since the EU’s REACH passed in 2006, the regulatory paradigm has been shifting to a new assumption, that ‘a substance is unsafe, unless it can be proven safe’ (Krimsky 2017).
	In addition, many of the established dose–response relationships address single toxic agents, as do the regulations that set exposure limits and standards. The cumulative impact of low-dose exposure to multiple toxic agents is often neglected. For example, according to the Environmental Impact Assessment Act in Taiwan, governmental approval of new industrial developments that exceed a certain production capacity requires a health risk assessment. Yet the risk assessments performed have addressed only the incremental additional health risk associated with the new development, ignoring the cumulative health risk associated with industrial and other factors across the entire geographic area (Lin et al. 2016). If low-dose and long-term exposures to multiple toxic agents continue, people who are initially considered as a low-risk group can eventually become a high-risk group.
	Although it is important to identify people at high risk in order to develop early prevention strategies (high-risk strategy), interventions for widespread environmental hazards should also cater to those at lower risk (population strategy) (Lanphear 2017); unless there is a compelling reason to exclude them. This is the concept of prevention paradox (see Box 7.4.5.)
	 	Box 7.4.5 The prevention paradox
	The prevention paradox, espoused by Geoffrey Rose in 1981, suggests that a large number of people exposed to low risk may generate more cases than a small number exposed to high risk. This is because when there is a small elevation in risk, the total burden of disease will increase more in the large group than in the small group. Conversely, an intervention that offers large benefits to the overall population might offer little benefit to the individual (Rose 1981). Two types of prevention strategy are the high-risk strategy and the population strategy. The high-risk strategy focuses on identifying high-risk individuals and providing individual protection. The population strategy focuses on controlling determinants of incidence and shifting the mean of hazard exposure to a lower level (Rose 2001).
	An estimate of population health gains resulting from 22 new preventive interventions in the Netherlands from 1970 to 2010 suggested that three-quarters of the gains were attributed to the population strategy and one-quarter to the high-risk strategy (Mackenbach et al. 2013). It should be noted that these two strategies are not always in competition. Choices can be made between the two strategies when establishing risk prevention policies, but the primary concern should be controlling the causes of incidence (Rose 2001).
	Risk assessments should not be one-off activities, but instead involve continued monitoring for potential or encountered adverse health effects through, for example, the development of new risk assessment tools or post-marketing surveillance. This is illustrated in the case study in Box 7.4.6.
	 	Box 7.4.6 Case study: safety of genetically modified crops
	Advances in genetically modified (GM) technology in foods, or genetically modified organisms 2.0, have brought on a rapid revolution of crops to meet the global demand for food both quantitatively and qualitatively. In the United States, common GM crops include canola, corn, cotton, soy, and sugar beet. Two types of health risks have arisen: direct risk from the intake of GM foods, and indirect exposure to herbicides used on GM crops.
	Currently, the health risk from dietary intake of GM foods is believed to be low. Two National Academy of Sciences reviews, in 2000 and 2004, concluded that genetically modified organisms pose no unique hazards to health. However, the reviews also recommended the development of new risk assessment tools and post-marketing surveillance.
	In contrast, the herbicides used on GM crops carry substantial health risks such as carcinogenicity. There has been a sharp increase of herbicides applied to GM crops in the past few decades. For example, the herbicide most widely used on GM crops is glyphosate, and its use in the United States increased by more than 250 times in the past 40 years (from 0.4 million kg used in 1974 to 113 million kg in 2014). The global use of this herbicide has increased by more than 10 times.
	As glyphosate-resistant weeds became more widespread, Enlist Duo—a combined herbicide product containing glyphosate and 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D)—was introduced by a chemical manufacturing company. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) first approved the use of Enlist Duo in 2014, and its use is projected to increase. The following year, in 2015, IARC classified glyphosate as a probable human carcinogen (Group 2A) and 2,4-D as a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B). In 2015, the US EPA revoked its approval of Enlist Duo, stating that the herbicide might be more toxic than previously thought. However, in 2017, the US EPA approved Enlist Duo once again, despite the lack of any significant change in its environmental and health assessments. These ever-changing developments raise new concerns about the safety of GM crops (Guyton et al. 2015; Landrigan and Benbrook 2015).
	An important goal of evaluating human health risks is to reduce the population’s exposure to toxic agents and improve environmental quality. While conventional risk assessments focus on the mechanism of toxic agents on human health, cumulative risk assessments should include both environmental sources of toxic agents and social determinants of exposure. An abundance of scientific literature shows that environmental health risks cause more burden in socioeconomically disadvantaged populations and communities—the same communities which have long been excluded from the decision-making processes resulting in environmental laws, regulations, and policies (Mohai et al. 2009; Kalnins and Dowell 2015).
	Incorporating social determinants of health into risk assessment can promote environmental justice. While uneven exposure to environmental hazards is now well recognized and awareness of environmental justice is rising, the pollution gap between rich and poor communities remains and has even widened. Take the emission of toxic release inventory in the United States: people living in the poorest counties have seen a decrease in emissions of 18%, yet those in the richest counties had a 68% reduction in emissions (Kalnins and Dowell 2015).





Risk management and risk communication


	Following risk assessment—which is evaluating the consequences of exposure to environmental agents—risk management becomes important. Risk management is a decision-making process of selecting and determining how to manage the identified environmental risks and how to implement the regulatory response (Commission on Risk Assessment and Risk Management 1997). This process can also help governments prioritize how they allocate resources to risks (Rocks et al. 2017).
	However, in the real world, there is often a gap between risk levels, governmental priorities, and public interest (Commission on Risk Assessment and Risk Management 1997). Thus, understanding the risk perceived by the general public and properly communicating potential hazards to stakeholders can lead to more effective risk management (Commission on Risk Assessment and Risk Management 1997; Rocks et al. 2017). For environmental emergency scenarios, communication of risk to the general public should start as early as possible to ensure comprehensive understanding and prevent panic (Bol 2016).
	Risk communication is the exchange of information about environmental risks among risk assessors, managers, news media, interested groups, and the general public (National Research Council 1989). An example is the concern over adverse health effects following the large-scale nuclear accident at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant in Japan in March 2011. The first concern raised was about health risks to the local population due to radiation exposure. Although such risks were found to be limited (World Health Organization 2013), related information should have been delivered to residents in a timely and appropriate way to prevent anxiety and mistrust of the authorities.
	In addition to reporting the level of toxic agents and the risk of developing disease, risk communication should also aim to prevent potential stigma from attaching to polluted areas. Development of a health literacy toolkit that translates scientific and medical jargon into terms understandable by the general population can help medical professionals answer people’s questions and monitor their health (Murakami et al. 2017; Goto et al. 2018).
	Another concern related to the Fukushima Daiichi event was food safety, both inside and outside the region, due to radioactive materials leaking from the nuclear plant. This also posed a challenge to international trade and public health in other countries. The general public have expressed concerns about the indirect and long-term health risks from dietary exposure to contaminated food (Hasegawa et al. 2015; Cho et al. 2017). Right after the accident, the Japanese government set limits for radioactive elements and restricted the sale and distribution of food products from Fukushima and other areas with significant contamination. The immediate actions (e.g. announcing new guidelines) and timely communication (e.g. providing food safety education and disclosing information to the public) were key to relieving concerns about radiation residues in food products, promoting food safety, and securing food supply stability (Gilmour et al. 2016; Cho et al. 2017).





The precautionary principle


	A key issue facing risk management is how to proceed in the presence of hazard data with limited or no evidence of human toxicity. Applying the precautionary principle while additional scientific information is being gathered is one approach. The precautionary principle was given impetus by the 1992 Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, which provided the following statement: ‘In order to protect the environment, the precautionary approach shall be widely applied by States according to their capabilities. Where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation’ (United Nations Environmental Programme 1992). The Rio Declaration forces the consideration of precautionary intervention but does not necessarily require such intervention. It includes qualifying language such as ‘according to their capabilities’ and ‘cost-effective measures’. Furthermore, the triple negative notion—that the absence of rigorous proof of danger does not justify inaction—is viewed by some as rather weak (World Commission on the Ethics of Scientific Knowledge and Technology 2005).
	There are many variants of the precautionary principle, and extensive literature devoted to developing a more rigorous definition. To some, the precautionary principle is merely a means to build more public health protection into quantitative risk analysis, with additional prudent defaults and safety factors to protect at-risk populations and a further focus on uncertainty. To others, the precautionary principle is a new way of addressing environmental risk and dealing with complexity and uncertainty. Its use is more likely to provide timely and preventive interventions (Kriebel and Tickner 2001; Martuzzi 2007). Some of the important approaches advocated by the precautionary principle, such as transparency and involvement of stakeholders, have also been frequently advocated under the rubric of risk assessment and management.
	The United States banned the production of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) in 1976, despite industry opposition, then and now, on the grounds of uncertain science. The continual decline in body burden of PCBs and dioxins has thus been accomplished based on regulatory decisions. Yet advancing the science needed for public health decision-making must remain a major goal, despite the usefulness of the precautionary principle (Foster et al. 2000; Goldstein and Carruth 2003, 2004; Grandjean et al. 2004).
	The working definition of the precautionary principle proposed by UNESCO (see Box 7.4.7; italics in the original) includes the firm statement that actions based upon the precautionary principle should be subject to continuous analysis and review (World Commission on the Ethics of Scientific Knowledge and Technology 2005). A number of major concerns have been raised about the precautionary principle, for example, what does it add to standard public health concepts? Is it true that complex scientific questions are unsolvable and, if so, is the precautionary principle needed to promote action in the face of scientific uncertainty? In view of its alleged use to justify trade barriers, is it still possible to advocate the precautionary principle as an antidote to biased decision-making?
	 	Box 7.4.7 Working definition of the precautionary principle
	‘When human activities may lead to morally unacceptable harm that is scientifically plausible but uncertain, actions shall be taken to avoid or diminish that harm. Morally unacceptable harm refers to harm to humans or the environment that is
	 	• threatening to human life or health, or
	• serious and effectively irreversible, or
	• inequitable to present or future generations, or
	• imposed without adequate consideration of the human rights of those affected.
	The judgement of plausibility should be grounded in scientific analysis. Analysis should be ongoing so that chosen actions are subject to review. Uncertainty may apply to, but need not be limited to, causality or the bounds of the possible harm. Actions are interventions that are undertaken before harm occurs that seek to avoid or diminish the harm. Actions should be chosen that are proportional to the seriousness of the potential harm, with consideration of their positive and negative consequences, and with an assessment of the moral implications of both action and inaction. The choice of action should be the result of a participatory process.’
	Reproduced with permission from COMEST (World Commission on the Ethics of Scientific Knowledge and Technology), The Precautionary Principle, Copyright © 2005 United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, available from http://unesdoc.unesco. org/images/0013/001395/139578e.pdf.
	The precautionary principle is said to be pertinent in situations where the scientific evidence is uncertain. One example is the management of the health and environmental risks of endocrine disruptors. This is particularly challenging due to the need to consider the interactive effects of multiple chemicals with a wide range of additive, synergistic, and antagonistic interactions (Kortenkamp 2007). A case study is shown in Box 7.4.8.
	 	Box 7.4.8 The precautionary principle and bisphenol A
	Worldwide, over 3 million tonnes of bisphenol A (BPA) are produced annually. BPA can be found in many consumer products. These include reusable water bottles, baby bottles, implantable medical devices, and dental sealants. BPA is also a component of epoxy resins, which are used to overlay the inside of food and beverage cans, in cardboard and papers used for food wrapping, in some plastic water pipes, and in paints and cigarette filters. Of concern is the fact that BPA leaches out from these consumer products, even under normal use conditions. The leaching increases under high temperatures, and with exposure to acidic or basic solutions.
	Animal studies have shown that BPA may alter male and female reproductive tract development, the brain, and the mammary glands. In large-scale human population studies in various parts of the world, BPA has been detected in urine, blood, saliva, breast milk, and tissues and fluids associated with pregnancy at levels similar to those that have been shown to cause damage in animals. In a study of over 5,000 people in Canada, over 90% had detectable levels of BPA in urine, with a geometric mean concentration of 1.16 ng/mL (Bushnik et al. 2010). Health Canada has stated that precaution is warranted, since it is not possible to dismiss the potential harmful effects of BPA (Health Canada 2010). With this statement, Canada became the first country to declare BPA a health hazard, but additional regulatory action has yet to be taken (Vandenberg 2011).
	Practical insight into the debate about the precautionary principle versus risk assessment can be found in the way the EU and other countries evaluate the safety of chemicals. The EU promulgated the REACH regulations, after much debate, with its proponents focusing on the precautionary principle as a rationale for the new legislation. REACH requires industry to develop data, assess risk, and provide information about virtually all chemicals in use, including constituents of product mixtures. No distinction is made between newly developed chemicals or those long available in commerce—a contrast with the US Toxic Substances Control Act, whose weakness in this regard led to the inadequate testing of compounds such as the gasoline additive methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE) before its inappropriate release into the environment (Erdal and Goldstein 2000).
	The cost of implementing REACH is estimated at US$3–6 billion for obtaining data and registering compounds over the first 11 years. Risk assessment, based on both toxicity and exposure, will be used extensively throughout the process, including for setting priorities for data needs and making decisions on regulatory approaches. Unfortunately, there appears to be no uniform coordinated effort to develop the research where toxicological data is scant.
	Unfortunately, the precautionary principle has been tainted through disagreements over application. The United States, Canada, and other countries disagreed with the EU on the extent of risk to health from consumption of hormone-treated beef or genetically modified foods. The EU’s use of the precautionary principle to establish a stringent aflatoxin standard, to the detriment of exports of sub-Saharan countries, has been criticized as the misuse of public health principles for trade protectionism (Goldstein 2007). The risk of exposure to electromagnetic fields from the use of mobile phones is another contentious and confused issue, resulting in advice based on a mix of the precautionary principle and the scientific evidence.
	The primary missing ingredient in the approach to ever more complex environmental challenges, including such broader issues as global warming, is a systems-based approach incorporating the best science and focusing on the most important questions. We need to have a more systematic and coordinated effort to respond to the challenges of fragmented national and international approaches to environmental issues that produce piecemeal efforts which may lead us to fall further behind in protecting public health and the environment.





Conclusion


	Understanding the web of environmental cause and effect relations is an increasing challenge in an ever more connected world. Advances in toxicology, filtered through an appropriate appreciation of the optimal approaches to analysing and presenting risks to an involved public, are crucial to protecting public health and the environment.
