Urbanization, governance, and health


	The physical and social characteristics and dynamics in cities that influence health do not happen randomly or by accident. Cities and metropolitan regions more generally are not shaped by faceless forces of natural succession and competition. People and organized groups or coalitions actively accomplish cities and urban neighbourhoods, and the process is rarely the same from here to there. There are real winners and losers in the political struggles of place making, and static definitions of physical and social variables rarely captures this dynamic of places. The political processes of urban place-making and remaking are what I refer to as ‘urban governance’. (Burris et al. 2007) As Szreter (2005) notes (see Chapter 1.2), social movements were critical in reshaping public health priorities, whose knowledge is considered, and how civil society plays an important role in democratic decision-making.
	The term governance is broadly understood as attentive to the relationships between the overlapping spheres of political, economic, and social life, as each aim to influence collective action. Governance is not government, but is inherently about the struggle and conflict between formal institutions and organizations and informal norms and practices. Urban governance includes a complex mix of different contexts, actors, arenas, and issues, where struggles over power can be manifested in public discourses or tacit day-to-day routines. An urban governance approach to urban health is attentive to both processes and outcomes, and must ask questions such as: what conditions lead to planners using or abusing power, responding to or even resisting market forces, working to empower some groups and dis-empower others, promoting multiparty consensual decision-making discourses or simply rationalizing decisions already made? (Corburn 2013). The governance approach views urban planning as a process that includes the shaping of public agendas and attention, available evidence, and norms of inquiry, inclusive or exclusive deliberations, and responses (or lack thereof) to bias, discrimination, inequality, and a recalcitrant state. An attention to governance moves health equity planning away from only focusing on vulnerable people or places to also include altering the political processes and institutions that work to maintain the social inequities driving urban health inequities (Friel et al. 2011).





Toward a twenty-first century science for urbanization and health: addressing toxic stress


	Twenty first century urbanization must embrace the now well-documented idea that social stress can be toxic to the human body, especially when place-based stressors are chronic and cumulative across one’s lifetime (McEwen and McEwen 2017). While stress can be life saving for most—think of the fight-or-flight mechanism—constant adversity is toxic, meaning that the prolonged activation of the stress response systems can disrupt the development of the brain architecture and other biologic systems. Some of the multiple, chronic stressors experienced by the poor and marginalized populations in cities appear in Figure 7.6.1 (Hajat et al. 2015). These stressors often begin in-utero, and individual behaviour changes alone cannot redress their impacts.
	Fig. 7.6.1 Urban toxic stressors that adversely impact human health.
	Corburn, J. 2013. Healthy City Planning: From Neighbourhood to National Health Equity. London: Routledge.
	As shown in Figure 7.6.2, under ‘normal’ stressful situations the human body undergoes a range of physical and chemical responses, but primarily the hormones epinephrine (adrenaline) and cortisol are released to heighten one’s awareness, but these eventually ‘shut off’ when the threat is over and the body returns to homeostasis (Fig. 7.6.2, solid line). The body’s ability to maintain stability under stress has been called allostasis (McEwen and McEwen 2017). In toxic stress situations, stressors are constant and the ‘allostatic load’ continues to increase and the release of ‘fight-or-flight’ hormones does not properly regulate or shut-off (Fig. 7.6.2, dashed line). Increased allostatic load wears away at the immune system as it overworks to manage the hormonal releases and attempt to return to homeostasis. Under toxic stress circumstances, the oversecretion of cortisol and adrenaline trigger other biologic responses like poor immune response, poor glucose regulation, and constant feelings of hunger that can contribute to chronic diseases such as overweight and obesity, diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, stroke, asthma, and mental health disorders (Velasquez-Manoff 2012). Some known toxic stressors include chronic poverty, racial, gender, and other forms of discrimination and marginalization, physical or emotional abuse, exposure to violence and housing instability (Berger and Sarnyai 2014). Allostaic load has been linked with changes in the length of telomeres, which are DNA-protein complexes capping the ends of chromosomes that protect them against damage. Telomere shortening is considered a marker of cellular ageing (Price et al. 2013).
	Fig. 7.6.2 Chronic stress and its biologic impacts.
	Since populations in many deprived and impoverished areas of cities are likely experiencing multiple ‘toxic stressors’, twenty-first century urbanization and health must be attentive to the physical and social stressors in places, such as chronic poverty and discrimination, housing instability, and exposure to violence. The toxic stress idea suggests that a twenty-first century science for the healthy city can no longer view a person as, for example, one day an African immigrant, another day born low birth weight, another day raised in a home bearing remnants of lead paint, another day subjected to racial discrimination at work, and still another day living in a racially segregated neighbourhood without a supermarket or access to transport. Just as the body does not neatly partition these experiences—all of which may serve to increase risk of uncontrolled hypertension and related morbidity and premature mortality—the twenty-first century urban health planner can no longer separate these spheres and sectors in research or practice (Corburn 2013).





Twenty-first century urbanization and health governance


	Measuring and addressing urban toxic stress will demand new, interdisciplinary action-research into the context-specific factors that might be making particular urban residents unhealthy and more susceptible to disease, disability, and death. This work must privilege partnerships, participation, and power-sharing between scientists, the urban poor themselves, social movements, and state-level decision-makers. There is no one-size-fits all approach. I borrow a term from the Science Studies, economics, and development literatures to call this collaborative urban health approach co-production (Jasanoff 2004). In the co-production of urban health, science is understood as dependent on the natural world, as well as historical events, social practices, material resources, and institutions that contribute to the construction, dissemination, and use of scientific knowledge. Political decision-making, in the co-production framework, does not take ‘scientific knowledge’ as a given, but seeks to reveal how science is conducted, communicated, and used. The co-production model problematizes knowledge and notions of expertise, challenging hard distinctions between expert-lay ways of knowing. Acting to understand and improve urban health, under the co-production approach, requires a negotiation among the always partial and plural positions of professionals and lay people. The co-production model also destabilizes the dominant view in science policymaking that science can be uncritically accepted as ‘fact’ and ‘truth’. The destabilizing stories and emphasis on the need for ‘negotiating expertise’, suggest that a deliberative science is necessary for the co-production of slum health knowledge for action (Corburn 2005).
	Adaptive ecosystem management offers a model of co-producing scientific research and practice for global urban health. Adaptive management acknowledges the failures of linear processes where narrow disciplinary scientists have aimed to develop complex models, predict long-term outcomes, and suggest one-time policy standards. Instead, adaptive management begins with an acknowledgement of the inherent complexity and uncertainty within systems, that this complexity demands an iterative, ongoing learning process among a range of expert stakeholders, and policy interventions must be adjusted to reflect newly acquired knowledge (Corburn 2013). Another difference between adaptive management and conventional science policy is that adaptive management does not postpone actions until definitive causality is known about a system, but rather emphasizes the importance of action in the face of uncertain science and couples these decisions tightly to rigorous monitoring.





Urban climate change adaptation


	Perhaps the key twenty-first century urban health challenge is ensuring the poor and most vulnerable residents and communities are able to adapt to a changing climate. The urban poor are some of the most vulnerable to the human health impacts of global climate change since, for instance, low-income, urban neighbourhoods may have less green space, housing located on flood-prone land, and fewer economic and social resources to escape and recover from heat, weather, and other climate-related stressors. Urban climate justice demands co-produced climate change adaptation plans that reduce risk and improve the health status of the poor and already vulnerable communities. This will demand new investments in urban infrastructure, such as housing, water, and sanitation, social and healthcare services, in urban communities that already experience health inequities. As many local governments, particularly in the Global South, experience severe capacity and resource constraints, co-produced adaptation demands a leadership role for the urban poor and civil society actors. Using this approach, urban climate justice would aim to not just reduce existing risks but also build-upon local institutional strengths and civic capacities.
	One such approach, used in Quito, Ecuador, resulted in the city’s Climate Change Action Plan that articulated the needs of marginalized groups, facilitated a youth-led Convention on Climate Change, incorporated local traditional and indigenous knowledge in the process, and defined ongoing civil society participation for climate action. Based on recommendations from Quito’s plan, the municipality has invested in socially vulnerable groups by building new water and sewerage infrastructure, social housing that enabled the poor to avoid living in unsafe structures on steep hillsides, reforested areas of the municipality as an ‘ecosystem service’ that could reduce mudslides and cool temperatures, and community-and school-based organic farming (AGRUPAR, Agricultura Urbana Participativa) that improves nutrition and food security for the urban poor (Chu et al. 2016). Quito’s food programme has multiple co-benefits; reducing malnutrition and vulnerability to climate-induced food supply disruptions for the urban poor, increasing employment and incomes, improving learning for children, enhancing water conservation and reuse, and reducing carbon emissions by limiting the travel distance along the food supply chain.





Health in all urban policies


	Health in All Policies (HiAP) is an approach to decision-making that aims to put the adaptive and co-production approach into practice (Shankardass et al. 2018). HiAP recognizes most public policies have the potential to influence health and health equity, either positively or negatively, but policymakers outside of the health sector may not be routinely considering the health consequences of their choices and thereby missing opportunities to advance health. HiAP emerged, in part, from the WHO’s Declaration of Alma-Ata in 1978 and reflects numerous international calls for policy action to address the SDOH (Freiler et al. 2013). The European Union endorsed HiAP in 2006 and the governments of Finland, Norway, Sweden, United Kingdom, Canada, South Australia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, Iran, and Brazil have all adopted some form of HiAP within governmental practice. The Dutch government actively supports municipalities to draft and implement HiAP strategies, but very few have managed to complete and implement these strategies, noting the difficulty in getting government actors and institutions outside the health sector to consider health impacts in their work (Storm et al. 2014). Some cities are actively working to integrate HiAP into their land use and planning decision-making. For example, Washington, DC passed the Sustainable DC Transformation Order in 2013, creating a HiAP Task Force and the Chicago Department of Public Health created the Healthy Chicago Interagency Council to integrate health across all city departments.
	The City of Richmond, California, in the San Francisco Bay Area, became the first city in the US to pass a HiAP ordinance in 2014 (Corburn et al. 2014). Richmond’s HiAP Ordinance is aligned with their General Plan and Budget, and includes intervention areas focused on how city policy, management, and service decisions can reduce the multiple toxic stressors residents and planners identified in Richmond. The HiAP Ordinance address six planning areas, including: (1) Governance and Leadership; (2) Economic Development and Education; (3) Full Service and Safe Communities; (4) Neighbourhood Built Environments; (5) Environmental Health and Justice; and (6) Quality and Accessible Health Homes and Social Services. In addition, HiAP includes a racial equity evaluation for all city projects, policies, and plans (Corburn et al. 2014).





Conclusions: pursuing greater urban health equity in the twenty-first century


	Contemporary inquiry into global urbanization and health can learn from the past to better understand how current trends gained resonance and what alternative futures might be possible. Alternative paradigms can be both practical and socially just, as the examples here suggest. However, more work needs to be done to avoid overgeneralizations and investigate specific contexts, how culture and politics shapes urbanization and appropriate health interventions. As global efforts to prioritize urban health continue, such as through the SDGs, a historical perspective is necessary to critically re-engage with urbanization as a structural determinant of health (WHO and UN Habitat 2016).
	As suggested here, re-orienting urbanization and the institutions behind it toward health will require moving toward integrated, multisector partnerships that target equity. Urban planners have a specific role to play by explicitly expanding the narrow framing of the ‘built environment and health’ to include social and political determinants of health, such as an attention to how racial discrimination contributes to place-based toxic stressors. This also demands that planners work with epidemiologists and others to break-down issue and sector fragmentation and the tendency in medicine and public health to focus only on one disease, risk factor, or behavioural change at a time. Civil society involvement, such as through activist social movements and ‘citizen scientists’, is crucial to ensure twenty-first century urbanization serves the well-being of the most vulnerable and marginalized populations and places.
	As discussed here, those concerned with urban health cannot wait until the science of health equity is definitive, but instead can rely on over a century of evidence that simultaneously addressing social, environmental, and economic inequalities can promote greater urban health equity.

8.1


Epidemiology and prevention of cardiovascular disease


	Nathan D. Wong and Wenjun Fan





Introduction


	Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) comprise the leading cause of morbidity and mortality, with recent 2015 estimates noting 422.7 million cases and 17.9 million deaths (Roth et al. 2017) and expected to grow to 23.6 million by the year 2030; 80% of these deaths occur in lower and middle income countries (WHO 2011). It is the largest contributor to non-communicable diseases (NCDs) that are now responsible for the largest share of morbidity and mortality worldwide. The incidence of CVD, including coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, heart failure, and stroke, as well as the prevalence of key risk factors, varies greatly according to geographical region, gender, and ethnic background. Multiple longitudinal epidemiological studies have provided valuable insights into the natural history and risk factors associated with the development and prognosis of CVD. Randomized clinical trials have demonstrated the value of management of several key risk factors for both the primary and secondary prevention of CVD. This chapter discusses the epidemiology of CVD, its associated risk factors and evidence for their control, assessment of CVD risk, and the evidence behind the control of CVD risk factors for the prevention of CVD.





Definitions, incidence, and distribution


	Cardiovascular disease comprises many conditions, including coronary heart disease, heart failure, rheumatic fever/rheumatic heart disease, stroke, and congenital heart disease. Ischaemic heart disease is typically the predominant manifestation of CVD and responsible for 46% of deaths due to CVD in men and 38% in women, followed closely by cerebrovascular disease at 34% and 37%, respectively (WHO 2011). Certain regions of the world, however, show ischaemic heart disease to be the cause of cardiovascular deaths in more than 50% of persons, with significant regional variations (Roth et al. 2017) (Fig. 8.1.1). While the burden of CVD was highest in Western countries during much of the 20th century, the highest mortality rates of CVD now occur among certain central Asian and Middle Eastern regions (Roth et al. 2017) (Fig. 8.1.2). By country, total death rates (per 100,000) from CVD, CHD, and stroke for the years 2012–2015 are highest in the Russian Federation for both men (1,041, 709, and 204, respectively) and women (433, 286, and 106, respectively) and among the lowest in Israel for men (96, 45, and 20, respectively) and in France for women (40, 9, and 12, respectively), with intermediate rates in the US (234, 124, and 27, respectively, in men and 117, 48, and 20, respectively, in women) (Benjamin et al. 2018).
	Fig. 8.1.1 Relative distribution of age-standardized cardiovascular deaths by cause for 21 global burden of disease regions.
	From Roth GA, Johnson C, Abajobir A, et al. Global, Regional, and National Burden of Cardiovascular Diseases for 10 Causes, 1990 to 2015. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2017 Jul 4;70(1):1–25 under a CC BY 4.0 license.
	Fig. 8.1.2 Age-standardized death rate from cardiovascular diseases by country, 2015.
	From Roth GA, Johnson C, Abajobir A, et al. Global, Regional, and National Burden of Cardiovascular Diseases for 10 Causes, 1990 to 2015. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2017 Jul 4;70(1):1–25 under a CC BY 4.0 license.
	In the United States, the overall prevalence of CVD in the years 2011–2014 (including hypertension) increases dramatically from 13.5% in men between the ages 20 and 39 years to 84.4% for men above 80+ years old; the corresponding figures for women were 11.5% and 86.5% (Benjamin et al. 2018).
	Of note, however, is the substantial reduction in CVD mortality rates in the US over the past three decades, both in men and in women, although absolute mortality from CVD in women, since 1985 has exceed that observed in men, until recent years when the number of deaths has been fewer in women than in men. These declines have been attributed both to improved treatments for CVD and its associated risk factors and to improvements in lifestyle factors such as substantial declines in cigarette smoking, although the increasing obesity epidemic is expected to negate some of these reductions in CVD.
	Myocardial infarction, angina pectoris, and sudden coronary death are the major clinical manifestations of CHD. CHD initially presents as sudden coronary death in approximately one-third of cases. Other forms of documented CHD include procedures done as a result of documented significant atherosclerosis, such as coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) or percutaneous coronary interventions (PCIs), including angioplasty and stenting. Persons with documented significant disease from a coronary angiogram, echocardiogram, nuclear myocardial perfusion, magnetic resonance imaging, or computed tomography angiographic or coronary calcium scan can also designate the presence of CHD; however, because the definitions used to define significant CHD vary and these findings often do not result in hospitalization or hard CHD events, such persons are not normally counted as incident or prevalent CHD, particularly for the purposes of endpoints in epidemiologic studies or clinical trials. Non-fatal or fatal myocardial infarction or sudden coronary death are most typically included as ‘hard’ CHD endpoints, while ‘total’ CHD may additionally include angina requiring hospitalization a well as PCI or CABG.
	CHD prevalence rates vary dramatically by age and gender in the United States. The most recent statistics from 2011 to 2014 showed that 16.5 million US adults aged 20 years and older have CHD; this varies widely by race and gender within the United States. For example, for males, while the overall prevalence was 7.4%, the prevalence in non-Hispanic white males was 7.7%, in black males 7.1%, in Mexican-American males 5.9%, and in Asian males 5.0%. The corresponding figures for females were 5.3% overall, 5.3% in non-Hispanic white females, 5.7% in black females, 6.1% in Mexican-American females and 2.6% in Asian females. An American experiences a heart attack every 40 seconds. CHD makes up more than half of all CVD deaths in men and women <75 years of age, with a lifetime risk (≥2 major risk factors) of developing CHD after age 55 years, of 37.5% for men and 18.3% for women (Benjamin et al. 2018).
	Other important manifestations of CVD include cerebrovascular disease (including stroke and transient ischaemic attacks), heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and peripheral arterial disease, in particular. Somewhat less common but still of significance are valvular heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, and bacterial and valvular endocarditis.
	Cerebrovascular disease includes stroke and transient ischaemic attacks (TIA). Stroke prevalence in the United States ranges from <1% in those <40 years of age to 14% in both genders in those aged 80 years and over. An estimated 7.2 million Americans aged 20 years and over have had a stroke; each year an estimated 795,000 persons experience a new or recurrent stroke, with approximately 610,000 of these cases being first attacks. Of all strokes, about 87% are ischaemic and 10% are intracerebral haemorrhagic strokes, and 3% subarachnoid haemorrhage strokes (Benjamin et al. 2018). The self-reported prevalence of physician-diagnosed TIAs is about 2.3%, translating to approximately 5 million persons, but the true prevalence is likely to be greater as many with neurological symptoms consistent of TIA fail to report them to their healthcare provider. About 12% of all strokes are preceded by a TIA.
	While mortality rates due to total CVD, and especially CHD and stroke, have declined substantially over the past 30 years, hospitalizations due to total CVD have increased, much of this fuelled by the more than doubling in the number of hospitalizations due to heart failure between 1980 and 2010 (1,023,000 in 2010 in the United States). It is projected that this will increase by another 25% by the year 2030. The prevalence of heart failure ranges from <1% in those under age 40 to 14.1% of men and 13.4% of women aged 80 years and over.
	Peripheral arterial disease is highly prevalent affecting approximately 8.5 million Americans aged 40 years and over and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality; it is most common in older persons over age 55 and is asymptomatic in most cases, being diagnosed by a Doppler tool measuring the ankle brachial index, where a value of <0.9 is diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease. The estimated prevalence in the US population is 7.2%; only about 10% of those with peripheral arterial disease actually have the classic symptoms of intermittent claudication (or leg pain) (Benjamin et al. 2018).
	Estimates of the prevalence of valvular heart disease, which includes aortic, mitral, and tricuspid valve disorders range from 0.3% in those under the age of 45 years to 11.7% in those aged 75 years and over. Rheumatic heart disease while uncommon in developed countries, affects more than 15 million individuals in Africa, Asia, and the Pacific, causing over 200,000 deaths annually. Infective endocarditis is relatively rare and results from formation of non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis on the surface of a cardiac valve, bacteraemia, and adherence of the bacteria in the bloodstream; the estimated risk in the general population is as low as 1 case per 14 million dental procedures (Benjamin et al. 2018).





Risk factors for cardiovascular disease


	The Framingham Heart Study, the seminal epidemiologic study of CVD, is a large longitudinal investigation begun in 1948 in the small town of Framingham, Massachusetts, USA. The original cohort of 5,209 participants aged 30–62 years of age received biennial physical examinations, risk factor assessments, and surveillance for CVD events (Wong and Levy 2013). The Framingham study was instrumental in the original identification of many of the factors that are associated with an increased risk of CVD, and in 1961, coined for the first time, the term ‘risk factors’ that is widely utilized in many different fields of medicine today (Kannel et al. 1961). The increased awareness of major risk factors for CVD initially identified by the Framingham Heart Study and by other researchers provided the impetus for important public health initiatives against smoking in the 1960s, hypertension in the 1970s, and hypercholesterolemia in the 1980s. More recently, obesity and physical inactivity have also been recognized as key risk factors for CVD. Diabetes is also now widely regarded as a CHD risk equivalent and the importance of a clustering of major cardiometabolic risk factors, commonly referred to as the metabolic syndrome, has received significant attention from the research and clinical community (Grundy et al. 2005). Risk factors often cluster together, and the number of risk factors present and their co-occurrence and is directly related to the incidence of CHD (Fig. 8.1.3). Importantly, it was the Framingham Heart Study that first introduced the concept of multivariable or global risk assessment for coronary heart disease (see also section to follow on global risk assessment) (Wilson et al. 1998).
	Fig. 8.1.3 Estimated 10-year CHD risk in 55-year-old adults according to levels of various risk factors: Framingham Heart Study
	Source: data from Wilson PWF et al. Prediction of Coronary Heart Disease Using Risk Factor Categories. Circulation 1998 97: 1837–47.
	Family history and genomics. A family history of premature CHD is a well-established, but unmodifiable risk factor for future CHD, and can sometimes be the crucial and single most important risk factor in predisposing an individual to early CHD (Hopkins et al. 2000; Williams et al. 2001). A large proportion of heart attacks or strokes occurring at a young age are felt to be attributable to inherited or familial predisposition. Hence, knowledge of an individual’s family history can help guide preventive efforts. A family history of premature CHD is generally defined as having a male first-degree relative experiencing a first manifestation of CHD under the age of 45, or a female first-degree relative experiencing CHD under the age of 55. The number of affected relatives with premature CHD is also felt to be an important factor, since those with 1 affected relative can be shown to have a fourfold greater risk of CHD, while those with 2 or more affected relatives may have more than a 12-fold greater risk of CHD compared to those without any affected relatives (Hopkins et al. 2000). Moreover, it has been shown that 35% of all early CHD occurs in just 3.2% of families, all of whom have a strong positive family history of CHD. Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is an autosomal dominant condition associated with very high levels of total and LDL-cholesterol (total cholesterol levels exceeding 500 are commonly reported) where individuals inherit from one or both parents (homozygous) a defective LDL-cholesterol receptor gene. Affected individuals have been known to have heart attacks and die by age 20 and FH is among the most widely studied genetic conditions responsible for CHD. Other genetic defects responsible for hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and other major cardiovascular risk factors have also been identified and are the subject of major investigations (Williams et al. 2001).
	In recent years, with the ability to sequence the entire human genome, key single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) have been identified and linked to the likelihood of CHD, although with a much higher threshold required to confirm a statistically significant relationship (p = 10–8) (Schunkert et al. 2011). One that has received significant attention is 9p21 because of its strong association with CHD (Palomaki et al. 2010). However, the utility of such SNPs in improving the ability to predict CHD over traditional risk factors is only modest and current guidelines have not recommended genomic screening due to the thus far limited demonstrated clinical utility.
	Of great recent interest is the emerging role of Mendelian randomization studies to estimate the effect of lifetime exposure to a given risk factor (or absence of risk factor) on risk of CHD. For instance, in one meta-analysis of studies involving 312,321 participants, examining the effect of long-term exposure to lower LDL-cholesterol on the risk of CHD mediated by 9 polymorphisms in 6 different genes found such naturally random allocation to lower LDL-C was associated with a 55% lower risk of CHD for each mmol/l lower LDL-C, which is approximately three times greater than that observed from statin treatment started later in life (Ference et al. 2012).
	Diabetes and metabolic syndrome. Diabetes mellitus is a major risk factor for CVD, and is associated with a greater risk for CHD, stroke, chronic kidney, and peripheral vascular disease (Kaseta and Sowers 2005). There are wide variations in prevalence according to gender and ethnicity. In 2011–2014, among US adults, the prevalence of physician-diagnosed diabetes mellitus was lowest in whites (7.4% in females and 8.0% in males) and highest in non-Hispanic Blacks (13.6% in females and 14.1% in males) (Benjamin et al. 2018).
	More than three-fourths of those with diabetes die of cardiovascular complications, most notably myocardial infarction and stroke, although peripheral arterial disease and heart failure are among the most common initial first CVD manifestations in persons with diabetes. Given this point, the National Cholesterol Education Program designated diabetes as a CHD risk equivalent (Expert Panel on Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment of High Blood Cholesterol in Adults 2001) because the risk of CHD in those with diabetes without known heart disease had been shown to be similar to recurrent CHD events in those with CHD (but without known diabetes), although more recent studies are showing that this is not always the case, with recent meta-analyses showing those with diabetes (without CHD) have about half the risk of future CHD events as those with CHD (but without diabetes). Population-based studies such as Framingham show about a 2–3-fold greater risk of CVD events in men with diabetes as compared to men without diabetes, but that in women, the corresponding figure is a 3–7-fold greater risk.
	Diabetes is typically diagnosed by a glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) level of 6.5% or greater, fasting glucose >126 mg/dl (7 mmol/l) or glucose level of >200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l) from the non-fasting state or after a 2-hour post-load glucose challenge test (American Diabetes Association 2018a). Pre-diabetes is diagnosed by a fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dl or casual glucose of 140–199 mg/dl.
	Clinical trial evidence to show whether intensive glycaemic control in persons with diabetes lowers CVD event rates has shown mixed results. The United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) originally showed a borderline, non-significant (p = 0.052) 16% reduction in risk of myocardial infarction among those with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes who were treated with intensive glucose-lowering therapy, but the 10-year post-interventional follow-up of this study, which was recently published, showed that these benefits continued with a 15% significant (p = 0.01) reduction in risk of myocardial infarction (Holman et al. 2008). A similar, extended post-interventional follow-up of the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial of Type 1 diabetes, which did not initially show a significant reduction in CVD events at the end of the randomized trial, showed years later a continued effect of the original intensive glucose-lowering treatment, with a 42% reduction in the risk of any cardiovascular event (The Diabetes Control and Complications Trial 2005). Such a continued post-trial effect of the randomized glycaemic therapy has been termed a ‘glycaemic legacy’ effect. More recently, however, three important randomized clinical trials (the Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes (ACCORD), ADVANCE and the Veterans Affairs Diabetes Trial (VADT)) failed to show that intensive glucose-lowering to a HbA1c range of 6–6.5%, significantly reduced CVD event rates, as compared to more standard maintenance of the HbA1c in the 7–9% range. In fact, those randomized to the intensive therapy group in ACCORD actually had a higher rate of CVD mortality (The Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes Study Group 2008), although this increased risk was restricted to those with prior macrovascular disease and where there was unsuccessful lowering of the glucose as a result of the intensive therapy. Those with less complicated diabetes (e.g. patients who were more recently diagnosed and without prior macrovascular disease) actually showed a benefit in the primary endpoint. Moreover, an important lipid substudy of ACCORD tested the efficacy of adding the fibric acid derivative fenofibrate or placebo to ongoing statin therapy and found no benefit in terms of reducing CVD event rates (although there was a benefit seen in the subgroup with high triglycerides and low HDL-C) (ACCORD Study Group 2000a). In addition, in the blood pressure substudy of ACCORD, intensive blood pressure therapy to achieve a systolic blood pressure <120 mmHg, as compared with <140 mmHg, was also found to provide no significant benefit in terms of CVD risk reduction, although there was a significant benefit in stroke reduction (ACCORD Study Group 2010b).
	Most recently, however, newer diabetes agents, in particular recent trials of SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists have finally demonstrated benefit in cardiovascular outcomes trials. SGLT-2 inhibitors lower blood glucose by urinary excretion and have other positive benefits, such as on blood pressure, arterial stiffness, and weight/adiposity, and oxidative stress. The first of these, empagliflozin, was tested in the EMPA-REG outcomes trial among persons with diabetes and established CVD, demonstrating a significant 14% reduction in the primary composite cardiovascular outcome, but a greater 38% reduction in cardiovascular death and 35% reduction in heart failure hospitalizations (Zinman et al. 2015). Later, the CANVAS trial involving canagliflozin showed a similar benefit in the primary composite cardiovascular outcome and in heart failure hospitalizations, but no significant benefit in cardiovascular mortality (Neal et al. 2017). GLP-1 receptor agonists are incretin-based therapies that stimulate insulin secretion and suppress glucagon secretion and may have other effects including reducing inflammation, blood pressure, body weight, and improving beta-cell function. The LEADER trial involving liraglutide is the first cardiovascular outcomes-driven trial of a GLP-1 reception agonist to show a benefit with a significant 13% reduction in the primary composite cardiovascular outcome (Marso et al. 2016).
	While the concept of the metabolic syndrome has waned over recent years, this condition referring to a constellation of cardiometabolic risk factors that are associated with a greater risk of developing future diabetes and CVD has been useful for the purposes of defining those with multiple risk factors who may benefit from a more intensified, unified approach at risk factor modification. Studies have documented that 30–40% of adults have metabolic syndrome in the United States, with even higher prevalence rates in some regions such as in the Middle East. Certain definitions of the metabolic syndrome place insulin resistance or abdominal obesity as the necessary condition, with additional conditions including elevated blood pressure, low HDL-cholesterol, elevated triglycerides, and impaired fasting glucose making up the definition. The American Heart Association/National Heart Lung and Blood Institute definition (Grundy et al. 2005) requires the presence of at least three of the following five criteria: abdominal obesity defined by a waist circumference >35 inches in women or >45 inches in men; HDL-cholesterol <40 mg/dl in men or <50 mg/dl in women, fasting triglycerides >150 mg/dl; elevated blood pressure of >130 mmHg systolic or >85 mmHg diastolic or on hypertensive therapy; or impaired fasting glucose defined as >100 mg/dl (5.6 mmol/L) or on hypoglycaemic therapy. It is important to recognize that other definitions exist, such as that from the International Diabetes Federation which requires the presence of abdominal obesity as measured by lower waist circumference cut-off points in European Caucasians (>94 cm in men and >80 cm in women), and among most Asian groups and those of Central and South American ancestry (where >80 cm in women and >90 cm in men define increased waist circumference) (Alberti et al. 2005).
	Numerous studies have shown an increased risk of future CVD events in persons with the metabolic syndrome. Among United States adults (Malik et al. 2004), a stepwise increase in risk for CHD, CVD, and total mortality has been shown relating to the presence of metabolic syndrome alone, metabolic syndrome with diabetes or pre-existing CVD, and metabolic syndrome with both CVD and diabetes (Fig. 8.1.4).
	Fig. 8.1.4 Relative risks for mortality from coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease, and all causes in United States Adults associated with the presence of metabolic syndrome with and without diabetes: NHANES II: 1976–80 follow-up study (mean 13 years follow-up).
	From Malik S, Wong ND, Franklin SS, et al. Impact of the metabolic syndrome on mortality from coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease, and all causes in United States Adults. Circulation; 2004: 110: 1239–44, with permission from Wolters Kluwer.
	Hypertension. Elevated blood pressure, and particularly systolic blood pressure, is strongly and positively related to the risk of future CHD and stroke. Hypertension is currently defined as a systolic blood pressure of 130 mmHg or higher, diastolic blood pressure of 80 mmHg or higher (or on pharmacologic treatment to lower blood pressure). Levels of 130–139 mmHg systolic or 80–89 mmHg diastolic are defined as Stage 1 hypertension, and levels of 140 mmHg or higher systolic or 90 mmHg or higher diastolic are defined as Stage 2 hypertension based on the new 2017 ACC/AHA guidelines (Whelton et al. 2018). Based on US NHANES data from 2011 to 2014, this results in the identification of 45.6% of US adults (103.3 million) with hypertension, of which 36.2% (81.9 million) would be recommended for treatment, and among those treated 53.4% (29.2 million) would still be above target blood pressure goal (Muntner et al. 2018). There is a strong age-related increase in prevalence of hypertension, and based on the older cut-point of 140/90 mmHg, prevalence ranges from under 10% in those <35 years of age and progressively increases with age to more than 70% in those aged 75 years and over with higher prevalences in men before age 55, but higher prevalences in women after age 65 (reaching 81.2% among those aged 75 years and over). Of note, isolated diastolic hypertension (systolic blood pressure of <140 mmHg but diastolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg or higher) is the most common form of hypertension under age 50, while isolated systolic hypertension (systolic blood pressure of 140 mmHg or higher, but diastolic blood pressure <90 mmHg) predominates over the age of 60 years (Franklin et al. 2001).
	For every blood pressure increase of 20/10 mmHg (systolic/diastolic) above 115/75 mmHg, the risk of death from CHD, stroke, or CVD doubles. Numerous clinical trials have shown that lowering blood pressure substantially decreases the risk of future cardiovascular events, stroke, and end-stage renal disease. A large meta-analysis of active treatment (with initial low dose diuretic, beta blocker, ACE inhibitor or calcium antagonist) compared to placebo showed significant reductions in the risk for heart failure (36%), stroke (33%), CHD (16%), CVD death (15%), overall CVD (25%) and total mortality (12%) (Prospective Studies Collaborative 2002; Elliott 2005). Of note, the recent landmark Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial (SPRINT) showed those non-diabetic but higher cardiovascular risk participants targeted to a systolic blood pressure <120 mmHg compared to <140 mmHg (with actual achieved blood pressures of 121 mmHg and 136 mmHg, respectively) was stopped early due to definitive benefit with the intervention group showing a 25% reduction in the primary composite CVD endpoint with a substantial 38% reduction in heart failure hospitalization and 43% reduction in cardiovascular mortality. All-cause mortality was also significantly reduced by 27% (SPRINT Research Group et al. 2015).
	Dyslipidaemia. Increased levels of total and low density lipoprotein (LDL)-cholesterol have long been recognized as major risk factors for CHD. A direct curvilinear relation exists between total and low density lipoprotein (LDL)-cholesterol and the risk of CHD. For example, compared to those with total cholesterol levels of 200 mg/dl, those with levels of 240 mg/dl are at approximately twofold greater risk, while those with levels of 300 mg/dl have a fourfold increased risk. However, there is significant overlap in total or LDL-cholesterol levels between those who experience CHD events versus those who do not and approximately one-third of heart attacks occur in persons with “normal” levels of total cholesterol below 200 mg/dl. Importantly, a low level of high density lipoprotein-cholesterol (typically defined as <40 mg/dl in men and <50 mg/dl in women), regardless of level of total cholesterol, is strongly associated with an increased risk of CHD (Castelli et al. 1986). For example, across levels of total cholesterol from <200 mg/dl to >260 mg/dl, the 14-year incidence of CHD varies only from 11.2 to 12.5%, whereas when HDL-C >60 mg/dl, these rates are 3.7% to 3.8%, respectively.

	Other lipid abnormalities include elevated serum triglyceride levels (the normal level is considered to be <150 mg/dl), small particle size LDL-cholesterol (known as small dense LDL-cholesterol) and elevated lipoprotein (a) levels. There has also been recent interest in non-HDL-cholesterol since it captures all the atherogenic apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins and does not require, unlike LDL-cholesterol, measurements to be made after fasting. Several epidemiological studies have demonstrated a stronger relationship of non-HDL-C compared to LDL-cholesterol with incidence of CHD.
	Table 8.1.1 shows the prevalence of elevated total and LDL-cholesterol and low HDL-cholesterol levels among US adults aged 20 years and over in 2011–2014 (Benjamin et al. 2018).
	Numerous primary and secondary prevention clinical trials have documented the efficacy of lowering LDL-cholesterol, particularly with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor drugs (‘statins’), which can lead to approximately 25–35% reductions in CHD and CVD incidence, where the lower the LDL-C achieved, the lower were the event rates (Rosensen 2004). These trials also showed no threshold level of LDL-C reductions where the CVD event rates begin to flatten. A large meta-analysis of 14 statin trials comprising 90,056 subjects showed that over a 5-year treatment period, every mmol/L reduction (approximately 40 mg/dl) in LDL-cholesterol achieved, was associated with reductions in all-cause mortality of 12%, coronary mortality of 18%, myocardial infarction and CHD death of 23%, stroke incidence of 17%, all major vascular events of 21%, and with no difference (relative risk 1.00) in cancer incidence (Baigent et al. 2005). Importantly, several trials have shown the additional benefit of reducing the LDL-C, with high dose statin therapy, to levels below 100 mg/dl. The largest of these, the Treat to New Targets (TNT) study showed that the achieved LDL-C of 77 mg/dl with high dosage atorvastatin therapy, when compared to achieved LDL-C of 101 mg/dl with low dose atorvastatin therapy, resulted in an additional 22% reduction in major cardiovascular events (LaRosa et al. 2005).
	Given that most randomized clinical trials of LDL-C lowering have demonstrated no more than 40% reductions in CVD incidence, addressing the remaining ‘residual’ risk has been of great interest. One factor that has been specifically investigated has been whether the raising of HDL-C levels will provide further benefit in reducing CVD events beyond that afforded by LDL-C lowering, given the strong protective effect of increased HDL-C levels suggested by observational studies. The AIM-High Trial (AIM-HIGH Investigators et al. 2011) was designed to be a rigorous test of the HDL hypothesis, randomizing 3,414 men and women with a prior CVD event and low HDL-C, and who had well-controlled LDL-C levels averaging 74 mg/dl on a statin, to extended-release niacin or placebo. LDL-C levels were kept similar between the groups, and the on-treatment HDL-C level averaged 5 mg/dl higher in those on niacin. However, the trial was discontinued early due to futility, with no significant reduction in CVD events observed (HR = 1.02, p = 0.79). The failure of this trial, as well as that of a second much larger niacin trial, HPS2-Thrive as well as the failure of three of four major trials of cholesterol ester transferase protein (CETP) inhibitors have raised significant questions as to the benefit of raising HDL-C levels, particularly in patients who are already well-controlled on statins.
	In recent years, evidence has accumulated regarding the cardiovascular benefits of newer non-statin therapies. In the IMPROVE-IT trial of persons with a recent (within 10 days) acute coronary syndrome, the addition of the cholesterol absorption inhibitor ezetimibe to simvastatin compared to simvastatin alone resulted in a 6% relative risk reduction for the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint, although given the high-risk study population, the absolute risk reduction was 2%, resulting in a number needed to treat of 50 for the prevention of a CVD event (Cannon et al. 2015). In addition, with the availability of proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin type 9 (PCSK9) monoclonal antibody therapies evolocumab and alirocumab, which provide average 50–60% reductions in LDL-C above maximal tolerated statin therapy, recently reported cardiovascular outcomes trials (Sabatine et al. 2017; American College of Cardiology 2018) have demonstrated further 15% relative risk reductions for the composite CVD endpoint, with greater benefit being observed with time and in those with higher risk features (e.g. more recent myocardial infarction or number of prior cardiovascular events).
	Cigarette smoking. Tobacco smoking is among the leading preventable causes of death globally. Numerous studies have linked tobacco use to the incidence of, and mortality from, CVD, with approximately a half-million deaths annually in the United States being attributed to tobacco use. Further, environmental tobacco smoke (‘second-hand smoke’) is responsible for approximately 40,000 deaths from heart disease annually in the United States. Cigarette smokers are 2 to 4 times more likely to develop CHD than non-smokers. Also, their risk of stroke is doubled and risk for peripheral vascular disease is more than 10 times higher than that of non-smokers (Luepker and Lando 2005). The most recent data among US adults in 2015 show an overall prevalence of smoking of 15.1%, with a wide variation by ethnic groups, ranging from 7% in Asian to 21.9% in American Indian/Alaska Natives (Benjamin et al. 2018).
	Obesity and physical inactivity. Recent estimates showed that two-thirds of US adults are overweight or obese (body mass index of 25 kg/m2 or higher), with 30% being obese (body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher). Since the 1960s, there has been a dramatic nearly threefold increase in obesity prevalence among men from 10.7% to 34.4% and more than a twofold increase in women from 15.7% to 36.1%. Moreover, 17.4% of children aged 6–11 and 20.6% aged 12–17 are defined to be obese based on latest survey data from NHANES 2013–2014. Further recent estimates from NHIS 2015 showed that half (49.7%) of the US adult population (52.9% of men and 46.7% of women) met nationally recommended amounts of physical activity (150 minutes of moderate, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity or an equivalent combination per week) (Benjamin et al. 2018).
	Obesity has been shown by numerous studies to be associated with an approximate 1.5-to 2-fold increase in risk of death from CHD, with the increase in risk beginning below the 25 kg/m2 cut-off point for overweight. Numerous studies also show approximately 20–40% lower risks of mortality and cardiovascular events associated with increased levels of physical activity or measured fitness. Several cardiovascular risk factors are linked to obesity, including hypertension, dyslipidaemia (including low HDL-cholesterol levels), type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnoea, and hyperinsulinemia. Increases in physical fitness have also been shown to be linked to increases in HDL-cholesterol levels and reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, insulin resistance, and glucose intolerance. Abdominal obesity, most commonly indicated by a waist circumference of >40 inches in men or >35 inches in women, is a major component of the metabolic syndrome (McCowen and Blackburn 2005). Measures of cardiovascular health and CVD risk. In recent years, the American Heart Association (AHA) (Benjamin et al. 2018) has promoted a goal to improve the cardiovascular health of all Americans by 20% while reducing mortality from heart disease and stroke by 20% by the year 2020. These goals introduce the concept of promoting cardiovascular health which is more positive and motivating than the concept of preventing cardiovascular disease, and have focused on examining the proportion of individuals (and the relation to CVD risk) who achieve one or more “ideal levels” based on the following seven metrics (also known as AHA’s Life’s Simple Seven™ ): (1) cigarette smoking (non-smoking is ideal); (2) physical activity (150 minutes or more moderate intensity or equivalent exercise per week is ideal); (3) body mass index (<25 kg/m2 is ideal); (4) healthy diet (achieving at least 4 of 5 key dietary components focusing on fruit/vegetable, fish, fibre, and sodium intake and sweetened beverage intake); (5) cholesterol (<200 mg/dl ideal in adults, <170 mg/dl in children), 6) blood pressure (<120/80 mmHg is ideal); and (7) fasting plasma glucose (<100 mg/dl is ideal). Fewer than 20% of adults and only about 40% of children meet five or more of these criteria for ideal cardiovascular health and fewer than 1% of adults are at ideal levels of all seven metrics of cardiovascular health. Moreover, CVD incidence varies more than 10-fold according to the number of cardiovascular health behaviours and factors that are present (Folsom et al. 2011) (Fig. 8.1.5).
	Fig. 8.1.5 Incidence of CVD according to the number of ideal health behaviours and health factors.
	Reprinted from Folsom AR, Yatsuya H, Nettleton JA, et al. Community prevalence of ideal cardiovascular health by the American Heart Association definition and relation with cardiovascular disease incidence. J Am Coll Cardiol 2011; 57: 1690–6 with permission from Elsevier.





Risk factors for stroke


	Important risk factors for stroke include elevated blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, disorders of heart rhythm, low HDL-cholesterol, cigarette smoking, family history, and chronic kidney disease (WHO 2011). Elevated blood pressure is the most important risk factor for both ischaemic stroke and intracranial haemorrhage, with about 77% of those with a first stroke having a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher. The Framingham Heart Study demonstrated the importance of mid-life antecedent hypertension as well as systolic hypertension as important predictors of stroke (Romero and Wolf 2013). Even prehypertension is associated with incident stroke. Randomized clinical trials consistently show the efficacy of blood pressure control for prevention of stroke. Diabetes is also a strong predictor of stroke, although mainly before age 55 years of age in blacks and before age 65 years of age in whiles. Atrial fibrillation is another powerful risk factor for stroke, independently increasing risk approximately fivefold at all ages, with nearly one-quarter of strokes attributable to atrial fibrillation in the ninth decade of life. While elevated total cholesterol levels are not strongly predictive of stroke, some studies have found low HDL-cholesterol levels to predict risk, but clinical trials of statin therapy consistently show benefits of such therapy for preventing stroke. Prospective studies have also shown moderate to vigorous physical activity to be associated with an overall 35% reduction in risk of ischaemic stroke compared with no physical activity. A family history of parental ischaemic stroke before the age of 65 has also been shown to be associated with a threefold increase in ischaemic stroke in offspring, even after adjustment for other risk factors. Finally, increased levels of creatinine and reduced glomerular filtration rate (eFGR) have been shown to predict future stroke and symptoms.





Risk factors for heart failure


	Hypertension is among the most prominent of risk factors for heart failure, followed by a preceding myocardial infarction, elevated B-type natriuretic peptide levels, and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio. In the Physicians Health Study, the lifestyle risk of heart failure was greater in those with hypertension and less in those with healthy lifestyle factors, including normal weight, not smoking, regular exercise, moderate alcohol intake, consumption of breakfast cereals, fruits, and vegetables (Djousse et al. 2009). The Framingham Heart Study was key in demonstrating the poor prognosis associated with heart failure in the community, with 1 of 2 individuals dying within 5 years of diagnosis and the strong association of hypertension conferring nearly an eightfold risk in men and fourfold risk in women for developing heart failure. They also documented other predictors of new onset heart failure, including elevated plasma natriuretic peptide levels, asymptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and increased left ventricular diastolic dimension (Mahmood and Wang 2013).





Risk factors for peripheral arterial disease


	Peripheral arterial disease shares many of the same risk factors that coronary heart disease does, although diabetes and cigarette smoking are stronger risk factors for peripheral arterial disease than for coronary heart disease with odds ratios in the range of 3 to 4. Another study showed hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and smoking were associated with incident peripheral arterial disease. Meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies indicated people at with low ankle brachial index (ABI) (<0.9) had around threefold risk of all-cause death as well as cardiovascular death in both sexes.





Cardiovascular disease risk assessment


	Global risk scores for cardiovascular disease risk assessment. In order to understand an individual’s risk of CVD or CHD, it is important to understand an individual’s “global risk” of developing the condition. Most risk scores developed over the past few decades, including those from the Framingham Heart Study in the United States as well as those from other countries have involved the determination of the future risk of developing CHD in the next 10 years. These have been used to stratify a person’s risk for consideration or intensification of risk factor management, especially for lipid-lowering therapy. More recently, algorithms for total CVD risk from Framingham have been developed, which are more global as they incorporate the combined risk for CHD, stroke, heart failure, and peripheral arterial disease (D’Agostino et al. 2008). In late 2013, the ACC/AHA released the pooled cohort risk calculator, which allows for the prediction of 10-year risk (in those aged 40–79 years of age) and lifetime risk (in those aged 20–59 years of age) of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) comprising of non-fatal or fatal myocardial infarction or stroke (Goff et al. 2014), and which is currently the standard for risk assessment recommended today for clinical practice.
	Fig. 8.1.6 Pooled cohort risk calculator.
	From https://clincalc.com/cardiology/ascvd/pooledcohort.aspx.
	In those where a global risk estimate is obtained, depending on the risk status, the appropriate intensity of treatment for given risk factors is considered (see next under cholesterol management). While estimation of global risk as described earlier is recommended, it may be best considered a starting point in risk assessment and a strong emphasis is to use the risk calculator as part of the patient-clinician ‘risk discussion’ on the best ways to lower cardiovascular risk through both lifestyle and use of appropriate preventive therapies. In addition, the presence of other risk factors not included in the risk algorithms, such as abdominal obesity, elevated triglycerides (if severe enough), impaired fasting glucose, or a strong positive premature family history, if present, however, could be used by the clinician to stratify an individual’s risk or required intensity of treatment upward. The ACC/AHA 2014 Guideline on Cardiovascular Risk Assessment (Goff et al. 2014) specifically notes that if the treatment decision is uncertain on the basis of the risk calculator that the following additional measures can be used for consideration to further inform the treatment decision: (1) family history of premature CVD (which should always be done as part of patient evaluation); (2) high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (with a level of >2 mg/L indicating higher risk); (3) coronary calcium scoring (with a score of >300 mg/dl or >75th %tile for age and sex warranting a high risk level); or (4) ABI (with a level of <0.9 indicating higher risk and diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease) (see next).
	Inflammatory measures for cardiovascular disease risk. High levels of inflammatory markers, including high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), a marker of systemic inflammation, as well as lipoprotein phospholipase associated A2 (LpPla2), a measure of vascular inflammation have been shown in numerous studies to be independently related to the risk of future cardiovascular events. IL-6, other interleukins, myeloperoxidase, and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) also have inflammatory activity and have been shown to be associated with cardiovascular events in some studies, as have other biomarkers such as brain naturietic peptide (BNP) and troponin levels. Levels of C-reactive protein exceeding 2 mg/L have been recommended as a higher risk level that could inform the treatment decision beyond global risk scoring (Goff et al. 2014). There are no current recommendations for the measurement of other inflammatory markers or biomarkers for the assessment of CVD risk in asymptomatic adults, however. The recent CANTOS trial recently provided proof of concept for the role of reducing/modifying inflammation in high risk individuals for the reduction of CVD events (Ridker et al. 2017). In this trial, high risk persons with known CVD were randomly assigned on top of optimal treatment to the monoclonal antibody to Il-1β, canakinumab for a median follow-up of 3.7 years and showed a significant 15% relative risk reduction in the primary CVD endpoint.
	Subclinical cardiovascular disease assessment. The ability to image or directly measure the atherosclerotic burden has been of great interest but whether these measures provide added value over less expensive and easier traditional office-based risk factor measures (including global risk assessment scores) has been an important question in cardiovascular epidemiology and prevention over the past 15 years (Greenland et al. 2010). Such measures must have a high level of sensitivity and specificity for detection of the disease, must be reproducible and cost-effective, and should provide added clinical utility over current office-based risk assessment.
	Increased carotid intima medial thickness (CIMT) as measured from carotid B-mode ultrasound, has been shown to be related to the risk of future CVD events from numerous prospective epidemiologic studies over the past 25 years, including the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC), Cardiovascular Health Study (CHS), and the Multiethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). CIMT has also been used as a surrogate endpoint in numerous clinical trials involving lipid-lowering and other interventions. Moreover, the presence of carotid plaques provides additional information and together with CIMT measurements have modest clinical utility for reclassification of risk in asymptomatic intermediate risk adults. While the most recent ACC/AHA Guidelines on Cardiovascular Risk Assessment do not recommend the measurement of CIMT alone for the assessment of CVD risk (Goff et al. 2014), due to its modest improvement in risk prediction from recent meta-analyses, more recent European guidelines have emphasized the assessment of carotid plaque together with CIMT.
	ABI measured from ankle and arm blood pressures utilizing a Doppler, provides for an assessment of peripheral arterial disease, which is diagnosed to be present when the ABI is less than 0.9. A low ABI has also been shown to be related to increased total and CVD mortality in numerous observational studies. However, as ABI tends not to be low until after the age of 60 years, it is therefore most useful as a screening tool for peripheral arterial disease in older persons. It is also a recommendation for further informing the treatment decision if uncertain from global risk assessment alone (Goff et al. 2014).
	Measures of coronary artery calcium as assessed by computed tomography (CT), have been shown in numerous prospective studies, to be associated with the future risk of CHD and CVD events, independent of standard risk factors (Greenland et al. 2010). Coronary calcium measures also provide incremental predictive value and added reclassification of risk over global risk assessment for the prediction of cardiovascular events. In the MESA study, it has been shown to provide greater incremental risk prediction among intermediate risk individuals (from C-statistic improvement) than any other major biomarker or subclinical disease screening test (Detrano et al. 2008). CAC testing is also felt to be the most useful of the current approaches for improving risk assessment in intermediate risk subjects (Goff et al. 2014).
	There are also numerous other tests which have varying levels of evidence relating them to CVD event risk. These include assessments of endothelial function, pulse wave velocity, brachial artery reactivity, and imaging of soft plaque such as by CT coronary angiography. Most of these other tests, however, do not have the quantity, strength, or consistency of evidence that CIMT, ABI, or CAC assessment do, and hence there is not the same level of consensus for recommending their use for the screening of asymptomatic adults.





Preventive strategies for cardiovascular disease risk reduction


	Cardiovascular epidemiology and disease prevention encompass an extensive field investigating the distribution and variation of CVD conditions, most notably coronary heart disease and stroke, their risk factor determinants, and strategies at the population and individual level aimed at preventing the development or recurrence of CVD. Epidemiologic approaches to studying CVD provide us with the tools for preventive efforts at the individual and population level. Primordial prevention is aimed at prevention of the risk factors for CVD, such as efforts aimed to prevent hypertension, obesity, or dyslipidaemia. Primary prevention, which focuses on the modification of these and other known risk factors, is aimed at preventing the clinical manifestations of CVD, such as myocardial infarction and stroke. Secondary prevention focuses on those who already have manifestations of disease, but where aggressive control of risk factors can have a major impact in preventing recurrences of disease. Concerted efforts between governmental agencies, the community, and the private sector are required to best address the continuing epidemic of CVD.
	Preventive strategies can be considered using the ‘ABCDE’ approach addressing aspirin/antiplatelet therapy (A), blood pressure and hypertension (B), cholesterol and dyslipidaemia (C), diet and nutrition (D), and exercise and physical activity (E). For secondary prevention among persons with pre-existing CVD, guidelines have been published by the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (Smith et al. 2011).
	Aspirin and Antiplatelet Therapy. Aspirin prophylaxis (81–162 mg/day) has been recommended for persons at intermediate risk, for the prevention of CHD in men and prevention of stroke in women, including those with diabetes or metabolic syndrome. Additionally, among those with pre-existing CVD, aspirin is recommended in combination with clopidogrel due to the added benefit in prevention of secondary events. The use of alternative antiplatelet therapies is also discussed (Smith et al. 2011).
	Blood pressure control. The most recent AHA/ACC guidelines (Whelton et al. 2018) have recommended the standard blood pressure goal of treatment of those with hypertension to be <130/80, with consideration of a diuretic, calcium channel blocker, or ACE inhibitor/ARB as the initial therapy in most patients, with the recommendation to add a second agent, including as a fixed-dose combination as needed to reach goal, especially when the blood pressure exceeds 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic from target. Such pharmacologic treatment is recommended in most persons with hypertension at or above 140/90 mmHg, or 130/80 mmHg when the 10-year ASCVD risk from the pooled cohort risk calculator is at 10% or greater, thus persons between these numbers need such an assessment of their ASCVD risk. These recent guidelines also place a greater emphasis on home or ambulatory blood pressure monitoring for the evaluation of possible white coat or masked hypertension.
	Cholesterol and lipid control. The 2014 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Blood Cholesterol (Stone et al. 2014) has emphasizes defining four ‘statin eligible’ groups of patients: those with (1) clinical ASCVD; (2) LDL-C of 190 mg/dl or greater; (3) diabetes; and (4) 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% or greater based on the pooled cohort risk calculator. It has specifically removed LDL-C targets that were present in prior guidelines because of the lack of clinical trial evidence for the use of such targets. Instead, the focus is on adequate intensity of statin medication, where for those with clinical ASCVD <75 years of age, LDL-C of 190 mg/dl, or diabetes and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% or greater, a high intensity statin is recommended with the expectation of a 50% or greater LDL-C reduction. In older persons with ASCVD, diabetes with <7.5% 10-year risk of ASCVD, or primary prevention subjects of 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% or greater, a moderate intensity statin is suitable. A recent non-statin consensus pathway update to these guidelines (Lloyd-Jones et al. 2017) has provided further guidance as to when these ‘targets’ of percentage (e.g. >50%) LDL-C reduction or specific values (e.g. <70 mg/dl in higher risk persons) have not been achieved that non-statin therapies such as ezetimibe or PCSK9 monoclonal antibody therapy can be recommended.
	Cigarette smoking prevention and intervention. Smoking cessation has long been documented to reduce the risk of CVD. The risk of CHD is reduced by 50% within one year of smoking cessation and to that of a never-smoker within 15 years. It is recommended that at each consultation with a healthcare provider the visit should be used as an opportunity to address the 5A’s of smoking cessation counselling which include ‘Ask’ (assess tobacco use at every visit); ‘Advise’ (strongly urge quitting); ‘Attempt’ (try to identify smokers ready to quit); ‘Assist’ (aid the patient in quitting); and ‘Arrange’ (for follow-up contacts). Interventions for smoking are varied. For youth, school, and community-based prevention programmes, state, and federal initiatives, as well as cessation assistance are available. For adults, behavioural treatment, self-help approaches, and pharmacologic therapy are used, with varying levels of success. For example, quit rates vary from 6% with physician advice only to 40% in those who participate in group programmes (40).
	Diabetes control. Recommendations for the treatment of diabetes to optimize cardiovascular risk reduction is available from a variety of sources. For example, the latest recommendations from the American Diabetes Association (2018b) addresses antiplatelet therapy, glycaemic control, blood pressure control, lipid control (discussed earlier), weight control, and lifestyle management. Moreover, similar guidelines have been published by the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD). Multifactorial intervention focusing on lipid, blood pressure, and glycaemic control has been shown to decrease the risk of future CVD events by more than 50% (Gaede et al. 2008). This is a very important message given that in recent reports, only one tenth of those with diabetes have achieved target treatment levels for HbA1c, blood pressure, and LDL-C (Wong et al. 2012). While the goal of glycaemic control is a HbA1c level of less than 7% in most uncomplicated diabetics, and even 6–6.5% if achievable without side effects, given the results of recent trials, HbA1c levels of <8% are accepted as an appropriate goal for those with pre-existing micro or macrovascular disease or difficult-to-control diabetes (American Diabetes Association 2018b). Appropriate intensity statin therapy similar to the ACC/AHA guidelines discussed earlier is also considered appropriate. In addition, in persons requiring additional HbA1c reduction beyond initial therapy (especially when 9% or greater), for those with known ASCVD, these most recent ADA guidelines recommend the use of a drug shown to have cardiovascular outcomes benefit such as empagliflozin, canagliflozin, or liraglutide (although possible benefit is considered for metformin and pioglitazone).
	Obesity management. The ACC/AHA/Obesity Society guideline for the management of overweight and obesity (Jensen et al. 2014) provides guidelines for maintaining ideal body weight. In particular, it notes even modest weight reduction can have beneficial effects on many of the cardiometabolic risk factors. It also recommends up to 14 sessions with a lifestyle interventionalist to provide maximum benefit in terms of weight reduction.
	Exercise and physical activity. The recent ACC/AHA Guideline on Lifestyle Management (Eckel et al. 2014) recommends 150 minutes per week of moderate intensity physical activity in at least 3–4 sessions per week each lasting approximately 40 minutes, for LDL-C and blood pressure reduction. Regular physical activity can help maintain healthy blood pressure, weight, lipid levels, low levels of inflammation (C-reactive protein) and insulin sensitivity. A pedometer can be an effective tool for intervention with one guideline, for example, recommending walking at least 10,000 steps a day. For secondary prevention, a prescribed exercise programme is recommended, and participation initially in a supervised cardiac rehabilitation programme is advised for those recovering from a recent CHD event.
	Food and nutrition. Lifestyle management remains the cornerstone for reducing CVD risk including achieving and maintaining optimal risk factor levels. The ACC/AHA Guideline on Lifestyle Management (Eckel et al. 2014) recommends the consumption of a dietary pattern that emphasizes intake of vegetables, fruits, and whole grains; includes low-fat dairy products, poultry, fish, legumes, non-tropical vegetable oils and nuts; and limits intake of sweets, sugar-sweetened beverages, and red meats. It notes this dietary pattern should be adapted to appropriate calorie requirements, personal and cultural food preferences, and nutrition therapy for other medical conditions (including diabetes) and to consider following plans such as the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) dietary pattern, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food Pattern, or the AHA Diet. It is also recommended to consume no more than 6% calories in saturated fat, and to avoid when possible the intake of trans fats. Moreover, a sodium intake of no more than 2,400 mg per day is recommended, with an alternative target being to reduce sodium take by 1,000 mg per day.
	Specific additional recommendations for secondary prevention of CVD. Besides lipid control, blood pressure, antiplatelet, diabetes control, and lifestyle recommendations discussed earlier, guidelines for secondary prevention also include therapy with a beta blocker, renin angiotensin, and aldosterone system blockers, as well as annual influenza vaccination (Smith et al. 2011). Specific systems implemented in the hospital setting, such as pre-printed discharge instructions, reminders on charts (which can be automated in the case of electronic medical records systems) are key to ensure maximal adherence to recommended therapies for secondary prevention of CHD.





Conclusions


	CVDs account for the greatest burden of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and both in developed and in developing countries. Key cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension, cigarette smoking, high blood glucose, physical inactivity, obesity, and elevated cholesterol are (in that order) the top leading causes of death worldwide. It has been estimated that elimination of obesity, unhealthy diets, and physical inactivity could reduce up to 80% of heart disease, stroke, and diabetes (Roth et al. 2017).
	In a recent Presidential Advisory (Smith et al. 2012) issued by the presidents of the World Heart Federation, European Society of Cardiology, AHA, and other leading cardiac societies, the call to reduce non-communicable deaths by 25% by the year 2025 was noted (of which nearly half are due to CVD) and key global targets recommended for adoption were: (1) a 10% reduction in the prevalence of insufficient physical activity; (2) a 25% reduction in the prevalence of raised blood pressure; (3) a 30% reduction in salt/sodium intake with recommended goal of achieving <5 grams salt intake (2,000 mg sodium) per day; and (4) a 30% relative reduction in the prevalence of current tobacco smoking. Also receiving support was a reduction of saturated fat intake by 15%, halving the prevalence of obesity, reducing alcohol intake by 10%, reducing elevated cholesterol by 20%, increasing by 50% the number of eligible persons to receive drug therapy to prevent heart attacks and strokes, and increasing availability of basic technologies and generic essential medicines for prevention of CVD.
	Concerted global efforts aimed at coordinating care for those with pre-existing CVD (secondary prevention), primary prevention, identifying persons with cardiovascular risk factors and getting them the necessary treatments, as well as primordial prevention aimed at prevention of obesity and other major risk factors in the first place, are critical for reducing the morbidity and mortality associated with CVDs.
