8.3


Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma


	Craig M. Riley, Jessica Bon, and Alison Morris





Introduction


	The most common non-malignant respiratory conditions characterized by airway dysfunction are referred to collectively as obstructive airway diseases and include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma. Both conditions are highly prevalent and have increased dramatically worldwide in the past few decades. COPD is now the fourth leading cause of death worldwide (WHO 2007), and both COPD and asthma have a profound impact on quality of life for patients and their families. In this chapter, we review definitions, epidemiology, and risk factors for COPD and asthma.





Definitions


COPD


	Traditionally, COPD has been defined as irreversible airflow obstruction due to chronic bronchitis and emphysema that progresses over time (Petty 2006). The Ciba Guest Symposium (Ciba Foundation Guest Symposium 1959) and the American Thoracic Society symposium (Committee on Diagnostic Standards for Nontuberculous Respiratory Diseases 1962) proposed the first formal definitions of chronic bronchitis and emphysema respectively. Current definitions are still largely based on these initial definitions; that is, chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as the presence of chronic productive cough for at least 3 consecutive months in 2 consecutive years, and emphysema is a pathological diagnosis of an increase in the size of the distal airspaces and destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis (American Thoracic Society Committee on Diagnostic Standards 1962). The most recent definitions of COPD as reported in the American Thoracic Society (ATS), European Respiratory Society (ERS), and the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) guidelines (Agusti et al. 2017) emphasize the inflammatory response to noxious particles and gases as the predominant pathological feature of the disease and have parted from the definition of COPD as being a syndrome of chronic bronchitis and emphysema. The widely accepted GOLD definition (Agusti et al. 2017) states that COPD is:
	 	a common, preventable and treatable disease that is characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation that is due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases. (Agusti et al. 2017)
	Although no longer specifically included in the definition, chronic bronchitis and emphysema remain important causes of the chronic airflow limitation characteristic of COPD. The three main components (inflammation, airflow limitation that is not fully reversible, and a gradual loss of lung function over time) represent the major pathophysiological events leading to the symptoms typically expressed by those with COPD: chronic and progressive cough, sputum production, and dyspnoea.





Clinical assessment of COPD


	Spirometry is an essential tool in the clinical diagnosis of COPD. COPD is still traditionally diagnosed based on the post-bronchodilator ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1, the volume of air exhaled in the first second of expiration) to the forced vital capacity (FVC, the maximum volume of air that can be forcibly expired). A cut-point of 70% continues to be widely used (Agusti et al. 2017), but increasing attention has been paid to utilizing the lower limit of normal as a cut-off for the FEV1/FVC ratio to define obstruction (Vaz Fragoso et al. 2016). Use of this cut-off has the potential advantage of limiting underdiagnosis in younger adults and overdiagnosis in the elderly, but to date, a clear clinical advantage to utilizing the lower limit of normal over a fixed cut-off has not been demonstrated (Calverley et al. 2018). Bronchodilator treatment prior to spirometry is important as it establishes whether obstruction is irreversible and thus helps to distinguish COPD from asthma. In COPD with mild or moderate obstruction, the FVC is generally unaffected, or only marginally affected; however, FEV1 is reduced. In severe obstruction, air-trapping may lead to a reduction in FVC as well as FEV1, which can be differentiated from restriction by analysis of flow volume loops or lung volume measurements by nitrogen washout or plethysmography. Patients with COPD also frequently have a low diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLco) because of the destruction of lung tissue resulting in decreased gas transfer.
	The degree of severity of obstruction in those with FEV1/FVC less than 70% is usually based on the patient’s FEV1. The 2018 GOLD criteria classify obstruction severity in COPD into four stages (Agusti et al. 2017) (Box 8.3.1). While the degree of obstruction is useful for monitoring the progression of disease and correlates strongly with mortality (Mannino et al. 2003), FEV1 is less predictive of other patient-centred outcomes including symptom burden and acute exacerbations (Han et al. 2013). As these patient-centred outcomes are the major targets of common treatment modalities, recent GOLD guideline updates have developed risk-stratification tools and treatment algorithms that incorporate symptom scores and exacerbation risk independently of spirometry discussed next (Agusti et al. 2017).
	 	Box 8.3.1 GOLD criteria of COPD severity
	 	• Stage I, mild: FEV1 ≥ 80% predicted.
	• Stage II, moderate: 50% ≤ FEV1 ≥ 80% predicted.
	• Stage III, severe: 30% ≤ FEV1 ≥ 50% predicted.
	• Stage IV, very severe: FEV1 < 30% predicted.
	Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD). Global Strategy for the Diagnosis, Management and Prevention of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: 2018 Report.





Epidemiologic assessment of COPD


	The methodology used to assess COPD prevalence in epidemiologic cohorts and population-based studies often leads to underestimation of the true prevalence. In population-based surveys, COPD is often defined on the basis of: (1) self-report of a doctor diagnosis of COPD, bronchitis, or emphysema; (2) self-report of respiratory symptoms; and (3) spirometry with or without prior bronchodilator treatment. Self-report of a clinical diagnosis significantly underestimate the true disease prevalence (Halbert et al. 2006). More accurate approaches incorporate both spirometry, exposure history, and respiratory symptom assessment (Buist et al. 2007).
	The variable use of bronchodilators significantly complicates large population-based spirometry surveys, and many studies unfortunately do not collect post-bronchodilator measurements. Failing to check for reversibility of airflow obstruction (using pre-and post-bronchodilator spirometry) may result in an overestimation of the prevalence of COPD. In population studies comparing pre-and post-bronchodilator spirometry to examine COPD prevalence, using post-bronchodilator values lowered the estimated rate of airflow obstruction by 30–50% (Tilert et al. 2013). Therefore, the use of post-bronchodilator spirometry to determine the diagnosis of COPD in population-based studies is strongly recommended.





Asthma


	The word ‘asthma’ comes from a Greek word meaning ‘panting’ (Keeney 1964), but reference to asthma-like symptoms can also be found in ancient Egyptian, Hebrew, and Indian medical writings (Ellul-Micallef 1976). There were clear observations of patients experiencing attacks of asthma in the second century, and evidence of disordered lung anatomy as far back as the seventeenth century (Willis 1678). The definition of asthma initially proposed at the Ciba Foundation conference in 1959 (Ciba Foundation Guest Symposium 1959) and endorsed by the ATS in 1962 (American Thoracic Society Committee on Diagnostic Standards 1962) is that ‘asthma is a disease characterized by wide variation over short periods of time in resistance to flow in the airways of the lung’. Although these features receive lesser prominence in some current definitions given the now-recognized importance of airways inflammation, they are still integral to the current Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) description of asthma as:
	 	a heterogeneous disease, usually characterized by chronic airway inflammation. It is defined by the history of respiratory symptoms such as wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness and cough that vary over time and in intensity, together with variable expiratory airflow limitation. (GINA 2018)
	This definition of asthma encompasses both the pathophysiological mechanisms (in chronic airway inflammation and variable airflow obstruction due to bronchial hyperreactivity) and their downstream effects on patients by which providers clinically identify and diagnose this disease.





Clinical assessment of asthma


	There is no single test or pathognomonic feature that defines the presence or absence of asthma. Furthermore, the variability of the condition means that evidence of it may not be present at the initial assessment. Thus, a diagnosis of asthma is made on the basis of the clinical history in combination with physical examination and respiratory function tests over a period of time. As a result, asthma is subject simultaneously both to significant under-and overdiagnosis. Studies have shown both a significantly lower prevalence of physician-diagnosed asthma in the community as compared to the prevalence of asthma-like symptoms, suggesting that 20–70% of asthmatics are undiagnosed (Aaron et al. 2018). Furthermore, there are several disorders that have signs and symptoms (such as wheeze) that can be confused with or mimic aspects of asthma and lead to overdiagnosis in approximately 1/3 of cases (Aaron et al. 2017); common conditions mistaken for asthma include gastroesophageal reflux disease, chronic bronchitis, lower respiratory tract infections, bronchiectasis, vocal cord dysfunction, obesity, and COPD.
	There are a number of tests that facilitate the diagnosis and monitoring of asthma. Measurements of lung function are the most frequently used and provide important information on airflow variability, reversibility, and severity. Airflow limitation is generally measured using spirometry or a peak expiratory flow (PEF) meter. PEF meters are inexpensive and easy to use, but they are less precise than spirometry and may underestimate the degree of airflow limitation. Therefore, spirometry is preferred for diagnosis when available. Because of the importance of bronchial hyperreactivity and bronchodilator reversibility, guidelines emphasize the importance of conducting spirometry or PEF measurements both before and after bronchodilator treatment when assessing lung function in asthma (GINA 2018). Pre-and post-bronchodilator testing is important since it establishes if obstruction is irreversible and allows distinction from COPD. Reversibility of FEV1 of ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL from the pre-bronchodilator value is generally accepted as a valid indication of asthma (GINA 2018). However, due to the highly variable nature of the condition, repeated lung function tests are required, as some patients may not display reversibility when their asthma is well-controlled, and reversibility may be present in non-asthmatics.
	In individuals with asthma symptoms and normal lung function, bronchial hyperresponsiveness (BHR) testing may be used as a diagnostic aid. BHR constitutes airway narrowing to non-specific stimuli, such as exercise, cold air, and chemical irritants. Although BHR is related to asthma, it may occur independently of asthma, and vice versa, which makes BHR testing insufficient to diagnose asthma in isolation.
	An increasing number of tests are available to measure non-invasive markers of airway inflammation, including sputum induction tests, exhaled nitric oxide, and measurements of inflammatory markers in exhaled breath condensate. While these tests may be useful in establishing asthma phenotypes and identifying patients who are more likely to respond to optimal treatment, they have as yet to be convincingly demonstrated to aid in asthma diagnosis (Colak et al. 2018).
	There have been several approaches used to categorize asthma (Wenzel 2012). Until recently, asthma has most commonly been clinically classified on the basis of severity using GINA criteria (GINA 2006), which subdivided asthma into four categories (intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, and severe persistent). More recent guidelines (GINA 2018) have suggested that clinical categorization should be based on the current level of asthma control (controlled, partly controlled, and uncontrolled), which may more adequately address the individual clinical needs of the patient. Other categorizations of asthma exist based on type of inflammation seen such as atopic, eosinophilic, or TH-2 high (Tran et al. 2016). Although these asthma endotypes may overlap, they may represent different mechanistic pathways and respond differently to treatment.





Defining asthma in epidemiological surveys


	Defining and diagnosing asthma in population-based epidemiological surveys poses even greater difficulties than defining asthma in individuals. As a result, asthma prevalence surveys usually focus on self-or parental-reported ‘asthma symptoms’ rather than diagnosed asthma. This approach allows a large number of participants to be rapidly surveyed without great cost. Of the symptoms clinically associated with asthma, epidemiological studies have shown that wheezing is the most important symptom for the identification of asthma, and thus questionnaires used to assess asthma prevalence are often based on wheezing. An alternative approach to symptom questionnaires has been to use more ‘objective’ measures such as BHR testing, either alone or in combination with questionnaires. BHR may not be more reliable than questionnaire alone, in part due to the variability of BHR at the time of assessment.





Overlap syndrome


	Although reversibility of airway obstruction (or the lack thereof) is the primary clinical characteristic used to define either asthma or COPD, it is increasingly recognized that patients may have features of both diseases (Woodruff et al. 2017). It is often difficult to clearly distinguish and diagnose the two conditions, particularly in older patients. These observations have led to the description of asthma-COPD overlap (ACO), in which obstructive respiratory disease shows features of both asthma and COPD (Woodruff et al. 2017). The epidemiology of ACO is not well-understood, and attempts to characterize its prevalence and associations have been limited by different definitions across various studies. Approximately 17% of patients diagnosed with either asthma or COPD would meet criteria for ACO, and these patients are at higher risk for exacerbation, hospitalization, and disability compared to either population alone (Vaz Fragoso et al. 2017; Woodruff et al. 2017). Further work needs to be done to clearly define this syndrome to better identify long-term outcomes and efficacious treatment strategies as ACO patients have generally been excluded from treatment trials of asthma and COPD.





Epidemiology, risk factors, and prevention of COPD


Epidemiology of COPD


	COPD is a major global cause of mortality and morbidity, with exacerbations leading to frequent hospitalization. Despite the large personal, societal, and economic burden, it has been difficult to accurately estimate the true prevalence and it is often underdiagnosed. According to the World Health Organization, the global burden of COPD is estimated at 210 million people with 65 million suffering from moderate to severe disease (WHO 2007). It is also a major cause of healthcare costs and lost productivity.
	European epidemiological studies of COPD show prevalence estimates for COPD of 2 to greater than 10% (WHO 2007) (Fig. 8.3.1). These differences in prevalence estimates are presumed to be attributable to differences in risk exposures or population characteristics, but methods and definitions used to measure COPD may also play a role. Definitions of COPD used in these studies vary from a doctor’s diagnosis of COPD, to more rigid definitions based on pathology and/or pulmonary lung function testing.
	Fig. 8.3.1 Prevalence rate (1/100,000) of COPD in Europe.
	Reproduced with permission from World Health Organization, Global surveillance, prevention and control of chronic respiratory diseases, http://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/handle/10665/43776/9789241563468_eng.pdf
	Halbert and co-workers (Halbert et al. 2003) assessed the reasons for conflicting prevalence estimates in the literature. They selected studies that had estimated population-based COPD prevalences and clearly described methods used to obtain these estimates. In total, 32 studies, representing 17 countries and eight WHO regions, presenting prevalence data for COPD were identified and reviewed. Prevalence estimates were based on spirometry (11 studies), respiratory symptoms (14 studies), patient-reported disease (10 studies), or expert opinion. The reported prevalence of COPD ranged from 0.23 to 18.3%, with the lowest prevalences (0.2 to 2.5%) being those based on expert opinion. Sixteen studies had measured rates that could confidently be extrapolated to an entire region or country. All 16 studies were conducted in Europe or North America, and in most, the prevalence was between 4% and 10%. However, in some studies, COPD prevalence may be higher. For example, preliminary data from 13,301 participants in the LifeLines cohort study performed in the Netherlands showed that 1920 out of 13,301 subjects had GOLD stage I or higher (14%) (i.e. 1,402 had GOLD stage I, 494 GOLD stage II, and 24 GOLD stage III/IV). In a later study, Halbert et al. (Halbert et al. 2006) identified 101 COPD prevalence estimates from 28 countries during the 1990–2004 time period. The pooled prevalence of COPD was 7.6%; the prevalence of chronic bronchitis alone was 6.4%, and the prevalence of emphysema alone was 1.8%. The pooled prevalence of COPD based on spirometry was 8.9%.
	Although the most accurate prevalence data are from high-income countries (HCs), the WHO estimated that almost 90% of the 3.22 million deaths estimated to be attributable to COPD in 2015 occurred in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) (WHO 2013). Few epidemiologic studies have provided truly comparable international prevalence estimates for COPD. The establishment of the Burden of Obstructive Lung Disease (BOLD) Initiative to assess the global burden of COPD allows more valid comparisons of the prevalence of COPD over time and across ethnopolitical regions (Buist et al. 2007). This study included 9,425 participants from 12 centres in 12 countries including China, Turkey, Austria, South Africa, Iceland, Germany, Poland, Norway, Canada, the United States, Philippines, and Australia. The study showed considerable variation in COPD prevalences, with GOLD stage II or higher COPD in women ranging from 5.1% in Guangzhou, China, to 16.7% in Cape Town, South Africa. In men, it ranged from 8.5% in Reykjavik, Iceland to 22.2% in Cape Town, South Africa. Using a similar study design, the Latin American Project for the Investigation of Obstructive Lung Diseases (PLATINO) studied the prevalence of COPD in 5,315 study participants in five Latin American centres (Mexico, Venezuela, Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay) (Menezes et al. 2005). Crude prevalence rates of COPD ranged from 7.8% in Mexico City, Mexico, to 19.7% in Montevideo, Uruguay. Age and smoking did not fully explain the international variation in disease prevalence, suggesting a role for additional risk factors.





Future prevalence and burden of COPD


	Assessing the future prevalence and burden of COPD requires the consideration of changing population distributions and smoking habits. A recent study (Burgel et al. 2018) modelled COPD prevalence by 2025 based on data from France and predicted a fourfold increase in prevalence of more severe COPD with disproportionate increases in women and individuals over the age of 75. Globally, COPD is projected to be the third-leading cause of death in both men and women with an estimated 4.57 million deaths annually, a 42% increase (WHO 2007). While this increase is driven primarily by LMICs where the mortality share of COPD is expected to increase primarily due to increases in smoking, the population mortality rate of COPD is projected to increase in every economic group studied (WHO 2013). Mortality rates are at risk to substantially increase with economic progress and the adoption of Western practices, particularly in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East (Bilano et al. 2015). In addition to mortality, COPD morbidity is on the rise. COPD is projected to be the seventh cause of morbidity worldwide by 2030 (WHO 2007). Analysis from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries and Risk Factors 2015 study suggests that sub-Saharan Africa and South and Southeast Asia suffer from the highest disability-adjusted life year burdens of COPD (GBD 2015 Chronic Respiratory Disease Collaborators 2017).
	What is most striking about the epidemiology of COPD has been the change in prevalence in women (Aryal et al. 2013). Due to increased smoking rates in women and women taking up smoking at younger ages in recent decades, women now are about equal to men in COPD prevalence with similar mortality (WHO 2007). This trend is expected to be continue in LMICs in response to both increases in smoking, continued biomass exposure, and increasing air pollution. Nonetheless, women with COPD remain less likely to be diagnosed and treated (Miravitlles et al. 2005).





Risk factors for COPD


Cigarette smoking


	COPD usually occurs with exposure to an inhalational irritant. In developed countries, this exposure is predominantly cigarette smoke. Cigarette smoke contains thousands of toxic chemicals including nicotine, acetone, and tar. Smoke inhalation stimulates an inflammatory reaction with recruitment of inflammatory cells to the lung that results in loss of lung parenchyma and airway obstruction. Smoking also leads to impaired mucociliary clearance, increased oxidative stress, and protease/antiprotease imbalance. Second-hand smoke (SHS) exposure increases risk of COPD and negatively impacts lung function by similar mechanisms.
	There is a well-established association between current and cumulative smoking and COPD, and adult smokers experience a faster FEV1 decline than non-smokers. This excess decline in lung function may return to normal levels of ageing-related decline after smoking cessation, emphasizing the importance of early tobacco cessation interventions. Few data are available on the incidence of COPD according to detailed smoking habits. Analysis of the Copenhagen City Heart Study confirmed a higher incidence of COPD in smokers than non-smokers, with 27% of participants who continued to smoke over a 25-year period developing COPD as defined by GOLD stage II–IV COPD, compared with 5.7% of non-smokers (Lokke et al. 2006). The longitudinal Vlagtwedde/Vlaardingen Cohort Study (with a follow-up of 25 years) also showed that persistent cigarette smokers, recidivist smokers, variable pipe/cigar smokers, and subjects who stopped smoking had an increased risk of developing COPD compared to never smokers. The risks of developing COPD in sustained ex-smokers, starters, brief smokers, and persistent pipe/cigar smokers were not significantly different.
	Less is known about the relative risk of non-cigarette smoking habits, including cigars, traditional pipes, water pipes, marijuana, and electronic cigarettes and vaporizers. Observational studies of these modalities will be challenging given the heterogeneity of exposure burden across brands and devices; however, it is likely that relative risk is significant given similar immune and inflammatory effects to cigarette smoking. At this time, evidence about safety and risk is insufficient to recommend alternate inhaled substances as a means of tobacco cessation.





Indoor biomass exposures


	Although cigarette smoking is the most common inhalational exposure related to COPD, biomass exposure from fuels burned for heating and cooking (WHO 2007) can lead to COPD as well. Such indoor air exposures are important risk factors in low-income countries where biomass fuels (wood and crop residues) and coal fuels are often used for heating and cooking without appropriate ventilation. WHO estimates that approximately 3 billion people, predominantly in LMICs, cook with solid fuels and kerosene resulting in household air pollution and increased COPD risk (WHO 2007). It is estimated that this exposure results in 25% of premature deaths from COPD in LMICs (WHO 2007). Recently, it has been recognized that poor inner-city and rural areas of wealthier countries have similarly high rates of indoor biomass exposure (Levy et al. 2018). While COPD is also thought to be related to outdoor pollution levels, current evidence is not conclusive regarding the magnitude of this risk (Schikowski et al. 2014).





Occupational exposures


	Occupational exposure to dusts, gases, and fumes are also associated with the rate of decline in FEV1 and the development of COPD. Some examples of occupational risk factors for COPD are coal dust, silica dust, oil mists, welding fumes, and organic dusts including cotton, grain, and wood. It is estimated that 15 to more than 20% of COPD is caused by occupational factors (Lytras et al. 2018). For example, the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey in the United States found that approximately 20% of COPD cases in the United States were attributable to work-related exposures (Hnizdo et al. 2002). The proportion was even higher (approximately 30%) in never smokers. Individuals who have occupational exposures and also smoke have an even greater COPD risk.





HIV


	Pulmonary disease has been a cause of significant morbidity and mortality in HIV-infected individuals since the beginning of the AIDS epidemic. COPD and emphysema were reported to be more common in HIV-infected individuals prior to the advent of effective antiretroviral therapy (ART)(Diaz et al. 2000) and prevalence of lung function imparirment has not decreased significantly in recent years. Population studies in the Veterans Administration found that a diagnosis of COPD was more common in HIV-infected individuals than in similar HIV-uninfected individuals in the current era (Crothers et al. 2011), and studies of pulmonary function have demonstrated that HIV is an independent risk factor for impairment of diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, a lung function abnormality that reflects emphysema/COPD as well as pulmonary vascular disease (Crothers 2013; Fitzpatrick et al. 2013). In addition, over half of outpatient HIV-infected cohorts report respiratory symptoms (Gingo et al. 2014). Although COPD occurs in HIV-infected individuals who have never smoked, it is still most common in smokers, making smoking cessation critical in this population.





Genetic risk factors


	The contribution of genetics to COPD is exemplified by the heritable disorder alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD). Individuals with AATD have a mutation in the SERPINA1 gene that results in abnormal structure of or decreases in endogenous levels of alpha-1 antitrypsin, a critical antiprotease whose absence can lead to breakdown of lung tissue and COPD in early life (Piitulainen and Eriksson 1999). The interplay between inhalational exposure and genetics is well-illustrated by the observation not all patients with AATD will develop COPD, and those who smoke experience lung function decline 2–4 times faster than never smokers with AATD (Piitulainen and Eriksson 1999). Similarly, not all individuals with a heavy cigarette smoking burden develop COPD.
	Other than the single gene AATD, genetic factors in COPD are likely multifactorial and have been difficult to study. Since COPD is predominantly expressed in later years, the parents of individuals with COPD have often already died, and the children of individuals with COPD are likely to be too young to have significant fixed airway obstruction. Initial genetic studies on COPD included small numbers of subjects and applied different definitions of disease, hampering a valid comparison between studies and increasing the likelihood of spurious results. Many positive results from genetic studies of COPD have therefore not been replicated. Furthermore, lack of replication might also be due to the apparent difficulties of extrapolating results from one population to another, such as Asians and Caucasians.
	Most studies on genetics of COPD have focused on genes that are involved in the processing of various tobacco smoke products, oxidative stress, or in the protease/antiprotease balance. In particular, variations in the genes encoding enzymes that detoxify cigarette smoke products (and are thus protective against oxidative stress) may explain why only a proportion of smokers develop COPD. Candidate genes identified in this way include EPHX1, ADAM33, MMP1, GSTP1, GSTT1, GSTM1, HMOX1, and SERPINA1 (Postma et al. 2011).
	Genomewide association (GWA) studies are applied to identify genetic loci that are associated with disease using markers throughout the genome, rather than selected on the basis of their assumed biological function. The first COPD GWA study identified variants in the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) subunit genes, CHRNA3/5 (Pillai et al. 2009) which were confirmed in later studies (Kim and Lee 2015). SNPs in this nicotinic cluster have previously been related to smoking habits and addiction, raising the question of whether these genes are directly involved in lung function loss leading to COPD per se, or act indirectly through effects on nicotine addiction. Other GWA studies have identified IREB2, which regulates cellular iron that is associated with pulmonary artery enlargement in COPD, AGER, the soluble protein product of which (sRAGE) is a potential biomarker for emphysema presence and progression, and hedgehog interacting protein (HHIP) which plays a role in lung development and injury response (Kim and Lee 2015). A recent whole genome sequencing study of patients with severe COPD confirmed findings of variants of HHIP and CHRNA3 genes as influential (Prokopenko et al. 2018). GWA studies have also been complemented and validated by quantitative trait loci (QTL) analyses, which allow incorporation of gene expression, methylation, and many other data types (Morrow et al. 2018). To date, discovery of these genetic variations has not led to novel therapies.





COPD prevention


	The mainstay of COPD prevention is reducing exposure to cigarette smoke and to indoor air pollutants. Barriers to prevention efforts include the underdiagnosis of COPD, lack of public awareness of the disease, and inadequate policies for preventing exposures. In LMICs, respiratory disease prevention efforts may be more focused on communicable pulmonary diseases such as tuberculosis and pneumonia. The Centers for Disease Control identified four main goals for COPD prevention (CDC 2011) (Box 8.3.2). The WHO recommends five policies for decreasing tobacco use that would be expected to impact COPD incidence (Box 8.3.2).
	 	Box 8.3.2 Centers for Disease Control goals for COPD prevention
	 	• Surveillance and evaluation: Improving public health data
	• Public health research and prevention strategies: Improving understanding of COPD
	• Programmes and policies: Improving collaboration among stakeholders
	• Communication: Improving awareness of COPD
	World Health Organization policies for controlling tobacco use
	• Promotion of smoke-free environments
	• Support for tobacco cessation programmes
	• Health warnings on cigarettes
	• Bans on tobacco advertisers
	• Higher taxes on tobacco products
	From Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Public Health Strategic Framework for COPD Prevention. Atlanta, GA: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; 2011. Available at www.cdc.gov/copd; World Health Organization. World Health Statistics 2008.
	Public health efforts aimed at reducing smoking rates and encouraging smoking cessation are of great importance. Improved ventilation measures to reduce indoor pollutants in houses decrease both the prevalence and morbidity of COPD (Zhou et al. 2014). For example, a systematic review and meta-analysis of improved biomass cookstoves found decreased COPD and respiratory symptoms in women (Thakur et al. 2018). The greatest benefits in COPD prevention may be in targeting those patients at risk for impaired lung development or rapid lung function decline in the setting of harmful exposures—assuming that they can be identified a priori, which remains the topic of ongoing research efforts.





Epidemiology, risk factors, and prevention of asthma


Epidemiology of asthma


	Like COPD, asthma is prevalent worldwide with an estimated 300 million people affected (WHO 2007). Its prevalence varies by country (Fig. 8.3.2), and it is increasing worldwide, with exact rates depending on environmental exposures, lifestyle factors, and urbanization (WHO 2007). Given the strong relationship of asthma with allergy, its increasing prevalence mirrors that of allergy. Despite availability of multiple therapeutic agents for asthma, mortality is about 250,000 deaths worldwide each year (WHO 2007). Asthma is also highly morbid, leading to both missed workdays and missed school given its frequency in children. Both morbidity and mortality from asthma can be linked to lack of access to medical care and adequate therapies.
	Fig. 8.3.2 World map of the prevalence of clinical asthma.
	Reproduced with permission from World Health Organization, Global surveillance, prevention and control of chronic respiratory diseases. http://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/handle/10665/43776/9789241563468_eng.pdf
	Two multidecade survey studies, the European Community Respiratory Health Survey (ECRHS) and the International Study of Asthma and Allergies in Childhood (ISAAC), started in the early 1990s and provided insight into changing asthma prevalence trends. Both studies showed striking international differences in asthma symptom prevalence with a particularly high prevalence of reported asthma symptoms in English-speaking countries including the British Isles, New Zealand, Australia, the United States, and Canada (Asher et al. 1995; Burney et al. 1996; Asher et al. 1998; Beasley et al. 1998). Among the non-English-speaking European countries, both studies showed high asthma prevalence in Western Europe, with lower prevalences in Eastern and Southern Europe. These studies also provided insights into asthma in Africa and Asia. These areas generally showed relatively low asthma prevalence (Fig. 8.3.2). In particular, prevalence was low in developing countries such as China and Indonesia whereas more affluent Asian countries such as Singapore and Japan showed relatively high asthma prevalence rates. The ISAAC survey also showed that centres in Latin America had particularly high symptom prevalence. Interestingly, Latin America showed higher prevalences than Spain itself, in contrast to the general tendency for more affluent countries to have higher prevalence rates.





Future prevalence and burden of asthma


	Global asthma trends have exhibited either slight increases or plateaus in prevalence. While many theories have been proposed for divergent studies, there is no clear explanation. Countries with similar socioeconomic and genetic compositions have experienced divergent prevalence rate progression (de Korte-de Boer et al. 2015; Backman et al. 2017). The asthma prevalence in many affluent countries has peaked or even begun to decline, whereas asthma symptom prevalence continues to rise in less affluent countries. Changes in prevalence of asthma may result from changes in methods of diagnosis, but changes in environmental risk factors may also play a role.





Risk factors for asthma


Atopy


	Atopy, or the presence of IgE antibodies to specific allergens, is strongly associated with asthma within populations. About half of asthma cases are linked to atopy (Arbes et al. 2007), although there is a lower population attributable risk (~20%) in less affluent populations and risk is variable (Weinmayr et al. 2007). IgE levels in serum are associated with a diagnosis of asthma and with presence of airway hyperresponsiveness. Although atopy is a risk factor for asthma, it represents a biological response to various exposures (e.g. allergen exposure) which may be modified by susceptibility factors (genetic and/or environmental).





Allergen exposure


	In sensitized asthmatics, allergen exposure can trigger asthma attacks and prolonged exposure can lead to the prolongation and exacerbation of symptoms; however, a causative role of allergen exposure in development of asthma is less clear. The key study linking allergen exposure in infancy to the subsequent development of asthma is that of Sporik et al. (1990) who followed 67 children with a family history of atopy. Subsequent longitudinal birth cohort studies found little or no association between early dust mite allergen exposure and asthma later in childhood (Tepas et al. 2006). A recent systematic review reported that visible mould or mould odour was associated with respiratory symptoms, wheezing, and development of asthma in children (Caillaud et al. 2018).





Gender and ethnicity


	There are a variety of demographic factors that are associated with asthma including age, gender, and ethnicity. Asthma incidence and prevalence are consistently lower in females than in males before age 12 years, whereas during adolescence and adulthood there is evidence of higher incidence and prevalence in females (Kimbell-Dunn et al. 1999). The reasons for this disparity are unclear, but could be related to later age of asthma onset in childhood and adolescence in females and differences between boys and girls in exposures, airway size, atopy, and frequency and severity of lower respiratory tract illnesses. These differences could also be due to hormonal influences. Hormones likely play a role as demonstrated by premenstrual asthma which manifests as worsening of asthma symptoms around the time of menstruation and the observation that pregnancy can often increase or decrease asthma control. Ethnicity also appears to influence asthma risk. For example, Puerto Ricans in the US have a high rate of asthma while Mexicans in the US have very low rates, a finding that has been termed the ‘Hispanic paradox’ (Rosser et al. 2014).





Socioeconomic status


	The impact of socioeconomic status on asthma is conflicting. Studies in the 1960s and 1970s suggested that asthma is more common in children in the higher socioeconomic status (SES); however, severe asthma appears to be more common in children in lower income groups (Stewart et al. 2001) and in some disadvantaged ethnic groups (Rosser et al. 2014). These findings could represent either a greater prevalence of asthma in disadvantaged groups, or increased severity due to environmental factors (e.g. SHS, nutrition, occupational exposures) or inadequate disease management and poor access to healthcare.





Obesity


	Studies have shown an association between body weight and asthma in both adults and children with prospective studies suggesting that obesity precedes asthma (Ronmark et al. 2005; Noal et al. 2011). However, findings supporting this association have not been entirely consistent (Noal et al. 2011). The evidence linking obesity and atopy is also conflicting with some studies suggesting that obesity is associated with asthma independent of atopy (Visness et al. 2010; Holguin et al. 2013) and with the identification of asthma clusters containing predominantly obese, nonatopic patients (Moore et al. 2010).





Diet


	Diet throughout the lifespan may impact asthma risk and severity. Many studies including several infant cohort studies have investigated the effects of breastfeeding on allergies and asthma with some studies showing protective effects, some showing no effect, and others suggesting that breastfeeding is a risk factor (Friedman and Zeiger 2005; Kramer et al. 2007; Matheson et al. 2007). Other nutritional factors may also play a role in the aetiology of asthma. In particular, it has been speculated that the increase in asthma prevalence may be due to a change in dietary patterns in the past few decades, that is, as cultures have become more ‘Westernized’ they have shifted from growing and consuming locally grown foods to consuming more processed foods and less fresh produce. This hypothesis is supported by results from the ISAAC Phase II and other studies (Chatzi and Kogevinas 2009; Nagel et al. 2010) that found that fruit, vegetable, and fish consumption was associated with a lower prevalence of current wheeze and asthma. Development of some atopic disorders has been associated with exposures to n-6 versus n-3 fatty acids, but this finding was not consistent for all atopy/allergies (Almqvist et al. 2007; Notenboom et al. 2011). Maternal folate supplementation during pregnancy has also been suggested as a risk factor for asthma in childhood.





Vitamin D


	There has been conflict in studies suggesting an association between vitamin D deficiency and asthma risk. Several studies based on dietary questionnaire findings have associated higher levels of maternal vitamin D with lower rates of asthma in children (Muehleisen and Gallo 2013) and low serum vitamin D levels in asthmatic children and adults with asthma severity and poor asthma control (Korn et al. 2013). A meta-analysis of double-blind, randomized, controlled trials of vitamin D found that vitamin D resulted in decreased rate of asthma exacerbations that required corticosteroid treatment (Joliffe et al. 2017), but not all trials examining vitamin D supplementation have not been successful in decreasing asthma rates or improving outcomes.





Outdoor air pollution


	The role of outdoor air pollutants (particulate matter (PM), ozone, nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and sulphur dioxide) in asthma has been extensively studied (Guarnieri and Balmes 2014). An association between measures of distance to major roads or traffic density and asthma symptoms has been demonstrated in a number of European countries (WHO 2005). Also, a large number of studies have reported associations between direct measurements of air pollution levels and exacerbation of pre-existing asthma, both in children and adults (WHO 2005). Some studies, including a birth cohort study (Brauer et al. 2007), have also suggested that air pollution may cause new onset of asthma and allergic disease. In particular, several large prospective studies have suggested a role for ozone (McDonnell et al. 1999; McConnell et al. 2002), although significant associations with some asthma outcomes were also shown for PM2.5, soot, and NO2 (Brauer et al. 2007).





Indoor air pollution


	Little is currently known about the contribution of indoor air pollutants (other than SHS) to the incidence and prevalence of asthma. Nitrogen dioxide from burning fossil fuels has received the most attention while sulphur dioxide from burning sulphur-containing coal or gas, mosquito coil smoke, and formaldehyde from wood preparation have also been considered. Particulates from open or closed wood and coal burning fires have received less attention in HCs (Oluwole et al. 2017), but have been studied in LMICs where very high indoor levels have been encountered. Damp indoor environments and indoor fungal exposure may also play a role as demonstrated in a large number of studies conducted across many geographical regions (Douwes and Pearce 2003; Karvonen et al. 2018). Further study is needed to determine whether programmes to decrease indoor PM concentrations or humidity levels can prove effective in decreasing asthma prevalence in addition to decreasing respiratory morbidity (Beasley et al. 2015).





Tobacco


	Although smoking is a primary risk factor for COPD, it may also influence asthma, both if asthmatic patients smoke or if they are exposed to SHS either before or after birth. The evidence for a role of tobacco smoke in asthma is strongest for increases in severity in children who already have asthma; however, an increasing number of studies also show positive associations between SHS and incidence of asthma (Accordini et al. 2012). Several meta-analyses concluded that household SHS exposure was associated with the incidence of new-onset asthma and incidence of wheezing in younger and older children (Vonk et al. 2003; Burke et al. 2012).





Occupational exposures


	Occupational asthma is the most common occupational respiratory disease in HCs. Estimates of the total proportion of adult occupational asthma range from 2 to 15% in the United States, 15% in Japan (Chan-Yeung and Malo 1994), 5% in Spain (Kogevinas et al. 1996), 2–3% in New Zealand (Fishwick et al. 1997), and 2–6% in the United Kingdom (Meredith and Nordman 1996). A study in the United States estimated that new-onset asthma may be caused by occupational exposures in as many as one of six adult patients (Mazurek et al. 2013). More than 250 agents have been identified as causes of occupational asthma. Some of the most common occupational asthmagens include flour/grain dusts, wood dusts, latex allergens, and isocyanates (Schenker et al. 1998).





Infections


	The increase in allergy and asthma contrasts strongly with a reduced prevalence of infectious diseases and corresponding decreased exposure to non-infectious micro-organisms. This reduction in exposure to micro-organisms has been hypothesized as a possible explanation for the allergy and asthma epidemic (Lambrecht and Hammad 2017) and is commonly referred to as the ‘hygiene hypothesis’. The hygiene hypothesis has been prompted by evidence that overcrowding and unhygienic conditions were associated with a lower prevalence of atopy, eczema, hay fever, and asthma. The hygiene hypothesis may not fully explain the current time and geographical trends in asthma prevalence, but the changes associated with Westernization may be contributing to the global increases in asthma susceptibility and prevalence. It remains unclear as to what is the most important factor in protection from allergies and asthma: dose, route (oral–faecal versus airborne), type of infection (viral versus bacterial versus parasitic) or location (upper versus lower airways or digestive tract).





Viruses


	Viral infections are common causes of exacerbations of asthma and associated with hospital admissions in both children and adults. In fact, respiratory viral infections are detected in the majority of asthma exacerbations; of these, about 60% are rhinoviruses (Johnston 2007). Viral infections may also be involved in the development of asthma, but the evidence is less clear. Longitudinal studies have shown that both respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus infection increases the risk of subsequent recurrent wheezing and asthma in early childhood (Lemanske et al. 2005; Feldman et al. 2015). The mechanisms of viral-induced asthma are poorly understood, but some evidence suggests that neutrophilic inflammation, impaired innate immune responses and TH17 signalling dysregulation play crucial roles (Johnston 2007; Das et al. 2017).





Bacteria


	Exposures to different types of non-pathogenic bacteria may have differential effects on atopy and asthma beginning at birth. Perinatal microbial exposure with vaginal vs. caesarean delivery is associated with decreased likelihood of developing childhood asthma (Kim et al. 2019), but the specific bacteria involved and whether the relationship is causal is not yet known. Additionally, studies in farming and non-farming environments have suggested that diversity of microbial species, rather than exposure to one particular microbial component, may be particularly protective (Heederik and von Mutius 2012). Consistent with these findings are observations that daycare centres—known to be associated with a lower prevalence of allergies and asthma in attending children—are associated with considerable bacterial diversity (Lee et al. 2007) as have households with daycare attendees, or with cats and dogs (Maier et al. 2010). Live bacterial exposure may not be required as levels of pro-inflammatory microbial agents (such as bacterial endotoxin) have a significant inverse association between indoor endotoxin levels and atopic sensitization, hay fever, and atopic asthma (Stein et al. 2016).





The microbiome


	With the advent of next generation sequencing, we are able to identify many more microbes in environments in the human body than previously detected by traditional culture-based methods. The microbiome, i.e. the total microbes and their genetic content in the human body, may impact asthma development and progression (Lynch and Boushey 2016). It is possible that the microbial composition and function of the lung microbiome alter local immune response and contributes to asthma. Enrichment of certain bacteria in the lungs is associated with inflammation, and studies have found differences in lung bacterial communities in individuals with asthma compared to health controls with enrichment of bacteria such as Prevotella and Haemophilus (Depner et al. 2017; Durack et al. 2017, 2018). The gut microbiome may also impact asthma as the microbial communities in the gut have profound effects on systemic immunity and can lead to tolerance or inflammation. Dysbiosis during infancy and childhood is associated with wheezing, atopy, and development of asthma (Fujimara et al. 2016). While efforts to change the gut microbiome with probiotics have shown some success in eczema and potentially atopy (Wickens et al. 2013; Cabana et al. 2017), similar benefits in asthma have not been demonstrated and no attempts to directly alter the lung microbiome have been performed. Whether therapeutic alterations in the microbiome or direct targeting of regulatory T cell processes may benefit asthma control or prevention requires further study.





Genetic factors


	Asthma is multifactorial in origin and influenced by multiple genes and environmental factors. The heritable component of asthma has been variably estimated to be between 35 and 95% (Ober and Yao 2011). It is not inherited in a simple Mendelian fashion, and particular genetic factors may affect one or more aspects of the complex etiological processes potentially involved in asthma including atopic sensitization, BHR, airway inflammation, and innate immunity. Investigating possible genes for these individual etiological factors is also fraught with difficulties, as control of these factors is also multifactorial. Multiple genes may lead to the same phenotype in different individuals or multiple genes contribute to asthma in a single person. Asthma development, exacerbations, and progression may all involve different environmental triggers and genetic factors, further complicating genetic studies.
	Despite the considerable heterogeneity observed, a number of genome linkage and GWA studies have identified several chromosomal regions significantly associated with asthma susceptibility. Several genes on the 17q21 locus including the ORMDL3/GSDMB genes have been identified in multiple populations as associated with asthma (Moffatt et al. 2007; Moffatt et al. 2010). In many cases, the involvement of the products of these genes in asthma pathophysiology is feasible, as they are associated with a variety of inflammatory or epithelial/cell-contact pathways and include genes for cytokines such as IL-13 and IL-33. As with COPD, the biological plausibility of these associations has also more recently been strengthened with epigenomic QTL studies (Nicodemus-Johnson et al. 2016; Dijk et al. 2018). However, even when incorporating epigenetic factors, these genes make only a small contribution to overall disease risk on an individual basis, and there may be issues due to the use of different asthma classifications in different studies. While recent meta-analyses of GWA studies have leveraged large cohort sizes into discoveries of further novel disease-associated loci (Demenais et al. 2018), some gene variants may only be associated with certain asthma subtypes and will be difficult to identify with present methodology.





Asthma prevention


	Risk factors for asthma may be more difficult to modify than those for COPD, and the heterogeneous nature of the disease complicates public health initiatives. As most asthma begins in childhood, the majority of prevention efforts have been focused on younger children, although asthma can also present in adulthood. Given potential roles for exposures to indoor allergens and chemicals, strategies targeting the home environment may be effective although these programmes have not been proven as primary prevention (Tanno et al. 2017). Secondary prevention efforts are targeted at improving asthma control and include efforts aimed at decreasing environmental triggers and in providing appropriate asthma controller medications. Encouraging parental smoking cessation is clearly important in both primary and secondary prevention as well as in prevention of COPD in the parent. Programmes targeting improvement in training health professionals, establishing treatment guidelines, and improving public awareness may decrease healthcare costs for asthma. Given the links of asthma with the microbiome, use of probiotics may be helpful as a primary or secondary prevention measure, but their efficacy has not been demonstrated in large-scale studies. As with COPD, prevention efforts face different obstacles in LMICs and HCs.





Treatment of COPD and asthma


	The initiation and evaluation of treatment for patients with COPD or asthma is complex. Specific recommendations regarding therapy can be found in disease-specific international (GOLD, GINA, etc) and regional guidelines (Agusti et al. 2017, GINA 2018). All patients with chronic respiratory disease benefit from avoidance of inhalational irritants (particularly cigarette smoke), immunization against common respiratory pathogens (i.e. pneumococcus, influenza), and careful evaluation for comorbid conditions. Patients with mild, intermittent symptoms from either asthma or COPD can be managed with short-acting, as-needed bronchodilators that can be taken during or before activities or exposures that provoke respiratory symptoms. Persistent asthma is managed with inhaled corticosteroids as first-line therapy, with long-acting bronchodilators and other medications including low-dose theophylline and leukotriene receptor antagonists often added in stepwise fashion until disease control is achieved. In individuals with poorly controlled asthma despite these therapies, tiotropium, a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, has been shown to modestly improve lung function and to increase the time to severe exacerbation requiring oral steroid use. Anti-immunoglobin E treatment and anti-interleukin 5 treatment can likewise be considered in individuals with poorly controlled allergic or severe eosinophilic asthma, respectively (GINA 2018). In contrast, daily COPD pharmacotherapy starts with long-acting bronchodilators; inhaled corticosteroids are typically added for recurrent exacerbations. ACO treatment, due to increased disease severity and combined features of persistent airflow obstruction and airway inflammation (Vaz Fragoso et al. 2017), usually includes both long-acting bronchodilators and inhaled steroids. Patients with functional status limitations can benefit significantly from specialized pulmonary rehabilitation programmes, though the benefits are better established in COPD (Mendes et al. 2010; McCarthy et al. 2015) than asthma.





Conclusions


	What do these epidemiological findings tell us about the future of asthma and COPD? The prevalence of COPD is still increasing, and future projections indicate that the global burden of COPD will increase even further. Cigarette smoking remains the greatest cause of COPD, and increasing use in the developing world will ensure that tobacco remains one of the most significant threats to global public health throughout the twenty-first century. Other major causes of COPD including occupational and indoor exposures, particularly among the poor in all countries, remain underappreciated and inadequately addressed. The downstream impact of evolving social trends like electronic cigarettes remains unclear, but demands further study. Different genetic susceptibility to lung function decline from inhalational exposures leads differential likelihood of developing COPD. International differences in COPD prevalence are likely to persist, and research into these disparities may help in targeting smoking cessation and other public health measures towards the highest-risk subgroups.
	Global asthma rates continue to increase with wide variation between countries and regions, and the main drivers of asthma development remain incompletely understood. Current public health efforts are thus limited to improving asthma control rather than targeted towards disease prevention. Shifting global patterns in exposure, diet, and occupation are all likely involved in altering the interplay between immunity and environment—through the “hygiene hypothesis” or otherwise—and further study is required to parse these complex interactions to understand how public health interventions can more effectively decrease the global burden of asthma.

8.4


Obesity


	Anna Peeters and Tim Lobstein





Introduction to obesity


	Globally, the numbers of adults experiencing obesity has increased over sixfold since 1975, from some 100 million to around 670 million in 2016 (Anonymous 2017). In the same period the numbers of children and adolescents living with obesity have risen more than tenfold (from 11m to 125m). While viewed as a condition affecting developed economies, over 15%, some 105m of adults with obesity, live in China and India. Over 20% of children with obesity live in China alone.
	Many middle-income countries are now experiencing a nutritional “double burden” of obesity and undernourishment (stunting, underweight, and/or micronutrient deficiencies) simultaneously. These trends are of major concern for population health and healthcare costs and capacity around the world, with obesity increasing the risk of a range of chronic diseases, disability, and early death. There is increasing international agreement on the need to take action to improve population diets and body weight, and a number of countries are now implementing obesity prevention policies such as warnings on food labelling and taxes on sugary drinks. However, further action at global political as well as local community levels are needed to avoid the projected future burden on health, well-being, and productivity.





Definitions of obesity


Commonly used measures for population health


	The World Health Organization (WHO) defines obesity as ‘abnormal or excessive fat accumulation that may impair health’ (WHO 2000). While a number of methods measure an individual’s body fat percentage with a high degree of accuracy, such as doubly labelled water, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, and magnetic resonance imaging, the cost of these methods usually prohibits their use in population surveys (Peeters et al. 2016). Instead, such surveys usually rely on anthropometric markers which are simple and reproducible to measure and have a high correlation with percentage body fat. The primary anthropometric measures are weight, height, and waist and hip circumferences. Most commonly, weight and height are recorded and combined to create an index of body mass (the BMI), calculated as weight (in kilograms) divided by the square of height (in metres).
	While body mass index (BMI) is valuable for estimating risk of obesity in population groups and for showing trends across time or disparities between groups, BMI alone should not be relied on for diagnostic purposes for individuals: high levels of muscle mass may raise BMI without indicating a risk of excess adiposity, while low levels of muscle mass may put someone at risk of excess adiposity within the ‘normal’ BMI range.





Adults


	Obesity was originally defined by analysis undertaken by the US Metropolitan Life Insurance Company relating BMI values to mortality (James 1976). A BMI of approximately 25 kg/m2 was identified as the cut-off above which mortality rates increased, with a BMI of 30 kg/m2 at 20% above this upper ‘normal’ BMI limit of 25 kg/m2. In 1995, WHO accepted BMI as the method for assessing degrees of underweight and overweight and took a BMI lower limit of 18.5 kg/m2 for distinguishing normal from underweight (Table 8.4.1) (WHO 1995).
	However, it is recognized that all common epidemiological measures of obesity at a population level have limitations. From a public health perspective, the precise choice of cut-off point is arbitrary: the health hazards are progressive, age dependent, and not substantially changed at any particular cut-off point. The classic comorbidities intrinsically linked to an excess BMI, for example, diabetes, hypertension, gall stones, and coronary heart disease are linearly related to BMI from a BMI nadir of about 19 or 20 kg/m2.
	While anthropometric measures such as weight and height provide simpler, less expensive, assessment of body composition than methods, such as imaging and bioelectrical impedance analysis, they do not provide a direct measure of body fatness, and as such which method is best has been much debated (Tanamas et al. 2016). Furthermore, for the same BMI, Europids generally have less body fat than Asians, but more than Africans or Pacific Islanders, which has led to suggestions that a lower BMI threshold should be used to define overweight and obesity in Asians, or that further subcategories of BMI should trigger public health action in different populations (WHO Expert Consultation 2004).
	Furthermore, as people age, fat mass tends to increase while muscle mass decreases. As a consequence, BMI may remain stable as people age despite an increase in body fat, particularly among the elderly. Sometimes referred to as sarcopenic obesity (Stenholm et al. 2008) the implication is that lower thresholds of BMI should trigger interventions for obesity prevention and treatment in older populations.
	Various alternative or additional measures have been advocated to improve estimates of adiposity and/or to provide better prediction of ill-health and risk of chronic diseases. These include waist circumference (WC), waist–hip ratio (WHR), waist-height ratio, neck circumference, conicity index, and body adiposity index. Most of these involve computation of convenience-ratios, which do not correspond to biological interpretation. They are also hard to visualize, a particular obstacle to public understanding in applications for health promotion. Where the range of body fat is very large (as in most population surveys), WC correlates surprisingly strongly with total body fat, explaining 70.4–77.8% of variance, so it is a little better than BMI, at least in men.(Lean et al. 1996) It is also a slightly better predictor of metabolic risk and chronic diseases than BMI, partly by better identifying individuals at increased health risk through greater total body fat, and partly by also including those with central adiposity who are not identified by BMI (Lean et al. 1995). The simplicity of BMI remains its major strength, resulting in recommendation by the WHO that ‘BMI provides the most useful population-level measure of overweight and obesity’ (WHO 2011). However, recent data has indicated that the overlap between those populations categorized as high risk adiposity by WC and BMI are increasingly differing over time, suggesting further consideration may be needed of new, combined measures (Gearon et al. 2018).
	Table 8.4.1 provides the international cut-points for BMI and WC in adults. While there are known ethnic differences in level of risk at different cut-points, the WHO recommends all countries report against these cut-points to allow for international comparisons (WHO Expert Consultation 2004).

Children


	Classifying overweight and obesity in children is more difficult that with adults due to their rapid growth and body changes as they age. Classification systems based on national population surveys have been developed and are in use in several countries. The International Obesity Task Force (IOTF) published a multinationally based classification system for children in 2000, and extended in 2012, which has been in widespread use since (Cole et al. 2000; Cole and Lobstein 2012). More recently the WHO developed a set of classification standards for children under 5 years, and a further set of classification reference values for older children (WHO 2018c, WHO 2018d). The two international classification systems show broad agreement but the prevalence of overweight and obesity in a given population can differ somewhat according to age and sex across these classification systems. It is recommended that estimates of excess adiposity in child populations should be reported using both IOTF and WHO classification systems to allow backward comparability and estimates of trends.





Obesity as a disease


	Over the past five years a number of national medical associations have identified a need to classify obesity as a disease. In the WHO’s expert report Obesity: Preventing and Managing the Global Epidemic (WHO 2000) obesity is described as a chronic disease, but the description has been challenged, not least because it would classify millions of adults and children as ill. In 2013, the American Medical Association published its support for describing obesity as a disease, arguing that while such a declaration would have no legal implications, it would pave the way for those with obesity to be better treated within the American medical system.
	This position statement reflected the growing opinion globally that people with obesity are not receiving the timely, affordable, evidence-based treatment that would improve their health and quality of life. While treatment options and pathways of care exist, it has been shown that many people with obesity do not receive adequate treatment and management due to reasons ranging from discrimination by health professionals to inadequate health system funding (All-Party Parliamentary Group on Obesity 2018).
	The rationale for identifying obesity as a disease includes the potential to drive broader healthcare coverage for both the prevention and treatment of obesity, in part through increasing recognition of the biologically irreversible nature of weight gain.
	In 2017, the World Obesity Federation released a position statement supporting the identification of obesity as a chronic relapsing progressive disease process (Bray et al. 2017). This position statement argued that ‘obesity fits the epidemiological model of a disease process except that the toxic or pathological agent is food rather than a microbe’. As such they argued for improved treatment and management globally due to the continuous effort needed to control the relapsing disease process of obesity.
	At the same time the World Obesity Federation published an accompanying article acknowledging that declaring obesity to be a disease could have a variety of benefits (Lobstein et al. 2017). It argued for the beneficial effects for people living with obesity who require access to medical advice and support, and that declaring obesity a disease would strengthen the argument for dealing with the social determinants, obesogenic environments, and systemic causes of individual weight gain. Furthermore, it may help to counter the commonly held assumption that obesity was a ‘lifestyle choice’ and entirely an individual’s responsibility.
	As more health organizations around the world declare obesity as a disease, it will be important to monitor whether this action supports the achievement of better prevention, management, and treatment of overweight and obesity.





Global trends in overweight and obesity


Trends in the prevalence in obesity


	As at 2016, some 390 million women and 281 million men were living with obesity globally, and a further 1.3 billion adults were overweight, non-obese (BMI 25–30 kg/m2) (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration 2017). Among children and youth (ages 5–19y) some 50 million girls and 74 million boys were living with obesity, and a further 213 million overweight, non-obese youth (Box 8.4.1).
	 	Box 8.4.1 Estimates of global obesity prevalence
	The figures cited in this chapter are based on the World Health Organization’s Global Health Observatory database (see http://www.who.int/gho/ncd/risk_factors/overweight/en/), provided by the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (see http://ncdrisc.org/index.html). The methods used to make national and regional estimates include interpolations between studies undertaken at different times and cross-matching countries for their demographic similarities. Adjustments are made for survey data which rely on self-reported weights and heights. Classification of BMI in childhood is based on the WHO-recommended cut-offs. Similar methods have been used for the Global Burden of Disease analyses (see http://www.healthdata.org/gbd) although in this case the classification of BMI in childhood is based on the IOTF cut-offs.
	When did obesity become a major public health concern? If we look back through the literature we find Kannel and Gordon in the USA (Kannel and Gordon 1974) suggesting in 1974, ‘There is a massive preoccupation with obesity in affluent countries and both the afflicted and their physicians have been engaged in frustrating efforts to correct it’. In the same year, Garrow in the UK (Garrow 1974) stated ‘Obesity is by far the most common and serious nutritional disease in Britain and other affluent societies’.
	In that year obesity (as currently defined) was affecting around 13% of the adult population in the USA, and under 7% of adults in the UK. In the next four decades obesity rates in those countries more than trebled, and by 2016 the disease was affecting over 36% of adults in the USA and 28% in the UK, along with 29% in Australia, 27% in South Africa, 29% in Mexico and 35% in Egypt.
	These latter two figures are perhaps the most alarming, as the rate of increase in several middle-income economies has been far steeper than that in high-income countries. As Figure 8.4.1 shows (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration 2017) traditionally affluent countries have shown a gradual rise in obesity prevalence from the early 1970s, whereas in several middle-income countries the rise in adult obesity prevalence is more recent, and more dramatic, and is taking place in a context where weight management services may be less accessible and healthcare pathways less developed.

	As the principle drivers of obesity—including sedentary behaviour, urbanization, and unhealthy and ultraprocessed food consumption—become more globalized, so the rise in obesity prevalence can be seen in populations exposed to these drivers. Estimates undertaken for the Global Burden of Disease study indicate that in the last decade the countries experiencing the most rapid increase in obesity prevalence are the emerging markets of SE Asia, Latin America, and parts of Africa (Table 8.4.2).

Childhood obesity


	Although obesity is still uncommon among children, its prevalence has shown a similar pattern of increase across countries to that of adults (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration 2017) We have noted that there are several methods for defining obesity in children, and while direct comparisons between surveys may not always be robust, trends using the same definitions are strongly indicative of the rising scale of the problem.
	As with adults, long-term increases in childhood obesity can be seen for most high-income countries, and more rapid increases found in low-and middle-income economies. Several regions are of particular concern: the countries of Latin America, from Mexico southwards, have shown a doubling of childhood obesity levels in just 20 years, while adolescents in the Middle East from Egypt through to the Gulf are showing obesity prevalence levels around 15–20%, and some Pacific islands are experiencing adolescent obesity prevalence above 30% (Table 8.4.3).
