Age and social disparities


	While variations in prevalence levels between countries have been high, and can partly be explained by a country’s stage of economic development, disparities between population subgroups within countries reveal additional factors of public health concern.
	The clearest variation across population group is by age (Fig. 8.4.2). Obesity prevalence increases by age in virtually all countries studied, with a decline in prevalence shown only in the age groups above 65 years in most high-income countries. This accumulation through the life course reflects the difficulty in losing weight once gained, along with the rising prevalence in all age groups from one decade to the next. It means that national averages can mask a more serious crisis: in the UK the average obesity prevalence level is 26% but among adults aged 55–64y it is 34% (NHS Digital 2017a) and therefore, all else being equal, over a third of adults can expect to become obese during their lives. In the USA the figure for older adults rises above 45% for the general population, and over 57% for non-Hispanic black women.
	Fig. 8.4.2 Increasing BMI by age to late middle-age in the UK.
	Source: data from NHS Digital (2017), ‘Health Survey for England 2016: Adult Overweight and Obesity’, (London: Health and Social Care Information Centre).
	Note that these data reflect cross-sectional surveys in the years shown, and therefore the decline in average BMI after age 60y could be due to several effects apart from an early demise of those people suffering highest levels of overweight. For example, it could reflect the perpetuation of lower BMI among previous generations persisting through each decade, or a specific cohort effect for those who were growing up in the 1920s or 1940s. Equally, it could reflect a significant change in circumstances, for example, moving from earned income to a pension-based income, or to reduced muscle mass rather than reduced adiposity. The decline applies to both genders, so it is unlikely to be due to a difference in gender survival rates.
	Differences in obesity prevalence according to socioeconomic status (measured by level of educational achievement or household income) can be seen in many countries: in high-income countries the risk of developing obesity tends to be higher in less affluent or less educated population groups, with the gradient from highest to lowest socioeconomic (SES) group tending to be most clearly seen for women and for children, and less so for men (McLaren 2007). The data for children are very clearly shown in the UK’s National Child Measurement Programme, a survey measuring virtually every child in the country when they enter and leave primary school (aged around 5y and 11y, respectively) (Fig. 8.4.3) (NHS Digital 2017b). Classified by levels of deprivation in the school environs, the data show a clear near-uniform decrease in obesity for each decile decrease in deprivation score.
	Fig. 8.4.3 UK National Child Measurement Programme data on obesity according to decile of index of deprivation. Obesity defined by UK growth reference cut-offs.
	Source: data from NHS Digital. National Child Measurement Programme—England, 2016–17. London: Health and Social Care Information Centre 2017.
	In low income countries, the gradient tends in the opposite direction, with wealthier or better educated families experiencing a higher risk of developing obesity, possibly in part to their greater exposure to labour-saving, urbanized, processed food environments. This gradient has been shown to reverse as countries progress through the nutrition and epidemiologic transition. The classic papers by Monteiro et al. in 2004 (Monteiro et al. 2004a, 2004b) demonstrate the ‘cross-over point’ to be at around ($2,500 national per capita GDP at the time).
	Other subpopulation groups may show disparities after adjusting for SES. Background racial or ethnic status can determine obesity risk status, and this may interact with gender. In the USA, obesity prevalence is lower for Hispanic males and higher for Hispanic females than it is for the overall population, while for groups of Asian origin prevalence is generally significantly lower than the average, but for black or African-American population groups obesity risk is higher than average for both men and especially women, with the obesity affecting more than 50% of women in this group (Ogden et al. 2014).
	Significant disparities are found between ethnic groups in many other countries. In New Zealand, higher than average rates of obesity are found among Maori and especially Pacific Islander groups (Ministry of Health—Manatū Hauora) and the same is the case for Australia’s indigenous Aboriginal and Torres Islander peoples (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2018).
	While increasing urbanization appears linked to obesity prevalence generally, in some countries—e.g. the USA and Australia—residence in rural or periurban areas confers a greater risk of obesity than residence in inner-urban areas. It is not clear if this holds true after SES differences are taken into account. It should also be noted that there are other population groups likely to be at increased risk of obesity, including recent immigrant populations and refugees dependent on food aid (Grijalva-Eternod et al. 2012; Wandell 2013).
	Lastly, nations differ in many respects, but one which opens interesting questions for public health policy is the degree of inequality manifest in a society. Measurements of disparities in wealth, e.g. using the Gini Index, have been found to have a close relationship with various measures of health status in the population, including obesity in adults and children (Pickett et al. 2005; Knai et al. 2012). Thus countries may differ in obesity prevalence in association with their differences in wealth distribution despite having similar average per capita GDP.





Future prospects


	Projecting future prevalence rates from past trends is fraught with difficulty. Past trends differ considerably between countries as we have shown. Changes in prevalence are non-linear, and presumably are self-limiting at some maximum level below 100%, although this may differ between countries and subpopulation groups. Modellers must attempt to distinguish age, cohort, and period effects alongside subgroup differences and changing demographics. While past trends can be helpful to predict future prospects, local and national responses to the obesity crisis may lead to policies which alter the trajectory in one direction, while economic crises, changing market dynamics, trade policies fuel prices, or the impact of global warming on food supplies may alter the trajectories in another.
	Despite the problems, some attempt at predicting future trends over the coming decade are helpful, not least for authorities responsible for healthcare services facing rising demand for treatment for the chronically disabling diseases consequent on obesity. Interventions to treat obesity rather than waiting to treat its consequences can be cost-saving, and although guidelines vary between countries, a threshold for intervention most commonly occurs at BMI levels above 35 kg/m2. Crude projections of the numbers of adults with BMI above 35 kg/m2 have been made in Table 8.4.4 for some of the world’s larger countries.

The social and health costs of overweight and obesity


Language of ‘cost’


	Before considering the costs of obesity we need to be clear what we mean. Firstly, there is a move to resist the phrase ‘cost of obesity’ (or ‘burden of obesity’) if it is used in the context of weight-biased language that implies people living with obesity are the cause of social and economic costs to the wider population. In the present discussion we use ‘direct costs of obesity’ to refer to the costs of either treating the disease, or treating the consequences of obesity such as diabetes, liver disease and cardiovascular disease; and ‘indirect costs of obesity’ to refer to the economic losses due to ill-health or premature death. There are also consequential costs to individuals and their families in terms of lost educational opportunity and lowered quality of life.





Adverse health outcomes


	Obesity brings a significant change in body function, with alterations in hormonal activity involving insulin, growth hormone, prostaglandins, androgen and oestrogen, and other steroid hormones, changes in joint and muscular physiology, along with raised risks of liver damage, adverse cardiovascular function, poor control of blood sugar and blood lipids, and consequential risk of osteoarthritis, heart disease, stroke, diabetes, liver dysfunction and a range of cancers (WHO 2000).
	Additionally, obesity is highly stigmatized in many countries in terms of both the perceived ‘undesirable’ bodily appearance and the apparent character defects it is supposed to indicate, leading to social discrimination. Compared to non-obese peers, people living with obesity are likely to complete fewer years of schooling, are less likely to gain tertiary education and, among women particularly, less likely to enter better-paid employment. Perhaps not surprisingly in these conditions, people living with obesity are more likely to see their own bodies as unattractive and to exclude themselves from social interaction.

	Higher health risks are reflected in greater need for healthcare. Estimates of the relative increase in the need for health services by BMI status have been made in several countries and are shown in Table 8.4.5.

	The metrics are not identical across studies, and clearly do not include a number of relevant costs, but the relative increment according to weight status is clear. 	These estimates may prove conservative. An assessment by the Milken Institute in the USA suggested that the direct costs for medical treatment for health conditions causally related to obesity and overweight were valued at US$427.8bn in 2014, or 14% of US healthcare spending (Waters and DeVol 2016).

	The Milken Institute report cited here also estimated the indirect costs due to absence or underperformance at work due to ill-health associated with obesity and its consequences, which the Institute estimated at an extraordinary US$988.8bn for 2014. Added to the Institute’s estimate of direct costs, the total of $1.4 trillion was equivalent to 8.2% of US gross domestic product for the year.
	Other forms of indirect cost have been considered. Additional food has to be grown and transported to meet the needs of heavier populations. Over the three decades 1985–2016 the average adult’s BMI in Australia increased by 10.1%, in the UK by 10.4% and in the USA by 12.6%.(NCD Risk Factor Collaboration) Simply to maintain body function at a stable level this implies a 10% increase in food intake for the average adult, implying a significant increase in food supplies beyond that needed for a rise in the numbers of adults. The majority of people do not accumulate excess adiposity until well into adulthood, so it is of concern that for children and adolescents the increases in average BMI over the same period for these three countries were 6.8%, 5.7%, and 8.1%, respectively.
	Further costs include the additional costs to infrastructure, both in hospitals and broader industries. A calculation of airline fuel use in the USA suggested that the additional BMI of the USA population in the period 1990–2000 led to a 2.4% increase in fuel requirements for domestic services, or 350m gallons of jet fuel, and added 3.8m tonnes of CO2 emissions to greenhouse gas emissions (Dannenberg et al. 2004). Calculations have been made for automobile transport in the USA (Jacobson and King 2009) which suggest that in 2008 around 1.1 bn gallons of fuel were used to transport the excess weight of the US population in private vehicles, releasing some 9 m tonnes of CO2.





The double burden of nutrition


	The last century has seen an extraordinary ‘nutrition transition’ which has led to energy-dense foods and beverages high in sugar and fat becoming widely available to developed and urbanized populations around the globe. A potential double burden of ill-health may occur in populations where the healthfulness of food supplies remains poor: surveys in Vietnam, Brazil, and South Africa have found evidence of overweight children showing lack of growth—stunting—and indeed children in lower-income households in the UK are more likely to be overweight and more likely to be below average height, compared with children in higher-income families (Lobstein et al. 2015).
	We are not aware of estimates of the costs of this specific issue. However, there have been recent attempts to estimate the direct and indirect costs for whole populations failing to meet dietary recommendations. A UK study estimated the healthcare costs of poor diets at £5.8 bn for 2006–2007 (Scarborough et al. 2011). An analysis of the economic costs of failing to meet Canadian food recommendations in terms of disease consequences estimated that poor diets were responsible for CA$5.1 bn annually for direct healthcare and CA$8.7bn for indirect costs (Lieffers et al. 2018). This is in addition to the costs associated with overweight and obesity, which have been estimated at CA$23.5 bn annually (Krueger et al. 2015).





Causes of overweight and obesity


A complex system of determinants


	For individuals, obesity results from an imbalance between energy intake and expenditure, whereby energy intake is consistently greater than energy expenditure. Behind this apparently simple equation, obesity is best contextualized as resulting from a complex set of interactions between a wide range of drivers, reflective of the broader socioecological model (Dahlgren and Whitehead 1991; Swinburn et al. 2011; Ohri-Vachaspati et al. 2015).
	Obesity results from complex interactions between an individual’s physiology, psychology, physical activity, and food consumption, and the social and environmental factors that surround them, including the broader social psychology, the physical activity environment, and food production and trade processes (Vandenbroeck et al. 2007). This complexity was mapped in an obesity system map for the UK Foresight report in 2007 (Vandenbroeck et al. 2007)—which is colloquially referred to as the ‘spaghetti map’ (Allender et al. 2015) due to the number of interconnections within and across each of the factors (Fig. 8.4.4).
	Fig. 8.4.4 The Foresight obesity system map.
	Reproduced from Vandenbroeck, IP et. al. (2007), ‘Foresight. Tackling Obesities: Future Choices—Obesity System Atlas’, (Government Office for Science, UK Government’s Foresight Programme) under the Open Government License.
	In the centre of these models is the set of individual characteristics such as age, sex, race/ethnicity, and genes that influence an individual’s propensity for weight gain. These individual characteristics are then influenced by a range of lifestyle behaviours, including diet, physical activity, and sleep. At the level of social and community networks and environments, influencers include sociocultural, socioeconomic, workplace, recreation, and transport environments, all of which amplify or attenuate the individual level drivers. These in turn are influenced by, and influence, the high-level systemic drivers such as food and transport systems and the broader socioeconomic, commercial, and political determinants of health.





The obesity epidemic


	The obesity epidemic, now seen across the world, has resulted from a series of large changes to how we live, including greater urbanization, a food system providing more accessible, affordable, and heavily marketed products and automation leading to decreased activity in our daily lives. While, as indicated earlier, for an individual there are a number of factors contributing directly to the development of obesity at the individual level, the major cause of the global pandemic of obesity is thought to be the global changes in food and diet (Swinburn et al. 2011).
	The increases in the prevalence of obesity first seen in high-income countries are now being observed in low-and middle-income countries as they rapidly urbanize and food companies increase their investment in these regions (Friel and Baker 2009; Baker and Friel 2014). China is an illustrative example having recently experienced a transition from a history of undernutrition to a rapid increase in obesity (Gordon-Larsen et al. 2014). Over the past two decades the national health survey in China documents rapid changes in diet, activity, and obesity, all reflective of large social change (Popkin 2014). Through analysis of the China Health and Nutrition Survey, Popkin et al. have documented changes to the food supply, cooking and eating behaviours, transportation modes, and physical activity patterns, all reflective of the tripling in the prevalence of overweight in adults observed between 1991 and 2009 (Popkin 2014).
	Globally, these changes to our food and activity environments have been termed the development of ‘obesogenic’ environments (Swinburn et al. 1999) The recognition that our environments encourage and incentivise the very behaviours that contribute to obesity was pivotal in broadening the search for solutions from individual education and behavioural change to transformation of our social, economic, political, food, and physical activity environments.





Causes of causes


	As well described by Friel et al. (2007), ‘Focusing only on direct action to make people eat more healthily and be more physically active misses the heart of the problem: the underlying unequal distribution of factors that support the opportunity to be a healthy weight. Unless this oversight is addressed the obesity epidemic and its inequities will persist and possibly increase.’ These causes of causes, or upstream determinants of health, set the context for our obesogenic environments. Housing, income, trade, and societal norms all affect the likelihood of overconsumption and sedentary behaviour.
	The policy and economic context strongly influences both the level of growth and consumption, and the resources (social, economic, knowledge, and skills) that citizens have at their disposal to maintain healthy lifestyles. While direct action will need to be taken at the level of food and activity environments, this will need to include consideration of the upstream ‘causes of causes’ in order to identify effective and equitable intervention targets.





Diet and physical activity


	In 2011 Swinburn et al. postulated a ‘tipping point’ for the obesity epidemic, identifying diet to be the primary direct driver of current obesity trends (Swinburn et al. 2011). While acknowledging that all the factors identified in the Foresight map contribute both at an individual and societal level to weight gain and obesity, they illustrate that the obesity epidemic since the 1970s can be explained from two distinct phases: ‘the so-called move less, stay lean phase (1910–60), characterized by decreasing physical activity levels and energy intake, and a population that remained lean; and the subsequent so-called eat more, gain weight phase, characterized by increasing energy intake and a concomitant rise in population weight’ (Swinburn et al. 2011). Here we explore the characteristics of diet and physical activity that have been shown to affect the propensity of an individual, and a population, to gain weight.
	The evidence demonstrates that an individual’s diet is driven by factors across multiple levels of the socioecological model: the microlevel (interpersonal and intrapersonal factors)—such as an individual’s knowledge and skills and their social networks and social norms; the mesolevel (food environment)—such as the marketing of foods and beverages and their perceived and actual availability and affordability; and the macrolevel (broader sociopolitical factors)—such as marketing regulations and agricultural policies (Peeters 2018).
	There are many studies demonstrating links between specific foods, nutrients, and dietary patterns and obesity. A review in 2016 by Mozaffarian (Mozaffarian 2016) concludes that robust evidence exists to recommend increased fruits, non-starchy vegetables, nuts, legumes, fish, vegetable oils, yogurt, and minimally processed whole grains; and fewer red meats, processed (e.g. sodium-preserved) meats, and foods rich in refined grains, starch, added sugars, salt, and trans fat, when considering the outcomes of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Further studies have suggested prospective associations between factors including diet quality and weight maintenance (Romaguera et al. 2010; Bertoia et al. 2015; Fung et al. 2015; Schulze et al. 2018) and between soft drink consumption and weight gain (Malik et al. 2006; Malik et al. 2013; Singh et al. 2015; Bucher Della Torre et al. 2016).
	Levels of physical activity and sedentary time are similarly driven by factors across multiple levels of the socioecological model: the microlevel (interpersonal and intrapersonal factors)—such as an individual’s knowledge and skills, perceptions of safety, and their social networks, and social norms; the mesolevel (physical activity and transport environments)—such as the walkability of a neighbourhood, the availability of public transport and the availability and affordability of physical activities; and the macrolevel (broader sociopolitical factors)—such as urban planning and transport policies (Durand et al. 2011; Hesketh et al. 2017). While there are clear links between activity levels and weight gain for the individual, population studies demonstrate that levels of PA have not changed substantially since the 1980s in many countries (Swinburn et al. 2011; Rodgers et al. 2018).
	A number of observational studies and reviews demonstrate the link between the number of hours spent sitting, the number of hours spent watching television, or screens in general, levels of moderate and vigorous physical activity, and transport mode with weight gain and obesity (Dunstan et al. 2005; Turrell et al. 2018).





Genes and biology


	The recent World Obesity Federation position statement on obesity articulated a perspective of obesity as a chronic, relapsing disease process. In this process the primary driver of current weight gain, food (particularly foods that are high in energy density such as fat, or in sugar-sweetened beverages), interacts with the other drivers of weight gain, including low physical activity and inadequate sleep, and with the individual’s genetic susceptibility.
	There are a few known genes with a strong effect on the development of obesity, such as that for leptin, and there are a large number of genes with contributing effects to weight gain susceptibility. In addition to direct genetic effects, we also now know that both epigenetics and the body’s weight maintenance physiology play a role in an individual’s susceptibility to weight gain and capacity for weight maintenance and weight loss.
	In the past decade, our understanding of the role of epigenetics in the development of obesity has increased rapidly (van Dijk et al. 2014). A recent review of studies investigating the association between obesity and either global, site-specific, or genome-wide methylation of DNA has demonstrated that, while there was evidence for a number of obesity-associated differentially methylated sites, there was no consistent evidence for a relationship between global methylation and obesity. Still an emerging field, the current evidence suggests there are epigenetic modifications in utero that may both assist in predicting future obesity risk, and represent modifiable targets to reduce this risk (van Dijk et al. 2014; van Dijk et al. 2015).
	For those who attempt weight loss, the physiology of the body is a powerful driver of weight regain. As described in detail by Sumithran et al. (Sumithran and Proietto 2013), in the hypothalamus, hormonal signals from the gastrointestinal tract, adipose tissue, and other peripheral sites are integrated to influence appetite and energy expenditure. In those who lose weight intentionally there are several physiological changes that encourage weight regain, including alterations in energy expenditure, metabolism, and hormone pathways involved in appetite regulation, many of which may persist long term.





Obesity in a ‘syndemic’ of epidemics


	Obesity, together with undernutrition and other dietary risks, are currently by far the largest cause of poor health globally, but are likely to be overtaken by the consequences of climate change. These three pandemics—obesity, undernutrition, and climate change—represent a ‘syndemic’ or synergy of epidemics because they co-occur in time and place, interact with each other to produce complex sequelae, and share common underlying societal drivers. Although beyond the scope of the present chapter, this global syndemic represents the paramount public health challenge in the twenty-first century. It is discussed in greater detail in the forthcoming report of the Lancet Commission on Obesity (Lancet Commission on Obesity 2019).





Prevention of overweight and obesity


	A range of public health strategies are needed to ensure reductions in risk of obesity throughout the life course (Baker et al. 2017). Specifically, strategies are needed to reduce intergenerational transfer and development of susceptibility, to reduce weight gain and support weight maintenance throughout life for those at a healthy weight, to support weight maintenance and moderate weight loss in those with a weight just outside the healthy weight range, and to support weight maintenance after weight loss for those with obesity.
	In addition, public health strategies are needed to mitigate the harms of obesity. Specifically, to reduce the stigma associated with obesity (Puhl and Heuer 2010) and to reduce the impact of obesity on people’s capacity to lead a fulfilling life, including opportunities in employment, housing, and marriage (Black et al. 2018). The advantage of a well-constructed, multisectoral, and multifactorial public health approach is that it can address all these issues concurrently.





Current recommendations for a public health approach to obesity


	There is currently significant coherence in the recommendations national and internationally for a successful public health approach to obesity. Many of the recommendations fall under the remit of government, but it is clear that to enable the cultural, political, and economic change required for reduced obesity rates into the future, action is required from the full range of societal stakeholders, from citizens through community and non-government organizations to the private sector (Huang et al. 2015). In addition, it is clear that there is a role for multiple levels of government, from local through state to national governments, as well as multiple sectors of government (Sacks et al. 2009).
	Whether the recommendations focus on childhood or whole of society it is clear that we need to enact a range of levers to re-orient our food and activity environments, empower and upskill our citizens, and rethink our societal conversations about obesity (Fig. 8.4.5) (Moodie 2008; McGuire 2012; Commission on Ending Childhood Obesity 2017; WHO 2017b, 2018c). In 2012 WHO set a target of reducing premature mortality from noncommunicable diseases by 25% by the year 2025 and for there to be no increase in adult and adolescent overweight and obesity (WHO 2013) In 2017, this was followed by a report from the Commission on Ending Childhood Obesity including the high-level policy actions governments will need to take to achieve this latter target (Commission on Ending Childhood Obesity 2017). WHO has also developed recommendations for action for the private sector (WHO 2004).
	Fig. 8.4.5 A framework to categorize obesity determinants and solutions.
	Reprinted from Swinburn, B. A., et al. (2011), ‘The global obesity pandemic: shaped by global drivers and local environments’, Lancet, 378 (9793), 804–14, with permission from Elsevier.
	The government recommendations identified by the WHO as the best buys to reduce unhealthy diets and increase physical activity span the key public health levers from pricing, through labelling and guidelines to public education campaigns (Box 8.4.2). Obesity prevention is likely to require government intervention in further areas, such as international trade and food procurement policies (Friel et al. 2013; Hawkes et al. 2013) and is likely to require development of national nutrition, physical activity, and/or obesity plans (Commission on Ending Childhood Obesity 2017; Peeters 2018; WHO 2018c, d) accompanied by ongoing community consultation, research and monitoring (Swinburn et al. 2013).
	 	Box 8.4.2 Key elements of a public health approach to obesity by government





Reduce unhealthy diet


	 	• Implement the global strategy on diet, physical activity, and health
	• Implement the WHO recommendations on the marketing of foods and non-alcoholic beverages to children
	• Reduce sugar consumption through effective taxation on sugar-sweetened beverages
	• Promote and support exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, including promotion of breastfeeding
	• Implement subsidies to increase the intake of fruits and vegetables
	• Limiting portion and package size to reduce energy intake and the risk of overweight/obesity
	• Implement nutrition education and counselling in different settings (e.g. in preschools, schools, workplaces, and hospitals) to increase the intake of fruits and vegetables
	• Implement nutrition labelling to reduce total energy intake (kcal), sugars, sodium, and fats
	• Implement mass media campaign on healthy diets, including social marketing to reduce the intake of total fat, saturated fats, sugars, and salt, and promote the intake of fruits and vegetables





Reduce physical inactivity


	 	• Implement the global strategy on diet, physical activity, and health
	• Implement community-wide public education and awareness campaign for physical activity which includes a mass media campaign combined with other community-based education, motivational and environmental programmes aimed at supporting behavioural change of physical activity levels
	• Provide physical activity counselling and referral as part of routine primary healthcare services through the use of a brief intervention
	• Ensure that macrolevel urban design incorporates the core elements of residential density, connected street networks that include sidewalks, easy access to a diversity of destinations and access to public transport
	• Implement a whole-of-school programme that includes quality physical education, availability of adequate facilities and programmes to support physical activity for all children
	• Provide convenient and safe access to quality public open space and adequate infrastructure to support walking and cycling
	• Implement multicomponent workplace physical activity programmes
	• Promotion of physical activity through organized sport groups and clubs, programmes, and events
	Source: data from World Health Organization. (2017). Tackling NCDs: ‘best buys’ and other recommended interventions for the prevention and control of noncommunicable diseases. World Health Organization. https://apps.who.int/iris/handle/10665/259232.
	A number of international bodies have also provided detailed recommendations to improve population diets and physical activity levels. The World Cancer Research Fund, International hosts the NOURISHING framework (Hawkes et al. 2013). This framework summarizes the policy domains required to improve population diets and an accompanying database collates information about implemented polices to promote healthy diets and reduce obesity. WHO’s Global database on the Implementation of Nutrition Action (GINA) serves a similar purpose, including how programmes are implemented, country adaptations, and lessons learnt (WHO 2018a). The Global Physical Activity Network hosts a knowledge database focusing on physical activity policies and including summaries of related evidence and implementation (WHO 2018b).
	Further, to see such recommendations enacted there will need to be an increase in the political and societal will for action (Huang et al. 2015; Baker et al. 2017). A recent review by Baker and colleagues (Baker et al. 2017) posits that it is possible to build and galvanize political commitment to obesity prevention. They identify a significant role for public health professionals in this process, suggesting that the catalysts will include ‘strategic actions by cohesive, resourced and strongly led nutrition actor networks’ (Baker et al. 2017). Such actions can be supported by evidence that supports a political ideology and feasible policy options (Clarke et al. 2016). Successful implementation of recommendations will also require a response to the substantial industry opposition to many of the recommended policies. For the first time the Director General of the WHO spoke about the critical role of regulation to contain the food and drink industries, stating ‘it is not just Big Tobacco anymore. Public health must also contend with Big Food, Big Soda, and Big Alcohol. All of these industries fear regulation, and protect themselves by using the same tactics’ (Chan 10 June 2013). One consequence of this recognition is the development of strong and transparent conflict of interest guidance documents (Buse et al. 2017; WHO 2017a).
	Finally, it is important to recognize that while a public health approach to obesity is urgently needed, without an integrated and concurrent focus on greater accessibility and availability of appropriate treatment options, the burden of obesity will continue for many decades.





Evidence of impact


	Many of the proposed population obesity prevention strategies have been implemented, evaluated, and modelled for population impact and cost-effectiveness. Comparative cost-effectiveness analyses have demonstrated that some of the regulatory population approaches, including a sugary drinks tax, restricting marketing of unhealthy food and drink and increasing availability of healthy food options relative to unhealthy food options, are likely to be cost-saving at a societal level, leading to reductions in obesity and its sequelae over the lifetime (Table 8.4.8) (Gortmaker et al. 1993; Carter et al. 2009; Vos et al. 2010; Dobbs et al. 2014). Large population benefit has also been identified as a consequence of strategies that change the behavioural defaults, such as food reformulation and decreases in standard portion sizes.

	The impact of a population strategy to improve one element of the food or activity pathways currently driving obesity will necessarily take a number of years to effect weight gain and obesity. In addition, the effect of any given pathway may be difficult to identify among the range of societal changes affecting obesity. In order to support evidence-based decision making it will be important to ensure the full range of evidence is collected and integrated. Approaches integrating logic pathways and systems dynamics will facilitate conclusions on whether a given policy, intervention, or programme is having its intended effect on the direct target behaviours, any unintended effects, and eventually its intended effect on weight gain and obesity (Peeters 2018). Recent evaluations have begun to adapt approaches from systems science (Rutter et al. 2017; Owen et al. 2018). While these methods are still evolving, by identifying and integrating a variety of evidence sources, such approaches have the potential to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of obesity prevention policies.
	One approach that has underpinned a number of intervention evaluations has been the quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight by Hall and colleagues (Hall et al. 2011). This mathematical modelling approach simulates energy expenditure adaptations during weight loss using findings from human metabolism studies. In addition to informing multiple modelling studies, this approach identified an important characteristic of the obesity epidemic: that a very small average daily energy imbalance between intake and expenditure of about 30 kJ per day can explain the observed average weight gain. This is equivalent to less than a biscuit a day, demonstrating the potential of effective prevention strategies to impact on population obesity rates.
	For long-term impact, implemented policies and programmes will need not only to be effective, but also to be sustained and to be equitable. Recent analyses of population obesity trends have shown no reduction in inequalities in obesity in high-income countries (Devaux and Sassi 2013; Chung et al. 2016). Further, there is some evidence that while obesity rates may be improving in some population groups, these improvements are occurring more often in less disadvantaged groups than more disadvantaged groups (Chung et al. 2016). To ensure that implemented policies benefit the most disadvantaged citizens, who are also likely to carry the highest burden of risk, a more comprehensive understanding of differential effectiveness across different population groups is required. A selection of population obesity prevention policies have been evaluated for such differential effectiveness, demonstrating that a sugary drinks tax and whole of community interventions are likely to be effective across the socioeconomic spectrum. However, the majority of recommended policies have not been evaluated for the equity impact. It will be important to continue to build evaluations of the equity effect of such policies (Backholer et al. 2014; Peeters and Backholer 2015). It will also be critical to continue to build the evidence regarding synergistic effects with other related and substantial population issues, including undernutrition climate change (Lancet Commission on Obesity 2019).





Conclusions


	A successful public health approach to obesity will require strong political commitment and leadership, accompanied by community and organizational support. Re-orienting our food and physical activity environments alongside supporting and upskilling our citizens will drive the culture change required to reverse the obesity epidemic. A comprehensive, integrated multisectoral approach will be required to reduce intergenerational transfer and excess weight gain, as well as to support weight maintenance in those who have experienced intentional weight loss. Evaluation techniques will need to continue to evolve to ensure implemented interventions are effective, equitable, and sustainable.
