8.5


Physical activity and public health


	Nyssa T. Hadgraft, Neville Owen, and Paddy C. Dempsey





Introduction


	Physical activity has well-established health benefits. However, large proportions of the adult populations of developed countries, and rapidly urbanizing developing countries are insufficiently physically active for health benefits. Additionally, many people’s lives are characterized by large amounts of time spent sitting. This represents a formidable set of public health challenges.
	Although the relationships of exercise and physical activity with health have been topics of interest for millennia (Tipton 2014; Myers et al. 2015), the modern era of physical activity and public health arguably dates back to the early 1950s with the seminal epidemiological studies of Morris and colleagues. These involved employees of the London Transport Executive (bus drivers compared to conductors) and Post Office (civil servants compared to postal workers). The main findings were that the largely sedentary bus drivers had almost double the age-adjusted rate of fatal coronary heart disease, when compared with conductors who spent much of their workday climbing stairs, walking, and standing. Similarly, the incidence of coronary heart disease was lower in the active postal workers compared to sedentary civil service clerks and executives (Morris et al. 1966, 1953). From a broader public health perspective, it is interesting to note that one of the initial hypotheses considered by Morris and colleagues was the potential effects of stress on the cardiovascular health of bus drivers, whom it would be assumed would be more socially isolated in their jobs than would the conductors.
	Some 70 years on from the Morris studies, residents of developed and developing countries have been subject to a broad set of demographic, epidemiological, economic, social, and technological transitions. Widespread urbanization, particularly in low-and middle-income countries, has meant large segments of traditionally rural populations are moving into cities. Many previously manual tasks in the occupational and household sectors have become automated, making life easier and safer in many respects. A pervasive consequence of these changes is that the living environments of large numbers of people globally are becoming less supportive of structured and incidental physical activity, and more conducive to large amounts of time spent sitting. For this reason, physical inactivity has been called a ‘global pandemic’ (Kohl et al. 2012); one requiring multidisciplinary and multisectoral approaches (Reis et al. 2016).
	In this chapter, we focus on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (put simply, too little exercise and too much sitting), in the contemporary public health context, highlighting:
	 	• the key definitions and distinctions around physical activity, exercise, and sedentary behaviour
	• current evidence on relationships with health outcomes, and current physical activity recommendations
	• current evidence on prevalence and trends in physical activity and sedentary behaviour, and some of the key issues for surveillance and measurement
	• how physical activity and sedentary behaviour may be understood in ways that will inform public health approaches
	We emphasize the importance of an interdisciplinary and intersectoral strategy—working with constituencies beyond the public health field, such as urban planners, architects, and policymakers, in order to create activity-friendly built environments that provide socially equitable opportunities for physical activity to be part of everyday living.





Physical activity and sedentary behaviour: definitions, health consequences, and guidelines


Definitions


	When thinking about what constitutes physical activity and where it takes place, images that might come to mind are people working out in a gym, or playing sport. However, physical activity is broader than structured exercise. Although often used interchangeably, ‘physical activity’, ‘exercise’, ‘physical fitness’, and ‘sedentary behaviour’ are terms that describe related but distinct concepts. Clear definitions and distinctions are important for research and practice in this field (see Table 8.5.1) (Caspersen et al. 1985; Pate et al. 2008; Brown et al. 2012; Tremblay et al. 2017).
	 	Table 8.5.1 Key terms and definitions: physical activity and sedentary behaviour
	 			Physical activity
	Any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that expends energy. The term ‘physical activity’ usually refers to the subset of activity that produces substantial health benefits—e.g. moderate-intensity to vigorous intensity activity in bouts of at least 10 minutes at a time. This can be from leisure-time physical activity, transportation (e.g. walking or cycling), occupational or household work, play, games, sports, or planned exercise.
		Exercise
	Asubset of physical activity that is purposeful, planned, and structured—with an objective more geared towards improving facets of physical fitness (see next); the term ‘exercise’ is at times used synonymously with ‘physical activity’.
		Physical fitness
	A set of attributes that people have or achieve that are health or skill-related, such as cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility, balance, and body composition. The degree to which people have these attributes can be measured with specific tests.
		Baseline activity
	All light-intensity activities of daily life, such as standing, walking slowly, and lifting light weight objects. It may also include short episodes of moderate or vigorous activity, such as climbing a few flights of stairs.
		Sedentary behaviours
	Any waking behaviour characterized by an energy expenditure ≤1.5 metabolic equivalents (METs), while in a sitting, reclining, or lying posture. Note that this is different from ‘physical inactivity’ (see earlier).
	As noted earlier, there is now increased interest in the distinct health effects and determinants of sedentary behaviour—sitting. While ‘sedentary’ was often historically used to describe someone who did not engage in sufficient physical activity (i.e. physically inactive), more recently it has been specifically defined to refer to any waking behaviour characterized by an energy expenditure ≤1.5 metabolic equivalents (METs), while in a sitting, reclining or lying posture (Sedentary Behavior Research Network 2012; Tremblay et al. 2017).
	Physical activity and exercise can be quantified using the constructs of intensity (how hard?), duration (how long?), frequency (how often?), and mode (what type?), for example, walking, running, swimming, cycling, etc. (Powell et al. 2004). These constructs are used to determine whether someone meets physical activity guidelines (see Box 8.5.2).





Health consequences: why physical inactivity and sedentary behaviour are crucial public health issues


	Strong evidence demonstrates that physical inactivity is a modifiable risk factor for a wide spectrum of health conditions, including non-communicable diseases that are a rapidly growing public health concern in developed and developing countries. It has been estimated that 6–10% of all deaths from non-communicable diseases (including 7% of deaths associated with type 2 diabetes, 6% of coronary heart disease deaths, and 10% of breast/colon cancer deaths) worldwide can be attributed to physical inactivity, making it the fourth leading cause of death worldwide (Lee et al. 2012).
	Physical inactivity is related not only to increased risk of illness and premature mortality, it also results in a substantial economic burden worldwide. In the first global estimate for the economic burden of physical inactivity (based on data from 142 countries, representing 93.2% of the world’s population), it was conservatively estimated that the effect of physical inactivity cost the world economy more than $67.5 billion through healthcare expenditure and productivity losses in 2013. Low-and middle-income countries had the largest disease burden from physical inactivity (Ding et al. 2016).
	There are numerous benefits to health from physical activity; including reducing the risk of excessive weight gain, type 2 diabetes, injurious falls, depression, and loss of cognitive function (Warburton et al. 2010; WHO 2010; Warburton and Bredin 2016; Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee 2018); see Box 8.5.1).
	There is also moderately strong evidence that physical activity maintains functional ability in older adults, helps maintain weight loss, improves sleep quality, and reduces the risk of hip fracture and osteoporosis.
	Different types of physical activity acting through multiple physiological pathways influence a broad array of health outcomes. The acute and chronic physiological adaptations that can lead to ill-health largely depend on the type of activity performed. For example, aerobic activities tend to cause many changes to the heart and vascular system (e.g. increased stroke volume, increased capillary density, reduced peripheral resistance). Resistance activities (e.g. weight training or working against body weight) have modest effects on the cardiovascular system, but do improve muscle strength and endurance (Powell et al. 2004; Garber et al. 2011). This highlights that any single activity is unlikely to be optimal for comprehensive health benefits and will depend upon the health outcome of most interest to the population subgroup of concern.
	At the lower end of the activity spectrum, accumulating research also indicates that reducing and replacing sedentary behaviours with light-intensity activities is beneficial in a variety of populations, on a smaller scale, for metabolic and cardiovascular health outcomes (Dempsey et al. 2016; Chastin et al. 2017; Chastin et al. 2018). Consistent evidence from prospective observational studies across numerous countries now also indicates that excessive sedentary behaviour (sitting) is also associated with an increased risk for all-cause mortality, heart disease, diabetes and some cancers (Wilmot et al. 2012; Biswas et al. 2015), and may be further exacerbated in those who are insufficiently active or unfit (Biswas et al. 2015; Bouchard et al. 2015; Ekelund et al. 2016). A recent meta-analysis (Chau et al. 2013) estimated that some 6% of all deaths could be attributed to daily self-reported sitting time.
	Since much of the world’s population is physically inactive (Hallal et al. 2012), and time spent sedentary (with a high proportion of that time spent in sitting in prolonged bouts) accounts for a majority of adults’ waking hours (Matthews et al. 2008; Healy et al. 2015), many of the aforementioned figures are likely underestimating the global economic and disease burden associated with physical inactivity and excessive sitting time. From a public health perspective, whether there is a minimum volume of physical activity that may reduce some of the health risks associated with prolonged sitting, or a threshold above which the benefits of physical activity are attenuated, is a topic of contemporary research interest (Powell et al. 2004).
	 	Box 8.5.1 Strength of the evidence on the health benefits of physical activity





Strong evidence of reduced rates of:


	 	• all-cause mortality
	• coronary heart disease
	• high blood pressure
	• stroke
	• metabolic syndrome
	• type 2 diabetes
	• breast cancer
	• colon cancer
	• depression
	• falling





Strong evidence of:


	 	• increased cardiorespiratory and muscular fitness
	• healthier body mass and composition
	• improved bone health
	• increased functional health
	• improved cognitive function





Moderately strong evidence that physical activity:


	 	• helps maintain functional ability in older adults, helps maintain weight loss, improves sleep quality, and reduces the risk of hip fracture and osteoporosis





Physical activity and sedentary behaviour guidelines


	Evidence supporting the importance of physical activity for population health may be found in a number of landmark documents, including:
	 	• the 1996 US Department of Health and Human Services’ Surgeon General’s Report on Physical Activity and Health (US Department of Health and Human Services 1996)
	• the 2008 US Department of Health and Human Services Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans (US Department of Health and Human Services 2008; Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee 2018)
	• the 2010 World Health Organization (WHO) Global Recommendations on Physical Activity for Health (WHO 2010)
	• and, in 2010, the Toronto Charter for Physical Activity was ratified at the 3rd International Congress for Physical Activity and Health (Bull et al. 2010), calling for global action to prioritize physical activity for all.
	Based on extensive evidence syntheses and reviews compiled by national and international bodies, there have been generally consistent recommendations developed in relation to adults’ physical activity. The WHO’s recommendations for adults aged 18–64 are to perform at least 150 min/week of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity (e.g. brisk walking, gentle bicycling), or at least 75 min/week of vigorous intensity aerobic physical activity (e.g. jogging, running, hard bicycling), or an equivalent combination of moderate and vigorous. In addition, it is recommended that individuals should engage in muscle-strengthening activities at least 2 days/week (see Box 8.5.2) (WHO 2010). More than the suggested minimum total of 150 min/week of activities (up to 300 min/week are suggested) is likely to provide additional benefits. The WHO recommendations were developed with the goal of primary prevention of non-communicable diseases (Vuori 2018).
	For those who are inactive or highly sedentary, any physical activity is beneficial. There are health benefits from volumes of physical activity less than half the recommended amount (Powell et al. 2004; WHO 2010). Indeed, a curvilinear reduction in risk occurs for a variety of diseases and conditions across volume of activity, with the greatest improvements in health and mortality risk tending to occur when those who are very inactive/sedentary become more physically active (Powell et al. 2004; Haskell et al. 2007; Garber et al. 2011).
	Recommendations for older adults (aged 65 or over) are generally the same as for adults, as much as abilities allow, with particular emphasis of avoiding excessive inactivity and sedentary time. For children/adolescents, the recommended amount of moderate-vigorous physical activity is at least 60 min/day, with muscle/bone strengthening exercises recommended at least three times per week.
	Recommendations on sedentary behaviour have recently been introduced into some country-specific guidelines, but are less specific than are those for physical activity. For example, Australia’s Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour Guidelines recommend that adults ‘minimise the amount of time spent in prolonged sitting’ and ‘break up long periods of sitting as often as possible’ (DoH 2017).
	 	Box 8.5.2 Recommended guidelines for physical activity and sedentary behaviour
	 	• Adults should accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity, or at least 75 minutes of vigorous intensity physical activity throughout the week, or an equivalent combination of moderate and vigorous intensity activity (e.g. running, brisk walking, bicycling, playing tennis, dancing, and swimming).
	• For additional health benefits, adults should increase their moderate-intensity physical activity to 300 minutes per week, or equivalent.
	• Muscle-strengthening activities involving major muscle groups should be done on 2 or more days a week, e.g. weight training, calisthenics (body weight resistance such as half-squats, push ups, pull ups, sit ups), carrying heavier loads, heavy gardening (such as lifting, digging, or shovelling).
	• Avoid inactivity and minimise the total amount of time that is spent sitting, particularly in sitting prolonged bouts; e.g. replace prolonged periods (~30–60 minutes) of sitting (e.g. at work, watching television) with more standing and more incidental activity.
	The WHO has provided leadership in recent decades in advocating for action on physical inactivity by member states (Vuori 2018). The WHO Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases 2013–2020, endorsed by the World Health Assembly in 2013, identifies physical inactivity as one of four risk factors for non-communicable diseases, alongside tobacco use, alcohol consumption and unhealthy diets (WHO 2013). In 2018, WHO launched the Global Action Plan on Physical Activity 2018–2030: More Active People for a Healthier World, which aims to provide countries with up-to-date guidance on physical activity and a framework for policy responses (WHO 2018). The plan sets a target of a 15% relative reduction in the prevalence of physical inactivity in adults and adolescents by 2030 (WHO 2018).





Physical activity and sedentary behaviour: prevalence and trends


Physical activity


	Country comparisons provide insight into variations in physical activity and sedentary behaviour across the world. When assessing self-reported physical activity against the guidelines outlined earlier, the proportion of adults globally who are not meeting guidelines has been estimated at 31.1%. However, country-and region-specific averages vary substantially. For example, only 4.7% of the population are considered inactive in Bangladesh, through to a high of 71.9% in Malta (Hallal et al. 2012). Higher levels of inactivity have been found in the eastern Mediterranean region (43.2%) and the Americas (43.3%), compared to Southeast Asia (17.0%) and Africa (27.5%) (Hallal et al. 2012). In general, higher levels of inactivity are found in higher-income compared to lower-income countries (Dumith et al. 2011). It has been suggested that this may be because the contribution of physical activity from work tends to be lower in higher-income countries (Hallal et al. 2012).
	Within individual countries, average physical activity levels also vary across subpopulations—differences that have implications for health inequities and developing appropriately targeted health promotion programmes. One contributing factor may be that safe and affordable spaces to be physically active are less accessible to some population groups, including those of low socioeconomic position, those with disabilities, and girls, women, and older adults (WHO 2018).
	Gender differences in physical activity levels have been observed across most countries, with women more likely to be physically inactive than men (Hallal et al. 2012; Bauman et al. 2009, 2012). These differences can be attributed to a range of economic, social, and cultural factors. Women often spend more time in household activities, which are not always captured by physical activity questionnaires (Hallal et al. 2003). However, women across the world also tend to have lower levels of leisure-time physical activity than men (Brown et al. 2016). This may be due to social and cultural factors, such as in countries where women’s participation in physical activity can be restricted (e.g. those in the Gulf Cooperation Council) (Mabry et al. 2010). However, gender differences also exist in high-income countries where cultural barriers to participation are less apparent, suggesting that social norms may also play a role. For this reason, gender-specific strategies may be needed to address the physical activity gap (Brown et al. 2016).
	Physical activity levels also appear to vary by socioeconomic status. Leisure-related physical activity levels tend to be greater among those in higher socioeconomic positions, while occupational physical activity is higher for those with a lower socioeconomic position (Gidlow et al. 2006; Beenackers et al. 2012). There is some evidence to suggest that occupational physical activity (which often involves heavy lifting and prolonged, static postures) may not be as beneficial for improving health outcomes as volitional physical activity performed during leisure (Holtermann et al. 2012; Coenen et al. 2018), which has been suggested as a possible pathway through which health inequities manifest (Coenen et al. 2018). This emphasizes the need to consider the mode and setting when assessing population levels of physical activity and designing interventions, as discussed later in this chapter.





Sedentary behaviour


	Recent findings highlight the extent to which adults around the world engage in high volumes of sitting time, but less is known about international prevalence of sedentary behaviour, relative to what is known about physical activity. Cross-country studies have found that self-reported daily sitting time can range from 2.5 to 3 hours per day in countries such as Portugal, Brazil, and Columbia, through to 6 hours/day in Denmark and the Netherlands, and seven hours/day in Japan and Saudi Arabia (Bauman et al. 2011; Loyen et al. 2016). However, data obtained from studies using accelerometers (a type of activity monitor) suggest that these self-report figures may be underestimates of actual time spent in sedentary behaviour, with some reporting adults spend 55–70% of their waking hours engaged in sedentary behaviours (Matthews et al. 2008; Hagstromer et al. 2010) or over 8 hours/day (Bauman et al. 2018).





Physical activity and sedentary behaviour trends


	Evidence from high-income countries suggest that the direction of physical activity trends over time vary depending on the setting in which the activity is being assessed. While leisure-related physical activity levels have tended to remain steady or slightly increased over time, physical activity during work, the domestic environment and transportation has decreased in recent decades (Hallal et al. 2012; Ng and Popkin 2012). Across the globe, fewer people now work in occupations that require them to be physically active (Ng and Popkin 2012). In the United States, the proportion of workers in manufacturing jobs has declined sharply over the last 50 years, while service-related jobs have become more prevalent. In 2008, only 20% of occupations required at least moderate intensity physical activity, down from 48% in 1960 (Church et al. 2011). Many adults now work in desk-based occupations, where over two-thirds of the workday can be spent sitting (Clemes et al. 2014; van Dommelen et al. 2016). Figure 8.5.1, adapted from Ng and Popkin (Ng and Popkin 2012) provides compelling estimates of past, recent, and projected trends across domains of physical activity and sedentary behaviour.
	Fig. 8.5.1 UK adults’ metabolic equivalents of task (MET)-hours per week of time in sedentary behaviour, and hours per week of all physical activity in different domains (active-leisure, travel, occupational and domestic physical activity): based on time-use surveys measured for 1961–2005 and forecasted for 2006–2030.
	Reproduced from Ng SW, Popkin BM. Time use and physical activity: a shift away from movement across the globe. Obes Rev. 2012;13(8):659–80, with permission from John Wiley and Sons.
	While much of the evidence on physical activity trends has come from high-income countries evidence from China and Brazil suggests that these countries have also experienced reductions in occupational and domestic physical activity in recent decades (Ng and Popkin 2012; Ng et al. 2014). For example, national surveys in China reveal that physical activity levels dropped by 32% between 1991 and 2006 (Ng et al. 2009), with much of this decline due to falling levels of occupational and domestic physical activity (Ng et al. 2014). At the same time, leisure-time physical activity levels have generally remained stable for the majority of the population (Ng et al. 2014).
	New technologies are changing, shifting, and refining our perspectives on physically active and sedentary behaviours and creating new research agendas. The rapidly growing use of consumable wearable technologies and smart phones/watches (which have inbuilt accelerometers) is also providing unique opportunities to monitor, and potentially intervene, on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (Althoff et al. 2017; Phillips et al. 2018). Until recently, surveillance studies examining the population prevalence of physically active and sedentary time (such as those described earlier) have typically relied on time-use and self-reported moderate-vigorous physical activity during leisure time, or people’s estimates of overall daily sitting or television/screen viewing time. However, activity monitoring using accelerometers (which can record time, duration, frequency, and intensity of movements) and inclinometer-accelerometers (which can provide more accurate data on sitting, standing, and stepping) are starting to provide more accurate and precise measurement of activity levels across the day. It is important to note that both self-report and sensor-assessed methods have their strengths and limitations. Self-report is prone to recall and response bias, social desirability, or under-or over-reporting, while sensor-assessed measurements can be expensive in larger studies and are typically unable to differentiate between the different contexts of physically active and sedentary behaviours (Sallis and Saelens 2000; Prince et al. 2008; Healy et al. 2011).
	A challenge for monitoring global physical activity levels is the variability between countries in the availability of current and representative data. Measures used to access physical activity can differ across countries, which creates challenges in comparisons (Varela et al. 2017). Regular, national surveillance of physical activity levels is generally concentrated in highly developed countries, while a number of low-and middle-income countries in Africa, parts of Latin America, and central Asia have limited or no data on their population’s physical activity levels (Hallal et al. 2012). The Global Observatory for Physical Activity (GoPA!) recently developed a series of Country Cards to amalgamate information on country-specific indicators for physical activity surveillance, policy, and research data (Varela et al. 2017). The cards are intended to be used as an advocacy tool to promote greater awareness of, and investment in public health policy, research, and programmes relating to physical activity, which may be particularly valuable for low-and middle-income countries (Ramirez Varela et al. 2018).





Understanding and influencing physical activity and sedentary behaviour: an ecological perspective


	Physical activity is broader than activities that constitute structured exercise or sport. It can also, and predominantly does, take place in a variety of different settings—including during leisure, transportation, and in the workplace or school environment. Similarly, when we think about sedentary behaviour, sitting occurs at desks in the workplace, watching television in the home, or driving a car for transport. Understanding the settings in which physical activity and sedentary behaviour take place, and the factors that influence these behaviours, is particularly important for identifying opportunities for public health interventions that do not exacerbate existing social disadvantage. Box 8.5.3 outlines three major settings in which physical activity and sedentary behaviour typically take place.
	 	Box 8.5.3 Physical activity and sedentary behaviour settings
	Leisure: Physical activity and sedentary behaviour performed during leisure is generally performed with a degree of volitional control relative to other settings such as the workplace or school environment. For many adults, physical activity comprises a small proportion of their total leisure time, if any. Instead, the majority of leisure time is spent in sedentary pursuits, such as watching television, using a computer, or socializing with friends.
	Work: Physical activity performed at work is often termed ‘occupational physical activity’. Jobs which require heavy lifting and other manual tasks have higher levels of occupational physical activity. With increasing automation within many industries and a large number of the workforce ‘desk-bound’, occupational physical activity has been decreasing over recent decades. Many workers (such as those in desk-based jobs, parts of manufacturing, transport) spend much of the day sitting. The workplace has therefore become a key target setting for reducing sedentary behaviour.
	Transportation: Physical activity performed during transportation is often termed ‘active transport’. Examples of this include walking or cycling to get to and from destinations, including public transport stops. The rates of active transport vary substantially across the world. For example, over a third of the population walks or cycles to work in China and the Netherlands, while fewer than 5% do so in Australia or the United States (Hallal et al. 2012). Cycling in particular, is very common in China, the Netherlands, and Denmark (Hallal et al. 2012), while the vast majority of people in Australia and the United States use cars to get to and from work. In addition to less time spent in physical activity, high car dependency means more time spent in prolonged bouts of sitting.
	Conceptual models and theories can be helpful for public health practitioners who are interested in understanding why a behaviour does, or does not occur, and therefore how to best intervene for positive health outcomes. Ecological models are helpful frameworks that have been applied to assist our understanding of a variety of health behaviours (Owen et al. 2011). A strength of ecological models is that they can incorporate multiple theories within an overarching framework, and thus allow for a broader approach to understanding potential determinants of major health risks and multilevel approaches for change (Sallis and Owen 2015).
	Rather than focusing primarily on changing behaviour at the individual level—which poses limitations beyond the individual’s control, ecological approaches also consider extrinsic influences on behaviour (see Fig. 8.5.2). The ultimate goal being to create environments and policies that make it safe, convenient, attractive, and economical to make health-promoting choices, and then motivate and educate people to take up those healthy options.
	Fig. 8.5.2 A summary version of ecological models of physical activity and sedentary behaviour.
	Reprinted from Owen N et al (2011) ‘Adults’ Sedentary Behavior Determinants and Interventions’ Am. J. Preventive Medicine 41(2):189–96, with permission from Elsevier.
	Ecological models have five key principles as outlined to follow (Sallis and Owen 2015), which have relevance to approaches for influencing both physical activity and sedentary behaviour:
	 	1. There are multiple levels of influence on health behaviours
	2. Environmental contexts are significant determinants of health behaviours
	3. Influences on behaviours interact across levels
	4. Ecological models should be behaviour specific
	5. Multilevel interventions should be most effective in changing behaviours
	Considering these principles in the context of physical activity and sedentary behaviour, the influences on these behaviours are complex and multifaceted. These might include individual factors (such as preferences, abilities or motivation), social factors (e.g. extent of social support for activity, social norms), environmental factors (e.g. availability of equipment or proximity to pleasant surroundings for activity), and policy factors (e.g. workplace policies around active transport) (Owen et al. 2011). As these influences are hypothesized to interact across levels, interventions or strategies that focus only on one level of influence (such as individual, behavioural factors) are likely to be limited in their success at changing behaviour (Hadgraft et al. 2018).
	A public health approach to addressing physical inactivity and sedentary behaviour recognizes that strategies premised on the idea of ‘individual choice’ will only go so far, and it is important to recognize and address the broader structural barriers many in the population face to being physically active. This includes the broader social and environmental conditions in which we live and work (Owen et al. 2014). The WHO emphasizes the importance of a systems-based approach for addressing physical inactivity; one that focuses on addressing both upstream policy approaches and downstream individual-focused strategies (WHO 2018).





Developing public health strategies to increase physical activity and reduce sedentary time


	Following the release of the Toronto Charter for Physical Activity, an evidence review identified seven ‘best investments’ for physical activity that are considered to be applicable across population groups (see Box 8.5.4) (GAPA-ISPAH 2012). Importantly, these approaches target the multiple levels of influence of physical activity, incorporating upstream social and environmental approaches, with downstream individually focused approaches (WHO 2018).
	 	Box 8.5.4 Seven best investments for physical activity
	 	1. Supportive school environments: Prioritizing and resourcing physical activity (structured and unstructured) across the entire school day, through approaches that engage the entire school community.
	2. Transport policies and systems: Promoting active transport by prioritizing walking, cycling, and public transport.
	3. Urban design infrastructure and regulations that support physical activity: the built environment should support transport and recreational walking, cycling, and recreation, across different age groups.
	4. Physical activity integrated into primary healthcare systems: physical activity should be promoted within primary healthcare as an important modifiable risk factor for non-communicable diseases.
	5. Education and awareness raising: multiple approaches, such as traditional media, social media, and public education campaigns should be used to promote physical activity awareness and knowledge and shift societal norms.
	6. Whole-of-community approaches to physical activity: Physical activity should be promoted across the life course, and programmes should be integrated across the multiple settings in which people spend their time (e.g. workplaces, schools, community settings).
	7. Making sport programmes accessible for all: promoting physical activity through sport by making sure it is enjoyable and accessible for people of different ages, gender identities, abilities, and across the socioeconomic spectrum.
	Many of the best investments for physical activity may also have a positive effect on reducing sedentary behaviour; for example, mass media campaigns, infrastructure, and policies that promote walking and cycling, rather than car use (Scheepers et al. 2014). While there is a smaller body of knowledge about what works for reducing sedentary behaviour relative to physical activity, evidence suggests that environmental modifications in the workplace environment, such as the implementation of sit-stand workstations, can lead to significant reductions in sitting time (Neuhaus et al. 2014; Chu et al. 2016). In line with the ecological model of health behaviours, these types of interventions appear to be more effective when included as part of a multicomponent approach that targets multiple levels of influence (Chu et al. 2016).
	In accordance with a key principle of ecological models, it is important that public health strategies for increasing physical activity and reducing sedentary behaviour are specific to the context in which these behaviours occur. As outlined earlier, physical activity and sedentary behaviour can occur in multiple settings and contexts. The main factors that influence time spent in physical activity and sedentary behaviour in each of these settings are not necessarily the same, and understanding these differences is important for intervention development (Owen et al. 2011). Designing effective interventions requires identifying the settings-specific determinants or influences on these behaviours, to enable the development of appropriately targeted strategies. Importantly, consideration should also be given to the equity of physical activity initiatives, including providing no-or low-cost strategies where possible (Boxes 8.5.4 and 8.5.5).
	 	Box 8.5.5 Examples of settings-based approaches for increasing physical activity and/or reducing sedentary behaviour





Workplace


	 	• Introduction of sit-stand workstations to address the significant influence of desk-based work on sitting time (Neuhaus et al. 2014)
	• Modifying the internal physical environment to promote stair use (e.g. through attractive design, point of decision prompts) and providing end-of-trip facilities to support active transport (Oldenburg et al. 2002)





School


	 	• Walking School Bus programmes to encourage children to walk to school rather than being driven (Mendoza et al. 2011).
	• Incorporating physical activity into academic classes and promoting physical activity breaks during lessons (Watson et al. 2017)





Transport


	 	• Building safe and separated bicycle lanes to encourage active transport (Pucher and Buehler 2008)
	• Reducing the availability of free car parking to promote use of active and public transport (Scheepers et al. 2014).





Community


	 	• Organized activities in public spaces (e.g. tai chi, dance class, yoga) (Heath et al. 2012)
	• Community walking groups (Kassavou et al. 2013)
	It is worth noting that much of the evidence on ‘what works’ for increasing physical activity and reducing sedentary behaviour has arisen from controlled research studies in high-income countries, with relatively short-term follow up durations (Foster et al. 2005). Evidence for the effectiveness of community-wide interventions is somewhat inconsistent, potentially due to methodological issues of studies and the challenges inherent with population-level approaches (Baker et al. 2015). To increase our knowledge about the types of population-level physical activity interventions that are both effective and cost-effective, funding and resources should be prioritized towards conducting longer-term and more rigorous evaluations of these types of approaches (Laine et al. 2014; Reis et al. 2016). In particular, it is important to access the efficacy of approaches in a diversity of populations, including those from low-middle-income countries, less privileged backgrounds, those with disabilities, and those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds.





Cities and transport systems, physical activity, and sedentary time


	One significant set of challenges (and potential opportunities) for public health has been the rapid urbanization of developing countries around the world. As greater proportions of the population transition from rural to urban living, there can be benefits to public health through better access to healthcare and reduced incidence of infection (Leon 2008). However, these benefits are counteracted by a rise in non-communicable diseases, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease (Yusuf et al. 2001), brought about by risk factors such as poor nutrition, insufficient physical activity, and high levels of sedentary time (Popkin 2004).
	While traditional approaches to urban transport have considered how we can design safer roads for cars, there is now increasing interest in the ‘walkability’ of urban environments, or how features of the built environment may promote or discourage physical activity (Giles-Corti et al. 2016). Evidence from large cross-country studies has shown that particular urban design features can significantly influence the amount of time people spend in physical activity (Sallis et al. 2016). Higher connectedness of streets, higher density (to support mixed development and public transport), and the availability of local destinations are associated with higher levels of walking for transport (Giles-Corti et al. 2016). Cycling is also more common in areas where there is supportive infrastructure—such as networks of separated bicycles lanes and bicycle parking (Pucher and Buehler 2008; Hallal et al. 2012). An advantage of walking and cycling is that they are low to no cost, meaning that they are broadly accessible to a large proportion of the population (i.e. those who have the physical capacity to walk or cycle). This makes walking in particular a feasible and accessible strategy for people as they age.
	Increasing the number of trips that are conducted by active transport and reducing the amount of time that people spend in cars may also have broad-ranging benefits for public health beyond impacts on physical activity levels. Car time, for example, has been associated with a number of risk factors for chronic disease, including higher waist circumference, BMI, fasting plasma glucose and a clustered cardiometabolic risk score (Sugiyama et al. 2016). Reducing car emissions will also have broader environmental and health benefits (Woodcock et al. 2009).





The International Physical Activity and the Environment Network


	In addressing key elements of the environmental and policy agenda advocated earlier, the International Physical Activity and the Environment Network (IPEN) project was established in 2004. IPEN has been working as an international team from 12 countries (Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Columbia, Czech Republic, Denmark, China, Mexico, New Zealand, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States), carrying out studies to identify neighbourhood environmental factors associated with physical activity and sedentary behaviour.
	Several findings with important public health implications have emerged. The IPEN project has measured physical activity using accelerometer devices, has examined variations by country in activity levels and participants’ perceptions of a range of built-and natural-environment attributes of their neighbourhoods, and has employed geographic information system databases to provide objective indices of environmental factors (see Fig. 8.5.3 for country-specific examples).
	Fig. 8.5.3 Examples of country-specific activity levels and related environmental attributes, from the IPEN project.
	Source: J. F. Sallis et al. The Lancet 387, 2207–2217 (2016).
	In identifying associations of neighbourhood environmental attributes with physical activity and health, using the ‘walkability’ construct (a composite measure employing indices of net residential density, intersection density, land use mix, and net retail area ratio) has been particularly informative.
	Through the IPEN project, interesting findings have emerged on the role that the built environment may play in promoting or discouraging physical activity. Based on data from 14 cities in 10 countries, several neighbourhood environment attributes were related consistently to accelerometer-assessed moderate to vigorous physical activity. These included:
	 	• residential density
	• number of public transport stops
	• number of street intersections
	• and, number of parks within walking distance
	The relationships were linear; for example, the higher the level of residential density was related to a correspondingly higher level of physical activity. Those living in the most ‘activity-friendly’ neighbourhoods did 68–89 minutes more of physical activity per week than those in the least activity-friendly neighbourhoods (Sallis et al. 2016).
	The IPEN project has identified considerable similarity of findings across the cities investigated, adding strong evidence to support previous calls for policy changes in urban planning, public transport, and development of parks and recreational facilities as ways to increase physical activity. It is of considerable interest that ‘activity-friendly’ neighbourhood characteristics were found to be related to physical activity in a linear fashion—suggesting that every improvement in the built environment of a city can be expected to help to increase physical activity, whether or not residents are starting at a low or high level. These findings, however, are from a set of developed countries. Comparable findings have emerged from studies in Japan (Liao et al. 2016). Whether such environmental attributes are similarly important in low-and middle-income countries remains to be determined.
	Creating environments in cities that promote, rather than discourage, activity will require the involvement of (among others) urban planners, engineers, and policy makers at different levels of government, alongside public health practitioners. Shared decision making and building trust with stakeholders from the variety of sectors involved is important for effective intersectoral action to create healthy cities (Barr et al. 2008).





Conclusions


	While efforts to understand and influence physical inactivity have been a public health priority for several decades, progress in improving the physical activity levels of populations has been modest (Heath et al. 2012). Understanding how to address low levels of physical activity in populations that are increasingly urbanized, automobile dependent, and captured by screens in their domestic and workplace environments is a complex issue, like many public health challenges.
	Public health initiatives focused on creating healthy and enabling environments, such as through targeting urban planning and the built environment attributes of cities, offer great potential to improve health outcomes. Such approaches would not only have positive benefits on and through physical activity, but also through influencing other adverse exposures such as air pollution, noise, stress, and limited access to good-quality food (Giles-Corti et al. 2016).
	The causes of low levels of physical activity and high levels of sedentary behaviour are multifactorial, and different approaches are likely to be necessary depending on the setting and the population group of interest. To achieve large-scale change, interventions and policies will need to be developed using intersectoral and systems-based approaches, as well as perspectives that incorporate broad-ranging expertise and recognize the influence of traditional non-health sectors on health risk behaviours and outcomes.

8.6


Diabetes mellitus


	Farah Naz Khan, Nida Izhar Shaikh, K.M. Venkat Narayan, and Mohammed K. Ali





Introduction


Diabetes: definition, classification, and diagnosis





Definition and classification


	Diabetes mellitus is a complex chronic disease characterized by elevated blood sugars. The term diabetes has Greek origins and was meant to describe the passing of urine, while mellitus stems from the Latin word for sweet. Elevated blood sugars or hyperglycaemia seen in diabetes can be attributed to either impaired insulin production, impaired insulin action, or both (American Diabetes Association 2018). Produced by the beta cells in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, insulin is the main hormone responsible for regulating glucose. In response to elevated blood sugars after food intake, the pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin, thereby facilitating the utilization of glucose and keeping blood glucose within an acceptable normal range. Prolonged hyperglycaemia over many years can cause damage to both large (macrovascular) and small (microvascular) blood vessels. The macrovascular complications from diabetes include coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral arterial disease, and microvascular complications encompass retinopathy (which can lead to vision loss), neuropathy (which can contribute to foot ulcers), and nephropathy (which can culminate in end-stage renal disease). Epidemiological studies examining the sugar levels at which the risk of macrovascular and microvascular complications increase have influenced the thresholds that we use to define and classify hyperglycaemia and diabetes.
	The American Diabetes Association (ADA) and the World Health Organization (WHO) provide widely recognized recommendations on the classification and diagnosis of diabetes (WHO 2006); however, it is important to note that the distinctions between the types are somewhat arbitrary and factors separating them exist on a spectrum as shown in Figure 8.6.1. Notably, those with type 1 diabetes will require insulin for survival, whereas other classifications may potentially be managed with non-insulin therapies. The main categories of diabetes classification that will be discussed are type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, and gestational diabetes.
	Fig. 8.6.1 Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia.
	Reprinted from World Health Organization and International Diabetes Federation (2006). ‘Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycemia. A report of a WHO/IDF Consultation.’ With permission from the WHO. Available from http://www.who.int/diabetes/publications/diagnosis_diabetes2006/en/.
	Type 1 diabetes is caused by the destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells. Most commonly, this is due to autoantibodies against the beta cells, but can been seen in post-pancreatectomy patients and in patients with chronic pancreatic inflammation or injury. Type 1 diabetes accounts for only a minority of diabetes across the world.
	A milieu of impaired metabolic functions contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes including: impaired pancreatic insulin secretion, increased hepatic gluconeogenesis, decreased incretin effects, decreased skeletal muscle glucose uptake, increased lipolysis, neurotransmitter dysfunction, and increased renal glucose reabsorption (Defronzo 2009).
	Gestational diabetes is similar to type 2 diabetes in that it occurs as a result of insulin resistance and impaired insulin secretion as opposed to the beta cell destruction seen in type 1 diabetes. Diagnosed either in the second or third trimester of pregnancy, gestational diabetes usually resolves after delivery. However, women with gestational diabetes have over 7 times higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared to women with normoglycemic pregnancies (Bellamy et al. 2009).
	There are also other (relatively) rare and specific forms of diabetes that include: (i) exocrine pancreatic insufficiency related diabetes such a cystic fibrosis-related diabetes; (ii) monogenic diabetes syndromes such as neonatal diabetes and maturity-onset diabetes of the young; and (iii) medication-related diabetes such as steroid-induced diabetes.





Diagnosis


	Diagnosis of diabetes relies on blood glucose levels, which can be done to reflect fasting serum glucose levels, 2-hour post-load glucose levels, or a combination of the two. These can be done as part of an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). OGTTs detect impaired glucose metabolism as the test measures blood glucose before and then 2 hours after the ingestion of a glucose load. The OGTT is often considered too cumbersome and more costly than using a fasting glucose alone, which is why the ADA prefers the use of fasting plasma glucose or glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) for diabetes diagnoses. Glycated haemoglobin is a non-fasted test that reflects the average blood glucose over the previous 8–12 weeks (Nathan et al. 2007). This being said, the OGTT remains the best test to detect those with impaired glucose tolerance who have normal fasting blood sugars (Balkau 2000), so it is still favoured as the diagnostic method of choice by the WHO. The latest ADA and WHO criteria for diagnosis of diabetes are summarized in Table 8.6.1 (WHO 2006; American Diabetes Association 2018), which includes the WHO 2011 special consultative report that also endorsed the HbA1c as a diagnostic test (WHO 2011).
	 	Table 8.6.1 ADA and WHO diabetes and non-diabetes hyperglycaemia diagnostic criteria
	ADA
	WHO
			Diabetes
		Fasting glucose

		2-hour glucose
	≥11.1 mmol/L
