8.12


Sexually transmitted infections


	Noah Kojima and J.D. Klausner





Introduction to sexually transmitted infections


	Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) refer to many pathogens that are commonly spread through sexual contact including vaginal and anal intercourse and oral sex. Chlamydia trachomatis (chlamydia), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhoea), and Treponema pallidum (syphilis) cause the majority of worldwide bacterial STIs. Viral STIs include: human papillomavirus (HPV), herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2 (genital herpes; HSV-1 and HSV-2), hepatitis A, B, and C (unrelated viruses that can cause liver disease), as well as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Parasites like Trichomonas vaginalis, the causative agent of trichomoniasis, are also a major contributor to the global burden of STIs. In total, there are over 30 organisms and hundreds of those organism subtypes that have been recognized as sexually transmissible (Table 8.12.1). The newest agents recognized as sexually transmissible include Zika and Ebola viruses.
	STIs are common. The global annual incidence of curable (bacterial and protozoal) STIs estimated by the World Health Organization (WHO) was 357.4 million cases in 2012 (WHO 2015). Furthermore, among countries with public health surveillance systems, STIs are among the most frequently reported infections. However, compared to bacterial or protozoal STIs, viral STIs are far more prevalent with an estimated 708 million cases of Herpes Simplex Virus and HPV infection.
	Given the high numbers of STIs that exist in almost every nation, it is not surprising to find that regardless of a nation’s resources, STI-related symptoms can account for a large number of healthcare visits and substantial costs. STIs are also stigmatized and may also result in psychosocial consequences such as anxiety, shame, and stress. Additionally, sequelae like infertility, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and malignancies, and the morbidities of STIs increase healthcare costs.
	Although STIs are commonly associated with genital sores, discharges, or rashes, most STIs are asymptomatic. Many countries around the world continue to use syndromic management (the identification and management of persons with symptoms) as a way to manage STIs clinically, however many non-specific symptoms can lead to overtreatment for suspected STIs and lack of symptoms can lead to under treatment. Therefore, in countries with available infrastructure, screening asymptomatic people at risk for STIs is important for individual prevention and public health. While STI case rates are highest in adolescents and young adults, the most serious health outcomes occur later in life and are disproportionately borne by women and infants. For those reasons, STI prevention and control is an important public health investment for every country.
	There are many methods that can be used to reduce the risk of STI acquisition. Vaccinations protect against some viral STIs, like hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and wart or cancer-causing HPV types. Additionally, barrier protection, e.g. male and female condoms, reduce or even eliminate the risk of STI spread or acquisition.
	There are many diagnostic tests for STIs. Various fluids, including saliva, urine, blood, vaginal or anal secretions, and self-collected tip of the urethra swabs, can be used for testing. It is important to test any orifice that may have been exposed to an STI during sexual activity because STIs are often localized mucosal infections that are not detected systemically in the blood or urine. Additionally, tests utilize many different biochemical mechanisms that can allow rapid point-of-care testing for some STIs, like HIV and syphilis. Other testing systems, like polymerase chain reaction (PCR), normally require specialized laboratory equipment although new point-of-care PCR-based systems enable detection of STIs in 60–90 minutes.
	Bacterial STIs and trichomonal infections are curable. Unfortunately, individuals do not gain immunity to an STI, and are equally susceptible to reinfection. In contrast to bacterial STIs, viral STIs are not medically curable with the exception of hepatitis C infection (rarely sexually transmitted). Other STIs like genital herpes and HIV infection are incurable, although medicines exist to manage chronic infections and reduce the risk of transmission. Some viral STIs and their sequelae are preventable with vaccines, e.g. HPV, hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis A virus (HAV). Others, like HPV, HBV, and HCV infection can spontaneously clear without medical intervention.
	The field of STIs is constantly changing. New threats, like the Zika virus are emerging, and some cases were sexually transmitted, while known STIs continue to cause challenges, for example, antibiotic-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae. At the same time, new infection prevention tools are being created. For example, pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV infection as well as post-exposure prophylaxis for syphilis and chlamydia. Additionally, new methods for diagnosis, like point-of-care HIV and syphilis testing, are being mobilized around the world.
	In this chapter we summarize the global epidemiology of STIs and their associated health consequences, and report on factors affecting the spread of STIs in the community. We also discuss STI prevention and control as a public health intervention, relying on many interrelated interventions working together to reduce STI incidence and prevalence in the community. Finally, we consider some of the most likely challenges and opportunities in STI prevention anticipated over the next few decades.

Sexually transmitted infections


	The global burden of STIs includes the overall number of cases of infection, a host of short-and long-term adverse health outcomes in individuals including death, and the financial consequences (healthcare and other costs) associated with STIs and their associated health, and psychosocial impact for both individuals and economies.





Global STI numbers


	The WHO estimated that approximately 357 million new cases of four curable STIs, i.e. Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Treponema pallidum, and Trichomonas vaginalis, occurred in 2012 (WHO 2015). There were 130.9 million cases of chlamydia, 78.3 million cases of gonorrhoea, 5.6 million cases of syphilis, and 142.6 million cases of trichomoniasis. The majority of countries, 108 of 198, have an STI surveillance system in place, however STI surveillance has not been globally standardized, so it is difficult to assess the spread of concerning infections, like untreatable Neisseria gonorrhoeae. While new cases of STIs were common, the areas with the highest rates of STIs were Africa, the Americas, and the Western Pacific. Compared to prior STI prevalence estimations, the overall global prevalence of curable STIs seems to be decreasing. However, due to differences in STI surveillance practices, many STI prevalence estimations are poor because they are limited to small studies among accessible populations and case-based surveillance reports.
	Compared to the WHO report on curable STIs from 2008, there were fewer overall cases of STIs estimated in 2012 (357 million versus 498.9 million, respectively). While the number of cases of chlamydia increased from 105.7 million cases to 130.9 million cases, the worldwide number of cases of gonorrhoea, syphilis, and trichomoniasis decreased (Fig. 8.12.1). In accordance with the WHO global strategy for STI prevention and control, over 90% of countries worldwide have adopted syndromic management of STIs. The WHO has recommended monitoring two syndromes: urethral discharge among men and genital ulcer disease among men and women. Urethral discharge is most commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection and Chlamydia trachomatis infection. Genital ulcer disease is classically caused by syphilis and chancroid, however viral infections, like herpes simplex virus, can also cause this syndrome. Genital ulcers facilitate HIV transmission. In 2014, 56 countries reported data on genital ulcer disease (Fig. 8.12.2). From those data, the African Region had the highest burden of genital ulcer disease, followed by the Americas and the Western Pacific.
	Fig. 8.12.1 New cases (millions) of four curable STIs in 2008 and 2015.
	Fig. 8.12.2 Proportion of genital ulcer disease burden by geographic regions, 2014.
	While syndromic management is a useful strategy to treat STIs in those presenting to clinics and estimate disease burden, laboratory-based STI testing has superior STI sensitivity and specificity. However, the accessibility and feasibility of laboratory-based STI testing is more limited worldwide due to the lack of political will, absence of infrastructure, and the cost of testing. There are many different laboratory-based methods to test for STIs, mainly Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection and syphilis. Microscopy with Gram stain and bacterial culture can detect Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Newer nucleic acid-amplification-based tests have become increasingly useful in the detection of Neisseria gonorrhoeae due to their higher sensitivity and specificity. Point-of-care, rapid syphilis tests have become useful in initial syphilis screening, however that test must be used on those without a known history of syphilis or treatment, because the test cannot distinguish between past or current infection. The confirmation of a diagnosis of syphilis necessitates two tests, treponemal and non-treponemal tests, which are not always available worldwide. Therefore, national syphilis estimates can be discordant with the actual burden of syphilis.





Viral STIs


	In contrast to bacterial STIs, the only curable viral STI is hepatitis C. Other STIs like genital herpes and HIV infection are incurable; however, they can be managed with antiviral medicines. While HIV infection may be the most well-known viral STI and contributes to a total of 36.9 million people living with a chronic infection, there are an estimated 417 million cases of herpes simplex virus type-2 infection, and roughly 291 million women are infected with human papillomavirus at any given time, worldwide.
	Genital herpes infection is a chronic, life-long viral infection caused by HSV-1 or HSV-2. It was estimated that in 2012, there were 417 million people aged 15 to 49 years living with HSV-2 infection. More women had HSV-2 infection when compared to men (267 million persons versus 150 million persons), and this was attributed to women being more susceptible to infection than men. Worldwide, Africa had the highest prevalence of HSV-2 infection, followed by the Western Pacific and Southeast Asia (Fig. 8.12.3) (Looker et al. 2015). Genital herpes disease and transmission can be reduced with medical therapy.
	Fig. 8.12.3 Estimated prevalence (millions) of Herpes simplex virus-2 infection by region, 2012.
	Source: data from Looker K. et al ‘Global Estimates of Prevalent and Incident Herpes Simplex Virus Type 2 Infections in 2012’. PLoS One, 10, e114989.
	Roughly 291 million women worldwide are infected with human papillomaviruses, a group of viruses that consist of over 100 different subtypes of viruses, of which about 30 primarily infect the oropharynx (throat) and genitals. Among those viruses, there are at least 13 cancer-causing varieties, which are classified as ‘high-risk’ viruses. Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women worldwide. In 2012, nearly 270,000 women died from cervical cancer, and nearly 230,000 of those deaths occurred in low-and middle-income countries. In low-income countries, the relevant disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost to cervical cancer are second only to oropharyngeal cancer (American Cancer Society 2015). Two human papillomaviruses, type 16 and 18, cause 70% of cervical cancers and precancerous cervical lesions. Worldwide, human papillomaviruses type 16 is the most prevalent, followed by type 18 (Bruni et al. 2010). In the United States, there are 35,000 HPV-associated cancers annually (61% in females and 39% in males), with an annual cost of US $8 billion for screening and treatment of HPV-associated health outcomes (Jemal et al. 2013).
	HIV infection continues to cause significant morbidity and mortality. Since access to antiretroviral drugs expanded in the early 2000s, an estimated 20 million have been treated and 5.2 million AIDS-related deaths have been averted in low-and middle-income countries (UNAIDS 2013b). Furthermore, children have seen the largest decrease in HIV incidence, which has been reduced by over half in the last 10 years (UNAIDS 2013a). While great progress has been made in the reduction in the spread of HIV, 36.9 million people are living with chronic HIV infection. Sub-Saharan Africa continues to carry the largest burden of those living with, dying from, and acquiring HIV infection (Fettig et al. 2014).
	Viral hepatitis caused 1.34 million deaths in 2015, with an increasing trend (WHO 2017a). Many unrelated viruses that all cause liver disease are grouped together as viral hepatitis. While sexual transmission of hepatitis A, B, C, and D have been observed; hepatitis B is the most commonly sexually transmitted hepatitis virus. Most deaths caused by the viral hepatitis were due to chronic liver disease (720,000 deaths due to cirrhosis), and followed by primary liver cancer (470,000 deaths due to hepatocellular carcinoma). Hepatitis B and C were responsible for 96% of all hepatitis related mortality. Globally, it is estimated that 257 million people are living with chronic hepatitis B infection and 71 million people were living with a chronic hepatitis C infection in 2015. Hepatitis B has the highest prevalence in Africa and Western Pacific, whereas hepatitis C has the highest prevalence in the Europe. In May 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed a Global Health Sector Strategy on viral hepatitis 2016–2021 to reduce new infections by 90%, and mortality by 65% by 2030. Other viral hepatitides are described in Table 8.12.2.
	 	Table 8.12.2 Viral hepatitis
	 			A
	Caused approximately 11,000 deaths in 2015. A vaccine is available. It is primarily transmitted through exposure to contaminated food or water. It can be acquired through sexual activity.
		B
	Caused over 880,000 deaths in 2015. A vaccine is available. It is primarily transmitted through blood or semen.
		C
	Caused over 400,000 deaths in 2015. Medicine is available to cure chronic hepatitis C infections. It is primarily transmitted through blood.
		D
	Older interferon-based medicines can be used to treat this virus with suboptimal results. It is an incomplete virus and can only infect persons with a current hepatitis B infection. It is transmitted mostly through exposure to blood. Persons with hepatitis B infection with a hepatitis D coinfection lead to worse health outcomes. Most experts estimate that 5% of persons infected with hepatitis B are coinfected with hepatitis D.
		E
	Caused approximately 44,000 deaths and 20 million infections in 2015. A vaccine to prevent hepatitis E infection has been developed and licensed in China; however, it does not have a wide global availability. Hepatitis E is transmitted via the faecal-oral route, primarily by contaminated water. It has a higher case fatality among pregnant women.
	While most STI acquisition occurs during sexual activity, mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of STIs can occur in utero or perinatally. In 2018, UNAIDS estimated that 180,000 children acquired HIV infection, predominantly through perinatal transmission or contaminated breast milk (UNAIDS 2018). Antenatal HIV screening and maternal treatment programmes have greatly reduced the frequency of MTCT of HIV infection, when compared to the estimated 420,000 children that acquired HIV infection at the peak of the epidemic in 2003. In eastern and southern Africa, the area with the highest frequency of MTCT of HIV infection in the world, 93% of the 940,000 pregnant women with HIV infection received antiretroviral prophylaxis in 2017, reducing the average frequency of MTCT of HIV to less than 10%.
	T. pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis, can readily cross the placenta during pregnancy and can cause morbidity and mortality among mothers and newborns. Between 2008 and 2012, the estimated total number of maternal infections and adverse pregnancy outcomes attributed to congenital syphilis decreased by 38% from 520,000 to 350,000 cases, which consisted of 143,000 early fetal deaths/stillbirths, 62,000 neonatal deaths, 44,000 preterm/low weight births, and 102,000 infants with syphilis (WHO 2015). While declines in congenital syphilis were seen in all regions, the largest declines were observed in South-East Asia. As of 2018, many countries have been successful in the dual elimination of MTCT of HIV and syphilis, including Cuba, Thailand, Belarus, Anguilla, Antigua, and Barbuda, Bermuda, Cayman Islands, Montserrat, and St. Kitts and Nevis (WHO 2014; WHO 2017b). The WHO acknowledged Armenia for eliminating MTCT of HIV and the Republic of Moldova for eliminating MTCT of syphilis. Strategies to eliminate MTCT of HIV include prevention of unintended pregnancies, increased access to testing and counselling, medical therapy, safe delivery practices, and appropriate infant feeding practices (WHO 2014). Strategies to eliminate of MTCT of syphilis include early antenatal testing and treatment. Other STIs, like Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and HSV infections, can be transmitted from mothers to newborns as a result of exposure to the pathogen as the neonate passes through the birth canal. Strategies to control those infections are discussed later.
	More research has emerged since the 2015 Zika virus outbreak in Brazil. Zika virus is now recognized as sexually transmissible, although its primary route of transmission (>99%) is through mosquitoes (Baud et al. 2017). Among pregnant women, Zika virus infection has been associated with severe adverse infant outcomes including miscarriage, stillbirth, and microcephaly. Additionally, new research supports that MTCT of Zika virus can occur perinatally (Blohm et al. 2018).
	For neonatal HSV-1 and HSV-2 infection, a devastating infection of newborns with > 50% mortality, it is estimated that approximately 14,000 cases occurred annually globally between 2010 and 2015 (4,000 cases for HSV-1 and 10,000 cases for HSV-2) (Looker et al. 2017). In the Americas, Europe, and Western Pacific, HSV-1 contributed to more cases than HSV-2, whereas in Africa, HSV-2 contributed to more infections. For congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, an infection causing deafness and neurodevelopmental problems, it is estimated that the incidence of congenital CMV infection among all live births ranges from 0.6% to 0.7% in developed countries and 1% to 5% in developing counties (Marsico and Kimberlin 2017), far more common than Zika virus.





STI-associated morbidity


	The presentation of an STI can range from an asymptomatic infection to a life threatening one. See Table 8.12.1 for a list of STI-related diseases or syndromes. The acquisition of STIs can also lead to stigma, shame, and psychological harm (Cunningham et al. 2009). Additionally, many STIs can lead to longer-term health problems, which can be categorized into four broad categories: female reproductive health disorders, e.g. infertility; adverse pregnancy outcomes, e.g. neonatal death; malignancies, e.g. cervical cancer associated with HPV; and increased risk of HIV infection acquisition.
	Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections are important causes of infertility (CDC 2018c). While it is possible to test for and treat those infections, 10–15% of women with chlamydial infection who go untreated will develop pelvic inflammatory disease. Infections in the upper genital tract can cause permanent damage from inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes, uterus, and surrounding tissues leading to infertility. Scarring of the fallopian tubes also increases the risk of ectopic pregnancy, which can be a serious medical or surgical emergency. Chlamydia trachomatis infection has also been associated with HPV-induced cervical cancer (Madeleine et al. 2007). Screening programmes have been shown to be effective in reducing rates of chlamydial and gonorrhoeal female reproductive health disorders (Workowski et al. 2015). Among women with HIV infection, Trichomonas vaginalis infection has been associated with increased risk for pelvic inflammatory disease.
	Many STIs are associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, causing morbidity and mortality among newborns. One of the most devastating STIs in pregnancy is syphilis. It is estimated that fetal loss and still birth were 21% more frequent, neonatal deaths were 9.3% more frequent, and prematurity or low birth weight were 5.8% more frequent among pregnant women with syphilis versus pregnant women without syphilis (Gomez et al. 2013). Additionally, 15% of newborns of mothers with untreated syphilis had clinical evidence of congenital syphilis. For Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections, exposure to the pathogen occurs during delivery. Untreated Chlamydia trachomatis infection causes significant perinatal morbidity including blindness and pneumonia. Untreated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection can cause rhinitis, vaginitis, urethritis, blindness, sepsis, arthritis, and meningitis. After delivery, prophylactic antibiotic ointments prevent eye infections from those infections. Prenatal screening and treatment prevent chlamydial and gonococcal infections among neonates (Workowski et al. 2015). Apart from the well-characterized features of HIV infection, many other viral STIs cause morbidity and mortality among newborns. Neonatal herpes is associated with skin, eye, and mouth disease, lasting neurological impairment, disseminated infection, and, has an estimated 60% fatality rate among newborns without treatment (Looker et al. 2017). Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis can be a serious disease among newborns that acquire perinatal HPV infection (CDC 2017). Among pregnant women with hepatitis B virus, without post-exposure prophylaxis, roughly 40% of infants develop a chronic infection. Among those infants, approximately one-fourth of those will eventually die from sequela of chronic liver disease (CDC 2018d). More recently, it has been found that Zika virus infection during pregnancy is associated with microcephaly, abnormal brain and eye development, hearing loss, and damage to muscles and bones (CDC 2018b).
	STIs are also associated with certain malignancies, which can occur during a chronic infection. Major STI-associated malignancies include anogenital cancers associated with HPV, hepatocellular carcinoma associated with chronic hepatitis, some lymphomas are associated with HIV infection, and Kaposi’s sarcoma is associated with human herpes virus type 8 infection. Low-and middle-income counties have a higher STI-related cancer burden than high-income counties.
	Where there are more than 100 types of HPVs, 13 HPVs have been identified as cancer causing (WHO 2018). Among the cancer-causing HPVs, HPV type 16 and 18 cause 70% of all cervical cancers and precancerous cervical lesions. HPV is also linked with cancers of the anus, vulva, vagina, and penis (Crosbie et al. 2013). Worldwide, cervical cancer is the fourth most frequent malignancy among women. In 2012, there were an estimated 530,000 new cases of cervical cancer among women, with approximately 270,000 deaths (WHO 2018). Over 85% of those deaths occurred in low-and middle-income counties. The progression from chronic HPV infection to cervical cancer is insidious, taking 5 to 10 years to develop among women with weakened immune systems, e.g. infection with HIV, and 15 to 20 years to develop among women with normal immune systems. In high-income counties, routine screening and treatment prevents up to 80% of cervical cancers. As of 2018, cervical cancer can be screened with conventional Pap testing and liquid-based cytology, visual inspection with acetic acid, and molecular testing for cancer-causing HPV types. Highly effective and safe vaccinations are available for cancer-causing HPV types. Increased use of HPV vaccines has great potential to prevent HPV-associated cancers among women and men worldwide.
	In 2015, it was estimated that 470,000 deaths were due to hepatocellular carcinoma secondary to viral hepatitis (WHO 2017a). The majority of cases of hepatocellular carcinoma are associated with chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis C virus infection (El-Serag 2012). Nearly all childhood and approximately half of all cases of hepatocellular carcinoma can be attributed to chronic hepatitis B infection. Additionally, it is estimated that 2.7 million people are living with a hepatitis B and HIV coinfection (WHO 2017a). The prevalence of hepatitis B is highest in the Western Pacific, Africa, and followed by South-East Asia. For prevention, the global coverage of hepatitis B vaccination reached 84% in 2015 reducing rates of transmission in the first five years of life. While challenges are still present, the WHO has created strategies to eliminate viral hepatitis by 2030 by increasing global surveillance, scaling up testing and treatment infrastructure, and the development of new diagnostics and treatments.
	Patients with HIV infection are at increased risk of many cancers due to immunosuppression (Yarchoan and Uldrick 2018). AIDS-defining malignancies include non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, Kaposi’s sarcoma, and cervical cancer. Patients with HIV infection are also at increased risk of developing lung cancer, anal cancer, Hodgkin’s lymphoma, oral cavity cancer, pharyngeal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, vulvar cancer, and penile cancer, however those are non-AIDS-defining malignancies.
	STIs can also increase risk of transmitting and acquiring HIV infection. STIs that cause genital ulcers, like syphilis or genital herpes, can increase the risk of acquiring or transmitting HIV infection by two to three times (WHO 2016). Other STIs, like Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Trichomonas vaginalis infections, and STI-related conditions like bacterial vaginosis, seem to increase risk of HIV transmission and acquisition due to mucosal inflammation (Galvin and Cohen 2004; Ward and Ronn 2010). STIs, like syphilis, have been observed to increase HIV viral load and decrease CD4 T-cell counts (Buchacz et al. 2004).





Global STI management costs


	The WHO Global Health Sector Strategy to manage global STIs was proposed in 2016, and set goals to end STI epidemics as a major public health concern by 2030. To achieve those targets, 70% of counties need to have a STI surveillance system in place; 70% of countries need to have 95% of pregnant women screened for syphilis and HIV, with 95% of those with syphilis receiving treatment; 70% of key populations need access to STI and HIV services; 70% of countries need to provide or have access to STI services in all HIV, reproductive health, family planning, and ante-and post-natal care services; 70% of countries need to deliver HPV vaccines, and those countries that provide that service need 90% national coverage in at least 80% of districts; and 70% of countries report antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections (WHO 2016). While some targets, like HPV vaccination, will generate significant returns on investment, initial implementation of those goals will be expensive. A recent analysis estimated that the total implementation cost will be US $18.2 billion over 2016 to 2021 in 117 low-and middle-income counties, with an initial $3.26 billion for HPV vaccination, $3.69 billion for HPV screening, $2.54 billion for chlamydial screening, and $1.4 billion for syphilis screening (Korenromp et al. 2017). Clinical STI management will add another $3 billion, with $1.4 billion going to diagnostic testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection and $0.8 billion going to service delivery.





Transmission of sexually transmitted infections


	Many risks factors have been associated with acquiring a STI that include behavioural risks as well as biologic risks. Behavioural risk factors include age of sexual initiation, number(s) and type(s) of sex partner(s), and use of barrier protection. Biological risk factors include sex, age, and developmental physiological changes. In addition to personal risk factors, community risk factors are also present, like the local prevalence of STIs, availability of screening and treatment services as well as social, economic, demographic, and cultural risk factors.





STI transmission dynamics


	An important mathematical model to understand the population dynamics of STI transmission was proposed by May et al. in 1987 for HIV infection (May and Anderson 1987). The model states that the average number of new infections caused by each infected person is determined by three factors: (a) the likelihood that an infected person will transmit the pathogen to an uninfected partner during sexual activity; (b) the average number of new sex partners formed between infected and non-infected people, and (c) the average amount of time an infected person can transmit the pathogen. Increasing any of those factors increases the population prevalence and vice versa.
	With that model in mind, approaches of STI prevention programmes used to control the spread of STIs can be categorized. Commonly, STI prevention programmes aim to reduce the average amount of time an infected person can transmit the pathogen by testing and treating STIs, however many different interventions have been described and implemented. A list of different STI control strategies is included in Box 8.12.1.
	 	Box 8.12.1 Strategies to control STIs
	 	• Clinical testing and treating
	• Community-based screening
	• Comprehensive sexual education
	• Vaccination
	• Barrier protection, e.g. condoms
	• Medical male circumcision
	• Pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV and other STIs
	• Expedited partner therapy





Medical male circumcision


	Medical male circumcision has been proven to reduce risk of male acquisition of HIV and other STIs (CDC 2018a). It is hypothesized that male circumcision reduces the risk of HIV and other STI acquisition because by removing the foreskin, the exposed penile skin thickens creating an effective barrier to infection. Additionally foreskin removal reduces the number of susceptible mucosal immune cells as well as alters the genital microbiota. Three randomized clinical trials showed that adult medical male circumcision lowered the risk for HIV infection acquisition by 51% to 60% among heterosexual males (Auvert et al. 2005; Bailey et al. 2007; Gray et al. 2007). Additionally, male circumcision reduced the risk of genital ulcer disease prevalence by 47% and cancer-causing HPV prevalence by 23% to 47% (Auvert et al. 2009; Tobian et al. 2009; Serwadda et al. 2010; Mehta et al. 2012). Partners of circumcised men also receive protection from STIs. A large randomized trial performed in Kenyan and Ugandan involving HIV-serodiscordant heterosexual couples, found a reduction in the incidence of syphilis incidence by 42% among men and 59% among women (Pintye et al. 2014). The literature also supports that male circumcision is associated with reduced risk of other STIs among women including oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) genotypes and of contracting cervical cancer (Svare et al. 2002; Drain et al. 2006; Wilson et al. 2013; Grabowski et al. 2016). The evidence of the benefits of male circumcision is mixed for some other conditions like herpes simplex virus type 2 (Borkakoty et al. 2010; Mugo et al. 2011; Mujugira et al. 2011; Davis et al. 2017), genital ulcers (Gray et al. 2009), Chlamydia trachomatis infection (Castellsague et al. 2005; Nayyar et al. 2014; Russell et al. 2016) and Trichomonas vaginalis infection (Gray et al. 2009).





Sexual networks and core groups


	Sexual networks are a type of social network that are defined by sexual activity among a group of individuals. Sexual networks can be determined by social, economic, cultural, migratory, or political forces, in addition to the physical or virtual spaces in which those networks can take place (Doherty et al. 2005). STI transmission within a sexual network depends on the number of sexual linkages within a sexual network and temporality of partnerships (concurrently versus sequentially). Bathhouses are an example of a physical space in which a sexual network can form. In the 1970s and 1980s, it was common for some men who have sex with men to find sex partners in bathhouses. Epidemiologic studies on the sexual networks formed in those bathhouses were used to trace the spread of HIV and other STIs. Now, the Internet has given rise to new virtual spaces facilitating sexual contacts through mobile applications and social media sites.





Future directions and challenges


	New global initiatives have been enacted with the goal to end STI epidemics as a public health concern. Recently, new methods to prevent HIV infection have been developed, the use of HPV vaccines has increased, and more countries have successfully eliminated of MTCT of HIV and syphilis. However, multi-drug resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection continues to spread and challenge STI control programmes.





Global and regional initiatives


	In 2016, the WHO debuted a new Global Health Sector Strategy on Sexually Transmitted Infections 2016–2021: Towards Ending STIs, which sets a vision, goals, targets, guiding principles, and priority actions to end STIs epidemics as a public health problem (WHO 2016). The strategy emphasized the importance of accelerating and focusing comprehensive prevention efforts through scaling up evidence-based behavioural, biomedical, and structural approaches, facilitating individual’s access to information of their STI status, improving access to treatment and comprehensive long-term care, and challenging pervasive stigmatization and discrimination. The 2030 targets for the strategy were (1) a 90% reduction of Treponema pallidum infection incidence globally from a 2018 global baseline, (2) a 90% reduction in Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection incidence globally from a 2018 global baseline, (3) ≤ 50 cases of congenital syphilis per 100,000 live births in 80% of counties, and (4) to sustain 90% coverage and at least 80% in every district in countries with HPV vaccine in their national immunization programme.
	The WHO also made the dual elimination of MTCT of HIV and syphilis a global health priority, with a few countries also aiming to eliminate MTCT hepatitis B infection. So far, 11 countries have been validated by the WHO for eliminating MTCT of HIV or syphilis (WHO 2014; WHO 2017b). Criteria required for validation include 95% of pregnant women receiving antenatal care, 95% of pregnant women receiving HIV and syphilis testing in pregnancy, and 95% of pregnant women diagnosed with HIV or syphilis receiving treatment, with targets of ≤50 new paediatric HIV infections per 100,000 live births and a transmission rate of either <5% in breastfeeding populations or <2% in non-breastfeeding populations and ≤50 cases of congenital syphilis per 100,000 live births. The WHO also requires that this process be conducted within a context of human rights, gender equality, and community engagement.





Antimicrobial resistance


	Since the introduction of effective antibiotic treatments for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection with sulfa drugs in the 1930s, the bacterium has become resistant to every antibiotic used for treatment (Hook and Kirkcaldy 2018). Neisseria gonorrhoeae developed resistance to sulfonamides, penicillins, early-generation cephalosporins, tetracyclines, macrolides, and fluoroquinolone drugs (Alirol et al. 2017). Most recently, Neisseria gonorrhoeae has been developing resistance to extended-spectrum cephalosporins, which is the last remaining empiric monotherapy for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Furthermore, there has been a report of Neisseria gonorrhoeae antibiotic resistance to dual therapy (ceftriaxone and azithromycin). In 2015, the WHO adopted a Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, which launched the Global Antibiotic Research and Development Partnership. This group aims to accelerate the development of new antibiotics, evaluate the potential of existing antibiotics and various combinations of them for more effective treatment, develop fixed-dose drug combinations, and develop simplified treatment guidelines for antibiotic-resistant bacterium. There are also three new drugs that are being developed to treat antibiotic-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection.





Advancement in technology


	While use of mobile geosocial networking applications used for meeting sex partners may increase the risk of STI acquisition (Beymer et al. 2014), other advances like pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV infection have been shown to be effective in preventing HIV acquisition (WHO 2016). Increased use of STI self-testing and rapid testing has also been shown to be helpful in increasing linkage to care, quality assurance, and partner services (Tucker et al. 2013). Additionally, digital innovations like mobile health-based messaging, Internet-based outreach, and combined interventions have been found to be acceptable, feasible, and impactful. Those interventions have also been useful in engaging harder to reach traditionally healthcare adverse populations (Daher et al. 2017). Finally, innovations in diagnostics may make it feasible to perform home or clinic-based STI testing for multiple organisms including the characterization of antimicrobial resistance in some organisms in as few as 20 minutes.





Conclusions


	STIs continue to be a major global cause of morbidity, mortality, and increased healthcare costs. This chapter outlined major issues regarding STI transmission, prevention, and programmes aimed to reduce global STI burden. While there are new challenges in the field of STIs, advancements in technology and global initiatives set by WHO could help reduce STIs as a public health epidemic in the near future. More effort is needed in research, implementation, and global collaboration and financial investment to eliminate many STIs as major public health problems.

8.13


Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)


	Quarraisha Abdool Karim, Urisha Singh, Cheryl Baxter, and Salim S. Abdool Karim





Introduction


	In May 2016, about 35 years since the first reported cases of AIDS, United Nations (UN) member states adopted the Declaration of ending AIDS by 2030, at a specially convened high level meeting in New York. The impetus for this remarkable announcement emanated from the confluence of new human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) knowledge, centrally around the use of antiretrovirals for treatment and prevention.
	Given that a vaccine or cure, much needed tools for elimination and eradication of HIV respectively are still in development, what does ‘ending AIDS’ mean? Epidemiologically it can be defined as the reduction of disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity, or mortality to a locally acceptable level as a result of deliberate intervention measures. While an epidemiological metric for achieving epidemic control has yet to be defined, it is defined mathematically as the reproductive rate of infection (R0) reaching below one. There is some consensus that this goal can be reached at an HIV incidence rate of 1/1,000 per annum.
	In order to track progress on achieving epidemic control, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) developed the Fast Track Strategy that monitors progress towards elimination of AIDS-related stigma and discrimination; AIDS-related mortality and reduction in HIV incidence rates. The intermediate 2020 targets include: (a) 90% of those who are infected know their status; 90% of those who are infected are initiated on antiretroviral (ARV) treatment and 90% of those on ARV treatment are virally suppressed; also referred to as 90–90–90; (b) a 90% reduction of incidence rates compared to 2010 and iii. Reduction in stigma and discrimination.
	This chapter traces the history of HIV from its origins, the remarkable scientific advances, and unprecedented global responses through to the current state of the epidemic, progress towards ending AIDS and remaining challenges.





In the beginning


	Acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) was first recognized in 1981 when a cluster of five previously healthy homosexual men from Los Angeles presented with Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP) (now Pneumocystis jirovecii) and additional clusters of homosexual men in California and New York presented with Kaposi’s sarcoma (CDC 1981; Gottlieb et al. 1981; Greene 2007). Within the next 18 months, additional cases of previously healthy homosexual men with PCP and Kaposi’s sarcoma were reported in various large cities in the United States (CDC 1982a). The main presenting symptoms of these men included severely depressed cell-mediated immunity coupled with opportunistic infections and rare malignancies (CDC 1981). The prognosis of the illness was poor with the outcome being rapid death following the manifestation of these symptoms. The predominance of this new disease entity in young homosexual men and linked cases, which suggested it was sexually related, led to the belief that it was a lifestyle-based illness and it was termed gay-related immune deficiency (GRID) or ‘gay plague’. A month later, the illness was detected in Haitians and then haemophiliacs which initially led to the belief that it originated in Haiti (CDC 1982b). However, the identification of cases of a new wasting illness in Uganda, which mimicked symptoms of AIDS, termed ‘slim disease’ placed doubt on the origin of the illness (Serwadda et al. 1985). Between 1982 and 1983, the first case of mother-to-child transmission of AIDS and the first AIDS-related death of an infant, aged 20 months, was reported. Additionally, reports of AIDS infection in haemophiliacs, injecting drug users (IDUs), recipients of blood transfusions and female partners of men with AIDS were released, providing the first indication that AIDS infection was likely also spread through blood and heterosexual sex (CDC 1982b; Greene 2007). At this time the new disease entity was renamed AIDS, all major routes of transmission were identified, however, its cause, diagnosis and treatment remained elusive (Marx 1982; Gottlieb et al. 1983).
	The lack of information on the causative agent of AIDS coupled with a lack of treatment and testing methods for the illness imparted great fear, uncertainty, and stigma towards those infected. Many people believed that AIDS could spread through holding hands or sharing a toilet seat. Parents with infected adult children refused to see them, nurses and auxiliary staff refused to take meals to infected patients, doctors argued whether treating infected patients was a moral obligation, and faith communities titled those infected as ‘abominations’ with the belief that AIDS was a form of ‘divine punishment for those with sinful lifestyles’ (Fee and Krieger 1993; Smith and Whiteside 2010). People living with AIDS (PLWA) were; physically attacked, unfairly dismissed from their jobs, unlawfully evicted from their homes and denied various health services. This drove the development of several organizations and activist groups aimed at advocating for and filling the gaps in care for PLWA and initiating civil rights protection policies (Gostin 1990; Herek and Capitanio 1993). The gay rights movement campaigned for AIDS to be viewed as a human rights issue with the argument that, other than the risk of infection with AIDS, there was also a high risk of harmful discrimination against those found to be infected (Bayer and Fairchild 2006). A multitude of public health officials supported this argument and raised additional concerns of stigma being a barrier to testing for the illness and for those with AIDS from accessing health services (Smith and Whiteside 2010). Media coverage of AIDS remained low with social movements and activism propagating the early response to AIDS and encouraging the discovery of its causative agent and diagnostic tests.





The discovery and spread of HIV


	The identification and isolation of the causative agent of AIDS was challenging due to the manifestation of clinical signs and symptoms years after infection by which time patients also presented with various additional infections.
	In 1983, Luc Montagnier and Francoise Barre-Sinoussi from the Pasteur Institute in France announced the isolation of a new retrovirus; lymphadenopathy-associated virus (LAV), and suggested that it was the cause of AIDS, however, proof of causality was not established. Eighteen months later, Robert Gallo’s group from the US National Cancer Institute announced the identification and isolation of a second retrovirus, the human T-lymphotropic virus type-III (HTLV-III), and provided sufficient evidence of causality of AIDS (Popovic et al. 1984). Three months later Jay Levy’s group in San Francisco isolated an ‘AIDS-associated retrovirus’ from 22 AIDS infected patients confirming the link between a retrovirus and AIDS (Levy et al. 1984). By 1985, LAV, HTLV-III and the AIDS-associated retrovirus were confirmed to be variants of the same retrovirus (Ratner et al. 1985; Marx 1988), which was then established as the cause of AIDS and renamed HIV (Coffin et al. 1986). A second, less prevalent and virulent strain of HIV was isolated from patients in West Africa in 1986, providing further confirmation of causality. This virus was named HIV-type 2 (HIV-2) with HIV subsequently renamed HIV-type 1 (HIV-1) (Clavel et al. 1986).
	Following the identification of the causative agent, its origins were investigated using phylogenetics and statistical modelling of the earliest available HIV sequences obtained between 1950 and 1960. Studies showed that HIV-1 and HIV-2 originated in central West Africa from separate zoonotic transfer of simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) from primates to humans where primates were butchered and consumed as bush meat (Fig. 8.13.1) (Sharp and Hahn 2008; Tebit and Arts 2011). Cross-species transfer of SIV from old world monkeys to chimpanzees then from chimpanzees to gorillas resulted in variations of SIV that gave rise to HIV-1 in humans. The HIV-1 groups M and N have been associated with SIV from Pan troglodytes, a subspecies of chimpanzee, HIV-1 group P and O have been associated with western gorillas and HIV-2 has been associated with SIV from Cerocebus atys, a subspecies of the sooty mangabey (Nerrienet et al. 2005; Santiago et al. 2005; Keele et al. 2006; Sharp and Hahn 2008; Plantier et al. 2009).
	Fig. 8.13.1 Origins of HIV.
	Reprinted from Denis M Tebit, Eric J Arts. Tracking a century of global expansion and evolution of HIV to drive understanding and to combat disease. The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 11(1):45–56 with permission from Elsevier.
	It has been estimated that HIV-1 group M, N and O originated in 1908 (range: 1884–1924), 1963 (range: 1948–1977), and 1920 (range: 1890–1940) respectively, while the origin of HIV-2 group A and B has been estimated to be 1932 (range: 1906–1955) and 1935 (range: 1907–1961) respectively (Korber et al. 2000; Wertheim and Worobey 2009; Tebit and Arts 2011; Sharp and Hahn 2008, 2011). Faria et al. (2014) demonstrated that HIV group M, the oldest lineage of HIV-1, originated in Kinshasa and attributed its spread through central Africa to extensive use of railway transport that linked various regions and enabled interactions between individuals from these regions (Faria et al. 2014). Additional studies cite the growth of cities, migration, urbanization, and improved travel as the main contributing factors towards the exponential spread of HIV and its uneven distribution of subtypes and circulating recombinant forms of HIV (Tebit and Arts 2011; Sharp and Hahn 2008; Faria et al. 2014).





The development of the HIV antibody test and HIV/AIDS surveillance


	Shortly after the discovery of HIV, diagnostic tools started to be developed to identify individuals infected with HIV. By March 1985, an enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was approved as the first HIV diagnostic test. This test recognized the IgG antibody produced in response to HIV-1 only. Blood banks in the USA and elsewhere in the world began routine screening of donated blood (Roberts 1994). Although sensitive and useful in the screening of blood products, the ELISA test had an antibody-negative window of at least 12 weeks post-infection and had a high rate of false negative results in response to other infections, pregnancy, autoimmune diseases, and various unknown conditions (Chappel et al. 2009). By 1986, two confirmatory tests, the western blot immunoassay (CDC 1989) and the HTLV-III immunofluorescence assay were approved with an antibody-negative window of approximately 6 weeks (Hedenskog et al. 1989; Chappel et al. 2009). These confirmatory tests were used in conjunction with the ELISA test and required that tests be performed in duplicate. Second generation HIV tests developed in the late 1980s, were designed to further reduce the antibody-negative window period to 4 weeks and improve the specificity of testing by including: the HIV-1 specific P24 antigen, an HIV-2 specific protein and an HIV-1 group O antigen to the antigen milieu in order to detect antibodies to these antigens. Third and fourth generation tests were subsequently developed, each with reduced antibody-negative windows, however, each of these tests were still used in combination with the confirmatory western blot immunoassays or the HTLV-III immunofluorescence assay. Fifth generation tests developed in 2015, eliminated the need for confirmatory testing as they provided results for the P24 antigen and the HIV antibody and reported separate results for HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies (Alexander 2016). Rapid HIV test kits became available in 2002 with 99.6% accuracy and results available within 20 minutes, it is now the predominant test of choice for an initial diagnosis in most settings.
	These diagnostic tests enabled surveillance systems to be established to monitor the evolving HIV epidemic. By the end of 1985, every region in the world reported at least one case of AIDS. HIV surveillance (Detels et al. 2012) has remained essential and critical to quantify the magnitude of the epidemic; monitor trends in new infections, identify risk factors associated with infection, target interventions; and importantly, compare clinical manifestations of each case of AIDS that lacked aetiological explanations. In the USA, reporting by name of each newly diagnosed case of AIDS became a state health-department requirement shortly after the initial Centre for Disease Control (CDC) case reports of AIDS in 1981. While AIDS reporting was widely accepted and implemented with ease, HIV case reporting sparked community protest due to the use of name-based reporting of HIV infection (Goston et al. 1997). Gay rights organizations and civil libertarians expressed concern of invasion of privacy and the possibility of information reaching entities that would institute prejudice on those infected concerning employment, insurance, and housing (Gostin et al. 1997). Health officials justified the use of name-based reporting on the basis that it would assist health departments to: monitor those infected and ensure they remain linked to care, enable contact between health departments and those infected to enable counselling on prevention of further transmission of HIV and to monitor the prevalence and incidence of HIV. However, continued protest against the use of names for reporting on HIV incidence resulted in the implementation of confidential case-report systems that used code-identifiers instead of names for reports early in 2003 (Institute of Medicine (US) Committee on the Ryan White CARE Act 1994). These systems laid the basis for unlinked, anonymous HIV surveillance globally.
	Each year, UNAIDS releases a report on the global status of the HIV epidemic based on data gathered from member states. Today HIV is found in every part of the world. About 77.3 million people have become infected with HIV and 35.4 million people have died from AIDS-related illnesses since the start of the epidemic. In 2017, there were about 37 million people living with HIV; 960,000 AIDS-related deaths occurred and 1.8 million new HIV infections. Sub-Saharan Africa continues to bear a disproportionate (65%) burden of infection. About three-quarters of all HIV infections are in 15 countries with the majority in sub-Saharan Africa (Fig. 8.13.2).
	Fig. 8.13.2 Overview of burden of HIV globally.
	These global data mask the diversity of epidemics within and between countries. Southern and Eastern Africa for example account for 52% of all new HIV infections that occur globally. Globally about a third of all new infections are taking place in young people between 15 and 24 years of age. In sub-Saharan Africa, adolescent girls and young women account for about 40% of all new HIV infections. Globally, key and priority populations such as men who have sex with men (MSM); transgendered persons, IDUs, and sex workers bear a disproportionately high burden of HIV infection and experience substantial challenges in access to services particularly in settings where they are marginalized or worse if criminalized.





Viral structure


	HIV is a retrovirus, so named because it encodes the enzyme reverse transcriptase. This unique enzyme allows a DNA copy to be made from viral RNA. Reverse transcription is a highly error prone process and is the major source of genetic variability that typifies HIV.
	Viral particles are spherical with a diameter of approximately 100 nm and as such can only be viewed under an electron microscope (Fig. 8.13.3a). The outer lipid membrane is derived from the human host and contains the two major envelope glycoproteins, gp120, and gp41 (‘gp’ stands for glycoprotein and the number is the molecular weight in kilodaltons) (Fig. 8.13.3b). These proteins are linked together and exist as trimers on the viral surface facilitating binding and entry to the host cell. The envelope protein is referred to as ‘Env’. Other major structural proteins are the group-associated antigens or Gag proteins. The matrix protein (p17), which lies just beneath the envelope, provides structure to the particle, while the capsid protein (p24) encloses the viral RNA. The capsid protein is clearly visible under the electron microscope as a dark conical structure in the centre of the particle (Fig. 8.13.3a). HIV encodes three unique enzymes that are major targets for antiretroviral therapies. These are reverse transcriptase (RT), integrase, and protease, collectively called polymerases or ‘Pol’ for short. All three enzymes are carried inside the viral particle where they remain active. In addition to the major structural proteins, HIV also produces a number of regulatory and accessory proteins that are only produced once the virus infects cells and are not present inside viral particles. These include Tat and Rev, which enhance levels of gene expression and Vif, Vpr, Vpu, and Nef, which function to increase viral production and infectivity.
	Fig. 8.13.3 (a) Electron micrograph image showing mature HIV particles; (b) schematic representation of HIV-1 particle.





Treating AIDS


	Prior to 1986, the clinical management of AIDS included prophylactic treatment against AIDS-related illnesses and opportunistic infections with patients usually experiencing slow, painful lingering deaths usually within two years of presentation at health facilities. The discovery of HIV, characterization of the virus and the development of diagnostic assays to detect HIV led to a turning point for AIDS patients in 1986 through the discovery of azidothymidine (AZT), the first drug able to suppress HIV replication in culture that emanated from an unprecedented collaboration between the United States National Cancer Institute and the Burroughs Wellcome pharmaceutical company (Mitsuya et al. 1985; Broder 2010). This nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI), originally synthesized in 1964 for cancer treatment, was found to act as a DNA polymerase chain terminator with selectivity to the HIV RT (Furman et al. 1986; De Clercq 2005). It was approved for use in treatment of patients with HIV by the USA Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1987 and provided the initial proof-of-concept for HIV treatment (Broder 2010). Monotherapy with AZT was the primary treatment for HIV from 1987 to 1995. The discovery of AZT was followed by the development of various additional nucleoside analogues including: didanosine (ddI) (1991), zalcitabine (ddc) (1992), stavudine (d4T) (1994), and lamivudine (3TC) (1995) (Table 8.13.1). By 1995, the first protease inhibitor (PI), saquinavir (SQV), was approved and in 1996 the first non-nucleoside RT inhibitor (NNRTI), nevirapine (NVP) (De Clercq 2009) was approved.
	The FDA approval of additional nucleoside analogues, PIs, and NNRTIs following AZT approval, changed the face of HIV treatment, which transitioned from monotherapy (1987–1995) to dual therapy (1992–1996) to the game-changing triple therapy/highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), now referred to as combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) (1996-present) (Arts and Hazuda 2012). cART demonstrated significant reductions in plasma viral load in patients treated for at least six months and became the standard of care since 1996 (Carpenter et al. 1997).
