	To combat HIV drug resistance, the development of new drugs continues to progress with the first fusion inhibitor/gp41 inhibitor (enfuviritide (T-20)) developed in 2003, the first CCR5 inhibitor/entry inhibitor (maraviroc (MVC)) developed in 2007 and the first integrase inhibitor (raltegravir (RAL)) developed in 2007. These drugs provide alternate treatment options for patients with complications (i.e. toxicity or incompatibility with other medications) or drug resistance (Arts and Hazuda 2012).
	Following the initiation of cART as the standard of care for HIV patients globally, the development of fixed-dose combination (FDC) drugs containing two or three-drug combinations emerged as methods to improve adherence and thus reduce treatment failure and the development of drug resistance. Combivir™, a single pill containing a combination of AZT and 3TC was the first FDC pill developed in 1997. This was followed by the development of additional two-drug combination pills; Kaletra (lopinavir (LPV) and ritonavir (RTV)) in 2002, Epzicom/Kivexa (abacavir (ABC) and 3TC) in 2004 and Truvada (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and emtricitabine (FTC)) in 2004. The first three-drug combination pill, Trizivir, was developed in 2000 and contained a combination of ABC, 3TC, and AZT while Atripla, a combination of TDF, FTC and efavirenz (EFV) was developed in 2006 (Table 8.13.1). Atripla was the first complete FDC regimen for treatment naïve patients and has been the most commonly used FDC treatment (De Clercq 2009; Este and Cihlar 2010).
	The face of AIDS in the United States (US) between 1996 and 1997 changed subsequent to the introduction of cART from an inevitably fatal condition to one that is chronic and manageable, however, AIDS-related deaths in resource-constrained settings only started to decline in 2007 (UNAIDS 2013). In sub-Saharan Africa, home to about 70% of the global burden of HIV disease, access to cART was limited due to the high prices of HIV drugs enforced through trade law agreements preventing generic manufacture of patented drugs. In South Africa, for example, the mean income in 1986 was $2,600 per annum while the cost of ARVs at the time was $1,000 per month. Countries like Thailand and India that were excluded from such trade law agreements imposed by the World Trade Organization (WTO) were able to develop and market generic ARVs at a fraction of the price of the patented ARVs enabling their citizens access to affordable cART and realize its life-saving benefits. In contrast to the estimated $10,000 per annum per person cost of patented drugs, the average cost of generic ARVs were $365 per annum per person (approximately $1 per day) (Fisher and Rigamont 2005). Africa still could not gain access to generic ARVs, due to the rights to exclusivity, resulting in millions of people dying from AIDS with substantial reductions in life expectancy and hundreds of thousands of orphans. By the year 2000, a combination of global solidarity, activism, and the establishment of the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria and the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) facilitated access to life-saving ARVs for millions of Africans.
	Through the discovery of ARVs and increased global access to ARVs, AIDS has evolved globally from an inevitably fatal condition to one that is chronic and manageable. In 2017, approximately 22 million HIV-infected people globally were on cART. An estimated 40% still need to have access to treatment. While mortality rates have been reduced substantially, we still continue to see approximately 1 million AIDS-related deaths each year. Continued stigma and discrimination; limited access to healthcare services and untreated tuberculosis remain critical barriers to realizing the survival benefits of cART for many and ongoing efforts to increase access to cART need to pay more careful attention to these factors.
	HIV-infected individuals on cART are living longer, and are experiencing new health challenges associated with ageing. Wing et al. (2016) reported that HIV-positive patients on cART experience more rapid development of dementia, chronic neurological complications, frailty, and geriatric syndromes than HIV-negative individuals (Wing 2016). Long-term ARV use has also been associated with hyperactivation of the immune system, premature immunological ageing, and chronic inflammation (Appay and Kelleher 2016). Various studies suggest that these immune and inflammatory changes drive more rapid ageing, this however remains controversial (Justice and Falutz 2014; Pathai et al. 2014).
	The gradual deterioration of immune function, increased occurrence of geriatric syndromes and frailty, increased rates of metabolic syndrome (i.e. chronic comorbidities) and continuous increase in inflammatory markers (referred to as inflammaging), all of which occur at younger ages in HIV positive vs. negative patients, supports the argument that HIV accelerates the ageing process (Franceschi et al. 2000). In contrast, some researchers suggest that adherence to cART translates to HIV-positive patients having suppressed viral loads and CD4 counts of >500cells/µl which supports life expectancy no different to that of HIV-negative individuals and thus HIV does not accelerate ageing (Althoff et al. 2015; Rasmussen et al. 2015). Further research is required to provide clarification.
	In addition to the possible association with accelerated ageing, the long-term use of ARVs has also been associated with an increased risk of non-AIDS defining illnesses (or AIDS comorbidities) at all ages (Smit et al. 2015). These comorbidities include diabetes (Kalra et al. 2011; Medapalli et al. 2012), obesity (Freitas et al. 2012) and cardiovascular disease and stroke (Shahbaz et al. 2015). Like with ageing, studies on the association between diabetes and HIV have also been controversial with early studies showing a clear link but later studies demonstrating variations in this link (Ford et al. 2010; Rasmussen et al. 2012; Jarrett et al. 2013; Monroe et al. 2015). While the association between abacavir use and cardiovascular disease also remains controversial (Martin-Iguacel et al. 2015) the Veteran Aging Cohort Study (Freiberg et al. 2013; Sico et al. 2015) and additional studies (Obel et al. 2007; Klein et al. 2015) reported a non-age-dependant increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke in HIV-positive individuals even among those with supressed viral loads. Recently, a link between diet and ARVs has also been elucidated whereby ARV use coupled with a high-fat diet was found to impair energy balance, glucose metabolism, inflammatory transcriptional pathways and cause metabolic dysfunction (Pepin et al. 2018).
	Collectively these data highlight that notwithstanding the benefits of cART in the treatment of AIDS; given its requirement for lifelong use and long-term effects, the need for a cure remains paramount.





Preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV


	The prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) has been a significant milestone in the HIV epidemic and represents one of the greatest successes in the field of human therapeutics. Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) was first described in 1982 and was attributed to infection in utero, intrapartum or postpartum through breastfeeding (CDC 1982a; CDC 1983; Greene 2007). The first PMTCT recommendations were issued by the US public health services late in 1985 and suggested counselling for HIV-positive pregnant women on how to live with HIV and take care of a child with HIV. These guidelines also advised against breastfeeding to prevent postnatal transmission of HIV due to early reports suggesting breastmilk as a route of transmission (CDC 1985; Ziegler et al. 1985). By 1987, the World Health Organization (WHO) confirmed breastfeeding as a route of HIV transmission (WHO 1987) and perinatal transmission of HIV was classified as the main cause of HIV in children. Prevention efforts focused on trying to prevent HIV infection in women of reproductive age through education and advising HIV-positive women against breastfeeding. This, however, did not address HIV acquisition in utero or intrapartum for children born to HIV-positive mothers or lack of access to clean water supplies in some regions of the world and, not surprisingly, the incidence of HIV in children continued to increase.
	By April 1991, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in collaboration with the National Institute of Health and Medical Research and the National Agency of Research on AIDS in France sponsored the paediatrics AIDS Clinical Trials Group (ACTG) Protocol 076 (ACTG 076), a randomized double-blinded clinical trial investigating the efficacy of AZT (also referred to as zidovudine) in PMTCT, based in the USA and France (CDC 1985). Oral AZT was administered from week 14–34 of gestation throughout the pregnancy, intravenous AZT was administered during labour and oral AZT was administered to the baby for six weeks following delivery (CDC 1994). Interim results released in December 1993 demonstrated a 67.5% reduction in risk of perinatal HIV transmission among the selected HIV pregnant women and their infants without significant toxicity (CDC 1994; Connor et al. 1994; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases 1994). These results led to the termination of the placebo arm enrolment and existing placebo patients were offered AZT. By 1994, the use of AZT for HIV PMTCT was approved with an understanding that the long-term effects of AZT were still unknown and the research on which this recommendation was based was incomplete and required completion with time (CDC 1993). It soon became a standard of care in industrialized countries however, the low-income regions struggled to implement this regimen due to poor infrastructure, drug costs, and local policies among other issues.
	Four additional AZT/ZDV clinical trials investigating AZT/ZDV against placebo were conducted; one in Thailand (Shaffer et al. 1999), two in Africa (Wiktor et al. 1999) and one in Cote d’Ivoire/Burkina Faso (i.e. the ANRS 049 DITRAME trial) (Dabis et al. 1999; Msellati et al. 1999). Variations in trial protocols made direct comparison of trials difficult. However, one African study (based in Cote d’Ivoire) and the Thai study had identical protocols and showed efficacies of 37% and 50% respectively. Irrespective of variations in protocols, all AZT/ZDV studies demonstrated a reduction in MTCT with AZT/ZDV. The PHPT-1 trial, a PMTCT trial in which mothers did not breastfeed, investigated the impact on varied durations of AZT/ZDV therapy to the mother and infant and found that longer antenatal treatment with AZT/ZDV was more effective than the shorter treatment, however, longer postnatal treatment provided no added benefit to the infant (Lallemant et al. 2000).
	The HIVNET 012 perinatal HIV prevention trial, which began in 1999 in Uganda, aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of neonatal and intrapartum single-dose NVP and AZT/ZDV (Guay et al. 1999). Additionally, the trial also aimed to compare the efficacy of single-dose NVP (sdNVP) to short-course AZT/ZDV treatment. The trial reported lower rates of vertical transmission with NVP than AZT without added side-effects or changes in mortality (Guay et al. 1999; Jackson et al. 2003). Aspects of the trial including record-keeping, methodologies and data analysis presented some controversy resulting in the NIH requesting the US Institute of Medicine (IOM) to conduct an independent review of the HIVNET 012 trial which was completed by 2004 and confirmed that the results which were reported were accurate (Delvaux 2004).
	By this time, a short course of AZT or a single-dose of NVP administered to mother and infant demonstrated success in reducing vertical transmission of HIV by 50% and presented cost-effective methods for PMTCT in resource-constrained settings, with few side-effects (Guay et al. 1999; Shaffer et al. 1999). Although utilized, at the time, additional clinical trials to elucidate efficacious methods for PMTCT were under investigation, particularly to address drug resistance in HIV, such as that associated with NVP monotherapy (Wainberg and Friedland 1998).
	The ANRS 075 trial (no breastfeeding) (Mandelbrot et al. 2001) and the PETRA trial (included breastfeeding) conducted in South Africa, Tanzania, and Uganda (Petra Study Team 2002) assessed the efficacy of combination therapy (AZT/ZDV and 3TC) on PMTCT. While results showed efficacy in PMTCT, both trials demonstrated the development of drug resistance, specifically to 3TC, with the ANRS 075 trials having higher levels of drug resistance due to longer treatment duration with 3TC. Interestingly, the South African SAINT trial, which compared the efficacy of AZT/ZDV+3TC (administered intrapartum and for one week following birth) to sdNVP (one dose given intrapartum and one dose given during labour to the mother and within 72 hours of birth to the infant) on PMTCT, found no significant difference in outcomes (Moodley et al. 2003).
	The PHPT-2 Thai trial (Lallement et al. 2004), ANRS1201 DITRAME PLUS study in Cote d’Ivoire (Dabis et al. 2005) and the Malawi based open-label randomized trial (Taha et al. 2004) all investigated the effects of using NVP in addition to AZT/ZDV regimens for PMTC and found no added benefit.
	While making comparisons between trials is difficult, the trend showed that a longer course of treatment was associated with improved outcomes and that sdNVP was the most efficacious and cost-effective regimen for prevention of HIV in the infant. Further, the addition of sdNVP to a AZT/ZDV inclusive regimen only showed added benefits in the case where infants were breastfed.
	Until 2009, the most commonly used regimen in developing countries was short-course AZT/ZDV with sdNVP given to mother and newborn during labour and 72 hours after birth respectively, with mothers from high-income settings advised to refrain from breastfeeding. In 2009, the WHO released guidelines advising the administration of cART to all pregnant women with a CD4 count <350 cells/ml (from 14 weeks of gestation) and the daily administration of NVP to infants from birth to 6 weeks if they are to be breastfed, or a course of daily AZT or NVP would be used for infants that were not breastfed. The guidelines also advised 12 months of daily NVP therapy for infants if they are to be breastfed for the duration, as is commonly the case in developing regions. These guidelines changed a few years later, advising the initiation of all pregnant women with CD4 <500 cells/ml (from 14 weeks of gestation onward) on cART. Currently the option B+ treatment strategy states that all pregnant women, irrespective of CD4 count, be placed on lifelong cART as soon as possible to reduce their viral load and prevent MTCT and all breastfeeding women should also receive lifelong cART (Chappell and Cohn 2014).
	The use of antiretroviral drugs in PMTCT has led to substantial reductions in MTCT of HIV, however; the goal to eliminate MTCT (EMTCT) is still paramount. The Global Plan launched by the WHO in 2011 targets a reduction in MTCT by 90% (WHO 2011) with the WHO developing guidelines in 2014 on integrated approaches for EMTCT and methods for validation of EMTCT (WHO 2014). The EMTCT of HIV is defined by the WHO as less than 50 paediatric infections per 100,000 live births and a transmission rate of either <5% for breastfed babies or <2% for non-breastfed babies. Additionally, 95% of pregnant women must be receiving antenatal care, HIV testing, and subsequent treatment if HIV positive. Cuba was the first country to receive validation for the EMTCT of HIV in 2015 Caffe et al. 2016), followed by Belarus, Thailand, and Armenia in 2016 (WHO 2016). Showing positive results in PMTCT, were Botswana, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, and Uganda (six priority countries identified by the WHO), which all achieved the Global Plan target of reducing PMTCT by 90% in 2015 (UNAIDS 2016a). An additional 14 priority countries still require achievement of the Global Plan and/or EMTCT goals. Interestingly, all these countries, except Nigeria, rolled out option B+ for PMTCT in 2015 and consequently experienced a decline in AIDS-related deaths among females of reproductive age between 2009–2015 (UNAIDS 2016a).
	In addition to a decline in PMTCT by 90% in 2015, the Global Plan also set a target for countries to achieve a reduction in MTCT rate to <5% among women that breast fed and <2% among non-breastfeeding women. The 21 Global Plan priority countries collectively demonstrated a decrease in MTCT among breastfeeding women from 22.4% to 8.9% between 2009 and 2015 (UNAIDS 2014) showing decline in the direction of the target.
	There are still various challenges that need to be addressed in order to achieve EMTCT, particularly in low-and middle-income settings. The main issues hindering EMTCT in these regions include: delays in seeking pre-natal care, misperceptions over exclusive breastfeeding, HIV discrimination and stigma, lack of resources at a clinic and country level, long waiting times for HIV results for infants, side-effects of treatment, gender dynamics and cultural beliefs (UNAIDS 2014, 2016). These challenges highlight the need for interventions that go beyond the implementation of therapeutics and speaks to the need for a vaccination or cure. Furthermore, it highlights the fact that to achieve EMTCT a decline in incidence of HIV in adults is essential.





Preventing sexual transmission of HIV


	There is no risk of HIV infection among those who practice sexual abstinence or lifelong mutual monogamy. Serial monogamy, where there are multiple sequential individual short-lived monogamous partnerships, is associated with an increased risk of HIV, but not to the same extent as the substantial increase in risk of transmission emanating from multiple concurrent sexual partnerships. Reduction in the number of concurrent sexual partnerships and the use of condoms are key components of HIV prevention messages, widely promoted as part of ‘ABC’ campaigns promoting Abstinence, Be faithful, and Condom use. Since 2010, this prevention mantra has been expanded to include knowledge of HIV status; medical male circumcision, preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and test and treat.





Male and female condoms


	Condoms are a pivotal component of the fight against HIV/AIDS. They are inexpensive and relatively easy to use and provide protection against acquisition and transmission of HIV, a wide range of other sexually transmitted infections as well as pregnancy (i.e. an available multipurpose technology).
	When used correctly and consistently, the male and female condom is highly effective in preventing the sexual transmission of HIV. The strongest evidence for the role of condoms in preventing the transmission of HIV comes from serodiscordant couple studies, which uniformly show that increased condom use is associated with a substantially reduced risk of HIV transmission.
	Despite their increasing accessibility and proven effectiveness in prevention of HIV, a wide range of factors have been implicated as barriers to condom use; the most common being the widespread perception that condoms reduce sexual pleasure and that suggesting the use of condoms represents self-acknowledgement of HIV infection or a lack of trust in the partner. In the context of a marital relationship or stable partnership where pregnancy is desired, or where subordination of women limits their ability to negotiate safer sex practices, attempts to introduce or promote condom use have had limited success.
	Several studies have demonstrated that alcohol consumption is associated with inconsistent condom use; this poses a challenge to individuals who meet high-risk sexual partners in social settings where alcohol is available. Condom use is lower in partnerships where an effective form of contraception is being used. This points to the need for interventions that promote dual method use (the simultaneous use of condoms with another form of contraception) among high-risk women.





Sexually transmitted infections


	HIV transmission and acquisition during intercourse is enhanced in the presence of sexually transmitted infections, particularly ulcerative infections such as syphilis, chancroid and herpes simplex type 2 virus (HSV-2) infection (Wald and Link 2002; Freeman et al. 2006). Genital ulceration or inflammation caused by sexually transmitted infections increase the infectiousness of HIV-positive individuals and the susceptibility of HIV-negative individuals. Although only one randomized controlled trial has been able to demonstrate a significant reduction in HIV incidence rates following treatment of sexually transmitted infections (Grosskurth et al. 2000), the significant sexual and reproductive health challenge posed by the high burden of curable sexually transmitted infections needs to be addressed in any HIV prevention effort.





Medical male circumcision


	Medical male circumcision is a proven HIV prevention option for men, reducing the risk of female-to-male transmission of HIV by up to 60% (Siegfried et al. 2009). Medical male circumcision has become a priority component of HIV prevention globally. Introduced in 2007, the number of medical male circumcisions has increased from just 5,190 in 2008 to approximately 14.5 million in 2016. Evidence of a population level impact of circumcision in South Africa has recently become available from Orange Farm, where an increase in the male circumcision rate from 12% in 2007 to 53% in 2010 was associated with a 57% reduction in HIV incidence rates (Auvert et al. 2013).





Use of antiretrovirals as PrEP for HIV prevention


	In addition to treatment benefits, the prophylactic use of antiretroviral drugs has generated new hope in the HIV prevention landscape. Since July 2010, when ARVs were first shown by the CAPRISA 004 trial (Abdool Karim et al. 2010) to prevent sexual transmission of HIV, the HIV prevention landscape has been transformed, principally through oral tenofovir (TFV)-containing PrEP (Grant et al. 2010; Baeten et al. 2012; Thigpen et al. 2012; Van Damme et al. 2012a; Marrazzo et al. 2015; McCormack et al. 2015).
	Although daily oral TDF/FTC has been demonstrated to be consistently effective in MSM and transgender women globally (Grant et al. 2010; McCormack et al. 2015), the results of clinical trials in African women have been inconsistent, most likely due to varying levels of adherence (Thigpen et al. 2012; Baeten et al. 2012; Van Damme et al. 2012a; Marrazzo et al. 2015). In the FEM-PREP trial (Van Damme et al. 2012b) for example, only 24% of the women allocated to the daily oral TDF/FTC group had detectable drug levels. Similarly, in the VOICE trial, only 25%, 29%, and 30% of women allocated to the daily tenofovir gel, daily oral TDF/FTC and daily oral TDF groups respectively had detectable drug levels (Marrazzo et al. 2015). The challenge of adherence, however, is not simply a behavioural issue. Women are more likely than men to require near-perfect adherence to oral PrEP in order to be protected against HIV (Donnell et al. 2014), indicating that biological factors may also be important to consider. Genital inflammation has been shown to be an independent risk factor for HIV acquisition (Masson et al. 2015) and affects PrEP effectiveness in women (McKinnon et al. 2018). Deep sequencing techniques have shed light on the cause of genital inflammation showing that anaerobic vaginal bacteria, which is common in a dysbiotic vaginal microbiome, is associated with both genital inflammation and HIV risk (Williams and Passmore 2016). Using proteomics, it was recently shown that a dysbiotic vaginal microbiome, comprising <50% Lactobacillus spp., directly influenced topical PrEP efficacy (Klatt et al. 2017).
	Despite the adherence challenges, oral PrEP is an important HIV prevention option and is now being implemented as part of a comprehensive HIV prevention package in several countries. In industrialized countries, high drug costs remain a major barrier. An increase in sexually transmitted infections has been observed among PrEP users underscoring the importance of barrier protection in addition to PrEP use. Important research is currently underway with novel ARVs and delivery mechanisms that are less user dependent.





Treatment as prevention


	There is now compelling evidence from the landmark HPTN 052 trial that antiretroviral treatment of HIV-infected individuals can prevent sexual transmission of HIV (Quinn et al. 2000). Early antiretroviral treatment initiation in the HIV-positive partner showed that HIV transmission was reduced by 96% in HIV discordant couples from nine countries (HPTN052) (Cohen et al. 2016). Taken in conjunction with other observational data, which show significant reductions in HIV transmission among serodiscordant couples receiving ART, onward transmission of HIV can be significantly reduced if viral load is suppressed through ART. This added benefit of cART and viral suppression for preventing HIV infection in uninfected persons is also increasingly being used as a prevention option captured as ‘undetectable equals uninfectious’ or abbreviated to U=U.





Modern technologies


	In recognition of stigma and discrimination as a barrier to test and treat for HIV, modern communication strategies have been introduced to encourage HIV testing, treatment, and support ARV adherence. These strategies include the eHealth and mHealth technologies (Muessig et al. 2015). eHealth is designed to deploy educational messages, to people at risk, either electronically or via a message on a website which the person frequents. To date, eHealth has targeted the MSM population with gay organizations utilizing the tool to develop websites frequented by gay individuals to deliver both educational information and referrals to gay-friendly test and treat sites (Sullivan et al. 2013; Muessig et al. 2015).
	Similarly, mHealth, utilizes social media applications (apps) to deliver tailored HIV/AIDS messages to users via their mobile devices or tablets. This technology has for example been incorporated into the Blued app (Blued app 2009), a Chinese gay dating app, which allows the delivery of HIV/AIDS educational messages and messages encouraging testing for HIV via the use of ‘non-judgemental community mobilization campaigns’. In addition to this, mHealth also offers options to encourage ARV adherence, by reminding patients to take pills and asking patients to indicate if pills were taken. The technology also provides reminders to patients for clinic visits.
	Phylogenetics, the use of viral sequences from recently infected individuals in a common social network (Villandré et al. 2019) or geographically defined area (de Oliveira et al. 2017), is being used to understand transmission dynamics better and enhancing surveillance efforts and informing more targeted and efficient approaches for responding to HIV.
	Microbiome analysis (Williams and Passmore 2016) and proteomics (Klatt et al. 2017) is advancing our understanding of the role of biology in rendering some women more vulnerable to HIV compared to others or the role the microbiome plays in reducing the potency of prophylactic use of ARVs.





Injecting drug use


	IDU represents a major risk factor for HIV infection, often of the opiate heroin. It has been estimated that one in ten new HIV infections is caused by sharing of contaminated needles (AIDS Alliance 2016). Approximately one-third of all new HIV infections in regions outside of sub-Saharan Africa occur among people who inject drugs (PWID) (Harm Reduction International 2016a; UNODC 2016). Collectively, China, Russia, and the USA account for 50% of all PWID worldwide and contribute the most to HIV infections among this group (Harm Reduction International 2016a). Eastern Europe and central Asia also have high burdens of PWID, with half of all new HIV infections in these regions occurring among PWID (Harm Reduction International 2016b). Despite PWID categorized as a priority group for HIV prevention and treatment, they represent a group with the least access to treatment, prevention, and testing programmes. This is driven by the legislation, criminalization, and stigma associated with drug use, which detracts PWID from utilizing healthcare and harm reduction programmes (UNAIDS 2016b). The high susceptibility to HIV in this group, is further driven by the criminalization associated with distribution or possession of syringes or needles for non-medical purposes in some regions, which encourages sharing of used needles (Beletsky et al. 2012a, 2012b).
	Despite PWID representing a key population independently, there is also bridging between sex workers and drug addiction. Mongolia, Afghanistan, and central Asia have reported a 20 times increased risk of HIV infection in sex workers who inject drugs compared to those who do not inject drugs (Baral et al. 2013). This overlap demonstrates the importance of HIV treatment and prevention programmes for this key population as they place other populations at risk for HIV acquisition as well.
	To date, interventions aimed at reducing the risk of HIV acquisition in PWID include needle and syringe programmes (NSPs), opioid substitution therapy (OST) and the use of PrEP, often referred to as harm reduction initiatives, with evidence suggesting a combination of these approaches should be used in PWID (Degenhardt et al. 2010).
	NSPs aim not only to reduce the transmission of HIV, but also that of other blood borne infections such as hepatitis C and B. Some programmes provide 200 sterile needles per drug user per year, some sites also provide equipment to prepare drugs such as sterile water, filters and mixing containers. In addition to this, some programmes employ interventions to reduce harm associated with IDU such as; provision of advice on how to inject drugs safely, information on how to prevent and manage overdoses, information on how to handle and safely dispose of needles and syringes and provision of referrals for HIV testing and treatment and other health services (NICE 2014). Some NSPs are delivered via; fixed sites, mobile units, peer-NSP programmes, street outreach, backpacking services, home delivery, syringe vending machines and pharmacies (Obadia et al. 1999; Riley et al. 2000; WHO 2007; Bryant et al. 2010; Jain et al. 2014). Despite demonstrating success in reduction of HIV incidence among PWID (Jones et al. 2010; Palmateer et al. 2010; Abdul-Quader et al. 2013; Aspinall et al. 2014; MacArthur et al. 2014), the NSP has only been implemented in 90 countries out of the 158 in which it is required in (Harm Reduction International 2016b).
	While all 29 regions in eastern Europe and central Asia have NSPs, the success of these programmes are hindered by hostile political reactions and inadequate government support which has forced some NSPs to shut down (Harm Reduction International 2016b). Within Asia and the Pacific, only 17 countries have NSPs with the lack of NSPs in this region driven by harsh drug policies, inflexible working hours, reduction in funding and human resource issues (Harm Reduction International 2016b). The coverage of NSPs is high in western and central Europe and North America, particularly in Canada were an estimated 94.5% of PWID reported to have used a clean needle on last injection. Many countries within Europe though are seeing declines in the number of operational NSPs and have various PWID that are not reached due to people <18 years of age being denied access to services and immigrants not being reached due to underdeveloped services in areas where they live. Latin America, the Middle East, and North Africa all have limited NSPs, which are not adequate for reaching the required number of PWID in the region. Here, criminalization of drug use, restriction of operating hours, inadequate resources, and poorly trained staff contribute to the inadequacy of the existing programmes. Within sub-Saharan Africa, NSPs only exist in five out of 54 countries due to a lack of political will and government support and funding (Harm Reduction International 2016b).
	In addition to NSP, OST, a medication-assisted treatment (MAT), is also used to manage injecting drug use and reduce associated harm among PWID. OST provides illegal drug users with replacement medication (i.e. opioids), most often methadone maintenance therapy (MMT) and sometimes buprenorphine, administered orally in a supervised clinical environment. Various studies have demonstrated the success of OST in reducing the frequency of injection use, improving health and social functioning, improving ARV use, improving linkage to health services, and reducing crime and unsafe injecting practices, particularly in developed countries (Lawrinson et al. 2008; Weber et al. 2009; Gowing et al. 2011; Vorma et al. 2013). Studies also reported a 54% reduction in HIV transmission among PWID with the use of OST (Riley et al. 2000; Aspinall et al. 2014). Studies have also shown that the more time PWID spend on opioid therapy the more positive their health outcomes and less likely they are to engage in risky behaviour (Kumar et al. 2009). Despite the success of OST, it is estimated that only 8% of PWID have access to this intervention. A recent systematic review of coverage of interventions to prevent and manage HIV among PWID shows that there is a high coverage of both NSP and OST in Australia, the Netherlands, Austria, and Norway, moderate coverage in Canada, New Zealand and Vietnam and low coverage in China, Indonesia, Tanzania and several other developing regions while places like the Russian federation have very limited access to NSP and do not provide OST (LArney et al. 2017). This has been attributed to social and structural discrimination, stringent laws that criminalize drug use and the lack of political will to implement interventions like OST due to the belief that abstinence of drug use is the only successful method to treat drug addiction (Connock et al. 2007; Jurgens et al. 2010; Kermode et al. 2011).
	Oral PrEP, a daily course of ARVs, which protects HIV-negative individuals from HIV acquisition prior to exposure to the virus, is also a recommended method to reduce HIV transmission among PWID. Oral PrEP typically comprises of a combination of TDF and FTC combined as a single pill Truvada. The success of oral PrEP in reducing HIV transmission among PWID has been reported, however, the high cost of oral PrEP is a major factor hindering its large-scale implementation for PWID (Choopanya et al. 2013; Fu et al. 2018).
	Although there is strong evidence to show that NSPs and OST reduce injecting use behaviours and HIV transmission by 48% and 54% respectively, there are still barriers to their implementation in most regions (Aspinall et al. 2014; MacArthur et al. 2014) predominantly driven by the criminalization and stigma associated with drug use and the lack of political support and government funding. While oral PrEP offers an alternate route that is somewhat less controversial and possibly more accessible than OST and NSP, it comes with its own setback of high costing and does not lower the prevalence of HCV and drug-related infections unless additional drugs are included. It must be recognized that prevention of HIV among PWID has far-reaching consequences on sex workers and on the general population as these individuals overlap and thus reducing incidence of HIV in one group could likely translate to reducing its incidence in various other groups.





Conclusion


	Notwithstanding the enormous scientific progress and programmatic success in initiating almost 22 million infected persons on cART and reducing vertical transmission rates to <1%; in 2017, globally there were about 1 million AIDS-related deaths, 1.8 million new HIV infection and about 37 million people living with HIV. These data underscore the challenges that continue to face us. Much more needs to be done to prevent new HIV infections and reach and facilitate access to services by key and priority populations.
	While globally, we are on track with meeting the 2020 intermediate targets for treatment; prevention of new infections remains a major challenge with only about 15% reduction in new HIV infections we are way off the 2020 target of 500,000 new infections. Stigma and discrimination, real or perceived, remains a major barrier to knowledge of HIV status or seeking prevention or care services by key and priority populations.
	Several countries have reached their 2020 targets and are well on their way to reaching their 2030 ending AIDS goal. Most countries are at different stages of progress towards reaching this 2020 intermediate goal. There is increasing recognition that 90–90–90 treatment targets alone will not be sufficient to get us to the 2030 UN goal of ending AIDS.
	Despite huge progress on prevention science research, preventing HIV infection remains a major challenge with little impact on reductions in incidence rates in the past 6 years. With approximately 5,000 new HIV infections occurring each day globally, ending AIDS will remain an elusive goal. Combinations of stigma and discrimination, marginalization, moral and judgemental attitudes, and criminalization of populations on the basis of sexual orientation, occupation or age remain barriers to knowledge of HIV status and access to HIV testing and much needed treatment and prevention services. According to the 2018 UNAIDS report, it is estimated that as much as 9.4 million HIV-infected individuals globally and much higher proportions in some countries do not know they are infected and, therefore, get neither tested nor treated. It is recognized that transmission persists because of these untested infected individuals and inadequately treated individuals continuing to engage in high risk activities. Peer-led interventions that engage and partner with key and priority populations and communities is critical to reach those we are not reaching with typical healthcare delivery systems and approaches. Given the diversity of epidemics within and between countries in terms of magnitude, modes of transmission and populations at risk no single approach will address all the challenges and implementation science and programming needs to identify optimal combinations of interventions and strategies needed at a local level for prevention success.
	Investments in novel prevention approaches need to continue including for the development of a vaccine and a cure to realize the 2030 ending AIDS goal as well as eventually eliminating and eradicating HIV. At the heart of our response and success to date are courageous advocates and people whose rights have to be respected and who have to continue to be part of our responses for success.
