8.14


Tuberculosis


	Roxana Rustomjee





Introduction


	Tuberculosis (TB) is the greatest of human scourges, leaving no population in the world unaffected and wreaking havoc since time immemorial. It has exacted a death toll of over a billion human lives since the 1900s, more than any other disease, despite being a treatable and preventable condition (Paulson 2013). This global health catastrophe represents the biggest failure in public health delivery, together with one of the slowest efforts in discovery of new drugs and a paucity in the fundamental understanding of various disease processes. As a result, TB research has suffered from the lack of novel interventions, with a single new diagnostic introduced in 1998 and only two entirely new drugs since the 1950s. Reaching elimination targets, as set out by the World Health Organization (WHO) End TB Strategy therefore presents as a formidable challenge (WHO End TB Strategy http://www.who.int/tb/strategy/en/).
	Over the past two decades, addressing the impact of the HIV epidemic on TB disease burden; together with a redoubled effort at TB control; including the implementation of new diagnostics and treatments, has led to a reduction in the global burden of disease (Maher et al. 2007). Nevertheless, the road ahead is not for the faint-hearted. Solutions for ending TB are complex and rooted as much in closing the knowledge gap in understanding pathogenesis as they are in the rapid discovery and deployment of diagnostics drugs and vaccines. In addition, remedying and reorienting the health systems and addressing the economic, social, and behavioural drivers of disease are imperative. It is time to dispel dogma and to take bold and unchartered measures in effecting change, starting with appropriately allocating resources and rapidly translating research findings into policy and practice. TB is an ‘indicator disease’ of global poverty and inequality (Fox et al. 2017). Prior to the discovery of antibiotics, the ‘Papworth Experiment’ (1918 to 1943) found that improving the social context through improvements in employment, nutrition, and housing reduced TB incidence in children. In contrast the TB incidence rate rapidly, increased post World Wars when populations faced widespread poverty (Fox et al. 2017). The WHO’s ‘End TB Strategy’, which aims to end the global TB epidemic by 2035 while reducing TB deaths by 95% and incidence rates by 90% between 2015 and 2030, emphasizes the role of poverty alleviation, human rights and equity within an effective biomedical and public health response (WHO End TB Strategy http://www.who.int/tb/strategy/en/; Lonnroth et al. 2010; Lonnroth and Raviglione 2016; Fox et al. 2017). This chapter while focussing on biomedical intervention does not minimize the relative contribution of improved socioeconomic status and behavioural interventions in bringing TB to an end.





Burden of TB and global trends


	The WHO reported 6.3 million newly notified cases of TB worldwide in 2016 and estimated that TB incidence and mortality appear to be on the decline by about 3% and 2% per year, respectively (WHO 2017). TB incidence is falling at about 2% per year and 16% of TB cases die from the disease. These estimates fall short of the projected 4–5% per year and 10%, respectively, required to reach the 2020 milestones of the End TB Strategy. While the fastest decline in TB incidence has been in the WHO European Region (4.6% from 2015 to 2016); notably, the decline since 2010 has also exceeded 4% per year in several high-TB burden countries, including Ethiopia, Kenya, Lesotho, Namibia, the Russian Federation, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Twenty-two high-burden, low-to middle-income countries, collectively account for 80% of the global TB burden. The annual number of incident TB cases was under 10 per 100 000 population in most high-income countries; to 150–300 in most of the high-TB burden countries; and above 500 in a few countries including the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Lesotho, Mozambique, the Philippines, and South Africa. Alarmingly, almost 39% of cases remain unreported bringing the estimated incidence of TB in the world to approximately 10.4 million; of which 90% were adults and 10% were people living with HIV (PLHIV). In southern Africa, HIV stands out as the key driver of the TB epidemic as it creates a large pool of susceptible individuals who are either vulnerable to infection or progression from latent infection to active disease (WHO 2017).
	Drug-resistant (DR) TB is a continuing threat with 600,000 new cases of resistance to rifampicin (RRTB), the most effective first-line drug, of which 490,000 had multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and 6.2% of those cases identified as extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) (WHO 2017). Almost half (47%) of DR cases were in India, China, and the Russian Federation, the majority of whom (72%) remain untreated. A total of 129 689 individuals are initiated on treatment for drug-resistant TB, representing only 22%, with treatment success remaining at a 54% global low. Under-reporting and linkages to care remain a key challenge, particularly for countries in Asia and Africa (WHO 2017).





TB infection


	A further 1.7 billion people (close to a quarter of the world’s population) are estimated to be infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, representing a huge reservoir of potential TB disease (Houben and Dodd 2016). ORCID http://orcid.org/0000-0001-5825-9347 This substantial number of infected cases highlights ongoing transmission of TB in households and communities and underscores an urgent need for transmission blocking strategies. Progression to active TB occurs in 5–15% of individuals (http://www.who.int/mediacentre/factsheets/fs104/en/). The precise mechanism of disease progression and the complex host-pathogen interactions that are associated with this remain unknown. Traditionally, we have distinguished ‘latent infection’ from ‘active TB’ and responded distinctly to these two compartmentalized states both in individual treatment and public health responses. We prefer to describe the disease process as a spectrum of five different states ranging from immunity to TB disease to lack of immune control and active disease (Barry et al. 2009). Following exposure to M. tuberculosis, infection may either be eliminated by the innate immune response (without the need for T-cell priming) or eliminated following development of an acquired immune response. Among those who are unable to prevent or eliminate infection following exposure, the majority establish and maintain immune control. Such individuals typically have evidence of T-cell priming and maintain low bacillary numbers that are difficult to detect or quantify using current diagnosis. A subsequent shift in the host-pathogen balance may permit active mycobacterial replication, leading to subclinical active infection (or incipient TB). The relationship between ‘latent’ and active infection is likely to be a dynamic one over time with bidirectional shifts between the two. Loss of immune control and escalating mycobacterial load, may subsequently lead to the development of symptoms and overt clinical disease as we outline in Figure 8.14.1. Thus, what has been referred to as latent TB infection may represent a dynamic balance between the organisms in a range of metabolic states and variations in immune control. Understanding ‘latent TB infection’ as a spectrum of immune responses, mycobacterial metabolic activity, and organism load redefines approaches to screening, diagnosis, and prevention of TB. An appreciation of these complexities directs the goals for the development of new vaccines and biomarker discovery and emphasizes the effect of HIV on TB reactivation. Also important is the pivotal role of antiretrovirals in regaining immune control of active infection in HIV-infected people. HIV infection is the most potent risk factor for the development of active TB disease. Recurrent TB, due to exogenous re-exposure to M. tuberculosis in high-TB prevalence settings is also very likely to play a key role, further increasing bacillary numbers and enhancing the likelihood of progression to disease. Here we consider implications of latent infection for disease control strategies because any strategy aimed at TB elimination needs to address this reservoir of potential infection and disease. Central to this is increasing the fundamental understanding of host factors, including host genetics as well as where bacteria are located during the early stages of TB infection, and whether different locations and environments affect bacterial behaviour and treatment response. Another important question that arises is how similar is the bacterial metabolism along the spectrum between infection and disease? If there are differences, how do we define vulnerable drug targets for latent TB infection? Answering these questions is limited by the inability to meaningfully sample bacteria from latently infected individuals. These knowledge gaps should be addressed simultaneously, as interventions to prevent TB progression evolve.
	Fig. 8.14.1 Unmet needs and key developments for TB eradication. Shown are the unmet needs and key developments for specific stages of disease. TB transmission is a complex process and blocking transmission is critical to eliminating TB. After infection, a spectrum of infected states is expected to prevail. These vary in bacterial load and immune responses with increasing bacterial loads reflecting a progression to active disease. Early identification of those individuals that will progress to active disease, using biomarkers, will allow for targeting preventive treatment to the most vulnerable populations. Diagnosis of active TB and rapid engagement into care requires novel diagnostics and addressing gaps in the healthcare system. New TB drugs that shorten duration of therapy and achieve non-relapsing cure are urgently needed.





Interventions to prevent TB progression


	Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) has been used successfully since the 1950s as part of a comprehensive control strategy to halt transmission at the population level and reduces the risk of active TB by 60%, at the individual level. The Thibela TB trial (2006–2011), where South African mining workforces were randomized to mass IPT or standard of care (mine health services provided comprehensive free medical care. This included tuberculosis diagnostic and treatment services, HIV testing, and antiretroviral therapy), was aimed at interrupting TB transmission by mass screening linked to treatment of either active disease or latent infection (Churchyard et al. 2014). However, the intervention did not reduce TB incidence or prevalence, most likely due to multiple factors including uptake and adherence. Several studies evaluating prevention of drug-susceptible TB infection are underway and use novel drugs or drug combinations (Tiberi et al. 2018). These innovative therapeutic approaches propose to either decrease treatment duration or improve on drug delivery mechanisms. A recent trial (A5279 study; NCT01404312) demonstrated that a 1-month course of weekly isoniazid/rifapentine (INH/RPT), was found to be safe and effective when compared with the usual 9-month course of isoniazid alone in people with HIV infection (Swindells et al. 2018). These results offer HIV-positive individuals who are at risk of developing active TB an additional, shorter-duration prevention option that is safe, effective, and more convenient. Results from other trials simplifying preventive therapy are expected in 2018 including a three-arm comparison between 3-month HP (H-isoniazid, P-pyrazinamide), 9-month H and intermittent 3HP (the WHIP3TB study; NCT02980016) among PLHIV; as well as, a 4 months of rifampicin (4R) vs. 9 months of isoniazid (9H) in adults and children with TB infection (NCT00931736). Further, supervised weekly 3HP is being compared to isoniazid among pregnant and post-partum women (P2001; NCT02651259). The results of these studies are long awaited and if successful, will greatly simplify preventive therapeutic options.
	Nevertheless, the main limitation of widespread TB prophylaxis remains the scalability to entire populations where more than 80% of the adult population is likely to be infected with only a small proportion (<10%) are at risk for progression to active disease. Recent advances in the discovery of correlates of risk, identify inflammatory signals in blood cells from healthy persons that reveal the process of progression from infection to active TB enabling a targeted ‘test and treat’ approach to TB infection. The CORTIS (Correlate of Risk Targeted Intervention Study) is evaluating the effectiveness of 3HP for high-risk individuals, with the treatment decision based upon a 16-gene, blood-based transcriptional (RNA) biomarker (NCT02735590) (Zak et al. 2016). This approach enables the prospective evaluation of treatment to be targeted to those at elevated risk of developing active TB. If successful, it may result in a point-of-care tool that would have potential to majorly impact the global burden of TB.
	With the high prevalence of strains resistant to first-line anti-TB drugs, where isoniazid and rifampin derivatives are of limited utility, different approaches will be needed especially in the absence of international prophylaxis guidelines. If an index case has MDR or XDR-TB, testing of household contacts has revealed significant numbers already infected with latent or active TB infection. Not all household contacts are infected by the same strain as the index case however, significant numbers (10–80% depending on the study) may have been infected by a discordant (sometimes sensitive) strain in the community (Moore 2016). Several drugs or combinations of drugs including fluoroquinolones, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and ethionamide have been assessed in small trials but none can, at present, be recommended. Most are toxic and even 6 months of treatment cannot be completed by the majority of patients (Moore 2016). For drug-resistant infection, three randomized controlled trials are underway. Six months of daily levofloxacin is being compared to placebo for individuals with presumptive multidrug-resistant TB in the VQUIN MDR Trial (ACTRN12616000215426), in adults, and the TB CHAMP study (ISRCTN92634082), in children under 5 years). In the PHOENIX MDR-TB Trial (https://www.actgnetwork.org/newsletter/oct2015/phoenix), six months of delamanid plus isoniazid will be compared with 6 months of isoniazid alone for patients with MDR-or extensively drug-resistant TB. Results are expected around 2021. In planning interventions to interrupt transmission through preventive therapy, the epidemiological and health system context must be considered. Population-level impact may not follow unless other interventions (including active case finding linked to effective treatment) are deployed.
	The assessment of complete sterilization of TB infection is a far greater challenge because unlike in active disease, where the bacterial burden reduces measurably from high detectable levels to little or no bacteria, the levels of bacteria and antigen present in latent TB infection are very low and discerning clearance is more challenging. Identifying a signature of persistence versus bacterial clearance could aid in identifying those individuals at highest risk for progressing to TB and direct them for TB infection treatment.





Interventions to halt the transmission of TB


	Ultimately, it is not simply enough to decrease TB incidence by preventing cases through prophylaxis targeted at close contacts, it is also necessary to understand the strategy and type of interventions most likely to avert the largest proportion of transmission events at the population level. There should be a specific focus on those events that result in secondary cases of infectious TB. As an example, in settings where transmission originates largely from specific and identifiable populations (e.g. young adult men) (Dodd et al. 2016), it may be feasible to target case-finding efforts in those groups. Where reactivation is common in high-risk groups, e.g. HIV-positive individuals (Pretorius et al. 2014), people with risk factors such as diabetes or malnutrition (Odone et al. 2014), elderly populations (Prince et al. 2015), it may be critical to target preventive therapy to those populations. In congregate settings (e.g. prisons or healthcare institutions), infection control and modification of the environment can have major impact in reducing transmission. The key issues include addressing drivers of transmission, measuring transmission, and identifying novel transmission blocking strategies (Shah et al. 2017). The variable success of preventive therapy interventions, alongside a growing number of studies demonstrating that close contacts only account for a minority of transmission events (Verver et al. 2004; Mathema et al. 2006; Chamie et al. 2015; Glynn et al. 2015; Shah et al. 2017) indicate that our current tools and approach for interrupting transmission are inadequate. Additional gaps in our understanding of the biology and local determinants of transmission underscore the need for more effort in this area.





Drivers of TB transmission


	Recent evidence from endemic countries, with varying levels of HIV and drug-resistant TB, implicate ongoing transmission as the driving force maintaining high levels of TB incidence (Li et al. 2007; Becerra et al. 2011; Shah et al. 2017). Drivers of transmission can be seen as a cascade in three stages: (1) sharing of air between infectious and susceptible individuals; (2) infectiousness of an index case; and (3) susceptibility to disease of other exposed individuals (Dowdy et al. 2014). These stages are heterogeneous at regional and national levels and the relative role of each stage is heavily dictated by local attributes including access to healthcare, population age structure, population density and migration (Wood et al. 2010; Liu et al. 2012). Variations in individual host susceptibility, in line with the local prevalence of HIV, diabetes mellitus, and silicosis, can also dramatically alter the transmission cascade (Murray et al. 1996; Hanifa et al. 2009). The strength of local TB control programmes in terms of case finding and treatment strategies is yet another factor that can affect local transmission dynamics. A larger proportion of undiagnosed or untreated patients will contribute to ongoing transmission in a community. This heterogeneity of transmission poses a substantial challenge to TB control. To design efficacious and efficient TB control strategies, it will be necessary to delineate the relative contribution of the various drivers of TB in different settings. Ultimately, drivers of transmission, including, but not limited to infectiousness of index cases, susceptibility of contacts as well poverty, overcrowding, health seeking behaviour, and institutional drivers must be studied and understood at a local level.





Measuring levels of TB transmission


	The prolonged natural history of TB means that observed cases of disease reflect a combination of recent transmission and recurrent disease, the latter made up of reactivation and exogenous reinfection. In addition, most cases observed via passive case finding systems (self-referral of patients to healthcare providers), underestimate the number of undiagnosed, but diagnosable, infectious individuals in the community. Current methods to measure transmission include examining case notification rates and trends in tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA). However, real-time, definitive diagnosis of recent exposure to M. tuberculosis at the individual level is not possible with any of the currently available tests (e.g. TST, IGRA, chest X-ray, sputum analysis). A biomarker of recent exposure as described, but not limited to, the CORTIS trial, would enable precisely targeted preventive therapy and accelerate identification of TB ‘hotspots’—areas of high-TB incidence—for earlier and more effective implementation of infection control measures (Wood et al. 2014). Such hotspot detection and elimination represent an immediate measure to interrupt transmission and reduce the global burden of TB while new drugs, diagnostics, and vaccines are progressing through the product development pipeline. These hotspot communities could also serve as priority areas for piloting new transmission interventions, as they become available (Lee et al. 2015).
	More recently, molecular epidemiology utilizing whole-genome sequencing has greatly facilitated studies of patient-and population-level transmission (Verver et al. 2004; Mathema et al. 2006; Glynn et al. 2015) Several studies have aimed to estimate the proportion of transmission that occurs within households by comparing genotypes of cases occurring within households or community settings. These studies have found that in medium-and high-TB burden settings, the majority of TB transmission occurs outside of households or with known close contacts (Chamie et al. 2015; Guerra-Assuncao et al. 2015). As such, the yield of contact investigations as a TB control activity may be lower than traditionally anticipated in such settings. Congregate locations that facilitate air exchange between infectious cases with non-infected individuals, such as transport hubs, churches, school classrooms, and prisons have been implicated as ‘hotspots’ or institutional amplifiers of transmission and may offer opportunities for targeted interventions (Dowdy et al. 2012; Zelner et al. 2016). However, it is unknown whether other, less obvious sites of congregation, may also be driving ongoing transmission. An integrated approach that combines traditional epidemiology with methods drawn from spatial, demography, and whole-genome analysis will undoubtedly be required to identify such drivers (Davies et al. 2015; Vynnycky et al. 2015).
	Halting TB transmission need not be limited to biomedical interventions. Historical data from western Europe, where TB incidence declined 10% annually after the Second World War, demonstrates the impact of socioeconomic development on reducing TB transmission. A broader approach regarding how socioeconomic development may interrupt transmission is desperately need together with systematic testing of interventions for impact, including engaging other government sectors equipped with the power and knowledge needed to accelerate economic development for TB-affected communities.
	In addition to the devastating impact of TB on families and communities, ongoing nosocomial TB transmission in clinics and hospitals represents a life-threatening risk to the global healthcare workforce. TB has become an occupational lung disease for providers from high-burden countries, including frontline community health workers, nurses, medical students, and physicians (Naidoo and Jinabhai 2006; Barnagarwala 2014). TB as a personal risk associated with a professional choice is unacceptable in the twenty-first century and must be addressed by national and international professional associations, lest their workers succumb to TB.
	Ultimately, both established and new interventions will be required to end TB. Given the variable and possibly non-durable success of preventive therapy, particularly in settings where transmission and the force of infection is very high (Comstock et al. 1967; Hanson et al. 1967; Comstock et al. 1979; Ayles et al. 2013; Churchyard et al. 2014); it is conceivable that any new interventions, including a preventive vaccine, which may protect against a single exposure or a low inoculum; may be ineffective against repeated, high-dose exposures. TB control programmes should therefore reduce ongoing transmission using all available methods. Synergy in reducing TB transmission may be attainable by combining interventions that shrink the reservoir of latent TB infection (preventive therapy), shorten time to treatment (case finding and diagnosis), and prevent transmission in key settings.
	Ultimately, there is cause for optimism. There are effective interventions available to target each component of TB transmission (and the analytical tools to demonstrate their effectiveness). Furthermore, the lack of an animal reservoir facilitates focus on human populations, behaviours, and environments. The increasing commitment from researchers, funders, and policymakers to address transmission of TB is supported by a focus on developing innovative approaches to meet the end TB targets.





New approaches to TB diagnosis


	Rapid, early, and accurate diagnosis is critical to timeous anti-TB treatment initiation, monitoring, and ultimately TB control. However, 39% of the estimated 10.4 million estimated cases were either undiagnosed or unreported (WHO 2017). Diagnosis of extrapulmonary TB and TB in children, PLHIV, and pregnant women remains particularly problematic. Furthermore, only 41% of TB cases notified globally were tested for rifampicin resistance and just 22% of the estimated drug-resistant TB incidence were initiated on appropriate treatment (WHO 2017). Diagnostic tools should ideally: (1) identify more TB with highly accurate point-of-care tests and replace smear microscopy; (2) include a simple, low-cost point-of-care triage test to exclude TB; (3) enable universal, rapid DST that informs regimen selection (Denkinger 2017); (4) offer point-of-care (POC) alternatives to sputum-based technologies with capability to detect all forms of TB especially paediatric (Kik et al. 2014). Nevertheless, addressing all these critical gaps in current diagnostic tools, without identifying and treating individuals with TB infection who may later progress to active TB disease (Pai et al. 2016) will greatly hamper progress in reaching TB elimination targets. Therefore, we add a further stipulation (5) to identify and differentiate TB across the spectrum of TB infection.
	Sophisticated bioinformatic computational tools and systems biology approaches are being applied to the discovery and validation of biomarkers, resulting in substantial progress in the understanding of T-cell responses and T-cell function, protein, and gene expression studies. Alternative diagnostic strategies under investigation as potential screening and triaging tools include non-sputum-based detection with breath-based tests and automated digital radiography. Reviewed herein are current TB diagnostics for disease and infection their application and performance, newer technologies in the pipeline and identify weaknesses and areas of progress that need to be addressed if we are to enhance TB control programmes and transition efforts towards TB elimination.
	Microscopy, culture, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) are currently the three validated diagnostic methods for the detection of active TB while chest radiography is sometimes used for screening of active TB (Pai et al. 2016). Major drawbacks associated with smear and culture are well described and will not be discussed here except to note the substantially reduced capability to diagnose TB in a large proportion of people living with HIV has enormous public health implications further contributing to disease transmission, morbidity and mortality (Dorman 2010). Because culturing tubercle bacilli is a pre-requisite for detailed phenotypic DST and genotyping (Pai et al. 2016), the protracted time interval required to detect bacterial resistance, technical expertise needed, biosafety requirements and high cost per test are some of the limitations of this method of diagnosis (Dorman 2010).
	NAATs are molecular assays that detect M. tuberculosis through the amplification of particular regions of DNA (Denkinger and Pai 2017). NAATs are both highly sensitivity and specific, detecting about 100% of smear positive pulmonary TB while differentiating between M. tuberculosis and non-tuberculosis mycobacteria (Flores et al. 2005). Sensitivity is however considerably reduced in smear-negative patients, extrapulmonary specimens, and in HIV prevalence settings and as a result, NAAT tests can therefore not be utilized as a rule out test (Denkinger and Pai 2017). There are several NAAT tests on the market and others in development (see https://www.finddx.org/tb/).
	Of the NAATs, GeneXpert MTB/RIF (Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) allows for rapid and simultaneous detection of M. tuberculosis complex DNA and rifampin resistance in just 2 hours directly from clinical specimens and exhibits both high sensitivity and specificity and is the most widely used. GeneXpert MTB/RIF is considerably more sensitive at identifying M. tuberculosis, requiring 131 colony forming units per millilitre of sputum in contrast to 10 000 bacilli per millilitre of sputum required for smear microscopy (Steingart et al. 2014). In late 2010, the WHO endorsed the GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay for use in TB endemic settings (WHO 2014). Despite high sensitivity overall, GeneXpert sensitivity is only 60–80% in smear-negative TB. Sensitivity is also reduced in children (66%) and PLHIV (79%) and is variable in extrapulmonary specimens (Detjen et al. 2015; Pai et al. 2016). Despite its revolutionary approach, GeneXpert MTB/RIF was not designed to penetrate all levels of the healthcare system nor can it meet all the diagnostic demands for TB elimination (Pai et al. 2016). The cost of GeneXpert MTB/RIF coupled with the inability to detect latent TB and resistance to multiple drugs are just some of its notable shortcomings. Moreover, the inability to distinguish between live and dead bacilli, sensitivity to high temperatures and need for a continuous power supply are some of the important limitations of this diagnostic tool that hampers widespread roll-out (Pai et al. 2016).
	A new molecular test, GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra, exhibits improved sensitivity to GeneXpert MTB/RIF, requiring just 16 bacilli per millilitre of sputum, and similar sensitivity to liquid culture. In March 2017 the WHO recommended its use as a replacement for the current GeneXpert MTB/RIF cartridge (WHO 2017). The Ultra assay should significantly increase TB detection in smear-negative patients and provide more reliable rifampin resistance detection. In addition, GeneXpert Omni, a portable, and POC device is expected to become available in 2018 (Pai et al. 2016). Unlike the other GeneXpert platforms, the Omni is battery operated and can withstand significant temperature variations, enabling it to be used as point of care in clinics for the rapid diagnosis of drug-sensitive and drug-resistant TB, allowing patients to be promptly initiated on effective treatment. This has the potential to improve patient outcomes and, ultimately, reduce TB transmission. The rapid uptake of such new tools in the highest burden countries, where health systems are often under strain, is essential. Ongoing, multicountry evaluations of the accuracy and feasibility are underway (https://www.finddx.org/news/find-ultra-study/).
	Line probe assays (LPAs) like that of the GenoType MTBDR (Hain Lifescience, Germany) allow for rapid differentiation of mycobacteria and simultaneous detection of drug-resistant mutations from culture using polymerase chain reaction and reverse hybridization methods (Denkinger and Pai 2017). The MTBDRsl test allows for rapid detection of mutations associated with resistance to fluoroquinolone, aminoglycosides, and cycloserine, drugs used to treat MDR-TB. LPAs have demonstrated excellent sensitivity and specificity for rifampin resistance but variable results for isoniazid resistance (Ling et al. 2008; Bwanga et al. 2009). LPAs are more rapid than conventional phenotypic DST methods and offer a lower biosafety risk but require skilled laboratory personnel, good quality control and rely on culture methods thereby limiting its role in resource-poor settings (Pai et al. 2016; Denkinger and Pai 2017). The GenoType MTBDR is endorsed by WHO and with rapid scale-up in high-burden countries through the EXPAND-TB project (Denkinger and Pai 2017). Given the high proportion of drug-resistant TB attributable to ongoing transmission (Kendall et al. 2015) and the substantial delays often experienced in diagnosing and treating drug-resistant TB, the impact of improved case finding, and diagnosis should be even greater. Broader implementation of a rapid molecular test—even only for passive case detection—has been projected to avert substantial morbidity and mortality due to rifampin-resistant TB in settings like India (Salje et al. 2014).
	The massive reservoir of latently infected adults generates an enormous pool for future reactivation cases. In fact, it is estimated that even if prevention of all new TB infections was achieved, the incidence of TB, arising from the 1.7 billion individuals in the global reservoir, would be 16.6 per 100,000 person-years in 2035, making the 2050 target to eradicate TB unattainable. The TST, and interferon-γ release assays (IGRAs) developed in the early 1900s and 2005, respectively, are the two diagnostic tools currently in use for latent TB infection. Both tests evaluate the presence of M. tuberculosis-specific T-cell responses to recent sensitization and are therefore unable to distinguish between latent, active, or past TB, or the progression thereof, relapse after treatment or protection after vaccination (except for newer generation IGRAs) (Denkinger and Pai 2017). There is therefore a critical need for the early identification of TB cases with the use of novel non-sputum-based diagnostics. A blood-based triage test, as described in the CORTIS trial, that enables targeted investigation of individuals with active and subclinical TB disease, including asymptomatic individuals with the highest risk of progression from latent infection to active disease status, has the potential to reduce the time to treatment initiation as well as prevent incipient TB disease prior to the onset of symptoms. Recent studies performed in latent TB infection subjects showed that M. tuberculosis-specific CD4 T-cells have a characteristic chemokine expression signature with increased numbers of these cells in latently infected subjects compared to healthy participants suggesting a role for subsets of CD4 T-cells in containing TB (Arlehamn et al. 2014). These signatures may have important implications in the identification of individuals with the greatest need for preventive therapy and to determine if targeted short-course preventive therapy can prevent TB disease among individuals found to exhibit the RNA signature (Penn-Nicholson et al. 2016).
	While more rapid diagnosis should intuitively result in more rapid treatment initiation—and hence reduction in disease transmission—the current paradigm of passive case finding constrains the potential transmission impact of improved diagnostic tools (Dowdy et al. 2017). TB patients are generally symptomatic for weeks to months prior to presentation to healthcare providers (Dheda et al. 2016), and they may have detectable bacilli in their sputum for many additional months before developing symptoms (Dowdy et al. 2013). A randomized controlled trial, while shortening the time to diagnosis, did not demonstrate a significant treatment benefit of GeneXpert MTB/RIF over smear microscopy (Theron et al. 2014). By contrast, active case finding (ACF) can detect infectious cases much earlier and hence potentially interrupt disease transmission. A recent randomized trial (XACT I) evaluated the feasibility and impact of GeneXpert MTB/RIF for ACF in South Africa and Zimbabwe, using mobile vans with on-board GeneXpert capacity and staffed by three healthcare workers each (Calligaro et al. 2017). Relative to sputum smear microscopy, GeneXpert MTB/RIF was associated with a 53% increase in the number of patients initiating anti-TB therapy. This trial demonstrates that ACF using newer molecular tools is feasible and substantially increases the proportion of patients initiating treatment in high-burden settings. Importantly, as demonstrated in another cluster-randomized trial in South Africa (Churchyard et al. 2015), scale-up of GeneXpert MTB/RIF is unlikely to impact mortality—or transmission—unless also accompanied by better linkage to care. Multiple ongoing studies are evaluating diagnostic tests of higher sensitivity for example, GeneXpert Ultra and/or greater portability in the context of ACF (https://www.finddx.org/news/find-ultra-study/). Targeted ACF interventions are needed.
	In summary, early data suggest that newer molecular diagnostic tools—if combined with ACF—may help reduce TB transmission in high-burden settings. Additional needs include trials to evaluate the effectiveness of more sensitive and/or scalable diagnostic tests (especially in the context of ACF), studies of comparative cost-effectiveness and feasibility, new tools to identify patients with highest transmission risk, and conclusive studies demonstrating that earlier diagnosis and treatment initiation can reduce TB burden at the population level. Despite these promising developments, there remain several unanswered questions regarding interventions to halt TB transmission through diagnosis and case finding. These include cost-effectiveness, feasibility, and impact in different settings, optimal combination of screening tools, and characterization of TB transmission from immunological, clinical, and healthcare-seeking behaviour perspectives. Ultimately, new diagnostic tools capable of detecting TB at earlier stages will likely only have transformative impact on transmission when used in the context of broader screening and ACF (Dowdy et al. 2017).





TB diagnostics pipeline


	Resistance mutations are not fully characterized for all TB drugs, and they are particularly deficient for the second-line and newer drugs used to treat MDR and XDR-TB. Next-generation whole-genome sequencing (NGS) remains the most attractive tool for TB drug resistance testing, with the potential to generate antibiotic susceptibility profiles for all drugs in a single analysis (Dookie et al. 2018) and might eventually become the reference standard for drug resistance identification. Reduced costs and the establishment of high-throughput sequencing centres and easy-to-use analytical tools have greatly increased access to NGS, which is being implemented as a routine service in several countries. However, in most high-burden countries it remains only a means for research with the analysis undertaken overseas. Proof of principle for NGS directly from sputum has been shown, but for comprehensive analysis the need to first isolate and culture the organism to obtain sufficient bacterial DNA hinders its application to patient management. Recent studies have shown some success in this regard (Votintseva et al. 2015; Votintseva et al. 2017; Dookie et al. 2018).
	The TB diagnostic pipeline is at its most robust and focused on novel technologies equipped with a better understanding of the variable host immune response and non-sputum-based options (Walzl et al. 2018, https://www.finddx.org/news/find-launches-diagnostic-pipeline-tracker/). Novel approaches being investigated include testing breath for TB metabolites and the application of nanotechnology and microfluidics to increase detection capacity and reduce hands-on sample manipulation (Walzl et al. 2018). Promising results have been reported on the use of new, more sensitive technology to detect lipoarabinomannan and circulating antigen peptides. New platforms capable of assessing molecules of variable size and composition or that detect multiple proteins are under development to support the measurement of host-response biomarkers. Competitors for the GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay are undergoing assessment for regulatory approval and are closest to launch (FIND). These competitors are devices designed for low-technology microscopy centres or high-throughput instruments with extended drug resistance detection intended for the reference laboratory. Most tests are sputum-based but some aim to use blood or urine, which might detect extrapulmonary TB and TB in children. Ending the epidemic will demand both innovative technologies and an enabling environment. It is hoped that by 2020 the following measures will be implemented: (1) a triage test and highly sensitive detection at the first point of contact; (2) TB confirmation with rapid integrated DST for critical drugs to drive treatment regimen decisions at a dedicated unit, and; (3) comprehensive DST at a reference level compatible with health system strengthening (Denkinger 2017).





The need for new drugs against tuberculosis


	Currently treatment for TB is long and toxic, ranging from a 4-month standard regimen for patients who are sputum smear and culture negative with minimal pulmonary disease in the USA, to the WHO standard 6 month short-course treatment for drug-susceptible TB. Short-course chemotherapy for drug-susceptible TB comprises an initial 2-month intensive phase (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol daily), continued by isoniazid and rifampin for the last 4 months. In the case of drug-resistant TB, 18–24 months treatment with second-line, less potent and more toxic drugs is required, involving an intensive phase of 6–9 months with aminoglycosides (amikacin/kanamycin) and cycloserine, terizidone, ethionamide, protionamide, capreomycin, aminosalicylic acid, and fluoroquinolones. Treatment success is approximately 85% for drug-sensitive TB, 50% for MDR-TB, and 30% with XDR-TB. To improve on these outcomes, an ideal new regimen should be safe, rapidly bactericidal and possess potent sterilizing activity against subpopulations of persisting bacteria that are drug tolerant in the face of continued chemotherapy. The global vision is to introduce an ultra-short, simple, and affordable TB regimen that works in virtually all people with TB, including children. This requires a multidrug regimen comprised entirely of new drugs. Such a regimen would unify the treatment of all current forms of TB under one cure. There is therefore a shift in focus from single drug development to regimen building. Drug combinations are needed to eradicate various bacterial subpopulations and prevent the development of resistance.
	To develop new drug candidates in order to have a sufficient number and combination of drugs for a new regimen, a multipronged approach has been adopted, which entails the discovery of new antitubercular agents, together with repurposing of previously approved antimicrobials and the development of host-directed therapies. An integrated approach with high-throughput screening of chemical libraries has been used to identify new lead compounds, followed by deconvolution of the drug target, assessing the effects on metabolism and identifying possible mechanisms of resistance (Evans and Mizrahi 2018). This approach, in combination with others, has allowed for repopulation of the TB drug development pipeline, with 14 chemical compounds having progressed along the clinical development pathway, including new chemical classes in preclinical (eight compounds) and clinical (nine compounds) phases (Tiberi et al. 2018). Novel mechanisms of action with activity against both replicating and non-replicating bacteria, reduced drug-drug interactions particularly with P450 enzymes; oral bioavailability with acceptable pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic safety and tolerability profiles are desirable attributes of new TB drug candidates. However, many more candidate drugs are needed to populate a pipeline robust enough to build entirely new regimens. An ideal drug combination should consist of at least three drugs that are active against MDR and XDR tuberculosis, and have potent, synergistic, and complementary activities against various subpopulations of M. tuberculosis. Such a combination should be equally effective against drug-susceptible and drug-resistant tuberculosis and produce a stable cure in a much shorter period than does the standard treatment. New antituberculosis drugs that do not interact with protease inhibitor-based treatments are also needed for the effective treatment of the HIV co-infected population. For this to be successful innovative trials need identify suitable drug candidates, to be inclusive of children and supported by sufficiently resourced trial capacities and regulatory guidance.





Lead optimization and clinical evaluation


	Bedaquiline, the first novel TB drug developed in five decades, with a novel mode of action by binding to the FoF1 ATP synthase, which catalyses the production of ATP using the proton motive force generated by the mycobacterial electron transport chain (Andries et al. 2005). Bedaquiline is highly potent against drug-susceptible and drug-resistant strains of M tuberculosis and is approved for treatment of drug-resistant TB. For drug-sensitive TB, bedaquiline will be combined with rifampin, delamanid, and linezolid in five different combinations in the TRUNCATE-TB28 (NCT03474198), Phase 2c open-label trial (Diacon et al. 2009; Belard et al. 2015; Tiberi et al. 2018). Bedaquiline also features in Next-5001, STREAM, and end-TB trials. The success of bedaquiline also highlighted the mycobacterial electron transport chain as a rich source of possible new drug targets, as evidenced by the developed of other similar agents such as Q203 (Bald et al. 2017; Iqbal et al. 2018).
	Delaminid and pretomanid are nitroimidazoles that undergo conversion by a F420-dependent nitroreductase to form metabolites that inhibit the synthesis of mycolic acids in the mycobacterial cell wall (Xavier and Lakshmanan 2014). Both these agents are currently in Phase 3 trials for drug-resistant TB and to assess the potential for treatment shortening, for example, through combination with bedaquiline (Tiberi et al. 2018). SQ109, a 1,2-ethylene small molecule that is structurally related to ethambutol, inhibits the incorporation of mycolic acids into the M. tuberculosis cell wall (Protopopova et al. 2005; Tahlan et al. 2012; Boeree et al. 2017). Encouraging data from the early bactericidal activity assessment confirm safety, tolerability, and no adverse cardiac effects. In the presence of an optimized background regimen, SQ109 has demonstrated promise in the treatment of drug-resistant TB (Tiberi et al. 2018). Benzothiazinones represent another interesting class of compounds that target the mycobacterial cell wall, in this particular case through inhibition of arabinogalactan biosynthesis (Makarov et al. 2009). One molecule, PBTZ169, a piperazinobenzothiazinone derivative of BTZ043, which has a relatively easy chemical synthesis and promising pharmacodynamics, has been advanced to Phase 2 clinical trials.
	Oxazolidinones represent a new class of orally bioavailable inhibitors of protein synthesis that act by binding to the 23s subunit of the ribosome and interrupting protein synthesis., linezolid, is recommended by the WHO to treat drug-resistant tuberculosis as a medicine with ‘unclear efficacy’. Two randomized controlled trials in patients with XDR-TB demonstrated improved rates of sputum culture conversion but linezolid was poorly tolerated which has limited its widespread application (Lee et al. 2012; Maartens and Benson 2015; Tang et al. 2015). Sutezolid follows in this class, with favourable pharmacokinetic properties (Rausch et al. 2018). However, advancing sutezolid to Phase 2 clinical trials (Wallis et al. 2014) is pending review after recent safety concerns arose from a 6-Month Toxicity Study of sutezolid in rats. Delpazolid (LCB01-0371), a new oxazolidinone with a cyclic amidrazone moiety, and contezolid (also known as MRX) are currently being advanced in the clinical development pipeline.
	GSK070, a new candidate drug with an entirely novel model of action, inhibits mycobacterial Leucyl-tRNA synthetase (LeuRS), an enzyme required for protein synthesis. The LeuRS system allows for aminoacylation of tRNAs, together with a proof reading site to remove incorrectly charged amino acids and inhibition of this process affects translation (need ref). GSK070 is currently entering Phase 1 clinical trials.





Regimen building


	Various combinations of new agents, together with existing drugs are being tested to develop short-course regimens with low toxicity. Based on promising results from a Phase 2b trial, the NC-005 regimen, BPaMZ (bedaquiline + pretomanid + moxifloxacin + pyrazinamide) will be assessed in the Phase 3 trial (NCT02193776) to provide a more effective, shorter regimen for both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB. The Nix-TB trial (NCT02333799) will assess a shorter, orally administered treatment for XDR-TB with pretomanid, bedaquiline, and linezolid. This combination promises to provide a new alternative for drug-resistant TB. Similarly, the ZeNix trial (NCT03086486) will also assess the potential for improved safety with a shorter, oral regimen consisting of pretomanid, bedaquiline, and lower dose linezolid (BPaL).
	Clofazimine (CFZ). CFZ, a riminophenazine, has been historically used for the treatment of lepromatous leprosy (Sharma et al. 2017). The drug has several advantages including intracellular accumulation within macrophages, a low prevalence of resistance, anti-inflammatory properties and contributes substantially to the sterilizing activity of TB regimens in mice and to the relapse-free cure of MDR-TB regimens in humans. However optimal dosing, pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, safety and tolerability rates, and treatment duration have not been definitively tested. Reversible but potentially stigmatizing skin discoloration along with known QT prolongation has tempered enthusiasm. Nevertheless, CFZ has demonstrated significant M. tuberculosis killing activity and treatment-shortening potential in murine models. This will be investigated in a 3-and 4-month regimen of standard TB treatment (rifampin/isoniazid/pyrazinamide/ethambutol) with the addition of CFZ (ACTG trial A5362) early efficacy (12-week culture conversion) and treatment shortening in dug-susceptible TB (Treatment Action Group 2017).





Host-directed therapies


	Host-directed therapies (HDT) are novel approaches in the field of anti-infectives for overcoming antimicrobial resistance and restoring cellular pathways that are perturbed by the causative pathogen, M. tuberculosis (Wallis and Hafner 2015; Yang 2017; Kaufmann et al. 2018). HDT for TB, aims to (i) modulate host cell factors that are required by a pathogen for replication or persistence; (ii) enhance protective immune responses against a pathogen; (iii) reduce exacerbated inflammation; and (iv) balance immune reactivity at sites of pathology. In TB, HDT aims to enhance the antimicrobial activities of phagocytes and to curtail inflammation through modulation of secreted factors (such as eicosanoids and cytokines) or cell membrane proteins (such as co-stimulatory molecules) and modulate granulomas to allow the access of antimicrobials or to restrict tissue damage (Kaufmann et al. 2018). By directly targeting the host, rather than the pathogen, HDTs may be less susceptible to the development of resistance to these therapies. Most HDT approaches are not considered to be stand-alone therapies but are combined with conventional therapy. Several HDTs have been directed at each stage of the macrophage life cycle of M. tuberculosis to overcome resistance to microbial killing by: (i) Triggering activation: IFN and TNF modulators and phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitors; (ii) inducing antimicrobial peptides: (vitamin d; histone deacetylase [hdac] inhibitors; and phenylbutyrate); (iii) inhibiting lipid formation: (statins and vitamin D); (iv) triggering autophagy (gefitinib, vitamin D, mTOR inhibitors, metformin, statins, verapamil, fluoxetine, nitazoxanide, carbamazepine, valproic acid); and (v) promoting phagosome maturation (metformin, kinase inhibitors, and statins) (Parihar et al. 2014; Singhal et al. 2014; Pauwels et al. 2017). Thus far few have progressed to clinical evaluation with successful results. Notably the clinical evaluation of metformin has not yielded promising results (Dutta et al. 2017). Results from a large Phase 2 trial designed to examine the safety and preliminary efficacy of multiple adjunctive host-directed TB therapies CC-11050 (PDE-4 inhibitor), auranofin, everolimus (mTOR inhibitor), and vitamin D, to assess their potential to shorten TB treatment and/or prevent permanent lung damage are expected in 2019 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02968927). Preclinical evaluation of anti-IL-1 blockade; autophagy targets; statins and Imatinib have concluded, and the statin and Imatinib projects are now proceeding to proof-of-concept clinical studies for M. tuberculosis treatment in the context of HIV co-infection (Mayer-Barber et al. 2010; Napier et al. 2011; Dutta et al. 2016; Gupta et al. 2016).
	While progress is slow and difficult, HDT will undoubtedly feature in the future of TB therapy. Further refinement in the identification of potential genetic predispositions in patients, discovery and validation of host or pathogen biomarkers that may indicate disease stage; treatment responses; type of inflammatory response; will potentially permit targeted HDT. Significant barriers include the potential for some of these agents to be cytotoxic or induce a worsened inflammatory response; lack of supportive preclinical and clinical data in assessing potential efficacy and selecting suitable candidate; and not least the potentially higher cost of adding these agents to already expensive treatments for MDR and XDR-TB.





Vaccines for TB


	Vaccination is the most effective intervention for the prevention, control, and/or eradication of an infectious disease. Mathematical modelling estimates that without new interventions, particularly those that blocks transmission such as protective vaccines, it will not be possible to reduce the incidence of TB to less than 10 per 100,000 by 2035. The growing burden of extensively resistant and untreatable TB as well a compelling argument for the return on investment emphasizes the need, and incentive for the development of an effective vaccine to prevent TB. This section highlights key challenges and recent advances in TB vaccine research. The current discovery, preclinical, and clinical pipeline have been described in detail elsewhere. Recent advances offering a broader diverse repertoire of TB vaccine candidates together with an enthusiasm to leap-frog TB vaccine development and include broadening both antigen selection and the range of vaccine-mediated immune responses as well as experimental design in both in animal models and smaller human clinical trials offer an unprecedented opportunity to expand demonstration of vaccine efficacy for the prevention and possibly the treatment of TB.
	Based on animal and human studies of TB, a robust cellular immune response is required for protection against Mtb infection and disease (Evans et al. 2016) whereas, most successful, licensed vaccines available today induce neutralizing antibodies that provide protective immunity. For this reason, the majority of current clinical TB vaccine candidates are based on a variety of vectors, adjuvants and antigens that induce CD4 or CD8 T-cell responses with TH1 cytokines such as IFN-γ or TNF-α. These clinical candidates are based on a variety of vaccine approaches, such as inactivated whole cell or whole cell extracts (Mycobacterium indicus pranii, Mycobacterium vaccae, DAR-901 (Mycobacterium obuense), RUTI and Mycobacterium smegmatis), viral-vectored candidates (vaccinia-based MVA85A, influenza, and human adenovirus 5 and 35 and chimpanzee adenovirus), fusion protein subunits with TH1-inducing adjuvants (M72/AS01, Hybrid 1/CAF01, Hybrid 1/IC31, H4/IC31, H56/IC31 and ID93/GLA-SE), and live recombinant BCG or attenuated TB vaccines (VPM 1002, Aeras 422, rBCG30, and MTBVAC). DNA vaccines are being developed in different countries, notably emerging economies, but have not yet entered into human clinical trials. To date, clinical trials characterizing these candidate vaccines have included studies of safety and immunogenicity in diverse populations, including healthy, TB-naïve adults, and infants, latently infected adolescents, and adults, HIV-infected adults, as well as patients undergoing drug treatment for TB (Evans et al. 2016).
	Vaccination against TB can be divided into one of three categories: (1) preventive pre-exposure vaccines (or priming vaccines) typically administered to neonates for prevention of infection (POI); (2) preventive post-exposure vaccines (or boost vaccines) that can be administered to adolescents and adults with latent TB infection or those that have previous vaccination and (3) therapeutic vaccines which are administered together with TB drugs to shorten and ameliorate the course of therapy and prevent recurrent disease. Different vaccines may be required to induce immune responses in diverse populations, such as infants, young adults, those already latently infected with M. tuberculosis or on treatment for TB, and those co-infected with HIV.
	The first candidate to be tested for efficacy, MVA85A (a modified vaccinia Ankara virus vector expressing the antigen 85A), failed to show protection (Tameris et al. 2013), other candidates remain in the clinical pipeline, with efficacy results expected (2018) from a Phase 2b prevention of disease trial with M72/AS01, the GSK adjuvanted fusion protein vaccine in 3,600 HIV-uninfected, adults latently infected with M tuberculosis.
	Iterative approaches focused on prevention of disease by viral-vectored vaccine candidates are yet to yield promising results. Innovation in trial design, vaccine approaches, constructs and routes of administration aimed at demonstrating biologic activity of vaccine candidates using more focused populations specifically selected to reduce sample size, are providing encouraging new evidence and pathways for vaccine developers. In a prevention-of-infection Phase 2 trial conducted in South Africa, revaccination with BCG significantly reduced sustained TB infections in high-risk adolescents. An experimental vaccine candidate, H4:IC31, a fusion protein of the immunodominant antigens TB10.4 and Ag85B, formulated with IC31 adjuvant, also reduced sustained infections, although not at statistically significant levels. However, the trend observed for H4:IC31 is the first time a subunit vaccine has shown any indication of ability to protect against TB infection or disease in humans. These results indicating that sustained QFT-GIT conversions are preventable by BCG revaccination, provide novel insights into possible mechanisms of protection in humans. Results from a concluded Phase 3 trial investigating the efficacy of killed M. vaccae lysate vaccine to prevent TB in adults with latent disease from Guanxi province China are expected while a ‘Prevention of Recurrence’ trial with the vaccine candidate ID93 is designed to determine whether the vaccine can prevent the 4–6% relapse and/or reinfection rate typically observed following successful treatment of active TB. All these experimental designs follow a non-traditional clinical development path, but attempt increase efficiencies by reducing sample size requirements of demonstrating biological signals earlier than conventionally phased product development plan.
	Recently a novel vaccine approach using a weakened form of a common herpes virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV) as a vector expressing M. tuberculosis Ag85A demonstrated complete protection in 41% and reduced overall TB disease by 68% in vaccinated rhesus macaques. Cytomegaloviruses persist lifelong in vivo and induce powerful adaptive and innate immune and increasing (‘inflationary’) responses (Beverley et al. 2014).
	The BCG control group showed no evidence of protection. It is critical to rapidly understand the mechanisms by which this re-engineered CMV creates and maintains a high state of immunity against the pathogen in vaccinated monkeys especially because this approach has the potential to work better than standard vaccines. The results demonstrate that a small Ag-specific response may be highly effective in synergy with the correct innate activation, in this case involving IL-21 and natural killer (NK) cells and hold promise for future development of this candidate vaccine. Human trials are expected by 2019.
	The development of appropriate preclinical models to prioritize the best vaccine candidate for advancement in human studies represents a key unmet need. Many TB vaccine animal challenge models have a narrow dynamic range of responses that do not allow for easy differentiation among candidates. This limitation is being addressed by refinement of the mouse, guinea pig, and macaque models to better approximate natural infection by M tuberculosis and better mimic human disease. The use of low dose challenge, sophisticated PET/CT imaging techniques, and novel vaccine candidates (such as H56, Cytomegalovirus [CMV] approaches, aerosolized adenovirus vaccines and IV administration of BCG) have recently shown that the macaque model may potentially be useful to delineate correlates of vaccine-induced protection.
	The lack of known correlates of protection and surrogate biomarkers of immune responses associated with different stages of TB infection and disease has been a barrier against the clinical evaluation of the vaccine candidates (Abubakar et al. 2016). We have discussed the implications of gene expression patterns of inflammatory biosignatures correlated with risk for TB disease progression, in both active and latent TB cases (Evans et al. 2016). Similarly, a broad unbiased systems biology approach in which gene expression signatures are compared in samples from various time points (Evans et al. 2016) and then correlated to either specific measures of immunogenicity, or to protection in efficacy studies are likely to yield potential correlates of vaccine-induce protection.
	Given no validated immunological correlates of protection, significant limitations of animal models and the strained capacity to fund and perform efficacy trials, a TB human challenge model would facility vaccine development by offering an option to investigate candidate selection, route of vaccination, dose optimization, and the identification of immune correlates despite the need to overcome significant safety, measurement/reporter, ethical, and regulatory challenges. If successful potential TB vaccines are tested in healthy donors challenged with attenuated M. tuberculosis strains that are viable, capable of replicating but do not cause infection or disease or be transmittable. Experiments in non-human primates are scheduled to start in mid-2019. A safer option, using BCG challenge has been pursued, while vaccines that target antigens unique to M tuberculosis would not be suitable for the BCG challenge model promising results have been demonstrated.
	Exponential advances in TB vaccine development have occurred over the past 5 years. Results from efficacy trials will provide insights into what is needed from a vaccine to deliver protective immunity and new tools will accelerate TB vaccine development, not only by providing a less expensive and rapid method for assessing potential vaccine efficacy, but also by permitting more rapid progress towards the identification of an immune correlate of protection. While the challenges in developing TB vaccines are great, the research community is embracing this challenge.





Closing the Gap—addressing global threats


	Financing for TB care and prevention has been increasing for more than 10 years, but a crippling funding gap still exists, estimated at US$ 2.3billion in 2017. Total health spending also falls short of the resources needed to achieve universal health coverage. TB kills more people than any other bacterial agent and when this fact is contrasted with the reducing investments in TB research, it becomes clear that the governments of endemic countries, together with those of donor nations, have yet to commit appropriate resources to realize the End TB Strategy. Closing these gaps requires more resources from both domestic sources (especially in middle-income countries) and international donors (especially in low-income countries). Given this complex funding landscape, TB is particularly susceptible to sudden changes in the global political landscape. The UK referendum to leave the European Union has created a risk that the sixth largest contributor to TB research will most likely adopt a trade-focused approach and withdraw support from global health efforts. Similar concerns prevail in the USA where the low incidence of TB makes it an issue of international development and foreign aid, rather than a concern for public health. TB also ranks low in terms of the research and development agenda globally, especially in the context of emerging infectious diseases such as Ebola, which grab international attention and resources. In this context, political will from endemic countries become mission critical to nucleate international support and must therefore feature centrally in efforts to eliminate TB.
	Profits from TB research and development are perceived to be minimal, owing largely to the fact that the disease is mostly prevalent in the poorest settings, which are unable to provide a financially lucrative market to drive drug discovery and development. TB research and development n is being currently driven by collaborative efforts involving public–private partnerships. Although the total funding for TB research and development increased from US $ 358.1 million in 2005 to 620.6 million in 2015, this has been insufficient to meet costs of discovery. Since 2009, approximately 2.8 billion US$ has been spent on TB research by public institutions, with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) contributing more than half this amount. Other sources of funding for TB research include Japanese pharmaceutical company Otsuka contributing 60% of industry spending, the Gates Foundation contributing 89% of philanthropic funding, and Unitaid contributing 47% of total multilateral funding. It is noteworthy that the largest multilateral supporter of TB research and development to date has been the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria, contributing US$ 120.2 million from 2002 to 2015 on TB operational research There have been substantial advances in HIV/AIDS within three-four decades, from huge investments by governments and donor agencies. Relative this this, investments in TB research and development has remained vastly inadequate and should be prioritized.





Conclusion


	TB has defined the fabric of modern medicine in the developing world and continues to claim the lives of the economically and socially disadvantaged. To address this, the WHO has set bold goals in the End TB Strategy and to achieve these, a higher level of annual decline in incidence is required. While a bold approach is needed to eradicate TB, it is questionable whether achieving these milestones places an unreasonable burden of performance on the crippled healthcare systems of endemic countries, which may require a slower, but steady, rate of sustainable decline. This can already be achieved through more effective deployment of current tools, together with safe-guarding the fidelity of available antibiotics using medical practices that limit the emergence of resistance. That said, new tools for diagnosis and treatment of TB are urgently required, in addition to an integrated approach for bolstering the healthcare system. Identifying and addressing gaps in the cascade of care for TB is critical and central to this is strong political will, which is required to create resources, build infrastructure, and attract much needed funding. Another challenge that needs to be addressed is the implementation of TB control programmes in the context of limited laboratory capacity and treatment barriers, which threaten to undermine any gains that the introduction of new interventions may bring. Hence, strengthening healthcare delivery and linkage to care is pivotal for TB eradication. As with many other infectious diseases, a cross-disciplinary approach to the development of health interventions promises success and, in this regard, it is critical to support research and development efforts across the value chain to advance new drugs and vaccines and to lay the foundation for future elimination efforts. Furthermore, considering comorbidities such as HIV infection and diabetes is required to ensure future control programmes consider those most at risk for progressing to active disease. While the treatment of drug-sensitive disease is affordable for most endemic countries, treating drug-resistant TB is prohibitive. This creates a research and development environment which calls on all stakeholders, including academic institutions, governments, and big pharma to shift cost paradigms and invest in the development of novel, cheaper regimens. For success in these endeavours, coordination between donors is essential to leverage the best value for money in terms of prioritizing research questions and for attracting further funding to the field. Finally, the world can no longer afford to ignore the growing menace of antimicrobial resistance. Considering that more than half of the recorded cases of bacterial resistance involve drug-resistant M. tuberculosis, the inability to eliminate TB threatens to plunge humanity back into the pre-antibiotic era. As a society, we simply cannot let this happen.
