8.15


Malaria


	Frank Baiden, Keziah L. Malm, and Fred Binka





Introduction


	Malaria is a life-threatening infectious tropical and subtropical disease of major global health concern. It is caused by parasites that are transmitted through the bites of infective female Anopheles mosquito. According to the 2018 World Malaria Report released by the World Health Organization, there were 219 million cases of malaria in 2017. These resulted in 435,000 deaths, nearly 61% of which were in children below 5 years of age. The World Health Organization (WHO) Africa Region carries the highest burden of malaria cases (92%) and deaths (93%).
	In 2017, five countries accounted for nearly half of all malaria cases. The countries are Nigeria (25%), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11%), Mozambique (5%), India (4%), and Uganda (4%) (Fig. 8.15.1). Malaria is an important cause of underdevelopment and poverty in these and other countries in malaria-endemic sub-Saharan Africa. It reduces gross domestic product in sub-Saharan Africa by about 1.3% per year. In continued high transmission settings, malaria could be reducing life expectancy at birth by more than six years (Bawah and Binka 2007; WHO 2018a).
	Per global population, the number of cases and deaths from malaria has seen steady decline since the 1990s. The period from 2000 to 2015 witnessed year-on-year reduction in the number of cases. Since 2015 however, this trend has stalled and there is a real threat that gains made over the past two decades could be reversed if urgent steps are not taken. Malaria thus remains an important threat to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (Rowe 2017).





Malaria: past to present


	The earliest evidence of malaria parasites was found in fossils of mosquitoes that dates to approximately 30 million years old. Hippocrates described the manifestations of malaria, and related them to where patients lived, and time of the year. His description is preceded by references to malaria and its symptoms by Nei Ching (Chinese Canon of Medicine) in 2700 BC and in the Cuneiform tablets of 6th century BC (Ross 1923; Neghina et al. 2010).
	The pioneering work of Alphone Laveran in Algeria in 1879 led to vastly improved understanding of the infectious basis of the disease. His discovery of black pigment in the blood of people suffering from malaria ultimately led to the knowledge of plasmodium as the infectious agent (Sundberg 2007; Cox 2010). Experiments conducted by Donald Ross in the late 1800s led to an understanding of the life cycle of the parasite. The use of the microscope to identify the plasmodium parasite and the deployment of interventions to break the chain in the life cycle of the parasite have remained the basis for the diagnosis, treatment, and control of the disease (Dobson 1999; Cox 2017).
	Interventions for the prevention and treatment of malaria preceded a full understanding of the plasmodium parasite and its life cycle. The perception of association between malaria and stagnant waters (ultimately to be appreciated as the breeding grounds for mosquitoes) led the Romans in 1930s to undertake drainage programmes (Majori 2012). Derivatives of the Artemisia annua, used in early traditional Chinese Medicine, remain an importance part of malaria treatment to date (Krishna et al. 2008). Peruvian Indians used the bitter bark of the Cinchona tree, later processed as quinine, in the treatment of fever. Quinine continues to be an important drug in the treatment of malaria. Between 1955 and 1969, a Global Malaria Eradication Programme (GMEP), resulted in the elimination of malaria from many regions in south Europe and parts of the Americas. There was however very little success from the rather limited efforts in sub-Saharan Africa (Bruce-Chwatt 1974; Krishna et al. 2008; Najera et al. 2011; Cohen et al. 2012; Majori 2012). The launch of Roll Back Malaria (RBM) in 1998 by Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, then Director-General of the WHO set in motion a momentum of increased investments and support to endemic countries (Nabarro 1999; Remme et al. 2001).
	Compared to the 1980s and 90s, malaria transmission has substantially reduced in many countries; to a point there is now a push for country-by-country elimination and eradication (Mendis et al. 2009; Alonso et al. 2011) (Fig. 8.15.1).
	Fig. 8.15.1 Countries and territories with indigenous cases in 2000 and their status by 2017.
	Reprinted from World Malaria Report 2018. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2018. License: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO, with permission from the World Health Organization.
	Countries with zero indigenous cases over at least the past 3 consecutive years are eligible to request certification of malaria-free status from WHO. All countries in the WHO European Region reported zero indigenous cases in 2016. Kyrgyzstan and Sri Lanka were certified malaria free in 2016.





Human Plasmodium parasites


	Malaria is caused by the protozoa that belongs to the genus Plasmodium. Out of the over 100 species of Plasmodium which infect mammals, five are so far known to cause disease in humans. These are the Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium malariae, Plasmodium ovale, and Plasmodium knowlesi.





Plasmodium falciparum


	Plasmodium falciparum (P. falciparum) is responsible for over 90% of cases and deaths worldwide. It is the most dominant form of malaria in sub-Saharan Africa. Children, pregnant women, and non-immune adults are vulnerable to the severe forms of the disease. According to the 2018 World Malaria Report, children under 5 years of age are the most affected, and account for 61% of the total deaths (WHO 2018a). Repeated infections in people who live in high transmission settings lead to the development of some partial immunity. This is the reason adults living in high transmission are less vulnerable to the severe forms of P. falciparum malaria. P. falciparum malaria is associated with the development of Burkitt’s lymphoma, a B-lymphocyte cancer (Thorley-Lawson et al. 2016). P. falciparum lacks a fixed structure. It undergoes continuous change during its life cycle as part of survival strategies (Dhangadamajhi et al. 2010). The incubation period for P. falciparum malaria ranges from nine to 14 days.





Plasmodium vivax


	Plasmodium vivax infection is the most geographically widespread of the five human malarias, with about 35% of the world’s population being at risk. It infects 19–50 million people each year mostly in the Asia Pacific region, Latin America, and parts of Africa. It causes significant morbidity and can be associated with severe malaria and death. Clinically, P. vivax malaria presents as an acute debilitating illness that is characterized by recurrent paroxysmal fever and relapses from dormant liver stages (hypnozoites). These symptoms can occur even when blood parasite density is low. P. vivax can be present and be infectious to mosquito vectors, while infected persons show no symptoms. The liver stage of P. vivax can lie dormant for weeks to years after first infection before causing relapses of symptomatic malaria. Primaquine is the only licensed antimalarial drug that targets the liver stage of the lifecycle. It used to be thought Plasmodium vivax depended on the Duffy antigen to invade red blood cells and individuals who do not express the Duffy antigen were refractory to P. vivax infection. Reports of P. vivax infections in Duffy negative patients raise the possibility of an alternative invasion mechanism (Menard et al. 2010; Howes et al. 2016). The incubation period for P. vivax malaria ranges from 12 to 18 days.
	P. vivax presents a particular challenge to malaria elimination for the following reasons: (1) It can survive in cooler climates hence its wider geographical coverage; (2) it is more difficult to detect using current diagnostic techniques; (3) a single infection can give rise to multiple episodes of malaria; (4) treatment of liver-stage parasites requires a 14-day course of primaquine; and (5) primaquine treatment can produce serious side effects in persons with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency (WHO 2015a; Baird et al. 2016).





Plasmodium malariae


	Plasmodium malariae is a widely distributed Plasmodium species. It is endemic in parts of Africa, South America, Asia, and the Western Pacific, and is responsible for a mild form of malaria. Malaria caused by P. malariae is often referred to a benign, quartan malaria. This is because it rarely results in severe disease, and the associated fever tends to occur at three-day intervals unlike the others which are usually tertian (i.e. 2-day interval for the occurrence of fever). P. malariae has a tendency for low-dose chronic, asymptomatic infection, which when untreated can lead to nephrotic syndrome and albuminuria (Gilles and Hendrickse 1963; Ehrich and Eke 2007). There are no animal reservoirs for P. malariae. A large case series reported from southern Papua in 2015 shows that P. malariae is responsible for a minority (2.6%) of clinical malaria cases but has potential to cause a severer form of anaemia. The mean haemoglobin in patients with P. malariae infection was 0.3–0.6g/dl lower than the other locally prevalent Plasmodium species, with an associated 2.3-fold greater odds of severe anaemia compared to individuals without malaria (Langford et al. 2015). The incubation period for P. malariae malaria is highly variable and ranges from 16 to 59 days (Collins and Jeffery 2007). Late recrudescence may occur with P. malariae malaria.





Plasmodium ovale


	Plasmodium ovale is primarily found in sub-Saharan Africa (Collins and Jeffery 2005). Molecular methods have led to the elucidation of two distinct sympatric species termed P. ovale curtisi and P. ovale wallikeri. P. ovale also causes mild (benign) malaria and is relatively unimportant as a cause of severe malaria morbidity and mortality. A systematic review of clinical presentation, treatment, and relapse characteristics of P. ovale malaria reported in 2017 identified 22 severe cases, five fatalities, and two cases of congenital malaria. Most cases were from sub-Saharan Africa, Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and India (Groger et al. 2017). Comparatively, P. ovale has received little attention in medical research and knowledge gaps exist in the optimal drug for its treatment. The incubation period ranges from 18 to 40 days.





Plasmodium knowlesi


	Plasmodium knowlesi is a malaria parasite found in monkeys which can infect humans via mosquito bites (Moyes et al. 2014). Human infection was first reported in 1964. It was however not until 2004 that reports of a large focus of naturally acquired human infections in Sarawak, Malaysia brought this species to greater global attention (Singh et al. 2004). P. knowlesi causes life-threatening malaria yet it is grossly under-reported and often misreported as P. malariae. It is the most common cause of malaria in Malaysia. Cases have also been reported in Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, and Myanmar. Infection with P. knowlesi is associated with high levels of parasitaemia. The risk of severe disease in adults appears as high as that of P. falciparum. For many years, misdiagnoses were associated with delayed administration of treatment and high fatality rates. Increased awareness of pathogenic potential has led to improvement in treatment and reduction in case fatalities (Rajahram et al. 2012; Jeremiah et al. 2014). Local transmission of P. knowlesi in sub-Saharan Africa is unknown and this may be due to lack of a monkey reservoir. Intravenous artesunate is highly effective in severe knowlesi malaria while chloroquine and artemisinin-combination therapy (ACT) are highly effective for uncomplicated P. knowlesi malaria (Barber et al. 2017). There is uncertainty about human-to-human P. knowlesi infection.





Life cycles of the malaria parasite and vector


	Two life cycles are important in discussing how the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito (vector) transmits Plasmodium (parasite) and causes malaria. These are the life cycles of the Plasmodium parasite, and of the female Anopheles mosquito. A good knowledge of the essential aspects of these life cycles is important for an appreciation of how preventive and therapeutic interventions have emerged and how they have been applied to date, their limitations and prospect for the development of new tools (Acharya et al. 2017).





Life cycle of the Plasmodium parasite


	Malaria infection is initiated when an infected female Anopheles mosquito bites a human host. It injects into the host saliva that contain anophelin, an anticoagulant. This material counteracts the host’s haemostatic response and prevents the sucked blood from clotting. In the process, the female Anopheles mosquito ingests sporozoites of Plasmodium parasite into the blood stream of the victim. The stage of the parasite life cycle that is transmitted in the bite is the sporozoite. Within 30 to 60 minutes of ingestion, sporozoites migrate through the venous circulation to the liver. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK215619/). While within liver cells, sporozoites undergoes a series of asexual multiplications that lead to the development of schizonts that contain the next stage of the parasite called merozoites. This process is called sporogonic schizogony and because it takes place in liver, it is also called the hepatic or pre-erythrocytic stage (Mota et al. 2002; Mota and Rodriguez 2002) (Fig. 8.15.2).
	Upon their maturation, merozoites burst out of schizonts and into the bloodstream where they attack red blood cells (RBCs) to begin the erythrocytic phase of development. Within the RBCs, merozoites differentiate further into ring form called trophozoites. Trophozoites undergo further asexual multiplication and develop into schizonts. This process is called erythrocytic schizogony. Schizonts burst on maturation to release more merozoites into the bloodstream. The rupture of erythrocytic-stage schizonts out of RBCs coincides with the emergence of symptoms. While within RBCs, the developing parasite digests haemoglobin and converts the waste product into hemozoin (also called malaria pigment) which are packaged in vesicular compartments called digestive vacuoles. The burst of schizonts leads to the release of digestive vacuoles (DVs) into the bloodstream, a triggering of immune response and the emergence of symptoms. While DVs get phagocytosed, merozoite largely escape the attack of the immune system, attack more RBCs, and further aggravate the illness.
	Typically, it takes 10–14 days from the time of sporozoite injection to the emergence of symptoms. This is called the incubation period. The cycles of release from RBCs and DVs, attack on new cells, and further RBC destruction underline bouts of fever, chills, and other symptoms of the disease (Mueller et al. 2015; Tannous and Ghanem 2018).
	Fig. 8.15.2 The lifecycle of the malaria parasite.
	Source: CDC, available freely at https://www.cdc.gov/malaria/about/biology/mosquitoes/. This does not constitute its endorsement or recommendation by the U.S. Government, Department of Health and Human Services, or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
	This does not constitute its endorsement or recommendation by the U.S. Government, Department of Health and Human Services, or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention During the intraerythrocytic stage, some merozoites differentiate into male (microgametocytes) and female (macrogametocytes) gametocytes. Gametocytes are the sexual forms of the parasite and they are the stage of development that can infect mosquitoes. During a blood meal, the female Anopheles mosquito ingests gametocytes and this reinitiates the sporogonic stage of parasite development. In the gut of the mosquito, male and female gametocytes develop into gametes which merge, and over 2 to 3 weeks develop into sporozoites in the salivary glands. Higher climatic temperatures accelerate parasite development within the mosquito (Afrane et al. 2012) (https://www.cdc.gov/malaria/about/biology/mosquitoes/). This is one of the anticipated effects of climate change on malaria.
	While the aforementioned is the classical presentation of the life cycle of the Plasmodium parasite, it important to appreciate that important difference exist in the life cycles of the different Plasmodia. In the case of P. vivax and P. ovale, a dormant stage (hypnozoites) can persist in the liver and cause relapses by invading the bloodstream weeks, or even years later after infection (Olliaro et al. 2016). Once in the bloodstream, P. vivax tends to attack reticulocytes (young RBCs) and remain in the ring form. The ability of P. vivax to attack RBCs is due to the presence of Duffy blood group antigens on the red cells of susceptible populations. For many years, it was thought that the absence of this antigen is the reason populations in sub-Saharan Africa are less susceptible to P. vivax infection. This is now firmly disputed.
	Generally, the level of parasitaemia with P. vivax infection is much lower than occurs with P. falciparum infection. Gametocytaemia also tends occur earlier in the course of P. vivax malaria. This makes patients infectious almost at the onset of symptoms.
	The different stages in the life cycle of plasmodium present a range of antigenic challenges to the host immune system. Antigen expression has been implicated in the aetiology of severe malaria (Pal et al. 2016, 2017). An improved understanding of the nature of antigen expression, facilitated by emerging genetic technology, should lead to the development of new diagnostic and therapeutic options for the management and control of the disease.





Life cycle of the Anopheles mosquito


	Anopheles is a vector that belongs to the class of mosquitoes named by J.W. Meigen in 1818. While over 100 of the Anopheles species can transmit human malaria, only 30–40 commonly do so. Anopheles gambiae is one of the best studied because of its role in malaria transmission (Afrane et al. 2012).
	The anopheline mosquito develops through four stages: egg, larva, pupa, and imago. This begins with the laying of eggs in fresh or stagnant water by the female anopheline mosquito. Cans, buckets, discarded tyres, clogged rain gutters that hold stagnant water are common sites for the laying of eggs. The eggs develop into larva which further develops into the pupa. All three stages are aquatic and last about 5 to 14 days. This length of time depends on the species of anopheline, the level of humidity and ambient temperature (Beck-Johnson et al. 2013).
	The adult stage emerges from the pupa on the surface of the breeding water. Female anopheline mosquitoes seek blood meals to derive vitally needed nutrients to fertilize its eggs. In the process it acts as vector for malaria and transmits the parasite into man.
	Although the adult female has the potential to live for up to a month, it typically lives for no more than two weeks. For malaria transmission to be possible therefore, the Anopheles mosquito needs to live long enough to enable the sporogonic stage of Plasmodium development to be completed. One of the postulated effect of global warming is that it will shorten the sporogonic phase of parasite development and enhance the ability of the mosquito to transmit malaria (Afrane et al. 2012; Caminade et al. 2014).





Pathogenesis of malaria


	All the mechanisms through which infection with P. falciparum leads to malaria are associated with the erythrocytic stage of parasite development (Buffet et al. 2011; Sanyal et al. 2012). When RBCs are infected by malaria parasites, they (RBCs) undergo configurational changes. These include loss of the normal discoid shape, increased rigidity of the membrane, elevated permeability to a wide variety of ionic and other species and increased adhesiveness (Mohandas and An 2012).
	Sticky RBCs more easily adhere to other normal RBCs (rosetting) and to the inside walls of capillaries (cytoadhesion). Clumping, rosetting, and cytoadhesion occur, blocking small vessels and causing ischaemic cell injury in several organs of the body (Moxon et al. 2011). Most notable are the lung, heart, brain, and kidney. This explains why malaria is a multisystem disease with wide range of unspecific clinical manifestations. The effect in the brain forms the basis of cerebral malaria. The rupture of parasitized RBCs and clearance of deformed parasitized and unparasitized erythrocytes by cells of the immune system including the spleen is the principal cause of malarial anaemia (Autino et al. 2012; Safeukui et al. 2015; White 2017). The release of toxins (packaged as digestive vacuoles referred to earlier) from ruptured RBCs into the bloodstream leads to cytokine expression and unspecific symptoms like fever, headache, loss of appetite, and vomiting.
	In pregnant women, parasitized RBCs adhere to chondroitin sulphate A in the placenta. The accumulation of RBCs compromises the efficiency of the placenta and this leads to clinical manifestations such as abortion, intrauterine growth retardation, low birth weight, and stillbirths.
	Cells that are attacked by RBCs express antigen on the surfaces as part of activation of the immune system. It is the repeated triggering of the immune system through antigen expression that forms the basis of immunity and tolerance to malaria (Matuschewski 2017). It is the reason the severity of malaria generally declines with increasing age and gravidity (in the case of pregnancy) in persons who live in malaria-endemic countries (Mendonca and Barral-Netto 2015). It is also the reason why individuals who have lived in endemic settings loss some immunity when they move into non-endemic settings.
	An important aspect of the immune response of the body is the mobilization of all possible capacity to destroy parasitized RBCs. The major organs in the body responsible for the destruction of parasitized and damaged RBCs are the spleen and liver. Hyperactivity due to repeated attacks leads to enlargement of these organs, most particularly the spleen. Community-based prevalence of palpable spleen enlargement was in the past used as a measure of the endemicity of malaria (Snow et al. 2012).





Clinical presentation


	The clinical presentation of malaria is closely related to the stages in its pathogenesis as outlined earlier. The liver phase of the malaria lifecycle occurs without clinical symptoms. Symptoms emerge following invasion and rupture of RBCs. In an ‘interruptible’ continuum, there are two forms of clinical presentations. These are uncomplicated and complicated or severe malaria.





Uncomplicated malaria


	Uncomplicated malaria is characterized by symptoms such as fever, headache, vomiting, and general malaise. In most high transmission settings, these symptoms often trigger suspicion of malaria and the initiation of treatment, when available. Unfortunately, the symptoms of uncomplicated malaria are so unspecific that they could as well be caused by other infections, particularly viral infections. In the absence of a test, the false diagnosis of malaria leads to treatment with antimalarials. If correctly diagnosed and effectively treated at this stage, good and complete recovery is nearly always assured. Most cases of malaria are uncomplicated and do not progress to severe or complicated malaria unless treatment is delayed or wrongfully administered.





Severe or complicated malaria


	When treatment of malaria is delayed or ineffectively administered, a cascade of pathophysiological events leads to progression to severe or complicated malaria. For epidemiological and research purposes, severe malaria is defined as one or more of the conditions defined in Table 8.15.1, occurring in the absence of an identified alternative cause, and in the presence of P. falciparum asexual parasitaemia (WHO 2014) (Table 8.15.1).
	Sustained RBC destruction and multiorgan damage leads to severe or complicated malaria. Although all organs of the body are affected, the most sensitively affected at early complicated stage is the brain. Brain involvement manifests a syndrome of presentations, the most common of which is cerebral malaria. Cerebral malaria refers to the syndrome in which altered consciousness is associated with a malarial infection, and cannot be attributed to convulsions, sedative drugs, or hypoglycaemia alone, or to a non-malarial cause. Commonly associated symptoms are severe loss of appetite, inability to tolerate oral feeds, repeated vomiting, disorientation, and convulsions.
	Sustained red cell destruction results in severe weakness, pallor, jaundice (yellowing of the eyes and skin), and kidney failure. At this stage, urgent and effective treatment is needed to prevent death. The highest mortalities occur in children aged less than 5 years, pregnant women, and non-immune adults.
	In these persons, malaria takes a rapid course from uncomplicated to complicated state. The state of consciousness commonly assessed in children in sub-Saharan Africa with the Blantyre coma score (BCS) is a good indicator of prognosis.
	In Gambia, a BCS of 2 or less was found in a review of 2,901 children with severe malaria to be the most sensitive and specific predictor of death or development of neurological sequelae (Jallow et al. 2012). Children who survive severe malaria may develop long-term neurological deficits that impact development and performance in school (Fernando et al. 2003; Brooker et al. 2008; Clarke et al. 2008; Gomes et al. 2009; Dondorp et al. 2010). Multiorgan failure including renal failure occurs more commonly in non-immune adults than in children in highly-endemic areas.

Malaria in pregnancy


	Malaria in pregnancy is a major cause of maternal morbidity and perinatal mortality in high transmission countries. Up to 9.5 million pregnant women in sub-Saharan Africa are estimated to be at risk of Plasmodium falciparum infection. In the absence of interventions, malaria in pregnancy results in 900,000 (95% CI 530,000–1,240,000) babies who are born with low birth weight (Walker et al. 2014).
	The state of pregnancy increases the risk of malaria infection and an estimated 125 million pregnant women get infected annually. The risk of severe malaria is particularly high in primigravidae in areas of higher transmission. The development of partial immunity leads to an attenuation of the risk in successive pregnancies. This pattern is less marked in areas of low transmission. The risk of malaria is highest in the second trimester. In the first trimester, malaria increases the risk of miscarriage by 60% and the rate of mortality from severe malaria in pregnancy can be as high as 50%. Younger women are particularly at risk of malaria during pregnancy (WHO 2015b; Tarning 2016).





Pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and diagnosis


	The increased susceptibility of pregnant women to malaria is due to the sequestration of malaria-infected erythrocytes in the maternal placenta. This sequestration is highest with P. falciparum infections. The affinity of parasitized RBCs for placenta is mediated by the expression of the parasite-derived protein VAR2CSA on the surface of infected RBCs. These cells bind to chondroitin sulphate A (CSA) in the placenta and induce placental inflammation. This inflammatory process leads to the aggregation of monocytes in the placenta, with compromise to the efficiency of the placenta as a medium of feto-maternal transfer.
	Parasite sequestration in the placenta can occur in early pregnancy and lead to poor placenta development. This is evident in poor villous vasculature and small placenta size. This early effect can lead to miscarriages, intrauterine growth retardation, and death. In high transmission settings, placenta parasite sequestration can occur in the absence of malaria symptoms during early pregnancy. Concurrent parasite sequestration in the brain however results in severe malaria with possible dire consequences.
	A challenge to the diagnosis of malaria in pregnancy is the fact that it may present without symptoms and blood smear microscopy will be negative even in the presence of a high parasite load in the placenta (Geelhoed et al. 2001; Kakuru et al. 2016). The sensitivity of microscopy to detect malaria parasites in peripheral blood in pregnant women can be as low as 42%. The use of antigen-based diagnosis and Polymerase Chain Reaction increases sensitivity to about 80% and 97%, respectively (Mockenhaupt et al. 2002).





Diagnosis of malaria


	Practically considered, there are three approaches to the diagnosis of malaria. These are
	 	(1) The presumptive approach
	(2) Rapid diagnostic test
	(3) Blood smear microscopy





The presumptive approach


	The presumptive approach relies on the clinical judgement of an attending clinician, and it is based on the symptoms and signs that a patient presents with. For many years, fever was used as proxy indicator of malaria infection in high transmission settings. This was justified because transmission was high and that made malaria either a direct or underlying cause of most fevers. It was also because it was impractical to have microscopy in many settings where malaria was treated and most of the antimalarials in common use at the time were also relatively inexpensive.
	The symptoms of malaria are very unspecific, and they could be caused by virtually many other acute infectious diseases. The presumptive approach was therefore associated with considerable overdiagnosis, inappropriate use of antimalarials, and selection of resistance strains. The approach also led to delayed diagnosis and management of the definitive causes of fevers. A shift away from the presumptive approach only began in the late 2000s and this was made conceivable by the development, global validation, and deployment of rapid diagnostic test kits. Today the management of malaria solely based on symptoms and signs is frowned upon and considered inconsistent with the WHO recommended strategy of ‘TEST-TREAT-TRACK’ (next). The presumptive approach should therefore be used only when parasitological testing is not available.





Rapid diagnostic test


	The dipstick technology for the rapid diagnosis of malaria was developed in the early 1990s. It was however not until the 2000s that they came into widespread use (Bell et al. 2006a, 2006b; Baiden et al. 2012). Rapid diagnostic tests for malaria (mRDT) are a point-of-care device that can be used to confirm parasite infection in about 15 to 30 minutes (Perkins and Bell 2008). Their availability has revolutionized the diagnosis of malaria and improved the targeting of antimalarials. The technology depends on the detection of antigens produced by the plasmodium parasite. These are histidine-rich protein-2 (HRP-2), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and adolase. Whereas the LDH and aldolase are expressed by all Plasmodium species, HRPS-2 antigen is specific to P. falciparum. This has made it possible to develop RDTs that distinguish P. falciparum from non-P. falciparum infections.
	Important advantages with the use of mRDTs include the fact that non-laboratory technicians can use it with minimal training. It can also be deployed in all settings irrespective of infrastructural capacity. A drawback to the use of mRDTs is the fact that it does not afford a quantitative measure of the degree of parasitaemia. Additionally, antigen persistence in the bloodstream means HRP-2-based mRDT positive results can remain positive for up to 3–4 weeks after successful treatment (Baiden et al. 2012; Mbabazi et al. 2015; de Oliveira et al. 2009). HRP-2-based mRDTs can therefore not be used to monitor therapeutic response and, therefore blood smear microscopy should be used in the diagnosis and management of severe malaria.
	An emerging challenge is the deletion of Plasmodium falciparum hrp2 and hrp3 genes from the genome of some parasites. This can affect the performance of HRP2-based mRDTs. These have been reported in South America, India, Eritrea and Kenya and are likely to spread as parasites with hrp2 and hrp3 genes will escape detection during test (Nima et al. 2017). Although the prevalence of HRP2 gene deletions in most high transmission countries remains low, effective surveillance is needed (Gamboa et al. 2010; Beshir et al. 2017; WHO 2018a).





Blood smear microscopy


	Microscopy has been the mainstay for the definitive diagnosis of malaria since the work of Alphone Laveran. It involves taking venous blood, preparing a blood smear on a glass slide, processing it, and reading under a light microscope. A technically competent technician is required to read the slide. The process requires much sophistication in terms of infrastructure, logistics, and technical competence. In most parts of the malaria-endemic world, the capacity to perform malaria microscopy could not be sustained beyond regional and district levels. Even in facilities that have the capacity to perform malaria microscopy, results may become available after treatment has been initiated due to the time it takes to perform this test. In the hands of a well-trained microscopist, microscopy is the gold standard for the diagnosis of malaria.
	A major advantage of microscopy is the fact that it affords species differentiation and quantification of parasite load. It can therefore be used to monitor parasite load as part of response to treatment. A major reason why the capacity for blood smear microscopy needs to be sustained is the fact that the possibility of diagnosis of other infectious diseases adds to the utility and cost-effectiveness of blood smear microscopy.





Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in malaria diagnosis


	Another approach to detecting malaria infection is the use of PCR-based assays. PCR-based assays for the detection of malaria parasites were developed in the 1990s. They have over a 100-fold greater sensitivity than microscopy for the detection of malaria parasitaemia. High cost and technical sophistication however limit its use as a point-of-care device. They are extremely useful for surveys in areas where malaria is approaching elimination and where low levels of parasitaemia make microscopy and mRDT less useful. A setting where PCR-based assays could be extremely useful is detecting malaria infection during pregnancy.





T3: Test-Treat-Track


	On World Malaria Day 2012, WHO launched T3: Test. Treat. Track, with a call on malaria-endemic countries, donors, and the global malaria community to scale-up diagnostic testing, treatment, and surveillance for malaria. The T3 strategy was premised on the vastly improved availability of quality-assured mRDTs, the substantially reduced levels of malaria transmission and the need for prudent use of the available range of antimalarials (WHO 2010, 2015b).
	Consistent with the strategy, it is now required that all cases of suspected malaria be confirmed through parasitological testing before treatment is initiated. In various trials and operational research, this approach has been shown to lead to significant reduction in the use of antimalarials. Reductions of between 30% and 60% have been reported (Skarbinski et al. 2009; D’Acremont et al. 2010; Kyabayinze et al. 2010; Thiam et al. 2011; Yukich et al. 2012). In a trial in a high transmission setting in Ghana however, the reduction in antimalarial use was a rather modest 12%. It was found in this trial that relying on the results of mRDTs to manage under-5 children presenting with fever (compared with the presumptive approach) improved the targeted use of antimalarials without compromise to clinical outcomes (Baiden et al. 2016). The use of mRDTs in the management of uncomplicated malaria has also been found to be cost-effective in diverse transmission settings (Yukich et al. 2010; Tawiah et al. 2016).
	Improved targeted use of antimalarials has come at some considerable cost. In the absence of tools to establish the aetiology of other fevers, there has been a shift towards increased presumptive use of antibiotics in the management of non-malaria febrile illnesses (Baiden et al. 2011; Iroh Tam et al. 2016). An improved understanding of the aetiology of fevers in malaria-endemic countries is needed if clinicians in sub-Saharan Africa are to be better-guided (Baiden et al. 2012; D’Acremont et al. 2014; Hopkins et al. 2017).





Treatment of malaria


	The primary goals of malaria treatment are:
	 	• To achieve cure and complete recovery in patients
	• To reduce the risk of transmission of the infection to others, by reducing the infectious reservoir and
	• To prevent the emergence and spread of resistance to antimalarial medicines
	The effectiveness and utility of antimalarials are assessed on their intrinsic potential to achieve these goals.





Antimalarial drugs


Artemisinins


	The remarkable story of the discovery of artemisinin and the establishment of its antimalarial activity by Chinese scientists represents one of the great discoveries in medicine in the latter half of the twentieth century (Krishna et al. 2008). The artemisins are a class of antimalarials derived from the Chinese plant, Artemisia anua, or sweet wormwood.
	It is a herb that has been part of traditional medicine in China for over 1,000 years. In 1972, Youyou Tu, a scientist at the China Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine, extracted the artemisinin from Artemisia anua (Liu and Liu 2016). Today, treatments containing artemisinin derivatives are part of the standard treatment for malaria.
	In 2015, Youyou Tu was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine for her pioneering work. The artemisinins and its semi-synthetic derivatives are described as a gift of Chinese traditional medicine to the world. The account about how the artemisinins have today emerged as the most important class of antimalarials is a classic in global health. It is one that calls for respect for oriental alternative and complementary medicine (Guo 2016; Ikram and Simonsen 2017).
	Artemisinin is a sesquiterpene, lactone-containing a distinctive peroxide bridge that is hypothesized to be responsible for its antimalarial properties. Once in the bloodstream, artemisinin derivatives kill the majority of parasites within a few minutes while getting rapidly metabolized. The poor level of artemisinin bioavailability limits its effectiveness. Semi-synthetic derivatives have been developed to overcome this limitation. Dihydroartemisinin is the active metabolite of all the artemisinin compounds. It is now available as a drug in the form of dihydorartemisinin-piperaquine (Baiden et al. 2015; Adjei et al. 2016; Oduro et al. 2017). The side effects of the artemisinins are minor and include nausea, vomiting, persistent cough, and dizziness. Very little is known about the teratogenicity of the artemisinins. They are therefore not recommended for routine use in first trimester pregnancy. This is likely to change soon.
	It was initially thought that the short half-lives of the artemisinins will limit the possibility of resistance development. Recent reports however confirm the emergence of artemisinin resistance in the Southeast Asia region. Artemisinin resistance is now a major global public health concern (Mbengue et al. 2015; Woodrow and White 2017). Derivatives of the artemisinins that are in common use are artesunate, artemether, and arteether.
	Artesunate is a water-soluble ester derivative of the artemisinin. It is used in combination with antimalarials like amodiaquine, sulphadoxine-pyrimethanine and mefloquine in the treatment of uncomplicated malaria. Artesunate in combination therapy is first-line drug for the treatment of uncomplicated malaria in many countries in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. As monotherapy, it is administered intravenously or intramuscularly to treat severe malaria. In a series of clinical trials conducted among Asian and African populations, the superior efficacy of artesunate (compared to quinine and artemether) was established (Dondorp et al. 2005, 2010; Esu et al. 2014). Rectal artesunate is a particularly useful formulation for the home and community-level management of severe malaria in children who are so sick they cannot tolerate oral medications. Where reaching the nearest health facility is likely to be delayed because of remoteness, rectal artesunate has been demonstrated to reduce the risk of death and neurological sequelae in children less than five years of age (Gomes et al. 2009).
	Artemeter is a semi-synthetic, lipid-soluble methyl ether of dihydroartemisinin. When administered intramuscularly, peak plasma concentration is achieved within 6 hours. Artemeter has very rapid schizontocidal activity against blood forms of P. falciparum and P. vivax. It is combined with lumefantrine in the popular antimalarial brand Coartem (Artemeter-Lumefantrine). It is also among the first-line drugs for the management of uncomplicated malaria in most malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Intramuscular injection of Artemeter is used in the treatment of severe malaria.
	Arteether comes in two forms: artemotil and alpha/beta arteether, both of which are given as an intramuscular injection once a day. It is the least commonly used among the artemisinin derivatives.
	Artemisinin-combinations are the most effective antimalarial medicines available today. Five ACTs are currently recommended by WHO for use against P. falciparum malaria. Individual country choice of ACT should be based on the knowledge of the local strains of P. falciparum and ACT efficacy. Unfortunately, artemisinin is produced in small quantities and this leads to a shortage of global supply and increase in price (Peplow 2016; Ikram and Simonsen 2017).





Chloroquine


	Chloroquine is a 4-aminiquinolone that was discovered in 1934 and had over 60 years of widespread use in the treatment of malaria. Chloroquine is administered through oral and intramuscular routes. A bitter taste and itching are its major side effects. Once in the bloodstream however, chloroquine kills asexual forms of the parasite. It has no activity against mature gametocytes and does not have effect on either sporozoites or hypnozoites of Plasmodium vivax. Its terminal elimination half-life is 45–55 days. Its major plasma metabolite desethylchloroquine has a longer half-life of 59–67 days. Chronic use (as in the treatment of skin conditions) can result in retinopathies. Ease of production, monotherapy and sustained presumptive use led to the emergence of parasite resistance which by the late 1990s had surpassed the WHO recommended threshold of 25% in many malaria-endemic countries (Abuaku et al. 2005; Oduro et al. 2005; Takala-Harrison and Laufer 2015).
	The WHO no longer recommends chloroquine for the treatment of malaria in sub-Saharan Africa. It is however retained (in combination with primaquine) for treatment for vivax or ovale malaria in travellers that aim at radical cure. Recent reports however suggest chloroquine efficacy is re-establishing in some areas in sub-Saharan Africa where resistance was initially high, and where chloroquine has not been used for many years (Kublin et al. 2003; Frosch et al. 2014; Galatas et al. 2017; Ndam et al. 2017). It is possible that chloroquine will regain efficacy and be reintroduced for malaria prevention and treatment.





Amodiaquine


	Amodiaquine is a 4-aminoquinolone that is similar in structure and activity to chloroquine. It has been used as an antimalarial since 1948 and remains active against many of the chloroquine-resistance strains of the parasite. It is considered safe for use in post-first trimester pregnancy although tolerability precludes its use in intermittent presumptive treatment (Clerk et al. 2008). In combination with artesunate, amodiaquine is among current first-line drugs for the treatment of malaria in some sub-Saharan African countries. Like chloroquine, amodiaquine can be produced synthetically and is considered an affordable antimalarial. It has a bitter taste and the main side effects are headache, drowsiness, and visual disturbances. Cardiac arrest may occur with overdose (Olliaro and Mussano 2003).





Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine


	This is a combination drug that contains sulfadoxine (a sulfonamide) and pyrimethamine (an antiprotozoal). It has been used for decades in the treatment and prevention of malaria. The combination acts synergistically to inhibitor protozoan folate synthesis. While the sulfadoxine competes with p-aminobenzoic acid, pyrimethamine serves as selective inhibitor of dihydrofolate. For many years sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine was used in the treatment of uncomplicated malaria, and over a brief period in the early 2000s it was used in combination with artesunate for the treatment of uncomplicated malaria in India, and some countries in east and southern Africa. Growing parasite resistance has lowered the efficacy of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa. Currently sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is almost exclusively used in intermittent preventive treatment (IPT) during pregnancy (Owusu-Boateng and Anto 2017). Its use for this indication is however threatened by resistance mutations in the parasite dhps gene. Hypersensitivity can result in Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is synthetically produced and is considered an affordable antimalarial.





Primaquine


	Discovered in 1946, primaquine is an 8-aminoquinoline used in the treatment and prevention of malaria caused by P. vivax and P. ovale. Primaquine is recommended for primary prophylaxis prior to travel to P. vivax-endemic regions. In low transmission settings, a single dose of 0.25 mg/kg body weight of primaquine combined with ACT is recommended to patients with P. falciparum malaria except pregnant women, infants aged less than 6 months and women breastfeeding infants less than 6 months of age. This is intended to reduce the risk of transmission.
	Until recently primaquine was the only antimalarial drug capable of eliminating hypnozoites, the dormant liver form of Plasmodium vivax. It was therefore used to prevent malaria relapse in persons who travel to P. vivax-endemic regions. Primaquine has rapid and potent ability to kill the gametocytes of P. falciparum and P. vivax. In early 2018, the Food and Drugs Agency (FDA) of the United States of America approved Krintafel (tafenoquine), as a single dose antimalarial for radical cure (prevention of relapse) of P. vivax malaria. It is approved for use in patients aged older than 15 years and who are receiving appropriate antimalarial therapy for acute P. vivax infection.
	Primaquine kills gametocytes and because of this, WHO in 2012 recommended that a single dose of 0.25 mg/kg primaquine be added to malaria treatment schedules in areas with artemisinin resistance and where the intent is to stop malaria transmission. The side effects of primaquine include nausea, vomiting, and stomach cramps. Primaquine is contraindicated in persons with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD). In such persons, primaquine cause dose-dependent oxidant haemolysis in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency (Watson et al. 2018). It is similarly for this reason primaquine is contraindicated in pregnant women and lactating mothers. There is synthetic production of primaquine and it is considered an affordable antimalarial. A case report in 2018 has highlighted the important role CYP-4502D6 mutation plays in primaquine treatment failure (Dijanic et al. 2018).





Quinine


	Quinine is a basic amine that was first isolated in 1820 from the bark of a cinchona tree and has remained an effective antimalarial drug to date. Prior to its laboratory isolation, the bark of the cinchona tree was used in the treatment of fever for well over a century. Quinine is hypothesized to act against P. falciparum by interfering with the parasite’s ability to dissolve and metabolize haemoglobin in RBCs. Quinine in its various salts is administered orally, intravenously, and intramuscularly. Until recently, quinine was the drug of choice for the treatment of severe and complicated malaria. Although it remains among drugs listed in many national guidelines for the management of severe malaria, intramuscular artemether, intravenous and intramuscular artesunate are preferred (see next). The common side effects of quinine are headache, palpation, nausea, tinnitus, hearing impairment, dizziness, blurred vision, and disturbance in colour perception. An important side effect of intravenously administered quinine is the risk of hypoglycaemia. Quinine toxicity can lead to cardiac arrest. Although quinine can be synthetically produced, the cinchona tree remains the most economically-viable source of it (Shanks 2016; Gachelin et al. 2017).





Treatment of malaria during pregnancy


	Except in the first trimester, the drugs recommended for use in malaria in non-pregnancy adults can also be use pregnant women. This includes artemisinin-based derivatives. The use of the artemisinin-based derivatives in the first trimester however remains restricted to situations where the benefits of its use outweighs the risk or where safer options are not available. There are increasing calls on WHO to reverse the current restriction and recommend the use of artemisinin derivatives for the treatment of malaria during the first trimester (Moore et al. 2016). The antimalarial medicines considered safe in the first trimester of pregnancy are quinine, chloroquine, clindamycin, and proguanil. WHO recommends the combination of oral quinine and clindamycin for the treatment of malaria in the first trimester of pregnancy (Table 8.15.2).

Vector control


	An important part of malaria control involves killing the mosquitoes and or destroying breeding sites. This approach is referred to as vector control. Vector control interventions that have proven to be efficacious and are in common use are sleeping under an insecticide-treated net (ITNs) and in-door residual spraying (IRS). Both interventions rely on the use of chemical insecticides (Alonso et al. 2011; Williams et al. 2018).





Insecticide-treated nets


	Investigation into the efficacy of ITNs began in the late 1980s and early 1990s with series of studies in different parts of sub-Saharan Africa that assessed the effect of ITN use on morbidity and all-cause child mortality. ITN use has been demonstrated to reduce overall childhood mortality by between 17 and 33% (Alonso et al. 1991; D’Alessandro et al. 1995; Binka et al. 1996; Nevill et al. 1996; Habluetzel et al. 1997; Lengeler et al. 1998; Phillips-Howard et al. 2003; Binka and Akweongo 2006). The use of ITNs was subsequently shown to provide community-wide protection by reducing the number of infective mosquitoes in the vicinity where ITNs are used (Binka et al. 1998).
	An important basis for the development of ITNs was the fact that most biting by the vector mosquitoes occurred at hours of the night when most people were in bed. The peak-biting activity of Plasmodium-transmitting mosquitoes in sub-Saharan Africa was known to be between 22.00 hrs and 05.00 hrs. Sleeping under an ITN therefore reduced the risk of bite and enhanced the killing of mosquitoes that are likely to transmit parasites. At about the mid-2000s however, evidence emerged of change in the biting pattern of Anopheles funestus following massive deployment of long-lasting insecticide nets (LLINs). Evidence is now firmly established, and this adaptive behaviour of the vector now poses a challenge to the use of ITN in malaria vector control and elimination.
	Notwithstanding the aforementioned, sleeping under an ITN remains one of the most cost-effective interventions in malaria control. In rural northern Ghana, the estimated cost per discounted healthy life-year gained is US $73.5 (Binka et al. 1997). In other areas, the cost per death averted could be as high as US $1,449 (Yukich et al. 2009).
	To promote widespread use of ITNs, free distribution is undertaken in several endemic countries. Between 2014 and 2016, a total of 582 million ITNs (505 million in sub-Saharan Africa) were delivered by manufacturers globally. In Africa 75% of ITNs were distributed through mass distribution campaigns. Household ownership of at least one ITN has increased from 50% in 2010 to 80% in 2016. More people at risk of malaria in Africa are sleeping under an ITN. In 2016, 54% of the population was protected by this intervention, an increase from 30% in 2010 (WHO 2018a). The scale-up in the distribution of ITNs is reported to account for the substantial reduction in malaria transmission, and related morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa (Bhatt et al. 2015).
	Two major challenges confront the continued effectiveness of ITN use in malaria control. First is the emerging gap between ITN possession and use (Lengeler and Snow 1996). In rural northern Ghana, ITN use is found to depend on cost and time of the year (Binka and Adongo 1997). Free mass distribution of ITNs has overcome the problem of cost in many places and has led to high levels of household possession though there is still inadequate access to ITNs even in the household with these ITNs. These high levels of possession are however not matched with usage (Doda et al. 2018).
	A second major challenge is the spread of insecticide resistance to the chemicals used to impregnate nets (Ranson and Lissenden 2016; Kisinza et al. 2017; Rakotoson et al. 2017). Pyrethroids are the most commonly used insecticides. Resistance to pyrethroids is now widespread in An. Gambiae and An. Funestus mosquitoes, the major malaria vectors. A breakthrough in efforts to overcome ITN insecticide resistance was recently reported in a trial led by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. The trial involved 15,000 children in Tanzania and it found that compared with nets impregnated with pyrethroid, nets impregnated with piperonyl butoxide reduced malaria infections by 44% (Protopopoff et al. 2018). This finding has prompted WHO to revise its recommendations on ITN production and use. It now recommends the use of nets sprayed with piperonyl butoxide in areas in Africa where mosquitoes are pyrethroid-resistant. A trial that is evaluating the effects of using combinations of nets in currently underway in Burkina Faso.





Indoor residual spraying


	IRS is one of the oldest interventions in malaria control and elimination. Literally put, it is a ‘recycled’ and ‘repackaged’ malaria control intervention. With dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) as insecticide, IRS was the principal method by which malaria was eliminated in many countries between the 1940s and 1960s. An estimated 700 million people mainly in Europe, Asia and Latin America were freed of the risk of malaria within a 20-year period (Mabaso et al. 2004; Africa WHOROf 2007). IRS involves spraying the inside walls of dwellings with insecticides. The technical basis is that the inner walls of dwellings retain doses of insecticide that are sufficiently lethal to kill mosquito that rest on these walls.
	In the years that followed the WHO-led efforts in the 1940s through the 1960s, IRS got used sparingly amid concerns that DDT use in sub-Saharan Africa would cause damage to ecology and poisoning within the food chain. Eventually DDT was banned from use as an IRS insecticide. The development of pyrethroids as alternative re-ignited interest in IRS but this was short-lived as insecticide resistance reduced effectiveness. An epidemic of malaria in South Africa in 1999–2000 however compelled authorities in the country to obtain international exemption to use DDT in an IRS-based malaria elimination programme. The success of this programme re-ignited interest in the use of IRS and DDT in countries in the southern Africa region (Mabaso et al. 2004; Channa et al. 2012a, 2012b). Insecticides that are currently being used in IRS include DDT, pyrethroids (lambdacyahlothrin, deltamethrin, alphacypermethrin), organophosphates (malathion, pirimiphosmethyl) and carbamates (bendiocarb). In the southern Africa Region DDT remains effective and populations-at-risk in Botswana, Namibia, South Africa, and Swaziland are being protected with this intervention (Smith Gueye et al. 2016a, 2016b). Resistance to cheaper insecticides and the need to shift to more expensive chemicals is slowing IRS implementation in the rest of sub-Saharan Africa (WHO 2018a). According to the 2018 World Malaria Report, IRS protection declined from a peak of 5% in 2010 to 3% in 2017, with decreases seen across all WHO regions. In the WHO African Region, coverage dropped from 80 million people at risk in 2010 to 45 million in 2016 (WHO 2018a). The intervention is also particularly popular with households because it can be disruptive of normal life.





Larval source management


	Larval source management (LSM) refers to the targeted management of mosquito breeding sites, with the objective of reducing the number of mosquito larvae and pupae. It is considered by WHO to be a supplementary measure in malaria vector control. The four types of LSM are:
	 	• Habitat modification, i.e. permanent alteration to the environment, e.g. land reclamation;
	• Habitat manipulation, i.e. a recurrent activity, e.g. flushing of streams;
	• Larviciding: the regular application of biological or chemical insecticides to water bodies;
	• Biological control: the introduction of natural predators into water bodies.
	For reason that are not always clear, LSM receives very little mention in global malaria control and elimination. This is even though LSM was a major intervention in malaria eradication efforts in southern Europe in the early 1970s, Cuba, other parts of Latin America and parts of north Africa. Its effectiveness has been demonstrated in areas in Africa where it has been well-implemented. In 2009, the Governments of Cuba and Venezuela entered into agreement with countries in the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), to expand larviciding activities through the provision of financial technical support, including the establishment of African based factories for larviciding products (Newman et al. 2013). Beyond the current efforts spearheaded by Cuba, there appears to be very little global interest in the implementation of LSM. There is only one mention of LSM in the 2018 World Malaria Report.





Chemoprophylaxis


	Antimalarials play an important role in malaria control when they are used in chemoprophylaxis. This is targeted at the most vulnerable including non-immune travellers to malaria-endemic countries. Current major interventions in this regard are intermittent preventive treatment in pregnant women (IPTp) and seasonal malaria chemoprophylaxis (SMC).





Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy


	The risk malaria poses to mother and child during pregnancy has always been appreciated and chemoprophylaxis has been part of the management of pregnancies in endemic countries for many years. In the era when chloroquine was effective, weekly subtherapeutic doses was recommended to prevent malaria during pregnancy (Geelhoed et al. 2001). The mass presumptive use of subtherapeutic doses and limited adherence contributed to parasite resistance to chloroquine.
	Trials conducted in the late 1990s to early 2000 to explore alternative drugs led to the choice of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP). In clinical trials, the use of SP in IPTp reduced the risk of moderate-to-severe anaemia, antenatal parasitaemia, placental parasitaemia, spontaneous abortions and low birthweight by 40%, 62%, 55%, 39%, and 19%, respectively (Wilson et al. 2011; Desai et al. 2018). Currently WHO recommends that in areas of moderate-to-high malaria transmission, IPTp with SP is given to all pregnant women at each scheduled antenatal care visit after the first trimester. The first IPTp-SP dose should be administered as early as 13 weeks’ gestation and each subsequent dose should be at least one month apart. The last dose may be administered up to the time of delivery (WHO 2015b).
	Logistic and other reasons continue to hamper effective implementation of ITPp-SP in many countries in sub-Saharan Africa. According to the 2018 World Malaria Report, an estimated 22% of eligible pregnant women received the recommended three or more doses of IPTp in 2017. This was up from 17% in 2015, 19% in 2016, and 0% in 2010. Coverage varies considerably by country. It is only Zambia that has coverage of the third ITPp dose (IPTp3) was 50% or more as at 2017 (WHO 2018a).
	With continued concern about parasite resistance to SP, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine looks the most promising as potential alternative or replacement antimalarial. Trials have demonstrated that it is well tolerated, effective, and acceptable, although it is also vulnerable to development of artemisinin resistance (Chico and Moss 2015; Kakuru et al. 2016; Tarning 2016; Rogerson et al. 2018).





Seasonal malaria chemoprevention


	In many parts of the world where malaria is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, transmission is highly seasonal. This pattern offers the opportunity to implement interventions that are targeted at the time of the year when incidence of malaria is highest. This principle underlines SMC. This is an intervention in malaria control where young children are provided with a treatment course of an effective antimalarial combination at monthly intervals for 3 or 4 months during the peak period of malaria transmission.
	In clinical trials, this approach reduced the incidence of uncomplicated malaria by 82% and of severe malaria by 82%. The WHO in 2012 recommended that SMC with SP and amodiaquine (AQ) be used in children aged ages 3–59 months in areas of sub-Saharan Africa where malaria transmission is highly seasonal, and parasites are sensitive to these drugs (Cairns et al. 2012; Matangila et al. 2015; Coldiron et al. 2017; Greenwood 2017) (Fig. 8.15.3). There is growing evidence of the need to extend this intervention to older children due to the benefits being shown in that particular age group and the observed increasing burden of malaria in children older than 5 years. A similar principle has been proposed for the deployment of malaria vaccines that have high initial efficacy, but which provide only a short period of protection. An ongoing trial in Burkina Faso and Mali is exploring this hypothesis (Greenwood 2017; Greenwood et al. 2017).





Intermittent preventive treatment in infants


	Intermittent preventive Treatment for Infants (IPTi) is the administration of a full therapeutic course of SP delivered through the Expanded Programme on Immunization at defined intervals corresponding to immunization schedules (usually at 10 weeks, 14 weeks, and nine months of age) to infants at risk of falciparum malaria in areas of high-to-medium transmission (Gosling et al. 2009).
	IPTi reduces clinical malaria, anaemia, and severe malaria in the first year of life. Despite WHO recommending IPTi in 2009, only Sierra Leone has incorporated it into policy and implemented the intervention; albeit on a limited scale.
	Fig. 8.15.3 A map of sub-Saharan Africa showing the areas where malaria transmission is likely to be highly seasonal.
	Reprinted from Greenwood B. et al (2017) ‘Seasonal vaccination against malaria: a potential use for an imperfect malaria vaccine’. Malar. J. 18(162) under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0).





Mass drug administration


	Mass drug administration (MDA) consists in the administration of a full dose of antimalarial treatment, irrespective of the knowledge of symptoms or presence of infection, to an entire population in a given area, except those in whom the medicine is contraindicated. In the context of transmission reduction, MDA aims to provide therapeutic concentrations of antimalarial drugs to as large a proportion of the population as possible in order to cure asymptomatic infections and to prevent re-infection during the period of post-treatment prophylaxis. To impact on transmission, MDA requires high coverage of the target population which, in turn, demands a high level of community participation and engagement.
	MDA has played an important role in the control and elimination of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) such as trachoma, lymphatic filariasis, and onchocerciasis. WHO recommends MDA to achieve the following: (1) Interrupt falciparum malaria transmission in areas where elimination is the target; (2) To reduce the risk for spread of multidrug resistance in the Greater Mekong area; (3) Reduction in malaria burden during malaria epidemics and exceptional complex emergencies. Examples of exceptional complex emergencies was the MDA undertaken during the Ebola outbreak in West Africa (2014–2016) and the outbreak that followed in the Democratic Republic of Congo.





Malaria and travel medicine


	There are 91 countries where international travellers may be at risk of malaria (WHO 2018a). For non-immune travellers to tropical regions, the risk of malaria is an ever-present danger. Non-immune here refers to persons who are ordinarily resident in temperate, non-malaria-endemic countries. Persons who were originally resident in malaria-endemic countries but have travelled and stayed out in a non-endemic country for more than six months are also considered as non-immune. For such persons, little or no immunity exist against malaria and they are at risk of malaria developing in the very severe forms. The disease can take a rapidly deteriorating course and may develop into cerebral malaria with a few hours to a day.
	Non-immune travellers to tropical countries need to seek expert advice. They may be required to begin antimalarial chemoprophylaxis while at their countries of origin, continue during the period of stay in the tropical region and then for a period when they are back to their countries of regular residence. Malarone, containing atovaquone and proguanil is one of the most commonly used antimalarial prophylaxis. Other antimalarials used in antimalarial prophylaxis are mefloquine and doxycycline. An emerging alternative to malaria chemoprophylaxis is ‘standby emergency treatment’ (SBET). This consist of providing travellers with emergency malaria treatment for self-administration in case of fever when no medical attention is available, or eventually for use under medical supervision after a confirmed malaria diagnosis (Genton and D’Acremont 2017).
	As much as feasible pregnant women and children aged less than 5 years should put off non-essential travel to malaria-transmission areas. Where travel is unavoidable, appropriate advice should be sought on the best forms of malaria protection and chemoprophylaxis before, during and after travel (Irvine et al. 2011). This includes avoiding mosquito bites through the use of ITNs, protective clothes, and mosquito repellents.





Malaria vaccines


	The current highly invigorated efforts to control, eliminate, and possibly eradicate malaria will have a greater likelihood of success if an effective vaccine were to become available to complement other interventions. The anticipation that this will be achieved has never been greater as gene technology is leading to identification of more target plasmodium antigens. The three main mechanisms being explored in malaria vaccine development are: (1) anti-infection; (2) transmission-blocking; and (3) antidisease. The most advanced malaria vaccine to date is the anti-infection RTS,S/AS01 vaccine developed by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK).





RTS,S/AS01 vaccine


	The RTS,S/AS01 vaccine is an example of an anti-infective mechanism in malaria vaccine development. It is a monovalent recombinant protein vaccine that targets a fragment of the circumsporozoite protein parasite antigen. It has been evaluated in large phase 3 trials in 11 sites across Africa. These trials took place between 2009 and 2013 and showed the vaccine to offer partial protection against clinical malaria in the older age group (5–17 months). Efficacy in children who received three doses plus a booster on months 0, 1, 2, and 20 was 36.3% between month 0 and study end (median 48 months per child). This was a decline from 50.4% achieved 14 months from the first dose. No significant efficacy against severe malaria was noted in the 6–12 week age group; not even with a booster over the duration of the trial (Moorthy and Okwo-Bele 2015; Rts 2015). The RTS,S/AS01 vaccine has received a positive scientific opinion from the European Medicines Agency in July 2015 and WHO has recommended limited, pilot deployment in Ghana, Kenya, and Malawi. The deployment is being undertaken under the banner of the Malaria Vaccine Implementation Programme (MVIP) and is targeted at children who are at least 5 months of age. The objective is to assess the feasibility of administering the needed four doses of the vaccine in children, and whether administrative will be safe and effective in reducing the incidence of malaria among vaccinated populations. The programmes in Malawi and Ghana were launched in April 2019.





Transmission-blocking vaccines (TBV)


	TBV are designed to target the sexual stages of parasite development in the mosquito. They utilize antigens expressed by gametocytes, gametes, zygotes and ookinetes to induce antibodies capable of attacking the parasite in the mosquito and impairing its viability and further development. TBVs that have reached human trials include Pfs25 and its Plasmodium vivax ortholog Pvs25, and Pfs230 (Ogobara et al. 2018).
	The antigen Pfs25 has been the most evaluated. It is made up of a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-linked protein which is expressed on the surface of ookinetes. Its configuration is complex and eluding full elucidation. An improved understanding of the structural conformation of the antigen and the finding of a good matching adjuvants will likely make Pfs25 and other TBVs important additions to existing tools for malaria elimination and eradication.





Pre-erythrocytic vaccines


	Pre-erythrocytic vaccines target the sporozoite and liver stages of Plasmodium and are designed to prevent disease and interrupt transmission. The leading approach in this mechanism is the vaccination using whole sporozoites which are genetically attenuated parasites, radiation attenuated sporozoites, and/or wild-type sporozoites administered in combination with chemoprophylaxis. The principle of immune response following vaccination with whole sporozoites have been established (Coelho et al. 2017). As with the TBVs, the principal challenge is improving upon the level of immune response that is induced.
	The PfSPZ is a non-replicating irradiated whole sporozoite vaccine which has entered human trials. In Mali, it proved to be efficacious against naturally transmitted parasites. A phase 3 programme is currently being developed.
	It has been proposed that an imperfect malaria vaccine may still be useful if used in seasonal vaccination against malaria (Greenwood et al. 2017). While the findings of the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine moves the world closer to the goal of an effective enough malaria vaccine, the rapid waning of immunity and the lack of effect in children aged 6–12 weeks proved that it did not get the human immune system to do more than it will naturally do. Proving the principle is nevertheless a significant breakthrough and there is optimism that the world is not too far away from achieving the target of a truly effective and practical malaria vaccine.





Surveillance


	Public health surveillance is the continuous, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health-related data needed for the planning, implementation, and evaluation of public health practice. An effective surveillance aims to achieve the following:
	 	• Provide early warning for impending public health emergencies;
	• Benchmark set goals and track progress in the outcome of intervention(s); and
	• Accurately define the epidemiology of the health problem to enable priority-setting and informed public health policy and strategies.
	The Global Technical Strategy (GTS) for Malaria 2016–2030 emphasizes the need for universal coverage of core malaria interventions for all populations at risk and highlights the importance of using high-quality surveillance data for decision-making. Surveillance is one of the three pillars of the GTS for Malaria 2016–2030, transformed from a routine activity of the health system into a core intervention in all settings of malaria endemicity. The new 12 core principles of malaria surveillance are:
	 	• Accurate parasitological diagnosis of a malaria case should be the foundation of a malaria surveillance system.
	• Major components of a malaria surveillance system should be integrated within routine health management information systems (HMIS).
	• National standard operating procedures should be based on country needs and WHO recommendations.
	• Front-line staff involved in the detection, recording, and reporting of cases should be the first users of data from the malaria surveillance system.
	• Surveillance systems should address the within-country heterogeneity of malaria.
	• Necessary investments in surveillance and system transition in response to changing malaria burden should be made.
	• All malaria surveillance data should be linked to a decision at appropriate levels in the health system.
	• Concerted effort should be made to include data from all sectors, including the private sector.
	• Malaria surveillance may become the broad responsibility of general health services following the interruption of transmission. Malaria programme surveillance systems should however be supported to ensure monitoring.
	• Innovation and advances in technology should be incorporated in malaria surveillance based on empirical evidence of additional benefits, cost, and sustainability.
	• Malaria surveillance should incorporate regular monitoring of the efficacy of antimalarial drugs used in treatment.
	• Malaria surveillance systems should be assessed routinely for accuracy, reliability, completeness, precision, timeliness, integrity, and actions taken based on the results of surveillance.
	The sources of data for malaria surveillance are be routine (health facility based and/or community based) or sentinel sites. Cases can be identified through an active or passive approach. The intensity of either or a mix of both is determined by the malaria transmission setting. Active approaches are increasingly adopted as transmission levels decline.
	A set of 46 indicators have been recommended. These indicators consider varying levels of resources availability for malaria control (programme financing, commodities), levels of service provision (intervention coverage), performance of systems for surveillance, monitoring, and evaluation; and trends in transmission, infection, and disease. Twelve (one for input, six for outcome, and five for impact) out of the 46 indicators are regarded as core. These are outlined in Table 8.15.3.
	With surveillance a core malaria intervention, WHO in March 2018 published a thoroughly detailed reference manual for malaria surveillance, monitoring, and evaluation. This manual addresses the evidence-base for making malaria surveillance a core intervention, how malaria surveillance systems should be established, new concepts and practices of malaria surveillance, surveillance for antimalarial drug efficacy and drug resistance, approaches to entomological surveillance, and vector control monitoring and evaluation. It also addressed issues of malaria early warning, detection, and response to outbreaks, monitoring, and evaluation of national programmes. This manual is a highly-recommended text for all health professionals whose work impact the continuum of malaria control through elimination (WHO 2018b).
