Measures of malaria frequency


	The number of malaria cases per at-risk population (incidence) and the proportion of a population carrying malaria parasite in the blood (prevalence) are the most commonly used proxy indicators of the intensity of malaria endemicity. The advantage these two indicators have over other indicators are that they are relatively simple to compute and inexpensive to determine, and report within a short time. The input for the two indicators can be obtained from routine health information systems and population-based surveys. For reasons elaborated further in this section, both indicators are imprecise measures of malaria transmission (Oduro et al. 2011, 2016).





Incidence of malaria


	Although absolute numbers of malaria cases, inpatients and deaths can be used to estimate trends over time and to identify places in which the problem of malaria is greatest, these are less useful for assessing which populations are at highest risk for acquiring malaria because of different population sizes. Incidence of malaria gives indication of risk of acquiring malaria and it is given by dividing the number of new cases of malaria over a given period by the population at risk. The ascertainment of both measures has challenges in most malaria-endemic countries.
	Coverage in diagnostic testing is still not universal and, in many places, there is a considerable mix of confirmed and unconfirmed cases counted among malaria cases. It is not always clear from routine health service records the number of cases of confirmed malaria and what proportion of unconfirmed cases could be estimated to be truly malaria. Another challenge is the so-called iceberg phenomenon. Access to health facilities remains a challenge in many rural and urban communities in malaria-endemic countries. Access is often limited by financial, geographical, and cultural constraints and only a fraction of people who fall sick seek care from health facilities. Health service data that are used to compute the incidence of malaria therefore tends to be biased towards underestimating the risk of disease.
	To determine the population that is risk, WHO recommends the use of estimates of population size published by a relevant government department such as a statistics office, planning bureau, or census office. However, the breakdown in vital registration and the lack of systems for continuously tracking populations makes it difficult to report with certainty that figures obtained from such official sources truly represent at-risk populations. Despite these limitation, incidence of malaria when applied over a reasonable length of time and over large populations gives an accurate measure of the magnitude of risk of infection. Trend data also conveys a strong enough impression of the direction of risk.





Prevalence of malaria


	The second measure of malaria frequency that is readily determined is the prevalence of parasitaemia in the population. Traditionally this represents the proportion of children aged 2–10 years who are found to have malaria parasites in their blood during surveys. National malaria programmes routinely use this to monitor the effect of interventions. The procedures have been incorporated into various demographic and health surveys, multiple indicators clusters surveys, and malaria indicator surveys. The determination of parasitemia is made at point-of-interview by trained, unskilled field workers, and the availability of mRDTs has made the procedures less cumbersome and less sophisticated.
	A challenge with survey-determined malaria prevalence however is that it fails to adequately measure transmission and the burden of disease. In many high malaria transmission settings, a large proportion of children carry malaria parasites in their blood without being ill (White 2017). This phenomenon makes imprecise inferences between levels of parasitaemia and risk of disease. Another challenge is the inherent limitation in the use of mRDTs. The persistence of HRP2 antigen in the blood similarly undermines any inference that a positive mRDT connote risk of malaria. There have been attempts to establish modelling-based link between prevalence and infection rates. However, differences in model structure and calibration data has meant that no consensus yet exists on the optimal application in disease-burden estimation (Patil et al. 2009). With these caveats, the ease of application and ability to establish a trend through year-on-year consistency in procedures make the determination of parasite prevalence an attractive and pragmatic proxy measure of endemicity and impact of interventions.





Entomological surveillance indicators


	The main entomological indicators are categorized into five groups:
	 	• Adult vector composition (species occurrence and density);
	• Adult vector behaviour (human blood index, human biting rate, biting time, biting location, resting location);
	• Adult vector resistance to insecticides (resistance frequency, status, intensity, and mechanisms);
	• Immature vector aquatic habitats (habitat availability and occupancy, larval density); and
	• Proxies for transmission (sporozoite rate, entomological inoculation rate (EIR), receptivity).
	Two key indicators with direct implication on malaria transmission are the EIR and vectorial capacity.





Entomological inoculation rate


	The most direct measure of malaria transmission is the EIR. The EIR measures the average number of infectious bites that a person receives per year in a specified population. To compute it, two parameters need to be established. These are the human landing rate (HLR) and sporozoite carriage rate. Determining the HLR involves an elaborate process of capturing all mosquitoes that land on a person (human biting rate) throughout the night and expressing this per person per night. All captured mosquitoes are sent to the laboratory where the salivary glands of each is dissected to determine the proportion of mosquitoes that carry sporozoites (sporozoite rate—SR) (Morrow and Moss 2017). The EIR is the arithmetic product of HLR and SR. The process of determining the EIR in a given location is expensive and technically demanding. It is therefore not part of routine malaria surveillance in endemic countries. Often EIRs are only available in the context of research, or specific well-funded programmes. The day-biting characteristics of some species of the vector is becoming an increasing problem.





Vectorial capacity


	Vectorial capacity (VC) is another basic indicator of malaria transmission. It is the number of new infections that the population of a given vector would induce per case per day at a given place and time, if the human population is and remains fully susceptible to malaria. It measures the rate of potentially infective contact and depends on mosquito longevity and susceptibility to Plasmodium infection.
	It is critical for malaria transmission for the female Anopheles mosquito to live long enough to enable the sporogonic phase of the life cycle of the Plasmodium parasite to be completed and for sporozoites to be injected during a blood meal. Like EIR, VC provides a good measure of malaria transmission, but it is very technical to compute and therefore not routinely used.





Gametocytes carriage and its implications


	The gametocyte is the stage in the life cycle of the Plasmodium parasite that is infective to the mosquito. Gametocytes are therefore vital to malaria transmission. However, because gametocyte carriage is asymptomatic (may be symptomatic in P. vivax malaria), this stage of arrested development in humans serves as reservoir for sustained malaria infection and re-infection. Developing antimalarial drugs that target gametocytes is an important part of the agenda to eliminate malaria. Of recent interest is the gametocidal activity role of methylene blue (Lu et al. 2018). Adding a single dose of 0·25 mg/kg primaquine to amodiaquine and SP or 3 days of 15 mg/kg per day methylene blue to dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine has been found to prevent P. falciparum transmission (Dicko et al. 2018). The ‘tolerant’ existence of the gametocyte stage in human provides insight into how natural immunity evolves in malaria. It has been hypothesized that some level of gametocytaemia is required to sustain natural immunity (Stone et al. 2018).





Control, elimination, and eradication: the continuum


	There are four distinct phases in the path towards country and global malaria-free status. These are control, pre-elimination, elimination, and prevention of reintroduction. A well-detailed process exists at WHO to define countries or regions as having transited from one phase into the other. This calls for clear, correct, and uniform use of the related descriptive terms. These have been supplied by WHO as follows:
	Control: This is the reduction of disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity, or mortality to a locally acceptable level as a result of deliberate efforts. Continued intervention is required to sustain control.
	Elimination: It is the interruption of local transmission (that is, reducing the rate of malaria cases to zero) of a specified parasite in a defined geographic area. Continued measures are required to prevent the re-establishment of transmission.
	Eradication: It is the permanent reduction to zero of the worldwide incidences of infection caused by human malaria parasites as a result of deliberate efforts. Once eradication has been achieved, intervention measures would no longer be needed. The interchangeable use of the terms, elimination and eradication is no longer acceptable.





Malaria elimination


	In 2016, WHO identified 21 countries (so-called E-2020 countries) with the potential to eliminate malaria by the year 2020 (Table 8.15.4). By 2018, 11 of these countries remained on track to achieve their elimination goals, while 10 had reported increases in indigenous malaria cases in 2017. Globally however the elimination net keeps widening, with more countries moving towards zero indigenous cases. In 2017, 46 countries reported fewer than 10,000 such cases, up from 44 countries in 2016 and 37 countries in 2010. Between 2016 and mid-2019, the WHO Europe region, Paraguay, Algeria, and Argentina have been certified as malaria-free.

Certification


	This is the WHO certification of a country as malaria-free. This certification is granted when local transmission of malaria by Anopheles mosquitoes has been halted for at least three consecutive years and an adequate system for preventing re-establishment of the disease has been established. The process of certification is managed at WHO by the Global Malaria Programme. It is a process that countries voluntarily submit to through application and providing the necessary proof. It is the WHO Director-General who grants the certification of malaria elimination (WHO 2016).





Malaria eradication


	Over the past few years, discussions about malaria on the global scale has been dominated by issues related elimination and possible eradication, and what it would take to achieve this feat. For many years after the failed attempt of the 1960s, the eradication of malaria was considered technically impossible. Of recent however, and particularly after the American billionaire-philanthropist Bill Gates declared eradication as a target of his foundation’s malaria programme, a surge in momentum has brought back malaria eradication on the global agenda (Star 2015). Discussions have dramatically shifted from a blanket declaration of non-feasibility to which tools, if available, could make this target achievable. There is also a roll-back to an aspiration that malaria eradication can be achieved through elimination of the disease, country-by-country, region-by-region. This aspiration is given impetus in the vision of the GTS for Malaria 2016–2030, ‘World-Free of Malaria’. The strategy targets elimination of malaria in 10, 20, and 35 countries by 2020, 2025, and 2030, respectively (WHO 2015c).
	The Malaria Eradication Research Agenda (malERA) initiative has brought together some of the world’s best malariologists to design a path in malaria research that is targeted at eradication. In the opinion of this group, malaria eradication is not feasible with current tools and state of knowledge (Alonso et al. 2011; Drugs mCGo 2011; Strategies mCGoI 2011). Among others, they advocate the need for drugs with the capacity to achieve Single Encounter Radical Cure and Prophylaxis (SERCaP). The target product profile (TPP) of such a drug should include radical cure, defined as elimination of all parasites (including the long-lived hypnozoites of P. vivax or P. ovale in the liver), suitability for mass administration (including administration to healthy subjects and the subsequent need of a very good safety profile), and prophylaxis for at least 1 month after treatment, to outlast the typical development period of Plasmodia parasites in anopheline mosquitoes. There is also the need to develop vaccines that will reduce and contribute to interruption of transmission, so-called TBVs. The vaccines in current development do not meet this standard as they aim at reducing morbidity and mortality, and not at blocking transmission (Drugs mCGo 2011; Vaccines mCGo 2011). To address in-country heterogenicity as the incidence of malaria declines will required new well-targeted tools for control and surveillance (Greenwood and Targett 2011). The drive towards malaria eradication is further buoyed by the formation of the Lancet Commission on Malaria Eradication in April 2018. This is a Commission of 24 experts from around the world, put together to develop a roadmap for malaria eradication (Chen et al. 2018).





Less-used terminologies


	For many years, four levels of classification are used to describe malaria endemicity. These are holoendemic, hyperendemic, mesoendemic, and hypoendemic (coinciding with reducing levels of intensity and EIRs). Neither the 2018 World Malaria Report nor the WHO manual on malaria surveillance refers to this approach to classification. Currently, these terminologies are so much less-used that they are best to be avoided.





Global programme and strategy


Global Malaria Programme


	The Global Malaria Programme (GMP) is WHO’s lead agency in the fight against malaria. It is responsible for coordinating global efforts to control and eliminate malaria. The GMP supports Member States to achieve the GTS targets through:
	 	• Setting and disseminating global guidance and policies on malaria control and elimination;
	• Supporting countries as they adapt, adopt, and implement WHO global norms and standards for malaria control and elimination;
	• Assisting countries as they formulate national malaria strategic plans;
	• Helping countries develop robust malaria surveillance systems;
	• Responding to requests from countries to address biological and operational emergencies and bottleneck issues.
	The GMP publishes the World Malaria Report each year. This is the most comprehensive report on the status of malaria in the world. It provides global and, country-by-country account of progress made to achieve set global targets. The GMP also produces a newsletter every two months that highlight latest news and developments in the work of the GMP. Subscription is available at https://www.who.int/malaria/news/sign_up_form/en/





Malaria Policy Advisory Committee


	The Malaria Policy Advisory Committee (MPAC) was established in 2011 following an extensive review of the policy-setting process for malaria control and elimination, initiated by the WHO GMP (D’Souza and Newman 2012). It provides independent strategic advice to WHO on the following:
	 	• Appropriate malaria policies and standards based on data from malaria programme implementation by Member States and malaria control partners as well as reviews of the best available evidence;
	• Engagement of WHO in malaria-related initiatives;
	• Major issues and challenges to achieving global malaria goals; and
	• The identification of priority activities to address identified challenges.
	The MPAC convenes twice a year in Geneva and is made of some of the world’s foremost experts on malaria. It is supported by the GMP Guidelines Development Group and ad hoc Evidence Review Groups which support the policy making process. Among important policy and initiatives over which the MPAC has had profound influence has been those related to updated policy recommendations on the use of sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine for ITPp, as well as the use of single dose primaquine as a Plasmodium falciparum gametocytocide. It is on the recommendation of the MPAC that the current limited deployment of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine has been implemented in Ghana, Kenya, and Malawi.





GTS for Malaria 2016–2030


	The GTS for Malaria 2016–2030 is a document produced by the GMP and adopted by the World Health Assembly in May 2015. It provides a comprehensive framework to guide countries and agencies in efforts to accelerate progress towards malaria elimination. The strategy has set the most ambitious targets for reductions in malaria cases and deaths since the malaria eradication era began. (Table 8.15.5) The timeline of 2016–2030 is aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, endorsed in 2015 by all United Nations Member States. The path towards achieving these targets are anchored on three pillars and two supporting elements. The pillars are
	 	• Pillar 1. Ensure universal access to malaria prevention, diagnosis, and treatment
	• Pillar 2. Accelerate efforts towards elimination and attainment of malaria-free status
	• Pillar 3. Transform malaria surveillance into a core intervention
	The two supporting elements of the GTS are (1) innovation and research and (2) a strong enabling environment.

8.16


Viral alcoholic and fatty liver diseases


	Ehud Zigmond and Daniel Shouval





Introduction


	The burden of liver diseases continues to rise worldwide. The aetiology of acute and chronic liver disease (CLD) varies among continents. Viral hepatitis B and C comprise the main causes for CLD in Africa and Asia, while alcoholic and nonalcoholic fatty liver diseases (NAFLDs) dominate in Europe and the United states. However, the ongoing wave of immigrants from Asia and Africa towards European countries is expected to have an impact on the epidemiology of these liver diseases worldwide. Prevalence and mortality data suggest that the increasing numbers of patients with cirrhosis and HCC in Europe, the US, Africa and East Asia are linked to increase in alcohol consumption and fatty liver disease (in the Western hemisphere) and to chronic viral hepatitis C and B in Asia and Africa (El-Serag and Kanwal 2014; Gower et al. 2014; Beste et al. 2015; Pimpin et al. 2018; Williams et al. 2018). In the present chapter we will present the evolving information on the epidemiology, natural history, prevention, and treatment of these selected liver diseases.





Hepatitis B


Aetiologic agent


	Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a double-stranded, enveloped virus of the Hepadnaviridae family.
	The hepatitis B virion consists of a surface and a core, which contains a DNA polymerase and the e antigen. The ~3,200 bp DNA structure is double-stranded and circular with four major genes: the S (surface), the C (core), the P (polymerase), and the X (transcriptional transactivating)genes. The S gene consists of three regions: S, pre-S2, and pre-S1—that encode the small, middle, and large envelope proteins called in total the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). HBsAg is a lipoprotein of the viral envelope that circulates in the blood as spherical and tubular particles. The C gene is divided into two regions, the pre-core and the core, and codes for two different proteins, the core antigen (HBcAg) and the e antigen (HBeAg).
	HBV strains are classified into ten genotypes designated A to J, based on divergence in nucleotide sequences of >8%, most of which have a characteristic geographical distribution (Cao 2009; Tanwar and Dusheiko 2012; Sunbul 2014). E.g. genotype A is highly prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa, Northern Europe, and Western Africa. Genotypes B and C are the major variants in South and South East Asia and the Pacific region. Genotype D is prevalent in Africa, Europe, the Mediterranean region, and India. Genotype E is restricted to West Africa. Genotype F is found in Central and South America. Genotype G has been reported in France, Germany, and the United States and genotype H is found in Central America (Kurbanov et al. 2010; Lin and Kao 2011). Genotypes A, B, C, D, and F have further been subdivided in up to four major subgenotypes and several minor genotypes, now identified by Arabic numerals. In recent years, massive immigration waves generate an impact on the geographic distribution of genotypes worldwide.
	HBV infection is controlled by cellular and humoral immune responses (Tan et al. 2015; Corti et al. 2018). It can be tracked through serological detection of the viral antigens or the antibodies raised by the immune system to target the virus. The presence of antibodies to the hepatitis B surface and/or hepatitis B core antigens (anti-HBs and anti-HBc) in the absence of HBsAg is generally taken (with few exceptions) to indicate resolution of infection and provides evidence of previous HBV infection. Persistence of HBV infection (chronic carrier state) is diagnosed by the detection of HBsAg in the blood on two occasions, six months apart or through continuous detection of HBV DNA even in the absence of detectable HBsAg in patients with occult HBV infection (OBI) (Raimondo et al. 2013). HBeAg is a secretory protein processed from the pre-core gene and considered as a marker for high viral replication and infectivity. HBV DNA is used as an indicator for viral replication expressed as IU/ml. There is a clear association between serum hepatitis B viral load and prognosis. Thus, the cumulative annual incidence of cirrhosis or HCC being 4.5 and 1.3%, respectively, in persons with DNA levels <50 IU/ml, while it is 36.2 and 14.9%, respectively, in persons with DNA levels of > to 2 × 105 IU/ml). This relationship supports the rationale for treating patients with high levels of HBV DNA with antiviral agents (Chen et al. 2006).





Epidemiology and transmission


	Globally, hepatitis B is one of the most common infectious diseases (MacLachlan et al. 2015; Schweitzer et al. 2015). There are however wide variations in published global estimates of persistent HBV infection ranging between 240 and 350 million HBsAg carriers (Basnayake and Easterbrook 2016), (up to ~3.5% of the world population). Estimates indicate that about 2 billion people (i.e. about 30% of the world population) have ever been infected with HBV worldwide (WHO 2012) residing mainly in Africa, Asia, and the Western Pacific regions. One recent burden estimate in 2015 proposed that 257 million people are living with chronic HBV infection while 2.7 million persons are co-infected with HBV and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
	On the basis of sero-epidemiological surveys, the WHO classified countries into four levels of endemicity according to the prevalence of chronic HBsAg carriage. Thus, HBV prevalence can be defined as low (<2.0%), lower intermediate (2.0–4.99%), higher intermediate (5.0–7.99%), and high >8.0%) (Fig. 8.16.1).
	Fig. 8.16.1 Global HBsAg endemicity (1957–2013).
	Reproduced from Schweitzer, A., Horn, J., Mikolajczyk, R.T., Krause, G., and Ott, J.J. (2015). Estimations of worldwide prevalence of chronic hepatitis B virus infection: a systematic review of data published between 1965 and 2013. Lancet 386, 1546–55, with permission from Elsevier.
	HBV is transmitted by either percutaneous or mucous membrane contact with infected blood or other body fluid. The virus is found in highest concentrations in blood and serous exudates. The primary routes of transmission are vertical and perinatal, early childhood exposure (often called horizontal transmission), sexual contact, and percutaneous exposure to blood or infectious body fluids (i.e. injections, needle stick, blood transfusion, tattoos).
	Most perinatal infections occur among infants of pregnant women with chronic-persistent HBV infection. The likelihood of an infant developing chronic HBV infection following vertical or horizontal transmission in the first year of life is 70–90% for those born to HBeAg-positive mothers (corresponding to high viral load) and less than 15% for those born to HBeAg-negative mothers. Most early childhood infections occur in households of persons with chronic HBV infection. The most probable mechanism involves unapparent percutaneous or permucosal contact with infectious body fluids (e.g. bites, breaks in the skin, dermatological lesions, skin ulcers). Sexual transmission has been estimated to account for 50% of new infections among adults in industrialized countries. The most common risk factors include multiple sex partners, men who have sex with men (MSM), history of a sexually transmitted infection and illicit drug injection. Finally, unsafe injections and other unsafe percutaneous or permucosal procedures (such as cocaine snorting) are a major source of bloodborne pathogen transmission of HBV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), and HIV in many countries. The risk of HBV infection from needle stick exposure to HBsAg-positive blood (in patients and healthcare workers alike), is approximately 30% and worldwide unsafe injection practices account for approximately 8–16 million HBV infections each year.
	In areas of high endemicity, the lifetime risk of HBV infection is more than 60%, and most infections occur during the perinatal period or during early childhood. In areas of intermediate endemicity, the lifetime risk of HBV infection varies between 20 and 60%, and infections occur in all age groups through the four modes of transmission, but primarily in infants and children. In areas of low endemicity, infection occurs primarily in adult life by sexual or parenteral transmission (e.g. through drug use). Acute infection is more often clinically overt in adults, while asymptomatic acute infection often remains unnoticed in young and older children. Infected infants and pre-school age children are at greatest risk of becoming chronic HBsAg carriers, thereby increasing the risk of cirrhosis and primary HCC later in life. The precise mechanism by which carrier rates are influenced by age of infection is unknown but probably relates to the effect of age on the immune system’s ability to clear and eliminate the infection due to evolving immune tolerance to the virus.
	Approximately 75% of the world’s chronic HBV carriers live in Asian countries. In 2018, China ranks highest, with at least 87 million hepatitis B carriers, and India the second highest, with a carrier pool of 35 million (Tandon 1997; WHO Hepatitis Data and Statistics https://www.wpro.who.int/hepatitis/data/hepatitis_data_statistics/en/). Importantly, chronic carriers of HBV are not only at risk of developing long-term progression of the infection but also represent a significant source and reservoir of infection to others.
	A model developed in 2005 estimated that for the year 2000, 620,000 persons died worldwide from HBV-related causes: 580,000 (94%) from chronic infection-related cirrhosis and HCC and 40,000 (6%) from acute HBV infection. Infections acquired during the perinatal period, in early childhood (<5 years old), and at 5 years of age and older accounted for 21%, 48%, and 31% of deaths, respectively (Goldstein et al. 2005).
	Besides the acquired age of infection, some of the variation in outcome of HBV infection may be related to the genetic heterogeneity of the virus. Progression to chronic infection appears to occur more frequently following acute infection with genotypes A and D than with the other genotypes (Tanwar and Dusheiko 2012). Chronic infection with genotype A and B appears to have a better prognosis than genotype C and D which are often caused by pre-core mutations of HBV, most common in Asia, Mediterranean countries, and Southern Europe.





Clinical manifestations and immuno-pathogenesis of HBV infection


	Acute hepatitis B has a long incubation period ranging from 15 to 180 days (90 days on average). Individual responses to the infection vary greatly. One-third of the individuals have subclinical infection; one-third experience a mild ‘flu-like’ illness without jaundice; and the remaining one-third develop jaundice with dark urine, extreme fatigue, anorexia, and abdominal pain. Jaundice usually peaks within 1–2 weeks and then gradually subsides. About 90–95% of infected adults and only 10–50% of infected newborns and babies recover spontaneously while the remaining subjects develop persistent HBV infection. Clinical recovery from acute infection is defined by normalization of ALT and AST associated with anti-HBs antibody seroconversion. Latent-occult HBV infection, also called OBI, manifested as intranuclear covalently closed circular (ccc) HBV DNA in the host hepatocytes, may persist for decades post so-called clinical recovery and anti-HBs antibody seroconversion (Rehermann et al. 1996). Such patients who may enter a dormant phase of persistent HBV infection are at risk for HBV reactivation when treated with immune-suppressive agents, including chemotherapy for malignant diseases or anti-inflammatory biologic agents, e.g. for inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, or rheumatoid arthritis (Shouval and Shibolet 2013). HBV reactivation rarely leads to immune clearance of HBV and more often to progression to cirrhosis and even fulminant liver failure. A small proportion (0.1–0.5%) of acutely infected adults develop fulminant hepatitis B, an exceptionally severe form of the disease which can be fatal requiring in two-thirds of cases an emergency liver transplant unless promptly treated with nucleos(t)ide analogue (Roche and Samuel 2014). About 5–10% of acutely infected adults and 50–90% of newborns will become chronically infected and remain infectious (Kumar et al. 2007).
	The immuno-pathogenesis of acute and chronic hepatitis B in infected newborns and babies as compared to adults may lead to different outcomes. Following acute infection, babies and young adults infected during the early years of life, often develop immune tolerance to HBV, associated with a high viral load and minimal liver injury. When immune tolerance to HBV is lost, the host immune system causes hepatocyte injury manifested by necro-inflammation and fibrosis, followed by an attempt at immune clearance of HBV, at a time when ALT levels often rise. A long-term, ongoing immune clearance phase causes more fibrosis and may lead to cirrhosis and compromised liver function. Once the host immune system is successful in inducing immune control against the virus, viral replication drops, and histologic evidence for liver injury may stabilize or resolve. However, resolution of the inflammatory process in the liver does not necessarily signifies cure since HBV DNA may still be present in the hepatocyte nucleus as cccHBV-DNA or undergo integration into the host hepatocyte genome. Thus persistent HBV infection is characterized by either overt viremia with detectable HBV DNA and HBsAg in serum or occult infection (OBI) extending to an inactive phase of the infection.





Extrahepatic manifestations of HBV infection


	Extrahepatic manifestations following acute and chronic HBV infection occur in 10–20% of patients. These include serum sickness like syndrome, rash, arthralgia, glomerulopathies, and very rarely aplastic anaemia.
	The natural history of chronic HBV infection can vary between individuals. Risk factors, which affect progression to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and HCC include male gender, viral load, elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT), genotype, and degree of fibrosis on liver biopsy. Patients with acute HBV infection are at risk for progression to a chronic carrier state. These patients, who may be still potentially infectious, may be asymptomatic with normal ALT and AST levels. A subgroup of HBsAg carriers may have clinically insignificant or minimal liver disease and never develop complications. Others will have clinically apparent chronic hepatitis with transition to cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Chronic infection with HBV can be either ‘replicative’ or ‘non-replicative’. The ‘replicative’ phase or immune tolerance phase, characterized by positive HBeAg and high viral load (> 2000 IU/ml and often >106 IU/ml), is often present in newborns and children of HBsAg-positive mothers. In ‘non-replicative’ infection, the rate of viral replication in the liver is low, serum HBV DNA concentration is generally low, and HBeAg is not detected. In these inactive HBsAg carriers, reactivation of HBV and liver injury can occur either spontaneously or following reduction in dose of immune-suppressive agents (e.g. chemotherapy for malignant conditions) (Lalazar et al. 2007). Patients with chronic HBV and replicative infection generally have a worse prognosis and a greater chance of developing cirrhosis and/or HCC (Chen et al. 2006). In patients with HBV pre-core mutations, replicative infection can occur in the absence of detectable serum HBeAg. Finally, super or co-infection with the hepatitis delta virus (HDV) or HCV remain a constant threat for HBsAg-positive patients irrespective if they have an active inflammatory liver disease at time of exposure or not. (See later).





Treatment


	Success in HBV treatment in CLD depends on the phase of chronic HBV infection. Viral replication by itself is not cythopathic and liver injury occurs only after the activation of host cellular and adoptive immune responses by the replicating virus, causing hepatocellular damage. Guidelines for treatment of chronic and acute HBV infection were developed by the American and European Associations for the Study of the Liver (European Association for the Study of the Liver 2017; Terrault et al. 2018). Treatment is indicated if ALT is elevated >X2 ULN, HBV DNA is >2,000 IU/ml or, if there are signs of moderate or severe liver fibrosis, or in case of treatment with chemotherapeutic or immune-suppressive agents.
	The short-term goals of therapy for chronic HBV infection are suppression of viral replication and HBeAg seroconversion in HBeAg-positive patients or only viral suppression in anti-HBe positive patients. In some patients, HBsAg titres will drop or become undetectable by conventional assays but anti-HBs seroconversion, and loss of HBsAg which is an ultimate goal for therapy, is relatively rare. The long-term goals include prevention of cirrhosis and HCC. However, although control of inflammation and progression to cirrhosis are often attainable, complete resolution of infection with elimination of cccHBV-DNA is rarely achieved in patients with persistent HBV infection. At present, treatment usually consists of a well-tolerated nucleos(t)ide analogue (p.o.) for an indefinite period and possibly lifelong. There are nowadays several licensed antiviral agents which are administered p.o., including lamivudine, telbivudine, entecavir, and tenofovir. Among these, entecavir and tenofovir are usually preferred, because of the higher genetic barrier (low probability of resistance) and higher potency. Treatment with the less tolerated interferon alpha by s.c. injections for about 48 weeks, is effective in inducing anti-HBe seroconversion in about a quarter of HBeAg-positive patients with chronic HBV; has the advantage of leading to prolonged suppression of viral replication when successful but is associated with significant adverse effects and still rare permanent resolution of infection. In summary, treatment of chronic HBV infections with oral antiviral agents is highly effective in suppression of viral replication and liver inflammation but rarely leads to anti-HBs seroconversion and complete resolution of infection. The recent detection of the sodium taurocholate co-transporting polypeptide (NTPC) which is an HBV receptor on the cell surface of hepatocytes is expected to trigger the development of new and more efficacious antiviral agents against HBV (Ni et al. 2014; Li 2015; Lin and Kao 2016).





Prevention


	All major health authorities agree that the most effective approach to reducing the burden of HBV is primary prevention through universal vaccination as close to birth as possible and control of disease transmission. Interrupting the chain of infection requires knowledge of the mode of disease transmission and modification of behaviour through individual education to practice safe sex and good personal hygiene. Screening of all donated blood and maintenance of strict aseptic techniques with invasive health treatments using universal precaution measures, have reduced the likelihood of contracting HBV.
	Safe and effective HBV vaccines have been available since the 1980s, and immunization with HBV vaccine remains the most effective means of preventing HBV disease and its consequences worldwide (Zanetti et al. 2008). Although the vaccine will not cure chronic hepatitis B, it is ~95% effective in preventing chronic infections, and is the first vaccine against a major human cancer.
	After the development and licensure of plasma-derived vaccines in the 1980s, recombinant DNA technology has allowed the expression of HBsAg in bacteria, yeasts, mammalian cells and even plants (1986 and onwards). As a result, different manufacturers have successfully developed recombinant DNA vaccines against HBV, which are currently the backbone for most vaccination programmes worldwide (Shouval 2003).
	Moreover, apart from monovalent vaccines against hepatitis B, a combination vaccine against hepatitis B and A as well as a broad range of combination penta and hexavalent vaccines that include an HBV component are available especially for vaccination during infancy and early childhood. Such vaccines, shown to be safe and immunogenic simultaneously, provide protection against a number of aetiologic agents including, diphtheria, tetanus, polio, pertussis (with either a whole-cell or an acellular component) and haemophilus influenza b.
	More recently, the so-called third-generation hepatitis B vaccines—based on the S-, pre-S1-, and pre-S2-antigens, or using new adjuvants have been developed (Barry and Cooper 2007; Leroux-Roels 2015; Shouval et al. 2015). These vaccines generate a more robust humoral immune response against HBsAg as compared to conventional recombinant HBV vaccines leading to an enhanced immune response, especially in immune-compromised persons and non-responders to vaccination.
	Immunization against hepatitis B requires the intramuscular administration of three doses of vaccine given at 0, 1, and 6 months. More rapid protection (i.e. for healthcare workers exposed to HBV or the susceptible sexual partner of a patient with acute hepatitis B) can be achieved through the adoption of an alternative schedule using three doses of vaccine administered at 0, 1, and 2 months followed by a booster dose given at 12 months. The extensive and long-term use of both plasma-derived and recombinant HBV vaccines has confirmed their excellent safety and tolerability. In 1998, several case reports from France raised concern that hepatitis B vaccination may lead to new cases or relapse of multiple sclerosis (MS) or other demyelinating diseases, including Guillain–Barré syndrome; however, no causal relation has been established (Duclos 2003). Hepatitis B vaccination is not contraindicated in pregnant or lactating women when absolute necessary.
	Seroprotection against HBV infection is defined as having an anti-HBs level >10 IU/L after complete immunization (CDC 1987). Reviews on the use of HBV vaccine in neonates and infants report seroprotective levels of anti-HBs antibodies at 1 month after the last vaccine dose for all schedules in 98–100% of vaccinees (Venters et al. 2004). While HBV vaccines generally induce an adequate immune response in over 95% of fully vaccinated healthy persons, a large interpersonal variability has been demonstrated in the anti-HBs immune response. The antibody response to hepatitis B vaccine has been shown to depend on the type, dosage, and schedule of vaccination used, as well as on the age, the gender, genetic factors, comorbidity, and the status of the immune system of the vaccinee (Hadler and Margolis 1992; Hollinger 1989). Immune-deficient patients i.e. with HIV, or those undergoing haemodialysis or immunosuppressant therapy, may require higher doses of vaccine and more injections (i.e. at months 0, 1, 2 and 6) to achieve an adequate and sustained immune response.
	Follow-up studies have shown that vaccine-induced anti-HBs antibodies persist over periods of several decades and that duration of anti-HBs positivity is related to the antibody peak level achieved after primary vaccination (Jilg et al. 1988; Leuridan and Van Damme 2011). Follow-up of successfully vaccinated people has shown that the antibody concentrations usually decline over time, but clinically significant breakthrough infections are rare. Those who have lost antibody over time after a successful vaccination usually show a rapid anamnestic response when boosted with an additional dose of vaccine given several years after the primary course of vaccination or when exposed to the HBV. This means that the immunological memory for HBsAg can outlast the anti-HBs antibody detection, providing long-term protection against acute disease and the development of the HBsAg carrier state (Banatvala and Van Damme 2003). Hence, for immune-competent children and adults, the routine administration of booster doses of vaccine does not appear necessary to sustain long-term protection (Consensus-Group 2000). Such conclusions are based on data collected during the first 10–20 years of vaccination in countries of both high and low endemicity (Kao and Chen 2005; Zanetti et al. 2005).
	Since the availability of hepatitis B vaccines in industrialized countries, early strategies for HBV control have stressed immunization of high-risk groups (e.g. MSM, healthcare workers, patients in sexually transmitted infection clinics, sex workers, IV drug users, people with multiple sex partners, household contacts of chronically infected persons) and babies born to HBsAg-positive mothers. However, such vaccination strategies, directed at specific risk groups, had little impact on the overall burden of HBV in endemic countries and gradually were replaced by effective universal vaccination programmes of newborns.
	In 1991, the WHO called for all children to receive the HBV vaccine. Substantial progress has been made in implementing this WHO recommendation: by the end of 2012, 179 countries had implemented or were planning to implement a universal HBV immunization programme for newborns, infants, and/or adolescents. In 2015, the global coverage with the third dose of hepatitis B vaccine reached 84%, which is not far from 90% goal, declared for the year 2020 by the WHO (WHO 2017). This high coverage leads to a major reduction in the incidence of chronic HBV infection in children below the age of 5 years worldwide as well as HCC. However, there are regional differences in coverage, especially in early administration of the birth dose of HBV vaccines in endemic countries. Thus, African, Eastern Mediterranean, and some European regions remain below the global average. Early vaccination within hours from birth, and high coverage with the primary vaccine series among infants had the greatest overall impact on the prevalence of chronic HBV infection in children (WHO 2004). According to model-based predictions, universal HBV infant immunization, (even without administration of a birth dose of vaccine to prevent perinatal HBV infection), would prevent up to 75% of global deaths from HBV-related causes, depending on the vaccination coverage for the complete series. Adding the birth dose would increase the proportion of deaths prevented up to 84% (Goldstein et al. 2005).
	In countries with high or intermediate disease endemicity, the most effective strategy is to start immunization at birth (< 24 hours). In such regions a birth dose of a monovalent HBV vaccine is recommended even if vaccination protocols include later administration of combination vaccines, which also contain an HBV component. Countries with low HBV prevalence may consider immunization of children or adolescents as an alternative to newborn immunization (WHO 2004, 2006).
	Indeed, the effectiveness of hepatitis B newborn and infant immunization programme has already been demonstrated in a variety of countries and settings (Andre and Zuckerman 1994; Lee 1997; WHO 2001). The results of effective implementation of universal hepatitis B programmes have become apparent in terms of reduction not only in the incidence of acute hepatitis B infections, but also in the carrier rate in immunized cohorts and in hepatitis-B-related mortality from HCC and cirrhosis (Coursaget et al. 1994; Chang et al. 1997; Liaw 2013). In Taiwan, the HBsAg prevalence in children under 15 years of age decreased from 9.8% in 1984 to 0.7% in 1999 (Chan et al. 2004). In the Gambia, childhood HBsAg prevalence decreased from 10% to 0.6% since the introduction of the universal infant immunization programme (Viviani et al. 1999). Data in Hawaii show a 97% reduction in the prevalence of HBsAg since the start of the infant hepatitis B vaccination programme in 1991. The incidence of new acute hepatitis B infections in children and adults was reduced from 4.5/100,000 in 1990 to 0 in the period 2002–2004 (Perz et al. 2006b). In Bristol Bay, Alaska, 3.2% of children were HBsAg-positive before universal hepatitis B immunization; 10 years later, no child under 10 years of age was HBsAg-positive (Wainwright et al. 1997). Finally, surveillance data from Italy, where a universal programme was started in 1991 in infants as well as in adolescents, have shown that the incidence of acute hepatitis B progressively decreased from 1991 to 2005, with a 24-fold and 50-fold decrease in the 15–24-year and 0–14-year age groups, respectively (Mele et al. 2008).





Public health impact


	HBV infection is a serious global health problem, which is under continuous surveillance by the WHO (WHO 2017). Prevention and elimination efforts of chronic HBV infection have utilized various estimates to assess the global burden of chronic HBV infection (Wiktor and Hutin 2016). Of the approximately 2 billion people who have been infected worldwide by 2012, more than 250 million are chronic carriers of HBV according to one estimate (WHO 2012). Approximately 15–40% of infected patients will develop cirrhosis, liver failure, or HCC. According to various estimates, HBV infection accounts for 600,000–900,000 deaths each year, mainly due to the consequences of chronic hepatitis, such as cirrhosis and liver cancer (Goldstein et al. 2005; Lavanchy 2004; Perz et al. 2006a; Schweitzer et al. 2015). Because these complications mainly occur in adults infected with HBV during childhood, most of the benefits of vaccination initiated 20–30 years ago have yet to be realized. Another consequence of persistent HBV infection, which is often underestimated, is the stigma that HBV carries to the individual, in the family setting, as well as in social and professional life.





Hepatitis delta virus


	HDV is a transmissible RNA pathogen that generally requires the help of a hepadnavirus like HBV for its own replication—similar to viroids or plant virus satellite RNAs (Hughes et al. 2011; Rizzetto 2015). Thus, in a natural setting, HDV is only found in patients who are also infected with persistent HBV since the HDV requires simultaneous presence of HBV for complete virion assembly and secretion. However, under rare circumstances, HDV may also replicate in immune suppressed, transplanted livers in the absence of overt HBV.





Aetiologic agent


	The HDV genome is a small single-stranded RNA composed of approximately 1,680 bases with a unique circular conformation that is replicated using a host RNA polymerase. The HDV genome contains an open reading frame translated to HDV antigens—the small (S-HD) and large (L-HD) proteins which differ by 19 amino acids. The L-HD amino acid sequence is identical to S-HD with the addition of a carboxy-terminal extension of 19–20 amino acids following the editing of the S-HD stop codon during the viral RNA replication cycle. The S-HD is required for viral replication and might promote RNA polymerase II elongation of nascent HDV RNA, while L-HD is essential for HDV particle assembly (Tseng and Lai 2009).





Epidemiology and transmission


	There are three types of HDV infection: simultaneous co-infection of HDV where HBV is transmitted by the same inoculum, super-infection of an HBV carrier with HDV (Rizzetto and Verme 1985) and isolated HDV infection without overt HBV reinfection (e.g. in immunosuppressed patients). A co-infection usually evolves into complete recovery, but the risk for severe acute hepatitis, even fulminant hepatitis, is higher than in the case of acute HBV mono-infection. A super-infection evolves towards chronicity in about 90% of cases. In isolated HDV infection, liver function tests are usually within normal range without significant histologic inflammatory activity.
	According to the WHO, at least 5% of people with chronic HBV infection are co-infected with HDV, resulting in a total of 15–20 million persons infected with HDV worldwide (http://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hepatitis-d) (Fig. 8.16.2).
	Fig. 8.16.2 Worldwide prevalence of HDV and the geographic distribution of its genotypes.
	Reproduced from Hughes, S.A., Wedemeyer, H., and Harrison, P.M. (2011). Hepatitis delta virus. Lancet 378, 73–85, with permission from Elsevier. Idilman, I.S., Keskin, O., Celik, A., Savas, B., Elhan, A.H., Idilman, R., and Karcaaltincaba, M. (2016).
	However, this is a broad global estimate since many countries do not report the prevalence of HDV. Worldwide, the overall number of HDV infection has been declining since 1980s. This trend is mainly due to a successful control of transmission and more importantly, global HBV vaccination programmes. Eight HDV genotypes have been characterized to date on the basis of a small number of complete genome sequences with 19–38% divergence at the nucleotide level of complete genomes (Hughes et al. 2011). The most frequent genotypes are: genotype I (includes the European, North American, African, and some Asian HDV isolates), genotype II (found in Japan, Taiwan, and Eastern Europe), genotype III (found exclusively in South America), genotype IV (found mainly in West Africa) and genotype V (found in Central Africa). The global distribution of the different genotypes of HBV and HDV is rather well known, although less is known on the types circulating among populations in remote areas. Little is also known on the viral transmission mechanisms driving the circulation of the endemic strains and epidemic outbreaks. Yet, on an individual basis, it appears that new and cell-to-cell transmission between hepatocytes is facilitated through the NTCP receptor.
	In contrast to the US and Western Europe, the prevalence of HDV infection is relatively high in the equatorial subtropical and tropical zones, concentrating in certain population groups (Torres 1996). A putatively more severe form of HDV has been reported in Brazil and is, endemic in the Western Amazon states (Parana et al. 2008; Viana et al. 2005). HDV infection is also endemic in several Eastern European and Balkan countries as well as in Turkey. In Western Europe, HDV is becoming rare, affecting around 5% of chronic carriers (Rizzetto and Ciancio 2012). HDV infection is associated with an increased risk of developing advanced CLD, early cirrhosis development, and HCC (Farci 2003; Smedile and Bugianesi 2005).
	In endemic areas, all HBV carriers should be tested for HDV. The diagnosis of HDV infection is based on serologic identification of anti-HDV (IgG) as evidence for previous or current exposure and anti-HDV(IgM) for identification of active /recent super or co-infection of an HBsAg carrier. Confirmation for delta virus viremia is obtained through HDV RNA testing by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which may also be utilized quantitatively for evaluation of HDV treatment protocols.





Prevention and treatment


	There is currently no vaccine for prevention of HDV. Consequently, it is imperative to prevent exposure of HBsAg carriers to contacts with HDV patients when applicable. Furthermore, no effective means are so far available for treatment of HDV infection. Long-term interferon alpha treatment may suppress HDV RNA in some patients and slow down progression of fibrosis but usually does not lead to resolution of HDV infection. The most effective means for controlling HDV infection is prevention of HBV infection through immunization. It is too early to judge if recently developed experimental pharmacologic agents against HDV i.e. blocking the NTCP receptor (Yurdaydin 2019), will reach licensure (Hughes et al. 2011; Yurdaydin 2019). Finally, for those patients with HDV co-or super-infection who develop decompensation and liver failure, survival after liver transplantation is superior as compared to patients with HBV mono-infection (Roche and Samuel 2012).





Hepatitis C


	Hepatitis C is a liver disease caused by the hepatitis C virus: the virus can cause both acute and chronic hepatitis infection, ranging in severity from an initially mild illness, lasting a few weeks to a lifelong illness with variable severity. Following acute HCV infection, 50–80% of patients will develop persistent infection and chronic hepatitis of variable severity, of whom ~20% will progress to cirrhosis with an annual risk for developing HCC of 4–5%.





Aetiologic agent


	HCV is classified in the family Flaviviridae. Like other flaviviruses, HCV is an enveloped RNA virus with an inner nucleoprotein core. Its envelope contains two glycoproteins, E1 and E2, which form heterodimers (to form a functional subunit) at the surface of the virion (Dubuisson and Cosset 2014; Panel 2015). Efforts to identify the HCV succeeded by direct cloning and sequencing of its genome. Although the virus was identified almost three decades ago (Choo et al. 1989), its replication cycle is still only partially understood. An important feature of HCV is that the viral genome displays extensive genetic heterogeneity at an individual as well as the global level. Thus, even within the same host, the HCV genome population circulates as ‘quasispecies’ of closely related sequences. Worldwide, a high degree of genetic variation exists, resulting in at least six major genotypes and more than 100 distantly related subtypes (Forns and Bukh 1999). It has been reported that until recently, virus pathogenicity and sensitivity to current standards of treatment appear to vary with different subtypes (i.e. genotypes 2 and 3, responding better to interferon alpha treatment than genotype 1 and 4). This relative resistance to treatment with antiviral drugs has practically been overcome through the development of new direct antiviral agents.





Epidemiology and transmission


	Estimates on the global prevalence of HCV and its consequences vary significantly (Alter 2007; WHO 2012; Basnayake and Easterbrook 2016; Polaris Observatory 2017). An extensive literature survey reports a wide range in estimates of the global prevalence of HCV carriers, ranging between 71 and 200 million of whom at least 2.28 million are co-infected with HIV (http://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hepatitis). Yet reliable data from several countries remain unavailable. A review of the epidemiology and genotype distribution of HCV infection revealed a mean global prevalence of anti-HCV antibodies of 1.6% (range 1.3–2.1%) corresponding to 115 million past or present viraemic infections. Globally, genotype 1 was the most common variant (46%) followed by genotype 3 (22%). Genotype 4 is the most common genotype in African HCV patients. A significant number of those who are chronically infected will develop cirrhosis or liver cancer (Gower et al. 2014).
	Figure 8.16.3 summarizes one estimate of the global prevalence of HCV. The highest prevalence of HCV has been reported from Egypt with a seroprevalence in the Nile delta ranging from 19% in the 10–19-year-old age group to 60% in the 30-year-old age group, and also associated with a high prevalence of liver cirrhosis. The high prevalence in the Nile delta is reported to be linked to parenteral anti-schistosomiasis therapy, which was carried out with inadequately sterilized injection material (Frank et al. 2000). Estimates in the United States reveal that 3.9 million Americans are chronically infected with HCV, with prevalence rates as high as 8–10% in African Americans (Smith et al. 2012). Haemodialysis patients, haemophiliacs, drug addicts, and people transfused with blood before 1990 are particularly affected by the disease. In Europe, 0.1–3.3% of the population has been infected, with the highest prevalence observed in Southern Europe (Italy) and Romania (Blachier et al. 2013).
	Fig. 8.16.3 Estimated prevalence of HCV.
	Reproduced from Polaris Observatory, H.C.V.C. (2017). Global prevalence and genotype distribution of hepatitis C virus infection in 2015: a modelling study. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2, 161–76, with permission from Elsevier.
	Despite infection control precautions, healthcare workers remain at risk for acquiring bloodborne HCV infections due to accidental exposure. Therapeutic injections are reported as accounting for 2 million new HCV infections each year. Many of these injections are performed in less than ideal conditions, often with reuse of needles or multidose vials and mainly, but not exclusively, in low-and middle-income countries. The residual risk of transmitting HCV through screened blood transfusions is very low in industrialized countries but safety of blood supply remains a major source of public concern in low-and middle-income countries.
	Up to 60–70% of intravenous drug users living in urban areas are seropositive for HCV antibodies. The rate of infection depends on the length of drug use, with 25% of infections occurring during the first year of addiction, 50% after 5 years, and up to 90% after more than 5 years of intravenous drug use.
	The global epidemic of HCV infection emerged in the second half of the twentieth century and has been attributed, at least in part, to the increasing use of parenteral therapies and blood transfusion during that period. In high-income countries, the rapid improvement of healthcare conditions and the introduction of anti-HCV screening for blood donors have led to a sharp decrease in the incidence of iatrogenic HCV (Prati 2006). Injectable drug use remains the main route of transmission, accounting for nearly 90% of new HCV infections. Mother-to-child transmission has been documented but is lower as compared to HBV. The risk of perinatal infection in children from HCV-infected mothers ranges from 3% to 10% in different populations. Transmission is believed to occur in utero, as a consequence of a high viral load in the mother; in particular, from co-infected HIV positive mothers (Kato et al. 1994). There is no contraindication for infected mothers to breastfeed the newborn. Sexual transmission is thought to be relatively infrequent (up to 2–3%); as such, it is not recommended in monogamic and stable couples to use condoms. However, the large reservoir of HCV carriers provides multiple opportunities for exposure to potentially infected partners. Individuals with multiple sexual partners, MSM, prostitutes and their clients, patients with common sexually transmitted infections, and partners of HCV and HIV co-infected persons are at the highest risk of acquiring HCV sexually. In many cases of HCV infection, no recognizable transmission factor or route is identified (Memon and Memon 2002).





Clinical manifestations


	The incubation period for hepatitis C before the onset of clinical symptoms ranges from 6 to 7 weeks on average. In acute infections, the most common symptoms are fatigue and jaundice; however, the majority of cases (between 60 and 70%), even those who develop chronic infection, are asymptomatic for years. Fulminant hepatitis C is very rarely observed. While most patients with acute HCV infection have mild symptoms or no symptoms, 50–85% of those infected develop chronic disease. Chronic disease is difficult to recognize because symptoms are mild and infection passes silently and insidiously from the acute to the chronic phase. Serological diagnosis of acute HCV infection is mainly based on recent HCV antibodies (anti-HCV) seroconversion. Persistence of HCV infection is diagnosed by the presence of HCV RNA in the blood for at least 6 months. The mechanisms leading to HCV persistence are currently unknown, although it is known that HCV chronicity develops despite humoral and cellular responses to HCV proteins (Park and Rehermann 2014). Factors associated with development of chronic disease appear to include older age at the time of infection, male gender, and an immunosuppressed state such as HIV infection (Lauer and Walker 2001).





Extrahepatic manifestations of hepatitis C


	Hepatitis C virus infection provokes B-lymphocytes dysfunction with extrahepatic manifestations of autoimmunity. Several autoimmune and metabolic conditions and diseases have been associated with HCV infection: lichen planus, granuloma annulare, porphyria cutanea tarda, and psoriasis (Andrade et al. 2012). One important expression of autoimmunity in HCV carriers is HCV-related cryoglobulinaemia, which can cause purpura, vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, and peripheral neuropathy (Atta et al. 2010). Cryoglobulinaemia has been found in HCV carriers with lympho proliferative disorders, mainly B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (Yu and Lin 2013). Furthermore, HCV infection has been associated with higher risk of insulin resistance and diabetes (Naing et al. 2013). On the other side, diabetes is a confirmed risk factor for the evolution to hepatocellular carcinoma.
	The presence of non-organ specific autoantibodies is another expression of autoimmunity found in HCV carriers, which has been associated in some studies with advanced fibrosis and failure in the treatment of hepatitis C with the combined therapy of interferon-α plus ribavirin. Antibodies to self-antigens such as nucleoproteins (ANA), smooth muscle (SMA), liver–kidney microsomal type-1 antigen (LKM-1), immunoglobulin G (RF), neutrophil cytoplasm (ANCA), and phospholipids (APL), which are routinely used as biomarkers of autoimmune diseases, can be found in HCV carriers with varying prevalence. Their induction seems mainly to involve immune cross-reactions caused by molecular mimicry between HCV polyprotein and human auto antigens (Atta et al. 2010).





Treatment


	The primary goals for treatment of HCV infection include eradication of infection as well as reduction of morbidity and mortality from CLD and HCC. Specifically, such effects are believed to occur through normalization of liver function tests such as ALT/AST, complete clearance of HCV, decline in disease progression leading to improved quality of life, and reducing the reservoir of chronic carriers, thereby controlling further transmission. In contrast to hepatitis B, chronic HCV infection is potentially completely curable. Virological cure or sustained viral response (SVR) is currently defined by undetectable HCV RNA for at least 24 weeks (SVR 24) after ending therapy (Gurusamy et al. 2013).
	Treatment is recommended for HCV-infected patients who are at risk of developing cirrhosis or with potential harmful extrahepatic manifestations of HCV as well as for liver transplant recipients with graft reinfection of HCV.
	In patients with cirrhosis, the benefits of therapy consist of reduction in of the risk of dying from a liver-related death including the risk of decompensation, liver failure, and development of HCC (Veldt et al. 2007).
	Historically, and until 2011 effective SVR has been obtained in up to 50% of HCV patients with genotype 1 and 80% of patients with genotypes 2 or 3 who had received combined weekly pegylated interferon-based treatment with daily ribavirin for 24–48 weeks (Chevaliez and Pawlotsky 2007; Tan and Lok 2007). Following the development and licensure in 2011 of the first generation of direct antiviral protease inhibitors Telaprevir and Boceprevir, SVR rates in response to various combination protocols rose to 70–80%, in treatment naïve patients, albeit associated with significant adverse events (Kwo et al. 2010; Jacobson et al. 2011). Since 2014, several new, efficacious, safe, and well-tolerated direct antiviral agents (DAAs) have been developed and licensed worldwide for interferon free treatment of chronic HCV infection (i.e. various combinations of sofosbuvir, ledispasvir, simeprevir, daclatasvir, ritonavir-boosted paritaprevir, ombitasvir as well as dasabuvir, elbasvir and grazoprevir), leading to SVR rates >90% for the various genotypes treated for 8–12 weeks in treatment naïve patients (European Association for Study of the Liver 2015; Panel 2015; AASLD-IDSA Hepatitis C Guidelines, 2020).
	The remarkable breakthrough in identification of HCV which lead to the development of efficacious antiviral agents was recently acknowledged by the Swedish Nobel Prize committee. Thus the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine was awarded to three scientists who have made the decisive contributions to the fight against bloodborne hepatitis, Harvey J. Alter, Michael Houghton and Charles M. Rice. Yet, the exceedingly high cost charged by the pharma industry for antiviral drugs has mellowed somewhat the excitement generated by the development of the new generation of DAAs. In spite of proven cost-effectiveness, low-and middle-income countries and even health insurers in the US and Europe face difficult challenges in coverage of the very high cost of curative treatment for the millions of patients around the globe (Chhatwal et al. 2015), (http://www.who.int/hepatitis/publications/hep-c-access-report/en/). The WHO is currently promoting an effort to simplify curative treatment protocols for developing countries (http://www.who.int/hepatitis/news-events/hep-c-access-report-2018/en/).





Prevention


	There is currently no licensed vaccine against HCV. The high mutation rates of the HCV genome complicate vaccine development and there is no consensus yet regarding the potential candidates for receiving such a vaccine once proven to be efficacious (Baumert et al. 2014; Mehta et al. 2014). Although 20–35% of patients with acute HCV infection clear the virus spontaneously, lack of knowledge of any effective protective immune response following HCV infection impedes vaccine research. Although some studies have shown the presence of virus-neutralizing antibodies, it is not fully clear whether and how the immune system is able to eliminate the virus. From a global perspective, an important impact on HCV disease burden will likely be achieved by a combination of efforts including public health measures as well as treatment of large cohorts of HCV carriers with the highly effective (but also very expensive) DAAs with a special emphasis on specific risk groups. It is imperative to continue and focus efforts on reducing the risk of HCV transmission from nosocomial exposures (e.g. screening of blood, rigorous implementation of infection control, reducing unsafe injection practices) and high-risk behaviours (e.g. injection drug use). Adherence to fundamental infection control principles, including safe injection practices and appropriate aseptic techniques, is essential to prevent transmission of bloodborne viruses in healthcare settings. Educational programmes aimed at the prevention of drug use and, for those already addicted, aimed at the prevention of shared needles and other equipment can decrease this source of infection. Some countries have established needle exchange programmes that provide easy access to sterile needles and syringes, accompanied by counselling and health education and instructions on the safe disposal of used syringes.





Public health impact


	The WHO estimates that ~400,000 die each year from HCV infection and its complications; (http://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hepatitis-c). It is estimated that 3–4 million persons are newly infected each year and that ~20% of those infected with HCV progress to cirrhosis within the first 10 years after infection (Alter 2007; Gerberding and Henderson 1992). Although the prevalence of chronic HVC reached a peak in 2001 (according to a multiple cohort model) in the United States, the prevalence of hepatitis C cirrhosis and HCC is expected to continue to increase through the next decades (Davis et al. 2010). Furthermore, chronic HCV disease is the primary indication for liver transplantation in industrialized countries (Adam et al. 2012). In Europe the overall prevalence of chronic hepatitis C in the last decade was 0.13–3.26% and ~1% in countries of the European Union and Economic area (https://ecdc.europa.eu/en/hepatitis-c). It is of great concern that the majority of subjects infected with HCV and HBV globally are unaware of their status (Blachier et al. 2013).





Alcoholic liver disease


	Alcoholic beverages have been used in human societies since the beginning of recorded history. In 2005, a study estimated that just over 40% of the world’s adult population consumes alcohol and the average consumption per drinker is 17.1 L per year (Shield et al. 2013). The level of alcohol consumption worldwide in 2010 was estimated at 6.2 litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15 years and over (equivalent to 13.5 g of pure alcohol per day) (WHO 2014).
	It has long been known that alcohol consumption is responsible for increased illness and death. Worldwide, alcohol causes ~3.3 million deaths each year (5.9% of all deaths), while liver cirrhosis and its complication accounts for 16.2% of the cases (WHO 2014). Furthermore, 139 million disability-adjusted life years (5.1% of the global burden of disease and injury), were attributable to alcohol consumption (WHO 2014). The burden is not equally distributed among countries. The highest disease load attributable to alcohol is found in the heavy-drinking countries of Eastern Europe and in Latin America (Figure 8.16.4). Of note, alcohol consumption over the last 20 years in the UK and Finland has increased significantly, while other countries such as France, Spain and Portugal were able to reduce the number of liver-related deaths (Sheron 2016; Williams et al. 2018).
	Fig. 8.16.4 Total (recorded and unrecorded) alcohol consumption per capita (aged 15 years and over), in litres of pure alcohol within a calendar year, by WHO region, projected estimates for 2012.
	Reproduced from WHO (2014) ‘Global status report on noncommunicable diseases 2014’ with permission from the World Health Organization.
	Alcoholic liver disease constitutes the commonest reason for admitting patients with liver disease to a hospital and is responsible for at least 41% of the liver deaths in Europe (Sheron 2016). Between 2004 and 2013, the number of new liver transplants registrations for this aetiology in the US increased by 45% (Wong et al. 2015). In Europe, the proportion of patients transplanted for alcoholic liver disease increased by 8.3% between the time periods 1988–1995 and 1996–2000 (Burra et al. 2010). Alcohol (38%), viral hepatitis (43%), or both (6%) are the leading indications for liver transplantation following cirrhosis.
	The costs to society from alcohol abuse cannot be overemphasized. In 2006, overall costs in the United States reached US$223.5 billion, out of which healthcare expenses accounted for 11%. Almost three-quarters of these costs were due to binge drinking (Bouchery et al. 2011). In Europe in 2003, alcohol consumption resulted in estimated costs of €125 billion, equivalent to 1.3% of gross domestic product, while the reported contribution of the alcohol industry to the European economy was about €9 billion (Rabinovich et al. 2009).
	In 2010, 5.5% of the global burden of disease was attributable to alcohol, almost similar to the burden of tobacco-associated illness (6.3%) (Lim et al. 2012). Alcohol use is the leading risk factor for global disease burden in Eastern Europe, most of Latin America, and southern sub-Saharan Africa.





Morphology and natural history of alcoholic liver disease


Fatty liver (steatosis)


	The first and most predictable hepatic change attributable to alcohol is the development of large droplet (macrovesicular) steatosis. This disorder usually resolves within 2 weeks if alcohol consumption is discontinued (Diehl 1997). Of note, about 5–15% of patients with alcohol-induced steatosis will develop cirrhosis during a 10-year follow-up period (Sorensen et al. 1984).





Alcoholic steatohepatitis


	The spectrum of alcoholic steatohepatitis includes fatty infiltration of hepatocytes associated with hepatocellular injury including ballooning degeneration, Mallory bodies, inflammation with neutrophils and/or lymphocytes, and fibrosis with a perivenular, perisinusoidal, and pericellular disposition. These changes are present in 10–35% of all alcoholics. It is estimated that the probability of developing cirrhosis in patients with alcoholic liver disease is 10–20% per year and overall, 70% of patients with alcoholic hepatitis will eventually develop cirrhosis (Diehl 1997) and some will proceed to fatal liver decompensation.





Cirrhosis


	In 2010, alcoholic cirrhosis accounted for 48% of cirrhosis-related deaths globally (Rehm et al. 2013). The long-term prognosis of alcoholic cirrhosis improves with abstinence. The 5-year survival in compensated cirrhosis patients who continue to drink is 70%, but can rise to 90% if patients abstain from further alcohol intake. In patients with decompensated cirrhosis, the 5-year survival drops to 30% in individuals who continue to drink, but is 60% in those who stay abstinent (Alexander et al. 1971; Diehl 1997).





Hepatocellular carcinoma


	Alcohol is considered both as a primary cause of HCC as well as a co-factor for the malignant transformation. As hepatitis C is relatively frequent in alcoholics, the proportional contribution of alcohol in the reported HCC incidence rates in earlier studies is likely to be overestimated. Although the exact annual incidence rate of HCC in alcoholic cirrhosis is unknown, it is clear that alcoholic cirrhosis is a significant risk factor for HCC, sufficient to warrant surveillance for HCC (Bruix et al. 2005).





Factors influencing the risk of alcoholic liver disease


	Most authors agree that persons who drink heavily (50–60 g of ethanol daily) are at increased risk of developing liver disease (Becker et al. 2002). However, the absolute risk of acquiring alcoholic hepatitis or cirrhosis is relatively low (6.9% in the mentioned study) which suggests that genetic factors and/or environment may play a role in the pathogenesis.





Amount of alcohol


	Excessive alcohol consumption is associated with an increased risk of cirrhosis. However, a specific dose–response relationship for cirrhosis has not been agreed upon. Evidence suggests that there is an increased risk for alcoholic liver disease with the ingestion of 60–80 g/day of alcohol in men and 20 g/day in women (Day 2000). ‘Safe’ limits of alcohol consumption for the liver are up to two drinks per day for women, and up to three drinks per day for men, with at least three alcohol-free days per week (Rehm et al. 2010; European Association for the Study of the Liver 2018).





Drinking behaviour


	A survey of 30,630 persons from Denmark revealed that beer or spirits are more likely to promote liver disease than wine (Becker et al. 2002). At present, it is uncertain whether wine per se is responsible for this reduced risk of liver disease compared to the other alcoholic beverages, or whether it represents a surrogate for other healthy behaviours such as increased consumption of fruits/vegetables (Everhart 2003). Binge drinking, a mode of social behaviour nowadays, is the exaggerated form of non-mealtime drinking. It has been reported to increase the risk of alcoholic hepatitis fivefold (Barrio et al. 2004) and to increase the risk of all-cause mortality in men and women (Tolstrup et al. 2004). Importantly, a report from the OECD countries revealed that 30% of men and 12% of women binge-drink at least once per month (OECD 2017). Also drinking multiple types of alcohol has been shown to be related to the risk of cirrhosis and non-cirrhotic liver disease (Naveau et al. 1997). Nevertheless, there are still controversies regarding the risks of binge drinking. A Danish survey of 55,000 participants showed that daily drinking was associated with the highest risk of liver cirrhosis (Askgaard et al. 2015), while a Finnish population-based health study of 6,366 subjects without baseline liver disease revealed that binge drinking was associated with an increased risk of liver disease independently of average alcohol intake (Aberg et al. 2017).





Gender


	The proportion of global deaths attributable to alcohol differs based on gender, with 7.6% of deaths among males and 4.0% of deaths among females in 2012 (WHO 2014). Nevertheless, it is well recognized that women are more susceptible to alcohol-induced health disorders than men. Men and women have similar sized livers and similar metabolic rates when the rate of alcohol metabolism is normalized to liver mass. However, blood alcohol levels after comparable doses of alcohol will usually be higher in women than in men because of their lower body volume and the higher percentage of their body mass consisting of fat. Evidence from animal models has suggested that oestrogen increases the gut permeability to endotoxin and accordingly upregulates endotoxin receptors of Kupffer cells leading to an increased production of tumour necrosis factor alpha in response to endotoxin (Enomoto et al. 1999). It is also known that the gastric alcohol dehydrogenase activity can be different in men and women (Parlesak et al. 2002).





Comorbid conditions


	Individuals with comorbid conditions affecting the liver exhibit a greater tendency to develop liver disease in response to alcohol consumption than persons being otherwise healthy (Fattovich et al. 2004). This was clearly demonstrated in the case of hepatitis C (Corrao and Arico 1998), hepatitis B, hereditary haemochromatosis (Fletcher et al. 2002), and obesity (Naveau et al. 1997), and most probably applies to other causes of chronic hepatitis.





Genetic polymorphisms


	Strong epidemiological evidence suggests the existence of heritable susceptibility to alcoholic liver disease. This appears related to several gene polymorphisms, some of which impact alcohol metabolism and others that influence hepatic immune responses.





Prevention


	The overall management of alcoholism and of alcoholic liver disease and its complications is beyond the scope of this chapter. Nevertheless, general measures include alcohol withdrawal and providing nutritional support. A number of public health policies to reduce alcohol consumption have been shown to be helpful and cost-effective (Wagenaar et al. 2009; Wagenaar et al. 2010).
