9.2


Substance use and misuse


	Considerations on global public health
	Giang Le Minh and Steve Shoptaw





Psychoactive drug use and public health: introduction


	Use and misuse of psychoactive drugs present major public health problems in most countries. Nicotine (in the form of tobacco products) and alcohol are the most commonly used and misused psychoactive drugs, and account for the greatest mortality and morbidity related to psychoactive drug use. Since nicotine and alcohol are discussed in Chapters 9.1 and 9.3, this chapter provides an overview of the epidemiology of psychoactive drugs, in particular cannabis, opiates, amphetamine-type stimulants (ATS), and cocaine.
	The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) compiles annual prevalence estimates of the use of various illicit psychoactive drugs and assesses trends over time. In the most recent World Drug Report published in 2019 the UNODC estimated that 271 million people, or 5.5% of the adult population (persons aged 15–64), used an illicit drug in 2017 (UNODC 2019). Of these, about 13% of persons using drugs were considered to use at levels that cause problems or drug use disorders (UNODC 2019). Prevalence of drug use disorders globally was relatively stable from 2009 to 2016; however, a small increase was observed in 2017 in large part due to findings of increased drug use in Nigeria and India (UNODC 2019). With respect to the use of specific illicit drugs, the UNODC estimated that cannabis was by far the most commonly used drug in 2017 with 3.8% of adults having used it in the previous year, followed by opioids (1.1%), ATS (0.6%), and cocaine (0.4%). Yet production continues to increase worldwide. In 2017, opium production reached 10,500 tonnes, breaking the record since the beginning of twenty-first century (according to UNODC estimates). Cocaine manufacture also reached its highest level ever—1,410 tonnes in 2016. The quantities of other drugs such as amphetamines or new psychoactive drugs intercepted worldwide in the same year increased several times as well.
	Involvement in substance use introduces serious consequences to health of individuals and societies among all nations. The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study (https://www.theLANCET.com/gbd) estimates the numbers of deaths and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), which is the sum of years of life lost due to premature death and years lived with disability by specific countries and by specific diseases. In 2017, there were approximately 585,000 deaths and 42 million years of ‘healthy’ life lost as a result of the use of drugs worldwide. Years of life lost due to premature death were attributed to approximately half of DALYs. Globally, the number of DALYs and deaths attributed to drug use has increased by 134 and 81%, respectively, over the past three decades (UNODC 2019). Despite the modest numbers of adults who use illicit drugs compared to alcohol and tobacco, they generate many costs to society, including lost productivity, increased disability and deaths, disruption of family and other social relationships, and costs of increased law enforcement and incarceration.
	Research over the last two decades has increased understanding of the mechanisms of development and sustained expression of substance use disorder over the lifespan. This includes: (1) there is great individual variation in reactions to drugs; (2) repeated drug use leads to changes in brain cells (neurons) and the ways they communicate, particularly in systems related to reward, reinforcement and decision-making; (3) outcomes to treatment of substance use disorders (SUDs) involve ceasing (or cutting down) substance use and returning to abstinence following lapse or relapse; (4) SUDs are chronic and relapsing—there is no ‘cure’—though effective treatments exist; (5) globally and across cultures there are strong similarities in how SUDs present; and (6) drug use is contemporary, with always changing complexities of the specific drugs used, their combinations, and the interventions that ameliorate harmful effects of drugs on the brain and behaviour. While knowledge of mechanisms underlying SUDs is likely to continue to increase rapidly, it is unrealistic to expect that there will be any ‘magic bullet’ breakthroughs for either the treatment or prevention of SUDs in the near future. As such, the public health challenge is to support policymakers in understanding and responding to SUDs using models for managing other chronic diseases that in parallel fashion require ongoing treatment over the lifespan.





Global epidemiology and social determinants of substance use and substance use disorders


	Geography is not necessarily destiny with respect to what drugs a person might use, but there are strong geographical patterns in the use of different drugs. The information on geographic differences in use of specific drugs that follows is summarized from the World Drug Report (UNODC 2019). The World Drug Report is based on reports from various participating countries producing variation in data quality; consequently, these data should be interpreted as estimates. Law enforcement information, particularly on seizures of drugs, is also used in assessing trends in international drug use. Despite some limitations, the World Drug Report is the best available single source on global use of illicit drugs.





Cannabis


	Cannabis is the most prevalent of illicit substances used globally with 188 million individuals estimated to use cannabis worldwide in 2017. Cannabis products are most often smoked, but can be taken orally. In addition to the use of cannabis for its psychoactive properties, many around the world use cannabis and related products (e.g. cannabidiol) for relief of a range of medical complaints and conditions. Cannabis cultivation has increased in recent years, although many of the increases are small-scale growing operations. While the cannabis herb is prevalent in most countries, cannabis resin, or ‘hashish’, is more common in locations including Afghanistan, the Middle East, and small pockets of Western Europe and northern Africa. Among adults, the highest level of cannabis use is reported in North America (13.8%), followed by Oceania (10.9%), and West and Central Africa (10.0%). The prevalence of cannabis use among adults in Asia is low (1.8%); however, given the very large population of the region, it remains the largest population of individuals using cannabis worldwide. The relationship between cannabis exposure and health and psychosocial deficits is documented, though a causal relationship is uncertain (Hasin 2018). For these reasons, and in the face of the failure of prohibition, decriminalization and legalization of cannabis use are increasingly advocated for in Europe and North America in the face of the failure of prohibition (van Ours 2012).
	A novel health threat to cannabis and tobacco use involves lung health problems linked to using ‘vapes’, equipment that vaporizes oils and waxes for inhalation instead of burning combustible materials to produce smoke. Marketers of these devices promote fewer health risks to vaping cannabis and tobacco as smoke is not inhaled into the lungs. Even when considering the negative consequences to smoking combustible cannabis and tobacco, observations of severe lung disease, lung infections, and deaths that correspond with use of vaping devices elevate health concerns. These vaping instruments and cannabis and tobacco products are all unregulated complicating attribution of cause for severe illnesses and deaths linked with their use. In light of these factors, current medical opinion is to avoid vaping to administer cannabis and tobacco products (Christiani 2020).





Opioids


	Among the 53 million people who used opioids worldwide in 2017, risk for overdose and death is high with two-thirds of deaths from drugs occurring in people who use opioids. Opioids are prescribed to relieve pain (predominantly oral medications), but opioids also can be injected or smoked for their euphoric properties (predominantly heroin). The highest levels of opioid use among adults were in North America (4.0%), Oceania (2.5%), South-West Asia and the Near and Middle East (2.3%), and South Asia (1.8%), all of which were higher than average global prevalence. It is important to note that those using prescription opioids outnumber those using heroin in North America and Australia, while in South-West Asia and the Near and Middle East and South Asia heroin is the main opioid of use. Deaths from the opioid epidemic in the US are alarmingly high and are now accounted mostly by increased use of synthetic opioids (such as fentanyl), often in combination with cocaine and methamphetamine (Hedegaard et al. 2018). In Europe, heroin use was the opioid used for most of the individuals who sought drug treatment.





Amphetamine-type stimulants (ATS)


	Illicit use of ATS, which includes amphetamine, methamphetamine, and methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA, ecstasy) is difficult to measure globally, complicated by small-scale local producers of these drugs, but was estimated to involve almost 50 million adults globally in 2017. The quantity of ATS seized from 1998 to 2017 increased more than tenfold, substantially more than cannabis, opioids, and cocaine, though, opioid seizures dominated drugs seizures from 2013 to 2017 (UNODC 2019).
	ATS (excluding ecstasy) is most prevalent in Oceania—especially Australia (Farrell et al. 2019)—and North America, while there is evidence of increasing use in Asia, especially given increased seizure of methamphetamine in the region (UNODC 2019). ATS can be taken orally, smoked (e.g. ‘ice’/crystal methamphetamine) or injected (excepting ecstasy, which is taken orally), and with strong positive attributes (especially for cocaine and methamphetamine) that include inducing euphoria, brightening mood, dampening appetite, increasing energy, sharpening body experiences (especially during sex), and focusing attention. Methamphetamine is considered to be the most worrisome ATS due to its neurotoxicity, addictiveness and the high burden of care associated with methamphetamine use disorder (Courtney and Ray 2014; Farrell et al. 2019). Despite lack of data in East and South-East Asia, there is a growing concern about methamphetamine use and methamphetamine-related issues in this region. East and Southeast Asia are the largest manufacture regions of methamphetamine worldwide. Trade routes often used for cocaine trafficking are increasingly also being used for ATS trafficking, with evidence of spillover into West Africa. At a prevalence of 0.4%, ecstasy use globally is comparable to cocaine use in the adult population, but higher rates are observed in specific regions including Oceania (1.7%), North America (0.9%), and Western and Central Europe (0.9%). Ecstasy, in particular, tends to be prevalent in young people and has recently seen a resurgence in use among the younger demographic after a period of stability or even decline from 2007 to 2012.





Cocaine


	Cocaine consumption among adults has remained relatively stable with approximately 18 million users worldwide in 2017 (UNODC 2019). Cocaine is taken intranasally (powder) or smoked (crack), but also can be injected. Cocaine use is most prevalent among adult populations in North America (2.1%), Western and Central Europe (1.3%), and Oceania (1.7%). While cocaine use decreased or stabilized in the Americas and Europe by 2010, there have been increases in these regions as of 2017. Cocaine use increases correspond with increases in cocaine bush cultivation in South America a region where cocaine use accounts for a third of patients in treatment for SUDs. While limited data exist in Africa and parts of Asia, there are indications that there is increasing and emerging use of cocaine in those regions; this may reflect the increased trafficking of cocaine through these areas. Although increased cocaine use globally may be occurring, treatment for cocaine use makes up a small proportion of all drug admissions in all locales except Central and South America.





New psychoactive substances


	New psychoactive substances (NPS), relative potency plant-based, or synthetic chemical compounds that mimic the effects of most types of drugs such as cannabis, opioids, hallucinogens, or stimulants, first emerged since the early 2000s in Western countries and late 2000s in Asia (Zawilska and Andrzejczak 2015; UNODC 2019). Examples of NPS include cathinones, phenethylamines, aminoindanes, and bath salts. NPS are worrisome for their neurotoxicity and lethality (Hohmann et al. 2014). Currently, East and Southeast Asia are perceived as the production factory of global NPS (UNODC 2019). Although the share of NPS in the drug market might be still limited (they account for only 3% of drug seizure cases), global NPS have been increasing in number, type and availability (Zawilska and Andrzejczak 2015). Although most countries have tried to regulate NPS, a significant number of these drugs remain uncontrolled (Lee et al. 2018). NPS are developed and appear on the market frequently with changes to molecular structure that present challenges to legal actions due to the sheer number and types of new compounds.





Poly drug use


	Poly drug use is a frequent condition worldwide, often with mixtures of drugs used specifically for the subjective effects of the drugs together. Speedballs or goofballs are combination opioids (usually heroin) taken with cocaine, amphetamine, or methamphetamine, which brings energy to the mellow opioid ‘high’ experience. Marijuana often is used with stimulants to dampen the harshness of coming down from these drugs. Concurrent use of alcohol and cocaine metabolizes in the body to produce, cocaethylene, a compound that produces a high that is subjectively distinct from either cocaine or alcohol alone. As permutations vary by drug availability and preference, prevalence of poly drug use is difficult to measure in distinct combinations. Instead, estimates count those who report poly drug use and tally the constituents of the reported poly drug mixtures, which may bias prevalence estimates for each of the constituent drugs in the mixture.





Historical interpretation and implications for public health


	There are identifiable patterns in drug use in different regions of the world. Some patterns reflect cultural differences, when drug is used in cultures and national societies for specific purposes, with acceptance and approval of those drugs (Jay 2010). Production, distribution networks and markets also affect ways drugs function culturally and reflect the way in which the reinforcing nature of the drug is woven into spiritual, religious, or hedonistic purposes. As drug use is integrated into culture, production and distribution of the drug can also be protected by local culture, including corruption of local authorities.
	Supply-side responses at the level of the society to interrupt and prosecute global drug distribution networks have little impact on overall use (Csete et al. 2016). Where there are societal, cultural, and/or individual factors that produce a demand for drug, a distribution system and market will arise to meet the demand. On the other hand, demand-side efforts at prevention, harm reduction, and treatment are sorely needed to reduce the demand for drugs drives production and distribution.





Social determinants of substance use disorders


	SUDs are complex with multiple etiological and risk factors that can be classified into three levels: individual, interpersonal, and contextual. Individual risk factors include biological predispositions, mental health disorders (major depression, anxiety), family characteristics, and socioeconomic status that correspond with SUDs (Stone et al. 2012). People with drug use disorders are almost four times more likely to have major depressive disorder (OR 3.80, 95% CI 3.02–4.78) and three times more likely to have an anxiety disorder (OR 2.91, 95% CI 2.58–3.28) (Lai et al. 2015). Interpersonal risk factors for SUD include family dysfunction ranging from parenting styles to childhood trauma including child physical and sexual abuse. Important contextual factors that facilitate the development of SUDs include level of disorganization for the neighbourhood and social environment (Stone et al. 2012; Ford et al. 2017).
	These factors heavily shape social norms for young adults and adolescents during development. Social networks that develop around youth who grow up in proximity to peer substance users can normalize perceptions of substance use, increasing likelihood youths will use substances (Arbour-Nicitopoulos et al. 2010).
	Policies in law and taxation that shape availability of specific drugs strongly affect the prevalence of drug use and drug use disorders, especially in youth and others susceptible to socioeconomic forces. Laws that restrict legal drinking age and when alcohol can be sold can reduce alcohol consumption (Stone et al. 2012). Increasing prices of drugs leads to long-term reductions in SUDs, even among abusers (Pacula and Chaloupka 2001).





Public health consequences of substance use and misuse


Differentiation between substance use and substance use disorders


	There are different adverse consequences of substance use and misuse, for individuals, their families, and for society as a whole. Though most people do not use substances or use at levels that do not cause problems, for those who occasionally use substance heavily or in hazardous situations can experience negative consequences that are aversive enough to modify behaviour—most cut down or stop using substance. The range of negative consequences with heavy use of substances include individual (e.g. physical and psychological discomfort following binge use—a ‘hangover’), interpersonal (e.g. a family member complains substance use is causing problems), employment (e.g. a supervisor fires the employee who repeatedly misses Mondays) and legal consequences (e.g. citation for driving under the influence). For the minority of people who continue to engage in chronic, heavy levels of substance use, adverse consequences usually increase in frequency and severity. Still more people will cut down or stop using the substance in response. Only a minority continues to use substance at levels that define addiction, especially in light of negative consequences.





Defining the substance use disorder diagnosis


	There are no biological markers that confirm substance use disorder diagnoses. Tests that screen for substances or their metabolites in urine, saliva, breath, blood, or nails reliably document recent substance use, which confirms the key symptom underlying substance use disorder: active substance use. Instead, SUDs are defined by behavioural criteria. Major diagnostic manuals are the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) of the American Psychiatric Association and the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) system of the World Health Organization (WHO). The criteria for defining SUDs have undergone considerable evolution in both of these classification systems since their first presentation. The current DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association 2013) and the ICD-11 (WHO 2018) are the latest versions that detail the diagnostic criteria of SUDs and substance dependence, respectively.
	A major diagnostic change occurred in 2013 when the DSM-5 integrated two diagnostic categories, abuse and dependence, into one diagnosis that represents a spectrum disorder that ranges in severity determined by number of diagnostic criteria present. The DSM-5 now defines substance use disorder as having at least two of the following characteristics over a 12-month period that cause clinically significant impairment or distress: (1) hazardous use, (2) continued use despite social or interpersonal problems, (3) neglect of major roles in order to use, (4) withdrawal, (5) tolerance, (6) using in larger amounts or for longer periods than intended, (7) repeated efforts to stop or control use, (8) time spent getting, using and recovering from drug, (9) continued use despite knowledge of negative consequences, (10) important activities given up in order to use, and (11) craving. Those with 2–3 criteria are classified as mild SUD, 4–5 as moderate SUD, and 6 or more as severe SUD.
	The ICD-11 was released in 2018 and will take effect in 2021. The ICD-11 substance dependence diagnosis is based on three central features that are shared with DSM-5 and is used when there is evidence of at least two of these central features over a 12-month period—or continuous use over a one-month period: (1) impaired control over substance use; (2) increasing central role of substance use over other activities and responsibilities; and (3) physiological features as manifested by (i) tolerance, (ii) withdrawal symptoms following cessation or reduction in substance use, or (iii) repeated substance use (or pharmacologically similar substance) to prevent or alleviate withdrawal symptoms.
	Public health and clinical impact of using these diagnostic systems have strengths in informing research and clinical efforts that contribute to scientific knowledge and treatment delivery. Globally, severity of diagnoses for SUD corresponds with likelihood to succeed with treatments for SUD, with those with mild disorder being more likely to meet substance goals in treatment than those with severe SUD. Use of diagnoses confirms a medical understanding of addiction, which confers far less stigma than non-medical model concepts. By doing so, rigour and precision in measuring fidelity of treatment delivery and rigour in measuring outcomes from treatment increase.





Infectious diseases


	Substance-related infectious disease transmission occurs when persons who use substances engage in behaviours to get (e.g. exchange sex) or use those drugs (e.g. share injection drug equipment). Injection drug behaviours, including sharing of injection equipment and paraphernalia used to prepare drug for injection have high efficiency in transmitting infections during drug administration, particularly for Hepatitis C virus. Substance use can facilitate infectious disease transmission when psychoactive properties inhibit inhibitions or otherwise enhance condomless sexual experiences such as ‘chemsex’ (sex under influence of substance), extreme sexual behaviours (multiple partner), or exchange sex). While lower transmission efficiency compared to injection drug use, far more people globally use their drugs but do not inject, which increases risks for sexually transmitted infections (Shoptaw et al. 2013).





HIV/AIDS


	Given the efficiency of infectious disease transmission when sharing injection drug use equipment and paraphernalia, it is not surprising that in the beginning of the US HIV epidemic, people who inject drugs (PWID) represented a group with high incidence and prevalence. Early studies in New York City showed approximately half of PWID in the city had HIV infection (Des Jarlais et al. 1996). Sharp reductions in HIV incidence and prevalence began in the 1990s among PWID that corresponded with several developments. Public health officials recognized effective medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD), particularly agonist (methadone) and partial agonist (buprenorphine, buprenorphine/naloxone) medications reduced heroin injection and thereby reduced transmission events for this group. There are solid reasons for this action: methadone promotes ART adherence among PWID (Uhlmann et al. 2010), even among PWID living with HIV/AIDS who are homeless (Palepu et al. 2011). Since 2005, methadone and buprenorphine are included on the WHO essential medications list for their effectiveness as treatments for opioid use disorder and their ability to prevent infectious disease transmission (WHO 2019).
	Also occurring during the 1990s, there were thrilling developments in treating HIV/AIDS, with development of multiple classes of medications that, when used in combination, dramatically slowed mortality, dampened transmission, and improved health for those living with HIV/AIDS. Policymakers recognizing this ensured access to HIV medications to all, including PWID living with HIV/AIDS. Concurrently, civil societies (grassroots groups of PWID and their allies) mounted effective campaigns at local, national, and global levels to ensure access to harm reduction (NSP—needle and syringe programmes) for individuals who use injection drugs. Modelling studies show that simultaneous access to these three elements (opioid agonist treatment, ART, and NSPs) will slow or stop new HIV transmissions among PWID (Degenhardt et al. 2010). Recognition of these elements and six other elements were compiled into a global consensus document that promotes a framework for countries to use to prevent HIV transmission by ensuring access and by measuring outcomes of HIV prevention among PWID (World Health Organization, UNODC, United Nations AIDS 2012). Interventions also included HIV testing and counselling, prevention, and treatment of sexually transmitted infections, condom distribution programmes for PWID and their sexual partners, targeted information, education and communication, prevention, vaccination, diagnosis, and treatment of viral hepatitis infection and prevention diagnosis and treatment of tuberculosis. With these effective prevention interventions, there is no good reason for an additional incident case of HIV among PWID. Indeed, additional new cases identify a lack of political will to ensure PWID have access to the combination prevention services framework.





Sexual transmission of HIV among persons who use drugs


	Around the world, far more people use non-injection methods to use drugs. Risks for HIV transmission linked with non-injection use of substances are indirect in that their use facilitates condomless sex with HIV-positive or status unknown sex partners. Non-injection substances can increase HIV transmission along four domains. Drugs (methamphetamine, cocaine) can directly interact with characteristics of cells to alter immune function and enhance HIV transmission dynamics. Substances can alter HIV transmission behaviours as well. Binge alcohol drinking (beer goggles) diminishes inhibitions; stimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine, ecstasy) enables sex at the extremes (longer, rougher sex sessions) and enable ‘chemsex’ or ‘high fun’, a unique sexual experience that occurs only when under the influence of these drugs among men who have sex with men (MSM). Substances can interact with individuals to support behaviours that enhance risks for HIV transmission (exchange sex) and that promote sex in high-risk environments (venues where sexually transmitted infections are common).
	Groups of users around the world have preferences that can enhance risks for HIV transmission. Binge alcohol drinking is the predominant substance linked with HIV transmission behaviours among MSM in South America among others. Use of stimulants by MSM (especially methamphetamine) significantly corresponds with HIV incidence (Plankey et al. 2007). Non-injection substance use interferes with consistent ART adherence, which can interfere with sustained viral suppression among those who are living with HIV/AIDS.
	Over the past decade, HIV transmission was slowed or halted using pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) medications (emtricitabine/tenofovir) for HIV-negative persons among high-risk groups (serodiscordant couples, MSM). Landmark research showed that people living with HIV with sustained undetectable viral load levels were unable to transmit HIV to their partners (Cohen et al. 2011). Undetectable equals untransmittable. Efforts to test biomedical HIV prevention among PWID have shown that providing opioid substitution therapy for PWID living with HIV not only reduces mortality and morbidity for the individual, but prevents HIV transmission to sexual partners (Miller et al. 2018). Research findings also show that providing PrEP to PWID who are HIV-negative prevents HIV infection in parallel fashion to groups who do not use drugs (Choopanya et al. 2013). Research has yet to show findings in parallel fashion to PWID for persons who use non-injection substances. Conceivably, non-injection use of these substances interferes with consistent adherence to ARVs among those who are living with HIV (treatment) or who are high-risk HIV-negative individuals who use substances (prevention).





Hepatitis C virus (HCV) among persons who inject drugs


	While HIV and HCV are transmitted through sharing of drug injection equipment, HCV is dramatically more infectious than HIV. Less efficient transmission of HCV can occur when coming into direct contact with blood (sharing a toothbrush used by someone with bleeding gums) and when having condomless sex with multiple sexual partners. A minority of individuals exposed to HCV spontaneously clear the infection. About 75 to 85% of persons with HCV progress to chronic phase with about 20% developing end-stage liver disease. Given this, it is not surprising that more PWID are living with HCV infection than are living with HIV—and coinfection with HCV and HIV can accelerate HIV disease progression.
	Untreated HCV infection represents the leading risk for morbidity and mortality for PWID. In meta-analysis, the time to significant liver damage is 26–38 years after time of infection, with cirrhosis 34–46 years afterwards (Smith et al. 2015). In the decade prior, treatment for HCV involved use of ribavirin and pegylated interferon. This combination produced sustained viral suppression (cure) for some individuals, with better outcomes for persons with select genotypes of HCV and less or no efficacy for others. Another drawback to the ribavirin/interferon combination involved significant side effects including moderate to severe depression and exhaustion that led many to abandon the treatment. In 2013 direct acting antiretrovirals (DAAs) were developed. These medications act by disrupting viral replication and infection processes. The result is these medications shortened treatment periods, reduced side effects of the treatment and produced cure rates for most persons, independent of HCV genotype. Concerns over reinfection among PWID following successful treatment for HCV are not borne out by data (Martinello et al. 2017). The key drawback to using DAAs is their high cost—so high as to likely interfere with their use by PWID. Use of DAAs early in HCV infection for PWID, while expensive, prevents liver damage and corresponding higher-cost treatments later in life. As well, HCV cure for PWID earlier in life prevents potential for HCV transmission via drug or sexual transmission behaviours, which further reduces costs for healthcare. Despite the high efficacy for DAAs as treatment for HCV, the high costs will likely continue to dampen policymakers’ willingness to scale them up even in the US and across the world for use among PWID until costs come down. One hopeful sign is that for most states in the US, DAAs are covered by Medicaid formularies, which portends access to these drugs for PWID.





Drug-induced (overdose) deaths


	In 2015, 450,000 persons were determined to have died from drug use. Deaths from overdoses are a unique and extreme major adverse consequence to drug use. In North America, especially the US, drug overdose is the leading cause of accidental death. Over 72,000 fatalities were tallied in 2017 in the US (Ahmad et al. 2018) of which 47,600 were attributed to opioid overdose (Statistics 2018). This opioid epidemic has become North America’s most widespread behavioural public health problem, with a higher number of deaths due to drug overdose in 2016 compared to deaths due to HIV at the peak of the AIDS epidemic in the US (CDC 2017). Cause of death due to overdose is attributed by medical examiners based on results from drug screening tests and recorded on certificates of death. Reports on overdose deaths that rely on death records have some inherent unreliability as autopsies are not conducted on all deaths. When poly substance use is present at death, it may be difficult to determine which substance is the cause of death. Stimulant drugs such as cocaine and methamphetamine can also induce deaths, especially when these drugs are combined with opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol, and other drugs.





Methodological toolbox for studying illicit substance use


	As illicit drug use is, by definition, illegal there are many difficulties in collecting rigorous data on the topic. The difficulties include: (1) social desirability responding (Pauls and Stemmler 2003) in which persons who use drugs may deny (or minimize) their drug use in order to present a desirable image to the researchers and/or to themselves; (2) locating survey participants, as many persons who use drugs at high levels may be homeless or unstably housed; and (3) the effects of drugs on memory (though greatest memory problems may be associated with alcohol use). Various techniques have been developed to reduce these problems including: (1) audio-computer assisted self-interviewing (ACASI) (Des Jarlais et al. 1996), in which questionnaires are programmed into computers so that the research participant listens to the questions over headphones and responds to the questions using either the keyboard or a touch screen. ACASI does not require participants to be literate and the questions can be presented identically to all individuals; (2) respondent-driven sampling (Heckathorn 1997), in which participants are reimbursed for recruiting others. Restrictions are placed on the numbers of participants that any individual can recruit, and additional data is collected in order to increase generalizability to the underlying population; and (3) timeline follow back (Sobell and Sobell 1992), a method in which major events in an individual’s life are used to anchor to the recall of events over long time periods.





Surveys and sampling strategies


	There are several major methods for studying the epidemiology of illicit drug use. These include household surveys of the general population, school surveys of drug abuse among young adults, and special studies aimed at examining drug use among particular groups, such as those who use drugs at high frequencies.





Household surveys of the general population


	Surveys of random samples of household members provide what is usually considered to be the best estimates of the use of different drugs in a country. Such surveys are quite expensive but provide data that cannot be obtained through any other method. The US National Survey of Drug Use and Health is conducted annually with a sample of over 67,500 respondents age 12 years or older. In that year, 10.6% of adults reported illicit drug use in the previous month (the measure of current drug use). The most commonly used illicit drug reported was marijuana followed by opioids. Specifically, there were an estimated 11.5 million people who reported non-medical use of pain relievers in 2016; a fivefold increase from 2012.





School surveys


	Surveys can also be conducted in schools. School-age youth are of particular interest because illicit drug use typically begins during adolescence, and trends in the use of different drugs are often much more pronounced in this age group. Thus, school surveys may be particularly useful for generating predictions about future drug use. ‘Monitoring the Future’ is the largest and longest running school survey in the US (Johnston et al. 2006). In the 2018 survey of the 44,400 students who were interviewed, 38.8% reported using illicit drugs in the previous year, with marijuana being the most commonly used illicit drug, (35.9%), and narcotics (other than heroin) being the second most commonly used illicit drug (6.0%).





Administrative data


	Persons who use illicit drugs frequently come into contact with both law enforcement and health agencies. They may be arrested for possession of drugs and/or they may seek treatment for both their substance abuse disorder and for related health problems, such as overdose and infections. Administrative data can be useful to detect temporal trends in criminal justice and treatment services. For example, According to the Treatment Episode Data Set (TEDS) (TEDS 2017), there were slightly more than 2 million admissions to publicly funded drug and alcohol treatment programmes in the US in 2017. Among those aged 12 and older who sought treatment, five substances accounted for 93% of admissions: opiates (34%, primarily heroin), alcohol (29%), marijuana/hashish (13%), stimulants (12%, primarily methamphetamine), and cocaine (5%). Over the past decade, administrative data using TEDS highlighted the way opiates exceeded alcohol as the primary driver of treatment admissions in the US with stimulants/methamphetamine taking the spot from cocain06 in the rankings of publicly funded treatment admissions for these five illicit substances.





Special studies


	While carefully framed surveys can provide data about the breadth of drug use in the general and school populations, and administrative data can provide useful information about problems associated with illicit drug use, these types of studies do not provide the depth of information needed to understand the problems associated with specific forms of illicit drug use. Special studies usually recruit persons who use drugs at high frequencies. PWID with or at risk for HIV infection are an example. Special studies may also recruit subjects from clinical (drug treatment programme) settings from the community. They may be cross-sectional (one-time data collection) or cohort studies (with the same subjects followed over time).
	This review of survey and method tools provides guidance and initial recommendations on how to use methods to collect data at the population level and within special populations that to advise prevalence, incidence, and potential interventions with important groups of persons who use substances.





Interventions: approaches to treatment and prevention of substance use disorders


	While there are effective methods for reducing transmission of infectious pathogens and for reducing overdoses among persons who use drugs, the ideal method for addressing these problems would be to eliminate drug use among persons with SUDs. Current treatments can be used to produce periods of abstinence from weeks to months, but there are currently no treatments that can produce permanent abstinence. This reality best frames SUDs not only as spectrum disorders, but as disorders that are chronic and relapsing over the lifespan. Multiple treatments often are required before abstinence is achieved.
	For prevention, there exists an accepted framework for PWID drafted by the WHO, UNODC, and the Joint United Nations Program on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS). This technical guide outlines a comprehensive package for prevention and treatment for PWID (World Health Organization, UNODC, United Nations AIDS 2012) that includes methods for setting country targets and for measuring progress in providing these services. Services include needle and syringe programmes, opiate substitution treatment, HIV testing and counselling, antiretroviral treatment, prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections, condom programmes for PWID and their sexual partners, targeted information, education, and communication for PWID and their sexual partners, prevention, vaccination and treatment of viral hepatitis, and prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of tuberculosis.





Opiate substitution treatment/medication for opioid use disorder


	Effective pharmacological treatment is available only for opioid dependence. Solid evidence supports agonist maintenance treatments including methadone and buprenorphine (mono formula or in combination with naloxone) (Connery 2015). Still, as SUDs interrelated to various psychological and social factors, evidence suggests medication should be combined with other treatment components including cognitive behavioural therapies, motivational interviewing, contingency management, harm reduction, social support services, and integrated care to achieve optimal outcomes.
	Methadone. Scale-up of methadone maintenance treatment (MMT) has been a major turning point in global public health for PWID. Methadone is a full opioid agonist (as is heroin) that activates opioid mu receptors on nerve cells located in areas of the brain that are the basis for analgesic and pleasure effects from opioids. This binding of methadone at mu receptors prevents opioid withdrawal symptoms, largely without producing euphoria. Methadone stops (or reduces) use of supplemental opioids, allowing the treated patient to avoid behaviours of drug use and to engage prosocial behaviours. Notable country outcomes following rapid scale-up of MMT in China and Vietnam demonstrate dramatic improvements in drug-related public health and social issues, especially reductions in HIV transmission. For most countries a drawback to providing MMT include requirements to deliver the care in highly regulated, specialty care settings to prevent diversion of the drug. There are successful models where methadone is prescribed at outpatient pharmacies with few medical or social harms, though policymakers are slow to engage this option. MMT is a primary HIV prevention strategy for PWID: 40% of reduction in the risk of incident HIV from sharing of injection drug and equipment (MacArthur et al. 2012; Karki et al. 2016). Given the strong advantages to MMT, retention in care is the primary treatment goal (Karki et al. 2016)
	Buprenorphine. Buprenorphine is an optional treatment to methadone approved in the US since 2002. Buprenorphine is an opioid partial mu agonist that is manufactured as a mono-product and a co-formulated product containing a naloxone tag that reduces concerns over injection use. The mono and combo products are available in oral (daily) form. Injection (weekly, monthly) and implant (6 months) formulations of buprenorphine are available in high-income countries. Buprenorphine tightly binds at the mu opioid receptor (preventing withdrawal symptoms), but binds so tightly that buprenorphine effectively blocks effects of supplemental opioid use. A key advantage to buprenorphine is the ‘partial’ agonist blockade function that is so effective that it protects against most risks for overdose (especially respiratory distress) when treated patients use supplemental opioids. This safety profile allows the medication to be prescribed in outpatient clinic settings. Systematic reviews that compare MMT with buprenorphine and placebo therapy show that both MMT and buprenorphine maintenance therapy (BMT) are more effective and cost-effective than no treatment and MMT is slightly more effective in retaining patients and suppressing illicit opioid use than buprenorphine (Mattick et al. 2014).
	Naltrexone. Naltrexone is a long acting opioid antagonist that tightly binds at the mu receptor sites. It is available in oral (daily), injection (monthly) and implant (6 months) formulations. The antagonist action of naloxone is complete and blocks any opioids from producing euphoria, which stops opioid use completely. The binding of naltrexone at the mu receptor is so strong that it will displace any opioid from the mu receptor site that may be remaining in the body (precipitating opioid withdrawal). This effect also is so strong that a liquid formulation (naloxone—injection, nasal spray) is used widely to reverse opioid overdoses in emergency settings. Naloxone also is distributed widely (often by syringe and needle programmes) among friends/family members of opioid users to use in cases of overdose. While naltrexone is on board, the medication blocks any opioid use, preventing relapse to opioids. When the medication has worn off, however, risks for overdose exist as individuals become overwhelmed by prior doses of opioids as tolerance is lost with sustained treatment by antagonists (Miotto et al. 1997). Outcomes show use of oral naltrexone yields no difference from treatment with placebo (Minozzi et al. 2011). The main failure of oral naltrexone is a high dropout rate (Minozzi et al. 2011). In 2010, the extended released injectable naltrexone was approved in the US, attempting to solve the issue of the oral formula. This monthly injection provides patients with opioid dependence with more freedom in managing their condition. It has been proved to be equally effective as buprenorphine/naloxone treatment for patients who have been detoxified (Jarvis et al. 2018; Lee et al. 2018).
	There are no medications approved for use to treat stimulants. Recent developments in medication development have yielded promising results for use of mirtazapine for methamphetamine use disorders (Colfax et al. 2011; Coffin et al. 2019). These trials replicated a statistically significant and meaningful reduction of methamphetamine use by 15–18% compared to placebo over a period of 12 weeks. These effects were observed in the context of regular counselling sessions, underscoring the likelihood that any medication for stimulant use disorder will require both medication and psychosocial interventions. Improvements in trial design and conduct in evaluating putative medication candidates for stimulant use disorder signal a strong possibility of development of one or more medications for cocaine and methamphetamine use disorders in the next decade.





Cognitive behavioural therapy


	Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), a multisession psychoeducation therapy, teaches persons with substance use disorder steps to initiate substance abstinence (dispose of drug and paraphernalia, set a quit date), to respond to cravings and urges using psychological and imagery skills and to return to abstinence in the setting of lapse or relapse. Most models of CBT stem from the original work of Marlatt and Gordon’s model of relapse prevention (Marlatt and Donovan 2005).
	The signal size of CBT for drug use disorder is in the moderate range (d=0.45). CBT has larger effect sizes when evaluated for treatment of cannabis use disorder with small effect size for poly substance use disorder (McHugh et al. 2010), findings verified in a second meta-analysis (Magill and Ray 2009). Moreover, CBT effects are measurable in trials at up to one-year follow-up evaluations (Rawson et al. 2004). CBT is a mature behavioural treatment for substance use disorder—so much so that elements of CBT are widely integrated into many ecumenical and 12-step approaches to counselling for SUDs.





Contingency management


	Contingency management (CM) is a treatment for SUDs that involves providing voucher incentives in increasing value for successive biological samples documenting drug abstinence. As such, the treatment is based in operant conditioning (Skinner 1938). Its application began in delivery of methadone maintenance therapy by providing take-home medications to individuals who provided evidence of no illicit opioids while in treatment (Stitzer et al. 1977). The treatment was first used to treat cocaine use disorder in the early 1990s (Higgins et al. 1993). The treatment is used with a range of SUDs successfully. Several meta-analyses reliably show effect sizes for CM range between d = 0.4 to d = 0.6 (Prendergast et al. 2006; Dutra et al. 2008; Benishek et al. 2014; Davis et al. 2016).
	CM can be delivered using two distinct methods. One provides vouchers of increasing value for successive samples documenting drug abstinence while the other provides opportunities to draw from a fishbowl for chances to win a small, medium, or large size prize. With successive samples marking drug abstinence, additional draws from the fishbowl are earned. The differing procedures have roughly equal efficacy.
	There are no treatments for stimulant use disorder with greater effect sizes than CM, yet adoption of the treatment remains lacklustre. In the US, the Veterans Administration Healthcare System has recently adopted providing the treatment for veterans diagnosed with cocaine use disorder. Early outcomes from this work indicate that the treatment is feasible and shows similar effects as in efficacy trials (DePhilippis et al. 2018). Evidence for increasing scale-up of CM more broadly is provided in a recent meta-analysis showing significantly greater effects in producing outcomes in treatment for stimulant use disorder than CBT or other modalities (De Crescenzo et al. 2018).





Motivational interviewing


	Motivational interviewing (MI) is an approach based in client-centred therapy that has the basic assumption that people change thinking and behaviour about their substance use along a series of stages (Miller and Rollnick 2013). A hallmark of this assumption is that individuals can enter into treatment at any of these stages. The therapy style for MI emphasizes the psychological basis of addiction being ambivalence—the simultaneous thoughts that substance use both is and is not a problem. Individuals frequently shift between beliefs that substance use is not a problem (followed by substance use) and beliefs that substance use is a problem (followed by an attempt to quit or cut down). Therapists trained in MI techniques elicit a process of ‘natural’ change (i.e. change that is identified, initiated, and maintained by the individual) using non-directive interventions. Outcomes show that MI engages individuals in longer term treatment and promotes specific behaviour changes. From this approach, ‘denial’ is not confronted by therapists. Instead, MI techniques focus on articulating ambivalent beliefs in individuals about their substance use and work to develop discrepancies in their beliefs with the goal of developing ‘change talk’. Statements from individuals that emphasize disadvantages of the status quo, that emphasize need to change, that express optimism for change and that disclose intention to change are defined as change talk and correspond with positive outcomes in treatment (Magill et al. 2019).
	Meta-analysis of MI outcomes for substance use disorder treatment show weak to moderate effect sizes (Sayegh et al. 2017). As with CBT, stronger effect sizes for MI are observed for cannabis use disorder and weaker effect sizes for alcohol, tobacco, and poly substance use.





Detoxification


	For most who become addicted to opioids, detoxification becomes a goal at some point. Many fail during multiple attempts at detoxification before a minority of individuals successfully maintain opioid abstinence. As noted, this raises risks for overdose following return to opioid use following the detoxification attempt. Some seeking detoxification services may not wish to become abstinent, but instead reduce their tolerance level to a more affordable level. Treatment for detoxification for opioid use disorder involves starting individuals on methadone then tapering methadone dose over a period of 2–3 weeks. During some point of the taper, withdrawal symptoms will cause many to discontinue early and return to opioid use, though often at a level somewhat lower than at the start of the taper). Despite the many individuals worldwide who start detoxification, the literature describing outcomes using this approach is uneven and poorly articulated, presumably because the high early discontinuation interferes with drawing conclusions in randomized controlled trials. One meta-analysis on opioid detoxification concludes that variable and poor quality studies prevent comparisons and instead recommends patients be counselled toward opioid maintenance treatment (Amato et al. 2004). Detoxification outcomes can be improved some, however, by integrating psychosocial counselling approaches while conducting the taper during detoxification programmes (Amato et al. 2008).





Residential treatment


	Residential treatment for SUDs involves providing direct service with multiple components within a licensed facility that can evaluate, diagnose, and treat the symptoms and disabilities linked with substance use disorder. Individuals in residential treatment receive services 24 hours as needed. Services range in intensity, from mild through intensive levels, with focus on instilling abstinence, preventing relapse, coping with triggers, mood management, 12-step involvement, physical exercise, congregant living skills, and activities of daily life (Reif et al. 2014b). Individuals who begin residential treatment generally receive more intensive services and as abstinence is established, mood improves and impulsive behaviour inhibited, intensity of services decrease allowing the individual to engage independent behaviours. Lengths of stay at residential treatment facilities range from 28 days through several months. Toward discharge from residential treatments, individuals have opportunities to establish drug-free routines outside the facility. Many engage work, family, and other social activities, then return to the residential treatment facility to end the day.
	Efficacy of the residential treatment approach shows that the approach has value, though the quality of the evidence prevents arriving at statistics that describe the extent of that value. Still this essential treatment approach for those with severe SUDs merits consideration as policymakers determine the mix of service intensities and modalities that are available to persons seeking treatment. Recovery housing provides a stepped down level of care that still provides direct service with multiple components that includes supervised, short-term housing to individuals with SUDs or co-occurring mental and SUDs after residential treatment. Recovery housing for persons with SUDs have positive effects on long-term substance use outcomes and improvements in functioning, including employment and criminal activity (Reif et al. 2014a).





12-step and related social programmes


	The 12 Steps of Alcoholics Anonymous is a fellowship of people who share the problems that have become unmanageable due inability to control use of alcohol (AA), narcotics (Narcotics Anonymous—NA), cocaine (Cocaine Anonymous—CA), Crystal Meth Anonymous—(CMA) and other substances. Twelve Step programmes rely on the original or derivative programme of recovery set forth by the Alcoholics Anonymous: The Big Book (Anonymous 2002a) and the Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions (Anonymous 2002b). A key distinction to these 12-step programmes is that they are not considered treatment for substance use disorder formally. Instead 12-step groups are a social fellowship in which persons with addiction meet, work the programme set forth in the Big Book, and provide and receive social support. As these programmes fiercely protect their anonymous nature, there are no randomized controlled trials that would describe their efficacy in producing or sustaining abstinence from substance. Despite efficacy indicators, the ubiquity of these groups around the world undoubtedly have the greatest effectiveness of any therapy or programme designed to instil and maintain substance abstinence worldwide.
	The programme of the 12-Steps of Alcoholics Anonymous is built around a concept of a ‘God’ that can be defined in many ways that is central to admitting powerlessness over control of substance use. Discomfort with the God-concept among many has contributed to development of secular versions of the 12-Steps. These include: Rational Recovery, SMART Recovery, Women for Sobriety, Secular Organizations for Sobriety, and Moderation Management. These groups use differing conceptualizations about addiction and its treatment from the 12-Steps and from each other. Many of these emphasize CBT and related psychological constructs to support recovery. Some work toward a secular adaptation of 12-Step groups.





Harm reduction


	Harm reduction among people who use drugs grew out of shared recognition among these individuals and their allies that due to stigma and lack of political support, health promoting and harm reducing strategies and interventions would not happen unless they banded together to demand them. The initial work of this grassroots movement was helping to institute and scale-up syringe and needle programmes worldwide. With the advent of the HIV/AIDS epidemic and the efficiency of transmission of virus via injection methods, efforts to broaden access to syringe and needle programmes gained acceptance in communities (Des Jarlais et al. 1996). This grassroots movement professionalized and developed organizations, leaders, and impact, especially on the global public health stage. Today, this involves a well-supported and effective ‘civil society’ movement. This movement has been able to organize civil disobedience and to build alliances with academic and community partners to achieve major accomplishments in ensuring harm reduction and health promoting interventions are available, worldwide, for persons who use drugs. In addition to syringe and needle programmes, harm reduction approaches have developed to include supervised injection facilities, primarily in response to the growing worldwide spread of fentanyl among PWID. Fentanyl is 50–100 times more potent than heroin, so the risks for overdose are now higher than perhaps any time in history. The supervised injection facility ensures that rescue medications and medical personnel are onsite for reversing unintended overdose. These harm reduction spaces also are designed to be spaces that provide sterile injection supplies, that provide access and/or linkages to medical care (especially wound/abscess care, treatment for sexually transmitted infections) and linkages to formal treatment for SUDs.
	Systematic review of trials on efficacy of syringe and needle programmes show these programmes provide social and physical environments that mitigate drug-related harms and increased access to social and material resources (McNeil and Small 2014). The specific elements of this support include refuge from street-based drug use settings, promotion of safer injecting in providing equipment and guidance for this objective, provide linkages to healthcare services and resources and protect from law enforcement. Given the stigmatized and victimized experiences common to PWID, provision of these safe spaces continue to be at the same level of priority as providing MOUD and access to naloxone reversal kits for persons living with opioid use disorder.
