9.6


Collective violence


	War
	Barry S. Levy





Introduction


	There are three categories of violence: self-directed violence, interpersonal violence, and collective violence. Collective violence is ‘the instrumental use of violence by people who identify themselves as members of a group—whether this group is transitory or has a more permanent identity—against another group or set of individuals in order to achieve political, economic, ideological, or social objectives’ (Krug et al. 2002, p. 215). Collective violence includes armed conflict (such as war), state-sponsored violence (such as genocide, repression, disappearances, and torture), and organized violent crime (such as gang warfare and banditry). This chapter focuses on war. (Chapter 8.7 focuses on self-directed violence. Chapter 9.5 focuses on interpersonal violence, including gang warfare. Chapter 8.19 covers bioterrorism.)
	During 2019, there were 32 armed conflicts: 15 in sub-Saharan Africa, 7 in the Middle East and North Africa, 7 in Asia and Oceania, 2 in North American and South America, and 1 in Europe. Most of these were intrastate conflicts (mainly ‘civil wars’), occurring within a low-or middle-income country between government forces and one or more armed non-state groups. There were three wars with 10,000 or more battle-related deaths in 2019—in Afghanistan (approximately 41,900), Yemen (25,900), and Syria (15,300) (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute 2020).
	There are multiple underlying and precipitating causes of war. Many wars are caused by disputes over government power, territory, or environmental resources. Risk factors for war include: (a) demographic factors, such as high infant mortality and high population density; (b) social and community factors, such as inequality among groups, availability of small arms and light weapons, and racial, ethnic, or religious tensions; (c) political factors, such as inadequate public role in decision-making, rapid regime change, and unequal access to power; (d) economic factors, such unequal access to or distribution of resources; and (e) other factors, such as deterioration in public services and cycles of violent revenge (Krug et al. 2002, pp. 213–39; Carnegie Commission on Preventing Deadly Conflict 1998). Conflicts over access to freshwater, which are increasing (Gleick 2018), can lead to war (Levy and Sidel 2011). Climate change, by causing increased temperature and extremes of precipitation with associated consequences, may increase the risk of armed conflict (Levy and Patz 2015). Ethnic tensions, militarism, and the arms trade contribute to the risk of war.





The health and environmental consequences of war


	The consequences of war include morbidity and mortality due to weapons; damage to the health-supporting infrastructure of society; contamination of air, water, and land; forced displacement; violation of human rights; diversion of financial and human resources; and promotion of additional violence (Levy and Sidel 2008, 2013). Each of these consequences is described in more detail next.





Morbidity and mortality due to weapons


	Many people, including an increasing percentage of civilians, have been killed or injured by weapons during war. An estimated 191 million people died directly or indirectly as a result of conflict during the twentieth century (Ferguson 2006). More than half of those who died were civilians and tens of millions of people died as a result of mass murder and genocide (Rummel 1994; Power 2002). In addition to physical injuries and illnesses, wars cause—both among military personnel and civilians—mental health consequences, including anxiety, depression, posttraumatic stress disorder, alcohol and drug abuse, violence inflicted on family and friends, and suicide (Blore et al. 2015; Bonde et al. 2016).
	From the early twentieth century to the start of the Second World War, the vast majority of deaths during war were among uniformed combatants, usually members of national armed forces. Although non-combatant civilians suffered from the social, economic, and environmental consequences of war, they were usually not targeted. However, since 1937, when Nazi forces bombed Guernica, a city in Spain, military operations, in addition to causing ‘collateral damage’ to non-combatant civilians as a result of attacks on military targets, have increasingly targeted—and injured and killed—non-combatant civilians (Tirman 2011).





Damage to the health-supporting infrastructure of society


	Much morbidity and mortality during war, especially among non-combatant civilians, results from damage to the health-supporting infrastructure of society. In some wars, such as the civil war in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (in which more than five million people died during the war and its aftermath), the vast majority of deaths among non-combatant civilians have been caused by infectious diseases, malnutrition, and pregnancy-and neonatal-related conditions—largely due to damage to the societal infrastructure (Coghlan et al. 2008). This damage includes adverse effects on medical care and public health services. Physicians, nurses, and other health workers are injured or killed or they flee; clinics and hospitals are physically damaged; public health services are reduced or eliminated; and there is inadequate or no access to essential medicines and vaccines. Damage to the societal infrastructure also includes adverse impacts on food and water supply systems, sewage disposal systems, power plants and electrical grids, and transportation and communication systems.





Contamination of air, water, and soil


	The physical environment may be contaminated during war—or the preparation for war—by military exercises on land, in air, and in water and by the production, testing, use, and disposal of weapons. Hazardous wastes from military operations can contaminate air, water, and soil. For example, groundwater contamination occurred due to disposal of petroleum products and other hazardous materials at the Otis Air Force Base in Massachusetts. Pesticides, solvents, other chemicals, and radioactive materials were dumped for over 30 years at the Rocky Mountain Arsenal in Colorado. Benzene, arsenic, chromium, and mercury have been detected at the McChord Air Force Base in Washington State (Westing 2008). In addition, release of hazardous and toxic substances from damaged industrial facilities can contaminate the environment. For example, during the Iraq War, environmental contamination occurred due to hazardous materials from a metal-plating facility, pesticides, and petrochemicals warehouses, a sulphur mining complex, and a military scrapyard site (United Nations Environmental Programme 2005).
	Conventional weapons have accounted for the overwhelming majority of adverse environmental consequences in war. During the Second World War, for example, extensive carpet bombing of cities in Europe and Japan caused many deaths and injuries, as well as widespread devastation of urban environments. During the Gulf War, more than 600 oil fires in Kuwait caused widespread environmental devastation and respiratory disorders among people who were exposed to the smoke from these fires. Bombing during the Vietnam War destroyed mangrove forests; resultant bomb craters remained long afterward, often filling with stagnant water that enabled breeding of mosquitoes that transmit malaria and other diseases.





Forced displacement


	War uproots people. Many of the approximately 26 million refugees globally were forced by war to leave their native countries; the five leading countries of origin of refugees in late 2019 were Syria, Venezuela, Afghanistan, South Sudan, and Myanmar, all of which had experienced war or internal conflict. Refugees often flee to neighbouring low-and middle-income countries, which are often already facing significant challenges in addressing the public health needs of their own populations. Seven of the eight countries sheltering the most refugees in late 2019—Turkey, Colombia, Pakistan, Uganda, Germany, Sudan, Iran, and Lebanon—are low-and middle-income countries already challenged in meeting the needs of their own citizens. Many of the approximately 46 million internally displaced persons and approximately 8 million stateless people were also forced to leave their homes as a result of war. In 2019, there were approximately 11 million people newly displaced, mainly by conflict and violence; the leading countries in which they were internally displaced were Syria, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Yemen, Afghanistan, Somalia, and Nigeria—all of which had experienced significant conflict and violence. The vast majority of all these uprooted people are women, children, and elderly people, many of whom are at increased risk of injury and illness, threats to their safety and security, and death. Internally displaced persons are generally worse off than refugees because they frequently do not have security or access to safe food and water, healthcare and public health services, shelter, and other basic human needs.





Violation of human rights


	Human rights have often been violated during war. These violations have included assaults on civilians, including sexual assaults on women and abduction of children into military forces; mass killing; torture of prisoners and other violations of the Geneva Conventions; and violations of medical neutrality. There are more than 250,000 children forcibly engaged in armed conflict. They have been abducted to join fighting forces or to serve as ‘sex slaves’. These children suffer physical injuries and illnesses, including mental health problems (Song and de Jong 2015).
	The Geneva Convention IV mandates the protection of civilian populations during war. This convention states that civilian populations and individual civilians shall not be the objects of attacks. It prohibits acts or threats of violence whose primary purpose is to spread terror among civilian populations. It prohibits indiscriminate attacks on civilians, such as those that are not directed at a specific military objective or those that may be expected to cause incidental civilian deaths or injuries and/or damage to ‘civilian objects’. In addition, it bans reprisal attacks against civilian populations or civilians.





Diversion of resources


	Former United States President Dwight D. Eisenhower said: ‘Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket signifies, in the final sense a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and not clothed’ (Eisenhower 1953). Military expenditures, which often constitute a high percentage of national budgets, often divert financial—and human—resources away from health and human services and other beneficial activities. In many countries, the total amount of military expenditures approximates the amount spent on healthcare and public health. In 2019, the United States spent $732 billion on military expenditures, representing 38% of global military expenditures—more than the next 10 countries (China, India, Russia, Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea, and Brazil) combined (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute 2020, p. 226). As a reflection of diversion of resources, the United States ranks first among the nations of the world in arms exports, military expenditures, and military technology, but ranks 30th in life expectancy and 43rd in infant mortality rate.
	As another example of the impact of the diversion of resources, the first $204 billion spent by the United States on the Iraq War could have achieved all of the following goals for three years: a 50% decrease in world hunger, a comprehensive global programme to address HIV/AIDS, complete immunization of all children in ‘less-developed countries’, and meeting all needs globally for clean water and sewage treatment (Bennis et al. 2005).





Promotion of additional violence


	Violence often promotes further violence. In the aftermath of war, a number of factors can lead to additional violence, such as persistent hatred and unresolved disputes among warring countries or groups, militarism, and the international arms trade. There are many examples in which, in the aftermath of war, persistent hatred and unresolved disputes have led to further armed conflict, such as in the Middle East. Additional violence can result from militarism, which is defined as a philosophy or a system of beliefs and attitudes that a country should develop and maintain strong military power and aggressively deploy it consistent with its values and national interests. The international trade in conventional weapons also heightens the risk of violence especially in low-and middle-income countries. The volume of international transfers of major arms increased 5.5% between the 2010–2014 and 2015–2019 periods. During the 2015–2019 period, the five largest suppliers of major weapons were the United States (36%), Russia (21%), France (7.9%), Germany (5.8%), and China (5.5%), and the Middle East region received 35% of imports of major weapons (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute 2020, p. 278 and p. 295).
	The United Nations General Assembly, in 2013, took a major step towards regulating the international trade in conventional weapons by overwhelmingly approving the Arms Trade Treaty, which links purchases of arms to the human rights records of the purchasing countries. The treaty is designed to prevent exported weapons from contributing to human rights violations, terrorism, or organized crime, and to prohibit arms shipments that are deemed to be harmful to women or children.





Types of weapons


Conventional weapons


	Conventional weapons consist of small arms and light weapons, heavy conventional weapons (such as tanks, artillery, combat aircraft, warships, and missiles), explosives, and incendiaries. Small arms and light weapons, which include pistols, rifles, machine guns, and other hand-held or easily transportable weapons, are the weapons that are most often used in war. They have occasionally been described as ‘weapons of mass destruction’ because the number of deaths that they cause ‘dwarf that of all other weapons systems—and in most years greatly exceed the toll of the atomic bombs that devastated Hiroshima and Nagasaki’ (Annan 2000).
	Armed drones are a category of conventional weapons. Since 2004, the United States has been conducting armed drone strikes in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, and Yemen, in attempts to kill suspected terrorists. The Bureau of Investigative Journalism has reported that, through 2020, most of the people who had been killed in 14,040 armed drone strikes in these countries had been militants, but at least 910 of them were civilians.





Nuclear and radioactive weapons


	The detonation of nuclear bombs over Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 during the Second World War immediately killed about 200,000 people, primarily non-combatant civilians, and later caused many more deaths from malignancies and other diseases. These attacks injured and disabled many more people, and caused massive devastation—and radioactive contamination—of the environment in these two cities (Sutton and Gould 2008).
	As of 2020, there were 13,400 nuclear warheads possessed by nine nations—in order of decreasing number of warheads, Russia, the United States, China, France, the United Kingdom, Pakistan, India, Israel, and North Korea (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute 2020, p. 326). The United States (with 5,800 nuclear warheads, 1,750 of which are deployed) and Russia (with 6,375 nuclear warheads, 1,570 of which are deployed) possess the vast majority of nuclear weapons. Both countries have hundreds of nuclear warheads on alert on land-based intercontinental ballistic missiles and submarine-launched ballistic missiles. All of the nuclear-armed countries are planning major programmes to upgrade and modernize their nuclear weapons and delivery systems. In addition to the possible intended or accidental use of nuclear weapons by these countries, it is increasingly recognized that non-state actors, such as terrorist groups, could acquire and detonate nuclear weapons.
	Atmospheric testing of nuclear weapons by the United States, the former Soviet Union, and other countries caused environmental contamination, with increased rates of leukaemia and other cancers among downwind populations. In addition, production of nuclear weapons caused environmental contamination. For example, the Techa River in the Chelyabinsk Region of Russia was heavily contaminated with radioactive materials from the nuclear weapons production facility there (Burmistrov et al. 2006). Leakage from stored radioactive wastes at the nuclear weapons production facility at Hanford, Washington, has also caused environmental contamination (Westing 2008).
	There are several international treaties concerning nuclear weapons. The Partial Test Ban Treaty (PTBT) of 1963, promoted in part by concerns about radioactive contamination of the environment, banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, under water, and in outer space. The expansion of the PTBT, the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban-Treaty (CTBT)—a key step towards nuclear disarmament and preventing proliferation of nuclear weapons—was opened for signature in 1996 but has not yet entered into force. The CTBT bans explosions of nuclear weapons, for either military or civilian purposes, but it does not ban computer simulations and subcritical tests, which some nations use to maintain the option of developing new nuclear weapons. The CTBT has been ratified by 168 nations and signed, but not ratified, by another 16 nations. Entry into force requires ratification by the 44 nuclear-capable nations; by 2018, only 36 had ratified the CTBT and the following eight nuclear-capable nations had not: China, Egypt, India, Iran, Israel, North Korea, Pakistan, and the United States.
	The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (the ‘Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty’, or NPT) attempts to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons by restricting transfer of certain technologies. It relies on a control system operated by the International Atomic Energy Agency, which also promotes nuclear energy. In exchange for the non-nuclear-armed countries’ commitment not to develop or otherwise acquire nuclear weapons, the NPT commits the nuclear-armed countries to good-faith negotiations on nuclear disarmament. The NPT was opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970. A total of 191 countries have ratified the treaty. All of the five nuclear-armed countries recognized under the NPT—China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States—have ratified it. Every 5 years since 1970, the states-parties to the treaty have held a review conference to assess implementation of the treaty. In 1996, the International Court of Justice (the World Court), in an advisory opinion, urged that the nations possessing nuclear weapons move expeditiously towards nuclear disarmament, as is required by the NPT.
	All of the nuclear-armed countries can help stop the spread of nuclear weapons by actively supporting and adhering to these treaties, and can renounce the first use of nuclear weapons and the development of new nuclear weapons. The United States and Russia can collaborate in dismantling their nuclear warheads and can secure nuclear materials better so that they will not be acquired by non-state actors.
	Attention is increasingly being focused on the total elimination of nuclear weapons. In 2017, the United Nations adopted the Treaty of the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW), which comprehensively bans nuclear weapons, including their possession. The TPNW is akin to the chemical and biological weapons conventions. Under the treaty, it is illegal for its parties to develop (or finance to develop), test, produce, acquire, possess, store, transfer, transport, plan or threaten to use, or use nuclear weapons. Nuclear-armed countries that join the treaty will need to destroy their nuclear weapons and terminate their nuclear weapons programmes. The treaty also mandates that parties to the treaty assist victims of nuclear weapons testing and use and it requires environmental remediation of areas contaminated by nuclear weapons. By the end of 2020, the treaty had been signed by 86 countries and ratified by 51.
	Possible deployment of ‘dirty bombs’, which are conventional explosive devices mixed with radioactive materials, and possible attacks on nuclear power plants represent other risks. So does depleted uranium (DU), from which the uranium isotope usable for nuclear weapons or for fuel rods in nuclear power plants has been removed. DU is used militarily as a casing for armour-penetrating shells. An extremely dense material, uranium increases the ability of shells to penetrate the armour of tanks; uranium also bursts into flames on impact. DU-encased shells were used by the United States during the Gulf War, the Iraq War, and the war in Kosovo; similar shells were used by the United Kingdom in the Iraq War. DU, which is both radioactive and toxic, can contaminate soil and groundwater (Bešić et al. 2018). Use of DU is considered legal by the nations that have used it, but its use is considered by other nations to be illegal under the Geneva Conventions and other international treaties.





Chemical weapons


	Chemical weapons, which were first used during the First World War, have been used on several occasions since then. The government of Syria under President Bashar al-Assad has used chemical weapons during the civil war in Syria many times against civilians, causing many deaths (Arms Control Association 2020). A Japanese cult, Aum Shinrikyo, used sarin in the subway system of two Japanese cities in the mid-1990s, killing 19 people and injuring thousands.
	The Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), which came into force in 1997, prohibits development, production, acquisition, stockpiling, transfer, and use of chemical weapons. It requires each participating country to destroy its chemical weapons and chemical weapons production facilities, as well as any chemical weapons it may have abandoned on the territory of another participating country. The CWC has been signed by 193 nations; one nation has signed, but not yet ratified it; and three nations have neither signed nor ratified it. The verification provisions of the CWC affect not only the military sector but also the civilian chemical industry with restrictions and obligations regarding production, processing, and consumption of chemicals that are considered relevant to the convention. These provisions are verified by reporting requirements, routine onsite inspection of declared sites, and short-notice challenge inspections. The CWC established the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) in The Hague to ensure implementation of its provisions (Lee et al. 2012). Stockpiles of chemical weapons, which remain in a number of countries, pose a continuing threat to health and the environment.





Biological agents


	Biological agents, which consist of bacteria, viruses, other microorganisms, and their toxins, can produce illness in humans and can be used against other animals or plants, thereby adversely affecting agricultural resources, food supplies, and human health. Biological agents have been used as weapons since ancient times (Barras and Greub 2014). In the sixth century BC, Persia, Greece, and Rome tried to contaminate drinking water sources with diseased corpses. In AD 1346, Mongols besieging the Crimean seaport of Kaffa placed cadavers of plague victims on hurling machines and threw them into the city. During the French and Indian War in the United States in the mid-eighteenth century, a British commander sent blankets infected with smallpox to Native Americans. During the First World War, Germany dropped bombs containing plague bacteria over British positions and used cholera in Italy. During the 1930s, Japan contaminated food and water supplies of several cities and sprayed the cities with cultures of microorganisms. In 1942, a test use of anthrax spores by the United Kingdom and the United States contaminated Gruinard Island, off the coast of Scotland (Harris and Paxman 1962). During the 1950s and 1960s, secret large-scale open-air tests at the US Army Dugway Proving Ground in Utah used the microorganisms that cause Q fever and Venezuelan equine encephalitis (Cole 1988). In 1979, the accidental release of anthrax spores near Sverdlovsk in the Soviet Union resulted in at least 77 cases of inhalation anthrax, at least 66 of which were fatal (Meselson et al. 1994).
	Biological agents could be used as terrorist weapons. In 2001, anthrax spores were disseminated through the US Postal Service, causing 23 cases of inhalational and skin anthrax, five of which were fatal. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has identified three categories of diseases caused by biological agents, according to level of concern that they may be used as terrorist weapons. Category A consists of the agents that can be easily disseminated or transmitted from person to person, result in high mortality rates and have the potential for major public health impact, might cause public panic and social disruption, and require special action for public health preparedness. Category A agents include those that cause anthrax, botulism, plague, smallpox, tularaemia, and viral haemorrhagic fevers, such as the Ebola, Marburg, and Lassa viruses. Category B consists of the agents that are moderately easy to disseminate, result in moderate morbidity rates and low mortality rates, and require specific enhancements of CDC’s diagnostic capacity and enhanced disease surveillance. Category B agents include those that cause brucellosis, glanders, melioidosis, psittacosis, Q fever, typhus fever, viral encephalitis, water safety threats, and food safety threats (such as Salmonella and Shigella species, and Escherichia coli O157:H7), as well as epsilon toxin of Clostridium perfringens, ricin toxin from castor beans, and staphylococcal enterotoxin B. Category C agents include emerging pathogens that could be engineered for mass dissemination in the future because of availability, ease of production and dissemination, and potential for high morbidity and mortality rates and for major health impact (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2018).
	The 1975 Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention (BWC), prohibits the development, production, transfer, or use of biological weapons. The BWC has been signed and ratified by 183 countries; signed, but not ratified, by four countries; and neither signed nor ratified by 10 countries. The verification measures included in the BWC are weak and attempts to strengthen them have been unsuccessful. The United States has blocked attempts to strengthen the verification measures of the BWC, stating that such measures might lead to exposure of US industrial or military secrets.





Antipersonnel landmines and unexploded ordnance


	Antipersonnel landmines, which are designed to be exploded by the presence, proximity, or contact of a person, can incapacitate, injure, or kill one or more people. Together with unexploded ordnance (UXO), they represent significant hazards in many countries and continue to account for much morbidity and mortality (Frost et al. 2017). Millions of antipersonnel landmines are still deployed in many countries. Antipersonnel landmines injure or kill thousands of people annually; the vast majority of landmine victims are civilians, primarily poor people, including children, living in rural areas. It is estimated that half of all landmine victims die of their injuries before they reach appropriate medical care. Although a mine may cost only a few dollars to produce, it may cost more than US$1,000 to remove, and its economic impact on human health and well-being can be substantially higher.
	Antipersonnel landmines, in addition to maiming and killing people, make large areas of land uninhabitable. Remaining in place for many years, they pose long-term threats to people, including refugees and internally displaced persons returning to their homes in the aftermath of war. Since the Mine Ban Treaty entered into force in 1997, production of landmines has been markedly reduced and millions of landmines that had been implanted in the ground have been removed (International Campaign to Ban Landmines n.d.). However, about 36 countries continue to retain antipersonnel landmines and millions of landmines are still deployed in 58 countries; additional resources will be required to unearth and destroy them, tasks that pose inherent risks to demining personnel (Sirkin et al. 2008). A total of 164 nations are parties to the Mine Ban Treaty. Thirty-two nations have neither signed nor ratified it, including the United States, Russia, and China.





Prevention


	Public health workers and other health professionals can play important roles in minimizing the health and environmental consequences of war and preventing war itself (Levy and Sidel 2008; Wiist and White 2017). Categories of preventive measures include: (1) documentation; (2) education and awareness-raising; (3) advocacy and support for policies and programmes to minimize the consequences of war and to prevent war; and (4) provision of preventive services.





Documentation


	It is important to document the health and environmental consequences of war in order to inform policymakers and the public about these consequences, provide necessary services to affected populations, document violations of international law, protect human rights, and reduce the likelihood of future war or other forms of violent conflict. Documentation can be performed by surveillance, epidemiological surveys, and rapid assessment (Levy and Sidel 2016).
	Public health surveillance includes the systematic collection, analysis, and dissemination of data. Before, during, and after war, surveillance can provide information on morbidity and mortality as well as hazardous exposures and other factors that place non-combatant civilians at increased risk of injury, illness, or death. Even before a war has begun, surveillance may be able to identify population-based risk factors that may lead to interventions that may prevent the war from occurring.
	Epidemiologic studies may provide critically important information on the nature, severity, and magnitude of morbidity and mortality, as well as on related risk factors. These studies are usually cross-sectional, but prospective and retrospective studies generally provide more accurate morbidity and mortality data.
	Rapid assessment is often performed intensely during a short period, but can still be used to obtain preliminary information on a disastrous event or situation during war or its aftermath. It is also used to estimate the nature and magnitude of future health and related problems so that appropriate services can be provided.
	Challenges to documenting accurately the adverse effects of war include inadequate or absent data systems, social breakdown, forced displacement, biases in reporting of data, problems in distinguishing combatants and non-combatant civilians, inadequate concern for the health of ‘enemy’ civilians, and ‘the fog of war’.





Education and awareness-raising


	Much can also be accomplished by health professionals educating and raising the awareness of other health professionals, policymakers, and the general public about the health and environmental consequences of war. A multifaceted approach can include presentations and publications by professional organizations and citizens’ groups, reports by the news media, and use of social media and other forms of communication. Health professionals who have witnessed war and its consequences and non-combatant and military personnel who have suffered from the consequences of war can be very effective in raising awareness about the impact of war.





Advocacy and support for policies and programmes


	Health workers can advocate for and support policies and programmes to minimize the consequences of war, such as protecting the health-supporting infrastructure of society during war and its aftermath, preventing the exploitation of women and children, protecting the rights of displaced persons and prisoners of war, and maintaining safe zones for hospitals and other healthcare facilities. Advocacy is often most effective when conducted by professional associations, such as the American Public Health Association, or advocacy organizations, such as the International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War and its national affiliate organizations, including Physicians for Social Responsibility and Medact.





Provision of preventive services


	Health professionals can directly provide preventive services during war and its aftermath. These may include providing healthcare, including mental health services, for displaced individuals and populations; providing immunizations and other preventive services for children, women, and other civilians; and assisting in the restoration of healthcare and public health services.





Roles of the United Nations


	Since its founding in 1945, the United Nations has had as its primary mission the maintenance of international peace and security. The United Nations works to accomplish its mission by preventing conflict, helping nations and other groups involved in conflict achieve peace, providing peacekeeping activities, and promoting conditions in which peace can be sustainably maintained and flourish.
	The Security Council of the United Nations determines the presence of a threat to peace or an act of aggression. It asks parties to a dispute or conflict to settle it by nonviolent means and it often recommends terms of settlement. The Security Council can implement a number of measures, such as economic sanctions and international military action, to restore or maintain peace and security among nations.
	The United Nations General Assembly provides a forum for member nations to express their perspectives on issues and to try to find consensus on challenging matters. It makes decisions concerning issues of peace and security.
	By using special envoys, political missions, and other forms of diplomacy, the United Nations tries to resolve conflicts before they become violent. In addition, it engages in peacekeeping activities to assist member countries in transitioning from conflict to peace. With troops and police contributed by member states, it maintains peace and security and also promotes peaceful political processes, protects civilian populations, and promotes disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration of former combatants. It also supports constitutional processes, helps to organize elections, protects and promotes human rights, and helps restore the rule of law. The United Nations has deployed 71 peacekeeping missions since 1948 and currently has 13 peacekeeping missions. The United Nations also engages in peacebuilding activities for countries that have recently been engaged in conflict, supports sustainable peace and development, coordinates efforts to counter terrorism, and works to eliminate weapons of mass destruction and regulate conventional arms.





Roles of non-governmental organizations


	Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) can be important partners for health professionals in preventing the health and environmental consequences of war. These civil society organizations can help by intervening to mitigate the consequences of war (such as by providing humanitarian assistance to victims of war), performing research on the health and environmental impacts of war, educating the general public and policymakers, and advocating for policies and programmes to prevent war and promote peace.





Levels of prevention


	The public health framework of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention can be applied to the prevention of war and its health and environmental consequences. In this context, primary prevention refers to preventing war before it begins, secondary prevention refers to prevention and minimizing the consequences of war after it has begun, and tertiary prevention refers to treating or ameliorating the health and environmental consequence of war.
	Health professionals can contribute to the primary prevention of war in a number of ways. As previously described, they can educate policymakers and the general public about the health and environmental consequences of war on civilian populations. They can help identify the presence of risk factors for war, including socioeconomic inequalities and other forms of social injustice (Levy 2019). They can promote disarmament and the reduction and elimination of weapons of mass destruction. They can promote international cooperation through partnerships with health professionals in other countries. And they can promote a culture of peace, in which conflicts and disputes are settled by nonviolent means.
	When war occurs, its consequences can also minimized by secondary prevention measures to limit injuries, illnesses, and deaths (especially among non-combatant civilians), by preventing damage to the environment, and by supporting a prompt end to hostilities. Secondary prevention measures include strengthening and ensuring compliance with the Geneva Conventions.
	During war and its aftermath, health professionals can promote and support:
	 	• Protection of non-combatant civilians.
	• Prosecution of targeting of civilians as a war crime.
	• Protection of the health-supporting infrastructure of society.
	• Evaluation of non-combatant civilians who are at risk of illness, injury, or death.
	• Maintenance of medical neutrality.
	• Transformation of the public mindset about civilians during war, including demonstrating that non-combatant civilians are not enemy supporters or members of the enemy’s military and addressing social and psychological forces that permit and encourage military forces to injure and kill civilians.
	In the aftermath of war, many tertiary prevention measures are critically important. For example, it is necessary to rehabilitate and reintegrate people who have incurred disabilities due to the war; repair the damage to the physical, social, cultural, and economic environments; and take measures to prevent further violence. After conflict is over, health workers have important roles to play, such as advocating for prompt return and restoration of communities and livelihoods and opposing forced relocation or return to insecure environments. They can also help to restore essential health services, which may include recruiting and training health workers. They can help to address mental health problems that may be otherwise overlooked. They can help restore food and water supply systems that were disrupted during war. And they can also promote and support programmes for truth, justice, and reconciliation. These programmes may include processes for determining the truth about crimes committed during war, ensuring trials and punishment for these crimes, compensating victims for their losses, and establishing memorials to commemorate the victims of these crimes.





Host-agent-environment model


	The traditional host-agent-environment framework for prevention in public health (Fig. 9.6.1) can be adapted as an approach to the prevention of war, with people representing the ‘host’, weapons and the military representing ‘agent’, and the conditions in which people live representing ‘environment’ (Fig. 9.6.2). This framework can enable development of war-prevention strategies, such as the following:
	 	1. Strategies aimed at people, including promoting understanding and tolerance, economic and social interdependence among countries, nonviolent resolution of disputes and conflicts, and developing the popular and political will to prevent war and promote peace
	2. Strategies aimed at weapons and the military, including controlling the international arms trade, eliminating weapons of mass destruction, reducing military expenditures, and intervening in disputes to prevent war
	3. Strategies to improve the conditions in which people live, including protecting human rights and civil liberties, reducing poverty and economic disparities, improving education and employment opportunities, and ensuring personal security and legal protections.
	Fig. 9.6.1 Host-agent-environment model used to develop preventive measures in public health.
	Fig. 9.6.2 Host-agent-environment model applied to the prevention of war.
	The only way to prevent all of the health and environmental consequences of war, however, is to prevent war.
