	Lower overall life expectancies for women and men within and between countries, indicates inequity in health, between the wealthier and the poorer and marginalized. Life expectancy is much higher for women and men in high-income countries (HIC) than LMIC. Poverty-related factors: poor nutrition, sanitation, low household income, and weak health systems underpin differences. Improvements in social, economic, and environmental conditions and access to good, quality healthcare have increased life expectancies in HIC. Even in HIC there are sharp differences in life expectancies, with poorer, more marginalized populations experiencing substantially shorter life expectancies.
	Situations of war and conflict in certain regions and countries have led to lower life expectancies for populations overall, but particularly for men. High maternal mortality lowers female women’s life expectancies in regions with poor maternal healthcare. Before antiretroviral therapy became universally available, AIDS-related mortality caused dramatic decreases in life expectancy in sub-Saharan African countries. In Eastern Europe and Russia, lower male life expectancy peaked in the period leading up to and after the dissolution of the USSR. These were attributed to gender-related male lifestyle practices such as excessive alcohol consumption, in response to the tremendous socioeconomic and political upheavals (Pietilä and Rytkönen 2008, p. 1,070).
	The Burden of Disease (BOD) is a good indicator of the health quality of life people enjoy or lose. Amatya Sen captures this: ‘we are not able to do much if we are disabled or ceaselessly bothered by illness’ (Sen 2004, p. 28 in Sprague 2018, p. 126). The WHO adopted the concept of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) to take account of illnesses and disabilities. It uses disability-adjusted-life years (DALY), quality-adjusted life years (QALY), and disability-adjusted life expectancy (DALE) as measures to quantify quality of health (Sprague 2018, p.128). This occurs throughout the life cycle with childhood and adolescence setting much of the scene for later adult health status. Perceptions of health vary between individuals and societies. Actions taken to decrease the BOD and promote enjoyment of health recognizes the special nature of health as a ‘social good’ (Sprague 2018).
	LMIC countries especially in sub-Saharan Africa continue to struggle to contain major infectious or communicable health conditions such HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and Malaria. Interventions to address these are human resource and skills intensive. Many LMICs have limited infrastructure, human resources, and technical expertise to contain epidemics and devote resources to other health and social, economic, education, and development needs (Box 10.2.6).
	 	Box 10.2.6 Key messages
	 	• Overall, women enjoy a longer life expectancy than men.
	• This varies within and between countries, reflecting the influence of a complex mix of sex, gender, age, behavioural, and social determinants of health.
	• Lower female than male life expectancy signifies higher levels of societal gender discrimination.
	• The WHO uses a number of measures for compromised health quality of life—the burden of disease.
	• Child and adolescent health influence the health trajectory in adulthood.
	• LMIC countries struggle with a dual epidemic of communicable and non-communicable diseases.





The impact of sex and gender on specific health problems


HIV/AIDS


	HIV is one of the most significant threats to women and men’s health in many parts of the world. The primary modes of HIV transmission are through unprotected vaginal or anal sex, use of contaminated needles during injecting drug use, and vertical transmission. We will on focus on the impact and variation in HIV’s impact on women and men’s health in LMIC in Southern Africa that bear the greatest burden of HIV infection (Abdool Karim et al. 2010; Ramjee and Daniels 2013).
	Sprague’s (2018) model in Figure 10.2.2 is valuable in showing graphically, the biological and structural factors impacting on HIV acquisition.
	Fig. 10.2.2 Pathways in vulnerability and consequences of HIV acquisition.
	Adapted with permission from Prof Finn Diderichsen from his and his colleagues framework that appears as figure 2.2. in Sprague (2008, p 47).





Biological HIV vulnerability


	Women are biologically significantly more vulnerable than men to HIV infection. This is on a physical, genetic, and immunological level. The female vaginal tract (and the anus) has a larger mucosal surface exposed to the virus during condomless sex. It is also exposed to HIV for a longer period (Abdool Karim et al. 2010; Ramjee and Daniels 2013). The greater susceptibility of the vaginal, cervical (and anal) mucosal surface to microabrasions during sex facilitates HIV entry. This may be due to inflammations, ulcerations, lesions, and pre-existing sexually transmitted infections (STI). Undiagnosed STI are commoner in women, due to low knowledge, greater difficulties in symptom diagnosis problems and access to STI healthcare is more stigmatized for women (Abdool Karim et al. 2010). The herpes simplex type 2 virus is linked to increased transmission risk ((Ramjee and Daniels 2013) and bacterial vaginosis (BV) and syphilis are also implicated. This is particularly significant for sub-Saharan Africa that has high levels of HSV-2, BV, and HIV.
	Young women, aged 15–24 years, are up to 8 times more likely to be HIV-infected than their male peers (Dellar et al. 2015, p. 64). Gendered social and economic factors are combined with heightened biological risk of HIV transmission, due to young women’s cervical immaturity and higher levels of genital inflammation (Abdool Karim et al. 2010; Ramjee and Daniels 2013). Hormones and immunological responses may also play a role. Increased levels of oestrogen after ovulation may increase HIV infectivity (Ramjee and Daniels 2013). Women’s hormonal and physiological changes during pregnancy and lactation may be linked to higher rates of HIV acquisition (Ramjee and Daniels 2013). There are increased risks of maternal mortality as a result of untreated HIV-related infections (Kendall et al. 2014). There is potentially enhanced HIV risk for women using the injectable progesterone contraceptive Depo-Provera (Abdool Karim et al. 2010). This is currently under intensive study (Harper 2015; Tasker et al. 2018).





Gender and other social factors impact on HIV vulnerability


	Biological factors interact with social, economic, and behavioural factors, to increase HIV infection vulnerability. Gender inequity is a key factor underscoring HIV infection vulnerability (Abdool Karim et al. 2010; Jewkes and Morrell 2012).
	Hegemonic patriarchal cultures of masculinity underpin men frequently dominating in in heterosexual intimate relationship decision-making. Women have lesser say in whether to engage in condomless sex than men. Hegemonic forms of masculinities promote men having multiple concurrent sexual relationships and older men engaging in sex with younger women. This heightens young women’s HIV vulnerability (Dellar et al. 2015, p. 67). Women may experience violence if they refuse sex or insist on condom use (Jewkes and Morrell 2010; Ramjee and Daniels 2013). Sexual violence can be a cause and a consequence of HIV (Jewkes 2014).
	Young women’s disadvantaged socioeconomic status is associated with earlier and coerced sexual debut, less condom use, multiple partners, and having transactional sex with more likely to be infected older men (Abdool Karim et al. 2010; Ramjee and Daniels 2013).
	Social constructions of masculinity may lead to increased male risks of HIV infection. Social expectations that ‘real’ (heterosexual) men show their masculinity through condomless sex and multiple partners places pressure men to engage in riskier sexual behaviour. Traditional social norms combine with a health system with poor integration of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and HIV. Men’s involvement in SRH, apart from for STI, is not encouraged. As Gutmann (2007, p. 11) states men are ‘the missing (f)actors in reproductive health’. Social context and barriers within health services hinder Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Intersex, Questioning, and other gender identities (LGBTQI+) individuals and groups from seeking SRH care.
	There are marked differences in women and men’s use of HIV care. Gender norms make it more acceptable for women to seek healthcare. Women seek care for reproductive health and child health needs. In parts of the world where the HIV epidemic is most severe, prevention of infant HIV transmission programmes has added to women’s greater health-seeking behaviour. This has created its own set of problems for women. Because they are frequently the first partner in an intimate relationship to test for HIV, if infected, they could face stigma and blame. However, women’s access to testing and diagnosis for HIV and access to ART has led to greatly improved healthcare access and outcomes for women living with HIV. Gender norms, that perceive seeking healthcare as a display of ‘weakness’, may discourage men from seeking healthcare until very ill (Stern et al. 2014b; Jewkes et al. 2015). Men are less likely to test for and be diagnosed with HIV infection, initiate ART, be retained in care and more likely to die of AIDS-related illnesses (Cornell et al. 2017). Men are less likely to participate in social support structures for people living with HIV (Madiba and Canti-Sigaqa 2012) (Box 10.2.7).
	 	Box 10.2.7 Key messages
	 	• Biological and gender-related factors make women, particularly younger women, more vulnerable to HIV infection.
	• They are more likely to be tested, diagnosed with HIV, and access and remain on ART due to greater health service access. However, this can lead to stigma and blame.
	• Hegemonic masculinities promote riskier sexual behaviour. This and less health service contact deter men from health-seeking and testing, being diagnosed with HIV, and accessing and remaining on ART.





Cardiovascular disease


	Non-communicable diseases (NCD) represent a significant BOD in the twenty-first century (Mendis and Chestnov 2014). Of the estimated 36 million deaths globally approximately 63% in 2008 were caused by NCD. Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) has the largest individual proportion of NCD deaths (48%) (Mendis and Chestnov 2014). Coronary Heart Disease and Stroke are the leading causes of CVD death and disability. Key risk factors include high blood pressure, overweight or obesity, and higher cholesterol levels. These appear to have similar effects on CVD outcomes for women and men.





The Gendered nature of CVD


	Despite CVD perceived for decades as a ‘male’ disease, it is commoner in women (Appelman et al. 2015), likely due to stroke being commoner and due to women’s longevity. Women present with CVD on average 7–10 years later than men. This has led to speculation that oestrogen plays a protective role against CVD for women. However, recent research fails to support this (Riska 2010) and has shown no benefit in prevention of CVD through hormonal replacement therapy (Spence and Pilote 2015, p. 209).
	Younger women have specific sex-related risk factors for CVD associated with pregnancy-related health problems such as gestational hypertension, diabetes and preeclampsia and endocrine disorders (Appelman et al. 2015). Risk factors such as migraine, commoner in women than men, appears to be associated with stroke in women. While smoking is commoner in men than women, multiple studies show that prolonged heavy smoking in women increases their relative risk of CVD compared to men (Appelman et al. 2015, p. 213).





NCD in LMIC


	NCD have become increasingly common in LMIC, influenced by lifestyle changes due to the health transition (Kengne et al. 2013). CVD shows a prevalence of pre-transitional diseases such as rheumatic fever and idiopathic cardiomyopathies, with high levels of hypertensive disease and stroke and health transition diseases. Common individual risk factors include tobacco use, physical inactivity, and unhealthy diets. Risk factors vary by sex, with tobacco use commoner in men and obesity in women (Mayosi et al. 2009). The African region has the highest age standardized death rate from NCD, 779 per 100,000 (Mendis and Chestnov 2014). The double burden of infectious diseases and NCD is referred to as ‘colliding epidemics’ (Mayosi et al. 2012, p. 5). NCD are the second leading cause of death in Sub-Saharan Africa comprising 30% of deaths in 2011 (Airhihenbuwa et al. 2016). Hypertension is a major underlying cause of CVD. The numbers of people with hypertension is expected to increase by 68% from 7.5 million in 2008 to 126 million in sub-Saharan Africa by the year 2025 (Airhihenbuwa et al. 2016). An analysis of country variation in strokes show that the poorest countries have the highest BOD (Mayosi et al. 2009, p. 936). The WHO estimates the burden of NCD in South Africa is two to three times higher than that in HIC and deaths due to CVD are likely to double by 2040. This is similar to that in other sub-Saharan Africa countries and central European countries, increasing in rural and poor urban communities. This is ‘driving a rise in the demand for chronic disease care’ (Mayosi et al. 2009, p. 935). Prevention and treatment of NCD in LMIC including CVD, is neglected due to the overwhelming burden of infectious illnesses (Mayosi et al. 2009, p. 934). HIV has exacerbated the burden of NCD. This demonstrates an important role for improved health services in reducing health inequities that underpin these conditions (Mayosi et al. 2009, p. 936).





CVD and healthcare


	Health systems factors play an important role in the gender differences in women’s perceptions of and presentation with possible symptoms of heart disease. Women present more frequently with symptoms of tiredness, weakness, light-headedness, palpitations, or loss of appetite rather than chest pain (Aggarwal et al. 2018, p. 3). When women report with symptoms of chest pain, this is more often attributed to unexplained chest pain (Crea et al. 2015, p. 159), because these do not conform to typical male symptoms (Crea et al. 2015; Aggarwal et al. 2018). Diagnostic tests for women and men with potential heart disease have differed. The Euro Heart Survey, in which 42% of patients were female, found physicians are more likely to conduct exercise ECG and coronary angiography on men with reported chest pain or discomfort than women. It found gender biases in the use of evidence-based medical treatment for women, leading to under or inappropriate treatment (Crea et al. 2015, p. 160).
	The risk of heart disease has been underestimated in younger women in whom, in-hospital post-acute myocardial infarction mortality is higher than among their male peers (Crea et al. 2015, p. 157). Factors related to younger women and ethnicity in the United States (black, Latino and south Asian women) create subgroups of women who are more disadvantaged and marginalized in recognition of heart attack symptom recognition and treatment (Aggarwal et al. 2018, p. 5). Angina and heart attacks are perceived as ‘male diseases’, with poorer recognition of symptoms and quality of care in women. Previously a greater proportion of men reportedly died from sudden, pre-hospital cardiac attacks. This is no longer the trend (Crea et al. 2015, p. 161). This is viewed as due primarily to gender biases in perceptions of cardiac attack symptoms.
	Less post-cardiac rehabilitation occurs in women. This may be due to health service and socioeconomic related factors, such as poorer promotion and referral by healthcare providers, cost and transport problems, inadequate social support systems, and the burden of family responsibilities (Aggarwal et al. 2018, p. 5). Socioeconomic factors are similarly likely to affect women’s prevention activities and health-seeking behaviour with respect to CVD (Spence and Pilote 2015, p. 209).
	Further research into potential biological risk factors for CVD in women and men can improve our understanding of the aetiology of CVD and assist in tailoring specific interventions for detection, treatment, and management (Appelman et al. 2015) (Box 10.2.8).
	 	Box 10.2.8 Key messages
	 	• Contrary to perceptions that CVD is a ‘male disease’ due to higher levels of hypertension and strokes, it is commoner in women.
	• Younger women and those with HIV have specific CVD risks.
	• Difference risk factors including socioeconomic influences lead to different CVD outcomes in women and men.
	• Healthcare professionals’ gender bias in detection, diagnosis, testing and treatment has had negative outcomes for women.
	• LMIC have ‘colliding epidemics’ of infectious diseases and NCD.





Gender-based violence


	GBV covers a wide range of categories of violence (Box 10.2.9).
	 	Box 10.2.9 Gender-based violence
	The United Nations defines Gender-based violence against women (VAW) as: Any act of GBV that harms of may result in harm (physical, sexual, or emotional/mental) or suffering to women (Sprague 2018, p.63). This may include threats or acts which coerce or deprive women of freedom. Physical violence includes being slapped, punched, choked, having objects thrown at one, pushed or shoved, beaten, intentionally burnt, or threatened with a weapon. This can be in either the private or public sphere. Rape or sexual violence includes any form of forced sexual act, including those due fear of harm or intimidation (WHO 2013, p. 6) It can be perpetrated regardless of the relationship of the perpetrator to the survivor, in any place. It includes penetration with a body part or object (Sprague 2018, p. 63). GBV includes femicide, homicide, and intimate partner (domestic) violence. These are most commonly perpetrated by men against women.





Violence against women


	There is pervasive violence against women internationally. Thirty-five percent of women report physical or sexual violence by a male intimate or non-intimate partner (WHO 2013). Women are most likely to be exposed to violence in the home or its surroundings. Most physical and sexual violence against women is by an intimate partner (WHO 2013). While physical and sexual violence is more visible, intimate partner emotional abuse or violence, especially from male intimate partners, including ‘verbal abuse, threats of violence, engendering fear, humiliation, destruction of property, enforcement of social isolation, taking or withholding earnings, and flaunting other sexual partners’ (Jewkes 2010, p. 851) is less recognized and addressed (Matheson et al. 2015). Emotional abuse’s reported prevalence is between 9 and 70% (Jewkes 2010, p. 851). People experiencing abuse frequently face unsympathetic criminal justice services (Meyer 2016) and unprepared health services (Global Burden of Disease Study 2013 Collaborators et al. 2015).
	Violence, including femicide against lesbian or gender non-conforming women, those living and not living with HIV, is a specific form of violent hate crime (Cooper et al. 2016). In some regions there is violent abduction of women for sex and/or marriage. For example in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa, a specific form of sexual violence, known as ukuthwala occurs—this includes abduction, forced marriage, and rape of young girls. It is a distortion of a past custom for consenting, eloping young adults (Monyane 2013).





Male-on-male violence


	Almost all violence against men is perpetrated by other men. It is estimated that for every violence male death, there are 29 male-on-male assaults serious enough to warrant healthcare (Krug et al. 2002).
	Gender-related factors promoting notions of toughness, competitiveness, and a desire for dominance over other men, as positive attributes of ‘being a man’ (Jewkes et al. 2015) are most prominent in underpinning male-on-male violence. These occur against a backdrop of other socioeconomic risk factors for male-on-male violence. Like male-on-female violence, these include socioeconomic deprivation, urban concentrations of poverty, and substance abuse (Global Burden of Disease Study 2013 Collaborators et al. 2015).





Interpersonal violence


	The global prevalence of interpersonal violence (IPV) against women is estimated as 15 to 71% (Sprague 2018, p. 63). IPV was responsible for 8.5% of deaths in 2013 (Global Burden of Disease Study 2013 Collaborators et al. 2015). GBV-related DALY differs by sex, age, and region. Injuries are higher among men than women, except in the older age group and apart from road accident injuries are due to male-on-male assault and homicide. Homicide in adult males aged 15 years to 49 years, in DALY are 2,651 per 100,000 population in western Europe and 10 780 in Eastern Europe (Global Burden of Disease Study 2013 Collaborators et al. 2015, p. 6). Interpersonal violence is responsible for 317/100,000 DALY. This is commoner in LMIC, with boys under the age of 15 years having a low rate of 468.4 per 100,000 DALY in Western Europe and a high rate of 6,471.4 in central Africa. Male-on-male interpersonal violence has reached epidemic proportions, among young men in a country such as South Africa, that is not at war (Norman et al. 2010).
	No convincing biological factors underpin interpersonal violence. Testosterone in men doesn’t explain why all men are not violent. Greater physical strength in men than in most women enables them to engage in more physical violence. GBV against women and in male-on-male violence is highly gendered.
	While several other factors cross-cut gender in influencing male violence against women, a key driver is gender power inequity in interpersonal relationships and society (Jewkes 2002). This manifests in male controlling behaviour, notions of male entitlement and power to ‘punish’ women that is condoned by individuals, within communities, the criminal justice system, and among policy makers and service providers (Seedat et al. 2009). There is an interaction between women’s experiences of violence and mental health problems. Violence against women has important negative mental health consequences such as depression and anxiety (Jewkes 2010). Physical health effects of violence include injury or death and limited sexual and reproductive control and health-seeking behaviour. This can lead to unintended pregnancies, with poorer maternal and perinatal health outcomes and risk of STI.
	Same-sex IPV has been under researched. However, research among gay men link emotional, physical, and sexual abuse in intimate partnerships to dominant forms of masculinities in which one partner exercises controlling behaviour and power over another (Coles 2009; Creighton and Oliffe 2010). Given that men are the main perpetrators of IPV, gay men may suffer disproportionately among men (Oliffe et al. 2014). Like men generally, they frequently view physical and mental injuries as ‘part of being a man’ (Oliffe et al. 2014, p. 574). This has health system and services implications due to reluctance to seek medical or other assistance (Oliffe et al. 2014) (Box 10.2.10).
	 	Box 10.2.10 Key messages
	 	• Violence against women and male-on-male violence among young men is of epidemic proportions. Males are generally the perpetrators.
	• Interpersonal violence is commonest for women and men, particularly from non-strangers.
	• Several socioeconomic factors influence GBV, but gender power inequity in interpersonal relationships and society, with males more powerful, is the key GBV driver.
	• GBV has severe negative physical and mental consequences.
	• Unsympathetic criminal justice systems and unprepared health service present major problems in detecting and addressing GBV.





Mental health


The burden of mental health and gendered aspects—commonalities and differences


	The burden of mental, neurological, and substance (MNS) use problems have increased by between 1990 and 2010. It currently accounts for one out of 10 healthy years of life lost globally. This causes excess mortality, impacting socially and economically on those affected, caregivers, and society. Historically, mental health research has focused on women’s issues (Smith et al. 2016). This focus may have led to a neglect of men’s mental health problems. Gender differences in mental health problems can be viewed through a gender conception and practices lens. During the industrial revolution, men left home for work, while women assumed child caring responsibilities in the home.
	This gendered labour division influenced on how men and women were viewed and expected to behave in society. Productive work in the public sphere became associated with men and masculinity, while socioemotional and domestic work became associated with women and femininity. Women were normatively viewed as fragile and emotional beings, with children requiring their mothers’ special care for moral and psychological development (Rosenfield and Smith 2010). While the current global shifts in ideological norms empower women striving for equality especially in the workplace, gender power divisions between men and women, in responsibilities, remain relevant for women and men’s mental health. Given dominant feminine role expectations, women tend to put others’ interests first more often, promoting internalizing problems (Doyal 1995). Childcare and household responsibilities often take a psychological toll on women, ultimately resulting in high stress levels. Where childcare is secure and home responsibilities are shared with spouses, women’s depressive and anxiety symptoms resemble the lower levels diagnosed among men. Gender norms encourage women to maintain social ties that are emotionally intimate. They enjoy higher levels of feeling that others care deeply about them (Taylar and Turner 2001). However, close ties that bring support can also be sources of negative interactions with conflicting demands (Taylar and Turner 2001). Negative interactions can offset the benefits of supportive interactions, leaving women with higher distress levels. Neurological differences in women and men’s mental health are contested and social factors, including gender play a dominant role in mental health problems.
	Large-scale epidemiological studies assessing mental health problems in the United States (Kessler et al. 2005) and elsewhere (Andrews et al.1999; Seedat et al. 2009), found no differences in men and women’s overall rates of psychopathology. The differences lay in the diagnoses (Rosenfield and Smith 2010). Men exhibiting problems of substance abuse and antisocial behaviour, are likelier to be destructive and problematic to others as well as themselves. Alcohol and drug addiction can lead to serious psychological or physical consequences. Research shows that men are likelier to take their lives in violent ways, hence suicide death rates are higher for all ages of men than women (Zarit and Zarit 2011). Antisocial personality disorder is more commonly diagnosed in men, as are schizoid and paranoid personality disorders. In contrast, histrionic, dependent, and avoidant personality disorders (female stereotyped), are more commonly diagnosed in women (Torgersen et al. 2001). Eating disorders are diagnosed as 10 times commoner in women than men (Byrne and McLean 2001). These occur mostly in late adolescence and early adulthood. Rates of dementia, perhaps related to longevity, are higher for older women, leading to older women having a greater need for mental health services.
	For women and men mental health problems are commonly comorbid with physical disorders such as CVD, cancers, metabolic disorders, and HIV (De Hert et al. 2009; Murthy 2004).
	Notions of hegemonic masculinities encourage males to suppress emotions (feelings of helplessness, worry, and insecurity) defined these as feminine and weak. These expectations ultimately prescribe how men and women express their feelings. Men and women develop coping mechanisms, which for men may lead to hiding their feelings, often turning to substance abuse. Some describe substance abuse as a male version of depression (Rosenfield et al. 2005). Men may experience negative mental health consequences through greater gendered difficulties in forging close long lasting social ties (Castillo et al. 2007).





The health system and gendered mental health practices


	Health system-related, health services and health practitioners’ behaviour, and clinician measurement bias has likely influenced much of the scholarship and current findings on gender and mental health. This has led to problematic assumptions about gendered mental health symptoms (Currin et al. 2011). Health professionals tend to perpetuate gender stereotypes about men and depression, by being less likely to correctly diagnose men presenting with symptoms of depression or anxiety (Borowsky et al. 2000). Men’s mental problems tend to be underestimated. Clinicians are less likely to use standard psychological measurement tools to assess men’s symptoms (Martin et al. 2013). Research comparing men’s and women’s mental health has tended to focus on different outcomes of stress instead of similarities and differences in men and women’s mental health experiences (Elliott 2013) (Box 10.2.11).
	 	Box 10.2.11 Key messages
	 	• Four conventional explanations for gender differences in mental health are gender socialization, help seeking, coping, and symptom stratification (Currin et al., 2011).
	• Understanding factors underlying mental health problems among women and men involves adopting a holistic consideration of the biological social, cultural, economic, and personal contexts of their lives (Judd et al. 2009).
	• Researchers, policymakers, and clinicians should reassess the validity and reliability of current measurement tools for detecting symptoms for men and women, and focus on what factors might be particularly relevant for men’s experiences (Smith and Hemler 2014). This can more effectively address mental health in women and men.





Maternal health


	In 2015, the maternal mortality ratio (MMR) (the number of female deaths during pregnancy, childbirth and immediately after childbirth per 100,000 live births) was an estimated 216. The overall MMR declined by 44% and 2.3% annually from 1990 to 2015. It would need to decrease to a minimum of 7.3%, to reach the SDG target of 70 by 2030 (WHO 2016a).





Differences between women and women: region, class, and ethnicity


	The overall decline in global MMR, belies huge differences in the position of pregnant women based on class, race, age, and within and between world regions. High levels of maternal morbidity and mortality are key indicators of global inequity reflecting structural inequity between women in different parts of the world. Women’s higher maternal morbidity and mortality in LMIC are linked to poverty. The World Bank’s 2018 Health Equity database found that people in 35 and 34 countries faced catastrophic and impoverishing health expenditure, respectively (Wagstaff et al. 2018). Poor maternal health and related problems remain important causes of women’s death and disability in LMIC. In HIC the risk of maternal death is 1 in 3,700 compared to 1 in 38 in in sub-Saharan African countries (United Nations Development Programme 2015). LMIC accounted for roughly 99% of global maternal deaths in 2015, with sub-Saharan Africa accounting for approximately 66%, followed by Southern Asia (WHO et al. 2015, p. xi). Eighteen sub-Saharan African countries had a MMR ranging between 500 and 1,000 deaths per 100,000 live births (WHO et al. 2015). India, Nigeria, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Ethiopia, and the DRC together had more than half of the global number of maternal deaths (Hogan et al. 2010). MMR in LMIC regions such as in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia are similar (351 and 336 per 100,000 live births, respectively).





The health system and healthcare


	Gender-related factors hinder women’s maternal healthcare in some regions, where women need permission from or be accompanied by a male partner, to attend health services. However, most differences in maternal health outcomes are due to preventable conditions related to health system and service issues, such as skilled birth attendance (WHO 2016a). While overall skilled birth attendance was estimated to be 73% by 2013, in Africa and Southeast Asia, more than 40% of births took place without skilled healthcare. Poor healthcare provider attitudes in maternal care, low healthcare provider knowledge and inadequate training underpin problems with access to skilled maternal healthcare (Sprague 2018, p. 98).
	Younger, poorer women and those in lower income or rural areas have poorer access to or are less likely to use effective methods of contraception. Globally, more than 10% of all women do not have access to or are not using an effective method of contraception, with much higher proportions in LMIC countries. Less than half of those in the WHO African Region had their contraceptive needs met (WHO 2016a). It is estimated if unmet need for contraception was met, it could decrease maternal deaths by nearly a third (United Nations Development Programme 2015).
	Most maternal health complications are preventable if women enjoy sufficient economic resources to satisfy educational and informational and health needs and are able to delay age at first pregnancy. The main direct causes of maternal morbidity and mortality include obstetric haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, and sepsis during pregnancy (WHO 2016a). Indirect causes include the following: Women with untreated AIDS-related health conditions have an eightfold increased risk of maternal death than HIV negative women (Kendall et al. 2014, p. S251). In the absence of HIV approximately 281,500 global maternal deaths could have been avoided in 2008 (Hogan et al. 2010). Inadequate access to skilled maternal healthcare, especially emergency obstetric care is a major problem. This is due to unavailability of adequate maternal health services, distances, costs in travelling to maternal health services, and inadequately skilled healthcare providers.





Unsafe abortion’s impact on maternal health


	Unsafe abortion is a ‘preventable pandemic’ (Grimes et al. 2006, p. 1). Unsafe abortion is on a continuum unsafe care, with abortions conducted either by unskilled individuals or in an unsafe medical environment (Sedgh and Adewole 2016). Unsafe abortion contributes significantly to maternal morbidity and mortality. An estimated 19–20 million unsafe abortions occur annually, with 97% in LMIC. An estimated 68,000 women die annually from unsafe abortion and millions have complications, often with long-term, poor maternal health consequences. Key outcomes from unsafe abortion are haemorrhage, infection, and poisoning from substances used in induced abortions (Grimes et al. 2006, p. 1). There has been a decline in abortions, in Eastern Europe, but no significant decreases in LMIC (Singh et al. 2017, p. 5). An estimated 55% were safe; 31% less safe and 14% least safe. Countries with the most restrictive abortion laws were responsible for the majority of unsafe abortions (Singh et al. 2017, p. 7).





Men and maternal health


	While maternal mortality and morbidity affects only women physically and emotionally, it should not be regarded as only a women’s health issue. The importance of men as partners in maternal health (attending antenatal, childbirth, and postnatal care) cannot be overemphasized (Brittain et al. 2015; Sibanda et al. 2017; Konje et al. 2018) (Box 10.2.12).
	 	Box 10.2.12 Key messages
	 	• Maternal mortality highlights health inequity between women in different world regions.
	• Most maternal deaths are preventable through good quality, skilled maternal care, and availability of emergency care.
	• Improved access to contraception and safe abortion would decrease maternal deaths.
	• Men as partners in maternal health should be promoted.





Interventions and initiatives to address women and men’s health


Biomedical interventions





HIV


	Biomedical interventions to decrease HIV infection have been the focus of much research. These include promotion of male and female condoms as barrier methods to protect against HIV acquisition.
	Biologically, uncircumcised men have higher female-to-male HIV infection risk than circumcised men. Randomized controlled trials in Kenya, Uganda, and South Africa show that medical male circumcision can provide partial protection against risk of female-male HIV transmission by up to 60% as well as to penetrative partners in same-sex male intimate relationships. The WHO and UNAIDS have recommended medical male circumcision as part of an HIV prevention strategy for men, particularly in countries with a high HIV prevalence and low circumcision rates (WHO/UNAIDS 2008). ART’s critical role in HIV treatment and in ‘treatment as prevention’, through pre-exposure prophylaxis, reducing HIV infectivity and transmissibility. People living with HIV (PLWH) with undetectable viral loads, have minimal risks of transmission (McNairy and El-Sadr 2014). Research for a microbicide, applied to the vaginal or anal tract to reduce HIV transmission, has had limited success in women, over the past 30 years. However there is active ongoing research (Karim et al. 2010; Doggett et al. 2015). This has highlighted HIV prevention’s gender-related factors—gender hierarchies in sexual decision-making and gender norms influencing younger women’s lack of adherence to microbicides (Doggett et al. 2015). There is also research for a vaccine to prevent or ameliorate the effects of HIV transmission (Bekker and Gray 2017).





CVD


	Key changes that have occurred to address gender issues in CVD. These include addressing knowledge among individuals and in communities and important health system changes in the delivery of care by health professions. In the United States in 2014, overall male mortality from CVD overtook female mortality for the first time since 1984. This is attributable to increased awareness of women’s symptoms, presentation, and appropriate treatment for possible heart attacks (Aggarwal et al. 2018, p. 2). Primary and secondary prevention has been largely responsible for a decline in CVD over the past decades (Appelman et al. 2015). Since 2014, an American Heart Association consensus statement has recommended the full battery of non-invasive diagnostic tests for women with suspected heart attack symptoms (Aggarwal et al. 2018, p. 4).





Maternal health


	Measures addressing poor maternal health have been introduced at an individual, community, and health systems level. These include improving knowledge of skilled care antenatally, during birth and postnatally at an individual, partner, and community level; and training of health professionals, particularly in rural areas to deal with complications and emergency care and ensuring emergency care facilities are available and well-functioning. Programmes like Momconnect in South Africa (Barron et al. 2016); and Maternal Waiting houses for pregnant women, operating in a variety of LMIC settings such as Lesotho, Cambodia, Malawi, Nigeria, Papua New Guinea, Timor, and Zambia (WHO 1996; Wild et al. 2012; Siv et al. 2014) are examples of health systems initiatives to improve maternal healthcare. Given that apart from HIV and respiratory illnesses, health-system-related causes are the commonest preventable maternal deaths causes, health system initiatives need to be prioritized.





Mental health


	Numerous medical and pharmaceutical interventions are effective in treating MNS problems. However psychological and social interventions are important to prevent and treat MNS disorders (Patel et al. 2016).





Transformative gendered initiatives to improve women and men’s health


	Multiple theories and interventions of change to address the impact of gendered factors on health have emerged. Gupta’s (2000) work on HIV introduced interventions along a continuum, to address the gender aspects of the epidemic. These include interventions that are: (1) gender exploitative; (2) gender neutral; (3) gender sensitive, or accommodating; or (4) gender transformative (Rolleri 2014). An example of gender exploitative programming in HIV prevention is one that uses an aggressive image of masculinity to promote condoms, taking advantage of patriarchal masculinity norms, reinforcing gender stereotypes (Rolleri 2014). Gender-neutral programmes take account of specific needs of women or men but miss opportunities to address gender determinants of health. An example is where fidelity messages are promoted to prevent HIV, without reference to gendered power relations in many women and men’s intimate sexual relationships (Gupta 2000). Gender-sensitive approaches address specific needs, such as introducing male-friendly reproductive healthcare services at convenient times for men. They recognize and respond to gender norms and inequities, but do not work structurally changing harmful norms or power imbalances (Rolleri 2014). Gender transformative programmes aim to increase awareness of inequitable gender norms, question these and promote, individually and structurally, equitable gender norms, and relations (Rolleri 2014). An example is changing inequitable norms in which men hold power in decision-making in sexual relationships to those in which women and men engage in equitable decision-making (Greene and Levack 2010).





Individual agency


	Some women living in contexts in which hegemonic patriarchal patterns prevail, engage in a variety of individual actions to assert their agency (Jewkes and Morrell 2012; Stern et al. 2016). Jewkes and Morrell’s (2012) research in rural South Africa shows that women resist male control and potential male IPV. Some women avoid initiating such relationships, while others accommodate them but simultaneously seek respect and non-violence. Some women in countries such as South Africa and Botswana avoid formal marriage, in part to avoid male control over their lives (Cooper et al. 2013).
	While many men conform to dominant masculinity associated with high risk sexual behaviour, some have adopted health-seeking behaviours protective towards their own and their partners’ health (Stern and Cooper 2014; Morrell et al. 2016). As not all masculinities are equally powerful, some men go against prevailing gender norms even if they face sanction. Some men act out their masculinity individually through reflecting discomfort with harmful hegemonic forms through caring fatherhood (Morrell et al. 2016). A study among 18–49-year-old men in South Africa found 84% reported helping their children with school homework; only just over half (54%) reported discussing personal matters with their children. Men who were more gender egalitarian in their attitudes were more likely to be caring fathers (Morrell et al., 2016, p. 81).





Structural changes


	Sexual and Reproductive Rights are a fundamental human right. Less restrictive abortion laws decrease unsafe abortions. The South African Choice of Termination Act of 1996 is a good example of this, with abortion-related morbidity and mortality decreasing by 91% between 1997 and 2002 (Cooper et al. 2016). Legalizing abortion is a first step, with social stigma, political will for implementation and healthcare provider unwillingness to provide abortions, remaining major problems (Harries et al. 2014). As the US and South African experience show, it is important even when abortion is legal to prevent rolling back gains made (Cooper et al. 2016). In all countries, but particularly those where abortion is illegal, post-abortion care is crucial in protecting women’s health (Singh et al. 2017). A 16-country study showed that factors most influencing access to safe abortion services were having abortion services integrated into comprehensive SRH care, strong country-based women’s rights organizations, supported by international agencies and professional medical associations; involvement of non-governmental organizations in provision of services; task sharing among providers so that provision of abortion services is more ‘normalized’; and availability of new and less complicated techniques (such as the use of misoprostol and misoprostol-mifepristone in medical abortion). Political will was a key factor for legalization, provision, and ensuring access to abortion services (Chavkin et al. 2018). Although the need for abortion will always remain, better knowledge and access to contraception is critical in preventing pregnancy in the first place.
	A number of social interventions prevent and treat MNS problems. Initiatives with good results include legislation measures to restrict access to means of self-harm/suicide and reduce the availability of and demand for alcohol. At health service and community levels, parenting programmes and life skills training in schools can be effective in building social and emotional competencies. At the health service level, self-management, web-based psychological therapy for depression and anxiety disorders; and primary care and community outreach programmes are positive initiatives. This may include psychological and pharmacological management for specific conditions.
	Hospitals play a role in providing specialist services for MNS disorders, providing for severe emergencies and for integrating mental healthcare into broader other healthcare services. At a specialist care level, the management of complex and severe cases of MNS disorders, and the integration of primary care level interventions in other medical care platforms, such as maternal and HIV care have shown positive results. The PRIME programme has focused on a district health systems level. It involved partnerships with stakeholders in Ethiopia, India, Kenya, Nepal, South Africa, and Uganda. It developed a district health framework for dealing with mental health problems. Research to test implementation of pilot projects and estimate costs and evaluate their outcomes and processes was conducted. It was aimed at health ministries’ scale-up of mental health services at district level in order to improve individuals’ and communities’ psychological well-being. It has prioritized LMICs, where there is a significant gap in addressing prevention, treatment, and care for mental health problems (Lund et al. 2016, p. S1). These would be cost-effective interventions, if scaled up. Less than 1% of development assistance for health and government spending on health is allocated to MNS problems, estimated at US$1–2 per capita per year in LMIC, and US$ 3–5 per capita in upper-middle-income countries. National Health Insurance or Universal coverage policies should include addressing these issues through allocation of public health resources (Patel et al. 2016, p. 1).





Advocacy and group/community initiatives


HIV and GBV


	A number of examples of gender transformative programmes have been introduced to address HIV and violence against women.
	A gender transformative HIV and GBV prevention programme, the Stepping Stones programme (Welbourn 1995), was developed in Uganda and adapted and used in 40 countries. Targeting women and men, it sought to improve sexual health through building stronger, more gender-equitable relationships (Jewkes et al. 2007). A randomized controlled trial evaluating the Stepping Stones programme in rural South Africa among young men and women (15–26 years old), showed of short term success in reducing sexual risk-taking and violence perpetration by young male participants. Similar changes did not occur among young female participants. This speaks to the difficulties women face in implementing individual behaviour change, in the absence of community or structural changes in gender norms and relationships (Jewkes et al. 2007).
	The International AIDS Alliance strategy (2016–2020) on HIV, health and rights conducts a programme based on a ‘people centred’ approach. It works through community action in partnership with PLWH, based on the premise that they are best able to assess their own needs. It promotes equity through focusing on those systematically excluded or marginalized; activities that are criminalized (such as women who use drugs in Kenya and sex workers); and people with diverse sexual orientations or gender identities. It analyses the social determinants, including gender’s, effect on peoples’ lives, and health (International AIDS Alliance 2017, p. 1). Its Vihaan project in India, promotes community-based organizations and PLWH taking a leadership role in care, treatment, and support programmes (International AIDS Alliance 2017, p. 3). In Kenya work with women using drugs involves issues of concern for young women as lovers, mothers, keeping safe, HIV, SRH and rights and childcare (International AIDS Alliance 2017, p. 2).
	Recent transformative research interventions aimed at girls involve cash transfer programmes to address one of the root economic HIV vulnerabilities in young women. These were implemented and evaluated in South Africa (Cluver et al. 2013) and other southern and eastern African countries affected by HIV (Samson 2009). They showed some success in encouraging younger women to complete schooling, be economically independent and engage in more positive sexual health behaviours.
	Over the past few decades, a substantial number of male-oriented initiatives have addressed the gender effects of HIV and GBV. These focused on changing patriarchal masculinities among men that are harmful to men and women’s health.
	Examples of transformative individual, community, and structural initiatives that engage primarily with men on GBV, HIV, and fatherhood include the Sonke Gender Justice Network and Primundo (Dworkin et al. 2012; Ricardo et al. 2011). Sonke Gender Justice Network’s the ‘One Man Can’ campaign, is a rights-based gender equality health initiative, recognized as best practice by the WHO. Its programme has been translated into over 10 languages and subsequently implemented across the African continent (Van den Berg et al. 2013). It organized men’s community-based workshops to reflect on human rights, women’s rights, how masculinities are defined and practised and can be more caring (Dworkin et al. 2013). It assisted establish community action teams to address GBV and HIV (Dworkin et al. 2012). Evaluations showed increased actions among male participants against GBV, engaging in safer sex and accessing HIV testing and ART (Dworkin et al. 2013).





Pharmaceuticals and patent laws—structural initiatives


	In India, people living with HIV struggled and won changes in India’s medicine patent laws to allow access to cheaper antiretroviral medication (People’s Health Movement 2018). The Treatment Action Campaign in South African launched and won a similar struggle as well as pressurizing the government into providing antiretroviral treatment in public sector health facilities (Colvin 2014). These initiatives confronted structural determinants of health and involved the support of health professionals and healthcare providers.





Mental health


	The ‘Emerging mental health systems in LMICs’ (Emerald) programme has aimed at improving health outcomes of people with MNS problems in Ethiopia, India, Nepal, Nigeria, South Africa, and Uganda. It generated evidence that was used to boost health system performance in providing improved mental healthcare and enhance the capacity of policymakers, and planners. It focused on strengthening health service use and caregiver capacity to support efforts within mental health systems. The programme sought to deal with stigma and discrimination as key barriers to health-seeking behaviour and provision of mental health services (Semrau et al 2015).





Other informative initiatives that could inform women and men’s health


	The Genuino Clandestino is an Italian network of collectives, associations, and individuals engaged in dealing with the struggles for food and control over land. Founded in 2009, with origins in small-scale producers of food, it links its activities to the specific needs of local communities, promotes small-scale organic food markets, certification of products, self-organized kitchens, and land access. Its strong grassroots community base has enabled it to take on local struggles important to female and male nutrition and land issues and to confront the interests of large multinational food and land companies (People’s Health Movement 2018).





Changing gender power relations


	There has been ongoing tension on place of men and boys in changing gender power relations (Tolhurst et al. 2012). Initial approaches for male involvement stressed their strategic importance for women’s health. This raised questions about whether gender was only about women’s interests. Later approaches emphasized male involvement as important in its own right and to improve female health (Tolhurst et al. 2012). These approaches argued that transforming gender relations acts in the interests of both women and men’s health. Yet others have drawn critical attention to women and men not being equally vulnerable or privileged. Hence addressing gender inequity in power relations likely involves the relinquishment of personal and structural hegemonic patriarchal forms of power and privilege, vested in institutions such as the legal, political, and economic system (Box 10.2.13).
	 	Box 10.2.13 Key messages
	 	• Biomedical interventions have been important in HIV, CVD, mental health, and maternal health improvements.
	• There are multiple theories of gender change, with gender transformation being the most far-reaching.
	• Individual agency, structural changes and advocacy and community initiatives are important in transforming gender power relations that can improve women and men’s health and healthcare.
	• Several evaluated transformative initiatives have shown promise in improving women and men’s health.





In conclusion


	Researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and policy implementers should recognize health as a complex interplay between many determinants, of which gender is one key social determinant. These operate at individual, interpersonal, systems (such as the healthcare system) and structural levels. This has key implications for how we conceptualize health problems, how we address them, how we approach research and design a health system and services. It involves work intersectorally to promote facilitators of health and engage in advocacy activities to transform the legal, policy, social, political, and economic structures, in which health is embedded.

10.3


Child health


	Tyler Vaivada, Amira Khan, Omar Irfan, and Zulfiqar A. Bhutta





Current situation of child health globally


	Within the life course, the period of life before attaining adulthood is divided into three age subgroups based on epidemiology and healthcare needs: the first 5 years (under-5 children), the next 5 years (older children), and the second decade of life (adolescents). The first 5 years of life are further subdivided into the neonatal period (the first 28 days of life), infancy (the first year of life), and preschool years (from 1 to 5 years). This chapter focuses on the health of under-5 children, in addition to older children from 5 to 10 years.
	The most important indicators of health status of children relate to their mortality, morbidity, nutrition, growth, and development. Poor health and survival are linked to social and economic development and child mortality is one of the most sensitive barometers of this relationship. An overview of the health situation and inequalities among children in the world is presented in this section.





Global burden and epidemiology of mortality in children under 5


	There has been remarkable progress in the reduction of the under-5 mortality burden, with the under-5 mortality rate (U5MR) decreasing from 93 per 1,000 livebirths in 1990 to 39 per 1,000 livebirths in 2017; a reduction of nearly 56% (UN IGME 2018). Much of this success in reducing under-5 deaths is attributable to falling infectious disease mortality. Despite progress made, 5.4 million children died in 2017—a staggering 2.5 million of them were neonates. Nearly half of under-5 deaths occur within the first month of life, and the risk of death is the highest on the day of birth; it then decreases over the subsequent days, months, and years. Unfortunately, as compared to the 60% reduction in the 1–59-month mortality between 2000 to 2017, mortality in the neonatal period has only decreased by 41% (UN IGME 2018).
	More than 80% of all under-5 deaths are clustered in just two regions of the world: sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Sub-Saharan Africa leads with the highest global U5MR of 76 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2017 with the chances of an under-5 child dying being 1 in 13. It is noteworthy that globally 50% of all under-5 deaths are concentrated in six countries: India, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Democratic Republic of Congo, Pakistan, and China.
	Most children eventually die from only a small number of diseases and conditions. Globally, the leading causes of under-5 mortality are those occurring in the neonatal period, such as preterm birth complications (18%), intrapartum-related events (12%), and neonatal sepsis or meningitis (7%). Although global data on preterm birth rates are sparse, in 2014, an estimated 10.6% (14.84 million) of live births occurred before 37 weeks’ gestation, of which 80% were in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia (Chawanpaiboon et al. 2018). Birthweight is a key indicator of maternal and foetal health during pregnancy, and in 2015, an estimated 14.6% (20.5 million) of newborns had low birthweight (LBW), defined as less than 2500g (Blencowe et al. 2019). LBW can be the result of intrauterine growth restriction, preterm birth, or both. Children born too soon or too small are at considerable increased risk of mortality and morbidity. Pneumonia (16%), diarrhoea (8%), and malaria (5%) are the leading causes of infection-derived post-neonatal under-5 mortality (UN IGME 2018).
	The so-called epidemiological transition has a complex, dynamic course which reflects changes in demographic, socioeconomic, cultural, biological, technological, and environmental domains. As a result, important modifications are seen in the patterns of causes of death that usually shift from acute infectious diseases and deficiency-related conditions to non-communicable diseases (NCDs), leading to a relative increase in conditions such as perinatal causes (prematurity, birth asphyxia, and trauma), congenital abnormalities, and injuries. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that, between 2000 and 2012, childhood measles, diarrhoea, and pneumonia mortality reduced by 80, 50, and 40%, respectively (WHO 2018a).
	Poverty, maternal health and education, gender, race, and poor-quality healthcare are some of the underlying determinants of under-5 deaths. Levels, trends, and progress in both infant and under-5 mortality are unequally distributed between and within communities, regions, and countries. The likelihood of a child dying in the poorest household, before their fifth birthday, is nearly double that of the most affluent. Similarly, those in rural areas have a 1.5 times greater chance of under-5 death than children in urban settings. More than one-third of under-5 mortality is concentrated in the least developed countries. Unless this inequity is addressed, it is estimated that between 2016 and 2030, 69 million under-5 children will die with nearly half of them in sub-Saharan Africa (Watkins et al. 2016). Figure 10.3.1 illustrates the distribution of under-5 deaths by cause in 2016. Figure 10.3.2 shows trends in child mortality rates.

Global burden and epidemiology of morbidity in children under 5


	Measurement of morbidity is more complex than that of mortality, thus data on the distribution of morbidity burden among the under-5 population is scarce. Despite data limitations, it is known that the main causes of morbidity highly correlate with the major causes of death in under-5 children (Table 10.3.1). Pneumonia, the second-leading cause of under-5 mortality is the leading cause of under-5 deaths in sub-Saharan Africa—nearly 490,000 annually. The global incidence of pneumonia in the 0–4 age group is nearly 0.19 episodes per child per year, with the highest incidence in Southeast Asia (0.26) and Africa (0.27) (Walker et al. 2013). In 2010, 120 million episodes of pneumonia occurred in children less than 5 years of age, of which 14 million progressed to severe illness (Fischer Walker et al. 2013).
	Recent estimates of diarrheal disease burden show that diarrhoea incidence and mortality decreased by nearly 6 and 21%, respectively, between 2005 and 2015 (GBD Diarrhoeal Diseases Collaborators 2017). Of the 1.3 million deaths caused by diarrhoea in 2015, nearly 0.5 million were in children under-5, accounting for 8% of the total under-5 mortality. Nearly 90% of these diarrhoeal deaths in children occurred in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. Persistently high rates of diarrhoea morbidity have long-term detrimental effects on child growth and cognitive development.
	Incidence of both pneumonia and diarrhoea are closely associated with poor home environments, undernutrition, and lack of access to health services. The prevalence of pneumonia and diarrhoea can be more than twice as high among the poorest children as among the richest ones. Malnutrition is an underlying determinant of nearly 45% of all under-5 deaths. With changing environments and lifestyles, rates of childhood overweight and obesity are rising. In many instances, overweight and obesity coexist with undernutrition and stunting, thus giving rise to the double burden of malnutrition.
