Global burden and epidemiology of mortality and morbidity in school-age children


	Although a great deal of progress has been made since 1990, there are still considerable differences in the risk of mortality between younger and older children (Fig. 10.3.2). The disparities in child mortality between the least developed countries and the global average have also narrowed, but a substantial gap remains that can be addressed by evidence-based interventions targeted at highly marginalized groups. Between 1990 and 2016, the global mortality rate for children between 5 and 10 years decreased from 10.3 to 4.5 deaths per thousand children (Masquelier et al. 2018). Despite this global trend, the mortality rates of older children remained high in 2016 in sub-Saharan Africa at 11.9 deaths per thousand. In 2016, there were still an estimated 585,000 deaths globally among children 5–9 years, with approximately 351,000 and 192,000 occurring in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, respectively.
	Mortality rates are substantially lower, and the breakdown of causes of mortality in children over the age of 5 are quite different from that of younger children, with NCDs and injury-related causes increasing in importance to different degrees between countries (Fig. 10.3.3). The relative proportion of total mortality due to these causes increases in adolescence, and in higher income countries. A high proportion of infection-related mortality, characteristic of early childhood, extends into later childhood for those countries with higher levels of under-5 infectious morbidity. For example, the nutritional and communicable disease-related death rate of children 5–14 in India in 2016 was 32.6 and 26.2 per 100,000 for girls and boys, respectively, but the same rates for China were only 1.7 and 1.5 (Fadel et al. 2019). Furthermore, while NCDs and injuries in this age group were the principal causes of death in China, Brazil, and Mexico, India still experienced higher mortality rates due to these causes. Here, the typical epidemiological transition has not yet occurred, resulting in a substantial double burden of communicable and NCDs in older children, putting significant strain on health systems.
	While their mortality risk is lower, older children bear the consequences of ill health and adversities that were experienced in their earlier years. Early and continued nutritional deficits and recurrent infections can lead to poor school performance, in addition to predisposing children to deleterious metabolic changes. The main causes of morbidity and mortality in children under 5, including respiratory infections, diarrhoea, and malaria, remain a significant burden for school-age children in the poorest low-and middle-income countries (LMICs). NCDs that become increasingly prominent and cause significant morbidity and disability include hemoglobinopathies, asthma, rheumatic heart disease, and sensory and neurological disorders. Additionally, school-age children experience a higher burden of injuries caused by drowning, road traffic accidents, poisoning, burns, and maltreatment.
	Fig. 10.3.3 Breakdown of the causes of mortality among children 5–14 in Brazil, China, India, and Mexico from 2005 to 2016.
	Source: data from Fadel, S.A. et al (2019). Trends in cause-specific mortality among children aged 5–14 years from 2005 to 2016 in India, China, Brazil, and Mexico: an analysis of nationally representative mortality studies. The Lancet, 393(10176), pp.1119–27.





Determinants and indicators of child health and well-being


	The determinants of child survival, growth, and development can be broadly categorized as the social and physical environment in which a child resides, or their biological characteristics. Social and environmental determinants constitute the underlying risk factors further up the causal chain that can influence child health status. Biological determinants are often directly related to these underlying risks and include maternal risk factors (which influence a child’s health even before they are born), birth conditions, and the health and nutritional status of child. The key adversities that have the highest impact on child health vary along the life course but are most critical in infancy and early childhood when most preventable child deaths occur. It is important to note that these risk factors affect entire populations of children to varying degrees, and those that contribute to a proportion of child deaths also contribute to a spectrum of morbidities, disabilities, and suboptimal growth and development trajectories in a much larger proportion of children.





Social and environmental determinants of child mortality and morbidity


	Economic marginalization and poverty are the underlying determinants of much of the inequity in child health globally. Household food insecurity and reduced access to a diverse range of nutritious foods is strongly associated with poverty and predisposes children to malnutrition. When parents lack the means to provide a nurturing environment for their children, the risk of child mortality rises, child health suffers, and the consequences extend through adulthood and into the next generation. Parental educational achievement, particularly of the mother, is strongly linked to child health through multiple pathways. Community and household living conditions are also important determinants of childhood exposure to infectious diseases, chiefly water quality, sanitation infrastructure, and hygiene practices. Children raised in a safe, secure, and stimulating home environment, with responsive caregivers, early educational opportunities, and good access to health services, are best placed to survive to adulthood and achieve their developmental potential. Supporting optimal child health is necessary to optimize human capital development within a population. When a child cannot reach their full intellectual and social potential, lifetime educational achievement and earnings are reduced, and the intergenerational cycle of poverty is perpetuated.
	Gender and women’s empowerment also play a key role in child health, the impacts of which begin even before birth. Adolescent girls who enter marriage and become pregnant at an early age are at higher risk for malnutrition, and subsequent foetal growth restriction and poor birth outcomes. Although female infants have a biological advantage over male infants in early life (who generally experience higher mortality rates than female infants in most regions of the world), inequitable gender preferences can put infant girls at a disadvantage with regards to infant feeding and care practices. These discriminatory parenting practices reflect societal gender inequality that manifests itself at the earliest stages of life.
	Geographical disparities in child health stem, in part, from inequitable access to food, health services, and education—particularly in rural regions. Geography also dictates the physical environment in which children and their families live, and to which pathogens and pollutants they are exposed. Climactic conditions and agricultural productivity can affect household food security, especially in regions susceptible to the effects of climate change. Children are especially vulnerable to environmental shocks that disrupt the normal functioning of infrastructure, health systems, and food distribution. Migration, political instability, conflict, and natural disasters create adversities in the living conditions of children that increase the risk for malnutrition and disease.





Biological risk factors for child mortality and morbidity


	There are several key maternal risk factors in the context of pregnancy that influence child health. Adolescent pregnancy is associated with poorer birth outcomes, and untreated infectious diseases in expectant mothers can cause serious birth complications or child death. Adequate maternal nutrition status, both before conception and during pregnancy, are required for optimal growth and development of the foetus. Preterm birth and intrapartum-related complications such as birth asphyxia, in addition to severe neonatal infections, cause the majority of neonatal deaths. Those infants that survive are at substantially increased risk for developmental delay and disability (Mwaniki et al. 2012). Early childhood malnutrition and exposure to pathogenic organisms are the immediate causes of the majority of preventable child mortality, morbidity, and poor growth and development beyond the neonatal period. The subclinical condition known as environmental enteric dysfunction, or environmental enteropathy, is characterized by intestinal inflammation and changes to the intestinal lining. It is linked to poor sanitation conditions and chronic pathogen exposure, primarily through the repeated ingestion of faecal matter, and is proposed to represent an important link on the causal pathway to child stunting and suboptimal cognitive development, though the exact mechanism by which this occurs is still being investigated (Keusch et al. 2014).





Nutrition and growth in childhood


	The nutritional status of under-5 children is usually assessed through three standard indicators: stunting, wasting, and underweight. In the case of stunting, a child’s linear growth falls below minus two standard deviations (−2 SD) from the median height-for-age of the WHO Child Growth Standards (WHO 2006a). Stunting is usually a result of chronic undernutrition over a lengthy period of time, often in the context of a high burden of infectious pathogens that are associated with enteric dysfunction and nutrient malabsorption. A child is considered wasted when they fall below −2 SD from the median weight-for-height of the WHO Standards. Wasting usually reflects an acute nutritional deficiency, due either to reduced food consumption or acute weight loss during an illness. A child is said to be underweight if his/her weight falls below −2 SD from the median weight-for-age of the WHO Standards, which can be a result of stunting, wasting, or both. Conversely, overweight is defined as 2 SD above the median weight-for-height of the WHO Child Growth Standards.
	While childhood malnutrition is a consequence of risk factors related to the social determinants of health, poor nutritional status itself is strongly associated with vulnerability to disease, delayed physical and mental development, and increased mortality risk. Undernutrition is usually associated with inadequate maternal education and reduced child well-being. Despite declines in recent decades, in 2018, 21.9% (149 million) of children under 5 years globally experienced stunted linear growth, down from 32.5% (198.2 million) in 2000. In 2018, 5.9% (40.1 million) were overweight, up from 4.9% (30.1 million) in 2000. In 2018, an estimated 7.3% (49.5 million) of children under 5 experienced wasting (UNICEF/WHO/World Bank 2019). These global metrics mask striking inequities between regions; in 2018, 14.6% of children under 5 in Southern Asia experienced wasting, representing more than half of all wasted children globally. In Eastern Africa, 35.2% (24 million) of children under 5 were stunted (UNICEF/WHO/World Bank 2019).
	An increasing number of countries are experiencing a ‘double burden’ of malnutrition, in which high rates of undernutrition, and overweight and obesity coexist. While Asia and Africa account, respectively, for 55 and 39% of all stunted children under 5, they also account for 47 and 24% of all overweight children under 5. Obese children are at increased risk for adult obesity, diabetes, liver disease, and poor social and economic performance in later life.
	Micronutrient deficiencies are also a concern in children, sometimes causing serious deficiency-related morbidity, and affecting growth, development, and immune function. Deficiencies in iron (one cause of anaemia), vitamin A, iodine, and zinc are particularly harmful to child health, and are common in LMICs.
	The nutritional status of children over 5 years globally is insufficiently measured and studied compared to the under-5 group. In addition to malnutrition and growth deficits that are carried forward from early childhood, micronutrient deficiencies such as iron deficiency anaemia can contribute to poorer school performance in school-age children.





Early child development


	The first years of life provide the greatest opportunities for optimizing developmental trajectories. Young children have maximum plasticity of neuronal systems and are highly vulnerable to the negative effects of poor environments, and thus can benefit the most from interventions aimed at addressing risk factors in the critical period of early childhood. Estimates using stunting and poverty as proxy measures suggest that 43% (250 million) children under 5 in LMIC are at risk of not achieving their developmental potential (Lu et al. 2016; Black et al. 2017). Large regional disparities exist, with 66% (94.8 million) of children in the sub-Saharan African region at risk, versus 18% (9.7 million) in Latin America and the Caribbean.
	A child’s environment and activities while growing shape their cognitive, motor, and socioemotional development. Optimal child development can only occur with adequate nutrition, prevention and timely management of illness, responsive caregiving, and adequate psychosocial stimulation. Chronic malnutrition, poverty, illness, disability, and severe psychosocial deprivation represent key adversities that hamper a child’s optimal development. Children experiencing these adversities have more difficulty learning, are less active, and may be less able to receive the attention needed from those who care for them. Later in childhood, school performance may suffer, and subsequent educational attainment and future earnings may be reduced.
	Effective interventions that impact child development are available along the life course, and aim to improve maternal health and birth outcomes, caregiver–child interactions, responsiveness, and stimulation through play and communication. Through stimulation and interactions, these interventions intend to enhance the child’s ability to learn socially and intellectually and grow physically. The frequent contact of mothers, their babies, and young infants with health services provides a unique opportunity for these services to actively promote and support early child development.





Key supportive actions for child health


	Actions to improve child health do not exist solely within the health sector. This section briefly outlines a package of intersectoral and cross-cutting actions, rights frameworks, and policy improvements that support child health at the structural level. These actions address the most basic and distal social and environmental determinants of child health and are completely essential if actions within the health sector are to be effective.





Cross-cutting actions and supportive interventions to address the social determinants of health


	There are a host of actions that must be taken at the national and subnational level to help to address the basic and underlying risk factors for child mortality and morbidity, and suboptimal development across the life course (Box 10.3.1). These include policies and programmes that aim to address poverty, food insecurity, illiteracy, gender inequality, poor infrastructure, unsafe home and community environments, suboptimal caregiving practices, and barriers to health service access. When specifically tailored and targeted with marginalized populations in mind, these actions have high potential to impact child health at the population level and should be the foundation of national strategies for improving child health and well-being across the life course.
	 	Box 10.3.1 Key cross-cutting actions, programmes, and policies supporting child health, and health throughout the life course
	 	• Poverty alleviation and cash transfer programmes
	• Social protection services and safety nets
	• Health insurance schemes
	• Infrastructure and education for improved water, sanitation, and hygiene
	• Improving living conditions and housing quality
	• Reducing indoor and outdoor air pollution and exposure to toxins (e.g. lead, arsenic, aflatoxin)
	• Food fortification with micronutrients
	• Agricultural policies supporting food security
	• Education and empowerment for women and girls
	• Improved access and quality of health services
	• Improved access to parenting programmes and comprehensive early child development services
	• Universal primary education





Recognizing the rights of the child


	Efforts to ensure effective accountability for children’s health are further enhanced by the recognition that availability of and access to health information and services for children and their caregivers are basic human rights. Recognition of need for legal entitlements of every child, regardless of his/her status or situation, elevates associated responsibilities and political commitments to legal obligations. This paradigm shift thus enables the establishment of not merely a normative but indeed legal foundation for addressing the health needs of children.
	The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), adopted in 1989 and ratified by all but two UN Member States, is the principal legal instrument for the protection of children’s well-being, and outlines the core obligations of States in relation to children’s health. Article 24 directly addresses the child’s right to health and healthcare, while other provisions refer to the many underlying determinants of children’s health. The CRC thus provides a valuable holistic blueprint of all essential needs and legal entitlements of children needed to ensure their survival, health, and optimal development.





Governance


	Supportive laws and policies are prerequisites for strengthening the health sector’s capacity to provide quality healthcare to a population. Governance in the context of a functional health system involves developing strategic policy frameworks, regulation, and system design and accountability. Examples of evidence-based policies that play a role in child health and that are currently being promoted in countries to tackle the burden of ill health and excess mortality are (WHO 2012b):
	 	• Maternity protection in accordance with the International Labour Organization Convention 183.
	• Policy on midwives authorized to administer a core set of life-saving interventions.
	• Policy on postnatal home visits in the first week of life.
	• The International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes.
	• Policy on community treatment of pneumonia with antibiotics.
	• Policy on low osmolarity oral rehydration salts and zinc supplementation.
	• Policy on rotavirus and pneumococcal vaccines.
	In order to facilitate the effective implementation of these policies in countries, advocacy and policy dialogue with a wide range of stakeholders is needed. Both public funding of healthcare and the quality of governance matter for the reduction of childhood mortality but remain inadequately monitored and evaluated. Some policies gain wide adherence rapidly while others lag behind. For example, among the 75 countries with the highest burden of maternal and child mortality, the number of those with a policy allowing community health workers (CHWs) to treat pneumonia has more than doubled from 18 to 38 between 2008 and 2012. CHWs with appropriate training and supervision, and access to essential drugs and supplies have contributed significantly to improved pneumonia treatment (Kalyango et al. 2013). In contrast, by 2017 less than a third of the 81 Countdown countries had fully adopted the legislation on International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, which was endorsed in 1981 with consensus by the member states of the WHO.





Key child health issues, critical periods, and age-specific health sector interventions for prevention and management


	Children living in resource-poor environments require protective interventions to prevent the major causes of mortality and morbidity summarized in prior sections. There are two main types of interventions: first, health promotion for morbidity reduction and prevention of specific disease conditions; second, case management interventions to treat disease, help reduce illness severity, and improve child health and survival. Maternal and newborn care interventions


	Although neonatal mortality rates have reduced by 51% between 1990 and 2017, accelerated efforts are still needed to achieve Sustainable Development Goal targets for 2030 (Hug et al. 2019). Improved coverage and quality care along the continuum from pregnancy, childbirth, and the newborn period, into childhood and adolescence are critical for optimizing newborn health and survival. Such goals must focus on the most effective evidence-based interventions and intentional investment and implementation, which has so far been insufficient. Newborn health interventions can be classified into those relevant for all mothers and newborns, and those relevant for those newborns with conditions that require additional care (Table 10.3.2).





Routine care for mothers and newborns


	Improving newborn health and survival necessitates addressing social determinants, the education and empowerment of women in society, and especially the health and well-being of girls. This includes education and nutrition, prevention of harmful practices such as female genital mutilation, delaying age at first pregnancy, prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections, enhancement of pre-pregnancy nutrition status and optimization of interpregnancy intervals. Routine care during pregnancy holds particular importance for newborn survival and well-being. Evidence-based interventions for newborn health (Bhutta et al. 2014) provided during antenatal care include maternal vaccination (Haemophilus influenzae type b, influenza, pneumococcal), infection prevention, screening, and treatment, prevention of Rhesus disease, and maternal nutrition enrichment in populations with inadequate dietary intakes.
	Antenatal care provides the platform for continued care during and after childbirth by planning for skilled birth attendance, preparing for any unforeseen complications, and by helping the family prepare for immediate newborn care practices, such as early initiation of exclusive breastfeeding.
	The presence of skilled birth attendants and the provision of immediate obstetric care represent the cornerstone of modern obstetrics. A Delphi process involving expert consultation suggested that basic emergency obstetric care could reduce neonatal deaths during the intrapartum period by 40% and comprehensive emergency obstetric care could do so by 40% (Lee et al. 2011).
	Skilled childbirth care in first-level health facilities, with the backup of a hospital that can manage complications, should be available and accessible to expectant mothers 24 hours a day, every day, as the complications that may occur cannot be predicted and may very rapidly become fatal. It is crucial to have access to a skilled attendant and a companion who can stay with the mother and child for the first 12–24 hours to ensure a successful home birth. Knowledge and recognition of maternal and newborn danger signs is crucial for women and families who cannot access a skilled attendant, and a plan needs to be in place for a clean delivery and early care-seeking.
	Vaccines are highly effective and cost-effective prevention tools for the prevention of morbidity and mortality in early life. Given their proven benefits, availability and accessibility of routine neonatal vaccines should be a public health priority. Several key vaccines are mentioned in Table 10.3.2.
	Care for newborns at the time of birth and during the period that follows includes several relatively simple and effective interventions that do not require advanced technology (Table 10.3.2). The most critical time to deliver these interventions is immediately after birth and in the first 24 hours of life as a large proportion of maternal and neonatal mortality is reported during this window. Hence, at least one additional contact with a health provider within the first week, is required.





Care of at-risk and sick newborns


	Fifteen million premature babies are born every year of which nearly 1 million die due to complications of preterm birth. About 75% of these deaths could be prevented if current cost-effective measures are made available to all (Liu et al. 2016). Such key interventions include tocolytics to delay birth, antibiotics for preterm premature rupture of membranes, and corticosteroids given to eligible mothers during preterm labour to promote lung maturation of the baby. Additional care of preterm and LBW infants is critical for improving newborn survival. Basic newborn care packages should involve identification of LBW infants within the first hours after birth. In settings where measuring birth weight is not feasible, such as for home births, all newborns perceived to be ‘small’ should receive additional care, much of which can be provided at home and in first-level health facilities. However, care for babies weighing less than 1,500 g, who have difficulty feeding or breathing due to lung immaturity, is best provided in a hospital.
	In addition to basic newborn care, LBW infants need more attention, including immediate drying, adequate nutrition, provision of warmth, hygiene, early detection and management of infections, vitamin K administration, and growth monitoring. Kangaroo mother care or skin-to-skin contact is supported by strong evidence to reduce mortality and improve breastfeeding. Mothers who are unable to breastfeed directly should be taught to express breast milk and to feed from a cup.
	Perinatal asphyxia is responsible for 10% of all under-5 deaths. Monitoring of progress and feto-maternal well-being in labour using a partograph has been proven to help reduce morbidity and mortality due to perinatal asphyxia. When foetal distress is suspected, assisted vaginal or Caesarean birth may be needed, which requires functional referral mechanisms. The second key intervention for prevention of asphyxia-related mortality and morbidity is neonatal resuscitation. All birth attendants should be skilled and equipped to perform neonatal resuscitation, which can include positive pressure ventilation, use of endotracheal intubation and laryngeal mark, in addition to thorough drying and stimulation.
	The timely detection and optimum treatment of suspected neonatal bacterial infections, such as pneumonia and sepsis can substantially reduce neonatal mortality. It is therefore important to have community-and health-facility-based activities which focus on screening and management. Newborns with severe infections should receive parenteral antibiotics, along with intravenous fluids or alternative feeding methods and other supportive therapy such as oxygen in a hospital. Although the evidence for the use of injectable and muscular antibiotics in community settings has shown significant reductions in mortality in the infected newborns, implementation at scale has been scarce.





Care during Infancy and early childhood


	The first 5 years of life is a critical period of rapid growth and development when children are particularly sensitive to adversity. The focus during this period is on supporting optimal nutrition, minimizing the burden of infectious diseases, and providing a nurturing, responsive, stimulating environment to optimize growth and development.





Malnutrition


	The World Health Assembly (WHA) has declared 2016–25 as the ‘decade of nutrition’ and the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2 aspires to end hunger, achieve food security, and eliminate all forms of malnutrition by 2030. Interventions to prevent malnutrition include promotion of optimal feeding of infants and young children, prevention and treatment of illness, and amelioration of micronutrient deficiencies in the diet. Early initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding up to 6 months of age, and continued breastfeeding along with complementary foods up to at least 2 years of age are key interventions to combat undernutrition. Early initiation of breastfeeding, ideally within the first hour after birth, is associated with a reduced risk of neonatal mortality (Khan et al. 2014) and exclusive breastfeeding during the first 6 months of life is associated with a significantly lower risk of all-cause and infection-related mortality compared to those who were predominantly, partially, or not breastfed (Sankar et al. 2015). Safe and appropriate complementary feeding started at 6 months of age can reduce the prevalence of malnutrition and contribute to reduced mortality. Promotion of safe and appropriate complementary feeding has been shown to significantly improve weight-for-age and height-for-age scores (Lassi et al. 2013).





Prevention and management of acute malnutrition


	Malnutrition, as a term, covers both being undernourished or overweight. Acute malnutrition is characterized by an acute loss of weight as a result of inadequate food intake or disease. However, there are many underlying and basic causes that contribute to the development of undernutrition. Several social factors such as decreased access to care, poor living conditions, inadequate care and feeding practices, and household food insecurity exacerbate this issue. In low-resource settings, children experiencing wasting are particularly vulnerable to infections, such as diarrhoea, pneumonia, and malaria, which can worsen malnutrition and further increase risk of disease, creating a vicious cycle of deteriorating health. The risk of mortality in acutely malnourished children is elevated, and nutrition-related factors directly or indirectly contribute to 45% of deaths in children under 5 years of age (Black et al. 2013).
	To improve the nutritional status of children and prevent them from becoming severely malnourished, the dietary management of moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) (weight-for-height between –3 and –2 SD of the median of the WHO Child Growth Standards or 11.5 cm < mid-upper-arm circumference [MUAC] < 12.5 cm) should be based on optimal use of locally available nutrient-dense foods. Inadequate nutrient content of habitual diets can be augmented through a number of approaches, including dietary diversification and fortification of certain staple foods with vitamins and minerals. Supplementary feeding in children with MAM should be complemented with essential nutrition actions such as breastfeeding, nutrition counselling, and addressing the underlying social determinants of undernutrition.
	Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children 6–59 months of age is defined as weight-for-height criterion less than −3 SD below median WHO Growth Standards, or MUAC less than 11.5 cm, or the presence of bilateral oedema. For infants less than 6 months, there is no agreed cut-off value for MUAC. Children with SAM should be clinically assessed for presence of medical complications and for their appetite. Children who pass the WHO-defined appetite test and are clinically well and alert are treated as outpatients while those with medical complications, danger signs, or who fail the appetite test should be treated as inpatients. Young infants less than 6 months with SAM are always treated as inpatient. Outpatient management involves providing the child with therapeutic feeding, micronutrient supplementation, antibiotics, and regular monitoring.
	Inpatient management is generally organized in two phases: the stabilization phase (usually 3–7 days) includes careful evaluation and management of hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, infections, electrolyte imbalance, and feeding initiation; and the rehabilitation phase (usually 4–6 weeks) which consists of the provision of nutritional and psychosocial support to achieve full nutritional recovery. Therapeutic feeding should start early in the stabilization phase and include giving a low-protein milk-based formula diet with additional vitamins and minerals such as the WHO-recommended F-75 (75 kcal/100 mL). In the rehabilitation phase, a milk formula with higher protein and energy content such as F-100 should be given and additional iron is needed to address deficiencies. Ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTFs) have replaced liquid F-100 in a variety of settings because they do not contain free water and can therefore be used without risk of bacterial contamination. Most RUTFs are lipid-based pastes combining milk powder, electrolytes, and micronutrients to meet recommended nutritional values and offer the malnourished child the same nutrient intake as F-100. RUTFs also contain 10–14 mg/100 g of iron, therefore no additional intake of iron is necessary.
	In combination with community-based screening, RUTFs are highly effective in the treatment of SAM in children 6–59 months of age without complications (WHO 2013c). These children can be managed in the community without the risks of nosocomial infections or any other disruptions regarding hospital care to the family. Often ignored is the sensory stimulation component of management where it is recommended that children with SAM be provided with structured play therapy and tender loving care in the rehabilitation phase.
	In children less than 6 months of age who have SAM, care should focus on managing sepsis and other underlying complications and on re-establishing breastfeeding where this has been ineffective.





Prevention and management of chronic malnutrition


	Chronic malnutrition in children is a global public health concern that is strongly linked to poverty. The process of nutritionally associated linear growth faltering begins in utero in the presence of maternal malnutrition, contributing to intrauterine growth restriction and low birthweight. During infancy, chronically suboptimal feeding practices, deficits in macronutrient and micronutrient intake, and a high burden of infectious diseases contribute to poor growth. A high prevalence of linear growth stunting within a population of children is a visible and easily measurable indicator of widespread chronic malnutrition. Children who experience this growth delay also suffer both higher mortality and suboptimal cognitive and motor development. Chronically malnourished children are at substantially higher risk of dying from common childhood infections such as diarrhoea, pneumonia, and malaria. Nutrition-related factors directly or indirectly contribute to 45% of deaths in children under 5 years of age, with an estimated 17% of mortality in children under 5 years attributable to stunting (Black et al. 2013).
	The exact causes of stunting within a population are multifactorial, and still not well-understood. As such, a broad spectrum of interventions to prevent and address both undernutrition and high infectious disease burden is necessary to minimize the risk of growth faltering. This includes the promotion of optimal infant and young child breastfeeding and complementary feeding practices described earlier, ensuring adequate micronutrient intake in those at risk of deficiency, and high coverage of the infection prevention strategies described in the following sections.
	Analyses of cohort data have shown that every unit increase in height-for-age z-score in children ≤2 years was associated with a 0.22 SD improvement in measures of cognitive function at 5 to 11 years (Sudfeld et al. 2015), demonstrating the lingering effects chronic malnutrition in young children. This has serious implications not only for population health in countries with a high burden of chronic childhood malnutrition, but also for the fulfilment of their intellectual and economic potential. Countries that prioritize the implementation and scale-up of nutrition-sensitive and nutrition-specific policies and programmes stand to make the greatest improvements in human capital development and economic productivity, as these actions generally have very high benefit-cost ratios (Hoddinott et al. 2013).





Micronutrient deficiencies and hidden hunger


	Sometimes described as ‘hidden hunger’, common micronutrient deficiencies such as those of vitamin A, iron, iodine, and zinc, both at clinical and subclinical levels, contribute to illness, suboptimal growth and development, and mortality in children. Strategies to prevent these deficiencies include supplementation (WHO 2011a, 2011b, 2016c), point-of-use fortification (WHO 2016d), mass food fortification of staple foods (WHO 2016e, 2018c), and dietary diversification (Pan American Health Organization and WHO 2003; WHO 2005b). See Table 10.3.3 for a summary of nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive interventions for the prevention and treatment of micronutrient deficiency in mothers and children, as recommended in the 2013 Lancet Series on Maternal and Child Nutrition (Bhutta et al. 2013; Ruel et al. 2013).
	 	Table 10.3.3 Summary of interventions to prevent and treat micronutrient deficiencies in mothers and children.
	 			Individual level
	Population level
			 	 	• Education and support for optimal infant and child breastfeeding and complementary feeding practices
	• Promotion of dietary diversification
	• Point-of-use fortification of complementary foods (e.g. micronutrient Sprinkles)
	• Single micronutrient supplementation (e.g. vitamin A capsules)
	• Multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMN)
	• Balanced energy protein supplementation (BEP)
	• Lipid-based nutrient supplements (LNS)
	• Delayed cord clamping
	• Deworming
	• Improved water, sanitation, and hygiene
	 	 	• National nutrition-sensitive policies and programmes
