	• Social safety nets





Acute respiratory infections


	Acute respiratory infections (ARIs), particularly pneumonia, are the second-leading cause of under-5 mortality, causing 16% of all child deaths worldwide. However, in children beyond the neonatal period, pneumonia continues to be the leading killer, responsible for nearly 13% of these deaths (Liu et al. 2016). Half of all childhood pneumonia deaths are attributable to Pneumococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Other common causative organisms include viruses, most prominently respiratory syncytial virus, in addition to bacterial infections with Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Pneumocystis jirovecii is a significant cause in areas with high HIV burden. Interventions to control ARIs can be divided into preventive interventions such as immunization against specific pathogens, improvements in nutrition, reduction in household air pollution, and case management interventions.
	Widespread use of vaccines against Pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, pertussis, diphtheria, influenza, and measles has the potential to substantially reduce the incidence of ARIs in children in LMICs. Two particularly important vaccines are those against Pneumococcus and Hib pathogens, as they account for the largest burden of disease. Pneumococcus and Hib were estimated to cause more than 300,000 and 30,000 under-5 deaths, respectively, in 2015 (Wahl et al. 2018).
	Two types of pneumococcal vaccines are currently being used internationally: a polysaccharide vaccine effective against 23 different strains of Pneumococcus (primarily recommended for adults) and different formulations of polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccine (PCV), of which WHO recommends the use of the 10-and 13-valent types (PCV10 and PCV13, respectively), for all infants. The serotypes included in these vaccines account for the majority of serious pneumococcal disease in children worldwide. PCVs are increasingly available in low-income, high-mortality countries, but gaps in vaccine uptake within countries could reduce their impact. A total of 141 countries have included the vaccine in their national immunization programmes; these include 7 of the 10 countries with the highest burden of pneumococcal disease.
	The use of Hib conjugate vaccines in developed countries has resulted in the virtual elimination of invasive Hib disease (meningitis and bacteraemic pneumonia) because of immunity in vaccinated children and a herd effect in those not vaccinated. There are several Hib conjugate vaccines available, all of which are effective when given in early infancy and have virtually no side effects. The success of these vaccines is seen in most low-income countries which have introduced Hib vaccines. Recent research has estimated that the use of PCV has prevented 250,000 pneumococcal deaths from 2000 to 2015 (90% of these after 2010), while Hib vaccine prevented 1.2 million deaths in the same period (Wahl et al. 2018).
	Vaccination should be seen as complementary to other strategies for pneumonia control, such as improved care-seeking and case management, better nutrition (including exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life), hand washing promotion, and measures to reduce indoor air pollution. Many studies have shown that young children exposed to smoke from the use of household biomass fuel had twice the risk of developing acute lower respiratory infection than unexposed children. A systematic review on household air pollution control strategies for child survival concluded that reducing exposure could reduce the risk of fatal pneumonia, especially if WHO guidelines are followed (Bruce et al. 2013).
	Diagnosis and clinical guidelines for ARI case management rely on two simple clinical signs: fast breathing and lower chest wall indrawing. Chest indrawing is the inward movement of the lower chest wall when a child breathes in. As per the revised WHO classification, children 2–59 months, with cough and/or difficult breathing plus fast breathing and/or chest indrawing are now classified as non-severe pneumonia that can be treated at home with oral amoxicillin (WHO 2014a). Severe pneumonia can be recognized by the presence of one or more danger signs (such as central cyanosis, severe respiratory distress, inability to drink, lethargy, or convulsions), and such cases must be managed in a hospital with parenteral antibiotics and supportive care including oxygen therapy. The updated guidelines to manage ‘chest indrawing’ pneumonia (previously labelled ‘severe pneumonia’) at home is significant, especially in settings when referral is difficult and also in reducing the use of unnecessary parenteral antibiotics. The role of CHWs in identifying and treating non-severe pneumonia is critical, especially in low-resource settings with poor access to facilities (Bhutta et al. 2013).





Diarrhoea


	Diarrhoea remains one of the leading causes of under-5 child mortality in LMICs that lack sufficient resources and a strong infrastructure. Strategies for the control of diarrhoeal diseases have remained substantially unchanged since the early 1980s. A package of proven prevention and treatment measures is available that, if taken to scale, will lead to a significant reduction in the morbidity of diarrhoeal disease. It consists of a seven-point plan for diarrhoea control and includes promotion of early and exclusive breastfeeding, vitamin A supplementation, rotavirus and measles vaccinations, promotion of hand washing with soap and improved water supply quantity and quality, community-wide sanitation promotion, fluid replacement to prevent dehydration, and zinc treatment (UNICEF and WHO 2009). The package should be implemented as part of a concerted process alongside targeted and integrated behaviour change strategies which aim improve uptake by families and communities.
	Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life reduces the risk of infection-related neonatal mortality when compared to partial or no breastfeeding (Gülmezoglu et al. 2016). Components of breast milk such as antibodies, hormones, and growth factors provide optimal protection to the growing child. It is recommended that appropriate complementary feeding be introduced at 6 months of age alongside continued breastfeeding until at least 24 months. This improves the nutritional status of infants and young children, optimizing physical and cognitive development and immune function.
	Rotavirus is the leading cause of diarrhoea mortality among children younger than 5 years. It is estimated that introduction of the rotavirus vaccine was responsible for a 2.6% decrease in diarrhoea-related mortality in children younger than 5 years between 2000 and 2016 (Troeger et al. 2018). The international market has two rotavirus vaccines: the monovalent (RV1) and the pentavalent (RV5), which show 80 to 90% efficacy against severe infection in countries with very low or low mortality, and 40 to 60% efficacy in countries with high mortality in children and high or very high mortality in adults. WHO recommends the first dose of rotavirus vaccine be administered as soon as possible after 6 weeks of age, along with diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP) vaccine. RV1 and RV5 are administered in 2 dose and 3 dose schedules respectively, with 4 weeks each between the doses (WHO 2013a, b).
	An estimated 800,000 children die each year from preventable diseases caused by lack of quality water, sanitation, and proper hygiene (Mills and Cumming 2016). Human faeces are the primary source of diarrhoeal pathogens. Water filtration and disinfection, and hand hygiene can significantly reduce diarrheal disease risk (Darvesh et al. 2017). However, behaviour change components are complex and often difficult to sustain. Poor-quality and quantity of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) and related measures can hinder linear growth in children under 5 years of age (Dangour et al. 2013). Thus, resources should also be directed towards extending and sustaining water, sanitation, and hygiene services at the community level. SDG 6 includes targets for universal access to drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene.
	Most diarrhoea-related deaths are due to dehydration, and dysentery (bloody diarrhoea) and electrolyte imbalance in severe cases. Management of diarrhoea includes:
	 	• Oral rehydration salts (ORS) solution administration to replenish fluid loss, or an intravenous electrolyte solution in cases of severe dehydration.
	• Mothers and health workers should supplement children with 20 mg per day of zinc for 10 to 14 days (10 mg per day for children under the age of 6 months).
	• Continuing or increasing breastfeeding during, and increasing feeding after, the diarrhoeal episode.
	• Using antibiotics only during episodes of bloody diarrhoea.
	The use of oral rehydration solution has shown to reduce diarrhoea-specific mortality by 93% (Munos et al. 2010). Two noteworthy advances in the management of acute diarrhoea are: zinc supplementation, and newly formulated ORS containing lower concentrations of glucose and salts. Over the years, ORS formulation therapy has proven safe and effective in the prevention and treatment of dehydration. However, acceptance of standard ORS by mothers and health workers has been suboptimal because watery stools persist, and the duration of diarrhoea is not reduced. Efforts over the past decades have led to the development of a new ORS formulation with reduced osmolarity (low sodium and glucose). This new formulation reduces stool output, vomiting, and the need for any intravenous therapy. The new ORS is safe and effective in both non-cholera diarrhoea and cholera in children and adults. WHO and UNICEF now recommend the use of ORS containing 75 mEq of sodium and 75 mmol of glucose per litre (total osmolarity of 245 milliosmol per litre) everywhere (WHO 2005a). In addition to fluid replacement, optimal nutrition status can enhance fluid absorption and strengthen immune function.
	A recent review of relevant clinical trials from areas with prevalent zinc deficiency showed benefit of zinc supplementation in children aged 6 months or more by reducing the duration of diarrhoea (Lazzerini and Wanzira 2016). Moreover, studies from India show that supplementing zinc in the management of acute diarrhoea can reduce the rate of hospital admissions for diarrhoeal disease (Mazumder et al. 2010). The addition of zinc to ORS in the treatment of diarrhoea has also increased the compliance of ORS and has reduced unwarranted use of prescription drugs of unknown identity and antibiotics (Bhandari et al. 2008).
	Dysentery is an inflammatory disorder of the lower intestinal tract with a clinical picture of abdominal cramping, fever, and severe diarrhoea, often accompanied by the passage of bloody and mucoid stools. Shigella is the leading and most severe cause of bloody diarrhoea. The primary treatment for shigellosis is the use of antibiotics, which can decrease dysentery-related mortality by more than 99% (Traa et al. 2010).
	Antibiotic resistance is an emerging challenge in the management of shigellosis, and with ciprofloxacin-resistant strains already emerging, this increases the urgency for the development of a Shigella vaccine. Ciprofloxacin is the current treatment drug of choice due to its effectiveness, safety, ease of oral administration, short course, and low cost. For severe cholera cases, WHO recommends the use of oral antibiotics to which strains of Vibrio cholerae in the area are known to be sensitive; possible choices include tetracycline, erythromycin, doxycycline, co-trimoxazole, and chloramphenicol. Antibiotic treatment of cholera has shown a 63% reduction in rates of clinical failure and a 75% reduction in rates of bacteriological failure (Das et al. 2013).





Enteric infections and neglected tropical diseases


	Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) are a group of bacterial, parasitic, and viral infections highly endemic to the poorest regions of the world, where NTDs caused over 500,000 deaths per year (Naghavi et al. 2017). Several conditions disproportionately affect children compared to adults, who are often infected with multiple pathogens. Some of these infections are chronic, and contribute to substantial and prolonged illness and disability.
	The WHO recognizes 17 core NTDs: rabies, trachoma, dengue, Chagas disease, Buruli ulcer, endemic treponematoses, human African trypanosomiasis (HAT), leprosy, echinococcosis, leishmaniasis, taeniasis/cysticercosis, dracunculiasis, trematodiases, lymphatic filariasis, schistosomiasis, onchocerciasis, and soil-transmitted helminthiases. From a programmatic point of view, WHO classifies NTDs into two groups: preventive chemotherapy and transmission control (PCT) NTDs, and innovative and intensified disease management (IDM) NTDs. The most prominent examples of PCT group NTDs are lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminthiasis; they are mainly controlled by the administration of drugs to entire at-risk populations. IDM focuses on NTDs that lack appropriate tools for large-scale use. These include Buruli ulcer, Chagas disease, HAT, and leishmaniasis. Climate change is contributing to the intensifying spread of many vector-borne infections, including malaria, dengue fever, Chagas disease, leishmaniasis, onchocerciasis to name a few (Mitra and Mawson 2017).
	Disease control strategies, in line with WHO’s 5 general strategies may involve: (i) prevention, including combined and concurrent preventive chemotherapy; (ii) improved access to clean water and sanitation; and (iii) control of insect vectors by use of environmentally safe insecticides, treated bed nets, and other personal protective measures, vegetation clearance, and improved sanitation to disrupt breeding sites (Mackey et al. 2014).
	Food-borne enteric infections are also major causes of morbidity and mortality in LMICs, with outbreaks of Salmonella, Escherichia coli, and spongiform encephalitis occurring due to suboptimal sanitation, hygiene, and food processing practices. Typhoid and paratyphoid fevers are caused by infection with Salmonella typhi and paratyphi, respectively. After malaria and diarrhoea, typhoid fever is the most common cause of death in older children. An estimated 14.3 million cases of typhoid and paratyphoid fevers occurred globally in 2017, with 12.6% of cases reported among children younger than 5 years, and 55.9% among children less than 15 years. The highest mortality rates were reported in South Asia, accounting for 69.6% of worldwide mortality from typhoidal illness in 2017 (Stanaway et al. 2019). Antibiotics such as cephalosporins and azithromycin are primarily used in the affected regions. In December 2017, WHO endorsed the first conjugate vaccine for typhoid. This new vaccine has longer-lasting immunity than older vaccines, requires fewer doses and can be given to younger children. Provision of safe water and adequate sanitation, good hygiene among food handlers, and vaccination are all effective in preventing typhoid fever.
	E. coli are normal inhabitants of the human intestine. Virulent strains are responsible for diarrhoea, neonatal meningitis, sepsis, and urinary tract infections. Transmission occurs via contaminated food and water or direct contact with an infected individual. Outbreaks have been associated with ground beef, exposure to animals in public settings, and contamination of water in recreational areas. Children who are suspected of having a systemic infection with E. coli should receive intravenous antibiotic therapy after diagnostic culture of the organism. Aminoglycoside or a third-generation cephalosporin is recommended as the empirical therapy. Preventive measures for E. coli infections involves hand hygiene, food safety, and contact isolation of infected individuals.
	Dengue virus is estimated to infect 50 to 100 million people worldwide and is a significant cause of childhood morbidity and mortality (WHO 2013d). It is endemic to more than 125 countries across all WHO regions (excluding Europe) and has increased in incidence about 30-fold in the past 50 years. The factors that facilitate local outbreaks are shared with other NTDs, and include a lack of vector control, rapid urbanization, climate change, global travel to endemic regions, and social infrastructure weaknesses. Its arthropod vector is the Aedes aegypti mosquito. Public health interventions for dengue focus on vector and environmental management. Complications can lead to dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF), which in some severe cases, such as in those who suffer from dengue shock syndrome (DSS), can be fatal.
	Soil-transmitted helminths (STH) are a group of worms transmitted through soil contaminated with infected human faeces. Of particular importance are the hookworm Necator americanus, the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, and the whipworm Trichuris trichiura. Most STH infections result from ingestion of contaminated soil or through skin penetration. Endemic to tropical regions worldwide, STH infections are particularly burdensome in poorer areas of Asia, Africa, and Latin America, with most cases occurring among the extreme poor living in some of the large LMICs of Asia, such as India, Bangladesh, China, and Indonesia. Children usually suffer from Ascaris and Trichuris infections, whereas hookworms can be seen among both children and adults. In sub-Saharan Africa, an estimated 50 million children are infected with hookworm alone, and in Southeast Asia nearly 120 million preschool and school-age children require treatment for STH infections (Hotez et al. 2015). The predisposing factors include poor personal hygiene and sanitation, poverty, and overcrowding. Infections can result in anaemia, growth retardation, and impaired cognitive development, and are also responsible for school absenteeism and a substantial burden of disability-adjusted life years (Vandemark et al. 2010). A recent study reported deficits in children’s cognitive development as a result of untreated STH infections (Pabalan et al. 2018). According to the WHO, administration of drugs like albendazole and mebendazole, education, and adequate sanitation are required for STH infection management.
	Schistosomiasis is caused by schistosomes that penetrate the skin of those that have frequent contact with contaminated water bodies, which are often children and adolescents. More than 90% of schistosomiasis cases occur in Africa alone. Schistosoma infection and non-treatment is significantly associated with educational, learning, and memory deficits (Ezeamama et al. 2018).





Malaria


	Malaria accounts for 5% of child deaths worldwide. More than 300,000 children under 5 (1–59 months) were killed by malaria in 2015 (Liu et al. 2016), accounting for nearly two-thirds of all malaria deaths. The African region bears 90% of the global malaria burden, however from 2000 to 2015 the leading cause of under-5 mortality in sub-Saharan Africa shifted from malaria to pneumonia. Chapter 8.15 describes malaria interventions in greater detail.
	Owing to effective preventive measures, the global malaria death rate has decreased by 60% since 2000. Vector control remains the most effective measure to prevent malaria transmission in all ages. Insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs), and more specifically long-lasting insecticidal bed nets (LLINs), are particularly effective in reducing uncomplicated malaria incidence and parasite infection prevalence in pregnant women and young children. The WHO’s Global Technical Strategy for Malaria 2016–2030 aims for universal coverage with effective vector control using LLINs or indoor residual spraying (IRS) of all households at risk for malaria (WHO 2015).
	Prompt parasitological confirmation by microscopy or alternatively by rapid diagnostic tests in all patients suspected of malaria should happen prior to treatment. Treatment solely on the basis of clinical suspicion should only be considered when a parasitological diagnosis is inaccessible. Once diagnosed, the child should be treated early with a safe and effective antimalarial medicine as delaying treatment could result in progression to severe disease, which is associated with a high case-fatality rate.
	Malaria case management has been greatly affected by the emergence and spread of chloroquine and sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine resistance. To counter the threat of drug resistance of Plasmodium falciparum to monotherapies and to improve treatment outcomes, the use of artemisinin-based combination antimalarials is recommended for treatment of uncomplicated malaria. In areas with poor access to health facilities, early recognition, prompt, and appropriate treatment require treatment in the home or community. The development of new chemical formulations to target mosquitoes and the upcoming first global malaria vaccine (WHO 2018b) hold potential to reduce the burden of malaria further.





HIV and AIDS


	In 2017, an estimated 1.8 million children under 15 globally were living with HIV, with just over half receiving antiretroviral (ARV) treatment. In 2015, HIV/AIDS accounted for about 1.4% of under-5 deaths globally (Liu et al. 2016), the vast majority of which occurred in sub-Saharan Africa. Although the proportional mortality due to HIV/AIDS among children under 5 remains unacceptably high in some African countries, it has declined significantly in the last decade due to scaling-up of interventions to prevent infections in children. In 2015, an estimated 45% of new HIV infections among children occurred in Central and West Africa. In children less than 18 months HIV infection diagnosis is established by the presence of HIV DNA through HIV nucleic acid-based testing (NAT) and beyond this age by detecting antibodies to HIV through an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. This is because maternal antibodies to HIV can pass through the placenta and remain present in HIV-exposed but uninfected children until the 18 months of age.
	About 90% of HIV-infected children are infected through the mother-to-child transmission (MTCT), which may occur during pregnancy, birth, or through breastfeeding. Without any interventions, there is risk of transmission between 20 to 45%, but this can be reduced to less than 2% with a combination of evidence-based interventions (WHO 2010a). Antiretroviral (ARV) drug interventions given to pregnant HIV-infected women are very effective at preventing peripartum MTCT and also protects the health of the mothers (WHO 2010a). In 2013, about 49% of women continued to take antiretrovirals (ARVs) while breastfeeding, compared to 62% of women who took them during pregnancy. This demonstrates the urgent need to increase awareness about the importance of continuing treatment after birth.
	Postnatal ARV interventions are now recommended to reduce the risk of maternal HIV transmission through breastfeeding. ARVs can be given either to the mother (Shapiro et al. 2010; Kesho Bora Study Group 2011) or to the infant (Coovadia et al. 2012). Based on the strength of this evidence and programmatic considerations, national authorities are advised to support one infant feeding practice for HIV-infected mothers, namely, either breastfeeding while on ARVs or to avoid breastfeeding altogether and use replacement feeds (WHO 2010b). In settings where diarrhoea, pneumonia, and malnutrition continue to be significant causes of child mortality, breastfeeding is likely to give HIV-exposed infants the greatest chance of HIV-free survival (Kagaayi et al. 2008; Peltier et al. 2009). Mothers should exclusively breastfeed their infants for the first 6 months of life, introducing appropriate complementary foods thereafter, and continue breastfeeding for at least the first 12 months of life, and up 24 months and beyond while being actively supported for ARV adherence (WHO 2016a). It has been challenging to achieve high coverage of these interventions in resource-poor countries. Moreover, CD4 count testing to establish which pregnant women are eligible for lifelong ARV treatment or prophylaxis has hindered scale-up in many settings. There is recognition that women in high-burden countries are likely to have repeated pregnancies that would each require ARV interventions, either prophylaxis or treatment. To this end, and to protect mothers, several national programmes have opted to start all HIV-infected pregnant women on lifelong treatment (e.g. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2013). The questions of whether all affected pregnant women will want to start lifelong regimen and how best to support women to remain in care and achieve high rates of adherence remain unanswered.
	In countries where infectious diseases and malnutrition do not contribute significantly to child mortality, mothers known to be HIV-infected may be advised to give their infants replacement feeds and avoid all breastfeeding. Commercial infant formula milk should be given as the replacement feed to the HIV-uninfected infants only when the following specific conditions are fulfilled:
	 	• Clean water and sanitation are assured at the household level and in the community, and
	• The mother or other caregiver can reliably provide sufficient infant formula milk to support normal growth and development of the infant; and
	• The mother or caregiver can prepare it cleanly and frequently enough so that it is safe and carries a low risk of diarrhoea and malnutrition; and
	• The mother or caregiver can, in the first 6 months, exclusively give infant formula milk; and
	• The family is supportive of this practice; and
	• The mother or caregiver can access healthcare that offers comprehensive child health services.
	Pneumocystis jirovecii (previously known as carinii) infection often occurs before HIV status has been confirmed, and can cause life threatening pneumonia in HIV-infected or exposed individuals. Co-trimoxazole is a fixed-dose antimicrobial combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim targeting a broad range of aerobic Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms, fungi, and protozoa including Pneumocystis. The drug is widely available in both syrup and solid preparations at a low cost, even in resource-limited settings. Regular prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) has been shown to reduce mortality of HIV-infected children by up to 40% even in the absence of ART (Chintu et al. 2004). Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis may also reduce the risk of malaria-related mortality in both HIV-infected and exposed children (Sandison et al. 2011), though its role in HIV unaffected children is questionable. Because of difficulty in diagnosing HIV infection in infants, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for all HIV-exposed children around 4 to 6 weeks after birth and continuing until HIV infection has been cleared and the infant is no longer at risk of acquiring HIV through breastfeeding (WHO 2014b).
	HIV-exposed and HIV-infected children should receive all childhood vaccines as early in life as possible, except Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) and yellow fever vaccines. In asymptomatic children, the decision to give late BCG should be based on the local risk of tuberculosis. Infants with symptomatic HIV infection should not receive yellow fever vaccines.
	Antiretroviral therapy (ART) can substantially improve survival of HIV-infected children. The availability of ARV drugs with other formulations such as ‘sprinkles’ make earlier initiation and adherence to treatment by children more convenient. The particular needs of adolescents infected with HIV such as access to adolescent-friendly sexual and reproductive health services are increasingly recognized as priorities.
	The Global Health Sector Strategy on HIV for the period 2016–2021 (WHO 2016b) suggests the health sector response to HIV as critical for achieving universal health coverage, which is a key target of the SDGs. The strategy proposes a set of global targets aligned with the multisectoral UNAIDS strategy. It also identifies five strategic directions: strengthening national HIV programmes; defining a package of essential interventions; adapting services for underserved populations for equitable coverage; implementing funding mechanisms to reduce costs to patients; and embracing innovation.





Prevention and management of suboptimal development and disability


	Experiencing repeated adversities between conception and early childhood disrupts normal brain development, social functioning, and learning. Developmental delay or disability can result from repeated exposure to infection or malnutrition, and from adversities related to insufficient stimulation, trauma, and maltreatment. Global data on direct measures of child development are still very sparse, although it is known that many children are at risk for poor development due to the conditions of poverty and chronic malnutrition.
	The Nurturing Care Framework (Black et al. 2017) outlines five key domains for intervention that must be addressed in order to ensure children reach their full developmental potential: good health, adequate nutrition, responsive caregiving, safety and security, and early educational opportunities. The efforts of parents, families, and communities, within an enabling environment, make this possible. Many of the evidence-based interventions supporting child health and nutrition discussed in prior sections have the potential to support healthy development through a reduction in risk factors for suboptimal development (Britto et al. 2017; Vaivada et al. 2017). Interventions in multiple domains of the Framework can also be packaged together for delivery, such as combined stimulation and nutrition interventions to support optimal development.
	It is imperative to provide extra support for children with motor, developmental, and learning disabilities, especially in LMICs, where these children are particularly vulnerable (WHO 2012a; 2010b). Primary care providers are well placed to support child development in LMICs, as they are often the only health service providers that have contact with young children and families. There is a notable lack of research examining the effectiveness of interventions for prevention of developmental delay in early childhood.





Strengthening integrated service delivery


	Despite the fact that effective interventions exist against all major conditions from which children die, the coverage of these interventions generally remains low. The key to achievement of substantial child mortality reduction is quality universal coverage of the interventions previously described.
	Before the mid-1990s, child health programmes in LMICs focused on immunization, control of diarrhoeal diseases, ARIs, and nutrition. Their implementation led to reduction in under-5 mortality in many countries, but this approach encountered limitations. The narrow focus on single interventions has failed to consider the child in a holistic manner, leading to many missed opportunities for care in contacts with a health practitioner. It was also difficult to resolve upstream health-system constraints such as management or human resource policies using this approach. Solving these problems involves ensuring access to an integrated package of interventions that are organized around the continuum of care. It also means that care should span across the home, community, health centre, and hospital. The advantages of delivering interventions as packages include the following:
	 	• Many interventions go naturally together because they are delivered by the same person at the same time.
	• Packaging is more cost-effective in terms of training, implementation, and supervision.
	• Packaging meets the needs of the individual caregiver and the child much better than isolated and uncoordinated single-intervention delivery, thus reinforcing the continuum of care.
	Potential obstacles to packaging of interventions may be related to policy, programmes, and the organizational structure of ministries and health services. For example, managers responsible for single issue-focused programmes may feel that packaging their interventions with other maternal and child health services lessens their delivery efficiency. Another concern about packaging interventions is that vulnerable groups may not get any of the interventions if insufficient attention is given to equitable delivery of the package.
	Delivery platforms relevant to child health ideally target the specific health needs of children at different stages of life with tailored packages of interventions for health promotion, prevention, screening, and treatment. Community delivery platforms aim to address the health needs of mothers and children where health facilities are sparse, often through the use of CHWs to facilitate outreach services, initiatives such as women’s groups, and campaigns such as Child Health Days. Financial platforms such as conditional cash transfers can incentivize health seeking behaviours and school attendance, and user fee removal can increase health service utilization. School-based platforms target the needs of school-age children with vaccinations, nutrition interventions, and health education. Digital and technology-based platforms leverage the broad reach of mobile phones and the Internet to deliver both health messaging and healthcare. A tailored and context-specific mixture of these delivery strategies is necessary to achieve optimal coverage of essential interventions for child health.





Integrated management of neonatal and childhood illness (IMNCI) and integrated community case management (iCCM)


	Integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI) was developed as an integrated delivery approach to managing common childhood diseases based on the principles of primary healthcare (PHC) as set out in the Alma Ata Declaration. Focusing on countries with a high under-5 mortality burden (>40/1,000 live births), the approach aims to enhance health workers’ skills in treatment of common childhood diseases, strengthen health systems for appropriate management of childhood illnesses, and improve family and community practices to promote child health.
	Over the years the approach has been expanded to include newborn care—IMNCI and integrated community case management (iCCM). Recognizing the key role CHWs can play when appropriately trained, equipped, and supervised, the equity-focused iCCM strategy involves training these workers to identify and treat children in remote areas for pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria using appropriate treatment methods such as ORS and zinc, oral antibiotics or artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) (WHO 2017b). A Cochrane review on the impact of IMCI concluded that the implementation of IMCI, especially with the neonatal care component, led to a decrease in infant and under-5 mortality rates (Gera et al. 2016).





Health system building blocks


	It is crucial to address the challenges that affect health systems in many low-income countries in order to effectively scale-up child health interventions. The programmes which address newborn and child health are implemented through ‘complex public and private organizations that rely on systems to provide medicines, finance health services, assure quality, and efficiency of care, manage the health workforce, and generate information needed for effective operational decisions’ (Countdown Working Group on Health Policy and Health Systems et al. 2008). Key input components to the health system include an adequate and skilled health workforce, evidence-based policies, and sufficient health funding—critical determinants of access, quality, and demand for effective interventions. Improving child health services globally relies heavily on decisions made using health information systems (HIS). However, in most resource-limited settings, HIS are prone to lack of coverage, incomplete record-keeping, poor data quality, limited analysis, and fragmented systems that can hamper delivery of quality health services. Service delivery, together with medical products and technologies, reflect the immediate outputs of the health system: the availability and distribution of care (WHO 2010c).
	Over the past two decades, increasing economic hardships and financial crises have disrupted healthcare delivery in many countries. Due to deteriorating infrastructure and a resource-limited public health sector, subject to structural adjustment and macroeconomic ceilings, challenges faced by healthcare sectors persist. As a result, human resources in the health sector have been destabilized and undermined. In many countries, households spend considerable amounts on healthcare and out-of-pocket expenditures for health services, sometimes two to three times greater than the total health expenditure by governments and donors. To establish an efficient, functional health system, it is important to address inequality in access to health services and provide financial risk protection. As part of the SDGs and universal health coverage (UHC) agendas, many developing countries have implemented health programmes to improve access to basic health services for all and provide financial risk protection to reduce out-of-pocket (OOP) health expenses.
	The higher the proportion of health-related user payments, the greater the relative financial burden on the poor, rendering many unable to afford necessary healthcare services. Household expenditure surveys show that more than 150 million individuals globally face severe financial crisis each year due to healthcare costs. The full assessment of such financial burden needs to evaluate a multidimensional framework to examine the broader impacts of illness or injury on the household economy, such as loss of work (Ruger 2012). Prepayment systems involve collection of funds in advance through tax-based insurance or social health insurance schemes. Both provide financial risk protection and promote equity through prepayment of healthcare costs and pooling of health risks. OOP expenditures should be gradually added into prepayment schemes, including community finance programmes.
	Health workers are ‘all people engaged in actions whose primary intent is to enhance health’. This includes health service providers such as doctors, midwives, nurses, pharmacists, and CHWs. It also includes health management and support workers who dedicate all or part of their time to improving health (WHO 2006b). The availability of a competent workforce is vital to successfully delivering healthcare services. Critical shortages, inadequate skill mix, and uneven geographical distribution of the health workforce are major barriers to achieving global goals for child health. The minimum threshold necessary to deliver essential maternal and child health services is estimated as 23 doctors, nurses, and midwives per 10,000 population. Countries that fall below this threshold struggle to provide adequate skilled care at birth to pregnant women, as well as emergency and specialized services for newborns and young children, influencing the burden of women and children mortality directly. Among countries categorized as low-income economies by the World Bank, only five met this minimum threshold in 2010.
	In almost all countries, a poor mix of the types of health workers and their range of individual skills, combined with a shortage of qualified health workers in remote and rural areas, impedes access by women and children to life-saving interventions and services. To address these challenges, countries are exploring and applying different solutions. Community-based health workers can provide a number of life-saving child health interventions, such as management of non-severe pneumonia and immunizations. As a result, governments in various countries are instituting new cadres of CHWs or upgrading the skills of existing community resource persons to deliver an essential package of health services that include child health interventions. Similarly, midwifery personnel are enabled to perform life-saving interventions such as resuscitation of the asphyxiated baby. The process of sharing tasks at various levels of service delivery, sometimes referred to as task-shifting, is being investigated and applied in a number of countries.





Supporting children in humanitarian emergencies and conflict settings


	The total number of people affected by humanitarian emergencies has been on the rise. In 2017 alone, there were an estimated 65 million forcibly displaced people, over half of whom were less than 18 years old (UNHCR 2018). A recent analysis commissioned by Save the Children was conducted by the Peace Research Institute in Oslo (PRIO) which mapped the numbers of children living in areas affected by armed conflict globally (Østby et al. 2018). The research reported that in 2017, 420 million children were living in areas defined as ‘conflict zones’ or ‘conflict-affected areas’—nearly one in every five children worldwide. Armed conflicts violate children’s rights, as established in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) (Hodgkin and Newell 2007).
	Environmental factors, including climate change, can encourage conflict and intensify the severity of natural calamities (IPCC 2014). Large-scale disasters and warfare can increase the probability of family separation dismantling any existing support systems, putting children at risk for abuse, violence, and neglect. Such emergencies can create economic hardship and create further vulnerabilities for children. In Lebanon, over one million Syrian refugees have been registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR 2017), and child labour and marriage have been reported as families face financial insecurity (Bartels et al. 2018). Moreover, children in situations of economic and physical instability are also at increased risk of sexual abuse, human trafficking, and recruitment by extremist groups or armed forces.
	The consequences of armed conflict on children can be both direct and indirect. ‍Direct effects include physical injury or disability, developmental delay, mental health sequelae, or death. Armed violence has the intended and unintended consequence of killing and maiming children. ‍Indirect effects are associated with the destruction of resources required by children for their optimal survival and growth, in addition to effects on the social determinants of health, such as living conditions, education, nutrition and health of caregivers (Guha-Sapir and D’Aoust 2011). Such conflicts can also displace children, and about 68.5 million people globally were forcibly displaced in 2017, with 25 million being refugees; over half of these refugees were children (UNHCR 2018).
	The UN Security Council identifies six grave violations against children in situations of armed conflict (United Nations 2013):
	 	• killing and maiming of children
	• recruitment and use of children as soldiers
	• sexual violence against children
	• abduction of children
	• attacks on schools and hospitals
	• denial of humanitarian access
	Given the prevalence of armed conflict globally and its deleterious effects on children, it is critically significant that child health experts respond both domestically and globally. Child health professionals should recognize children’s traumatic life experiences and respond to the consequences of such trauma on children’s health and well-being by providing holistic, multidisciplinary, culturally acceptable, and age-appropriate services that reflect children’s need for physical, mental, emotional, and sexual and reproductive healthcare (Marsac et al. 2016).
	Governments should develop systems to register all children at birth, so that no child remains stateless, and children separated from family have opportunities to reunite. A plan needs to be in place to regularly review plans for children in custody of the State. Doing so overcomes the barriers to accessing health services, education, and employment. There is a need to facilitate dialogue between states, the UN, NGOs, and non-state armed groups to protect children. It is important for the governing bodies to support international mechanisms to prosecute cases of children’s rights violations in conflict.
	Educational opportunities for children affected by armed conflict should be provided ensuring their swift reintegration into society. There is strong evidence supporting the role of education for boys and girls at all levels in reducing political violence (Østby and Urdal 2010).‍ Interventions for optimal feeding including breastfeeding become even more critical for survival in humanitarian emergencies. During such displacements children may face risks from diarrhoeal diseases, pneumonia, and undernutrition. Moreover, unhygienic water and sanitation, overcrowding, food insecurity, and overburdened health facilities can further exacerbate the worsening situation for children.
	Children should be protected from landmines, small arms, and light weapons through strict control on their ownership, sale, and safe storage. Environmental hazards, such as landmines, injure and kill children long after conflicts have ended. As a complement, initiatives for child protection may also take the form of direct implementation, such as the establishment of ‘Child Friendly Spaces (CFS)’ that allow children safe zones to play, parent trainings that emphasize alternatives to physical punishment and reunification for separated children. Domains for further research include the physical, developmental, and psychosocial health consequences of armed conflict exposure on children; the associations if any, between social determinants and these effects; the burden of child morbidity and mortality attributable to armed conflict; interventions; and child health assessments for humanitarian response.





Global initiatives to accelerate progress on child survival, good health, and optimal development


	Several global initiatives related to specific causes of child mortality have been launched to help accelerate progress in closing the gap in child health outcomes between high-income countries and LMICs. Countries that have rapidly increased coverage for multiple interventions across the continuum of care have accelerated child survival. Their success can mainly be attributed to improvements in service quality—bringing them closer to home and expanding access to essential care.
	The UN has launched the updated Every Woman Every Child’s Global Strategy for Women’s and Children’s Health for the period 2016–2030 (WHO 2017c). The aims of this ‘Global Strategy’, which are universal in scope, are to end all preventable mortality for mothers, newborns, and children, and promote this vision as part of a plan for accelerating progress in achieving the SDGs. The strategy has helped catalyse new attention and investment to some of the most frequent causes of women’s and children’s mortality. Other recent global initiatives and events are tackling different aspects of implementing the ‘Global Strategy’, including the Child Survival Call to Action, The Family Planning Summit, and the UN Commission on Life-Saving Commodities for Women and Children, Every Newborn Action Plan, and the Global Action Plan for Pneumonia and Diarrhea.
	To accelerate progress and achieve improved health outcomes for all children, it is important to ensure universal access to good-quality basic care, clean water, sanitation, and other social sector services such as education. This also includes creating the national legal, policy, and budget frameworks to promote the realization of children’s rights to these services.





School-age children


	Children between 5 and 10 years of age normally attend primary school, and thus can be targeted by school-based health programmes. School feeding programmes and targeted micronutrient supplementation are effective strategies to prevent malnutrition. Education and messaging regarding the lifelong benefits of healthy eating habits and an active lifestyle can begin in this age group, coupled with supporting a healthy food environment. The school setting also provides an opportunity for the promotion of good oral hygiene practices and oral health screening. Furthermore, vision screening and the provision of corrective lenses for those children that require them help them learn more effectively. The WHO Health Promoting Schools initiative provides a framework of preventive actions that aim to promote healthy living habits and better learning conditions, and provide a safe learning environment with access to health services for schoolchildren.





Overweight and obesity


	An estimated 38.3 million children under 5 worldwide were overweight or obese in 2017. Nearly half of these children live in Asia and about a quarter in Africa (WHO/UNICEF 2018). Past the age of 5, obesity rates climb even further: 340 million children and adolescents between 5 and 19 years experienced overweight or obesity in 2016. Overweight and obesity increases a child’s risk of developing type 2 diabetes, hypertension, asthma, and liver disorders. Moreover, they have a higher likelihood of suffering from depression and low self-esteem.
	To assess, prevent, and manage childhood obesity, the WHO recommends primary care providers take anthropometric measurements for all young children to determine weight-for-height and assess the presence of wasting or overweight (WHO 2017a). They should also counsel caregivers on optimal infant and young child feeding, promote intake of healthy food and adequate physical activity, and develop a management plan for children identified to be obese. As childhood stunting raises the risk of becoming overweight or obese, it is not recommended to provide formulated supplementary foods to children who are only moderately wasted or stunted, unless there is household or community food insecurity or other medical considerations.





Non-communicable diseases and injuries


	With the global epidemiological transition and change in lifestyles, NCDs are on the rise globally, especially in industrialized countries. Contrary to common perception, NCDs and their risk factors have a significant impact on the health of children and adolescents. Congenital disorders, diabetes, cancer, sickle cell disease, epilepsy, chronic respiratory diseases such as asthma, and rheumatic heart disease are some key NCDs that affect children and require a functioning health system providing quality care to effectively detect and manage. Childhood overweight and obesity, unhealthy diet, exposure to pollution, certain infectious diseases, and epigenetics can all increase the risk of developing an NCD in the short-and long-term.
	While many NCDs are chronic and require ongoing management, some preventive actions do exist. Preventing obesity is a key strategy to prevent the development of several NCDs, both during childhood and later in life. Improving indoor and outdoor air quality can help prevent asthma exacerbations. Prompt detection and treatment of rheumatic fever can help prevent progression to rheumatic heart disease.
	Supporting positive developmental progress, resilience, and self-efficacy is vital for children to achieve their full potential. As mental disorders can begin to surface in childhood, routine screening and counselling for conditions such as anxiety, depression, and conduct disorder should be provided.
	As rates of unintentional injuries rise as children become older, injury prevention is key to reducing injury-related mortality and disability. This includes requiring the use of helmets on bicycles and mopeds, and seatbelts in automobiles. Swimming lessons and education on water safety provided to children can reduce the risk of drowning. Burns can be prevented through the use of safer types of improved cookstoves, compared to open flames. Improving access to emergency services and trauma care in the event of injury is necessary to minimize injury-related mortality and morbidity.





Communicable diseases


	Ensuring complete and up-to-date vaccinations status in school-age children is the most effective prevention strategy for infectious diseases. For children 5–10 years, these include universal vaccination for human papilloma virus (HPV) (age 9+) and tetanus, targeted vaccination for typhoid, cholera, dengue where indicated, and catch-up and booster vaccines as needed. Routine deworming treatment in endemic regions is also recommended for reducing the risk of anaemia. Improving WASH conditions in the school setting as well as the household also remains crucial for preventing infection transmission. School-age children also still require many key interventions that are carried over from the under-5 period for specific high-burden conditions, including ARIs, diarrhoea, and malaria. Typhoid fever in particular becomes increasingly prevalent in older children and requires prompt screening and treatment.





Child health in the SDGs era


	In 2015, the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development was adopted by all United Nations Member States (UNGA 2015), representing a comprehensive plan for peace and prosperity, not only for people, but also for the planet. As part of this agenda, 17 SDGs (Box 10.3.2) were agreed upon, building on the legacy of the prior Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), whose purview ended in 2015. The MDGs contained specific targets for reductions in maternal and under-5 mortality, emphasizing massive inequities between low and high-income regions, and were successful in bringing the global health and development community together with a common goal. Countries that have rapidly increased coverage for multiple interventions across the continuum of care have accelerated child survival. The most pronounced falls in under-5 mortality occurred in four regions: Latin America and the Caribbean; East Asia and the Pacific; Central and Eastern Europe and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CEE/CIS); and the Middle East and North Africa. All have more than halved their regional rates of under-5 mortality since 1990. Their success was attributed mainly to improvements in service quality—bringing them closer to home and expanding access to essential care.
	While all of the SDGs are relevant to child health from a societal and environmental perspective, two specific goals contain ambitious and explicit targets for key indicators of child health. These include achieving global targets for stunting and wasting reduction by 2025, ending all forms of malnutrition by 2030 (Goal 2.2), and ending preventable newborn and under-5 deaths by 2030 (Goal 3.2), with targets for neonatal and under-5 mortality of 12 and 25 per 1,000 live births, respectively.
	 	Box 10.3.2 The Sustainable Development Goals
	 	• Goal 1. End poverty in all its forms everywhere
	• Goal 2. End hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture
	• Goal 3. Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages
	• Goal 4. Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all
	• Goal 5. Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls
	• Goal 6. Ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all
	• Goal 7. Ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable, and modern energy for all
	• Goal 8. Promote sustained, inclusive, and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment, and decent work for all
	• Goal 9. Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation
	• Goal 10. Reduce inequality within and among countries
	• Goal 11. Make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient, and sustainable
	• Goal 12. Ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns
	• Goal 13. Take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts*
	• Goal 14. Conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas, and marine resources for sustainable development
	• Goal 15. Protect, restore, and promote sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, sustainably manage forests, combat desertification, and halt and reverse land degradation and halt biodiversity loss
	• Goal 16. Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable, and inclusive institutions at all levels
	• Goal 17. Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development





Measuring progress in child health


	The Countdown to 2030 initiative aims to provide a framework through which to improve the monitoring and measurement of child, women, and adolescent health. The main focus is on measuring and reporting, at the national level, on the coverage of many of the key interventions described in this chapter, in addition to highlighting geographic and socioeconomic inequities in this coverage within countries.
	There are 81 countries tracked as part of the Countdown initiative, and despite progress in recent years towards universal coverage, there is still a large gap in coverage of essential interventions along the continuum of care (Boerma et al. 2018). In order to achieve the ambitious targets set out by the SDGs, a great deal of investment is still required. Countdown aims to provide accurate data on coverage, quality, and inequalities so as to guide these investments towards those countries, regions, and populations who have the greatest need. To this end, efforts to strengthen the collection of high-quality vital statistics data are required to improve accountability to commitments made to improve child health. Furthermore, developing a deeper understanding of the drivers of this coverage change, through quantitative analysis of coverage data coupled with assessment of national policy impacts, is also needed to develop evidence-based recommendations tailored to each Countdown country context. Ideally, this involves strengthening individual countries’ capacity for conducting these analyses.





Conclusion


	ARIs, diarrhoea, malaria, and injuries are the main causes of illness and death in children 1–59 months. Among newborn babies, most deaths are the result of preterm birth complications, intrapartum-related events such as birth asphyxia, and infections. Undernutrition is associated with 45% of all under-5 deaths. Despite the substantial progress made in reducing under-5 mortality, 5.4 million children under 5 died in 2017, 2.5 million of these being neonates.
	Poor health and survival are linked to social and economic disadvantages. Child deaths are unequally distributed in the world. Within countries, child morbidity and mortality tend to be higher in the rural areas and within the poorer and least educated families. Poorly nourished, LBW, sick, and disabled children all are at particular risk of adverse outcomes and have special needs for care. Global progress in child health is attributable to a broad range of factors that include high coverage of good-quality, effective interventions, development programming, and strategic integrated delivery of packaged health services, along with improvements in education, child protection, respect for human rights, and economic gains in developing countries.





Key points


	 	• Approximately two-thirds of under-5 deaths could be prevented by universal coverage of a small set of existing interventions that do not require expensive technology. Among these interventions, the promotion of breastfeeding, management and prevention of neonatal conditions, ARIs, diarrhoea, malaria, and HIV infection, in addition to improved feeding, have the highest impact in reducing child mortality.
	• Reducing stillbirths and neonatal mortality requires high-quality coverage of key interventions delivered during pregnancy, childbirth, and in the postnatal period.
	• Many more children today survive infancy yet remain in impoverished conditions. Infections and chronic malnutrition during infancy and childhood delay growth and development, and thus promoting interventions for survival alone is inadequate.
	• Supporting early child development during critical time periods facilitates optimal developmental trajectories in which children grow into adults that can realize their full potential.
	• Coverage of key interventions remains unacceptably low. Integrating interventions into packages of care organized along a continuum through pregnancy, birth, the neonatal period, and childhood, and delivered at all levels—from the home and community to first-level facilities and hospitals—would contribute to improved efficiency in intervention delivery and to the achievement of high coverage.
	• Strengthening health systems is a prerequisite for increasing the coverage and quality of health interventions.
	• The development of an operational plan to which programmes can be held accountable, along with a good financing and human resource strategy, will yield long-term benefits for the child and the health system at large and is an essential element to follow the development of a child survival strategy.
