10.4


Adolescent health


	George Patton, Peter Azzopardi, Natasha Kaoma, Farnaz Sabet, and Susan Sawyer





Introduction


	The current generation of 10-to 24-year-olds is the largest in human history. Their health and wellbeing are increasingly shaped by the global forces of urbanization, migration, global communications, economic development, and the sustainability of planetary ecosystems. Over the past two decades we have come to new understandings of adolescence as a critical developmental phase in life for achieving human potential (Patton et al. 2016). It is characterized by maturation of all physiological systems including reproductive, musculoskeletal, cardiometabolic, and neurocognitive. Health during adolescence shapes patterns of growth and the acquisition of social and emotional capabilities, sets trajectories for health across the life-course and, because this is the next generation to parent, lays a foundation for the healthy development of the next generation (Patton et al. 2016). Thus investments in adolescence have the potential to bring a ‘triple dividend’, an understanding that has brought a fresh prominence to adolescent health in global policy (Every Woman Every Child 2015). However, the challenge for governments in investing in adolescent health is a relative lack of capacity extending from the health workforce to healthcare systems, monitoring frameworks and evidence base for policy and programming, and processes relative to other fields of health (Patton et al. 2016). This chapter outlines current understandings of adolescent health, growth, and development, the available evidence for effective interventions and priorities for research, and technical investment.





Concepts of adolescence


	Adolescence is generally conceptualized as the phase of life that spans childhood and adulthood. It is a phase of major growth with neurocognitive maturation extending well into the third decade. Through history, adolescence has been considered to begin with puberty and end with transitions into marriage and parenthood (Worthman and Trang 2018). In today’s contexts, the endpoint is often less clear-cut, particularly in higher income and urban settings where the adoption of other adult roles such as the transition to employment, financial independence, as well as the formation of life partnerships commonly mark the end of adolescence. These events occur at different ages in different parts of the world influencing local cultural concepts of adolescence, which vary greatly.
	Sawyer et al. recently reviewed the range of different English terms have been used to describe the adolescent phase of life or parts of it (Fig. 10.4.1) (Sawyer et al. 2018). Within the UN system, adolescence has been generally defined as the second decade from 10 to 19 years and youth commonly refers to 15 to 24 years. The terms ‘adolescents and young adults’ and ‘young people’ are also used to refer to the 10–24-year-old age group (World Health 1989; Sawyer et al. 2012).
	The Convention on the Rights of the Child defines a child as below the age of 18 years unless, under the laws applicable to the child, majority is attained earlier (Assembly 1989). Eighteen is commonly viewed as the legal age of majority, the point at which an individual is considered an adult in many countries, although not universally. In law there is no single definition of adulthood but rather a collection of laws that at differing ages, for different activities, bestow the status of adulthood. These include laws that have major consequences for health and health risks including those related to the age of consent to sexual intercourse or medical treatment, the minimum age that young people can legally work, leave school, drive, buy alcohol, marry, and be held accountable for criminal actions. In addition to ‘young adults’, ‘emerging adulthood’ is a term that has been used to describe the phase of life from the late teens to the late twenties when an individual acquires some of characteristics of adulthood without having necessarily reached the milestones that historically define fully-fledged adulthood.
	This chapter focuses on this age range from 10 to 24 years, coinciding with the major years of physical, cognitive, and social development and the key social role transitions that mark adulthood. When we use the terms ‘adolescence and young adulthood’, or simply ‘adolescence’, we are referring to these years.
	Fig. 10.4.1 Different terms used to describe the adolescent and young adult years.
	Reprinted from Sawyer, S. M., et al. (2018), ‘The age of adolescence’, Lancet Child and Adolescent Health, 2(3):223–8, with permission from Elsevier.





Adolescent growth and development


Timing of adolescent growth and development


	Later childhood and adolescence are increasingly viewed as sensitive developmental phases where an individual’s interaction with the physical, nutritional, social, and cultural environment shapes patterns of physical, social, and emotional growth (Patton et al. 2016). These aspects of the environment affect the timing and form of puberty. The effects of this changing environment are evident in secular trends in the age of menarche in girls. Over the past 150 years there has been a fall in the age of menarche of around 4 to 5 years in Western Europe and North America, which is thought to arise from better childhood health from improved nutrition and reduced infectious disease (Worthman and Trang 2018). Occurring over a shorter period, similar trends have been observed in countries undergoing rapid economic development or in children whose families have moved from low-resource to high-resource settings (Houghton et al. 2014). In high resource settings the mean age for menarche is now 12–13 years, although the onset of puberty occurs much earlier with adrenarche (adrenal maturation) on average occurring around the age of 7–8 years and thelarche (breast budding) around 10 years (Patton and Viner 2007).
	The timing of puberty predicts later life health as early puberty increases risks for premature all-cause mortality, cardiovascular deaths, type II diabetes and some mental disorders (Day et al. 2015). During adolescence, early puberty is also associated with higher rates of common mental disorders in girls; a mismatch between the social and sexual roles that accompany physical maturity and an individual’s underlying cognitive–emotional capabilities is one possible explanation (Brooks-Gunn and Warren 1989).
	In pre-industrial societies, the adolescent transition from puberty to adult roles, as defined by the transition to parenthood, ranged from around 2 years in girls to 4 years in boys (Schlegel and Barry 1991). In today’s developed economies, longer periods of education and the availability of effective contraception means that adolescence commonly persists for well over a decade. The lengthening of adolescence means that it occupies a greater proportion of the life-course than ever before. It is also associated with a more diverse set of influences on adolescent health, growth, and development in many places. These include a longer duration of education and training, with the acquisition of professional capabilities and independence increasingly being hallmarks of adult status (Patton and Viner 2007; United Nations Children’s Fund 2012). So too relationships with an adolescent’s family of origin have shifted in many places with an extension of time living at home into the third and even fourth decade in many places. Opportunities for engagement with the peer group and cultural influences beyond the local neighbourhood have also changed with the growth of mass media, and more recently, digital and social media. For these reasons, influences on adolescent health differ markedly today from those in previous generations. Equally the opportunities for using new platforms for health interventions have also expanded.





Psychosocial development


	Early adolescence (10–14 years) is dominated by puberty and the effects of the rapid rise in pubertal hormones on body morphology, and sexual and brain development. It is accompanied by a remodelling of the brain’s reward system, a sensitivity to peer influences, low levels of future orientation and altered risk perceptions, sometimes leading to risk-taking behaviour. It is a time of identity formation and development of new interests including sexual and romantic relationships. School and family environments have major effects on growth and development and are therefore important settings for health intervention.
	Mid-adolescence (15–19 years) is characterized by continued pubertal maturation, particularly prominent for males, whose growth spurt starts later and continues for longer. Brain development continues with maturation of the prefrontal cortex and increased connectivity between brain networks enhancing executive and self-regulatory skills. It is a phase of greater autonomy and, in poor resource settings where there are limited opportunities for educational engagement, a common point of transition into marriage and parenthood for girls. In higher resource settings, this phase of development is accompanied by a greater future orientation and an ability to weigh up the short-and long-term implications of decisions. Education settings are influential for those who remain in school: for those who leave school, work settings have a growing influence on health, particularly in hazardous work environments in low-income settings.
	Later adolescence or young adulthood (20–24 years) is accompanied by maturation of the prefrontal cortex and greater planning and self-regulation. It marks the end of a period of high brain plasticity. It often corresponds to the adoption of adult roles and responsibilities, including entering the workforce or tertiary education, marriage, childbearing, and economic independence.





Adolescent health in the global context


Demographic and epidemiological transitions


	The demographic transition from high birth and early-life death rates to low fertility and longer life expectancy has reshaped the relative proportion of adolescents in high-income countries since the post-war years. The demographic transition is now proceeding rapidly in most other countries with different countries at very different points in that transition (World Bank 2007). This acceleration of the demographic transition has resulted in today’s adolescent generation being the largest in history relative to other age groups. With a population of 1.8 billion, 10–24 year olds comprise over a quarter of the global population. Nearly 90% live in low-and middle-income countries where they may comprise more than a third of the population (Fig. 10.4.2). In contrast, in a growing number of high-income countries the proportion of 10-to 24-year-olds is now under 15%. Projecting forward to the end of the century, around a half of the world’s adolescents will be growing up in sub-Saharan Africa.
	Fig. 10.4.2 Percentage of the population aged 10 to 24 years across countries in 2020.
	Better childhood health and nutrition, extended time in education, delays in family formation and access to new technologies theoretically offer a prospect of this being the healthiest generation of adolescents ever. Indeed, many more adolescents are now growing up in non-communicable disease (NCD)-predominant countries with lower levels of reproductive health problems, infectious disease injury, and violence. Yet uneven demographic change means that across Asia and Africa many more young people are growing up with high risks for multiple health problems in the adolescent years (Azzopardi et al. 2019).
	The demographic transition has been accompanied by epidemiological and nutritional transitions with profound implications for adolescent health and health risks. The nutritional switch towards greater consumption of foods that are high in added sugars, salt, and unhealthy fats, and low in important micronutrients is fuelling a global rise in obesity but with continuing high levels of micronutrient deficits. Further global trends in youth unemployment, less stable families, environmental degradation, armed conflict, and mass migration also pose new threats to adolescent health.
	The epidemiological transition, that commonly accompanies the demographic transition and economic development, has changed health profiles for all age groups. Many adolescents have benefited from better control of infectious diseases including diarrhoeal disease, lower respiratory tract infections, tuberculosis, and malaria. Adolescent girls and young women in many settings have benefited from gains in maternal health, particularly in settings where early pregnancy has fallen markedly. However, the epidemiological transition has brought an increase in other health problems for adolescents, including road traffic injuries and suicide. In some countries and contexts, such as Latin America and Eastern Europe, these problems have extended to homicide, mostly in young males (Patton et al. 2009). A link to broader economic conditions was evident in the rise of mortality and alcohol-related disease burden in Eastern European countries following the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991 and is likely to be a factor underlying more recent civil unrest and armed conflict across the Middle East, North Africa, and sub-Saharan Africa (Yair and Miodownik 2014).
	Other adolescent health problems have become more prominent with the epidemiological transition, including more persistent mental and physical health problems. For these reasons, self-harm and suicide have assumed greater significance in adolescent health in recent decades, particularly in high resource settings (Collishaw 2015). Mental disorders have a particular significance in adolescent health as they commonly have their onset in late childhood and adolescence. Because many persist into adulthood, adolescent mental disorders make a greater contribution to adult disease than ever before (Patton et al. 2014).
	HIV is a further reason why adolescents and young adults, particularly in southern and eastern sub-Saharan Africa, have to date seen fewer benefits from the epidemiological transition. To a large extent, the burden of HIV has fallen on the young; new infections are concentrated in adolescent girls and young adults; the effectiveness of new antiretroviral medication has also brought the survival into adolescence and adulthood of a generation affected by maternal–child transmission. In this context of continuing high prevalence, adolescents and young adults have not had the same mortality declines as other age groups (Murray et al. 2014).
	With ageing populations and a convergence to a disease burden dominated by NCDs in later life, adolescent-prevalent NCDs and adolescent-onset NCD risks assume greater significance (Jamison et al. 2013). In part, the relatively high prevalence of adolescent NCDs reflect greater survival into adolescence of diseases that were previously fatal in early childhood (e.g. cystic fibrosis and childhood cancers): in part it reflects a changing epidemiology of mental and physical disorders with higher incidence rates in the adolescent years in developed settings, e.g. allergy and autoimmune conditions (Mayer-Davis et al. 2017). NCD risks that commonly emerge during adolescence include tobacco use, physical inactivity, obesity, alcohol, and illicit substance use and poor diets. Without specific policy interventions, the combination of increasing wealth and unrestrained marketing will see adolescent health risks continue to rise in prevalence.





Adolescent health by region


	We have adopted the conceptual model from the 2016 Lancet Commission on Adolescent Health and Wellbeing to describe global and national patterns of adolescent health (Fig. 10.4.3). The model considers:
	 	1. Current causes of disease burden and death across the adolescent years;
	2. Health risks that emerge during adolescence with consequences for health during these years, for later adult health and/or a healthy start to life for the next generation; and
	3. Important and structural determinants of health that affect health growth and development across the adolescent and young adult years (Sawyer et al. 2012). These include education and employment; marriage and parenthood; marketing and digital media; and the quality of universal health coverage.
	The model also depicts the corresponding responses to adolescent health problems and their determinants. The most effective actions for adolescent health and wellbeing are intersectoral, occur at multiple levels, and with multiple components. They may include structural, media, community, online, and school-based elements as well as the provision of preventive and treatment health services. Intersectoral coordination has, for example, been prominent in countries that have made progress in reducing road traffic injury. In addition to the specific interventions outlined earlier, essential underpinning elements have included strong information systems, clear governance, civil society advocacy and a capacity to implement effectively within different sectors (Jamison et al. 2013).
	Fig. 10.4.3 A conceptual framework for adolescent health.
	Reprinted from Patton, G, et al. (2016), ‘Our Future: A Lancet Commission on Adolescent Health and Wellbeing’, Lancet, 387, 2423–78, with permission from Elsevier.





Disease burden across adolescence


	Disease burden and mortality rates generally increase across the adolescent years into young adulthood, with those increases particularly marked for sexual and reproductive health problems and common mental disorders in females, and for injuries, violence, and substance use disorders in males.
	This is in turn reflected in increases in mortality across the adolescent years with particularly marked increases in deaths due to injury, violence, suicide in males and maternal causes for females in later adolescence and young adulthood (Patton et al. 2016). In comparison to younger children, adolescents have had lesser reductions in mortality in recent decades. In a study of 50 countries with longitudinal data, the mortality of children had declined by over 80% in the last 50 years (Grazzi 2004). In contrast, mortality among adolescents had improved only marginally. Indeed, there has been a reversal of historical mortality patterns in which early childhood mortality exceeds adolescent deaths. Over that time causes of death in adolescents have changed with a fall in infectious disease deaths in most high-and middle-income countries and a rise in deaths due to injuries, that now account for around 40% of all adolescent deaths globally.
	Azzopardi et al. recently populated 12 headline indicators presented in the 2016 Lancet Commission on Adolescent Health and Wellbeing to examine trends in adolescent health over the past quarter century together with differences between countries and regions (Azzopardi et al. 2019). In that analysis, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) estimates were used to assess variations in disease burden by country with disease burden grouped into three categories: group 1 conditions (infectious diseases, maternal health problems, undernutrition, and/or HIV) common in low-resource setting; injury and violence; and the NCDs of adolescence (chronic physical illness, mental disorders, and substance use disorders). Countries were classified as multiburden if they had high disease burden from all categories of disease: injury excess with high rates of injury and NCDs; and NCD predominant where the major disease burden around from chronic mental and physical health problems (Fig. 10.4.4).
	Fig. 10.4.4 Changing disease burden from 1990 to 2016 in 10-to 24-year-olds in countries classified as multiburden, injury excess, and NCD predominant.
	Reprinted from Azzopardi, Peter S, et al. (2019), ‘Progress in adolescent health and wellbeing: tracking 12 headline indicators for 195 countries and territories, 1990–2016’, The Lancet, under a CC BY 4.0 License.
	Figure 10.4.4 illustrates the extent of change in adolescent disease burden over the last 25 years. Particularly notable has been a reduction in adolescent injuries and violence in many places, with a majority of injury-excess countries in 1990 having become NCD predominant. There has been relatively less success in ensuring the transition of countries with a multiburden disease profile. Many of these countries are the countries that have seen the greatest increase in their adolescent population. For this reason the number of adolescents growing up in multiburden countries in 2016 was 35% greater than in 1990, suggesting that the challenges for health service systems in these places have become substantially greater.





Adolescent health risks


	Although adolescent health risks contribute to disease burden during the adolescent and young adult years, their greatest contribution is often towards disease burden later in life or in relation to adverse consequences for the health growth and development of the next generation. Tobacco use is illustrative. It overwhelmingly has its onset in adolescence but causes little or no disease burden during these years. However, it is a major risk factor for NCDs in older adults and maternal smoking during pregnancy is a well-established risk factor for poor foetal growth and later life illness in offspring (Patton et al. 2018).
	Overall tobacco use has declined in adolescents globally since 1990 in part due to the implementation of the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. However, progress has been mixed. Rates of daily smoking remain above 15% in 10–24-year-olds across many European countries with one in four smoking daily in the Russian Federation. Across countries, tobacco use is almost always more common in adolescent males than in females. A number of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East have seen rises and in some low-resource countries (e.g. Indonesia and Papua New Guinea), rates of tobacco use are unacceptably high. Notably, non-signatories to the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control have generally seen lesser falls in adolescent and young adult tobacco use.
	Alcohol use disorders typically begin during the young adult years, with a younger age of drinking onset being particularly hazardous (Bonomo et al. 2006; Viner and Taylor 2007). Alcohol use carries risks for injury, violence, suicide, and unwanted pregnancy during adolescence, is linked to a range of NCDs in adulthood (cancers, cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and pancreatitis) and greater use in pregnancy has prominent intergenerational harms (Riley and McGee 2005). Both alcohol use and binge drinking are generally more prevalent in males. Although still more common in resource rich countries, binge drinking is becoming prevalent in other places with the actual number of adolescent binge drinkers having increased slightly in recent decades (Azzopardi et al. 2019).
	Overweight and obesity increase markedly across adolescence and young adulthood with very high persistence, particularly for obesity (Patton et al. 2011). The risks in later life include premature mortality, chronic disability, type 2 diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, and cerebrovascular disease. Preconception maternal (adolescent) obesity increases risks for miscarriage, gestational diabetes, operative delivery, pre-eclampsia, infant perinatal mortality, and macrosomia (Yu et al. 2006). Adolescent overweight and obesity have increased markedly in prevalence across almost all countries since 1990, with dramatic annual increases of around 10% in China and Vietnam. The prevalence of overweight and obesity is around one in five young people in NCD Predominant and Injury Excess countries and is continuing to increase in all places. Since 1990, the increase in overweight and obesity in NCD-predominant and injury-excess countries has been 120% (Azzopardi et al. 2019).
	Sexual and reproductive health risks also typically emerge during adolescence, with risks shifting in an environment of greater access to digital technology and social media (e.g. sexting, higher risk sex with multiple partners). Globally there have been strong trends towards reduced adolescent fertility, but these trends are less prominent in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America. Rates of women giving birth before 18 years remain high across much of sub-Saharan Africa, and for a number of countries in South Asia. Overall around one in five women in multiburden countries report giving birth by the age of 18 years.
	There is continued debate around the extent to which adolescent mothers are at greater risk of adverse maternal and infant outcomes. Some recent reports using verbal autopsy methods have failed to find differences in mortality in young mothers (Blanc et al. 2013; Nove et al. 2014). However, a recent World Health Organization (WHO) multicountry survey of pregnancy complications found much greater pregnancy-related morbidity in adolescent mothers (Ganchimeg et al. 2014) and country level studies continue to report higher maternal mortality in young mothers, particularly from causes such as unsafe abortion that may be sensitive to reporting bias in household surveys. An estimated 22 million unsafe abortions occur annually, of which about 15% are among adolescent girls. Young women have a higher risk of abortion-related deaths than in those over 25, are more likely to terminate pregnancy after the first trimester, and are more likely to use unregulated providers (Woog et al. 2015). Even after controlling for various sociodemographic factors, knowledge of the legal status of abortion and partner support, adolescents had 77% lower odds of obtaining a safe abortion compared with women aged 30 and older.
	Beyond adolescent birth rates, limited information is available on adolescent sexual and reproductive health in many countries. Across sub-Saharan African and Latin American countries with available data, between 10% and 20% of 15–24-year-olds report having first sexual intercourse before the age of 15 years. Condom use in the context of having had two or more partners in the past year shows great variability between countries, but remains under 50% for adolescents in multiburden countries where rates of adolescent pregnancy, HIV, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are high and access to contraception and facilities for menstrual management are low.
	Data around adolescent mental disorder and mental health risks is perhaps some of the weakest in global health. One recent estimate of coverage of minimally sufficient data for estimating the prevalence of six major mental disorders of children and adolescents reported an overall global coverage of 6.5%; 124 countries had no usable data at all (Erskine et al. 2017). Yet mental health problems and mental health risks appear common in almost all places. Self-harm, for example, is a risk factor for premature death from suicide and accidental injury; in later life adolescents who self-harm also have higher mortality from cancer and cardiovascular disease (Bergen et al. 2012). At least 1 in 20 adolescents in the mid-teens in high-income countries report some self-harm, typically self-laceration, or self-poisoning, in the previous 12 months (Hawton and James 2005). Other risk factors for mental disorders including bullying, sexual, and physical abuse and intimate partner violence are rarely monitored in adolescence.





Responding to adolescent health needs


Health services


	Health services for adolescents play a number of roles ranging from acute healthcare such as the management of trauma; preventive healthcare such as the provision of preconception and antenatal care to young women; and the management of chronic health problems or health risks including HIV, mental and substance use disorders, and chronic physical illnesses.
	Adolescents and young adults commonly fail to access healthcare at the same level as other age groups. Unmet versus met need for contraception are potentially useful indicators of the extent to which adolescents are able to access a sensitive health service. Just under two-thirds of young women aged 15–24 years have their demand for modern contraception satisfied with modern methods, with rates substantially higher in NCD-predominant countries than in multiburden countries where around half of young women have their needs met. Given the rate of demographic change in multiburden countries, the actual numbers of young women with unmet need have substantially increased, suggesting that health services have not kept pace with rapid population growth, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. To a large extent, data on met need for contraception comes from girls who are married. Far fewer data are available on sexually active unmarried adolescents, particularly in the many countries where prescribing contraception to unmarried girls under the age of 18 years is illegal.
	Health service interventions may differ in their effectiveness in adolescents in comparison to older adults for a range of reasons (Cipriani et al. 2016). Rates of contraceptive failure are, for example, higher in adolescents than in older women, with younger women more likely to abandon contraception despite ongoing need (Blanc et al. 2009). Reasons include poor understanding of pregnancy risks, concerns about the effect of contraceptives on health or fertility and opposition from partners. Lack of knowledge of services, cost, shyness, stigma around early sexual activity and judgemental providers are further barriers. One study in the United States found contraceptive failure was almost twice as high in under 21 year olds using oral contraceptive pills, transdermal patches, or the vaginal ring. In contrast, the failure rate of long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) is extremely low in all age groups (Winner et al. 2012). Yet despite increased use of LARCs in the United States since 2007, 15–24-year-olds remain less likely to use them than 25–39-year-old women (Finer et al. 2012).
	Notwithstanding their increased prevalence across adolescence, most adolescents and young adults with mental health problems do not receive treatment from health professionals. One European study of mental healthcare in adults showed that about 6% of the sample was in need of mental healthcare but nearly half reported no formal healthcare use. Those aged 18–24 reported the least use of services (Alonso et al. 2007). Actions to reduce barriers include promoting mental health literacy and combatting stigma, particularly in LMIC where the scaling up of mental health services has not yet been a priority (Patel et al. 2007).





Barriers to healthcare


	Two sets of barriers diminish access to quality healthcare for adolescents. One set are external to health services and include legal frameworks governing health actions, out of pocket costs, and cultural and community attitudes. Though not unique to adolescents, these barriers assume greater importance in the young.
	Legal and financial barriers to health service access are greater for adolescents than other age groups and are increasingly out of step with the health risks that adolescents face. One example is lack of access to contraception in many countries for unmarried girls under the age of 18 who are sexually active. Even when national legislation allows a particular health response, provider attitudes and beliefs about the appropriateness of an action in the context of age, marital status, or partner/parental consent may affect their response to an adolescent (Calhoun et al. 2013). Financial barriers arise from adolescents’ limited independent eligibility for tax and insurance-based funding schemes. Where health insurance exists, it is often through parents (or partners), presenting risks to confidentiality when accessing healthcare for sensitive problems, e.g. mental health, contraception, or substance use (Waddington and Sambo 2015). Socially marginalized adolescents often fall outside of financing systems for healthcare and are particularly vulnerable to catastrophic medical events.
	Further barriers to access arise more from the developmental context of adolescence, including adolescents being less experienced users of healthcare. Adolescence brings an increasing desire for privacy and confidentiality, with embarrassment, shame, and fear of being judged presenting barriers to healthcare. In the United States, a leading concern of adolescents who had foregone healthcare was not wanting their parents to find out (Schoen et al. 1998). Inexperience in turn leads to many adolescents not appreciating that problems such as substance use, bullying or overweight can be discussed with health professionals (Sanci 2011).
	Adolescents value respect, good coordination of care, appropriate provision of information, high-quality communication, involvement in decisions about care, and healthcare providers listening to their needs (Luxford et al. 2010). As such, the skills of clinicians differ from those needed for the healthcare of younger children which is typically mediated through parents. One important task for health professionals is to set expectations with adolescents and parents about an adolescent taking greater responsibility for healthcare. With increasing age, providers need to explicitly engage the young person themselves, which ideally includes consulting with them alone which is difficult in many cultural settings.
	Improving access to quality healthcare requires actions beyond the health service sector. For making sexual and reproductive health services more adolescent-responsive, training of health workers alone does little to improve access or contraception use. However, high-quality training, combined with the provision of adolescent-responsive facilities, strategies to change community norms, and greater availability of LARCs can bring major shifts in access and quality (Chandra-Mouli et al. 2015). Further elements within a multifaceted approach might include promotion of adolescent health literacy, engagement of community leaders, having an appropriate package of services, monitoring provider competencies, promoting equity and non-discrimination, collecting data for quality improvement and engaging adolescents around practice policies (Nair et al. 2015).
	Ultimately access to healthcare depends on the availability of platforms which are responsive to the life context of adolescents. School-based health services will have greater relevance as secondary education participation grows in many countries. Service models range from fully equipped and permanently staffed school centres with medical, nursing, and counselling staff to clinics sited near schools but with strong links. The predominant focus of many school-based and school linked health services has been on provision of sexual and reproductive healthcare but there is clearly an opportunity for these services to extend to mental healthcare, treatment, and prevention of infectious diseases, management of anaemia, and other chronic physical health problems. Web-based technologies also have the potential to improve access to health services (Kauer et al. 2014).





Education settings as platform for health action


	Education is a powerful determinant of health and human capital and socioeconomic progress, one in which the adolescent years are central (Viner et al. 2012). Those who are more educated live longer lives with less ill-health (Cutler and Lleras-Muney 2012). In high-income countries (HICs), the benefits are generally greater for women in terms of mortality, self-reported health, mental health, and obesity (Miyamoto and Chevalier 2010). Among adolescents in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), higher education is associated with reduced teenage births and older age at marriage. The health and wellbeing benefits of expansion of secondary education accrue through multiple mechanisms, including healthier behaviours, greater cognitive capacity, and longer productive adult lives for the current generation, better health, and lower mortality among their children and overall greater productivity in the future workforce. Education brings profound intergenerational benefits; improved education for women may account for up to half of the global improvement in child mortality since 1970 (Patton et al. 2018).
	With primary education now widespread in LMICs, expansion of participation in secondary education offers an achievable strategy for improving health across the life-course and into the next generation (Miyamoto and Chevalier 2010). In countries that already have high secondary education participation, facilitating schools to more explicitly promote health has the potential for leverage above and beyond the health benefits of educational participation alone.
	However, many forces operate to divert adolescents from secondary education. Prominent among these are the costs of education and the opportunity costs to families of the loss of adolescent labour, especially in rural areas. For these reasons, poor adolescents in LMICs are less likely to attend secondary school. Early marriage accounts for higher dropout rates in girls in LMICs. Most interventions to increase access to and retention in education in these setting have been in younger adolescents, largely in primary schools. Scholarships, school fee reduction or removal, cash transfers conditional on remaining in school, providing school uniforms, decreases in grade repetition, school proximity, and mother tongue education are cost-effective strategies in different contexts for promoting school retention (Glewwe and Kremer 2006; UNICEF 2015). Addressing gender disparities in access, social norms around girls’ participation in education, and targeting resources to the poorest regions as well as to disadvantaged students are important elements of increasing adolescent educational engagement in the poorest groups. There is also value in greater non-formal or flexible learning strategies for adolescents without access to mainstream education (e.g. child labourers and married adolescents who have left school) (Yasunaga 2014). Health interventions complement these strategies to promote educational engagement: these might include comprehensive sexuality education, providing access to modern contraception, treatment of micronutrient deficiencies and anaemia and management of mental disorders (Rosenberg et al. 2015).
	The traditional way in which schools address health and health risks has been through health education delivered in classrooms. This approach can bring small to moderate benefits in knowledge and attitudes but implementation is often patchy and the effects are generally not sustained (Foxcroft and Tsertsvadze 2011). In contrast, the ways that schools operate more widely have great effects on health, behaviour, and wellbeing (Patton et al. 2003). For this reason actions that address the school ethos and environment have become much more a focus of recent evaluations and policy attention (Patton et al. 2006; Shinde et al. 2018). A school’s environment extends to the physical and social environment, management, and organization, teaching, discipline, pastoral care, school health services, whole-school health promotion, and extracurricular activities. Positive effects from these interventions extend to student substance use, violence, and victimization, and mental health, particularly in groups facing discrimination and disadvantage (Shackleton et al. 2016).
	The most effective actions for health in school settings will commonly be multicomponent with curriculum elements, a focus on a school’s social and physical environment (e.g. around water, sanitation, and menstrual management facilities), together with engagement of families and/or the community (Harden et al. 2009). These approaches consistently show positive outcomes for adolescent sexual health, violence, and tobacco smoking and may be beneficial for other health risks (Harden et al. 2009; Blank et al. 2010).





Peers, media, and marketing


	The emergence of strong peer relationships is a central feature of early adolescent development (Viner et al. 2012). Such relationships may have either positive or negative effects on health. Peer connection, peer modelling, and awareness of peer norms can be protective against violence, mental health problems, substance use, and sexual health risks (Salazar et al. 2009). Equally, peers may also increase risks, with peer participation in risk behaviours likely to increase smoking initiation and persistence, alcohol initiation and use, self-harm, sexual risks, and violence (Fisher et al. 2007; Kretman et al. 2009). Other peer characteristics, such as sexual partner communication and negotiation skills, influence risks of unwanted pregnancy, STIs, and HIV (Taffa et al. 2002; Salazar et al. 2009).
	Modern adolescent peer relationships differ markedly from a pre-industrial social context in both the number and diversity of peers. Prolongation of education and later marriage and parenthood have effectively expanded the role of peers within the lives of adolescents. Peer education, or the promotion of healthy behaviours for young people by young people, is one popular strategy adopted by the health sector. Such interventions have certainly shown positive outcomes for the young people conducting the programming (i.e. the peer educators themselves) (Maticka-Tyndale and Barnett 2010). Peer promoters themselves have greater self-confidence, improved communications, leadership and interpersonal skills, higher aspirations, and lower rates of health risk behaviours. However, there has been little testing of their effectiveness in changing health outcomes for the broader population of young people they are meant to reach, leading to suggestions that peer education is ineffective (Chandra-Mouli et al. 2015). This reflects a tension in resource-constrained settings between a wish to scale up promising approaches and the value of undertaking smaller scale interventions with rigorous methodologies (Maticka-Tyndale and Barnett 2010).
	Mass media and more recently social media are further expanding the role of peers and youth cultures in the lives of adolescents in all places (Larson 2002). Online spaces have changed adolescent developmental tasks such as relationship and identity building which were previously mainly negotiated in face-to-face engagement with peers. For many adolescents, identity formation incorporates local influences with new elements derived from global cultures. There is continued debate over whether exposure to digital media, including a greatly expanded social network, may adversely affect adolescent social, emotional, and cognitive development (Bell et al. 2015). To date, the development of the new media has been so rapid that research efforts to understand their effects have failed to keep pace.
	Few studies of the health effects of marketing to adolescents have extended either to LMICs or to new media. Much marketing through digital media extends beyond national borders and is more tailored to individuals. Given that marketing is likely to become even more powerful and increasingly cross-national borders, policy responses at both national and global levels will be needed. To date most research has been around mass media, where the effects on risks ranging from tobacco and alcohol use, to choice of diet and body image norms are clear. There are also good examples of interventions using mass media to promote adolescent health. The South African multimedia ‘edutainment’ programme Soul City, for example, helped change social norms around HIV/AIDS and domestic violence, contributed to increased individual knowledge about condom use and domestic violence and to the empowerment of local communities (Moyer-Gusé 2008).
	While trends in using digital media are global, the means of accessing information varies widely (e.g. mobile phones, personal or public computers). In sub-Saharan Africa growth in access to mobile phones has meant that digital media have become available even in remote places (Lester and Karanja 2008). Young people are generally the earliest adopters of information and communication technologies (ICT) such as mobile phones, instant messaging, the internet, and social media, a phenomenon seen in LMICs as well as in HICs. These new media have the potential to provide a powerful voice for adolescents and young adults to actively engage with each other and their communities. Even in disadvantaged groups and remote locations mobile phones may offer a platform for communication and engagement around health (Alami et al. 2019). These tools provide a platform for health education in their own right as well as the capacity to augment healthcare delivery and other preventive actions including those within schools. Social media offer the potential to reach diverse groups including those who are geographically isolated or facing discrimination and disadvantage.





Community interventions


	The lives of young people are affected by the behaviour, norms, and values of adults and other adolescents in their communities. Community interventions commonly involve local government, families, youth-focused and religious organizations, and schools. Positive youth development (PYD) broadly refers to experiences that provide optimal preparation for the attainment of adult potential and wellbeing. These programmes are often community based and seek to promote life skills and positive attitudes including self-confidence and empowerment, social and emotional skills, and good problem solving. They aim to build the agency of young people so that they can positively influence the environments in which they live, learn, and play. The strategies employed range from sport and outdoor education to theatre, music, and art, survival skills, leadership training, and mentorship. Certain interventions, such as the promotion of sport in girls, have the potential to bring benefits in physical health and fitness, as well as empowering girls to deal with harmful gender norms (Saavedra 2009). PYD programmes aim to strengthen assets and skills, increasing youth agency and contribution, and foster an enabling environment. The most effective have generally built on available community structures, used good information on adolescent health and wellbeing, adopted a multicomponent strategy and monitored progress. One example has been the Communities that Care (CTC) framework that has been trialled in a number of United States sites with clear benefits and evidence for cost-effectiveness (Catalano et al. 2012).
	One strength of PYD as a framework for intervention in LMICs is that it can be applied in different countries and contexts. One recent systematic review suggested that across LMIC, these programmes achieved gains across a range of youth outcomes, including education, sexual risk behaviour, early marriage, violence, and job skills and employment (Catalano et al. 2019). Several of the approaches also demonstrate promise that PYD increases gender equality.
	Conditional cash transfer programmes (CCT) are another example of a community-based intervention that commonly targets adolescents. Examples include payment of school fees and supplemental cash to poor parents on the condition that they send their child to school. Trials in Malawi and Kenya found reduced self-reported sexual activity, pregnancy, and marriage in one or both countries, and reduced school dropout among girls and young women who received the CCTs (Baird et al. 2010).





Structural interventions


	Legislation, taxation, and implementation of policies bringing investment in families, communities, schools, and health services are essential elements of adolescent health action in all places. Laws commonly govern both access to resources for health and protection from hazards. Some specifically address health (e.g. access to healthcare including effective contraception); others address health risks (e.g. consumption of alcohol, access to tobacco); and others address social determinants of health (e.g. age of marriage, protection from hazardous work). Inadequate and inconsistent legal frameworks undermine the health, rights, and potential of adolescents and young adults. Particularly significant are laws that penalize groups facing discrimination and disadvantage where adolescents are more vulnerable that older age groups. One example are laws that diminish the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) adolescents and young adults with particularly punitive laws in Nigeria, Somalia, and Sudan.
	It was not until the twentieth century that more consistent international legal frameworks emerged for adolescents. The 1989 United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) recognized children as bearers of human rights rather than parental property, with liberties and responsibilities appropriate to their age (United Nations General Assembly 1989). The overwhelming majority (195) of countries have signed and ratified the UNCRC, with the United States the only exception. The UNCRC embodies adolescent development suggesting that where freedoms and liberties are restricted, this should be consistent with human rights principles and evolving capacities (Ruck et al. 2016). As adolescents acquire greater competency and maturity, there is a lesser need for adult guidance and an increased capacity for autonomy.
	Despite these important developments in international legal frameworks, there remains great diversity in the laws that affect adolescents. Laws often fail both in their framing and implementation, reflecting neither the principles of the UNCRC or an understanding of adolescents’ actual capacities. Rather, they mirror historical economic, social, cultural, and sometimes religious priorities (Lansdown 2015). In areas where legislation has a proven role in protecting health (e.g. minimum age to smoke tobacco, working age), laws commonly do not exist. In others, such as legal frameworks around sexual and reproductive health, there is little consistency between countries in the age of marriage, access to contraception, availability of safe abortion, and legality of same-sex relationships.
	Child marriage jeopardizes the health, growth, and development of girls in many countries. Around 15 million girls around the world marry each year before 18 years and in lower-income countries, one-third of girls are married before 18, and one in nine before 15 years (UNICEF 2013). Too early marriage results in diminished opportunities for education, greater sexual exploitation, and violence that can sometimes extend to enslavement. Child brides are also exposed to health risks from early pregnancy, have greater maternal and infant mortality, and heightened vulnerability to HIV/AIDS and other STIs (Klugman et al. 2014).
	The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) requires states to ensure that men and women have equal rights to enter into marriage and to freely choose a spouse with their free and full consent. Yet 34 countries permit girls to marry below 18 years. Some still permit marriage below 15 years, and a few specify no minimum age (Forum on Marriage and the Rights of Women and Girls 2015).
	More rational legal frameworks governing adolescents would take greater account of evolving adolescent cognitive and emotional capacities. With access to knowledge, adolescents from the age of 14 years demonstrate similar or even greater cognitive capacity than adults to make good judgements in calm and emotionally neutral contexts (Steinberg 2007). Yet in emotionally charged situations of stress or excitement, particularly with peers, emotions are more likely to drive decision-making (Steinberg 2007; Van Duijvenvoorde and Crone 2013). Legal frameworks would ideally take both factors into account in framing legislation around age of consent. Restricting an adolescent’s right to smoke would therefore be justified from their greater vulnerability to poor decision-making in emotionally charged contexts with peers, as well as from a still evolving capacity to understand the future health consequences. Such approaches would also support and promote adolescent autonomy. Thus voting from 16 years both empowers adolescents and promotes civic engagement. Permitting access to effective contraception including LARCs for sexually active adolescents is one example of how the law can take development into account in protecting an adolescent’s health.
	Investments in adolescent health should ideally extend from those directed towards conspicuous health problems to health risks that emerge during these years and the broader social determinants of health (Fig. 10.4.3). This ideal is rarely achieved as a result of major barriers to health action, whether through health services, community platforms, or structural initiatives. Adolescents and young adults are the age group with the poorest level of universal health coverage (Tylee et al. 2007). Social, structural, and environmental determinants of adolescent health lie largely outside the health service sector (Viner et al. 2012). There are shifts in these determinants as young people mature through adolescence, such that strategies suited to younger adolescents may be inappropriate or ineffective with young adults. So too strategies that are effective and appropriate for girls may be less effective for boys. The settings for health actions mirror those of determinants and extend from health services, schools, and education settings, to families and communities, places of employment, road transport, media, legal, and policy environments.





Youth engagement and empowerment


	The United Nations defined youth participation as ‘the active and meaningful involvement of young people in all aspects of their own, and their communities’ development, including their empowerment to contribute to decisions about their personal, family, social, economic and political development’ (United Nations (DESA) 2007). It embodies the ideas that adolescents and young adults make essential contributions to the design and implementation of programmes and policies that affect them and that meaningful engagement will lead to more equitable communities (Suleiman et al. 2006). In essence, meaningful engagement is not only a fundamental right but essential to capture the unique contributions of youth (Ruck et al. 2016). Developmental perspectives further support meaningful engagement as essential for positive social and emotional development during adolescence. Adolescents are emotionally ‘primed’ to engage so providing the structures, processes, and support for meaningful engagement itself shapes positive trajectories of development (Dahl 2004). Even though the rationale for youth engagement around health is strong, there has been little systematic research into models of youth engagement, leadership and participation, and their effectiveness.
	The sociologist Karl Mannheim wrote early in the twentieth century about the capacity of youth to inspire social change and how the focus of efforts shifts across generations (Mannheim 1970). In recent years, adolescents and young adults have led movements for democracy in Asia and the Middle East, for lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) rights, for gender equality, and for action on climate change. Conversely, where opportunities for positive engagement are absent, we have seen adolescents and young adults drawn into violent extremism and gang violence with catastrophic health and societal consequences (Dahl 2004).
	Successful engagement emphasizes the capacities of adolescents and young adults to work in partnership with adults. This generally requires both processes to promote active youth participation (‘training young people to speak’) and the responses of adults (‘training adults to listen’) (Patton et al. 2016). Adolescents and young adults depend on systems and structures for engagement that are put in place and supported by adults. To engage most effectively, youth need resources (including financial), training, ongoing mentorship, sensitization to political and management processes. They also need platforms and mechanisms for engagement. Existing models range from tokenism to those that are completely youth-led (Wong et al. 2010). More egalitarian relations between young people and adults are essential for meaningful engagement but decisions are still often taken through an adult lens that overlooks young people’s perspectives (Gibbs et al. 2010). In general, the greater the level of youth control and responsibility, the greater is the effectiveness of engagement, whether around their own health or around policies and programmes that affect others (Wong et al. 2010).
	Youth engagement in health-related advocacy has increased over the past two decades, fostered at a global level by the UN and other international organizations. Similar processes have occurred at country and community levels within organizations delivering services to young people.
	There are reasons to be optimistic about the scope for extending meaningful youth engagement around their health and wellbeing. The growth of social networking and digital media make it possible to access information, communicate and mobilize with other advocates, as well as draw in resources in unprecedented ways. New media promote more active engagement as adolescents and young adults can independently generate their own content (Kaplan and Haenlein 2010). These possibilities allow broader collaboration which in turn can generate political leverage. Time, privacy, and the need to convince adolescents that their voices will be heard remain barriers. For these reasons capitalizing on these new possibilities is likely to require a shift in approaches to communication for both government and civil society organizations. Attitudes of adults towards young people and their capabilities, together with young people’s lack of confidence in engagement processes, are a common barrier (Coates and Howe 2014). Attitudinal barriers commonly arise from cultural contexts where young people are perceived as subordinate to adults, that exclude young women and that further stigmatize socially marginalized groups (Harden et al. 2001; Iwasaki 2014). Inflexible bureaucratic arrangements, insufficient investment to support ongoing engagement, and restrictive policies, such as limiting the participation of adolescents in research, may be further limiting factors (Villa-Torres and Svanemyr 2015).
	For these reasons, most youth engagement in health falls short of sustainability, and top-down, adult-driven approaches remain the most common.(Gibbs et al. 2010) In programmes that do engage young people, those selected are often already ‘confident, articulate and naturally identified leaders’. In practice, few efforts meaningfully involve the most marginalized adolescents, who may include ethnic minorities, HIV-positive youth, married adolescents, youth with disabilities, LGBT youth, youth living in poverty, those with lower educational levels, and very young adolescents (Paterson and Panessa 2008). In many circumstances, adolescent girls and young women face inequitable systems and structures which limit their participation.





The investment case and accountability


	There is also growing evidence for both cost-effectiveness and high benefit–cost ratios from investments in adolescent health. In the US, the benefits from evidence-based prevention programmes were estimated to range between $2 and $42 for every dollar invested (Catalano et al. 2012).
	A recent analysis of the investment case for adolescence in LMICs highlighted both high benefit–cost ratios from five investments (education, HPV vaccination, reducing rates of child marriage, prevention of road traffic injury and provision of youth-friendly healthcare) and their affordability even in low-resource setting (Sheehan et al. 2017). In providing health services for physical, mental and sexual health, an investment of US$4.65 per capita per annum had an unweighted mean ratio of benefit to costs (BCR) of over 10; for the prevention of road traffic injuries a BCR of 5.9 could be achieved through an annual per capita investment of US$0.60. Programmes to reduce child marriage (US$1.5 per capita per annum) showed a mean BCR of 5.7, with the benefits greatest in lower-income countries. Investment to improve secondary schooling were more expensive with a per capita investment of US$22.6 per annum generating a mean BCR of 11.8 (Sheehan et al. 2017).
	Yet recent analyses of developmental assistance for health across the life-course suggests that there is scant investment in 10–24-year-olds (Skirbekk et al. 2017; Li et al. 2018). Only 1.6% of developmental assistance for health is targeted to 10 to 24-year-olds, despite this age band making up 30% of the population in low-income countries. Overwhelmingly the investments have been in HIV and reproductive health with little or no investment in adolescent nutrition, mental health, or injury prevention (Li et al. 2018).
	The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s and Adolescents’ Health has outlined the need for better data to drive accountability for countries (United Nations 2014). Ideally, data should allow comparisons over time and tracking of inequalities within and between countries. In reality existing global data systems for adolescents remain poorly coordinated, inconsistent in coverage and timing, inadequately disaggregated, missing large groups of adolescents (e.g. out of school adolescents) and fail to deal with the spectrum of adolescent health problems and their determinants (Patton et al. 2012).
	The implementation of adolescent health policies often requires engagement across government ministries. In many countries, this extends to international agencies and global funders and ideally includes civil society groups outside of government (Bhamra et al. 2015). The relevant constituents include professionals working with adolescents, academics and private industry with young people and youth-focused organizations essential stakeholders in the implementation of effective policies and programmes. Their meaningful engagement can ensure a proper understanding of what data mean, inform the feasibility and appropriateness of potential actions, and support broader buy-in.
	The most effective actions for adolescent health and wellbeing are often intersectoral and multicomponent, tailored to local needs and capacities. Ideally such interventions will have been adapted and trialled in similar contexts. Yet in some areas such as mental disorders, nutritional interventions, and sexual and intimate partner violence, there are not yet clearly effective and scalable actions for adolescents. In other areas, health actions such as comprehensive sexuality education have been evaluated in HICs, but neither adequately adapted nor evaluated in LMICs. Many innovative approaches have been piloted and sometimes rolled out on a larger scale but without evaluation. Examples include interventions based on digital media that offer great promise but in the absence of more systematic evaluation their broader utility remains uncertain (Patton et al. 2016).





Conclusion


	Adolescent health now has a presence in global health and international development. The challenge now is to take responses to scale. We now have a good understanding of many approaches that are effective including the strategies for re-orienting health service responses to adolescents, intersectoral actions, and the value of partnerships with young people themselves. Next steps to more effective and accountable systems for adolescent health will need to include better information systems, development of a stronger evidence base for action and ensuring effective policy action around those facing the greatest levels of discrimination and disadvantage. The benefits will extend well beyond adolescence to health in later life and lay a foundation for the best possible start to life for the next generation.
