10.5


Intersectional and social epidemiology approaches to understanding the Influence of race, ethnicity, and caste on global public health


	Jennifer Beard, Nafisa Halim, Salma M. Abdalla, and Sandro Galea





Introduction


	Health at the individual, interpersonal, and community level is a product of multiple, intersecting characteristics that comprise identity and contribute to privilege and vulnerability. Health, illness, well-being, and misery for all humans are shaped by a confluence of biological, social, and cultural factors. While traditional epidemiological approaches have measured associations by considering variables in isolation, there is growing recognition that multiple variables are important determinants of identity and, therefore, of health and well-being.
	Social epidemiology, in particular, has aimed to more fully understand how multiple intersecting factors influence population health (Bowleg 2012; Bauer 2014; Larson et al. 2016). Social epidemiology the science of measuring the ways in which variables like race, ethnicity, sex, gender, sexual orientation, and physical ability are associated with illness and health at the population level (Berkman et al. 2014). It seeks to examine the role of material, behavioural, and psychosocial pathways which influence social inequality and health disparities over the life course, looking at early exposure to social toxins like racism and poverty (as well as biological toxins such as lead or air pollution) and their cumulative influence on health later in life (Cable 2014). Although the traditional methods of epidemiology remain limited to measuring single variables and their association with single outcomes, newer approaches have emerged that aim to understand the complexity of forces that shape health in populations (Galea, Riddle, et al. 2009; Diez Roux 2011). These innovations in social epidemiology are akin to intersectional approaches to understanding health disparities within and across populations.
	An intersectional approach challenges and complements traditional epidemiological methods by asserting the need to measure the impact of multiple, interlocking variables on the health of individuals and populations. As Amroussia et al. (2017) explain, ‘The intersections of these categories create a complex web of social inequalities that are all experienced together by individuals. It is not possible to explore inequalities grounded in each category in isolation from each other, since that is not the way they are experienced by individuals’ (Amroussia et al. 2017). Privilege, disadvantage, and bias exert pressure, influencing individual agency and power. These external forces are shaped by ambient societal factors like cultural and social norms, economic and political structures, institutions, and laws. For example, a Hispanic woman living in the US faces greater social inequities than a Hispanic man. That same man may face more social challenges than a White woman, particularly if he is poor, Black, or gay. Intersectionality takes all these ascribed, achieved, and external forces that shape identity and influence agency into consideration within a specific cultural, social, and historical context.
	This chapter examines the ways in which the individual characteristics we are born with or acquire over the course of our lives intersect to offer us privileges or hamper us with disadvantages that dictate our positions in the social hierarchy and our health. We define common terminology and explore the intersections between social determinants and health outcomes in an illustrative case focused on India. Finally, we offer recommendations for making intersectionality central to social epidemiology and global health.





Terminology and definitions


	Many of the concepts featured in this chapter (race, ethnicity, privilege, racism) are widely understood and used in common parlance, yet each is also abstract and nuanced. The following definitions aim to provide common understanding of the overlapping social positions and processes that contribute to individual and population health.
	Race and ethnicity: The Oxford English Dictionary (OED) defines ‘race’ as ‘a group of people, animals, or plants, connected by common descent or origin. In its widest sense the term includes all descendants from an original stock, but may also be limited to a single line of descent or to the group as it exists at a particular period’ (Oxford English Dictionary Online 2018). The breadth of this basic definition, referring to vague categorization of all living entities based on context and other subjective criteria may startle first-time readers. Most of us have deeply ingrained ideas about race as an objective system grouping human beings according to intrinsic physical characteristics including skin colour, facial features, and hair texture. Yet, researchers unravelling the human genome have concluded that these external markers have very little grounding in genetic difference (Rosenberg et al. 2002; Yudell et al. 2016). This conclusion is consistent with decades of sociological theory and research (Berger and Luckmann 1966). Race is a social construct built on and enforced by differences that have no biologic grounding (Scott and Marshall 2009). James Scott and Gordon Marshall, editors of the Oxford Dictionary of Sociology, describe it as a term that should always be marked by inverted commas to indicate that ‘this manner of categorizing individuals and population groups is not based on any biologically valid distinctions between the genetic make-up of differently identified “races’’ (Scott and Marshall 2009).
	The OED defines ‘ethnicity’ as ‘status in respect of membership of a group regarded as ultimately of common descent, or having a common national or cultural tradition; ethnic character’ (Oxford English Dictionary Online 2018). This definition closely mirrors that of ‘race’ but with emphasis on culture and other shared external identifiers such as country of origin, history, language, religion, and tribe. For many scholars and activists, ‘ethnicity’ is a more useful term than ‘race’ because it is free of biological connotations. But ethnicity is also a complex social construction dependent on external factors ranging from geopolitical boundaries to personal identification. For example, many Americans take great pride in their ancestors’ pre-migration national heritage and identify as Irish or Italian even though they have never been to said country and have no personal connections there. Ethnicity, like race, also has a long history of being used to justify social exclusion and brutality.
	Birth-ascribed status: The concept of birth-ascription is helpful for understanding aspects of identity into which one is born and upon which one is ranked within the social hierarchy. These demographic identifiers include race, ethnicity, sex, and caste. Gerald Berremann explains birth-ascription as a ‘consequence of birth or ancestry and hence immutable’, conferring a ‘societally defined and affirmed worth which is regarded as intrinsic to the individual that cannot be repudiated, relinquished, or altered’ (Berremann 1972). Birth-ascription, he suggests, is a prison without walls in which ‘everyone is sentenced for life to a social cell shared by others of like birth, separated from and ranked relative to all other social cells’ (Berremann 1972).
	Raj Bhopal has described race and ethnicity as ‘complex, intertwining, and important concepts used by societies to identify and evaluate social groups and individuals’ (Bhopal 2015). His use of the word ‘evaluate’ is apt. Birth-ascribed status is a form of social evaluation imposed by those with privilege and power. In the US, being identified as Black, Hispanic, or more broadly as ‘not-White’, functions as a form of social evaluation used to justify slavery, brutality, codified social exclusion, and both explicit and implicit bias. In India, caste and sex are the primary drivers of social hierarchy.
	Achieved status and agency: Achieved status, is a sociological term referring to ‘any social position held by an individual as a result of his or her personal accomplishments in open formal or market competition with others’ (Scott and Marshall 2009). Achievement refers to education, profession, income, marriage, parenthood, and other social positions that one earns, accomplishes, or chooses. The Oxford Dictionary of Sociology notes that the distinctions between achieved status and ascribed status are not absolute as one’s place within the social hierarchy based on race, ethnicity, gender, and caste further or limit opportunities for and scope of accomplishment. Agency or the ‘the capacity for willed (voluntary) action’, can be bolstered or diminished by education, social network, family relationships, professional path, and income (Scott and Marshall 2009). A Dalit woman living in a poor, rural region will face more barriers than her counterpart living in an urban area that will limit her agency or ability to transcend the social rank into which she was born.
	Social position and identities: Social identity theory posits that individuals develop their sense of identity based on groups to which they belong. The development of social identity is a three-part process that starts with social categorization of the people around you as ‘us’ or ‘them’ (Tajfel and Turner 985). Step two, social identification, involves assuming the identities of the different groups to which we belong. Step three, social comparison, is the impulse to define oneself and one’s group as different from and better from other groups. Brenda J. Allen outlines six primary identity groups: gender, race, social class, sexuality, ability, and age (Allen 2011). Some groups (male, White, wealthy, heterosexual, able-bodied, and adult) are typically more powerful than others and have historically built their identity around subjugating others.
	Intersectionality: Intersectionality was first articulated by women of colour as a critique of the feminist, civil rights, and anticolonial movements of the last half of the twentieth century (Collins and Bilge 2016). Kimberlé Crenshaw, a Black feminist legal scholar, is generally credited with first using the term ‘intersectionality’ in 1989. Mainstream feminism in the US, she argued, was a movement created by and for White middle-class women. And the civil rights campaign to end racial discrimination likewise erased the compound sex-and race-based subordination of Black women with its focus on middle-class Black men (Crenshaw 1989). Although Crenshaw is often credited with first articulating the need for an intersectional approach to understanding ‘multiply-burdened marginalization’ (Crenshaw 1989), she was by no means alone. Her voice was one in a global chorus of women of colour frustrated with the binary thinking of social change movements that categorized marginalization as race- or gender-based, without considering what Patricia Hill Collins and Sirma Bilge describe as the ‘many axes that work together and influence each other’, enhancing the privilege and power of some and deepening the oppression of others (Collins and Bilge 2016).
	Figure 10.5.1 illustrates intersectional identities as a cluster of interlocking ascribed, achieved, and geopolitical identities that lock together to form the position of each individual. Privilege, disadvantage, and bias exert pressure influencing each individual’s agency and power. These external forces are shaped by ambient societal factors like culture, norms, economic and political structures, institutions, and laws.
	Fig. 10.5.1 Intersectional identities.
	Racism and racialization: The Oxford English Dictionary definition of ‘racism’ provides a detailed overview of discriminatory social processes, beliefs, and actions based on race, ethnicity, an other defining characteristics:
	 	A belief that one’s own racial or ethnic group is superior, or that other such groups represent a threat to one’s cultural identity, racial integrity, or economic well-being; (also) a belief that the members of different racial or ethnic groups possess specific characteristics, abilities, or qualities, which can be compared and evaluated. Hence: prejudice, discrimination, or antagonism directed against people of other racial or ethnic groups (or, more widely, of other nationalities), esp. based on such beliefs. (Oxford University Press 2018, emphasis added)
	From this broad perspective, skin colour and other physical features are inadequate as universal determinants of racialized discriminatory behaviour.
	Racialization is the imposition of a ‘racial interpretation’ on groups of people seen as other, even when both parties share similar physical and social characteristics. In European and United States migration history, Caucasian Jews, Irish, and Italians have been depicted and shunned as separate and inferior races despite similar White skin and other physical attributes. In colonial Rwanda, Tutsis were favoured by German and Belgian colonizers over the more ‘African’ Hutus. Both ethnic groups are Black, but colonial rulers promoted the former as being closer to White because of their lighter skin, tall and slim stature, and facial features. Racialized discrimination has played out in its most extreme forms in, for example, the genocides in Europe, Rwanda, and Darfur, ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya from Myanmar, and tribal violence in Kenya. In India, the caste system has imposed discriminatory social stratification rendering millions ‘untouchable’ (Berremann 1972). In the US, structural racism is sometimes described as a caste system that has led to mass incarceration and police shootings of unarmed Black men (Alexander 2010; Sampath 2015; Demby 2018).
	Privilege and disadvantage: Social privilege and disadvantage are the unearned consequences of birth-ascribed rank. Many variables are at play in the ratio of advantage and disadvantage each of us carry, including skin colour, religion, sex, gender, sexual orientation, body-type, and physical ability. The degree to which these qualities confer unearned advantage or disadvantage is dependent on the biases and norms of the context in which we live. In the 1989, Peggy McIntosh famously used the analogy of an ‘invisible knapsack’ filled with free passes, passports, and licences to describe White privilege and male privilege (McIntosh 1989). Intersectional approaches to understanding oppression shed light on many other determinants of privilege, power, disadvantage, and oppression. As McIntosh explained more recently: ‘We are all put ahead and behind by the circumstances of our birth. We all have a combination of both. And it changes minute to minute, depending on where we are, who we’re seeing, or what we’re required to do’ (Rothman 2014).
	Social determinants of health: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention define social determinants of health as ‘conditions in the places where people live, learn, work, and play that affect a wide range of health risks and outcomes’ (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2018). These daily conditions of life include the houses we live in, the type of food we eat, the schools we attend, the amount of money we have to meet our needs, the way we are treated by our parents as children, the degree to which we feel socially accepted, and more (Commission on Social Determinants of Health 2008). Likewise, race-based privilege, oppression, and other birth-ascribed attributes like ethnicity, sex, and caste are critical factors contributing to the health of individuals and populations. In the US, for example, infant mortality is two times higher for Black babies (11.7 deaths per 1,000 births) compared to White (4.8 per 1,000) (Riddell et al. 2017). And, in Brazil, low-birth weight is significantly higher among infants of African ancestry (12.4%) compared to Brazilians with European-only ancestry (8.10%) (Nyarko et al. 2013).





Intersectionality in global health research: conceptual framework and methodologies


	Figure 10.5.2 illustrates the pathways connecting intersectional identities and health status across the life course. As articulated in Section 2, an individual’s social position depends on his/her birth-ascribed and achieved attributes. Further, the individual’s birth-ascribed attributes depend on his/her own characteristics (i.e. gender, birth-order, skin tone, sexual orientation) and the characteristics of his/her parents (wealth, income, religion, caste, race, and ethnicity). Intersectional theory posits that ‘multiple social categories (e.g. race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, socioeconomic status) intersect at the micro level of individual experience to reflect multiple interlocking systems of privilege and oppression at the macro, social-structural level (e.g. racism, sexism, heterosexism)’ (Bowleg 2012). Birth-ascribed attributes largely shape an individual’s achieved attributes later in life. Individuals are endowed with privileges and disadvantages along different dimensions, the net of which determine each individual’s social position. History, culture, and social and economic context determine the identities associated with privileges and those with disadvantages.
	Fig. 10.5.2 Pathways linking intersectional identity and health outcomes throughout the life course.
	Social positions affect health and well-being across the life course, as illustrated in the constructs on the far left in Figure 10.5.2. Depending on social position, each individual will or will not experience bias and discrimination in interactions with healthcare providers, educators, employers, and others. For example, clinicians influenced by unconscious bias may make assumptions and care decisions about poor patients, patients of another race or ethnicity, patients of a different caste, patients who are gay or lesbian, or patients with non-binary gender. Parents may rely on internalized social norms to make decisions on whether to invest in daughters as much as sons. And, educators or employers may perceive members of their own race or religion as having more positive attributes (e.g. cooperative, competent, honest, compliant, hard-working, ‘pure’) than those of another race or caste with whom they may associate negative qualities (e.g. competitive, incompetent, dishonest, deviant, lazy, ‘polluted’). These decisions or interactions can lead to discrimination and exclusion over the life course, affecting foetal growth, birth outcomes; childhood nutrition and development; sexual contraception choices and contraception use during adolescence, and pregnancy outcomes or life expectancy during adulthood.
	The extent to which clinicians, educators, employers, and others engage in discriminatory practices will be shaped by the enactment and enforcement of national and international laws criminalizing discrimination. Whether or not a Black pregnant woman in the US and many other countries with a history of institutional racism or a low-caste pregnant woman in India and other South Asian countries will be able to leverage or negotiate respectful treatment will depend on her position. Leveraging or negotiating refers to using advantages along some social positions to compensate for disadvantages along others. For example, a wealthy Black pregnant woman in the US or a Brahmin pregnant woman in India will be better able to demand respectful treatment than a poor woman who is Black or from a Scheduled Caste. The more disadvantages individuals have, the less ability they will have to leverage power in social interactions. The ratio of disadvantages to privileges one carries, influences stress burden, perceived agency, and, ultimately, health and well-being.





Study design, measurement, and modelling


	The advantages of incorporating intersectional approaches in health research have been widely acknowledged (Hankivsky et al. 2010; Bowleg 2012; Bauer 2014; Lopez and Gadsden 2016; Larson et al. 2016; Green et al. 2017). Yet, intersectionality frameworks have been underutilized due to limited progress in developing methodologically sound approaches for applying intersectionality in health research. Intersectional theory challenges and offers nuance to standard epidemiological methods for measuring associations between variables like race, ethnicity, caste, gender, economic status, and health outcomes by placing each individual at the centre of a busy thoroughfare with multiple roads leading in from all angles. Another helpful image is that of a knotted tangle of many strands of yarn in which each is spun from multiple types of fibre representing social identifiers and varying levels of access to privilege and power. The traditional methods of social epidemiology stop short of measuring and analysing what Lisa Bowleg has described as ‘multiple and interlocking social identities’ (Bowleg 2012), which is the goal of an intersectional approach.
	Applying an intersectional approach to population health research requires using analytical methods that examine the complex characteristics of individuals that blur the fixed lines that define a population (Green et al. 2017). A number of social epidemiologists have incorporated intersectionality into their research, using it to inform study design, determine variables to measure, approach measuring multiple social positions, and analyse data (Weber and Parra-Medina 2003; Schulz and Mullings 2006; Warner 2008). An overview of some intersectional approaches to population health research follows:
	Study approach/design: Eco-epidemiology is a methodological parallel to the intersectionality framework concerned with the determinants of disease in individual cases as well as the social contexts within which individuals live. To measure how race produces ill-health, for example, an eco-epidemiology approach takes into consideration that study subjects experience of racism at individual (i.e. internalized racism), interpersonal and community (discrimination and exclusion), and societal levels (institutionalized racism). Similarly, an eco-epidemiology approach to data analysis incorporates contextual factors pertinent to neighbourhoods and states:
	 	• Neighbourhood factors include violence rates, incarceration rates, income/wealth inequality, affordable housing, housing occupancy rates, and liquor outlet density;
	• State factors include public funding for healthcare and social programmes, human rights protections, discriminatory laws or policing practices, and employment protections.
	Eco-epidemiology generally requires a large sample size, with samples organized across multiple levels (individuals; neighbourhoods; etc.) of the socioecological spectrum (Bauer 2014).
	Operationalization of intersectional social positions: Intercategorical and anticategorical intersectionality are two methods researchers have used to measure multiple, interacting variables and their possible influence on health (McCall 2005; Wemrell et al. 2016; Green et al. 2017; Wemrell et al. 2017). The intercategorical approach uses traditional social categories such as race and gender as proxies of the social forces of racism or sexism. The anticategorical approach, emphasizes ‘the inherent fluidity and malleability of social categories, as… socially contingent constructions rather than mirrorings of fixed realities’ (Wemrell et al. 2017).
	Wemrell et al. adopted the ‘anticategorical’ approach to measuring intersectional social positions and risk for ischaemic heart disease by combining categories such as immigration status (yes, no), socioeconomic status (high, medium, low), marital status (yes, no), and mental illness (yes, no) separately for men and women. The research team constructed 48 variables, 24 for men and 24 for women (Wemrell et al. 2017). These variables included:
	 	• Males who had been registered inhabitants of Sweden for at least 10 years, had high income, cohabitated, and had been prescribed psychotropic medication.
	• Females who had been registered inhabitants of Sweden for at least 10 years, had high income, cohabitated, and had not been prescribed psychotropic medication. (Wemrell et al. 2017)
	Modelling: Eco-epidemiologists primarily alternate between two approaches to model health effects of intersectionality. Green et al. (2017) advocate use of multilevel modelling approaches, which entail setting up the data in a way that nests individuals (level 1) within each intersectional identity (level 2) (Green et al. 2017). The authors suggest adding two sets of covariates to regression models: individuals’ (a) gender, race, and other dimensions of social identity; (b) intersectional identity. This differs from traditional approaches of modelling intersectionality. In a traditional approach, a researcher uses an interaction variable for an intersectional identity (e.g. an interaction variable indicating being both Black and female) along with two variables, each for one identity (i.e. a variable indicating being female, and another indicating being Black).
	Complementary use of complex systems approaches has strong potential utility for dealing with the complexities associated with intersectional health production processes (Galea et al. 2009). Individual and societal factors influence one another in the process of the production of health. For example, an individual’s alcohol use and residence in a neighbourhood with a high density of alcohol shops can each adversely influence health. Yet, individuals who tend to engage in high levels of alcohol use may choose to live in neighbourhoods where alcohol outlets are easily accessed. Or, neighbourhoods where alcohol outlets are readily available may influence moderate or non-alcohol users to increase their use to the point of alcohol addiction. Each situation is an example of individual and neighbourhood-level factors influencing each other, and thereby confounding the associations estimated by regression models between single-level factors and health outcomes. Such relationships between determinants are commonly referred to as dynamic relationships.
	Individual, interpersonal, community, and societal indicators can be consequences as well as the causes of health outcomes. An individual’s health can be a consequence as well as a ‘complicating cause’ of alcohol use disorder (Galea et al. 2009). An individual living with a chronic disease may turn to alcohol dependence among other harmful behaviours as a coping mechanism. Or many individuals’ high demand for alcohol may influence availability of liquor stores in the neighbourhood. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as ‘reciprocity’ between health exposures and outcomes.
	Complex systems computational models have the potential to simulate dynamic reciprocal interactions and interrelations between individuals, exposures, and outcomes that change over time and across the life course (Galea et al. 2009). Computer simulations that specify rules by which individual agent’s interactions can be used to observe how intersecting variables at the individual level can translate into population health outcomes. In model specifications, researchers can let agents be adaptive (i.e. agents change their behaviours over time) or prescriptive (i.e. agents behave using pre-set rules). Agents may interact based on spatial proximity or memberships within a social network; can be clustered into groups at different levels (i.e. households, neighbourhoods, states); and, can be influenced by group-level factors (Galea, Riddle, et al. 2009; Galea, Hall, et al. 2009; El-Sayed et al. 2012).





Case study: intersectionality and health inequities in India


	India is home to 1.2 billion people, ranked hierarchically by gender, religion, caste, and economic class, among other axes of power (World Bank Group 2017). Steady economic growth of 3–4% annually replaced the stagnation of the British colonial era, making famines a distant memory (Drèze and Sen 2013). India’s economic growth has accelerated over the last three decades at an annual rate of 9%, making it one of the world’s fastest growing economies (Paul and Mas 2016).
	At independence in 1947, after two centuries of British colonial rule, India committed to using legislative policy within the framework of a representative democracy to improve the lives of women and historically disadvantaged minority groups. To reduce caste-based inequalities, India has adopted a number of progressive laws designed to reduce structural inequities and equalize political representation. All 30 states have set aside 22.5% of seats in the legislature and government-sponsored educational institutions and public-sector jobs for the Scheduled Castes (16–17% of the population) and the Scheduled Tribes (7–8% of population) (Deshpande 2000; Pande 2003). Further, India enacted a number of laws and regulations aiming to eliminate gender-based discrimination and, thereby, improve women’s status in society.
	The 2006 Prohibition of Child Marriage Prevention Act criminalizes child marriage and imposes a jail sentence or fine. The 1994 National Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostics Techniques (PNDT) Act bans sex-selective abortions. And, since 1993, Indian states have been constitutionally required to reserve for women one-third of all chief positions (Pradhan) in local village councils (Gram Panchayats). Notably, in a landmark ruling in 2014, India’s Supreme Court recognized transgender people as members of a third gender, which shows the country’s gradual progress toward gender inclusiveness.
	Still, Amartya Sen has argued that health in India is in ‘dire straits’ due to severe underinvestment (India Express News Service 2017). In 2011, India spent 3.9% of its gross domestic product on health, a 28% decrease from 1995. India’s health inequalities by gender, caste, and class are glaring, and particularly at the intersection where all three meet. A child from a Scheduled Caste, for example, is twice as likely to die in the first year of life compared to a Brahmin child (Thresia 2018). A female child is 1.7 times more likely to die in the first year than a male child (Chowdhury et al. 2017). Infants and children from the lowest standard of living quintile respectively have 2.73 and 4.61 higher odds of mortality than those from the highest quintile (Subramanian et al. 2006). Even Kerala, the southern-most Indian state with health indicators comparable to those in high-income countries, is beset by pervasive health inequalities (Thresia 2018).





Positions


	Caste, gender, and class are the most salient axes of social position and power in present-day Indian society. Table 10.5.1 compares race in the US and caste in India as systems of social stratification.

	* Endogamy refers to marriage within one’s own group based on kinship and/or shared customs, values, and beliefs (such as tribes or castes).
	Ancient Hindu society stratified the population into four mutually exclusive, exhaustive, birth-ascribed, and endogamous castes (varna) (Desai and Kulkarni 2008; Vaid 2014), each associated with a type of occupation:
	 	• Brahmin (priests and teachers),
	• Kshatriya (rulers and warriors),
	• Vaishya (traders)
	• Shudra (artisans and manual labourers).
	Each caste is further stratified into many smaller subcastes (jatis), and each subcaste into even smaller sub-sub castes (Vaid 2014). Scheduled Castes, the lowest in the hierarchy, tend to be employed in occupations considered profane (e.g. skinning animal carcasses, butchering animals, removal of human waste, attendance at cremation groups, washing clothes, fishing). The historical justification for ‘untouchability’ is ‘they are so low that they do not deserve to be assigned a caste’ (Desai and Kulkarni 2008).
	The ritual of purity-pollution underlies the religious rationale for the caste system. Dharma (right conduct), karma (just deserts) and rebirth are the philosophies rationalizing caste assignments. At nearly 3,000 years, India’s caste system is among the world’s oldest forms of social stratification (Beteille 1969; Von Fürer-Haimendorf 1982; Galantar 1984; Omvedt 1993). Caste discrimination was legally abolished in 1950, but continues to vitally affect opportunities, rewards, and social roles. India’s gender-based social stratification entitles men to more rights, resources, and responsibilities compared to women, regardless of ability. India’s gender stratification and preference for sons has resulted in many families adopting sex-selective abortion skewing pro-male sex-ratio at birth and neglect of female infants and children (Miller 1989; Jeffery and Basu 1996; Murthi et al. 2018).
	Patrilocality (i.e. a married couples living near or with the husband’s parents), patrilineality (i.e. names and property pass to the next generation through male descendants), the role of sons in religious rituals, old-age support from sons, the dowry system, and desire to protect female safety and purity are the key cultural factors legitimizing gender stratification (Jayachandran 2015).





Intersectional processes


	Returning to Figure 10.5.2, gender and caste interact in complex ways affecting illness and health in India. For the purpose of illustration, consider gender and caste as simple dichotomies. Compared to Priya, a Brahmin woman, Amitabh, a Brahmin man will likely be less vulnerable and susceptible to health risk factors. He will have better access to assets and services that promote good health, and he will suffer fewer consequences of illness, violence, or disability. On the other hand, Priya will likely perform better than Prakash, a Scheduled Caste/Schedule Tribe (SC/ST) man, who will likely perform better than Anju, an SC/ST woman. While Amitabh and Anju hold extreme social positions on a continuum of intersecting gender and caste identities, Priya and Prakash belong to the middle group. Amitabh has only privileges accorded to him due to his male and Brahmin identities and Anju has only disadvantages. Priya can leverage her caste privileges to compensate for her gender disadvantages. And Prakash can leverage his gender privileges to partially compensate for his caste disadvantages. Although, both Priya and Prakash exist in the middle of the social continuum, Priya belongs to a dominant middle group and Prakash to subordinate middle group since gender identity is more fluid than caste identify in present-day India.





Intersectional health research in India


	To date, only a handful of studies have adopted an intersectionality framework to explain health disparities in India. Sen and Iyer (2012) used household survey data on health seeking behaviour from 60 villages of Koppal district, Karnataka. They found that, of the six groups based on two categories of gender (male, female) and three categories of class (poorest, poor, and non-poor), middle-groups (non-poor women and poor-men) shared striking similarities in key health outcomes (Sen and Iyer 2012). Using the National Family Health Surveys of India 1992/93—2005/06, Joe found severe immunization shortfalls among SC/ST children from rural areas, particularly for girls (Joe 2015). Using the National Family Health Surveys of India 1992/93–2005/06, Mukhopadhyay (2015) found that ‘class inequality dominates caste inequality and caste inequality dominates gender inequality’ in childhood stunting in rural North India (Mukhopadhyay 2015). Finally, Scaria (2017) used data from a household survey from Wadakkanchery village of Kerala and found that morbidity is highest among women from Scheduled Castes and Tribes, followed by women from Other Backward Classes, and Christian and Muslim women (Scaria 2017).





Looking forward: embracing intersectional social epidemiology


	Intersectionality offers social epidemiologists an opportunity to explore innovative research methods for exploring the systems driving health inequalities. It also offers a pathway for using our research to improve the underlying social and structural conditions contributing to disparate health outcomes (Galea 2013; Galea and Link 2013; Bauer 2014).
	Embracing intersectionality will require a range of approaches, from ecological thinking to systems thinking. Complex systems approaches will require data tracing multiple positions and processes within and across levels (Galea 2017). At a minimum, we need to maximize our access to data on social positions (e.g. race, ethnicity, caste, etc.) and social processes (e.g. privilege/disadvantage, racial discrimination/racialization) across multiple levels of social-ecology. Big data from social media, consumer health-record platforms, and troves of administrative and corporate records presents unique opportunities to explore causes of disease, factors that protect health, and sources of resilience.
	The conceptual nuance of measuring the contribution of multiple intersecting identities to both individual and population health offers social epidemiologists an opportunity to embrace theory and deepen our understanding of historical, structural, social, and cultural drivers of health and illness (Galea and Link 2013). Finally, and, perhaps most importantly, social epidemiologists need to continue to ask questions of consequence (Galea 2013). This means continuing to pursue knowledge of disease causality but not simply for the sake of knowing. Rather, we need to pursue this knowledge with the aim of intervening to mitigate or enhance individual and community-level factors driving health outcomes, both good and bad.





Conclusion


	Global health activists and practitioners have been using intersectional approaches since at least 1978 and the Alma-Ata Health for All Declaration, which urged the world to eliminate ‘gross inequality in the health status of the people, particularly between developed and developing countries as well as within countries’ by promoting ‘maximum community and individual self-reliance and participation in the planning, organization, operation and control of primary healthcare’ (WHO and United Nations Children’s Fund 1978). As defined by Alma-Ata, primary care put equal emphasis on addressing social drivers of health and access to healthcare.
	We have not yet achieved health for all. Health disparities continue to widen in countries at all income levels. The social margins team with individuals and populations excluded from economic productivity and good health based on their position in the social hierarchy and processes that assign privilege and disadvantage based on race, ethnicity, caste, sex, gender, sexual orientation, education, income, geography, and other characteristics. Social epidemiology and global public health have an opportunity to hasten social change by embracing intersectional complexities innovating our current research methods, and conducting research that facilitates social change. We must also recruit a new generation of public health researchers who represent multiple intersecting identities and encourage them to think critically and creatively about what our current research methods miss.

10.6


The health of Indigenous peoples


	Papaarangi Reid, Donna Cormack, Sarah-Jane Paine, Rhys Jones, Elana Curtis, and Matire Harwood





Defining Indigenous


	The United Nations (UN) reports there are more than 370 million Indigenous peoples worldwide, residing in around 90 countries (UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues (UNPFII) 2009, p. 1), with greater numbers in the Africa, Asia, and South America regions. These population statistics are fraught with significant challenges in how Indigenous peoples are defined, whether Indigenous peoples are recognized in all nation states, and data completeness and quality (Ohenjo et al. 2006; Gracey and King 2009; Davis 2016).
	Defining the term ‘Indigenous peoples’ is contested and while it is often taken as an umbrella for other names such as Aboriginal, Native, First Nations, tribal peoples or original inhabitants (Gracey and King 2009), these terms are not universal and may fail to acknowledge the many and varied histories of coloniality across different continents in different eras (Ohenjo et al. 2006; Mohindra 2017). In discussing the challenges of defining Indigenous peoples, the UNPFII notes:
	 	Today, the prevailing view is that a single formal universal definition of the term is unnecessary for the recognition and protection of the rights of indigenous peoples, and will fail to capture the diversity, range and complexity of the situations of indigenous peoples throughout the world. (2015, p. 6)
	The UN reiterates the importance of self-identification in recognition that some states may deny the existence of Indigenous peoples, and suggests that on an individual level:
	 	… an Indigenous person who self-identifies with an Indigenous population (group consciousness) and is recognised and accepted as one of its members (acceptance by group), which in turn reserves the sovereign right and power to decide who belongs without external interference. (UNPFII 2015, p. 4)
	Despite the fundamental right for Indigenous peoples to be recognized, some states refuse to do so (Ohenjo et al. 2006), choosing instead to describe peoples as being marginalized by geographic, socioeconomic, linguistic or lifestyle factors (UNPFII 2015). Defining who is Indigenous is central to claiming Indigenous identity, history and rights and is also fundamental to ‘being counted’ within nation states. Reluctance to acknowledge Indigenous peoples amplifies challenges with data completeness and quality.





‘Counting’ Indigenous peoples in data


	Indigenous peoples are often undercounted, miscounted, or not counted in state data systems (Anderson et al. 2016; Axelsson et al. 2016a; Davis 2016). In many jurisdictions, data for Indigenous peoples are not collected, not reported, or aggregated into broader groups, limiting visibility for Indigenous communities within the data. The ability to count, in a practical and technical sense, is deeply connected to the right to be counted as Indigenous peoples and nations (Robson and Reid 2001) and affirmed in human rights frameworks and conventions, including the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) (UN 2007). Appropriate data collection and disaggregated data for Indigenous populations is an ‘urgent priority’ (UNPFII 2004).
	Variable availability and quality of data across Indigenous populations also impacts on understanding the complex inequities in Indigenous health globally. Available data are not always relevant for Indigenous peoples’ own priorities (Walter 2018), and limited by a focus on narrow biomedical measures rather than Indigenous conceptualizations of health and wellbeing (UNPFII 2009; Walker et al. 2017). This limits the ability to explore questions of importance to our own Indigenous communities, or to hold states to account for their failures to recognize Indigenous rights and to eliminate inequities.





The state of health of Indigenous peoples


	UNDRIP reaffirms Indigenous rights, including the right to be actively involved in the planning, development, and implementation of health services and programmes, the right to traditional medicines and health practices and the right to equal health within the country of residence (UN 2007; UNPFII 2013; Axelsson et al. 2016b).
	In contrast to this clear articulation of rights, and corresponding obligations for states to ensure the realization of these rights, many Indigenous peoples experience stark inequities in health, reflected in lower life expectancy, increased mortality and morbidity, and disproportionate numbers living with disability relative to other populations (Anderson et al. 2006; Ohenjo et al. 2006; UNPFII 2013; Axelsson et al. 2016b; Mohindra 2017). These outcomes are heavily influenced by the environments in which we live, including unequal access to conditions that are important for good health, such as safe water, secure and nutritious food, sanitation, and other social determinants of health (UNPFII 2013). Indigenous peoples experience multiple obstacles to healthcare, as well as discriminatory, inequitable, and culturally incompetent care (Allan and Smylie 2015; UNPFII 2015). Further threats to the health of Indigenous peoples include the ongoing impacts from the destruction of Indigenous systems and institutions, natural environments, and the effects of climate change (Gracey and King 2009; UNPFII 2013).
	While there are publications describing important health issues across Indigenous communities, comprehensive health outcomes data, and peer-reviewed studies of Indigenous health at the state level predominantly focus on high-income countries, especially Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United States (Anderson et al. 2016; Axelsson et al. 2016a), with less research published for low-and middle-income countries (Mohindra 2017). Challenges also arise from international comparisons between Indigenous peoples that may not account for variations in territorial histories, social, political, and economic arrangements, and risk focusing attention on whose health status is worst among Indigenous communities. However, international comparisons can be useful in representing the international failure of many nation states to realise Indigenous peoples’ rights to health. Mindful of these challenges, this section summarizes key health measures and outcomes for Indigenous peoples globally.
	Stark, inequitable health outcomes for Indigenous peoples have been documented globally (e.g. Montenegro and Stephens 2006; Ohenjo et al. 2006; Hayman et al. 2015). An international collaboration recently published the most comprehensive review on Indigenous health to date, drawing on data from 28 populations in 23 countries, covering around 154 million Indigenous peoples globally (Anderson et al. 2016). The review confirmed previous work, documenting poorer outcomes for Indigenous peoples globally when compared with non-Indigenous populations, sustained across many health and social outcomes (Anderson et al. 2016). The review also identified variations in the magnitude of inequities between countries. Worse outcomes for Indigenous were typical but not universal, with some instances identified where there were no differences or, very rarely, better outcomes for Indigenous communities (Anderson et al. 2016). For example, data on Life-Expectancy-at-Birth (LEaB), covering 18 Indigenous populations from 14 countries, showed generally lower LEaB for Indigenous peoples. Inequities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples varied from extreme inequities in some populations of 10 years or more, to eight Indigenous populations with gaps between 5 and 10 years, with the remaining countries having differences of two years or less, except for Sami in Sweden where the difference was not statistically significant (Anderson et al. 2016).
	The review also reported that the health of Indigenous mothers and infants generally echoed socioeconomic conditions of their communities. In general, infant mortality rates were lower (less than 50/1,000 live births) in higher income countries than in lower income countries (more than 50/1,000 live births). In almost all populations where data were available, Indigenous infant mortality rates were higher than for non-Indigenous peoples with particularly high ratios in some countries (Anderson et al. 2016).
	Maternal deaths should be infrequent and reflect the availability, accessibility, affordability, and safety of local health services. Data was unavailable or unstable for many nations in the review but consistent disparities in maternal deaths were noted in Australia, New Zealand, Panama, and Columbia (Anderson et al. 2016). The receipt of lower levels of maternity services by Indigenous mothers has been reported elsewhere (Rumbold et al. 2011; Paulino et al. 2019). In some nation states, Indigenous women in remote communities have to relocate to give birth (UNPFII 2015), which may leave them without social support in health services that may be culturally unsafe.
	Indigenous peoples continue to be disproportionately impacted by infectious diseases with mortality and morbidity generally reported to be higher, especially for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, syphilis, viral hepatitis, and rheumatic fever (Montenegro and Stephens 2006; Gracey and King 2009; UNPFII 2009; Russell et al. 2019). Infectious diseases have a significant impact, especially in lower income countries, among marginalized communities living in poverty, and where the disease or its risk factors are stigmatized. Indigenous health inequities for rheumatic fever exist in both developing (Steer et al. 2002) and wealthy countries (Carapetis et al. 2005; Abouzeid et al. 2019). Indigenous children in high-income countries also experience inequitably high rates of respiratory disease (Chang et al. 2009). The socioeconomic and health disadvantage common among Indigenous communities drives much of these inequities (UNPFII 2009, 2015), which are further exacerbated by inequitable health service access and care (Baker et al. 2012).
	Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are now deeply problematic for Indigenous peoples. NCDs account for significant mortality and morbidity globally (di Cesare et al. 2013), contributing to both health inequities within nations (di Cesare et al. 2013) and to the wellbeing and economic security of Indigenous communities (NCD Alliance 2012). The four most common NCDs are cardiovascular diseases, cancers, diabetes, and chronic respiratory diseases (WHO 2013), contributing significantly to inequities in life expectancy between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of mortality for most Indigenous peoples. Deaths from ischaemic heart disease, twice those of non-Indigenous peoples (Ministry of Health 2011; Espey et al. 2014), account for more than half of CVD deaths, followed by stroke, heart failure (Woods et al. 2012) and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) (Watkins et al. 2017). CVD inequities are evident between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in age of onset and the underlying cause of the heart disease. For example, RHD causing heart failure is more common in young Indigenous Australians and Africans; hypertensive and ischaemic heart failure is more common in older non-Indigenous people (Bukhman and Ochieng 2017).
	Cancer is underemphasized as a health issue for Indigenous peoples, particularly in low income countries, possibly due to overwhelming rates of infectious diseases. Cancers have a broad range of risk factors including infections (e.g. Hepatitis B and C, HPV, HIV, and Helicobacter pylori), metabolic conditions, diet, and exposure to toxins and carcinogens (WHO 2019). The relative frequency of exposure to these factors has led to variation in the types of cancer impacting Indigenous peoples in different regions (Moore et al. 2014). However, the risk of dying from all cancers is significantly higher for Indigenous peoples in general (Cunningham et al. 2008; Parkin et al. 2008; Ministry of Health 2015). Timely access to cancer screening, diagnostic and treatment services (Moore et al. 2014) by Indigenous peoples show consistent inequities in regions where measured (UNPFII 2015).
	Respiratory conditions, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma, are also common causes of mortality, morbidity, and hospitalizations for Indigenous peoples. Asthma is the second leading cause of hospitalization among Indigenous Australians and death rates are 3.2 times higher (NCD Alliance 2012). COPD hospitalization and mortality rates for Indigenous peoples are higher in most higher income nations (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2014; Gershon et al. 2014; Ministry of Health 2015) with differences in exposure to tobacco and environmental pollution, differences in disease management, and differential access to health services, explaining most of these inequities (NCD Alliance 2012; Chang et al. 2014). While allergic disorders are rare in traditional rural settlements, urbanization, and the concurrent move to overcrowded living conditions and increased exposure to environmental pollutants has seen increased rates for Indigenous communities (Mbugi and Chilongola 2010).
	Disorders of nutrition, including undernutrition, malnutrition, and overnutrition, are also important. Anderson et al. (2016) note that child malnutrition is still a significant issue for Indigenous peoples, reporting higher levels of childhood malnutrition with stunting among Indigenous peoples residing in a number of nation states in South America. Rates of obesity among children and adults are increasing, including among those populations where childhood malnutrition is still disproportionately high (Anderson et al. 2016).
	Type 2 diabetes is currently estimated to affect more than 50% of Indigenous adults aged over 35 years, with incidence rates climbing (NCD Alliance 2012). Indigenous peoples experience disproportionate rates of diabetic complications including renal failure, lower extremity amputations, eye disease and macrovascular outcomes (Naqshbandi et al. 2008). While the high incidence of end-stage renal failure among Indigenous peoples is reported in major population centres across Oceania, Indigenous peoples receive fewer kidney transplants than non-Indigenous peoples and many experience geographic and economic difficulties accessing optimal treatments (Weil and Nelson 2006).
	Diabetes inequities exist across the life course. For example, gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) incidence rates among Native American (7.9%), Canadian First Nations (11.5%), Australian Aboriginal (8.4%), and Māori in New Zealand (6%) are higher than those for non-Indigenous women of those respective countries and the total international incidence (2–5%) (Lawrence et al. 2008; Porter et al. 2012; Jowitt 2016). GDM is a risk factor for the development of NCDs in the lifetime of both mothers (Nolan 2011) and their offspring (O’Reilly 2014). Despite suggestions that this might be a driver for the high prevalence of intergenerational diabetes (Osgood et al. 2011) and other NCDs in Indigenous peoples, screening for and management of GDM among Indigenous women is currently inadequate (McGrath et al. 2007; Daly et al. 2017). It is critical to acknowledge the lived context of Indigenous peoples who often have been excluded from traditional territories and food sources and reside in obesogenic environments and situations of food insecurity (Gracey and King 2009).
	Finally, mental wellbeing is a global health priority for Indigenous peoples (Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) 2018). Mental health conditions are ‘a complex challenge because of increased visibility, pervasive structural stigma, outdated practices and organizational fragmentation’ (PAHO 2018, p. 2). Mortality data underestimate the importance of these conditions on the wellbeing and livelihoods of individuals and their families. In 2015, it was estimated that globally NCDs accounted for around 60% of Disability-Adjusted Life Years, of which mental, neurological., substance-use disorders, and self-harm (MNSS) accounted for 12% (PAHO 2018).
	The legacies of colonization, dispossession, marginalization, systematic discrimination, and denial of Indigenous rights are linked to disproportionately high rates of stress and mental distress, highlighting the downstream impacts of these trauma on a number of parameters of Indigenous wellbeing. Anderson et al. (2016) note that the lack of morbidity data for Indigenous peoples, including data on mental health conditions, was a key issue especially for countries outside of North America and Oceania, limiting the ability to fully explore the impacts of mental illness on Indigenous wellbeing.
	Mental health conditions are disproportionately prevalent among young Indigenous peoples (WHO 2014). Suicide is a leading cause of death in young Indigenous peoples, particularly in Australia, Brazil, New Zealand, Taiwan, and circumpolar countries (Patel et al. 2007; WHO 2014). Indigenous youth are more likely to be exposed to risk factors for mental illness such as growing up in poverty, adverse conditions such as scarcity of food, poor nutrition, violence and aggressions, inadequate education, substance abuse and sexual and reproductive health challenges (Patel et al. 2007).
	NCDs are clearly a challenge for Indigenous peoples and one that needs Indigenous voice, active participation, and leadership. Despite these inequities, international efforts to prevent and control NCDs have been slow to ensure Indigenous participation. Leaders in Indigenous health remain frustrated by this and note that working with Indigenous peoples is critical to ensure a reduction in NCD risk factors and NCD burden, and to avoid increasing inequity (NCD Alliance 2012; Finlay and Armstrong 2018).
	Inequities have also been documented in both intentional and unintentional injury among Indigenous peoples, with higher rates of death, morbidity and disability reported by a number of countries illustrating differential exposure to violence and conflict (Montenegro and Stephens 2006), differential access to safe living and working conditions, and appropriate injury prevention strategies (Berger 2002).
	Access to, and quality of, healthcare is an issue for Indigenous peoples globally (Montenegro and Stephens 2006; Ohenjo et al. 2006; UNPFII 2015). For some Indigenous peoples, healthcare is inaccessible for geographic and financial reasons, or because of discrimination (Montenegro and Stephens 2006; Ohenjo et al. 2006). In addition, many countries have healthcare systems that privilege non-Indigenous approaches to health and wellbeing, and marginalize Indigenous ways of healing, including denying access to traditional medicines. The decentring of Indigenous health knowledges and practices, coupled with discrimination, means that even where care is available, Indigenous peoples often experience culturally inappropriate or unsafe services.





The representation and framing of Indigenous health


	Alongside the urgent need for improved data for Indigenous peoples, Indigenous scholars are concerned with the ways in which Indigenous peoples are represented in health research and statistics (Walter 2016, 2018). Representations of Indigenous health, often controlled by non-Indigenous peoples, invoke deficit, racialized narratives that contrast sharply with Indigenous narratives (Walter 2016). Moreover, data available to describe the health of Indigenous peoples often do not reflect historical and embodied contexts and circumstances, nor contemporary lived realities. In many states, non-Indigenous models of health are dominant in health systems (UNPFII 2015) and data, displacing Indigenous approaches to health and wellbeing.
	Indigenous models of health recognize the interdependence of peoples, the connections between peoples and environments, and the importance of balance (Bird 2002; Smylie and Anderson 2006; Kaholokula et al. 2009; UNPFII 2009), and take into account how histories fundamentally shape social, cultural, political, legal, and economic institutions in societies, with flow on effects for social categorization and hierarchies such as socioeconomic status, and exposure to health-protective or health-damaging factors for individuals and communities (Walters et al. 2011). Current inequities in health are understood to be intimately linked to colonialism and racism, and the disruption to connections between people and environments from forced removal from lands, dispossession or destruction of territories and resources and environmental degradation and pollution (UNPFII 2009). The disruption of connection parallels a disruption to Indigenous systems of knowledge, ways of being, social institutions and processes of intergenerational transmission, and is understood as a root cause of current health inequities (Bird 2002; King et al. 2009; Wirihana and Smith 2014). Increasingly, Indigenous models of health are also articulating historical trauma and its intergenerational transmission, as a fundamental determinant of health for Indigenous peoples (Walter et al. 2011; Paradies 2016).





Interventions for equity in Indigenous health


	Given the complex and self-replicating processes that contribute to the health inequity experienced by Indigenous peoples, effective interventions need to be comprehensive, connected, long-term, tailored, and responsive to change. The following are a range of important considerations for progress towards health equity for Indigenous peoples.





Self-determination


	Self-determination is an essential component of Indigenous health development. It is affirmed as a prerequisite for the protection, promotion, exercise, and enjoyment of all other human rights and fundamental freedoms (UNPFII 2009). It is a preexisting human right and is not dependent on the views of, or permission from, nation states (UNPFII 2009). Self-determination is intimately linked to a peoples’ democratic entitlement and thus underpins the integrity of all relationships between Indigenous peoples and respective nation states. UNDRIP reaffirms Indigenous rights to self-determination, active participation in decision-making and the need of states to ‘obtain free, prior and informed consent’ before adopting and implementing legislative or administrative measures that may affect Indigenous peoples (UN 2007). Self-determination also applies to the right of Indigenous peoples to determine the structure and form of health systems and institutions in our territories.





Decolonisation of Indigenous knowledge and knowledge production


	Human rights and fundamental freedoms detailed in international rights instruments do not always fully align with Indigenous worldviews. Indigenous values have greater focus on collective rather than individual rights, and these being balanced against responsibilities (UNPFII 2009). Further, Indigenous values including respect, cooperation, reciprocity, spirituality, deference to elders, and the importance of language and traditions are not captured. Most Indigenous peoples acknowledge the life force of all things, animate and inanimate and see as limited, international rights instruments that only acknowledge humans.
	Royal (2009) promotes that the central tenet of indigeneity is an active and ongoing kin-based relationship between humankind and the natural environment, noting that this is not about claiming resources but rather an affirmation that the earth is truly our mother. This alters relational dynamics between humans and the natural environment from one permitting extractive activities that degrade and endanger to one where humans are expected to respect and protect the environment. These worldviews are supported by Indigenous knowledge systems that are neither static nor finite, but have been undermined by processes of colonisation.
	Indigenous knowledges form an essential part of the diverse knowledge systems on earth and are critical for important health challenges. UNDRIP specifically notes the right to protect Indigenous knowledges and manifestations of these knowledges including human and genetic resources, while also acknowledging rights to supporting customary processes, philosophies, and relationships.





Interventions on oppressive pathways


Acknowledge historical trauma, promote healing, and prevention


	Historically, Indigenous peoples have survived horrific traumatic events, including genocides, ethnocides (destruction of cultures, languages, and ways of living), epistemicides (destruction of traditional knowledges and ways of knowing), and ecocides (destruction of environments including food sources) (Walters et al. 2011; Walters 2016). For many, these events have continued into recent history (forced adoptions or removal of children to boarding schools, long-term poverty, and discrimination) and the present (deforestation of tribal territories, pollution of waterways, continuous racialized microaggressions). Indigenous scientists are seeking to understand the role of historical trauma, and how contexts, processes and outcomes become embodied and contribute to patterns of illness among Indigenous peoples and subsequent health inequities (Walters et al. 2011).
	Two growing bodies of evidence are important. First is the evidence that traumatic events are important in the life course by negatively and directly affecting the health of individuals and communities, especially if events are repeated (Walters et al. 2011). The second body of evidence demonstrates that significant trauma can have an intergenerational effect. These effects are mediated by both epigenetic pathways, affecting the way in which genes are regulated and expressed, as well as physiological mechanisms, usually mediated by stress hormones and metabolic or immune responses. It is thought these mechanisms contribute to the disparate rates of diseases among Indigenous peoples including metabolic diseases, cardiovascular diseases as well as stress and coping disorders such as depression, anxiety, and substance abuse (Walters et al. 2011).
	While the theory and evidence relating to historic trauma is still evolving, especially methodological issues (Walters et al. 2011), the complexities of the relationships become obvious. These complexities demand sophisticated research and we ought to rise to this challenge rather than dismiss the role of historic trauma in Indigenous health status.
	While Indigenous peoples continue to exhibit courageous resilience in the face of these traumas, healing will require a dual focus. First, eliminating exposure to further stressors that could become embodied, such as poor nutrition, especially during pregnancy and childhood, poverty, lower quality services especially in education, health, justice, and welfare services, exposure to racisms, and higher levels of violence and loss. Second, Indigenous peoples must be permitted to heal and restore from these traumas. Some authors have noted the importance of traditional knowledge and practices to support this healing and how culture can be medicine (Walters et al. 2011, 2020).





Acknowledge racism, and intervene to mitigate and eliminate


	Indigenous communities and scholars note the role of racism as a fundamental determinant of Indigenous health (Paradies et al. 2008; Allan and Smylie 2015; Paradies 2016; 2018). As a system of oppression, racism shapes health for Indigenous peoples through its structuring of histories as well as social, cultural, political, and economic institutions. Racism also operates through racially discriminatory practices at the level of individuals, intersecting with other oppressive systems to negatively influence health across the life course and intergenerationally (Paradies 2016).
	Interventions are necessary to eliminate racism at interpersonal and structural levels, including action to address the role of racialized beliefs and assumptions among health providers in shaping interactions with patients and influencing clinical decision-making and healthcare outcomes (Paradies et al. 2013; Fitzgerald and Hurst 2017). There is an urgent need for the fundamental role of racism to Indigenous health to be acknowledged as a global public health issue, and for nation states to combat racism against Indigenous peoples within the health sector and more broadly in society. Further, whether or not there are health impacts, Indigenous peoples have a right to freedom from all forms of discrimination (Paradies 2018).





Acknowledge and address health system bias, make (health) systems culturally safe


	Although Indigenous peoples have long identified relationships between imposed colonial health systems and healthcare delivery, and health outcomes, these relationships have been underexamined in health research generally (Smedley et al. 2003), and for Indigenous peoples specifically (Paradies 2018). Acknowledgement of the contingent and culturally-embedded nature of health systems demands critical reflection on how organizational structures, policies, environments, practices, and provider behaviours reproduce and maintain colonial logics and power structures.
	Cultural competency and cultural safety are proposed as possible interventions to eliminate ethnic health inequities. In some countries, they have been incorporated into regulatory and legislative frameworks governing healthcare workers (Bacal et al. 2006). However there are important differences in definitions of these terms, how they are interpreted, incorporated into practice, and what these interventions are hoping to achieve. While cultural competency interventions often focus on teaching healthcare workers awareness of Indigenous languages, cultures, and practices, these teachings do not address the fundamental causes of inequities and risk promoting stereotypes and therefore undermine the decolonizing and transformative work necessary to address biases (Truong et al. 2014).
	Interventions are necessary that ensure health professionals develop a critical consciousness about historic processes and how they play out in contemporary practice today. Cultural safety was articulated by Dr Irihapeti Ramsden who insisted health workers reflect on their privilege and power within the health system and use it to eliminate injustice and inequity (Papps and Ramsden 1996). Cultural safety insists health workers reflect on themselves as power bearers and on their ‘own culture’ and ask what we need to change in our practice to achieve equitable outcomes for all patients. Ramsden’s work contributed to the current standards of critical self-reflection and reflective practice in the training of healthcare providers.
	The importance of health systems where healthcare, interventions and policy are grounded in Indigenous culture and knowledge systems has been acknowledged (Walters et al. 2020). There are many examples where Indigenous knowledge and healing practices have been incorporated into current health systems, and have contributed significantly to what is now called Westernized medicine (Oguamanum 2004; Maskarinec et al. 2014; Baddock et al. 2017). However, this incorporation can be problematic and damaging where it is extractive, performative, or tokenistic. While culturally grounded health services have been posited as a response to inequities in healthcare access and quality, they should be more rightly understood as a fundamental right of Indigenous peoples to have access to health services, interventions, and systems that are based on Indigenous knowledge and worldviews, and are designed and controlled by Indigenous peoples.





Build an Indigenous health workforce


	A health workforce that reflects the community it will serve is a critical component of high quality and equitable healthcare (Betancourt et al. 2003; Lancet 2016). Indigenous health workforce development contributes both to Indigenous development and reducing ethnic inequities in health (Curtis 2016) and aligns with international workforce initiatives. There is evidence that if patients and healthcare workers are of the same ethnicity, described as ethnic or racial concordance (Burgess et al. 2004), interactions are marked by better communication, shared decision-making, improved respect, affiliation, and trust (Cooper et al. 2006), greater satisfaction with the care received and less likelihood of the patient perceiving racism in the interaction (LaVeist and Nutu-Jeter 2002).
	Indigenous health workforce development also increases the potential for cultural competency of both health workers and health systems (Betancourt et al. 2005) as it requires healthcare providers to critically reflect on their own culture and biases and the impact these have on clinical interactions and health service delivery (Kumagai and Lypson 2009). Becoming an Indigenous health professional is also generally associated with improved financial independence (Curtis 2016), community respect and support, positive role modelling and intergenerational effects, access to health expertise and better system navigation (Ratima et al. 2007). Seeing Indigenous peoples as health professionals, as opposed to recipients of care, helps challenge colonial stereotypes and increases the potential for positive collegial interactions which may in turn reduce implicit bias among non-Indigenous health workers (van Ryn et al. 2015).
	Some countries are investing in Indigenous health workforce development and their experience has reinforced the need to adopt a ‘whole pathway’ approach that includes recognition of socioeconomic, cultural, and geographical barriers to accessing quality education at all levels, appropriate careers advice, and comprehensive academic, pastoral. and cultural support within tertiary contexts (Curtis et al. 2014).





Mitigate biases in research


	Research is the process of knowledge production but knowledge, who is knowledgeable and knowledge creation are all situated—politically, economically, socially, culturally, and historically. Smith (2012) writes that many Indigenous peoples consider ‘research’ a dirty word. This references the alignment of research with colonization and its processes of appropriation and claiming. Colonization included the brutal suppression of Indigenous cultures, languages, customs, traditional knowledges and ways of knowing, and in this process, colonizers rebranded themselves as discoverers and authorities of Indigenous lives.
	Colonial processes sought to replace what Indigenous peoples know with a belief in a single Euro-centric knowledge system. Imperialism now seeks to govern the way we think about knowledge, controlling what questions we ask, what we see and what we know (Smith 2012). Research is thus understood as a mechanism for establishing and maintaining power and control as part of the colonial project. Even supposedly ‘objective’ scientific methods can produce evidence that supports racist beliefs and further marginalizes Indigenous peoples (Te Rōpū Rangahau Hauora a Eru Pōmare 2002; Reid et al. 2017).
	Indigenous researchers are increasingly rejecting approaches that seek to further entrench colonialism, deny the Indigenous experience, and reaffirm discriminatory views about Indigenous peoples. Further, Indigenous academics have been active in challenging Euro-centric research, revitalizing Indigenous research methodologies and supporting research institutions to do more for Indigenous peoples and communities (Smith 2012). However, it is necessary for all researchers, research organisations, and funding authorities to reject research projects and processes that fail to respect Indigenous knowledges, histories, ambitions, stories, voices, data, bodies, genes, and rights (Reid et al. 2017; Walker et al. 2017). UNDRIP affirms the rights of Indigenous peoples to maintain, control, and protect traditional knowledges, develop, and incorporate traditional knowledges into our contemporary practices, advance new practices, and create new Indigenous knowledges.





Identify and mitigate future external risks to inequity


	Climate change is the greatest threat to global health for the twenty-first century (Costello et al. 2009) working through multiple pathways both direct and indirect (Smith et al. 2014). Climate change acts as a threat multiplier, amplifying the health effects on structurally oppressed communities (Watts et al. 2018), with marginalized populations who already experience poorer health facing disproportionate risk (Levy and Patz 2015; Woodward and Porter 2016; Paavola 2017). Those who have contributed least to global greenhouse gas emissions (e.g. those in developing countries, low-lying island nations, and Indigenous peoples) will be hit first and worst.
	Indigenous peoples are also more likely to depend on natural ecosystems for daily living and economic wellbeing. In addition, the capacity to respond and adapt to climate change is restricted by conditions of greater socioeconomic deprivation, ongoing social marginalization, and exclusion from political processes and structures (Ramos-Castillo et al. 2017).
	Actions to tackle climate change could negatively impact Indigenous health and equity (Walpole et al. 2009; Robbins 2015) and further undermine Indigenous rights (Jones et al. 2014). However, climate action is also an opportunity for health development (Watts et al. 2015) and reducing health inequity. Despite the central importance of climate change to Indigenous wellbeing, international decision-making bodies and processes have not centralized Indigenous voices (Nilsson 2008).
	Indigenous peoples have affirmed the pivotal importance of Indigenous ways of knowing and being to climate action. Whyte (2016) has shown that Indigenous cultural and political systems have in-built flexibility that allows societies to constantly adapt to environmental changes. The International Indigenous Peoples’ Forum on Climate Change ((IIPFCC) 2012), stated, ‘we reiterate the need for recognition of our traditional knowledge, which we have sustainably used and practised for generations; and the need to integrate such knowledge in global, national, and subnational efforts. This knowledge is our vital contribution to climate change adaptation and mitigation’ (p. 1).
	To Indigenous peoples, climate change represents an extension and intensification of colonialism (Whyte 2017). Activities and industries that are major producers of greenhouse gas emissions have depended on the dispossession and appropriation of Indigenous lands and resources (Cameron 2012). Indeed, the values, systems, structures, and processes foundational in the colonization of Indigenous peoples also underpin the environmental changes that threaten local and global ecosystems (Wood 2015). That these same systems are being relied on provide solutions for the climate crisis is of concern to Indigenous peoples, as these systems have historically been tightly bound to philosophies that see the planet in extractive and exploitative ways (Jones 2019).
	Indigenous worldviews, especially relationality with the natural environment, challenge systems where human rights dominate. The time has arrived to mitigate unprecedented damage to our planet and solutions based on Indigenous sciences provide balance to current debate, processes, and interventions.





Conclusion


	Describing the health of Indigenous peoples has many challenges including definitions, enumeration, and analysis. Making sense of health data is also challenging as we seek to recognize the complex, layered, and multifactorial influences that play out through time and across geographies for Indigenous peoples. This chapter canvasses the inequitable health outcomes for Indigenous peoples globally, shaped by shared experiences of dispossession and oppression, and the significant and ongoing health impacts resulting from differential exposure to social, political, economic, and cultural determinants of health, particularly colonialism and racism. These data also speak to the ongoing resistance of Indigenous peoples, and aspirations for the recognition of our rights and restoration of relationships with our territories, environments, and relations. The state of Indigenous health challenges us to have a critical view of colonial histories and how these have become embedded in our lives. We also recognize the potential of Indigenous knowledge systems, ontologies, and values to drive positive health and wellbeing into the future.

10.7


People with disabilities


	Anne Kavanagh, Marissa Shields, and Alex Devine
