	‘Disability doesn’t make you exceptional, but questioning what you think you know about it does’, Stella Young, 2014
	(Palenzuela 2014)





Introduction


	The health of people with disabilities has, until recently, been largely ignored by public health researchers, practitioners, and policymakers. We argue this is because public health largely concentrates on the prevention of disability and conceives of disability as a health deficit. This chapter will show why the health of people with disabilities is a significant public health issue that requires urgent attention.
	People with disabilities are a substantial minority of the world’s population. Approximately 15% of the world’s population has a disability; that’s over one billion people. Globally, people with disabilities are one of the most disadvantaged populations. They are more likely to have low levels of education, be unemployed, socially excluded, live in poverty, experience homelessness, and live in poor-quality housing (OECD 2010; WHO 2011). These disadvantaged circumstances impact on their physical and mental health. In many countries, in part due to their exclusion from public health and broader society, people with disabilities smoke at higher levels than their peers without disabilities (Courtney-Long et al. 2014; Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016b), are more likely to be overweight and physically inactive (Neter et al. 2011; Kim et al. 2015; Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016b).
	People with disabilities are also more likely to experience discrimination, bullying, and physical and sexual violence (Hughes et al. 2012; Krnjacki et al. 2016; Krnjacki et al. 2017; Pinquart 2017). This is further compounded by difficulty accessing quality health promotion and care. Remedying the disadvantage, discrimination, violence, risky health behaviours and poor access to healthcare and disability services people with disabilities experience will lead to improvements in their health. This means that much of the poorer health of people with disabilities is avoidable rather than a consequence of their underlying impairment.
	In this chapter, we describe how disability is conceptualized and measured; what is known about the prevalence of disability internationally; the health outcomes for people with disabilities and the impact of the social determinants of health. We also discuss some of the extant literature on improving health outcomes for people with disabilities. The chapter concludes with a call for people with disabilities to be a priority population for public health and outlines an agenda for future public health research, policy, and practice.





Evolving conceptualizations of disability


	Disability is a complex and contested concept. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) describes disability as resulting from:
	 	‘the interaction between persons with impairments and attitudinal and environmental barriers that hinders their full and effective participation in society on an equal basis with others.’ (United Nations 2006, Article 1)
	The importance of this definition is that it distinguishes between an impairment, such as paraplegia or vision loss, and barriers to participation such as discrimination, physical inaccessibility, and limited employment opportunities. The disability is not solely caused by an impairment per se but rather by the presence of the impairment and other characteristics of society that prevent, or make it difficult for, people with disabilities to participate in key life domains, attain their rights, and realize their aspirations.
	The CRPD is the first human rights treaty to specifically define the rights of people with disabilities and outline state obligations to promote, protect and uphold these rights (United Nations 2006; Keogh and Down 2014). Among these rights is the recognition that people with disabilities have the right ‘to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health without discrimination on the basis of disability’ (United Nations 2006, Article 25).





Conceptualization of disability within public health


	Public health researchers, practitioners, and policymakers have traditionally focused on the prevention of disability and ill-health through policy and programmes which reduce the risk of acquiring disability. Examples include seatbelts and speed limits to reduce road accident injuries, immunization, and smoking taxation. Prevention of injury and ill-health, alongside promoting health and wellbeing is central to public health and should remain so. Like the rest of the population, people with disabilities can benefit from such public health interventions. However, in most public health programmes disability is considered a ‘failure’ of public health. Further, interventions which work among the general population are often assumed to apply to and be effective for people with disabilities. This is despite limited evidence or knowledge on appropriate research designs which could measure the benefit of mainstream public health interventions for people with disabilities (Berghs et al. 2016).
	Antiquated assumptions that conceptualize disability as a burden or deficit can reinforce this exclusion from public health. Burden of disease studies for example position disability as a health deficit. This means that years lived with disability are valued far less than years lived without disability. This positioning assumes that people with disabilities cannot be healthy, and, when used for resource allocation or cost-effectiveness analyses, emphasizes that the lives of people with disabilities are less effective at the outset (Arnesen and Nord 1999). Effectively, this means that an intervention targeted at women with disabilities such as mammographic screening would be considered less cost-effective than in the general population because their lives are assigned lesser value.
	Addressing health deficits and disability aligns broadly with what is often referred to as the medical model of disability. The literature distinguishes between the medical (or individual) model of disability and the social model. Proponents of the social model portray the ‘medical model’ as conceiving of disability as a deficit in individual bodies that is addressed through prevention, medical treatments and, preferably, cured (Oliver 1981; 1990; 1996a; b). The social model, positioned as a radical departure from this approach, identifies physical, social, cultural, and economic barriers that are disabling. The social model draws attention to the ways in which governments, organizations, workplaces, and communities can respond to overcome barriers to an individual’s participation in society.
	The social model has been important politically and widely embraced by advocacy groups as it calls government and societies to account and has helped pave the way towards the formal recognition of the rights of people with disabilities as articulated in the CRPD. Others have drawn attention to the shortcomings of both models, pointing out that while the social model is an important counterpoint to the medical model, it ignores the fact that individual bodies have limitations, experience pain, fatigue and that can indeed impact on participation (Shakespeare 2014).





The International Classification for Functioning, Disability, and Health


	The International Classification for Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF), developed by the World Health Organization (WHO 2002), is one of the most widely used frameworks for conceptualizing disability. The framework is illustrated in Figure 10.7.1. This framework is designed to guide measurement, research, service delivery, and policy development. It distinguishes between functional limitations related to an impairment affecting body functions and structures (e.g. loss of arm function), activity (e.g. execution of a task or action such as dressing) and participation in life (e.g. employment).
	The ICF emphasizes that acting on the impairment through medical treatment alone is not sufficient. Society can reduce activity restrictions through technologies and other adaptions (e.g. screen readers, wheelchairs, hearing loops) and reducing participation restrictions (e.g. by reducing discrimination, referred to as environmental factors in the ICF). These domains are classified as bodily, individual, and societal perspectives in the ICF, respectively. In the ICF the ‘functioning’ refers to all body functions, activities, and participation, while disability is an umbrella term for impairments, activity limitations, and participation restrictions. The ICF also lists environmental (e.g. discrimination, policies) and personal (e.g. age) factors that interact with all these components.
	Fig. 10.7.1 Disability framework for the International Classification for Functioning.
	WHO (2002) Towards a common language for functioning, disability, and health: The international classification of functioning, disability and health. Geneva: World Health Organization. p.9).





Measurement of disability


	A recent scoping review of research using the ICF found that the ICF has been widely adopted in research and has led to better quality statistics on disability. Of particular note is the important role the ICF has played in monitoring community-based rehabilitation in low-resource settings and its use in policy and programme design and evaluation (e.g. education and social policy). Many countries have used the ICF in new surveys of disability, in particular conceptualizing the activity and participation domains of functioning. However, the authors of the review note that environmental factors have not been well conceptualized or measured (Madden and Bundy 2019).
	Despite the widespread acceptance of ICF as a useful model for the collection of data on disability, it has been operationalized in many different ways, resulting in challenges in the interpretation of disability statistics (Madans et al. 2015; Sabariego et al. 2015). For example, at an international level the Washington Group has developed a short and extended set of questions that can be used in censuses and surveys (see http://www.washingtongroup-disability.com/about/) (Madans et al. 2011; Madans and Loeb 2013). Over 30 countries have used the short set in their census, with the questions now globally endorsed for use in monitoring the Sustainable Development Goals. In parallel, the WHO developed the ‘Model Disability Survey’ (MDS). The MDS is considered a very comprehensive survey with approximately 320 questions and has been piloted in a small number of countries to allow for a more in-depth understanding of disability (WHO 2017a).
	At a country level, a number of countries have developed instruments that broadly capture functioning in an ICF framework. For example, Ireland has developed a National Disability Survey which captures all elements of the ICF, including environmental factors which affect functioning, such as attitudes and flexible working arrangements (Kostanjsek et al. 2013). In Australia, the Australian Bureau of Statistics conducts a comprehensive survey of disability every three years—the Survey of Disability, Ageing, and Carers. This survey includes over 150 questions and provides a comprehensive picture of all aspects of the ICF. They have also produced a short module on disability which is used in a number of other surveys they administer (Harper 2010).





Prevalence of disability


	Comparisons of different surveys designed to collect disability prevalence reveal markedly different prevalence estimates and have demonstrated that the concordance between surveys is poor (Mont 2007). For example, in Australia the prevalence of disability from the Survey of Disability, Ageing, and Carers was 18.3% compared to 6.7% when disability was measured using the Washington Group questions (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2016b). A Norwegian study investigated the prevalence of disability and the concordance based on eight different instruments applied to the same sample. They found that prevalence varied between 10 and 25% with instruments with more questions tending to yield higher estimates (Molden and Tossebro 2010).
	The varying prevalence estimates, and the lack of comparability between the different instruments used to measure disability, presents major challenges for monitoring and evaluation. There is a need for methodological research that seeks to harmonize the different approaches so that disability is consistently captured.
	Figure 10.7.2 shows the prevalence of disability across a selected range of countries that have measured disability using census or survey data. As discussed earlier, the Survey of Disability, and Carers in Australia yields a high prevalence of 18.5%. However, many other countries did not use such a comprehensive set of questions and prevalence was less than 2% in Togo, Iran, Philippines, and Nepal. These low prevalence estimates were ascertained through a single question on the country’s census, which asked if the respondent or a person in the household had a disability, however the exact question varied between countries. For example, in Iran the respondent to the census was asked ‘Is there anybody in the household with at least one of the following disabilities?’ with nine different disability types to select from. In Togo the respondent was asked for each household member ‘Does [person] have a handicap?’ Until more consistent approaches to disability measurement are applied across countries it will be very difficult to make meaningful comparisons between countries.
	Fig. 10.7.2 International prevalence of disability across selected countries.
	* Source data from Loeb (2016, Appendix 1). ^ Source: data from UNESCAP (2015, p.4).





The health of people with disabilities


	People with disabilities generally experience poorer physical and mental health outcomes and have a higher prevalence of health conditions than the general population. People with disabilities are often at higher risk of experiencing secondary health conditions, compounding existing health conditions and disability, as well as increasing the likelihood of experiencing comorbidities such as diabetes and other non-communicable diseases (WHO 2011).
	While it is clear that people with disabilities experience poorer physical and mental health outcomes compared to people without disabilities, there is uncertainty as to the true prevalence of health conditions among people with disabilities due to poor-quality research and data. For example, a systematic review on the prevalence of diabetes among people with intellectual disabilities found that the prevalence ranged from 0.4% to 25% across studies from Europe, North America, New Zealand, Australia, China, and Hong Kong (MacRae et al. 2015). Similarly, a systematic review of mental health conditions among people with intellectual disabilities found the prevalence ranged from between 14% to 75%, again underscoring the challenges in ascertaining true and comparable prevalence estimates (Buckles et al. 2013).
	Despite concerns regarding prevalence measurement of particular conditions, people with disabilities consistently report poorer self-rated health and increased psychological distress. Over half of adults with severe or profound disabilities in Australia reported fair or poor health, compared to only 6% of people without disabilities. Prevalence of psychological distress was also elevated in this group, with 34% experiencing high or very high distress. Only 5% of the population without disabilities experience such high levels of distress, clearly indicating a disparity in mental health (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016b). These findings were replicated in the United States, as researchers found the number of conditions people experienced was directly associated with increased feelings of psychological distress (Okoro et al. 2014). While these perceptions of health and wellbeing are important in their own right, poor psychological wellbeing is associated with a higher prevalence of physical health conditions among people with disabilities, such as coronary heart disease, diabetes, and hypertension (Okoro et al. 2014).
	Health outcomes are also related to health seeking behaviour, which in turn is influenced by disability. In a population-based case-control study in Cameroon and India, people with disabilities were significantly more likely to report significant health problems compared to people without disabilities, yet delayed seeking healthcare. The researchers found that awareness of and access to rehabilitation services were extremely low among people with disabilities (Mactaggart et al. 2016).





Health outcomes among specific groups of people with disabilities


	Health outcomes within population of people with disabilities can vary however, with some population groups experiencing poorer health outcomes than others, depending on the type of disability, severity of disability, and geographic and cultural context. Adults with severe or profound disabilities in Australia for example are over three times as likely to have three or more health conditions, such as back problems, arthritis, and cardiovascular disease, as compared to people without disabilities (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016b). Individuals with particular disability types, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), or intellectual disability, have also been shown to have poorer physical health outcomes relative to the general population. A review of international literature found people with ASD had elevated levels of cardiovascular risk factors and more multimorbidities compared to people without ASD (Cashin et al. 2018).
	People with intellectual disabilities in Scotland were also more likely to have poorer physical health outcomes, with only 39% of individuals reporting no physical health conditions. Overall, people with intellectual disabilities had a higher prevalence of 14 conditions, such as epilepsy, visual impairment, and hearing loss, in comparison with the general population (Cooper et al. 2015). These comorbidities are likely to become even more prevalent as individuals with disabilities age, as shown by research from the Netherlands wherein 80% of adults with intellectual disabilities over the age of 50 reported two or more physical health conditions, compared to 56% of community-dwelling older adults without disabilities (Hermans and Evenhuis 2014).
	As highlighted by a national survey of psychosis in Australia, people with psychosocial disabilities experience higher risk of diabetes, metabolic disorders, heart disease, and obesity. They also have a significantly elevated mortality rate from all these conditions, compared with the general population. Their health outcomes are also impacted upon by the side effects of medication, as well as higher prevalence of drug and alcohol misuse which may aggravate mental health conditions (Morgan et al. 2012; National Mental Health Consumer and Carer Forum 2011; Simonsen et al. 2013). Compounding this is the insufficient resourcing of most mental health systems, and the fact that health practitioners do not always have the skills or resources to address the co-occurring health needs of people with disabilities.
	Not only are people with psychosocial disabilities more likely to experience the ill-effects of co-occurring health conditions, but people with other types of disabilities are disproportionately impacted by certain co-occurring mental health conditions. Approximately 40% of mothers with disabilities in the United States for example, experienced depression prior to their pregnancy, and nearly one-third of women with disabilities reported symptoms of postpartum depression following birth, compared to 16% of women without disabilities (Mitra et al. 2015). Adults with intellectual disabilities in Scotland have a sevenfold increase in the odds of schizophrenia and are twice as likely to have anxiety. Fifteen percent of people with intellectual disabilities were found to have depression, compared to 10% of the general population (Cooper et al. 2015). More generally, half of people with severe or profound disabilities in Australia had at least one mental health condition, compared to 8% of individuals without disability or restrictive long-term health conditions (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016b).





Increased likelihood of engaging in risky health behaviours


	People with disabilities are more likely to engage in some risky health behaviours, which in turn, contribute to poor health outcomes. Important health behaviours impacting people with disabilities include tobacco use, alcohol and substance misuse, and physical inactivity.





Smoking


	Internationally, people with disabilities have higher rates of tobacco use compared to the general population. Across all disability types in the United States, 40% of men and 38% of women with disabilities aged 18–49 were regular smokers, while only 21% of adults without disabilities smoked regularly (Courtney-Long et al. 2014). Patterns are similar in Australia, where 30% of adults with severe or profound disabilities smoke; twice that of the general population (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016b). People with disabilities are also less likely to report trying to quit smoking. In the Republic of Korea for example, 55% of adults without disabilities who smoked regularly made a past-year quit attempt, while only 45% of individuals with disabilities did (Lee et al. 2014b). Less than 20% of people with mobility impairments in the United States attempted to quit in the last year, compared to 27% in the general population (Borrelli et al. 2014).





Alcohol use


	By contrast, people with disabilities appear to consume less alcohol than the general population (Glazier and Kling 2013; Pinquart and Pfeiffer 2015; Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016b; Mitra et al. 2016). However, people with disabilities have an increased use of other substances. In the United States, the prevalence of any substance misuse in the past month, including prescription or illicit drugs, binge alcohol, or habitual cigarette smoking, is 40% for people with disabilities, and 34% for people without disabilities.





Substance misuse


	Individual with disabilities in the United States have higher odds for using substances such as heroin, oxycodone, sedatives, and methamphetamine (Glazier and Kling 2013). Research into substance misuse has been less indicative for people with specific disability types, such as intellectual disabilities. While evidence from the United States suggests the overall prevalence of substance misuse is low among people with intellectual disabilities, the risk of developing a substance-related problem is comparatively high (Carroll Chapman 2013). As lower cognitive function is associated with increased drop-out from treatment (Brorson et al. 2013), issues relating to substance abuse may be particularly challenging to measure and treat among people with intellectual disabilities, as well as other disability groups.
	When asked about substance misuse and treatment, people with physical disabilities in the United States were less likely to have received helpful treatment for substance misuse issues, with 50% reporting useful treatment compared to 57% of the general population (Anderson et al. 2014).





Physical inactivity


	Participation in physical activity is an additional key concern for people with disabilities, as many individuals have very limited support or opportunity to engage in physical activity. Across all people 15–64 years with severe or profound disabilities in Australia for example, 46% reported no past-year physical activity. By comparison, 31% of people without disability reported no physical exercise (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016b). Similarly, 30% of adults with disabilities 20 years and older in the Republic of Korea did not participate in physical activity within the last year (Kim et al. 2015). Rates of physical activity are especially poor for people with particular types of disability, such as people with intellectual disabilities. Only 9% of adults with intellectual disabilities met minimum physical activity guidelines, according to a recent systematic review (Dairo et al. 2016). This pattern extends to children with disabilities, who also have lower rates of physical activity. For example, 70% of children with disabilities in the Netherlands did not participate in organized sports, and 80% played sports either not at all, or for less than 1 hour per week (Neter et al. 2011).





Disability and the social determinants of health


	So why are the health behaviours and outcomes of people with disabilities so much poorer than people without disabilities? This can be answered in part by exploring the social determinants of health for people with disabilities. As discussed, disability is not simply the result of a particular impairment or condition. Rather, the experience of disability is largely determined by society and the environment. The social determinants of health reflect this by illuminating external factors which impact the circumstances, opportunities, and perception of a particular person (Emerson et al. 2011). Social determinants, such as violence, poverty, education and employment, and stigma and discrimination are crucial in understanding the experiences and health outcomes of people with disabilities.
	It is likewise imperative to understand the processes by which people with disabilities are excluded from health systems, including public health, to the detriment of their health, wellbeing, and disability. International research continues to highlight that people with disabilities experience ongoing inequalities in relation to socioeconomic status, employment, educational attainments, lack of access to accessible and appropriate housing and surrounding environments, and restricted access to services (Groce et al. 2011; WHO 2011; Byrne 2018). These inequalities play a major role in influencing health behaviours and outcomes for people with disabilities.
	Emerson et al. (2011) offer a useful explanation of how the relationship between disability and the social determinants of health are often established at an early age and differ across the life course. For young children, the most relevant social determinants often relate to ‘material and psychosocial’ hazards (e.g. poor housing, poor diet, economic insecurity, family violence, stressful life events, lack of supportive relationships with adults). As children age, these social determinants may be exacerbated by the costs of caring for a child with disabilities. Adults with disabilities face exclusion from the labour force which may exacerbate existing social and economic challenges. While the mechanisms for these associations are not fully understood, it is clear that children and adults with disabilities are at increased risk of exposure to poorer living and working conditions and greater economic insecurity, which are associated with poorer health outcomes (Emerson et al. 2011).





Poverty and disability


	Globally, people with disabilities are more likely to live in poverty compared to people without disabilities, and the situation appears to be worsening. In the United States, the overall poverty rate has increased for all individuals, but most dramatically for people with disabilities. Twenty-five per cent of people with disabilities were in poverty in 1981, rising to 32% in 2014 (Brucker and Houtenville 2015).
	The link between poverty and disability is also evident in low and middle-income countries (LMICs), where a systematic review found over 80% of included studies identified a positive relationship between disability and poverty. Notably, the severity of disability was associated with the severity of economic poverty. The authors found the observed relationship remained despite adjustment for age, gender, area of residence, and education. This trend was consistent throughout regions across the globe, impairment types, study designs, and age groups (Banks et al. 2017).
	Poverty among people with disabilities in LMICs has persisted despite many countries making gains in addressing poverty more broadly. In Cambodia for example, the country has made significant progress in addressing poverty through sustained economic growth and the implementation of social protection programmes. Poverty rates have declined over the past decade from estimates of 47% of the population in 2007, to current estimates of 13.5% (National Institute of Statistics et al. 2015; World Bank 2018a; b). However, reductions in poverty are not equal across households with and without family members with disabilities.
	This situation was highlighted in a study analysing the Cambodian SocioEconomic Survey data from 2009 to 2014 (National Institute of Statistics et al. 2015). Analysis found that the poverty rate among households with members with disabilities was 18%, compared to 13.6% for households without any members with disabilities. When the cost of disability incurred by households was included in the analysis, the poverty rate for households with a member with disabilities increased to 34%. An additional 17% of household income was required in order to achieve the same standard of living as similar households without disabilities (Palmer et al. 2016). The limited household resources of families who have a family member with a disability make it more difficult to meet the costs of accessing services, such as health and education (UNESCAP 2015).
	Poverty, health, and disability are clearly inter-related. In the UK, it has been found that the greater risk of exposure to socioeconomic disadvantage may constitute 20–50% of the risk of decreased physical and mental health among children with intellectual disabilities (Emerson et al. 2011). Similarly, a cross-sectional survey of English men and women with mild and moderate intellectual disabilities found that self-rated health was strongly associated with material hardship, with individuals who had experienced material hardship in the past year more likely to report ‘not good health’ (Emerson and Hatton 2008). Most high income countries have income support for people with disability who are unable to work however many low-to-middle-income countries do not have such a safety net putting people with disability at even higher risk of poverty and ill-health (WHO 2011).





Access to nutrition


	People with disabilities, especially children, experience poorer nutritional status than people without disabilities. Malnutrition and disability are intimately linked—with malnutrition contributing to the risk of impairment, and children with disabilities thought to be more at risk of experiencing malnutrition. The risk of malnutrition is often assumed to be linked to difficulty with feeding, or that children with disabilities are more likely to be unwell which impacts on their ability to eat. While these are important factors, a study conducted in Kenya in 2013 found malnutrition was also related to neglect, lack of awareness of the need for greater nutritional intake that some children with disabilities have, and intentional underfeeding (Groce et al. 2014; International Centre for Evidence in Disability et al. 2014). Identifying malnutrition in children with disabilities can also be challenging given certain impairments may impact on physical growth. As such it can be difficult to accurately use traditional malnutrition assessments such as measuring the mid-upper arm circumference. This may hinder the identification of malnutrition among children with disabilities and reduce the likelihood of timely and adequate treatment for malnutrition.
	Possible outcomes of poor diet and malnutrition include poorer health outcomes, missing or delay in developmental milestones, acquiring avoidable secondary conditions, stunting and wasting, and preventable death (Groce et al. 2014; International Centre for Evidence in Disability et al. 2014). Researchers in Iran found that more than 40% of girls and boys with disabilities assessed were underweight, while stunting was present in 42% of children with disabilities in the study. Notably, only 6% of children without disabilities were underweight. Further, 90% of the children with disabilities did not receive adequate vitamins and minerals, such as iron and calcium (Neyestani et al. 2010). In the Netherlands, children with disabilities were less likely to have breakfast, and were four and a half times less likely to eat fruit on all weekdays (Neter et al. 2011). Children with intellectual disabilities in France were also found to have poorer diets, with nearly half consuming soft drinks with meals at school, compared to only a quarter of students without disabilities (Mikulovic et al. 2011). Young people with intellectual disabilities in Taiwan also had a poorer diet, eating fewer fresh fruits and vegetables than their peers without disabilities (Yen and Lin 2010).
	Poorer diet and lower rates of physical activity contribute to the higher prevalence of obesity and being overweight observed among adults and children with disabilities, particularly in high income countries. Forty-five per cent (45%) of adults with upper or lower limb disabilities in the Republic of Korea for example are reported to be obese (Oh et al. 2012), and nearly 80% of adults aged 18–65 with intellectual disabilities in the United States are reported to be overweight or obese (Barnes et al. 2013). Among school children in Northern Ireland, 33% of students with intellectual disabilities were overweight or obese, compared to 24% of their peers without disabilities (Slevin et al. 2014). In the Netherlands, 31% of children with disabilities were overweight, compared to 10% of children without disabilities. The difference in the prevalence of obesity was likewise striking, as 11% of children with disabilities were obese, compared to only 2% of children without disabilities (Neter et al. 2011).





Exclusion from education and work


	People with disabilities in both LMICs and high-income countries (HICs) experience many barriers to education and to gaining and maintaining work (Saleh and Bruyere 2018). In relation to education, these inequalities arise due to negative attitudes or low expectations of the benefits of education for children with disabilities, the absence of necessary adjustments and accommodations, and limited access to inclusive education. In terms of employment, low expectations about the capacity of people with disabilities within the workplace, restricted access to important career development opportunities such as training and skills development, insufficient support to gain and maintain work, and precarious engagement with labour market (e.g. underemployment, insecure employment, exploitation) are major barriers (Saleh and Bruyere 2018).
	People with disabilities in Guatemala for example, expressed their frustration at the unattainability of education, a result of poverty, social invisibility and stigma, and structural barriers to access. Lack of education was perceived as a primary barrier to alleviating poverty (Grech 2014). Alternatively, evidence from Nepal, Bangladesh, Cambodia, and the Philippines suggest that longer years of education significantly increase the opportunity for people with disabilities to get a job and engage in full time, white collar jobs, reducing the risk of poverty, improving participation and access to better health (Lamichhane 2015).
	From the employment statistics of people with disabilities in the United States, it is clear that barriers to employment are still present. Full time, full year employment for people with disabilities has decreased markedly over time, from 12% in 1981 to less than 6% in 2014. For those employed, median earnings are $10,000 USD less for people with disabilities (Brucker and Houtenville 2015).
	Similarly, of the 18.3% or 4.2 million Australians living with disabilities, only 53.4% are currently in the labour force (e.g. employed or looking for work). This is compared to 83.2% of Australians without disabilities. The unemployment rate for Australians with disabilities is 10%, nearly double the rate of that for Australians without disabilities (5.3%) (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2016a). Stigma and discrimination are recognized as one of the major barriers to improving employment outcomes for Australians with disabilities (Australian Human Rights Commission 2016). When people with disabilities are employed, they are often in insecure work, have poorer working conditions, less perceived fairness of pay and are more likely to be underemployed (LaMontagne et al. 2016; Milner et al. 2015; Milner et al. 2017).
	Likewise in the UK, adults with intellectual disabilities are more likely to be in non-standard employment and experience job insecurity. They are also more likely to transition into economic inactivity from standard employment (Emerson et al. 2018). Stigma and structural barriers also constituted major barriers to employment in Brazil. People with disabilities who did gain employment were typically paid less and given less skilled work, as their abilities were persistently doubted (Toldra and Santos 2013).
	Additionally, people with disabilities struggle to enter the workplace, as shown by a study of young people with disabilities in Canada. Overwhelmingly, young people with disabilities had significantly poorer work and job search experiences. Eighty-three per cent of young people with learning or memory impairments were refused an interview, and 63% of young adults with mobility impairments were denied workplace accommodations. 77% of young people with learning or memory impairments reported discrimination at work due to their disability (Lindsay 2011).
	Using longitudinal data from the US, the authors found that a third of young people with ASD had attended college (34.7%) and just over half had been in paid employment within the first 6 years after high school (55.1%). Over half of youth with ASD who had left high school in the past two years had no participation in employment or education. The authors found that young people with ASD had the lowest rate of employment participation and the highest rates of no participation as compared to young people with other disabilities (Shattuck et al. 2012).





Housing and the surrounding environment


	Accessible, affordable, and secure housing are key determinants of health (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016a). Conversely, reduced access to safe and accessible housing disproportionately impacts on the social and health outcomes of people with disabilities (Beer and Faulkner 2009). Researchers from Victoria, Australia found that people with disabilities were substantially less likely to own a home and were much more likely to experience housing stress and live in rental accommodation than the general public. People with disabilities may be additionally hampered in their access to safe and accessible housing due to restrictions imposed by availability of transportation systems and access to services. Housing that is safe, accessible, and close to transportation and services may require people with disabilities to move away from family and friends, thereby leading to isolation from support networks (Beer and Faulkner 2009).
	Community living is known to be essential for social inclusion and a key element of quality of life. Deinstitutionalisation has continued to occur in most countries, but this has not been sufficiently replaced with resources to support independent living within the community for people with disabilities. As such, adequate housing within the community remains out of reach for many people with disabilities, particularly for people with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities (Siska et al. 2018).
	The surrounding environment to where people live and work is also important. A qualitative survey of adults with a variety of different disabilities and functional limitations in the US analysed the environmental factors influencing participation at the individual community, and societal levels. The eight major categories of factors were: built environment, natural environment, transportation, assistive technology, IT access, social support and societal attitudes, systems and policies, and economic environment. Particularly poignant was one participant’s description of the immense process and organization that facilitates participation, wherein having physical access (such as a ramp) is not enough when one must consider the weather, if the personal assistant will come, if sidewalks and ramps are clear outdoors, and if transportation will arrive. This work highlights the interconnected nature of environmental barriers on health and participation. Individuals expressed a desire to work but were concerned that they would lose their disability pension, and if they lost their job, they would have no income at all. Individuals discussed challenges with negative, disabling societal attitudes, and of the importance of social facilitators such as a supportive family. The researchers emphasize that barriers can, and must, be addressed at the societal, community, and individual levels in order to positively influence participation (Hammel et al. 2015).





Violence


	Globally, people with disabilities are disproportionately affected by violence. Despite this, violence prevention and response programmes all too often have neglected the needs or excluded people with disabilities, or do not understand how to accommodate or respond to the people with disabilities who have experienced violence (Devine et al. 2017). Twenty-eight per cent of people with disabilities in the United States have experienced intimate partner violence (Mitra and Mouradian 2014), and evidence from a systematic review of violence found people with disabilities were 50% more likely to experience violence compared to people without disabilities (Hughes et al. 2012). One-quarter of people with mental illness have experienced recent physical, sexual, or intimate partner violence (Hughes et al. 2012).
	Women with disabilities are particularly at risk. In Australia, women with disabilities have a twofold increase in the odds of experiencing physical violence, intimate partner violence, emotional abuse, and stalking and harassment compared to women without disabilities (Krnjacki et al. 2016). In the United States, women with disabilities were fourfold as likely to experience rape and threefold as likely to experience other sexual violence as compared to women without disabilities (Breiding and Armour 2015).
	Violence against people with disabilities is similarly prevalent in lower income countries. Eighty-four per cent of women with disabilities involved in a survey of disability and violence in Bangladesh had experienced at least one act of violence or abuse (Hasan et al. 2014). These experiences were echoed in Nepal and Cambodia, where nearly 60% of women with disabilities had ever experienced violence (Astbury and Walji 2014; Puri et al. 2015). Despite the alarmingly high prevalence of violence towards people with disabilities, especially women, a recent evaluation of interventions found that there is currently no clear evidence on the type of approaches that work to reduce violence (Mikton et al. 2014).





Stigma and discrimination


	Stigma and discrimination play a key role in all the barriers encountered by people with disabilities. The negative attitudes of society at large exclude people with disabilities from education, employment, and healthcare, as shown throughout this chapter. Stigma deprives people with disabilities of their independence and rights, as discussed by individuals in a study from Croatia, who typically have little say in their education, employment, or sexual and reproductive health (Buljevac et al. 2012). Negative attitudes have also been found to be the major barrier for people with disabilities in the Philippines to participate in work, community meetings and social activities (Marella et al. 2016). Stigma also contributes to neglect and exclusion, such as in the Solomon Islands, where children with disabilities are seen as a punishment for violating a taboo (Gartrell et al. 2018).
	Stigma and exclusion trap people with disabilities in poverty (Grech 2014; Trani et al. 2015). For example, a study on people with severe mental illness in India highlights this ‘negative feedback loop’ wherein individuals with severe mental illness face stigma, especially for individuals from lower castes. This stigma, combined with the educational and employment limitations imposed on people from lower castes, feeds persistent poverty, decreases social involvement and self-esteem, and poses additional responsibilities on carers, further contributing to stigma and discrimination (Trani et al. 2015).
	In summary, while public health action is needed across a multitude of health-related areas, eliminating the disparities in the social determinants and resultant health of people with disabilities can only be done through addressing stigma, prejudice, and discrimination and the subsequent exclusion experienced by people with disabilities.





Inclusion of people with disabilities within public health


	The number of people living with disabilities is likely to increase in both LMIC and HIC over time due to communicable and non-communicable diseases; road traffic accidents and injuries; longer life expectancies/ageing; conflict; natural disasters; and growing socioeconomic inequities experienced in many countries (Marmot et al. 2010; WHO 2011; Mannan and MacLachlan 2013; Krahn et al. 2015; Durham et al. 2016). Exclusion from public health interventions, combined with the greater unmet health needs and barriers to health services of an increasing number of people with disabilities, will lead to poorer health outcomes at an individual and population level (Durham et al. 2016; Marella et al. 2016). This highlights the urgent need for public health and health systems more broadly to ensure people with disabilities are better included in and benefit from all aspects of public health.
	This will require both disability-specific initiatives and disability-inclusive programmes. Disability-specific initiatives are designed to target people with disabilities directly, for example capacity development for people with disabilities to better understand the risks of certain health behaviours, promoting access to physical activity and recreation for people with disabilities, or, providing outreach screening programmes for people with disabilities who are not able to travel to health services. Disability-inclusive programmes are mainstream activities designed to ensure that they are accessible to people with disabilities and that they benefit people with and without disabilities equally (Kleinitz et al. 2011; Piatta and Guy 2010). Examples include health promotion messaging designed to include representation of people with disabilities which is accessible in a range of communication formats (e.g. Braille, easy-to-understand) (Piatta and Guy 2010; Kleinitz et al. 2011). Even with appropriate messaging, people with disabilities may experience additional barriers to making healthy choices due to issues such as mobility (e.g. unable to access parks, public transport, shops), difficulty to reading information (e.g. food labels) due to vision or cognitive impairments and community attitudes towards people with disabilities accessing resources in their community.
	It also requires barriers to all aspects of public health and health systems experienced by people with disabilities to be identified and addressed. The section to follow focuses on key components of public health, outlining some of the barriers experienced by people with disabilities, as well as examples of how these barriers can be addressed.





Health promotion and prevention


	Disease prevention, including screening for cancer and immunization, are crucial components of primary healthcare for all people. However, people with disabilities do not always receive disease prevention services to the same extent individuals without disabilities do. Access to disease prevention, especially screening, is often difficult, particularly for women with disabilities. Costs for screening may not be available through universal healthcare and costs may be prohibitive. Women with disabilities frequently report that medical professionals do not understand their disabilities, putting women in a position where they must explain themselves and advocate for their own care (Ramjan et al. 2016). Disability-specific information is typically unavailable for screening processes, (Angus et al. 2012) and most healthcare providers report they need substantial additional training in order to provide adequate preventive care for people with disabilities (Merten et al. 2015).
	Data from a national health survey in the United States revealed that women with disabilities are less likely to be up-to-date with cervical and breast cancer screening. Only two-thirds of women with mobility impairments were estimated to have received a Pap test within the previous three years, and 61% of women with cognitive limitations received a mammogram within the last two years. By comparison, 81% of women without disabilities had an up-to-date Pap test, and 73% had had a recent mammogram (Steele et al. 2017). Women in the United States with more complex, and more severe, disabilities are consistently less likely to be up-to-date with cancer screening (Horner-Johnson et al. 2014).
	While breast and cervical cancer screening rates among women with disabilities are still lower than those of women without disabilities, there is some evidence for the effectiveness of educational programmes in increasing cancer screening rates among women with disabilities. Women Be Healthy 2, an educational programme about mammography and Pap tests, was appropriate for women with disabilities as materials were created to be hands-on, multimodal, and accessible to people with low literacy (Swaine et al. 2014). Similarly, a DVD about mammography preparedness for women with intellectual disabilities starred an actress with intellectual disability confidently navigating her first mammography appointment (Greenwood et al. 2014). Both programmes showed increases in cancer screening knowledge among participants. Despite small sample sizes, these programmes suggest that appropriate educational and support resources can help women with disabilities increase their knowledge of, and ability to access, cancer screening. For another example of disability-inclusive screening programmes, see the Case Study 10.7.1 next.
	Encouraging research from the United States on colorectal cancer screening suggests similar rates of testing between people with and without disabilities, and that where disparities exist, people with disabilities are actually screened more (Iezzoni et al. 2016). While the exact explanation for good uptake of colorectal cancer screening among people with disabilities are unclear, increased contact with physicians, who may follow-up to ensure screening is completed, may be an important driver of this trend.
	 	CASE STUDY 10.7.1 Just checking: increasing cancer screening for people with disabilities
	While people with disabilities have generally lower cancer screening rates, the literature indicates mixed outcomes regarding immunization rates. Older people with disabilities in the United States were more likely to have received a flu vaccine in the past year and a pneumonia vaccine than their peers without disabilities (Pharr and Bungum 2012). Researchers in remote Ecuador found that children with disabilities were immunized at rates comparable with their siblings without disability, highlighting the effectiveness of the national immunization programme and importance of positive cultural attitudes towards disability (Groce et al. 2007). The relative ease of giving vaccinations, which typically do not require special equipment, may positively influence vaccination rates. However, some groups of people with disabilities, such as individuals with intellectual disabilities, may have vaccination rates lower than the general population. Data from Taiwan has shown that teenagers with intellectual disabilities were vaccinated against Hepatitis B at lower rates than the general population (Yen and Lin 2011). Young people with intellectual disabilities in Taiwan were also less likely to have received a flu vaccine than older people and very young children, although individuals with moderate and severe intellectual disabilities were more likely to have received the vaccine than individuals with mild intellectual disabilities (Yen et al. 2012; CDC 2010 cited in Yen et al. 2012). This suggests that although regular contact with the medical system may positively influence vaccination rates, people with disabilities do not consistently receive the same level of immunization as the general population.
	Despite these factors, people with disabilities may be less likely to receive vaccinations associated with sensitive issues, such as sex and sexuality. Providers of the human papilloma virus (HPV) vaccination in the United States reported the main reason children with disabilities were not vaccinated was due to parental refusal (Cody and Lerand 2013). As such, immunization rates may differ between people with and without disabilities depending on the acceptability of particular vaccinations and (mis)perceptions about the relevance for people with disabilities. Identifying barriers to HPV vaccination among people with disabilities is critical and strategies to improve uptake of HPV need to be developed.
	Health promotion is an area which requires significant new research and investment to improve diet, increase physical activity and reduce smoking rates. Despite the higher prevalence of smoking among people with disabilities, there are few programmes and little literature on successful tobacco cessation approaches and programmes, contributing to the decreased rate of quit attempts by people with disabilities. It is clear, however, that people with disabilities have a desire to quit: nearly 90% of people with mobility impairments in a study from the United States planned to quit within six months (Borrelli et al. 2013).
	Some initial evidence from small tobacco cessation programmes in the United States emphasizes the importance of tailoring programmes to people with disabilities, through disability-specific examples and discussion of disability-relevant issues, such as the interaction between nicotine replacement therapy and medication (Pomeranz 2014; King et al. 2016). While these suggestions provide a foundation for creating effective cessation programmes, it is obvious people with disabilities are underserved in this area.
	A recent review of intervention research focused on improving physical activity levels found that research in this area is increasing. Interventions were predominantly individually focused on behaviour change with mean incorporating technologies (e.g. information and interactive technologies). Most studies showed positive outcomes however 60% of studies were of groups were multiple sclerosis (41%), stroke (15%), and spinal cord injury (12%) limiting the generalisability of findings (Lai et al. 2017). Further research is needed with people with other types of disability. Research should also concentrate on how population-based interventions in the general population can be adapted to be more appropriate and relevant to people with disability.





Access to health services


	Access to healthcare services is a substantial issue for people with disabilities across the globe. The poorer physical and mental health outcomes of people with disabilities, as well as poorer health behaviours and discrepancies in disease prevention services, are related to barriers to health services. While the experiences and health of people with disabilities may vary widely across countries, issues of transport, lack and/or inaccessible health facilities and equipment (including toilets), discrimination by health workers, and cost of services and travelling to services are routinely reported as major barriers. Similarly, lack of knowledge on when, where and how to access health services, and inaccessible information and health messaging compound these barriers (MacLachlan et al. 2011; Kleinitz et al. 2012; Van Rooy et al. 2012; Vaughan et al. 2016).
	Research from various contexts demonstrates these barriers. Nearly 15% of people with disabilities in the Republic of Korea for example reported difficulty accessing healthcare in the preceding year, with approximately 60% citing cost as their primary barrier to care (Lee et al. 2014a). Qualitative work in Namibia found cost was also a significant barrier to care for people with disabilities, although interviewees cited transport as the main barrier. Nearly 90% of respondents with disabilities reported walking, sometimes hours, to healthcare centres due to prohibitively expensive transport fees. For those who were able to reach the clinics, additional obstacles to care included language differences, a shortage of healthcare workers, and inaccessible facilities (Van Rooy et al. 2012).
	Further qualitative work in Sudan, Namibia, Malawi, and South Africa reinforced these barriers, and respondents discussed problems with inaccessible equipment and poor availability of services (Eide et al. 2015). Children with disabilities and their parent carers in rural and remote Australia reported similar challenges in accessibility of health services due to long travel times and lack of services (Dew et al. 2013).
	In addition to these barriers to general medical care, individuals often face further difficulties to effective sexual and reproductive care. Often policies and strategies do not recognize the unique needs of males and females with disabilities and community perceptions may hold that people with disabilities are asexual or hypersexual. In Ghana, men and women with disabilities are typically grouped together as a homogenous group, despite differences in needs. The use of derogatory language, like ‘idiot’, when describing men and women with disabilities was found to further contribute to stigma and control over their sexual and reproductive health needs (Mprah et al. 2014).
	Stigmatizing attitudes may also prohibit people with disabilities from having access to information about sexual health and reproduction, as was reported by people with physical disabilities in Vietnam (Nguyen et al. 2018). These negative attitudes, and the ubiquitous belief that sexuality and reproduction are taboo for people with disabilities can be further seen in a study of access to services in Uganda. Women with disabilities reported extreme stigma surrounding their pregnancy and sexuality due to their disabilities. Male partners with disabilities described total exclusion from the pregnancy and childbirth, as they were offered no assistance to reach antenatal and birthing wards on upper floors of the hospital (Ahumuza et al. 2014).
	Pregnant women in higher income countries, such as the United States, still face humiliation and embarrassment in the doctor’s office, such as when being transferred to inaccessible equipment, such as examination tables that cannot be adjusted for height (Iezzoni et al. 2015). For a case study on an effective sexual and reproductive health programme for women with disabilities, please refer to Case Study 10.7.2.
	 	CASE STUDY 10.7.2 Promoting inclusive public health programmes





Women with Disability taking Action on REproductive and sexual health—W-DARE project


	Compounding disability and gender based discrimination often mean that women with disabilities experience exclusion from the socioeconomic and political lives of their communities. Similarly, women with disabilities face barriers to accessing public health programmes such as health information, screening, prevention, and care services, as well as violence prevention and response programmes. As a result, women with disabilities experience poorer health outcomes across their life cycle when compared to women without disabilities, including in relation to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and violence (MacLachlan and Swartz 2009; Lee et al. 2015; Vaughan et al. 2015; Marella et al. 2016; Vaughan et al. 2016; Devine et al. 2017).
	Limited data, particularly from LMIC, on the prevalence of disability and the lived experience of women with disabilities in relation to their health and access to programmes, also makes it difficult to plan and resource disability-inclusive public health programmes. The W-DARE project in the Philippines is one of the few examples of inclusive action research that has been undertaken to increase demand for and supply of quality SRH services and information for women with disabilities.
	W-DARE was a 3-year project conducted by the University of Melbourne in Australia and De La Salle University in the Philippines, in collaboration with the Likhaan Center for Women’s Health; Center for Women’s Studies Foundation at the University of the Philippines; and two national disabled people’s organizations (DPOs)—WOWLEAP (Women with disabilities Leap social and economic progress) and PARE (Persons with disability Advocating for Rights and Empowerment). Women with disabilities were resourced as co-researchers across the project, ensuring their lived experience informed the design, implementation, and evaluation of the project (Vaughan et al. 2015).
	Key findings from phase one of the research highlighted women with disabilities reported poorer wellbeing when compared to women without disabilities, and were more likely to report reduced access to health services, work, education, and social activities. Barriers to inclusion reported included cost of services, lack of information about services, and difficulty getting to health facilities. Levels of SRH knowledge were generally low, especially among women who are Deaf or hard of hearing and women with intellectual disabilities. Specific barriers to SRH services reported by women with disabilities included discrimination; limited capacity of service providers; inaccessible transport; economic barriers; and difficulty accessing sign language interpreters. Reports of violence and abuse against women with disabilities were common. What was also evident was the resilience of many of the women with disabilities interviewed.
	In response, the W-DARE team developed and implemented a number of interventions aimed at promoting access to quality SRH programmes. Demand side interventions included peer-facilitated Participatory Action Groups for women with disabilities to enhance knowledge and demand for SRH services and develop networks of peer support. Supply side interventions included workshops for service providers to increase awareness of the needs and rights of women with disabilities; collaboration with the Department of Health to increase disability inclusion in primary healthcare settings; project partner exchange visits to share experiences of disability inclusiveness within local health and development programmes; and, working with violence prevention and response services to strengthen disability inclusion including through referral practices. Recognition that sustained change requires a major shift in society’s perception of disability, led to the production of a number of social media videos of women with disabilities talking about their lives and their rights.
	The W-DARE interventions led to positive outcomes for women with disabilities and highlighted that increased access to information on rights and disability inclusion for both women with disabilities and service providers; enhanced social networks and opportunities for social inclusion for women with disabilities; and consumer participation in the design of more inclusive health services, are essential for upholding the right to SRH for women with disabilities.
	For the W-DARE project to have a sustained impact however, it is vital address systemic barriers to participation in all other life domains experienced by women with disabilities such as education, employment and general health programmes are addressed This will require governments, service providers, DPOs, public health and development programmers to work collaboratively with women with disabilities to identify context-specific barriers and solutions to promote inclusion of people with disabilities within their communities.





Health-related rehabilitation


	While not relevant for all people with disabilities, health-related rehabilitation is not only an important right articulated in the CRPD, but recognized as a key component of Primary Health Care and a critical part of the broader health system (Pryor et al. 2017; Bezmez et al. 2018). However, many people with disabilities, particularly those living in LMICs, have limited access to health-related rehabilitation services, resulting in unmet health and rehabilitation needs, reduced social and economic participation, and reduced quality of life (Gargett et al. 2016; Pryor et al. 2017; WHO 2017b).
	Similar to broader health services, individual level barriers to rehabilitation services in LMICs include difficulty travelling long distances to services when roads and transport are often inaccessible or unaffordable and services are mainly located in urban areas, such as was identified by Gargett et al. in their review of rehabilitation workforce needs in the Pacific (Gargett et al. 2016); the prohibitive cost of rehabilitation services and assistive devices as identified by Palmer et al. in their study of the economic challenges experienced by people with disabilities in Vietnam (Palmer et al. 2015); and lack of knowledge on when, where, and how to access rehabilitation services, such as highlighted by Mactaggart in their study of access to health and rehabilitation services in Cameroon and India (Mactaggart et al. 2016).
	At a systems level, access to rehabilitation is hampered by the neglect of rehabilitation within broader health systems strengthening efforts (Pryor et al. 2017); lack of rehabilitation specialists within an already limited pool of health workers who can respond to the rehabilitation needs of people with disabilities (Gargett et al. 2016); limited inclusion of measures of disability and rehabilitation within Health information Systems in many low-and middle-income countries (McPherson et al. 2017); and extensive gaps within referral processes across and within health systems (WHO 2017b).
	As like all public health interventions that aim to improve the capacity to meet the needs of people with disabilities, health-related rehabilitation services need to actively and respectfully involve people with disabilities in all aspects of decision making and service delivery; and, ensure a holistic understanding of rehabilitation that responds to the complex needs of individuals (Bezmez et al. 2018).





Health information systems and data transparency for monitoring and evaluation


	There is still a need for greater context-specific information on the lived experience of people with disabilities in relation to their health and inclusion within the public health sphere (Vaughan et al. 2016). Very few health systems in LMIC and HIC collect information on people with disabilities and their access to health. For example, a study of health information systems in Lao found indicators related to disability or functioning were not included, and overall health data was often incomplete, inaccurate or poorly used (Durham et al. 2016). This makes it difficult to monitor progress in access or health outcomes. Enhancing the focus on disability within public health could provide an opportunity to strengthen health information systems (Durham et al. 2016).
	Similar to the issue of measurement of disability more broadly, this requires an accepted definition of disability and standard measure of disability that health information systems can readily and affordably adopt. As highlighted earlier, better disability measures within population and health surveys are also required to better monitor health behaviours, health outcomes, access to health and impact of disability on other key domains such as education and employment (Durham et al. 2016). In Australia the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare have developed a set of questions that can be routinely implemented in administrative data (such as primary care and hospitals). It is hoped in the future that the implementation of these questions will enable enhanced monitoring and evaluation of health service use for people with disabilities (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2016c).





Disability services and supports


	Disability services and supports (both within and external to health systems) for people with disabilities are critical for health and wellbeing. Services and supports include personal assistance with self-care (e.g. dressing, eating, showering) as well as support to participate in the community and paid and unpaid work. Access to therapeutic supports such as speech therapy is also critical to enabling people with disabilities to attain their potential. Basic supports such as hearing aids and wheelchairs are also critical for full participation in society. New technologies such as robots (van den Heuvel et al. 2017), IT assisted technologies including smartphone apps (Mavrou et al. 2017), and technological innovation in assisted and augmented communication (Miksztai-Rethey and Farago 2018) hold considerable promise for improving participation and access to health. In all settings, including education, workplaces, and health services, reasonable adjustments and accommodations are critical to enable people with disabilities to access and participate. This can range from ramps and lifts to improve the physical accessibility, to flexible working conditions, such as working from home. Further, ensuring the development, implementation and monitoring of workplace disability strategies (including mental health) will not only promote healthier workplaces, but will promote better understanding of the importance of inclusion (International Labour Office et al. 2014).
	Internationally, disability services are often underfunded and poorly resourced with considerable inequities in access to services. Approaches to the funding and delivery of services vary widely. Given the barriers that many people with disabilities experience in accessing mainstream services, one of the most important approaches to improving health and social outcomes in LMIC is community-based rehabilitation (CBR). CBR is a multisectoral approach to improve the equalization of opportunities for, and social inclusion of, persons with disabilities. CBR is implemented through the combined efforts of people with disabilities, their families and communities, and relevant government and non-government health, education, vocational, social, and other sectors (WHO 2010).
	In Cambodia for example, a number of non-government organizations have been working with communities in rural and remote areas to improve understanding of disability, promote early identification, and, develop locally based approaches to support people with disabilities and their families to address impairment related conditions (i.e. through training families on appropriate rehabilitation techniques and exercises that they can do with their family members with disabilities), and, working with local authorities and other stakeholders to promote community inclusion (i.e. promoting access to local schools). The government of Cambodia has been working with these organizations to develop National CBR guidelines. As with many countries of all income levels, sustainable financial and human resources is an ongoing challenge (Bailey and Nguon 2014).
	A review of disability services in Australia by the Productivity Commission found that services were ‘inequitable, underfunded, fragmented, and inefficient and give people with disabilities little choice’. The Commission recommended a doubling of funding and significant changes to how services were provided (Productivity Commission 2011). This led to the introduction of the National Disability Insurance Scheme which provides individuals with disability-individual budgets and they can purchase the services and support they need. See Case Study 10.7.3.
	 	CASE STUDY 10.7.3 Australia’s National Disability Insurance Schemes
	Prior to the introduction of the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) in Australia, the disability services were delivered by state and territory government and access, quality and coverage varied significantly between states. Funding was provided by the federal government to the states and territories to fund disability services but the delivery of services was a state or territory responsibility. This meant that service access varied according to what state people lived in and whether they lived in cities or rural and remote areas and there was no guarantee of long-term security of funding. People also had little choice of the services they were provided.
	The Productivity Commission of Australia was tasked with reviewing the current disability service system and to consider alternative models of delivery. In particular they considered the implementation of personalized budgets, such as introduced in the United Kingdom, where people with disabilities and their families and carers are provided with individual budgets, depending on their particular support needs, to buy the services and supports they need (Needham and Dickinson 2017). The Commission also recommended the adoption of an insurance approach whereby people with disability are assured of funding to cover the lifetime costs of their disability. The Productivity Commission recommended the implementation of the National Disability Insurance Scheme and a doubling of funding to the disability service sector (Productivity Commission 2011).
	The Productivity Commission recommended that the NDIS include three tiers of support.
	Tier 1 provides insurance (i.e. guaranteed support) for all Australians who acquire a significant disability. Tier 1 was also designed to promote opportunities for people with disability to participate in the community.
	Tier 2 included anyone with a disability and their primary carers (estimated by the Productivity Commission at around 4.8 million people). Tier 2 involves working with mainstream services, provided information and referral services.
	Tier 3 involves the provision of long-term care and support, through individualized funding packages, to people with a significant and ongoing disability and who were less than 65 years of age and Australian citizens or residents. At the time of Commission’s report this was estimated be around 410,000 people, about ten percent of the disabled population. To be eligible for Tier 3 support the disability needs to be permanent as well as associated with ‘significantly reduced functioning in self-care, communication, mobility or self-management and require significant ongoing support’ and/or be assessed as belonging to a group ‘for whom there was good evidence that [early] intervention would be safe, significantly improve outcomes and would be cost-effective’. To be eligible for packages individuals are assessed to identify their goals and needs, are provided with certainty of funding based on needed and have choice over the services and supports they purchase (Productivity Commission 2011). The services and support were to be provided by a range of not-for-profit, governmental, and private organizations.
	The NDIS reform received strong support from both major political parties as well as State and Territory governments. It was implemented in four trial sites across Australia from 1 July 2013, with another three sites commencing on 1 July 2014. It began full roll-out across Australian in July 2016 with full roll-out due to be completed in 2019/2020 (Buckmaster and Clark 2018).
	The NDIS is the largest social policy reform implemented in Australia since the introduction of Medicare—the universal health scheme. It has faced a number of significant implementation issues including clarity around eligibility for individualized services and supports particularly for people with psychosocial disabilities, ICT issues, lack of services for people with disabilities to choose from (‘market failure’), problems with the processes of planning with participants and difficulties faced by individual’s navigating the complexities of the new system. There are also concerns related to the different capacities of individuals to negotiate and navigate such a complex system resulting in significant inequities in funding packages (Carey et al. 2017). A further tension is in the role of governments from ‘light touch’ ‘market regulation’, where government identifies fraudulent practices and sets some minimum standards, to ‘market stewardship’, where government plays an active role in supporting innovation, stimulating markets particularly where there are shortages, and ensuring equity and choice and control. While it is clear that there are gaps in the NDIS in terms of access to services for people with different types of disability or people regional and remote Australia, partly driven by lack of financial sustainability, the role of government in supporting markets to develop in these areas is underdeveloped with the potential for considerable inequities to arise (Carey et al. 2017; Carey et al. 2018).
	The initial evaluation of the scheme showed that participants were generally satisfied (Mavromaras et al. 2018) however it will be many years before we know just how well Australia’s bold reforms in the funding and delivery of disability services delivers on its aspirations.





Public health research and disability


	To date, research on the health of people with disabilities has been sparse, however it is clear that public health research could do much to advance the evidence-base about the health of people with disabilities as well as identify evidence-based interventions and strategies to improve their health. For example, public health researchers could advance the measurement and reporting of disability-related information, the development of interventions and programmes to address health disadvantage (e.g. targeted tobacco cessation programmes) and policy analysis. Importantly this research needs to be conducted from multiple disciplinary perspectives and employ both qualitative and quantitative methods. It is also critical that people with disabilities are central to all research conducted and at the core of solutions to problems identified. Best practice in this area involves co-design of research projects where people with disabilities are appropriately resourced to conduct the research.
	The W-DARE project, presented earlier, is an example of co-designed research. As such, women with disabilities were resourced as co-researchers to work alongside researchers without disabilities at all stages of the project.
