This included initial two-way capacity development, design and implementation of all stages of the research, ongoing training of health workers and other women with disabilities on attaining the rights to sexual and reproductive health, analysis of data, and presentation of findings. Not only did this ensure the research benefit from insider knowledge of the lived experience of women with disabilities in the Philippines, but it also demonstrated the capabilities of women with disabilities as central to research that is about them (Vaughan et al. 2015).
	The Centre for Research Excellence in Disability and Health is example of a multidisciplinary programme of research on the health of people with disabilities that draws on the disability sector to drive its research priorities and dissemination activities. See Case Study 10.7.4.
	 	CASE STUDY 10.7.4 National Health and Medical Research Council, Centre for Research Excellence in Disability and Health
	The Centre of Research Excellence (CRE) in Disability and Health ((http://credh.org.au/) is funded by Australia’s National Health and Medical Research Council. It is a world first; it aims to gather the evidence needed to guide social and health policy reform in Australia.
	The CRE brings together an interdisciplinary group of researchers with stakeholders from the health and disability sectors, state and federal governments, and disability consumer representative groups—who are embedded in the research design and development. In collaboration with people with disabilities, service providers, non-government organizations and other stakeholders, the CRE will identify the key and emerging issues affecting Australians with disabilities. The research is designed to respond to the priorities identified by stakeholders in the disability sector.
	The research involves four work programmes:
	 	1. Mapping the spatial distribution of social, economic, and health inequities between people with and without disabilities
	2. The application of cutting-edge epidemiological methods to establish the main social determinants of health of people with disability
	3. The construction of the first ever cost-effectiveness model to estimate the health impacts and value for money of policy interventions for people with disabilities
	4. An innovative policy lab where stakeholders are embedded in the research process where they are interviewed throughout the life of the CRE, given the opportunity to reflect on others’ input and respond to the findings of the other three work programmes.
	The CRE-DH is also engaged in developing a skilled research workforce in disability and health by training new early-career researchers and PhD students as well as building the research capacity of academics and policymakers across sectors to respond to the pressing problem of people with disabilities’ poor health.





Conclusion and ways forward


	In this chapter we have shown that while the evidence-base on the health of people with disability is incomplete, there is enough evidence to conclude that people with disabilities have poorer mental and physical health, on average, than nondisabled people. These poorer health outcomes are in part due to the underlying health conditions but are also a result of socioeconomic disadvantage, higher levels of health damaging behaviours, poorly targeted health promotion, and preventive healthcare, lack of access to quality health, disability and rehabilitation services, and higher exposure to discrimination, stigma, and violence.
	Turning around the health disadvantage for people with disabilities requires population-based and targeted approaches that address the specific circumstances of people with disabilities. As one of the leading researchers into the social determinants of health highlights: ‘To reduce the steepness of the social gradient in health, actions must be universal, but with a scale and intensity that is proportionate to the level of disadvantage.’ (Marmot et al. 2010). It can therefore be argued that people with disabilities have a greater need for all public health functions (e.g. immunizations, support for healthy behaviours) and it is time for public health researchers, policymakers and practitioners to address the exclusion of people with disabilities within public health and the broader health system (United Nations 2006; WHO 2011; Mannan and MacLachlan 2013; Krahn et al. 2015).
	Public health approaches to improving the health of people with disabilities requires a social determinants approach to primary prevention, health promotion and support for healthy lifestyles, through to care and rehabilitation for those who experience health conditions and/or disability. Public health approaches must also consider social protection and welfare programmes which aim to reduce poverty and more effective interventions that promote the social and economic participation of people with disabilities (Skempes and Bickenbach 2015; Carey 2016).
	Health and rehabilitation system strengthening is required to improve health outcomes of people with disabilities. Systems strengthening must have good governance; coherent and explicit policies which articulate and resource for targeted programmes for people with disabilities; appropriate resourcing to implement inclusive policies and programmes; better coordination of care and referral process throughout health and rehabilitation systems; reduce the current gap in public health human resources for health that can support coordination of care as well as provide services that meet the needs of people with disabilities (Krahn et al. 2015; Mannan and MacLachlan 2013; McVeigh et al. 2016).
	Essential to all of these processes is greater recognition that people with disabilities have the same (and often additional) health needs and rights as people without disabilities. The right to health is enshrined in the CRPD (United Nations 2006). A critical illustration of why this right and all other intangible rights of people with disabilities required its’ own UN convention, is the fact that people with disabilities were excluded from international action, including public health action, in response to the Millennium Development Goals. With significant advocacy by and with people with disabilities and their representative organizations, the inclusion or people with disabilities is clearly articulated in the Global Goals for Sustainable Development 2015–2030 (SDGs) (Marella et al. 2016).
	Global commitment to the CRPD, the SDGs, as well as platforms such as the WHO Alma-Ata Primary Health Care Principles (WHO 1978), mandates public health practitioners, researchers, and policymakers in all countries to ensure people with disabilities are both meaningfully included and benefit in all aspects of public health. This will require more inclusive approaches to address existing barriers to inclusion within mainstream public health policy and programming (i.e. health promotion messaging, disease outbreak and disaster responses), as well as disability-specific actions (i.e. promotion and resourcing of CBR in low-and middle-income countries (United Nations 2006; WHO 2011; MacLachlan et al. 2012; MacLachlan and Mannan 2014; Krahn et al. 2015).
	We have described how the measurement of disability and the quality of information collected on disability is poor. There is an urgent need for better context-specific information and data on the lived experience of people with disabilities in relation to their health and inclusion within the public health sphere (Vaughan et al. 2016). Improved context-specific disability data collection and disaggregation including within Health Information Systems is critical to monitor progress towards inclusion, as well as identify barriers to improving health outcomes for people with disabilities (Durham et al. 2016). This includes identifying gaps in knowledge, practices, and attitudes of public health practitioners to improve their capacity for inclusion, alongside strategies to enhance the knowledge and capacity of people with disabilities to improve their access to public health programmes (Mannan and MacLachlan 2013; Krahn et al. 2015; Vaughan et al. 2016).
	Meaningful leadership and participation of people with disabilities in policy development is needed so that policy is responsive to the needs of people with disability (Love et al. 2018). Furthermore, we need to ensure that people with disabilities are supported to understand their rights to health, as well as provided with information, resources, and support to access public health programmes (Devine et al. 2017). In terms of research, we need to build the capacity of people with disabilities to take leaderships roles in public health research and ensure that all research projects are responsive to the priorities of people with disabilities.
	Public health has much to contribute to alleviating the health disadvantage that people with disabilities face. To do this, public health needs to move beyond understanding disability as a health deficit and take a social determinants approach to the health of people with disability. Reducing disability-related health inequalities requires addressing the root causes of poor health including social determinants such as poverty and discrimination. Doing so would enable public health to more truly achieve its goals of promoting the health of all individuals and their communities.

10.8


Health of older people


	Samir K. Sinha and Brittany Ellis





Introduction to health of older people


	This chapter considers the phenomenon of population ageing, the unique health needs of older people, and specific approaches to providing health and social care for them. Ageing reflects biological, psychological, and social processes that occur across the life course, and at individual rates. Indeed, these processes are associated with ageing, but are not synonymous with chronological age. They vary between individuals according to many factors such as gender, ethnic background, lifestyle, socioeconomic, geographic location, and historical factors. This helps to explain why certain countries or populations are ageing faster than others.
	How ‘old age’ has been defined continues to vary across settings, over time, and from person to person. In the past, the United Nations (UN) and other international agencies used 60 years or older (60+) to define ‘the elderly’, but more recently there has been a growing consensus that 65+, or even older ages, should be used in general to describe this segment of the population, while recognizing that disadvantaged populations may experience processes associated with ageing earlier.
	While the process of ageing is universal, it is considered by many to be anything but uniform. Indeed, regardless of any current chronologically based descriptions, it is clear that people over 65 years of age are not one homogenous group and that there exists a great variance of experience, capacity, and health status between individuals at any age. As people age, some will age well and with little disability for significant periods of their later years while others may experience most of their later years as living with increasing frailty and a higher degree of dependence. It is essential to recognize this heterogeneity in defining the health and social needs of our ageing populations, designing and evaluating interventions, and planning for the future for this rapidly growing and increasingly diverse segment of our populations.





Demographic projections related to population ageing


	The age of the world’s population is rapidly increasing both structurally and numerically, and by 2050 the number of people aged 60 years or older worldwide is expected to exceed the number of people aged 15 years or younger. In 2019, there were an estimated 694 million people who were aged 65 years or older worldwide, representing 9% of the total population. This population is projected to number an estimated 1.55 billion persons, representing 15.9% of the total population in 2050 (UN DESA 2019).
	Population ageing, which refers to an increasing median age, is occurring. In 2015, the median age of the world’s population was estimated to be 30 years. The country with the youngest population by median age was Niger (14 years), and the countries with the oldest populations by median age were Germany, Italy, and Japan (46 years). By 2050, it is anticipated that the world median age will increase to 36 years, with Taiwan and the Republic of Korea projected to both reach a median age of 54 years (UN DESA 2017).
	While much attention is focused around population ageing in high-income countries, this phenomenon is currently occurring far more rapidly in lower-income countries. Indeed, between 2017 and 2050, the number of older adults in high-income countries is expected to increase by 38%, which is much less than the expected 260% increase for lower-income countries (UN DESA 2017). In general, the more developed a country is, the more likely it is that population ageing will occur within an affluent environment, with higher levels of overall health and social care resources and infrastructure being available to support this phenomenon. However, in developing countries, ageing can still occur successfully even in the context of the emerging burden of chronic diseases, industrialization, and changing living patterns.
	Figures 10.8.1 and 10.8.2 illustrate the global phenomenon of population ageing at the country level in the year 2020 and again in 2050. As can be appreciated across these two figures, a significant number of more developed and developing countries will be experiencing major demographic shifts over the coming decades with older people representing greater proportions of their ageing populations.
	Fig. 10.8.1 Percentage of population aged 65 or over in 2020.
	Source: data from United Nations (2019) Department of Economic and Social Affairs: Population Dynamics, available from https://population.un.org/wpp/Maps/.
	Fig. 10.8.2 Percentage of population aged 65 or over in 2050.
	Source: data from United Nations (2019) Department of Economic and Social Affairs: Population Dynamics, available from https://population.un.org/wpp/Maps/.





Determinants of population ageing


	The achievement of population ageing can be considered a major success story, having come largely as a result of gains in infant and child survival, and, more recently, to gains in life expectancy at older ages accompanied by reductions in fertility.
	The earliest observed influence on population ageing occurred in Europe as a result of declines in fertility and childhood mortality which began in the nineteenth century and accelerated in the twentieth century initially due to improved living conditions and sanitation, and then to better nutrition, immunizations, and antibiotics. From the middle of the twentieth century, reductions in deaths from heart disease, stroke and cancer have further significantly extended adult life expectancy, primarily in developed countries.
	In developing countries, fertility and mortality rates have also fallen, but to a lesser degree than among their more developed counterparts. The adoption of modern health practices, including successful infant and child health programmes, are probably most responsible for the rapid rates of mortality decline achieved at younger ages. As a result, globally, over two-thirds of adults over the age of 60 years are now living in developing or low-and middle-income regions (UN DESA 2017).
	The dramatic declines in fertility being witnessed throughout the world have mainly been attributed to urbanization, industrialization, and social mobility which have all had an influence on family structures. In addition, the ‘emancipation’ of women resulting in their greater chances for education, later age of marriage, and access to contraception have all contributed as well (Kinsella and He 2009). China’s one-child policy, introduced in 1979, also had a dramatic impact on fertility rates in that country which fell from 4.77 between 1970 and 1975 to 1.51 between 1995 and 2000 only increasing slightly to 1.60 in between 2010 and 2015—further contributing to its more accelerated rate of population ageing (UN DESA 2017a).
	Currently, close to half of the world’s people live in a region in which fertility rates are below what is considered the population replacement level of there being at least 2.1 children per woman (UN DESA 2019). Currently, the country with the highest fertility rate is Niger (7.2) and the lowest is Taiwan (1.2) while fertility rates are considered to be below replacement levels in North America (1.9), Europe (1.6), and many countries in Latin America, Asia and the Caribbean (UN DESA 2017a).
	As fertility rates decline, life expectancy begins to have a greater impact on the rate of population ageing. While human life expectancy has increased dramatically over the twentieth century and the beginning of this century, new data is starting to show a deceleration and even more recently a demonstrable decline in life expectancy in some developed countries like Canada, the United States, and the United Kingdom. For example, in 2016 the average life expectancy in the United States of America reportedly decreased for a second year in a row, driven largely by a 50% gradual rise since 2005 in what are being coined ‘deaths of despair’—the combined deaths from suicide, alcohol and drug use (Radley et al. 2018). Nevertheless, current conventional thinking predicts that our actual potential life-span as humans remains at around 120 years, with centenarians—those living to ages greater than 100 years—still representing the fastest growing age group in many developed countries.
	In some populations, including Canada and the United States, international migration has also had a role in changing age (and gender) distributions, with large influxes of relatively young immigrants helping to influence population ageing rates. In the case of many of these countries, progressive immigration policies have been developed to help partially address the issue of declining fertility and population ageing rates. Furthermore, dramatic shifts have been seen in some nations as social and political conflicts have led to significant emigration. Nowhere was this more recently evident than in Syria where death and emigration have led to a population decrease by over three million people or roughly 20% of the country’s population between 2010 and 2019 (UN DESA 2019). However, in most countries, migration has had less of an overall impact than changing fertility and mortality rates.





Specific factors that further influence population ageing


Ageing and gender


	Women have always tended to live longer than men, and globally, with the exception of Mali and Swaziland, this continues to be the case with the current average life expectancy of women 75.0 years and men 70.2 years (UN DESA 2019). The reasons behind this difference in life expectancy between men and women is complex and likely results from an interplay between differences in attitudes, social roles, biological risks, and particular behaviours including the higher incidence of alcohol and drug use and smoking in men, leading to their higher rates of accidents, violence, and cardiovascular disease. Many theories behind biological risk differences exist, however, all lack firm evidence. They include more active female immune functioning, the protective effect of oestrogen, compensatory effects of the second X chromosome, and the influence of oxidative stress (Austad 2006). Regardless, as a result of their tendency to live longer, women are more likely to experience a greater burden of the disease and disability associated with advanced age.
	While conditions that affect people at older ages are similar among men and women (except for breast cancer and reproductive cancers), there are specific gender differences in the incidence of these conditions and their peak age of onset. For instance, men experience their peak incidence of coronary artery disease earlier than women. Lung cancer is more common among men who have long had higher rates of smoking, although lung cancer has now become the second most common cancer among women, reflecting their increasing smoking rates. Also, while there are few differences noted on self-rated health, older women have higher rates of reported functional disability than men, likely due to the higher prevalence of arthritis, asthma, depression, anxiety, and cognitive impairment that occur among women as they age.
	Women continue to also be at increased risk of violence and abuse, both as children and adults, and these acts, which come in a variety of forms from domestic and sexual violence, to human trafficking, honour crimes and female genital mutilation, are associated with an increased incidence of anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (Oram et al. 2017) and risk of premature death. It has been further argued that research in this area continues to be flawed as it often reports issues in a gender-neutral fashion, not recognizing the important differences between men and women, while regularly excluding important variables such as intimate partner violence (Howard et al. 2017).
	Gender differences in terms of evolving social roles and human rights will continue to have significant effects on current and future experiences of ageing for women as well. For example, during the life course women are still more likely to be excluded from schooling, receive lower quantities of nutritious food, have no control over household decisions, and receive no health insurance from an employer. Their greater longevity also means that they are more likely to experience the death of their spouse and to spend a greater proportion of their later years widowed, very often with an accompanying loss of social status and reduced economic circumstances. The highest levels of widowhood (above 40% among women aged 60–64) are found in some sub-Saharan countries that have experienced political unrest or high prevalence rates of HIV (UN DESA 2015). Furthermore, in parts of Africa, widowed women have no rights to own their late husband’s land, which often leaves them in poverty. Older women are also especially vulnerable in the event of crises such as war, natural disaster, and famine, partly because they generally control fewer economic resources than older men, and also because much of the care of children and other vulnerable people tends to fall on older women.
	Finally, historically, clinical research, including disease modelling, management, and pharmacologic treatment, has been conducted in predominantly younger male populations and had its findings generalized to women and older people. For example, despite the facts that women are twice as likely to live with two or more chronic diseases when over 80 years old, and that heart disease kills more women than men, protocols for diagnosing and treating heart disease have been largely based upon research with middle-aged, white, male patients with only 27% of participants being female (Kim et al. 2008). As a result, women tend to be diagnosed later with more advanced disease and have poorer treatment outcomes.





Ageing among ethnic minorities and indigenous peoples


	With increasing numbers of immigrants reaching old age in their host countries, racial and ethnic minorities are now beginning to constitute the fastest growing segment of the older populations within many Western countries (Zubair and Norris 2015). These demographic changes will continue to have important implications, especially since morbidity and mortality rates among older populations have also been shown to be unevenly distributed across racial and ethnic groups. In the United Kingdom, for example, data from the Black and Minority Ethnic Elders Study demonstrated that older adults from ethnic minority groups, particularly those of African/Caribbean or South Asian ethnicity, were more likely to report worse health outcomes than the white ethnic majority population (PRIAE Policy Research Institute on Ageing and Ethnicity 2005). Many older people in these ethnic groups are first-generation immigrants and may have encountered particular issues as they age that relate to migration stress, their reasons for having had to leave their country of birth, and having to cope with language limitations and the separation from family members and networks in their country of origin.
	Noted differences for older ethnic minority populations in general have also been extended to physiological ageing, access to social and healthcare services, income and educational levels, health habits, disease prevalence, progression, and response to treatment. Similar disparities among health and disease in older people in ethnic minority groups are evident in both the Netherlands (Denktaş et al. 2009) and the US (Federal Interagency Forum on Aging-Related Studies 2016). Despite these recurrent findings, there remains a lack of understanding as to the exact causes of these differences as, historically, ‘minority’ ethnic groups have been excluded from studies or their heterogeneity diminished through being classified occasionally as part of broader ‘non-majority’ ethnic groups.
	Other research has demonstrated that minority ethnic communities sometimes have little confidence that mainstream services will meet their diverse cultural, linguistic, or religious needs and uncertainty around what services exist and how to access them. The challenge of having public sector providers assuming, often incorrectly, that minority ethnic communities have strong community/family support networks that they can rely upon is an additional barrier towards accessing the care and support needed (PRIAE 2005).
	Significant health disparities also exist among indigenous minority groups throughout the world especially where their continued lower socioeconomic status, as compared to the majority non-indigenous population, and persisting effects of colonialism, remain two of the key drivers of their disparities. Their achievement of a poorer overall health status has been linked to being disproportionately plagued by factors like poverty, malnutrition, inadequate housing, and overcrowding. This in turn has been exacerbated by the transition from a traditional to more modern lifestyle, systemic racism, and discrimination, and has led to high rates of chronic diseases including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obesity, and mental health disorders and functional limitations at an earlier age than the general population.
	Access to care issues for indigenous populations has been associated with a significant health divide especially characterized by a decreased life expectancy of between 5 and 10 years compared to the general population in Canada (Statistics Canada 2005) and of similar ranges in both New Zealand and Australia (Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) 2011; Phillips et al. 2017). Nevertheless, while the life expectancy gap is expected to continue to shrink over time in Canada, the numbers of older indigenous people greater than 65 years of age is expected to triple over the next two decades, compared to only a doubling of this age cohort for the overall population (Government of Canada 2009). Indeed, shifting demographics, coupled with the more vulnerable health status of older indigenous peoples, will demand that their needs are responded to with increasingly culturally safe and appropriate health interventions to further address and reduce health disparities.





Ageing among LGBTQ peoples


	While between an estimated five to ten per cent of the population identifies as being lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer (LGBTQ), many may have lived a portion or their entire lives, to varying degrees, in hostile environments, prior to experiencing more inclusive modern-day standards. For some, this could result in feelings of great stigma and shame that continue to shape their lives, often requiring them to keep their sexual orientation hidden as a strategy for survival. In part due to their increased experiences of victimization and discrimination, individuals who identify as LGBTQ often face greater health disparities than those who do not. Older LGBTQ persons are more likely to live in poverty and may also have fewer future caregiver options as they are more likely to live alone, are less likely to have children or grandchildren (Barker et al. 2006), or they may remain isolated from their families of origin. Furthermore, current or past negative experiences with health, social, and community care professionals may also lead to hesitation on the part of older LGBTQ adults to seek appropriate supportive services, leaving some with specific healthcare needs that also go largely unrecognized by healthcare professionals (Brotman and Ryan 2008).
	There are certain medical issues that require particular attention in LGBTQ older adults such as regular screening for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections among gay and bisexual men; greater risks of cardiovascular disease due to higher rates of obesity and metabolic syndrome, smoking, and alcohol use for lesbian and bisexual women (Valanis et al. 2000); and a higher prevalence of psychological disorders and distress overall (Mays and Cochran 2001). This latter issue is particularly important as experiencing social stressors such as prejudice, stigmatization, violence, and internalized homophobia over long periods of time can result in higher risks of depression, suicide, risky behaviour, and substance abuse for LGBTQ older adults. These disparities will likely continue as they age, but it is unclear if these disparities will increase, remain stable, or decrease with time. Further recognition of these challenges and work in this area is needed.





Ageing in rural areas


	In 2010 the World Health Organization (WHO) recognized that, for the first time in history, the majority of the world’s population were now living in urban settings. As early as 1960 it was estimated that 66% of the global population lived rurally, but this has been steadily declining to 45% by 2018 (UN DESA 2018). Rapid urbanization has led to difficulties in providing appropriate urban infrastructure as many urban centres struggle to manage issues related to pollution, sanitation, transportation, and the provision of health and education. Health challenges with rapid urbanization have included increases in rates of non-communicable diseases (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancers, and chronic respiratory disease), violence, physical inactivity, substance abuse, and communicable diseases.
	The shift of younger generations to urban environments principally to find work, coupled with the greater movement of some older people into rural areas in retirement, has led to unusually high levels of population ageing in rural regions. Further, living in rural areas has been associated with greater economic hardship, less access to basic health and social services and quality housing, and higher commodity prices (Phillipson and Scharf 2005). Although older people in rural settings might report higher levels of social cohesion, they may live more undersupported lives as their younger family members, who previously may have acted naturally as unpaid caregivers for them, migrate to urban areas in search of greater economic opportunities.





Demographic and epidemiological transitions


	Population ageing and changes in mortality and life expectancy have also been accompanied by changes in patterns of prevalent and incident diseases. Omran (1971) described the epidemiological transitions we have been experiencing over time as (i) the age of pestilence and famine; (ii) the age of receding pandemics; and (iii) the age of degenerative and man-made diseases. These transitions have been witnessed at an accelerated rate in rapidly developing countries like Brazil, China, and India, as they have experienced substantial changes in economic development, increasing urbanization, and changes in the health status of their citizens resulting in rapid population ageing.
	Globally, non-communicable diseases, particularly cardiovascular diseases and cancers, now represent the current leading causes of morbidity and mortality with prevailing risk factors for developing these conditions including an unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, obesity, hypertension, and tobacco use (Li et al. 2012). Even though the proportion of later-life fatalities caused by heart disease, strokes, and cancer significantly fell over the last 25 years, this decrease was partially offset by a concurrent increase in the number of deaths attributable to other chronic non-communicable diseases, such as diabetes, chronic lung disease, renal disease, and dementia (Table 10.8.1).

	Nevertheless, stark differences in mortality causes in older people between developed and developing regions do remain. For example, in higher-income countries over 90% of deaths among people aged 60 years or over are due to non-communicable diseases, whereas in lower-income countries almost 20% of deaths in this age group are still due to communicable diseases. Many rapidly ageing lower-income countries are also still experiencing high overall levels of communicable diseases including childhood infections and HIV/AIDS (WHO 2011).





Variations in life expectancy


	While mortality rates tend to increase at older ages, in recent decades they have slowed at all ages. Life expectancy is defined as the average number of additional years of life that a person at a given age could expect to live, providing age-specific mortality levels remain constant. Table 10.8.2 shows life expectancy at age 60 for males and females in different regions of the world. In 2015, a woman in Africa who had already lived to 60 years could expect to live to 77.5 years, while one in Oceania could expect to live to 85.4 years. Similar differences are reflected in male life expectancy at age 60.
