	Inequalities in life expectancy exist between countries and regions, and between different population groups within countries. Between-country reductions were largely achieved between 1950 and 1990 due to improved access to safe water and sanitation, childhood immunization, improved childhood nutrition, and declining fertility (Hosseinpoor et al. 2012). However, large inequalities in life expectancy still remain, with life expectancy remaining low at 63 years across lower-income countries (UN DESA Population Division 2017a).
	Within-country differences in life expectancy have been further observed according to gender, socioeconomic status, and other factors. A major study of 1.7 million people across seven countries compared the impact of low socioeconomic status with other major risk factors on health, such as physical inactivity, smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity, and high alcohol intake. It found that when compared with their wealthier counterparts, people with low socioeconomic status were almost 1.5 times (46%) more likely to die before they were 85 years old—estimating that low socioeconomic status was associated with a reduced life expectancy of 2.1 years, similar to being inactive (2.4 years) and more impactful than respectively having high blood pressure, obesity and high alcohol consumption (1.6, 0.7, and 0.5 years) (Stringhini et al. 2017).





Healthy life expectancy


	As well as adding years to life, it is also important to add life to years. Healthy life expectancy (or health-adjusted life expectancy (HALE)) estimates life expectancy, but with an adjustment for time spent living with a disability and/or other impairment to good health. Within the context of population ageing, age-associated limitations in performing everyday activities can have substantive effects on healthcare utilization. Healthy life expectancy estimations can therefore help answer questions raised regarding whether extra years of life achieved are being spent in poor or good health and their resulting associated impact around the demand for health and social care services.
	The level of inequalities in both life and healthy life expectancies that can exist across a region is well studied. One study looking at these two data points across 25 countries in the European Union observed a greater variation in healthy life expectancy than for life expectancy. It found that, on average, a 50-year-old man could expect to live until 67.3 years free of activity limitations, and a woman to 68.1 years with observed variations in healthy life expectancy ranging from a low of 9.1 to a high of 23.6 years, respectively, for men in Estonia and Denmark. Higher healthy life expectancies were associated with higher gross domestic product, lower unemployment, and with life-long learning (Jagger et al. 2008).
	When healthy life expectancy increases relative to life expectancy, then people will spend a greater proportion of their life in good health and a ‘compression of morbidity’ will be experienced (Fries et al. 1989). If people live longer due to a reduction in fatal illness, but with an increase in disability due to chronic or degenerative diseases, then there will be ‘expansion of morbidity’ experienced. A third scenario, that of ‘dynamic equilibrium’, could, for example, occur if the population prevalence of some chronic diseases increases with ageing, but the progression of some degenerative diseases reduces.
	While the achievement of a compression of morbidity may be prevailing in some populations, data to test this hypothesis are difficult to find and hard to interpret. Very few countries are capable of making reliable assessments over time, between geographic regions or socioeconomic groups. In some settings, there is evidence that the prevalence of disability at older ages may be decreasing, but other studies are finding an increase in disability. For example, a study which assessed disability trends in 12 Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries among individuals aged 65 years and over, reported mixed results (Lafortune et al. 2007). Disability declined among elderly people in five out of the 12 countries (Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, the United States, and Italy). At the same time, three countries demonstrated increased rates of severe disability (Belgium, Sweden, and Japan), indicating that increased longevity can still lead to increased numbers of older people in poor health and in need of long-term care.
	If a widespread compression of morbidity is to occur at a population level, greater health promotion and risk reduction activities will be needed for groups that have high levels of health risks. For example, preventing smoking is likely to result not only in more years of life, but also more years in good health. However, even if preventive activities were highly successful in reducing or postponing disability, it is expected that increasing numbers of people living to very old ages would mean that there will also be greater numbers of people eventually living with disabling conditions. At a population level, even if a compression of morbidity dominates, there will still be an increasing need for health and other forms of care as the population ages.





Differential, usual, and successful ageing


	Ageing is believed to be a slow, continuous process. Therefore, some of its effects can be observed only when they have progressed sufficiently to induce identifiable alterations that can be validated by available testing methods. An illustrative example is atherosclerosis, the consequences of which manifest during middle and older ages even though an atherosclerotic lesion may start early in life. Whatever organ or tissue is considered, timetables of ageing represent an approximation, as the onset of ageing cannot be pin-pointed precisely by a specific physiological sign.
	While a number of functions undoubtedly decline as we age, the extreme heterogeneity of an overall achieved functional status, even in the oldest cohorts, supports the view that ageing must be evaluated on an individual basis. In addition to genetic makeup, an older individual’s health and social status, economic, and environmental conditions all contribute to how they age. Ageing processes have thus been distinguished across three distinct categories: categories (1) ‘disease/disabled’, characterized by the presence of pathology, disability, or both; (2) ‘usual’ (normal) ageing, characterized by the absence of overt pathology but the presence of functional declines; and (3) ‘successful’ ageing, characterized by few or none of the physiological losses seen in the usual ageing group. This concept of differential ageing is based on (1) the substantial heterogeneity that exists among older individuals; (2) the common observation that ageing is not a uniform or inevitable process of disease or disability; (3) the persistence of ‘plasticity’ well into advanced age, that is, a continuing capacity for adaptive and compensatory rehabilitation; and (4) the identification of predictors of various patterns of ageing, especially factors that contribute to more successful trajectories of ageing (Seeman 1994).
	Extrinsic factors appear to also play an important role in age-associated functional decline. In one study, factors promoting the maintenance or improvement of functioning included younger age, higher income, higher education, high cognitive performance, being Caucasian, being of lower body weight, maintaining good lung function, living without diabetes or hypertension, participating in exercise, and receiving emotional support (Seeman 1994). Other correlates of improved survival at later ages even among those with chronic conditions were the absence of smoking, regular participation in physical activities, and the maintenance of a strong social network (Rizzuto et al. 2012). Taking all such factors into account, the prospects for avoidance, or eventual reversal, of functional loss with age are vastly improved, while the risks of adverse consequences are reduced (Rowe and Kahn 1987). Furthermore, it is increasingly appreciated that interventions may be beneficial at all ages provided they are customized to the individual. Indeed, physical exercise, dietary, surgical, and pharmacological interventions have proved successful in enhancing health even at older ages and thus should never be restricted on the basis of age alone. Our growing ability to identify those factors that can maximize health and physiological competence can support an overall enhancement of an older person’s quality of life, a reduction in their burden of disease and disability, while decreasing the potential need for healthcare resources.





Societal perceptions of ageing


Images and stereotypes related to ageing


	‘Ageism’ was defined in 1969 by US gerontologist Robert Butler as a combination of prejudicial attitudes towards ageing and older people, discriminatory practices against older people, and institutional practices and policies that perpetuate older age stereotypes (Butler 1969). A report by the American Association of Retired Persons (AARP) concluded that many Americans had misconceptions about ageing and older people, including that they are senile, asexual, and miserable (Abramson and Silverstein 2006). Although some changes have occurred for the better in terms of depictions of ageing, older adults are still generally viewed less favourably than the young.





Older people’s own perceptions of ageing


	The Growing Old in America report (Taylor et al. 2009) explored ‘markers of old age’. The study reported that ‘turning 85’ was the most commonly endorsed marker of what it meant to be old, with the second and third markers being ‘can’t live independently’ and ‘can’t drive a car’, respectively. Other markers included ‘has trouble walking up stairs’, ‘retires from work’, and ‘has grey hair’. The English Longitudinal Study of Ageing found that self-assessed health was strongly related to how old individuals felt, with study participants often reporting being in better health and feeling younger than their actual age (Demakakos et al. 2007).
	Interviews with older adults in Australia demonstrated the wide acceptance of ageist stereotypes. Participants aged 65 and 89 years described oldness as ‘not trying, withdrawn, isolated, irritating, self-oriented, living outside the mainstream, unattractive, uninteresting, frail, senile, silly, over the hill, narrow-minded, a burden, lonely, vulnerable, dowdy, and unproductive’ (Minichiello et al. 2000). Such ‘internalized ageism’ can, however, be dangerous in that older adults may, as a result, experience worse functional health and even a reduced will to live. Levy et al. (2002) found that older individuals who held more positive self-perceptions of ageing (measured over 20 years earlier) tended to live 7.5 years longer than individuals with less positive self-perceptions of ageing. This advantage remained after accounting for age, gender, socioeconomic status, feeling lonely, and level of functional health. Within the context of Western societies, where older age is portrayed more negatively, while the post-war ‘baby boomers’ are said to be challenging old age stereotypes, there still remains a high level of diversity in the health and social circumstances of these birth cohorts.





Evolving concepts of later-life productivity and social contribution


	With a societal emphasis pointed towards the anticipated demands that the ageing population will make, the significant value of the contributions older people make through continued paid employment, but also as unpaid caregivers, volunteers, and mentors are easily overlooked. Indeed, the way in which population ageing is evolving and being experienced is helping to challenge well-established concepts. The ‘old-age dependency ratio’, for example, is a common demographic metric which compares the ratio of the economically ‘dependent’ part of the population, or those 65 years or older, with those who are 20–64 years old, who are considered to be working age and therefore economically ‘active’. The metric, while providing some utility, is increasingly leading to erroneous conclusions as it specifically underestimates the contributions of individuals over the age of 65 years where increasing numbers of older people are remaining in paid employment, or still acting as significant economic contributors through their spending, while also neglecting to consider that not all persons of traditional working ages are active in the labour force, with some being economically dependent. The concept also negates the value of the contributions older people who perform unpaid work, including organized volunteer positions, child-minding, and unpaid caregiving activities, all of which have significant overall economic and societal benefits and implications. Several alternative measures are now being proposed to better account for the growing diversity of capacities and dependencies across age (UN DESA 2017a).





Ageing-related concepts in health


Multimorbidity and polypharmacy


	The prevalence of diseases and morbidity among older people has increased over time, partly due to the improved and earlier diagnosis of diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, and dementia, but also due to the rise of disabling non-fatal chronic conditions such as arthritis.
	Multimorbidity is commonly defined as the co-occurrence of two or more chronic conditions whose prevalence increases with age and negatively associated with many important health outcomes such as increased health service utilization and decreased life expectancy. It also profoundly affects an individual’s overall well-being, quality of life, and ability to function normally. Patients with multimorbidity further struggle to manage the associated polypharmacy and medication burden of having to take the multiple medications prescribed to them, leading to difficulties with treatment adherence and a worsened quality of life.
	Despite the increasing numbers of individuals living with multimorbidity, clinical practice guidelines and care delivery models are still primarily built around the management of single diseases rather than the interplay between them. Thus approaches to the care and treatment need to shift to become more relevant to the actual needs and preferences of patients with multimorbidity, which will require complex treatment decisions to be made sometimes in the absence of high-quality or direct evidence.
	While medications can be beneficial in the management of specific health problems, they also have the potential to cause serious adverse effects. Older people have a reduced volume of distribution for drugs, and slower rates of drug metabolism and elimination, and so are more vulnerable to overdosing or the side effects of certain medications that can make them less appropriate to prescribe in older adults. Furthermore, polypharmacy increases the risk of adverse drug reactions or related events including hospitalization and death.
	In high-income countries like Sweden a recent study reported a prevalence of polypharmacy of 44.0% (5+ medications), and excessive polypharmacy (10+ medications) of 11.7% among older adults (Morin et al. 2017); while another study from Canada noted that nearly 40% of older adults were currently taking one inappropriate medication while 12% were taking multiple inappropriate medications (CIHI 2014). Adverse drug reactions have been associated with around 30% of the hospital admissions among older people and it is estimated that up to half these adverse reactions could have been prevented (Simonson and Feinberg 2005). With the support of medication reviews that promote more appropriate prescribing and even de-prescribing that is aligned with an older person’s actual treatment objectives and preferences, increased compliance with an overall treatment regimen could likely be achieved, accompanied by a concomitant decrease in the risk and occurrence of adverse events and their associated morbidity and mortality.





Disability and function


	As people age they are more likely to experience challenges with their ability to function, which can impact their capacity to mobilize, stay socially engaged, and live independently. Activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs) are two classes of functional measures that have been developed, based on an individual’s ability to perform specific tasks, and are widely utilized to describe one’s capacity for independent living. ADL tasks refer to those that are required to carry out basic self-care activities, such as transferring out of a bed or a chair, walking, toileting, bathing, dressing, and eating, while IADL tasks refer to those that are required to maintain an independent household, such as doing light housework, preparing meals, using the telephone, shopping for personal items, managing money, and getting around the community.
	ADL dependency is less common than IADL dependency, and in one survey of community-dwelling population, 85 years of age and older, only 16% reported requiring help with one ADL, 10% with two or three ADLs, and 9% with four or more ADLs, while just under half reported needing help in performing one or more IADLs (Kane et al. 2003). The monitoring of an individual’s IADL and ADL performance, which generally demands a combination of both cognitive and physical abilities, has also become a useful way to measure and monitor disease severity, progression of certain neurodegenerative conditions such as dementia, and in certain cases recovery as well such as after a stroke.
	Finally, the WHO estimates that approximately 33% of adults over 65 years of age have a disabling hearing impairment, while 81% of the world’s visually impaired people are aged 50 years and above (WHO 2019). Both hearing and visual impairments can impact a person’s ability to function independently, and can also negatively affect their economic opportunities, quality of life, mental health, physical health, and mortality risk. Furthermore, the burden associated with dual sensory impairment, which is prevalent in between 5 and 20% of people over the age of 70 years, is likely more profound (Brennan and Bally 2007).





Frailty


	Frailty is a term that is increasingly being used to describe older people who are at risk of poor outcomes due to their diminished adaptive reserve and resiliency. Fried et al. (2001) developed an operational definition of frailty—a ‘frailty phenotype’ that includes decreased resiliency and reserve, cycles of decline across multiple systems, negative energy balance, sarcopenia, and decreased strength and exercise tolerance. Another common way to define frailty, uses the concept of a ‘frailty index’ to include the accumulation of a broader range of limitations and deficits that accumulate exponentially with age and corresponds with an increasing level of vulnerability to stressors (Rockwood and Mitnisky 2011). While frailty is not age specific, it more commonly occurs with increasing age. Furthermore, at any given age, women on average compared to men have been found to be living with more deficits than do men. However, women appear to tolerate their deficits better than men, and appear to have a lower risk of adverse outcomes in association with higher frailty index scores.
	Increasingly, frailty is becoming recognized as an important risk factor for increased morbidity and mortality across a range of clinical settings. From emergency departments, to inpatient medical and surgical stays, increasing frailty has been associated with an increased risk of experiencing falls, disability, hospitalization, the need for long-term care and mortality (Clegg et al. 2013). However, more work needs to be done to develop better ways to more easily measure and detect frailty and determine the levels at which certain therapies or interventions may or may not be useful in an individual’s care.





Healthcare for older people


	As ageing populations carry the greatest overall burden of illness and disability, healthcare planners are often challenged by concerns about increasing demands and rising costs of health and social care in the face of population ageing. Older adults visit doctors more often, use more medications, have more admissions to hospital, tend to have longer stays in hospital and pose the most complex diagnostic and therapeutic problems, but also have the potential to benefit the most from the provision of appropriate and timely health and social care. As greater consideration is given about how and for whom treatment interventions should be extended to mitigate morbidity and mortality within older populations, overcoming ageism around treating illness at later ages will be just as important.
	For many, health concerns and symptoms in the elderly are overlooked or dismissed as part of the normal ageing process and thus may go underdiagnosed and undertreated. While healthcare professionals do not necessarily intend to behave in a discriminatory fashion, it is clear that a lack of skills and confidence in working with older people can lead to behaviour which may be perceived as discriminatory. Furthermore, denying access to services on the basis of age alone is becoming increasingly recognized as not being acceptable. Decisions about treatment and healthcare should always be made on the basis of a patient’s health needs, the overall health status of the individual, their own wishes and aspirations and, where appropriate, those of their caregivers, and the patient’s ability to benefit.
	Increasingly, strategies that can both promote healthy ageing, prevent, and treat functional decline and enable people to more successfully manage and live with their chronic health conditions and functional impairments are becoming recognized and understood. These can both improve an older person’s longevity and their overall quality of life and help them compensate for functional impairments, maintain their independence, and prevent future complications. Furthermore, as the health needs of older people living with multimorbidity can be particularly complex to manage, their care should be approached when possible from a multidisciplinary perspective and include them and their families and caregivers as partners in their own health management to enable the delivery of more efficient and effective care.





Health promotion activities to support healthy ageing


	A useful framework for promoting healthy ageing has been described in three stages by Kalache and Kickbusch (1997). The first is increasing capacity for health in early life and includes good maternal nutrition, and optimizing the development of vital organs such as brain, muscle, bone, and blood vessels during childhood and early adulthood to build resources that may affect later capacity (such as increasing peak bone density to protect against osteoporosis). The second stage occurs in adult life and involves strategies to reduce damage (such as avoiding smoking), to protect against damage (such as eating a balanced diet) or to prevent loss through lack of use (such as with regular physical activity). The third stage is in late life and involves the continued primary prevention and minimizing the secondary progression of disease and disability, protecting against increased environmental demands or stresses, and compensating for lost capacity. Examples of these approaches in health promotion include routine immunization, exercise and strength training and rehabilitation when necessary, maintaining and strengthening social supports, correction of deficits in vision and hearing, making modifications to domestic and outdoor environments to enable more independent living and trying to address as possible important social determinants of health such as poverty.
	Indeed, several key health behaviours are associated with diseases that are common in older age and thus suggest a primary preventive approach is likely to be the most effective way to reduce their incidence. A common example of this is the prevention of smoking which is linked to cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, many cancers, and ultimately a decreased life expectancy. While older people may find it difficult to maintain high levels of exercise, regular physical activity is strongly associated with lower rates of obesity, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, depression, and osteoporosis, and an increased life expectancy in many observational studies. Observational studies also suggest an association between good nutrition and better health at older ages (Tucker et al. 2005) as well as the importance of staying socially connected with others and an increased life expectancy (Rizzuto et al. 2012)
	Much of the evidence for promoting vaccinations among older adults comes from observational studies and may reflect other differences between vaccinated and non-vaccinated groups. As the ageing process is associated with immunosenescence and subsequently an increased risk of infection, as well as diminished response to vaccination, the value of still promoting vaccinations in later life becomes apparent. Accordingly, it is currently recommended that in addition to updating routine vaccinations that may have been missed in earlier life, routine vaccinations for all older people over 65 years should include: influenza, pneumococcal, shingles (zoster) and tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (TdaP of Td) (CDC 2019).
	It is a common assumption that prevention in general—and screening in particular—is always in the patient’s best interest. In young healthy populations, benefits of early cancer detection and treatment are considered to outweigh its harms. In older populations, mortality benefits may be less pronounced, as the screening tests themselves may pose a greater threat to one’s health, while the presence of comorbidities may make treatment options untenable (Eckstrom et al. 2013). Furthermore, older adults are often underrepresented in both cancer screening and treatment trials, making recommendations around either, especially older adults with multimorbidity, functional impairments, and shorter life expectancy more difficult.
	Currently in the US routine screening for cervical and breast cancers in women is still recommended for those up to the age of 65 and 74 years, respectively; screening for colorectal cancer is recommended for all adults over the age of 50 and up to the age of 75 years depending on the person’s health and comorbidities; meanwhile, in men 70 years and older there remains insufficient evidence to support prostate cancer screening using the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test (US Preventive Services Task Force 2019). In any case appropriate testing should occur for appropriate symptomology in line with an individual’s overall goals of care.





Specific conditions predominantly affecting older people


	A number of conditions affect older people with greater frequency and impact than those who are younger. This includes dementias, falls and osteoporosis, incontinence, frailty, and loneliness, as well as elder abuse. Further, older adults are also at risk of diseases that affect all populations, including mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety. The unique manifestations and impact of these conditions in older people has long been neglected in research, and it is increasingly evident that such issues impact the lives of older people in significant ways.





Dementia


	The growing global prevalence of dementia is partially the result of population ageing, combined with improving awareness and diagnosis of the disease. With the greatest risk factor for developing dementia, with Alzheimer’s disease being the most common form, being age, women remain more likely to develop dementia than men, due to their greater longevity. It is currently estimated that there are more than 50 million people currently living with dementia worldwide, and that this figure will reach 131.5 million in 2050 (Alzheimer’s Disease International 2019).
	Advances in the prevention and management of cardiovascular diseases over the past few decades, and improvements in educational attainment, has likely contributed to a lower current prevalence of vascular and some others forms of dementia (Livingston et al. 2017). While there currently exists no cure for dementias, key reasons to support early diagnosis include the ability to provide pharmacological and social interventions that can help manage the manifestations of dementia, and better support for involved caregivers and individuals with dementia to live with as much independence as possible.





Falls and osteoporosis


	Falls are a common and major cause of disability in older adults, with both the risk of falls and the risk of injury from falls increasing with both age and frailty. Approximately 30% of community-dwelling older adults report sustaining a fall on an annual basis, while between 5 and 10% of falls result in serious injuries such as osteoporosis-related fractures (Gillespie et al. 2012). Falls are often attributed to a complex interaction of risk factors that include chronic and acute illnesses, mobility or balance issues, medications, and cognitive impairment. Falls are also a growing concern because injuries from falls can threaten an older person’s mobility, independence, and confidence. A number of interventions have been shown to reduce the risk of falls, including health/environment risk factor screening/intervention programmes, muscle strengthening, and balance retraining, and home hazard assessment and modification (Gillespie et al. 2012). Furthermore, the increased recognition of osteoporosis as a preventable and treatable disease common in older men but especially older women would aid in the dissemination of proven medical therapies that could significantly reduce a person’s future risk of sustain a fragility fracture.





Incontinence


	While urinary and faecal incontinence are not diseases of older age per se, the likelihood of having these conditions significantly increases with age, especially in older adults. The prevalence of any degree of urinary incontinence in older adults is reported to be as high as 5.4% for men and 29% for women (Herschorn et al. 2008), while the overall prevalence of faecal incontinence is 15.3% (Whitehead et al. 2009). Incontinence impacts all parts of a person’s, and by extension, their caregiver’s life, including staying active and socially engaged, and can lead to increased social isolation, depression, physical deconditioning, falls, fractures, and skin breakdown. Despite the high prevalence of these issues, older adults often do not seek treatment due to embarrassment and social stigma, or because they assume this is a normal aspect of ageing, and left untreated, incontinence can worsen over time. Educating both the public and professionals on how to engage more around this issue will allow more persons with these issues to be supported.





Elder abuse and neglect


	Elder abuse is defined as ‘a single, or repeated act, or lack of appropriate action, occurring within any relationship where there is an expectation of trust which causes harm or distress to an older person’ (WHO/INPEA 2002). It can take various forms: physical, verbal, psychological/emotional, sexual, and financial, and also reflect intentional or unintentional neglect, as well as self-neglect. The self-reported global annual prevalence rate of elder abuse in 2015 was found to be 15.7% affecting an estimated 140 million older people (Yon et al. 2017). Psychological and financial abuse were the most commonly reported forms (11.6% and 6.8%, respectively), with neglect, physical, and sexual abuse representing 4.2, 2.6, and 0.9% of cases (Yon et al. 2017).
	The most likely persons to commit elder abuse are family members and friends which creates especially complex situations when an older person is also dependent on their abuser for having their living or care needs met. With population ageing, the likelihood exists that elder abuse will increase unless it is more comprehensively recognized and addressed, especially when it can result in higher rates of depression, anxiety, hospitalization, nursing home placement, and mortality (Lachs and Pillemer 2015).





Depression and anxiety


	The WHO estimates 15% of people over the age of 60 live with mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety (WHO 2017), which in older people can present atypically and is likely under-recognized. There are a number of reasons to expect why people may experience poorer mental health in later life, including the presence of more potential psychosocial stressors such as financial stress, social isolation, a lack of social support and losses, as well as the increasing likelihood with age of experiencing chronic illnesses, multimorbidity, and living with frailty. It is worthwhile, to screen for depression and anxiety, as there are many effective non-pharmacological and pharmacological treatments.





Models of care to support older people


Primary care for older people


	It is essential that the evolving needs of older people are reflected in the routine provision of primary care by ensuring its practitioners are appropriately trained to have a solid understanding of normal ageing as well as the common problems and issues including those that can present more atypically in older adults. In addition to becoming more aware of effective disease prevention interventions, understanding the importance of screening for and how to manage common geriatric issues like dementia, falls, osteoporosis, incontinence, constipation, frailty, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy, will be essential towards the provision of effective primary care of older people. Indeed, the reality is that when older persons with complex needs are paired with the inadequate provision of primary care, this tends to lead to more physician visits, more prescribed medications, more visits to emergency departments, more hospital admissions, and worse overall outcomes (Nie et al. 2008.).
	Traditional clinic-based primary care models will also need to adapt to better support older adults with more complex health and social needs to receive ongoing care by the same providers and where possible with an interprofessional team-based approach to care. The advent of primary care models like the ‘patient-centred medical home’ as well as the provision of ‘house calls’ are becoming increasingly recognized as a cost-effective alternative way of providing primary care for patients for whom this form of care is a necessity rather than a convenience that can not only improve healthcare experiences and outcomes but also their overall healthcare costs (Stall et al. 2014). Lastly, the advent of new technologies that support remote patient monitoring and the provision of ‘virtual’ care using various technologies is also gaining prominence as a way to better deliver care to frail older populations who are unable to access conventional models of care.





Specialty care for older adults


	In more developed nations the medical specialities of geriatric medicine and psychiatry have emerged to meet the changing needs of particularly frail older adults across the continuum of care. These fields’ increasing expertise lay in their ability to understand the differences between normal and abnormal ageing and how typical ways of approaching the care of older persons may need to be further adapted to achieve the most optimal outcome. The value of a Comprehensive Geriatrics Assessment (CGA), the main skilled activity geriatricians provide has also become well-established as a highly effective way to minimize overall functional decline, help older adult remain living in the community rather than in an institution and improve an older person’s chance of survival and overall quality of life (Ellis et al. 2017).
	Despite their growing perceived value as specialist providers, even in most developed countries an extreme shortages of geriatricians still exist. In Canada for example, while older Canadians began to outnumber younger Canadians in 2016, there are currently nine times the number of as paediatricians as there are geriatricians. As the specialties of geriatric medicine and psychiatry gain more traction and support for their growth, other medical subspecialty areas of care are quickly emerging like geriatric cardiology, surgery, oncology, and emergency medicine. Furthermore, the advent of specialist gerontological nurses, social workers, therapists, and pharmacists is also occurring as well in order to fill the rapidly growing need for more specialist expertise in the care of older adults.





Long-term institutional and community-based care


	Many older persons as they age will require some form of long-term care during the course of their life. A common approach until recently to address the growing need for long-term care associated with population ageing in middle and high incomes countries was to prioritize the provision of long-term care in more institutional-based residential care settings like nursing homes as opposed to through the provision of more home and community care. While there will always remain a role for the provision for some long-term care in institutional settings, technological advances to better support home diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring is enabling a much broader range of care to be provided in one’s home. In high-income countries, as a result of evolving societal preferences and the realization that community-based care can be far more cost-effective that institutional-based care, there is a trend towards care being increasingly provided in community settings. In many countries, a growing shortage of available paid long-term care providers and available family caregivers is placing additional demands on other health services such as acute care hospitals when inadequate long-term care capacity exists. As a result, more funding is being prioritized to better support the development and provision of more cost-effective and sustainable home and community-based long-term care.





Acute care for older people


	Older adults compared to the rest of the population, not only use hospital services more often, but also on a more urgent and critical basis and are at least twice as likely as younger populations to be admitted to the hospital with acute presentations (Keim and Sanders 2004). While older adults represent the greatest users of hospital services overall, a number of longitudinal studies have consistently demonstrated that only a small proportion of older adults are actually high users of hospital services. Furthermore, three factors appear to characterize these high users: multimorbidity, having pre-existing functional impairments that make one more dependent, and being socially frail in having inadequate social and community supports at home (Wolinsky et al. 1995).
	In recognizing that typical older patients that present to hospitals are characterized with more complex and often inter-related health and social care issues, compared to younger patients, we can appreciate that the management of their acute care needs often necessitate a different overall approach. Indeed, frail older adults have been found to be at greater risk of experiencing functional decline, delirium, longer lengths of stay, and a greater risk of becoming institutionalized or dying during or after a hospitalization. In response, the Acute Care for Elders (ACE) model of care has emerged as a response designed to improve functional outcomes and to improve the processes for the care of older patients. This model emphasizes: an environment of care designed to promote improved function for older patients; an interdisciplinary team that works together to identify/address the vulnerabilities of older patients; nursing care plans to for the prevention of disability; early planning to help prepare the patient to return home; and a review of medical care to prevent iatrogenic illness (Malone et al. 2015). Implementing specific models and point-of-care interventions and practices that encompass ACE principles in locations such as the emergency department, inpatient, transitional, outpatient, prehospital, or community settings can improve overall outcomes and reduce lengths of stay, admissions, readmissions, and inappropriate resource use (Sinha et al. 2018).
	A growing interest in helping frail older patients to minimize their need to receive acute care in hospitals has led to the emergence of more proactive prehospital models of care such as ‘community paramedicine’ that have been shown to meaningfully reduce emergency calls and in turn emergency department visits and hospitalizations (Verma et al. 2017) or alternative delivery models of acute care such as ‘hospital at home’ can result in less clinical complications such as hospital-acquired infections, delirium and functional decline, lower mortality rates, and for less overall costs (Shepperd and Iliffe 2005). These two examples represent just some of the emerging acute care models that could allow both more and less developed countries with their growing and evolving acute care systems to re-think their traditional acute care approaches in order to promote the achievement of better outcomes through the better use of limited healthcare resources.





Rehabilitative care and reablement services


	The loss of one’s functional abilities can represent the largest threat to an older individual’s independence which can often necessitate increased support to maintain one’s overall capacity for independent living. Although care that prioritizes ‘early mobilization’, can mitigate some degree of the functional loss that is commonly associated with episodes of acute or chronic illness, some frail older patients will inevitably suffer from a loss of function to such a degree that, without restorative interventions, they may not be able to return to their previous level of functional independence. Therefore, having timely access to targeted and appropriate preventive, and restorative care services is critical to minimizing the frequency and extent of functional loss experienced by at-risk older adults.
	Traditionally, individuals needing more intensive rehabilitation could only receive it in hospitals or other institutional settings, but more recently community-based rehabilitation options like geriatric day hospitals, in-home and community-based therapy options including exercise and falls prevention programmes are being developed and demonstrating their ability to better prevent and manage function decline. Furthermore, the provision of traditional home care services for those with functional limitations is increasingly being delivered using a ‘reablement’ approach that recognizes the ‘resiliency’ of many and enables them re-learn or develop new skills to once again complete their functional tasks independently. Not only does this approach further enable ageing-in-place, but it has appropriately reduced the need for ongoing long-term care services and their associated costs (Tessier et al. 2016).





The growing importance of unpaid caregivers and social support


	Within the context of ageing populations, the role of unpaid caregivers is paramount, but often still remains socially and politically invisible. In Canada, for example, half of all Canadians aged 15 and over have provided care to a family member or friend, at some point in their lives (Sinha 2013). The contributions of unpaid caregivers represent an important component of many national economies. In the United States, the provision of unpaid care has an estimated annual economic value of $470 billion, which in the same year was more than six times the total amount spent on paid home care and health services (Reinhard et al. 2015).
	With current societal, political, and economic imperatives encouraging a shift away from institutional care and towards ‘care at or closer to home’ there exists an assumption that in addition to having enough accessible and affordable housing and community-based healthcare providers, families and friends will be willing and able to continue to provide a substantial level of unpaid care. However in many countries, as their overall populations age, their population of potential unpaid caregivers is predicted to shrink. What is further complicating matters is that constantly shifting economic opportunities and the growing ease of mobility is contributing to the growing distance between family members and lessening their potential to be family caregivers.
	While both caregivers and care recipients generally regard home-based care as preferable to institutionalization, caregiving can be physically, emotionally, and financially taxing. Legg et al. (2013) reported an association between provision of care and self-reported poor health of caregivers, that also increased with the amount of care being provided. Women, who tend to spend more of their time than others providing unpaid care, are also more likely to feel the financial effects of caregiving, contributing to higher rates of later-life poverty.
	The tradition of being able to rely on family support to care for older people is changing in many countries as a result of changing economic and political conditions, the increased participation of women in paid work, and the impact of certain diseases. Economic development, urbanization, and internal and international migration, leading to demographic transitions and changing social norms are all significantly impacting on the traditional provision of intergenerational support. In what some view as an extreme response to this challenge, a new Chinese ‘Elderly Rights Law’ was instituted in 2013 requiring grown children to provide physical and emotional care for their elderly parents, including a requirement to visit their parents regularly and look after them financially, or face fines or jail sentences. HIV/AIDS has so significantly affected middle-aged populations in many regions that it has left both older people and children without support and further led to the care of orphaned children being undertaken by their grandparents.
	There is a growing recognition that caregivers must ideally be able to access training, services, and financial supports to enable and encourage them to take on and maintain caregiving roles that enables the delivery of more personalized care and enable lower health system expenditures. The UK, New Zealand, and Australia have all implemented national strategies to better support caregivers, which include information services, financial supports, community supports, legislation to allow caregivers to request flexibility in the workplace, and working with employers to show the financial and organizational benefits of better supporting caregivers in the workplace. Indeed, recognizing the important role of unpaid caregivers, and ensuring that their evolving needs are taken into account in planning and allocating resources will be needed to enable the care of ageing populations.





Age-friendly cities and communities


	The WHO over the past decade has been actively promoting the creation of age-friendly cities and communities to promote a more thoughtful approach that could promote the health and well-being of people of all ages across the life course. An age-friendly community is defined as one that recognizes the great diversity among older persons, promotes their inclusion and contributions in all areas of community life, respects their decisions and lifestyle choices, and anticipates and responds flexibly to ageing-related needs and preferences (WHO 2007). Through its work, the WHO has identified eight domains of community life that influence the quality of life and health of older persons and people of all ages: respect and social inclusion; social participation, communication, and information; civic participation and employment; outdoor spaces and buildings; transportation, housing, and community support and health services. The consideration of these eight domains into the design and development of communities, has supported the needed transformation of communities into age-friendly ones that encourage active and healthy ageing by optimizing opportunities for health, participation, and security.
	The development of the WHO Global Network for Age-friendly Cities and Communities was recently identified as one of its ten priorities to enable healthy ageing. It currently has over 500 member cities and communities across 37 countries. Among communities that have taken part in age-friendly community development activities at various levels, many have learned to assess their level of ‘age-friendliness’, how to integrate ageing perspectives into urban planning efforts, and how to create age-friendly environments that consider not only design and physical features, but also infrastructure, policies, and service provision. Further increased concern towards ensuring older people have appropriate and affordable housing and transport options and that pedestrian safety and safety from violence and crime are better addressed will ensure that the social involvement and the health and well-being of older people can be better supported.





Public health implications of population ageing


	As seen in this chapter, population ageing is a major global phenomenon that will continue to have a major impact on disease and disability patterns and on the use of health and social services. A coordinated and appropriate public health response, therefore, is essential if this phenomenon is to translate into an opportunity for longevity and healthy ageing, rather than a threat to global health and resources.
	Public health is important in monitoring trends and transitions in risk factors, disease, and disability, encouraging effective health promotion practices that promote healthy ageing, and in setting policy for equitable and efficient use of healthcare resources for this growing population that requires different and more customized approaches to their care. The fact that vaccinations rates among the elderly lag far behind those of children speaks to just some of the significant public health gaps that currently exist. For example, no country other than South Korea has achieved the WHO-recommended target influenza vaccination rate of 75% for older adults (National Institute on Ageing 2018).
	Health promotion to support healthy ageing begins in early life and continues throughout the life course to the oldest ages. As noted earlier, exercise, not smoking and maintaining strong social networks can allow older adults to live significantly longer that others who do not engage in these practices. Increasingly, it is also becoming recognized that dementia is not an inevitable consequence of ageing and that nine potentially modifiable health and lifestyle factors from different phases of life that, if eliminated, might prevent the development of dementias (Livingston et al. 2017). Much more knowledge is needed as to how we can optimize the conditions and experiences of ageing.
	Finally, better acknowledgement and recognition of the continued contributions made by older people themselves, as well as unpaid caregivers, to their families and communities and national economies is also of fundamental importance in addressing ageism and better meeting the challenges of an ageing population and their associated health needs.





Summary


	 	• Ageing is universal, unavoidable, and not uniform.
	• Population ageing is occurring at far greater rates in low-and middle-income countries than in high-income countries, and is placing considerable strains on health and social care sectors in varying ways.
	• Increased longevity has not been experienced uniformly across socioeconomic and ethno-cultural groups or in different countries.
	• Severe disability is becoming less common in successive cohorts of older people indicating that a compression of morbidity and disability is occurring, although not with certainty in a growing number of cases.
	• Advances in healthcare for older people have more recently had dramatic effects in improving survival and reducing disability associated with the inevitable increases in chronic diseases at older ages, but has also allowed the emergence of new chronic diseases like Alzheimer’s and other related and incurable dementias that now appears to be emerging as one of the greatest global challenges for health and social care in the twenty-first century.
	• Families and increasingly friends in all countries are increasingly providing a major part of the care needed by older people—as unpaid caregivers—but do require more knowledge and support of formal health and social services.
	• Public health has major roles in surveillance, disease prevention and the promotion of healthy ageing, and in the development of health and social services for older people.

10.9


Forced migrants and other displaced populations


	Catherine R. Bateman Steel and Anthony B. Zwi





Introduction to forced migrants and other displaced populations


	Migration and displacement have always been features of human life but the intensification of globalization, and increased ease of travel and interconnectedness, has seen the effects of displacement reaching far beyond the immediate contexts in which they occur. Forced migration is displacement that involves coercion and the implication that those involved have moved against their will. The previous few decades with the end of the cold war, rapid globalization, increasing inequality between and within nations, ongoing wars, and conflict (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) 2006), have created a landscape where forced migration affects all populations to some extent, whether as displaced or as hosts to the displaced. Health professionals will undoubtedly be confronted with the effects of forced migration and called upon to engage in responses for those affected regardless of where they practice. This chapter aims to provide a global overview of forced migration and the public health challenges facing populations forced to move from their usual homes, in order to assist the public health professional in framing their own responses. It begins by presenting a brief history of forced migration and the legal definition of ‘refugee’. We describe the emergence of categories of forced migrants that do not meet the legal definition of ‘refugee’, describe how these groups are treated by states, and the implications for people’s lives and health. The chapter then explores the social and political factors that have influenced the treatment of refugees by states. We lay out some of the major health issues that refugees face in both developing and developed countries. The wide variety of actors involved in both protecting forced migrants and providing health services is presented, along with a discussion of the contextual conditions that have an impact, often detrimental, on the health of forced migrants. As well as describing the structural factors that create and limit health outcomes, this analysis seeks to highlight the agency and voice of forced migrants, exploring the importance of understanding and projecting these, and of appreciating the rationales for how forced migrants may act in the often chaotic situations in which they find themselves. We consider how interactions with other actors, within the complex social, political, and legal context of forced migration, may lead to seemingly unhealthy choices, and at times, barriers to engaging with services. Yet, forced migrants make choices, when possible, seeking to protect their well-being and fight for better, and healthier, outcomes.





Causes of displacement


The global context


	Forced migration reached record levels in 2011 with more people becoming refugees in that year than in any year since the start of the new millennium. Humanitarian crises in countries such as Sudan, Libya, Somalia, and Côte d’Ivoire, as well as ongoing instability in Afghanistan and Iraq among others, contributed to a staggering 4.3 million people being newly displaced from their homes (UNHCR 2011). While war, violence, and natural disaster are major contributors, and the causes most commonly associated with forced migration, it is important to consider the broader global dynamics that shape and create the forced migration situation.





Globalization, inequality, and perceptions of crisis


	Forced migration cannot be fully understood without considering the global context and the shifting global forces that shape the form and patterns of migration. Globalization and its role in shaping the dynamics of forced migration need to be considered. Although globalization is a contested concept with disputed definitions, most people accept it as a global process of integration which affects sociocultural, economic, and political domains (see Chapter 1.5). The increased ease of travel, and the cultural interconnectedness that projects visions of opportunities in distant lands, provides a context which may facilitate migration among those with powerful forces driving them from their homes.
	The economic implications of the globalized landscape are also worthy of mention in any analysis of forced migration. There is a polarized debate over the effects of globalization on human development and health. Some commentators argue, like Feachem (2001), that the forces of economic globalization may be beneficial to the poor, increasing wealth and therefore health; while others (Baum 2001; MacDonald 2007) highlight the poor health situation in many developing countries and the vast inequities present, and suggest that globalization plays a part in generating these conditions by creating an uneven playing field and weighting the economic benefits towards those that already have power and wealth. They argue that globalization cannot be separated from economic policies that serve the interests of the wealthy, reinforcing or exacerbating inequalities, fuelling conflicts, and contributing to public health crises in developing countries. This analysis suggests that the only way to improve health is to seriously restructure the dominant international financial institutions. Taking the middle ground, Lee (2004) suggests that rigorous, ongoing analysis is required to assess the positive and negative impacts on health within the overall conceptual domain of globalization. Zwi and Alvarez-Castillo (2003) argue that globalization has often led to poor health outcomes for vast populations and that this in turn is responsible for fuelling forced migration. Regardless of our standpoint on globalization, what it is, how it impacts on health, and its influence, what is clear is that global inequities exist and are dramatic, the impact of such inequities cannot be ignored as major contributors to forced migration, whether or not associated with violence.
	Castles (2004) provides an analysis that calls for careful examination of the global context when describing forced migration dynamics. He argues that the current perception of a global ‘asylum crisis’ should be seen more as a crisis of North–South relationships, within which ‘asylum’ is but one aspect. The current picture of forced migration, he argues, is a result of disparities between ‘North’ and ‘South’. Although the North–South conceptualization does not perhaps accurately represent the divisions we see today, we can see the dynamics he describes as ‘North–South’ as being between the wealthy and less-wealthy nations. While disparities exist and people search for a better life, or simply for survival, forced migration will continue. The disparity is also reflected in how the effects of forced migration are absorbed globally, further deepening the crisis in North–South relations. He shows that while there has repeatedly been a perception of impending asylum crises ever since the 1800s, which largely do not fully emerge as feared, there are some new features. He cites the increase in endemic violence and human rights violations as a feature that has increased the volume of forced migration in recent times. Castles (2004) shows, however, that for the North, there is no significant economic or social crisis resulting from forced migration and contrary to popular belief, the North has not had to absorb large influxes of people. The situation is nonetheless construed by those in the North as a crisis because it highlights the ‘erosion of nation-state sovereignty’. The South, however, has absorbed the vast majority of forced migrants from neighbouring countries (Allotey and Reidpath 2003). This combined with increasingly restrictive policies of wealthy countries that seek to limit refugee absorption from the South, leads to a tension in North–South relations, and opens space for people smuggling and trafficking, further threatening the sense of control over borders that the North is seeking to maintain, and therefore deepening the sense of crisis perceived by the North. Hence the burden has been left largely with the South, while in the North, incomplete pictures of fear that exclude vulnerable people have been painted and promoted (Grove and Zwi 2006). In their review of globalization, forced migration, and health, Zwi and Alvarez-Castillo (2003) suggest that public health professionals have a responsibility to examine the context and whole picture, and in so doing, to break down these ‘incomplete pictures of fear’ and advocate for a more humane globalization that has a chance of decreasing the poor health outcomes associated with forced migration.





Immediate drivers of displacement


	There is general agreement on the range of factors that contribute to displacement and forced migration. However, the importance of particular factors, and the linkages between them, varies in different contexts. Identification of specific causes has implications for both the states involved and the migrants themselves, given that the perceived cause of displacement has an impact on the international response, the level of funding support provided, and the attitudes of host populations to those seeking protection. The health consequences of forced migration will be shaped by not only the causes of displacement, but also by the perceptions of all actors regarding these causes and their relationship to them. In this respect, the terms and context within which forced migrants are described and ‘presented’ greatly affects the societal response and opportunities, or constraints, operating.
	Forced migration has traditionally been associated with war and violence. The conception of a refugee as defined by the United Nations (UN) Convention, fleeing from persecution to a place of safety in another country, was clear-cut and well understood. As Moore and Shellman (2004) describe, the central model was one of:
	Violence in = Forced migration out.
	However, while the main causes of involuntary displacement remain armed conflict, repression, and war, other factors such as natural disasters and development projects are also important, as are the more complex set of economic, social, and political circumstances that may lead to trafficking and people smuggling.
	Martin (2002) focuses attention on natural and man-made disasters and border changes leading to statelessness, as factors which lead to forced migration, alongside the well-recognized factors related to persecution, human rights violations, repression, and conflict. Environmental factors, such as rising sea levels and extreme weather conditions, are also increasingly recognized as important. Some argue that these causes may, over time, supersede conflict as a primary cause of forced migration (Myers and Kent 1995). Resource constraints, including depleted access to land and water, and conflict over precious minerals, are likely to become increasingly important, especially as the global population increases from around 6 billion people at present to nearly 9 billion by 2050.
	While all these factors are important, quantifying their effects is difficult. Data are available regarding numbers of ‘Convention’ refugees (see ‘Categories of forced migrants’ section) and also, more recently, regarding internally displaced persons (IDPs). These data may give some indication of the level of displacement produced by conflicts and violence, alongside immediate natural disasters such as tsunamis and earthquakes. However, more insidious environmental and economic effects are far harder to quantify.
	The increased complexity of recent times in describing and understanding factors that cause displacement raise new concerns that go beyond the simple ‘violence migration’ model therefore calls for new approaches. Major challenges include an increased focus on economic migrants and those who are forced to move as a result of environmental and climate changes; there is also a rise in ‘mixed migration’, a term which recognizes that many migrants fall somewhere on the spectrum between forced and voluntary migration and are hard to categorize as one or the other.
	Particularly important is a call for a shift in policies of protection for host countries to developing policies which address the root causes within countries from which people are forced to migrate; and a growing recognition that understanding causes may allow predictions of impending displacement as well as the identification of the means to avert large-scale displacement. Some analyses continue to support the primacy of violent conflict, or threat of conflict as the major predictor of populations leaving their homes. Moore and Shellman (2004) analysed a global sample of 40 countries and using a model that incorporated a wide range of indicators (government threat, dissident threat, government-dissent interaction, ethnic or non-ethnic civil wars, war on territory, income opportunity, political freedom and the rule of law, and cultural and family ties), they found that the first three were the primary determinants of forced migration flows. These were more important than other factors such as size of economy or type of political institution. Apodaca (1998) analysed a variety of models developed to predict forced migration and concluded that human rights violations are one of the most important predictors.
	Economic migration has often been portrayed in the media as freely chosen migration that should not confer a responsibility to protect on accepting states. However, analysts such as Castles (2003) argue that forced migration is linked to economic migration and that the two are ‘closely related (and indeed often indistinguishable) forms of expression of global inequalities and societal crises’. These inequities have intensified since the end of the cold war. He argues that studies of the causes of forced migration have neglected the overarching economic and social structures which should be seen in relation to ‘US political and military domination, economic globalization, North–South inequality and transnationalism’ (Castles 2003).
	Debates regarding causes of displacement have particular salience in relation to the protection offered to forced migrants. As subsequent sections of this chapter describe, the nature and extent of protection is often determined by perceived cause. Therefore, understanding these debates is crucial as they may have effects on what and how protection, if any, is offered to forced migrant populations.





Categories of forced migrants


	Definitions of forced migration have been debated for more than 50 years, dating back to the first UN Convention on Refugees in 1951. The legal framework that emerged under the Convention centred on ‘refugees’ as a specially defined group and is based upon the 1951 Convention and a subsequent 1967 protocol. According to these, a refugee is a person who:
	 	owing to a well-founded fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality membership of a particular social group, or political opinion, is outside the country of his nationality, and is unable to or, owing to such fear, is unwilling to avail himself of the protection of that country. (UNHCR 2009)
	This definition has been modified by regional instruments in Africa and Latin America, as described in a later section. The International Association for the Study of Forced Migration (IASFM), however, defines forced migration much more widely as:
	 	a general term that refers to the movements of refugees and internally displaced people (those displaced by conflicts) as well as people displaced by natural or environmental disasters, chemical or nuclear disasters, famine, or development projects. (Forced Migration Online 2008)
	This definition encompasses a wide range of forced migrants, and these can be distinguished into several distinct groups (Table 10.9.1).
	The definitions of other forced migrant groups, and their sources, are outlined in the following subsections. They highlight the increased attention devoted to describing, as well as defining, the many forms of forced migration that exist. The discourse and narratives presented have a marked impact on how people see, and respond to, those forced to leave their usual homes and livelihoods.





Internally displaced persons


	Unlike refugees, there is no legal definition of an IDP. It is generally accepted that if a person meets the definition of a refugee, but their displacement does not take them across an international border, then they are internally displaced. The Secretary General of the UN has appointed a representative to deal with IDPs and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) has produced a set of Guiding Principles to address the specific needs of IDPs who are described as:
	 	persons or groups of persons who have been forced or obliged to flee or to leave their homes or places of habitual residence, in particular as a result of, or in order to avoid the effects of, armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights or natural or human-made disasters, and who have not crossed an internationally recognized State border. (Deng 1998)





Asylum seekers


	Asylum seekers are those who are fleeing persecution and are seeking refugee status in another country. According to the UNHCR, an asylum seeker is:
	 	Someone who has made a claim that he or she is a refugee, and is waiting for that claim to be accepted or rejected. The term contains no presumption either way—it simply describes the fact that someone has lodged the claim. Some asylum seekers will be judged to be refugees and others will not. (UNHCR 2009)
	The application referred to relates to being recognized under the 1951 Convention as a refugee and therefore being entitled to the protection and support stipulated by the Convention. They may or may not arrive in a country with authorization, nevertheless, they have a legal right to claim asylum and are therefore not ‘illegal’.





Trafficked persons


	The 2003 Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, especially women and children, describes trafficking as:
	 	recruitment, transportation, transfer, harbouring, or receipt of persons, by means of the threat or use of force or other forms of coercion, of abduction, of fraud, of deception, of the abuse of power or of a position of vulnerability or of the giving or receiving of payments or benefits to achieve the consent of a person having control over another person, for the purpose of exploitation. Exploitation shall include, at a minimum, the exploitation of the prostitution of others or other forms of sexual exploitation, forced labour or services, slavery or practices similar to slavery, servitude or the removal of organs. (UN 2003, Resolution 25)

Smuggled persons


	Smuggling of aliens or ‘illegal migrant smuggling’ is defined by the UN 2000 Protocol Against Smuggling of Migrants by Land, Sea and Air, which supplemented the UN Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime, to mean:
	 	the procurement, in order to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit, of illegal entry of a person into a state, party of which the person is not a national or permanent resident. (UN 2000, Article 3(a))





Environmentally displaced persons


	The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s online Glossary of Statistical Terms describes an environmental refugee as ‘a person displaced owing to environmental causes, notably land loss and degradation, and natural disaster’ (United Nations 1997). However, the term was first described by El-Hinnawi (1985), a researcher from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) in 1985, who defined environmental refugees as:
	 	those people who have been forced to leave their traditional habitat, temporarily or permanently, because of a marked environmental disruption (natural and/or triggered by people) that jeopardized their existence and/or seriously affected the quality of their life.
	‘Environmental disruption’ in this definition is taken to mean any physical, chemical, and/or biological changes in the ecosystem (or resource base) that render it, temporarily or permanently, unsuitable to support human life. The validity of the term ‘environmental refugees’ has been debated greatly since that time. Actors emerge from a realm of perspectives including environmentalists, economists, and refugee advocates, each with a different interpretation of the term. Some prefer to use the term ‘environmental migrant’ or ‘environmental displacee’; different terms establish different implications for both the individuals and states involved.





Development displacees


	There is no legal definition for development displacees; however, Forced Migration Online suggests they are:
	 	people who are compelled to move as a result of policies and projects implemented to supposedly enhance ‘development’. These include large-scale infrastructure projects such as dams, roads, ports, airports; urban clearance initiatives; mining and deforestation; and the introduction of conservation parks/reserves and biosphere projects. Affected people usually remain within the borders of their country. People displaced in this way are sometimes also referred to as ‘oustees’, ‘involuntarily displaced’ or ‘involuntarily resettled’. (Forced Migration Online 2008)
	Interestingly, large-scale agricultural projects do not seem to be specifically mentioned.





Forced migration statistics


	Assessing the volume of global flows of forced migrants is valuable in identifying trends and the patterns of distribution with respect to where the burden for providing assistance and care lies. In specific countries and contexts, where people are forced to migrate from their place of origin, the first step in addressing public health and other more general concerns is often to define the size of the population at risk. Donors, governments, aid agencies, and community organizations require basic demographic and related data to inform planning and service delivery. The collection of data is complicated and surrounded by controversy, having the potential to immediately reframe what looks like a technical issue into a political one.
	The two main sources of statistics on forced migrants are the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI). These organizations produce differing estimates for different types of forced migrants in different geographical contexts. The logistic difficulties of collecting reliable data from shifting forced migrant populations leaves space for political interests to enter, and seek to shape, the field. This is compounded by disagreement over definitions of forced migrants and which groups to include in which categories, as mentioned earlier, with significant implications for the rights and entitlements of such groups, as well as for who bears the responsibilities for addressing their needs. Despite contested data, available sources provide valuable information on trends and distribution.





UNHCR forced migration statistics


	The UNHCR provides data based on ‘persons of concern’, an increasingly wide-ranging term. ‘Persons of concern’ includes refugees (as defined by the 1951 Convention or the 1969 Organization of African Unity (OAU) Convention); persons granted complementary protection (alternative forms of protection for those that fall outside of the terms of the 1951 Convention) and those with forms of temporary protection; asylum seekers who in the year of data collection are still pending a final decision on an application for protection; stateless persons; refugees who returned to their country of origin in the year of data collection; and IDPs (see Table 10.9.2). For the purposes of UNHCR the latter are limited to conflict-generated IDPs to whom UNHCR protection or assistance is extended, but does not include all IDPs.
	UNHCR reported that in 2011 the number of forcibly displaced persons exceeded 42 million for the fifth consecutive year (UNHCR 2011). This figure included refugees, IDPs, and asylum seekers. It was estimated that 4.3 million people were newly displaced in 2011 due to conflict or persecution, with 800,000 of these displaced across international borders. This was a 20% increase since 2010 of new displacement. There was also an increase of 700,000 in refugees and IDPs protected by the UNHCR and 7.1 million, three-quarters of the UNHCR refugee population, were reported to be in a protracted refugee situation. Developing countries hosted four-fifths of the world’s refugees (UNHCR 2011). The countries of origin for refugees are shown in Figure 10.9.1. Afghanistan produced the greatest number of refugees followed by Iraq and Somalia. UNHCR statistics demonstrate that the majority of refugees remain within their region of origin. Pakistan was the country that hosted the most refugees in 2011, followed by Iran and Syria. Almost half of the world’s refugees falling under the UNHCR mandate were hosted in countries with a GDP per capita of less than $3,000.
