10.10


Prisoners


	A wicked problem for public health
	Tony G. Butler and Peter W. Schofield





Background


	The relationship between incarceration and population and individual health outcomes is influenced by a vast array of contextual factors. Broad determinants include national or regional differences in criminal justice system policies and their application—which influence how many individuals are incarcerated—or in the nature of the healthcare system as it functions for the general public and in prison. At the level of the individual, factors such as pre-offending medical history, indigenous or minority status, gender, education and occupational status, financial resources, and family history may each influence the impact of criminal justice system interventions on health outcomes. Incarceration can be evaluated for its immediate impact on health (i.e. among prison inmates) as well as for the consequences for health upon release. Furthermore, from a public health perspective, it is appropriate to consider the health consequences of incarceration not only upon prisoners themselves, but on their family and friends. The challenge in confronting the health needs of those incarcerated indeed constitutes a ‘wicked problem’, embodying huge social complexities, including striking health inequities, for which optimal data are frequently lacking (Plamondon and Pemberton 2019).





Historical perspective on prison public health


	Prison health reformers such as John Howard and Sir George Onesiphorous Paul in the 18th century recognized that infectious conditions could easily spread from those detained in gaols to the wider community, with dire consequences (Howard 1973). The main point of contact between the incarcerated population and the community occurred when those in detention were brought up from the bowels of squalid prisons to attend court. Well-documented cases exist whereby infectious diseases spread from prison to the community during so-called assizes (courts set up by judges who travelled across various circuits in England and Wales). Notable outbreaks (dubbed ‘Black Assizes’), included the Oxford Black Assize outbreak of 1577 resulting in over 300 deaths. The Black Assize of Exeter 1586 was caused by the filthy condition of Exeter Prison situated underneath the court. By the time the assize occurred, some individuals had been in gaol for a long period; so weak and thin, they had to be carried into the courtroom and subsequently spread disease to the judges and locals in attendance, and infected the population of the Westcountry for many months after. Typhus, known as ‘gaol fever’, was responsible for these deaths.
	In 1759, an English authority estimated that each year one-quarter of prisoners died from gaol fever and that ‘Imprisonment until the next term of court’ was often equivalent to a death sentence. This concept of prisons as a public health threat and the need for interventions to improve health is eloquently expressed by the eighteenth-century reformer and philanthropist, Sir George Onesiphorous Paul, who in 1784 stated that prison hygiene procedures were:
	 	‘Not for the benefit of the prisoners but rather to increase the ‘salutary humiliation’ of prison life and to prevent the spread of epidemic disease beyond the prison walls and to the general citizenry’.
	The spread of disease from prisons to the wider community can take place prior to release because of the substantial contact that occurs between prisoners and the general community during incarceration from legal interactions such as court appearances, via the vast number of prison guards, teachers, administrators, health staff, and welfare workers employed in prisons, and by relatives and friends during visits and day-release. All provide a potential bridge between prison and the community. Furthermore, the cycle of incarceration ensures that many individuals relentlessly cycle back and forth between prison and the community (Andolsek 1997).
	This notion of the prison as an incubator of disease originates from these historic examples but persists today in the consciousness of prison public health officials. While ‘gaol fever’ is not the focus of concern, new threats such as tuberculosis, influenza, Ebola, HIV, viral hepatitis, and COVID-19 have replaced it. A striking example of prisoners’ health impacting on the general community occurred in the countries of the former Soviet Union around the turn of the twentieth century where the epidemic of tuberculosis (TB) among the prisoner population was linked to its re-emergence in the community (Farmer et al. 1999; Stern 1999, 2000; Kenyon 2009). In 1997, an amnesty of 40,000 prisoners occurred, of whom 4,000 were estimated to have TB with a further amnesty releasing up to 120,000 prisoners to relieve chronic prison overcrowding (Gentleman 2000). This example illustrates two salient factors in prisoner healthcare—the need to ensure that appropriate infection control measures are in place in prison during incarceration to prevent the spread of infection within the prisoner population, and secondly that prison health services should be aligned with those of the community to ensure the standard of healthcare in prison is the same as that afforded to those in the community. This latter point is referred to as the ‘principle of equivalence’ and is underpinned by the United Nations’ Principles for the Treatment of Prisoners (United Nations 2015).





Prisoner populations: an international perspective


	Offender populations, most notably prisoners, comprise some of the most stigmatized and socially excluded groups in society, and are characterized by extreme socioeconomic, health, and psychological disadvantage. Those exposed to the criminal justice system are typically poorly educated, unemployed, socially isolated, and financially dependent. Epidemiological surveys of prisoners consistently find high levels of physical and psychiatric ill health, exposure to communicable diseases such as bloodborne viruses and sexually transmissible infections, and engagement in health risk behaviours including tobacco use, violence, harmful alcohol consumption, and illicit drug use. It is unsurprising therefore that studies have found increased mortality compared with community peers, particularly in the areas of drug overdose and suicide (Kariminia et al. 2007a, 2007b). Over the past 15 years, numerous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have unambiguously highlighted the extreme health needs of the offender population across all health domains (Fazel and Baillargeon 2011; Dolan et al. 2016; Fazel and Seewald 2018). While this information provides an important platform for health policy formulation it does not supplant the need for better, more effective interventions to prevent events such as suicide and drug overdose. Without question, enormous challenges face prison medical services and those involved in prison health provision and research with respect to prioritizing the use of limited resources.





Prisoner populations


	Overall, the world’s prisoner population increased in absolute terms between 2000 and 2015 to over 10 million (Coyle et al. 2016), this 20% increase in the world’s total prison population is broadly in line with the increase in the overall population (18%) over this period (see Figs. 10.10.1 and 10.10.2 from Coyle et al. 2016). However, at regional level, the prisoner populations of the Americas, Asia and Oceania all outstripped natural population growth whereas in Africa and Europe the prisoner population grew at a lesser rate than the overall population. In percentage terms, Europe is the only region showing a trend towards decarceration.
	Fig. 10.10.1 Prison population totals, 2000 and 2015*: entire world and by region.
	*Data are aggregated national prisoner population totals for the year 2000 or nearest available year. Figures for 2015 are based on World Prison Brief data as of November 2015 and vary as to the specific dates to which they refer. Source: data from Coyle A, Fair H, Jacobson J, Walmsley R. Imprisonment worldwide. The current situation and an alternative future. Policy Press, Bristol. 2016.
	Fig. 10.10.2 Percentage change in general population total and prison population totals, 2000 to 2015: entire world and by region.
	Source: data from Coyle A, Fair H, Jacobson J, Walmsley R. Imprisonment worldwide. The current situation and an alternative future. Policy Press, Bristol. 2016.
	The United States of America (USA) is the world’s largest incarcerator with over two million individuals currently behind bars (Drucker 2011). Although crime rates have fallen in recent times in many countries, the prisoner population has increased due to myriad changes in justice approaches such as: ‘three strikes and you’re out’ (in some states in the USA), mandatory minimum prison terms, better police detection methods allowing cold-case prosecutions, commissions of inquiry into historic sexual abuse of those in care, and a trend towards bail refusal (in the case of Australia) (Coyle et al. 2016).
	Internally, prisoner populations are far from static with significant prisoners movements occurring due to security reasons including splitting up gangs, for a prisoner’s safety and protection, moving prisoners to and from courts, attending medical appointments either in the community or at other correctional facilities better equipped to address certain health problems, moving individuals closer to their family in the community, to attend rehabilitation programmes at other sites, as a punishment by moving a prisoner to a facility with a harsher regime or different security classification, and moving closer to a city or town in anticipation of release.
	While the static prisoner population represents a cross-sectional count on a census date, the throughput (or churn) of prisoners is large and significant. In the USA for example, the cross-sectional population is around 2 million, but an estimated 12 million individuals cycle through USA correctional facilities each year. Globally, while around 11 million individually are incarcerated at any one time, an estimated 30 million people are released from prisons annually (Coyle et al. 2016). By further example in New South Wales (Australia’s most populous state and the jurisdiction with the highest prisoner population), the static population is around 13,000 with an estimated 180,000 prisoner movements per year. This presents challenges to prison health services in ensuring continuity of treatment within the prison system.
	In Australia, the number of adult former prisoners returning to prison within two years of their release increased from 33% in 2000 to 51% in 2015 (Corrective Services 2016). Over two-thirds of state prisoners in the USA were arrested at least once within 3 years of their release in 2005 (Durose et al. 2014), and in the United Kingdom (UK) the reoffending rate is approximately 46% after 1 year of release from prison (Ministry of Justice 2016). These figures indicate the challenges faced by departments of corrective services in preventing recidivism suggesting the need for innovation and multipronged approaches involving a range of government agencies, including the health, welfare, and justice sectors.





Indigenous incarceration


	Beyond the socioeconomic characteristics that define prisoner populations as over-representing the poor and disadvantaged, closer examination reveals that key ethnic groups are also over-represented in custodial settings. In the USA in 2017, Blacks represented 12% of the general adult population but 33% of the sentenced prisoner population while Whites accounted for 64% of adults in the community but 30% of prisoners (Bronson and Carson 2019). Expressed as a rate, there were 1,549 Black prisoners for every 100,000 Black adults but for Whites the rate is 272 per 100,000. Similarly, in the UK, 27% of prisoners identified as coming from an ethnic minority, compared with 13% in the general population (Ministry of Justice 2019). Black or British Black people comprised 13% of the UK prisoner population (Ministry of Justice 2019) but approximately 3% of the UK general population (UK Office for National Statistics 2018).
	Indigenous or first nations people have also been identified as over-represented in the prison systems of Canada, New Zealand, and Australia. In Canada, ‘In 2016/2017, Aboriginal adults accounted for 28% of admissions to provincial/territorial correctional services and 27% for federal correctional services, while representing 4.1% of the Canadian adult population’ (Malakieh 2018). While forming 12.5% of the general population aged 15 and over in New Zealand, 50% of prisoners identify as Māori, with Māori women accounting for 60% of the female prisoner population (New Zealand Department of Corrections 2007). In Australia, the pattern is similar with Aboriginal people comprising around 2% of the general population aged 18 years and over but 28% of the adult prisoner population (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2018). The overall crude incarceration rate in Australia is 164 per 100,000 but for Aboriginal people the rate is 2,481 per 100,000 (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2018). The rate varies considerably across Australia from 672 per 100,000 in Tasmania to 4,257 per 100,000 in Western Australia. It is believed that Australia has the highest incarceration rate of Aboriginal people in the world.
	Explanations for these high rates among Aboriginal people include offence criminalization with Aboriginal people more likely to be imprisoned for certain, often petty, crimes than a non-Aboriginal person, poverty, unemployment, inadequate legal representation, a lack of diversionary options for Aboriginal people, intergenerational offending, and colonization and dispossession. A comprehensive set of recommendations from a socio-legal perspective have been developed by the Australian Law Reform Commission covering Justice Reinvestment, bail, sentencing, use of community-based sentences, mandatory sentencing, prison programmes and parole, access to justice, fines and driver licences, alcohol, police response, and child protection and adult incarceration (Australian Law Reform Commission 2017). All have been identified as important in issues in the overincarceration problem.





Why is the prisoner population so unhealthy?


	Wilkinson and Pickett have drawn attention to a consistent, positive association of national or regional levels of inequality with poor health and adverse social outcomes (such as homicide or rates of incarceration) (Wilkinson and Pickett 2009) citing evidence for the potency—for its negative impact on those experiencing social inequality—of ‘social evaluative stress’ related to individuals’ perceptions of their relatively lower positions within the social hierarchy. Chronic stress can have direct effects, mediated by the autonomic nervous and endocrine systems as well as, most importantly, the brain directly, such that early experiences and exposures become biologically embedded with lifelong consequences with respect to health, behaviour and resilience to future life challenges (see next).
	Another influential theory, that of ‘fundamental causes’ posits that higher socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with better health because ‘SES embodies an array of resources, such as money, knowledge, prestige, power, and beneficial social connections that protect health no matter what mechanism are relevant at any given time’ (Phelan et al. 2010). Thus, relative to those of higher SES, individuals with less privilege are less likely to be informed about health practices, less likely to adopt them, and to have poorer access to health or preventive healthcare leading to later detection and treatment of illness when it occurs. The fundamental theory has some explanatory relevance for the disproportionate rates of incarceration—representing an unwanted outcome through contact with the criminal justice system—among those least privileged in the community.
	Finally, it is apposite to reference one of the most influential theories of crime causation, which considers low self-control as a fundamental mechanism and for which there is very considerable empirical support (Hirschi and Gottfredson 1995). The theory claims to explain more than just why individuals break the law. Poor self-control is suggested as a key cause of ‘practically everything that ( … ) provides short-term benefit at the risk of long-term cost’ (Hirschi 2004). For this reason, gambling, smoking, heavy drinking, or misusing prescription medication—examples of conduct conceivable as analogous to crime—are part of the behavioural package that the theory seeks to explain (Moffitt et al. 2011; Wills and Stoolmiller 2002; Hirtenlehner 2019). Consistent with this theory, incarcerated populations display high rates of substance abuse, illnesses related to risky sexual practices, and traumatic brain injury related to other risk taking or impulsive behaviour. These theories each contribute a perspective on why offenders, and the incarcerated in particular, are some of the most socially disadvantaged and unhealthy individuals in society.
	Enormous advances in our understanding of how early life experiences may influence later life health and behaviour have come from the study of epigenetics (Moore 2015). The extent to which specific genes are accessible to the machinery by which they are transcribed (leading to protein synthesis and the attendant biological effects) can be significantly influenced by specific events or exposures, especially in early life. For example, epigenetic changes adjacent to the gene encoding the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) implicated in the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenocortical (HPA) axis which plays a major role in the stress response have been shown to occur in the context of adverse exposures, leading to reductions in cortisol which have been shown to be associated with impaired stress response and poor self-regulation (Conradt 2017). Highlighting how early exposures of relevance may occur, in one study, intimate partner violence during pregnancy was shown to be associated with changes in the expression of the GR in the children born to that pregnancy (Radtke et al. 2011).
	The data deriving from these sophisticated genetic techniques, together with that from structural and functional brain imaging which have demonstrated important adverse biological correlates of low SES and of criminality, serve to emphasize the importance of optimizing early childhood development and reducing toxic adversity as likely to be the most effective long-term measures to reduce the individual and social harms associated with offending behaviour, often the product of individuals exposed to early life disadvantages (Hackman et al. 2010; Lange et al. 2010; Lawson et al. 2013).





A snapshot of mental and physical ill health in prisoners


	Prisoner populations are characterized by very high rates of mental morbidity and illness with rates of major mental illness such as psychosis and depression substantially exceeding community rates (Butler et al. 2006; Torrey et al. 2010; Fazel and Seewald 2018). Increased rates are seen also for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), personality disorder, ADHD and substance abuse (Fazel and Seewald 2018). The evidence for major depression and psychotic illnesses is the strongest (Fazel et al. 2016; Fazel and Seewald 2018). Despite the high level of need, these disorders are frequently underdiagnosed and poorly treated (Wilper et al. 2009). The extent to which, at the prisoner population level, incarceration itself is a cause of mental ill health is not clear but in some individuals it has an adverse impact with the development of depression with or without suicidality (Baillargeon et al. 2009; Mears and Cochran 2012).
	Mental illness has been shown to be a risk factor for suicide, premature mortality on release from prison (Kariminia et al. 2007b) and recidivism (Baillargeon et al. 2009; Fazel and Yu 2011). Issues that naturally arise in relation to this high burden of psychiatric morbidity include its optimal and efficient detection, appropriate management, and its impact on the incarceration experience and on release (Wilper et al. 2009). Upon entry into prison, immediate risks related to existing psychiatric conditions include suicidality, the health consequences of withdrawal from substances (e.g. alcohol, amphetamine, or opiates), or the sudden discontinuation of medication for which adverse consequences might ensue (e.g. anticonvulsants, antidepressants, antipsychotics). Approaches to screening for significant mental illness vary considerably both within and between countries, but as with other illnesses, incarceration presents an opportunity to identify and treat mental illnesses that may have been either unrecognized or untreated previously. The stigma and practical adverse consequences in terms of securing employment, relationship/family breakdown, or resumption of addictive behaviours can make the post-release period particularly challenging psychologically.
	Of the psychiatric illnesses prevalent among the incarcerated, there is evidence to suggest that depression and psychosis are risk factors for offending and that adequate treatment may reduce offending risk (Fazel et al. 2014; Albalawi et al. 2019). Substance abuse is also associated with an increased offending risk. The situation with respect to acquired brain injury, in many instances due to trauma, is complex. A consistent finding throughout the international literature is of a very high prevalence of self-reported traumatic brain injury (TBI) within populations of offenders and prisoners, ranging up to 85% of male prisoners in some studies (Schofield et al. 2006, 2011; Durand et al. 2017). The frontal lobes of the brain, important for regulating behaviour, are known to be especially susceptible to damage by trauma, and therefore the possibility that TBI may be causally implicated in subsequent offending behaviour arises. Several retrospective cohort studies using record linkage have identified an increased risk of offending following a TBI (Fazel et al. 2011; Schofield et al. 2015); however a study in which non-head trauma cases served as controls failed to find evidence of offending risk associated with TBI, although in that study only mild TBI was evaluated (Kennedy et al. 2017). Indeed, many of the TBIs reported by offenders may be mild, following which the likelihood of significant brain damage impacting brain function is low. In some unknown proportion of offenders who report a TBI which preceded their offending, the TBI may have been a consequence of an underlying predisposition towards impulsive or risky behaviour (Schofield et al. 2019).
	With respect to physical health, prisoners have a substantial excess of morbidity relative to the general community. One study from the USA, in which adjustment was made for age, gender, race, education, employment, the USA as birthplace, marital status, and alcohol consumption found elevated rates of hypertension, asthma, arthritis, cervical cancer, hepatitis but no increased odds of diabetes, angina, myocardial infarction and a lower odds of obesity (Binswanger et al. 2009).
	For some individuals, incarceration may be associated with health benefits, related to the provision of increased access to healthcare compared with the community, abstinence from illicit drugs, alcohol and tobacco, and reduced risk of accidents or violence. The benefits may differ according to racial/ethnic group and by country (Fazel and Benning 2006; Kariminia et al. 2007a; Spaulding et al. 2011). Thus, in the USA, compared to community controls, African American (but not white) men were reported to have substantially reduced mortality for the period of time in prison although the effect largely disappeared when adjustment was made for the compassionate release of prisoners with terminal illnesses (Spaulding et al. 2011). By contrast, in the UK and France, in prison mortality was reduced overall among prisoners, although deaths by pneumonia and other infective illnesses were higher (Clavel et al. 1987). More consistent are the findings of increased mortality in the months after release from prison, related to factors including suicide, overdose either deliberate or unintentional, violence or liver disease (Kariminia et al. 2007b; Spaulding et al. 2011).





Drug use in prisoner populations


	Alcohol and other drug (AoD) use is a defining characteristic of prisoner populations (Butler et al. 2006; Fazel et al. 2006), and the association between AoD use and offending behaviour, including violent offending, is well established. In New South Wales, Australia, 60% of prisoners surveyed as part of the highly regarded New South Wales’ Inmate Health Survey report they were drunk, ‘high’, or ‘stoned’ at the time of committing the offence for which they were currently imprisoned, most commonly on amphetamine or methamphetamine (49.1%), alcohol (43.8%), and cannabis (27.1%) (Justice Health & Forensic Mental Health Network 2015). Methamphetamine use in the 12 months prior to incarceration has now surpassed cannabis use in Australia (Butler and Simpson 2017).
	Approximately half of all prisoners report histories of injecting drug use (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2015; Justice Health & Forensic Mental Health Network 2015; Butler and Simpson 2017). While most injecting drug users (IDUs) suspend this behaviour during incarceration, approximately half of IDU continue to do so during incarceration (Fetherston et al. 2013). Only a small proportion of individuals report commencing injecting drug use during imprisonment (Butler et al. 2003). Drug use in prison is fairly common with over half of participants (56%) reporting that drugs were either ‘quite easy’ or ‘very easy’ to obtain in NSW prisons (Justice Health & Forensic Mental Health Network 2015). Injecting drug use is the overwhelming risk factor associated with hepatitis C transmission (Luciani et al. 2014). However, in the prison context other risk behaviours implicated in the transmission of infectious diseases include: amateur tattooing, sharing barbering equipment, and blood-to-blood contact during fights (Luciani et al. 2014).
	Problematic alcohol use receives far less attention than illicit drugs in the prison context, possibly due to its legal status, yet two-thirds of those reporting alcohol use in the 12 months prior to incarceration (67%) had consumed hazardous or harmful quantities of alcohol (Justice Health & Forensic Mental Health Network 2015). Despite the widespread and problematic use of alcohol among those in prison when in the community, a lack of evidence-based prison-based alcohol treatment programmes is apparent in the peer reviewed literature (de Andrade et al. 2018; Doyle et al. 2019). This is important given the link between substance use and reoffending and suggests a need for more prison-based drug treatment options for this population (de Andrade et al. 2018).
	Apropos the high rates of drug use in this population, histories of injecting drug use, prison drug use, and also injecting drugs in prison, it is notable that few jurisdictions internationally have allowed the provision of clean injecting equipment despite its proven effectiveness in reducing the spread of bloodborne viruses in the community (Stöver and Hariga 2016). Reasons for this include arguments that it will effectively arm prisoners with a weapon to be used against prison personnel. However, to our knowledge only one case of a prison officer being stabbed with a needle has been reported in the literature. This occurred in Australia and tragically resulted in the officer dying from AIDS. This incident has harmed efforts to consider the provision of clean injecting equipment both in Australia and beyond. This day is still remembered by custodial officers in New South Wales over 20 years since the incident occurred. It is also argued that introducing needle exchanges in prison would be viewed as condoning drug use and this should be avoided. Interestingly, similar arguments are used by opponents of condom provision to prisoners, i.e. if filled with liquid and frozen they can be used as a cudgel, and symbolically they are seen as condoning and promoting sex between prisoners (even providing sexual predators with protection from sexually transmissible infections). However, evidence suggests that condom introduction in the Australian context did not increase sex between prisoners but, when sex did occur, promoted safe sex between prisoners (Butler et al. 2013).





Smoking


	Tobacco smoking is recognized as one of the deadliest health risk behaviours, responsible for killing up to half of its users and more than seven million deaths each year (WHO n.d.). More than six million of these deaths are the result of direct tobacco use while around 890,000 are the result of non-smokers being exposed to second-hand smoke (WHO n.d.). Successful public health campaigns have contributed to reducing daily smoking rates in the general population in many developed countries, but these reductions are generally not reflected among prisoners. For example, smoking rates fell from 19% in the general Australian population in 2001 to 12% in 2016 (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare n.d.) However, among prisoners, there has been no corresponding downward trend and the rate of current tobacco smoking has remained stubbornly high at around 84%. This is due to high rates of tobacco use in key marginalized groups who are over-represented in prisoner populations—IDUs, those with mental illness, and Aboriginal people (in the case of Australia) (Baker et al. 2006).
	The main response to tobacco control in prisons has been to ban smoking altogether (Spaulding et al. 2018). Whether this is in response to concerns for smokers’ health or a fear of litigation by non-smoker prisoners and staff is unclear. While banning smoking undeniably improves air quality (Proescholdbell et al. 2008) and reduces the health risk posed to non-smokers, this measure is not without consequences such as the creation of another black market borne out of tobacco scarcity and the problems associated with this, and smoking other noxious substances as a substitute (Puljevic et al. 2018). The issue of smoking bans can present a dilemma for public health officials who by nature are opposed to tobacco smoking yet believe that the human rights of one of the most vulnerable groups in society ought to be respected. The effectiveness of smoking bans as a cessation strategy is questionable with several studies indicating that many of those released to freedom go on to relapse. One USA study found that 63% of former prisoners relapsed on their first day of release, 82% after 1 week, 86% after 4 weeks, and 97% had resumed smoking at 6 months (Lincoln et al. 2009). These figures illustrate several important points for those working in public health in prison and the extreme challenge posed by this population. Firstly, the scale of the problem is staggering with few, if any, other population group in the community having such high levels of tobacco smoking. Secondly, the high rates suggest an absence of appropriately tailored and effective interventions specific to the needs of this population to achieve sustained abstinence. Thirdly, going from total bans that promote drastically reduced tobacco smoking during incarceration to almost all relapsing after fairly short periods in the community suggests existing interventions are ineffective for this population or don’t reach them, or that continuity of care is lacking with respect to health promotion activities aimed at tobacco smoking in the transition from prison to the community.





Women prisoners


	The number of women and girls in prison worldwide has been reported to have increased by 53% since 2000, against a global population growth (from 2000 to mid-2016) of 21% (ICPR 2017). Consistent with the situation in other countries, in Australia women represent a substantially smaller proportion of the total prisoner population than men (9% vs. 91% in Australia), but there was an 85% increase in women prison numbers between 2008 and 2018 (vs. 55% in men) (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2018). The increase has been particularly marked among Aboriginal women with a 117% increase between 2008 and 2018 (versus a 74% increase in non-Aboriginal women in Australia). Many of these women have endured significant abuse and trauma and much of their substance use, mental health issues, and violence likely has its origins in past traumatic events (Wilson et al. 2017). Higher levels of psychiatric morbidity and substance use are found among women prisoners relative to men (Fazel et al. 2016). In Australia, 2 in 5 (38%) women coming into prison reported they had children in the community who were dependent on them for their basic needs (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2015). The rate of women incarcerated for violence offences is increasing (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2018). Recognizing that ‘women prisoners are one of the vulnerable groups that have specific needs and requirements’, and that prison system worldwide have been developed around men, in 2010 the ‘United Nations Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners and Non-custodial Measures for Women Offenders’—the Bangkok Rules (UNODC 2010)—were passed by the UN. This resolution encourages member states ‘to adopt legislation to establish alternatives to imprisonment and to give priority to the financing of such systems, as well as to the development of the mechanisms needed for their implementation’.





Family members


	There is a growing literature attesting to the adverse health effects of incarceration upon family members. Significant increases in the frequency of adverse physical and mental health problems, as well as increased mortality, have been found in the children of prisoners (Wildeman 2014; Wildeman et al. 2014; Wildeman and Wang 2017) and rates of obesity and cardiovascular disease may be elevated in women who have a family member incarcerated, even after controlling for socioeconomic status (Roettger and Boardman 2012; Lee et al. 2014). Because African Americans in the USA, and those of indigenous background in the USA and other countries, are far more likely to be imprisoned, the burden of such health consequences is more likely to affect women and children of the same racial or ethnic background, compounding pre-existing levels of disadvantage. The impact on children of having a parent incarcerated can be extensive, prolonged, and insidious, including developmental problems affecting learning behaviour, and psychological issues (Lee et al. 2013).





The ageing offender


	In the USA, the incarceration epidemic has been associated with a substantial increase within the prison system of older inmates, and other countries are experiencing similar developments, albeit in lower absolute numbers. In comparison with the non-offender population, related at least in part to the greater burden of chronic disease, prisoners as a group display features of accelerated ageing due to poor health, mental illness and lifestyle factors, including drug and alcohol misuse, and other social determinants such as trauma, homelessness and victimization (Angus 2015). In the USA, from 1996 to 2008, the number of older adults in jail who were aged 55 or older increased 278% compared to a 53% increase in the overall jail population. Data from Canada indicate that 25% of the federal prison population are aged 50+, a 50% increase over the preceding decade (Darrell and Beck 1997; Beck and Berzofsky 2010; OCI 2019).
	Based on figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the number of prisoners aged 65 years and over has increased by 348% between 2001 and 2017 (Ginnivan et al. 2018). The increase was over 700% in the case of women prisoners in the same age group. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended restructuring prisons to accommodate the environmental needs of elderly prisoners (WHO 2014). Recommended provisions include grip rails, seats in showers, bunk bed ladders, ramps and widened doorways to accommodate wheelchairs, and better access to bathroom facilities. The WHO has also urged institutions to adopt appropriate screening for conditions associated with ageing, such as sensory impairment, mobility problems and arthritis (WHO 2014).
	The serious nature of some older prisoner’s crimes (e.g. historic sexual offences or murders) often precludes their diversion into the community, release at the end of their allotted sentence, or compassionate release on diagnosis of a terminal illness. Those released at the conclusion of their prison sentence face difficulties finding accommodation in aged care facilities who are often reluctant or unable to accommodate ex-offenders, placing this group at an increased risk of homelessness.
	In a recent USA study using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) to evaluate cognition, 70% of 310 individuals who had been incarcerated for at least 48 hours aged 55 years and older met criteria for cognitive impairment (defined by a MoCA score of <24) (Ahalt et al. 2018). Those scoring within this range were more likely to be non-white, report fair or poor health and, on six month follow-up, were more likely to make multiple visits to the emergency room and to be rearrested.
	Some of the most difficult and controversial issues with respect to the application of criminal justice system procedures, including the appropriateness of incarceration, arise in relation to violent or other serious illegal acts by individuals who have sustained brain damage or disease affecting parts of the brain that mediate or regulate behaviour. Such individuals include those suffering from frontotemporal dementia (FTD), a condition associated specifically with behavioural dysregulation and loss of insight (Liljegren et al. 2015). The growing recognition that cognitive impairment, like psychiatric problems, when present in individuals who come to the attention of the criminal justice system, may better be managed through the health system than the criminal justice system has, in some settings, been reflected in changes in legislation. For example, in New South Wales, Australia, the Mental Health Act was recently changed to allow for the possible diversion of individuals with cognitive impairment away from courts and legal sanction to healthcare settings for further assessment and management. The operational consequences of such legislation, however, include practical challenges with respect to how best to screen for cognitive impairment. One distinct challenge relates to the fact that impairments of self-control and insight of major relevance to offending behaviour (so-called executive impairment), may not be accompanied by any formal test abnormalities but are typically detected based upon history from an informant.





Research challenges in the prison setting


	An extensive literature describes the myriad health problems facing prisoners, but a dearth of evidence exists regarding interventions for this population. Information regarding health status is important but it needs to be complemented by culturally sensitive treatments and interventions that are customized to this population and the unique environment. A search of PubMed in June 2019 covering the period 1980 to 2019 using the terms ‘prisoners’ + ‘randomized trial’ returned only 34 results while ‘prisoners’ + ‘review’ or ‘meta-analysis’ yields 1,641 results. The small number of randomized trials in this setting reflects the poor evidence base in this area and also the considerable challenges of undertaking research in the prison environment.
	Difficulties undertaking research in the prison setting and challenges associated with the population may explain this trend towards descriptive rather than applied research and the employment of study designs such as randomized trials. Challenges include a protracted ethics approval processes and a culture among ethics committees of being overly protective of this population who they characterize as inherently vulnerable and incapable of providing informed consent. This perception of prisoners has likely been formed on the basis of well-documented abuses by researchers of this population in the past (Hornblum 1997). However, these are unlikely to apply today but nonetheless are still projected onto this population by zealous ethics committee members. As Beecher (1966) comments ‘the harms that are apt to result from social scientific research are rarely of the same magnitude as those produced by research in the medical sciences, which have placed the lives of unwitting research subjects at risk by infecting them with dysentery and malaria and using them as guinea pigs for LSD research’ (Beecher 1966).
	Another challenge is a tendency for the prison system not to like being examined by an external organization, including researchers. Researchers cannot simply design a study and approach participants via telephone or methodologies that rely on direct recruitment or mail-out surveys as might occur in the community. Any of these research approaches in the correctional setting requires a rigorous ethics approval process which can sometimes take several years to reach a resolution. Even with ethics approval, site-specific concerns from local prison management may prevent the research from progressing should it be deemed disruptive to the smooth running of the prison.
	Issues raised by ethics committees include whether or not prisoners should be paid for participation in research, and what form of payment (Moreno 2001). Payment is often cited by ethics committees as an inducement despite its widespread use in the community to compensate research participants. However, as Moreno states ‘none of the landmark scandals that have marred the history of medical ethics— the concentration camp experiments, the radiation experiments, the Jewish Chronic Disease Hospital case, the Willowbrook hepatitis studies, the Tuskegee syphilis study—did financial inducement figure’ (Moreno 2001).
	‘Vulnerability’ of prisoner research participants is also a widely used concept to stymie research but is often poorly articulated by ethics committees in adopting a protectionist view of this group. Fitness to provide fully informed consent is often raised as a concern. However, it is our experience across numerous surveys that most prisoners can comprehend the research being undertaken, the reason it is being conducted, and hence make an informed decision whether or not they wish to participate in a study. Recent work has established that prisoners feel insulted at the thought that a third party can decide on their behalf that they are incapable of making such a decision.
	Numerous physical barriers exist in the prison setting which present a challenge to the conduct of research including: locked doors, X-ray scanners, biometric scanners, sniffer dogs, and a reliance on custodial officers to locate research participants. However, once inside the prison walls, prisoners are mostly willing to participate in research often for altruistic reasons of genuinely wanting to improve the lot of prisoners and as a form of civic duty (Lafferty et al. 2016). Response rates in the order of 80% are not uncommon in the prison setting if participants are approached with respect and the research is explained properly. Contrary to popular perception, prisoners are reliable survey respondents. We validated self-reports of TBI in a sample of 200 men and found we could locate evidence of the reported head injury in over 80% of cases using hospital medical records (Schofield et al. 2011).
	Many individuals in prison have never been involved in surveys or invited to express opinions and often relish the opportunity to participate; they often report involvement in research as a cathartic experience. For many, involvement in research is often the first time they have ever told anyone about their background, upbringing, etc. and feel valued at being consulted. It is important that treatment pathways are put in place by researchers as part of a duty of care to participants including counselling for those who may be distressed, follow-up testing for bloodborne viruses and sexually transmissible diseases, access to hepatitis treatments, vaccinations, and other forms of treatment and care.
	The process whereby ethics committees make research on prisoners more difficult has been referred to as ‘ethics creep’ and results in research being hampered or even abandoned (Gill 2019). As Haggerty (2004) states ‘The range of potential research related harms envisioned by REBs at times seems to be limited only by the imagination of different reviewers’ (Haggerty 2004).
	While we recognize the important and necessary role that ethics committees play, a more realistic approach should be adopted to facilitate a better understanding of the population they serve, and greater recognition be given to the positive benefits that can accrue from research in this field.





Cost of incarceration


	Taken in its broader context, the vast sums of money spent on incarceration indirectly impact on public health as the criminal justice system absorbs funding that could otherwise be spent on health and education (Settumba et al. 2018). Justice Reinvestment is one approach that has been touted as a solution to this conundrum and posits that funding used for incarceration and running the justice apparatus might be better spent on programmes and infrastructure that keep people out of prison (Willis and Kapira 2018). Despite the enthusiasm of Justice Reinvestment advocates, the evidence base is small which could explain the lack of uptake by jurisdictions internationally.
	Synergizing health services between prisons and the community is important to ensure continuity of healthcare on reception into prison and on release from prison into the community. The provision of health services to prisoners is most effective when it meets the same standards as those of the broader community in terms of both the scope of services provided and the standard of healthcare. During discussions on the provision of health services to prisoners in the UK, it was commented by the Inspectorate of Prisons for England and Wales that:
	 	Prisoners were members of the wider community before their reception into prison and their health care was the responsibility of the NHS (National Health Service); the vast majority will return to that community and to the NHS on release. It is illogical that, during the time they are prisoners, their health care is provided through separate channels. (Inspectorate of Prisons for England and Wales 1996)





Public health opportunity


	Contact with the justice system via the police, courts, and prisons provides an important point of contact to connect and engage with this underserved population to identify health and social problems and initiate treatments to improve health, social, and justice outcomes. It has been suggested that imprisonment, while unfortunate, represents an important but largely overlooked public health opportunity to improve the health of this group (Glaser and Greifinger 1993). Evidence for this comes from studies showing that some prisoners are more likely to use health services when in prison than in the community (Butler and Milner 2003; Indig et al. 2009). Australia is unique in terms of having a national prisoner health data collection that collects indicators on various aspects of prisoner health and health service use on entry to prison, during incarceration, and at the time of release (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2015). Indicators from this survey show that almost all those entering prison received a health assessment, one-fifth referral to mental health services, few reporting needing to see a health professional but did not; almost all could see a health professional in prison if they wanted to; and eight out of ten prisoners reported their health either improved or stayed the same while in prison (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2015). 	Using the incarceration opportunity to tackle a major public health problem is currently being trialled in a world-first study in New South Wales (Australia) as part of efforts to eliminate hepatitis C (HCV). The Surveillance and Treatment of Prisoners with Hepatitis C (STOP-C) project aims to halt the transmission of HCV in prisons and hence the community when otherwise infected individuals are released from prison back to the community (Hajarizadeh et al. 2017). As the global burden of HCV infection continues to rise with an estimated 71 million people affected worldwide interventions that target hard-to-access populations are needed (The Polaris Observatory HCV Collaborators 2017). People who inject drugs represent the core of the HCV epidemic in developed countries, accounting for most new (80%) and existing (60%) cases (Shepard et al. 2005). HCV is particularly prevalent among prisoners with around half reporting a history of injecting drug use and one-fifth exposed to hepatitis C (Sarah et al. 2013; Butler and Simpson 2017). Significant interest exists in whether treating those in prisons with HCV can impact on the wider HCV epidemic in Australia. The treatmentas-prevention approach adopted by the STOP-C trial comes from the HIV field where it has been shown that using antiretroviral therapy can prevent HIV transmission (Cohen et al. 2011). STOP-C leverages off the new treatments for HCV which have 90–95% cure rates, few side effects, and taken for only 8–12 weeks. If successful, the possibility exists to scale-up HCV treatment thus representing one of the first attempts to use the incarceration opportunity to impact on a major public health problem affecting the wider community. If successful, this approach could be adopted for other public health problems prevalent in this population.





International covenants and protections for prisoners’ health


	Numerous statements and covenants exist that theoretically protect the health of prisoners and those held in detention; many of these have an HIV prevention focus. The most famous is the United Nations’ Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners which was first adopted in 1955 and revised following consultation as the Nelson Mandela Rules in 2015 (United Nations 1955, 2015). While not legally binding, the Mandela Rules provide broad guidelines for best practice for citizens held in prisons and other forms of custody covering physical and mental health, disability, confidentiality of healthcare, accommodation, clothing, exercise, nutrition, etc. (United Nations 2015). Although not enforceable, they do provide principles against which countries can be judged in terms of their treatment of prisoners. Similarly, the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture (OPCAT) provides a framework under the United Nations’ human rights system for oversight of places of detention and closed environments (United Nations 2002). It requires signatories to establish an independent national preventive mechanism to conduct inspections of all places of detention. As of June 2018, 88 countries have ratified the protocol (Wikipedia n.d.). However, three of the world’s largest incarcerators—the USA, Russia, and China—who together account for over 4 million prisoners—have not ratified the protocol. Brazil, the world’s third largest incarcerator has signed the protocol.
	Recent statements by the cities of San Francisco and London calling for public health approaches to be adopted to tackle incarceration (San Francisco) and violence (London) give rise to the view that traditional approaches to crime prevention have not been effective and new thinking is required to address these problems. In specifying how this approach might operate to fight violence, the public health approach is spelled out as one which:
	 	• takes a population approach, not one which just focuses on high risk individuals;
	• is preventive: by tackling ‘upstream’ risk factors, it aims to lessen ‘downstream’ consequences;
	• takes a system wide multiagency approach including involving business and volunteers;
	• takes brave decisions that require a long-term commitment;
	• recognizes the complexity of the issue, and seeks to build an evidence base that reflects that (Catch 22 2018).
	While this [preventive] thinking is the bread and butter of public health, it represents an important conceptual shift in thinking in the fight against crime which has traditionally been downstream focused and tackled by justice agencies once contact with criminal justice system has occurred.
	The public health approach to violence outlined here is important in highlighting the role of upstream factors in crime prevention which includes genetic and biological drivers of offending behaviour which to date have received little attention given the focus on sociological approaches. Traditional approaches to offending have often relied on sociological theories. Indeed, as Raine (2013) states in ‘The Anatomy of Violence’, ‘The dominant model for understanding criminal behaviour has been, for most of the twentieth century, one built on social and sociological models. … . . sole reliance on these social perspectives is fundamentally flawed’ (Raine 2013).
	The father of criminology, Cesare Lombroso, sought to identify criminal characteristics in physiognomy (Lombroso 2006). His work has long since been discredited, but advances in techniques such as brain imaging and genetics have resulted in a resurgence of interest into the biological influences on offending. The emergent discipline of ‘biosocial criminology’ seeks to explain crime and antisocial behaviour by exploring both biological and environmental factors and their interactions (Beaver 2009).
	Clearly, ‘brave decisions’ need to be made in addressing crime. Politicians frequently adhere to a perceived punitiveness on behalf of the community adopting a ‘tough on crime’ stance, driven by a populist press motivated by delivering sensationalist headlines to their readership. However, recent deliberative work that takes a more considered approach than that offered by snap opinion polls challenges this view of the community as punitive and driven by a desire for revenge and retribution. This important work, incorporating Citizens Juries and deliberative roundtables, suggests that the public, when provided with relevant information regarding the costs of incarceration and its limited deterrent and therapeutic qualities, favours the development and implementation of effective interventions to treat this population (Simpson et al. 2014). Public health can contribute to this area by promoting the use of rigorous research methodologies such as randomized control trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, and systematic reviews in the criminal justice area.
	Multiagency approaches will be required to tackle crime and hence reduce the numbers held in prison. This approach will necessarily have to harmonize biological and social factors for optimal success. To this end, the approaches of these two cities (San Francisco and London) is both refreshing and forward thinking.





Future challenges


	Consistent with our intention of preserving relevance for an international readership, we recognize that prioritization, in terms of advancing health outcomes of individuals who come in contact with the criminal justice system will differ by country, or region. Thus, a major priority within the USA concerns the imperative to halt and reverse the epidemic of incarceration, particularly among Blacks (Drucker 2011). In relatively less developed regions, such as Latin America, improvement in the physical conditions of prisons and the better recognition and treatment of psychiatric conditions may be paramount. Setting region-specific considerations aside, we consider that the following challenges are likely to have broad relevance regardless of setting: creating and operating diversionary programmes, reducing the impact of incarceration on families, dealing with cognitive impairment and other ageing-related illnesses, optimizing transition to the community and health maintenance on release from prison and, of crucial importance, more rigorous research as mentioned in the previous section (Adams 2018).
	Prisons represent individual, societal, and institutional failures at multiple levels. They are costly and have limited efficacy in terms of their rehabilitative properties. To this end, they represent one of society’s greatest challenges and one requiring a concerted effort by agencies spanning health, welfare, justice, law, and education. The prisoner population represents one of the most unhealthy in the community across all health metrics and one that presents numerous challenges, including the attitude of the community towards a group that has transgressed the rules of society. What has not occurred to date is the ‘ownership’ of this population by mainstream public health agencies, although recent moves have sought to remedy this, calling on public health professionals to apply the arsenal of methodologies and evidenced-based approaches to tackle offending behaviour. This will require a ‘genes to gaol’ approach that will not come quickly and will require effort, funding, innovation, and dedication.
