11.2


The political economy of noncommunicable diseases


	Lessons for prevention
	Anne Marie Thow, Raphael Lencucha, and K. Srinath Reddy





Introduction to noncommunicable diseases


	Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are the major cause of death and disability globally, and the prevalence of these diseases continues to rise, particularly in low and middle-income countries (LMIC) (WHO 2013). Annual deaths from NCDs increased by 14.1% between 2005 and 2015 (Wang et al. 2016). Cardiovascular disease—mainly ischaemic heart disease and stroke—is the largest contributor to global mortality, accounting for 17.9 million deaths in 2015 (Sacco et al. 2016). The number of adults with diabetes, worldwide, has quadrupled since 1980 (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration 2016), and the number of deaths from cancer increased by 17% between 2005 and 2015, with tracheal, bronchus, and lung cancer the leading causes of cancer deaths (Wang et al. 2016). Obesity prevalence doubled between 1980 and 2008, from 6.4% to 12%, with half of this rise occurring between 2000 and 2008 (Stevens et al. 2012; WHO 2016). In 2014, one in three adults aged over 18 years were overweight (Stevens et al. 2012; WHO 2016).
	A large proportion of NCD deaths are premature (over 40% occur before the age of 70), and 80% of these premature deaths occur in LMIC (WHO 2014b). The four major NCDs (cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic respiratory disease, and diabetes) are responsible for over 80% of NCD deaths (WHO 2014b). Although NCDs are still often thought of as diseases of the wealthy, the burden of these diseases in LMIC has escalated rapidly over the past few decades and people with these diseases in LMIC are far more likely to die than those in high-income countries (Sommer et al. 2015). The World Health Organization’s (WHO) South East Asia and Western Pacific Regions (including India and China respectively), account for approximately half the diabetes cases in the world (WHO 2016). Between 1970 and 2008, the proportion of newly reported cancers occurring in LMIC increased from 15% to 56%; by 2030, the proportion is expected to be 70% (Wagner and Brath 2012). By 2020, it is estimated that chronic respiratory disease will be the fourth leading cause of lost ‘disability-adjusted life years’ in LMIC (Checkley et al. 2014).
	These diseases have a devastating impact at the personal and household level; in addition to causing death, chronic diseases have a high burden of morbidity. For example, the complications of diabetes include blindness, kidney failure, and lower limb amputation—all of which impact significantly on quality of life as well as participation in employment (WHO 2016). As a result of their associated premature mortality and morbidity, NCDs pose a substantial household and national economic burden, both from the cumulative healthcare costs associated with chronic conditions and lost economic productivity. The economic losses due to cardiovascular disease, chronic respiratory disease, cancer, diabetes, and mental health between 2005 and 2025 are projected at US$ 47 trillion, representing 75% of global GDP in 2010 (US$ 63 trillion) (Bloom et al. 2011). Not only this, but the investment required to prevent NCDs is significantly less than the costs currently associated with these diseases: a 10% reduction in mortality from ischaemic heart disease and stroke would reduce economic losses in LMICs by an estimated US$25 billion per year (three times greater than the investment required) (WHO 2011). Recent estimates suggest that investment of an additional $1.50 per capita for prevention in the 20 countries with the highest NCD burden would avert 15 million deaths, 8 million incidents of ischaemic heart disease, and 13 million incidents of stroke in the 20 countries (Bertram et al. 2018).
	Despite the rising tide of NCDs, it is widely accepted that these diseases are largely preventable. For example, at least one-third of the 12 million cancer cases that occur annually are preventable (Boyle and Levin 2008). In this chapter, we focus on five major modifiable risk factors for NCDs: tobacco use, alcohol use, unhealthy diets, physical inactivity, and air pollution (Lim et al. 2013; WHO 2017). In 2016, tobacco use was responsible for 7.1 million deaths, mainly from cancer and respiratory disease, with most of these deaths occurring in China, India, the United States, and Russia (Global Burden of Disease 2017). In 2010, dietary risk factors (particularly diets low in fruits and vegetables and those high in sodium, but also including diets high in fats and sugars) were the largest contributors to the global disease burden—and particularly risk for cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and some cancers Lim et al. 2013). Alcohol use/consumption is the seventh leading risk factor for NCDs, in terms of the morbidity burden as measured by disability-adjusted life years—and globally, alcohol exposure has increased by 15.2% since 1990 (Global Burden of Disease 2017). Physical inactivity is associated with an increased risk of cancer (breast and colon), diabetes, ischaemic heart disease and stroke, and even low amounts of activity are beneficial in reducing risk (Kyu et al. 2016). In 2014, the prevalence of physical inactivity in high-income countries was almost double that of LMIC. However, with changes to work and leisure, the prevalence of physical inactivity is increasing in LMICs (WHO 2016). In 2017, air pollution was estimated to cause one-quarter of all adult deaths from heart disease and stroke, 43% from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and nearly a third from lung cancer, and is also associated with diabetes (WHO 2016; Global Burden of Disease 2017; Bowe et al. 2018).
	In this chapter, we discuss how these four major risk factors emerged in a context whereby economic interests converge with public policy to produce environments of risk. The important thread running through this chapter is that the global rise in NCDs is conditioned by modifiable political and economic patterns. This chapter concludes by presenting a number of strategies that public health practitioners can take to remedy this situation.





Policy action on risk factors is essential for NCD prevention


	The World Health Organization (WHO) Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases 2013–2020 was agreed by member states at the World Health Assembly in 2013 (WHO 2013). The NCD global action plan sets out a clear vision and targets for addressing the heavy global burden of NCDs, including nine voluntary global targets with a strong focus on all of these modifiable risk factors:
	 	1. A 25% relative reduction in the overall mortality from cardiovascular diseases, cancer, diabetes, or chronic respiratory diseases
	2. At least 10% relative reduction in the harmful use of alcohol, as appropriate, within the national context
	3. A 10% relative reduction in prevalence of insufficient physical activity
	4. A 30% relative reduction in mean population intake of salt/sodium
	5. A 30% relative reduction in prevalence of current tobacco use in persons aged 15+ years
	6. A 25% relative reduction in the prevalence of raised blood pressure or contain the prevalence of raised blood pressure, according to national circumstances
	7. Halt the rise in diabetes and obesity
	8. At least 50% of eligible people receive drug therapy and counselling (including glycaemic control) to prevent heart attacks and strokes
	9. An 80% availability of the affordable basic technologies and essential medicines, including generics, required to treat major noncommunicable diseases in both public and private facilities
	The member states of the WHO have also agreed on a comprehensive package of effective policy options to support achievement of these targets by reducing the prevalence of all four major risk factors for NCDs (WHO 2013):
	 	• Policy options for tobacco control focus on implementation of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), which includes mandating smoke-free environments, graphic health warning labels on tobacco products, bans on advertising, promotion and sponsorship, and taxes on tobacco products.
	• Policy options for promoting a healthy diet include breastfeeding promotion, restrictions on the food marketing, creating incentives for reformulation of food to reduce sugar, salt, and fat content, promoting healthy food environments, social marketing, nutrition labelling, and taxes and subsidies.
	• Policy options for reducing the harmful use of alcohol include strengthening health services’ response and community action, addressing drink–driving and availability of alcohol, restrictions on marketing, and taxation. A critical component of global recommendations for all four risk factors is protection of policy making from influence by vested interests.
	• Policy options identified for promoting physical activity include promotion of ‘active transport’, recreational activity and sport, including through urban planning and transport policies, creation of healthy built environments which support physical activity, and public campaigns to promote activity.
	Growing recognition of the link between environmental risk factors—and, in particular, air pollution—has resulted in emerging global consensus regarding the need for policy action in this sphere for effective NCD prevention (Lelieveld et al. 2015; WHO 2017). This will require policy change across health, transport, housing, and energy sectors to reduce air pollution from particulate matter. Innovation by countries has included support for clean household energy, cleaner vehicle standards and support for public transport (WHO 2018).
	Achieving the Sustainable Development Goal targets related to NCDs and the global NCD targets will require structural, policy-led change that addresses environments in which people live, work, and play, with attention to contextual and regional differences (Reddy 2015). These environments have a significant impact on peoples’ capacity to engage in healthy behaviours, and can either support and incentivize the healthier choices, or the opposite. For example, redesigning streets to form squares and one-way streets, implementing traffic calming measures and creating bicycle lanes, creating or renovating playgrounds, improving lighting, and enhancing aesthetics are associated with increased physical activity, as measured by an increase in the percentage of people engaging in active transport and other measures of activity, and will also have benefits in reducing traffic-related air pollution (Heath et al. 2006). Similarly, there is a growing body of evidence that indicates that food environments have a major influence on food choice and consumption, such that shifts in access, pricing, portions, marketing, and other powerful drivers of eating can have major effects on weight (Wansink and Sobal 2007; Brownell et al. 2010).
	However, there has not yet been widespread system policy implementation to create supportive environments for health promotion and NCD prevention. This lack of action stems from policy tensions that arise when government attempts to control health-harming products come up against powerful economic interests. Companies that produce alcohol are notorious for resisting any type of regulation. This resistance often utilizes arguments and corresponding tactics that locate the cause of NCDs at the individual, rather than environmental level (Roberto et al. 2015). These tensions are also seen with industries with interests contrary to reducing car use, in relation to interventions aimed to reduce physical inactivity and pollution. As we will discuss, this emphasis on individual responsibility has important implications for how governments and the public health community addresses NCD prevention. The message of personal responsibility often translates into public health approaches such as health communication campaigns and voluntary standards to guide industry practices. Alone, these approaches are largely ineffective when environments continue to make the healthy choice the more difficult choice (Golden et al. 2015).
	The structural, environment-focused policies required to prevent NCDs—including labelling, taxation, restrictions on marketing, and reform of transport and planning policy—require change in finance, commerce, trade, planning, and communications policies. Achieving health oriented policy change in these sectors, especially those that govern unhealthy commodities and physical environments, has proved challenging because of the overt or covert influence of industry over government decision-making or more nuanced misalignments between the mandates of government sectors and health objectives (Miller and Harkins 2010; Lencucha et al. 2015; Schram 2017). Governments that do implement strong environmentally focused NCD prevention policy consistently face challenges in national and international economic forums; for example, tobacco, alcohol and nutrition labelling measures have all been challenged at the World Trade Organization (WTO) (Lencucha and Drope 2015; Global Burden of Disease 2017; Mitchell and Casben 2017; Thow et al. 2017). It is for this reason, that a political economy perspective is indispensable in understanding and acting on product and environmental risk.





Global political economy and environments of risk


	A political economy perspective on health is one that links individual health risk (e.g. choice or biology) with political and economic structures and practices. This perspective asks: ‘How do economic interests intersect with political decisions to shape the environments in which individuals live?’. In its simplest form, this perspective brings together and analyses political and economic structures and how these structures shape the conditions for health. For example, as we discuss in more depth, political decisions driven by pressures to free the commercial sector from regulation have led to product environments where healthy choices are difficult.
	Political structures refer to public policy, what a government decides to do or not do, and the institutions, namely rules, norms, and strategies established by government, that form and enact policy (Dye 1972; Ostrom 1986). Importantly, observers note that the contemporary political economy is also marked by a deliberate retreat of the state from public life, whereby non-state actors, whether powerful individuals, companies, or other groups, play an important role in shaping the economic patterns of society (Strange 1996; Zohlnhöfer et al. 2018). By considering the political economy of NCDs prevention one can examine how structural factors can impact the incidence and prevalence of disease. This perspective serves as a backdrop to understand why health-harming products continue to dominate the consumer environment despite their known risk for NCDs. The same perspective can elucidate how political decisions and economic interests shape how we move about the built environment (e.g. by foot, by bike, or by car) and how this movement is conditioned by the existence of road systems, forms of public transportation, and access to safe alternative transportation (e.g. curbed bike lanes on busy streets).
	When ‘environments of risk’ are considered from a political economy perspective, it enables public health actors to critically assess sociopolitical factors that generate product environments characterized by health-harming products, built environments that condition physical inactivity over physical activity, and marginalization of pollution reduction. This type of analysis positions these five modifiable risk factors, not as ‘behavioural’ risk factors, but in a context wherein individual choice is bounded by political economic structures that often make the healthy choice the difficult choice.
	To begin, we examine these global political economic patterns and the underlying (or at least purported) rationality informing these patterns. Neoliberalism has emerged as a dominant way of thinking about the relationship between governments, markets, and society. Benatar and colleagues note that ‘neoliberalism has triumphed as the prevailing and dominant paradigm of global capitalism’ (Benatar et al. 2018). Early proponents of neoliberalism were driven by the goal of economic freedom, both in terms of individual freedom to make economic choices from a wide range of options, and the ability of companies to provide a wide range of appealing options available to consumers (e.g. Friedman 2002). As Gill notes ‘these (neoliberal) policies are cast within a neoliberal discourse of governance that stresses the efficiency, welfare, and freedom of the market, and self-actualization through the process of consumption’ (Gill 1995, p. 401). In this view, economic freedom has intrinsic value, as an expression of the human aspiration and capacity to express one’s agency, and instrumental value, a means of upholding political and economic freedom (Friedman 2009). This neoliberal vision has been largely, if not uniformly, institutionalized since the 1980s (Labonté and Stuckler 2016). David Harvey notes that neoliberalism is ‘in the first instance a theory of political economic practices that proposes that human well-being can best be advanced by liberating individual entrepreneurial freedoms and skills within an institutional framework characterized by strong private property rights, free markets, and free trade. The role of the state is to create and preserve an institutional framework appropriate to such practices’ (Harvey 2007).
	As indicated, a key tenet of neoliberalism is the separation of market from state control, with the idea that consumer decisions, not government control, will correct market failures. The ongoing result of the neoliberal paradigm is an acute tension between those who believe that government should take an active role in protection and promotion of health by intervening in the market, and those who seek a clearer separation between government and market whereby responsibility is left to individuals to make healthy choices (or not) and thus shape the market through these decisions. In sum, the dominant neoliberal paradigm has created a situation where governments struggle, or neglect, to regulate in the public interest because of a dominant paradigm that argues for the virtue of separating market and state, and a legacy of pressure from powerful institutions to conform to a set of policies that drives a separation of market and state. Opponents of the current neoliberal orthodoxy argue that ‘We need to work harder to reclaim the narrative: we do not have a fiscal crisis. We have a crisis of inadequate taxation. We are not living in conditions of economic scarcity. We are living in conditions of extreme inequality’ (Labonté and Stuckler 2016, p. 316). This argument is tied to the widespread recognition that although neoliberalism is thought of as a theory and practice involving freeing markets from state control, in reality neoliberalism is largely perpetuated by state decisions and often brings seemingly paradoxical state interventions to protect market activity (e.g. government bailouts to large companies) (Brenner et al. 2010).
	In this context, the intent of public health regulation to reduce consumption of commodities associated with NCD risk gives rise to a very real tension for governments, with a perceived choice between profits and public health interests. The companies that benefit from the continuation of behaviours associated with NCD risk are all major contributors to GDP and employment in many countries. In addition to this, risky commodities are often more profitable than healthier alternatives. For example, highly processed foods generally have higher profit margins due to their long shelf life when compared to fresh, unprocessed foods, and there is minimal profit to be had from active transport. However, it is important to note that profitability does not directly translate to economic benefits for government or society, and often leads to wealth concentration and heightened economic inequality (Goda and Lysandrou 2013; Saez and Zucman 2016). An example of this tension is seen in the public discourse regarding taxation of tobacco, alcohol, pollution, and unhealthy foods and beverages. If finance ministers see this as a revenue measure with diminishing returns (as consumption/pollution falls), neoliberal opponents can sway them with the ‘freedom from nanny state’ and ‘regressive impact on poor’ arguments. If taxation is projected as a public health imperative, with a particular focus on the socioeconomic aspect of the NCD burden, broader public support can be built up (Sassi et al. 2018; Thow et al. 2018a).
	Tobacco, food, and alcohol companies, as well as companies with a vested interest in individually-oriented transport, are strongly transnationally integrated, both vertically and horizontally, and are valued in the billions. The world’s top ten food companies, which produce primarily highly processed foods, own almost all the familiar international brands and in 2017 had combined sales of over 400 billion dollars (Top 100 food and beverage companies n.d.). This is more than the GDP of Thailand, and equivalent to half of Indonesia’s GDP. In 2016, seven of the top 10 biggest companies in the world were petroleum and car companies, including China National Petroleum (#3), Royal Dutch Shell (#5), Exxon Mobil (#6) and Volkswagen (#7) (Fortune Global 500 List 2017).
	Despite a global decline in tobacco consumption, transnational tobacco companies continue to generate increasing profits. For example, Philip Morris International saw a rise in profits from roughly 7 billion Canadian dollars (CAD) to over 9 billion CAD from 2006 to 2012. The same increases can be seen with British American Tobacco and Japan Tobacco (Physicians for a Smoke Free Canada n.d.). The total profits for the big six tobacco companies rose from 35 billion USD in 2012 to over 60 billion USD in 2015 (Bowers 2012). It is this massive wealth that drives the tobacco industry to employ every means to fight tobacco control efforts.
	This perception of profit doesn’t take into account the negative externalities that arise from consumption of tobacco, alcohol and unhealthy foods, or that are associated with living in built environments that disincentivize physical activity or generate air pollution—namely poor health, social costs, and lost productivity—but it is nevertheless an influential perception (Kankeu Tchewonpi et al. 2013; Lencucha et al. 2018b). The economic paradigm just described creates a framework for decision-making in which costs that are harder to quantify are less likely to be considered in decision-making; for example, costs in the form of quality of life, social capital, or rising inequality (Stiglitz 2017). The vertical integration of these industries can also result in significant inequality in the way that profits accrue, geographically. The profits from value adding often accrue to companies based in high-income countries, with a strong extractive element evident in the GDP and employment gains in LMICs. For example, although tobacco is a significant contributor to GDP for many countries in Africa, such as Malawi, the economic gains to tobacco farmers is dwarfed by the huge profits made by transnational tobacco companies (Makoka et al. 2017).





Industry power and the political economy of noncommunicable disease risk


	The enormous size and reach of these ‘industries of risk’ translates into significant political power. In a global political economy largely driven by the ideas and corresponding policies of neoliberalism, industry is positioned as creator of wealth and the voice of industry is often given preference. Thus, when the health sector talks about policy change in economic sectors that will reduce consumption of profitable commodities, their voice is often drowned out by others with a vested interest in these commodities. In this section, we explore three key ways in which industry exercises power in politics and policy making, to the detriment of governments efforts to reduce consumption of harmful commodities and create built environments that foster activity. Drawing on Lukes’ conception of power, we consider ways in which industry actively exerts power in formal decision-making forums (‘decision-making power’), shapes the agenda in political debates (‘non-decision-making power’), and exercises ideological power (Lukes 2005).
	Decision-making power focuses on policy preferences revealed through political action.
	Industry actors invest heavily in shaping government policy through establishing relationships, and direct lobbying efforts. The power of these relationships is widely recognized in the area of tobacco control. The tobacco industry is notorious for employing different tactics to aggressively influence policy; namely to prevent the regulation of their products (Saloojee and Dagli 2000). In the United States, industry actors are formally consulted on the negotiating text of trade agreements by the Office of the US Trade Representative, while public health actors are not. It is common for governments to consult with industry on economic policy decisions and this practice often conflicts with the aims of health sectors to protect health policy from industry influence. For example, the Philippines InterAgency Committee on Tobacco was established to coordinate tobacco control policy within government but is chaired by a representative from the trade ministry who views the tobacco industry as a legitimate stakeholder and thus the industry has a reserved seat at the agency (Lencucha et al. 2015).
	The influence of relationship building and policy lobbying has also been used effectively by the alcohol industry (McCambridge et al. 2018). For example, the alcohol industry in sub-Saharan Africa—taking the mantle of ‘technical expert’—has supported governments in the drafting of their national alcohol policies (Bakke and Endal 2010). Evidence from Lesotho, Malawi, Uganda, and Botswana shows that the resulting policies minimized a public health approach to alcohol and maintained a narrow focus on the economic benefits from trade and alcohol. In terms of addressing alcohol problems, the policy content focused on individual drinkers, with no mention of effective environmental interventions (Bakke and Endal 2010). Similarly, in Thailand, there has been little action on environment-focused alcohol policy—in part because alcohol company executives sit in the national policymaking body (Treerutkuarkul 2017).
	Industry also exerts direct power in decision-making through involvement in the negotiation of trade and investment agreements, and through using dispute settlement mechanisms in these agreements to influence policy. For example, the Government of Thailand proposed graphic warning labels on alcohol that highlighted the associated harms, similar to approaches used in tobacco control (Cecchini and Belloni 2015). This policy proposal was withdrawn in 2010 after Specific Trade Concerns were raised at the World Trade Organization (O’Brien 2013). Similarly, despite neoliberal commitment to free trade arguably increasing access to medicines and health technologies in developing country markets, commercial interests prevent affordable access to these products through a variety of trade provisions (United Nations 2016). In particular, strict patent protection that benefits international pharmaceutical companies mean that affordability of NCD treatments remains a challenge in LMICs.
	Investor-State Dispute Settlement mechanisms are included in many international trade and investment agreements and enable foreign investors to directly contest government policy (this is in contrast to traditional ‘state-state’ mechanisms of dispute settlement, where only governments can bring challenges regarding national policies that inhibit trade or investment). These mechanisms create avenues for industry to contest regulation that undermines ‘reasonable expectations’ of profits—which resonates with the tension between risky products and public health regulation described earlier (Hawkins and Holden 2016). For example, the tobacco multinational Philip Morris brought a claim against Australia under an International Investment Agreement (IIA) between that country and Hong Kong Special Administrative Region in China, in 2011. This claim challenged Australia’s mandatory ‘plain packaging’ of tobacco products as an unreasonable measure that would expropriate trademarks and undermine good will indirectly (Allens Arthur Robinson 2011). Philip Morris International filed a similar claim in 2010 against Uruguay’s decision to expand graphic health warning labels on tobacco products (Lencucha 2010; Porterfield and Byrnes 2011).
	Non-decision-making power is that which sets the agenda in debates and makes certain issues unacceptable for discussion in ‘legitimate’ public forums. A key element of exercising non-decision-making power is framing discourse and public debate regarding an issue. The tobacco industry has consistently attempted to shape the discourse on government regulation by drawing on the powerful value of personal freedom. Early efforts to dissuade governments from regulating tobacco products, were supported by the message that individuals should have the freedom to choose the products that they want to consume. That the government should not intervene with the personal decisions of its citizens. The following statement by the Institute of Economic Alternatives, an ardent supporter of the tobacco industry, on tobacco product regulation reflects the logic used to oppose public regulation: ‘We argue that the interests of consumers are nearly always better advanced by the provision of accurate information and free choice than by prohibitions and restrictions on commercial speech. Markets can correct themselves more quickly than governments … Restrictions on product development and marketing in the nicotine industry have led to … failures of both government and the market. Buttressed by political grandstanding, corporate rent-seeking, rigid ideology, and old-fashioned puritanism, the result has been a disaster for the only group of people whose interests are of direct relevance: smokers’ (Snowdon 2013, p. 41). These frames, however, don’t acknowledge the disproportionately high experience of NCD risk factors, and concomitant NCD morbidity and mortality, among people of low socioeconomic status. The narrow definitions and frames of ‘benefit’ ignore the significant impact of NCDs on economic productivity and on inequalities (Nugent et al. 2018).
	Another of the powerful messages used by industry in opposition to government regulation of their products is that such regulation will create economic ripples that will harm employment throughout the supply chain. In LMICs this message is tied to economic development. Industry argues that regulation will result in loss of employment, with particular emphasis to the most vulnerable, the farmers. The tobacco industry has long argued that tobacco regulation will hurt tobacco farmers and have convinced government officials of this point. We see this argument being made by industry representatives in the media (Karombo 2018; Khan 2018) and by government officials in high-level policy venues such as the World Trade Organization (Lencucha et al. 2016). These arguments harken back to the ideas of economic freedom and growth that underpin the neoliberal paradigm.
	However, recent research has questioned the evidence base for the claims that farmers are prosperous from crops such as tobacco. A study conducted in Malawi in 2014 found that smallholder tobacco farmers who were on contract with tobacco leaf buying companies, after accounting for family labour costs, were making roughly 220 USD per year, less than one dollar per day (Makoka et al. 2017). In the same study independent tobacco farmers were finding themselves in debt at the end of the season. This is in a context where the CEO of British American Tobacco tops 20 million USD in salary and bonuses in one year (Treanor 2012). Similar arguments are evident in the food industry’s opposition to taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages, which are linked to increased risk of diabetes and obesity, on the basis of their potentially regressive fiscal impact on poor households (Thow et al. 2018a). For example, in the Philippines, the industry argued consistently that the proposed sugar-sweetened beverage tax should be reduced because it was anti-poor, and would be ‘crucial to the fate of millions of low-income Filipino consumers’ (PhilStar.com 2017). This argument has been found to ignore the disproportional health benefits that accrue to low-income consumers, as their higher price sensitivity leads them to decrease their consumption more than their higher income counterparts (Thow et al. 2018a).
	Strong frames that create tension between profits and public health regulation are also evident in public industry submissions to government. For example, food industry submissions regarding the proposed TransPacific Partnership Agreement assumed that trade liberalization would raise living standards and benefit the economy and country; food was framed exclusively as an economic commodity with implications for revenue generation, with no connection to nutritional health (Friel et al. 2016).
	Ideological power shapes thoughts and behaviour by invoking strong values, emotions, and ethical principles. Marketing and other strategies that seek to create brand loyalty and influence habit formation in children can be a source of ideological power. Powell has argued that the food industry has used the school system to integrate and normalize messages of personal responsibility over diet and the idea of energy balance (i.e. emphasizing physical activity as a remedy for unhealthy diet). He shows how Coca-Cola systematically worked to shape the discourse towards healthy choice and consumer responsibility by implementing over 250 ‘anti-obesity’ programmes in schools. Powell and Gard interrogate a number of programmes that Coca-Cola designed to stimulate physical activity among the children. Underlying these types of programmes is a message that there is no bad food but bad choices. For example, messages that consumption of a ‘high energy’ product like Coca-Cola, must be followed by the decision to exercise in order to balance the energy in with energy out. Food industry interests have pushed these types of messages at all levels. Brownell and Warner provide the example of how the Sugar Association in the United States enlisted the support of US government officials to oppose the WHO draft strategy to address issues of diet and physical activity. The Association pushed the message that there should be greater emphasis on personal responsibility, a focus on physical activity, and the oft made assertion that there are no good and bad foods just bad choice (Brownell and Warner 2009).
	Ewing and Cervero (2010) conducted a meta-analysis of over 200 studies that examined the relationship between transportation and the built environment. One prominent finding is that Vehicle Miles Travelled (VMTs) was positively associated with the accessibility of the destination, such as work. They also found that mixed-use settings, such as retail outlets, schools, grocery stores, had a negative relationship with VMTs. For example, they also found that having a bus stop nearby was positively associated with public transportation usage. These factors are examples of how the way that the built environment is designed shapes modes of transportation. If we take one step back, we can think about how policy can shape these environments and one step further to see how certain economic interests can shape this policy. For example, the rise of car culture in the United States was partly driven by ideas of personal freedom tied to convenient mobility (Seiler 2009). The rise of affordable personal use vehicles was supported by public policy that lead to car-friendly infrastructure developments in cities, such as roads and parking lots, and policies that facilitated access to cheaper fuel sources, through subsidized fuel extraction, refinement, and transport to urban centres.





How public health can support strong policy for noncommunicable disease prevention


	Despite the power wielded by industry interests in the policy process, there has been innovation and meaningful policy change for NCD prevention. In this section, we examine cases of public health success—where governments have successfully regulated in the face of strong economic interests. In many cases, this innovation is led by LMIC; in part due to the devastating burden of NCD morbidity and mortality in these countries. These case studies provide the opportunity to draw lessons from experience and consider how public health actors can protect policy space and support regulation to promote healthy product and built environments.





Strong, local evidence


	Assembling strong, local evidence to underpin policy is essential to convince policy makers of the need to take action, and of the solutions needed—even though alone it is insufficient for policy change. The power of evidence of effectiveness is clear from the decision by the Government of Peru to scale up strong environmentally focused regulation regarding the hours alcohol can be sold. Data on the impact of a local ban in the district municipality of La Victoria in Lima on the sale of alcohol (Sundays to Wednesdays up to midnight and Thursdays to Sundays up to 03:00) over 2 years showed that, compared to a district without a ban, violent incidents had halved. Subsequently, a similar ban was established in the entire Metropolitan area of Lima, and the national police began an intensive action campaign for zero tolerance to driving under the influence of alcohol. A year later, the number of violent deaths had decreased by 11%, homicides by 19%, and the number of victims of alcohol-attributable traffic crashes by 28% (WHO 2014a).
	It is not just quantitative evidence that it required to underpin policy change. A turning point in tobacco control legislation was brought about by evidence that the tobacco industry had acted unethically in promoting their products, undermining the assumption by policy makers that consumers had full access to information about the harms and benefits of the product. Availability of adequate, accurate information regarding products is an important assumption in a market-based economy—and asymmetry of information is a recognized aspect of market failure. For example, a free choice may involve knowing the risk and benefits of consuming a medicine whereby the consumer can decide if the benefits outweigh the risks. In the United States in the mid-1990s, a series of lawsuits were filed against the tobacco industry in an attempt to retrieve damages caused by tobacco to consumers and the pressing burden of tobacco-related illness on the health system (Schroeder 2004). One of the important outcomes of these suits, and particularly the Master Settlement Agreement, was the requirement that the tobacco companies release internal documents for public scrutiny. At the time, the CEOs of the major tobacco companies were testifying that tobacco was not addictive and posed no, or at least minimal, harm to users. Contrary to this testimony the internal documents revealed that the tobacco industry was well aware of the harms of tobacco use and more importantly, despite this knowledge, had been aggressively and deceptively marketing their products to consumers. This is a history of the most sinister cases of corporate deception where ‘The tobacco industry knowingly and successfully deceived the public for 50 years about the connection between smoking and cancer’ (Leahy 2014). The example of tobacco industry deception illustrates how economic interests can shape consumer decisions by controlling the information available to consumers.
	As discussed earlier, the frames and norms surrounding a product have dramatic implications on the extent to which the companies producing the product have access to the policy making arena. For example, there is now no question as to the risk posed by tobacco products, to the extent that Philip Morris, one of the largest tobacco companies, acknowledges the harms of tobacco consumption on their website. The National Cancer Institute in the United States asserts that ‘there is no safe tobacco product, and there is no safe level of exposure to tobacco smoke’ (National Cancer Institute n.d.). This categorical position informs decisions to exclude tobacco interests from accessing arenas where health policy, and now even other social policy, is being made. For example, the World Bank instituted a policy in 1991 that prohibits the organization from any involvement with tobacco (World Bank n.d.). Article 5.3 of the FCTC implores governments to protect health policy from tobacco industry interference (WHO 2003), given the aforementioned efforts of the tobacco industry to shape policy in their favour (Bialous and Peeters 2012; Gilmore et al. 2015). In contrast, we still see companies like Pepsi Co partnering with health groups in the fight against NCDs (Yach et al. 2010). Evidence regarding both the scale of the problem and the influence of industry in policy making will help to change norms and frames regarding other NCD risk factors.





Coalitions


	Theories of the policy process highlight the influence of strong coalitions of actors with shared interests, in shaping policy outcomes (Sabatier 1987; Weible et al. 2012; Shiffman 2016). Key features of strong actor coalitions in a health context include their ability to construct compelling frames of the issue and convincing reasons to act. It is also critical that they engage with the politics of the issue, and develop relationships outside of the health sector (Shiffman 2016). An example in relation to policy action on NCDs is CLAS (the Healthy Latin America Coalition) (NCD Alliance 2017). CLAS is a coalition with 250 member organizations who has developed a rapid-response system for nutrition policy advocacy, based on consensus position statements. When there is a nutrition policy crisis in a Latin American country then the Coalition can coordinate a strong public health voice to protect good policies—they don’t have to gain consensus every time, as they can speak on the basis of the agreed statements. For example, when the Mexican health commission wanted to lower the rate of the sugar-sweetened beverage tax, the coalition organized a coordinated lobby to retain the tax.
	Strong coalitions across sectors have also been effective in supporting urban planning policies that promote and support physical activity. Cities that encourage physical activity through active transport are now seen as a priority from both sustainability and health perspectives (Giles-Corti et al. 2015). In Australia, draft urban planning legislation incorporated health considerations because of concerted lobbying by health actors (Harris et al. 2017). Health was explicitly identified as a relevant issue for planning policy in submissions by health-focused agencies, who also connected health to wider planning concerns including economic issues, transport, public open space, and environmental sustainability.





Prepare for push-back from industry


	As described in detail earlier, effective policies to prevent NCDs will be contested by the industries that stand to lose with decreased consumption or use of their products. Pro-active consideration of these arguments and development of thoughtful responses is a critical component of protecting policy space for NCD prevention. Industry is predictable in their focus on the economic and profit implications of policies to prevent NCDs, and strategic counterarguments to industry lobbying can help to minimize their impact. For example, when South Africa proposed their soft drink tax, industry argued strongly against it on the basis of job losses: they stated that 3,400 jobs would be lost in the sugar-sweetened drinks production; 25,200 jobs would be lost in ‘upstream’ jobs; 19,200–29,000 jobs in retail and 15,400 job losses directly and indirectly as a result of reduced demand for drinks (Wilkinson and Bhardwaj 2017). Data from an independent think tank showed that these estimates were vastly overestimated, as the industry analysis assumed that producers would not shift to producing healthier, untaxed drinks (which would result in more jobs) and did not consider that with the funds raised from the tax, treasury spending would also result in some jobs being created. This balanced data helped to keep the policymakers focused on the health concerns, and the tax was passed (Cullinan 2017). Economic interests have the ability to wield massive resources to move such arguments into the public discourse. In the case of tobacco, health proponents have recognized that it is crucial to intercept such messages by instituting rules within government that either prevent industry access to government decision-makers or ensure that such access is transparent and the information about any such consultations is open to public scrutiny.





Healthier economic policy


	Finally, it is essential for public health actors to identify specific opportunities for economic policy change that creates healthy environments for NCD prevention. Using tools such as Health Impact Assessment can be vital in identifying specific points at which economic policy can negatively impact on health and NCDs (Hirono et al. 2016). At a practical level, it is important that health policy actors strategically frame health policy objectives in ways that ensures that they are able to defend necessity and non-discrimination as key principles for trade compliance. For example, analysis of concerns regarding nutrition labelling for NCD prevention at the World Trade Organization revealed a lack of clarity regarding the necessity of the measures, as well as practical concerns, such as the use of stickers to label imports (Thow et al. 2017). However, it is also important to go beyond simply health focused policy measures to consider broader, whole-of-government objectives that determine how governments balance competing objectives. It is essential for governments to clearly identify national interests in relation to NCDs and, more broadly, public health, to set the context for economic policymaking—including (and in some ways, especially) the negotiation of international trade and investment agreements. For example, policy incoherence with respect to nutrition in South Africa has its roots in whole-of-government priorities that preference economic indicators over nutrition (Thow et al. 2018b). It is also important to recognize that government has numerous tools that can be used to foster healthy product environments. The regulatory role of government can be complimented by targeted interventions to ensure that healthy products, such as fruits and vegetables are accessible and affordable. Governments can leverage economic resources to subsidize or incentivize healthy food production, including subsidies to small retail outlets to carry products like fruits and vegetables (Story et al. 2008; Lencucha et al. 2018a).
	Despite the dominant neoliberal economic paradigm that often preferences industry interests over public health, significant changes to economic policy can and have been made in the interests of public health. After the Phillip Morris challenge to plain packaging, the Government of Australia made a decision not to agree to investor-state dispute settlement (Voon and Mitchell 2016). Similarly, the Governments of Brazil, South Africa, and India have terminated a number of their bilateral investment agreements, due to the constraints they place on domestic policy space (UNCTAD 2016). Strategic engagement by public health actors with the sectors that govern NCD risk—as well as recognition of the political economy of NCD risk—can support meaningful policy change for environments that promote health.

11.3


Immunization and vaccination


	Eleonora A.M.L. Mutsaerts and Shabir A. Madhi





Introduction


History of vaccination


	The origins of vaccine-derived immunity date back to 900 AD when the Chinese observed that individuals surviving smallpox were immune to renewed illness. This led to the earliest documented experiments on vaccination by inoculating smallpox into scarified skin, a process called variolation. Although variolation was effective in conferring immunity to smallpox, it carried a significant risk of severe disease or even death in some recipients. The practice of smallpox inoculation spread to Africa and Turkey, before arriving in Europe and the Americas. In eighteenth-century Britain, Edward Jenner observed immunity to smallpox in cow-maids who developed cowpox after close exposure to cows. In 1796, he experimented inoculating a 13-year-old boy with vaccinia virus (cowpox) and challenged the child with smallpox virus to prove the concept of immunity. This led to the first smallpox vaccine being developed in 1798; ultimately resulting in eradication of smallpox 200 years later.
	Subsequent to the success of developing a smallpox vaccine, Louis Pasteur developed the rabies vaccine in 1885, followed by antitoxins and vaccines against cholera, typhoid, plague, diphtheria, tetanus, anthrax, and tuberculosis through the 1930s. It was however only after the mid-1940s, that systematic immunization became common practice. The Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) was launched in 1974 by the World Health Organization (WHO). The goal of EPI was to immunize children worldwide with six core vaccines: diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, measles, polio, and tuberculosis. Vaccination of children is now regarded as one of the most successful public health interventions of the 20th century and continues to have vast impact on preventing infectious disease and death worldwide.





Challenges to immunization programmes


	Following initiation of the EPI programme, only 5% of children in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) received the full series of vaccines in the 1970s, which increased to around 80% by the late 1980s. However, global vaccine coverage reached a plateau and even declined in some places by the mid-1990s. Consequently, approximately 19.9–30 million children born each year would be underimmunized or unvaccinated. This is further accentuated by inequity in vaccine coverage, with children from the lowest economic quintile in many LMIC being 2–3 fold less likely to be fully immunized than those from the highest quintile. This paradox is manifest by the increased susceptibility of children from poverty-stricken backgrounds to developing vaccine-preventable diseases, as well as having less access to curative healthcare services.
	Reasons for underimmunization of children are multifactorial and include lack of political commitment to prioritize immunization programmes; lack of access to health facilities in marginalized and poverty-stricken communities; vaccine hesitancy due to social, cultural, and religious issues and mis-information; logistical issues in vaccine supply such as maintaining cold-chain and sterile needle and syringe availability; as well as high pricing of newly developed vaccines. Furthermore, vaccine hesitancy, especially in high-and middle-income settings are fostered by antivaccine lobby groups, often based on unsubstantiated concerns.
	To address some of these barriers, which prevent the full public health value of vaccines being realized, the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (Gavi) was established in 2000 as a partnership of governments, private sector, philanthropists, and civil society. The mission of Gavi is to reduce the number of unvaccinated children, as well as expedite the inclusion of new life-saving vaccines into public immunization programmes in low-income countries.





Public health impact of vaccination


	Even at current vaccine coverage rates of approximately 83% of children being fully immunized, childhood vaccination is estimated to save 2 to 3 million lives annually. The benefit of immunization is evident from the decline in global mortality attributed to many pathogens for which vaccines have been deployed. See Figure 11.3.1.

	Notable successes of vaccination:
	 	• Eradication of smallpox by 1979 after a global immunization campaign. Until the 1960s, smallpox killed two million people per year.
	• Reduction of the number of polio cases from 350,000 per year in 1988 (endemic in 125 countries) to 74 cases in 2015 (endemic in three countries).
	• Eradication of neonatal tetanus in two-thirds of developing countries, with annual neonatal tetanus attributed deaths being reduced from 1.2 million in 1980 to less than 50,000 in 2015. The reduction in neonatal tetanus is a result of increase in tetanus toxoid vaccine coverage in pregnant women, coupled with changes in birthing and practices and prenatal care of newborns.
	• Reduction in the number of measles deaths by 79% between 2,000 (n = 580,000) and 2015 (<50,000), thereby preventing more than 20 million measles deaths during this period.
	• Eradication of rinderpest disease in animals.
	Note: In addition to immunization, broader social and economic development, including improved sanitation, increased access to healthcare facilities, and improved infant nutrition are also likely to have played a role in the decline in childhood deaths due to vaccine-preventable disease.





Broader impact of vaccination


	Immunization of infants is widely heralded as a cost-effective healthcare intervention, second only to access to potable water. It is estimated that the economic benefit of vaccination is approximately 44-fold greater than the up-front cost of immunization, inclusive of direct treatment cost and the life-time loss of productivity averted by prevention of disease. The benefits of immunization extend beyond the prevention of disease in the individual, with health benefits also potentially accruing to society at large by the interruption of transmission of some pathogens (indirect immunity) or person-to-person circulation of some live-attenuated vaccines (herd immunity). Furthermore, the societal valuation of vaccines could include broader outcomes, including the effects on comorbidities, nosocomial infections, educational attainment, cognitive development, labour productivity, income, savings, investment, and fertility.





Advances in the vaccine landscape


	Since the 1970s, significant advances have occurred in the development of new vaccines. Vaccine development was fostered by progress in biotechnology and enhanced understanding of immunity against different pathogens, including newly designed adjuvant technology. The number of vaccines that have been licensed in the past two decades or are in the final stages of clinical development, exceeds the total number of vaccines that were developed in the previous two centuries; Table 11.3.2.

Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG)


	Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB), is now the leading vaccine-preventable cause of death worldwide. An estimated 1.7 billion people are infected with MTB globally, contributing to 10.4 million active cases in 2016, 10% of which is related to HIV-infection. There were an estimated 1.2 million deaths resulting from TB in 2016. The risk of developing TB following MTB infection is greatest in children under 2 years of age, with 30–40% of those infected with MTB progressing to disease. MTB infection during childhood manifests either as pulmonary TB (PTB) or as the more severe spectrum of extrapulmonary TB (30–40% of cases). Childhood TB serves as an indicator of ongoing M. tuberculosis transmission in a population.
	Immunocompromised individuals are at heightened risk of progressing from MTB infection to disease, or having reactivation of underlying dormant MTB infection. HIV-infected individuals who are not treated with antiretroviral treatment (ART) have a 10% annual risk of TB disease, compared to a life-time risk of 10% among the general population. Although this risk is reduced if initiated on ART, it remains significantly greater in HIV-infected individuals than the general population. Other factors facilitating spread of and predisposition to TB include poverty, overcrowding, poor ventilation, tobacco use, and diabetes. The risk of TB is also increased in refugees, migrants, urban poor, and incarcerated individuals.
	Despite availability of treatment, around 40% of TB cases remain undiagnosed. To achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal of ending TB epidemics by 2030, there is an increased focus on early detection and treatment of TB cases; as well as provision of chemo-prophylaxis in high-risk groups such as HIV-infected adults, children with MTB infection less than 5 years of age, and household contacts of active TB cases. In addition, vaccination with BCG vaccine of infants at birth, or shortly thereafter, remains a key component to achieve the End TB strategy; as does the development of new TB vaccines.
	BCG was first introduced in humans in 1921, making it one of the oldest vaccines. It is a freeze-dried preparation of a live-attenuated strain of M. bovis. Currently, more than 10 manufacturing strains exist. Despite ongoing research for the development of new anti-TB vaccines, the absence of an established immunological correlate of protection is a major impediment to vaccine development. As such, BCG is the only available TB vaccine and also provides protection against leprosy. However, BCG vaccine effectiveness varies considerably between different manifestations of TB, vaccine effectiveness wanes over time and there is variability between different BCG vaccine strains. Neonatal BCG vaccination is reportedly associated with 59% (RR 0.41, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.29–0.58) protection against PTB, possibly being lower in countries closer to the tropics; and >80% against extrapulmonary TB during childhood. Recent evidence indicates that BCG vaccination might also protect against M. tuberculosis primary infection. The duration of protection following BCG vaccination at 10–15 years of age is uncertain. Currently, the additional benefit from booster doses is being re-investigated.
	BCG vaccination is recommended in settings with a high TB incidence and/or high leprosy burden. A single dose is recommended at birth to all healthy neonates. The vaccine is contraindicated in individuals known to be allergic to vaccine components, immunocompromised individuals including symptomatic HIV-infected, and ART naïve with CD4% ≤25%. Children infected with HIV, who are receiving ART, and are clinically and immunologically stable should be vaccinated with BCG.
	New TB candidate vaccines are currently being developed, prioritizing development of vaccines targeted at adolescents and adults, considering they contribute to >90% of TB cases and are the primary source of MTB transmission in communities.





Hepatitis B


	Hepatitis B virus (HBV) causes acute hepatitis and chronic hepatitis; the latter could progress to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Serological prevalence of the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is used to measure endemicity of active HBV infection. HBsAg seropositivity was estimated at 3.5% of the world population in 2015; including 257 million people living with chronic HBV. The prevalence of seropositivity is highest in the Western Pacific (6.2%) and Africa (6.1%). Global mortality due to HBV infection was estimated at 887,220 in 2015 including deaths due to HCC, cirrhosis, and acute hepatitis. HBV infection in infancy has a higher risk of causing chronic infection than when acquired later in life. In HBV endemic areas, co-infection with other viral infections commonly occurs, including co-infection with HIV, hepatitis C virus, and hepatitis D virus.
	Hepatitis B vaccines were first licensed in 1982 and contain the HBsAg surface protein. In 1986, recombinant vaccines were developed, which are now most widely used. Immunization with a complete primary series of three doses of HBV induces protective antibody levels (i.e. HBsAg antibody ≥10 mIU/ml) in >95% of infants; and protection is likely lifelong. Hence, no booster doses are recommended. Hepatitis B vaccines are available either as a monovalent vaccine or in combination with diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP) ± Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) and inactivated polio vaccine (IPV); only the monovalent vaccine should be used for immunization at birth. WHO recommends that hepatitis B vaccine should be given immediately after birth to prevent vertical acquisition from highly-infectious mothers (i.e. Hepatitis B antigen positive), which should be followed by two or three further doses to complete the primary series. As of 2018, 102 (53%) countries had introduced hepatitis B vaccination at birth. Neonatal vaccination provides partial (estimated 30–40%) prevention against perinatal infection.
	Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended in persons at high risk of HBV infection in older age groups, including patients who frequently require blood or blood products. If resources are available, catch-up campaigns in unvaccinated cohorts are recommended. HIV-infected adults, in whom there is possibly waning of immunity, may need re-vaccination. Other measures to prevent HBV transmission include hepatitis B immunoglobulin at birth (costly and unavailable in most low-income countries) and screening of donated blood for transfusion.
	Global coverage with three doses of hepatitis B vaccine was estimated at 84% in 2015. Routine HBV immunization has contributed to a reduction in prevalence of chronic hepatitis B infection in children aged 0–5 years from 4.7% in the pre-vaccination era to 1.3% in 2015. An estimated 14.2 million cases of chronic HBV infection were prevented by hepatitis B vaccine among children under 5 years of age worldwide in 2013.





Polio


	Poliomyelitis is an acute communicable disease caused by three poliovirus serotypes (1, 2, or 3). Prior to routine introduction of vaccination, poliovirus was the major pathogen causing permanent disability in children; 1 in 200 susceptible individuals developed paralytic poliomyelitis.
	Both oral, live-attenuated vaccines (OPV) and injectable, inactivated virus vaccines (IPV) are available. Live OPV vaccines contain attenuated virus strains, which may replicate and re-obtain their potential for transmission and neurovirulence, causing isolated cases or outbreaks of paralytic poliomyelitis. Since 2009, type 2 polio virus was removed from OPV, to eliminate vaccine-derived polio infections from this strain. The trivalent OPV has since been replaced by the bivalent OPV (bOPV containing type 1 and 3 Sabin viruses) in immunization programmes still using OPV.
	The EPI recommends three to four doses of bOPV and at least one dose of IPV. The advantages of bOPV compared with IPV include low cost, ease of administration, superior intestinal mucosal immunity, and potential for boosting immunity in household and community contacts. A sequential IPV-bOPV or IPV-only schedule can be used in countries with sustained high vaccination coverage and low importation risk from neighbouring countries. However, WHO does not recommend this switch in endemic countries and regions with high risk of wild poliovirus (WPV) importation.
	In 1988, the World Health Assembly aimed at eradicating poliomyelitis by 2000 through initiation of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative. Since then, global incidence of poliomyelitis dropped by >99%. Wild poliovirus (WPV) type 2 was eradicated in 2015 and no detection of WPV type 3 occurred since November 2012. Countries with endemic polio have dropped from 125 in 1988 to 2 in 2015 (Afghanistan, Pakistan).





Diphtheria


	Diphtheria is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. In the past, diphtheria was one of the most devastating infectious diseases with case-fatality rates up to 50%. Diphtheria toxoid-based vaccines were developed in the late 1940s, but only became widely accessible worldwide in the 1970s when EPI was initiated. Introduction of the vaccine contributed to a >90% reduction of reported diphtheria cases from 1980 to 2000. Nevertheless, diphtheria remains a considerable health problem in countries with low vaccine coverage; including among displaced populations and refugees. Approximately 86% of children globally receive three doses of diphtheria-containing vaccines. Due to increased vaccination coverage in children, a shift in age distribution to adolescents and adults has occurred.
	Diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccines contain a formaldehyde-inactivated preparation of diphtheria toxin, adsorbed onto alum to increase immunogenicity. Since the 1940s, a combination vaccine containing DTP has been widely used. Diphtheria toxoid, tetanus toxoid, and pertussis vaccine are also available in combination with HBsAg and Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccines (pentavalent vaccines), and IPV (hexavalent vaccines containing acellular pertussis vaccine). Routine infant immunization includes a three-dose primary series (starting at 6 weeks and 4 weeks apart) and a booster at 15–18 months. Presence of maternal diphtheria antibody interferes with immune responses following the first two doses during early infancy, however, protective antibody levels are reached after the third primary series dose. The diphtheria vaccine does not prevent infection, but inhibits diphtheria toxin’s effects, thereby preventing systemic illness.
	Immunity wanes over time after a three-dose primary vaccination schedule. In order to achieve protection, a booster dose is required. It is recommended that individuals ≥7 years of age should receive the low-dose diphtheria toxoid (Td) vaccine, to reduce risk of vaccine reactions.





Tetanus


	Clostridium tetani is the causative bacterium of tetanus. It is acquired through exposure to C. tetani spores in contaminated skin wounds or tissue injury. All age groups are at risk; although neonates contributed to the highest burden of tetanus related deaths in the past. Tetanus infection is associated with case-fatality rates up to 100% in the absence of medical care. In countries with suboptimal immunization programmes, including low coverage rates of tetanus vaccination during pregnancy, tetanus remains a considerable public health problem. Most cases of tetanus still occur in neonates in LMIC, as well as some cases in mothers. Poor hygiene during delivery/abortion, cultural practices, and cord care practices contribute to maternal and neonatal tetanus. Incidence rates are highest in rural and difficult to reach areas, where delivery predominantly takes place at home without sterile practices. In countries where maternal and neonatal tetanus is uncommon with high coverage rates in infants and pregnant women, the majority of cases occurs in adolescents and adults after injuries. Due to poor surveillance systems in LMIC, there is a lack of robust data on tetanus incidence. Nevertheless, it is estimated that approximately 34,000 neonates died from tetanus in 2015, a 96% reduction compared to 1988 (787,000 cases).
	Tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccines (TTCV) are incorporated in routine immunization programmes around the world. Use of combination vaccines containing diphtheria toxoid is recommended. Prevention of neonatal tetanus is targeted by immunizing women of childbearing age with TTCV, either during or outside of pregnancy. By doing so, both the mother and the newborn (through transplacental transfer of tetanus antibodies) are protected. Administration of TTCV is recommended to women of childbearing age in countries with high risk for neonatal tetanus. In any country, tetanus vaccination history should be verified in all pregnant women when visiting the antenatal clinic for the first time and any missing doses should be administered. In all settings, clean procedures during delivery are important.
	Recovery from tetanus disease does not induce natural immunity. Individuals who have been infected remain susceptible and thus need to be immunized. WHO recommends administration of three primary and three booster doses through routine childhood immunization (booster doses at 12–23 months, 4–7 years, and 9–15 yrs).





Pertussis


	Pertussis, also known as whooping cough, is caused by Bordetella pertussis and is endemic globally. Prior to the vaccine era, pertussis was a common childhood disease with infections occurring in most individuals and >50% presenting with clinical symptoms. Young infants are at highest risk of death due to pertussis infection. Pertussis can be prevented by vaccination and immunization programmes in children have been successful in reducing pertussis cases and deaths. Combined with diphtheria and tetanus toxoid, the pertussis vaccine was introduced in the EPI in 1974. Vaccination prevented >1.3 million pertussis related deaths worldwide in 2001 and 687,000 deaths in 2008.
	Two type of pertussis vaccines are available. Whole-cell (wP) vaccines contain killed Bordetella pertussis bacteria and are commonly used in most LMIC. Acellular (aP) vaccines contain subunit pertussis toxin in combination with 1–4 other immunogenic pertussis proteins, including filamentous haemagglutinin, pertactin, and fimbriae. Many high-income countries (HICs) have replaced wP with aP vaccines in order to decrease adverse events following vaccination.
	A rise in pertussis incidence in a number of countries using the aP vaccine has been reported. The increase in cases was partly attributed to cyclical patterns, improved surveillance, increased awareness, and more sensitive laboratory testing using polymerase chain reaction. However, aP vaccines have shorter duration of protection (4–5 years) than wP (10–12 years) and do not confer mucosal protection or prevent transmission as effective as wP. WHO recommends that countries currently using wP do not change to aP. In HICs, pertussis remains the least controlled vaccine-preventable disease; possibly contributed to by the transitioning from the wP to aP vaccines.
	Pertussis vaccination is aimed at reducing severity of pertussis in infancy. The global target is to vaccinate >90% of infants with three doses of pertussis vaccine. In some countries a booster dose of TdaP is recommended in adolescents and adults to prevent pertussis in this population. There is insufficient evidence whether the booster dose is able to reduce severe pertussis in children; however, a booster dose of aP might be required decennially considering the duration of protection from aP. Furthermore, vaccination of pregnant women has been a recent focus of pertussis immunization, aimed at protecting young infants against pertussis disease during the first 2–3 months of life when risk of severe pertussis disease and death is greatest; and they are too young to have derived immunity from direct vaccination. Vaccination of pregnant women has been demonstrated to be safe and has >90% effectiveness in preventing pertussis in their infants. It is recommended that vaccination occurs from the second trimester onward, and at least 30 days before the anticipated birth of the child to optimize transplacental transfer of antibody to the foetus. Maternal pertussis vaccination, however, has been shown to interfere with immune responses to aP and possibly pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) (due to diphtheria toxoid included in the dTap vaccine given to mothers—which is similar to the cross-reacting material (CRM) protein used to conjugate polysaccharide in PCV-CRM197 formulations). The clinical relevance of this interference in antibody responses in the infants of vaccinated women requires further investigation.





Haemophilus influenzae type b


	Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) bacteria are responsible for severe pneumonia, meningitis, and other invasive diseases. The greatest burden of disease prior to routine Hib polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccine (HibCV) immunization was in children aged 4–18 months, with younger children deriving immunity from maternal transfer of antibody and older children through natural immunity derived from Hib exposure. HIV-infected children have a 6-fold higher risk of Hib invasive disease compared to HIV-uninfected.
	Hib disease is difficult to diagnose because it requires immediate laboratory testing in patients, before receiving antibiotics; and sampling of cerebrospinal fluid in cases of meningitis. Furthermore, the highest burden of severe disease and mortality from Hib in LMIC is due to pneumonia, for which the sensitivity of blood culture in diagnosing cases is <5%, and there are no other pragmatic diagnostic tools by which to make a pathogen specific diagnosis.
	Prior to vaccine introduction in LMIC in 2000, Hib was estimated to cause 2–3 million cases of serious disease in children <5 and 386,000 deaths. In 2015, the number of Hib deaths dropped to around 30,000 (uncertainty range [UR] 18,400–40,700), a 90% reduction from 2000. HibCV is currently used in 191 (98%) WHO member states.
	Although HibCV was introduced into high-income immunization programmes since the late 1980s, there was a lag of approximately a quarter of a century before the majority of low-income countries (LICs) were able to include the vaccine into their public immunization programme. This introduction was enabled by Gavi support, as well as a HibCV price reduction from approximately $20 per dose when first licensed to less than $2 per dose nowadays as part of a combination vaccine with other vaccine epitopes. HibCV immunization has been associated with >90% reduction in invasive Hib disease (especially meningitis) in countries administering the vaccine in routine immunization programmes; as well as approximately 20% reduction in all-cause radiologically confirmed pneumonia.
	The vaccine consists of proline-rich protein, a cell wall component of the Hib polysaccharide, conjugated to a protein to stimulate a T-cell dependent immune response. This induces immunity in young infants and establishes memory cell repertoire. The vaccine can be administered singularly, but is nowadays mainly combined with DTP ±HepB ±IPV. WHO recommends HibCV in all infant immunization programmes. The vaccine may be administered as a three primary dose schedule without a booster (3p+0); 2 dose primary schedule with a booster (2p+1); or a three-dose primary schedule with a booster (3p+1), depending on local epidemiology and the national schedule. Booster doses are currently used in most resource-rich countries, but are not generally recommended in the EPI schedule. Booster dosing might, however, be required for HIV-infected children in whom waning of immunity has been shown in the absence of treatment with ART.





Pneumococcal vaccines


	Diseases caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae include pneumonia, meningitis, and bacteraemia, and other less severe but more frequent mucosal illnesses such as otitis media, sinusitis, and bronchitis. An estimated 294,000 (UR 192,000–366,000) HIV-uninfected children and 23,300 (15,300–29,700) HIV-infected children aged 1–59 months died of pneumococcal disease in 2015, predominantly in LMIC. The burden of pneumococcal disease is highest in children under 2 and the elderly.
	Introduction of PCVs into immunization programmes has resulted in a dramatic decline in vaccine-serotype invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) incidence, even in unvaccinated age groups due to the indirect effect of vaccination. This is achieved by PCV reducing nasopharyngeal acquisition of vaccine-serotypes among the young vaccinated children, who are also the main source of transmission in communities, and consequently interrupting the transmission of the vaccine-serotypes among unvaccinated age groups.
	Two PCV vaccines are currently recommended: a 10-valent (PCV10) and 13-valent (PCV13) vaccine. The vaccines are designed to cover the serotypes associated with severe pneumococcal disease in children. PCV10 includes protein D as the conjugating protein, which may provide some protection against non-encapsulated Haemophilus influenzae mucosal infection, a common cause of otitis media and possibly pneumonia. Similar to Hib conjugate vaccine, PCV also induces a T-cell dependent immune response resulting in memory responses; as well as protecting against nasopharyngeal colonization (50% efficacy). This indirect protection of unvaccinated individuals, including adults at high risk for pneumococcal disease, is achieved once infant vaccine coverage rates are approximately 50%.
	Vaccine efficacy of PCV is >85% against vaccine-serotype IPD, approximately 50% against vaccine-serotype acute otitis media, and 30% against all-cause radiologically confirmed pneumonia hospitalization. Although there is replacement by non-vaccine-serotypes in the nasopharynx, this has not translated into substantial increase in non-vaccines serotype IPD incidence in children. However, recent data from the United Kingdom, indicate that the indirect protection against vaccine-serotype IPD in the elderly following childhood vaccination, has been offset by an increase in non-vaccine-serotype IPD. Substantial increase in non-vaccine-serotype IPD has also been observed in HIV-infected adults in South Africa, following childhood PCV13 immunization.
	WHO recommends three doses, either as a three-dose primary series (3p + 0) or as a two-dose primary series and a booster dose at 9–15 months of age (2p+1 schedule), depending on locally relevant factors. A two-dose primary series at 6 and 14 weeks induces similar immunogenicity compared to a three-dose primary series schedule at 6, 10, and 14 weeks; with the advantage of using the third dose as a booster dose which is required in some settings to sustain durability of protection and might be more effective in preventing nasopharyngeal colonization.
	By 2018, PCV had been introduced in the national immunization programme in 138 countries and a further three countries are planning on vaccine introduction in 2018. High costs of PCV ($20 per dose in middle-income countries and approximately $3.50 per dose in LICs) pose a significant burden on national health budgets. As a result, reduced dosing schedules are being evaluated in settings with low pneumococcal circulation and continued monitoring for prevalence of S. pneumonia colonization.
	PCV vaccination is also licensed for use in high-risk adults, including HIV-infected adults and the elderly; for whom a single dose of vaccine appears to be adequate. In HIV-infected adults not on ART, PCV vaccination was associated with a 74% reduced risk for recurrent vaccine-serotype IPD; whereas in the elderly (>50 years of age), PCV immunization was associated with an efficacy of 46% (95%CI 22–63%) at preventing vaccine-serotype pneumonia. Currently, broader spectra for PCV sero-coverage are being developed, which would include 15–25 serotypes.
	Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccines (PPV) exist and contain 23 serotypes (PPV-23). PPV is not immunogenic for most serotypes in children <2 years of age and protective immunity in older individuals may be limited or short lived as it stimulates a T-cell independent response which does not result in memory induction. Furthermore, repeat dosing with PPV is associated with immune hyporesponsiveness.
