PPV-23 could be used 1–2 months after priming with PCV in specific groups at risk for severe infection such as sickle cell disease, chronic renal failure, immunosuppression, cerebrospinal fluid leaks, asplenia, diabetes mellitus, or chronic liver, heart, or lung disease. This could increase coverage for those serotypes not included in PCV. In resource-limited settings there is limited evidence to support routine immunization of the elderly and high-risk populations with PPV-23.





Rotavirus


	Rotaviruses are responsible for most cases of severe diarrhoeal disease in young children globally in the absence of vaccination. Approximately 215,000 deaths per year were due to vaccine-preventable rotavirus infections in children <5 years of age, according to WHO estimates from 2013. Almost every child is infected by rotaviruses by 3–5 years of age. The median age of primary infection ranges from 6 to 9 months in LIC, and 2–5 years in HIC. Most (90%) cases of rotavirus-associated deaths occur in LIC and are associated with lack of healthcare facilities. Rotaviruses are responsible for up to a half of diarrhoea related hospital admissions and approximately 40% of all-cause diarrhoea deaths in LMIC in the absence of vaccination.
	Rotavirus vaccine introduction has contributed to a 50% decrease in diarrhoeal deaths in children under 5 in Mexico and a significant decline in rotavirus gastroenteritis hospitalizations in the United States.
	Currently, two oral, live, attenuated rotavirus vaccines are available: Rotarix™ (derived from a monovalent strain of human rotavirus) and RotaTeq™ (a re-assorted pentavalent bovine-human rotavirus). Both vaccines are safe and highly effective in preventing severe gastrointestinal disease. There is a small increased risk of intussusception (~1–2/100,000 infants) mainly after the first dose of vaccine, but this risk is far outweighed by the benefits of immunization.
	In LIC, vaccine efficacy (45–70%) can be lower than in industrialized settings (>90%), however, rotavirus vaccination still results in large numbers of severe gastroenteritis cases and deaths being prevented, because of the high incidence of severe rotavirus disease.
	WHO recommends rotavirus vaccine introduction in routine immunization programmes either as a two-dose course (Rotarix™) or a three-dose course (RotaTeq™). In India (Rotavac, Rotasiil), Vietnam (Rotavin-M1) and China (Lanzhou lamb) additional rotavirus vaccines are licensed and produced, however these are not available internationally. The manufacturers recommend that the last dose is given no later than 32 weeks of age, because of theoretical concerns of increased risk for intussusception in older children, however, WHO recommends that the rotavirus vaccines may be given with DTP vaccines until two years of age. In 2018, 94 countries worldwide have introduced rotavirus vaccines. Due to the less than desired vaccine efficacy of current live-attenuated formulations in LMIC, research is ongoing on improved formulation –including the development of subunit systemically administered vaccines.





Measles


	The highly contagious measles virus caused epidemics every 2 to 3 years prior to vaccine introduction in 1963. Measles was responsible for 30 million cases of infection and >2 million deaths worldwide on an annual basis in the pre-vaccine era; with more than 95% of individuals infected before reaching 15 years of age. Despite availability of a vaccine since the 1960s, measles remained an important cause of death among children. In 2000 there were an estimated 850,000 deaths from measles, which decreased to an estimated 89,780 by 2016 due to a concerted effort at increasing vaccine coverage rates in routine immunization programmes, as well as undertaking periodic community-wide supplementary immunization activities. This resulted in more than 20.4 million deaths being prevented between 2000 and 2016.
	The age of measles acquisition varies with population immunity and birth rate. Infants and toddlers are at increased risk to acquire measles in LIC, refugee camps, countries with low population immunity, high birth rates, and high population density. Once vaccination coverage improves, a transition occurs from infection during childhood to adolescence or adulthood in cohorts that have not been vaccinated before.
	As part of the Global Vaccine Action Plan, the WHO targets measles elimination in 5 of 6 WHO regions by 2020. The definition of elimination is the interruption of transmission in a specific geographical area for ≥12 months and is confirmed after sustaining this for ≥36 months. Once sufficient immunity in the population is reached, measles virus transmission can be interrupted. Due to its high infection rates (Ro), measles requires the highest coverage rates (approximately 90–95%) for herd protection to materialize. Global coverage of the first measles dose by 12 months was 85% in 2016, and even lower (78%) in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
	The measles vaccine is a live-attenuated virus and may be given as a monovalent vaccine or in combination with rubella, +/– mumps, +/– varicella (MR, MMR, MMRV). The timing of measles vaccine administration depends on coverage, measles incidence, and age at which visits take place in the immunization schedule. For example, countries with weaker immunization programmes reaching suboptimal coverage and high measles virus transmission may offer doses at younger ages (6–9 months) and may need to use supplemental vaccination campaigns. All children should receive two doses of measles vaccine. In countries with ongoing transmission, the first dose should be administered during infancy (at 9 months) and the second dose between 15 and 18 months of age. In areas of high measles and maternal HIV incidence, an addition dose should be given at 6 months to mitigate against the lower transplacental acquisition of measles antibody in children born to HIV-infected women, as well as more severe disease in HIV-infected children. If measles transmission is low, the first dose may be administered at 12 months.
	Countries should reach ≥95% coverage with both doses in order to achieve measles elimination. During every contact with health services, children should be evaluated for missed doses and should be vaccinated if necessary.





Rubella


	Rubella virus causes an acute, but mild infection and usually affects children and young adults. The importance for public health is related to its teratogenic outcomes. Rubella infection in pregnant women may result in miscarriage, foetal death, or congenital defects. Congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) is associated with ophthalmic (e.g. cataract, glaucoma, microphthalmia); auditory (e.g. sensorineural deafness), cardiac (e.g. patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defects) and craniofacial (e.g. microcephaly) defects. Women of childbearing age who are susceptible to rubella are at highest risk of CRS. In countries that have not introduced rubella-containing vaccines (RCV), the burden of CRS is estimated to be similar as in 1996 when approximately 22,000 children were born with CRS in Africa (95%CI: 6,127–51,472), 46,000 (95%CI: 1,016–168,910) in South East Asia and 12,634 (95%CI: 1,545–21,396) in the Western Pacific Region. Many HIC and some LMIC have introduced rubella vaccination with high coverage rates and have almost reached rubella and CRS elimination.
	Rubella vaccine, a live-attenuated vaccine, is mostly based on the RA 27/3 strain. The vaccine is often given as part of combination vaccine with measles (MR), measles and mumps (MMR), ± varicella (MMRV). The main purpose of rubella immunization is to decrease incidence of primary infection in pregnant women and thus protect against CRS in their offspring. When vaccine coverage is low (e.g. only offered in private sector), viral circulation may decline, and result in a shift of primary infection occurring during childhood to adolescence and adulthood. This may result in a paradoxical increase in CRS cases.
	WHO recently recommended that countries that are providing two doses of measles vaccine should consider incorporating routine infant immunization against rubella when giving the second dose of measles vaccine. This approach (ideally accompanied by an initial immunization campaign targeting a wide range of adolescents and women of childbearing age) is preferred to the alternative strategy of immunizing adolescent girls and females of childbearing age, as this may be undermined by low vaccine coverage and ongoing circulation of the virus. Due to high response rates of a single dose of rubella vaccination and long-term persistence of protection, a booster dose is not required.





Human papilloma virus


	Human papilloma virus (HPV) is a group of viruses, of which at least 13 types could cause precancerous lesions that may progress to cancer. HPV commonly causes infections in the reproductive tract, the majority resulting in asymptomatic infection with spontaneous resolution. HPV is transmitted through sexual contact and most people are infected shortly after the onset of sexual activity. HPV-16 and HPV-18 are responsible for 70% of cervical cancers and precancerous cervical lesions. HPV is also associated with anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers. In LMIC, cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in women. An estimated 630,000 new cases of HPV-related cancer occurred in 2012, of which 84% were cervical cancer. Most deaths due to cervical cancer (85%) were in LMIC.
	Three HPV vaccines are licensed and available: bivalent (HPV types 16 and 18), quadrivalent (HPV types 16, 18, 6, and 11), and non-avalent (HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58) vaccines. All of the vaccines are recommended to be administered prior to onset of sexual activity and prevent cervical cancer. The quadrivalent and non-avalent HPV vaccines also protect against common genital wart-causing strains.
	WHO recommends inclusion of HPV vaccination in all national immunization programmes. HPV is indicated primarily for girls aged 9–14 years with a two-dose schedule to prevent cervical cancer. Vaccination of females ≥15–25 years or males is only recommended if feasible, cost-effective, and affordable. The risk of HPV infection in boys is reduced if a vaccination coverage >80% is achieved in girls. A three-dose vaccine schedule in women 15–25 years of age with precancerous cervical lesions has recently been shown to be effective in preventing progression to cervical cancer; but not in older women.
	By May 2018, 80 (41%) countries had introduced HPV vaccine in their national immunization programme. The implementation of HPV vaccine in immunization programmes is technically and logistically a departure from the services used for EPI vaccination; as the targeted age groups rarely visit childhood immunization centres. Introduction of HPV vaccine should be part of a larger comprehensive strategy for the prevention of cervical cancer and other HPV-related diseases. As part of this strategy, health personnel should be trained, people should be educated about behaviours leading to HPV acquisition, and women should be informed about screening, diagnosis, and treatment of precancerous lesions and cancer. Also, availability of cervical cancer screening and treatment of invasive cancers should be addressed. It is important that HPV vaccination does not replace the need for screening during adulthood, because older age groups will not have been vaccinated and the vaccine does not prevent all high-risk HPV types.





Vaccines recommended when living in certain regions


Japanese encephalitis


	Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is the main cause of viral encephalitis in Asia. Japanese encephalitis (JE) is a zoonotic viral disease. The virus amplifies in pigs and wading birds and is spread primarily by Culex mosquitoes. The most important vector, Culex tritaeniorhynchus, breeds in flooded rice fields and water pools and usually bites at night time. Elimination of JEV is not possible due to the animal reservoirs. However, control is possible by vaccination of humans in endemic regions. Because viraemia in humans is too low for transmission, they are a dead-end-host. The season for JEV transmission is from April/May to September/October in temperate climates. In the tropics or subtropics, transmission increases during the rainy season. However, during the dry season transmission may be possible if irrigation systems are in place.
	The burden of JE is unclear due to lack of surveillance and difficulty of laboratory confirmation. An estimated 68,000 clinical cases occur every year, with approximately 13,600 deaths. Most cases of JE are mild, but case-fatality rates can be as high as 30% in case of encephalitis. Encephalitis may result in permanent neurologic or psychiatric sequelae in 30–50% of cases. 24 countries are endemic for JE, all of them in the WHO Southeast Asia and Western Pacific regions. People living in rural areas, close to rice fields, and in close proximity to pigs are at increased risk for JE.
	Safe and effective vaccines can prevent JE. In all areas where JE disease is a public health concern, JE vaccination is recommend as part of the national immunization schedule. Three JE vaccines are currently available and recommended: inactivated Vero cell-derived vaccines, live-attenuated vaccines, and live recombinant (chimeric) vaccines. Inactivated Vero cell-derived vaccines are recommended as 2-dose (from 6 months of age), whereas live-attenuated (from 8 months of age) and live recombinant vaccines (from 9 months of age) are given as a single dose.
	JE vaccination does not induce herd immunity, so high coverage is required in populations at risk. If this is sustained, elimination of viral circulation can occur. A common immunization strategy in JE endemic areas should encompass a one-time campaign in the primary target population (depending on local epidemiology, commonly <15 years), and inclusion of JE vaccine into the national routine childhood immunization schedule. If the burden of disease in older age groups is high, they may also be targeted for vaccination.





Yellow fever


	Yellow fever (YF) is a viral disease transmitted by mosquitoes and affects humans and other primates. The virus is endemic in tropical areas in Africa (29 countries) and Central and South America (13 countries). YF can cause acute viral haemorrhage and is named ‘yellow’ due to jaundice being one of the clinical manifestations. The burden of YF is estimated at 84,000–170,000 cases of severe disease and 29,000–60,000 YF deaths in Africa in 2013. YF may be transmitted in sylvatic (jungle), intermediate, or urban cycles. Sylvatic YF is common in primates, other than humans. In humans it is predominantly seen in Central and South America in young men working in close proximity to the rain forest. Intermediate YF transmission occurs in humid settings in Africa infecting both humans and non-human primates. Urban YF transmission is associated with large epidemics, where Aedes aegypti transmits the virus from person-to-person in densely populated areas. Only a minor proportion of individuals who are infected with the virus develop severe symptoms. Among those with severe symptoms, around half die in 7–10 days. Most (>90%) of YF deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa, with children being at highest risk.
	YF can be prevented by a very effective live-attenuated vaccine. A single dose is adequate to confer sustained lifelong immunity against disease. Infant immunization at the same time as measles vaccination is recommended in YF-endemic countries. Additionally, mass immunization campaigns are recommended in settings with high risk of YF and low vaccination coverage.





Tick-borne encephalitis


	Tick-borne encephalitis can cause viral infections of the central nervous system. It is endemic in in eastern, central, and northern Europe, northern China, Mongolia, and the Russian Federation. An estimated 10,000–12,000 clinical cases of tick-borne encephalitis are reported every year. In general, infections occur after tick bites during outdoor activities in the forest.
	Vaccination using a formalin-inactivated strain of the virus could protect against tick-borne encephalitis if administered as a three-dose primary series. The need for public immunization varies between geographical areas, depending on the local incidence of tick-borne encephalitis. If the disease is highly endemic (incidence of clinical disease ≥5 cases/100,000 population per year prior to vaccination), WHO recommends vaccination in all age groups.





Vaccines recommended in high-risk populations


Typhoid


	The enteric bacterium Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi) causes typhoid fever, a life-threatening infection. Transmission occurs via the faecal-oral route through contaminated food and water. The only known reservoir of S. typhi are humans. S. typhi infection is associated with lack of safe water and sanitation, poor hygiene when handling food, high population density, overcrowding, low socioeconomic status, and low literacy rates.
	LMICs have a substantial burden of typhoid disease, which has however decreased with improved sanitation, hygiene, and access to potable water. Globally, the burden ranges from 11 to 21 million cases and around 128,000–161,000 deaths annually. The incidence of typhoid fever varies significantly between countries in Asia and Africa. Children have the highest incidence of typhoid fever, in particular between 5 and 15 years of age.
	Three types of typhoid vaccines are available: typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV), unconjugated Vi polysaccharide (ViPS), and live-attenuated Ty21a vaccines. The licensed TCV vaccines are preferred at all ages due to their increased immunogenicity, use in younger children, and longer duration of protection. TCV should be prioritized in countries with a high burden of typhoid disease or antimicrobial resistance. Countries could also consider routine use of ViPS vaccine in individuals ≥2 years of age, and Ty21a vaccine for individuals ≥6 years of age depending on costs and programmatic issues.





Cholera


	Cholera is a diarrhoeal disease that may cause rapid dehydration and is caused by toxigenic serogroups of the Vibrio cholera bacterium. Risk factors for cholera include lack of clean drinking water, poor sanitation, and poverty. In the past, cholera outbreaks caused millions of cases and hundreds of thousands of deaths. Some LMICs still experience major epidemics and cholera remains an important public health issue in many countries; especially in areas with fragile infrastructure during times of unrest/wars, natural disaster, and in refugee camps. Cholera endemicity is defined as the detection of cholera due to local transmission in a specific area in the last 3 years. A country with one or more endemic regions is classified as a cholera-endemic country. A cholera outbreak is defined as the detection of at least one confirmed case of cholera and proof of local transmission. Outbreaks occurred in Haiti and Yemen between 2010 and 2017 and regions in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa have shown surges in endemic disease. The burden of cholera is highest is Africa and southern Asia (99% of all cases). Risk of cholera is increased in humanitarian emergencies and around 50% of the cases and deaths occur in children under 5.
	Two types of oral cholera vaccines are available: WC-rBS, a killed whole cell monovalent vaccine with a recombinant B subunit of cholera toxin; and WC, a killed modified whole cell bivalent vaccine without the B subunit. WHO recommends that, along with other preventive measures, cholera vaccines should be used where disease is endemic and considered in areas at risk for outbreaks. The parenteral cholera vaccine has poor efficacy and is no longer recommended.





Meningococcal disease


	Meningococcal meningitis is a serious bacterial infection affecting the membrane around the brain and spinal cord. If untreated, case-fatality rates may go up to 50% or could cause severe neurological sequelae (10%). The Neisseria meningitidis bacteria may be responsible for meningococcal meningitis. There are 12 N. meningitidis serogroups, of which A, B, C, W, X, and Y can cause epidemics. The disease mainly affects children and young people and can occur as single cases, clusters, or epidemics.
	Depending on the serogroup, the geographical burden of disease differs; however, due to inadequate surveillance, estimates of global burden of meningococcal disease are uncertain. The meningitis belt, an area in sub-Saharan Africa stretching from Senegal to Ethiopia (26 countries), has the highest burden of meningococcal disease. Risk of meningococcal disease is increased when the nasopharyngeal mucosa is damaged in the dry season due to dust winds, colds nights, and upper respiratory tract infections in combination with transmission facilitated by overcrowding.
	Vaccines against specific serogroups are administered routinely or during outbreaks. There are three types of vaccines available: polysaccharide vaccines, conjugate vaccines, and protein-based vaccines. Polysaccharide vaccines can be bivalent (serogroups A, C), trivalent (A, C, W), or tetravalent (A, C, Y, W) and are usually given during outbreaks. However, protection decreases after several years and, apart from serogroup A, are poorly immunogenic in infants. These vaccines have largely been replaced by polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccines (Men-CV)
	Men-CVs confer longer-lasting immunity, induce herd immunity, and prevent nasopharyngeal colonization—hence also interrupting transmission of the bacteria. They are immunogenic in children from 1 year of age onward. Currently available vaccines include monovalent (A or C) or quadrivalent (A, C, Y, W) conjugate vaccines, also in combination with HibCV (HibMenC). Epitope specific protein based vaccines are available for serotype B.
	Mass immunization campaigns using meningococcal A conjugate vaccine in the meningitis belt have contributed to a 58% decline in the meningococcal meningitis A cases and 60% reduction in the risk of epidemics since 2010. More than 280 million individuals have been vaccinated in 21 countries located in the belt as of November 2017. However, epidemics due to meningococcal serogroups W, X, and C still occur, with a burden of 30,000 cases of meningococcal disease reported annually.





Hepatitis A


	Hepatitis A virus (HAV) can cause mild to severe liver disease. Most HAV infections are asymptomatic during childhood, but symptoms commonly occur when infected later in life. The virus is transmitted via the faecal-oral route by ingesting contaminated food or water, or through close contact with an infected person. The risk of hepatitis A infection is associated with socioeconomic factors such as income, availability of clean water, sanitation, and hygiene. The burden of hepatitis A is estimated to have increased from 117 million to 126 million in the period between 1990 and 2005, with deaths due to hepatitis A rising from 30,283 to 35,245 in the same period.
	In most LICs, anti-HAV antibodies are present in 90% of children by the time they reach 10 years of age. Asymptomatic childhood infection induces immunity and few are susceptible to symptomatic disease during adolescence and adulthood. Yet, middle-income countries often have intermediate HAV endemicity. As sanitation and hygiene improve, a number of individuals will not be infected during childhood, but may be at risk of symptomatic infection during adult life. Hence, when HAV endemicity decreases, the number of clinical cases of hepatitis A will increase. In HIC, the prevalence of anti-HAV antibody is low, as is circulation of the virus.
	Hepatitis A can be prevented by safe and effective vaccines. Inactivated and live-attenuated vaccines are available and result in long-lasting protection in adults and children. WHO recommends HAV vaccination to be integrated in the national routine immunization schedule for children ≥1 years of age in countries with high incidence of acute hepatitis A, who are transitioning from high to intermediate endemicity if it is cost-effective. Large scale vaccination in highly endemic countries is not recommended.





Rabies


	Rabies is a viral disease transmitted from animals to humans through bites or scratches. Dogs are responsible for 99% of rabies transmissions and are the main source of human rabies deaths. Rabies can also be found in domestic animals and wildlife. Rabies is present in more than 150 countries and causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths and approximately 3.7 million disability-adjusted life years lost on an annual basis. Once clinical signs appear, it almost always results in death due to acute progressive encephalitis.
	The majority of cases occur in Asia and Africa, with 40% in children under 15 years of age.
	The principle strategy for rabies control consists of vaccination of dogs and prevention of dog bites.
	Vaccination of humans and immunoglobulins exist, but they are usually not accessible to people living in remote areas. Vaccination is effective before or after exposure to rabies.





Dengue


	Dengue virus is transmitted to humans by female mosquitoes. The primary vector is the Aedes aegypti species and to some extent the Aedes albopictus species. People with dengue infection develop flu-like illness, but infected individuals may develop severe fatal complications. Four dengue serotypes exist: DEN-1, DEN-2, DEN-3, and DEN-4. Infection will result in lifelong protection against the specific serotype, but there is limited and temporary cross-immunity to other serotypes. Instead, new infection by other serotypes increases the risk of developing severe dengue. In Asia and Latin America, severe dengue is a significant cause of serious illness and death among children.
	In recent decades, dengue incidence has increased rapidly from 0.4–1.3 million in 1995–2005, to 2.2 million in 2020 and 3.2 million in 2015. Around 50% of the global population is at risk for dengue infection. Dengue is commonly found in the tropics and subtropics, predominantly in urban and semi-urban regions. Local risk factors include rainfall, temperature, and urbanization.
	Prevention and control of dengue can be achieved by successful vector control. The first dengue vaccine (Dengvaxia, CYD-TDV) was licensed in 2015 for use in persons 9–45 years of age living in endemic settings. Vaccination is not recommended when seroprevalence is <50% in the targeted age group. Recent findings showed that vaccination resulted in more severe disease and hospitalizations from dengue in individuals previously seronegative at time of first vaccination compared to unvaccinated individuals. WHO now recommends a ‘pre-vaccination screening strategy’, in which only dengue-seropositive persons are vaccinated, the logistics of which might prove challenging.
	Currently, other tetravalent live-attenuated vaccines are being developed in phase III clinical trials. Development of new vaccine candidates based on subunit DNA and purified inactivated virus platforms is also ongoing.





Vaccines recommended in certain immunization programmes


Mumps


	Mumps is a viral infection spreading between humans via airborne droplet or direct contact. It is also known as infectious parotitis because of infection in the salivary (parotid) glands. Infection with mumps during childhood causes mild disease, primarily affecting children aged 5–9 years. Infection in adults may occur and may cause more serious complications such as meningitis (up to 15% of cases), orchitis, or deafness.
	Mumps incidence infection rates ranges from 100 to 1,000 cases per 100,000 population in absence of vaccination. Vaccination against mumps resulted in a reduction of incidence. The vaccine has been incorporated in childhood immunization schedules of many middle-and high-income countries, usually combined with measles and rubella (MMR) immunization. WHO recommends mumps vaccination in countries with a high burden of mumps, an established routine vaccination programme and persistent high vaccination coverage with measles and rubella of more than 80%. Similarly to rubella vaccine, insufficient coverage of mumps vaccination during childhood can cause a shift in age distribution to infection at older ages, when the course of disease is more severe.





Seasonal influenza


	Influenza viruses can cause seasonal influenza epidemics as well as sporadic cases and outbreaks outside of the influenza season. Symptomatic influenza attack rates of 5–10% have been reported in adults and 20–30% in children; with as many of 50% of individuals demonstrating sero-conversion following seasonal epidemics. Persons with increased risk of severe disease and complications include pregnant women, children under 5 years of age, the elderly, and individuals with chronic conditions or immunosuppression. Healthcare workers are also at increased risk of influenza acquisition due to increased exposure and higher risk of spreading disease. In tropical areas, influenza occurs throughout the year, whereas temperate climates typically show a seasonal peak in incidence during winter.
	WHO recommends protection of high-risk groups against severe influenza illness and death by annual influenza vaccination. These risk groups include pregnant women who are considered as the highest priority group, children aged 6 months to 5 years, elderly persons (>65 years), individuals with chronic medical conditions and healthcare workers. Vaccine effectiveness is dependent on the closeness of the genetic match between the vaccine and wild-type circulating strains, and could vary from 0% to 70% year-by-year. Influenza viruses continuously evolve over time. Therefore, it is important to monitor wild-type circulating viruses and update the vaccine formulation bi-annually.
	Vaccination of pregnant women has been shown to protect the women (50% efficacy), as well as their infants <6 months of age (50% efficacy) against symptomatic influenza infection. Furthermore, a 20% reduction in all-cause pneumonia hospitalization has been reported in randomized controlled trials in the young offspring of vaccinated pregnant women.
	A number of challenges exist with influenza vaccine development, including dependency on egg-culture for vaccine virus propagation, uncertainty of predicting the drifts in the upcoming wild-type strains; and short duration of protection. This is being addressed by the search for universal influenza vaccines, at least against group A viruses, which cause the most severe seasonal epidemics. Furthermore, the threat of virus shift resulting in a pandemic from a new novel strain of influenza virus, warrants countries to have a pandemic plan in place, which includes how they will procure and dispense vaccines should such a pandemic arise. Ideally, a ‘universal’ influenza virus vaccine should also confer cross-protection against pandemic virus; however, this is less likely to be realized over the next 5–10 years.





Varicella and Zoster vaccines


	Varicella zoster virus (VZV) is a highly contagious virus that causes varicella (chickenpox), mostly during childhood, and herpes zoster (shingles) later in life. In absence of vaccination, almost all individuals are infected by the time they reach mid-adulthood. VZV epidemiology depends on climate, population density, and risk of exposure. The disease is generally mild, but severe disease may develop (e.g. cellulitis, pneumonia, encephalitis, death), especially in infants and immunocompromised individuals. After primary infection, the virus may establish latency in sensory nerve ganglia and reactivate later in life, causing herpes zoster. Typically, herpes zoster affects elderly and immunocompromised persons.
	Multiple formulations of live-attenuated varicella vaccine based on the OKA strain are available. It may be given as a monovalent dose or in combination with the MMR vaccine (MMRV). Routine immunization against VZV is employed in many resource-rich countries. Coverage of ≥80% is required to prevent a shift of infection to older age groups. Herpes zoster vaccination is currently not recommended due to limited availability of data. The recently licensed zoster vaccine in the United States showed efficacy for preventing herpes zoster of 70% (95%CI 54–81%).





Vaccination of special populations


Refugees, asylum-seekers, migrants


	Refugees, asylum-seekers, and migrants may have increased risk for acquisition of infectious diseases because of mass population movement; limited access to clean water, shelter, and sanitation. Children in these populations also have increased risk of respiratory infections, diarrhoea, and skin infections. Despite high vaccination coverage in the countries of origin, young children may have missed vaccinations due to interruptions by civil unrest and war. Also, individuals may not have access to healthcare, health insurance, or registration in the health system.
	Vaccination of refugees, asylum-seekers, and migrants may be challenging if populations are on the move. All vaccines should be administered according to the national routine immunization schedule of the country of stay. Priority vaccines include measles, mumps, rubella, and polio. Furthermore, refugees might benefit from early vaccination against cholera, especially if in or from settings where cholera is endemic.





HIV-infected


	HIV-infected individuals require special consideration because of increased susceptibility to severe disease from infections, including TB, pneumococcal disease, and measles. HIV-infected persons have reduced immunogenicity following vaccination when administered in advanced stages of AIDS, but HIV-positive adults and children are able to mount moderate to good vaccine responses. Waning of immunity may result in reduced protection over time for some vaccines. Individuals may require administration of booster doses, especially if children were vaccinated prior to initiation of antiretroviral therapy.
	HIV-exposed-uninfected children and HIV-infected children, who were vaccinated when already on antiretroviral therapy, have similar responses to vaccination as HIV-unexposed children. Except for BCG, asymptomatic HIV-infected individuals should receive all EPI vaccines at the indicated ages. BCG vaccination should be given to children receiving ART, who are clinically well and immunologically stable. In neonates newly diagnosed with HIV, BCG vaccination should be delayed until antiretroviral therapy is initiated and the infant is confirmed immunologically stable. If an HIV-infected child has an acute severe illness, vaccination should be delayed, as for any severely ill child.





Healthcare workers


	Healthcare workers have increased risk for acquisition of vaccine-preventable diseases. It is important that healthcare workers can maintain delivery of healthcare services during epidemics. They should also avoid spreading disease to vulnerable patient groups. Appropriate vaccination for BCG, hepatitis B, polio, diphtheria, measles, rubella, meningococcal, influenza, varicella, and pertussis is recommended, especially if at increased risk of exposure.





Emerging vector-borne diseases


	Vector-borne diseases require vectors, such as mosquitoes, ticks, or sand flies for transmission between hosts or rely on other animals as reservoirs or carriers. They account for an estimated 17% of all infectious diseases and have the highest burden in tropical and subtropical areas. Since 2014, major outbreaks of chikungunya, dengue, malaria, Zika, and Ebola have affected populations and claimed many lives around the world.





Ebola


	Ebola virus disease, previously called Ebola haemorrhagic fever, is a severe and often fatal illness in humans. The virus was first discovered in 1976, during outbreaks in South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The largest outbreak occurred in 2014–2016 in West Africa. Five Ebola virus species have been identified, of which the Zaire species was responsible for the recent outbreak.
	The virus is transmitted from wild animals to humans and can spread between humans. Case-fatality rates vary between 25% and 90%. Treatment consists of supportive care, including rehydration, but no cure is available.
	An experimental vaccine (rVSV-ZEBOV) was shown to protect against the virus in a trial in Guinea. WHO supports Ebola vaccination in high-risk populations in the Democratic Republic of Congo using a ring vaccination strategy. This involves tracing contacts of recently confirmed cases as well as contacts of contacts. Other preventive measures should target reducing the risk of transmission and containment of outbreaks.





Maternal immunization


	Despite considerable progress in the reduction of under-5 mortality, a significant number of deaths still occurs during the neonatal period and progress has been slower in this age group. Of 700,000 deaths in the first month of life, 28% is attributable to infectious diseases. It is therefore important to protect infants already in the first weeks of life. Yet, primary immunization schedules usually start at 6 weeks of age in most LMIC. Maternal immunization could reduce the morbidity and mortality from infectious diseases at birth. Transplacental transfer of maternal antibodies successfully protects newborns against tetanus, influenza, and pertussis after maternal immunization during pregnancy. New maternal vaccines currently being developed include immunization for group B streptococcus and respiratory syncytial virus.





Universal access to immunization


	In 2012, the World Health Assembly adopted the Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP), which sought to deliver universal access to immunization. This was expected to avert 24.6–25.8 million vaccine-preventable deaths in this decade alone. Key to the GVAP agenda is ensuring equitable access to immunization services, regardless of geographic location, ethnic or religious beliefs, and socioeconomic background. Efforts to achieve this include Gavi’s support for the introduction of new vaccines in the poorest countries by subsidizing vaccine procurement. As a result, the timelines by which PCV and rotavirus vaccines were introduced into public immunization programmes have been drastically reduced and 20 out of 25 countries within the meningitis belt have introduced the MenA conjugate vaccine. Furthermore, steady progress has been made in the field of polio and tetanus eradication/elimination.
	However, immunization equity analyses still show that economic disparities, place of residence, and education status continue to determine a child’s vaccination status. In many regions, vaccine supply remains a challenge with 16 countries reporting one or more stock-outs of vaccines lasting for more than one week in 2017. As a result, an estimated 19.9 million (15%) of the annual birth cohort of 132 million are either not vaccinated or underimmunized. The continued presence of vaccine-preventable deaths is primarily due to low immunization coverage rates. Understanding the mediators contributing to underimmunization and non-vaccination of children is, therefore, fundamental to derive the full benefits that vaccines stand to offer at an individual and societal level.
	In this context, there is a need for community-engagement and a bottom-up approach that includes societal, cultural, and religious considerations to address the barriers contributing to underimmunization of children.





11.4


Principles of infectious disease control


	Robert J. Kim-Farley





Principles of infectious disease control: overview


	Infectious diseases remain a leading cause of morbidity, disability, and mortality worldwide. Lower respiratory infections result in the highest mortality for any category infectious diseases and comprise the fourth leading causes of death worldwide (WHO 2020). Their control is a constant challenge that faces health workers and public health officials in both industrialized and developing countries. Only one infectious disease, smallpox, was eradicated and stands as a landmark in the history of the control of infectious diseases. The international community is now well down the path towards eradication of poliomyelitis and dracunculiasis (Guinea worm infection). Other infectious diseases, like malaria and tuberculosis, foiled eradication attempts or control efforts and are reemerging as increasing threats in many countries, including both developing and developed countries. Some infectious diseases, such as tetanus, will always be a threat if control measures are not maintained. Newer infectious diseases, like AIDS and COVID-19, demonstrate the truth of McNeill’s statement that infectious disease will remain ‘one of the fundamental parameters and determinants of human history’. The history of infectious diseases is an exciting story in itself and readers interested in the subject are referred to McNeill (1976) or the comprehensive work on the history of human diseases (Kiple 1993).
	This chapter provides a global and comprehensive view of infectious disease control through examination of the magnitude of disease burden, the chain of infection (agent, transmission, and host) of infectious diseases, the varied approaches to their prevention and control, and the factors conducive to their eradication as well as emergence and reemergence. Although this chapter provides many examples of infectious diseases that illustrate modes of transmission and approaches to infectious disease control, this chapter does not attempt to be comprehensive in listing all infectious diseases. Detailed recommendations on control measures for any specific disease are outlined periodically in the updated reports of the American Public Health Association, Control of Communicable Diseases Manual (Heymann 2014), the comprehensive two-volume work Mandell, Douglas and Bennett’s Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases (Bennett et al. 2020), and the textbook Infectious Diseases (Gorbach et al. 2004). For readers specifically interested in paediatric infectious diseases there is the comprehensive two-volume Feigin and Cherry’s Textbook of Pediatric Infectious Diseases (Cherry et al. 2014); for infectious diseases in emergency medicine settings there is the textbook Infectious Diseases: Emergency Department Diagnosis & Management (Red and White Emergency Medicine Series) (Slaven et al. 2006); and for tropical infectious diseases there is Tropical Infectious Diseases: Principles, Pathogens, and Practice (Guerrant et al. 2011). A comprehensive treatment of the worldwide distribution of infectious diseases is provided in Atlas of Human Infectious Diseases (Wertheim et al. 2012). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) publishes up-to-date disease surveillance information for the United States and recommendations for control measures in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Reports and provides annual summaries of notifiable infectious diseases in the Summary of Notifiable Diseases, United States (CDC 2016). Many other countries have similar types of publications. The World Health Organization (WHO) publishes worldwide surveillance information and recommendations for control measures in the Weekly Epidemiological Record. A more detailed background on infectious agents as determinants of health and disease is provided in Chapters 8.11–8.15.





Definitions of infectious diseases and their control


	Infection occurs when an infectious agent enters a body and develops or multiplies. Infectious agents are organisms capable of producing inapparent infection or clinically manifest disease and include bacteria, rickettsia, chlamydiae, fungi, parasites, viruses, and prions. An infectious disease, or communicable disease, is an infection that results in clinically manifest disease. Infectious disease may also be due to the toxic product of an infectious agent, such as the toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum causing classical botulism. As this is a textbook of public health, the infectious diseases considered are those that manifest in human hosts and are a result of the interaction of people, animals, and their environment. Infectious diseases may be due to infectious agents exclusively found in human hosts such as rubella virus, in the environment such as Legionella pneumophila, or primarily in animals such as Brucella abortus.
	Control of infectious diseases refers to the actions and programmes directed towards reducing disease incidence (new infections), reducing disease prevalence (infections in the community at any given point in time), or completely eradicating the disease. Control aimed at reducing the incidence of infectious disease or their risk factors can be considered as primary prevention of infectious disease. Primary prevention protects health through individual and community-wide measures, including such actions as maintaining good nutritional status, keeping physically fit, immunizing against infectious diseases, providing safe water, and ensuring the proper disposal of faeces.
	Control aimed at reducing the prevalence by shortening the duration of infectious disease can be considered as secondary prevention of infectious disease. Secondary prevention corrects departures from good health through individual and community-wide measures, including such actions as screening that result in early detection of disease, prompt antibiotic treatment, and ensuring adequate nutrition. It should be noted that such control efforts in secondary prevention in a group of infected individuals may also result in primary prevention in uninfected people. For example, prompt and specific drug therapy for tuberculosis patients resulting in sputum conversion to culture-negative status renders them no longer a source of infection to others and treatment of HIV-positive pregnant women reduces transmission of HIV to their newborns.
	Control aimed at reducing or even eliminating long-term impairments of infectious disease can be considered as tertiary prevention of infectious disease. Tertiary prevention reduces or eliminates disabilities, minimizes suffering, and promotes adjustment to permanent disabilities through such actions as providing orthopaedic appliances and its associated rehabilitation for victims of poliomyelitis, counselling and vocational training, and prevention of opportunistic infections. For example, the prevention of opportunistic infections in HIV infection can be considered as tertiary prevention (Osterholm and Hedberg 2005).





Global burden of infectious diseases


	A WHO analysis of the global burden of disease estimates that infectious diseases caused 12.3 million deaths, accounting for 21% of total global mortality of 56.8 million deaths in 2008 (WHO 2008). Five diseases—lower respiratory infections, AIDS, diarrhoeal diseases, tuberculosis, and malaria—account for some 81% of the total infectious disease burden. Most infectious disease (some 97%) deaths occur in the economically developing group of countries where approximately a quarter of deaths are due to an infectious cause (WHO 2008). However, infectious diseases are also of importance in more developed countries. In the United States, for example, influenza still ranks as an important cause of death.
	The current magnitude of morbidity and mortality due to infectious diseases worldwide is highlighted by the the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) as follows (http://www.healthdata.org/results/gbd_summaries):
	 	• Acute lower respiratory infections, including pneumonia and influenza, cause some 489 million episodes of illness each year and result in 2.49 million deaths annually. These infections are the highest cause of infant and child mortality in developing countries.
	• HIV newly infects about 1.9 million people each year and causes an estimated 864,000 AIDS-related deaths annually, down from a peak of 2.2 million that occurred in the mid-2000s. There were some 36.8 million people living with HIV in 2019.
	• Diarrhoeal diseases are also a major cause of morbidity and mortality in infants and children in developing countries. Each year there are some 6.6 billion episodes with 1.5 million deaths due to diarrhoeal disease, of which the vast majority are among children under 5 years of age.
	• Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, infects some 1.82 billion people, about one-fourth of the world’s population, and is the leading cause of death of a single pathogen. It was estimated that 8.5 million people who developed clinical disease and 1.18 million died of tuberculosis in 2019.
	• Malaria was estimated to cause some 231 million cases and 643,000 deaths in 2019, mainly in children under the age of 5 years.
	• Influenza epidemics, caused by influenza A and B viruses, are estimated to kill from 500,000 to 1 million people worldwide each year. Influenza pandemics, of which there were three in the last century, have killed as many as 40–50 million people (as occurred during the 1918–1919 ‘Spanish flu’ pandemic) and, as with the current concerns regarding highly pathogenic avian influenza H5 viruses, continue to threaten to re-emerge as a major public health emergency.
	• The COVID-19 Pandemic, ongoing at the time of writing this chapter, has become the most important infectious disease public health pandemic in the last 100 years. Deaths from COVID-19 are projected to exceed 3.5 million deaths worldwide by mid-2021.





Chain of infection: agent, transmission, and host


	The chain of infection is the relationship between an infectious agent, its routes of transmission, and a susceptible host. The prevention and control of infectious diseases depend upon the interaction of these three factors that may result in the human host clinically manifesting disease.





Agent


	The infectious agent is the first link in the chain of infection and is any microorganism whose presence or excessive presence is essential for the occurrence of an infectious disease. Examples of infectious agents include the following:
	 	• Bacteria: for example, spirochetes and curved bacteria such as Borrelia burgdorferi causing Lyme disease; Gram-negative rods such as Yersinia pestis causing plague; Gram-positive cocci such as Streptococcus pyogenes, group A causing erysipelas; and Gram-positive rods such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis causing tuberculosis.
	• Rickettsiae: for example, Rickettsia ricketsii causing Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and Rickettsia prowazekii causing epidemic louse-borne typhus fever.
	• Chlamydiae: for example, Chlamydia psittaci causing psittacosis (ornithosis), and Chlamydia trachomatis causing trachoma and genital infections.
	• Fungi: for example, Trichophyton schoenleinii and Microsporum canis causing tinea capitis (ringworm of the scalp), and Trichophyton rubrum, Trichophyton mentagrophytes, and Epidermophyton floccosum causing tinea pedis (ringworm of the foot, or athlete’s foot).
	• Parasites: for example, helminths such as Trichinella spiralis causing trichinosis, filaria such as Brugia malayi causing filariasis (which may lead to the symptom of elephantiasis), nematodes such as Enterobius vermicularis causing enterobiasis (pinworm disease), trematodes such as Clonorchis sinensis causing clonorchiasis (oriental liver fluke disease), cestodes such as Taenia solium causing taeniasis (beef tapeworm disease), and protozoa such as Trypanosoma cruzi causing American trypanosomiasis (Chagas’ disease).
	• Viruses: for example, Paramyxoviridae such as measles virus which causes measles, Togaviridae such as rubella virus which causes rubella, Picornaviridae such as the hepatovirus which causes hepatitis A, and arthropod-borne viruses (arboviruses) such as dengue viruses which cause dengue fever.
	• Prions: small proteinaceous infectious particles which cause such diseases as kuru, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (and its variant associated with exposure of humans to the bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or ‘mad cow’, agent), and the Gerstmann–Straussler–Scheinker syndrome.
	There is increasing evidence that some infectious agents, often with cofactors, are associated with human tumours. Examples include: Schistosoma haematobium with bladder cancer, Schistosoma japonicum with colorectal cancer, Clonorchis sinensis with cholangiocarcinoma, hepatitis B and C viruses with hepatocellular carcinoma, Helicobacter pylori with gastric cancer, and human papillomaviruses with cervical cancer. Some 2.2 million cancers cases are attributed by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) to infectious agents.
	Agents can be described by their ability to infect (infectivity), be transmitted (infectiousness), and cause disease (pathogenicity) as well as their ability to cause serious disease (virulence). The infectivity of an infectious agent is the extent to which the agent can enter, survive, and multiply in a host and is measured by the ratio of the number of people who become infected to the total number exposed to the agent. Rhinoviruses that can cause the common cold are examples of infectious agents with high infectivity.
	The infectiousness, or transmissibility, of an infectious agent is the extent to which the agent can be transmitted from one host to another. It is measured by the basic reproduction number (known as R0) which is determined by the number of secondary infections in a susceptible population that result from a primary infection. Epidemic-prone diseases such as measles and pertussis caused by measles virus and Bordatella pertussis bacteria, respectively, are examples of diseases due to highly infectious agents with an R0 of 10 or greater.
	The pathogenicity of an infectious agent is the extent to which clinically manifest disease is produced in an infected population and is measured by the ratio of the number of people developing clinical illness to the total number infected. Examples of highly pathogenic infectious agents are the measles virus and the human (α) herpesvirus 3 (varicella-zoster) causing measles and chickenpox, respectively, in which most infected susceptible people will manifest disease.
	The virulence of an infectious agent is the extent to which severe disease is produced in a population with clinically manifest disease. It is the ratio of the number of people with severe and fatal disease to the total number of people with disease. An example of a highly virulent infectious agent is HIV whereby nearly all untreated people with AIDS will die.
	Characteristics of infectious agents that affect pathogenicity include their ability to invade tissues (invasiveness), produce toxins (intoxication), cause damaging hypersensitivity (allergic) reactions, undergo antigenic variation, and develop antibiotic resistance. An example of an infectious agent with high invasiveness is the Shigella organism which can invade the submucosal tissue of the intestine and cause clinically manifest shigellosis (bacillary dysentery). An example of an infectious agent that has a high degree of ability to produce toxins is the Clostridium botulinum organism which can elaborate toxins in inadequately prepared food and cause classical botulism. An example of an infectious agent that is highly allergenic is the Mycobacterium tuberculosis organism which can cause tuberculosis. An example of an infectious agent that has a high degree of antigenic variation is the type A influenza virus which frequently experiences minor antigenic changes—antigenic ‘drift’. Influenza A viruses, on an irregular basis, may also undergo a major antigenic change creating an entirely new subtype—antigenic ‘shift’. Antigenic shifts that have the characteristic of high transmissibility between people may result in an influenza pandemic when large numbers of individuals are exposed to the new subtype for which they have no prior immunity. An example of an infectious agent that can develop antibiotic resistance that challenges control efforts is Neisseria gonorrhoeae that has both chromosomally mediated and resistance transfer plasmid-mediated genetic factors for antibiotic resistance.
	The infective dose of an infectious agent is the number of organisms needed to cause an infection. The infective dose may vary depending upon the route of transmission and host susceptibility. An example of an infectious agent that needs only a very low infective dose (as few as ten organisms) is Escherichia coli O157:H7 which causes enterohaemorrhagic diarrhoea. An example of an infectious agent that needs a relatively higher infective dose is Vibrio cholerae which requires around 100 million bacteria to be ingested to cause cholera disease in a healthy adult.
	Control measures for infectious diseases directed at inactivating the agent are designed according to the type of agent and its reservoirs and sources. For example, an agent like Vibrio cholerae can be inactivated through adequate chlorination of the water supply. This is a chemical method for provision of safe water to control cholera. An agent like hepatitis B virus can be inactivated through adequate autoclaving of injection and surgical equipment. This is a sterilization method to control hepatitis B. Details of these and other methods of control directed at the agent are provided in the sections in this chapter on control measures applied to the agent and the environment.





Routes of transmission


	Control efforts are often designed to break the routes of transmission, the mechanisms by which infectious agents are spread from reservoirs or sources to human hosts. A reservoir of an infectious agent is any person, other living organism, or inanimate material in which the infectious agent normally lives and grows. The source of infection for a host is the person, other living organism, or inanimate material from which the infectious agent came. Horizontal transmission refers to transmission between individuals whereas vertical transmission refers to the specific situation of transmission between parent to offspring (e.g. transplacentally in utero, during passage through the birth canal, or through breast milk). The routes of transmission have been summarized in the Control of Communicable Diseases Manual (Heymann 2014) as follows:





Direct transmission


	Direct and essentially immediate transfer of infectious agents to a receptive portal of entry through which human or animal infection may take place. This may be by direct contact such as touching, biting, kissing or sexual intercourse, or through direct projections (droplet spread) of droplet spray onto the conjunctiva or onto the mucous membranes of the eye, nose, or mouth during sneezing, coughing, spitting, singing or talking (risk of transmission in this manner is usually limited to a distance of about 1 metre or less from the source of infection). Direct transmission may also occur through direct exposure of susceptible tissue to an agent in soil, through the bite of a rabid animal, or transplacentally (Heymann 2014).





Indirect transmission


Vehicle-borne


	Contaminated inanimate materials or objects (fomites) such as toys, handkerchiefs, soiled clothes, bedding, cooking, or eating utensils, surgical instruments or dressings; water, food, milk, and biological products including blood, serum, plasma, tissues or organs; or any substance serving as an intermediate means by which an infectious agent is transported and introduced into a susceptible host though a suitable portal of entry. The agent may or may not have multiplied or developed in or on the vehicle before being transmitted (Heymann 2014).





Vector-borne


	Mechanical: includes simple mechanical carriage by a crawling or flying insect through soiling of its feet or proboscis, or by passage of organisms through its gastrointestinal tract. This does not require multiplication or development of the organism.
	Biological: propagation (multiplication), cyclic development, or a combination of these (cyclopropagative) is required before the arthropod can transmit the infective form of the agent to humans. An incubation period (extrinsic) is required following infection before the arthropod becomes infective. The infectious agent may be passed vertically to succeeding generations (transovarian transmission); trans-stadial transmission indicates its passage from one stage of the life cycle to another, as from nymph to adult (for example, ticks infected with Rickettsia rickettsii can remain infected with this agent as they pass from nymph to adult stages). Transmission may be by injection of salivary gland fluid during biting, or by regurgitation or deposition on the skin of faeces or other material capable of penetrating through the bite wound or through an area of trauma, often created by scratching or rubbing. This transmission is by an infected non-vertebrate host and not simple mechanical carriage by a vector as a vehicle. An arthropod in either role is termed a vector (Heymann 2014).





Airborne transmission


	The dissemination of microbial aerosols to a suitable portal of entry, usually the respiratory tract. Microbial aerosols are suspensions of particles in the air consisting partially or wholly of microorganisms. They may remain suspended in the air for long periods of time, some retaining and others losing infectivity or virulence. Particles in the 1-to 5-micrometre range are easily drawn into the alveoli of the lungs and may be retained there. Not considered as airborne are droplets and other large particles that promptly settle out (see ‘Direct transmission’).
	Droplet nuclei: usually the small residues that result from evaporation of fluid from droplets emitted by an infected host (see earlier). They also may be created purposely by a variety of atomizing devices, or accidentally as in microbiology laboratories, abattoirs, rendering plants, or autopsy rooms. They usually remain suspended in the air for long periods.
	Dust: the small particles of widely varying size that may arise from soil (e.g. fungus spores), clothes, bedding, or contaminated floors (Heymann 2014).
	Control measures for infectious diseases directed at interrupting transmission are designed according to the type of transmission for the agent. Direct transmission of an agent like Neisseria gonorrhoeae, for example, can be reduced by using condoms as a barrier method of control of gonorrhoea. Vector-borne transmission of an agent like Plasmodium falciparum can be reduced by using a residual insecticide against Anopheles mosquitoes as a chemical vector control method for malaria. Airborne transmission of an agent like Mycobacterium tuberculosis from sputum-positive pulmonary tuberculosis patients in hospital can be reduced using special ventilation to create a negative pressure in the patient’s room as an environmental method of control of tuberculosis. It should be recognized that some infectious agents may have more than one route of transmission. Poliovirus, for example, can be spread via direct transmission through the faecal–oral route and pharyngeal spread, or indirect transmission through contaminated food or other materials. Details of these and other methods of control directed at interrupting transmission are provided in the section on ‘Tools for control of infectious diseases’ in this chapter.





Host


	The human host is the final link in the chain of infection. The infectious agent may enter the host through the following portals of entry.
	 	• Respiratory tract: infectious agents can be inhaled into the respiratory tract and will be deposited at different levels of the pulmonary tree according to the size of the aerosol, droplet nuclei, or dust particles. For example, Mycobacterium tuberculosis in airborne droplet nuclei, 1–5 μm in diameter, may be inhaled into the alveoli of the lungs of a vulnerable host and result in tuberculosis.
	• Intact skin: some infectious agents, such as Necator americanus which causes hookworm disease, can penetrate the intact skin.
	• Gastrointestinal tract: an infectious agent, such as Vibrio cholerae which causes cholera, may enter via the gastrointestinal tract. People who have a compromised gastric function, such as gastric achlorhydria, may be at increased risk of disease.
	• Mucous membranes: infectious agents, such as measles viruses, may be deposited on mucous membranes, including the conjunctiva of the eye, by droplet spread or by direct contact with infected people or contaminated objects.
	• Genitourinary system: some infectious agents, such as Escherichia coli which causes urinary tract infections, can enter the urinary tract via an ascending route from the urethra colonized with the organism. Structural abnormalities of the urinary tract and procedures such as urinary catheterization may predispose the host to disease. Sexually transmitted infectious agents, such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae which causes gonorrhoea, may enter the male or female genital orifices.
	• Placenta: certain infectious agents, such as rubella virus which causes congenital rubella syndrome, can cross the placenta resulting in transplacental transmission, a direct route of transmission from the mother to the foetus that is a form of vertical transmission.
	Infectious agents also enter the host though mechanisms that get past the body’s natural barriers, including wounds that break the integrity of the skin or mucous membranes; invasive procedures, parenteral injections, parenteral infusions, blood transfusions, or organ transplants that may introduce an agent into the body; or insect vectors that may inject agents through the skin.
	The most important host factors regarding developing clinically manifest disease and the severity of disease are immune status and age. Infants, young children, and the elderly are at generally higher risk from more severe disease due to immaturity or deterioration of their immune systems, respectively. Host co-infections or other health conditions that diminish the immune status, for example, HIV infection or malnutrition, respectively, are also risk factors.
	Many host defence mechanisms help prevent infection or disease. Non-specific host defence mechanisms include the intact skin (by providing a natural barrier), sinus and nasal cilia (by moving mucus and particles towards the nasal cavity), tears, saliva, and mucus (by preventing drying and containing lysozymes and other components with antimicrobial properties), and gastric acid (by the antimicrobial and antiparasitic properties of hydrochloric acid). Specific host defence mechanisms include naturally acquired immunity from previous infection, transplacentally acquired passive immunity in the newborn from the mother, artificially acquired active immunity from immunization, and artificially acquired passive immunity from immunoglobulins and antitoxins.
	Host responses to infection that prevent or reduce the severity of infectious disease include: (1) polymorphonuclear leucocytosis stimulated by some bacterial infections that increases the number of phagocytic white blood cells; (2) fever that may slow the multiplication of some infectious agents; (3) antibody production that may neutralize some infectious agents or their toxins; (4) interferon production that may block intracellular replication of viruses; and (5) cytotoxic immune cell responses that kill cells infected with viruses.
	The manifestation of infection in the host may vary from inapparent (subclinical) infection to severe disease that may even result in death. The interaction between an infectious agent, routes of transmission, and host factors determine the spectrum of signs and symptoms. Sometimes the host may become an asymptomatic carrier of the infectious agent and be a source of infection for others.
	Control measures for infectious diseases directed at the host are designed according to the immune status of the host and the likelihood of host exposure to certain infectious agents. For example, measles disease can be prevented by active immunization with measles vaccine to develop host immunity. Pneumonic plague can be prevented in those in close contact with patients with plague pneumonia by chemoprophylaxis using antibiotics such as tetracycline or sulphonamide. Details of these and other methods of control directed at the host are provided in the section on control measures applied to the host in this chapter.





Tools for control of infectious diseases


	The primary concern of infectious disease control in public health, whether in developing or industrialized countries, is the reduction, elimination, or even eradication of infectious disease. This is accomplished by directing control measures to the agent, the routes of transmission, or the host. Such control measures include: (1) identifying and then reducing or eliminating infectious agents at their sources and reservoirs, (2) breaking or interfering with the routes of transmission of infectious agents, and (3) identifying susceptible populations and then reducing or eliminating their susceptibility.
	The tools for control of infectious diseases are related to recognition and evaluation of the patterns of diseases and the results of interventions to control them. In infectious disease control, the most important tool for recognition and evaluation is surveillance of disease defined as:
	the process of systematic collection, orderly consolidation and analysis, and evaluation of pertinent data with prompt dissemination of the results to those who need to know them, and particularly those who are in a position to take action. It includes the systematic collection and evaluation of:
	 	1. Morbidity and mortality reports
	2. Special reports of field investigations of epidemics and of individual cases
	3. Isolation and identification of infectious agents by laboratories
	4. Data concerning the availability, use, and untoward effects of vaccines and toxoids, immune globulins, insecticides, and other substances used in control
	5. Information regarding immunity levels in segments of the population
	6. Other relevant epidemiologic data
	A report summarizing the aforementioned data should be prepared and distributed to all cooperating persons and others with a need to know the results of the surveillance activities. The procedure applies to all jurisdictional levels of public health from local to international (Heymann 2014).
	Surveillance, therefore, is ‘information for action’. More detailed information on surveillance or on field investigations is given in Chapter 5.19.
	Tools for control related to interventions include:
	 	• Control measures applied to the host: active immunization, passive immunization, chemoprophylaxis, surgical intervention, behavioural change, reverse isolation, barriers, and improving host resistance.
	• Control measures applied to vectors: chemical, environmental, and biological.
	• Control measures applied to infected humans: chemotherapy, surgical intervention, isolation, quarantine, restriction of activities, and behavioural change.
	• Control measures applied to animals: active immunization, isolation, quarantine, restriction or reduction, chemoprophylaxis, and chemotherapy.
	• Control measures applied to the environment: provision of safe water, proper disposal of faeces, food and milk sanitation, and design of facilities and equipment.
	• Control measures applied to infectious agents: cleaning, cooling, pasteurization, disinfection, and sterilization.
	Achieving maximum impact on control of a specific infectious disease may involve more than one of these interventions. For example, the control of hepatitis A infection can be achieved through interventions that may include: active immunization, passive immunization, food preparation, and handwashing behaviours, provision of safe water, food sanitation, and proper disposal of faeces.
	The tools for control can also be considered according to the level at which they are applied: individual, institutional, or community based. At the individual level, control measures, usually initiated by a clinician, are directed towards the specific infectious disease threats to the specific person. Examples include chemoprophylaxis to prevent wound infection, pre-exposure prophylactic immunization against rabies for a veterinarian, and use of diphtheria antitoxin in a patient with diphtheria.
	At the institutional level, control measures, usually initiated by the officials of the institution, are directed to a group of people who are in close contacts with each other, such as people in day-care centres, schools, military barracks, hospital wards, nursing homes, and correctional facilities. Examples include: (1) administering amantadine hydrochloride or rimantadine for chemoprophylaxis or chemotherapy of influenza A in a high-risk institutional population; (2) quarantining institutionalized young children during a measles outbreak; and (3) hepatitis B immunization of staff and clients of institutions for the developmentally disabled.
	At the community level, control measures, usually initiated by local, state, or national public health agencies, are directed to the community at large. Examples include childhood immunization programmes, provision of safe water, regulation of food supplies, and recall of contaminated food products.
	It should be noted that some control measures, such as immunization, may take place at all levels while others, such as the provision of safe water to a community, are more specifically applied at a particular level.
	The tools for the control of infectious diseases and their relationship to the chain of infection are the focus of the remainder of this chapter.





Control measures applied to the host


	Control measures applied to the host range from relatively easily administered immunization to behavioural changes that may be extremely difficult for an individual to accept and practise. This section details the types of control measures applied to susceptible hosts and gives examples of their application in the control of selected infectious diseases.





Active immunization


	One of the most efficient control measures applied to a host is one that renders the host immune from infectious disease by an infectious agent. Active immunization is a cornerstone of public health measures for the control of many infectious diseases and is considered one of the most cost-effective methods of individual, institutional, and community protection for vaccine-preventable infectious diseases. The most powerful example of the potential impact of active immunization against an infectious disease is that of smallpox vaccination. Mobilization of political will on a worldwide basis, coupled with full application of the strategies of active surveillance and containment immunization against smallpox, ultimately resulted in the complete global eradication of the disease and cessation of transmission of the infectious agent, variola virus.
	Active immunization is usually considered synonymous with the term vaccination, and is the process of administration of an antigen that can induce a specific immune response that protects a susceptible host from an infectious disease. Some draw a distinction between the two terms. Narrowly defined, vaccination is the process of administration of an antigen and immunization is the development of a specific immune response. Administering an antigen without evoking an immune response is possible, since no vaccine is 100% effective. Conversely, someone can become immunized even if they were not administered an antigen. For example, the live, attenuated oral polio vaccine viruses can be transmitted from the recipient to other close contacts.
	Active immunization can be accomplished through different types of antigens, including the following:
	 	• Inactivated toxins: diphtheria toxoid is an example of a formaldehyde-inactivated preparation of diphtheria toxin that protects against clinically manifest disease, although the immunized person may still become infected with toxin-producing strains of Corynebacterium diphtheria. Tetanus toxoid and Clostridium perfringens toxoid (pig bel vaccine) are other examples of inactivated toxin preparations.
	• Inactivated complex antigens: whole-cell pertussis vaccine is an example of a heat or chemically treated preparation of killed whole pertussis bacteria that protects against clinically manifest disease, although the immunized person may still become infected with Bordetella pertussis. Inactivated polio vaccine and inactivated influenza vaccine are other examples of inactivated vaccines.
	• Purified antigens: acellular pertussis vaccine is an example of a vaccine composed of isolated and purified immunogenic pertussis antigens. Other vaccines with purified components include polyvalent capsular polysaccharide pneumococcal, polysaccharide meningococcal, protein-polysaccharide conjugate Haemophilus influenzae type b, and plasma-derived hepatitis B vaccines.
	• Recombinant antigens: hepatitis B recombinant vaccine is an example of a vaccine composed of hepatitis B surface antigen subunits made through recombinant DNA technology. Human papillomavirus vaccine is another example of a DNA recombinant vaccine.
	• Live, attenuated vaccines: measles vaccine is an example of a vaccine containing live infectious agents that are of reduced virulence, but induce protective antibodies against measles viruses. Other live, attenuated vaccines include oral polio, mumps, rubella, yellow fever, and bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG) vaccines.
	• Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines: some of the COVID-19 vaccines are examples of a new vaccine technology that utilizes mRNA to deliver one or more of the SARS-CoV-2 genes into the body’s cells that then cause those cells to make spike proteins that are subsequently released from the cell and provoke an immune response.
	Protective antibody responses usually take 7–21 days to develop. Although most vaccines must be given before exposure to be effective, some vaccines may protect even if administered after exposure to an infectious agent. For example, measles vaccine may provide protection against measles disease if given within 72 hours of exposure. This occurs since the percutaneous route of administration of the antigen evokes an immune response faster than the measles virus results in disease through the respiratory route of natural exposure.
	Duration of protection varies from only months, such as with killed whole-cell cholera vaccine, to years or even life with some live attenuated vaccines, such as measles vaccine. Some inactivated toxoids and vaccines, such as tetanus toxoid, may require a priming series of doses to be optimally effective and additional booster doses to maintain protective antibodies. Many new technologies are being explored that may increase the number and efficacy of vaccines available against infectious disease, including immune stimulating complexes, live viral or bacterial vector vaccines, and timed-release vaccines.
	It should be recognized that vaccines vary in their efficacy and no vaccine is 100% effective. Vaccine efficacies vary with type of vaccine, manufacturing techniques, storage, and handling conditions, skill of administration, age of vaccination, and other host factors. Vaccines for routine use are safe. However, no vaccine is 100% safe. Potential vaccinees, or their parents or guardians, should be screened for contraindications and be informed of potential side effects.
	Immunization schedules for the routine control of infectious diseases preventable by immunization vary between countries and are usually based on expert advice to governments and physicians.
