Sterilization of equipment for surgery and wound dressings; parenteral administration of drugs, vaccines, or nutrients; catheterization; and dental work are all important means of controlling infectious diseases by killing infectious agents. Sterilization can be accomplished through use of fire, pressurized steam (such as in an autoclave), heated air, certain gases (such as ethylene oxide), ultraviolet light, ionizing radiation, liquid chemicals, and filtration. The method of sterilization chosen depends on the type of equipment to be sterilized.
	The use of sterilized disposable equipment, such as disposable needles, syringes, and catheters, has the potential to reduce the risk of transmission of infectious agents. However, it must be assured that such equipment is disposed of properly and is not reused. For example, disposable syringes cannot be properly resterilized because the plastic from which they are made cannot withstand the heat necessary for sterilization. Technologies, such as the single-use disposable needle and syringe developed for immunization programmes, help assure such disposable equipment is not reused.





Control and prevention programmes


	The preceding sections have considered the issues and given examples of control measures for infectious diseases at individual, institutional, and community levels and the tools for control directed at the host, routes of transmission, and the agent. Control and prevention programmes using these tools must be developed according to a number of factors including: (1) the risk of disease; (2) the magnitude of disease burden (as measured by mortality, degree of disability, morbidity, and economic costs); (3) the feasibility of control strategies; (4) the cost of control measures; (5) the effectiveness of such measures (on current levels of disease and impact on future cases or outbreaks); (6) the adverse effects or complications of the control measures; and (7) the availability of resources. Public health planning for the control of infectious diseases must consider these issues to design optimal, evidence-based control and prevention programmes.
	The tools of disease surveillance for recognition and evaluation of the patterns of disease can provide information on the risk and magnitude of disease burden to individuals, people in institutions, subgroups of populations, and the community at large. Establishment and maintenance of the infrastructure for surveillance, including a system for the reporting of notifiable infectious diseases and unusual events, must be a high priority.
	Feasibility of possible control and prevention strategies must be assessed through operational research, pilot projects, or from field experience. The fact that a particular measure can help control a disease does not mean it can be applied on a sufficient scale to have the desired impact. The cost of control activities (in both human and material resources) can be assessed through costing studies that can also provide the data needed to conduct more rigorous cost–benefit and cost-effectiveness analyses. A costly measure, even if it provides a high degree of control for an infectious disease, may not be affordable to the society or reasonable to apply in the light of other less expensive alternative strategies. For example, use of sterile, disposable products may be costlier than reusable, sterilizable products. Effectiveness of control measures may be assessed through epidemiological studies to find out their impact on reduction in the incidence or prevalence of disease.
	The availability of resources for prevention and control programmes forces public health planners to set priorities by taking into account all these factors and then designing programmes that have maximum impact within available resources. Planners have a responsibility to mobilize additional necessary resources by raising public awareness and generating political will. Effective communication of disease burden and the results achievable through well-managed and effective control programmes can be a powerful tool for advocacy. Ideally, communities or their representatives should actively participate in the planning, execution, and evaluation of public health programmes.
	Prevention effectiveness is ‘the measure of the impact on health (including effectiveness, safety and cost) of prevention policies, programmes, and practices. The assessment of prevention effectiveness is the ongoing process of applying evaluation tools to prevention practices’ (CDC 1995). Recognizing that systems for assessing the effectiveness of prevention strategies (including prevention strategies for infectious diseases) are weak or non-existent in both developing and industrialized countries alike, the CDC has suggested the following objectives for prevention effectiveness activities: ‘evaluate the impact of prevention, use results of evaluation research to establish programme priorities, and establish or apply standardized methods to compare the benefits and effectiveness of alternative prevention strategies’ (CDC 1995).
	The current situation of international migration of many people worldwide presents an additional complexity to the design of programmes for the control of infectious diseases. Pertinent issues include refugee camps, legal status of migrants in recipient countries, and temporary return migration. Public health officials must consider the most effective mix of combined control measures applied to the host, agent, and routes of transmission when designing suitable control and prevention programmes (Gellert 1993). Particularly in terms of humanitarian emergencies, whether due to human violence or natural disaster, crowding can make diseases such as measles, acute respiratory infections (ARI)s and meningitis of particular concern for groups of displaced persons (Heymann 2014). A recent statement by the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene’s Executive Committee calls for US migration policy to be evidence-based, compassionate, and maintain international human rights law. They further argue that investment in the health needs of the world’s vulnerable populations is beneficial not only to these affected populations, but to the United States as well, as infectious diseases are a global issue (Rosenthal et al. 2017).
	International commerce and transportation are important areas of concern for public health infectious disease control programmes, especially as the speed of travel has increased. The tools of control include such measures as:
	 	• Spraying insecticides effective against mosquito vectors of malaria in aircraft before departure, in transit, or on arrival.
	• Rat-proofing or periodic fumigation to control rats on ships, docks, and warehouses to prevent plague.
	Specific international control measures relating to aircraft, ships, and land transportation for infectious diseases are detailed in the International Health Regulations (2005) (WHO 2005).
	The challenge facing infectious disease control programmes is to design an optimal set of interventions at local, institutional, community, national, and international levels supported and accepted by the political leadership and the people to whom these measures are applied.





Eradication


	A unique end point in the control of infectious diseases is that of eradication. Eradication is the cessation of all transmission of an infectious agent by extermination of that agent. To date, only one human infectious disease, smallpox, and one animal infectious disease, rinderpest, have been eradicated. The WHO World Health Assembly in May 1980 confirmed its global eradication some 3 years after the last naturally acquired case of smallpox in October 1977 (Fenner et al. 1988). The magnitude of this accomplishment is appreciated when one realizes that, in the early 1950s, it was estimated that 50 million cases of smallpox still occurred each year in the world, some 150 years after Edward Jenner had performed the first vaccination and wrote: ‘it now becomes too manifest to admit of controversy, that the annihilation of the Small Pox, the most dreadful scourge of the human species, must be the final result of this practice’ (Fenner et al. 1988). Rinderpest (known as cattle plague or steppe murrain) was an infectious viral disease of cattle and some other even-toed ungulates, that was associated with a high mortality rate. In 2011, after widespread vaccination campaigns, the United Nations declared the disease eradicated.
	The goal of global eradication has been set by the World Health Assembly for two other infectious diseases, poliomyelitis caused by wild poliovirus and dracunculiasis (Guinea worm infection), the latter caused by the infectious agent Dracunculus medinensis. A high level of sustained political will, aggressively applied disease surveillance, and effective control measures are the required elements to achieve eradication of the infectious agents for these diseases.
	Impressive progress has been made towards the global eradication of poliomyelitis since the 1988 World Health Assembly set the goal for its eradication. Polio cases have decreased by over 99% since that date, from some 350,000 cases in over 125 countries to only 22 reported cases in 2017. In 2018, only parts of three countries in the world (Nigeria, Pakistan, and Afghanistan) remain endemic for the disease (WHO 2018). Poliomyelitis control measures that will lead to eradication include the following:
	 	• Achieving and maintaining high levels of routine coverage of infants with at least three doses of oral polio vaccine.
	• Mass application of oral polio vaccine in countries where poliomyelitis is endemic through national immunization days, usually by providing oral polio vaccine to every child less than 5 years of age twice each year, separated by 4–6 weeks, and conducted during the low season of poliovirus transmission.
	• ‘Mopping-up’ operations after the use of national immunization days has reduced transmission of disease to defined focal geographic areas, usually by providing oral polio vaccine house-to-house to all children less than 5 years of age on two occasions separated by 4–6 weeks.
	• Aggressive action-oriented surveillance for acute flaccid paralysis. Such surveillance includes: (1) case investigation, (2) a laboratory network for isolation and characterization of polioviruses in suspect cases of poliomyelitis and people in close contact with them, and (3) limited outbreak response immunization providing one house-to-house round of oral polio vaccine to children less than 5 years of age living in the same village or neighbourhood of the patient.
	Significant strides in the eradication of dracunculiasis have also been made. Over the last three decades the total number of dracunculiasis cases has declined by more than 99%. In 2017, only 30 cases were reported from just two countries, Chad and Ethiopia (WHO 2018a). Dracunculiasis control measures that are leading to its ultimate eradication include the following:
	 	• Establishing a national programme office, conducting baseline surveys, and preparing and refining a national plan of action.
	• Educating the population in endemic areas that the source of Guinea worm comes from their drinking water.
	• Ensuring that people with blisters or emerging worms do not enter sources of drinking water through behaviour changes and by converting step-wells into draw-wells.
	• Promoting the boiling or filtering of water through a fine mesh cloth to remove copepods. Treating drinking water with chlorine or iodine will also kill the copepods and infective larvae.
	• Providing non-infected water through construction of wells or rainwater catchments.
	• In selected endemic villages, controlling copepod populations with temephos (Abate®) insecticide placed in reservoirs, tanks, ponds, and step-wells.
	• Implementing an intensified surveillance and aggressive case-containment strategy as programmes get close to achieving eradication.
	The eradication of a disease requires a unique set of conditions, including the following: (1) a defined, accessible reservoir of the infectious agent; (2) affordable and effective control measures that can interrupt the chain of infection directed at the host, agent, or route of transmission; and (3) a surveillance mechanism adequate to monitor and ultimately certify the disappearance of the infectious agent.
	It is likely that measles may be targeted for global eradication in the future. Some countries and geographic regions have already targeted measles for elimination—a term sometimes used to describe the eradication of a disease from a large geographic area. Other diseases that may potentially be targeted for eradication in the future include: mumps, rubella, hepatitis B, leprosy, and diphtheria.





Emerging infectious diseases


	New, emerging, and reemerging infectious diseases have become a focus for the attention of public health prevention and control programmes in both industrialized and developing countries. Such infectious diseases have thwarted any expectation that infectious diseases will soon be eliminated as public health problems and resulted in a widening spectrum of diseases, many of which were once thought to be almost conquered. Krause has reflected on this as follows:
	 	Bacteria reproduce every 30 minutes. For them, a millennium is compressed into a fortnight. They are fleet afoot, and the pace of our research must keep up with them, or they will overtake us. (Krause 1998)
	Many factors contribute to the emergence of new or reemergence of those previously known (Lederberg et al. 1992; CDC 1994; Murphy 1994), including the following:
	 	• Human demographic change by which people begin to live in previously uninhabited remote areas of the world and are exposed to new environmental sources of infectious agents, insects, and animals.
	• Breakdowns of sanitary and other public health measures in overcrowded cities and in situations of civil unrest and war.
	• Economic development and changes in the use of land, including deforestation, reforestation, and urbanization.
	• Climate change, including global warming, which may extend the favourable habitats for vectors such as mosquitoes.
	• Other human behaviours, such as increased use of child-care facilities, sexual and drug use behaviours, and patterns of outdoor recreation.
	• International travel and commerce that quickly transport people and goods vast distances.
	• Changes in food processing and handling, including foods prepared from many different individual animals and transported great distances.
	• Evolution of pathogenic infectious agents by which they may infect new hosts, produce toxins, or adapt by responding to changes in the host immunity.
	• Development of resistance of infectious agents such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae to chemoprophylactic or chemotherapeutic medicines.
	• Resistance of the vectors of vector-borne infectious diseases to pesticides.
	• Immunosuppression of people due to medical treatments or new diseases that result in infectious diseases caused by agents not usually pathogenic in healthy hosts.
	• Deterioration in surveillance systems for infectious diseases, including laboratory support, to detect new or emerging disease problems at an early stage.
	Examples of emerging infectious disease threats include the following:
	 	• Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) a severe acute viral respiratory illness caused by the the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in December 2019 in Wuhan, China. It clearly demonstrates the ability for a previously unknown virus with an animal origin (bat) to cross species and create a pandemic killing millions of susceptible people.
	• Toxic shock syndrome, due to the infectious toxin-producing strains of Staphylococcus aureus, illustrates how a new technology yielding a new product, super-absorbent tampons, can create the circumstances favouring the emergence of a new infectious disease threat.
	• Lyme disease, due to the infectious spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, illustrates how changes in the ecology, including reforestation, increasing deer populations, and suburban migration of the population, can result in the emergence of a new microbial threat that has now become one of the most prevalent vector-borne disease in the United States.
	• Shigellosis, giardiasis, and hepatitis A are examples of emerging diseases that have become threats to staff and children in child-care centres as the use of such centres has increased due to changes in the work patterns of societies.
	• Opportunistic infections, such as Pneumocystis pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly carinii), chronic cryptosporidiosis caused by Cryptosporidium species, and disseminated cytomegalovirus infections, illustrate emerging disease threats to the increasing number of people who are immunosuppressed because of cancer chemotherapy, organ transplantation, or HIV infection.
	• Foodborne infections such as diarrhoea caused by the enterohaemorrhagic strain O157:H7 of Escherichia coli and water-borne infections such as gastrointestinal disease due to Cryptosporidium species are examples of emerging disease threats that have arisen due to such factors as changes in diet, food processing, globalization of the food supply, and contamination of municipal water supplies.
	• Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome first detected in the United States in 1993 and caused by a previously unrecognized hantavirus illustrates how exposure to certain kinds of infected rodents can result in an emerging infectious disease.
	• Nipah virus disease first detected in Malaysia in 1999 and caused by a previously unrecognized Hendra-like virus demonstrates how close contact with fruit bats and pigs can result in an emerging infectious disease.
	• Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), a viral respiratory illness caused by the SARS-associated coronavirus (SARS-CoV) that was first reported in Asia in February 2003 and spread to more than 20 countries in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia affecting over 8,000 people and killing over 700 before the SARS global outbreak was contained in 2004, shows the need for continued vigilance in surveillance and outbreak response capacity (WHO 2003).
	• The emergence of the novel influenza A virus in birds, highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1), that has occasionally infected humans is an example of an antigenic shift in an influenza virus that, should it develop into a form easily transmissible from human to human, could potentially lead to a pandemic.
	• Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), a viral respiratory disease caused by a novel coronavirus (MERS-CoV) was first identified in Saudi Arabia in 2012. There have been 1,888 laboratory-confirmed cases and 670 deaths since 2012. It is an example of a virus that had infected an animal reservoir (camel) for over 20 years before being noted in humans (Cotton et al. 2014). The majority of cases (>85%) and deaths have been reported in the Arabian Peninsula. The virus was exported and resulted in the largest outbreak outside the region of origin, in South Korea, in 2015.
	• Ebola virus disease (EVD), a viral haemorrhagic fever that was first discovered in 1976 in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Sudan, was responsible for an outbreak of unprecedented magnitude it was discovered for the first time in West Africa in 2014. It is an example of a major outbreak of a disease that had been previously confined to more geographically isolated areas. There have been over 11,000 fatalities and the outbreak led to individual cases in a number of other countries due to international travel (CDC 2016a).
	• Zika virus, a vector-borne disease, was first isolated in Uganda in 1947 (Dick et al. 1952), but became a global concern with the outbreak of Zika virus in the Americas beginning in 2015. Zika virus can be transmitted via vector (Aëdes mosquitoes), vertical transmission from mother to foetus, via sexual contact or possibly blood transfusion. It is an example of an infectious disease being introduced into large susceptible populations with dramatic numbers of people affected. While cases are typically mild or asymptomatic, the disease can result in birth defects such as microcephaly (CDC 2016b).
	Antimicrobial drug resistance as a major factor in the emergence and reemergence of infectious diseases deserves special attention. Although significant reductions in infectious disease mortality have occurred since the introduction of antimicrobials for general use in the 1940s, antimicrobial drug resistance has emerged because of their widespread use in humans.
	Drugs that once seemed invincible are losing their effectiveness for a wide range of community-acquired infections, including tuberculosis, gonorrhoea, pneumococcal infections (a leading cause of otitis media, pneumonia, and meningitis), and for hospital-acquired enterococcal and staphylococcal infections. Resistance to antiviral (e.g. amantadine-resistant influenza virus and aciclovir-resistant herpes simplex), antifungal (e.g. azole-resistant Candida species), and antiprotozoal (e.g. metronidazole-resistant Trichomonas vaginalis) drugs is also emerging. Drug-resistant malaria has spread to nearly all areas of the world where malaria occurs. Concern has also arisen over strains of HIV resistant to antiviral drugs. Increased microbial resistance has resulted in prolonged hospitalizations and higher death rates from infections; has required much more expensive, and often more toxic, drugs or drug combinations (even for common infections); and has resulted in higher healthcare costs (CDC 1994).
	Antimicrobial drug resistance has also emerged because of the use of antimicrobials in domesticated animals. For example, the use of fluoroquinolones in poultry has created a reservoir of quinolone-resistant Campylobacter jejuni that has now been isolated in humans. The Food and Drug Administration’s Veterinary Feed Directive (VFD) (Final Rule effective 1 October 2015) was put into place to regulate drugs used in animal feeds, and stipulates that VFD drugs must be used only under supervision of a licensed veterinarian (FDA 2015).
	An aggressive public health response to these new, emerging, and reemerging infectious disease threats must be made to characterize them better and to mount an effective response for their control. For example, the 1999 outbreak of West Nile fever in New York City and surrounding areas that, within a 4-year period, spread throughout the United States demonstrates how a viral encephalitis, initially classified as Saint Louis encephalitis and later confirmed to be due to West Nile virus, can reach far beyond its normal setting.
	The WHO has outlined the following high-priority areas (WHO 1995):
	 	• Strengthen global surveillance of infectious diseases.
	• Establish national and international infrastructures to recognize, report, and respond to new disease threats.
	• Further develop applied research on diagnosis, epidemiology, and control of emerging infectious diseases.
	• Strengthen the international capacity for infectious disease prevention and control.
	(Emerging infectious diseases are addressed in detail in Chapter 8.17.)





Bioterrorism: the deliberate use of biological agents to cause harm


	Another unfortunate source of an infectious disease threat is the spectre of biological warfare or bioterrorism, especially in an age where terrorist acts are frequent events (Christopher et al. 1997). The 2002 World Health Assembly resolution urges member states ‘to treat any deliberate use, including local, of biological and chemical agents and radionuclear attack to cause harm also as a global public health threat, and to respond to such a threat in other countries by sharing expertise, supplies and resources in order rapidly to contain the event and mitigate its effects’ (WHO 2002).
	The WHO recommends the following (WHO 2004):
	 	• Public health authorities, in close cooperation with other government bodies, should draw up contingency plans for dealing with a deliberate release of biological or chemical agents intended to harm civilian populations. These plans should be consistent or integral with existing plans for outbreaks of disease, natural disasters, large-scale industrial or transportation accidents, and terrorist incidents.
	• Preparedness for deliberate releases of biological or chemical agents should be based on standard risk-analysis principles, starting with risk and threat assessment to determine the relative priority that should be accorded to such releases in comparison with other dangers to public health in the country concerned. Considerations for deliberate releases should be incorporated into existing public health infrastructures, rather than developing separate infrastructures.
	• Preparedness for deliberate releases of biological or chemical agents can be markedly increased in most countries by strengthening the public health infrastructure, and particularly public health surveillance and response, and measures should be taken to this end.
	• Managing the consequences of a deliberate release of biological or chemical agents may demand more resources than are available, and international assistance would then be essential.
	Many countries are developing rapid response capability to deal with such contingencies, especially in the light of the 2001 bioterrorist attack using anthrax in the United States.





Conclusion


	Only through worldwide concerted action will the effort to control infectious disease be effective. We are now in an era where, as Nobel Laureate Dr Joshua Lederberg has stated, ‘The microbe that felled one child in a distant continent yesterday can reach yours today and seed a global pandemic tomorrow’ (quoted in CDC 1994). As Hans Zinsser stated over 60 years ago:
	Infectious disease is one of the few genuine adventures left in the world. The dragons are all dead and the lance grows rusty in the chimney corner… About the only sporting proposition that remains unimpaired by the relentless domestication of a once free-living human species is the war against those ferocious little fellow creatures, which lurk in the dark corners and stalk us in the bodies of rats, mice, and all kinds of domestic animals; which fly and crawl with the insects, and waylay us in our food and drink and even in our love (Hans Zinsser 1934, quoted in Murphy 1994).

11.5


Medical screening


	Theories, methods, and effectiveness
	Tang Jin-ling and Li Li-ming





Introduction


	Since the middle of last century, cancer, and cardiovascular disease have overtaken infectious disease as the top killers of human life. Cardiovascular disease can be successfully prevented through modification of risk factors, whereas against cancer we rely largely on early detection and early treatment. On one hand, checks for risk factors of cardiovascular disease has become almost a clinical routine with a hope to prevent severe complications. On the other hand, screening for cancer has rapidly become a widespread medical practice in the past decades. Genetic testing, one of the most exciting scientific breakthroughs in biomedical sciences in the twentieth century, further raised the enthusiasm for screening. Screening in various different disguises has become an important part of modern public health and clinical medicine.
	Broadly speaking, screening exists in forms from firmly established and well-planned population screening programmes to ubiquitous use of diagnostic methods for early diagnosis to experiments with new diagnostic methods by individual clinicians in search of silent diseases. Well-organized screening programmes can indeed do more good than harm but the obsessive search of silent diseases may have often caused overdiagnosis and overtreatment. In this chapter, we will discuss the theories, methods, effects, and pitfalls of health screening in both the narrow and broad concepts with an aim to promote appropriate use of disease screening and efficient use of healthcare resources. Cancer will be used most of time as examples to illustrate when necessary.





What is medical screening?


	After decades of tremendous efforts fighting against chronic diseases, we have yet to find preventive and therapeutic methods that are as powerful as hygiene, antibiotics, and vaccines used for combating infectious diseases.
	Chronic diseases differ from infectious diseases in an important way that it takes years or even decades to become severe enough and cause symptoms, suffering, disabilities, or death. Moreover, rapid advances in biomedical technology, notably in testing and imaging, have made it possible to detect many chronic diseases when they are still asymptomatic. New diagnostic innovations are also applied to identify risk factors of chronic disease for primary prevention. It is further assumed that intervention on risk factors can prevent the occurrence of disease and treatment of silent disease can retard or stop disease progression, improve prognosis, and ultimately reduce suffering and mortality. Early detection and early intervention have formed the foundation for combating chronic disease in modern medicine. In public health, this strategy is known as medical screening, health screening or population screening (Wilson and Jungner 1968; Morrison 1992; NSC 1998; Raffle and Gray 2007).
	Screening is defined as the systematic application of a simple test or inquiry to well persons to detect those having a specific preclinical disorder or increased risk of disease for the purpose of early treatment or prevention with an ultimate aim of improving the health of the screened population. In brief, screening is early detection and early intervention aimed to improve health. Figure 11.5.1 uses Pap smears for screening cervical cancer to show the participants flow and main components of a screening programme.
	Fig. 11.5.1 Participants flow and components of a screening programme: Pap smear for screening cervical cancer.
	Public health tends to emphasize that screening be a systematic approach. Screening is not simply the application of a new test; it is a carefully planned, systematically organized, and regularly repeated, collective effort that combines early detection and early treatment with an ultimate goal of improving those who are screened. ‘Systematic’ also means that the decisions on issues such as whether or not to screen, who to screen, and how to screen, how to further confirm diagnosis, and how to treat should be carefully determined based on scientific evidence before a screening programme is implemented so as to make sure that it is desired by and will benefit the population to be screened.
	The ‘test’ is referred to a wide range of medical procedures that can be performed in order to detect a risk factor and a silent disease, such as laboratory tests and imaging techniques and endoscopic examinations. The ‘inquiry’ is referred to an interview or questionnaire used to obtain information about a person’s occupational history, family history, disease history, lifestyle, and other information that can be used to estimate current or future risk of disease. Information from tests and inquiries can be used independently or more often in combination to predict the risk of disease, for example, by using scores or multiple regression models such as the Framingham cardiovascular risk equation.
	Screening is offered to ‘well persons’ rather than patients. Well persons are not those who are totally free of any disorder. They may have disorders other than the one to be screened for and even the screened disorder but have not sought medical attention on account of symptoms of that disorder. Different from clinical practice, those who are screened are not those who have brought themselves to doctors for suspecting an illness but are those invited by healthcare professionals for checks and inquiries. This is a considerable deviation from the long-practised medical paradigm in which patients only see the doctor when they are sick and thus creates new ethical concerns.
	For cancer, screening is mostly targeted at a disease at its preclinical stage. The goal is to prevent more severe complications or death from the disease. Pap smears, mammograms, and faecal occult bleed tests are examples in case. Screening can also be targeted at risk factors for prevention of the first occurrence of disease. For example, smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and elevated blood glucose are often checked with a hope to prevent myocardial infarction and stroke through lifestyle and prophylactic interventions on these risk factors.
	Although we normally talk about screening for a single disease, a screening programme can be multiphasic and targeted at more than one disease or all major risk factors of a disease at the same time. In this sense, periodical health checks can also be viewed as a kind of screening although with more complexities. Health checks can identify overt diseases. But health checks for silent diseases and risk factors should be assessed with similar scientific rigour and managed with similar standards as we do for screening.
	Unlike drugs, a screening programme is a complex intervention with many components. Its potential benefits and harms are determined by multiple factors including the test, further diagnostic investigations, follow-up interventions, and the way they are organized. Screening will fail if any of the major components fail.
	Last but not least, screening must be able to achieve the ultimate goal of improving the health of the screened population. Against this goal, many screening programmes and similar efforts may not be justified.





Some historical accounts


	The aforementioned section depicts the picture of screening in the eyes of public health workers. However, screening can be a different concept to others including clinicians and the public. In fact, screening did not appear in this exact modern clothe at its onset. Screening is an evolving concept and new ideas are still being proposed and adopted.





Pre-modern screening before 1960


	The idea of screening is not new. As early in 1861, Dr Horace Dobell, an eminent British physician recommended that physicians should perform periodic checks on everyone, irrespective of whether they were seeking medical help. In 1990, Dr George Gould, an American physician, argued that ranchers check their cattle, merchants check their stock, accountants check their books, generals check their armies, governments check their budgets, but why physicians do not regularly check the healthy people——and they should. However, their recommendation for regular and non-specific medical examinations of healthy people did not take firm hold immediately.
	Historically, it is generally believed that the concept of modern screening originated in early last century from the practice of health checks organized by the army for selecting out those who were unsuited to the needs of the military machine, by insurance companies as a means of selecting premiums, and by large cooperations in selecting suitable employees (Raffle and Gray 2007). Early screening programmes also included testing for infectious disease, for example, tuberculosis, which was typically organized by the government. Most early screening activities, however, did not meet the stringent criteria for modern screening programmes. These criteria for screening are the results of scientific evaluation of health checks and early screening programmes and of better understanding of the natural history of chronic diseases in the past few decades.
	In the 1950s, screening was already firmly in place in the United States, whereas it was just beginning in Britain. For example, in 1957, the Commission on Chronic Illness in the United States recommended a wide range of screening, including diabetes, glaucoma, and cancer of the mouth, skin, breast, cervix, and rectum. However, scientific evidence for the effectiveness of screening was lacking and doubts about screening started to mount.





Modern screening era since 1960


	In particular, in 1968, two reports were published, one is by the Nuffield Provincial Hospital Trust and the other by the World Health Organization. Both questioned some of the general beliefs of screening. The Nuffield Trust evaluated 10 existing screening or proposed screening activities in the United Kingdom and concluded most of them were ineffective or even harmful. Wilson and Jungner’s report for the World Health Organization discussed various aspects of screening and proposed, importantly, 10 criteria a screening programme should meet. They further argued that even if these principles were all met, research was still needed to provide evidence on the benefit, harm, and affordability of a screening programme.
	Two randomized controlled trials were established to evaluate the effectiveness of screening, one at Kaiser Permanente in 1964 and the other in South-East London in 1967. Both trials failed to find a positive result on multiple outcomes including death that would support multiphasic screening. Decades later, these early reports and evaluation trials on screening have eventually reoriented the practice of screening from multiphasic health checks to specific disease screening: general health checks are not screening. Today, we have cumulated a great amount of evidence about modern screening and found often it was not effective or marginally effective. But they always cost and have arms.





Screening in the twenty-first century


	In the past, screening was decided by experts, delivered as a utilitarian programme, and complied with by dutiful and grateful patients. But things have changed in the twenty-first century. There are pressures for change in screening. Transition away from paternal paradigm of medical care, heightened expectations from patients, right of patients for information, increasing new technologies among other factors have been changing the concepts, principles, and practice of screening.
	The concept of screening that was firmly established in the late last century has never been universally accepted without challenges and variations. In fact, the early practice of screening has never truly disappeared; they continue to exist in different covers. In addition, new ideas of detecting silent diseases and checks for risk factors are being developed and adopted by millions of individual healthcare workers without demonstrated evidence on their benefits and harms. In the name of early diagnosis of disease, many variations of screening truly exist, from experimental use by individual clinicians, to improvised or opportunistic testing in clinics and hospitals, to popular health checks, and to well-organized efficacy-proven screening programmes for specific diseases.
	The rapid rise of general health checks with an increasingly large number of items included in it represents a worrying return to the early practice of screening before the 1960s. These new or so-called new ideas and atypical screening activities must also be brought into discussion as they constitute much of the inappropriate or even bad practice of screening and their effectiveness is uncertain. We should know what bad screening activities are like so we can prevent them from being introduced. It is particularly difficult to stop an ineffective intervention once they are already in practice. For example, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) was first introduced in the late 1980s in Western countries and is now still widely used although it has been proven ineffective (Hoffman 2011).





When would screening be potentially effective?


	The concept of identifying future risks or the potential of disease of individuals is remarkably attractive and has permeated to nearly all aspects of medicine. The ever-increasing technological and biological wizardry of medicine raises expectations and further tempts clinicians and the public. However, so few medical interventions are like screening that is so appealing at the first glance but disappointing at the end. In addition, screening is so complex and difficult to be provided with high standard and quality so that they will eventually realize the benefits promised. As a result, only a few screening programmes can truly do more good than harm and are thus worthwhile (only programmes that can do more good than harm at a reasonable cost should be recommended). When implemented, they should be managed in such a way as to achieve a level of quality which can ensure that the balance of good and harm demonstrated in research is reproduced in the ordinary service setting.
	What would make a screening programme potential beneficial? The potential benefits and harms of a screening programme are mostly determined by the following three factors: the disease, the screening test(s), and the treatment(s). We will explain why in the following sections.





The disease


	About the disease, three important aspects are relevant and should be assessed: (1) the disease to be screened for must have a long detectable preclinical phase; (2) the severity of the disease must be considered as a large health burden to the population in terms of suffering, disability, destitution and/or death; and (3) the preclinical phase of the disease must be relatively prevalent.
	The preclinical or asymptomatic phase of a disease is the time period from the onset of the disease to the time symptoms appear and a diagnosis is made routinely by a doctor (Fig. 11.5.2). A long preclinical phase is the prerequisite for the disease to be detected and treated early enough so that treatments would be more effective. For example, most infectious and acute diseases that have a very short asymptomatic phase are not suitable for screening, while most cancers may have a latent period of many years are often a suitable target for screening.
	Fig. 11.5.2 Screening test and lead time in a hypothetical case of colon cancer.
	Most cancers may have a long preclinical phase but the actual length of that period is normally unknown. First, it is almost impossible to know when a cancer started in a person. Second, most cancer patients currently diagnosed are asymptomatic and are almost always offered treatment and the natural progress of cancer is thus altered. This makes it impossible to know when symptoms would occur in these patients if there were no treatment. Lack of knowledge on the preclinical period of cancer makes it difficult to estimate accurately the effectiveness of screening and creates unsubstantiated belief and blind enthusiasm for screening.
	The burden of disease is a relative concept. Diseases such as cancer that causes severe suffering, disability, and death are generally more suitable for screening than diseases such as minor skin problems. The view on the burden of a disease may vary greatly across populations and over time in the same population. For example, in some African countries where infectious disease is the major threat to life, cancer would be deemed much less important than in Western countries where cancer has become the major killer. Screening and management of hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and diabetes mellitus for prevention of major cardiovascular complications were certainly less eminent a century ago than today in most populations.
	The prevalence determines the total number of cases that can be detected by screening in the screened population. If the disease is rare and too few cases can be identified, no matter how effective the treatment would be, screening would not be able to have an important impact on the health of the population. When would a disease be deemed prevalent and justified for screening? There is no universal answer to the question either. Again the answer may vary across populations and over time dependent on resources available, opportunity costs, and values of people at the time the decision needs to be made.
	The prevalence of a disease is positively related to the prevalence of the risk factors and the average duration of the preclinical phase. These relations suggest that screening be more likely effective in people with increased risk factors of the screened disease. Second, the prevalence of the undiagnosed but detectable preclinical disease also depends on whether or not the population has been screened recently. Recent screening in a population would reduce the number of undiagnosed asymptomatic patients. This suggests that in order for the screening programme to be cost-effective, two subsequent rounds of testing should not be kept too close to each other in time. For example, breast mammogram or Pap smear should be performed again in the same person every 3–5 years rather than more frequently.
	Risk factors and early-stage cancer can be considered similar in that both increase the future risk of severe complications, suffering, and death. Thus, cardiovascular risk factors that can increase the risk of myocardial infarction and stroke are often also screened and corrected with medications. These factors usually include hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and type II diabetes, which are common and can effectively controlled through lifestyle modification and therapeutic drugs.





The screening test


	The screening test refers to the test or a series of tests used in a screening programme to identify those who are likely to have the disease and warrant further confirmatory diagnostic investigations. Screening is feasible only if a good screening test is available. The test should be sufficiently accurate. Precisely, it should have relatively a high sensitivity and specificity. The ability of a test to correctly classify people who truly have the preclinical disease as test positive is called sensitivity and the ability to correctly classify those who are truly free of the disease as negative is called as specificity (Table 11.5.1).
	 	Table 11.5.1 Classification of disease status by the gold standard and screening test
	 			Test
	Gold standard
		Dis. (+)
	Dis.(–)
	Totals
			Test (+)
