	N = a + b + c + d
	If sensitivity and specificity are not perfect, which is always the case, errors will occur in the test results. Those who truly have the disease but are test negative, suggesting absence of disease are false negative results. False negative results will lead to missing the opportunity of early diagnosis and treatment. On the other hand, those who are truly free of the disease but test positive, suggesting presence of disease are false positive results. False positive results would result in unnecessary confirmatory diagnostic investigations and even further unnecessary treatments and harms. As screening can detect and treat conditions that will never cause symptoms and suffering in the rest of a person’s life, unnecessary treatment is much commoner than usually expected.
	Furthermore, the screening test should be able to give a sufficient lead time. Lead time is the period from the time an asymptomatic patient is detected by screening to the hypothetical time symptoms would appear and diagnosis be made by a doctor if the screening test had not been performed (Fig. 11.5.2). For a group of patients, this lead time can be approximated with some data and assumptions (Morrison 1992). For any individual patient, lead time is always a hypothetical concept and inestimable. For a screening programme to be effective in reducing morbidity and mortality in a population, there must be enough lead time in a sufficient number of cases detected. If lead time is insufficient, patients will not be treated in time to retard or stop the progression of the disease.
	Finally, the test should also be simple, rapid, inexpensive, and safe so that it can be applied to a large number of people at an affordable cost and people and clinicians will accept it and make efforts to do it (Cochrane and Holland 1971; Sackett and Holland 1975; Morrison 1992) Otherwise, screening could become either too expensive to be affordable or too unattractive so people will not come for it. For example, conduct of the test should be easy to learn. Those that can be administered by non-medical personnel will cost less than those that require skills from years of medical training. Moreover, screening that requires hospitalization for a few days to go through complex and invasive procedures are unlikely to be popular to eligible participants.





The treatment


	If screening can bring about any good, it will be from the treatment rather than the test and any other activities in it. Therefore, for a screening programme to be potentially beneficial, there must be treatments available that are effective and acceptable in asymptomatic patients. Neither do treatments used for late-stage patients necessarily help early-stage patients nor would treatments acceptable to symptomatic patients equally acceptable to asymptomatic patients. In brief, the treatments for early stage of patients must be re-evaluated in randomized controlled trials if they are to be used in screening for treating preclinical patients.





Performance of the screening test


	Screening is a combination of early detection and early treatment of preclinical diseases. Success of a screening programme is thus first determined by the test. The test is related to both the benefits and costs and harms of screening. This section will explain how they are related and how we can ‘manipulate’ the test so as to increase benefits and reduce costs and harms.
	What would make a good test for screening? As already described, a good test for screening should be accurate, feasible, and acceptable. We will now analyse the role of accuracy for screening. Accuracy is referred to the ability of a test to correctly classify true disease status, either presence or absence. It is thus commonly expressed in two separate parameters: sensitivity and specificity.





Sensitivity and specificity


	Sensitivity is the ability to detect the disease in those who truly have the disease, while specificity is the ability to rule out the possibility of disease in those truly free of the disease.
	Sensitivity and specificity are estimated through scientific research. Such research normally starts with two groups of people, one truly with the disease of concern and the other truly free of the disease. Then the test is applied to all participants in both groups. Normally, a positive test result will suggest the presence of disease and a negative result absence of disease. According to true disease status and test results, the participants can be classified into four categories: (a) true positive; (b) false positive; (c) false negative; and (d) true negative (Table 11.5.1).
	Sensitivity is expressed as the percentage of those having a positive result in those who truly have the disease and specificity is the percentage of those having a negative result in those truly free of the disease. Sensitivity can also be viewed as the probability of a true patient being detected by the test and specificity the probability of a person truly free of the disease being confirmed by the test. If sensitivity is not perfect, some true patients will turn out to be test negative. We call these negative results false negatives. Conversely, if specificity is not perfect, some of those truly free of the disease will turn out to be test positive. We call these positive results false positives (Table 11.5.1).
	For example, assuming there are 100 participants truly having the disease and 200 truly free of the disease included in a diagnostic study, 95 out of the 100 participants truly having the disease turned out to be positive (a = true positives) and 5 negative (c = false negatives); 180 out of the 200 people truly free of the disease turned out to be test negative (d = true negatives) and 20 positive (c = false negatives). This gives
	Sensitivity = a/(a + c) = 95/(95 + 5) = 95%
	Specificity = d/(b + d ) = 180/(20 + 180) = 90%





Predictive values


	Information on the accuracy of a test is not directly useful for practice, where we have only the test results with which we wish to find out the true disease status. In practice, the questions concerned are: (1) how likely is a person to truly have the disease given a positive test result, and (2) how likely is a person to be truly free of the disease given a negative test result? The answer to the first question can be estimated by the positive predictive value and the second by the negative predictive value. The positive predictive value (PPV) is the probability of truly having the disease given a positive test result and the negative predictive value (NPV) the probability of being truly free of the disease given a negative test result.
	However, predictive values cannot be estimated simply from sensitivity and specificity without knowing the prevalence of the disease in the population to which the test is applied. Put it differently, estimation of predictive values also requires knowledge on the prevalence of disease. Given sensitivity, specificity and prevalence, predictive values can be estimated by the following equations:
	PPV = P.SN / {P.SN + (1–P)(1–SP)}
	NPV = (1–P)SP / {P(1–SN) + (1–P)SP}
	Where SN = sensitivity
	SP = specificity
	P = the prevalence of the disease in the population tested
	From the aforementioned equations, we can see that predictive values are determined by characteristics of both the test and disease, precisely, the accuracy of the test and the prevalence of the disease in the population to which the test is applied. The prevalence of the disease is also called the pre-test probability of disease. The accuracy of the test is normally assumed to be a stable feature of a test and can be generalized from the research population to other populations, although this stability assumption may not be necessarily true in all circumstances. As a result, the same positive (or negative) test result may mean a different probability of having (or being free of) the disease in populations with a different prevalence of disease.
	Assuming that a test has both sensitivity and specificity of 95%, a very good test for screening, the predictive values will differ hugely as the prevalence varies (Fig. 11.5.3). As the prevalence increases, the PPV will increase but the NPV will decrease. As screening is normally conducted in populations with a relatively low prevalence of disease, results of a screening test will generally have a low PPV and high negative predictive.
	Fig. 11.5.3 Prevalence of disease and prediction error rate of test positive and negative results.
	For screening, a high NPV is good as those with a negative test result can be reassured free of the disease. But a low PPV will be of a concern as it would mean many or most of test-positive results are not true positive and further expensive and time-consuming investigations would have to be conducted in them without a gain. The false positive rate in test-positive results is one minus the PPV and is often over 50% and can be as high as 90% or higher in some screening programmes. Thus, much of the efforts in screening has to be made to reduce false positive results so as to minimize related costs and harms.
	Two methods of reducing the rate of false positive results are obvious. One is to screen in people with a relatively high risk of the disease concerned. For example, the prevalence of lung cancer is higher in people of older age and smoking cigarettes, two major risk factors of lung cancer, than in the general adult population. Thus, screening for lung cancer can reduce cost in those of older age and smoking cigarettes. More complex methods can be used to identify high-risk people by incorporating more risk factors of the screened disease (Tammemägi et al. 2013). For the same reason, breast cancer screening should be focused on women aged 40 or above.
	The other method is to ‘manipulate’ the sensitivity and specificity of the test so as to achieve a desired PPV for screening.





Balancing between sensitivity and specificity


	The results of a medical test are in nature normally quantitative rather than qualitative and often arbitrarily divided into a dichotomous result by using a cut-off value to facilitate clinical interpretation. Those with a result equal to or above the cut-off value are considered test positive, while those with a result below the cut-off are deemed negative. Different cut-off values can be used and will give rise to different combinations of sensitivity and specificity. The sensitivity and specificity of a test is inversely related: specificity decreases as sensitivity increases and vice versa. This means importantly we cannot increase both sensitivity and specificity at the same time by choosing a particular cut-off value unless the test is improved technically.
	Different combinations of sensitivity and specificity of a test may be used in different clinical settings. A high sensitivity test will help detect most patients, whereas a high specificity will help reduce false positive results and reduce the costs of further investigations. For example, in such settings as the emergency room, we may use a low cut-off value to have a high sensitivity so as not to miss even a small risk of a life-threatening problem. This will result in a high sensitivity but a large number of false positives will result due to the low specificity. Thus, those who are indicated free of a severe problem is certain but those who are indicated of having the problem will have to go through further investigations to confirm the diagnosis. Conversely, in such settings as down-syndrome screening, a relatively high cut-off value is used to achieve a high specificity and high PPV so as to minimize the number of amniocentesis which may cause unnecessary abortion.
	In screening, the prevalence is generally low and the percentage of those free of the disease which is complementary to the prevalence will be high. Consequently, a small error in the test results in those free of disease will generate a large number of false positives and considerably increase the costs and harms of further investigations in those who do not truly have the disease. Should we lower the cut-off so as to maximize the number of patients detected and potential benefits from treatments or should we increase the cut-off so as to minimize the costs and harms of further unnecessary investigations? They are the issues that need to be carefully debated in planning a screening programme. The choice of the cut-off value is central to balancing sensitivity and specificity and further to the consequent balance between benefits and costs of the entire screening programme.





How can we prove screening works?


	A high risk of a severe disease, a good test, and an effective treatment are the prerequisites for a screening programme to be eventually beneficial. However, these criteria are not a guarantee that potential benefits of screening will be realized in practice. How can we find out whether a screening programme can truly bring about more good than harm?
	Take cancer screening as an example, an intuitive method for evaluating the benefits of screening is to compare the survival between asymptomatic cases detected by screening and symptomatic cases diagnosed as a result of symptoms. Let’s call the former type of patients ‘screening-detected’ and the later ‘routinely diagnosed’. A higher survival rate in screening-detected patients than in routinely diagnosed patients is then considered as evidence that screening is beneficial in reducing fatality and increase survival.
	Such comparisons used to be widely conducted. However, they are severely flawed and their results misleading. A few biases almost certainly exist to cause a false conclusion. The major ones include lead time bias, length time bias, and selection bias.





Lead time bias


	Lead time is the duration of time from the time the disease is detected by screening to the time symptoms would appear in the same person if there were no screening (Fig. 11.5.2). Lead time always exists in screening; otherwise, screening will not detect patients any earlier and become equivalent to no screening. Purely due to lead time, screening-detected patients will surely survive longer than routinely diagnosed patients simply because the former was diagnosed and treated earlier and observed longer over time than the later. In other words, if early detection and early treatment is not effective and do not affect the natural progress of the disease, screening-detected patients will live longer by exactly the amount of lead time than routinely diagnosed patients. We call this false survival benefit lead time bias.
	To illustrate, in scenario A of Figure 11.5.4, the patient is diagnosed and treated as a result of appearance of symptoms in the absence of screening, in scenario B the patient is detected and treated early as a result of screening but does not live any longer than that in scenario A as screening is not effective, and in scenario C the patient is also detected by screening but has lived longer than that in scenario A, showing a benefit of screening. As lead time always exists, the patient in scenario B will always look like surviving longer than that in scenario A. The extra survival in the patient in scenario B is however purely a result of lead time. Screening is beneficial only when the extra survival in screening-detected patients is longer than the lead time such as in scenario C. But we can distinguish scenario C from B if and only if we know the lead time.
	Fig. 11.5.4 How lead time affects survival time after screening?
	But lead time cannot be estimated. It cannot be estimated by using the onset time of disease which is impossible to know for most chronic diseases. Nor can lead time to be estimated by the difference between the detection time by screening and the time symptoms appear as the two time points cannot be known in the same patient. In reality, the time symptoms appear cannot be known if screening is conducted and detected the patient. Conversely, the detection time by screening cannot be known if screening is not provided and diagnosis is made as a result of symptoms.
	Lead time bias is like asking two persons who will live a longer life. If one is 25 years’ old and the other 40 and they both will die at the age of 80, the younger person can live from now for another 55 years and the older only 40 years. The younger will live 15 years more than the older from now purely because of the lead time ——we see the younger 15 years earlier. Therefore, we cannot deduct from this observation that the younger will truly live a longer life as their life span is the same. In the context of screening, the younger person is like screening-detected patient and the older routinely diagnosed patient. Lead time is always a part, if not all, of the extra survival observed in screening-detected patients as compared with routinely diagnosed patients.
	In conclusion, all comparisons of survival between screening-detected patients and routinely diagnosed patients are flawed and subject to lead time bias.





Length time bias


	Length time bias is another inevitable bias in comparing the survival between screening-detected patients and routinely diagnosed patients. It occurs because the same cancer progresses at a different rate in different people.
	Screening detects relatively benign cancer rather than the worst. To illustrate, Figure 11.5.5 shows three types of patients with the same cancer: slow-progress cancer (a, b, and c), cancer with a moderate progress rate (d, e, and f), and fast-progress cancer (g, h, and i). Assume cancer started all at the same time. By the time of screening, the fast-progress cancer would have progressed to a stage at which symptoms have appeared and diagnosis made at a routine clinical setting. On the other hand, slow-progress cancer is still too small to be detectable by the screening.
	Screening tends to detect cancer that progresses more slowly and has inherently better prognosis than cancer that is routinely diagnosed. In addition, like slow-progress cancers, some screening-detected cancers may stop progress, regress, or even spontaneously resolve so that it will never cause a problem before people die from other causes. Thus, screening-detected patients are bound to have a better prognosis and survive longer than routinely diagnosed patients, even if screening is not effective. We call this false conclusion on the benefit of screening length time bias.
	Fig. 11.5.5 Length time bias: fast-progress tumours come to medical attention before screening is performed, whereas tumours with a moderate progress rate allow more time for detection.





Confounding


	Comparison of screening-detected patients with routinely diagnosed patients is inherently flawed for evaluation of the effectiveness of screening programmes. To avoid these biases, we can alternatively compare screened people with those who are not screened regardless of whether or not they are found to have the disease. The non-screened population can be those who are in the same community and offered screening but have not received screening or another population in which screening did not provide at all. Screening will be considered effective if the mortality of the screened disease in the screened population is found to be lower than that in the non-screened population. For example, the mortality of prostate cancer was reduced in screening region as compared with the rest of Australia, suggesting PSA screening be effective (Bartsch et al. 2008). However, such comparisons are like any other cohort studies and subject to the problem of confounding.
	Confounding is a bias that arises in comparison due to incomparability in factors that may affect the prognosis of the screened disease between screened and non-screened populations. We would like to think that those who were screened had the same characteristics as those who were not screened. However, there may exist many possible differences between screened and non-screened populations, which may cause confounding. For example, if people at a higher risk of the screened disease are more eager to be screened, e.g. women with a family history of breast cancer are more willing to get a mammography, a screening test will look worse than it truly is. This will cause underestimation of the true benefit of screening.
	Confounding can also make screening look better than it truly is. For example, if one has to travel a long distance to get tested, more young and healthy people will be screened and fewer people in the screened population would die and screening would seem to make a positive difference. As screening is not compulsory and people mostly volunteer themselves to screening, this bias is also called volunteer bias or referral bias, a form of selection bias. Due to selection processes, the screened and non-screened will not be comparable and confounding will inevitably occur.
	Like in clinical trials, the best way of tacking confounding, or selection bias some would like to call, is to conduct a randomized controlled trial. In randomized trials, people are randomly allocated to comparison groups so that any prognostic factors of the disease will be balanced among compared groups so that confounding will be eliminated.





Evaluation of screening by the randomized controlled trial


	Randomized controlled trials in screening differ from usual clinical trials. In order to minimize contamination of screening service between compared groups, communities, or clusters of people rather than individuals are randomized. Screening service is offered to those in the intervention communities but not the control communities. Such trials are known as cluster randomized controlled trials. A lower mortality from the screened disease in the screened group than the control group will suggest screening is beneficial.
	As illustrated in Figure 11.5.6, in a randomized controlled trial of screening for cancer, there are four categories of people in each of the compared groups: those free of cancer, fast-progress cancer, cancer with a moderate progress rate, and slow-progress cancer. Because of randomization, the proportion of each category will be comparable between screened and non-screened communities. Screening will affect the prognosis of only those with cancer at a moderate progress rate and mortality in the other 3 categories are comparable and will cancel each other. Thus, any lowered mortality in the screened group can be attributed to screening. As only those with cancer at a moderate progress rate are compared, lead time bias and length time bias are also be avoided at the same time confounding is controlled by randomization.
	Fig. 11.5.6 Randomized controlled trial designed to evaluate a screening programme.
	Now it is widely accepted that screening programmes for healthy people are justifiable only when randomized controlled trials have clearly demonstrated that benefits outweigh harms. The benefits should be estimated on important endpoint outcomes such as death rather than intermediate surrogate outcomes such as blood test and imaging results. For example, randomized controlled trials show that mammography can significantly reduce mortality from breast cancer in women over 50 years old (Wells 1998), whereas chest X-rays with or without sputum cytology do not affect mortality from lung cancer (Bech et al. 2003).
	Cluster trials on screening are normally large and expensive and difficult to organize. They have also a low statistical power as most people in such a trial do not contribute to the comparison so the benefit if any is greatly diluted. Alternatively, trials are conducted in which only screening-detected cancer patients are included and randomized to receive either a treatment or no treatment as control. It is generally considered unethical to give no treatment to cancer patients in the control group. Such trials are relatively rare. With a better understanding of the natural progress of cancers, many cancer patients are now willing to watchfully wait rather than to be treated immediately. This makes such trials more acceptable (Holmberg et al. 2002; Wilt et al. 2012). In theory, the control group can be given a treatment with proven benefit in screening-detected cancer. If there is such a treatment, it already forms evidence supporting screening.
	However, trials of screening-detected patients, at best, can only be viewed as efficacy trials like those for drugs as they do not take into account the organizational aspects of a screening programme. If poorly organized, a screening programme may still fail even if the test is sufficiently accurate and treatment effective. In reality, compromises are often made in ways people are selected for testing, the test is conducted, and treatments delivered. Compromised management standard and quality may make a screening programme eventually fail to bring about any good to the screened population (Raffle and Gray 2007). Thus, the overall effectiveness of a screening programme can only be reliably evaluated in randomized controlled trials that randomly allocate eligible people to screening or usual care.





Balancing the benefits, costs, and harms of screening


	Randomized controlled trial may show a screening programme is beneficial but the benefit comes at a cost. The costs include money, human resources and time, and inconvenience, worries and harms caused to the screened and incur at every stage of screening from the test to further investigations to the treatment.





Benefits


	Screening will be futile if early treatment does not bring about extra benefit and can be effective only when treatments of early detected patients has greater benefits than usual care. The total population gain in the benefit from a screening programme will be determined by the total number of cases detected as well as the effectiveness of treatment. The former is in turn determined by the prevalence of disease and sensitivity of the test. The higher the prevalence, the larger the number of patients can be potentially detected; the higher sensitivity is, the larger the proportion of patients can be eventually picked by screening. The total life years gained from screening is the product of the number of cases treated and the average extra survival gained from early treatments. Given that treatments are effective, the cost-effectiveness of screening can be increased by screening only persons at a high risk of the disease, by using a test of high sensitivity, by using a cut-off value that gives rise to a high sensitivity, and/or by testing the same persons more often.





Costs and harms


	The benefits of screening come at a cost and with harm. Costs and harms can result from the screening test, further diagnostic investigations, and treatment. Harms may occur in the following forms:
	 	• harms and inconvenience caused by the initial test;
	• negative labelling effects: stress and anxiety caused by a false positive result;
	• harms and inconvenience caused by unnecessary investigations in false positive persons;
	• harms and inconvenience caused by unnecessary treatment of those who do not have the disease or have the disease that would never progress to the clinical stage and would have not been treated if there were no screening;
	• prolonged stress and anxiety if detected patients cannot be effectively treated;
	• a false sense of security caused by false negative results which could delay final diagnosis.





Increasing benefits and reducing costs and harms


	The costs and harms of the initial test and of the final treatment are largely unavoidable. There is not much that can be done to reduce them. In contrast, confirmatory diagnostic investigations are where a large proportion of costs and labelling effects can be avoided. These further investigations are normally expensive and time-consuming, and are often invasive and can cause harm. Further investigations are unnecessary and the costs and harms incurred can be reduced if false positive results can be reduced. All screening programmes should make efforts to do so.
	As most people do not have the screened disease in the screened population, a relatively low specificity can result in a large number of false positive results which can outnumber many times the true patients detected. The lower the prevalence is, the higher the false PPV will be; the higher the specificity is, the lower the false PPV will be. The rate of false positive results can thus be considerably reduced by increasing the specificity and by screening in high people and at a longer interval between two tests. As sensitivity and specificity of a test are inversely related, specificity can only be increased with a compromise in sensitivity and missing diagnosis of a few more patients. This can be done by changing the cut-off value. A good screening programme must carefully choose the cut-off value so as to achieve a desirable combination of sensitivity and specificity, which will, in turn, help favourably balance the benefit against the cost and harm.
	In brief, avoidable costs and harms of screening occur largely as a result of false positive test results and can be reduced by screening in high-risk people and by using a relatively high specificity. Having said that, time is an important factor to consider as well. As technology advances fast, a few years of waiting may substantively reduce the costs of the initial test and end up with an improved test with greater accuracy as well.





Illustration 1: screening for prostate cancer


	In this section, we will use prostate cancer screening, in particular, data in the United States (US), as an example to demonstrate the rationale, principles, methods, and problems of screening.





Severity and prevalence of prostate cancer


	Cancer is a terrifying disease. It relentlessly metastasizes throughout the body. It causes death if not treated, and often even it is treated. And the best way to treat it is to catch it early. These views about cancer seem strong enough to lend support to screening activities for cancer. Prostate cancer seems no exceptional.
	Prostate cancer is common. It is a leading cause, and the second cause of death from cancer in men in the US. The lifetime risk of receiving a diagnosis of prostate cancer was approximately 9% in 1985 and reached 16% in 2007 (Altekruse et al. 2010). Silent prostate cancer is also prevalent. One of the early studies showed that the prevalence of latent carcinoma of prostate at autopsy was 12% (Breslow et al. 1977). More recently, a systematic review of 29 autopsy studies of men who died of other causes showed the prevalence of incidental prostate cancer increases with age (Bell et al. 2015). It was found in some 5% in men aged 30 years or below and as common as 59% in men aged 80 years or above.
	The median age at diagnosis is 67 years and the median age at death is 81 years (Altekruse et al. 2010). Some 60% of patients die from competing causes in 10 years after diagnosis of prostate cancer. These findings suggest prostate cancer be a slow progressing cancer and have a long preclinical phase. Studies estimated that asymptomatic prostate cancer can be detected with prostate-specific protein (PSA) by a lead time of 5–10 years (Draisma et al. 2009).
	About 80% of prostate cancer patients are local and has not spread outside of the prostate. The 5-year survival rate for these patients is nearly 100%. In contrast, patients diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer that has spread to distant lymph nodes, bones, or other organs, the 5-year survival rate is only about 29% (ACS 2018). The sharp contrast in survival of the local and distant cancers suggest that many patients can be detected early and their survival be greatly prolonged by early treatment.





The test—prostate-specific protein


	Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is the primary driving force for the rise of prostate cancer screening (AUA 2013; Hoffman 2018). PSA is a protein produced by normal as well as malignant cells of the prostate gland. The PSA test measures the level of PSA in a man’s blood. The blood level of PSA is often elevated in men with prostate cancer. PSA testing was introduced in the late 1980s. In the US, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved in 1994 the use of the PSA test in conjunction with a digital rectal exam to test asymptomatic men for prostate cancer.
	Before the 1980s, solid cancers could be diagnosed only by symptoms, signs, and imaging and rarely by a simple blood test. PSA was considered an exciting breakthrough and caused great enthusiasm for screening for prostate cancer. By the early 2000s, approximately 75% of men aged 50 years or above had undergone PSA testing and 90% of prostate cancer were detected by means of screening in the US.
	PSA testing is safe, quick, simple, and inexpensive and thus generally acceptable to healthy men and feasible for testing a large number of people. The major concern is its accuracy. Using the cut-off value of 4.0 ng/ml as is normally recommended, specificity is 91% but sensitivity is only 21% which will miss 79% of cancers. Twelve per cent (12%) of the tested will turn out to be positive and only 30% of test-positives are truly positive. Using a lower cut-off value of 3.0 ng/ml, sensitivity will be increased to 32% which is still relatively low but will lower specificity to 85% (Wolf et al. 2010). Eighteen per cent (18%) of the tested will turn out to be positive and only 28% of the positive results are truly positive. The further investigation is biopsy of the prostate. Approximately, 70% of the test-positive men will not benefit from biopsy but may have harms including stress, bleeding, pain, clot formation, infection, and urinary difficulties.





The treatment


	When prostate cancer is confirmed, the usual treatment is radical prostatectomy. PSA testing had become widespread before the benefits of aggressive treatment of asymptomatic prostate cancer was demonstrated in research. Till 2002, a Scandinavian randomized controlled trial of 694 men with asymptomatic prostate cancer and aged below 75 years showed radical prostatectomy as compared with watchful waiting could reduce the risk of death from 8.9% to 4.6%, a relative reduction of 48% during a median follow-up of 6.2 years (Holmberg et al. 2002). The mortality reduction persisted through 15 years of follow-up (Bill-Axelson et al. 2011). However, only about 5% of the cancer patients in this trial were detected by screening and over 75% were palpable. It is thus questionable whether this result is applicable to patients with prostate cancer mostly detected by screening and impalpable.
	Unfortunately, the PIVOT trial (Prostate Cancer Intervention Versus Observation Trial) in the US failed to confirm this benefit of radical prostatectomy in men with prostate cancer mostly detected by screening and of earlier stage than those in the Scandinavian trial (PIVOT 2009). The trial randomized 731 men to either radical prostatectomy or watchful waiting. After 12 years of follow-up, no statistically significant difference was found in overall and prostate-specific mortality (Phillips 2011).
	It remains controversial whether current treatment methods for early stage of prostate cancer can prolong life. These trials are relatively small and did not take into account the standard and quality of screening, which may further compromise the benefit. Large randomized controlled trials were eventually mounted to directly compare the screened and non-screened populations. They are tougher and ultimate evaluations of PSA screening.





Randomized controlled trials of PSA screening


	By 2010, six large randomized controlled trials on PSA screening have been completed and published with a total number of participants of 387,286 men studied (Djulbegovic et al. 2010). The median follow of the six trials ranged from 4 years to 15 years but was 9 years or longer in five trials. A systematic review of these trials showed that compared with usual care, PSA screening with or without digital rectal examination could on average detect 50% more, or 20 more in every 1000 screened, men with prostate cancer. The extra patients detected by screening are all stage I or stage II cancers. Harms are not reported in the majority of trials and found relatively rare if reported.
	Importantly, five trials with 302 500 randomized participants showed a relative risk 0.88 on mortality from prostate cancer, a result which is statistically not significant. Four trials with 256 019 randomized participants showed a relative risk of 0.99 on all-cause mortality, again statistically insignificant. There is large heterogeneity in the proportion of extra prostate cancers detected but all the trials showed homogeneously no effect on reducing mortality. These results suggest that the increased detection of early-stage prostate cancer has not translated into a benefit in reducing overall mortality and mortality specific to prostate cancer.
	In conclusion, some 30 years later since PSA was introduced for screening, the current best evidence does not seem to support that PSA screening is effective in reducing the outcomes that are important for patients. It may be argued that in some circumstances PSA may reduce mortality specific to prostate cancer. However, PSA screening may have increased the risk of death from other causes and thus led to no reduction in overall mortality, which constitutes strong evidence against PSA screening. Having made that conclusion, it still remains a possibility that the lack of effect of PSA screening is partly a result from a likelihood that many silent prostate cancer patients may have also been detected and treated in the usual care group in these trials.





Illustration 2: screening for cardiovascular risk factors


	Unlike cancers, cardiovascular diseases share many common risk factors. These factors are mostly well understood and can be effectively controlled with currently available interventions. The amenable cardiovascular risk factors include, notably, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, smoking, body weight, lack of physical activities, and type II diabetes mellitus. In this section, we will use hypertension to illustrate how screening can be used for risk factors for the purpose of primary prevention, although these cardiovascular risk factors are usually checked together.





Hypertension pressure—the most frequently checked condition


	Blood pressure has probably taken over the measurement of body temperature and become the most frequently checked clinical condition in today’s medicine. It is checked often in routine clinical encounters, in general, health checks, and even at home with automated sphygmomanometers. Searching for hypertension is normally not taken as a part of screening programme and thus has not been debated and challenged for the evaluation we ask for cancer screening. This has further abetted the culture of measuring blood pressure.
	Hypertension is common and its cardiovascular complications are severe and prevalent. Blood pressure can be easily measured. Blood pressure-lowering drugs can effectively reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications and are widely used. These all make hypertension suitable for screening. Indeed, worldwide hypertension has been widely screened and treated. However, treating hypertension is not merely for the sake of lowering blood pressure; it is for lowering the risk of severe cardiovascular complications and death.





Effectiveness of searching for hypertension


	It is not clear whether screening for hypertension in the general population would help reduce future risk of cardiovascular complications and deaths. A systematic review of randomized controlled trials of general health checks, all or most of which included measuring blood pressure, found general health checks in general practice could effectively reduce cardiovascular risk factors such as blood pressure and blood cholesterol but had no effect on both cardiovascular mortality and overall mortality (Si et al. 2014). This finding is consistent with a previous larger systematic review which also included randomized trials in non-primary care settings (Krogsbøll et al. 2012).
	That not all detected hypertensive patients are eventually treated may partly account for the lack of effect of routinely checking blood pressure and other cardiovascular risk factors on reducing mortality. In the context of screening, blood pressure checks should not be encouraged if the majority of detected patients are eventually treated. It is possible that blood pressure checks are already common in the general population so that the difference in the intervention and usual care groups is too small to be detectable. It is also possible that the benefit from checks for cardiovascular risk factors has been cancelled by harms of treatments and of checks for other diseases. More recently, a large randomized controlled trial provides evidence for checks for only cardiovascular risk. The trial randomized 59,616 participants from a general population and compared the effect of checks for hypertension and other major cardiovascular risk factors followed by repeated lifestyle interventions over 5 years. At the end of 10 years’ follow-up, screening did not show any effect on ischaemic heart disease, stroke, and mortality (Jørgensen et al. 2014).
	Screening for hypertension and other cardiovascular risk factors in the current medical context seems to have failed in the most important criteria for screening: screening should be able to reduce severe complications and deaths that the screened condition may cause. There is another important issue that needs to be addressed in searching for hypertension and in screening in general: what is the clinical condition we are screening for? If the condition screened is difficult to define, a screening programme is likely to be stretched and eventually become doubtful.





What constitutes hypertension?


	Regular checks for hypertension reemphasized the ultimate criteria for screening: screening programmes should be recommended when and only when they can produce more good than harm at an affordable cost for a population. However, the good and harm ratio for hypertension screening changes as the diagnostic criteria for hypertension change. Hypertension is, in essence, an ‘arbitrary’ condition which is reflected in the choice of cut-off value for defining it. This has important implications for screening for hypertension and screening in general.
	Epidemiological studies have shown beyond reasonable doubt that the risk of cardiovascular disease increases as blood pressure increases. The relation is largely linear for blood pressure between 120 mmHg and 180 mmHg systolic or between 70 mmHg and 110 mmHg diastolic, a range most adults’ blood pressure falls into. There is no clear turning point below which cardiovascular risk does not increase with blood pressure (Law and Wald 2002; Lacey et al. 2018). Compared with those with the lowest blood pressure values, all others are hypertensive; conversely, compared with those with the highest blood pressure values, all others are normal tensive. There is no blood pressure value that can be used objectively and undebatably for defining hypertension. Any cut-off value will be a result of the trade-off in balancing among various factors. A higher cut-off value will result in fewer hypertensive patients for whom treatment will be more effective, whereas a lower cut-off value will result in more hypertensive patients for whom treatment will be less effective. Where should the cut-off value be set?
	The fundamental requirement is that treatment of hypertension thus defined should be able to do more good than harm. Furthermore, resources available to, and the values of, the population concerned must also be taken into account (Jackson et al. 2005; MacMahon et al. 2005; Tang and Hu 2005). This was exactly how once the cholesterol cut-off for prescribing Statin was set in the United Kingdom (Pickin et al. 1999; Gaw and Packard 2000). Previously defined hypertension was widely accepted and treatments are effective. However, around the year 2000, the cut-off for hypertension was reduced to 90/140 mmHg. A systematic review of randomized controlled trials showed that antihypertensive drugs did not reduce risk of cardiovascular disease and related mortality in mild hypertension created by the new criteria (Lenzer 2012; Brunström and Carlberg 2018). This conclusion is very likely to be applicable to those who have an even lower blood pressure but will be diagnosed as hypertensive according to the new US guidelines in which the cut-off is lowered to 130/80 mmHg (Whelton et al. 2017). The new definitions will make any screening programmes for early, mild hypertension questionable.
	Importantly, changing of disease definitions has been happening to hyperlipidaemia, type II diabetes mellitus and many other risk factors and diseases including cancer (Welch et al. 2011; Doust et al. 2017; Yang et al. 2017). The implications of changing the definition of cancers for cancer screening will be discussed later in this chapter.





Health checks as multiphasic screening


	Modern concept and practice of systematic screening originated in early attempts of general health checks. Today we emphasize systematic planning and rigorous evaluation of benefits and harms of screening programmes through randomized controlled trials. Since the 1960s, many randomized controlled trials on screening of individual diseases have been conducted and the results are often disappointing. In the same time, general health checks, the old practice of screening has not disappeared. In fact, in recent decades it has been on a continuous increase and become a large business in many countries including China (Ren 2016). Modern general health checks may include hundreds of tests and examinations in one package. Many of them are new tests including genetic testing and have not been rigorously evaluated and proven to be able to do more good than harm.
	Health checks can be viewed as an application of many screening tests for many different diseases in one programme. On one hand, often only a fraction of people with identified problems are adequately followed up with further investigations and treatments and the benefit of the tests and examinations are not fully realized. On the other hand, further investigations and treatments of some detected problems may do harms without a benefit. Against the ultimate standard for screening that is a demonstration of benefits in reducing mortality and prolonging life in randomized controlled trials, are general health checks effective and worthwhile?
	In 2012, a systematic review identified 14 randomized controlled trials with a total 182,880 participants included and summarized the evidence for the effects of general health checks in adults on reducing morbidity and mortality (Krogsbøll et al. 2012). In this review, general health checks were defined as screening for more than one disease or risk factor in more than one organ system, regardless of whether they were performed once or repeatedly. Many trials included risk factors for cardiovascular disease and screening techniques for cancer.
	Nine trials provided data on total mortality, 8 on cardiovascular mortality, 8 on cancer mortality. It showed no benefit in reducing mortality from health checks: the risk ratio is 0.99, 1.03, and 1.10 respectively for total mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and cancer mortality. None of these results are statistically significant. The review also failed to find any benefits on hospitalization, disability, worry, additional physician visits, and absence from work. Although the debate may continue, it is almost certain that benefits of general health checks for reducing mortality, the ultimate aim of screening, would be trivial, if any at all.
	The authors of the review wrote in the Cochrane editorial as follows:
	 	In spite of the consistently negative results of screening and lifestyle counselling, general health checks remain a popular political tool for combating the burden of ischaemic heart disease and other chronic diseases. Lately, the British government has started a general health check for the population. Danish left wing parties went to the polls in 2011promising the same but changed their minds shortly after gaining power. In 1968 the World Health Organization proposed that several criteria should be fulfilled before systematic screening could be recommended. These criteria have often been interpreted as criteria for screening for early stages of diseases, but they also apply to systematic screening for high risk of diseases. Some of the main criteria are that the disease in question should be serious and that a valid screening instrument is available, both of which are fulfilled for ischaemic heart disease. However, the most important criterion is that screening should reduce morbidity and mortality in the target population.
	The authors made a rather strong recommendation that doctors should not offer general health checks to their patients, and governments should abstain from introducing health check programmes (Gøtzsche 2014).
	It was the early debates over the value of health checks that led to the modern concept of more organized screening programme focused on specific diseases (Raffle and Gray 2007). Given the widespread of different ideas and practices of screening that are often ineffective, it is time to revisit these debates. It is reasonable to argue that screening ideas such as general health checks should include only those tests and examinations that are clearly targeted at specific diseases and proven effective on important outcomes.





Early detection and overdiagnosis


Screening and overdiagnosis


	With the availability of rapid-growth new technologies, the idea of early diagnosis and early treatment have been increasingly applied in clinical settings often before they are demonstrated effective. This has caused overdiagnoses. Overdiagnosis occurs when people without symptoms are diagnosed with a disease that ultimately will not cause them to experience symptoms or early deaths (Moynihan et al. 2012). Screening and overdiagnosis are related. Screening is about early detection and early treatment, whereas overdiagnosis is often in the form of early diagnosis that does not lead to a benefit.
	Overdiagnosis can result from overdetection or overdefinition (Broderson et al. 2018). Overdetection is a major form of overdiagnosis in cancer and partly driven by advances in technologies (Orme et al. 2010). It can occur by identifying abnormalities that are never going to cause harm, which include those that do not progress, that progress too slowly to cause symptoms or harm during a person’s remaining lifetime, or that resolve spontaneously.
	Overdefinition is the major type of overdiagnosis for such conditions as hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes mellitus, and osteoporosis. It can occur by lowering the cut-off vale for disease diagnosis and by including more parameters in the diagnostic criteria without evidence that doing so helps people feel better or live longer.





Overdiagnosis in hypertension


	As just discussed, hypertension is not black and white disease entity. Rather, it is an arbitrarily defined clinical condition by using a cut-off. With a hope to prevent early and in more people, the cut-off value for diagnosing hypertension has been reduced a few times so more and more people are now diagnosed, alerted, or treated.
	In 1998, the cut-off value for hypertension was further lowered from 160/95 mmHg to 140/90 mmHg. In China, this change in the cut-off increased the prevalence of hypertension by 134% and created over 100 million new patients. A similar phenomenon was also observed for hyperlipidaemia and type II diabetes. It was estimated in 2002, the total drug costs for hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and type II diabetes could amount to 56% of the total healthcare expenditure of the government if all the patients were treated with drugs (Hu et al. 2017).
	In 2015, 23.2% or approximately 244.5 million of the Chinese adult population aged 18 years or above were hypertensive, and another 41.3% or approximately 435.3 million had pre-hypertension according to the current Chinese guidelines (Wang et al. 2018). In 2017, it was recommended in the US that the cut-off value for hypertension be further lowered to 120/80 mmHg (Whelton et al. 2017). Using these new criteria, the total number of hypertensive patients in China will be further doubled and increased to approximately 500 million or prevalence of 46.4% (Wang et al. 2018).
	Given that there is insufficient evidence that drug treatment of mild hypertension can reduce morbidity and mortality (Krogsbøll et al. 2012; Jørgensen et al. 2014; Si et al. 2014) the new cut-off value for hypertension will create sweeping overdiagnosis worldwide.





Overdiagnosis in cancer


	Cancer is usually considered a black and white disease entity. Once found, it kills. In fact, cancer is very much like hypertension which is a continuous condition and the risk of suffering and death increases as the severity or size of cancer increases. Early-stage, asymptomatic cancer is merely a ‘risk factor’ of future suffering and death rather than a current misfortune.
	The relation of cancer to mortality can be illustrated in Figure 11.5.7. Cancer does not start with a large lump of cancerous cells. Instead, it begins with cancerous mutations in cells when they divide. These cancerous cells may multiply and form an in situ cancer. The in situ cancer may further grow in size and even become invasive spreading into surrounding tissues and the lymph nodes nearby. Local cancer may further progress into the metastatic stage and spread to another organ. Although most patients may die of a cancer at the metastatic stage, early-stage cancers are not necessarily lethal. In fact, many may regress or even resolve spontaneously, stop progress, or grow so slowly that they will not cause harms before the individual die of other causes (Black 1998). This means that some early-stage cancer may not harm in a person’s lifetime. Indeed, autopsy studies found that subclinical cancer exists in a large proportion of people who died of accidents or other causes rather than cancer (Welch et al. 2010).
	Fig. 11.5.7 Stage of cancer and the chance of dying from that cancer.
	Now we can see that the relation between cancer and mortality is, essence, similar to that between hypertension and mortality. Again, where should we draw the cut-off for diagnosing cancer in such a circumstance? Unlike hypertension, we do not deliberately discuss and play with the cut-off value in diagnosis of cancer. But the truth is we keep pushing down the cut-off value in the size of the tumour: the cut-off is lowered every time more powerful diagnostic methods are made available. There is no doubt that cancers detected through current imaging technologies are much smaller those diagnosed through symptoms and physical examination. As a result, the definition of cancer has been changing as well but stealthily due to advances in diagnostic technology. Most cancer patients we diagnosed today are small and asymptomatic and would not have been diagnosed and treated in the days before the rise of modern technology. Have these advances in medicine truly helped reduce suffering and death? The evidence shows not necessarily.
	Again, take prostate cancer as an example. A meta-analysis of 19 autopsy studies found that the prevalence of unsuspected prostate cancer in men aged 70–79 years was as high as 36% in Caucasians and 51% in African-Americans (Jahn et al. 2015). After PSA was introduced in the late 1980s in the US, the incidence of prostate cancer quickly increased by over 100%. Between 1999 and 2006, the annual age-adjusted incidence of prostate cancer in men maintained above 150 per 100,000 men. About 80% of prostate cancers were, however, clinically confined to the prostate and only 4% had metastasized (Hoffman 2011). Given the great increase in the incidence, the mortality of prostate cancer, however, remained largely the same between 1975 and 2007. The combination of increasing incidence and stable mortality is a clear sign of overdiagnosis. Furthermore, evidence from six randomized controlled trials with a total of 387 286 participants do not support the routine use of PSA for screening prostate cancer (Djulbegovic et al. 2010).
	Thyroid cancer is more striking an example of overdiagnosis. While the chances of tests to detect a thyroid ‘abnormality’ are high, the risk it will ever cause harm is low (Tang and Hu 2005; Welch et al. 2011). In the United Sates, an analysis in 2006 showed many of the newly diagnosed thyroid cancers were the smaller and less aggressive forms not requiring treatment (Davies and Welch 2006) but carried a risk of damaged nerves and long term medication if treated. In South Korea, the rate of thyroid cancer was increased by 14 times from 1993 to 2011. Most of the increase are believed to be overdiagnosis, attributable to the early detection of papillary thyroid cancer by ultrasound (Ahn et al. 2014; Park et al. 2016). Furthermore, a systematic review found that it is unclear that ultrasonography plus follow-up cytology for screening thyroid cancer can decrease mortality rates or improve important patient outcomes (Lin et al. 2017).





Other diseases


	Overdiagnosis is not limited to hypertension and cancer and in fact is ubiquitous in medicine. Next are a few more examples.





Pulmonary embolism


	Pulmonary embolism is usually considered a ‘not to be missed’ diagnosis. Historically, pulmonary embolism was nearly universally fatal, diagnosis made on clinical grounds and often only discovered after death. Anticoagulants were established management standard. In the late twentieth century, computed tomography pulmonary angiography allowed to detect pulmonary embolism reliably and non-invasively. Progressively smaller pulmonary embolisms are now being found and the incidence of diagnosed pulmonary embolism has been doubled but the death rate remained largely unchanged, suggesting smaller subclinical pulmonary embolism is overdiagnosed (Prasad et al. 2012).





Abdominal aortic aneurysms


	Abdominal aortic aneurysms is another typical example of detecting clinically less important abnormalities. A study of 201 men aged between 60 and 75 with hypertension or heart disease compared the number of abdominal aortic aneurysms that can be identified by ultrasound and that by physical examination. In five people with aneurysm of 5 cm or greater, physical examination can find 4. In 5 with aneurysm between 4 and 5 cm, physical examination detected only 1. In 8 with aneurysm smaller than 4 cm, physical examination failed to identify any. Ultrasound could detect all of them, creating three times more subclinical aneurysms. Most of these aneurysms are below the size for which surgery is recommended and thus represent typical overdiagnosis (Lederle et al. 1988).





Stroke


	Silent stroke was found by MRI scans to exist in over 10% of people from the general population without clinically diagnosed stroke. The prevalence of silent stroke increases as age increases. It was 7%, 8%, 10%, and 15%, respectively, in those aged 30–49, 50–59, 60–69, and 70–79 years. It is not a certain treatment of silent stroke is beneficial (Das et al. 2008).





Chromic kidney disease


	The new US guidelines recommend that an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 and sustained for 3 months or longer is deemed abnormal. According to these criteria, more than 10% of adults in the US are now classified as having some form of chronic kidney disease (Levey et al. 2009).





Lessons from early detection


	Advances in diagnostic methods have made diagnosis of disease at their clinical stage much easier, more quickly, and more reliably, which has reduced unnecessary treatments and increased the effectiveness in those treated. However, at the same time, these advances are also being used widely to find diseases at their preclinical stage. Furthermore, diagnostic criteria for diseases are being expanded, making more and more people become patients. Modifying the definition of disease normally creates mild or early stage of diseases. However, it is often unclear whether the preclinical patients thus created and identified will benefit from treatment.
	From the perspective of screening, many of the activities for detecting and treating early or mild diseases do not seem justifiable. Early detection is happening extensively at a large number and still on an increasing trend. The number of early patients thus created or discovered is likely many times more than those found by appropriately organized screening programmes. If there is no benefit, it is a considerable waste. We thus argue that new diagnostic methods for detecting asymptomatic patients should not be introduced into practice before they are rigorously evaluated in the way we do for screening. Guidelines should also be made for defining a new disease or modifying the diagnostic criteria of a current disease so that a benefit will be guaranteed to result.





Conclusions


	Intuitively screening is highly appealing but in practice frequently ineffective.
	All screening programmes cost and have harms. Decades of epidemiological research show that it is much less often than many would expect that screening can do more good than harm. This reemphasizes urgently the ultimate criteria for screening: only those programmes that can do more good than harm at an affordable cost should be recommended. Policy makers should assess carefully as regards the disease, the test, and treatments to see whether they are suitable for screening. The ultimate evidence about the benefit and harm of a screening programme should be from randomized controlled trials. Screening programmes should also be organized in high standard and quality so that the benefit demonstrated in research can be reproduced in practice.
	But not all efforts for early detection and early treatment occur in the form of systematic screening. In fact, more often they take place in routine clinical services and increasingly in general health checks. In some places, health checks may account for most of early detection activities and should be planned and evaluated as carefully as we do for screening of specific diseases. Even if effective, a screening programme will benefit only a few at a large cost to the entire population. Even worse, the harm starts immediately but the benefit if any takes much longer to appear. Thus, the decision to introduce a new screening programme should be taken as seriously as we make important healthcare decisions like building a large new hospital.
	Finally, is the benefit of a screening programme worth its costs and harms? The answer to this question inevitably varies across populations that have different resources available, different health needs to address, and different views on the value of the benefit and harm. Screening should be recommended to a population only when a benefit–harm ratio is deemed desirable to that population.
