11.6


The practice of environmental health in an era of sustainable development


	Yasmin E.R. von Schirnding and Lynn R. Goldman





Introduction to environmental health practice


Roots of environmental health practice


	The practice of environmental health goes back to earliest times. For example, cleanliness, water supply and sanitation have played an important role in disease prevention throughout recorded history (Rosen 1958). Many of the world’s water and sanitation practices had their origins in the ancient civilizations of India, Egypt, and Mesopotamia—a testimony to their hydraulic engineering skills. It was the Romans who excelled in sanitary engineering however, with the Cloaca Maxima, the great sewer of Rome, still forming part of the drainage system of modern Rome. Personal hygiene and cleanliness were emphasized by early and prehistoric societies, and were regarded as a sign of spiritual purity (Rosen 1958).
	For thousands of years the theory prevailed that disease was linked to the gods, and only gradually did the idea evolve (for example, in the writings of the Greek physician Hippocrates in Airs, Waters and Places (400 BCE) that disease was linked to natural causes such as climate and the environment (Rosen 1958). Airs, Waters and Places also provided practical advice on how to address environmental health issues (perhaps an early example of health impact assessment) by suggesting that before a place was colonized, it was necessary for the character of the soil to be assessed.
	In the course of the subsequent demise of Greek-Roman civilization, much scientific knowledge was lost, and in the Middle Ages, unsanitary conditions prevailed, especially in cities, although regulations were implemented with penalties for pollution of water supplies and other environmental nuisances. Quarantine was also a way in which environmental health was practised, to protect from the corruption of air (the theory of miasma—‘bad air’), in addition to personal hygiene measures.
	During the mid-nineteenth century and beyond, awareness of threats to public health from poor sanitation grew, and with this ‘sanitary awakening’, widespread sanitary reform measures were implemented. These were spearheaded by an enquiry by Edwin Chadwick, a Poor Law Commissioner, who, in 1842, published a major report on sanitary conditions in England (Chadwick 1842). Chadwick’s investigation into the causes of poverty concluded that people often became poor as a result of ill-health from an adverse environment (that situation prevails today). In 1848, with the passage of the Public Health Act in the United Kingdom (Calman 1998), provision was made for the appointment of Inspectors of Nuisances—the predecessors of today’s environmental health officers. A national board of health, and district health boards were also recommended.
	It was John Snow who traced the origin of the cholera epidemics in London to contaminated water, and who thereby conducted one of the first comprehensive environmental epidemiology investigations—a key function of importance in the practice of environmental health. In the United States, the Shattuck report in 1850 (Winslow 1949) similarly drew attention to the links between poor living conditions and health, and recommended the establishment of state and local boards of health, as well as local sanitary associations and regular (environmental) health surveys.
	From its roots in antiquity to the sanitation movement of the 1800s, environmental health practice was fairly narrowly focused on sanitation, environmental hygiene, inspection and control, and has since gradually broadened to address health and environment concerns in the context of sustainable development (von Schirnding 2002a), with emphasis on ecosystems and ecology (Rapport et al. 2009). In the early-to mid-twentieth century, air pollution disasters (e.g. Meuse Valley, Belgium in 1930, Donora, Pennsylvania in 1948, and London, United Kingdom in 1952); industrial disasters like Bhopal, India; as well as mounting evidence of the carcinogenic, reproductive and other effects of chemicals (highlighted in Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring, 1962) led to increased awareness of toxic chemicals in the environment. This awareness was further heightened by such incidents as the Love Canal toxic waste site disaster in the United States in the 1970s.
	Environmental health has thus expanded beyond its horizons. Today environmental health practitioners have to concern themselves with a wide variety of issues, with virtually any aspect of the environment having the potential to affect human health. The environment can impact chronic diseases such as cancer, lung diseases, or birth defects, as well as infectious diseases like gastroenteritis, respiratory infections, or vector-borne diseases like malaria. Typical environmental health concerns include ambient and indoor air quality, food safety, water quality, sanitation, waste management, housing quality, noise pollution, electromagnetic radiation, occupational and industrial hygiene, vector control, and toxic chemical exposures.
	The environment has much broader impacts too—both positive and negative. For example it may provide protection and resiliency to natural disasters or predispose people to harm (for example from building in earthquake-prone areas). It may promote health through the provision of nutritious and safe food, drinking water, provision of recreational opportunities, interaction with nature, and so on.
	In particular, concern about health effects associated with natural ecosystems and global (climate) change has grown in recent years, necessitating the need to address health issues in the context of complex (eco) systems analysis (McMichael et al. 2006; Patz et al. 2008; McMichael 2013). With growing appreciation of the links between ecology and health, the integrity of natural ecosystems, and the transdisciplinary and intersectoral nature of environmental health, there have been calls for new epidemiological approaches to dealing with environmental health hazards (Soskolne et al. 2007). With the global spotlight on sustainable development, practitioners have begun to look at environmental health risks more holistically, from the viewpoint of various economic sectors like housing, transport, or energy, and settings or systems like the city at large.
	This approach can be tracked through the various United Nations (UN) conferences held on the environment and sustainable development going back over the past 40 or more years. These are briefly highlighted next, as well as some of the key principles and goals articulated therein.





Global initiatives


	Following the UN Conference on the Human Environment held in Stockholm, Sweden (UN 1972), in 1983 the World Commission on Environment and Development (UNCED) headed by former Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland (World Commission on Environment and Development 1987) linked the issue of environmental protection to economic growth and development. The Commission’s report ‘Our Common Future’ (World Commission on Environment and Development 1987) launched the concept of sustainable development into the mainstream of world debate.
	Sustainable development essentially means meeting people’s development needs in such a way as not to exceed the earth’s carrying capacity in the longer term. Although specific definitions for sustainable development vary, broadly speaking, the concept is concerned with balancing environmental, social, and economic objectives in order to maximize societal well-being, both now and in the future.
	The UN Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) (UN 1992)—a watershed event popularly referred to as the ‘Earth Summit’—resulted in the adoption of Agenda 21—a global action plan with concrete goals, targets, and outputs for measures needed to achieve environmentally sustainable development into the twenty-first century. It also resulted in the ‘Rio Declaration’ which encompassed important agreements on 27 principles adopted by 178 nations, including the Precautionary Principle, the Polluter Pays Principle, the Common But Differentiated Responsibilities principle (CBDR), and other principles such as the principle of intergenerational equity, the principle of access to information, and the decision-making process, and the principle of integrated decision-making (these are discussed further in Section 3). Several key conventions were also adopted, such as those on climate change (including the Kyoto Protocol) and on biological diversity (under which was negotiated the Cartagena Protocol).
	The Rio Declaration, in its preamble, alluded to the central role of health in sustainable development by stating that ‘Human beings are at the centre of concerns for sustainable development. They are entitled to a healthy and productive life in harmony with nature’. This concept was further developed during the World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD) (UN 2002a) which took place in Johannesburg, to review progress 10 years after UNCED.
	At WSSD, health was singled out as one of the five priority issues to be addressed, along with water, energy, agriculture, and biodiversity (Annan 2002; UN 2002b). In the Johannesburg Plan of Implementation (JPOI) which emerged from this conference, particular emphasis was placed on health issues in relation to environment and poverty concerns. Improving access to safe water, sanitation, clean air, improved waste management, and sound management of chemicals were among the key issues of importance for environmental health practitioners that received special attention in Johannesburg (von Schirnding 2005).
	This momentum was somewhat lost in the subsequent run-up to the twentieth anniversary of UNCED. ‘Rio+20’ (UN 2012) aimed to review progress over the past 20 years and to renew political commitments to sustainable development. While many new green economy policies were endorsed in the final Rio+20 document ‘The Future We Want’, no new international commitments nor legally binding agreements were made, albeit voluntary agreements were made by countries to meet their own sustainable development targets. Coming out of WSSD where health made a strong showing, and out of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) process (UN 2000) where health had a central position, health did not feature strongly at Rio +20. This confirmed the pressing need for the health community, and especially environmental health practitioners, to remain actively engaged in the sustainable development agenda (Kleinert et al. 2012; Singh et al. 2012).
	Of note, all three conferences (UNCED with its focus on environment, WSSD with its focus on the social dimension, especially—poverty, and Rio+20 with its focus on the green economy) failed to ensure the integration of the three pillars of sustainable development. The process of setting sustainable development goals in the follow-up process to Rio+20 (the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development), which was initiated at the Sustainable Development Summit in 2015 (Barbier 2012; UN 2015; Bhandary et al. 2015) aims to ensure that these three pillars of sustainable development are not considered separately from each other. Progress towards achievement of these goals is now reviewed under the newly constituted High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development (UN 2018), one of the important outcomes of the Sustainable Development Summit. Health, and environmental health in particular, can be used as a tool by practitioners to integrate across the three dimensions of sustainable development. Measurable targets (and indicators) are needed to ensure health remains a prerequisite for, and an outcome of, sustainable development—in all its dimensions. This is discussed further in Section 7.





Concept and scope of environmental health


	In considering the practice of environmental health, it is apparent from the foregoing discussion that the nature and scope of the discipline has undergone considerable transformation, especially in light of the emerging concept of sustainable development and sustainability. In its broadest context, environmental health is concerned with the health effects associated with the environment. This includes both the physical (natural or ‘built’) as well as the social environment. It is less concerned with the health of the environment per se, as it is with its impacts on human health. In this respect, environmental health is an integral part of the discipline of public health, with strong links to the environmental sciences.
	The World Health Organization (WHO) has defined environmental health in various ways to include ‘Those aspects of human health and disease that are determined by factors in the environment. It also refers to the theory and practice of assessing and controlling factors in the environment that can potentially affect health’ (WHO 1989). While health has been defined by the WHO as ‘A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity’ (WHO 1946), environmental health has tended to focus mainly on the physical environment, with less emphasis on the social environment and on social and mental well-being. Nevertheless, both the physical as well as the social aspects of the environment are important aspects of the realm of environmental health.
	An updated definition of environmental health by the WHO gives added emphasis to this social component and describes environmental health as comprising ‘those aspects of human health, including quality of life, that are determined by physical, chemical, biological, social, and psychosocial factors in the environment. It also refers to the theory and practice of assessing, correcting, controlling, and preventing those factors in the environment that can potentially affect adversely the health of present and future generations’ (WHO 2004). This definition incorporates, as well, a focus on sustainability, in so far as it alludes to the health of both present and future generations. Environmental health is thus not only concerned with the identification, control, and remediation of factors in the environment which can affect health, but also with disease prevention and enhancement of intergenerational human health.
	The intersectoral nature of environmental health is recognized in the WHO’s Constitution (WHO 1948), which states that the Organization shall ‘promote, in cooperation with other specialized agencies, where necessary, the improvement of nutrition, housing, sanitation, recreation, economic, or working conditions and other aspects of environmental hygiene’.
	The concept has its roots in a number of international strategies and fora, including the 1977 ‘Health-For-All’ strategy of WHO (and its renewal and subsequent updates: WHO 1977, 1981, 1998; Yach 1996), the Alma-Ata conference on Primary Health Care in 1978 (WHO 1978), the World Health Assembly (WHA) Technical Discussion on Intersectoral Action (WHO 1986a), the Ottawa Charter on Health Promotion (WHO 1986b), the Sundsvall meeting on Supportive Environments for Health (Haglund et al. 1996), the WHO Commission on Environment and Health (WHO 1992), and the international conference on ‘Intersectoral Action for Health—A Cornerstone for Health-for-All in the 21st Century’, held in Canada in 1997 (WHO 1997; Kreisel and von Schirnding 1998).
	Addressing the underlying multifactorial determinants of health is essential in order to ensure health improvements which are sustainable over the long term. Primary prevention is a key aspect of the work of the environmental health practitioner, and involves implementation of interventions before ill-health occurs. It includes health promotion interventions geared towards general health and well-being, as well as interventions on specific known causes of disease-for example the phaseout of lead—a well-documented neurotoxicant—in gasoline. Pollution prevention is an example of a primary preventive measure, involving strategies such as source reduction, waste minimization, reuse, recycling, emissions control, waste disposal, and clean-up. Secondary preventive measures can be implemented which are targeted at an early stage of exposure before health impacts manifest (for example lead screening), while tertiary preventive measures involve the early identification and treatment of people with a disease (Goldman 2016).
	By addressing health, environment, and development concerns in an intersectoral way, a win–win situation occurs: the health sector gains because disease prevention can move upstream and take advantage of the intersectoral approach to development and environmental improvements. The environmental sector gains because environmental issues can become grounded in matters of local and direct concern to people.
	In the following subsections, we look briefly at some of the major trends in health, environment, and development in recent years, before highlighting environmental health issues and the burden of environmentally related disease, which are of importance in directing the work of the environmental health practitioner.





Global trends


	Of overriding significance is the fact that on a global scale there has been unprecedented wealth creation and economic development in the past decades, coupled with intensified global efforts targeting major causes of death and disease throughout the world. The sanitary movement of the 1800s mentioned earlier had a major impact on the reduction of infectious disease mortality and resulted in major improvements (increases) in life expectancy. More recently this has been accelerated in part due to such initiatives as the MDGs process which set in motion an ambitious programme of goals and targets to eradicate poverty by the year 2015 (UN 2000), and its successor, the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) process.
	Life expectancies for men and women have increased, and a greater proportion of total deaths now occur among people over the age of 70 years, compared with 20 years ago. Infectious disease mortality rates have declined, and burdens of HIV, TB, and malaria have all fallen. Substantially fewer children under the age of five years are dying (Wang et al. 2013), with deaths in this age group having declined by almost 60% since 1970. Between 1990 and 2015, the under-5 mortality rate dropped from 90 to 43 deaths per 1,000 live births (UNDP 2015). Nonetheless, in 2015, 16,000 children continue to die every day, mostly from preventable and environmentally related diseases like pneumonia, diarrhoea, and malaria. This burden is greatest in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA).
	Despite huge progress in human development and poverty eradication over the past decades (over one billion people were lifted out of poverty since 1990), today, nearly one billion people still live in poverty, including a higher percentage of women than men, and big gaps in progress remain in some regions of the world, especially in sub-Saharan Africa and southern Asia. Moreover, the distribution of income at the country level has worsened in much of the world, despite narrowing in gaps in health and education (UNDP 2011). At the same time, global wealth has become increasingly concentrated in the wealthiest one percent of the population, who had 32% of global wealth in 2000, compared to 46% in 2010 (UNDP 2016).
	Human population growth is increasing by 75–80 million people a year (Sachs 2012) and is projected to grow to 9.7 billion by 2050 (UNDP 2016). In 2014, over half of the world’s population lived in urban areas (UNDP 2016), and, with the addition of another 2.5 billion people by 2050, this number may rise to two-thirds of the world’s population. Over half the population will be under the age of 18 years. Urban growth will be greatest in Africa and Asia, followed by Latin America and Oceania. By 2030 it is expected that there will be 41 mega-cities with populations of over 10 million inhabitants. The fastest growing cities are likely to have the highest concentration of slums or informal settlements. Already around 880 million people live in slums, and it is predicted that 40% of the world’s future expansion will occur in slums (UNDP 2016).
	With rapid economic development and urbanization in developing countries, cities are becoming increasingly overcrowded and polluted. Air and water pollution levels have been increasing, as has the generation of municipal and hazardous waste. In the last 30 years, however, in many industrialized nations stronger environmental laws have resulted in cleaner and safer drinking and recreational water as well as in improved air quality. On a global basis nevertheless, pollution of air and water supplies is worsening (Goldman and Torres 2009). Drinking water is under pressure from such factors as pollution, ageing infrastructure, population growth, and resulting increased demand and consumption. While demand is increasing, supplies are becoming more erratic and uncertain, with water-related impacts on agriculture, health, and income levels (UNDP 2016). In general, growth in incomes has been associated with deterioration in key environmental indicators such as carbon dioxide emissions, soil and water quality, and forest cover (UNDP 2011).





Environmental health issues


	The practice of environmental health is inextricably involved with disease prevention and control. Environmental health practitioners face a growing diversity of environmental hazards to deal with, in many different settings, in developed and developing countries alike. Traditional risks associated with poverty often coexist alongside risks associated with urbanization and industrialization, agriculture, and land-use practices. For example, water supplies may be contaminated by pesticides and faeces exposing consumers both to microorganisms and toxic substances, and air pollution may stem both from burning dirty household fuels such as coal, wood, and other sources of biomass fuel used for cooking and heating, as well as from the use of industrial fossil fuels. In poor countries, accidental chemical releases may occur more commonly, and there may be fewer means to protect people. Poor countries (and the poor in wealthy countries) may also be more vulnerable to the health effects associated with natural disasters and climate change.
	Problems may have to be dealt with simultaneously at the global, national, and local levels. Some problems may be of special relevance at the local or micro level (for example water supply and sanitation, waste disposal, or toxic chemicals) while other problems may be more important at the regional or global level (for example global climate change, or long-range transport of air pollution).
	Health impacts associated with global change and disturbances to natural ecosystems (disruption of bio-geophysical systems such as the climate system and associated rising temperatures, declining rainfall, extreme weather events, degradation of land and water, depletion of resources, and other effects) (McMichael 2013) have to be dealt with at all levels and, as indicated earlier, may impact severely on poor countries and on the poor in general. Potential impacts are numerous such as heat-related mortality, health impacts associated with extreme weather events, changes in vector-borne disease distribution, disruption of agricultural production, or threats to drinking water supply. While poor countries have contributed least to global climate change, they have experienced the greatest variability in weather (such as loss in rainfall in some regions and flooding and others) with implications for agricultural productivity and livelihoods (UNDP 2011). Without appropriate action, by 2030, over 100 million more people could be living in poverty (UNDP 2018).
	Problems may differ in urban and rural environments, although increasingly the divide between urban and rural is becoming blurred. While cities provide numerous benefits associated with increased job opportunities and provision of essential services and facilities, environment and health problems may nevertheless be profound, especially in cities that are not economically homogeneous. In informal settlement areas in particular, infectious diseases associated with inadequate water and sanitation, and dirty household fuels may be prevalent. Rich and poor people live in very different epidemiological worlds, even within the same city, and this situation occurs in both high-income as well as low-income countries (WHO and UN-Habitat 2010). Infant mortality rates are often higher among poor segments of urban populations in developed countries.
	Lead poisoning illustrates very well the unequal burden of risk borne by poor inner-city children who are not only more exposed to sources of lead in and around the home environment (from flaking lead-based paint, for example, or contaminated air and dust), but are also more vulnerable to the toxic effects of lead, being often nutritionally deprived and having inadequate access to healthcare facilities. This is true even of children living in such countries as the United States and parts of Europe (Tong et al. 2000). Within inner-city areas, studies from South Africa have shown substantial socioeconomic differentials in blood lead burden among inner-city children (von Schirnding et al. 1991).
	Poorer countries also have higher levels of household deprivation as evidenced by such factors as indoor air pollution, and inadequate access to clean water and sanitation. The environmental burdens of poverty fall directly on poor populations. As income levels rise, however, and with increased affluence and associated lifestyles and consumption patterns, these burdens tend to lessen, concomitant with environmental burdens which are more diffuse, indirect, and delayed, and affect a more temporally and spatially displaced public (UNDP 2011). Risks associated with community urban air pollution are an example.
	With further economic development, these more localized burdens tend eventually to lessen too (or be displaced elsewhere), while environmental risks associated with global effects—for example, greenhouse gas emissions—tend to rise with high levels of materials and energy consumption and waste generation (UNDP 2011). The most disadvantaged people carry a double (or triple) burden of deprivation—they are more vulnerable to the global effects of environmental degradation, have often to cope with new and emerging risks associated with rapid industrialization and urbanization, but also have to deal with threats to their immediate environment like indoor air pollution, dirty water, and poor sanitation.





Burden of environmentally related disease


	It has been estimated by WHO (WHO 2016) that in 2012, globally around 12.6 million deaths (23% of all deaths), were attributable to modifiable environmental risks, and 22% of the disease burden measured in DALYs (disability-adjusted life year—a measure of overall disease burden, expressed as the number of years lost due to ill-health, disability or early death) attributable to environmental factors. Children under 5, and older adults were most affected. Among children under 5, it was estimated that 26% of all deaths could be prevented if environmental risks were removed. Adults between the ages of 50 and 75 were found to be most affected by environmental factors. Diseases with the largest environmental fraction (in DALYs) included cardiovascular diseases, diarrheal diseases, and respiratory tract infections. These are related to such factors as ambient and household air pollution, and water, sanitation, and hygiene.
	Recent findings indicate a predominance of non-communicable disease risks compared with 1990. With advances in economic development and other factors, as alluded to earlier, there has been a shift away from infectious, parasitic, and nutritional diseases towards non-communicable diseases (NCD)s. In contrast, deaths associated with ambient air, chemical and soil pollution associated with modern industrial development are increasing (Landrigan et al. 2018)
	Nevertheless, still today, pneumonia and diarrhoea (associated with household air pollution or water and sanitation) are the leading killers of young children. Diarrhoea accounts for 20% of deaths among children under the age of 5 years, while lower respiratory infections account for account for around 18% of deaths in children under 5. Nearly all of these deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, reflecting uneven progress in reducing child mortality (UNICEF 2012). The highest fraction of deaths and disease that could be addressed by improving environmental conditions is in low-and middle-income countries. In 2015, 844 million people lacked a basic drinking water service, while 2.3 billion lacked a basic sanitation service (WHO and UNICEF 2017).
	The global burden of disease (GBD) estimates provide a sense of where environmental health practice could make a big impact in future. Continued support to improve access to water and sanitation services and a transition to cleaner household fuels is a high priority in much of sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. Nearly 90% of the deaths due to diarrhoea worldwide have been attributed to unsafe water, inadequate sanitation, and poor hygiene. In addition, around three billion people worldwide use solid fuels as their main cooking fuel (UNICEF 2012).
	Further information on the relevance of global burden of risk estimates for environmental health practice is provided in Box 11.6.1 and Table 11.6.1, which are based on the 2015 GBD study (Forouzanfar et al. 2016). It should be noted that while both the WHO study (WHO 2016) and the GBD study (Forouzanfar et al. 2016) found environmental factors to be a major cause of premature death, disease, and disability, the GBD estimates are slightly at variance with those reported earlier by WHO. WHO for example attributed 12.6 million deaths to unhealthy environments, and the GBD 2015 study 9 million premature deaths (16% of global mortality). This discrepancy is most likely the result of differing definitions of environment (Landrigan et al. 2018). In respect of specific risk factors like ambient air pollution, and household air pollution, resulting discrepancies are probably in part due to changes in computational methodology, and in regard to water and sanitation, differing definitions of access to safe water.
	 	Box 11.6.1 Global burden of risk estimates main priorities for environmental health practice, e.g. in prevention, research, and policy development
	The 2015 global comparative risk assessment of burden of disease and injury provides data on major environmental risks, discussed here (Forouzanfar et al. 2016). It should be noted however, that the 2017 comparative risk assessment of burden of disease and injury provides alternate estimates, based on, inter-alia, different modelling processes for air pollution (Stanaway et al. 2018).
	Of the 79 risk factors and risk clusters examined, several related directly to environmental factors, including water and sanitation, air pollution (ambient particulate matter pollution, household air pollution from solid fuels and ambient ozone pollution), residential radon, and lead exposure. It was estimated that 9 million premature deaths in 2015 were from environmentally related disease, contributing to 16% of total global mortality.
	In 2015 4.2 million deaths were due to ambient particulate air pollution, and 2.9 million deaths were associated with household air pollution from solid fuels.1.8 million deaths resulted from diseases related to unsafe water, sanitation, and handwashing.
	Environmental factors were responsible for 21% of all cardiovascular disease related deaths, 26% of deaths due to ischaemic heart disease, 23% due to stroke, 51% due to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and 43% due to lung cancer.
	Between 1990 and 2015, global exposure to such factors as unsafe sanitation and household air pollution each decreased by more than 25%, and attributable DALYs declined significantly for unsafe sanitation and water, and household air pollution.
	Environmental risks declined steadily in relation to the sociodemographic index (SDI).
	In 1990, household air pollution ranked fourth in leading risk factors, while in 2015 it ranked eighth. Ambient particulate matter pollution ranked sixth in 1990 and 2015. In 1990 unsafe water ranked second in leading risk factors, whereas in 2015 unsafe water ranked as the fourteenth leading risk factor. Unsafe sanitation ranked seventh in 1990 and nineteenth in 2015.
	From 2005 to 2015, global deaths which were attributable to unsafe water and no hand washing with soap, fell by more than 12%. DALYs decreased by more than 20%. Even greater declines occurred in deaths and DALYs for unsafe sanitation since 2005. Reductions in the attributable mortality and DALYs due to diarrheal diseases associated with unsafe water, sanitation, and hygiene where especially marked.
	In regard to household air pollution, since 2005, attributable deaths decreased by 13% to 2.9 million deaths in 2015, and the disease burden decreased by 20.3% over this period. Both ambient particulate matter and household air pollution where among the 10 largest contributors to global DALYs in 2015.
