11.9


Training of public health professionals in developing countries


	San Hone and Roger Detels





Introduction to training of public health professionals in developing countries


	Public health and medical systems and training are essential for the health of a country (Heller et al. 2007; Bangdiwala et al. 2010). This is particularly true for developing countries, in which great disparities in wealth exist and there are limited funds to invest in the health of their citizens. Developing countries have being exerting tremendous efforts towards achieving universal health coverage (UHC) through primary health-led approaches for which public health services and medical resources must be made available at national, provincial, subprovincial, and local district levels. The skills and requirements of public health and medical professionals at each of these levels differ and are unique within each level. The mandate of public health is broad, and therefore requires some level of specialization within the profession. Thus, various public health professionals are responsible for assuring access to primary healthcare, as well as maternal and child health services, protection of the environment, including provision of adequate and safe levels of water and safe disposal of human and other waste, implementation of community health programmes such as immunization coverage, prevention, and control of endemic and epidemic health threats from microbial agents, addressing increases in chronic illnesses, and administration/management of the broad and diverse public health workforce at each level. Thus, public health training requires providing training not only in medical sciences, but also in technical fields such as microbiology, chemistry, the physical sciences, management sciences, and behavioural, social, and political sciences, statistics, epidemiology, and research methodologies.
	The World Economic Forum launched a 4-year US$100 million fund to support two non-governmental organizations, Last Mile Health and Living Goods, to train 50,000 health workers in six countries, bringing global attention to the need to improve healthcare at the lowest levels (Winters et al. 2018). The focus is to demonstrate how technology can reinvent community healthcare at scale to ensure quality healthcare to marginalized populations in lower-/middle-income countries, using utilitarian but cutting edge strategies to train health workers; e.g. digital education in the implementation of ‘M Health’ discussed next.
	The public health workforce draws individuals from a variety of backgrounds relevant to their intended public health roles, including medicine, nursing, and the behavioural, management, and biological/physical sciences (Beaglehole and Dal Poz 2003). Generally, health training programmes provide training at the certificate level mainly for health professionals and others serving at the local level, which may include health volunteers (who are the core of many health systems and provide service at the village level), specialized training (e.g. midwife), as well as training at the master’s level (usually requiring 1–3 years of graduate study) and the doctoral level (requiring 4–6 years of graduate study) for those who become leaders of public health programmes and research. Training at the graduate level also includes specialized training in specific fields for those who focus on environmental, social, behavioural, and healthcare issues of public health essential for a broad mandate of public health. Although most public health training programmes provide basic initial training in public health, there is also an important need to provide postgraduate and refresher training to ensure that the public health workforce continues to utilize the most modern strategies and resources.
	In the opinion of some public health professionals, including the authors, there is too often a mismatch between the roles and responsibilities of public health professionals at each level and the training that they receive. Too often, public health curricula in developing countries were developed by the European colonialists based on the European system, and do not adequately address current health problems of the country. This mismatch reflects both the content of the training programmes and the strategies/content of the country’s public health system itself. Public health planners, managers, and administrators are confronted by a range of barriers to achieving optimal public health, including funding constraints, politics, and the scarcity of qualified personnel and public health leaders. It is the responsibility of public health trainers to develop strategies and curricula to overcome these barriers and to ensure that the training of public health professionals is appropriate and has the flexibility to provide trainees with the ability to devise new strategies to address constantly changing public health issues and problems. In some instances, this requires reconsideration of the current public health structure to ensure maximum effectiveness. Public health programmes need to ensure that health professionals in training see a clear career path for themselves, that there is an optimal distribution of health professionals, particularly to rural and remote areas, and that the system provides both monetary and non-monetary incentives to motivate them. In this chapter, we address each of these issues in greater depth and make suggestions for improvement and enhancement of health training in developing countries.





Typical public health structures in developing countries—health system structure in developing countries


	Typically, government health systems in developing countries have a tiered system for providing health, comprising the national, provincial, subprovincial, and local levels. In addition, in most developing countries there are private healthcare sectors that provide services primarily to the wealthy, and national and international non-governmental organizations that also provide public health services through community volunteers and clinical services. Sometimes these operate outside the purview of the government public health system which can create problems (see chapter 11.12). In this chapter we will focus on training relevant for the government-sponsored public health system.
	The greatest number of health personnel work at the lowest level, with decreasing numbers at the subprovincial, provincial, and national levels. The highest levels of training and responsibility focus on the national level. The duration and intensity of training for health workers increase with greater levels of responsibility for programme leadership.
	The public health systems in developing countries are usually divided into three levels: (1) the central administrative level that develops health policies, recommends strategies for the entire country and administers national programmes, national training institutions, and national hospitals that provide complicated tertiary care; (2) the middle level comprised of provincial and subprovincial health departments that are responsible for implementing national policies and programmes, and provincial hospitals that often see referrals from the local healthcare facilities and conduct regional training programmes for local health professionals and volunteer health workers; and (3) the local or district level that implements national and provincial programmes such as primary healthcare, maternal and child health programmes, and immunization campaigns (Fig. 11.9.1).
	Fig. 11.9.1 The health system.
	Reproduced by kind permission of Dr Lo Veasnakiry.
	The district level (health centres or health posts) usually provides a minimum package of primary healthcare and public health activities to a population of approximately 5,000–30,000 each and a referral hospital for low-level uncomplicated health problems. The health force at the village health centre includes primary/community healthcare workers, nurses and/or nurse midwives who receive training for one or more years and are responsible for primary healthcare services, including maternal and child, family planning, childhood immunizations, and delivery of treatment for non-communicable diseases, HIV and tuberculosis which required daily observed treatment. With the recent trend of moving towards the global elimination of certain communicable diseases such as malaria, vaccine-preventable childhood diseases (polio, measles), and elimination of mother to child transmission of HIV and syphilis, etc., the role of the primary health care providers has expanded.
	In some countries, these primary care providers are assisted by public health staff who receive about six or more months of training focusing on health education for the endemic and epidemic diseases and environmental sanitation activities. At the village or commune level, there are often volunteer health workers who are selected by the local population and provide minimal first aid and referral to the district health centre or hospital, and who assure directly observed therapy for tuberculosis and other diseases. They also help organize immunization sessions, give oral vaccinations (e.g. polio) and high-dose vitamin A to children, but are not allowed to give injections. In addition, they promote health education activities, including promoting environmental sanitation. The position carries with it a level of prestige that is its main reward, although some level of remuneration is usually advisable. Volunteer health workers usually receive training for several weeks. The characteristics of an ideal volunteer health worker have been outlined by Taylor et al. (2018), and include knowledge of the local population and culture, good interpersonal and communication skills, the ability to see the world from others’ perspectives, a non-judgemental attitude, ‘imbeddedness’ within the community, shared demographic characteristics, and a desire to assist people.





Responsibilities/roles of public health professionals at each level in developing countries


	Levels of training and duration vary, depending on the role that the graduate is expected to play in the health system. At the highest level, usually for bachelor’s or master’s programmes, the trainees receive instruction in administration of health programmes (although care is usually taught through the medical education system), content and strategies for health education, and behavioural modification to achieve a healthy lifestyle, strategies for assuring a safe water supply, appropriate disposal of human and other waste products, oral health, systems of health financing, control strategies for the major infectious diseases affecting the country (which usually include tuberculosis, malaria, parasite infections, and HIV, as well as any locally endemic diseases), and administration and strategies for immunization programmes. Some developing countries require a medical degree or other health science or technical degree as a prerequisite for entering into a master of public health (MPH) programme. Graduates of these programmes are expected to lead public health programmes. Programmes at this level usually require the trainee to complete an internship in the field at the local or rural level to ensure their understanding of the system and the culture of the populace at the point of delivery. Research methodologies, if available, are usually taught in the relatively few PhD/doctoral programmes in medical and public health institutions. However, many developing countries are only recently investing in schools of public health, and in most, research is not conducted. Recently there has been a movement to use the internet to provide distance learning for public health workers at the MPH level and for postgraduate/refresher courses that target developing countries, which are offered through various universities and government agencies (Mokwena et al. 2007). Although these programmes are probably quite useful for teaching methodology and public health strategies, they may have difficulties in training relevant to practising at the local level in different countries, as they cannot offer hands-on field experience. One strategy to overcome this difficulty is to have discussion sessions on specific topics through the web, which include practitioners from the local level. Because most developing countries do not have the resources to invest in research programmes, most public health programmes are not evidence-based.
	At the village level, many countries employ volunteer health workers who have had only a few weeks of training and perform very routine functions, such as tending to minor wounds, routine first aid, and encouraging villagers to take their medications as recommended by physicians and allied health workers at the district or higher levels. The role of the volunteer health worker may include home visits, first aid, treatment of simple and common ailments, health education, nutrition and surveillance, family planning, referrals, collection of data on vital events (births, deaths), and assisting more highly trained health professionals such as the nurse midwives. They usually have the best knowledge of the village and the villagers in terms of health status and needs, and are often selected by the communities themselves. To be successful they need to be an integral part of their community and have the support of that community. It is important that they receive some reward from the villages, as they are not usually paid by the government.
	A typical health structure at the district/township level is presented in Figure 11.9.2.
	Health professionals at the village health post include nurse midwives and allied health personnel and health workers who usually have one to three years of training. Nurse midwives are responsible for encouraging and implementing enrolment in prenatal programmes, staffing antenatal clinics, delivering babies, and providing postnatal guidance. They need to be able to recognize difficult pregnancies that will require more highly trained medical personnel to ensure safe delivery. These problem pregnancies are usually referred to a higher-level facility. Transportation to the hospital, particularly for emergency and complicated deliveries, can be a serious problem. Allied health personnel with nurse midwives usually perform the other medical, sanitation, and health education roles, and direct and facilitate health campaigns such as polio immunizations days. In some countries, nurse midwives perform both roles, although they may be assisted by assistant nurse midwives and/or public health staff who have had less but some training. Nurse midwives may be responsible for as many as 10–15 villages. The rural and urban health centres may have facilities for care of patients, including injuries requiring more than simple first aid. Patients with complicated illnesses, however, are referred to higher-level health facilities, and are diagnosed and treated by physicians.
	With the trend towards UHC, many countries are striving to identify feasible and cost-effective strategies for providing health services. Major strategies include decentralization of some services that were previously not available at the village health level; for example, performing HIV screening tests and introducing a package of disease reduction services for primary healthcare workers. Under these schemes, primary healthcare providers, nurse midwives, and lower-level health workers are also responsible for conducting packages of activities to target communicable diseases for which the government has pledged to achieve elimination by a specific time. These usually include active case surveillance, implementing appropriate screening tests, implementing immunization campaigns, introducing standardized treatment, and implementing timely reporting.
	The district hospitals may have a laboratory to perform routine procedures, but are usually not able to do more sophisticated biochemical and microbiological assays, which are usually done at the provincial level. One problem with the laboratories at each of the different levels is that quality control procedures are often not implemented and standardized. Few of these laboratories participate in quality control programmes, although some wealthier developing countries (e.g. China) have implemented quality control programmes at the county and provincial levels. Thus, there is a problem with achieving valid test results and safety in many of these laboratories (Callaway 2012). A second problem is staffing these laboratories with well-trained, competent technicians who need to periodically update their laboratory skills to ensure valid results and safe procedures.
	Fig. 11.9.2 Health structure/system at the district level.
	Complicated surgical procedures and medical management of serious health problems are usually performed only at the provincial and national/tertiary levels. A serious problem in developing countries with limited resources and populations residing in remote areas is diagnosis and timely transport of patients to tertiary care facilities to ensure successful treatment.
	Training of health workers may occur at each of the levels of the public health system, although training of higher levels of health professionals is usually limited to universities, medical schools, and schools of public health, dentistry, health sciences, and nursing.





Education for health professionals in developing countries


	In all developing countries, completion of medical school is required for healthcare professionals working in the various healthcare facilities at the national, provincial and district level hospitals. Many developing countries require graduating physicians to work a minimum number of years at the district level as a strategy for providing healthcare at the peripheral levels of the health system. A medical degree or a master’s degree in public health is often also required at the national and provincial levels for staff responsible for administering national programmes. Specialized and advanced medical training is usually only required at the national level healthcare facilities, and sometimes at provincial-level health facilities. Specialized training is usually required for health professionals conducting dental care and pharmaceutical services.
	Advanced training is required for health professionals who will design and direct health information systems such as disease surveillance, and who will design and conduct health research to inform policy decisions and evaluate health programmes. These activities are usually directed at the national level, although they may involve staff at the provincial, district, and local levels.
	Nurses usually require bachelor’s degree level training. However, midwives who work at the local level may receive an associate midwife degree, which may require only 1–2 years of certificate-level training, depending on the country. Some countries also have midwife assistants who receive shorter periods of training. Staff providing lower-level nursing, medical imaging, sanitary services, low-level laboratory services, and physical therapy usually have limited training.





Problems with providing public health training in developing countries


	Health professionals at the district level, who often have had only 1–3 years of training, are expected to assist in planning and management of public health programmes, recognition of the need for and initial conduct of outbreak investigations; implementation and monitoring of immunization programmes; prevention, treatment, and monitoring of tuberculosis and HIV programmes (e.g. directly observed therapy); implementing specific communicable disease elimination strategies (e.g. active case investigation for malaria elimination); and basic health education in strategies to prevent disease and promote healthy lifestyles. Their training may include the various skills and knowledge required to carry out these responsibilities, including the need for collection of accurate data that can be used to plan and support effective health systems (International Institute for Viral Registration and Statistics 1989). Thus, there is a need for congruency in the training of public health professionals and the responsibilities they will assume (Sudhinaraset et al. 2013). A major barrier to achieving proper training at all levels of public health training is the scarcity of qualified faculties in these programmes. Refresher training for health workers is important to ensure that they keep up with current and changing strategies and policies. The training of health professionals at the local level is often not integrated, so staff members know only their own responsibilities but do not have a holistic understanding of where their efforts fit into the broad public health system.
	Funding for public health programmes and training is often a low priority for political leaders and decision-makers. The majority of health programmes in developing countries are subsidized by international donors who have their own health agendas, which may differ from those of the country (see chapter 11.12).
	Clear public health career tracks are often not apparent for qualified individuals who wish to choose a career in public health. Complicating recruitment of public health professionals at every level is the low level of remuneration. Often physicians who are willing to work in public health must also have private practices to generate enough income to support their families (Chomitz et al. 1998; Ferrinho et al. 2004). Thus, they are not able to dedicate their full efforts to their public health responsibilities. Physicians are often reluctant to work in remote rural areas (WHO 2010a). Public health workers at the peripheral level are usually paid low wages or are expected to volunteer their services. In these situations, other reward structures must be created to motivate volunteers and low-level workers (Henderson and Tulloch 2008; Mangham and Hanson 2008).





Strategies to overcome barriers to optimal public health training


	The fundamental principles for designing public health training involve both academic and practical components. For training programmes to be responsive to needs, the needs must be clearly delineated. It is important that the tasks and responsibilities of health professionals at every level of the public health system be designed to meet the needs of the constituency and the level of responsibility expected at that level. A first step is to conduct needs assessments at each level, from the local and provincial levels to the national level, and from primary health care providers to researchers and policy-makers (Bangdiwala et al. 2010). The assessment should involve members of the community or constituency at that level. Formulation of the responsibilities and tasks at each level can then be clearly defined, and documentation of formal job descriptions provided so that an appropriate training curriculum may be developed for health workers expected to perform the required tasks at that level of the system. Training resources should then be identified and/or developed for the required training at each level of the public health system. At each level, the curriculum should be designed and evaluated for responsiveness to the job descriptions of the positions that graduates are intended to fill. The faculty of the training programmes at each level should include individuals who have had experience in delivering services at that level. The training should include providing an understanding of where the responsibilities of the health professional being trained fit into the public health system of the country.





Incorporating new technologies


	Development and widespread use of hand-held computers/phones, global positioning systems, and increasingly sophisticated communications systems, called ‘M Health’, provide opportunities for monitoring, mentoring, and enhancing health activities, particularly at the local level. Implementation of ‘M Health’ strategies can lower costs, while enhancing the quality of the health service delivered, and the completeness and ease of real-time events and disease reporting and transparency and accountability for both funders and donors. For example ‘M Health’ strategies can be used for training and updating of skills via videos sent to mobile devices for: connecting the primary health care providers with supervisory staff for assistance in health and logistic problems that they encounter in the field; accessing higher-level health personnel for advice about care; linking individuals with serious health problems to a higher level of care; reporting health activities such as immunizations and community outbreaks in real time; facilitating rapid public health responses; and increasing the confidence of local health workers because their mobile devices give them access to a higher level of support. Mobile phones used in conjunction with global positioning systems can be used to monitor primary health care providers performance by assuring that they are where they report being and having them check in and out for each home visit, etc. These low-cost strategies are particularly relevant for developing countries with limited budgets and many disease problems. It is important to deploy mobile devices (technology) to facilitate the global goal of UHC, which is dependent on the performance of community-based public health professionals. Updated mobile devices can serve as a platform for practise-based education, training and mentoring through which knowledge and skills for clinical service delivery can be transferred from super-tertiary centres to the community level, and thus ultimately ensure not only the quality of services but also the sustainability and feasibility of UHC (Project-ECHO 2017). In addition, the strategies of using mobile devices can be configured according to specific needs, such as a referencing job aids providing standardized health messages and guiding stepwise procedures for service delivery, a trigger point for initiating case investigation, and to advance the response for effective disease surveillance, etc. The use of these emerging strategies and technology to enhance the performance of health workers and meet the needs of villagers at low costs need to become part of health systems and part of the curriculum for training at every level (Rotheram-Boris et al. 2012; Tomlinson et al. 2013; Taylor et al. 2018).
	It is important for those designing public health systems to delineate clear career paths for health professionals at each level, which will inform and, if done well, attract potential students to pursue those careers. An important component of defining career paths is to include incentives for individuals in these career paths (Calcutta Declaration 1999). A problem in many developing countries is the high attrition rate of trained health volunteers, in part due to a lack of monetary incentive. In some developing countries, training, especially for nurses, may better prepare trainees for work in developed countries. Thus, migration of health professionals whose training was funded by the developing countries, particularly doctors and nurses, to better working conditions and pay in developed countries reduces the potential workforce (Stilwell et al. 2004; Naicker et al. 2009; WHO 2010b). In these situations, developing countries may be considered to be subsidizing healthcare in developed countries!
	Incentives for health workers should include monetary rewards, but it is important that they also include recognition of the importance of the health professionals at every level in the entire system for advancing the health of their constituencies. This recognition is particularly important at the lowest and least financially rewarding levels. Prestige and recognition of worth are powerful incentives!





Assuring that the public health system remains responsive to changing needs


	Finally, it is important to monitor and periodically evaluate the performance of the health system at each level. Over time, specific needs change due to a range of factors and new technologies are developed; therefore, training programmes at every level must adapt their curricula to meet current needs and rapidly emerging technologies. Previously trained health workers need to update their skills. Thus, it is important to also include continuing training at all levels for health workers that will assure that they can continue to meet the changing demands of the health system.

11.10


Transformative learning for health professional in the twenty-first century for the future health workforce


	Wanicha Chuenkongkaew and Suwit Wibulpolprasert





Why transforming health professionals learning?


	Since the 1910 Flexnor report, a set of studies of health professional education system has been proposed for a continuous reform. The empirical experiential apprenticeship was replaced by a science-based curricula at non-commercial and university-based medical schools. The reforms equipped health professionals with the knowledge and skills that doubled life expectancy during the twentieth century (Frenk et al. 2010).
	At the start of the twenty-first century, new complex challenges emerged that affect worldwide healthcare services systems. Inequities in term of healthcare access and quality underscore failure to share health advances both domestically and internationally. An unprecedented rate of technology development, rapid demographic transition towards aged and urban populations with increasing chronic noncommunicable diseases (NCD) and disability, rapid globalization favours easy spread of emerging such as COVID19-coronavirus pandemic and re-emerging infectious diseases, have moved the world into a situation of VUCA (Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, and Ambiguity). All these emerging challenges, together with the top political commitments to achieve Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030, require a totally new type of health professionals.
	The current health professional education systems have not been well adapted to address the global challenges. This is mainly caused by outdated, static and fragmented curricula, institutes, and faculty members. The graduates are thus equipped with insufficient knowledge, attitude, and competencies to match the present and future healthcare systems (Wasi 2000). There are many challenges including:
	 	• Poor teamwork and inadequate collaboration among health professionals
	• Gender inequity of professional status
	• Narrow attention on technique without understanding the broader context
	• Episodic encounters with patient illnesses rather than holistic continuous care
	• Emphasizing hospital-based care rather than community and home-based, primary care and disease prevention
	• Inadequate understanding of social determinants of health
	• Quantitative, qualitative imbalances, inequitable distribution, and inappropriate skill-mix in the professional labour market
	• Poor leadership in health system development
	Thus, the need to transform the health professional education systems is imminent. The movements must ensure that the new graduates fit well with the changing health challenges and health systems development.





Health challenges and future healthcare delivery system


	Global emerging challenges including rapid globalization, technologies development, demographic, and epidemiological transition have been affecting the healthcare delivery system. We can envisage more chronic diseases, both Communicable (CD) and NonCommunicable Diseases (NCD), and Public Health Emergencies, linked to social determinants of health (SDH). We see the rapid increases in health expense and equity. Socio-economic development has also resulted in changing demand and provider-patient relationships.
	The World Bank and the World Health Organization (WHO) reported in 2017 that half of the world’s population lacked access to essential healthcare. Moreover, almost 100 million people were pushed into extreme poverty, forcing them to survive on only $1.90 or less a day (Tracking Universal Health Coverage 2017). To end people’s extreme poverty, which is the greatest challenge and ambitious goal of SDGs, inclusive and sustainable economic growth is needed. This can be achieved through policy coherence of economic, social, and environmental sectors.
	Universal Health Coverage (UHC) is an effective social measure to tackle health disparity and medical impoverishment at the same time. The United Nation SDGs 3.8 aims to achieve UHC in 2030.
	UHC is defined as ‘all people can access the health services they need without incurring financial hardship. It includes the access to essential comprehensive health promotion, disease prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, long-term, and palliative care services and technologies, without financial barriers’.
	To achieve UHC, five criteria must be met.
	 	First, the availability of essential health services. This includes an adequate number of skilled Health Work Force (HWF) employed with decent working conditions.
	Second, affordability to ensure no financial hardship through minimizing out-of-pocket (OOP) payments at point of services.
	Third, accessibility with equitable geographical distribution and near home primary and community-based healthcare.
	Fourth, acceptability with culturally appropriate, gender sensitive, non-discriminatory and responsive to special needs of specific populations,
	Fifth quality and accountability, including quality of care, patient safety, and responsiveness to patients’ demand, as well as people’s engagement.
	Public health (PH) is defined as ‘… the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health and efficiency through organized community effort’ (Grant 2012).
	Essential PH functions include strengthening primary and community-based healthcare; increasing capability, accessibility, and quality of individual and people-based healthcare services; reinforcing evidence informed policy decision processes through Health Systems Researches; strengthening qualified and equitable HWF; protecting health and safety both in normal and crisis situations and creating social innovation for PH problems. With emerging threats from health in crisis, including man-made, natural disasters, and pandemics, PH capacity is even more essential to ‘prevent, detect, and respond’ to protect health and humanity.
	Thus, UHC and PH are closely linked and should be developed in parallel with good integration.





Investing on HWF is the key to achieve health-related SDGs


	To achieve SDG targets in 67 low-and middle-income countries (LMIC), more investment on health is needed. A prospective investment of $41-$57 per person, per year on health by 2030 could provide a 9:1 return of global economic growth. The International Labour Organization (ILO) determines a threshold of 41.1 HWF per 10,000 population to achieve UHC. The strategic investment should focus more in the frontline HWF (potentially for women) in rural and underserved communities.
	Currently, the world’s urbanized population is projected to double from 30% in 1950 to 66% in 2050. Despite the rapid urbanization projected for the next two decades, African and Asian rural populations are estimated to be almost 90% of the global rural population, mostly in India, China, and Nigeria (United Nations 2014), (Fig. 11.10.1). Only 22% of the global urban population has limited healthcare access, whereas 56% of the rural population lacks access to essential healthcare services (International Labour Office 2015) (Fig. 11.10.2). The rural dwellers in Africa are the most deprived group in healthcare access. The challenge to achieve health-related SDGs is to focus to a greater degree in the LMIC where small city growth becomes urbanized rapidly.
	Fig. 11.10.1 Annual rural population at mid-year (thousands).
	Fig. 11.10.2 Rural/urban population with lack of health coverage due to HWF shortages, 2015 (ILO HWF lack of access to healthcare services, percentages) The ‘urban’ population is defined as the definition using in each country. The definitions are applied by national statistical offices in completion of the latest available census.
	Accessibility, availability, financial protection of efficient healthcare services, OOP expenditure and maternal mortality ratios (MMR) are five indicators for measurement of key dimensions of healthcare coverage and access (Fig. 11.10.3).
	Fig. 11.10.3 The global inadequacy in access to quality healthcare service: rural/urban population 2015 (percentage) Regional averages weighted by rural and urban dwellers except for MMR, by skilled birth attendants.
	Source: ILO estimates, 2015.
	Although we are facing rapid urbanization, more than 50% of the world population is in the rural underserved areas (Fig. 11.10.2), where severe shortage of HWF is a major challenge (Table 11.10.1). Strengthening primary and community-based healthcare and mobilizing community partnerships are essential to address the urban/rural divide. It requires strong basic primary healthcare (PHC)-based health systems manned by qualified committed health volunteers and professionals. Its success depends on active engagement of families, local government, community leaders, and intersectoral collaboration. Empowering HWF through transforming learning and practice in the community is a key contribution to address the disparity in UHC.

	A priority approach is community-engaged health professional learning, a mechanism to envision learners how to work in and with communities, in other words, learning how to involve the people that live in community with local redevelopment. It is a key component to produce health professionals with skills and spirit to the community for the reduction of geographical inequities. An engagement of learning develops when the community and academic partnership sustainably collaborate on the design, delivery, and programme evaluation with equal value to empower the community by training qualified and motivated health professionals to provide community-based service for health equity.
	Transformative learning for effective community engagement needs socially accountable values including honesty, respect, authenticity, openness and transparency, and trustworthiness.





Global movement on transformative learning for health professional in the twenty-first century


	In 2010, the Global Commission on Health Professionals Education for the twenty-first century was launched, on the 100th anniversary of the Flexner Report. The Global Commission report strongly proposed a system-based approach to replace scientific based curricula in health professional learning. The report triggered global movements to promote transformation, for instance:
	 	• The Southeast Asia Regional Committee resolution, SEA/RC/R6 on ‘Strengthening health workforce education and training in the region’ (WHO 2012).
	• World Health Assembly resolution, WHA 66.23 on Transforming health workforce education in support of UHC (WHA 2013).
	• The WHO recommendations 2013 for transforming and scaling up health professional education and training (WHO 2013). Eleven recommendations include faculty development in term of continuous professional development (CPD); accreditation; and recruitment process for faculty and teaching staff, curriculum development, simulation method, direct entry of graduates, admission procedures, streamlined educational pathways and ladder programmes, interprofessional education, accreditation, and CPD. The global recommendations provide a guide for transformative learning which include policy and technical guidelines for establishing undergraduate and graduate programmes It gives guidance on how best to produce graduates in response to health needs of the populations.
	• In the Prince Mahidol Award Conference (2014 ) ‘Transformative learning for health equity’, several new movements to tackle the current inadequacies of health professional learning have been gathering pace across a range of different constituencies (WHO 2006).
	• In 2015, as replacement to ‘unfinished’ health-related MDGs, a SDG 3.C on substantially increasing health financing and the recruitment, development, training and retention of the HWF in developing countries is a primary aim for the attainment of UHC (SDG 2015). To achieve UHC, all people must have access to an essential national package of healthcare services and essential, safe, effective, and good-quality medicines without financial barriers.
	• In 2016, the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 (GSHRH 2030), reiterates and revisits through a contemporary lens the agenda to adopt transformative strategies in the scale-up of HWF learning. The strategy outlined a set of milestone and key indicators on HWF learning. These include the establishment of an accreditation mechanism for health training institutions by 2020, progress towards halving current levels of disparity in HWF distribution (disaggregated by place of employment, for instance subnational and/or urban/rural/remote) and reduction of the prequalification attrition rates in medical, nursing and allied health professional schools to 20% or less by 2030.
	Education strategies should focus on investment in trainers who have a high potential of social return as a priority. It should prioritize regulating curricula to balance on producing graduates in response to local needs and to international markets. A coordinated approach is essential to create close linkage between health professional planning, learning, and motivating interprofessional education (IPE) and interprofessional practice (IPP). National policies should include setting and monitoring the education standards and sufficient financial support. The collaboration between higher education and health sector should be implemented by the integration between health systems and competency-based learning.
	Health professionals should be equipped with knowledge, skills, values, and attitudes in term of SDH and public health systems to build the most collaborative and effective interprofessional team. Building PH capabilities on epidemic preparedness and the global health security agenda to prevent, detect, and respond to emerging threats is a priority in current education strategies. The high quality of health training institutes should be regulated through accreditation mechanisms.
	 	• The United Nation Secretary General appointed a High-Level Commission on Health Employment and Economic Growth (HEEG 2016) which reported 10 concrete recommendations. The commission brought in the active involvement, at the top level relevant Intergovernmental Organizations including the ILO, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), and the WHO. The commission recommends stimulation of the health and social sector jobs to drive inclusive economic growth for greater economic stability and security. The achievement can also make gains across SDG 1 (poverty elimination), SDG 3 (good health and well-being), SDG 4 (quality education), SDG 5 (gender equality) and SDG 8 (decent work and economic growth). The report also shows that between 2000 and 2014, in OECD countries, there was a 48% increase in health and social sector employment while the industrial and agriculture sector declined.
	The commission recommended an increase of at more than 40 million new jobs in health and social sectors to reduce projected shortage of 18 million HWF, especially in LMIC and LIC by 2030. More health demand will create more jobs. The global economic return on health investment is 9:1 and one extra year of life raises gross domestic product (GDP) by 4%. More than 70% of the global health and social service workforce are women, compared with less than 40% of those across all employment sectors.
	The commission also recommended 10 specific actions. Six actions are on health system and HWF reform, including job creation; gender and woman’s right; education, training, and skills; health service delivery and organization; technology; crisis management and humanitarian setting. The remaining four recommendations on enabling actions include financing and fiscal space; partnership and cooperation; international migration; data and information and accountability.
	Transforming and scaling up high-quality learning should shift away from narrow specializations to general practice. It should highlight more on lifelong learning to build highly competent HWF. It has to generate motivated HWF in response to local and global health needs. Furthermore, reduction of unnecessary entry barriers is needed. These include addressing geographical inequities, strengthening youth education for better chance of employment, and reinforcing the effectiveness of community-based health workers.





New skills for the future health professionals and leaders


	Addressing global emerging challenges, health professionals need to move towards better health promotion, health protection, disease prevention, people-centred care, and community-based and primary healthcare based health systems with extensive geographical coverage.
	In the twenty-first century, competency-based curricula and team-based learning will replace traditional time-based learning. As defined by OECD, ‘competency’ is not only ‘knowledge and skills’ but the ability to meet complex needs by making use of psychosocial resources in a particular context. Effective health promotion needs to integrate health literacy, communication skill, and personal attitude. A competency-based approach is tailored to identify learner’s outcome or performance to align learning and training with health needs of populations in different settings (Gruppen et al. 2012).
	Increasing social and economic development allow increasing and timely access to healthcare and knowledge. The patient–doctor relationship has gradually shifted from vertical patron–client, to contractual relationship with reducing trust and increasing cost. To bring back trust-based relationship, the communitarian relationship based of community family doctors would be the new direction.
	In the twenty-first century, basic skills should include learning, literacy, and life skills (Fig. 11.10.4) in the training process. In addition, health professionals are also required to understand the high intrinsic value of social justice; ethics; morality; human rights; equity in health; altruism and social accountability. These will facilitate their communication with patients and work with other professionals, families, and community reflecting a mutual respect. They need the skills to enquire, search, interpret, and use evidence for appropriate decision-making. They also need to comprehensively understand the influence of social, political, and economic effects on health status including a concept of Health in All Policies and the SDH.
	Fig. 11.10.4 Twenty-first century skills: learning, literacy and life skills.
	New health professional leaders need five key soft skills for change as illustrated in Table 11.10.2 (Piirto 2010).
	 	Table 11.10.2 Five ‘soft skills’ for changes
	 			Intelligent
	A good understanding or a high mental capacity; comprehend quickly
		Imagination
	A capacity to create a solution that is both novel and appropriate, divergent thinking, being a good critical thinker and problem solver
		Inspiration
	A sudden arrival of a novel idea, a ‘leap’
		Insight
	An ability to clearly understand the inner nature of things, particularly by intuition





An insight manifests itself suddenly, requires preparation of hard work, believe in reconceptualization, connects old and new information, and applies to ill-structured problems


		Intuition
	An immediate and effortless knowing from the collective unconscious (a dark or wild animal side and a social mask to get along with other people) of prototypes of the deep human experience





Many people do not trust intuition despite their presence but creative people trust and prefer using it. An intuitive person is more likely to operate the tasks by using trial and error instead of using an instruction


Transformative learning for health professional


	Transformative learning for health professional is the sustainable expansion and reform of health professionals’ learning to achieve required new skills. It aims to reduce health inequity and improve quality of care as well as addressing issues of health professionals’ competencies for the country health systems. Achieving this will ensure improvement of population health and health equity.
	Transformative learning theory was outlined by Jack Mezirow in 1978 (Jack Mezirow 2014). It comprises three dimensions:
	 	• psychological (changes in understanding of the self)
	• convictional (revision of belief systems)
	• behavioural (changes in lifestyle)
	The learning of health professionals is shifting from ‘informative’ to ‘formative’ and on to ‘transformative’.
	The ‘informative’ learning is the fundamental level of fact memorization and skill building to become experts.
	The ‘formative’ learning focuses at the higher level of critical reasoning and systematic thinking to produce professionals.
	The ‘transformative’ learning aims at the highest level of analysis, synthesis, and enlightenment to be leader for changes.
	Transformative learning requires reform of the health professional educational system. Reform includes both institutional and instructional reforms. The institutional reform focuses at reforming the structural and functional education system. The instructional reform specifies curricular design, learning process development, and outcome.





Institutional reform (structure and function)


	See Box 11.10.1.
	 	Box 11.10.1 Transformative health professional learning





Institutional reform (structure and function)


	 	• Professional reform
	• Leadership development and management reform
	• Collaboration among stakeholders
	• Legal and regulatory reform
	• Expenditure and financing reform





Instructional reform (process and outcome)


	 	• Recruitment reform
	• Curricula reform
	• Learning process reform, including Interprofessional education (IPE), application of IT and authentic learning





Professional reform that focus on faculty development


	Faculty development includes academic and career development, teaching improvement, research capacity, and leadership development to ensure teaching, research, and service congruence (Steinert 2012). Effective faculty development is a crucial component in promoting individual and organizational change for its ‘grounded in growth’ perspective.
	Parker Palmer addressed that ‘growth of any craft depends on shared practice and honest dialogue among the people who do it’ (Palmer 1998). One of the key components of faculty development is to share ‘community of practice’ dialogue. This would allow collective reflection on human issues of the profession rather than only technical ones. Among others, faculty development help to create values or merits as ‘role models’ or ‘inspirational teachers’, rewards system, and attempts for excellence.





Leadership development and management reform


	Leadership is critically significant to guide, direct, and influence others to bring about fundamental changes to the health systems. The institutional mechanism is empirically applied to: (1) emphasize fostering leadership development through transformative learning for health professional education and research at all levels; (2) connecting health professional development to evolving local health needs, national priorities and the SDGs; (3) building health equity and eliminating health disparity (WHO 2016) through collaborative institutional and instructional reforms; (4) generating and interpreting data with appropriate stakeholder input to inform evidence-based policy and evaluate innovative practice for education and training; and (5) developing a national HWF plan that harnesses market forces towards development of a workforce with adequate skill-mix for delivery of comprehensive PHC.
	Management reform of the education system is collectively pointing to decentralizing the educational administration to shift from central to local control in terms of authority and decision-making power based on good governance and social accountability.





Collaboration among stakeholders


	Synergy and coherence among multisectoral key stakeholders from professional educational institutions and councils and the systems that are collaboratively responsible for healthcare services is a necessary component to bring about transformative change and leadership through collective action in developing future health professionals who have a commitment to work in underserved areas where health inequities and inequalities remain. Such collaboration includes public-private partnerships for an inclusive and sustainable healthcare system.





Legal and regulatory reform


	In terms of legal and regulatory reform, quality assurance, accreditation and re-accreditation of training institute\ions and curriculum are key instruments to ensure quality and competency of graduates while national licensing examination, re-licensing process, and CPD are instruments are necessary to ensure continuity of health professionals’ competency. Accreditation of health professional learning should be introduced and strengthened. It can be achieved through implementation of accreditation procedures. The procedures should emphasize continuous improvement of quality educational processes and outcome, with inclusion of social accountability. Mutual learning with gradual movement towards mutual recognition among countries should be supported, for example the Mutual Recognition Arrangements on the medical, nursing, dental, and pharmacy professions among the South-East Asia Nations.
	Finally, with the increasing number of private health professional education institutes, the accreditation and licensing systems should be applied equally in both public and private institutions.





Reform of financing systems


	Health professional education requires big investment. Producing a medical doctor in Thailand, for example, costs around US$60,000. Most public institutes are highly subsidized. Students in the private schools may take publicly subsidized loans. The challenge is equity in access and efficiency in using the public resources. Students from low socio-economic families, especially in the rural settings, find it difficult to compete with those from urban better off families.
	‘Rural recruitment, local training and hometown placement’ is an important measure to ensure better equity both in the access to education and the distribution of the graduates.
	In some instances, local communities recruit and support their own students with the condition that students must return to work in their communities.
	An education financing reform should aim to restructure and reallocate resources to cover local communities through public-private partnerships.
	Demand-side financing schemes, where funds are channelled directly to the local communities or students, will empower them and create greater community responsiveness among the supply side.





Instructional reform


	See Box 11.10.1.





Recruitment reform


	Student enrolment and admission policies should focus more on increasing the socio-economic, demographic, psycho-physiologic, ethnic, and geographical diversity of students. It would reflect local population diversity and ensure their social return. As such, special systems should be in place to increase inclusion of students from disadvantaged, underserved populations, and marginalized groups. These systems should also align with the requisite academic standards and other desirable characteristics. In addition, special training programmes should be implemented to support underserved population groups to achieve admissions requirements and to reduce dropouts before completion of their training.





Curricula reform


	The existing conventional, and fragmented curricula should be transformed. They should focus on population health needs, new models of service delivery and health team skill-mix to support UHC for health equity. The ‘silo’ competencies across different relevant curricula have to be reviewed to ensure better alignment across different professionals.
	Essential new issues should include:
	 	• Broader and deeper competency-based learning with emphasis on social and contextual determinants of health in situ
	• Broader understanding of overall integrated people-centred health systems and roles of different health professionals
	• Continuous leadership development to be active ‘change agents’
	• Home-based comprehensive primary care, health promotion and disease prevention
	• Community engagement, inter-or transprofessional health teams, and immersion education experiences
	• Inclusion of community leaders, health service managers, and users from heath facilities on curriculum planning committees





Interprofessional education (IPE)


	WHO defines IPE as ‘Learning “With”, “From” and “About” different professions, for collaborative practice to improve healthcare quality’ (WHO 2010). It is one of the 11 WHO’s key recommendations. It supports and enhances the performance of community health systems. It deepens mutual understanding among different professions to bring about an effective collaboration and improve health outcomes in the community.
	In order to scale-up IPE, all health professions should be incrementally focusing on IPP in the real-life services (de Villiers and Naidoo 2011; IOM 2013).
	To optimize health professional learning, the transformation should also focus on team-based education in addition to the competency-based learning.
	The key challenges are:
	 	• Personal barriers, including failure to appreciate other professionals
	• Misunderstanding and miscommunication
	• Fear of change
	• Differences in income
	• Different power in the systems
	• Language or gender
	• Institutional barriers such as practice setting, structure, and priority





Information and communication technology (ICT) for transformative learning


	Digitalized Information Technology (IT) and social media skills are key elements of twenty-first century teaching and learning. It can provide a common platform for knowledge exchange and sharing. However, this platform does require substantial infrastructure support to connect all the basic facilities, services, and information together.
	ICT for Transformative learning has five objectives:
	 	• Fostering and deepening the learner-centred learning system and learning environment
	• Diminishing costs by mobilizing and sharing resources
	• Increasing the application of ICT in learning settings and sharing knowledge on informatics
	• Strengthening teachers’ and learners’ confidence, competency, and capacity in ICT utilization
	• Developing an online course from the existing course
	The four strategies for applying ICT in transformative learning include:
	 	• Fostering ICT across all disciplines
	• Increasing the use of technology platform s in courses
	• Promoting learner utilization of mobile devices
	• Implementing a comprehensive learning management system to achieve learning outcome improvement
	The key successful indicators are:
	 	• Percentage of teaching and technical support staff with ICT literacy
	• The number of electronic resources on learning, educational research studies, and innovations that can be applied to improve the learning process and achieve better learning outcomes
	• The number of ICT skilful faculty members
	In the technology-rich digitalized innovative environment, shortfalls in soft skills development can occur. To overcome such challenges, a few measures should be addressed:
	 	• Social interaction by means of communicating through dialogue
	• Encouraging
	• Explaining
	• Hugging and thanking
	We should always emphasize that ‘The digitalized technologies are helpful but artificial, the real health services depend on the ten digits of the health professionals that touch on the patients and people’.
	‘Appropriate Technology with High Human Touch’ is the most favoured service, not the ‘High Technology with Low Touch’ (Gade and Chari 2013).





Authentic learning


	Authentic learning or experiential based learning will engage learners to actually participate in solving real health challenges. The learners’ skills and attitude gained from experience and practice will keep them motivated to enhance their lifelong learning. This is to ensure sustainable quality of care and ultimately achieve community satisfaction. The key challenge is to create learning experiences to effectively provoke deep reflective thinking.
	Authentic learning should be supported by the effective and appropriate application of ICT.





Networks on transformative learning for health professional


	A number of global and regional transformative learning networks to actively enrich its momentum have been established, including:
	 	• The Joint Learning Initiative (2004)
	• The Global Health Workforce Alliance (GHWA)
	• The Asia Pacific Action Alliance on HRH (AAAH)
	• THEnet
	• The President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) supported Medical and Nursing Education Partnership Initiative (MEPI and NEPI) or AFREhealth
	• The Asia-Pacific Network on Health Professional Education Reform (ANHER)
	• The Pacific Open Learning Health Net (POLHN)





The Joint Learning Initiative (2004)


	The Joint Learning Initiative (2004) is a network of more than 100 great healthcare leaders who are determined to confront the global health system crisis by mobilizing and strengthening HWF primarily in low-income countries. Reflecting their initiative, the HWF shortage has become a common concern and the collective action to tackle the HWF crisis is needed.





The Global Health Workforce Alliance (GHWA)


	When the Rockefeller supported Joint Learning Initiative ended in 2005, one of its recommendations was to establish global and regional networks on HWF.
	In 2006, the GHWA was launched and hosted by WHO in response to the HWF crisis. It is a global network of various agencies including civil society, financing sectors, workers, national governments, international, academic, and professional organizations. In 2016, GHWA transitioned to the Global Health Workforce Network (GHWN), operated by WHO to support the national actions on the Global Strategies on HRH 2016–2030 and the recommendations of the UN High-Level Commission on Health Employment and Economic Growth.





The Asia-Pacific Action Alliance on Human Resources for Health (AAAH)


	At more or less the same time as the GHWA, the HWF leaders in Asia and Pacific established the AAAH. It is a regional partnership mechanism to strengthen country health workforce planning and development actions. AAAH’s prominent roles are to advocate HRH policy; monitor information system; strengthen capacity; generate, manage, and share knowledge; and coordinate technical issues. AAAH has convened annual conference, since 2006 and biennial since 2014. Network activities of 18 countries, in WHO SEAR and Western Pacific Regions (WPR), include training workshops and study visits. Intersession research workshops to drive national agenda by country partners through evidence generation and capacity building activities.





Training for Health Equity Network (THEnet)


	In 2008, Training for Health Equity Network (THEnet) aims to increase the impact of academic institutions on community health and develop more equitable health systems. The identification of successful strategies to indicate health workforce shortages is primary goal, THEnet is located in outreach areas worldwide and steps forward to convince schools and policymakers that socially accountable education can increase quantity and quality of HWF practising in rural and underserved areas.





The Medical Education Partnership Initiative (MEPI) and the Nursing Education Partnership Initiative (NEPI)


	In 2010, the United States (US) PEPFAR, supported the MEPI administered by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the NEPI administered by the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA). These two networks have together strengthened innovative evidence-based strategies for transformative health professional learning, training, and research in support of HIV epidemic control and achievement of UHC in Africa. Both MEPI and NEPI were a response to the critical shortage of HWF in sub-Saharan Africa by increasing the quantity, quality, and capacity of physicians, nurses, and midwives. From these two multicounty initiatives, a new African designed and led African Forum for Health Research and Education in Health (AFREhealth) has emerged which embraces interprofessional collaboration since 2016.





Asian Network on Health Professional Education Reform (ANHER)


	To envision the 2010 Global Commission’s report on Transformative Learning, Bangladesh, China, India, Thailand, and Vietnam, committed to implement and conduct distinct and suitable health professionals’ education reform. The strategies will be flexible with respect to the nation’s socio-economic and cultural situation and trends, as well as its domestic health service system. In 2011 at a meeting in Hanoi, they initiated ANHER. The network has agreed on joint actions including joint surveys on health professional learning, information sharing, and learning in medical nurse and public health professional reform, plus other internationally collaborative activities. The situation analysis survey focused on the introduction of innovative institutional and instructional reforms. The reforms aimed to improve quality, enhance teamwork among students, schools, and networks, improved curricula, and practicum to prepare health workers for the new challenges. The innovations are introduced into the learning systems such as e-learning methods and introduction of new skills in the curricula such as public health and management training. Articles on cross-country analysis and country experiences were published for experience learning and sharing and drive the reform (Chuenkongkaew et al. 2016; Pudpong et al. 2017; Zodpey et al. 2018).





The Pacific Open Learning Health Net (POLHN)


	The POLHN is a key programme of the WHO in collaboration with the Pacific Ministries of Health to increase health professional standards and quality by offering free, online, and blended courses. The network cooperates through 47 learning centres and a team of dedicated focal points in 15 countries. POLHN offers different specialized online accredited programmes from Fiji National University, Pacific Paramedical Training Centre, and Penn Foster Dental School. Since Internet access in the Pacific is getting better and an increasing number of online courses are available globally, online continuing education will be increasingly important in the Pacific. In this regard, POLHN needs to reinforce its role in overall CPD, including better regional coordination with more countries.





Conclusion


	The successes of health-related SDGs depend on the successes of the health system reform towards primary care-based, patient-centred health service. These reforms, in turn, depend on the successes of the Health Professional Education reform.
	The reforms will ensure adequate numbers and equitable distribution of competent, inspired, and motivated HWF with leadership capacity.
	Transformative health professional learning is a set of essential reforms, from hospital-based to health systems and community-based and authentic learning. The reforms focus on building skills and attitude on rationalizing appropriate technology with a high human touch. It moves from individual silo-based practice to integrated team-based practice. It also ensures the effective and constructive collaboration between the producers and users of HWF in the health systems.
