11.11


Humanitarian emergencies


	Craig Spencer and Les Roberts





A challenging moment in history: more people in need, more money, and more difficult tasks


	In recent years the humanitarian sector has been the target of intense criticism. The humanitarian community has been seen as driven by wealthy country agendas, inadequately developing and listening to local actors, and not being adequately accountable to international law and humanitarian principals (Agenda for Humanity n.d.). While all of these criticisms have a solid basis of complaint, they do not stem from a humanitarianism in decline. The lack of clarity of purpose of many humanitarian players has arisen in part as a result of the spectacular success of the humanitarian community.
	Fig. 11.11.1 Highest mortality periodically recorded over the last 30 years in >100,000 people lasting >1mo. Deaths/1,000/mo.
	Source: data from Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED) database.
	This may partially be explained by a 75% decline in the fraction of people living in poverty since 1981 when current World Bank measures began (Roser and Ortiz-Ospina 2018). Yet perhaps most of the decline is because of the near ubiquitous presence of humanitarian actors during the most acute of crises and their improvement in the science of keeping people alive.
	Our present moment in history also involves higher numbers of displaced people than have ever been recorded. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimates that more than 60 million people are displaced, with two-thirds of them still in their home country and therefore the responsibility of that government (UNHCR n.d.). One-quarter of today’s refugees have fled Syria, a middle income and highly educated country not similar to most of the origins of last century’s most acute crises shown in Figure 11.11.1. Those who do manage to cross borders now are not returning for longer periods than those in recent decades (Fig. 11.11.2).
	Fig. 11.11.2 Estimate of the percentage of the global population displaced over time.
	Reprinted with permission from the Pew Research Center 2016. http://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2016/08/03/nearly-1-in-100-worldwide-are-now-displaced-from-their-homes/ft_16-07-28_displaced_world/
	Making this time period more complex is the fact that more money is being spent on humanitarian assistance. The 2017 Global Humanitarian Assistance Report suggests that $27.3 US billion was spent in 2016 on humanitarian assistance, more than on development. This is in stark contrast to the 1970s–1990s when OECD countries typically spent more than ten times as much on development aid as on humanitarian assistance (Global Humanitarian Assistance 2000).
	Figure 11.11.3 shows the dramatic increase in violent deaths in the WHO Middle East and Northern Africa (MENA) region since 1990 (GBD 2018). In this region, violent deaths have increased in every demographic group, increasing 450% from 1990 to 2015.
	Fig. 11.11.3 Increased numbers of violent deaths MENA region, 1990–2015.
	Reprinted from GBD 2015 Eastern Mediterranean Region Intentional Injuries Collaborators (2018) ‘Intentional injuries in the Eastern Mediterranean Region, 1990–2015: findings from the Global Burden of Disease 2015 study’. Int J Public Health. 2018; 63(Suppl 1): 39–46, under a CC BY 4.0 license.
	During this time, violence has become the number one cause of death for children 10 to 19 years old. Thus, the core causes of morbidity and mortality in this region are not easily fixed by non-state actors like humanitarian aid workers. Adding insult to injury, violence against aid workers has become more common and expectations of neutrality and safety for health workers and aid workers has diminished (Jackson 2012). Over 1,000 hospitals and clinics have been attacked during the war in Syria, a level of attacks out of step with historical norms (Briody et al.). On one day in July of 2016, the last four remaining hospitals in the besieged city of Aleppo were bombed, presumably by Russian aircraft (AlJazeera 2016a). No United Nations (UN) condemnation or International Criminal Court (ICC) action was taken, and no apology form the Russians was offered. This event, like the invasion of Iraq as a pre-emptive war or the rise of anti-immigrant sentiment across the globe, implies that the humanitarian community is living in an era of incivility that adds significant barriers to their work.
	This period involving lower mortality crises means humanitarian assistance in the twenty-first century is less focused on the relatively easy to treat killers of measles, ARI, diarrhoea, and malaria deaths. Today, aid is more often being provided to more people from middle income countries who want long-term support and have health priorities that involve addressing issues like violence, depression, and unemployment. The Oxford Dictionary defines ‘humanitarian’ as ‘Concerned with or seeking to promote human welfare’. Thus, addressing whatever the most acute needs of a population are is innately the mandate of the humanitarian endeavour. But, the UN, church groups, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) who tend to lead major humanitarian efforts are innately better suited to preventing measles and malaria deaths than they are to addressing issues that require ongoing engagement and social change.
	To summarize, the twenty-first century will be a challenging era for the humanitarian community. There are more people in need, not only for food, water, and medicine to stay alive, but who are also experiencing more complicated and difficult needs in a period of rising expectations. While this sounds difficult, this is in many ways the apex of civilization. The challenges are vast because the expectations of service and compassion are now projected to more than just those at risk of death. The challenges are difficult because we are now expected to operate in environments where aid workers are targeted and where host governments responsible for those at risk are often the source of that risk. The challenges are complex because depression and domestic violence and many of the relief priorities today are issues not easily solved even in the wealthiest of countries. This chapter will review where the humanitarian community has been and will lay out some of the new efforts for dealing with these challenges.





Introduction to emergency public health and humanitarian assistance: where we have been


	During the Biafran War (1967–1970) perhaps half of the 2,000,000 population inside the shrinking breakaway enclave died of malnutrition and disease by the end of the conflict (Western 1972). During this crisis, profound advances in modern humanitarian relief arose. Unable to determine which children were starving and which children were just skinny or small, the Friends Overseas Service Committee triggered the development of the Quaker Upper Arm Circumference (QUAC) Stick, the first scheme for assessing nutritional anthropometry. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) tested the universally accepted theory that malnourished children could not produce an immunological response to being vaccinated by using intervention and control groups. They vaccinated some very malnourished children and followed up weeks later by drawing blood from the study children to see if immunity had developed. In this first known controlled trial in an emergency, it turned out that malnourished children could indeed be effectively vaccinated (Ifekwunigwe et al. 1980). Other developments included the first known public health adaptation of capture-recapture methodologies from wildlife biology in order to estimate the number of deaths (and thus the first real-time conflict mortality measurement), the first guidelines for such things as running feeding centres, and the creation of the medical relief organization Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF).
	In the crises that followed, more and more central insights into the science of keeping vulnerable people alive and healthy accumulated at an ever-increasing rate. The East Pakistan Crisis, by chance arising where an international diarrhoeal research centre was based, brought the advent of oral rehydration therapy (ORT) (Sack et al. 1970). Relief for Cambodians on the Thai border demonstrated the value of surveillance and rapid assessments (Glass et al. 1980). The famine and conflict in the Horn of Africa in the early 1980s provided the rationale for the caloric content of rations, a two-stage measles vaccination strategy for children less than 9 months, and a variety of other ‘best practices’ (Toole et al. 1988, 1989). By the 1990s, comprehensive outlines of priorities and best practices were in place based on the accumulation of these various lessons learned and documented (Toole 1990; CDC 1992; MSF 1997).
	Most of these guidelines were developed based on experiences in settings of extreme poverty and high mortality, where the excess (above the normal) mortality profiles were dominated by infectious diseases, primarily diarrhoea, respiratory infections, and malaria. While acute respiratory infections are often the leading cause of death in emergencies, it is relatively difficult to prevent infections and emergency response efforts usually focus on getting effective medical treatment to cases. In contrast, the next three major killers in emergencies in decades past, namely malaria, measles, and diarrhoea, can all be prevented by interventions commonly provided as part of humanitarian relief efforts. Figure 11.11.4 next shows the global rate of death from these three diseases from 1985 to 2015. Data are compiled from multiple sources (Rodolfo et al. 1993; Kosek et al. 2003; Boschi-Pinto et al. 2008; WHO n.d. 2011).
	Fig. 11.11.4 Global death rates for malaria, measles, and diarrhoea.
	Sources: data from (WHO n.d., 2011, Boschi-Pinto et al. 2008, Kosek et al., 2003, Rodolfo et al., 1993).
	In assessing why these dramatic reductions occurred, it is hard to separate what influence the reduced fraction of the global population in poverty has had compared to focused programmes like measles vaccinations and oral rehydration solution (ORS) promotion or newly available technologies like long-lasting insecticide impregnated bednets. It is most likely that all these factors are at work and simultaneously interacting with other improvements such as higher rates of literacy and improving function of health related institutions. In emergencies, people tend to die of the same causes that they die of in stable times, just at a higher rate. Therefore, when compared to the Cold War era, the lower mortality widely seen today may be in part a reflection that our global population is less vulnerable to death in general. The Cold War era crises often continued for many years with large numbers of people displaced and supported in camps for a variety of geopolitical and economic reasons. Crowded camps are ideal environments for spreading disease. Today, few of the world’s displaced stay in camps further diminishing the emphasis on infectious disease control.
	To summarize this overview of humanitarian relief evolution over the past half century, the world of humanitarian response today has little in common with the Biafran era. Today, most of the world’s displaced have not crossed a border and are displaced within their own country. Many and perhaps most of the world’s most vulnerable displaced persons are in urban settings. Finally, likely as a result of the developments of the relief community and greater global wealth, few crises in the twenty-first century to date have been associated with extended periods of high mortality, as were seen in Cambodia, Mozambique, Sudan, Somalia, Biafra, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo), and elsewhere in the last century. Rising international expectations of support have resulted in expanding humanitarian efforts focused more on issues of suffering, often from chronic or mental health-related disorders.
	To address these new realities, this chapter will look at those areas where the twenty-first-century humanitarian endeavour is likely to differ dramatically from the twentieth century, including: preparedness and planning, changing institutional structures and architecture, the growing international attention of disease outbreaks, the evolving public health profile of emergency relief needs, and the role of new and innovative technologies. The roles of emergency planning and relief workers have grown, professionalized, and become politicized at a dramatic rate in recent years and we attempt here to create a framework for understanding these transitions.





Definitions and classification


	There are few terms used more divergently in society today than the word ‘humanitarian’. Merriam Webster defines humanitarian as: ‘a person promoting human welfare and social reform, philanthropist—recognized as a great humanitarian for her work to end world hunger.’ The Oxford Online Dictionary says: ‘humanitarian (adjective) (1) Concerned with or seeking to promote human welfare. (2) Denoting an event or situation which causes or involves widespread human suffering, especially one which requires the large-scale provision of aid’. In this chapter, and with most humanitarian employers, humanitarian will signify seeking to promote human welfare while adhering to the Red Cross Code of Conduct, a set of 10 rules designed to promote indiscriminate compassion, impartiality, neutrality, and accountability (ICRC n.d.).
	There is currently no universally accepted definition of the term ‘disaster’. This lack of standardization can be attributed in part to the broad range of disciplines involved in disaster management. Nonetheless, common to most definitions is the concept of large-scale loss that exceeds a community’s own capacity to respond effectively, requiring some form of external assistance.
	The United Nations International Strategy for Disaster Reduction (UNISDR) defines a disaster as ‘a serious disruption of the functioning of a community or a society involving widespread human, material, economic or environmental losses and impacts, which exceeds the ability of the affected community or society to cope using its own resources’ (UNISDR 2010). This definition is also one of several recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO).
	Similarly, there is no standard classification system for disasters, although numerous have been proposed. Generally, disasters are associated with the hazards that cause them. They can be classified as either natural or human generated, with subclassifications of each. Natural disasters are often subclassified according to whether they are acute onset or slow/gradual onset, human-generated disasters as intentional or non-intentional. Generally there are not widely accepted definitions of these subclassifications. Moreover, military, political, and public health professionals have evolved to use words like emergency, disasters, and humanitarian with little functional criteria in common. Further undermining the utility of disaster classifications is the fact that often scholars from different disciplines understand the same crises in different ways. For example, while the 2011 Syrian war is largely painted as politically triggered over a short period by an Arab Spring uprising and a brutal government crackdown, Selby describes the conflict as a slow onset consequence of years of abnormally low rainfall creating migration and political instability (AlJazeera 2016b; Selby et al. 2017). Thus, we shall emphasize here epidemiologically based definitions and interpretations, as that will likely be the most useful approach for health professionals.





Epidemiology


	The epidemiology of manmade crises (war and most famines) differ dramatically from natural and technological disasters, which aside from drought, tend to have a rapid onset. We shall refer to the latter as disasters and data about their occurrence and mortality effects are far better than with manmade crises. Earthquakes and tsunamis are the deadliest of natural disasters followed by extreme temperature events and floods.
	According to the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters, during the period from 1996 and 2015, on average approximately 600 natural and technological disasters occurred globally each year resulting in 67,000 annual fatalities (CRED 2017). Over these two decades, the number of annual events has gone up slightly while the annual death toll has not. The most severely affected region was Asia, followed by Africa and the Americas.
	Those most vulnerable to the public health impacts of disasters are the poor. While 27% of disasters occurred in countries categorized as having low human development, they accounted for 47% of deaths, because of their limited capacities to mitigate, prepare for, and respond to disasters. Moreover, the economic costs run into billions of dollars and a single disaster can set back a nation’s development many years with obvious implications for public health programming and health outcomes. A CDC report cites World Bank estimates that the 2014 Ebola outbreak in Sierra Leone cost the country $2.2 billion in lost gross domestic product (GDP) from 2014 to 2016, roughly a 20% drop (CDC 2016).
	Globally, the most frequent types of disasters are transport accidents, followed by floods, windstorms, industrial accidents, earthquakes, and droughts/food insecurity (Table 1). Climate change is expected to affect the frequency and severity of floods, windstorms, and droughts, with their associated public health impacts (World Health Organization and World Meteorological Organization 2012). For example, severe droughts and associated food insecurity have occurred at more frequent intervals over the past decade in the Sahel and Horn of Africa. Monsoon-associated floods in Pakistan in 2010 and 2012 were among the most severe ever recorded.

	While such events are usually recorded well and seen as non-controversial, natural disasters have long-term effects such as inducing migration or prolonged interruptions of public services and the actual health effects may be more complex in nature and go unrecorded. An extreme example of this arose when Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017. Official government estimates placed the death toll at 64 deaths, a number repeated consistently by government officials in the months that followed (Shugarmen 2017). An examination of death certificates by the New York Times three months later placed the death toll at 2,000 and a population-based survey months later conservatively placed the death toll at about 4,600 (Kishore et al. 2018). This is the exception rather than the rule as acute disasters like transport accidents and earthquakes typically cause trauma deaths over seconds or hours.
	There is a growing body of evidence that climate change is interacting with a variety of factors to make populations more vulnerable. Thus it is difficult to distinguish which deaths are associated with climate change, overpopulation, or simply associated with natural disasters. Weather extremes and climate changes interact with other important global trends that threaten to increase the frequency and impact of disasters. Increasing urbanization, poor urban planning, poor land use, unregulated industrialization, new and emerging infectious diseases, and terrorism all have the potential to expose greater numbers of people to hazards (United Nations International Strategy for Disaster Reduction 2010; WHO 2011a; Bhui et al. 2012). The Christchurch earthquake of 2011, Bangkok floods of 2011, and Superstorm Sandy in New York City in 2012 all demonstrated that disasters striking densely populated urban areas have the potential for substantial public health and economic impact. The Nigeria floods of 2012 and on the Indian Subcontinent in 2017 that forced millions from their homes have brought attention to the issues of poor urban planning and settlements in flood-prone zones. The severe acute respiratory syndrome epidemic of 2003 and the H1N1 pandemic of 2009 have demonstrated the need for stronger public health surveillance and response mechanisms. Terrorist attacks across a range of countries have revealed security threats that need to be addressed in disaster planning and mass casualty response plans (WHO 2007). In spite of these complicating factors, because deaths tolls from disasters tend to be collected consistently, evidence suggests that since the 1920s there has been over an 80% reduction in the annual deaths from natural disasters (Richie et al. n.d.). Over this past century, deaths from droughts have dramatically declined while earthquakes have evolved to become the dominant cause of natural disaster deaths. Thus, the relatively consistent documentation of disaster death tolls has recorded the beneficial effects of the world’s efforts to attenuate drought and famine effects.
	In contrast, the impacts of armed conflicts are far more difficult to quantify. The World Bank estimated that 1.5 billion people live in countries affected by repeated cycles of political and criminal violence, and fragility (World Bank 2011). Most modern-day conflicts are protracted civil wars, in which civilians are often deliberately targeted and frequently displaced from their communities. Often called ‘complex emergencies’, they are associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality.
	In such conflicts, large numbers of deaths can result from violent injury, as in the Rwandan genocide, the Balkan conflicts of the 1990s, and the recent war in Syria. But in many instances, most deaths are due to the so-called indirect health consequences of conflict—increased rates of infectious diseases, acute malnutrition, and complications of chronic diseases that arise due to societal disruption, population displacement, and breakdown in health services. This has been well described in crises in DR Congo, Ethiopia, Somalia, and Sudan (Toole 1997; Coghlan et al. 2006).
	The number of ongoing conflicts can be difficult to quantify, as definitions vary. The Uppsala Conflict Database defines a conflict as a ‘contested incompatibility that concerns government or territory or both where the use of armed force between two parties results in at least 25 battle-related deaths in a year. Of these two parties, at least one has to be the government of a state’. Based on this definition there were 52 ongoing conflicts in 2016, of which 2/3rds were intrastate or civil wars (Uppsala Conflict Data Program n.d.). Since the Second World War, there has been a strong tendency for conflicts to become longer in duration and less intense in terms of rates of violence (Garfield et al. 2012). Passive efforts to monitor conflicts are almost always incomplete but tend to be more incomplete in the least socially networked countries. For example, a survey from MSF found that at least 9,400 Rohingya died over a one-month period of ethnic cleansing from August to September 2017 in Myanmar (MSF 2018). Virtually none of those deaths were recorded in the news of by social media. In contrast, five civil society groups in Syria are believed to have recorded the vast majority of violent deaths in that conflict (Price et al. 2014).
	Perhaps the most robust and standardized of systems for monitoring deaths from conflict is the previously mentioned Uppsala Conflict Database which attempts to evaluate press, relief agency, and expert opinion to make annual death toll estimates (see ucdp.uu.se ). Population-based estimates based on surveys or multiple systems estimations have shown the Uppsala system to be relatively complete in highly networked countries (Our World Data 2017). For example, the Human Rights Data Analysis Group (HRDAG) estimate suggests that the system is 60% complete in Syria (Price et al. 2014 vs. UNDP 2010). Likewise, looking at Algeria from 1997 to 2016 suggests that UCDP is 100% sensitive when compared to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) Excel database. In contrast, a 2011 comparison of death toll in South Sudan with the exact same ACLED database suggests a sensitivity of only 35%. In the violent and moderately connected setting of Iraq 2003–2010, a comparison of the conflict related deaths recorded in a household survey suggested the Uppsala data set was 12–17% complete (Burnham et al. 2006; Hagopian et al. 2013 vs. UCDP 2010). Further, surveys in CAR in 2009 suggest the UCDP was less than 2% complete there (Vinck and Pham 2011). This suggests that our global data and understanding of deaths from wars is likely of lower quality than our understanding of deaths from natural disasters.
	Garfield looked at both the major natural and manmade disasters from 2002 to 2006 (Garfield 2007) and found that while natural disasters tended to affect far more people, conflicts tended to kill far more people. These results are presented in Figure 11.11.5, next.
	Fig. 11.11.5 Relative measures of populations affected and killed in major emergencies 2002–2006.
	Reprinted from Garfield R (2007) ‘Measuring Humanitarian Emergencies’ Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness 1(2):110–116, with permission from Cambridge University Press.
	In terms of the demands on local societies and the humanitarian community, elevations in mortality rates can persist for years after the formal end of conflict, as documented in Angola, DR Congo, and South Sudan. An important aspect of crises that can expose the affected populations to increased public health risks is forced displacement. The United Nations Development Program (UNDP) has developed a Human Development Index, in an attempt to articulate how well a society is doing. The index is a composite of life expectancy at birth, an education index, and income. According to the Human Development Index for 2016, nine of the 10 least developed countries on the planet experienced significant levels of armed conflict in recent years. The only one of these countries that has not experienced major conflict, Guinea, is surrounded by conflict-affected countries. Similarly, of the ten countries with the highest maternal mortality, nine have recently endured conflict. According to the World Bank, no low-income fragile or conflict-affected country achieved even one of the eight Millennium Development Goals—three of which are health related.
	The process of displacement can increase the risk of infectious diseases (e.g. through housing in unsanitary conditions or exposure to disease-carrying vectors), food scarcity and malnutrition, physical violence, sexual abuse, and psychological trauma. Thus, the disruption associated with crises usually disproportionately affects the health and survival of small children. Access to health services is often limited and ongoing health programmes (e.g. vaccinations) disrupted. Higher disease rates are often documented among internally displaced persons (IDPs), as the well-developed mechanisms to provide protection and humanitarian assistance to refugees do not always apply directly in IDP settings (Salama et al. 2001).
	Thus, our knowledge and use of data is rather contrasting between disasters and conflicts. Wars induce far more deaths, and often involve protracted periods of crisis where outside support can be essential for averting deaths. Disasters, in contrast, affect far more people, and tend of create crises of shorter duration. Disaster related epidemiological data is most useful for making preventative plans and policies. This last concept leads us to the topic of disaster planning.





Preparing and planning for disasters


	Following the 2010 earthquake in Haiti, the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED) produced an assessment contrasting the previous 10 natural disaster events that struck the island of Hispaniola. Of note, the two countries that comprise this island each had similar populations of approximately 10 million people.
