	What is striking is that 10 storms hitting the same island by chance affected 2.5 times as many people in Haiti but induced 17 times more deaths in Haiti. There are likely many factors such as crowding and deforestation that work against the safety of the less wealthy Haitian population. But some factors, like construction quality, zoning codes and compliance, and government response plans also likely influenced the sevenfold risk of mortality associated with these storms for residents in Haiti.





Preparing for disasters—health emergency risk management


	The most effective means of reducing the public health risks and impacts of disasters is to employ a comprehensive emergency risk management approach. Emergency risk management (ERM) consists of a continuum of synergistic steps that can reduce the risks and consequences of disasters, including prevention (risk reduction and mitigation), preparedness, response, and recovery. These steps are so closely interconnected that for all practical purposes they should not be considered in isolation from each other. Risk assessments and risk reduction activities directly inform disaster preparedness and response, for example. Moreover, the manner by which agencies respond to an emergency will directly impact the recovery process (WHO 2011b).
	ERM for health draws on the disciplines of risk management, disaster management, and health systems. The approach emphasizes managing the risks prior to a disaster occurring so that potential public health consequences may be prevented or minimized. Specifically, ERM entails identifying and reducing hazards and associated vulnerabilities, preparing for and responding effectively to disasters, and recovering, rehabilitating, and reconstructing after a disaster has occurred. Experience has demonstrated that countries and communities that have invested sufficient resources in ERM have responded more effectively and have been more resilient to the effects of disasters. Strengthened ERM also has the potential to contribute to sustainable development.
	Bangladesh is one of the most natural disaster-prone countries on the planet. Large numbers of people live on a low, flat alluvial delta vulnerable to floodwater coming from the Brahmaputra basin to the north and the typhoon-prone Indian Ocean to the south. A typhoon in 1970 resulted in approximately a quarter of a million deaths (Bern et al. 1993). Over the next decades, the people of Bangladesh built 311 elevated typhoon and flood shelters that could hold 350,000 people and implemented community-based response strategies. A similar 1991 typhoon affecting a far larger population resulted in 138,000 deaths (Mallick et al. 2005). During the 1991 storm, seeking a storm shelter early and being in an official shelter were highly protective against death although only 17% of the affected populations sought shelter in response to the storm warning sirens. Since then, advances in storm warning, public communications and community response have resulted in Southern Bangladesh being held up as an example of disaster preparedness (UNDP 2010).





Guiding principles


	In addition to the emphasis on managing risks, ERM is guided by the following key principles (Brennan et al. 2009):
	 	• Addressing all hazards. Many of the key functions required to manage risks are common across all hazards, for example, assessments, communications, logistics, etc. Moreover, it is neither efficient nor cost-effective to develop separate plans, procedures, trainings, rosters, and response mechanisms for each individual hazard. While some hazard-specific considerations will rarely be required (e.g. radio-nuclear), an all-hazards approach allows for more efficient management of risks and responses.
	• Multisectoral approach. Many activities required to protect and preserve health are managed primarily by non-health sectors, for example, water and sanitation, shelter, food security, law and order, etc. Effective mechanisms for multisectoral collaboration and coordination are therefore necessary to ensure optimized ERM in the health sector. These should be established at national and local levels, wherever possible.
	• Prepared community. Communities are always the first to respond to disasters and can play a critical role in meeting emergent health needs. Community resilience can be strengthened by building their capacity to prevent, mitigate, prepare for, respond to, and recover from disasters. Local governments, civil society organizations, and individual citizens all have the potential of contributing to ERM.





Key components of emergency risk management


	Prevention, risk reduction, and mitigation come first.
	Table 11.11.2 regarding the impact of the 10 storms on the Dominican Republic vs. Haiti highlights the value of robust building zoning codes, urban planning, flood plain buffer zones, utility repair plans, evacuation plans, pre-recorded radio messages, and all of those things that prevent people from risk exposure which are planned years and months ahead of any disaster. The highest priority of disaster planning should be to keep people and potentially harmful exposures apart. While that statement is very broad (including evacuation orders and do not travel orders and hazardous waste regulations), it needs to be kept in the forefront of the disaster planner’s priorities.
	Disaster risk assessments are the lens through which prevention and risk reduction can happen.
	In 1993, a truck bomb was exploded in the parking lot under the World Trade Center killing 6 and injuring over 1,000 people (Lambert n.d.). In the aftermath of this explosion, electricity went out and smoke filled the vertical structure. With the electricity out, the elevators did not work. Because the stairwells had no windows and were dark and filled with smoke, it took many hours for people to go down those stairwells in the dark. The CDC sent a team to assess what had gone right and wrong during the event and the team’s top recommendation was that battery powered lights be placed in the stairwells in case the power was ever cut off again. In 2001 when the World Trade Center was struck by two airliners 8 years later, thousands and thousands of people were likely saved because those lights were in those stairwells in the minutes after the electricity went out and before the buildings collapsed. This is a particularly dramatic example of the value of a disaster risk assessment.
	Ideally, a disaster risk assessment should be multisectorial, multidisciplinary, and attempt to identify risks in advance to develop clear strategies to manage them (International Federation of the Red Cross 2006). The health component of a multisectoral risk assessment aims to determine the likelihood and potential public health impact of future disasters. Possible health consequences include direct impacts on people (e.g. injury, disease) or health facilities, and/or secondary effects due to damaged infrastructure (e.g. water and sanitation systems), population displacement, environmental damage, etc.
	A coastal community will have greater vulnerabilities to hurricanes than communities located at a distance from the shoreline. A community on a steep hillside will have different earthquake risks than a nearby village on the flat valley bottomland. Thus, the most important lessons and ideas that will help shape a community’s preparation for a disaster will often come from locals and will need to vary from place to place. The task of a disaster planner is to separate out those lessons that are universal (e.g. never drive a car into moving floodwaters, always assume electrical lines are ‘hot’ even if the electricity has stopped working) and those that are site-specific (e.g. when a tornado comes, go to the church basement).
	Strategies and programmes should be based on evidence and endorsed or formed on the level of the implementers.
	Disaster risk assessments, based on assessing past disasters, inspecting the environment, and speaking with key partners should be used to develop strategies and programmes to reduce the potential impact on public health by the identified hazards. These may include general health system strengthening measures to improve the coverage and effectiveness of existing health services (e.g. vaccinations, training and supervision of staff, improved drug management). They may also include specific health sector interventions that can mitigate the effects of disasters, such as the successful safe hospital programme in Latin America (Pan American Health Organization 2000, 2002) and early warning alert and response systems for outbreak control. In some places, radio messages or alarms are important to establish. In some situations such as the recent Latin American Zika outbreak, focusing support and efforts to key groups like health workers and pregnant women, may be appropriate. Once a strategy or programme is established, drills or simulations can be an invaluable tool to understand what parts of the response procedure are not working optimally.
	Get prepared. The UNISDR definition of preparedness is ‘the knowledge and capacities developed by governments, professional response and recovery organizations, communities, and individuals to effectively anticipate, respond to, and recover from, the impacts of likely, imminent or current hazard events or conditions’ (UNISDR 2009). Many emergency organizations also use the related term ‘readiness’ to describe their ability to rapidly and appropriately respond to a disaster. In those cases where emergencies are likely to be predicted or recur (e.g. hurricanes, floods, wildfires), preparedness plans need to be in places on the household level, as well as on the local governance and national levels.
	Sound preparedness clearly arises from an effective risk assessment and is linked to early warning systems. It should ensure the required resources and capacities can be rapidly deployed following the onset of a disaster. Clear emergency functions should be specified in advance and rosters of qualified and experienced staff developed. Stockpiles of essential drugs, equipment, and supplies should be established and maintained, including strong logistics procedures. All emergency staff should be trained in the relevant technical standards, performance standards, and response procedures (Sphere Project 2011). Standard operating procedures should address key administrative, financial, procurement, and communications functions. Coordination mechanisms should be developed in advance, both for improved health sector and intersectoral functioning. Contingency planning may take into account possible scenarios and triggers for response, and further strengthen coordination.
	Response is what gets noticed. When Ebola struck in DRC in 2018, WHO was more than 100 times more responsive than they had been during the 2013–2015 outbreak in West Africa in terms of person days delay in responding. WHO had prepared staff, a vaccine had been developed that was utilized in the field within a month of initial reports, and they had protective clothing and materials in stock. It is not by chance that WHO received scathing reviews for years after the 2013 outbreak and almost exclusively good press in 2018. This, in spite of the fact that over both periods responding to Ebola was likely much less than 10% of all that WHO was doing. This is nearly universal: governments and agencies are publicly evaluated on their response to crises more than for the crises they averted or non-emergency related good they do.
	This implies that the things needed to respond (knowledge, messages, materials, and people) need to be in place long before a crisis hits. Having preparedness plans, documented operating procedures, a flexible emergency funding strategy, and a rooster of workers are all tasks best achieved far in advance of a crisis, but will usually be what most influences the quality of response.
	Recovery is often neglected. Many organizations adhere to the so-called build back better approach. Recovery programmes are increasingly informed by post-disaster needs assessments (PDNA), which provide a measure of loss within each sector and a prioritized plan for recovery and reconstruction (World Bank Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery 2011). In reality, emergency responders are poorly suited to doing this and local players often do not have the resources. Most emergency funding lasts for months or a year at the longest and reconstruction rarely happens so quickly. While this is widely known and agencies and offices have attempted to address the void between emergency response and reconstruction, this remains a very problematic issue.
	In 1993, the US government created a funding office to fill the void between emergency response and development called the Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI). Critics have pointed out how this institution has done little to end the dropping of health supporting programmes when an acute crisis has passed. In the case of OTI, critics point out how it seems to spend much of its funding on civil society activities like democracy building (Blum 2013). For example, Wikileaks reported that in a 2006 cable, then-Ambassador William Brownfield, outlined a strategy to ‘penetrating Chavez’s political base’, ‘dividing Chavismo’, ‘protecting vital US business’, and ‘isolating Chavez internationally’ and OTI funding was a central part of this (Hart 2013). While this example is from the US, many other countries have interwoven political and humanitarian agendas and it is inevitable that ambassadors and funders will not be able to operate with the humanitarian tenants of impartiality and neutrality. Thus, when recovery and developments get together for a ‘Do Development Differently’ conference, they conclude that locals are not sufficiently engaged and empowered and that true recovery is often neglected (DDD n.d.). When the UN held a Humanitarian Summit in Istanbul in 2016, they conclude that locals are not sufficiently engaged and empowered and recovery is underfunded or neglected (Agenda for Humanity 2016). Thus, in spite of widespread understanding of the problem and good intent, for the foreseeable future there will be a tendency to provide funding when a crisis is underway; but, in the poorest of settings, for competing priorities to shift the focus from rebuilding post-crisis.





Coordination of response


	The coordination of responses occurs by a wide variety of mechanisms that vary widely. There is a tendency for natural disasters to be coordinated by a national emergency response mechanism. Sometimes this coordination is housed in the military, sometimes it is a permanent cabinet level office like in the UK and Japan, and sometimes it is a self-standing office like in Peru and Ghana. In such settings, assistance from abroad is typically coordinated by that entity. In some cases, the coordination structures can evolve or be complex. For example, during the 2014 Ebola outbreak in Sierra Leone, initially, the Ministry of Health directed the focus of response efforts through a National Ebola Response Committee (NERC) which met daily and coordinated most overseas assistance with the WHO. After 3 months, the military took over the national Coordination and the NERC, but the Ministry of Health continued coordinating the foreign assistance (LR personal observation).
	In complex emergencies and including wars, it is often difficult for the host government to play a coordinating role either because it is overstretched or weak, or because humanitarian actors are wedded to their concept of neutrality and are reluctant to cooperate with a warring party. In such settings the UN Cluster System is often established. Figure 11.11.6 is a visual display of this system.
	Fig. 11.11.6 UNOCHA depiction of the Cluster System.
	Reprinted under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license.
	The Cluster System is typically coordinated by the United Nations Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA n.d.) and operates as a constellation of coordinating bodies. There are 11 sectors that each have a coordination lead, usually a UN agency that attempts to share information, resources and optimize the distribution of assets. In some settings where needed, there are subclusters that attempt to coordinate for a subset of a sector’s activities. Typically, members of the humanitarian community gather for regular meetings, often with government agencies present. For a variety of reasons, some humanitarian actors such as MSF tend not to formally participate in Cluster processes. In 2018, 27 countries have ‘Health Clusters’ operating all led by the WHO. While the success of these clusters is widely debated, they are almost certainly going to be a mainstay of humanitarian coordination for the foreseeable future





Public health needs


	Oxygen, water, and food remain the essential priority human needs in almost all settings including the most acute of hardships. The initial handbooks overviewing the public health priorities in high-mortality, low-resource settings remain as relevant today as when they were written (CDC 1992; MSF 1997). Most were lacking in some areas now better appreciated, with obstetric care being perhaps the most dramatic example. Usually those handbooks defined an emergency in terms of a doubling or quadrupling of the baseline mortality rate. In settings of extreme hardship, those displaced and whose livelihoods and social order are disrupted will generally continue to die and suffer from the same ailments they experienced before the crisis but at a higher rate. In some categories of disasters such as natural disasters like earthquakes and floods, death profiles are briefly but dramatically altered but prolonged elevated mortality as seen in the 2017 Puerto Rico example earlier is rare. Thus, in the most typical disruption and displacement scenarios, acute respiratory infections, diarrhoea, and in some places malaria, dominate the prevention and treatment priorities. Yet, these kinds of crises, with mortality rates elevated fourfold or more, are accounting for a smaller and smaller fraction of all humanitarian aid.
	Most aid workers today can work an entire lifetime and never see the dramatically elevated mortality of ten or 20 times the baseline rates seen repeatedly in the 1960s through the Rwandan Crisis of 1994. For example, if we use the threshold of 2% of the population dying each month (ten times the highest of baselines) in a population over 100,000 people to define a humanitarian catastrophe, a review of both published and unpublished mortality reports suggests that from 1979 to 1994, as shown in Figure 11.11.1, there was such a catastrophe on average every 2 years, but none have been reported since that time (Roberts 2013). The camp-based relief setting has also become rare, forcing relief agencies to work in cities and with existing government institutions.
	This change away from relief typified by water and food delivery and life-saving primary healthcare approaches is being driven by four forces: the global transition from a disease burden profile typified by acute infectious illness to one dominated by chronic diseases, more aid funding and a downward trend in conflict inducing a lower threshold of what is considered a humanitarian crisis, changing motivations, and the rise of the rights-based framework within humanitarian relief.





Transition from acute infectious diseases to chronic conditions


	In recent years, international health crises like the 2013–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak and the 2015–2016 Zika epidemic have dominated the headlines. In both of these events, the WHO declared a ‘public health emergency of international concern’ to mobilize international support and governments and NGOs led a global response to increase preparedness and funding for these diseases that seemed to threaten global health security.
	Yet despite the outsized media coverage and financial contributions to combat them, outbreaks of acute infectious diseases are now responsible for a small proportion of global deaths. Lopez et al. have documented how globally, between 1990 and 2005 the human species transitioned from experiencing disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost primarily to infectious diseases to losing DALYs primarily from chronic and non-infectious causes (Lopez et al. 2006). In fact, globally more people will die in the next 3 hours from NCDs than the total number who died from Ebola in the 3-year-long West Africa epidemic (WHO 2018). Yet despite the fact that NCDs are responsible for 60% of all DALYs and 70% of all deaths, they currently receive only 2% of overseas development assistance for health (Allen 2017).
	The epidemiological transition occurring in developing countries from infectious diseases to noncommunicable diseases as a greater contributor to mortality has been well documented. For example, Lopez et al. contrast the causes of death among adults in various regions based on 1990 and 2001 data respectively (Lopez et al. 2006). Over those 11 years, the non-HIV infectious disease adult death rates declined markedly in Latin America and the Caribbean, the Middle East and North Africa, East Asia and the Pacific, and South Asia. In each locality, this reduction in infectious disease death rates corresponded with lower overall adult mortality. Only in the post-Soviet Europe and Central Asia region and Africa did adult mortality rise over this period; in the former, primarily from cardiovascular diseases and unintentional injuries, and in Africa primarily from HIV. In Africa, overall mortality still decreased over this period because of dramatic reductions in infant and child mortality.
	The impact of this epidemiological transition was evident in crises in Bosnia, Kosovo, and Iraq, where Ministries of Health and aid agencies were confronted with morbidity profiles dominated by non-infectious diseases. More recently, the high prevalence of NCDs in Syrians displaced by the ongoing civil war has challenged aid groups and health systems in neighbouring countries. Prior to the Syrian civil war, a 2007 survey found that cardiovascular disease was responsible for 45% of overall mortality in Aleppo, and a situational analysis conducted by the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office (EMRO) demonstrated that 79% of mortality among Syrians nationally was related to NCDs (Gardemann 2002; Rahim 2014). Providing NCD care for the millions displaced by the conflict has been complicated by the difficulties in humanitarian relief coordination within Syria and by the lack of access to primary healthcare in neighbouring countries where many Syrians have sought refuge.
	The growing prevalence of noncommunicable diseases in humanitarian settings highlights the disconnect between the health needs of those impacted by crisis and a humanitarian system that has been built to respond to crises characterized by high-mortality from communicable diseases.
	Adding to this need to transition medical preparedness for emergencies is the growing appreciation of HIV as a non-fatal chronic condition. An estimated 10.3 million Africans regularly received antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) in 2015, double that of 2011, covering 54% of the total number of Africans who are HIV positive 2011 (WHO et al. 2011; WHO 2016). As a disproportionate number of humanitarian operations occur in Africa, planning for the chronic disease support aspects of HIV needs to be part of the humanitarian public health portfolio (O’Brien et al. 2010).
	The future success of the humanitarian community will depend in part on how well it can develop the capacity to provide quality care for NCDs in humanitarian crises while simultaneously maintaining the ability to respond to outbreaks of acute infectious diseases that will undoubtedly continue to plague our increasingly connected world.





More aid, more in need, and longer armed conflicts


	Spending on humanitarian assistance has increased dramatically in recent decades. According to Global Humanitarian Assistance, formal humanitarian assistance spending increased fourfold from 1990 to 2010 (United Nations Children’s Fund 2013). Unfortunately, however, more aid is being taken up by the increasing numbers of people displaced by conflict, requiring relief after natural disasters, and to a lesser extent, technological disasters such as the Fukushima nuclear meltdown in 2011. This has the effect of lowering the mortality prioritization with regard to what is considered a humanitarian crisis. It also means since much humanitarian spending is in post-conflict settings, that humanitarian assistance is now inseparable from development work.
	At the same time, there was a downward trend in the number of armed conflicts in the world since the end of the Cold War, although this number has been on the rise since 2013, driven largely by ongoing conflict in the Middle East (Gleditsch et al. 2002; PRIO 2017). Although many of the ongoing conflicts are internalized within a state, a growing proportion are internationalized indicating the involvement of external states, which is significant because internationalized conflicts tend to last longer and more difficult to resolve (PRIO 2017). Further complicating the issue, conflict has become more protracted with the average conflict increasing from 19 years in 1990 to 37 years in 2013. Garfield et al. documented how the number of people living in conflict has increased over the past half century but a smaller and smaller portion of those people are in high-intensity conflict settings (Garfield 2012). With prolonged conflicts taking place in multiple geographic regions, the international community faces serious challenges.





Changing motivations and the rights-based framework


	Aid meant to induce development may be different in nature from humanitarian aid designed to prevent deaths and suffering in the short term. Donors are continuing to place increasing emphasis on sustainability of humanitarian interventions and demanding local participation and empowerment. These are natural changes in perspective that match a transition from death aversion to priorities involving improved quality of life. A few NGOs such as MSF maintain a philosophy that they work primarily to reduce death and suffering but most others now hold long-term impact and sustainability as central objectives. This creates several new conditions for relief work. Many relief efforts in the 1980s and 1990s defined success by the lowering of the crude mortality rate (CDC 1992). This is rare today. Sustainability efforts usually require training and supporting local officials and institutions, committing to multiyear engagements, and monitoring changes in behaviours. These require different skills from those prevalent in relief agencies in the twentieth century. Reconstruction activities following earthquakes and tsunamis often employ many times more construction and economic experts than health professionals and epidemiologists.
	In tandem with this shift in focus from just averting deaths, has been the rise of a rights-based approach to programming. The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) defines a human rights-based approach as ‘a conceptual framework for the process of human development that is normatively based on international human rights standards and operationally directed to promoting and protecting human rights’ (UNICEF 2013). This framework, while not fundamentally contradictory, is very different in focus and in programme implications from the ‘public health’ approach of the last century’s relief operations (CDC 1992; MSF 1997). This public health approach, sometimes called a cost-effectiveness approach, concentrated on how the relief community could reduce the most deaths and suffering with the assets available. This manifested in specific interventions like measles immunization, latrine construction, or primary healthcare clinics which brought broader benefits at low costs.
	The rights-based approach has the advantage that it more readily encompasses issues like psychological suffering which are harder to measure, and can project values such as that girls should have equal chances for advancement as boys. But the term ‘normatively based’ in the UNICEF definition is not well defined or constant. For example, UN resolutions or agency position statements often stress the need to have child re-unification programmes where benefit is difficult to demonstrate (Ager and Metzler 2012). In the public health approach the benefits and the cost-effectiveness of programmes are more readily established, and new ideas can be compared with established programmes. Rights-based programming, in contrast, has no equivalent incentive to demonstrate cost-effectiveness and in fact is more driven by the strength of resolutions or declarations. Thus, if one wants to advocate for the value of counselling rape victims, in a rights-based framework it would be more efficient to attempt to pass a UN resolution than to evaluate the effectiveness of programmes in the field. With the public health approach, the opposite would be true.
	In summary, humanitarian public health needs have broadened as the clientele served has begun to span a broader range of development levels, as the need to support people with chronic conditions including HIV has become more important. This may be an indication that the humanitarian endeavour has worked over the past half century. A Biafra-like scenario, where half the population died in a 4-year period, is rare today. Thus, the world’s growing sources of compassion and aid can serve more than just those on the verge of death.





New developments for the twenty-first century


	A host of new developments make it likely that relief work in the middle of the twenty-first century will look little like efforts in Biafra and South East Asia the century before. The advances of the past decades that will likely expand in the future can be considered in three broad categories: political trends, new approaches, and new technical advances. These categories interact with and influence each other, with technical advances often creating the potential for new orderings of social organization. While not comprehensive, this section seeks to imagine the likely changes to come in the field of humanitarian response.





Political trends


The melding of political and humanitarian agendas


	National governmental political agendas and humanitarian relief have never been completely independent. In 1919, the US Congress formed the American Relief Administration (ARA), supposedly an independent NGO-like entity, headed by future President Herbert Hoover, to act as an independent famine relief mechanism in Europe in the years following the First World War (Fisher 1927). Oxfam, among the most famous of NGOs for its politically neutral funding sources, was formed in large part to lobby the British government to loosen the Allied blockade of occupied Europe (Oxfam n.d.). MSF co-founder Bernard Kouchner later became the French Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and the Foreign Minister, allotting funding for his creation, MSF. That humanitarian and political interests overlap is not completely unhealthy if in a democracy the populace is privately choosing to fund humanitarian ventures while simultaneously influencing the priorities of their government to do the same. On the other hand, countries are often in open competition with each other, and the linking of aid to enhance economic, military, or political competitiveness would be antithetical to the humanitarian endeavour. Two documents have attempted to keep humanitarian aid ‘neutral’ in the eyes of combatants and beneficiaries over the last part of the twentieth century.
	Both the Third Geneva Convention of 1949 and the Red Cross Code of Conduct, to which most NGOs and the UN aspire to adhere, actively encourage the separation of humanitarian endeavours and self-interested agendas of individual states. The fourth tenet of the non-binding Red Cross Code of Conduct explicitly states, ‘We shall endeavour not to act as instruments of government foreign policy’ (International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies n.d.). The ICRC and MSF are particularly famous for keeping political and military forces at arm’s length even during the acute phases of crises. For example, during the 1992 crisis when Kurds fled northern Iraq but were not allowed into Turkey, MSF refused to move in public or cooperate with any military personnel carrying a weapon. Many military personnel, including the British and American forces who had just invaded Iraq and were thus belligerents in this conflict, operated within the displaced community without weapons so as to work with MSF and other NGO personnel. Thus, until 2001, while funding influenced where relief went and what kinds of relief efforts were funded, an honest effort was made on the part of most donors and most international NGOs to not undertake patently political activities to advance the agenda of one country.
	Nonetheless, a remarkable change in the landscape of humanitarian assistance has been the melding of political and humanitarian agendas after the terrorist attacks on New York City on 11 September 2001. Beginning with the invasion of Afghanistan, this narrowing separation of political and humanitarian ventures was often ignored or blurred. In October 2001, US Secretary of State Colin Powell addressed leaders of the American NGO community referring to their organizations as ‘force multipliers’ (International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies n.d.). In Afghanistan, US humanitarian aid was openly discussed as a military tool for winning hearts and minds. In May of 2003, USAID Administrator Andrew Ntasios told the American NGOs that they needed to do a better job of advertising that the goods and services they provide to the Afghan people were coming from the US government. He told the American NGOs that they were an ‘arm of the US government’ (Klien 2003). Military activities such as distributions and school construction often made it unclear what was being done by combatants and what was being done by NGOs (Falconer 2009). MSF, who had been working in Afghanistan for 33 years, was forced to pull out there and in Iraq after their aid workers were targeted for assassination (Katz and Wright 2004). This blurring of aid and political agendas was again demonstrated when the Central Intelligence Agency hired a physician to conduct a sham vaccination campaign in Pakistan as part of the hunt for Osama Bin Laden in 2011 (Roberts and VanRooyen 2013; Rubenstein 2013). Subsequent to this ploy, the Aid Worker Security Database demonstrated a drastic increase in the number of vaccinators attacked and killed as shown in Figure 11.11.7 next.
	Fig. 11.11.7 Vaccinators attached, 2002–14.
	Source: data from Humanitarian Outcomes (2015), Aid Worker Security Database, https://aidworkersecurity.org/Graphic provided courtesy of A. Stoddard.
	The responses to natural disasters are not devoid of political overtones or agendas either. Following the 2005 tsunami in a largely Muslim area of the Pacific, the US Secretary of State called the disaster a ‘wonderful opportunity’ for the United States (Anonymous 2005). Preferential responses to former colonies and near neighbours appear to be an inevitable aspect of bilateral giving following natural calamities.





Attacks on healthcare


	As a likely consequence of the blending of political and humanitarian agendas discussed earlier, there is growing worry within the humanitarian community that attacks on healthcare—including workers, structures, and transport—are occurring at an unprecedented rate.
	During armed conflicts, international humanitarian law protects healthcare facilities and personnel from being the targets of attack. This protection is enshrined in the Geneva Conventions and was re-iterated by the United Nations Security Council Resolution 2286 as recently as 2016 (UN 2016). Certain high-profile attacks—such as the destruction of MSF’s hospital in Kunduz, Afghanistan in 2015 by a US Air Force gunship—have provoked widespread concern among aid workers. Although there have long been documented attacks on healthcare—including Italian attacks on the Ethiopian Red Cross, and even attacks on Red Cross that incensed Henri Durant in the Franco Prussian War—there is a perception among aid workers of an increase in attacks on healthcare workers and facilities (International Crisis Group 2005; Verma 2017). While anecdotal evidence, especially in Syria suggest an increase, a historical lack of standardized data documenting these attacks makes it difficult to quantify any trends (Briody 2018).
	In response numerous organizations have established advocacy campaigns—including ICRC’s Health Care in Danger and MSF’s Medical Care Under Fire—to raise awareness and document such attacks while comprehensive databases have been established by independent research organizations like the Aid Worker Security Database of Humanitarian Outcomes to record attacks on healthcare workers (WHO 2015).
	The WHO-led trauma response during the 2016 Mosul offensive in Iraq provides an example of how healthcare is being provided in potentially more dangerous conditions that may expose aid workers to a greater risk of attack. A coalition of Iraqi and international forces launched military operations to retake the city of Mosul from ISIS but abdicated its responsibility under international humanitarian law to provide medical care to war-wounded combatants. Anticipating a high number of patients with complex trauma, the WHO assumed control of the trauma response and contracted medical NGOs and private medical actors to ‘co-locate’ or embed within military units on the frontlines of conflict to provide medical stabilization and coordinate a trauma referral system (Fox et al. 2018). Although there were no reported attacks on healthcare workers, there was concern in the humanitarian community that directly working with military forces on the frontlines of a conflict increases the risk to aid workers and compromises the principles of independence and neutrality.





Migration—a record number on the move


	An unprecedented 65.6 million people around the world have been forced from their home, and 20 more people are displaced every minute while fleeing violence, poverty, and persecution (Pew Research Center 2016).
	Most people on the move today are internally displaced, indicating they have not crossed a border and are still within their home country. Using the example of those displaced by the Syrian civil war, nearly half of the nearly 12 million Syrians on the move are still within that country. The majority of the rest are living in neighbouring countries—including Turkey (3.4 million), Lebanon (1 million), Jordan (660,000), and Iraq (125,000) (Pew Research Center 2018). Despite the increasingly anti-immigrant and nationalistic rhetoric of politicians in the Western world, relatively few on the people on the move are being hosted in the United States or Europe.
	In addition to the large displacement of Syrians since 2011, there are multiple other large populations on the move throughout the world. In Central America, violence in Honduras and El Salvador in 2016 caused 388,000 to flee the region to seek refuge further north in Mexico and the US. Beginning in 2017, nearly 700,000 of Rohingya—a stateless minority group living in Myanmar—fled across the border to Bangladesh to escape persecution. Across sub-Saharan Africa, hundreds of thousands of men, women, and children—primarily from West Africa—have travelled through the Sahel to reach Libya from which many try to reach Europe via the dangerous sea route.
	In the course of their journeys and regardless of whether they cross a border, displaced people are subject to numerous challenges, including human rights abuses, lack of access to healthcare, and restricted movement. For example, in Libya countless thousands are held in official and unofficial detention centres where rape, torture and abuse in an attempt to extract ransom are common (Amnesty International 2018). Similarly, many Rohingya report having been the victim of rape and indiscriminate attacks while in Myanmar or while fleeing across the border into Bangladesh.
	One aspect of the migration experience that is disturbingly underdocumented is the number who die while on the move. Efforts such as the ‘Missing Migrants’ project by the International Organization for Migration have attempted to quantify the mortality experience of migrants in different contexts, but these are limited by incomplete and unstandardized data collection, limited political funding and support, and the difficult physical environments through which many migrate. Using the Mediterranean Sea route as an example, the Missing Migrant’s Project reports that 6,869 people have died attempting this crossing between 2014 and 2017, making it the most dangerous sea journey in the world (IOM 2018). However, the number is undoubtedly much higher given that this estimate doesn’t include the untold number of people who drowned but whose bodies were never found.





Humanitarian accountability


	While aid agencies and the Red Cross Code of Conduct have always purported to support local empowerment and accountability of aid deliverers to beneficiaries and donors alike, many new developments have made that aspiration more common. The third edition of the Sphere Standards (Sphere Project 2011), perhaps the most widely followed guidelines for humanitarian practice, has an expanded emphasis on local participation and accountability to beneficiaries. In 2010, the UN passed an ‘Accountability Framework’ which may or may not result in more cost-efficient services on the ground, but certainly contributes to an international focus on recording transparently what is achieved by aid efforts and at what cost (UN 2010). Likewise, in 2011, the InterAgency Standing Committee (IASC) developed an operational framework on how to ensure accountability to affected populations in humanitarian emergencies which is widely cited among humanitarian players (IASC 2011). Thirdly, the rise of wealthy, highly functional governments in all regions of the world raises the expectations of aid delivery procedures. For example, in 2003, India became a net creditor to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Food Programme (WFP) (Bijoy 2011). The rise of local NGOs as a primary international delivery mechanism, the prevalence of social networking, and the economic downturn in post-2008 Europe and North America all point towards a future where local and more players have a larger role in what aid is provided and how it will be disbursed.





Growing participation of ‘non-traditional’ actors in humanitarian response


	At its root, today’s humanitarian system is fundamentally a Western construct based on European Enlightenment ideals of charity and limitations on the conduct of war. Although some form of the humanitarian impulse is likely as old as mankind, the formal structure we know today was first established in the late nineteenth century and was greatly expanded in the aftermath of World War II with programmes primarily targeted to provide assistance to Europeans displaced by war. The humanitarian community gradually extended its programmes globally to nearly all populations affected by crisis, and its core principles have largely remained unchanged since their beginnings, despite substantial global geopolitical and financial changes.
	However, there are indications that within the global aid community a number of ‘non-traditional’ actors—including China, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey—are playing a larger role in the humanitarian endeavour. While the majority of funding for humanitarian emergency response comes from ‘traditional’ government and intergovernmental sources—the US, European Commission and United Kingdom alone contribute more than 50% of the total government humanitarian contributions—recent years have shown greater contributions from outside the rich Western nations. Between 2012 and 2014, the largest increases came from Saudi Arabia and the Gulf States of Kuwait and Qatar (ALNAP 2015) and as shown in Figure 11.11.8, between 2004 and 2016 humanitarian contributions from China have increased fivefold (Hirono 2018).
	Fig. 11.11.8 Chinese GDP in trillions and humanitarian spending in millions 2004–2015.
	Sources: UNOCHA FTS, World Bank.
	In addition to their growing financial presence, non-traditional actors are also playing a bigger political role in the global humanitarian system. Turkey has used its growing economic influence and its strategic position between Europe and the conflicts in the Middle East to position itself as a significant contributor to humanitarian assistance worldwide. In recognition of its involvement in Somalia, its role in hosting millions displaced in the Syrian civil war, and its deal with the EU to reduce the number of asylum seekers entering Europe, Turkey was selected to host the first ever World Humanitarian Summit in 2016.
	Humanitarian response has largely been shaped by Western ideas and actors since its inception, yet that is currently changing as non-traditional actors constitute a larger part of the financial and political leadership of the humanitarian endeavour. It remains to be seen what impact this growing involvement of non-Western donors will have on the future of humanitarian action.





New approaches


	The growing appreciation of local capacities to provide exacting technical services combined with technical advances and greater emphasis on accountability, have paved the way in the past decade for exciting new ways of delivering aid. Among these are the following:





Home-based treatments


	In the 1980s, the promotion of ORT was championed aggressively by the UN and aligned agencies because it was seen as a way to overcome the primary barrier to successful treatment of acute illness, namely early detection and treatment. The logic was that if people did not have to go through the effort of transporting the patient and their things to a medical facility, far more people would get treated. This was partially the logic behind the barefoot doctors’ programme in post-revolution China and a variety of other initiatives such as mobile clinics (Gish and Walker 1977).
	Over the past decade, ambitions to provide antiretroviral treatments in areas of modest medical infrastructure and limited resources have resulted in a variety of models for drug distribution and patient monitoring using community or patient volunteers, or paid community health workers. The evidence suggests that patient management and monitoring schemes that are not physician based, where the monitoring occurs closer to the community level, are associated with better patient retention and survival (Callaghan et al. 2010). In focused settings of high malaria transmission, home-based treatment of fever has been shown to be an effective life-saving approach (Kidane and Morrow 2000).
	In emergency settings, no home treatment strategies have received more attention or inspired as much enthusiasm as home therapeutic feeding. Home therapeutic feeding usually involves training and equipping mothers of malnourished children to cure the child at home with a nutritious ready-to-use food such as eeZeePaste™NUT or Plumpy’Nut® which come precooked and are resistant to bacterial growth. These ready-to-use home treatment products cut down on attrition in feeding centres, are a less expensive means for treating moderately malnourished children, and have been shown to be highly effective in field trials (Patel et al. 2005).





Crowd sourcing and mobile phones


	The widespread availability of mobile phones and social media has made it possible to have the whole population participate in the monitoring of crises. One of the most well-known of these efforts is the Ushahidi platform, formed during the violent period following the 2008 Kenyan elections (Ushahidi n.d.).
	Perhaps the most dramatic application of the Ushahidi platform was in the February 2010 Chilean earthquake. The 8.8 magnitude quake was followed by a series of aftershocks that damaged thousands of buildings and ultimately killed an estimated 521 people. Within 48 hours of the initial quake, an Ushahidi–Chile platform was established and a team of graduate students in New York began mapping press reports and text messages to create a picture of damage and where people were trapped. One hundred ‘incidents’ were mapped in the first day of operation and 700 were mapped by the end of 3 days. In the weeks that followed, the Ushahidi platform updated local press members and the general public about food distributions, dangerous buildings, the occurrence of looting, and the progress of children re-attending school (Carlsen et al. 2011). Crowd sourcing strategies have also been used to inform Chinese authorities about acute situations in the aftermath of the Szechuan earthquake, to map the occurrence of sexual violence in Syria, and to map unsafe areas following the Japanese tsunami of 2011.
	Mobile phones by themselves are allowing for some exciting innovations. Somalis affected by conflict have received humanitarian aid in the form of phone credits which can be used to purchase goods in local shops (Global Communities n.d.). After the earthquake in Haiti, the largest mobile phone carrier used cellular networks to compare the movement of people before and after the earthquake to show that 630,000 people in Port-au-Prince left the capital in the 19 days following the earthquake (Bengtsson et al. 2011). In the Democratic Republic of Congo, community members in North Kivu were provided mobile phones to monitor trends in the number of children separated from their families and caregivers in emergencies (Guinote 2012; Rubenstein 2015). Many of these initiatives are exploratory and controlled trials will be needed to establish such procedures as effective protective investments. It is likely mobile-phones will be increasingly utilized by the humanitarian and health community in the years to come.





Monetary aid


	As part of the promotion of local and beneficiary empowerment, providing aid that allows beneficiaries to set their own priorities has become increasingly popular. The example of giving displaced Somalis mobile phone credit was discussed earlier. But, giving cash directly to beneficiaries in lieu of rations or material goods has several advantages. People are more likely to end up with what they want and the transfer costs are far lower. It has the potential to support the local economy including creating incentives for future increased local food production. It potentially has downsides such as driving local inflationary pressures and exposing people to increased risks of exploitation and extortion. A recent comprehensive review generally weighs the upsides as being greater than the downsides but suggests that implementers will need to choose the contexts carefully and develop methods for monitoring the success of direct cash assistance (Harvey 2007).
	Closely related to monetary aid is the distribution of credit vouchers or coupons. Sometimes these have a specific purpose such as paying for school fees or uniforms. The most common flexible distribution is non-food item (NFI) or food item fairs where a select collection of vendors selling at predetermined prices gather in one place and beneficiaries with coupons spend their coupons at this one place and time. This system has the advantages of giving beneficiaries choice over the aid items they receive, it supports local markets, and leaves beneficiaries less open to local extortion. A recent analysis of such a NFI fair aimed at recently displaced populations in South Kivu Province, DR Congo found that local authorities missed most IDPs when constructing vulnerable lists and included many locals. At the end of the NFI distribution process, the NFI ‘vulnerability score’ as defined by UNICEF was unchanged by the distributions (O’Keeffe and Zadravecz 2012). As with so many new practices, implementation and evaluation procedures will need to be developed locally to match each context in order to maximize the efficiency of distributions via fairs and similar voucher systems.





New technical advances


	A host of new technical advances or tools also create the potential for transformative advances in humanitarian relief in this century (Interagency Standing Committee 2013). Some technologies, such as the Global Positioning System (GPS), are so essential to relief efforts at present that it is hard to realize that the technology was almost non-existent 20 years ago. It is likely to evolve as a tracking tool for people, goods, and vehicles. One-dollar GPS transmitters will likely result in the tracking of individual cases of vaccines and drugs, and curb looting of warehouses by armed groups. Eye and fingerprint scanning technologies are reducing ration theft and false registrations across the globe. Advances in medicine, in diagnostic techniques, or protective devices such as long-lasting impregnated bednets, are constantly changing the practice of humanitarian relief. Some of the more promising new technical and medical breakthroughs are highlighted here.
	Satellite imagery and remote sensing has already changed humanitarian practice. UNHCR has used satellite images to count people moving from Darfur into Chad. For years, remote sensing has been used to predict crop failure and crop yields. The destruction of villages in Darfur and DRC has been documented with before and after remote images. But lately, satellite imagery has been used to undermine the impunity brought by national sovereignty. For example, during the 2017 period government violence against the Rohingya in Rakhine State in Myanmar, Human Rights Watch made extraordinarily detailed and timely documentation of village destruction by remote imagery (HRW 2017).
	Cloud computing and internet collaboration hold potential for a host of new ideas and innovations that may assist those responding to emergencies. Groups like Hackers for Humanity attempt to channel the efforts of internet talents to charities (Hackers for Humanity n.d.). A variety of efforts to solve ‘humanitarian problems’ have been addressed by crowdsourcing for a solution. A notable example is the use of open-source survey (OpenDataKit) and navigation (OpenStreetMap) software in the 2013–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak. Using local people with self-owned smartphones, surveyors were able to quickly update geographic and village information used by medical surveillance and response teams at a cost of €3.80 per village surveyed (Nic Lochlainn et al. 2018).
	Internet accountability mechanists: Google Earth and the internet are allowing for greater accountability of aid from the perspective of small private donors. A model held up as innovative but already being reproduced is that of Charity Water. Charity Water does not directly implement water supply and sanitation projects, but instead subcontracts with local operational partners to turn Western private donations into water and sanitation infrastructure (Charity Water n.d.). Charity Water provides donors with the latitude and longitude of the specific things people have paid to have built so that over time they can see if indeed a well was built or public tap installed, and they can monitor if it continues to be used over time. They even install monitors so that donors to a specific project can see at any given moment if water is flowing from it. While not all aid is remotely visible, this process of linking donors to beneficiaries visually or by social media will likely grow over time and the process of humanitarian assistance will be better for it (Srinivasan et al. 2012).
	Unmanned aerial vehicles: Although unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV)—‘drones’- are known primarily for their military uses, there has been increasing recognition of their potential to improve humanitarian and disaster response. UAVs have already delivered small packages to camps in Port-au-Prince after the 2010 Haiti earthquake and helped assess the damage caused by Typhoon Haiyan in the Philippines in 2013 (Oxfam 2013; Reuters 2014). Zipline, a US-based drone manufacturer and operator, has partnered with the Ministry of Health in Rwanda to trial delivery of blood for transfusion to remote areas throughout the country, and other countries have used UAVs to deliver emergency vaccines, HIV medication and antimalarial medication to difficult-to-access areas (Reliefweb n.d.). Confronted by high tuberculosis burden in a very remote location, Doctors Without Borders recently began using an unmanned maritime vehicles (UMV) to transport tuberculosis samples in Papua New Guinea (MSF 2018). Although they may face challenges from regulatory requirements and local opposition, UAVs may likely play a larger role in future humanitarian and disaster response.
	Telemedicine: Telemedicine—medical care provided from a distance—is being increasingly used in developed settings to remotely connect patients and healthcare providers. MSF has been using telemedicine since 2010 to connect field staff with experts based in Europe or the US who can provide advice from afar (Walji 2015). Although its use is still limited, the increasing presence of cellular and wireless connections and the lack of specialized healthcare providers in the most remote areas means telemedicine has promise for greater use in humanitarian response.





Conclusion


	The twenty-first century is likely to see an ever growing humanitarian movement that will become more focused on economic, emergency preparedness, and developmental issues. Aid will be more politicized, while simultaneously more locally controlled and with greater accountability for implementation. The post-Biafra humanitarian endeavour has been associated with a dramatic decline in extreme episodes of excess deaths associated with crises and the new face of humanitarian relief, which often looks a lot like development work of old, has largely been built on the successes of twentieth-century humanitarian relief.
