11.14


Global health in the era of sustainable development


	Fiona Fleck





Introduction: from millennial to sustainable development goals


	The world is experiencing demographic and epidemiological transitions that have resulted in a larger human population living much longer lives. In response to these changes, the World Health Organization (WHO) has expanded its initial focus on infectious causes of death to a much broader agenda, including noncommunicable diseases, violence and injuries, nutrition, antimicrobial resistance, health worker shortages, increasing pollution and decreasing biodiversity, climate change, mass migration and inequitable access to basic medicines and services (Vujicic et al. 2004; WHO 2010b).
	The WHO works through national governments and with many other agencies, initiatives, and public–private partnerships to improve human health. The final scorecard of the Millennium Development Goals summarizes the cumulative progress made in recent decades (UN 2000, 2015, 2017; PATH 2017; UNAIDS 2018).
	For example, from 1990 to 2015, the maternal mortality ratio declined by 45% and the percentage of births assisted by skilled health personnel increased from 59 to 71% (UN 2015). By 2017, the global under-5 mortality rate had declined to 39 deaths per 1,000 live births from a 1990 rate of 90 deaths per 1,000 live births (UN 2015; UN InterAgency Group for Child Mortality Estimation 2018). In 2017, about 85% of children worldwide received at least one dose of measles vaccine, an increase from 73% in 2000 (UN 2015; WHO 2018a).
	New human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infections fell from an estimated 3.5 million cases in 2000 to 1.8 million in 2017 (Jordan et al. 2017). In 2003, 800,000 people living with HIV were receiving antiretroviral therapy, compared to 21.7 million in 2017 (UN 2015; UNAIDS 2018). Between 1990 and 2015, global malaria incidence fell by an estimated 37% and mortality by 58%, however WHO estimates show that no further progress was made between 2015 and 2017 (WHO 2016a, 2018j). Tuberculosis mortality fell by 42% over between 2000 and 2017 (WHO 2018i).
	The WHO’s efforts to further improve health outcomes, described in its thirteenth general programme of work 2019−2023 (GPW 13), are closely aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. In adopting this agenda, Member States of the United Nations committed to meeting 17 goals and 169 targets, measured by 250 indicators (UN 2015a). Sustainable development is defined as a process that ‘meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs’ (World Commission on Environment and Development 1987).
	In the 2030 Agenda, governments agree to reconcile three conflicting demands: improved human welfare, environmental protection, and economic growth. Most high-income countries have tended to fare better on measures of human well-being (Sen 1999), but advances in each dimension of the human development index; life expectancy, education, and gross national income per capita, are associated with a large environmental footprint (Sneddon et al. 2006; Steffen et al. 2015).
	The mutually conflicting goals of industrialization (Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 9, industry, innovation and infrastructure) and climate change mitigation (Goal 13, climate action) and between biodiversity (Goal 14, life below water; Goal 15, life on land) and human welfare (Goal 1, no poverty) are clearly outlined, confronting policy makers with many interactions between and within the different goals. These can be divided into positive interactions (i.e. synergies), in which progress towards one goal contributes towards progress in another, or trade-offs, when progress towards one goal hinders progress in another. A few goals have no demonstrable association in either direction and are thereby unclassified (Worm et al. 2006; Pradhan et al. 2017). The 2030 Agenda challenges governments to uncouple the relationship between economic growth and environmental damage, at a time when most countries will experience a rapid increase in population.
	The WHO’s focus, Goal 3 (good health and well-being), is synergistic with Goal 1 (no poverty), Goal 5 (gender equality), Goal 10 (reduced inequalities) and Goal 6 (clean water and sanitation). The health goal has 13 targets, including some of the areas that were covered by the Millennium Development Goals—maternal, newborn, and child deaths, HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria. The new targets are for neglected tropical diseases, hepatitis, water-borne and other communicable diseases, noncommunicable diseases and mental health, narcotic drug abuse and the harmful use of alcohol, road traffic deaths and injuries, sexual and reproductive health services, hazardous chemicals, air, water and soil pollution and contamination, tobacco control, research and development on vaccines and medicines, health financing and workforce, and early warning of national and global health risks. The WHO and other health organizations have mapped their respective mandates and set mid-term milestones for targets of SDG 3 in the Global Action Plan for Healthy Lives and Well-being for All (WHO 2013a, 2018k).
	The WHO constitution established ‘the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health’ as ‘one of the fundamental rights of every human being without distinction of race, religion, political belief, economic or social condition’ (WHO 1948). The right to health underpins all SDG 3 targets, particularly 3.8: to ‘achieve universal health coverage, including financial risk protection, access to quality essential healthcare services and access to safe, effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all’.
	Based on the 2030 Agenda, the WHO’s current five-year strategy presents a vision of: one billion more people benefitting from universal health coverage, one billion more people better protected from health emergencies, and one billion more people enjoying better health and well-being (WHO 2018).





Towards universal health coverage


	Universal health coverage (UHC)—defined as ensuring that all people have access to needed health services of sufficient quality without incurring financial hardship—is the subject of sustainable development target 3.8. As a step towards this target, the WHO envisions an expansion of such coverage to an additional one billion people by 2023. In the absence of financial protection, an estimated 800 million people spend at least 10% of their household budgets on health expenses. For almost 100 million people each year, these expenses are high enough to push them into extreme poverty (WHO/World Bank 2017). At least half of the world’s population still lacks access to essential health services.
	Progress towards UHC is tracked by measures of coverage of health services, and by the impact that out-of-pocket expenditure on those services has on people’s living standards and their ability to spend on other basic needs. These measures reflect the twin imperatives of UHC: that people receive the health services they need without facing financial hardship (Sachs 2012; Wagstaff et al. 2017, 2018).
	The WHO and the World Bank evaluate the overall level and the extent to which UHC is equitable because national averages can mask low levels of coverage in disadvantaged groups. For example, only 17% of mothers and children in the poorest fifth of households in low-and lower-middle-income countries received at least six of seven basic maternal and child health interventions, compared to 74% for the wealthiest fifth of households (World Bank 2004; WHO/IBRD 2017).
	The International Health Partnership for UHC 2030 has 118 signatories—governments and multilateral, civil society, and philanthropic organizations—to its Global Compact. They have committed to building and expanding equitable, resilient, and sustainable health systems, funded primarily by public finance, and based on primary healthcare, that deliver integrated, comprehensive people-centred and quality health services for all, while taking necessary measures to protect households from financial hazards due to health expenditures.
	The WHO defines quality of care as the degree to which health services increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge (Kieny et al. 2018). The components of services comprise financing, workforce, governance, service delivery, information, medicines, technologies, and infrastructure.
	Primary healthcare is an essential component of national health systems that is needed to move countries closer towards UHC. Strong primary healthcare is vital for making progress on the unfinished agendas of communicable diseases, and maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health, as well as for the growing burden of noncommunicable diseases.
	Digital health approaches and other system innovations are also playing an important role in strengthening these services.
	Each national health system has scope to improve upon the components of its health services. For example, essential medicines and health technologies are often poorly distributed and unfairly priced (FAO 2018a). Repeated shortages continue to affect critical products, including insulin, antihypertensives, intravenous fluid, oral rehydration solution, analgesics, oral antidiabetics, and opioids for palliative care.
	Antiretrovirals for HIV, direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C and second-line treatments for drug-resistant tuberculosis when first marketed were too expensive for many countries. However, some countries have since negotiated price reductions, following voluntary licensing agreements and production of quality-assured generics (Andrieux-Meyer et al. 2015) and UN procurement has brought these medicines within reach of millions of patients.
	In some countries, the costs of caring for diabetes alone consume nearly 25% of the national health budget (Zhang et al. 2010). Globally, insulin can be accessed reliably by only half of the 100 million people who need it (Basu et al. 2019). In the United States of America, out-of-pocket expenses for insulin increased by 89% between 2000 and 2010. The US$21-billion global market in insulin is divided between three companies that together account for 99% in terms of value and 96% in terms of volume. Although more than 90 of 132 countries have no tariffs for insulin, the combination of taxes, steep mark-ups, and other supply chain costs have pushed up the drug price and hurt affordability (Health Action International 2015).
	The WHO has revised the methods used to measure pricing and affordability of essential medicines—particularly those used for primary care—in the context of the SDG monitoring. The WHO promotes policies and builds technical capacities in low-resourced health systems, develops international standards for the manufacturing and regulation of health products and provides guidance for health systems on how to deliver them safely and cost-effectively.
	Better access to medical products is pursued by negotiating price reductions for existing products and incentivizing product development for markets with limited purchasing power. Generic medicines, which do not need to recoup the investment needed for drug discovery, development, and marketing approval, are sold at prices closer to the costs of manufacturing, offering a significant means to reduce healthcare costs in all countries. A national policy that encourages the use of generic medicines can save an estimated 60% of the costs of medicines (WHO 2010, 2010a).
	In 1977, the WHO introduced the first Model List of Essential Medicines, its selection of the most effective and affordable medicines available at the time. The model list is intended to be adapted for use in any health system, especially those in low-and middle-income countries. The current list contains 433 products and is used by about 150 countries. In 2007, WHO developed the first Model List of Essential Medicines for children under 12 years of age. These lists are updated every two years (WHO 2013b).
	The WHO prequalification programme stimulates the supply of quality-assured medicines, including generics, and encourages competition between manufacturers (WHO 2013c). The programme was established in 2001 as a quality-assurance mechanism for products procured by UN agencies, the GAVI Alliance, and the Global Fund. Prequalification has resulted in more reliable supplies, better forecasting, and often substantial price reductions (WHO n.d.). Compliance measures include on-site inspections to ensure adherence to good manufacturing practices. Products can become de-listed if quality is not maintained; the prospect of de-listing has proven to be an incentive for manufacturers to maintain standards.
	In addition to financing, infrastructure, and medicines, UHC requires a health workforce of adequate size and skills. However, countries at all levels of socioeconomic development face difficulties in education and training, deployment, retention, and performance of their health workforce (Anand and Barnighausen 2004, 2007; Mullan et al. 2011).
	The WHO and the World Bank have developed an ‘SDG index threshold’ of 4.45 doctors, nurses, and midwives per 1,000 population as an indicative minimum density for health workers. In 2016 the global health workforce was over 43 million. The supply projections point out that despite significant growth leading to an aggregate number by 2030 of 67.3 million health workers, the projected global shortage of healthcare workers in 2030 will be more than 14.5 million (WHO 2016).





Disabilities


	The WHO estimates that over a billion people, about 15% of the world’s current population, have some form of disability. Its International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health defines disability as an umbrella term for impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions as the result of interaction between individuals with a health condition and personal and environmental factors. Therefore, the disability experienced by a person with lower limb paralysis in a setting where wheelchairs are available, and where homes, pavements, public transport, and the workplace are adapted to wheelchair access, is very different from the disability experienced by a person who has the same physical condition but who lives in an environment with none of these adaptations.
	People with disabilities report seeking more healthcare than people without disabilities and have greater unmet needs. However, all people with disabilities also develop the same health problems that affect the general population, and therefore need access to mainstream healthcare services. Article 25 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities reinforces the right of persons with disabilities to attain the highest standard of healthcare, without discrimination. The WHO also provides guidance to policy makers on mental health programmes. Of particular concern are the health services available to people with severe mental disorders; moderate to severe depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders. People with these conditions generally have a life expectancy that is 10–20 years less than the general population. Most of these premature deaths are due to physical health conditions. For the minority who can access healthcare, the care received is often of poor quality and physical health conditions are often overlooked.





Emergency preparedness and response


	Since its inception, WHO has coordinated the international response to outbreaks and other cross-border heath threats. Its International Health Regulations oblige Member States to report infectious disease outbreaks and other health incidents such as chemical spills and nuclear incidents, as well as to build core capacities for surveillance and response (WHO 2008a; Heymann et al. 2013). These reports are assessed, and responses are mounted in function of the severity, potential for spread, number of people affected, and the causative event or agent. The strongest rating is a ‘Public Health Event of International Concern’ defined as, ‘an extraordinary event which is determined to constitute a public health risk to other States through the international spread of disease and to potentially require a coordinated international response’ (WHO 2008a, 2018b, 2018c). Since the 2005 revision of the Regulations, there have been four such events: H1N1 influenza (2009), Ebola (2014), polio (2014), and Zika (2016).
	This approach to health emergencies was severely tested during the 2013–2016 Ebola virus disease outbreak in West Africa. Problems with the international response have been well documented (WHO 2015a; The Ebola Outbreak Epidemiology Team 2018). There were concerns that neither the affected countries nor the WHO sounded the alarm early enough; and that the rating of the outbreak as a public health event of international concern was overdue. Coordination between the WHO, Ministries of Health, United Nations agencies, and non-governmental partners was weak on many levels. The WHO lacked sufficient staff on location to respond adequately and the dynamics of transmission across the borders of Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone highlighted the need to strengthen health security (Moon et al. 2015; WHO 2015a, 2015b; Gostin and Katz 2016).
	The International Health Regulations require countries to avoid disruption to travel and trade, but during the 2013–2016 Ebola outbreak more than 40 countries implemented measures that significantly interfered with international traffic, outside the scope of the temporary recommendations issued by WHO. As a result, Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone faced severe political, economic, and social consequences, as well as barriers to receiving necessary personnel and supplies (WHO 2015a).
	The lessons learnt from the 2013–2016 outbreak catalysed the establishment of the WHO’s Health Emergencies Programme. A more effective response to outbreaks and emergencies is made possible by a unified structure and one line of accountability from headquarters through the WHO’s Regional Offices. Administrative and financial adjustments were made, including the creation of a contingency fund for emergencies. An incident management system is used to structure and manage response activities, as a core component of the Emergency Response Framework (WHO 2017a).
	The WHO now coordinates more closely with United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, joining other agencies that provide support for humanitarian crises in the field, such as the United Nations Refugee Agency, the World Food Programme, and the United Nations Children’s Fund (Nabarro 2015).
	As of February 2019, the WHO was responding to 41 graded health emergencies around the world and leading the health cluster in United Nations InterAgency Standing Committee cluster system in responses to outbreaks, emergencies, protracted conflicts, and natural disasters in 27 countries and territories.
	There are three WHO grades for emergencies, signifying the level of operational response required: Grade 1 (limited response); Grade 2 (moderate response); Grade 3 (major/maximal response) (InterAgency Standing Committee 2016). A graded emergency that persists for more than six months becomes a protracted emergency, which is an environment in which a significant proportion of the population is vulnerable to prolonged disruption of livelihoods, disease, and death.
	The WHO provides technical assistance to countries to help build their capacity to detect, report, and contain infectious disease outbreaks and other health events in line with the International Health Regulations. This assistance covers early warning alert and response systems, laboratory and surveillance, burden of disease, regulatory capacity building, risk communications, and planning for pandemic product deployment.
	The WHO has also developed standardized approaches that countries can take to respond to major epidemic-prone diseases, such as meningitis, yellow fever, and cholera. In 2016, the WHO launched a plan to immunize 1.4 billion people against yellow fever in 40 countries by 2026. In 2018, the World Health Assembly endorsed a goal to reduce cholera deaths by 90% in 47 countries (G20 2018).
	The WHO Emergency Medical Teams Initiative assists organizations and Member States to build capacity of clinical response teams and to better coordinate deployment of quality-assured medical teams in emergencies. The WHO also helps to identify dangerous and re-emerging pathogens and provides countries with the technical support they need to strengthen their biosafety, biosecurity, and readiness for outbreaks (Bermingham et al. 2012). To prevent epidemics, countries need resilient and inclusive health systems that extend to rural areas, a sensitive early warning system along with rapid response capacity, and informed communities that trust their health service providers. They also need effective and affordable vaccines, diagnostics, and treatments, reliable laboratory and logistics capacity, and safe treatment facilities, properly distributed, staffed, and equipped.





Preventing epidemics and pandemics


	During the 2013–2016 Ebola outbreak, the WHO coordinated field trials for candidate vaccines. In December 2016, the Ebola vaccine rVSV-ZEBOV was shown to confer nearly 100% protection for clinical trial participants in Guinea (Henão-Restrepo et al. 2017). To better anticipate the need for vaccines, diagnostics, and therapeutics, the WHO collects inputs to its R&D Blueprint (WHO 2016b). In 2018, the priority diseases were: Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, Ebola virus disease, Marburg virus disease, Lassa fever, Middle East respiratory syndrome, severe acute respiratory syndrome, Nipah and henipaviral diseases, Rift Valley fever, and Zika. The list also contains ‘Disease X’, representing the epidemic potential of an unknown pathogen (WHO 2018h). For each of the epidemic-prone diseases, research and development roadmaps, target product profiles, and generic protocols are developed. At the same time, the WHO works to strengthen national regulatory and ethics bodies so that research can be conducted during public health emergencies (WHO 2014).
	It is clearly preferable that Member States lead the response and coordination of health emergencies, drawing on the support from international partners as required. Increasingly, the WHO is assisting Member States to establish Emergency Operations Centres and develop their capacities for emergency management and coordination. Partnerships such as the Global Outbreak Alert and Response Network and the Global Health Cluster are vital to effective preparedness and response.
	Monitoring and evaluation are difficult in emergency situations but are needed for the improvement and adjustment of public health interventions (Roberts and Brennan 2015). Another challenge for emergency healthcare provision is security, as many outbreaks occur in a conflict setting. WHO is monitoring and compiling data on attacks on health facilities, transport, and staff, as well as engaging in campaigns such as #NotATarget, with Médecins Sans Frontières and the International Committee of the Red Cross (WHO n.d.).
	A century after the 1918 influenza pandemic—which killed an estimated 30–50 million people—the WHO is still responding to media coverage, public perception, and government policy on influenza. In 2011, the World Health Assembly approved the Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework (WHO 2011). The framework sets out obligations for the sharing of information and materials relating to influenza viruses, and of medicines and vaccines, once a pandemic is underway. The framework stipulates obligations for the WHO, its Member States, and WHO-appointed influenza laboratories, and the pharmaceutical industry (Gao et al. 2013; CDC 2018).
	In 2018, thirty-five countries had the systems needed to detect unusual respiratory disease events, a fivefold increase since 2014. In addition, 34 priority countries had functioning inpatient influenza surveillance: this doubled from 16 countries in 2014 and 29 priority countries have a human–animal interagency coordination mechanism (CDC 2018; WHO 2018l). Moreover, 91 countries shared epidemiological data on influenza, compared to 55 countries in 2014.
	However, the continued building of national, regional, and global capacities to prevent, prepare for, respond to, and recover from, health emergencies remains a vital international priority. With the sole exception of disease eradication, gains against infectious diseases are always fragile (Packard 1997). Reductions in transmission can be undone by complacency, diminished control efforts, changes in vector habitats or human behaviour, or by the spread of resistant pathogens.
	Antimicrobial resistance prevents effective treatment of a range of infections caused by bacteria, parasites, viruses, and fungi. Without effective antibiotics, trauma, surgery, organ transplants, childbirth, and immunosuppression can become life-threatening events. The high cost of healthcare for patients with resistant infections is due to a longer duration of illness, complications, additional tests, and the need to use more expensive drugs.
	Antimicrobial resistance occurs naturally over time, through genetic changes in pathogens. However, the misuse of antimicrobials in medicine and in agriculture is accelerating this process. Antimicrobial resistant-microbes are found in people, animals, food, and the environment. They can spread between people and animals, including from food of animal origin, and from person to person (Ong and Heymann 2007). Poor infection control, inadequate sanitary conditions, and inappropriate food-handling encourage the spread of antimicrobial resistance. Multidrug resistance is a particular concern for major health programmes focused on the control of malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV infection.
	The Global Action Plan on antimicrobial resistance was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2015 and its objectives guide the WHO in supporting Member States to develop and implement national action plans on antimicrobial resistance (WHO 2015b).
	The WHO also works with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) in a tripartite ‘One Health’ approach to promote best practices to avoid the emergence and spread of antibiotic resistance, including optimal use of antibiotics in humans, animals, and the environment.
	In 2016, the United Nations General Assembly signalled the world’s commitment to taking a coordinated approach to address the root causes of antimicrobial resistance across multiple sectors, especially human health, animal health, and agriculture.





Better health and well-being


	In 1800, the global population was less than one billion. Rapid population growth, peaking at 2.6% in 1962, resulted in the global population increasing from 1.5 billion in 1900 to 6.1 billion in 2000. That growth has now slowed, reducing by half since 1960. Life expectancy has risen globally for both men and women, a gain of more than 10 years since 1970, to a global average of 72 years in 2016. The WHO South East Asian region has seen a gain of more than 8 years in the past two decades alone. By 2100, average global fertility is predicted to decline to two live births per woman of reproductive age, average life expectancy to level out at 83 years for men and 85 for women and the global population to therefore stabilize at about 11.2 billion (UN 2017).
	Worldwide, the proportion of older people in the total population is increasing at more than three times the overall population growth rate. With some exceptions, populations are now ageing fastest in low-and middle-income countries. A transition towards an older society, which took place over more than a century in Europe, is now taking place in less than 25 years in countries like Brazil, China, and Thailand.
	By 2030, for the first time in history, the population of people aged 65 and older are expected to outnumber children under age 10 (1.41 billion versus 1.35 billion). By 2050, older persons are expected to account for 35% of the population in Europe, 28% in North America, 25% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 24% in Asia, 23% in Oceania, and 9% in Africa. These trends have major implications for healthcare, as most people will die from the complications of noncommunicable diseases.





The health impacts of climate change


	Quantifiable targets are required because the unprecedented improvements in health outcomes seen at the beginning of the century are fragile and easily reversed, including by the effects of climate change and environmental degradation (WHO 2008b). The WHO expects approximately 250,000 additional deaths per year between 2030 and 2050 to be attributed to the health effects of climate change; 38,000 due to heat exposure in elderly people, 48,000 due to diarrhoea, 60,000 due to malaria, and 95,000 due to childhood undernutrition. The direct costs to health are estimated to be between US$2–4 billion per year by 2030 (GBD 2016 Risk Factors Collaborators 2017; Postigo et al. 2007; WHO 2014, 2018g).
	Climate change affects human health directly through extreme weather events and in a more chronic fashion through changes in precipitation, crop yields, and sea levels. More than half of the world’s population lives within 60 km of the sea. Rising sea levels and storms destroy homes, medical facilities, and other essential services. Deaths in Europe alone from extreme weather events—heatwaves and cold waves, wildfires, droughts, river and coastal floods, and windstorms—are projected to increase from about 3,000 to about 150,000 per year by 2100 (Forzieri et al. 2017).
	Variable rainfall patterns affect the supply of fresh water, a shortage of which compromises hygiene and increases the risk of diarrhoeal disease. Floods contaminate freshwater supplies, heighten the risk of water-borne diseases, and create breeding grounds for insect vectors. They also cause drownings and physical injuries, damage homes, and disrupt health services. Rising temperatures and variable precipitation are likely to decrease the production of staple foods in many of the poorest regions. Crop failures are likely to increase the prevalence of malnutrition and undernutrition, which currently cause 3.1 million deaths every year (USFDA 2013; UNICEF 2018).
	Climatic conditions also affect water-borne and vector-borne diseases by lengthening their transmission seasons and altering the geographic range of vectors. As mosquito habitats change, more people are likely to be exposed to arboviral diseases such as yellow fever, dengue, chikungunya, and Zika, as well as to malaria. After years of declining incidence and deaths, progress in malaria control stalled in 2015, with an estimated 219 million cases and 435,000 related deaths in 2017 (Nayyar et al. 2012; WHO 2018f).
	People living near the coast are particularly vulnerable to climate change. Small island states and low-lying coastal countries, home to an estimated 65 million people, are already experiencing the adverse effects of climate change. With one-third of their population living on land that is less than 5 metres above sea level, the threat of sea-level rise, storm surges, and coastal destruction pose existential risks (UNDP 2017). Some small island states may eventually disappear with sea-level rise.
	At the 2017 United Nations Climate Change Conference, the WHO and the UN Climate Change secretariat launched a special initiative to protect people living in small island developing states from the health impacts of climate change (Ghebreyesus and Espinosa 2018).
	Adaptation measures on these islands are complicated by their unique and fragile biodiversity and their dependence on imported fuels and food. While contributing less than 1% to the world’s greenhouse gas emissions, these countries are among the first to experience the worst and most devastating impacts of climate change. Despite the lack of commensurate resources, some small island states are already improving population and health system resilience by diversifying crops, building cyclone-resistant health facilities, and using solar energy to power medical services (UNDP 2017).





Air pollution and a multisectoral approach


	Affecting a much larger proportion of the world’s population, air pollution is another factor mediating the health impacts of climate change. The WHO estimates that more than 90% of the world’s population lives in places where the air quality does not meet the recommended concentrations levels of major pollutants, of which particulate matter is a common proxy indicator. WHO air quality guidelines set limits for particulate matter, nitric dioxide, ozone, and sulphur dioxide—pollutants for which a revision is due in 2020—and other air pollutants. The WHO estimates that 4.2 million deaths from ambient air pollution and 3.8 million deaths from household air pollution are caused by the contribution of these pollutants to stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections (Prüss-Üstün et al. 2016).
	Multisectoral action is vital to global health efforts and central to the SDG agenda because of the many determinants acting upon people’s health, such as socioeconomic status, gender, and other social determinants. Such action is thus essential for tackling the various sources of air pollution. For example, when the Olympic Games were held in Beijing in 2008, stringent policies to reduce local and regional emissions were enacted: traffic was reduced, factories were closed, construction halted, and emission standards revised (Su et al. 2015). Air quality improved dramatically in Beijing and adjacent co-hosting Chinese cities. Observational studies showed significantly decreased cardiovascular deaths in the cities affected by the 6-month implementation period and researchers estimated that sustained improvements, consistent with WHO air quality standards, could avert almost 1.57 million premature deaths in China each year (Guojun et al. 2016).
	Ambient and household air pollution can be reduced by expanding access to clean household fuels and technologies to meet the domestic energy needs of cooking, heating, and lighting. Ambient air quality can be rapidly improved by the expansion of urban public transit networks, energy-efficient buildings, optimal waste management, and by producing electricity from clean, renewable energy. Policies to reduce air pollution can thus be beneficial for both climate and health, lowering the burden of disease attributable to air pollution, as well as contributing to climate change mitigation. These mutually beneficial policies, akin to the synergistic SDGs, are known as health co-benefits. For example, policies that favour electric vehicles and that promote public and active transport can reduce carbon emissions and traffic congestion, impermeabilization of urban land and noise exposure, while improving the urban environment, people’s physical fitness, and ambient air quality (UNEP 2013).





Noncommunicable diseases: determinants and risk factors


	The transition from infectious to noncommunicable causes of deaths is indicated by current estimates attributing 71% of all deaths to noncommunicable diseases, 15 million of which occur between the ages of 30 and 69 years. Deaths in adults occurring before the age of 70 are considered premature. In total, cardiovascular diseases account for 17.9 million deaths annually, cancers 9 million, respiratory diseases 3.9 million, and diabetes 1.6 million. These four groups of diseases account for over 80% of premature deaths due to noncommunicable diseases (WHO 2016). Road traffic crashes cause 1.35 million deaths per year and have become the leading cause of death of people aged 5 to 29. Approximately half of the people killed on the roads are pedestrians, cyclists, or motorcyclists (WHO 2018e).
	Four risk factors are associated with 70% of the premature deaths due to cardiovascular diseases, cancer, respiratory diseases, and diabetes: tobacco use; the harmful use of alcohol; energy-dense, nutrient-poor diets; and inadequate physical activity. In each area, the WHO gathers data, recommends evidence-based policies, provides technical support, and monitors the impact of interventions. In 2011, ‘best buy’ interventions were proposed to governments for the prevention and control of noncommunicable diseases, ranging from antihypertensives and antilipidemiants for cardiovascular disease to vaccines for human papillomavirus to prevent cervical cancer. These are interventions that have significant public health impact, and are cost-effective, inexpensive, and feasible to implement (WHO and the World Economic Forum 2011).
	To support countries in tackling the increasing burden of road traffic crashes that claim over 1.35 million lives each year, the WHO recommends passing laws to reduce speed and drink-driving, to make seat-belts and helmet mandatory, as well improving road infrastructure with safe pedestrian crossings and cycle lanes, making vehicles safer, improving post-crash care, and investing in public transport.
	Recent estimates show that 1.4 billion people worldwide do not meet the WHO recommendations on physical activity (Guthold et al. 2018). A large proportion of this inactivity is a result of the same road traffic conditions that cause the deaths of 351,000 cyclists and pedestrians per year. The WHO therefore recommends the provision of infrastructure, facilities, and public open spaces for walking, cycling, and other physical activity (WHO 2018e).





Nutrition—optimal quantity and quality


	Everyone has the right to adequate food and nutrition; however, this human right is continually violated as nearly one in three people suffer from at least one form of malnutrition. In 2017, 462 million adults worldwide were underweight while more than 1.9 billion were overweight, of whom more than 600 million were obese. In the same year, 38.3 million children under the age of 5 years were overweight or obese and 150.8 million were affected by stunting (low height-for-age) and 50.5 million were affected by wasting (low weight-for-height) (FAO 2014, 2018b; WHO 2018).
	By 2030, the global community has committed to ‘end all forms of malnutrition, including achieving, by 2025, the internationally-agreed targets on stunting and wasting in children under 5 years of age, and address the nutritional needs of adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women and older persons’.
	Poor nutrition continues to cause nearly half of deaths in children under 5, while malnutrition and unhealthy diets are key risk factors for noncommunicable diseases such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers in adults (Petemadi et al. 2017). People are consuming more processed foods high in calories, fats, sugars, and salt. Nearly two out of three infants under 6 months of age are not exclusively breastfed (Yang et al. 2014).
	Many diets are low in whole grains, in fruits, nuts and seeds, or vegetables. Diets are the result of personal factors such as gender, culture, knowledge, skills, and preferences. Diets are also determined by economic, political, and environmental factors including cost and availability of food, marketing, labelling, poverty levels, urbanization, geography, and climate change.
	To tackle malnutrition and prevent and control diet-related noncommunicable diseases everyone needs access to safe, affordable, and healthy diets. The Second International Conference on Nutrition Framework for Action provides a set of 60 policy actions and recommendations that governments, can use to improve nutrition (FAO/WHO 2014).
	These policy actions need to be translated into concrete actions such as restricting marketing of unhealthy foods to children, taxing sugar-sweetened drinks or banning industrial trans fats, mandating simplified front-of-pack nutrition labelling and introducing nutrition standards for food served or sold in schools, hospitals, and other public institutions (Hastings et al. 2003; McGinnis et al. 2006; Cairns et al. 2009; De Ruyter et al. 2012; Ebbeling et al. 2012; Qibin et al. 2012; WHO 2015, 2017).
	In this 2016–2025 Decade of Action on Nutrition, the response by governments is accelerating; but more action, consistent with the WHO’s recommendations, is needed (WHO 2017b).





Minimizing harms from tobacco and alcohol


	Tobacco use kills around 8 million people every year, accounting for 17% of adult deaths (GBD 2017). Since 2000, the prevalence of smoking has decreased from a global average of 27% to 20% in 2016. Currently 34% of men and 6% of women smoke, totalling 1.1 billion smokers aged 15 or more globally. While smoking rates have declined since 2000, the number of smokers has not. Over 24 million young people aged 13–15 smoke cigarettes. The number of smokeless tobacco users in 2016 stands at 367 million adults and 13 million young people aged 13–15 (WHO 2013, 2018).
	The epidemics of smoking-related diseases—lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and other respiratory conditions—are decreasing in countries where tobacco control measures have taken effect and the burden of disease is shifting to low-and middle-income countries.
	The World Health Assembly adopted its first resolution on tobacco control in 1970. Building on decades of progress, SDG target 3.4, calls upon countries to strengthen their implementation of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (WHO FCTC). The WHO FCTC was the first treaty negotiated under the auspices of the WHO and one of the most rapidly ratified treaties in the history of the United Nations (WHO 2012). Provisions in the treaty govern the production, sale, distribution, advertisement, and taxation of tobacco products as minimum requirements for tobacco control (WHO 2013d).
	To reduce demand for tobacco, many countries have passed tobacco control legislation restricting tobacco sales by age and type of outlet as well as by increasing taxes. Australia, France, Ireland, Russia, Turkey, the United Kingdom have introduced indoor smoking bans and other measures. In 2012, Australia became the first country to introduce plain packaging (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2012; National Health and Medical Research Council 2013). Plain packaging prohibits the use of logos, colours, brand images, and promotional information on tobacco products and packaging, other than brand and product names in a prescribed colour and font. Six other countries have since implemented plain packaging laws: France, Hungary, Ireland, New Zealand, Norway, and the United Kingdom. Australia and later France, Norway, and the United Kingdom successfully fought legal challenges to their plain packaging laws. Several other countries are enacting legislation, developing regulations, or approving plain packaging policies.
	The development of electronic cigarettes and heated tobacco products has raised a new set of issues for tobacco control, shifting the emphasis to building the scientific evidence and the regulatory capacity needed to quantify the harms of various tobacco and nicotine delivery devices and updating regulations as required. In addition, while many countries have stringent regulations concerning traditional marketing and advertising, many of these activities have shifted to unregulated online channels. The unfinished public health agenda includes building capacity in each country to counter the tactics of the tobacco industry, treating the diseases caused by tobacco use, finding sustainable alternatives to tobacco-growing and educating people about the health risks of smoking and other nicotine delivery devices.
	The harmful use of alcohol contributes to 3 million deaths globally every year and over 5% of the burden of disease and injury (WHO 2018d). It has a direct impact on many health-related targets of the SDGs, including those for maternal and child health, infectious diseases (HIV, viral hepatitis, lower respiratory infections, tuberculosis), noncommunicable diseases (cancer, cardiovascular diseases and diabetes), digestive diseases, mental health, violence, injuries, and poisonings. Alcohol per capita consumption per year in litres of pure alcohol is one of two indicators for SDG health target 3.5—’Strengthen the prevention and treatment of substance abuse, including narcotic drug abuse and harmful use of alcohol’ (UN 2015).
	Almost all countries have alcohol excise taxes and fewer than half use other price strategies, such as banning below-cost selling or volume discounts. Most countries have a combination of policy measures including taxes, limits on retail and wholesale distribution, advertising restrictions, age limits for consumption and legal limits for blood alcohol concentrations when driving (WHO 2018d).
	The WHO launched a new initiative in 2018 to address the lack of progress in reducing the health harms associated with alcohol consumption. The initiative provides governments with a technical package of five strategies: (1) strengthening restrictions on alcohol availability; (2) advancing and enforcing drink-driving countermeasures; (3) facilitating access to screening, brief interventions, and treatment; (4) enforcing bans or imposing comprehensive restrictions on alcohol advertising, sponsorship, and promotion; and (5) raising prices on alcohol through excise taxes and pricing policies.





Innovation, data, and statistics


	When the Millennium Development Goal reporting period ended in 2015, 80% of the world’s poor people were living in rural areas, 55% of whom had access to safe water for drinking, compared to 85% of the urban population. While considerable progress had been made, the richest and poorest people did not benefit equally. For example, between 2000 and 2015, skilled birth attendance rose from 80 to 89% in the richest quintile, but only from 33% to 43% in the poorest. Women continued to be more likely to live in poverty and to remain at a disadvantage in the labour market, earning 24% less than men globally. Equity is central to the sustainable development agenda. The world has learnt that national averages can hide gross disparities (Gurria 2011).
	Part of the reason for these persistent inequities is that population level statistics have traditionally suffered from incomplete coverage; certain ethnic groups are systematically excluded, institutional populations are not included in household surveys, administrative data only reflect those who can access the services and school-based surveys can only count the children who are able to attend school in the first place (Carrera et al. 2012).
	Disaggregated data are needed to track progress for the most vulnerable people, and it costs more to collect and analyse these data, to resolve issues of sample sizes, confidentiality, and transparency, particularly when indicators require multidimensional disaggregation, for example—’child labour in poorest quintile in urban areas’. The challenge is meeting the demand for high-quality, timely, disaggregated data across a very broad agenda. The UN General Assembly was clear: ‘Sustainable Development Goal indicators should be disaggregated, where relevant, by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability and geographic location, or other characteristics, in accordance with the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics’ (United Nations 2014).
	The WHO welcomes this emphasis, as health systems do not naturally evolve to ensure a fair distribution of services. Decisions aimed at increasing a country’s economic growth do not automatically protect the poor or promote their health. International trade agreements do not, by themselves, guarantee food security, job security, health security, or access to affordable medicines. All these outcomes require deliberate policy decisions that place equity at the forefront (Blas and Sivasankara Kurup 2010; Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2015; FAO 2016) and the ability to measure impact across the diverse groups that constitute a national population.
	To quantify its contribution to improvements in health outcomes, the WHO has developed an impact framework with three levels of measurements: health-adjusted life expectancy, an index for each goal and programmatic targets.
	The WHO impact framework specifies the baseline data and the indicators by which performance should be measured. Thus, for the first time, all components of WHO’s work—from guidelines and technical support, humanitarian response, policy dialogue, and health campaigns—will be measured in terms of the health impact delivered in countries and not merely by whether programmes delivered their planned outputs. This shift from output to impact responds to the demands made by governments and other donors for more transparency and accountability for public funds (OECD 2005, 2008, 2011).





Incentivizing innovation


	Innovation can improve any aspect of policies, systems, products and technologies, services and delivery methods that affect people’s health and well-being. The WHO is working
	towards a more innovative culture in global health that promotes digital technologies for health. In 2018, the organization established an innovation hub with the Programme for Appropriate Technologies in Health (PATH). In partnership, WHO and PATH have developed vaccine vial monitors that show when the cold chain has been breached, vaccines for malaria and Japanese encephalitis, classification and guidelines for digital health interventions, and the Global Digital Health Atlas, a technology registry platform designed to strengthen impact and facilitate scale of emerging health innovations.
	When an unmet health need is identified, an ideal product is defined, and a public–private partnership is formed to develop the product. These projects usually bring together expertise from academia, industry, and public health, with funding from philanthropic sources. Other examples include the Medicines for Malaria Venture, the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative, the Global Alliance for TB Drug Development, and the Drugs for Neglected Diseases Initiative.
	The Meningitis Vaccine Project illustrates the benefits of designing a product based on the needs of low-income countries (Meningitis Vaccine Project n.d.; CDC 2012). Ministers of health asked the WHO for a vaccine that could prevent annual epidemics in the 26 countries that form Africa’s meningitis belt, and defined its ideal characteristics, including the price they could afford to pay.
	In less than a decade, the new vaccine was developed by a consortium of scientists, licensed with support from Canada’s regulatory authority, and prequalified by the WHO. The technology for producing a conjugate vaccine was transferred from the United States of America and the Netherlands to the Serum Institute of India, which agreed to manufacture the vaccine at the target price of 50 cents per dose. The first campaigns using the new vaccine began in late 2011; more than 100 million doses had been administered by the end of 2012. Following these campaigns, some hyperendemic countries have recorded their lowest level of meningitis cases in more than a decade.
	The economic benefits are expected to be significant. A single case of meningitis can cost a household the equivalent of 3–4 months of income. Mounting a reactive emergency response to epidemics can absorb more than 5% of a country’s entire health budget. The project is ground-breaking in another sense. African countries usually wait years, if not decades, for new medical technologies to trickle into their health systems. In this case, Africa was first to receive the best technology that the world could offer.
	Technological innovation is needed for other aspects of the medicines supply chain. For example, the problems caused by substandard, spurious, falsely labelled, falsified, and counterfeit medical products have been difficult to resolve by the traditional approach of strengthening national drug regulatory authorities and quality-assurance laboratories (Cockburn et al. 2005). WHO estimates that only 20% of countries have well-developed systems for regulating medical products—of the remaining countries, around 50% implement drug regulation at varying levels of effectiveness, and the remaining 30% have either no drug regulation in place or a very limited capacity that barely functions. Online sales of medicines further complicate efforts to protect consumers from substandard or falsified medical products (WHO n.d. a).
	Past efforts to address the problem of counterfeit and substandard medicines have been hampered by the confusion of public health issues with issues of intellectual property rights and copyright infringements, and high-profile trade incidents in which legitimate generic medicines were seized, in transit, as counterfeits. In many countries, the only legal instrument available to address the public health problems caused by counterfeit and substandard medicines is legislation related to intellectual property rights (Attaran et al. 2012).
	The efficiency, effectiveness, quality, sustainability, safety, and/or affordability of products can always be improved. As shown by repeated shortages of insulin (discovered in 1923) and penicillin (in 1942), the fact that a medicine is long-established is not a guarantee of its availability.





Future directions


	While much progress has been made in recent decades, global health is a field in need of continued innovation. For the world to sustain a human population of 11.2 billion, major changes are needed in the way that people live, eat, work, and receive healthcare. The SDGs have an ambitious scope and several contradictions that need to be resolved. The health sector faces major challenges from epidemiological and demographic transitions and the difficult task of leaving no-one behind in its provision of high-quality health services. The WHO will need to keep building on its history of success in infectious disease control when working across all sectors to maximize the health benefit of their policies.
	Global health’s contribution to sustainable development can help to ensure equitable access to resources, a healthy interface with the natural environment, and negligible variation in life expectancies (FAO 2018c). The WHO will continue to track changes in the determinants of health and the patterns of disease, identify effective interventions, and measure the degree to which, over time, its recommendations improve health and longevity.
